(c) Each U_i is a plane, so \dim U_i = 2: U_1 = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2), U_2 = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_3), U_3 = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2 + \cvec{e}_3), each with an evidently independent spanning list. All three contain the x-axis \Span(\cvec{e}_1). - U_1 \cap U_2 = \{ y = z = 0 \} = \Span(\cvec{e}_1). - U_1 \cap U_3 = \{ z = 0, y = z \} = \{ y = z = 0 \} = \Span(\cvec{e}_1). - U_2 \cap U_3 = \{ y = 0, y = z \} = \Span(\cvec{e}_1). - U_1 \cap U_2 \cap U_3 = \Span(\cvec{e}_1). So each of these has dimension 1. Since U_1 + U_2 contains \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3, it is 
R^3, and so U_1 + U_2 + U_3 = 
R^3 has dimension 3. The inclusion–exclusion formula would give 2 + 2 + 2 - 1 - 1 - 1 + 1 = 4 
e 3, so it fails. In (b), the last term is (U_1 + U_2) \cap U_3 = 
R^3 \cap U_3 = U_3, of dimension 2, and indeed 2 + 2 + 2 - 1 - 2 = 3. The inclusion–exclusion guess replaces this 2 by \dim(U_1 \cap U_3) + \dim(U_2 \cap U_3) - \dim(U_1 \cap U_2 \cap U_3) = 1 + 1 - 1 = 1, which is wrong because (U_1 + U_2) \cap U_3 is much bigger than (U_1 \cap U_3) + (U_2 \cap U_3) = \Span(\cvec{e}_1).

title: 1.8 Infinite-Dimensional Spaces
content:
Infinite-Dimensional Spaces Every theorem about bases so far has assumed a finite spanning list. Yet several of our running examples have none: F[x] is not finite-dimensional (@thm-polynomials-infinite-dimensional), and neither are the sequences or the functions 
R 	o 
R. Do such spaces have a basis at all? This section shows that they always do, using a principle from set theory called Zorn’s Lemma, and then looks honestly at the price. The basis exists, but often nobody can write it down, and several finite-dimensional facts stop being true. Bases of infinite sets of vectors An infinite-dimensional space cannot have a finite basis, so a basis now has to be an infinite collection of vectors. We recall the conventions for arbitrary subsets, set up with the span (@def-span) and with independence (@def-linear-independence). A linear combination always involves finitely many vectors, because the axioms only let us add two vectors at a time. Let S \subseteq V be any subset, finite or infinite. - \Span(S) is the set of all linear combinations a_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + a_k\elem{v}_k with k \in 
N, a_i \in F, and \elem{v}_i \in S. - S is linearly independent if every finite list of distinct vectors of S is linearly independent in the sense of @def-linear-independence. - S is a basis of V if S is linearly independent and \Span(S) = V. For a finite set S = \{\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k\} of distinct vectors, these agree with the notions for the list (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k), since a sub-list of an independent list is independent. The empty set is independent: its only finite list of distinct vectors is the empty list. In the infinite case we lose the ordering of a basis, and we will not need it. [A Basis of F[x]] Show that \{ x^k : k \in 
N \} = \{1, x, x^2, \dots\} is a basis of F[x]. Spanning. By @def-polynomial, every polynomial can be written as a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_Nx^N for some N \in 
N. This is a finite linear combination of 1, x, \dots, x^N. Independence. Let x^{k_1}, \dots, x^{k_m} be distinct monomials and suppose a_1x^{k_1} + \dots + a_mx^{k_m} = 0. The left side is the polynomial whose coefficient of x^{k_j} is a_j, because the exponents k_j are distinct. The zero polynomial has every coefficient equal to 0, so by the definition of equality of polynomials, a_j = 0 for every j. Hence \{ x^k : k \in 
N \} is a basis of F[x]. The sequence space behaves differently. Let F^{
N} be the space of all sequences (a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots) with entries in F, with entrywise addition and scaling. For i \in 
N let \elem{e}_i be the sequence with 1 in position i and 0 everywhere else. [The Vectors \elem{e}_i Do Not Span F^{
N}] Show that \{ \elem{e}_i : i \in 
N \} is linearly independent in F^{
N}, but is not a basis of F^{
N}. Independence. Let i_1, \dots, i_m be distinct and suppose a_1\elem{e}_{i_1} + \dots + a_m\elem{e}_{i_m} = \elem{0}. Position i_j of the left side is a_j, since only \elem{e}_{i_j} has a nonzero entry there. Position i_j of the zero sequence is 0, so a_j = 0 for every j. Not spanning. A linear combination a_1\elem{e}_{i_1} + \dots + a_m\elem{e}_{i_m} has nonzero entries only in the m positions i_1, \dots, i_m. So every vector in \Span\{\elem{e}_i : i \in 
N\} has only finitely many nonzero entries. The sequence (1, 1, 1, \dots) has infinitely many, so it is not in the span. The same example shows that F^{
N} is infinite-dimensional. For each n, the list (\elem{e}_0, \dots, \elem{e}_n) is independent of length n + 1. If a list of length m spanned F^{
N}, then n + 1 \le m for every n by @thm-steinitz, which is impossible. It is tempting to write (1, 1, 1, \dots) = \elem{e}_0 + \elem{e}_1 + \elem{e}_2 + \cdots. In a vector space this sum means nothing: the axioms define sums of two vectors, hence of finitely many, and an infinite sum would need a notion of limit. So “the \elem{e}_i span” is false, even though every sequence is “made of” its entries. Infinite sums return only in spaces with a notion of distance, much later. Let V be the space of formal power series a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + \cdots over F, that is, F^{
N} with x^k standing for \elem{e}_k. Is \{1, x, x^2, \dots\} a basis of V? No. It is independent, by the argument of @exm-sequence-standard-vectors. But its span consists of the series with only finitely many nonzero coefficients, which are the polynomials. The series 1 + x + x^2 + \cdots is not among them, so the set does not span V. So does F^{
N} have a basis? In finite dimension we built bases by sifting (@thm-sift) or by extending one vector at a time (@thm-basis-extension). Both constructions stop after finitely many steps. For F^{
N} no step-by-step process can stop, and we need a different kind of existence argument. Zorn’s Lemma Look again at what a basis is in finite dimension: an independent list that cannot be enlarged (@thm-maximal-indep). “Cannot be enlarged” is a statement about the family of all independent sets, ordered by inclusion. Zorn’s Lemma is a general principle that produces objects which cannot be enlarged. To state it we need words for orderings. A partial order is a way of comparing elements in which some pairs may be incomparable. [Partial Order, Chain, Upper Bound, Maximal Element] Let P be a set. A partial order on P is a relation \le on P (@def-relation) such that, for all p, q, r \in P: 1. p \le p (reflexive); 2. if p \le q and q \le p, then p = q (antisymmetric); 3. if p \le q and q \le r, then p \le r (transitive). Let (P, \le) be a partially ordered set. - A chain in P is a subset C \subseteq P such that for all p, q \in C, p \le q or q \le p. - An upper bound of a subset C \subseteq P is an element u \in P with c \le u for every c \in C. - A maximal element of P is an element m \in P such that no p \in P satisfies m \le p and p 
e m. In words: a chain is a subset in which any two elements can be compared. An upper bound of C sits above everything in C, but it only has to lie in P, not in C. A maximal element has nothing strictly above it. It is not required to lie above everything else. [Inclusion as a Partial Order] Let X be a set and P the power set of X (@def-power-set), ordered by \subseteq. Check that this is a partial order, and describe chains, upper bounds, and maximal elements when X = \{1, 2\}. Then do the same for the subsets of \{1, 2\} with at most one element. Every set satisfies A \subseteq A, which is (P1). If A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A, then A = B by @thm-double-inclusion, which is (P2). Inclusion is transitive, which is (P3). For X = \{1, 2\}, the set C = \{ \varnothing, \{1\}, \{1, 2\} \} is a chain, while \{1\} and \{2\} are incomparable, so \{ \{1\}, \{2\} \} is not a chain. The set \{1, 2\} is an upper bound of every subset of P, and it is the only maximal element. Now let Q = \{ \varnothing, \{1\}, \{2\} \}, still ordered by \subseteq. Both \{1\} and \{2\} are maximal: nothing in Q strictly contains either. Neither is above the other. The subset \{ \{1\}, \{2\} \} has no upper bound in Q. Zorn’s Lemma Let (P, \le) be a nonempty partially ordered set in which every nonempty chain has an upper bound in P. Then P has a maximal element. We do not prove Zorn’s Lemma, and no proof is possible from the other everyday rules of set theory. It is equivalent to the axiom of choice, the principle already used to build right inverses of surjections in @thm-right-inverse-iff-surjective: from any family of nonempty sets one may choose one element from each. Mathematicians accept it as an axiom, and we do too. In this section we point out each place where it is used. “Maximal” is not “largest”. The partially ordered set Q in @exm-partial-orders has two maximal elements and no largest one. For bases this is the familiar fact that a space has many bases: in 
R^2, both \{\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2\} and \{(1, 1), (1, -1)\} are maximal independent sets, and neither contains the other. Every vector space has a basis We prove the more general extension statement first, since the existence of a basis is the case S = \varnothing. [Basis Extension, General Form] Let V be a vector space over F, and let S \subseteq V be a linearly independent subset. Then there is a basis B of V with S \subseteq B. ① Let P be the family of independent sets containing S, ordered by \subseteq. ② A chain has the union as an upper bound, because an independence test uses only finitely many vectors, and finitely many members of a chain all fit inside one of them. ③ Zorn gives a maximal B. ④ If some \elem{v} were outside \Span(B), then B \cup \{\elem{v}\} would be a bigger independent set, so B spans. Let P be the set of all linearly independent subsets T \subseteq V with S \subseteq T, partially ordered by \subseteq (see @exm-partial-orders). Since S is independent, S \in P, so P is nonempty. Step 1: every nonempty chain has an upper bound. Let C \subseteq P be a nonempty chain and let U =  igcup_{T \in C} T. Every T \in C contains S and C is nonempty, so S \subseteq U, and T \subseteq U for every T \in C. If T_1, \dots, T_k \in C with k \ge 1, then one of them contains all the others. We use induction on k. For k = 1 there is nothing to prove. Suppose the claim holds for k, and let T_1, \dots, T_{k+1} \in C. By the induction hypothesis some T_j contains T_1, \dots, T_k. Since C is a chain, T_j \subseteq T_{k+1} or T_{k+1} \subseteq T_j. In the first case T_{k+1} contains all of T_1, \dots, T_{k+1}, and in the second case T_j does. Now let (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k) be a list of distinct vectors of U. If k = 0, the empty list is independent. Otherwise, each \elem{u}_i lies in some T_i \in C, and by the Claim one of T_1, \dots, T_k, say T_j, contains all the \elem{u}_i. Since T_j is independent, the list (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k) is independent. Hence U is independent, so U \in P, and U is an upper bound of C. Step 2: a maximal element. By Step 1 and @thm-zorn, P has a maximal element B. Thus B is independent and S \subseteq B. Step 3: B spans V. Suppose not, and let \elem{v} \in V with \elem{v} 
otin \Span(B). Then \elem{v} 
otin B, since B \subseteq \Span(B). We show B \cup \{\elem{v}\} is independent. Take a list of distinct vectors of B \cup \{\elem{v}\}. If \elem{v} is not in the list, the list lies in B and is independent. Otherwise, after reordering (which does not affect independence, as addition is commutative), the list is (\elem{v}, \elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_m) with distinct \elem{w}_i \in B. Let a\elem{v} + b_1\elem{w}_1 + \dots + b_m\elem{w}_m = \elem{0}. If a 
e 0, then \elem{v} = -a^{-1}(b_1\elem{w}_1 + \dots + b_m\elem{w}_m) \in \Span(B), a contradiction. So a = 0, and then b_1 = \dots = b_m = 0 because B is independent. Hence B \cup \{\elem{v}\} \in P, it contains B, and it is not equal to B. This contradicts the maximality of B. Therefore \Span(B) = V, and B is a basis of V containing S. Notice where finiteness went. Steps 1 and 3 each look at only finitely many vectors at a time, which is all that linear algebra ever does. The one infinite step, “keep enlarging until you cannot”, is handed to Zorn’s Lemma. Every Vector Space Has a Basis Every vector space V over a field F has a basis. The empty set is linearly independent. By @thm-basis-extension-general with S = \varnothing, V has a basis. For V = \{\elem{0}\} that basis is \varnothing, since \Span(\varnothing) = \{\elem{0}\}. So F^{
N} has a basis, and so do 
R^{
R} and the continuous functions on [0, 1]. The theorem does not tell us what these bases are. Existence without construction: 
R over 
Q The real numbers form a vector space over 
Q: add reals as usual, and multiply a real by a rational. By @thm-every-space-has-basis this space has a basis, often called a Hamel basis. Nobody has ever written one down, and nobody will. It is known that the existence of such a basis cannot be proved without some form of the axiom of choice. What we can prove is that this basis is infinite. The tool is counting. A countable set is one whose elements can be listed as a sequence, possibly with repeats. [Countable Set] A set A is countable if A = \varnothing or there is a surjective function

R, not about linear algebra, and its proof needs one property of

In finite dimension, U \subseteq V with \dim U = \dim V forces U = V (@thm-dim-impl-eq). Now let U = \{ p \in F[x] : 	ext{the constant coefficient of } p 	ext{ is } 0 \}. By the argument of @exm-basis-of-polynomials, U has the basis \{x, x^2, x^3, \dots\}, and x^k \leftrightarrow x^{k+1} matches it one-to-one with the basis \{1, x, x^2, \dots\} of F[x]. Yet 1

R over

From here on the book is mostly about finite-dimensional spaces, where bases are finite lists and counting works. Every theorem that needs finite dimension says so in its hypotheses. Infinite-dimensional spaces return with more structure, such as inner products and limits, where infinite sums can finally be given a meaning. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define what it means for an arbitrary subset S of a vector space V to be a basis of V. 2. State Zorn’s Lemma, including the meaning of “chain” and “upper bound”. 3. (b) See @thm-zorn and @def-partial-order: a nonempty partially ordered set in which every nonempty chain (a subset whose elements are pairwise comparable) has an upper bound (an element of P above every element of the chain) has a maximal element. Going deeper [C1: Complements in Any Dimension] Let U be a subspace of a vector space V, of any dimension. Prove that there is a subspace W of V with V = U \oplus W, that is, every \elem{v} \in V can be written uniquely as \elem{u} + \elem{w} with \elem{u} \in U, \elem{w} \in W. Hint: @thm-basis-extension-general. By @thm-every-space-has-basis, U has a basis B_U. It is independent in V, so by @thm-basis-extension-general there is a basis B of V with B_U \subseteq B. Let W = \Span(B \setminus B_U), a subspace by @thm-span-subspace. Existence. Let \elem{v} \in V. Since B spans, \elem{v} = \sum_i a_i\elem{u}_i + \sum_j b_j\elem{w}_j, a finite sum with \elem{u}_i \in B_U and \elem{w}_j \in B \setminus B_U. The first sum lies in U and the second in W. U \cap W = \{\elem{0}\}. Let \elem{v} \in U \cap W. Since B_U spans U and B \setminus B_U spans W, we have \elem{v} = \sum_i a_i\elem{u}_i = \sum_j b_j\elem{w}_j with distinct \elem{u}_i \in B_U and distinct \elem{w}_j \in B \setminus B_U. Then \sum_i a_i\elem{u}_i - \sum_j b_j\elem{w}_j = \elem{0} is a combination of a list of distinct vectors of B, because B_U and B \setminus B_U are disjoint. Since B is independent, every a_i and b_j is 0, so \elem{v} = \elem{0}. Uniqueness. If \elem{u} + \elem{w} = \elem{u}' + \elem{w}' with \elem{u}, \elem{u}' \in U and \elem{w}, \elem{w}' \in W, then \elem{u} - \elem{u}' = \elem{w}' - \elem{w} lies in U \cap W = \{\elem{0}\}. Hence \elem{u} = \elem{u}' and \elem{w} = \elem{w}'. This proves V = U \oplus W. [C2: Bases of 
R over 
Q Are Uncountable] 1. Let A_0, A_1, A_2, \dots be countable sets. Prove that  igcup_{n \in 
N} A_n is countable. (You may use the axiom of choice.) 2. Let V be a vector space over 
Q with a countable basis. Prove that V is countable. 3. Deduce that every basis of 
R over 
Q is uncountable. Hint: for (b), write V as a union of spans of finite lists. (a) Let A =  igcup_{n} A_n. If A = \varnothing there is nothing to prove; otherwise fix a^* \in A. For each n with A_n 
e \varnothing, choose a surjection \sigma_n \colon 
N 	o A_n (this is where choice is used). Define h \colon 
N 	imes 
N 	o A by h(n, m) = \sigma_n(m) if A_n 
e \varnothing, and h(n, m) = a^* otherwise. Every a \in A lies in some nonempty A_n and equals \sigma_n(m) for some m, so h is surjective. By @lem-countable-sets (b) and (a), A is countable. (b) If the basis is empty, V = \{\elem{0}\} is countable. Otherwise list the basis as \sigma(0), \sigma(1), \dots for a surjection \sigma \colon 
N 	o B. Every \elem{v} \in V is a combination of finitely many basis vectors, all among \sigma(0), \dots, \sigma(n) for some n. Hence V =  igcup_n V_n with V_n = \Span(\sigma(0), \dots, \sigma(n)). The map 
Q^{n+1} 	o V_n, (q_0, \dots, q_n) \mapsto \sum_i q_i\sigma(i), is surjective, so each V_n is countable by @lem-countable-sets (d) and (a). By (a), V is countable. (c) By @thm-every-space-has-basis, 
R has a basis over 
Q. If some basis were countable, then 
R would be countable by (b), contradicting @lem-reals-uncountable. Hence every basis is uncountable.

title: 1.9 Changing the Field
content:
Changing the Field Every vector space comes with its field, and we have already seen that the field matters: \dim_
C 
C = 1 but \dim_
R 
C = 2 (@exm-dimensions). This section explains the pattern behind that example. Shrinking the field multiplies the dimension by a fixed factor, the tower law. Going the other way, every real vector space can be enlarged to a complex one, its complexification, without changing the dimension. Both moves are used later, most of all when real matrices need complex eigenvalues. Restricting the scalars Start with the standard example. The space 
C^2 over 
C has the basis (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2), so its dimension is 2. But nothing stops us from multiplying vectors of 
C^2 only by real numbers. The addition is the same, and the axioms still hold, because they hold for all complex scalars. So 
C^2 is also a vector space over 
R. What is its dimension now? [
C^2 as a Real Vector Space] Show that (\cvec{e}_1, i\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, i\cvec{e}_2) is a basis of 
C^2 over 
R, and write (1 + 2i, 3 - i) in it. Spanning. Let (z_1, z_2) \in 
C^2 and write z_k = a_k + b_ki with a_k, b_k \in 
R. Then (z_1, z_2) = a_1\cvec{e}_1 + b_1(i\cvec{e}_1) + a_2\cvec{e}_2 + b_2(i\cvec{e}_2), a combination with real coefficients. For example, (1 + 2i, 3 - i) = 1\cvec{e}_1 + 2(i\cvec{e}_1) + 3\cvec{e}_2 + (-1)(i\cvec{e}_2). Independence. Let a_1, b_1, a_2, b_2 \in 
R with a_1\cvec{e}_1 + b_1(i\cvec{e}_1) + a_2\cvec{e}_2 + b_2(i\cvec{e}_2) = \cvec{0}. The left side is (a_1 + b_1i, \; a_2 + b_2i). Each entry is 0, and comparing real and imaginary parts (@def-complex-numbers) gives a_1 = b_1 = a_2 = b_2 = 0. Hence \dim_
R 
C^2 = 4 = 2 \dim_
C 
C^2. The general setting has a big field L, a smaller field K inside it, and a vector space over L. [Subfield, Restriction of Scalars, Degree] Let L be a field. A subfield of L is a subset K \subseteq L that contains 0 and 1 and is closed under addition, multiplication, negatives, and inverses of nonzero elements. Let K be a subfield of L, and let V be a vector space over L. Keeping the addition of V and using scalar multiplication only for scalars in K makes V a vector space over K. We say V is obtained by restriction of scalars. In particular L itself, a vector space over L, is a vector space over K. If it is finite-dimensional, its dimension is the degree [L : K] \coloneqq \dim_K L. In words: a subfield is a field sitting inside L with the same operations. Restriction of scalars forgets how to multiply by elements of L outside K. There are two things to check. First, K with the operations of L is a field. Closure makes the operations land in K, the elements 0, 1, negatives, and inverses are in K by assumption, and the remaining axioms are identities that hold for all elements of L, so in particular for those of K. Second, V over K is a vector space. Scalar multiplication K 	imes V 	o V lands in V, and each axiom of @def-vector-space holds for all scalars in L, so in particular for all scalars in K. We always write \dim_K V or \dim_L V when both fields are in play. [Degrees of Some Fields] Find [
C : 
R], [
Q(\sqrt2) : 
Q], and [K : K] for any field K. Is [
R : 
Q] defined? [
C : 
R] = 2. Every z \in 
C is a \cdot 1 + b \cdot i with a, b \in 
R, and a + bi = 0 forces a = b = 0 by @def-complex-numbers. So (1, i) is a basis of 
C over 
R. [
Q(\sqrt2) : 
Q] = 2. The set 
Q(\sqrt2) = \{ a + b\sqrt2 : a, b \in 
Q \} is a subfield of 
R by @exm-q-sqrt2-field. The list (1, \sqrt2) spans it over 
Q by definition. For independence, let a + b\sqrt2 = 0 with a, b \in 
Q. If b 
e 0, then \sqrt2 = -a/b \in 
Q, contradicting @thm-sqrt2-irrational. So b = 0, and then a = 0. [K : K] = 1. The list (1) is a basis of K over K: every a equals a \cdot 1, and a \cdot 1 = 0 forces a = 0. This degenerate case says that restricting to the same field changes nothing. [
R : 
Q] is not defined, because 
R is not finite-dimensional over 
Q (@thm-reals-infinite-dimensional-over-rationals). Restriction only goes down. The set 
R with the operations of 
C is not a vector space over 
C: everything about addition works, but scalar multiplication leaves the set, since i \cdot 1 = i 
otin 
R. Enlarging the field needs a construction, which is the second half of this section. The tower law In @exm-c2-over-r we took a vector, wrote it in coordinates over 
C, and then split each complex coordinate into real coordinates. The same two-stage process works for any fields. [Tower Law] Let K be a subfield of L, and let V be a vector space over L. Suppose (a_1, \dots, a_m) is a basis of L over K and (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) is a basis of V over L. Then the list of the mn vectors (a_1\elem{v}_1, \dots, a_m\elem{v}_1, \; a_1\elem{v}_2, \dots, a_m\elem{v}_2, \; \dots, \; a_1\elem{v}_n, \dots, a_m\elem{v}_n) is a basis of V over K. In particular, \dim_K V = [L : K] \cdot \dim_L V. Coordinates in two stages. A vector is an L-combination of the \elem{v}_j; each L-coefficient is a K-combination of the a_i. Substituting gives a double sum \sum_j \sum_i b_{ij}\,a_i\elem{v}_j with b_{ij} \in K. For independence, run the same two stages backwards: regroup the double sum by j, use independence over L, then independence over K. Throughout we use two axioms of @def-vector-space for scalars in L: (c + c')\elem{x} = c\elem{x} + c'\elem{x} and c(c'\elem{x}) = (cc')\elem{x}. Spanning. Let \elem{x} \in V. Since (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) spans V over L, there are c_1, \dots, c_n \in L with \elem{x} = \sum_{j=1}^n c_j\elem{v}_j. Since (a_1, \dots, a_m) spans L over K, for each j there are b_{1j}, \dots, b_{mj} \in K with c_j = \sum_{i=1}^m b_{ij}a_i. Therefore \elem{x} = \sum_{j=1}^n \Bigl( \sum_{i=1}^m b_{ij}a_i \Bigr)\elem{v}_j = \sum_{j=1}^n \sum_{i=1}^m (b_{ij}a_i)\elem{v}_j = \sum_{j=1}^n \sum_{i=1}^m b_{ij}(a_i\elem{v}_j), where the second equality uses (c + c')\elem{x} = c\elem{x} + c'\elem{x} and the third uses c(c'\elem{x}) = (cc')\elem{x}. This is a K-linear combination of the vectors a_i\elem{v}_j. Independence. Let b_{ij} \in K with \sum_{j=1}^n \sum_{i=1}^m b_{ij}(a_i\elem{v}_j) = \elem{0}. Reading the display above from right to left, \sum_{j=1}^n \Bigl( \sum_{i=1}^m b_{ij}a_i \Bigr)\elem{v}_j = \elem{0} . Each coefficient \sum_i b_{ij}a_i lies in L, and (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) is independent over L. Hence \sum_{i=1}^m b_{ij}a_i = 0 for every j. For each fixed j, this is a K-combination of (a_1, \dots, a_m) equal to 0, and that list is independent over K. Hence b_{ij} = 0 for all i and j. So the mn vectors a_i\elem{v}_j form a basis of V over K, and \dim_K V = mn = [L : K] \dim_L V. The name comes from the picture of fields stacked in a tower, K \subseteq L, with V on top: dimensions multiply as you go down. The most important case is 
R \subseteq 
C. [Complex Spaces as Real Spaces] Let V be a vector space over 
C with basis (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n). Then (\elem{v}_1, i\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n, i\elem{v}_n) is a basis of V over 
R. In particular \dim_
R V = 2\dim_
C V. By @exm-field-degrees, (1, i) is a basis of 
C over 
R. By @thm-tower-law with a_1 = 1 and a_2 = i, the list (1\elem{v}_1, i\elem{v}_1, \dots, 1\elem{v}_n, i\elem{v}_n) is a basis of V over 
R, and 1\elem{v}_j = \elem{v}_j by @def-vector-space. The dimension is 2n. This is the result of @exr-dimension-c2, now as a case of the tower law. For example, \dim_
R 
C^n = 2n, and \dim_
R 
C[x]_{\le n} = 2(n + 1), with basis (1, i, x, ix, \dots, x^n, ix^n). A subset of 
C^n can be a subspace over 
R without being a subspace over 
C. The real vectors 
R^n \subseteq 
C^n contain \cvec{0} and are closed under addition and under multiplication by real scalars, so they form an 
R-subspace of dimension n. But \cvec{e}_1 \in 
R^n and i\cvec{e}_1 
otin 
R^n, so 
R^n is not a 
C-subspace. Always ask: a subspace over which field? What is \dim_
R M_{2 	imes 3}(
C)? What is \dim_
Q 
Q(\sqrt2)^2? M_{2 	imes 3}(
C) has dimension 6 over 
C (@exm-dimensions), so \dim_
R = 2 \cdot 6 = 12 by @thm-restriction-of-scalars-dimension. The space 
Q(\sqrt2)^2 has dimension 2 over the field 
Q(\sqrt2), and [
Q(\sqrt2) : 
Q] = 2 by @exm-field-degrees, so \dim_
Q = 2 \cdot 2 = 4 by @thm-tower-law. Complexification Now go up. A real matrix such as the rotation  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} moves every nonzero vector of 
R^2 off its own line. In 
C^2, however, it sends (1, -i) to (i, 1) = i(1, -i). To use such complex vectors for an arbitrary real space V, not just 
R^n, we need a complex space that contains V the way 
C^n contains 
R^n. The model is 
C^n itself. Every \cvec{z} \in 
C^n splits as \cvec{z} = \cvec{x} + i\cvec{y} with \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n, its real and imaginary parts, taken entry by entry. Multiplying by a + bi with a, b \in 
R gives (a + bi)(\cvec{x} + i\cvec{y}) = (a\cvec{x} - b\cvec{y}) + i(a\cvec{y} + b\cvec{x}). The right side only uses real scalars acting on real vectors. So we can copy it for any real space, exactly as 
C was built from pairs of real numbers in @def-complex-numbers. The complexification of V is the space of formal expressions \elem{u} + i\elem{v} with \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V, multiplied by complex numbers the way the rules of algebra dictate. Complexification Let V be a vector space over 
R. The complexification of V is the set V_
C \coloneqq V 	imes V with addition and scalar multiplication by 
C defined, for all (\elem{u}, \elem{v}), (\elem{u}', \elem{v}') \in V_
C and a, b \in 
R, by (\elem{u}, \elem{v}) + (\elem{u}', \elem{v}') \coloneqq (\elem{u} + \elem{u}', \; \elem{v} + \elem{v}'), \qquad (a + bi)(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) \coloneqq (a\elem{u} - b\elem{v}, \; a\elem{v} + b\elem{u}). We write \elem{u} + i\elem{v} for (\elem{u}, \elem{v}), and \elem{u} for (\elem{u}, \elem{0}). In words: addition is entry by entry. Multiplication by a + bi is the formula forced by i^2 = -1. The notation is honest: i(\elem{v}, \elem{0}) = (0\elem{v} - 1\elem{0}, \; 0\elem{0} + 1\elem{v}) = (\elem{0}, \elem{v}), by @thm-zero-scalar-mult and @thm-scalar-zero-vector, so (\elem{u}, \elem{0}) + i(\elem{v}, \elem{0}) = (\elem{u}, \elem{v}). Also a real scalar acts entrywise: a(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = (a\elem{u}, a\elem{v}). So V_
C, restricted to real scalars, is just two copies of V. Why V_
C is a vector space over 
C. The operations land in V 	imes V. Addition is entrywise, so (commutativity, associativity, zero, negatives) follow from the same axioms in each entry of V, with zero (\elem{0}, \elem{0}) and negative (-\elem{u}, -\elem{v}). We check the scalar axioms that involve the multiplication of 
C; below, a\elem{u} - b\elem{v} means a\elem{u} + (-b)\elem{v}, which is the same by @thm-negative-scalar-dist. Let \alpha = a + bi and  eta = c + di with a, b, c, d \in 
R, and \elem{z} = (\elem{u}, \elem{v}). - 1\elem{z} = \elem{z}: we get (1\elem{u} - 0\elem{v}, \; 1\elem{v} + 0\elem{u}) = (\elem{u}, \elem{v}), since 0\elem{v} = \elem{0} by @thm-zero-scalar-mult. - \alpha( eta\elem{z}) = (\alpha eta)\elem{z}: since  eta\elem{z} = (c\elem{u} - d\elem{v}, \; c\elem{v} + d\elem{u}), the axioms of V give  egin{aligned} \alpha( eta\elem{z}) &=  igl( a(c\elem{u} - d\elem{v}) - b(c\elem{v} + d\elem{u}), \; a(c\elem{v} + d\elem{u}) + b(c\elem{u} - d\elem{v})  igr) \ &=  igl( (ac - bd)\elem{u} - (ad + bc)\elem{v}, \; (ac - bd)\elem{v} + (ad + bc)\elem{u}  igr). \end{aligned} Since \alpha eta = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i, this is (\alpha eta)\elem{z}. - (\alpha +  eta)\elem{z} = \alpha\elem{z} +  eta\elem{z}: with \alpha +  eta = (a + c) + (b + d)i,  egin{aligned} (\alpha +  eta)\elem{z} &=  igl( (a + c)\elem{u} - (b + d)\elem{v}, \; (a + c)\elem{v} + (b + d)\elem{u}  igr) \ &= (a\elem{u} - b\elem{v}, \; a\elem{v} + b\elem{u}) + (c\elem{u} - d\elem{v}, \; c\elem{v} + d\elem{u}) \ &= \alpha\elem{z} +  eta\elem{z}. \end{aligned} The remaining axiom, \alpha(\elem{z} + \elem{w}) = \alpha\elem{z} + \alpha\elem{w}, is @exr-changing-the-field-b3. Here is the payoff: complexifying keeps the dimension, and even keeps the basis. [A Real Basis Is a Complex Basis of the Complexification] Let V be a vector space over 
R with basis (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n). Then (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n), that is, ((\elem{v}_1, \elem{0}), \dots, (\elem{v}_n, \elem{0})), is a basis of V_
C over 
C. In particular \dim_
C V_
C = \dim_
R V. A complex coefficient a_j + b_ji on \elem{v}_j puts a_j\elem{v}_j into the real part and b_j\elem{v}_j into the imaginary part. So one complex combination of the \elem{v}_j is the same as two real combinations, one for each part, and both questions (spanning, independence) split into two real questions about (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n). For a, b \in 
R and \elem{x} \in V, @def-complexification and @thm-scalar-zero-vector give (a + bi)(\elem{x}, \elem{0}) = (a\elem{x} - b\elem{0}, \; a\elem{0} + b\elem{x}) = (a\elem{x}, \; b\elem{x}). Call this identity (∗). Spanning. Let (\elem{u}, \elem{v}) \in V_
C. Since (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) spans V, there are a_j, b_j \in 
R with \elem{u} = \sum_j a_j\elem{v}_j and \elem{v} = \sum_j b_j\elem{v}_j. By (∗) and entrywise addition, \sum_{j=1}^n (a_j + b_ji)(\elem{v}_j, \elem{0}) = \sum_{j=1}^n (a_j\elem{v}_j, \; b_j\elem{v}_j) = \Bigl( \sum_{j=1}^n a_j\elem{v}_j, \; \sum_{j=1}^n b_j\elem{v}_j \Bigr) = (\elem{u}, \elem{v}). Independence. Let \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n \in 
C with \sum_j \alpha_j(\elem{v}_j, \elem{0}) = (\elem{0}, \elem{0}), and write \alpha_j = a_j + b_ji with a_j, b_j \in 
R. By the same computation,  igl( \sum_j a_j\elem{v}_j, \; \sum_j b_j\elem{v}_j  igr) = (\elem{0}, \elem{0}). Since (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) is independent over 
R, all a_j = 0 and all b_j = 0. Hence every \alpha_j = 0. Therefore (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) is a basis of V_
C, and \dim_
C V_
C = n. As a consistency check, restricting V_
C back to 
R gives \dim_
R V_
C = 2n by @thm-restriction-of-scalars-dimension, which matches the fact that V_
C over 
R is two copies of V. The same proof works word for word for an infinite basis set, since every combination involves finitely many vectors. [The Complexification of 
R^n Is 
C^n] Show that the map (\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) \mapsto \cvec{x} + i\cvec{y}, from (
R^n)_
C to 
C^n, is a bijection that respects addition and multiplication by complex scalars. Here \cvec{x} + i\cvec{y} is computed in 
C^n: its k-th entry is x_k + y_ki. Every \cvec{z} \in 
C^n has unique real and imaginary parts entry by entry (@def-complex-numbers), so exactly one pair (\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) of real vectors maps to \cvec{z}. Hence the map is a bijection. Addition is entrywise on both sides, so it is respected. For scaling, let a, b \in 
R. In (
R^n)_
C, (a + bi)(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = (a\cvec{x} - b\cvec{y}, \; a\cvec{y} + b\cvec{x}), which maps to the vector with entries (ax_k - by_k) + (ay_k + bx_k)i. In 
C^n, the k-th entry of (a + bi)(\cvec{x} + i\cvec{y}) is (a + bi)(x_k + y_ki) = (ax_k - by_k) + (ay_k + bx_k)i. The two agree, so the map respects scalar multiplication. It sends the basis (\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n) of (
R^n)_
C from @thm-complexification-basis to the standard basis of 
C^n. So (
R^n)_
C is 
C^n in disguise; in Chapter 2 such a bijection will be called an isomorphism. In the same way (M_n(
R))_
C is M_n(
C), and (
R[x]_{\le n})_
C is 
C[x]_{\le n}. The construction earns its keep in Chapter 9, where real matrices without real eigenvalues, like the rotation above, get complex ones, and in Chapter 12, in the spectral theory of real operators. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the degree [L : K] of a subfield K \subseteq L. 2. State the Tower Law. 3. What is \dim_
R 
C^3? Give a basis. 4. True or false: every 
C-subspace of 
C^n is an 
R-subspace. Justify your answer. 5. What is \dim_
C (M_2(
R))_
C? (a) [L : K] = \dim_K L, where L is regarded as a vector space over K by restriction of scalars (@def-restriction-of-scalars), when this dimension is finite. (b) See @thm-tower-law: if (a_i) is a basis of L over K and (\elem{v}_j) is a basis of V over L, then (a_i\elem{v}_j) is a basis of V over K, so \dim_K V = [L : K]\dim_L V. (c) 6, with basis (\cvec{e}_1, i\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, i\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3, i\cvec{e}_3), by @thm-restriction-of-scalars-dimension. (d) True. A 
C-subspace contains \cvec{0}, is closed under addition, and is closed under multiplication by every complex number, in particular by every real number. (e) 4: \dim_
R M_2(
R) = 4 (@exm-dimensions), and @thm-complexification-basis keeps the dimension. B. Practice [B1: A Tower over 
Q] Find \dim_
Q 
Q(\sqrt2)^3 and a basis of 
Q(\sqrt2)^3 over 
Q. By @exm-q-sqrt2-field, 
Q(\sqrt2) is a field, so 
Q(\sqrt2)^3 is a vector space over it with basis (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3) and dimension 3 (@exm-dimensions). By @exm-field-degrees, (1, \sqrt2) is a basis of 
Q(\sqrt2) over the subfield 
Q. By @thm-tower-law, (\cvec{e}_1, \sqrt2\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \sqrt2\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3, \sqrt2\cvec{e}_3) is a basis of 
Q(\sqrt2)^3 over 
Q. Hence \dim_
Q 
Q(\sqrt2)^3 = 2 \cdot 3 = 6. [B2: Complex Matrices over 
R] Let \E_{11}, \E_{12}, \E_{21}, \E_{22} be the matrix units of M_2(
C). Find a basis of M_2(
C) over 
R, and write \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 + i & 2 \ -i & 3i \end{pmatrix} in it. The matrix units form a basis of M_2(
C) over 
C (@exm-standard-bases). By @thm-restriction-of-scalars-dimension, (\E_{11}, i\E_{11}, \E_{12}, i\E_{12}, \E_{21}, i\E_{21}, \E_{22}, i\E_{22}) is a basis of M_2(
C) over 
R, so \dim_
R M_2(
C) = 8. Splitting each entry of \A into real and imaginary parts, \A = 1\E_{11} + 1(i\E_{11}) + 2\E_{12} + 0(i\E_{12}) + 0\E_{21} + (-1)(i\E_{21}) + 0\E_{22} + 3(i\E_{22}). [B3: Working in a Complexification] Let V be a vector space over 
R. 1. Verify that \alpha(\elem{z} + \elem{w}) = \alpha\elem{z} + \alpha\elem{w} for all \alpha \in 
C and \elem{z}, \elem{w} \in V_
C. 2. In (

title: Linear Maps
content: Linear Maps Chapter 1 studied vector spaces one at a time. This chapter studies the functions between them that respect the structure: linear maps, the functions that send sums to sums and scalar multiples to scalar multiples. Differentiation of polynomials, the trace of a matrix, a rotation of the plane, a shift of a sequence, and multiplication by a matrix are all linear maps, and one theory covers them all. The theory is built without coordinates, and that is the point of putting it here. Two subspaces measure how far a linear map is from being injective and from being surjective: its kernel and its image. The Rank–Nullity Theorem ties their dimensions to the dimension of the domain, and turns questions that look as though they need a computation into questions of counting — often it is enough to check one of injectivity and surjectivity and let the count supply the other. By the end we can say when two spaces are “the same”: finite-dimensional spaces are classified by a single number, their dimension. No basis is chosen anywhere in this chapter; Chapter 4 chooses one and turns all of this into matrices. What you need. From Chapter 0, functions and what injective, surjective, and bijective mean, composition and inverses (@def-injective-surjective-bijective, @def-composition, @thm-composition-preserves), and the counting fact this chapter has a linear version of: between finite sets of equal size, injective and surjective agree (@thm-finite-injective-iff-surjective). Also field arithmetic (@thm-field-basic-properties), polynomials with their degree and evaluation (@def-polynomial, @thm-degree-of-product, @thm-evaluation-respects-operations), which supply half the examples, and, for §04 alone, polynomials of a matrix (@thm-polynomial-of-matrix-properties). From Chapter 1, essentially all of it: vector spaces and the subspace test (@def-vector-space, @thm-subspace-test), span (@def-span, @thm-span-subspace), independence (@def-linear-independence), bases and coordinates (@def-basis, @exm-standard-bases, @thm-coordinates-linear, @cor-basis-existence), dimension with basis extension and the two counting theorems that replace a check (@def-dimension, @thm-basis-extension, @thm-right-size-basis, @thm-size-bounds, @thm-dim-impl-eq), and sums and direct sums with the dimension formula (@thm-direct-sum-criteria, @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim), whose proof pattern is the one Rank–Nullity reuses. Nothing in this chapter needs Chapter 3. Linear systems, row reduction, and the rank of a matrix come after it, and every proof here is written so that they can. Roadmap - Linear maps. The definition, a gallery of examples and nonexamples drawn from geometry, matrices, calculus, and algebra, and the fact that makes linear maps manageable: a linear map is determined by, and may be freely prescribed on, a basis. - Kernel and image. The two subspaces attached to every linear map, how to compute an image from a spanning list, and the kernel test that makes injectivity cheap to check. - The Rank–Nullity Theorem. \nullity T + \rank T = \dim V, proved by taking a basis of the kernel and extending it, and the corollaries that let a count replace a check. - The algebra of linear maps. Adding, scaling, and composing maps; \cL(V, W) as a vector space and \cL(V) as an algebra; polynomials in an operator, and the relations they satisfy. - Invertible maps and isomorphisms. When two spaces are “the same”, why dimension alone decides it in finite dimension, and the Invertible Operator Theorem, which collects nine ways to recognize an invertible operator. Named moves - Injective via the kernel. To show T is injective, show that T\elem{v} = \elem{0} forces \elem{v} = \elem{0}. One quantifier instead of two. - Count instead of check. When \dim V = \dim W is finite, injective, surjective, and bijective are the same property; check whichever is easier, usually the kernel. - Basis of the kernel, then extend. Take a basis of the smaller space, extend it to the whole, claim the added vectors do the remaining work, and count. This proves Rank–Nullity, and it proved the dimension formula for sums before it. - One equation is enough. Between spaces of equal finite dimension, ST = \id alone makes both maps invertible — the counting move again, in disguise. - Transport along an isomorphism. An isomorphism carries bases to bases and preserves every statement written in terms of sums and scalar multiples, so a question about V may be asked in any space isomorphic to it.

title: 2.1 Linear Maps
content:
Linear Maps Chapter 1 studied vector spaces one at a time. This chapter studies the functions between vector spaces that respect addition and scaling. This section defines them, collects examples from geometry, matrices, calculus, and algebra, and proves the fact that makes them manageable: a linear map is completely determined by what it does to a basis. Functions that behave like matrices Objects come first, then the maps between them that respect their structure. For sets the maps are functions; for groups they are homomorphisms (@def-group-homomorphism). For vector spaces the structure is addition and scalar multiplication, so we want functions that respect those two operations. The standard example is a matrix. For \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), the rules of matrix multiplication (@thm-matrix-multiplication-properties) give \A(\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}) = \A\cvec{x} + \A\cvec{y}, \qquad \A(c\cvec{x}) = c(\A\cvec{x}) \qquad 	ext{for all } \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in F^n,\ c \in F . Now look at three functions that are not given by matrices at all. - Differentiation on polynomials: (p + q)' = p' + q' and (cp)' = cp'. - Trace on square matrices: 	r(\A + \B) = 	r \A + 	r \B and 	r(c\A) = c	r \A (@thm-trace-properties). - Rotation of the plane about the origin: rotating a parallelogram gives a parallelogram, so the rotation of a sum is the sum of the rotations, and rotating a stretched arrow gives the stretched rotated arrow. The inputs are polynomials, matrices, and arrows, not columns. Yet all three obey exactly the two rules that matrices obey. Whatever we can prove from those two rules alone will hold for all of them at once. So we give the two rules a name. A linear map is a function that preserves linear combinations. The definition [Linear Map] Let V and W be vector spaces over the same field F. A function T \colon V 	o W is a linear map (or linear transformation) over F if 1. T(\elem{u} + \elem{v}) = T(\elem{u}) + T(\elem{v}) for all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V, and 2. T(c\elem{v}) = cT(\elem{v}) for all c \in F and all \elem{v} \in V. A linear map T \colon V 	o V from a space to itself is also called a linear operator on V. We often write T\elem{v} for T(\elem{v}). In words: (LT1), additivity, says that adding first and then applying T gives the same result as applying T first and then adding. The sum on the left is taken in V; the sum on the right is taken in W. (LT2), homogeneity, says the same for scaling: the scalar c can be pulled out of T. Both conditions must hold for every choice of vectors and scalars, so one counterexample is enough to show that a function is not linear. The phrase “over the same field” matters. Scalars from F act on both sides of (LT2), so both spaces must accept them. We will see below that one function can be linear over 
R and not linear over 
C. A general linear map is always named T, S, or R in this book, never f; a specific map may get a letter that recalls what it does, such as D for differentiation. Examples We check the examples against (LT1) and (LT2), grouped by where they come from. Matrices. [Multiplication by a Matrix] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). Show that T_\A \colon F^n 	o F^m, T_\A(\cvec{x}) = \A\cvec{x}, is a linear map. Let \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in F^n and c \in F. By the distributive law in @thm-matrix-multiplication-properties, T_\A(\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}) = \A(\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}) = \A\cvec{x} + \A\cvec{y} = T_\A(\cvec{x}) + T_\A(\cvec{y}), which is (LT1). By the scalar rule in the same theorem, T_\A(c\cvec{x}) = \A(c\cvec{x}) = c(\A\cvec{x}) = cT_\A(\cvec{x}), which is (LT2). Hence T_\A is linear. We will use the name T_\A for this map throughout the chapter. For F = 
R and n = m = 2, the map T_\A sends the unit square to the parallelogram spanned by \A\cvec{e}_1 and \A\cvec{e}_2, the columns of \A (@thm-matrix-times-vector-columns). The unit square (dashed) and its image under \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Drag the tips of the two arrows to change \A. [Maps Given by Formulas in Coordinates] 1. Show that T \colon F^3 	o F^2, T(a_1, a_2, a_3) = (2a_1 + a_3,\ a_2 - a_1), is linear. 2. Let \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) be a basis of a vector space V over F. Show that the coordinate map V 	o F^n, \elem{v} \mapsto \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB}, is linear. (a) The formula is a matrix product:  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \ -1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} a_1 \ a_2 \ a_3 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 2a_1 + a_3 \ -a_1 + a_2 \end{pmatrix}. So T = T_\A for this 2 	imes 3 matrix \A, and T is linear by @exm-matrix-transformation. The same argument shows that every map F^n 	o F^m whose output entries are combinations of the input entries, with constant coefficients and no constant terms, is linear. (b) By @thm-coordinates-linear, \coord{\elem{u} + \elem{v}}{\sB} = \coord{\elem{u}}{\sB} + \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} and \coord{c\elem{v}}{\sB} = c\coord{\elem{v}}{\sB}. These are (LT1) and (LT2). Geometry. [Projection onto an Axis] Show that T \colon 
R^2 	o 
R^2, T(a_1, a_2) = (a_1, 0), is linear. Let \cvec{u} = (a_1, a_2), \cvec{v} = (b_1, b_2), and c \in 
R. Then  egin{aligned} T(\cvec{u} + \cvec{v}) &= (a_1 + b_1, 0) = (a_1, 0) + (b_1, 0) = T(\cvec{u}) + T(\cvec{v}), \ T(c\cvec{u}) &= (ca_1, 0) = c(a_1, 0) = cT(\cvec{u}). \end{aligned} So (LT1) and (LT2) hold. The map drops each point vertically onto the x-axis, like a shadow cast by light from straight above. [Rotation of the Plane] Let 	heta \in 
R, and let R_	heta \colon 
R^2 	o 
R^2 rotate each vector counterclockwise about the origin by the angle 	heta. Find a formula for R_	heta, and deduce that it is linear. Write (a_1, a_2) = (r\cos\varphi, r\sin\varphi) in polar coordinates. Rotating adds 	heta to the angle and keeps the length r, so by the addition formulas for sine and cosine,  egin{aligned} R_	heta(a_1, a_2) &=  igl(r\cos(\varphi + 	heta),\ r\sin(\varphi + 	heta) igr) \ &= (a_1\cos	heta - a_2\sin	heta,\ a_1\sin	heta + a_2\cos	heta). \end{aligned} This is T_\A for \A =  egin{pmatrix} \cos	heta & -\sin	heta \ \sin	heta & \cos	heta \end{pmatrix}, so R_	heta is linear by @exm-matrix-transformation. Calculus. For a polynomial p = a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_nx^n \in F[x], define its (formal) derivative as p' = a_1 + 2a_2x + \dots + na_nx^{n-1}, where ka_k means a_k added to itself k times. Over 
R this is the derivative of calculus. [Differentiation] Show that D \colon F[x] 	o F[x], D(p) = p', is linear. Show also that D maps F[x]_{\le n} into F[x]_{\le n-1} for n \ge 1. Let p = \sum_k a_kx^k and q = \sum_k b_kx^k, and c \in F. The coefficient of x^{k-1} in D(p + q) is k(a_k + b_k) = ka_k + kb_k, which is the coefficient of x^{k-1} in D(p) + D(q). The coefficient of x^{k-1} in D(cp) is k(ca_k) = c(ka_k), which is the coefficient in cD(p). Both steps use only the field axioms. Two polynomials with the same coefficients are equal (@def-polynomial), so (LT1) and (LT2) hold. If \deg p \le n, the highest power in p' is at most x^{n-1}, so D restricts to a linear map F[x]_{\le n} 	o F[x]_{\le n-1}. [Integration] Show that J \colon 
R[x] 	o 
R[x], J(p)(x) = \int_0^x p(t)\,\dd t, is linear. On coefficients, J sends a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_nx^n to a_0x +  rac{a_1}{2}x^2 + \dots +  rac{a_n}{n + 1}x^{n+1}, so it does map polynomials to polynomials. By linearity of the integral from calculus,  egin{aligned} J(p + q)(x) &= \int_0^x  igl(p(t) + q(t) igr)\,\dd t = J(p)(x) + J(q)(x), \ J(cp)(x) &= \int_0^x cp(t)\,\dd t = cJ(p)(x) \end{aligned} for every x \in 
R. Hence J is linear. (The coefficient formula divides by k + 1; over a field such as 
F_2, where 1 + 1 = 0, it breaks down.) Algebra and sequences. [Multiplication by x] Show that M \colon F[x] 	o F[x], M(p) = xp, is linear. By the distributive laws in @thm-polynomial-ring-laws, x(p + q) = xp + xq, and x(cp) = c(xp) because the product of polynomials is associative and commutative and the constant c is a polynomial. These are (LT1) and (LT2). [Trace and Transpose] Show that the trace 	r \colon M_n(F) 	o F and the transpose M_{m 	imes n}(F) 	o M_{n 	imes m}(F), \A \mapsto \A	p, are linear. For the trace, @thm-trace-properties (1) says 	r(\A + \B) = 	r \A + 	r \B and 	r(c\A) = c	r \A, which are (LT1) and (LT2); the target is F, regarded as a vector space over itself. For the transpose, the (i, j) entry of (\A + \B)	p is a_{ji} + b_{ji}, the (i, j) entry of \A	p + \B	p; and the (i, j) entry of (c\A)	p is ca_{ji}, the (i, j) entry of c\A	p. [The Shift Maps on Sequences] On the space F^{
N} of sequences (@exm-vector-spaces), define the right shift and the left shift R(s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots) = (0, s_0, s_1, \dots), \qquad L(s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots) = (s_1, s_2, s_3, \dots). Show that both are linear. The operations on F^{
N} are termwise. The entry in position k \ge 1 of R(\elem{s} + \elem{t}) is s_{k-1} + t_{k-1}, which is the entry of R(\elem{s}) + R(\elem{t}); in position 0 both have 0 = 0 + 0. Similarly, R(c\elem{s}) has entries 0 = c \cdot 0 and cs_{k-1}, the entries of cR(\elem{s}). For L, the entry in position k of L(\elem{s} + \elem{t}) is s_{k+1} + t_{k+1}, and of L(c\elem{s}) is cs_{k+1}, as required. The right shift is the map promised in the warning of Chapter 1, §8, on what changes in infinite dimension: it matches F^{
N} one-to-one with the sequences whose first entry is 0, respecting addition and scaling. In the next section we measure exactly how R and L fail to be bijective. [Composition with a Fixed Function] Let X and Y be sets and g \colon X 	o Y a function. Show that C_g \colon F^Y 	o F^X, C_g(h) = h \circ g, is linear. Show also that 
R[x] 	o 
R[x], p(x) \mapsto p(x + 1), is linear. The operations on function spaces are pointwise (@exm-vector-spaces). For t \in X, C_g(h + k)(t) = (h + k)(g(t)) = h(g(t)) + k(g(t)) =  igl(C_g(h) + C_g(k) igr)(t), and C_g(ch)(t) = c\,h(g(t)) =  igl(cC_g(h) igr)(t). So (LT1) and (LT2) hold. The output is again a function, not a number; linearity is about the function h varying, while g stays fixed. For the second claim, write \sigma \colon 
R[x] 	o 
R[x] for p(x) \mapsto p(x + 1); in full, if p = \sum_k a_kx^k, then \sigma(p) = \sum_k a_k(x + 1)^k, a finite sum in 
R[x]. Linearity is now read off the coefficients. The coefficients of p + q are the a_k + b_k, so \sigma(p + q) = \sum_k (a_k + b_k)(x + 1)^k = \sigma(p) + \sigma(q) by @thm-polynomial-ring-laws, and \sigma(cp) = \sum_k ca_k(x + 1)^k = c\,\sigma(p) in the same way. So \sigma is linear. (It translates the graph of p one unit to the left.) One can also read \sigma as an instance of C_g with g(t) = t + 1, once a polynomial and the function it defines are identified; that identification needs an argument, which Chapter 3 supplies. The degenerate maps. Three maps are always available: the identity on any space, the inclusion of any subspace, and the zero map between any two spaces. They look too simple to matter. They matter because every general statement about linear maps must be true for them, so they are the first test of any conjecture. [Identity Map] The identity \id_V \colon V 	o V, \elem{v} \mapsto \elem{v}, is linear: \id_V(\elem{u} + \elem{v}) = \elem{u} + \elem{v} = \id_V(\elem{u}) + \id_V(\elem{v}) and \id_V(c\elem{v}) = c\elem{v} = c\,\id_V(\elem{v}). [Inclusion Map] If U is a subspace of V, the inclusion \iota \colon U 	o V, \iota(\elem{u}) = \elem{u}, is linear, because the operations of U are those of V. Its formula is the identity’s, but its codomain is bigger. For instance 
R[x]_{\le 2} 	o 
R[x] is an inclusion. [Zero Map] For any V and W over F, the zero map 0 \colon V 	o W, \elem{v} \mapsto \elem{0}_W, is linear: \elem{0}_W = \elem{0}_W + \elem{0}_W and \elem{0}_W = c\elem{0}_W (@thm-scalar-zero-vector). Three consequences of linearity The two axioms already force several other rules. The first is the quickest test for nonlinearity. [Linear Maps Send Zero to Zero] Let T \colon V 	o W be linear. Then T(\elem{0}_V) = \elem{0}_W. By (LT1), T(\elem{0}_V) = T(\elem{0}_V + \elem{0}_V) = T(\elem{0}_V) + T(\elem{0}_V). Adding -T(\elem{0}_V) to both sides gives \elem{0}_W = T(\elem{0}_V). The proof used only (LT1). Homogeneity with c = 0 would also give it: T(\elem{0}_V) = T(0\elem{v}) = 0T(\elem{v}) = \elem{0}_W. [Linear Maps Preserve Negatives] Let T \colon V 	o W be linear. Then T(-\elem{v}) = -T(\elem{v}) and T(\elem{u} - \elem{v}) = T(\elem{u}) - T(\elem{v}) for all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V. By @thm-negation-scalar, -\elem{v} = (-1)\elem{v}. So (LT2) gives T(-\elem{v}) = (-1)T(\elem{v}) = -T(\elem{v}), using @thm-negation-scalar again in W. Then (LT1) gives T(\elem{u} - \elem{v}) = T(\elem{u} + (-\elem{v})) = T(\elem{u}) + T(-\elem{v}) = T(\elem{u}) - T(\elem{v}). Checking two conditions separately is often longer than necessary. One combined condition suffices. [One-Line Test for Linearity] Let V and W be vector spaces over F, and let T \colon V 	o W be a function. Then T is linear if and only if T(c\elem{u} + \elem{v}) = cT(\elem{u}) + T(\elem{v}) \qquad 	ext{for all } c \in F 	ext{ and all } \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V . (\Rightarrow) Suppose T is linear. By (LT1) and then (LT2), T(c\elem{u} + \elem{v}) = T(c\elem{u}) + T(\elem{v}) = cT(\elem{u}) + T(\elem{v}). (\Leftarrow) Suppose the condition holds. Taking c = 1 gives T(\elem{u} + \elem{v}) = T(\elem{u}) + T(\elem{v}), which is (LT1). Taking \elem{u} = \elem{v} = \elem{0} and c = 1 gives T(\elem{0}) = T(\elem{0}) + T(\elem{0}), so T(\elem{0}) = \elem{0}. Now taking \elem{v} = \elem{0} gives T(c\elem{u}) = cT(\elem{u}) + T(\elem{0}) = cT(\elem{u}), which is (LT2). Finally, the slogan. Two applications of the axioms handle a combination of two vectors; induction handles any finite combination. [Linear Maps Preserve Linear Combinations] Let T \colon V 	o W be linear, let \elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k \in V and a_1, \dots, a_k \in F, where k \ge 0. Then T(a_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + a_k\elem{v}_k) = a_1T(\elem{v}_1) + \dots + a_kT(\elem{v}_k). We use induction on k. For k = 0 both sides are empty sums, so the claim is T(\elem{0}) = \elem{0}, which is @thm-zero-maps-to-zero. Let k \ge 1 and suppose the claim holds for k - 1 vectors. By (LT1), then the induction hypothesis and (LT2), T\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{k-1} a_i\elem{v}_i + a_k\elem{v}_k\Bigr) = T\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{k-1} a_i\elem{v}_i\Bigr) + T(a_k\elem{v}_k) = \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} a_iT(\elem{v}_i) + a_kT(\elem{v}_k). [Linear Maps Are Determined by a Basis] Let V and W be vector spaces over F, let \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) be a basis of V, and let \elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_n \in W be any vectors. Then there exists exactly one linear map T \colon V 	o W such that T(\elem{v}_i) = \elem{w}_i \qquad 	ext{for } i = 1, \dots, n . It is given by T(a_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + a_n\elem{v}_n) = a_1\elem{w}_1 + \dots + a_n\elem{w}_n for all a_1, \dots, a_n \in F. Uniqueness is the computation above: any linear T with these values must be given by the formula. Existence asks us to use the formula as a definition. The only danger is that a vector might have two expressions \sum a_i\elem{v}_i, giving two candidate values; the basis rules that out, because coordinates are unique. So: ① define T(\elem{v}) from the coordinates of \elem{v}; ② check (LT1), (LT2), using that coordinates respect the operations; ③ check T(\elem{v}_i) = \elem{w}_i; ④ prove uniqueness by @thm-linear-combination. Existence. Let \elem{v} \in V. By @thm-unique-representation, there are unique scalars a_1, \dots, a_n \in F with \elem{v} = a_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + a_n\elem{v}_n; they are the entries of \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} (@def-coordinates). Define T(\elem{v}) \coloneqq a_1\elem{w}_1 + \dots + a_n\elem{w}_n . Since the scalars are unique, this assigns exactly one vector of W to each \elem{v} \in V, so T \colon V 	o W is a well-defined function. Let \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V and c \in F, with \coord{\elem{u}}{\sB} = (b_1, \dots, b_n) and \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} = (a_1, \dots, a_n). By @thm-coordinates-linear, \coord{c\elem{u} + \elem{v}}{\sB} = c\coord{\elem{u}}{\sB} + \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} = (cb_1 + a_1, \dots, cb_n + a_n). Hence, by the definition of T and the vector space axioms in W, T(c\elem{u} + \elem{v}) = \sum_{i=1}^n (cb_i + a_i)\elem{w}_i = c\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\elem{w}_i + \sum_{i=1}^n a_i\elem{w}_i = cT(\elem{u}) + T(\elem{v}). By @thm-equivalent-condition, T is linear. Moreover, \elem{v}_i = 0\elem{v}_1 + \dots + 1\elem{v}_i + \dots + 0\elem{v}_n, so \coord{\elem{v}_i}{\sB} = \cvec{e}_i and T(\elem{v}_i) = \elem{w}_i. Uniqueness. Let S \colon V 	o W be any linear map with S(\elem{v}_i) = \elem{w}_i for all i. For \elem{v} = a_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + a_n\elem{v}_n \in V, @thm-linear-combination gives S(\elem{v}) = a_1S(\elem{v}_1) + \dots + a_nS(\elem{v}_n) = a_1\elem{w}_1 + \dots + a_n\elem{w}_n = T(\elem{v}). Since S(\elem{v}) = T(\elem{v}) for every \elem{v} \in V, the functions are equal: S = T. This proves the theorem. The theorem has two halves, and they are used differently. Uniqueness says that to check two linear maps are equal, check them on a basis. Existence says that to build a linear map, choose the images of a basis freely. The same holds for the infinite bases of Chapter 1, §8, because every vector is still a unique finite combination of basis vectors; we record this as @thm-linear-map-from-any-basis below. In Chapter 4 this theorem turns into the matrix of a linear map: once bases are fixed, the n vectors T(\elem{v}_i), written in coordinates, are the columns. [Linear Maps on an Arbitrary Basis] Let V and W be vector spaces over F, let B be a basis of V (possibly infinite, in the sense of @thm-basis-extension-general), and for each \elem{b} \in B let \elem{w}_{\elem{b}} \in W be any vector. Then there is exactly one linear map T \colon V 	o W with T\elem{b} = \elem{w}_{\elem{b}} for every \elem{b} \in B. Let \elem{v} \in V. Since B spans V and is independent, \elem{v} is a finite combination \elem{v} = \sum_{\elem{b} \in B} a_{\elem{b}}\elem{b} in which only finitely many a_{\elem{b}} are nonzero, and these coefficients are unique: two such expressions differ by a finite combination of distinct elements of B equal to \elem{0}, whose coefficients all vanish by independence. Define T\elem{v} = \sum_{\elem{b} \in B} a_{\elem{b}}\elem{w}_{\elem{b}}, a finite sum. The coefficients of \elem{v} + \elem{u} and of c\elem{v} are a_{\elem{b}} + a'_{\elem{b}} and ca_{\elem{b}} by uniqueness, so T is linear, and T\elem{b} = \elem{w}_{\elem{b}} because the coefficients of \elem{b} are 1 at \elem{b} and 0 elsewhere. If S is another linear map with S\elem{b} = \elem{w}_{\elem{b}} for all \elem{b}, then S\elem{v} = \sum a_{\elem{b}} S\elem{b} = T\elem{v} by @thm-linear-combination. This proves the theorem. If T(n\elem{v}) = nT(\elem{v}), then by additivity T((n + 1)\elem{v}) = T(n\elem{v} + \elem{v}) = T(n\elem{v}) + T(\elem{v}) = nT(\elem{v}) + T(\elem{v}) = (n + 1)T(\elem{v}). (b) Let n \in 
N. By additivity and T(\elem{0}) = \elem{0}, \elem{0} = T(n\elem{v} + (-n)\elem{v}) = T(n\elem{v}) + T((-n)\elem{v}), so T((-n)\elem{v}) = -T(n\elem{v}) = -nT(\elem{v}) = (-n)T(\elem{v}), using (a). Every integer is n or -n for some n \in 
N. (c) Let q = m/n with m \in 
Z and n \ge 1. By (b) applied to the vector q\elem{v}, and then to \elem{v}, nT(q\elem{v}) = T(nq\elem{v}) = T(m\elem{v}) = mT(\elem{v}). Multiplying by  rac1n \in 
Q gives T(q\elem{v}) =  rac{m}{n}T(\elem{v}) = qT(\elem{v}). So (LT2) holds for every scalar q \in 
Q, and with additivity, which is (LT1), T is linear. [C2: Over 
C, Additivity Is Not Enough] 1. Give an additive map 
C 	o 
C that is not linear over 
C, and explain which step of @exr-linear-maps-c1 fails for it. 2. Let V and W be vector spaces over 
C. Regarding them also as spaces over 
R, let T \colon V 	o W be linear over 
R, and suppose T(i\elem{v}) = iT(\elem{v}) for all \elem{v} \in V. Prove that T is linear over 
C. (a) Complex conjugation T(z) = \conj{z} is additive and not 
C-linear (@exm-complex-conjugation). The argument of @exr-linear-maps-c1 still shows T(q z) = qT(z) for rational q, and that is true for conjugation. What fails is that the rational numbers are not all the scalars: nothing in that argument reaches a scalar like i, which is not built from 1 by adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing. (b) (LT1) holds because T is linear over 
R. For (LT2), let c = a + bi \in 
C with a, b \in 
R, and \elem{v} \in V. By the vector space axioms, c\elem{v} = a\elem{v} + b(i\elem{v}). Using (LT1), then 
R-homogeneity, then the hypothesis,  egin{aligned} T(c\elem{v}) &= T(a\elem{v}) + T(b(i\elem{v})) = aT(\elem{v}) + bT(i\elem{v}) \ &= aT(\elem{v}) + b\,iT(\elem{v}) = (a + bi)T(\elem{v}) = cT(\elem{v}). \end{aligned} Hence T is linear over 
C.

title: 2.2 Kernel and Image
content:
Kernel and Image For any function, Chapter 0 asked two questions: is it injective, and is it surjective? For a function between sets, answering them means comparing outputs pair by pair and hunting for preimages point by point. For a linear map both questions reduce to a single subspace each. This section defines the two subspaces, the kernel and the image, shows how to compute them, and proves the test that makes injectivity cheap: a linear map is injective exactly when its kernel is zero. Two questions, two subspaces Let T \colon V 	o W be linear. Start with injectivity. Suppose two inputs collide, T(\elem{u}) = T(\elem{v}). By @thm-preserves-negation this is the same as T(\elem{u} - \elem{v}) = T(\elem{u}) - T(\elem{v}) = \elem{0} . So a collision between \elem{u} and \elem{v} is the same thing as their difference being sent to \elem{0}. To detect every collision at once, it is enough to know which vectors are sent to \elem{0}. For a general function this trick is unavailable, because there is no subtraction; linearity turns a question about all pairs into a question about one set. Surjectivity asks whether every \elem{w} \in W is an output, so the set to know is the set of all outputs. For the matrix map T_\A(\cvec{x}) = \A\cvec{x} both sets are concrete: the outputs are the vectors \cvec{b} for which \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} can be solved, and the inputs sent to \cvec{0} are the solutions of \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}. Chapter 3 computes both. The definitions below give the two sets a name for every linear map. They are defined for what they measure. The kernel is everything T sends to zero; the image is everything T reaches. [Kernel] Let T \colon V 	o W be a linear map over F. The kernel of T is the subset of the domain \ker T \coloneqq \{ \elem{v} \in V : T(\elem{v}) = \elem{0}_W \} \subseteq V . [Image] Let T \colon V 	o W be a linear map over F. The image of T is the subset of the codomain \im T \coloneqq \{ T(\elem{v}) : \elem{v} \in V \} = \{ \elem{w} \in W : \elem{w} = T(\elem{v}) 	ext{ for some } \elem{v} \in V \} \subseteq W . In words: a vector \elem{v} is in \ker T when \elem{v} lives in V and T sends it to the zero vector of W. A vector \elem{w} is in \im T when \elem{w} lives in W and there exists at least one input with output \elem{w}; the input need not be unique. In the language of @def-image-preimage, \ker T = T^{-1}(\{\elem{0}\}) is the preimage of the zero vector, and \im T = T(V) is the image of the function T. The kernel is also called the null space of T, and the image its range. For group homomorphisms, the kernel was defined the same way (@def-group-homomorphism), with \elem{0} playing the role of the identity element. There is nothing to check for well-definedness: both sets are described by conditions that either hold or fail. What does need checking is that they are subspaces, not just subsets. [The Kernel Is a Subspace] Let T \colon V 	o W be linear. Then \ker T is a subspace of V. We use the Subspace Test (@thm-subspace-test). (1) By @thm-zero-maps-to-zero, T(\elem{0}_V) = \elem{0}_W, so \elem{0}_V \in \ker T. (2) Let \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in \ker T, so T(\elem{u}) = T(\elem{v}) = \elem{0}_W. By (LT1), T(\elem{u} + \elem{v}) = T(\elem{u}) + T(\elem{v}) = \elem{0}_W + \elem{0}_W = \elem{0}_W. Therefore \elem{u} + \elem{v} \in \ker T. (3) Let \elem{v} \in \ker T and c \in F. By (LT2), T(c\elem{v}) = cT(\elem{v}) = c\elem{0}_W = \elem{0}_W, using @thm-scalar-zero-vector. Therefore c\elem{v} \in \ker T. [The Image Is a Subspace] Let T \colon V 	o W be linear. Then: 1. \im T is a subspace of W; 2. T is surjective if and only if \im T = W. (a) We use the Subspace Test (@thm-subspace-test). (1) \elem{0}_W = T(\elem{0}_V) by @thm-zero-maps-to-zero, so \elem{0}_W \in \im T. (2) Let \elem{w}_1, \elem{w}_2 \in \im T, say \elem{w}_1 = T(\elem{v}_1) and \elem{w}_2 = T(\elem{v}_2) with \elem{v}_1, \elem{v}_2 \in V. By (LT1), \elem{w}_1 + \elem{w}_2 = T(\elem{v}_1 + \elem{v}_2), and \elem{v}_1 + \elem{v}_2 \in V, so \elem{w}_1 + \elem{w}_2 \in \im T. (3) Let \elem{w} = T(\elem{v}) \in \im T and c \in F. By (LT2), c\elem{w} = T(c\elem{v}) with c\elem{v} \in V, so c\elem{w} \in \im T. (b) The inclusion \im T \subseteq W always holds. By @def-injective-surjective-bijective, T is surjective exactly when every \elem{w} \in W equals T(\elem{v}) for some \elem{v}, that is, when W \subseteq \im T. So T is surjective if and only if \im T = W. This pays off a pattern from Chapter 1, §2. The null space of a matrix (@exm-null-space-subspace), the symmetric matrices (@exm-symmetric-matrices) and the trace-free matrices (@exm-trace-free-matrices) were each shown to be subspaces by a separate check, and that section promised a single theorem. Each is the kernel of a linear map (T_\A, \A \mapsto \A - \A	p, and the trace), so @thm-prop-kernel covers them all at once. First examples. Start with the maps that have the most extreme kernels and images. [The Zero Map and the Identity] Find the kernel and image of the zero map 0 \colon V 	o W and of the identity \id_V \colon V 	o V. The zero map sends every vector to \elem{0}_W, so \ker 0 = V and \im 0 = \{\elem{0}_W\}. The identity sends \elem{v} to \elem{v}, which is \elem{0} only when \elem{v} = \elem{0}, so \ker \id_V = \{\elem{0}\}. Every \elem{v} is its own image, so \im \id_V = V. These two are the ends of the scale. The kernel is always between \{\elem{0}\} and V, and the image between \{\elem{0}\} and W. The zero map kills everything and reaches nothing but \elem{0}; the identity kills nothing and reaches everything. [Projection onto an Axis] Find the kernel and image of the projection T \colon 
R^2 	o 
R^2, T(a_1, a_2) = (a_1, 0), of @exm-projection. T(a_1, a_2) = (0, 0) exactly when a_1 = 0. So \ker T = \{ (0, a_2) : a_2 \in 
R \}, the y-axis. Every output has second entry 0, and every (a_1, 0) is an output, namely T(a_1, 0). So \im T is the x-axis. The kernel is the direction the light shines along; the image is the screen the shadow falls on. A nonexample by minimal change. Replace \cvec{0} by another vector: for the projection, \{ \cvec{v} : T(\cvec{v}) = (1, 0) \} = \{ (1, a_2) : a_2 \in 
R \}. This is the vertical line through (1, 0). It does not contain \cvec{0}, and it is not closed under addition, since (1, 0) + (1, 0) = (2, 0) lies off the line. So it is not a subspace. It is the kernel shifted by (1, 0). The same thing happens for systems in Chapter 3: the solution set of \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} is one particular solution plus the set of solutions of \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}, which is \ker T_\A. Why the preimage of \elem{0}? Because \elem{0} is the one output that every linear map is guaranteed to hit, so its preimage is never empty, and because all other preimages are translates of it. If T(\elem{p}) = \elem{w}, then T(\elem{v}) = \elem{w} exactly when T(\elem{v} - \elem{p}) = \elem{0}, that is, when \elem{v} \in \elem{p} + \ker T. The kernel describes the shape of every nonempty preimage at once. Keep track of where each subspace lives. The kernel sits inside the domain V; the image sits inside the codomain W. For T_\A \colon F^n 	o F^m, the kernel consists of columns with n entries and the image of columns with m entries, so “\ker T = \im T” does not even make sense unless V = W. And the image is not the codomain in general: the differentiation map D \colon 
R[x]_{\le 3} 	o 
R[x]_{\le 3} has codomain 
R[x]_{\le 3}, but x^3 is not the derivative of any cubic, so \im D 
eq 
R[x]_{\le 3}. Injectivity via the kernel The computation that opened the section now becomes a theorem. It is the reason to prefer the kernel over the definition of injectivity whenever a map is linear. [Kernel Test for Injectivity] Let T \colon V 	o W be linear. Then T is injective if and only if \ker T = \{\elem{0}\}. (\Rightarrow) Suppose T is injective, and let \elem{v} \in \ker T. Then T(\elem{v}) = \elem{0}_W = T(\elem{0}_V) by @thm-zero-maps-to-zero. Injectivity gives \elem{v} = \elem{0}_V. Hence \ker T \subseteq \{\elem{0}\}, and the reverse inclusion holds because \ker T is a subspace (@thm-prop-kernel). (\Leftarrow) Suppose \ker T = \{\elem{0}\}, and let T(\elem{u}) = T(\elem{v}). By @thm-preserves-negation, T(\elem{u} - \elem{v}) = T(\elem{u}) - T(\elem{v}) = \elem{0}, so \elem{u} - \elem{v} \in \ker T = \{\elem{0}\}. Hence \elem{u} = \elem{v}, and T is injective. Compare the work. The definition asks: for all pairs \elem{u}, \elem{v}, does T(\elem{u}) = T(\elem{v}) force \elem{u} = \elem{v}? The theorem asks only: for each \elem{v}, does T(\elem{v}) = \elem{0} force \elem{v} = \elem{0}? The second question is usually a homogeneous linear system or a coefficient comparison. For T_\A, the theorem says that \cvec{x} \mapsto \A\cvec{x} is injective exactly when \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} has only the trivial solution; Chapter 3 turns that into a test that elimination can run. Computing the image The image is defined by an existence condition, which is hard to check directly. When V has a spanning list, applying T to it gives a spanning list of \im T. [The Image Is Spanned by the Images of a Spanning List] Let T \colon V 	o W be linear, and suppose (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) spans V. Then \im T = \Span igl(T(\elem{v}_1), \dots, T(\elem{v}_k) igr). In particular, if V is finite-dimensional, then so is \im T, even when W is not. (\supseteq) Each T(\elem{v}_i) lies in \im T, which is a subspace by @thm-prop-image. By @thm-span-subspace (3), the span of these vectors is contained in \im T. (\subseteq) Let \elem{w} \in \im T, say \elem{w} = T(\elem{v}) with \elem{v} \in V. Since (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) spans V, \elem{v} = a_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + a_k\elem{v}_k for some a_i \in F. By @thm-linear-combination, \elem{w} = a_1T(\elem{v}_1) + \dots + a_kT(\elem{v}_k) \in \Span(T(\elem{v}_1), \dots, T(\elem{v}_k)). If V is finite-dimensional, some finite list spans V (@def-finite-dimensional), and its images form a finite list spanning \im T. So the recipe for the image is: apply T to a basis (or any spanning list) of V, then sift the results to a basis if one is wanted (@thm-sift). The images of a basis need not be independent; the projection sends the basis (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) to (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{0}). Examples We now compute kernels and images across the families: polynomials, matrices, and sequences. In each case we then read off injectivity from the kernel and surjectivity from the image. [Differentiation] Find the kernel and image of D \colon 
R[x]_{\le 3} 	o 
R[x]_{\le 2}, D(p) = p'. Kernel. Let p = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + a_3x^3. Then D(p) = a_1 + 2a_2x + 3a_3x^2, which is the zero polynomial exactly when a_1 = 2a_2 = 3a_3 = 0. Since 2 
eq 0 and 3 
eq 0 in 
R, this means a_1 = a_2 = a_3 = 0. So \ker D = \{ a_0 : a_0 \in 
R \} = \Span(1), the constants. Image. By @thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images applied to the basis (1, x, x^2, x^3),  egin{aligned} \im D &= \Span igl(D(1), D(x), D(x^2), D(x^3) igr) = \Span(0, 1, 2x, 3x^2) \ &= \Span(1, x, x^2) = 
R[x]_{\le 2}. \end{aligned} So D is surjective but not injective: p and p + 5 have the same derivative. Note \dim \ker D + \dim \im D = 1 + 3 = 4 = \dim 
R[x]_{\le 3}. [Trace] Find the kernel and image of 	r \colon M_2(
R) 	o 
R. Kernel. A matrix  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{pmatrix} has trace 0 exactly when d = -a, that is, when it equals  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ c & -a \end{pmatrix} = a egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} + b\E_{12} + c\E_{21}. So \E_{11} - \E_{22}, \E_{12}, \E_{21} span \ker 	r. They are independent: the combination above is the zero matrix only if a = b = c = 0. Hence they form a basis, and \dim \ker 	r = 3. Image. \im 	r is a subspace of 
R, and it contains 	r \E_{11} = 1. The lazy preimage r\E_{11} of any r \in 
R shows \im 	r = 
R. So the trace is surjective but not injective. Again 3 + 1 = 4 = \dim M_2(
R). The next two examples live in infinite-dimensional spaces, and the pattern “one property but not the other” goes the opposite way. [Integration] Find the kernel and image of J \colon 
R[x] 	o 
R[x], J(p)(x) = \int_0^x p(t)\,\dd t, of @exm-integration. Kernel. For p = a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_nx^n, J(p) = a_0x +  rac{a_1}{2}x^2 + \dots +  rac{a_n}{n + 1}x^{n+1}. This is the zero polynomial only if every  rac{a_k}{k + 1} = 0, that is, every a_k = 0. So \ker J = \{0\}, and J is injective by @thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel. Image. Let U = \{ q \in 
R[x] : q(0) = 0 \}, the polynomials with constant coefficient 0. Every J(p) has constant coefficient 0, so \im J \subseteq U. Conversely, if q = b_1x + b_2x^2 + \dots + b_mx^m \in U, then p = b_1 + 2b_2x + \dots + mb_mx^{m-1} satisfies J(p) = q. Hence \im J = U. Since 1 
otin U, J is not surjective. [The Shifts: Injective but Not Surjective, and Conversely] Find the kernels and images of the right and left shifts R, L \colon F^{
N} 	o F^{
N} of @exm-shift. Right shift. R(s_0, s_1, \dots) = (0, s_0, s_1, \dots) is the zero sequence only if every s_k = 0. So \ker R = \{\elem{0}\}, and R is injective. Every output has first entry 0; conversely, (0, t_1, t_2, \dots) = R(t_1, t_2, \dots). So \im R = \{ \elem{t} \in F^{
N} : t_0 = 0 \} 
eq F^{
N}, and R is not surjective: \elem{e}_0 = (1, 0, 0, \dots) is never an output. Left shift. L(s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots) = (s_1, s_2, \dots) is zero exactly when s_1 = s_2 = \dots = 0, with s_0 arbitrary. So \ker L = \Span(\elem{e}_0) 
eq \{\elem{0}\}, and L is not injective. Every sequence is an output, since L(R(\elem{t})) = \elem{t}. So \im L = F^{
N}, and L is surjective. This pays off the pointer from Chapter 1, §8: R matches F^{
N} one-to-one with its proper subspace \im R. For a map V 	o V on a finite set, injective and surjective are equivalent (@thm-finite-injective-iff-surjective). The shifts, and the pair J and D on 
R[x] (where D(J(p)) = p makes D surjective, while D(1) = 0 makes it not injective), show that for linear maps on an infinite-dimensional space this equivalence fails. The next section proves that it holds again when V is finite-dimensional. Find \ker T and \im T for the map T \colon 
R^2 	o 
R^3, T(x, y) = (2x - y,\ x + y,\ x - y), of @exm-map-from-basis-values. Is T injective? Surjective? If T(x, y) = \cvec{0}, then x + y = 0 and x - y = 0, so x = y = 0. Hence \ker T = \{\cvec{0}\}, and T is injective. By @thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images, \im T = \Span(T(\cvec{e}_1), T(\cvec{e}_2)) = \Span igl((2, 1, 1), (-1, 1, -1) igr), a plane in 
R^3. A span of two vectors has dimension at most 2 < 3, so \im T 
eq 
R^3 and T is not surjective. What injective and surjective maps do to lists Injectivity and surjectivity are statements about vectors. They translate into statements about lists: injective maps keep independent lists independent, and surjective maps keep spanning lists spanning. On a basis, the translation goes both ways. [Injective Maps Preserve Independence, Surjective Maps Preserve Spanning] Let T \colon V 	o W be linear. 1. If T is injective and (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) is linearly independent in V, then (T(\elem{v}_1), \dots, T(\elem{v}_k)) is linearly independent in W. 2. If T is surjective and (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) spans V, then (T(\elem{v}_1), \dots, T(\elem{v}_k)) spans W. 3. If (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) is a basis of V, then T is injective if and only if (T(\elem{v}_1), \dots, T(\elem{v}_n)) is linearly independent, and T is surjective if and only if (T(\elem{v}_1), \dots, T(\elem{v}_n)) spans W. (a) Let a_1T(\elem{v}_1) + \dots + a_kT(\elem{v}_k) = \elem{0}. By @thm-linear-combination, T(a_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + a_k\elem{v}_k) = \elem{0}, so a_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + a_k\elem{v}_k \in \ker T. Since T is injective, \ker T = \{\elem{0}\} (@thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel), so a_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + a_k\elem{v}_k = \elem{0}. The independence of (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) gives a_1 = \dots = a_k = 0. (b) By @thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images, \Span(T(\elem{v}_1), \dots, T(\elem{v}_k)) = \im T, and \im T = W because T is surjective (@thm-prop-image). (c) Injectivity. (\Rightarrow) is (a). (\Leftarrow) Suppose the images are independent, and let \elem{v} \in \ker T. Write \elem{v} = a_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + a_n\elem{v}_n. By @thm-linear-combination, \elem{0} = T(\elem{v}) = a_1T(\elem{v}_1) + \dots + a_nT(\elem{v}_n), so all a_i = 0 and \elem{v} = \elem{0}. Hence \ker T = \{\elem{0}\}, and T is injective by @thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel. Surjectivity. By @thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images, \im T = \Span(T(\elem{v}_1), \dots, T(\elem{v}_n)). By @thm-prop-image, T is surjective exactly when this span is W. Without injectivity, independence can be lost. The projection T(a_1, a_2) = (a_1, 0) sends the independent list ((1, 0), (1, 1)) to ((1, 0), (1, 0)), which is dependent. The kernel is to blame: (1, 1) - (1, 0) = (0, 1) lies in \ker T. Likewise, a map that is not surjective sends no list to a spanning list of W, since all the images lie in \im T 
eq W: the inclusion 
R[x]_{\le 2} 	o 
R[x]_{\le 3} sends the basis (1, x, x^2) to a list that misses x^3. Part (c) turns a question about a map into a question about n vectors in W, which for vectors in F^m is a question Chapter 3 settles by elimination. In the next section, counting dimensions will let us check only one of injectivity and surjectivity when \dim V = \dim W. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the kernel and the image of a linear map T \colon V 	o W. Of which spaces are they subspaces? 2. State the kernel test for injectivity. 3. True or false: if T(\elem{u}) = T(\elem{v}), then \elem{u} - \elem{v} \in \ker T. Justify your answer. 4. True or false: for D \colon 
R[x]_{\le 3} 	o 
R[x]_{\le 3}, D(p) = p', we have \im D = 
R[x]_{\le 3}. Justify your answer. 5. True or false: for a linear T \colon V 	o W and any \elem{w} \in W, the set \{ \elem{v} \in V : T(\elem{v}) = \elem{w} \} is a subspace of V. Justify your answer. (a) See @def-kernel and @def-image: \ker T = \{ \elem{v} \in V : T(\elem{v}) = \elem{0} \}, a subspace of V (@thm-prop-kernel); \im T = \{ T(\elem{v}) : \elem{v} \in V \}, a subspace of W (@thm-prop-image). (b) See @thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel: a linear map is injective if and only if its kernel is \{\elem{0}\}. (c) True. By @thm-preserves-negation, T(\elem{u} - \elem{v}) = T(\elem{u}) - T(\elem{v}) = \elem{0}. (d) False. Every derivative of a polynomial of degree at most 3 has degree at most 2, so x^3 
otin \im D. (e) False. If \elem{w} 
eq \elem{0}, the set does not contain \elem{0}, since T(\elem{0}) = \elem{0} 
eq \elem{w}. For example, for the projection of @exm-projection-kernel-image and \elem{w} = (1, 0), the set is the line \{ (1, a_2) \}. It is a subspace exactly when \elem{w} = \elem{0}, in which case it is \ker T. B. Practice [B1: Kernel and Image from the Definitions] For each map, find the kernel and the image, give a basis of each, and decide whether the map is injective and whether it is surjective. 1. D^2 \colon 
R[x]_{\le 3} 	o

R[x]_{\le 1}, and conversely b_0 + b_1x = D^2 igl(	frac{b_0}{2}x^2 + 	frac{b_1}{6}x^3 igr), so \im D^2 = 
R[x]_{\le 1}, again with basis (1, x). Since \ker D^2 
eq \{0\}, D^2 is not injective (@thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel); since \im D^2
