title: 2.3 The Rank–Nullity Theorem
content:
The Rank–Nullity Theorem The examples of the last section kept producing the same coincidence. Differentiation 
R[x]_{\le 3} 	o 
R[x]_{\le 2} has a kernel of dimension 1 and an image of dimension 3, and 1 + 3 = 4 = \dim 
R[x]_{\le 3}. The trace on M_2(
R) gives 3 + 1 = 4 again. This section proves that the same equation holds for every linear map on a finite-dimensional space, with no matrices at all, and then turns it into the most useful counting tool of the chapter. Chapter 3 meets the equation again for matrices, counted a different way. Rank and nullity The two numbers in the equation are dimensions of the two subspaces of @def-kernel and @def-image, so they are defined whenever those subspaces are finite-dimensional. [Nullity] Let T \colon V 	o W be a linear map with \ker T finite-dimensional. The nullity of T is 
ullity T \coloneqq \dim \ker T. [Rank] Let T \colon V 	o W be a linear map with \im T finite-dimensional. The rank of T is ank T \coloneqq \dim \im T. If V is finite-dimensional, both numbers are defined: \ker T is a subspace of V, hence finite-dimensional (@thm-subspace-dimension), and \im T is finite-dimensional by @thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images. The nullity counts the independent directions that T destroys; the rank counts the independent directions that survive in the output. [Rank and Nullity in Examples] Find the nullity and rank of (a) differentiation D \colon 
R[x]_{\le 3} 	o 
R[x]_{\le 2}; (b) the zero map and the identity on a space of dimension n. (a) By @exm-differentiation-kernel-image, \ker D = \Span(1) and \im D = 
R[x]_{\le 2}. So 
ullity D = 1 and ank D = 3. (b) By @exm-kernel-image-degenerate, the zero map V 	o V has nullity n and rank 0, and the identity has nullity 0 and rank n. A nonexample. The integration map J \colon 
R[x] 	o 
R[x] of @exm-integration-kernel-image has nullity 0, but its image contains the independent list (x, x^2, \dots, x^k) for every k, so the image is not finite-dimensional (@thm-size-bounds) and ank J is not defined. What separates J from the examples above is that its domain is infinite-dimensional. The theorem We want to prove that for every linear T \colon V 	o W with V finite-dimensional, \dim \ker T + \dim \im T = \dim V . This is a dimension formula, so we look for the proof pattern that proved the last one, the Dimension Formula for Sums (@thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim): take a basis of the smallest space, extend it, make a Big Claim about the vectors that were added, and count. Which space is the smallest? The kernel lives in V and the image lives in W, different spaces that cannot be compared. The only inclusion available is \ker T \subseteq V. So we start with a basis of \ker T and extend it to a basis of V. The image has to be reached by applying T, and the kernel vectors contribute nothing when we do. So the natural candidate for a basis of \im T is the images of the added vectors. [Rank–Nullity Theorem] Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space, let W be any vector space over the same field, and let T \colon V 	o W be linear. Then \ker T and \im T are finite-dimensional, and 
ullity T + ank T = \dim V . The picture is the whole proof. The \elem{u}’s all go to \elem{0}; the \elem{v}’s carry everything else. ① Take a basis (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k) of \ker T, the smallest space in sight. ② Extend it to a basis (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k, \elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_r) of V (Basis Extension). ③ Big Claim: (T\elem{v}_1, \dots, T\elem{v}_r) is a basis of \im T. Spanning: apply T to a general vector of V; the \elem{u}-terms die because they are in the kernel. Independence: the only way to use linearity is backwards, turning \sum b_jT\elem{v}_j = \elem{0} into T(\sum b_j\elem{v}_j) = \elem{0}. Then \sum b_j\elem{v}_j is in the kernel, where the \elem{u}’s are a basis, and the big basis of V finishes it. ④ Count: \dim V = k + r = 
ullity T + ank T. This is the move of @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim: basis of the smallest space, extend, Big Claim, count. The new ingredient is that the Big Claim is about the images of the added vectors. Step 1: bases. By @thm-prop-kernel, \ker T is a subspace of V. Since V is finite-dimensional, so is \ker T (@thm-subspace-dimension), and it has a basis (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k) with k = 
ullity T (@cor-basis-existence). This list is linearly independent in V, so by the Basis Extension Theorem (@thm-basis-extension) there are \elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_r \in V such that (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k, \elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_r) is a basis of V. Thus \dim V = k + r. Step 2: the Big Claim. The list (T\elem{v}_1, \dots, T\elem{v}_r) is a basis of \im T. Spanning. By @thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images applied to the basis of Step 1, \im T = \Span(T\elem{u}_1, \dots, T\elem{u}_k, T\elem{v}_1, \dots, T\elem{v}_r). Each T\elem{u}_i = \elem{0}, since \elem{u}_i \in \ker T, and deleting a zero vector from a list does not change its span, because \elem{0} lies in every span (@thm-span-absorb). Hence \im T = \Span(T\elem{v}_1, \dots, T\elem{v}_r). Independence. Let b_1, \dots, b_r \in F satisfy b_1T\elem{v}_1 + \dots + b_rT\elem{v}_r = \elem{0}. By @thm-linear-combination, T(b_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + b_r\elem{v}_r) = \elem{0}, so b_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + b_r\elem{v}_r \in \ker T. Since (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k) spans \ker T, there are a_1, \dots, a_k \in F with b_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + b_r\elem{v}_r = a_1\elem{u}_1 + \dots + a_k\elem{u}_k . Rearranging, (-a_1)\elem{u}_1 + \dots + (-a_k)\elem{u}_k + b_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + b_r\elem{v}_r = \elem{0}. This is a combination of the basis (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k, \elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_r) of V, which is linearly independent, so all its coefficients are 0. In particular b_1 = \dots = b_r = 0. Hence (T\elem{v}_1, \dots, T\elem{v}_r) is linearly independent. Step 3: count. By the claim, \im T has a basis of length r, so it is finite-dimensional with ank T = r (@def-dimension). Therefore 
ullity T + ank T = k + r = \dim V , as claimed. The proof reads correctly when k = 0 (injective T: the \elem{v}’s are a basis of V) and when r = 0 (\ker T = V: the claim says \im T has the empty basis). Notice what was not used: nothing about W beyond its being a vector space. The theorem counts only in the domain. Applied to the matrix map T_\A \colon F^n 	o F^m, the theorem says 
ullity T_\A + ank T_\A = n. In particular, the solutions of a homogeneous system \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} in n unknowns form a subspace of dimension n - ank T_\A, whatever method is used to find the rank. Chapter 3 proves this equation a second way, by counting the free and pivot columns of a reduced matrix; here we counted basis vectors, and no row operation appeared. In the online version you can test the count on any matrix map. from sympy import Matrix A = Matrix([ [1, 2, 0, 3], [2, 4, 1, 8], [-1, -2, 1, -1], ]) rank = A.rank() # dim im T_A nullity = len(A.nullspace()) # dim ker T_A: length of a basis of the kernel print("rank =", rank, " nullity =", nullity, " dim of domain =", A.cols) rank + nullity == A.cols Count instead of check Rank–Nullity links the two questions of the last section. Injectivity is about the kernel, surjectivity about the image, and the theorem says the two dimensions add up to a fixed number. So one controls the other. [Consequences of Rank–Nullity] Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F, and let T \colon V 	o W be linear. 1. T is injective if and only if ank T = \dim V. 2. T is surjective if and only if ank T = \dim W. 3. If \dim V > \dim W, then T is not injective. 4. If \dim V < \dim W, then T is not surjective. 5. If \dim V = \dim W, then T is injective \iff T is surjective \iff T is bijective. (a) By @thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel, T is injective if and only if \ker T = \{\elem{0}\}. A finite-dimensional space is \{\elem{0}\} exactly when its dimension is 0, because the empty list is a basis of \{\elem{0}\} and a basis of length 0 spans only \{\elem{0}\}. So T is injective if and only if 
ullity T = 0, which by @thm-rank-nullity means ank T = \dim V. (b) If T is surjective, then \im T = W (@thm-prop-image), so ank T = \dim W. Conversely, if ank T = \dim W, then \im T is a subspace of W of the same dimension, so \im T = W by @thm-dim-impl-eq, and T is surjective. (c) Since \im T is a subspace of W, ank T \le \dim W < \dim V by @thm-subspace-dimension. By (a), T is not injective. (d) By @thm-rank-nullity, ank T = \dim V - 
ullity T \le \dim V < \dim W. By (b), T is not surjective. (e) If \dim V = \dim W, then (a) and (b) have the same right-hand side, so T is injective if and only if it is surjective. Hence either property gives both, which is bijectivity; and bijective maps are injective by definition. Part (e) is the linear version of the pigeonhole principle for finite sets (@thm-finite-injective-iff-surjective), with dimension in place of the number of elements. It is a count instead of check: to show that a map between spaces of the same finite dimension is bijective, check only the kernel, usually the easier half, and let the count supply surjectivity. For T_\A with \A square, it says that if \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} has only the trivial solution then \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} is solvable for every \cvec{b}; Chapter 3 puts that equivalence at the center of its account of square systems. Parts (c) and (d) are the linear version of “no injection from a bigger finite set into a smaller one, and no surjection the other way”. Both finiteness and equal dimension are needed. Rank–Nullity requires V to be finite-dimensional; W may be anything, as for the inclusion 
R[x]_{\le 2} 	o 
R[x], with nullity 0 and rank 3. Part (e) fails when the spaces are infinite-dimensional, even for an operator V 	o V: the right shift R on F^{
N} is injective but not surjective, and the left shift L is surjective but not injective (@exm-shift-kernel-image). And the hypothesis \dim V = \dim W cannot be dropped: T(x, y) = (2x - y,\ x + y,\ x - y) from 
R^2 to 
R^3 is injective but not surjective. Answer each question with a count. 1. Can a linear map 
R^5 	o 
R^2 be injective? 2. Is there a linear map T \colon 
R^6 	o 
R^4 with 
ullity T = 1? 3. A linear operator T on 
R[x]_{\le 3} satisfies \ker T = \{0\}. Must T be surjective? (a) No, by @cor-rank-nullity-consequences (c): 5 > 2. Concretely, the rank is at most 2, so the nullity is at least 3. (b) No. By @thm-rank-nullity the rank would be 6 - 1 = 5, but \im T \subseteq 
R^4 has dimension at most 4. (c) Yes. The domain and codomain are both 
R[x]_{\le 3}, of dimension 4, and T is injective, so it is surjective by @cor-rank-nullity-consequences (e). Existence with conditions on derivatives The same argument works when some conditions are on derivatives, where no Vandermonde matrix is at hand. [Prescribing Values and Slopes] Show that for all a, b, c, d \in 
R there is exactly one p \in 
R[x]_{\le 3} with p(0) = a, \qquad p(1) = b, \qquad p'(0) = c, \qquad p'(1) = d . Hence find the cubic that rises from 0 at x = 0 to 1 at x = 1 with slope 0 at both ends. Define T \colon 
R[x]_{\le 3} 	o 
R^4 by T(p) =  igl(p(0),\ p(1),\ p'(0),\ p'(1) igr). Each entry is linear in p: evaluation respects sums and scalar multiples (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), and so does differentiation (@exm-differentiation). Hence T is linear by @thm-equivalent-condition. Kernel. Let p = c_0 + c_1x + c_2x^2 + c_3x^3 with T(p) = \cvec{0}. Then p(0) = c_0 = 0 and p'(0) = c_1 = 0. So p = c_2x^2 + c_3x^3, and the remaining conditions read p(1) = c_2 + c_3 = 0, \qquad p'(1) = 2c_2 + 3c_3 = 0 . Subtracting twice the first from the second gives c_3 = 0, and then c_2 = 0. Hence \ker T = \{0\}. Count. \dim 
R[x]_{\le 3} = 4 = \dim 
R^4, so T is bijective by @cor-rank-nullity-consequences (e). Surjectivity is existence for every (a, b, c, d), and injectivity is uniqueness. For the data (0, 1, 0, 0), try p = \alpha x^2 +  eta x^3, which already has p(0) = p'(0) = 0. Then p(1) = \alpha +  eta = 1 and p'(1) = 2\alpha + 3 eta = 0 give  eta = -2 and \alpha = 3. So p = 3x^2 - 2x^3; by uniqueness it is the only such cubic. Dimensions of subspaces cut out by conditions Many subspaces are defined as “all vectors satisfying some linear conditions”, which is to say as the kernel of a linear map. If the map is surjective, Rank–Nullity gives the dimension of the kernel at once, and surjectivity is often easy to see. [Dimension of a Kernel from a Surjective Map] Find the dimension of each subspace. 1. The trace-free matrices U = \{ \A \in M_n(F) : 	r \A = 0 \} (@exm-trace-free-matrices). 2. U' = \{ p \in 
R[x]_{\le n} : \int_0^1 p(t)\,\dd t = 0 \}. (a) U = \ker 	r, where 	r \colon M_n(F) 	o F is linear (@exm-trace-matrices). Its image is a subspace of F (@thm-prop-image) containing 	r \E_{11} = 1, so it contains c \cdot 1 = c for every c \in F; it is all of F, and ank 	r = 1. Since \dim M_n(F) = n^2 (@exm-standard-bases), @thm-rank-nullity gives \dim U = n^2 - 1. (b) U' = \ker \psi, where \psi \colon 
R[x]_{\le n} 	o 
R, \psi(p) = \int_0^1 p(t)\,\dd t, is linear by @exr-linear-maps-b3 (b). Since \psi(1) = 1, the image is a subspace of 
R containing 1, hence all of 
R, so ank \psi = 1. By @thm-rank-nullity, \dim U' = (n + 1) - 1 = n. Without the theorem, (a) needs an explicit basis of n^2 - 1 matrices together with a proof of independence and spanning. With it, one matrix of trace 1 is enough. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the rank and the nullity of a linear map. 2. State the Rank–Nullity Theorem, with its hypotheses. 3. True or false: there is an injective linear map 
R^4 	o 
R^3. Justify your answer. 4. True or false: if V is finite-dimensional and T \colon V 	o V is linear with \im T = V, then T is injective. Justify your answer. 5. True or false: every injective linear map F^{
N} 	o F^{
N} is surjective. Justify your answer. 6. Name the four steps of the proof of Rank–Nullity. (a) See @def-nullity and @def-rank: 
ullity T = \dim \ker T and ank T = \dim \im T, when these are finite-dimensional. (b) See @thm-rank-nullity: if V is finite-dimensional and T \colon V 	o W is linear, then 
ullity T + ank T = \dim V. (c) False. 4 > 3, so no linear map 
R^4 	o 
R^3 is injective (@cor-rank-nullity-consequences (c)). (d) True. T is surjective, and its domain and codomain are the same finite-dimensional space, so T is injective by @cor-rank-nullity-consequences (e). (e) False. The right shift R is injective but not surjective (@exm-shift-kernel-image). The count fails because F^{
N} is not finite-dimensional. (f) Take a basis of \ker T; extend it to a basis of V; prove the Big Claim that the images of the added vectors form a basis of \im T (spanning, then independence); count. B. Practice [B1: Verifying Rank–Nullity] For each map, find a basis of the kernel and a basis of the image, and verify that 
ullity T + ank T = \dim V. 1. T \colon 
R[x]_{\le 3} 	o 
R^2, T(p) = (p(0), p(1)). 2. T \colon M_2(
R) 	o M_2(
R), T(\A) = \A + \A	p. (a) T is linear by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations. Kernel: for p = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + a_3x^3, T(p) = \cvec{0} means a_0 = 0 and a_1 + a_2 + a_3 = 0, that is, p = a_2(x^2 - x) + a_3(x^3 - x). The list (x^2 - x, x^3 - x) spans \ker T, and it is independent by @thm-distinct-degrees-independent, so it is a basis. Image: T(1) = (1, 1) and T(x) = (0, 1) are independent, so they span a 2-dimensional subspace of 
R^2, which is 
R^2 (@thm-dim-impl-eq). So \im T = 
R^2 with basis ((1, 1), (0, 1)). Hence 2 + 2 = 4 = \dim 
R[x]_{\le 3}. (b) T is linear because the transpose is (@exm-trace-matrices). Kernel: \A + \A	p = \O means a_{11} = a_{22} = 0 and a_{21} = -a_{12}, so \ker T = \Span(\E_{12} - \E_{21}), with basis (\E_{12} - \E_{21}). So \im T is the space of symmetric matrices, with basis (\E_{11}, \E_{22}, \E_{12} + \E_{21}) (as in @exr-kernel-image-b2). Hence 1 + 3 = 4 = \dim M_2(
R). [B2: Bijective by the Kernel Alone] Let n \ge 0 and T \colon 
R[x]_{\le n} 	o 
R[x]_{\le n}, T(p) = p + xp'. 1. Show that T is a linear map into 
R[x]_{\le n} and that \ker T = \{0\}. Deduce that T is bijective. 2. Hence show that there is exactly one p \in 
R[x]_{\le 2} with p + xp' = 1 + x + x^2, and find it. (a) For p = \sum_{k=0}^n a_kx^k, xp' = \sum_{k=1}^n ka_kx^k, so T(p) = \sum_{k=0}^n (1 + k)a_kx^k \in 
R[x]_{\le n} . Linearity: T(cp + q) = (cp + q) + x(cp' + q') = c(p + xp') + (q + xq') = cT(p) + T(q), using @exm-differentiation. If T(p) = 0, then (1 + k)a_k = 0 for each k; since 1 + k 
eq 0 in 
R, every a_k = 0. So \ker T = \{0\}, and T is injective (@thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel). Domain and codomain have the same finite dimension n + 1, so T is bijective by @cor-rank-nullity-consequences (e). (b) With n = 2, surjectivity gives a solution and injectivity makes it unique. By the formula in (a), T(a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2) = a_0 + 2a_1x + 3a_2x^2, so we need a_0 = 1, 2a_1 = 1, 3a_2 = 1. Hence p = 1 + 	frac12 x + 	frac13 x^2. Check: xp' = 	frac12 x + 	frac23 x^2, and p + xp' = 1 + x + x^2. [B3: A Dimension via a Surjective Map] Let U = \{ p \in 
R[x]_{\le 4} : p(1) = p(2) = 0 \}. Use a surjective linear map to show that \dim U = 3. Hence find a basis of U. Define T \colon 
R[x]_{\le 4} 	o 
R^2, T(p) = (p(1), p(2)). It is linear by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, and U = \ker T. Its image contains T(1) = (1, 1) and T(x) = (1, 2), which are independent, so \im T is a 2-dimensional subspace of 
R^2 and equals 
R^2 (@thm-dim-impl-eq). Thus ank T = 2, and by @thm-rank-nullity, \dim U = 5 - 2 = 3. The polynomials (x - 1)(x - 2), x(x - 1)(x - 2), and x^2(x - 1)(x - 2) vanish at 1 and 2 and have degrees 2, 3, 4 \le 4, so they lie in U. They are nonzero of distinct degrees, hence independent (@thm-distinct-degrees-independent). There are 3 = \dim U of them, so they form a basis of U (@thm-right-size-basis). C. Going deeper [C1: A Lower Bound for the Rank of a Composite] Let U and V be finite-dimensional, let W be a vector space, all over F, and let T \colon U 	o V and S \colon V 	o W be linear. Write ST for the composite S \circ T, which is linear (see the note before @exr-kernel-image-c1). Let S' \colon \im T 	o W be the restriction of S to \im T, that is, S'(\elem{v}) = S(\elem{v}) for \elem{v} \in \im T. 1. Show that S' is linear, that \im S' = \im(ST), and that \ker S' = \ker S \cap \im T. 2. Deduce that ank(ST) = ank T - \dim(\ker S \cap \im T). 3. Hence prove Sylvester’s inequality: ank(ST) \ge ank S + ank T - \dim V. Hint: for (c), compare \ker S \cap \im T with \ker S. (a) S' satisfies (LT1) and (LT2) because S does and \im T is a subspace (@thm-prop-image) with the operations of V. A vector \elem{w} lies in \im S' exactly when \elem{w} = S(\elem{v}) with \elem{v} = T(\elem{u}) for some \elem{u} \in U, that is, when \elem{w} = ST(\elem{u}); so \im S' = \im(ST). A vector \elem{v} \in \im T lies in \ker S' exactly when S(\elem{v}) = \elem{0}; so \ker S' = \ker S \cap \im T. (b) \im T is finite-dimensional with \dim \im T = ank T, since U is finite-dimensional (@thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images). By @thm-rank-nullity applied to S' \colon \im T 	o W and by (a), ank T = \dim \ker S' + \dim \im S' = \dim(\ker S \cap \im T) + ank(ST). (c) \ker S \cap \im T is a subspace of \ker S, so \dim(\ker S \cap \im T) \le 
ullity S = \dim V - ank S, by @thm-subspace-dimension and @thm-rank-nullity for S. Substituting into (b), ank(ST) \ge ank T - (\dim V - ank S) = ank S + ank T - \dim V . [C2: When the Kernel Equals the Image] Let V be finite-dimensional and T \colon V 	o V linear with \ker T = \im T. 1. Prove that \dim V is even. 2. Give an example of such a T on 
R^2, and one on 
R^4. 3. Is there such a T on 
R^3? Justify your answer. (a) By @thm-rank-nullity, \dim V = 
ullity T + ank T = \dim \ker T + \dim \im T = 2\dim \im T, which is even. (b) On 
R^2, let T(x, y) = (y, 0). Then T(x, y) = \cvec{0} exactly when y = 0, so \ker T is the x-axis; and the outputs (y, 0) fill the x-axis, so \im T is the x-axis too. On 
R^4, let T(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4) = (x_2, 0, x_4, 0). Its kernel is \{ x_2 = x_4 = 0 \} = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_3), and its image is \{ (a, 0, b, 0) \} = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_3). Both maps are matrix maps, hence linear. (c) No. By (a), \dim V would be even, but \dim 
R^3 = 3.

title: 2.4 The Algebra of Linear Maps
content:
The Algebra of Linear Maps So far we have studied one linear map at a time: its kernel, its image, and the count that ties them together. But linear maps rarely come alone. The map p \mapsto p + p' is the identity plus differentiation, and rotating then projecting is one map followed by another. This section shows that linear maps can be added, scaled, and composed, that these operations obey almost all the rules of arithmetic, and that an operator can be plugged into a polynomial just as a square matrix can. Adding and scaling linear maps Look at three maps on 
R[x]_{\le 2} that have already appeared in this chapter or will soon: p \mapsto p + p', \qquad p \mapsto 3p', \qquad p \mapsto p' - 2p . Each is built from two simpler maps, the identity \id and differentiation D, by the recipe “apply both to p, then combine the outputs with the operations of the target space”. The first is “\id + D”, the second “3D”, the third “D - 2\id”. Instead of checking linearity for each such combination separately, we would like to check it once for the recipe. The recipe itself deserves a name. Linear maps into the same space can be added and scaled output by output, and the results are again linear maps. [The space of linear maps] Let V and W be vector spaces over the same field F. We write \cL(V, W) for the set of all linear maps V 	o W, and \cL(V) \coloneqq \cL(V, V) for the set of linear operators on V (@def-linear-transformation). For S, T \in \cL(V, W) and c \in F, the sum S + T and the scalar multiple cT are the functions V 	o W defined by (S + T)(\elem{v}) \coloneqq S\elem{v} + T\elem{v}, \qquad (cT)(\elem{v}) \coloneqq c\,(T\elem{v}) \qquad 	ext{for every } \elem{v} \in V . As in @def-linear-transformation, we write T\elem{v} for T(\elem{v}) when no brackets are needed. In words: to evaluate S + T at \elem{v}, evaluate both maps at \elem{v} and add the results in W; to evaluate cT, evaluate T and scale the result in W. The operations of V play no role in the definition. That is why S and T must have the same codomain: the sum S\elem{v} + T\elem{v} has to be computed in one space. Both maps must also be defined on the same V. We have used these operations before without naming them: the operations on F^X in @exm-vector-spaces (d) are defined by the same pointwise recipe, with values added in F instead of W. It turns out that the recipe never leaves the world of linear maps, and that \cL(V, W) is itself a vector space. This is the first sign that maps between vector spaces are as good as vectors. [\cL(V, W) Is a Vector Space] Let V and W be vector spaces over F. If S, T \in \cL(V, W) and c \in F, then S + T and cT are linear. With the operations of @def-space-of-linear-maps, \cL(V, W) is a vector space over F. Its zero vector is the zero map \elem{v} \mapsto \elem{0}_W, and the negative of T is (-1)T \colon \elem{v} \mapsto -T\elem{v}. There are two layers. The set W^V of all functions V 	o W, with the pointwise operations, is a vector space, for the same reason F^X is: each axiom is checked one input at a time, where it becomes an axiom of W. Then \cL(V, W) sits inside W^V, so the Subspace Test finishes the job, and its three conditions are exactly “the zero map is linear”, “a sum of linear maps is linear”, and “a multiple of a linear map is linear”. Let W^V be the set of all functions V 	o W, with the operations of @def-space-of-linear-maps applied to arbitrary functions. The verification in @exm-vector-spaces (d) goes through word for word with W in place of F: two functions V 	o W are equal when they agree at every \elem{v} \in V (@def-function), and at each \elem{v} every axiom for W^V becomes the same axiom in W, with zero function \elem{v} \mapsto \elem{0}_W and negative \elem{v} \mapsto -f(\elem{v}). Hence W^V is a vector space over F, and \cL(V, W) \subseteq W^V. We apply @thm-subspace-test. (1) The zero map is linear: \elem{0}_W = \elem{0}_W + \elem{0}_W and \elem{0}_W = c\,\elem{0}_W by @thm-scalar-zero-vector. So \elem{0} \in \cL(V, W). (2) Let S, T \in \cL(V, W), \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V, and a \in F. By the definition of S + T, the linearity of S and T, and the axioms of W, (S + T)(\elem{u} + \elem{v}) = S\elem{u} + S\elem{v} + T\elem{u} + T\elem{v} = (S + T)\elem{u} + (S + T)\elem{v}, (S + T)(a\elem{v}) = aS\elem{v} + aT\elem{v} = a\,(S\elem{v} + T\elem{v}) = a\,(S + T)\elem{v} . So S + T \in \cL(V, W). (3) Let c \in F and T \in \cL(V, W). Then (cT)(\elem{u} + \elem{v}) = c\,(T\elem{u} + T\elem{v}) = (cT)\elem{u} + (cT)\elem{v}, and (cT)(a\elem{v}) = c\,(aT\elem{v}) = (ca)T\elem{v} = (ac)T\elem{v} = a\,(cT)\elem{v}, using the axioms of W and commutativity of multiplication in F. So cT \in \cL(V, W). By @thm-subspace-test, \cL(V, W) is a subspace of W^V, hence a vector space over F with the same zero and negatives. The negative of T in W^V is \elem{v} \mapsto -T\elem{v} = (-1)T\elem{v}, by @thm-negation-scalar. This proves the theorem. The step that used commutativity of F is worth a second look: cT is linear because c can be moved past the scalar a. This is one place where “F is a field” is used silently. [Sums of Matrix Maps and Other First Examples] For \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), write T_\A \colon F^n 	o F^m, \cvec{x} \mapsto \A\cvec{x}, for the matrix map of @exm-matrix-transformation. 1. Show that T_\A + T_\B = T_{\A + \B} and cT_\A = T_{c\A} for \A, \B \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and c \in F. 2. Describe \cL(V, W) when V = \{\elem{0}\}, and when W = \{\elem{0}\}. 3. On 
R[x]_{\le 2}, write T(p) = p' - 2p in terms of \id and D, and compute T(1 + x^2). (a) Let \cvec{x} \in F^n. By @def-space-of-linear-maps and distributivity (@thm-matrix-multiplication-properties),  egin{aligned} (T_\A + T_\B)(\cvec{x}) &= \A\cvec{x} + \B\cvec{x} = (\A + \B)\cvec{x} = T_{\A + \B}(\cvec{x}), \ (cT_\A)(\cvec{x}) &= c(\A\cvec{x}) = (c\A)\cvec{x} = T_{c\A}(\cvec{x}). \end{aligned} The maps agree at every \cvec{x}, so they are equal. So adding and scaling matrix maps is adding and scaling matrices. (b) If V = \{\elem{0}\}, a linear map must send \elem{0} to \elem{0}_W, so the zero map is the only element: \cL(\{\elem{0}\}, W) = \{0\}. If W = \{\elem{0}\}, every function V 	o \{\elem{0}\} is the zero map, and it is linear, so again \cL(V, \{\elem{0}\}) = \{0\}. These degenerate cases matter because formulas like “\dim \cL(V, W) = \dim V \cdot \dim W”, which we prove in Chapter 4, must give 0 here, and they do. (c) T = D - 2\id, which is linear by @thm-linear-maps-vector-space. With p = 1 + x^2, p' = 2x, so T(p) = 2x - 2 - 2x^2. Here is a nonexample by minimal change. Keep D on 
R[x]_{\le 2}, but replace \id by the evaluation map E(p) = p(0) \in 
R. Both maps are linear and both are defined on 
R[x]_{\le 2}. But D lands in 
R[x]_{\le 2} and E lands in 
R, so D + E would require adding a polynomial to a number. The clause that fails is “S, T \in \cL(V, W)” with the same W: the sum is not defined. Composition Addition makes \cL(V, W) a vector space, but the operation that really matters for maps is doing one after another. For functions, Chapter 0 wrote this as S \circ T (@def-composition). For linear maps we drop the circle. Notation. For T \in \cL(U, V) and S \in \cL(V, W), we write ST \coloneqq S \circ T \colon U 	o W, so (ST)\elem{u} = S(T\elem{u}). The map written on the right acts first. For an operator T \in \cL(V), T^2 = TT means “apply T twice”, never “square the output”. Is ST linear, and how does composition interact with the sum? It turns out that composition behaves like a multiplication: associative, with identities, and distributive over addition on both sides. [Composition of Linear Maps] Let U, V, W, X be vector spaces over F. 1. (Linearity) If T \in \cL(U, V) and S \in \cL(V, W), then ST \in \cL(U, W). 2. (Associativity) If T \in \cL(U, V), S \in \cL(V, W), and R \in \cL(W, X), then R(ST) = (RS)T. 3. (Identities) If T \in \cL(U, V), then T\id_U = T = \id_V T. 4. (Distributivity) If T, T_1, T_2 \in \cL(U, V), S, S_1, S_2 \in \cL(V, W), and c \in F, then  egin{aligned} (S_1 + S_2)T &= S_1T + S_2T, \ S(T_1 + T_2) &= ST_1 + ST_2, \ (cS)T &= c(ST) = S(cT). \end{aligned} Parts (b) and (c) hold for all functions, so there is nothing new to do. Part (a) is a two-line check. The interesting point is in (d): the three identities are not equally cheap. In (S_1 + S_2)T the map T acts first and the sum is taken afterwards, so the identity is just the definition of the sum. In S(T_1 + T_2) the sum is taken before S acts, and pulling it out of S needs S to be linear. So we should watch where the linearity of the left factor is spent. (a) Let \elem{u}, \elem{u}' \in U and a \in F. Since T and then S are linear, ST(\elem{u} + \elem{u}') = S(T\elem{u} + T\elem{u}') = ST\elem{u} + ST\elem{u}', \qquad ST(a\elem{u}) = S(aT\elem{u}) = a\,ST\elem{u} . (b) and (c) hold for arbitrary functions, by @thm-composition-associative and the observation after @def-identity-function. (c) Each side is a function U 	o W, so we compare values at \elem{u} \in U. By @def-space-of-linear-maps, (S_1 + S_2)T\elem{u} = S_1(T\elem{u}) + S_2(T\elem{u}) = (S_1T + S_2T)\elem{u}, with no linearity used. Next, since S is linear, S(T_1 + T_2)\elem{u} = S(T_1\elem{u} + T_2\elem{u}) = ST_1\elem{u} + ST_2\elem{u} = (ST_1 + ST_2)\elem{u} . Finally (cS)(T\elem{u}) = c\,(ST\elem{u}) by definition, and S(cT\elem{u}) = c\,(ST\elem{u}) because S is linear. This proves the theorem. In short, \cL(V) carries a vector space structure and a multiplication (composition) that is associative, has the unit \id_V, distributes over addition, and lets scalars move freely through products. A vector space with such a multiplication is called an algebra over F; M_n(F) is the other algebra we know (@thm-matrix-multiplication-properties). The two will turn out to be the same algebra in disguise when we write operators as matrices in Chapter 4. [Rotate, Then Project] Let R \colon 
R^2 	o 
R^2 be the rotation by 90^\circ counterclockwise, R(x, y) = (-y, x), and let P \colon 
R^2 	o 
R^2, P(x, y) = (x, 0), be the projection onto the x-axis. Compute PR and RP. In PR the rotation acts first: PR(x, y) = P(-y, x) = (-y, 0), \qquad RP(x, y) = R(x, 0) = (0, x). At (1, 0): PR(1, 0) = (0, 0), while RP(1, 0) = (0, 1). So PR 
eq RP. Geometrically, PR rotates \cvec{e}_1 onto the y-axis and then squashes it to \cvec{0}; RP leaves \cvec{e}_1 alone under the projection and then rotates it to \cvec{e}_2. In matrix form, P = T_{\A} and R = T_{\B} with \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, and indeed \A\B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} 
eq  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \B\A. Composition is not commutative, and the order is read right to left. In @exm-rotation-projection-dont-commute, PR 
eq RP. It can be worse: for T \in \cL(
R^2, 
R^3) and S \in \cL(
R^3, 
R^2), both ST \in \cL(
R^2) and TS \in \cL(
R^3) are defined, but they live on different spaces, so they cannot even be compared. And for T \in \cL(
R^2, 
R^3), S \in \cL(
R^3, 
R^4), ST is defined but TS is not. The thing you do first goes on the right. Let T \colon 
R^3 	o 
R^2 and S \colon 
R^2 	o 
R^4 be linear. Which of ST and TS is defined, and between which spaces does it go? ST = S \circ T first applies T \colon 
R^3 	o 
R^2, then S \colon 
R^2 	o 
R^4, so ST \in \cL(
R^3, 
R^4). TS would apply S first, landing in 
R^4, where T is not defined; so TS is not defined. Because of the missing commutativity, school identities about products must be rechecked. By distributivity (@thm-composition-linear (d)), (S + T)^2 = (S + T)(S + T) = S^2 + ST + TS + T^2, which equals S^2 + 2ST + T^2 only if ST = TS. With P and R as above, PR + RP \colon (x, y) \mapsto (-y, x), while 2PR \colon (x, y) \mapsto (-2y, 0); so (P + R)^2 
eq P^2 + 2PR + R^2. This is the operator version of the matrix warning in Chapter 0, §9. Operators, powers, and polynomials Composition of operators on one space V never leaves \cL(V), so we may compose an operator with itself as often as we like. Repeated composition leads to powers, and combinations of powers to polynomials, exactly as for square matrices (@def-polynomial-of-matrix). [Powers and Polynomials of an Operator] Let V be a vector space over F and T \in \cL(V). The powers of T are defined recursively by T^0 \coloneqq \id_V, \qquad T^{k+1} \coloneqq T^k T \quad (k \in 
N). For p = a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_Nx^N \in F[x], the operator p(T) \in \cL(V) is p(T) \coloneqq a_0\id_V + a_1T + a_2T^2 + \dots + a_NT^N . In words: T^k applies T exactly k times, and T^0 does nothing. In p(T), the constant term becomes a_0\id_V, because an operator cannot be added to a scalar. Each T^k is linear by @thm-composition-linear (a) and induction, and p(T) is linear by @thm-linear-maps-vector-space. As for matrices, p(T) does not depend on how many zero coefficients we write, since 0 \cdot T^k is the zero map. Plugging in an operator respects sums and products of polynomials, just as plugging in a matrix does. [Polynomials in One Operator] Let T \in \cL(V) and p, q \in F[x]. Then: 1. T^jT^k = T^{j+k} for all j, k \in 
N; 2. (p + q)(T) = p(T) + q(T) and (pq)(T) = p(T)\,q(T); 3. p(T)\,q(T) = q(T)\,p(T). The proof of @thm-polynomial-of-matrix-properties used four matrix rules: associativity, identity, distributivity, and “scalars move through products”. @thm-composition-linear supplies exactly these four rules for operators. So the old proof transfers line by line. Part (c) is the surprise: T need not commute with other operators, but it commutes with every polynomial in itself. (a) Fix j and use induction on k (@thm-induction). For k = 0, T^jT^0 = T^j\id_V = T^j by @thm-composition-linear (c). If T^jT^k = T^{j+k}, then by @def-polynomial-of-operator and associativity (@thm-composition-linear (b)), T^jT^{k+1} = T^j(T^kT) = (T^jT^k)T = T^{j+k}T = T^{j+k+1} . (b) Let p = \sum_{i=0}^{m} a_ix^i and q = \sum_{j=0}^{l} b_jx^j. The statement for sums holds because (a_i + b_i)T^i = a_iT^i + b_iT^i in the vector space \cL(V) (@thm-linear-maps-vector-space). For products, the coefficient of x^k in pq is \sum_{i+j=k} a_ib_j (@def-polynomial-ring), so  egin{aligned} (pq)(T) &= \sum_k \Bigl( \sum_{i+j=k} a_ib_j \Bigr) T^k = \sum_{i=0}^{m} \sum_{j=0}^{l} (a_ib_j)\,T^iT^j \ &= \Bigl( \sum_{i=0}^{m} a_iT^i \Bigr)\Bigl( \sum_{j=0}^{l} b_jT^j \Bigr) = p(T)\,q(T), \end{aligned} where the second equality uses (a), and the third uses both distributive laws and (a_iT^i)(b_jT^j) = (a_ib_j)\,T^iT^j, all from @thm-composition-linear (d). (c) Since pq = qp in F[x] (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws), part (b) gives p(T)q(T) = (pq)(T) = (qp)(T) = q(T)p(T). This proves the theorem. In practice, (b) says that a factorization of p is a factorization of p(T): for instance T^2 - 3T + 2\id_V = (T - \id_V)(T - 2\id_V) = (T - 2\id_V)(T - \id_V). [Differentiation Is Nilpotent] Let n \ge 0 and let D \in \cL(F[x]_{\le n}) be (formal) differentiation (@exm-differentiation), D(a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_nx^n) = a_1 + 2a_2x + \dots + na_nx^{n-1}, where ka_k means a_k added to itself k times. Show that D^{n+1} = 0. Show also that D^n 
eq 0 when F = 
R. For 0 \le k \le n, D(x^k) = kx^{k-1} if k \ge 1 and D(1) = 0. So D sends each x^k to a scalar multiple of x^{k-1}, or to 0 when k = 0. Applying this k + 1 times, D^{k+1}(x^k) is a scalar multiple of D(1) = 0, so D^{k+1}(x^k) = 0. Since k \le n, also D^{n+1}(x^k) = D^{n-k} igl(D^{k+1}(x^k) igr) = D^{n-k}(\elem{0}) = \elem{0}, by @thm-polynomial-of-operator-properties (a). Now let p = a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_nx^n. Since D^{n+1} is linear, @thm-linear-combination gives D^{n+1}(p) = a_0D^{n+1}(1) + a_1D^{n+1}(x) + \dots + a_nD^{n+1}(x^n) = \elem{0} . Hence D^{n+1} = 0. Over 
R, D^n(x^n) = n(n-1) \cdots 1 = n! 
eq 0, so D^n 
eq 0. Over 
F_2 with n = 2, however, D(x^2) = 2x = 0, and D^2 = 0 already; the field matters for the exact power, but never for D^{n+1} = 0. An operator T with T^k = 0 for some k \ge 1 is called nilpotent. The example shows that a nonzero operator can have a power equal to zero, just as the matrix  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} can. Differentiation is the model nilpotent operator, and it returns when we study canonical forms. [Operators That Satisfy a Polynomial] With P and R as in @exm-rotation-projection-dont-commute, find nonzero polynomials p and q with p(P) = 0 and q(R) = 0. Also, for an arbitrary p \in F[x], compute p(\id_V) and p(Z), where Z \in \cL(V) is the zero operator. For the projection, P^2(x, y) = P(x, 0) = (x, 0) = P(x, y), so P^2 = P and p = x^2 - x satisfies p(P) = P^2 - P = 0. By @thm-polynomial-of-operator-properties (b), this says P(P - \id) = 0: whatever P - \id produces is killed by P, and indeed (P - \id)(x, y) = (0, -y) lies on the y-axis. For the rotation, R^2(x, y) = R(-y, x) = (-x, -y), so R^2 = -\id, and q = x^2 + 1 satisfies q(R) = R^2 + \id = 0. Rotating twice by 90^\circ is rotating by 180^\circ. Since q has no real roots, q has no real linear factor, so the trick “factor q, then factor q(R)” gives nothing over 
R. For p = a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_Nx^N: every power of \id_V is \id_V, so p(\id_V) = (a_0 + a_1 + \dots + a_N)\id_V = p(1)\,\id_V. Every power Z^k with k \ge 1 is the zero map, but Z^0 = \id_V, so p(Z) = a_0\id_V, the scalar p(0) times \id_V. The second computation is the reason for the convention T^0 = \id_V: with it, “the constant term” of p(T) is what survives when T is the zero operator. The constant term is a_0\id_V, not a_0. Writing “P^2 - P + 3” for an operator is a type error: P^2 - P is a map and 3 is a number. For p = x^2 - x + 3, p(P) = P^2 - P + 3\id, which is 3\id since P^2 = P. Forgetting the \id leads to “p(P) = 3”, which is not an operator at all. With P the projection above, compute p(P) for p = x^3 - 2x + 1. Since P^2 = P, also P^3 = P^2P = PP = P. So p(P) = P^3 - 2P + \id = P - 2P + \id = \id - P, which is the map (x, y) \mapsto (0, y): the projection onto the y-axis. Polynomial relations such as P^2 = P, R^2 = -\id, and D^{n+1} = 0 carry real information about an operator. In the next section we use one to write down an inverse without solving any equations, and later in the book the polynomials that kill an operator lead to the minimal polynomial and to canonical forms. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. For S, T \in \cL(V, W) and c \in F, define S + T and cT. Why must S and T have the same codomain? 2. True or false: for all S, T \in \cL(V), ST = TS. Justify your answer. 3. Let T \in \cL(
R^5, 
R^2) and S \in \cL(
R^2, 
R^5). Which of ST, TS are defined, and in which spaces do they lie? 4. For T \in \cL(V) and p = 4 (a constant polynomial), what is p(T)? 5. True or false: for all S, T \in \cL(V), (S + T)^2 = S^2 + 2ST + T^2. Justify your answer. (a) (S + T)(\elem{v}) = S\elem{v} + T\elem{v} and (cT)(\elem{v}) = c\,T\elem{v} for every \elem{v} \in V (@def-space-of-linear-maps). The sum S\elem{v} + T\elem{v} must be computed in a single vector space, so both values must lie in the same W. (b) False. In @exm-rotation-projection-dont-commute, PR(1, 0) = (0, 0) but RP(1, 0) = (0, 1). (c) Both are defined. ST applies T first: ST \in \cL(
R^5). TS applies S first: TS \in \cL(
R^2). (d) p(T) = 4\id_V, by @def-polynomial-of-operator. (e) False. By @thm-composition-linear (d), (S + T)^2 = S^2 + ST + TS + T^2, which differs from S^2 + 2ST + T^2 by TS - ST. With S = P, T = R of @exm-rotation-projection-dont-commute, RP - PR \colon (x, y) \mapsto (y, x) is not the zero map, so the identity fails. B. Practice [B1: Computing compositions] Let S, T \in \cL(
R^2) be given by S(x, y) = (x + y, \, y) and T(x, y) = (y, \, x). 1. Compute ST, TS, and 2S - T. 2. Compute S^2 and S^k for every k \in 
N. 3. Hence show that (S - \id)^2 = 0. (a) Applying the right-hand map first, ST(x, y) = S(y, x) = (x + y, \, x), \qquad TS(x, y) = T(x + y, \, y) = (y, \, x + y). So ST 
eq TS; for instance ST(1, 0) = (1, 1) and TS(1, 0) = (0, 1). By @def-space-of-linear-maps, (2S - T)(x, y) = (2x + 2y, \, 2y) - (y, \, x) = (2x + y, \, 2y - x). (b) S^2(x, y) = S(x + y, \, y) = (x + 2y, \, y). We claim S^k(x, y) = (x + ky, \, y) for all k \in 
N, by induction on k. For k = 0, S^0 = \id sends (x, y) to (x + 0y, \, y). If the claim holds for k, then S^{k+1}(x, y) = S^k igl(S(x, y) igr) = S^k(x + y, \, y) = (x + y + ky, \, y) = (x + (k + 1)y, \, y), where the first equality is @def-polynomial-of-operator, S^{k+1} = S^kS. (c) (S - \id)(x, y) = (y, \, 0), so (S - \id)^2(x, y) = (S - \id)(y, 0) = (0, 0). Hence (S - \id)^2 = 0, that is, S - \id is nilpotent. Expanding with @thm-polynomial-of-operator-properties (b), S^2 - 2S + \id = 0, which matches (b): (x + 2y, y) - 2(x + y, y) + (x, y) = (0, 0). [B2: Operators that preserve a subspace] Let U be a subspace of V, and let \mathcal{A}_U \coloneqq \{ T \in \cL(V) : T\elem{u} \in U 	ext{ for every } \elem{u} \in U \} . Prove that \mathcal{A}_U is a subspace of \cL(V), that \id_V \in \mathcal{A}_U, and that ST \in \mathcal{A}_U whenever S, T \in \mathcal{A}_U. We use @thm-subspace-test in the vector space \cL(V) (@thm-linear-maps-vector-space). (1) The zero map sends every \elem{u} \in U to \elem{0}, and \elem{0} \in U because U is a subspace. So 0 \in \mathcal{A}_U. (2) Let S, T \in \mathcal{A}_U and \elem{u} \in U. Then S\elem{u} \in U and T\elem{u} \in U, so (S + T)\elem{u} = S\elem{u} + T\elem{u} \in U, since U is closed under addition. Therefore S + T \in \mathcal{A}_U. (3) Let c \in F and T \in \mathcal{A}_U. For \elem{u} \in U, (cT)\elem{u} = c\,T\elem{u} \in U, since U is closed under scalar multiplication. Therefore cT \in \mathcal{A}_U. Hence \mathcal{A}_U is a subspace of \cL(V). Next, \id_V\elem{u} = \elem{u} \in U for every \elem{u} \in U, so \id_V \in \mathcal{A}_U. Finally let S, T \in \mathcal{A}_U and \elem{u} \in U. Then T\elem{u} \in U, and applying the hypothesis on S to the vector T\elem{u} \in U gives ST\elem{u} = S(T\elem{u}) \in U. This shows ST \in \mathcal{A}_U. [B3: A polynomial that kills D] Let D \in \cL(
R[x]_{\le 2}) be differentiation. 1. Find a nonzero polynomial p with p(D) = 0. 2. Show that no nonzero polynomial q of degree at most 2 satisfies q(D) = 0. 3. Hence, or otherwise, compute (\id + D)^3 as a combination of \id, D, D^2, and evaluate (\id + D)^3(x^2). (a) By @exm-differentiation-nilpotent with n = 2, D^3 = 0. So p = x^3 works. (b) Let q = a + bx + cx^2 with q(D) = a\id + bD + cD^2 = 0. Applying this operator to x^2, with D(x^2) = 2x and D^2(x^2) = 2, 0 = ax^2 + 2bx + 2c . A polynomial is zero exactly when all its coefficients are, so a = 0, 2b = 0, and 2c = 0. Hence a = b = c = 0 and q = 0. (c) The operator \id + D is q(D) for q = 1 + x. Applying the product rule of @thm-polynomial-of-operator-properties (b) twice, (\id + D)^3 = q(D)q(D)q(D) = (q^3)(D), and q^3 = 1 + 3x + 3x^2 + x^3. So (\id + D)^3 = \id + 3D + 3D^2 + D^3 = \id + 3D + 3D^2, using D^3 = 0 from (a). Therefore (\id + D)^3(x^2) = x^2 + 3 \cdot 2x + 3 \cdot 2 = x^2 + 6x + 6. C. Going deeper [C1: The Heisenberg relation] Let F be a field, let D \in \cL(F[x]) be formal differentiation, D(\sum_k a_kx^k) = \sum_{k \ge 1} ka_kx^{k-1} (@exm-differentiation), and let S \in \cL(F[x]) be multiplication by x, S(p) = xp (the map M of @exm-multiplication-by-x). 1. Prove that DS - SD = \id. 2. Let T \in \cL(F^n, F^m). Prove that T = T_\A, where \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) is the matrix with columns T\cvec{e}_1, \dots, T\cvec{e}_n. 3. Now suppose that F has characteristic 0 (@def-characteristic), and let n \ge 1. Deduce that there are no operators D', S' \in \cL(F^n) with D'S' - S'D' = \id. 4. Show that the assumption on the characteristic in (c) cannot be dropped. Hint: for (c), use (b) and consider traces. (a) Both sides are linear (@thm-linear-maps-vector-space, @thm-composition-linear). We first compare them on x^k, k \in 
N. We have DS(x^k) = D(x^{k+1}) = (k + 1)x^k. If k \ge 1, SD(x^k) = x \cdot kx^{k-1} = kx^k; if k = 0, SD(1) = x \cdot 0 = 0 = 0 \cdot x^0. In both cases (DS - SD)(x^k) = (k + 1)x^k - kx^k = x^k = \id(x^k). Every p \in F[x] is a finite combination p = \sum_k a_kx^k, so by @thm-linear-combination, (DS - SD)(p) = \sum_k a_k(DS - SD)(x^k) = \sum_k a_kx^k = p. Hence DS - SD = \id. (b) Let \cvec{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n) = x_1\cvec{e}_1 + \dots + x_n\cvec{e}_n \in F^n. By @thm-linear-combination and @thm-matrix-times-vector-columns, T\cvec{x} = x_1T\cvec{e}_1 + \dots + x_nT\cvec{e}_n = \A\cvec{x} = T_\A(\cvec{x}). Since \cvec{x} was arbitrary, T = T_\A. (c) Suppose, for a contradiction, that D', S' \in \cL(F^n) satisfy D'S' - S'D' = \id. By (b), D' = T_\A and S' = T_\B for some \A, \B \in M_n(F), and \id = T_{\I_n}. By associativity of matrix multiplication, T_\A T_\B(\cvec{x}) = \A(\B\cvec{x}) = (\A\B)\cvec{x}, so T_\A T_\B = T_{\A\B}, and similarly T_\B T_\A = T_{\B\A}. With @exm-sum-of-matrix-maps (a), T_{\A\B - \B\A} = T_\A T_\B - T_\B T_\A = \id = T_{\I_n} . Evaluating at \cvec{e}_j gives equal j-th columns (@thm-matrix-times-vector-columns), so \A\B - \B\A = \I_n. Taking traces and using @thm-trace-properties, n \cdot 1 = 	r \I_n = 	r(\A\B) - 	r(\B\A) = 0 . Since n \ge 1 and F has characteristic 0, n \cdot 1 
eq 0 by @def-characteristic. This is a contradiction, so no such D', S' exist. In words: over 
Q, 
R, 
C, or any field of characteristic 0, the relation DS - SD = \id of (a) has no analogue on F^n, n \ge 1. Since every n-dimensional space is isomorphic to F^n, as we show in the next section, the same holds on every nonzero finite-dimensional space. (On the zero space \id = 0, so the relation holds trivially there; that is why n \ge 1.) (d) Over 
F_2 (characteristic 2), take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} as in @exr-matrices-c1. There \A\B - \B\A =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \I_2, because -1 = 1 in 
F_2. By the computation in (c), D' = T_\A and S' = T_\B satisfy D'S' - S'D' = T_{\A\B - \B\A} = \id on 
F_2^2. So the conclusion of (c) fails without the characteristic assumption; the proof breaks exactly at n \cdot 1 
eq 0, since 2 \cdot 1 = 0 in 
F_2. [C2: Commuting nilpotent operators] Let S, T \in \cL(V). 1. Suppose ST = TS. Prove that (S + T)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n}  inom{n}{k} S^kT^{n-k} for every n \in 
N, where  inom{n}{k} S^kT^{n-k} means S^kT^{n-k} added to itself  inom{n}{k} times. 2. Deduce that if ST = TS, S^a = 0, and T^b = 0 for some a, b \ge 1, then (S + T)^{a+b-1} = 0. 3. Show that (b) fails without ST = TS: give nilpotent S, T \in \cL(
R^2) such that S + T is not nilpotent. Hint: for (c), try maps that send one standard basis vector to the other and the other to \cvec{0}. (a) First, T^jS = ST^j for all j \in 
N, by induction on j: it holds for j = 0, and if T^jS = ST^j, then T^{j+1}S = T^j(TS) = T^j(ST) = (T^jS)T = (ST^j)T = ST^{j+1}, using associativity (@thm-composition-linear (b)) and @thm-polynomial-of-operator-properties (a) in the form T^{j+1} = T^jT. Now induct on n. For n = 0 both sides are \id_V. Suppose the formula holds for n. By @thm-composition-linear (d), (S + T)^{n+1} = (S + T)^n(S + T) = \sum_{k=0}^{n}  inom{n}{k} S^kT^{n-k}S + \sum_{k=0}^{n}  inom{n}{k} S^kT^{n-k+1} . By the first paragraph, S^kT^{n-k}S = S^k(T^{n-k}S) = S^kST^{n-k} = S^{k+1}T^{n-k}. Shifting the index in the first sum, the coefficient of S^kT^{n+1-k} becomes  inom{n}{k-1} +  inom{n}{k} =  inom{n+1}{k} (Pascal’s rule, with  inom{n}{-1} =  inom{n}{n+1} = 0). This is the formula for n + 1. (b) By (a) with n = a + b - 1, (S + T)^{a+b-1} is a sum of multiples of S^kT^{a+b-1-k}, 0 \le k \le a + b - 1. If k \ge a, then S^k = S^{k-a}S^a = 0 by @thm-polynomial-of-operator-properties (a), so the term is 0 by @thm-composition-linear (d). If k \le a - 1, then a + b - 1 - k \ge b, so T^{a+b-1-k} = 0 likewise. Every term vanishes, so (S + T)^{a+b-1} = 0. (c) Let S(x, y) = (y, 0) and T(x, y) = (0, x). Then S^2(x, y) = S(y, 0) = (0, 0) and T^2(x, y) = T(0, x) = (0, 0), so both are nilpotent. But (S + T)(x, y) = (y, x), so (S + T)^2(x, y) = (x, y), that is, (S + T)^2 = \id. Then (S + T)^{2k} = \id 
eq 0 and (S + T)^{2k+1} = S + T 
eq 0 for every k, so S + T is not nilpotent. Here ST(x, y) = (x, 0) 
eq (0, y) = TS(x, y), so the hypothesis of (b) indeed fails.

title: 2.5 Invertible Maps and Isomorphisms
content:
Invertible Maps and Isomorphisms In Chapter 1 we noticed that a basis of length n turns every vector of V into a column in F^n, and that sums and multiples survive the translation. Then 
R[x]_{\le 2} and 
R^3 behave “the same”, although they are different sets. This section makes “the same” precise. We define invertible linear maps and isomorphisms, prove that finite-dimensional spaces are classified by one number, their dimension, and collect everything we know about invertibility of an operator into one theorem. When are two spaces the same? The naive notion of sameness is equality of sets, and it fails at once. The polynomial 3 - x + 2x^2 is not a column vector, so 
R[x]_{\le 2} 
eq 
R^3. Yet every computation in one space has a twin in the other. Match a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 with (a_0, a_1, a_2): (1 + 2x) + (x - x^2) = 1 + 3x - x^2 \quad \longleftrightarrow \quad (1, 2, 0) + (0, 1, -1) = (1, 3, -1). A reader who only sees one side cannot tell which space the computation happened in. Three features make this work. The matching is one-to-one and surjective, so nothing is lost or left over. It respects sums and multiples in the direction polynomial → column. And it respects them in the reverse direction too, so a conclusion drawn among columns can be carried back. In the language of this chapter: a linear map with a linear map going back. An isomorphism is a perfect dictionary between two vector spaces: every word has exactly one translation, and translating respects sums and scalar multiples in both directions. [Invertible Linear Map] Let V and W be vector spaces over F, and let T \in \cL(V, W). Then T is invertible if there exists a linear map S \in \cL(W, V) such that ST = \id_V \qquad 	extbf{and} \qquad TS = \id_W . In words: S undoes T on V (first T, then S, and we are back where we started), T undoes S on W, and the undoing map is itself linear. The definition asks for one map S doing both jobs. Well-definedness. If S exists, it is an inverse function of T in the sense of @def-inverse-function, and inverse functions are unique by @thm-bijective-iff-invertible. So we may speak of the inverse and write T^{-1} \coloneqq S. The same theorem says an invertible T is a bijection. Is the word “linear” in the definition doing any work? One could imagine a linear bijection whose inverse function is not linear, which would then fail the definition. It turns out this never happens: [The Inverse of a Linear Bijection Is Linear] Let T \in \cL(V, W) be bijective. Then its inverse function T^{-1} \colon W 	o V is linear. Consequently, a linear map T is invertible if and only if it is bijective. To show T^{-1}(\elem{w}_1 + \elem{w}_2) = T^{-1}\elem{w}_1 + T^{-1}\elem{w}_2, we cannot compute T^{-1} directly. But we can apply T, which we know is linear, to the right-hand side, and see that it lands on \elem{w}_1 + \elem{w}_2. Since T is injective, only one vector does that, namely T^{-1}(\elem{w}_1 + \elem{w}_2). Let \elem{w}_1, \elem{w}_2 \in W and c \in F, and put \elem{v}_i \coloneqq T^{-1}\elem{w}_i, so that T\elem{v}_i = \elem{w}_i. Since T is linear, T(\elem{v}_1 + \elem{v}_2) = \elem{w}_1 + \elem{w}_2, \qquad T(c\elem{v}_1) = c\elem{w}_1 . Applying T^{-1} to both equations gives T^{-1}(\elem{w}_1 + \elem{w}_2) = \elem{v}_1 + \elem{v}_2 = T^{-1}\elem{w}_1 + T^{-1}\elem{w}_2 and T^{-1}(c\elem{w}_1) = c\elem{v}_1 = c\,T^{-1}\elem{w}_1. Hence T^{-1} is linear. For the last statement: if T is invertible, it is bijective by @thm-bijective-iff-invertible. Conversely, if T is bijective, its inverse function S = T^{-1} satisfies ST = \id_V and TS = \id_W by @def-inverse-function, and S is linear by the first part. So T is invertible. This proves the theorem. So in practice we check invertibility by checking bijectivity, and never need to verify linearity of the inverse. Invertible linear maps are important enough to have a second name. [Isomorphism] Let V and W be vector spaces over the same field F. An isomorphism from V to W is an invertible linear map T \in \cL(V, W); equivalently, by @thm-inverse-is-linear, a bijective linear map. [Isomorphic Spaces] Vector spaces V and W over F are isomorphic, written V \cong W, if there exists an isomorphism V 	o W. In words: V \cong W says that some perfect dictionary exists; it does not name one. The name comes from Greek isos (equal) and morphe (form): the two spaces have the same form, though not the same elements. An isomorphism V 	o V is also called an invertible operator. [The Standard Isomorphisms] Show that each map is an isomorphism, and give its inverse. 1. \Phi \colon 
R[x]_{\le n} 	o 
R^{n+1}, a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_nx^n \mapsto (a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n). 2. \Psi \colon M_{m 	imes n}(F) 	o F^{mn}, (a_{ij}) \mapsto (a_{11}, \dots, a_{1n}, a_{21}, \dots, a_{mn}), listing the entries row by row. 3. \Theta \colon 
C 	o 
R^2, a + bi \mapsto (a, b), where 
C is a vector space over 
R. 4. T_\A \colon F^n 	o F^n, \cvec{x} \mapsto \A\cvec{x}, for an invertible \A \in M_n(F); and \id_V for any V. (a) Linear. Polynomials are added and scaled coefficient by coefficient, and so are columns, so \Phi(p + q) = \Phi(p) + \Phi(q) and \Phi(cp) = c\,\Phi(p). Bijective. The map (a_0, \dots, a_n) \mapsto a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_nx^n is a two-sided inverse function, because two polynomials are equal exactly when all their coefficients agree (@def-polynomial). By @thm-inverse-is-linear, \Phi is an isomorphism, and \Phi^{-1} is that map. Hence 
R[x]_{\le n} \cong 
R^{n+1}. (b) Matrices are added and scaled entrywise, and so are vectors of F^{mn}, so \Psi is linear. The map that writes the first n entries of a vector into row 1, the next n into row 2, and so on, undoes \Psi on both sides. Hence M_{m 	imes n}(F) \cong F^{mn}. (c) For a, b, a', b', c \in 
R: (a + bi) + (a' + b'i) = (a + a') + (b + b')i and c(a + bi) = ca + cbi, so \Theta is linear over 
R. Every complex number has unique real and imaginary parts (@def-complex-numbers), so (a, b) \mapsto a + bi is a two-sided inverse. Hence 
C \cong 
R^2 as real vector spaces. In the same way @exm-complexification-rn showed that (\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) \mapsto \cvec{x} + i\cvec{y} is a bijection (
R^n)_
C 	o 
C^n respecting complex scalars; in our new language, (
R^n)_
C \cong 
C^n over 
C. (d) T_\A is linear (@exm-matrix-transformation). Since \A(\A^{-1}\cvec{x}) = (\A\A^{-1})\cvec{x} = \cvec{x} and \A^{-1}(\A\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x} by @thm-matrix-multiplication-properties, the linear map T_{\A^{-1}} is a two-sided inverse: T_\A^{-1} = T_{\A^{-1}}. The identity \id_V is its own inverse. This degenerate example matters: it shows V \cong V, and even the zero space is isomorphic to itself, via the zero map \{\elem{0}\} 	o \{\elem{0}\}, which is \id_{\{\elem{0}\}}. Here is a nonexample by minimal change. Take (a) with n = 3, but keep only three coefficients: \Phi' \colon 
R[x]_{\le 3} 	o 
R^3, a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + a_3x^3 \mapsto (a_0, a_1, a_2). It is still linear, and still surjective, since (a_0, a_1, a_2) = \Phi'(a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2). But \Phi'(x^3) = \cvec{0} = \Phi'(0), so \Phi' is not injective. No S can satisfy S\Phi' = \id, because S\Phi'(x^3) = S(\cvec{0}) = 0 
eq x^3. The clause ST = \id_V is the one that fails. Why this definition. Could we drop one of the two equations? The next example says no. [One Equation Is Not Enough] On 
R[x], let D be differentiation and J(p) \coloneqq \int_0^x p(t)\,\dd t, so that J(x^k) =  rac{x^{k+1}}{k+1} (@exm-differentiation, @exm-integration). On the sequence space F^{
N}, let L(a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots) \coloneqq (a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots) and R(a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots) \coloneqq (0, a_0, a_1, \dots) be the left and right shifts of @exm-shift. Show that DJ = \id and LR = \id, but that none of D, J, L, R is invertible. All four maps are linear, by @exm-differentiation, @exm-integration, and @exm-shift. For each k \in 
N, DJ(x^k) = D igl(	frac{x^{k+1}}{k+1} igr) = x^k, so DJ and \id agree on every x^k. Every polynomial is a finite combination of the x^k, so DJ = \id by @thm-linear-combination. Directly, LR(a_0, a_1, \dots) = L(0, a_0, a_1, \dots) = (a_0, a_1, \dots), so LR = \id. But JD(1) = J(0) = 0
