e j. So \A(\I_n + \E_{ij}) = (\I_n + \E_{ij})\A, which gives \A\E_{ij} = \E_{ij}\A. Compare the entries in position (k, l): by @def-matrix-multiplication, (\A\E_{ij})_{kl} =  egin{cases} a_{ki} & l = j \ 0 & l 
e j \end{cases}, \qquad (\E_{ij}\A)_{kl} =  egin{cases} a_{jl} & k = i \ 0 & k 
e i. \end{cases} Taking l = j and k 
e i gives a_{ki} = 0. Taking k = i and l = j gives a_{ii} = a_{jj}. Since i 
e j were arbitrary (and every index i has some j 
e i because n \ge 2), all off-diagonal entries of \A vanish and all diagonal entries are equal to c = a_{11}. Hence \A = c\I_n. (b) Let \P =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, so \P^{-1} = \P. Then \N\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \P^{-1}\N\P =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \N	p. In terms of operators: T\cvec{x} = \N\cvec{x} has T\cvec{e}_1 = \cvec{0} and T\cvec{e}_2 = \cvec{e}_1. In the reordered basis \sB = (\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1), the first basis vector goes to the second and the second goes to \cvec{0}, so \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} = \N	p. The same operator has both matrices, as @thm-similar-iff-same-operator predicts. [C2: \A\B and \B\A] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F). 1. Prove that if \A is invertible, then \A\B \sim \B\A. 2. Show that (a) fails without the invertibility hypothesis, even though 	r(\A\B) = 	r(\B\A) always holds. (a) Since \A is invertible, \A^{-1}(\A\B)\A = (\A^{-1}\A)(\B\A) = \B\A by associativity. With \P = \A this is \B\A = \P^{-1}(\A\B)\P, so \A\B \sim \B\A. (b) Take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Then \A\B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, of rank 1, and \B\A = \O, of rank 0. By @prp-similarity-invariants (a), \A\B 
ot\sim \B\A. Both traces are 0, in agreement with @thm-trace-properties; the trace simply cannot detect the difference. [C3: Every nonzero 2 	imes 2 matrix with square zero] Let \N \in M_2(F) with \N 
e \O and \N^2 = \O, and let T \colon F^2 	o F^2, T\cvec{x} = \N\cvec{x}. 1. Explain why there is \cvec{v} \in F^2 with \N\cvec{v} 
e \cvec{0}, and show that \sB = (\N\cvec{v}, \cvec{v}) is a basis of F^2. 2. Compute \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}, and deduce that \N \sim  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. 3. Hence show that  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -4 \ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \sim  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} in M_2(
R), with an explicit \P. (a) Since \N 
e \O, some column \N\cvec{e}_j is nonzero (@thm-matrix-times-vector-columns); take \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_j. Let a\N\cvec{v} + b\cvec{v} = \cvec{0}. Multiplying by \N and using \N^2 = \O gives b\N\cvec{v} = \cvec{0}, so b = 0 because \N\cvec{v} 
e \cvec{0} (@thm-zero-product). Then a\N\cvec{v} = \cvec{0} forces a = 0 for the same reason. So \sB is linearly independent of length 2 = \dim F^2, hence a basis by @thm-right-size-basis. (b) T(\N\cvec{v}) = \N^2\cvec{v} = \cvec{0} and T\cvec{v} = \N\cvec{v} = 1 \cdot \N\cvec{v} + 0 \cdot \cvec{v}. The columns of \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} are therefore (0, 0) and (1, 0), so \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Also \mtx{T}{\sE}{\sE} = \N. By @thm-similar-iff-same-operator (a), \N \sim  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. (c) Let \N =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -4 \ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}. Then \N^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 4 - 4 & -8 + 8 \ 2 - 2 & -4 + 4 \end{pmatrix} = \O and \N 
e \O. Take \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_1, so \N\cvec{v} = (2, 1), and \sB = ((2, 1), (1, 0)). By @thm-change-of-basis-maps, \P = \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sE} =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} satisfies \P^{-1}\N\P =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Check: \P^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix} by @thm-two-by-two-inverse (here ad - bc = -1), \N\P =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, and \P^{-1}\N\P =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.

title: 4.3 Rank, Equivalence, and Factorizations
content:
Rank, Equivalence, and Factorizations Similarity compares two matrices of one operator, where the same basis is used for input and output, and the last section showed that deciding it is hard. This section asks what happens when the two bases may be chosen independently, as they may for any map T \colon V 	o W. The answer is strikingly simple: the rank is then the only thing that matters. On the way we meet the column–row factorization, which writes every matrix as a product through a space of dimension equal to its rank, and we collect the basic inequalities for the rank of a composition. The column–row factorization In Chapter 3 we computed the rank of a matrix by row reduction, and the reduction gave more than a number. It produced a basis of the column space, the pivot columns of \A (@thm-basis-column-space), and it expressed every other column in terms of them, with coefficients read off the reduced row echelon form. Recording both pieces of information as matrices gives a factorization. [Column–Row Factorization] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) have rank r \ge 1, with pivot columns j_1 < \dots < j_r. Let \C \in M_{m 	imes r}(F) be the matrix whose columns are the pivot columns \cvec{a}_{j_1}, \dots, \cvec{a}_{j_r} of \A, and let \R \in M_{r 	imes n}(F) consist of the first r rows of the reduced row echelon form of \A, that is, its nonzero rows. Then \A = \C\R . Moreover, the columns of \C are linearly independent and the rows of \R are linearly independent. Column l of \C\R is \C times column l of \R, that is, a combination of the pivot columns of \A with the entries of column l of the RREF as coefficients. For a pivot column the coefficients are a standard basis vector, and for a free column they are exactly the coefficients that @thm-basis-column-space (b) provides. So the factorization is that theorem written as a matrix identity. Let \E be the RREF of \A, with entries e_{kl}. By @thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank, \E has exactly r pivots, so its nonzero rows are rows 1, \dots, r. Fix a column index l. By @thm-matrix-times-vector-columns, column l of \C\R is \C egin{pmatrix} e_{1l} \ \vdots \ e_{rl} \end{pmatrix} = e_{1l}\cvec{a}_{j_1} + \dots + e_{rl}\cvec{a}_{j_r} . Case 1: l = j_i is a pivot column. By @lem-rref-columns (a), column j_i of \E is \cvec{e}_i, so the combination is \cvec{a}_{j_i} = \cvec{a}_l. Case 2: l is a free column. Let t be the number of pivot columns to the left of l. For k > t, the leading entry of row k of \E lies in column j_k > l, so e_{kl} = 0. The combination is therefore e_{1l}\cvec{a}_{j_1} + \dots + e_{tl}\cvec{a}_{j_t}, which equals \cvec{a}_l by @thm-basis-column-space (b). In both cases column l of \C\R is column l of \A; hence \A = \C\R. The columns of \C form a basis of \col(\A) by @thm-basis-column-space (a), so they are independent. The rows of \R are the nonzero rows of \E, which form a basis of ow(\A) by @thm-basis-row-space, so they are independent. This proves the theorem. In words: every matrix of rank r is a “tall” matrix with independent columns times a “wide” matrix with independent rows, and the middle size is exactly r. The factorization cannot be squeezed further. [Rank as the size of the thinnest factorization] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) be nonzero. Then ank \A is the smallest integer s \ge 1 such that \A = \B\D for some \B \in M_{m 	imes s}(F) and \D \in M_{s 	imes n}(F). Let r = ank \A; then r \ge 1 since \A 
e \O. By @thm-column-row-factorization, a factorization with s = r exists. Conversely, suppose \A = \B\D with \B \in M_{m 	imes s}(F). By @thm-rank-product-inequality, r = ank(\B\D) \le ank \B, and ank \B \le s because \col(\B) is spanned by s columns (@thm-size-bounds). Hence r \le s. This gives a second view of “row rank equals column rank”. Let \A 
e \O, and let \B be the matrix whose s = \dim \col(\A) columns form a basis of \col(\A). Each column \cvec{a}_j of \A is \B\cvec{d}_j for its coordinate column \cvec{d}_j (@thm-matrix-times-vector-columns), so \A = \B\D with \D =  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{d}_1 & \cdots & \cvec{d}_n \end{pmatrix}. Then every row of \A is a row of \B times \D, a combination of the s rows of \D (@thm-three-views-of-product (3) and the row form of @thm-matrix-times-vector-columns), so \dim ow(\A) \le s = \dim \col(\A). Applying the same argument to \A	p gives the reverse inequality. In the language of maps, the factorization says that \cvec{x} \mapsto \A\cvec{x} can be done in two steps, F^n 	o F^r 	o F^m: first a surjection onto a space of dimension r, then an injection. [A column–row factorization] Find the column–row factorization of \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \ 2 & 4 & 1 & 4 \ 3 & 6 & 1 & 7 \end{pmatrix} \in M_{3 	imes 4}(
R). Row reduce. Subtracting 2 times row 1 from row 2 and 3 times row 1 from row 3 gives rows (1, 2, 0, 3), (0, 0, 1, -2), (0, 0, 1, -2). Subtracting row 2 from row 3 gives the RREF  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. The pivot columns are columns 1 and 3, so r = 2, and by @thm-column-row-factorization \A = \C\R =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & 1 \ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}. Check by rows: row 2 of \C\R is 2(1, 2, 0, 3) + (0, 0, 1, -2) = (2, 4, 1, 4), and row 3 is 3(1, 2, 0, 3) + (0, 0, 1, -2) = (3, 6, 1, 7). The last column of \R says \cvec{a}_4 = 3\cvec{a}_1 - 2\cvec{a}_3, and indeed 3(1, 2, 3) - 2(0, 1, 1) = (3, 4, 7). Equivalent matrices Go back to the change-of-basis square for a map T \colon V 	o W (@thm-change-of-basis-maps): \mtx{T}{\sB'}{\sC'} = \mtx{\id}{\sC}{\sC'}\,\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sC}\,\mtx{\id}{\sB'}{\sB} . When V 
e W, nothing ties the basis of V to the basis of W. So the two outer matrices are unrelated invertible matrices, of sizes m 	imes m and n 	imes n. Any two matrices of the same map are related in this way, and this recurring shape deserves a name. Two matrices are equivalent when they describe the same linear map, with the input basis and the output basis each changed freely. Equivalent matrices Let \A, \B \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). We say \A is equivalent to \B if there exist invertible matrices \Q \in M_m(F) and \P \in M_n(F) such that \B = \Q\A\P . In words: we may multiply on the left by any invertible matrix and on the right by any invertible matrix, and the two need not be related. Both sizes are forced: \Q acts on the m rows and \P on the n columns. This is an equivalence relation on M_{m 	imes n}(F): \A = \I_m\A\I_n; if \B = \Q\A\P then \A = \Q^{-1}\B\P^{-1}; and if also \C = \Q'\B\P', then \C = (\Q'\Q)\A(\P\P'), where products of invertible matrices are invertible by @thm-inverse-matrix-properties (part 3). Examples. - Row equivalence. If \B is obtained from \A by row operations, then \B = \E\A with \E invertible (@thm-row-equivalent-iff-invertible-multiple), so \A and \B are equivalent with \Q = \E and \P = \I_n. Column operations correspond to multiplying on the right, and they are allowed too. - Similarity. If \B = \P^{-1}\A\P, then \A and \B are equivalent, with \Q = \P^{-1}. - The identity and a swap. \I_2 and S =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} are equivalent, since S = S\I_2\I_2. They are not similar, because \I_2 is similar only to itself. - Degenerate case. The zero matrix \O_{m 	imes n} is equivalent only to itself, since \Q\O\P = \O. It is the matrix of the zero map in every pair of bases. Nonexample by minimal change. Keep \B = \Q\A\P but drop the requirement that \Q be invertible. Then every matrix could be sent to the zero matrix with \Q = \O, and the relation would not even be symmetric: \O = \O \cdot \I_2 \cdot \I_2, but \I_2 
e \Q\O\P for any \Q, \P. The clause “invertible” is what makes \Q\A\P a change of basis rather than an arbitrary composition. Equivalent is much weaker than similar. The matrices \I_2 and J =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} are equivalent, since J = J\I_2\I_2 and J is invertible, but they are not similar (see the warning in the previous section). For square matrices, “equivalent” allows a different change of basis on each side, and that freedom destroys almost all the structure an operator has. How much structure survives? The rank does, since multiplying by invertible matrices does not change it (@thm-rank-product-inequality). The theorem below says that nothing else survives. The target is the simplest matrix of each rank. For 0 \le r \le \min(m, n), let \N_r \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) be the block matrix \N_r \coloneqq  egin{pmatrix} \I_r & \O \ \O & \O \end{pmatrix}, with 1 in positions (1, 1), \dots, (r, r) and 0 everywhere else. Its first r columns are \cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_r \in F^m, and its remaining columns are zero. [Rank Normal Form] 1. Let V and W be finite-dimensional with \dim V = n and \dim W = m, and let T \colon V 	o W be linear of rank r. Then there are bases \sB of V and \sC of W such that \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sC} = \N_r. 2. Every \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) is equivalent to \N_r, where r = ank \A. 3. Two matrices \A, \B \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) are equivalent if and only if ank \A = ank \B. Work backwards from the goal. \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sC} = \N_r says: T sends the first r vectors of \sB to the first r vectors of \sC, and sends the last n - r vectors of \sB to \elem{0}. So ① the last n - r vectors of \sB should be a basis of \ker T, and by Rank–Nullity that is exactly the right number; ② the first r vectors of \sB extend it to a basis of V; ③ their images are forced to be the first r vectors of \sC, and we must show they are independent, which follows by counting; ④ extend them to a basis of W. These are the bases of the proof of Rank–Nullity, one on each side. (a) By the Rank–Nullity Theorem (@thm-rank-nullity), \dim \ker T = n - r. Let (\elem{u}_{r+1}, \dots, \elem{u}_n) be a basis of \ker T, a subspace of V by @thm-prop-kernel. By the Basis Extension Theorem (@thm-basis-extension) there are \elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_r \in V such that \sB = (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_r, \elem{u}_{r+1}, \dots, \elem{u}_n) is a basis of V; the new vectors may be listed first, since reordering a basis gives a basis. Put \elem{w}_i = T\elem{u}_i for i = 1, \dots, r. By @thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images, \im T = \Span(T\elem{u}_1, \dots, T\elem{u}_n). Since T\elem{u}_j = \elem{0} for j > r, removing these vectors does not change the span, so (\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_r) spans \im T. This list has length r = \dim \im T, so it is a basis of \im T by @thm-right-size-basis (b); in particular it is linearly independent in W. By the Basis Extension Theorem there are \elem{w}_{r+1}, \dots, \elem{w}_m \in W such that \sC = (\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_m) is a basis of W. Now read off the columns of \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sC} (@def-matrix-of-linear-map). For i \le r, T\elem{u}_i = \elem{w}_i, whose \sC-coordinate vector is \cvec{e}_i. For j > r, T\elem{u}_j = \elem{0}, whose coordinate vector is \cvec{0}. These are the columns of \N_r. (b) Let T \colon F^n 	o F^m, T\cvec{x} = \A\cvec{x}, and let \sE_n, \sE_m be the standard bases. The j-th column of \mtx{T}{\sE_n}{\sE_m} is \coord{\A\cvec{e}_j}{\sE_m} = \A\cvec{e}_j, the j-th column of \A (@thm-matrix-times-vector-columns), so \mtx{T}{\sE_n}{\sE_m} = \A. By @thm-rank-map-equals-rank-matrix, ank T = ank \A = r. Take \sB, \sC as in (a). By @thm-change-of-basis-maps, \N_r = \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sC} = \mtx{\id}{\sE_m}{\sC}\,\A\,\mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sE_n}, and both outer matrices are invertible by @thm-change-of-coordinates (c). Hence \A is equivalent to \N_r. (c) (\Rightarrow) If \B = \Q\A\P with \Q, \P invertible, then ank \B = ank \A by @thm-rank-product-inequality. (\Leftarrow) If ank \A = ank \B = r, then by (b) both \A and \B are equivalent to \N_r. Since equivalence is symmetric and transitive, \A is equivalent to \B. This proves the theorem. So the equivalence classes of M_{m 	imes n}(F) are exactly the sets of matrices of rank r, for r = 0, 1, \dots, \min(m, n): there are \min(m, n) + 1 of them, whatever the field. Every linear map between finite-dimensional spaces looks like “keep r coordinates and delete the rest” once the bases on both sides are chosen well. The right pair of bases makes any single map trivial. Contrast this with operators. For T \in \cL(V) we must use one basis for input and output, and the relation becomes similarity. There the rank is far from the whole story: \I_2 and  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} have the same rank but are not similar. Classifying operators up to a change of one basis is a much harder problem, answered in Chapter 10 by the Jordan and rational canonical forms. The proof is also an algorithm. To find \Q and \P for a concrete matrix, compute a basis of 
ul(\A), extend it, and take images. [Bringing a 2 	imes 3 matrix to normal form] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \ 2 & 4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \in M_{2 	imes 3}(
R). Find invertible \Q \in M_2(
R) and \P \in M_3(
R) with \Q\A\P = \N_r. Subtracting 2 times row 1 from row 2 gives  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, so r = ank \A = 2, and the solutions of \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} satisfy x_3 = 0, x_1 = -2x_2. Hence 
ul(\A) = \Span((-2, 1, 0)), as Rank–Nullity predicts (3 - 2 = 1). Following the proof, let \cvec{u}_3 = (-2, 1, 0), and extend with \cvec{u}_1 = \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{u}_2 = \cvec{e}_3. The list (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_3, \cvec{u}_3) is independent: in a\cvec{e}_1 + b\cvec{e}_3 + c(-2, 1, 0) = (a - 2c, c, b) = \cvec{0}, the second and third entries give c = b = 0, and then a = 0. So it is a basis \sB of 
R^3. The images are \cvec{w}_1 = \A\cvec{e}_1 = (1, 2) and \cvec{w}_2 = \A\cvec{e}_3 = (1, 3), which already form a basis \sC of 
R^2 since r = m = 2. Therefore \P = \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sE_3} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -2 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Q = \mtx{\id}{\sE_2}{\sC} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \ -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, using @thm-change-of-coordinates (c) and @thm-two-by-two-inverse. Check: \A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 2 & 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix} (the columns are \cvec{w}_1, \cvec{w}_2, \cvec{0}), and \Q\A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \ -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 2 & 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \N_2 . The pair (\Q, \P) is far from unique; any choice of extension gives another. How many equivalence classes does M_{3 	imes 2}(F) have, and which is the class of  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}? Ranks in M_{3 	imes 2}(F) range over 0, 1, 2, so there are \min(3, 2) + 1 = 3 classes by @thm-rank-normal-form (c). The given matrix is nonzero and its second column is twice the first, so its rank is 1, and it lies in the class of \N_1: all matrices of rank 1. Rank inequalities for compositions The rank of a composition cannot exceed the rank of either factor, and it cannot fall too far either. Both facts come from the same observation: ST is S applied to the subspace \im T. For a subspace X \subseteq W and a linear map S \colon W 	o U, the restriction S|_X \colon X 	o U, \elem{x} \mapsto S\elem{x}, is linear, since its values are those of S. Its kernel is \ker S \cap X. [Rank of a Composition] Let T \colon V 	o W and S \colon W 	o U be linear, with V and W finite-dimensional. Then ank(ST) \le \min(ank S, ank T). Consider the restriction S' = S|_{\im T} \colon \im T 	o U. For \elem{v} \in V, (ST)(\elem{v}) = S(T\elem{v}) = S'(T\elem{v}), so \im(ST) \subseteq \im S'; conversely every S'\elem{w} with \elem{w} = T\elem{v} \in \im T equals (ST)(\elem{v}). Hence \im(ST) = \im S'. Since \im T is finite-dimensional (a subspace of W, @thm-subspace-dimension), Rank–Nullity (@thm-rank-nullity) applied to S' gives ank(ST) = \dim \im S' = \dim \im T - \dim \ker S' \le ank T . Also \im(ST) = \im S' \subseteq \im S, and \im S is finite-dimensional by Rank–Nullity for S, so ank(ST) \le ank S by @thm-subspace-dimension. This proves the theorem. The lower bound uses the same restriction, but now we control its kernel instead of ignoring it. [Sylvester’s Rank Inequality] Let T \colon V 	o W and S \colon W 	o U be linear, with V and W finite-dimensional. Then ank(ST) \ge ank S + ank T - \dim W . In matrix form: for \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \B \in M_{n 	imes p}(F), ank(\A\B) \ge ank \A + ank \B - n. Of the ank T dimensions that reach W, the map S can destroy only those lying in \ker S, and \ker S has dimension \dim W - ank S. Rank–Nullity for the restriction S|_{\im T} turns this sentence into an inequality. Let S' = S|_{\im T}, so that \im S' = \im(ST) as in the proof of @thm-rank-of-composition, and \ker S' = \ker S \cap \im T \subseteq \ker S. By Rank–Nullity for S' and then for S,  egin{aligned} ank T &= ank(ST) + \dim(\ker S \cap \im T) \ &\le ank(ST) + \dim \ker S = ank(ST) + \dim W - ank S, \end{aligned} where the inequality is @thm-subspace-dimension. Rearranging gives the claim. For matrices, apply it to S\cvec{y} = \A\cvec{y} on W = F^n and T\cvec{x} = \B\cvec{x} on V = F^p: the matrix of ST in standard bases is \A\B by @thm-matrix-of-composition, and ranks of maps and matrices agree by @thm-rank-map-equals-rank-matrix. If you worked @exr-rank-nullity-c1, you have seen this proof already; we record the result here as a theorem so that later arguments can cite it. A typical use: if \A\B = \O with \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \B \in M_{n 	imes p}(F), then 0 \ge ank \A + ank \B - n, that is, ank \A + ank \B \le n . For instance, there are no \A, \B \in M_3(
R) of rank 2 with \A\B = \O. The rank of a product depends on the order of the factors. For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \A\B = \B has rank 1 but \B\A = \O has rank 0. @thm-rank-product-inequality and Sylvester’s inequality bound ank(\A\B) from both sides; they do not determine it, and they say nothing that would make ank(\A\B) = ank(\B\A). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define what it means for \A, \B \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) to be equivalent. 2. State the Rank Normal Form theorem for a matrix \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). 3. True or false: equivalent square matrices are similar. Justify your answer. 4. True or false: ank(\A\B) = ank(\B\A) for all \A, \B \in M_n(F). Justify your answer. 5. How many equivalence classes does M_{2 	imes 5}(
F_7) have? 6. In the proof of the normal form for T \colon V 	o W, which vectors form the end of the basis of V, and which vectors form the start of the basis of W? (a) There are invertible \Q \in M_m(F) and \P \in M_n(F) with \B = \Q\A\P (@def-equivalent-matrices). (b) If r = ank \A, there are invertible \Q, \P with \Q\A\P =  egin{pmatrix} \I_r & \O \ \O & \O \end{pmatrix}; and two m 	imes n matrices are equivalent if and only if they have the same rank (@thm-rank-normal-form). (c) False. \I_2 and  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} both have rank 2, so they are equivalent, but \I_2 is similar only to itself. (d) False. With \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, ank(\A\B) = 1 and ank(\B\A) = 0. (e) The possible ranks are 0, 1, 2, so there are 3 classes. The field plays no role. (f) The last n - r vectors of the basis of V form a basis of \ker T. The first r vectors of the basis of W are the images of the first r basis vectors of V, and they form a basis of \im T. B. Practice [B1: A column–row factorization] Find the column–row factorization of \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 & 0 \ 2 & -2 & 5 & 1 \ 1 & -1 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_{3 	imes 4}(
R). Hence write the second and fourth columns of \A as combinations of its pivot columns. Subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2 and row 1 from row 3: the rows become (1, -1, 2, 0), (0, 0, 1, 1), (0, 0, 1, 1). Subtract row 2 from row 3, and then 2 times row 2 from row 1: 	ext{RREF} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 & -2 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. The pivot columns are 1 and 3, so ank \A = 2, and by @thm-column-row-factorization \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 5 \ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 & -2 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Check by rows: 2(1, -1, 0, -2) + 5(0, 0, 1, 1) = (2, -2, 5, 1) and (1, -1, 0, -2) + 3(0, 0, 1, 1) = (1, -1, 3, 1); row 1 is (1, -1, 0, -2) + 2(0, 0, 1, 1). Reading columns 2 and 4 of \R: \cvec{a}_2 = -\cvec{a}_1 and \cvec{a}_4 = -2\cvec{a}_1 + \cvec{a}_3. Indeed -2(1, 2, 1) + (2, 5, 3) = (0, 1, 1) = \cvec{a}_4. [B2: Normal form of a rank-one matrix] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \ -2 & 2 & -4 \end{pmatrix} \in M_{2 	imes 3}(
R). Find invertible \Q \in M_2(
R) and \P \in M_3(
R) such that \Q\A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, following the proof of @thm-rank-normal-form. Row 2 is -2 times row 1, and \A 
e \O, so ank \A = 1. The null space is \{ x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 = 0 \}; setting the free variables x_2, x_3 to (1, 0) and (0, 1) gives the basis \cvec{u}_2 = (1, 1, 0), \cvec{u}_3 = (-2, 0, 1). Extend with \cvec{u}_1 = \cvec{e}_1: in a\cvec{e}_1 + b\cvec{u}_2 + c\cvec{u}_3 = (a + b - 2c, b, c) = \cvec{0}, the last two entries give b = c = 0 and then a = 0, so \sB = (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{u}_2, \cvec{u}_3) is a basis of 
R^3. Its first image is \cvec{w}_1 = \A\cvec{e}_1 = (1, -2), which we extend to the basis \sC = ((1, -2), \cvec{e}_2) of 
R^2 (independent, since a(1, -2) + b(0, 1) = (a, -2a + b) = \cvec{0} forces a = b = 0). Then \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & -2 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Q =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Check: \A\P has columns \A\cvec{e}_1 = (1, -2), \A\cvec{u}_2 = \cvec{0}, \A\cvec{u}_3 = \cvec{0}, and \Q(1, -2) = (1, 0). So \Q\A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Both \Q and \P are invertible by @thm-change-of-coordinates (c). [B3: Rank-one pieces] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). 1. Use @thm-column-row-factorization to show that if ank \A = 1, then \A = \cvec{x}\cvec{y}	p for some nonzero \cvec{x} \in F^m and \cvec{y} \in F^n. 2. Show that if ank \A = r \ge 1, then \A is a sum of r matrices of rank 1, and that it is not a sum of fewer than r matrices of rank 1. 3. Write  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \ 2 & 4 & 1 & 4 \ 3 & 6 & 1 & 7 \end{pmatrix} as a sum of two rank-one matrices. (a) With r = 1, \C \in M_{m 	imes 1}(F) is a single column \cvec{x}, and \R \in M_{1 	imes n}(F) is a single row, which we write as \cvec{y}	p with \cvec{y} \in F^n. So \A = \cvec{x}\cvec{y}	p. Both are nonzero: the columns of \C and the rows of \R are linearly independent by @thm-column-row-factorization, and a list containing a zero vector is dependent. (This recovers one direction of @exr-rank-c2.) (b) Write \A = \C\R with columns \cvec{c}_1, \dots, \cvec{c}_r of \C and rows \cvec{r}_1, \dots, \cvec{r}_r of \R, and let c_{ik}, r_{kl} be the entries of \C, \R. The m 	imes n matrix \cvec{c}_k\cvec{r}_k has (i, l)-entry c_{ik}r_{kl}, so by @thm-three-views-of-product (1), (\C\R)_{il} = \sum_{k=1}^{r} c_{ik}r_{kl} = \sum_{k=1}^{r} (\cvec{c}_k\cvec{r}_k)_{il}, \qquad	ext{that is,}\qquad \A = \cvec{c}_1\cvec{r}_1 + \dots + \cvec{c}_r\cvec{r}_r . Each \cvec{c}_k\cvec{r}_k has rank 1 by the (\Leftarrow) direction of @exr-rank-c2, since \cvec{c}_k 
e \cvec{0} (a column of \C, whose columns are independent) and \cvec{r}_k 
e \cvec{0} (a row of \R, whose rows are independent). If \A = \A_1 + \dots + \A_s with each ank \A_i = 1, then by @exr-rank-c1 applied repeatedly, r = ank \A \le ank \A_1 + \dots + ank \A_s = s. (c) By @exm-column-row-factorization, \A = \C\R with \C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & 1 \ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and \R =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}, so  egin{aligned} \A &=  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 2 \ 3 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} +  egin{pmatrix} 0 \ 1 \ 1 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \ &=  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \ 2 & 4 & 0 & 6 \ 3 & 6 & 0 & 9 \end{pmatrix} +  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} C. Going deeper [C1: Frobenius’s rank inequality] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), \B \in M_{n 	imes p}(F), and \C \in M_{p 	imes q}(F). Write N = 
ul(\A) \subseteq F^n, and let S \colon F^n 	o F^m be S\cvec{y} = \A\cvec{y}. 1. Show that \col(\A\B) = \{ \A\cvec{y} : \cvec{y} \in \col(\B) \}, and deduce from Rank–Nullity for S|_{\col(\B)} that ank(\A\B) = ank \B - \dim(N \cap \col(\B)). 2. Show similarly that ank(\A\B\C) = ank(\B\C) - \dim(N \cap \col(\B\C)). 3. Prove that \col(\B\C) \subseteq \col(\B), and deduce Frobenius’s inequality ank(\A\B\C) + ank \B \ge ank(\A\B) + ank(\B\C). 4. Deduce Sylvester’s inequality for matrices from (c). Hint: for (d), look for a special choice of the middle factor. (a) By @thm-three-views-of-product, every vector \A\B\cvec{x} equals \A\cvec{y} with \cvec{y} = \B\cvec{x} \in \col(\B); conversely every \cvec{y} \in \col(\B) is \B\cvec{x} for some \cvec{x}, and then \A\cvec{y} = (\A\B)\cvec{x} \in \col(\A\B). So \col(\A\B) = \im(S|_{\col(\B)}). The kernel of S|_{\col(\B)} is N \cap \col(\B), and \col(\B) is finite-dimensional, so by @thm-rank-nullity, ank \B = \dim \col(\B) = ank(\A\B) + \dim(N \cap \col(\B)). (b) The same argument with \B\C in place of \B gives \col(\A\B\C) = \im(S|_{\col(\B\C)}), with kernel N \cap \col(\B\C), so ank(\B\C) = ank(\A\B\C) + \dim(N \cap \col(\B\C)). (c) Every vector \B\C\cvec{x} = \B(\C\cvec{x}) lies in \col(\B), so \col(\B\C) \subseteq \col(\B). Hence N \cap \col(\B\C) \subseteq N \cap \col(\B), and by @thm-subspace-dimension, \dim(N \cap \col(\B\C)) \le \dim(N \cap \col(\B)). By (b) and then (a),  egin{aligned} ank(\A\B\C) &= ank(\B\C) - \dim(N \cap \col(\B\C)) \ &\ge ank(\B\C) - \dim(N \cap \col(\B)) \ &= ank(\B\C) - ank \B + ank(\A\B). \end{aligned} Rearranging gives Frobenius’s inequality. (d) Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \C \in M_{n 	imes q}(F), and apply (c) with p = n and \B = \I_n. Then ank(\A\C) + n \ge ank \A + ank \C, since ank \I_n = n. This is @thm-sylvester-rank-inequality for matrices. [C2: Counting over 
F_2] 1. Show that M_2(
F_2) contains exactly 1 matrix of rank 0, 6 of rank 2, and 9 of rank 1. 2. Deduce the sizes of the equivalence classes of M_2(
F_2). 3. Compare with similarity: how many matrices of M_2(
F_2) are similar to \I_2? Is the class of \I_2 under equivalence a union of several similarity classes? (a) The only matrix of rank 0 is \O. A matrix has rank 2 exactly when its two columns span 
F_2^2, that is (@thm-right-size-basis), when they form a basis of 
F_2^2. The first column can be any of the 3 nonzero vectors of 
F_2^2. The second must lie outside the span of the first, which has 2 elements, so there are 4 - 2 = 2 choices. That gives 3 \cdot 2 = 6 matrices of rank 2. Since \lvert M_2(
F_2) vert = 2^4 = 16, the remaining 16 - 1 - 6 = 9 matrices have rank 1. (b) By @thm-rank-normal-form (c), the classes are the sets of matrices of a fixed rank, of sizes 1, 9, and 6. (c) \I_2 is similar only to itself, so its similarity class has 1 element, while its equivalence class, the invertible matrices, has 6. Since similar matrices are equivalent, each equivalence class is a union of similarity classes, and here the class of the 6 invertible matrices contains the similarity class \{ \I_2 \} together with others. For example  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} is invertible but not similar to \I_2, so there are at least two similarity classes inside.

title: 4.4 Products and Quotient Spaces
content:
Products and Quotient Spaces So far every new vector space in this book has been found inside an old one, as a subspace. This section builds new spaces in two other ways. The first glues spaces together side by side, making a product; it is the “external” direct sum promised in Chapter 1. The second, the quotient space V/U, is subtler and more important: it collapses a subspace U to a single point and keeps only what V knows beyond U. Quotients let us state precisely what a linear map remembers and what it forgets, in the three Isomorphism Theorems. Products of vector spaces In Chapter 1 we wrote V = U \oplus W for subspaces U and W of one space V (@def-direct-sum). The two pieces already lived in a common space, and “direct” was a property of how they sat there. But often we want to combine two spaces that have nothing to do with each other, such as 
R^2 and 
R[x]_{\le 1}, into one space in which each keeps its identity. There is no common space to add inside, so we build one. The model is F^2. A vector of F^2 is a pair (a, b) of scalars, and we add and scale pairs entry by entry. Nothing in that recipe needs the entries to be scalars: the entries could be vectors, taken from any vector spaces over F. The product of vector spaces is the space of lists with one entry from each space, added and scaled entry by entry. [Product of vector spaces] Let V_1, \dots, V_k be vector spaces over the same field F. Their product (or external direct sum) is the Cartesian product (@def-cartesian-product) V_1 	imes \dots 	imes V_k = \{ (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) : \elem{v}_i \in V_i 	ext{ for each } i \}, with addition and scalar multiplication defined entrywise: for a \in F,  egin{aligned} (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) + (\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_k) &\coloneqq (\elem{v}_1 + \elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k + \elem{w}_k), \ a(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) &\coloneqq (a\elem{v}_1, \dots, a\elem{v}_k). \end{aligned} In words: the i-th entry of a sum is the sum of the i-th entries, computed in V_i, and similarly for scalar multiples. Two elements are equal exactly when all their entries are equal. Every operation happens inside one V_i at a time, which is why all the V_i must share the field F: the same scalar a has to act on every entry. It is a vector space. Both operations land in V_1 	imes \dots 	imes V_k, since \elem{v}_i + \elem{w}_i \in V_i and a\elem{v}_i \in V_i. Each axiom of @def-vector-space is an equation between lists, so it holds when it holds in each entry, and in each entry it is the same axiom in V_i. For example, (VS6) reads  egin{aligned} (a + b)(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) &= ((a + b)\elem{v}_1, \dots, (a + b)\elem{v}_k) \ &= (a\elem{v}_1 + b\elem{v}_1, \dots, a\elem{v}_k + b\elem{v}_k) \ &= a(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) + b(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k), \end{aligned} using (VS6) in each V_i. The zero vector is (\elem{0}, \dots, \elem{0}), with the zero of V_i in the i-th entry, and the additive inverse of (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) is (-\elem{v}_1, \dots, -\elem{v}_k). The other axioms are checked in exactly the same way. Examples. - The standard example. F 	imes \dots 	imes F (n factors) is F^n with its usual operations. - Unrelated spaces. An element of 
R^2 	imes 
R[x]_{\le 1} is a pair ((a, b), c + dx), and ((1, 0), x) + ((2, 5), 3 - x) = ((3, 5), 3). - Augmented data. A linear system \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} with m equations in n unknowns is a single element (\A, \cvec{b}) of M_{m 	imes n}(F) 	imes F^m. - Degenerate cases. For k = 1 the product is V_1 itself, with entries written in parentheses. And V 	imes \{\elem{0}\} consists of the pairs (\elem{v}, \elem{0}); the map \elem{v} \mapsto (\elem{v}, \elem{0}) is a linear bijection V 	o V 	imes \{\elem{0}\}, so a zero factor adds nothing. Nonexample by minimal change. Take V_1 = 
C as a vector space over 
C and V_2 = 
R over 
R. The set 
C 	imes 
R is fine, but the entrywise rule i \cdot (z, t) = (iz, it) fails: it 
otin 
R for t 
e 0. The clause that fails is “over the same field”. Restricting the scalars of 
C to 
R (@def-restriction-of-scalars) repairs it, and 
C 	imes 
R over 
R is a vector space of dimension 3. Bases of the factors combine into a basis of the product. For \elem{v} \in V_i, write \iota_i(\elem{v}) for the list with \elem{v} in the i-th entry and \elem{0} in every other entry. The map \iota_i \colon V_i 	o V_1 	imes \dots 	imes V_k is linear, because the operations are entrywise. [Dimension of a Product] Let V_1, \dots, V_k be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F, and let (\elem{b}_{i1}, \dots, \elem{b}_{in_i}) be a basis of V_i for each i. Then the list of all vectors \iota_i(\elem{b}_{ij}), for i = 1, \dots, k and j = 1, \dots, n_i, is a basis of V_1 	imes \dots 	imes V_k. In particular, \dim(V_1 	imes \dots 	imes V_k) = \dim V_1 + \dots + \dim V_k . Spanning. Let (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) be in the product. Since the operations are entrywise, (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) = \iota_1(\elem{v}_1) + \dots + \iota_k(\elem{v}_k). Each \elem{v}_i is a combination \sum_j c_{ij}\elem{b}_{ij}, and \iota_i is linear, so \iota_i(\elem{v}_i) = \sum_j c_{ij}\,\iota_i(\elem{b}_{ij}) (@thm-linear-combination). Hence (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) is a combination of the vectors \iota_i(\elem{b}_{ij}). Independence. Let \sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i} c_{ij}\,\iota_i(\elem{b}_{ij}) = \elem{0}. The i-th entry of the left side is \sum_j c_{ij}\elem{b}_{ij}, because every \iota_{i'}(\elem{b}_{i'j}) with i' 
e i has \elem{0} there. So \sum_j c_{ij}\elem{b}_{ij} = \elem{0} in V_i for each i, and the independence of the basis of V_i gives c_{ij} = 0 for all j. The list has n_1 + \dots + n_k vectors, which gives the dimension (@def-dimension). For instance, \dim(
R^2 	imes 
R[x]_{\le 1}) = 2 + 2 = 4, so this product is isomorphic to 
R^4 by @thm-isomorphic-iff-same-dimension. How does the external product relate to the internal direct sum of Chapter 1? If U_1, \dots, U_k are subspaces of V, there is a natural linear map from the product to V: add up the entries. The sum is direct exactly when this map loses no information. [Internal and External Direct Sums] 1. Let U_1, \dots, U_k be subspaces of a vector space V, and let S \colon U_1 	imes \dots 	imes U_k 	o V, \qquad S(\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k) = \elem{u}_1 + \dots + \elem{u}_k . Then S is linear with \im S = U_1 + \dots + U_k. It is injective if and only if the sum U_1 + \dots + U_k is direct. In that case S is an isomorphism from U_1 	imes \dots 	imes U_k onto U_1 \oplus \dots \oplus U_k. 2. Conversely, let V_1, \dots, V_k be vector spaces over F. Then the images \iota_i(V_i) are subspaces of V_1 	imes \dots 	imes V_k, each isomorphic to V_i via \iota_i, and V_1 	imes \dots 	imes V_k = \iota_1(V_1) \oplus \dots \oplus \iota_k(V_k). (a) For lists (\elem{u}_i), (\elem{u}_i'), and a \in F, regrouping the finite sums gives S((\elem{u}_i) + (\elem{u}_i')) = \sum_i (\elem{u}_i + \elem{u}_i') = S((\elem{u}_i)) + S((\elem{u}_i')) and S(a(\elem{u}_i)) = \sum_i a\elem{u}_i = aS((\elem{u}_i)), so S is linear. Its image is \{ \elem{u}_1 + \dots + \elem{u}_k : \elem{u}_i \in U_i \}, which is U_1 + \dots + U_k by @def-sum-of-subspaces. Its kernel consists of the lists with \elem{u}_1 + \dots + \elem{u}_k = \elem{0}. By @thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel, S is injective if and only if the only such list is (\elem{0}, \dots, \elem{0}), which is condition (b) of @thm-direct-sum-k-criteria, equivalent to the sum being direct. In that case S, viewed as a map onto its image, is a linear bijection, hence an isomorphism (@def-isomorphism). (b) Each \iota_i is linear and injective (its kernel is \{\elem{0}\}, since \iota_i(\elem{v}) has \elem{v} as its i-th entry), so \iota_i(V_i) is a subspace (@thm-prop-image) and \iota_i is a bijection onto it. Every list satisfies (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) = \iota_1(\elem{v}_1) + \dots + \iota_k(\elem{v}_k), so the product is the sum of the subspaces \iota_i(V_i). If \iota_1(\elem{v}_1) + \dots + \iota_k(\elem{v}_k) = \elem{0}, then (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) = (\elem{0}, \dots, \elem{0}), so every piece \iota_i(\elem{v}_i) is \elem{0}. By @thm-direct-sum-k-criteria ((b) \Rightarrow (a)) the sum is direct. So internal and external direct sums are the same thing seen from two sides. An internal direct sum is a product that happens to live inside V; a product is an internal direct sum of copies of its factors. Many books write \oplus for both. This book keeps 	imes for the external construction, so that U \oplus W always refers to subspaces of one space. Use @thm-internal-external-direct-sum (a) and Rank–Nullity to explain why, for finite-dimensional subspaces U, W of V, the sum U + W is direct if and only if \dim(U + W) = \dim U + \dim W. The addition map S \colon U 	imes W 	o V has image U + W, and \dim(U 	imes W) = \dim U + \dim W by @thm-dimension-of-product. By @thm-rank-nullity, \dim U + \dim W = \dim(U + W) + \dim \ker S. So \dim(U + W) = \dim U + \dim W exactly when \ker S = \{\elem{0}\}, that is, when S is injective, which by the theorem means the sum is direct. This recovers @thm-direct-sum-criteria (a) \Leftrightarrow (c). Cosets The second construction starts from a picture you have already seen. In Chapter 1 we compared the line U = \{ x + 2y = 0 \} through the origin with the parallel line L = \{ x + 2y = 3 \}, which is not a subspace. In Chapter 3 we found that the solutions of a consistent system \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} form a set \cvec{p} + 
ul(\A), a subspace shifted by one particular solution (@thm-general-solution-structure). Both are translates of a subspace. They deserve a name. [Coset] Let U be a subspace of a vector space V, and let \elem{v} \in V. The coset of U through \elem{v} is the subset \elem{v} + U \coloneqq \{ \elem{v} + \elem{u} : \elem{u} \in U \} \subseteq V . Any \elem{w} \in \elem{v} + U is called a representative of the coset. In 
R^2, with U = \{ x + 2y = 0 \} = \Span((2, -1)), the coset through (3, 0) is the line \{ x + 2y = 3 \}: a point (3, 0) + t(2, -1) = (3 + 2t, -t) satisfies x + 2y = 3, and every solution of x + 2y = 3 is of this form with t = -y. In general (a, b) + U = \{ x + 2y = a + 2b \}, so the cosets of U are exactly the lines parallel to U. The picture shows three cosets of U: U itself (solid), the line through \cvec{v} = (1, 1) (dashed), and another parallel line (dotted). The points \cvec{v} = (1, 1) and \cvec{v}' = (3, 0) lie on the same dashed line, because \cvec{v}' - \cvec{v} = (2, -1) \in U; so they are two representatives of one coset. That observation is the whole theory of cosets. [When two cosets are equal] Let U be a subspace of V. By @thm-first-isomorphism applied to S, the rule \elem{u} + (U \cap W) \mapsto S\elem{u} = \elem{u} + W is a well-defined injective linear map with image \im S = (U + W)/W, hence an isomorphism. (Directly: if \elem{u} - \elem{u}' \in U \cap W, then \elem{u} - \elem{u}' \in W, so \elem{u} + W = \elem{u}' + W, and the value does not depend on the representative.) If U and W are finite-dimensional, then so is U + W (it is spanned by the union of bases, @prp-sum-of-spans), and @thm-dimension-quotient turns the theorem into \dim(U + W) - \dim W = \dim U - \dim(U \cap W). That is the dimension formula for sums (@thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim), now as a consequence of an isomorphism rather than of a basis computation. An exercise below asks for the details. The third theorem says that quotients can be taken in stages. [Third Isomorphism Theorem] Let U \subseteq W \subseteq V be subspaces. Then W/U = \{ \elem{w} + U : \elem{w} \in W \} is a subspace of V/U, and (V/U)/(W/U) 	o V/W, \qquad (\elem{v} + U) + W/U \mapsto \elem{v} + W is a well-defined isomorphism. Hence (V/U)/(W/U) \cong V/W. Let S \colon V/U 	o V/W, S(\elem{v} + U) = \elem{v} + W. Well defined. If \elem{v} + U = \elem{v}' + U, then \elem{v} - \elem{v}' \in U \subseteq W, so \elem{v} + W = \elem{v}' + W by @lem-coset-equality (b). By @thm-well-defined-on-quotient (a), applied to V 	o V/W, \elem{v} \mapsto \elem{v} + W, the rule defines a function on V/U. Linear and surjective.  egin{aligned} S((\elem{v} + U) + (\elem{w} + U)) &= S((\elem{v} + \elem{w}) + U) = (\elem{v} + \elem{w}) + W \ &= S(\elem{v} + U) + S(\elem{w} + U), \end{aligned} and similarly for scalars, by @def-quotient-space in both quotients. Every \elem{v} + W equals S(\elem{v} + U). Kernel. S(\elem{v} + U) = W means \elem{v} \in W. If \elem{v} \in W, then \elem{v} + U \in W/U. Conversely, if \elem{v} + U = \elem{w} + U with \elem{w} \in W, then \elem{v} - \elem{w} \in U \subseteq W, so \elem{v} \in W. Hence \ker S = W/U. In particular W/U is a subspace of V/U, by @thm-prop-kernel. By @thm-first-isomorphism applied to S, (V/U)/(W/U) \cong \im S = V/W, via (\elem{v} + U) + W/U \mapsto S(\elem{v} + U) = \elem{v} + W. The notation W/U is used with two meanings, and they agree: the quotient space of W by U, and the set of cosets \elem{w} + U with \elem{w} \in W, sitting inside V/U. The coset \elem{w} + U is the same subset of V in both readings, and the operations agree because both are computed with representatives. For example, with V = 
R^3, U the z-axis, and W the xz-plane, V/W \cong 
R through the y-coordinate, and the theorem says that first forgetting z and then forgetting x leaves the same thing as forgetting both at once. The universal property of the quotient The proofs of the three theorems repeated one move: a linear map that vanishes on U passes to V/U. We record that move once, in its general form. It is the standard way to define linear maps out of a quotient. [Universal Property of the Quotient] Let U be a subspace of V, \pi \colon V 	o V/U the quotient map, and T \colon V 	o W a linear map. 1. If U \subseteq \ker T, then there is exactly one linear map  ar T \colon V/U 	o W with  ar T \circ \pi = T, namely  ar T(\elem{v} + U) = T\elem{v}. Its image is \im T, and it is injective if and only if U = \ker T. 2. Conversely, if some function  ar T \colon V/U 	o W satisfies  ar T \circ \pi = T, then U \subseteq \ker T. (a) If \elem{v} - \elem{v}' \in U \subseteq \ker T, then T\elem{v} = T\elem{v}'. By @thm-well-defined-on-quotient (a) there is exactly one function  ar T with  ar T(\elem{v} + U) = T\elem{v}, and it is linear by the computation in the proof of @thm-first-isomorphism, which used only this formula. Any linear  ar T with  ar T \circ \pi = T satisfies this formula, so it is this one. The image is \{ T\elem{v} \} = \im T. The kernel of  ar T is \{ \elem{v} + U : \elem{v} \in \ker T \}; it is \{ U \}, the zero subspace, exactly when every \elem{v} \in \ker T lies in U, that is, when \ker T \subseteq U, which together with U \subseteq \ker T means U = \ker T. Apply @thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel. (b) Let \elem{u} \in U. Then \pi(\elem{u}) = U = \pi(\elem{0}), so T\elem{u} =  ar T(\pi(\elem{u})) =  ar T(\pi(\elem{0})) = T(\elem{0}) = \elem{0} by @thm-zero-maps-to-zero. Hence U \subseteq \ker T. In words: linear maps out of V/U are the same as linear maps out of V that kill U. The First Isomorphism Theorem is the case U = \ker T. For example, the map T \colon 
R^3 	o 
R, T(x, y, z) = x, kills the z-axis U, so it induces  ar T \colon 
R^3/U 	o 
R, (x, y, z) + U \mapsto x. Since \ker T is the yz-plane, strictly larger than U, this  ar T is not injective: it also kills the coset \cvec{e}_2 + U. Quotients will return in Chapter 9, where an operator T with T(U) \subseteq U induces an operator on V/U, and this is the engine of induction arguments on the dimension. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the quotient space V/U and its two operations. 2. State the condition, in terms of \elem{v} - \elem{w}, for \elem{v} + U = \elem{w} + U. 3. True or false: V/U is a subspace of V. Justify your answer. 4. State the First Isomorphism Theorem. 5. If U is a 2-dimensional subspace of 
R^5, what is \dim(
R^5/U)? What is \dim(
R^5 	imes U)? 6. What must be checked before the formula (\elem{v} + U) + (\elem{w} + U) = (\elem{v} + \elem{w}) + U can be used as a definition, and which property of U makes the check work? (a) For a subspace U of V, V/U = \{ \elem{v} + U : \elem{v} \in V \}, with (\elem{v} + U) + (\elem{w} + U) = (\elem{v} + \elem{w}) + U and a(\elem{v} + U) = a\elem{v} + U (@def-quotient-space). (b) \elem{v} + U = \elem{w} + U if and only if \elem{v} - \elem{w} \in U (@lem-coset-equality). (c) False. The elements of V/U are cosets, which are subsets of V, not vectors of V. (d) If T \colon V 	o W is linear, then \elem{v} + \ker T \mapsto T\elem{v} is a well-defined isomorphism V/\ker T 	o \im T (@thm-first-isomorphism). (e) 5 - 2 = 3 by @thm-dimension-quotient, and 5 + 2 = 7 by @thm-dimension-of-product. (f) That the right-hand side does not depend on the representatives: if \elem{v} - \elem{v}' \in U and \elem{w} - \elem{w}' \in U, then (\elem{v} + \elem{w}) + U = (\elem{v}' + \elem{w}') + U. This works because (\elem{v} + \elem{w}) - (\elem{v}' + \elem{w}') = (\elem{v} - \elem{v}') + (\elem{w} - \elem{w}') and U is closed under addition. B. Practice [B1: A basis of a quotient of 
R^4] Let U = \Span((1, 0, 1, 0), (0, 1, 0, 1)) \subseteq 
R^4. 1. Find \dim(
R^4/U) and a basis of 
R^4/U. 2. Write (3, 1, 4, 1) + U in your basis. 3. Decide whether (1, 2, 3, 4) + U = (3, 4, 1, 2) + U. (a) The two spanning vectors are independent (look at the first two entries), so \dim U = 2 and \dim(
R^4/U) = 4 - 2 = 2 by @thm-dimension-quotient. Extend by \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2. If a(1, 0, 1, 0) + b(0, 1, 0, 1) + c\cvec{e}_1 + d\cvec{e}_2 = (a + c, b + d, a, b) = \cvec{0}, then a = b = 0 from the last two entries and c = d = 0 from the first two. So the four vectors are independent, hence a basis of 
R^4 (@thm-right-size-basis), and by @thm-dimension-quotient (\cvec{e}_1 + U, \cvec{e}_2 + U) is a basis of 
R^4/U. (b) Solve (3, 1, 4, 1) = (a + c, b + d, a, b): a = 4, b = 1, c = -1, d = 0. Since the U-part becomes zero in the quotient, (3, 1, 4, 1) + U = -1(\cvec{e}_1 + U) + 0(\cvec{e}_2 + U). Check: (3, 1, 4, 1) + \cvec{e}_1 = (4, 1, 4, 1) = 4(1, 0, 1, 0) + (0, 1, 0, 1) \in U. (c) The difference is (1, 2, 3, 4) - (3, 4, 1, 2) = (-2, -2, 2, 2). A vector (a, b, a, b) of U has equal first and third entries, but -2 
e 2. So the difference is not in U, and the cosets are different by @lem-coset-equality. [B2: A map that factors through a quotient] Let T \colon 
R[x]_{\le 2} 	o 
R^2, T(p) = (p(1), p'(1)), and U = \Span((x - 1)^2). 1. Show that U \subseteq \ker T, so that T induces a linear map  ar T \colon

R^2 with  ar T(p + U) = T(p). 2. Prove that  ar T is an isomorphism. 3. Compute  ar T(x^2 + U), and find the coset  ar T^{-1}(0, 1). (a) T is linear, since evaluation and differentiation are. For q = (x - 1)^2, q(1) = 0 and q'(1) = 2(1 - 1) = 0, so T(q) = \cvec{0}, and hence T(cq) = \cvec{0} for all c. So U \subseteq \ker T, and @thm-quotient-universal-property (a) gives the linear map  ar T. (b) T(1) = (1, 0) and T(x - 1) = (0, 1), so T is surjective and ank T = 2. By @thm-rank-nullity, \dim \ker T = 3 - 2 = 1 = \dim U, so \ker T = U by @thm-dim-impl-eq. By @thm-quotient-universal-property (a),  ar T is injective with image \im T = 
R^2. Hence  ar T is a linear bijection, an isomorphism. (c)  ar T(x^2 + U) = T(x^2) = (1, 2). Since T(x - 1) = (0, 1),  ar T^{-1}(0, 1) = (x - 1) + U, the set of all x - 1 + c(x - 1)^2. [B3: Matrices modulo scalars] Let n \ge 1 and S = \{ c\I_n : c \in F \} \subseteq M_n(F). 1. Show that S is a subspace and find \dim(M_n(F)/S). 2. For n = 2, find a basis of M_2(F)/S. 3. Show that \A + S = \B + S if and only if \A - \B is a scalar matrix, and decide whether  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix} + S =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} + S. (a) S = \Span(\I_n) is a subspace by @thm-span-subspace, of dimension 1 since \I_n 
e \O. By @thm-dimension-quotient, \dim(M_n(F)/S) = n^2 - 1. (b) Extend (\I_2) by \E_{11}, \E_{12}, \E_{21}. If a\I_2 + b\E_{11} + c\E_{12} + d\E_{21} =  egin{pmatrix} a + b & c \ d & a \end{pmatrix} = \O, then a = c = d = 0 and then b = 0. So the four matrices are independent, hence a basis of M_2(F) (@thm-right-size-basis), and (\E_{11} + S, \E_{12} + S, \E_{21} + S) is a basis of M_2(F)/S by @thm-dimension-quotient. (c) This is @lem-coset-equality (b) for the subspace S. Here the difference is  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = 2\I_2 \in S, so the two cosets are equal. C. Going deeper [C1: The dimension formula from isomorphisms] Let U and W be finite-dimensional subspaces of a vector space V. 1. Using @thm-second-isomorphism and @thm-dimension-quotient, prove that \dim(U + W) = \dim U + \dim W - \dim(U \cap W). 2. Give a second proof: apply Rank–Nullity to the addition map S \colon U 	imes W 	o V, S(\elem{u}, \elem{w}) = \elem{u} + \elem{w}, after showing that \elem{u} \mapsto (\elem{u}, -\elem{u}) is an isomorphism from U \cap W onto \ker S. (a) U + W is finite-dimensional, being spanned by a basis of U followed by a basis of W (@prp-sum-of-spans), and U \cap W \subseteq U is finite-dimensional (@thm-subspace-dimension). By @thm-second-isomorphism, (U + W)/W \cong U/(U \cap W), and isomorphic finite-dimensional spaces have equal dimension (@thm-isomorphic-iff-same-dimension). Applying @thm-dimension-quotient to both sides, \dim(U + W) - \dim W = \dim U - \dim(U \cap W), which rearranges to the formula. (b) The map S is linear with image U + W by @thm-internal-external-direct-sum (a). Let J \colon U \cap W 	o U 	imes W, J\elem{u} = (\elem{u}, -\elem{u}); it is well defined because \elem{u} \in U and -\elem{u} \in W, and linear because the operations are entrywise. It is injective, since (\elem{u}, -\elem{u}) = (\elem{0}, \elem{0}) forces \elem{u} = \elem{0}. Its image lies in \ker S, since \elem{u} + (-\elem{u}) = \elem{0}. Conversely, if (\elem{u}, \elem{w}) \in \ker S, then \elem{w} = -\elem{u}; so \elem{u} = -\elem{w} \in W, hence \elem{u} \in U \cap W and (\elem{u}, \elem{w}) = J\elem{u}. Thus J is an isomorphism onto \ker S, and \dim \ker S = \dim(U \cap W). By @thm-dimension-of-product and @thm-rank-nullity, \dim U + \dim W = \dim(U 	imes W) = \dim(U + W) + \dim(U \cap W). [C2: The operator induced on a quotient] Let V be finite-dimensional, T \in \cL(V), and U a subspace with T\elem{u} \in U for every \elem{u} \in U. 1. Prove that  ar T(\elem{v} + U) \coloneqq T\elem{v} + U is a well-defined linear operator on V/U. 2. Let (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_m) be a basis of U, extended to a basis \sB = (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_m, \elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_s) of V. Show that \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \O & D \end{pmatrix}, where \A \in M_m(F) is the matrix of the restriction T|_U \colon U 	o U in (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_m), D \in M_s(F) is the matrix of  ar T in (\elem{w}_1 + U, \dots, \elem{w}_s + U), and \O is the s 	imes m zero matrix. 3. Check (b) when T is differentiation on 
R[x]_{\le 2}, with U = 
R[x]_{\le 1} and \sB = (1, x, x^2). Hint: for (a), apply @thm-quotient-universal-property to \pi \circ T. (a) The map \pi \circ T \colon V 	o V/U, \elem{v} \mapsto T\elem{v} + U, is linear as a composition of linear maps (@thm-composition-linear). For \elem{u} \in U, T\elem{u} \in U, so (\pi \circ T)(\elem{u}) = U, the zero of V/U; thus U \subseteq \ker(\pi \circ T). By @thm-quotient-universal-property (a) there is exactly one linear map  ar T \colon V/U 	o V/U with  ar T(\elem{v} + U) = T\elem{v} + U. (b) For j \le m, T\elem{u}_j \in U, so it is a combination of \elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_m only, and its \sB-coordinates are 0 in the last s places. These first m columns, restricted to their first m entries, are the columns of the matrix \A of T|_U (which maps U to U by hypothesis and is linear). For the remaining columns, write T\elem{w}_k = \sum_i b_{ik}\elem{u}_i + \sum_l d_{lk}\elem{w}_l. Passing to V/U, where \elem{u}_i + U = U is zero, gives  ar T(\elem{w}_k + U) = \sum_l d_{lk}(\elem{w}_l + U). So the s 	imes s matrix (d_{lk}) is the matrix D of  ar T in the basis (\elem{w}_1 + U, \dots, \elem{w}_s + U) of @thm-dimension-quotient, and the bottom-right block of \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} is D. (c) T(1) = 0, T(x) = 1, T(x^2) = 2x, so \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Differentiation maps U = 
R[x]_{\le 1} into itself. The block \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is the matrix of T on U in (1, x), the lower-left block is  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, and the block D is the 1 	imes 1 matrix \O_1: indeed  ar T(x^2 + U) = 2x + U = U, the zero coset, since 2x \in U. [C3: Counting cosets over a finite field] Let F = 
F_q be a finite field with q elements, V a vector space over F of dimension n, and U a subspace of dimension m. 1. Show that \lvert V vert = q^n. 2. Show that every coset \elem{v} + U has exactly \lvert U vert elements, and deduce \lvert V/U vert = q^{n - m} by counting. 3. Check that (b) agrees with @thm-dimension-quotient. (a) Choose a basis (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n). By @thm-unique-representation, (a_1, \dots, a_n) \mapsto a_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + a_n\elem{v}_n is a bijection F^n 	o V, and F^n has q^n elements. (b) The map U 	o \elem{v} + U, \elem{u} \mapsto \elem{v} + \elem{u}, is surjective by @def-coset and injective because \elem{v} + \elem{u} = \elem{v} + \elem{u}' implies \elem{u} = \elem{u}'. So \lvert \elem{v} + U vert = \lvert U vert = q^m by (a) applied to U. By @lem-coset-equality (c), the cosets partition V into \lvert V/U vert disjoint sets of size q^m, so q^n = \lvert V/U vert \cdot q^m, and \lvert V/U vert = q^{n - m}. (c) By @thm-dimension-quotient, V/U is a vector space over 
F_q of dimension n - m, so by (a) it has q^{n - m} elements, in agreement with (b). For example, 
F_2^3 modulo a line has 8/2 = 4 cosets.

title: 4.5 Projections and the Trace of an Operator
content:
Projections and the Trace of an Operator Chapter 1 ended its discussion of complements with a promise: a splitting V = U \oplus W should give a projection of V onto U along W, and different complements should give different projections. This section keeps that promise. Projections are the operators that are simplest in a well-chosen basis, and computing their matrices there leads to a second topic: the trace of an operator, a number attached to T \in \cL(V) that no choice of basis can change. We end with involutions, which split a space into two pieces in the same way. Projections Suppose V = U \oplus W. By @def-direct-sum, every \elem{v} \in V can be written as \elem{v} = \elem{u} + \elem{w} with \elem{u} \in U and \elem{w} \in W in exactly one way. So the rule “\elem{v} \mapsto \elem{u}”, keep the U-piece and throw away the W-piece, is a well-defined function V 	o V. In 
R^3 = \{	ext{the } xy	ext{-plane}\} \oplus \{	ext{the } z	ext{-axis}\}, it sends (a, b, c) to (a, b, 0): the shadow of a point on the floor when light falls straight down. What property does such a map have that singles it out? Apply it twice. The output \elem{u} already lies in U, and its splitting is \elem{u} = \elem{u} + \elem{0}, so applying the rule again returns \elem{u}. Doing it twice is the same as doing it once. We take this as the definition, because it can be checked without knowing U and W in advance. A projection is an operator that leaves alone everything it has already produced. [Projection] Let V be a vector space over F. An operator P \in \cL(V) is a projection if P^2 = P, that is, P(P\elem{v}) = P\elem{v} for every \elem{v} \in V. In words: P^2 is the composite PP (@def-polynomial-of-operator), so the condition says that P fixes each of its own outputs. Equivalently, P\elem{x} = \elem{x} for every \elem{x} \in \im P: if \elem{x} = P\elem{v}, then P\elem{x} = P^2(\elem{v}) = P\elem{v} = \elem{x}, and conversely this for \elem{x} = P\elem{v} is P^2(\elem{v}) = P\elem{v}. No inner product and no notion of angle is involved. The projections of this section are often called oblique projections, to distinguish them from the orthogonal projections met later, in the chapters on inner product spaces. Examples. - Onto an axis. P(x, y) = (x, 0) on F^2. Then P^2(x, y) = P(x, 0) = (x, 0), so P^2 = P. - A rank-one projection. T(x, y) = (2x - y,\ 2x - y) on 
R^2 from @exm-projection-adapted-basis. We saw there that its matrix \A satisfies \A^2 = \A; directly, T(2x - y, 2x - y) = (4x - 2y - 2x + y, \dots) = (2x - y, 2x - y). - Constant term. On F[x]_{\le n}, P(p) = p(0), the constant polynomial with value p(0). The constant polynomial c has value c at 0, so P(P(p)) = P(p). - Degenerate cases. The identity \id_V and the zero operator are projections, since \id_V^2 = \id_V and 0^2 = 0. They correspond to keeping everything and keeping nothing. Nonexample by minimal change. Change the first example to T(x, y) = (2x, 0) on 
R^2. Its image is still the x-axis and its kernel is still the y-axis. But T^2(x, y) = (4x, 0) 
e T(x, y) when x 
e 0: T does not fix the vectors of its own image, since T(1, 0) = (2, 0). So having “the right image and kernel” is not enough; the clause P^2 = P is what forces P to be the identity on its image. Likewise the reflection R(x, y) = (y, x) is not a projection: R^2 = \id 
e R. Here is the promised correspondence. It says that projections and direct sum decompositions are two descriptions of the same thing. [Projections and Direct Sums] Let V be a vector space. 1. If P \in \cL(V) is a projection, then V = \im P \oplus \ker P, P is the identity on \im P, and P is zero on \ker P. 2. Conversely, suppose V = U \oplus W. Then there is exactly one operator P \in \cL(V) with P\elem{u} = \elem{u} for all \elem{u} \in U and P\elem{w} = \elem{0} for all \elem{w} \in W, namely P(\elem{u} + \elem{w}) = \elem{u}. It is a projection, with \im P = U and \ker P = W. It is called the projection onto U along W. For (a), every vector splits as “what P keeps” plus “what P removes”: \elem{v} = P\elem{v} + (\elem{v} - P\elem{v}). The first piece is in the image by definition, and P^2 = P is exactly what puts the second piece in the kernel. For (b), uniqueness of the splitting makes the rule a function, and uniqueness again makes it linear. (a) Let \elem{v} \in V. Then \elem{v} = P\elem{v} + (\elem{v} - P\elem{v}), where P\elem{v} \in \im P and P(\elem{v} - P\elem{v}) = P\elem{v} - P^2(\elem{v}) = \elem{0} because P^2 = P. Hence V = \im P + \ker P. If \elem{x} \in \im P \cap \ker P, then \elem{x} = P\elem{x}, as shown after @def-projection-operator, and P\elem{x} = \elem{0}; so \elem{x} = \elem{0}. By @thm-direct-sum-criteria, V = \im P \oplus \ker P. We have also seen that P fixes \im P, and P is zero on \ker P by definition. (b) Existence. By @def-direct-sum, each \elem{v} \in V has exactly one splitting \elem{v} = \elem{u} + \elem{w}, so P\elem{v} \coloneqq \elem{u} defines a function V 	o V. It is linear: if \elem{v} = \elem{u} + \elem{w} and \elem{v}' = \elem{u}' + \elem{w}', then \elem{v} + \elem{v}' = (\elem{u} + \elem{u}') + (\elem{w} + \elem{w}') and a\elem{v} = a\elem{u} + a\elem{w} are splittings, because U and W are subspaces, so by uniqueness P(\elem{v} + \elem{v}') = \elem{u} + \elem{u}' = P\elem{v} + P\elem{v}' and P(a\elem{v}) = a\elem{u} = aP\elem{v}. For \elem{u} \in U the splitting is \elem{u} = \elem{u} + \elem{0}, so P\elem{u} = \elem{u}; for \elem{w} \in W it is \elem{w} = \elem{0} + \elem{w}, so P\elem{w} = \elem{0}. Properties.
