e i. By the hypothesis and linearity, \varphi(\E_{ik}) = \varphi(\E_{ii}\E_{ik}) = \varphi(\E_{ik}\E_{ii}) = \varphi(\O) = 0. (b) \E_{ii} = \E_{ij}\E_{ji} and \E_{jj} = \E_{ji}\E_{ij}. Hence \varphi(\E_{ii}) = \varphi(\E_{ij}\E_{ji}) = \varphi(\E_{ji}\E_{ij}) = \varphi(\E_{jj}). (c) Let c = \varphi(\E_{11}). For \A = (a_{ij}) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}\E_{ij}, linearity with (a) and (b) gives \varphi(\A) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}\varphi(\E_{ij}) = \sum_{i} a_{ii}\varphi(\E_{ii}) = c\sum_i a_{ii} = c\,	r \A . Conversely, c\,	r is linear and c\,	r(\A\B) = c\,	r(\B\A) by @thm-trace-properties. So the linear functionals with \varphi(\A\B) = \varphi(\B\A) are exactly the multiples of the trace.

title: Duality
content: Duality A linear map V \to F turns each vector into a single number. The i-th coordinate in a basis does this, and so do evaluating a polynomial at a point, integrating a function, and taking the trace of a matrix. These linear functionals are the measurements we can make on a vector space, and together they form a vector space of their own, the dual space V^{*}. The dual space mirrors V with every inclusion reversed. A subspace corresponds to the functionals that vanish on it. An injective map corresponds to a surjective one. The kernel of a map corresponds to the image of its dual map, whose matrix is the transpose. Passing to the dual turns a hard question into an easy one surprisingly often. It also explains facts we already know from a new angle: why a subspace of F^n is always the solution set of a homogeneous system, and why row rank equals column rank. What you need. From Chapter 0, the transpose and its arithmetic (@def-transpose, @thm-transpose-properties) and matrix multiplication read column by column (@thm-matrix-times-vector-columns), together with polynomials (@def-polynomial), which supply the infinite-dimensional example of §01. From Chapter 1, bases, dimension, and complements (@def-basis, @def-dimension, @thm-complement-exists), and bases of infinite-dimensional spaces (@thm-basis-extension-general) for the remarks on infinite dimension. From Chapter 2, linear maps and the space \cL(V, W) (@def-linear-transformation, @thm-linear-maps-vector-space) and the Rank–Nullity Theorem (@thm-rank-nullity). From Chapter 3, the row space and null space of a matrix (@def-row-space, @def-null-space) and inverses by row reduction (@thm-inverse-by-row-reduction). From Chapter 4, the matrix of a map and change of basis (@def-matrix-of-linear-map, @thm-change-of-coordinates), and quotient spaces with the First Isomorphism Theorem (@def-quotient-space, @thm-first-isomorphism). Roadmap - Linear functionals and the dual space. Measurements as vectors; dual bases; separating vectors by functionals. - Annihilators. The functionals that vanish on a subspace, and the formula \dim U + \dim U^{0} = \dim V. - The double dual. A natural isomorphism V \to V^{**} that needs no basis, and what “natural” means. - The dual map and the transpose. Pulling functionals back along a map; its matrix is the transpose; kernels and images trade places. - Duality for subspaces and quotients. The dual of a subspace is a quotient of the dual, and the dual of a quotient is an annihilator; hyperplanes and codimension. - Hyperplanes and linear systems revisited. Every subspace is cut out by equations; converting between parametric and implicit descriptions. Named moves - Test against functionals. To show a vector is zero, show that every functional (or every vector of a dual basis) sends it to zero. - Pass to the dual and count. Replace a subspace by its annihilator and use \dim U + \dim U^{0} = \dim V. - Natural or chosen? Ask whether an isomorphism needs a basis. V \cong V^{*} does; V \cong V^{**} does not. - Dualize a statement. Injective becomes surjective, kernel becomes image, a matrix becomes its transpose, and inclusions reverse.

title: 5.1 Linear Functionals and the Dual Space
content:
Linear Functionals and the Dual Space Chapter 2 studied linear maps V 	o W into arbitrary targets. The smallest nonzero target is the field F itself, and maps into it are everywhere: a coordinate, the value of a polynomial at a point, an integral, the trace. This section names these maps and shows that they form a vector space V^{*}, of the same dimension as V when V is finite-dimensional. It also proves the fact that makes them useful: every nonzero vector is detected by at least one of them. Measuring a vector by a number After studying vector spaces and the maps between them, we look at the simplest possible target. Here are four maps we have already met, from four different families. - A coordinate. Fix a basis \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) of V. The map V 	o F sending \elem{v} to the first entry of \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} respects sums and multiples, by @thm-coordinates-linear. - Evaluation. The map F[x] 	o F, p \mapsto p(3), satisfies (p + q)(3) = p(3) + q(3) and (cp)(3) = c\,p(3), by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations (a constant c is a polynomial with value c). - Integration. The map 
R[x] 	o 
R, p \mapsto \int_0^1 p(t)\,\dd t, is linear by the linearity of the integral from calculus. - Trace. The map 	r \colon M_n(F) 	o F is linear (@exm-trace-matrices). The inputs are columns, polynomials, and matrices. The outputs are always single scalars. Each map is a way of measuring a vector by one number, and each measurement respects sums and scalar multiples. The same expression keeps recurring, “a linear map whose target is F”, and we will see that these maps form a space with a structure of its own. So we give them a name. A linear functional is a linear measurement: it assigns a scalar to each vector, and the measurement of a linear combination is the same combination of the measurements. [Linear Functional] Let V be a vector space over F, and regard F as a vector space over itself. A linear functional on V is a linear map \varphi \colon V 	o F. That is, for all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V and all c \in F, \varphi(\elem{u} + \elem{v}) = \varphi(\elem{u}) + \varphi(\elem{v}), \qquad \varphi(c\elem{v}) = c\,\varphi(\elem{v}). [Dual Space] Let V be a vector space over F. The dual space of V is the set of all linear functionals on V, V^{*} \coloneqq \cL(V, F), with the pointwise operations (\varphi + \psi)(\elem{v}) \coloneqq \varphi(\elem{v}) + \psi(\elem{v}) and (c\varphi)(\elem{v}) \coloneqq c\,\varphi(\elem{v}) for \varphi, \psi \in V^{*}, c \in F, and \elem{v} \in V. In words: a linear functional is a linear map (@def-linear-transformation) whose codomain is the one-dimensional space F. Its values lie in the same field F over which V is a vector space. The first condition says that measuring a sum gives the sum of the measurements, and the second says that scaling a vector scales its measurement. The dual space collects every such measurement, and it adds them the natural way: the measurement \varphi + \psi reports the sum of the two readings. We write functionals with Greek letters \varphi, \psi, which keeps them apart from vectors of V. Well-definedness. Two things need checking: that \varphi + \psi and c\varphi are again linear, and that the vector space axioms hold. Both are the case W = F of @thm-linear-maps-vector-space. So V^{*} is a vector space over F. Its zero vector is the zero functional \elem{v} \mapsto 0, and the negative of \varphi is \elem{v} \mapsto -\varphi(\elem{v}). Note that V^{*} is a set of functions on V, not a subset of V. [Four Families of Functionals] Show that each map is a linear functional. 1. \varepsilon_c \colon F[x] 	o F, p \mapsto p(c), for a fixed c \in F (evaluation at c). 2. \iota \colon 
R[x]_{\le 2} 	o 
R, p \mapsto \int_0^1 p(t)\,\dd t. 3. 	r \colon M_n(F) 	o F. 4. The zero functional on any V. Also find the dual space of the zero space \{\elem{0}\}. (a) By @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, (p + q)(c) = p(c) + q(c), and, regarding ap as the product of the constant polynomial a with p, (ap)(c) = a(c)\,p(c) = a\,p(c), because the constant polynomial a has value a at c. These are the two conditions of @def-linear-functional. (b) By linearity of the integral, \int_0^1 (p + q) = \int_0^1 p + \int_0^1 q and \int_0^1 ap = a\int_0^1 p. On coefficients, \iota(a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2) = a_0 +  rac{a_1}{2} +  rac{a_2}{3}. (c) This is @thm-trace-properties (1): 	r(\A + \B) = 	r \A + 	r \B and 	r(c\A) = c	r \A. (d) 0 = 0 + 0 and 0 = c \cdot 0 in F, so the zero functional is linear. On \{\elem{0}\}, a linear functional must send \elem{0} to 0 (@thm-zero-maps-to-zero), and there is only one vector. So the zero functional is the only element, and \{\elem{0}\}^{*} = \{0\}. This degenerate case matters: it is the case n = 0 of the count \dim V^{*} = \dim V proved below. The family F^n can be described completely. A row vector times a column is a scalar, and every functional on F^n arises this way. [Functionals on F^n Are Row Vectors] For \cvec{a} = (a_1, \dots, a_n) \in F^n, define \varphi_{\cvec{a}} \colon F^n 	o F by \varphi_{\cvec{a}}(\cvec{x}) \coloneqq \cvec{a}	p\cvec{x} = a_1x_1 + \dots + a_nx_n . Then \varphi_{\cvec{a}} \in (F^n)^{*}. Every \varphi \in (F^n)^{*} equals \varphi_{\cvec{a}} for exactly one \cvec{a}, namely (\varphi(\cvec{e}_1), \dots, \varphi(\cvec{e}_n)). The map F^n 	o (F^n)^{*}, \cvec{a} \mapsto \varphi_{\cvec{a}}, is an isomorphism. The map \varphi_{\cvec{a}} is T_{\cvec{a}	p} for the 1 	imes n matrix \cvec{a}	p, with a 1 	imes 1 matrix read as a scalar, so it is linear by @exm-matrix-transformation. Let \varphi \in (F^n)^{*} and put a_i \coloneqq \varphi(\cvec{e}_i). Then \varphi_{\cvec{a}}(\cvec{e}_i) = a_i = \varphi(\cvec{e}_i) for each i. Two linear maps that agree on the basis (\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n) are equal by the uniqueness part of @thm-linear-transform-basis, so \varphi = \varphi_{\cvec{a}}. If \varphi_{\cvec{a}} = \varphi_{\cvec{b}}, then a_i = \varphi_{\cvec{a}}(\cvec{e}_i) = \varphi_{\cvec{b}}(\cvec{e}_i) = b_i for every i, so \cvec{a} = \cvec{b}. Hence \cvec{a} \mapsto \varphi_{\cvec{a}} is a bijection F^n 	o (F^n)^{*}. It is linear, since \varphi_{\cvec{a} + c\cvec{b}}(\cvec{x}) = \sum_i (a_i + cb_i)x_i = \varphi_{\cvec{a}}(\cvec{x}) + c\,\varphi_{\cvec{b}}(\cvec{x}) for every \cvec{x}. By @thm-inverse-is-linear it is an isomorphism. So in F^n a functional is a row vector acting by matrix multiplication, and its 1 	imes n matrix in the standard bases is  igl(\varphi(\cvec{e}_1) \ \cdots \ \varphi(\cvec{e}_n) igr). This is how we compute with functionals: rows act on columns. Nonexamples by minimal change. Each of the following changes one of the examples slightly. In each case something still works, and we name a condition that fails. - On 
R^2, the length (x, y) \mapsto \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} (@exm-norm). It sends \cvec{0} to 0 and respects positive scalars. But with c = -1 and \cvec{v} = (1, 0) it gives 1, not -1, so the scaling condition fails. - On 
R[x], squaring the evaluation at 0: p \mapsto p(0)^2. The outputs are still scalars. But for p = q = 1 we get (1 + 1)^2 = 4 
eq 1 + 1, so additivity fails. - On M_2(F), replace the trace a + d of \A =  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{pmatrix} by ad - bc. Then \E_{11} \mapsto 0 and \E_{22} \mapsto 0, but \E_{11} + \E_{22} = \I_2 \mapsto 1, so additivity fails. The expression ad - bc is linear in each row separately, which is a different property. Why this definition. Why single out the target F? Because nothing is lost. A linear map T \colon V 	o F^m is the same thing as m functionals: if \varphi_i(\elem{v}) denotes the i-th entry of T\elem{v}, then each \varphi_i is linear and T\elem{v} = (\varphi_1(\elem{v}), \dots, \varphi_m(\elem{v})); conversely any m functionals stacked this way give a linear map. So functionals are the “rows” of linear maps, and understanding them one at a time is a way of understanding all maps into F^m. The name comes from analysis, where the vectors were themselves functions and a map such as f \mapsto \int_0^1 f was called a “functional”, a function of a function. The word “dual” will explain itself in this chapter: every statement about V has a mirror statement about V^{*}. The values must lie in the field of scalars of V. Regard 
C as a vector space over 
C. The real part z \mapsto \operatorname{Re} z is additive, and it respects real scalars, but it is not a linear functional on 
C over 
C: with c = i and z = 1, \operatorname{Re}(i \cdot 1) = 0 
eq i \cdot \operatorname{Re}(1) = i. It is a functional on 
C regarded as a vector space over 
R. The dual space depends on the field. The first payoff is a count that holds for every nonzero functional: it hits every scalar, and in finite dimension it kills exactly one dimension. [A Non-Zero Functional Is Surjective] Let V be a vector space over F, and let \varphi \in V^{*} be nonzero. Then \varphi is surjective. If V is finite-dimensional, then \dim \ker\varphi = \dim V - 1. Since \varphi 
eq 0, there is \elem{u} \in V with c \coloneqq \varphi(\elem{u}) 
eq 0. For every a \in F, linearity gives \varphi(ac^{-1}\elem{u}) = ac^{-1}c = a, so \varphi is surjective. Hence \im\varphi = F and ank\varphi = 1. If V is finite-dimensional, the Rank–Nullity Theorem (@thm-rank-nullity) gives \dim\ker\varphi = \dim V - 1. For example, \ker	r in M_n(F) has dimension n^2 - 1, and the polynomials in F[x]_{\le n} with p(c) = 0 form a subspace of dimension n. Every nonzero functional cuts out a subspace one dimension smaller than the whole space. Later in this chapter these kernels, the hyperplanes, become the building blocks of every subspace. Which of the following are linear functionals? (a) p \mapsto p(0) + 1 on 
R[x]. (b) p \mapsto p(1) - 2p'(0) on 
R[x]. (c) \A \mapsto a_{12} on M_2(F). (a) No. It sends the zero polynomial to 1, but a linear map sends 0 to 0 (@thm-zero-maps-to-zero). (b) Yes. Evaluation at 1, differentiation, and evaluation at 0 are linear, and V^{*} is closed under linear combinations and composition with linear maps (@thm-linear-maps-vector-space, @thm-composition-linear). (c) Yes. It is the coordinate of \A at \E_{12} in the standard basis of @exm-standard-bases, and coordinates are linear (@thm-coordinates-linear). The dual basis Return to the coordinate functionals. Let \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) be a basis of V, and let \varphi_i(\elem{v}) be the i-th entry of \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB}. The basis vector \elem{v}_j has coordinate vector \cvec{e}_j, so \varphi_i(\elem{v}_j) = \delta_{ij} =  egin{cases} 1 & 	ext{if } i = j, \ 0 & 	ext{if } i 
eq j, \end{cases} with the Kronecker delta of @def-identity-matrix. Each \varphi_i reads off one coordinate and ignores the others. These n functionals are the natural candidates for a basis of V^{*}, and the theorem says they are one. The Dual Basis Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, and let \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) be a basis of V. 1. There are unique \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \in V^{*} with \varphi_i(\elem{v}_j) = \delta_{ij} for all i, j. For every \elem{v} \in V, \varphi_i(\elem{v}) is the i-th entry of \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB}. 2. The list (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n) is a basis of V^{*}. 3. For every \elem{v} \in V and every \varphi \in V^{*}, \elem{v} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \varphi_i(\elem{v})\,\elem{v}_i, \qquad \varphi = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \varphi(\elem{v}_i)\,\varphi_i . ① A functional is a linear map into F, and a linear map may be prescribed freely on a basis, so existence and uniqueness in (a) are one citation. ② Independence: apply a vanishing combination \sum c_i\varphi_i to \elem{v}_j; the delta kills every term but c_j. ③ Spanning: we cannot count, because \dim V^{*} is exactly what we do not know yet. So we guess the coefficients. If \varphi = \sum c_i\varphi_i, then applying both sides to \elem{v}_j forces c_j = \varphi(\elem{v}_j). With this guess, the two sides are linear maps that agree on a basis, hence equal. (a) For each i, apply @thm-linear-transform-basis with W = F and the prescribed values \delta_{i1}, \dots, \delta_{in} \in F. It gives exactly one linear map \varphi_i \colon V 	o F with \varphi_i(\elem{v}_j) = \delta_{ij} for all j. If \elem{v} = a_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + a_n\elem{v}_n, then by @thm-linear-combination \varphi_i(\elem{v}) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_j\varphi_i(\elem{v}_j) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_j\delta_{ij} = a_i , the i-th entry of \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} (@def-coordinates). (b) Independence. Let c_1\varphi_1 + \dots + c_n\varphi_n = 0 in V^{*}. Applying both sides to \elem{v}_j and using the pointwise operations of @def-dual-space, 0 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i\varphi_i(\elem{v}_j) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i\delta_{ij} = c_j for each j. Hence (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n) is linearly independent. Spanning. Let \varphi \in V^{*}, and put \psi \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^{n} \varphi(\elem{v}_i)\varphi_i \in V^{*}. For each j, \psi(\elem{v}_j) = \sum_i \varphi(\elem{v}_i)\delta_{ij} = \varphi(\elem{v}_j). So \psi and \varphi are linear maps V 	o F that agree on the basis \sB, and \psi = \varphi by the uniqueness part of @thm-linear-transform-basis. Hence \varphi \in \Span(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n), and (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n) is a basis of V^{*}. (c) The second formula was proved in the spanning step. The first is the definition of coordinates, since \varphi_i(\elem{v}) is the i-th coordinate of \elem{v} by (a). This proves the theorem. The two formulas in (c) are mirror images. A vector is recovered from its measurements by the dual basis; a functional is recovered from its values on the basis. [Dual Basis] Let \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) be a basis of a finite-dimensional vector space V over F. The basis (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n) of V^{*} given by @thm-dual-basis, characterized by \varphi_i(\elem{v}_j) = \delta_{ij}, is the dual basis of \sB. We write it \sB^{*}. Counting the dual basis gives the dimension of the dual space at once. [Dimension of the Dual Space] Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F. Then V^{*} is finite-dimensional and \dim V^{*} = \dim V. In particular V^{*} \cong V. Let n = \dim V and choose a basis of V (@cor-basis-existence). By @thm-dual-basis (b), its dual basis is a basis of V^{*} of length n. Hence \dim V^{*} = n, and V^{*} \cong V by @thm-isomorphic-iff-same-dimension. For instance \dim M_{m 	imes n}(F)^{*} = mn and \dim F[x]_{\le n}^{*} = n + 1. Many books write \elem{v}_i^{*} for the dual basis functional \varphi_i. We avoid that notation for two reasons. It suggests that \varphi_i is determined by \elem{v}_i alone, which is false (see the warning below). And in this book the star on a map is reserved for adjoints, which come much later. We write \varphi_i, and speak of “the dual basis of \sB”. How do we find a dual basis in practice? In F^n, functionals are rows, and the conditions \varphi_i(\elem{v}_j) = \delta_{ij} turn into a single matrix equation. [The Dual Basis Is Read Off the Inverse Matrix] 1. Find the dual basis of \sB = ((1, 1), (1, -1)) in 
R^2. 2. More generally, let \sB = (\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n) be a basis of F^n, and let \P =  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{v}_1 & \cdots & \cvec{v}_n \end{pmatrix}. Show that \P is invertible and that the dual basis of \sB is \varphi_i(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{r}_i\cvec{x}, where \cvec{r}_i is the i-th row of \P^{-1}. (a) By @thm-functionals-on-fn, \varphi_1(x, y) = px + qy for some p, q \in 
R, that is, \varphi_1(\cvec{x}) =  egin{pmatrix} p & q \end{pmatrix}\cvec{x}. The conditions \varphi_1(1, 1) = 1 and \varphi_1(1, -1) = 0 say  egin{pmatrix} p & q \end{pmatrix}\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} with \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. Likewise the row \cvec{r}_2 of \varphi_2 satisfies \cvec{r}_2\P =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Stacking the two rows into a matrix \R, the four conditions become \R\P = \I_2, so \R = \P^{-1}. By @thm-two-by-two-inverse, with ad - bc = -2, \P^{-1} =  rac{1}{-2} egin{pmatrix} -1 & -1 \ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac12 & 	frac12 \ 	frac12 & -	frac12 \end{pmatrix}. Hence \varphi_1(x, y) =  rac{x + y}{2}, \qquad \varphi_2(x, y) =  rac{x - y}{2}. Check: \varphi_1(1, 1) = 1, \varphi_1(1, -1) = 0, \varphi_2(1, 1) = 0, \varphi_2(1, -1) = 1. And the first formula of @thm-dual-basis (c) for \cvec{v} = (3, 1) reads (3, 1) = 2(1, 1) + 1(1, -1), which is true. The second formula expresses a functional in the dual basis through its values on \sB: for \psi(x, y) = x, the values are \psi(1, 1) = 1 and \psi(1, -1) = 1, so \psi = \varphi_1 + \varphi_2, and indeed  rac{x + y}{2} +  rac{x - y}{2} = x. (b) The columns of \P form a basis of F^n, so \P is invertible by @thm-invertible-tfae. Let \R \in M_n(F) have rows \cvec{r}_1, \dots, \cvec{r}_n, and let \psi_i(\cvec{x}) \coloneqq \cvec{r}_i\cvec{x}. By the entry formula for a product (@thm-three-views-of-product), \psi_i(\cvec{v}_j) = \cvec{r}_i\cvec{v}_j = (\R\P)_{ij}. Hence \psi_i(\cvec{v}_j) = \delta_{ij} for all i, j if and only if \R\P = \I_n, if and only if \R = \P^{-1} (multiply by \P^{-1} on the right). Now take \R = \P^{-1}: the functionals \psi_i(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{r}_i\cvec{x} are linear (@thm-functionals-on-fn) and satisfy \psi_i(\cvec{v}_j) = \delta_{ij}, so by the uniqueness in @thm-dual-basis (a) they are the dual basis. This agrees with Chapter 2: \P = \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sE} and \P^{-1} = \mtx{\id}{\sE}{\sB} (@thm-change-of-coordinates), so \P^{-1}\cvec{x} = \coord{\cvec{x}}{\sB}, and row i of \P^{-1} computes the i-th coordinate, as @thm-dual-basis (a) predicts. The columns of \P are the basis; the rows of \P^{-1} are the dual basis. A dual basis functional depends on the whole basis, not only on its own vector. In 
R^2, the basis ((1, 0), (0, 1)) has first dual functional \varphi_1(x, y) = x. The basis ((1, 0), (1, 1)) has the same first vector, but \P^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, so its first dual functional is \varphi_1(x, y) = x - y. Changing \cvec{v}_2 changed \varphi_1, because \varphi_1 must vanish on \cvec{v}_2. The same method works away from F^n, once we recognize the coordinates. [Dual Bases in 
R[x]_{\le 2}] 1. Show that the dual basis of (1, x, x^2) in 
R[x]_{\le 2} is (\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \varphi_2) with \varphi_0(p) = p(0), \varphi_1(p) = p'(0), and \varphi_2(p) = 	frac12p''(0). (We index from 0 to match the exponents.) 2. Let \ell_{-1} = 	frac12x(x - 1), \ell_0 = 1 - x^2, and \ell_1 = 	frac12x(x + 1). Show that (\ell_{-1}, \ell_0, \ell_1) is a basis of 
R[x]_{\le 2} whose dual basis is (\varepsilon_{-1}, \varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_1), the evaluations at -1, 0, 1. Deduce that p = p(-1)\ell_{-1} + p(0)\ell_0 + p(1)\ell_1 for every p \in 
R[x]_{\le 2}. (a) Each \varphi_k is linear, as a composition of differentiation (@exm-differentiation) with evaluation at 0, scaled. For p = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2, we have p(0) = a_0, p'(0) = a_1, and 	frac12p''(0) = 	frac12 \cdot 2a_2 = a_2. So \varphi_k(x^j) = \delta_{kj} for j, k \in \{0, 1, 2\}, and by the uniqueness in @thm-dual-basis (a) these are the dual basis. Over a general field F, the dual basis of (1, x, x^2) is still “the coefficient of x^k”, but the formula 	frac12p''(0) needs 2 
eq 0 in F. (b) The values of the \ell’s at the three points are  egin{aligned} &\ell_{-1}(-1) = 1,\ \ell_{-1}(0) = 0,\ \ell_{-1}(1) = 0; \ &\ell_0(-1) = 0,\ \ell_0(0) = 1,\ \ell_0(1) = 0; \ &\ell_1(-1) = 0,\ \ell_1(0) = 0,\ \ell_1(1) = 1. \end{aligned} That is, \varepsilon_i(\ell_j) = \delta_{ij} for i, j \in \{-1, 0, 1\}. Basis. Let c_{-1}\ell_{-1} + c_0\ell_0 + c_1\ell_1 = 0. Evaluating at j \in \{-1, 0, 1\} gives c_j = 0. So the list is independent, of length 3 = \dim 
R[x]_{\le 2}, hence a basis by @thm-right-size-basis. Dual basis. The evaluations are linear (@exm-linear-functionals) and satisfy \varepsilon_i(\ell_j) = \delta_{ij}, so they are the dual basis by the uniqueness in @thm-dual-basis (a). The first formula of @thm-dual-basis (c) now reads p = \sum_i \varepsilon_i(p)\,\ell_i = p(-1)\ell_{-1} + p(0)\ell_0 + p(1)\ell_1. The last formula rebuilds a polynomial from three of its values. It is a preview of the Lagrange interpolation formula of Chapter 6, and it explains where the \ell’s come from: they are the basis dual to the evaluations. Let (\elem{v}_1, \elem{v}_2, \elem{v}_3) be a basis of V with dual basis (\varphi_1, \varphi_2, \varphi_3). Compute \varphi_2(3\elem{v}_1 - \elem{v}_2 + 5\elem{v}_3) and (2\varphi_1 + \varphi_3)(\elem{v}_3). \varphi_2(3\elem{v}_1 - \elem{v}_2 + 5\elem{v}_3) = 3 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1 + 5 \cdot 0 = -1, the second coordinate. (2\varphi_1 + \varphi_3)(\elem{v}_3) = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 = 1. V \cong V^{*} is true in finite dimension, but no isomorphism is singled out. @cor-dimension-dual-space gives an isomorphism by sending \elem{v}_i \mapsto \varphi_i, and that depends on the basis. In 
R^2 with the standard basis, it sends (1, 0) to the functional (x, y) \mapsto x. With the basis ((1, 0), (1, 1)), it sends the same vector (1, 0) to (x, y) \mapsto x - y, by the warning above. A vector does not come with “its” functional. Later in this chapter we make precise the sense in which V^{*} needs a choice to be identified with V, while the double dual V^{**} does not. Testing against functionals In F^n a vector is zero exactly when all its entries are zero, and the entries are the values of the coordinate functionals. The same holds in any finite-dimensional space, and it gives a flexible way to prove that a vector is zero. [Functionals Separate Vectors] Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F. 1. If \elem{v} \in V and \elem{v} 
eq \elem{0}, then there is \varphi \in V^{*} with \varphi(\elem{v}) = 1. 2. If \elem{v} \in V satisfies \varphi(\elem{v}) = 0 for every \varphi \in V^{*}, then \elem{v} = \elem{0}. It suffices that \varphi_i(\elem{v}) = 0 for the functionals \varphi_i of one dual basis. 3. For \elem{u}, \elem{w} \in V: \elem{u} = \elem{w} if and only if \varphi(\elem{u}) = \varphi(\elem{w}) for every \varphi \in V^{*}. We need a functional that does not vanish at \elem{v}, and the only functionals we can build at will are dual basis functionals. The first one takes the value 1 on the first basis vector. So make \elem{v} the first vector of a basis: this is possible exactly because \elem{v} 
eq \elem{0}. (a) Since \elem{v} 
eq \elem{0}, the list (\elem{v}) is linearly independent: if a\elem{v} = \elem{0}, then a = 0 by @thm-zero-product. By the Basis Extension Theorem (@thm-basis-extension), there is a basis (\elem{v}, \elem{v}_2, \dots, \elem{v}_n) of V. Let (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n) be its dual basis (@thm-dual-basis). Then \varphi_1(\elem{v}) = 1. (b) The first statement is the contrapositive of (a). For the second, if (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n) is the dual basis of a basis (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) and every \varphi_i(\elem{v}) = 0, then \elem{v} = \sum_i \varphi_i(\elem{v})\elem{v}_i = \elem{0} by @thm-dual-basis (c). (c) If \elem{u} = \elem{w}, the values agree. Conversely, if \varphi(\elem{u}) = \varphi(\elem{w}) for every \varphi, then \varphi(\elem{u} - \elem{w}) = \varphi(\elem{u}) - \varphi(\elem{w}) = 0 for every \varphi, so \elem{u} - \elem{w} = \elem{0} by (b). This is the signature move of the chapter: to show a vector is zero, test it against every functional, and a dual basis suffices. It turns one equation in V into scalar equations, which are often easier to reach. Parts (a), (b) (first sentence) and (c) hold for every vector space V; only (a) needs a new construction. By @thm-basis-extension-general, \{\elem{v}\} extends to a basis B of V. Every \elem{w} \in V is a finite combination of distinct vectors of B, with coefficients that are unique because B is independent. Let \varphi(\elem{w}) be the coefficient of \elem{v} in this expansion (and 0 if \elem{v} does not occur). Adding or scaling expansions gives expansions, so by uniqueness coefficients add and scale, and \varphi is linear with \varphi(\elem{v}) = 1. The price is Zorn’s Lemma (@thm-zorn): for 
R over 
Q, no one has an explicit formula for such a functional. [A Matrix Killed by Every Trace] Let \A \in M_n(F) satisfy 	r(\A\X) = 0 for every \X \in M_n(F). Show that \A = \O. Deduce that every linear functional on M_n(F) is \X \mapsto 	r(\A\X) for exactly one \A \in M_n(F). The matrix units \E_{ij} form a basis of M_n(F) (@exm-standard-bases), and \A = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}\E_{ij}. By @thm-dual-basis (a), its dual basis consists of the coordinate functionals \varepsilon_{ij}(\A) = a_{ij}. We compute \varepsilon_{ij}(\A) as a trace. By @def-matrix-multiplication, (\A\E_{ji})_{kk} = \sum_l a_{kl}(\E_{ji})_{lk}, and (\E_{ji})_{lk} = 1 only for l = j and k = i. So the only nonzero diagonal entry of \A\E_{ji} is (\A\E_{ji})_{ii} = a_{ij}, and 	r(\A\E_{ji}) = a_{ij} = \varepsilon_{ij}(\A). Taking \X = \E_{ji} in the hypothesis gives \varepsilon_{ij}(\A) = 0 for all i, j. By @thm-functionals-separate-points (b), \A = \O. For the deduction, let \Theta \colon M_n(F) 	o M_n(F)^{*}, \Theta(\A)(\X) \coloneqq 	r(\A\X). Each \Theta(\A) is linear in \X, and \Theta is linear in \A, both by @thm-trace-properties (1) and the distributive laws of @thm-matrix-multiplication-properties. We just showed \ker\Theta = \{\O\}, so \Theta is injective (@thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel). Since \dim M_n(F)^{*} = n^2 = \dim M_n(F) (@cor-dimension-dual-space), \Theta is bijective by @cor-rank-nullity-consequences (e). This is the matrix analogue of @thm-functionals-on-fn. When V is infinite-dimensional The main results of the last two subsections assumed finite dimension, or used a finite basis. That hypothesis does real work. Consider F[x], with its basis \{1, x, x^2, \dots\} (@exm-basis-of-polynomials). For k \in 
N let \varphi_k(p) \coloneqq 	ext{the coefficient of } x^k 	ext{ in } p . These are the coordinate functionals, and \varphi_k(x^j) = \delta_{kj}, exactly as in @thm-dual-basis. But they are not a basis of the dual space. [The Coordinate Functionals Do Not Span F[x]^{*}] The functionals \varphi_k (k \in 
N) lie in F[x]^{*} and form a linearly independent set. But they do not span F[x]^{*}: the evaluation \varepsilon_1 \colon p \mapsto p(1) is not a linear combination of finitely many \varphi_k. Polynomials are added and scaled coefficient by coefficient (@def-polynomial), so each \varphi_k is linear. Independence. Let k_1, \dots, k_m be distinct and c_1\varphi_{k_1} + \dots + c_m\varphi_{k_m} = 0. Applying both sides to x^{k_j} gives c_j = 0, since \varphi_{k_i}(x^{k_j}) = \delta_{k_ik_j}. Not spanning. The evaluation \varepsilon_1 is linear by @exm-linear-functionals (a), and \varepsilon_1(x^N) = 1^N = 1 for every N \in 
N. Suppose, for a contradiction, that \varepsilon_1 = c_1\varphi_{k_1} + \dots + c_m\varphi_{k_m} for some m \in 
N, distinct k_j, and c_j \in F. Choose N \in 
N larger than every k_j. Then \varphi_{k_j}(x^N) = 0 for every j, so the right-hand side sends x^N to 0, while \varepsilon_1(x^N) = 1. This contradiction shows \varepsilon_1 
otin \Span\{\varphi_k : k \in 
N\}. Where did the proof of @thm-dual-basis break? In the spanning step. The candidate \sum_i \varphi(\elem{v}_i)\varphi_i for \varphi = \varepsilon_1 would be \varphi_0 + \varphi_1 + \varphi_2 + \cdots, an infinite sum, and infinite sums mean nothing in a vector space (the warning in Chapter 1, §8). A functional on F[x] may take nonzero values on infinitely many basis vectors, while a finite combination of the \varphi_k cannot. More is true, and we state it without proof. For every infinite-dimensional V, a basis of V^{*} is strictly larger, as an infinite set, than a basis of V; in particular V^{*} 
ot\cong V. So “\dim V^{*} = \dim V” is a genuinely finite-dimensional fact, and this is why finite dimension appears in the hypotheses of most theorems in this chapter. A first step towards seeing how large F[x]^{*} is appears in Exercise C4 below. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define a linear functional on a vector space V over F, and the dual space V^{*}. 2. True or false: p \mapsto p(1)^2 is a linear functional on 
R[x]. Justify your answer. 3. True or false: if (\elem{v}_1, \elem{v}_2) and (\elem{v}_1, \elem{w}_2) are bases of V, then the first functionals of their dual bases are equal. Justify your answer. 4. What is \dim M_{2 	imes 3}(F)^{*}? 5. State the formula that expresses \varphi \in V^{*} in the dual basis of (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n). 6. Name the move you would use to prove that a vector \elem{v} of a finite-dimensional space is \elem{0} without computing \elem{v} itself. (a) See @def-linear-functional and @def-dual-space: a linear functional is a linear map V 	o F, and V^{*} = \cL(V, F) with pointwise addition and scaling. (b) False. For p = 1 and c = 2, the polynomial cp = 2 is sent to 2^2 = 4, while c times the image of p is 2 \cdot 1^2 = 2. So the scaling condition fails. (c) False. By the warning after @exm-dual-basis-inverse-rows, in 
R^2 the bases ((1, 0), (0, 1)) and ((1, 0), (1, 1)) have first dual functionals x and x - y. (d) 6, by @cor-dimension-dual-space, since \dim M_{2 	imes 3}(F) = 6. (e) \varphi = \sum_{i=1}^n \varphi(\elem{v}_i)\varphi_i, by @thm-dual-basis (c). (f) Test against functionals: show \varphi(\elem{v}) = 0 for every \varphi \in V^{*}, or only for the functionals of one dual basis, and apply @thm-functionals-separate-points (b). B. Practice [B1: Finding dual bases] 1. Find the dual basis of ((1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1), (1, 1, 1)) in 
R^3. 2. Show that the dual basis of (1, x - 1, (x - 1)^2) in 
R[x]_{\le 2} is p \mapsto p(1), p \mapsto p'(1), p \mapsto 	frac12p''(1). Hence write p = 2 + 3x - x^2 in this basis. (a) Let \P have the three vectors as columns. Row reduction of [\P \mid \I_3] (@thm-inverse-by-row-reduction) gives \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \P^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 1 \ -1 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, and one checks \P^{-1}\P = \I_3. By @exm-dual-basis-inverse-rows (b), the dual basis is \varphi_1(x, y, z) = -y + z, \qquad \varphi_2(x, y, z) = -x + z, \qquad \varphi_3(x, y, z) = x + y - z . For instance \varphi_3(1, 0, 1) = 0, \varphi_3(0, 1, 1) = 0, and \varphi_3(1, 1, 1) = 1. (b) The three maps are linear, as combinations of differentiation and evaluation at 1. Call them \psi_1, \psi_2, \psi_3. On the basis:  egin{aligned} &\psi_1(1) = 1,\ \psi_1(x - 1) = 0,\ \psi_1((x - 1)^2) = 0; \ &\psi_2(1) = 0,\ \psi_2(x - 1) = 1,\ \psi_2((x - 1)^2) = 2(1 - 1) = 0; \end{aligned} \psi_3(1) = 0,\ \psi_3(x - 1) = 0,\ \psi_3((x - 1)^2) = 	frac12 \cdot 2 = 1 . So \psi_i takes the value \delta_{ij} on the j-th basis vector, and by the uniqueness in @thm-dual-basis (a) they are the dual basis. (The list (1, x - 1, (x - 1)^2) is a basis: it has distinct degrees 0, 1, 2, so it is independent by @thm-distinct-degrees-independent, and it has length 3 = \dim 
R[x]_{\le 2}, so @thm-right-size-basis applies.) For p = 2 + 3x - x^2: p(1) = 4, p'(1) = 3 - 2 = 1, 	frac12p''(1) = -1. By @thm-dual-basis (c), p = 4 + (x - 1) - (x - 1)^2 . Check: 4 + x - 1 - (x^2 - 2x + 1) = 2 + 3x - x^2. [B2: Which maps are functionals?] Determine which of the following are linear functionals. Justify your answer. 1.

R^3 	o

R) 	o 
R, \A \mapsto a_{12} - 3a_{21}. 4. 
R[x] 	o 
R, p \mapsto \int_0^1 t\,p(t)\,\dd t. 5. 
R[x]_{\le 2} 	o 
R, p \mapsto p(0) + p'(0) + 1. 6. 
C^2 	o 
C, (z, w) \mapsto z + \conj{w}, where 
C^2 is a vector space over 
C. (a) Yes: it is \varphi_{\cvec{a}} with \cvec{a} = (2, 0, -1), linear by @thm-functionals-on-fn. (b) No. (1, 1, 0) \mapsto 1, but 2(1, 1, 0) = (2, 2, 0) \mapsto 4 
eq 2, so the scaling condition fails. (c) Yes: it is \varepsilon_{12} - 3\varepsilon_{21}, a combination of coordinate functionals for the standard basis, and V^{*} is a vector space (@def-dual-space). (d) Yes. By linearity of the integral, \int_0^1 t(p + q)(t)\,\dd t = \int_0^1 tp(t)\,\dd t + \int_0^1 tq(t)\,\dd t and \int_0^1 t(cp)(t)\,\dd t = c\int_0^1 tp(t)\,\dd t. (e) No. The zero polynomial is sent to 1 
eq 0, contradicting @thm-zero-maps-to-zero. (f) No. With c = i and (z, w) = (0, 1): (0, i) \mapsto \conj{i} = -i, while i \cdot (0 + \conj{1}) = i. The map is additive and respects real scalars, but it is not linear over 
C. [B3: Coordinates of a functional] 1. Let (\varphi_1, \varphi_2) be the dual basis of ((1, 1), (1, -1)) from @exm-dual-basis-inverse-rows. Write \psi(x, y) = 3x + 5y as a combination of \varphi_1 and \varphi_2. 2. Let (\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \varphi_2) be the dual basis of (1, x, x^2) from @exm-dual-basis-polynomials. Write \iota(p) = \int_0^1 p(t)\,\dd t as a combination of them. (a) By @thm-dual-basis (c), \psi = \psi(1, 1)\varphi_1 + \psi(1, -1)\varphi_2 = 8\varphi_1 - 2\varphi_2. Check: 8 \cdot  rac{x + y}{2} - 2 \cdot  rac{x - y}{2} = 4x + 4y - x + y = 3x + 5y. (b) By @thm-dual-basis (c), \iota = \iota(1)\varphi_0 + \iota(x)\varphi_1 + \iota(x^2)\varphi_2 = \varphi_0 + 	frac12\varphi_1 + 	frac13\varphi_2. Check: for p = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2, the right-hand side is a_0 + 	frac{a_1}{2} + 	frac{a_2}{3} = \int_0^1 p. C. Going deeper [C1: Functionals with the same kernel] Let V be any vector space over F, and let \varphi, \psi \in V^{*} with \ker\varphi = \ker\psi. Prove that \psi = c\varphi for some c \in F. Is the converse true? Hint: if \varphi 
eq 0, fix \elem{u} with \varphi(\elem{u}) = 1 and consider \elem{v} - \varphi(\elem{v})\elem{u}. If \varphi = 0, then \ker\psi = \ker\varphi = V, so \psi = 0 = 1 \cdot \varphi. Suppose \varphi 
eq 0. By @prp-nonzero-functional-surjective there is \elem{u} \in V with \varphi(\elem{u}) = 1. Let \elem{v} \in V. Then \varphi igl(\elem{v} - \varphi(\elem{v})\elem{u} igr) = \varphi(\elem{v}) - \varphi(\elem{v})\varphi(\elem{u}) = 0, so \elem{v} - \varphi(\elem{v})\elem{u} \in \ker\varphi = \ker\psi. Therefore 0 = \psi(\elem{v}) - \varphi(\elem{v})\psi(\elem{u}), that is, \psi(\elem{v}) = \psi(\elem{u})\varphi(\elem{v}). Since \elem{v} was arbitrary, \psi = c\varphi with c = \psi(\elem{u}). The converse holds only for c 
eq 0: if \psi = c\varphi with c 
eq 0, then \psi(\elem{v}) = 0 \iff \varphi(\elem{v}) = 0. For c = 0 and \varphi 
eq 0, \ker\psi = V 
eq \ker\varphi. [C2: Functionals vanishing where others vanish] Let V be a vector space over F, and let \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_k, \psi \in V^{*}. 1. Prove that if \ker\varphi_1 \cap \dots \cap \ker\varphi_k \subseteq \ker\psi, then \psi \in \Span(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_k). 2. Deduce that if V is finite-dimensional, then (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_k) spans V^{*} if and only if \ker\varphi_1 \cap \dots \cap \ker\varphi_k = \{\elem{0}\}. Hint: for (a), consider the linear map T \colon V 	o F^k, \elem{v} \mapsto (\varphi_1(\elem{v}), \dots, \varphi_k(\elem{v})). (a) Let T be as in the hint; it is linear because each \varphi_i is. Its kernel is \ker\varphi_1 \cap \dots \cap \ker\varphi_k. Define S \colon \im T 	o F by S(T\elem{v}) \coloneqq \psi(\elem{v}). This is well defined: if T\elem{v} = T\elem{v}', then \elem{v} - \elem{v}' \in \ker T \subseteq \ker\psi, so \psi(\elem{v}) = \psi(\elem{v}'). It is linear, since S(cT\elem{v} + T\elem{v}') = S(T(c\elem{v} + \elem{v}')) = \psi(c\elem{v} + \elem{v}') = cS(T\elem{v}) + S(T\elem{v}'). Now extend S to F^k. The subspace \im T \subseteq F^k has a basis (\cvec{y}_1, \dots, \cvec{y}_r) (@thm-subspace-dimension, @cor-basis-existence), which extends to a basis (\cvec{y}_1, \dots, \cvec{y}_k) of F^k by @thm-basis-extension. By @thm-linear-transform-basis there is 	ilde S \in (F^k)^{*} with 	ilde S(\cvec{y}_j) = S(\cvec{y}_j) for j \le r and 	ilde S(\cvec{y}_j) = 0 for j > r. Then 	ilde S and S agree on a basis of \im T, so 	ilde S = S on \im T. By @thm-functionals-on-fn, 	ilde S(z_1, \dots, z_k) = a_1z_1 + \dots + a_kz_k for some a_i \in F. Hence for every \elem{v} \in V, \psi(\elem{v}) = S(T\elem{v}) = 	ilde S igl(\varphi_1(\elem{v}), \dots, \varphi_k(\elem{v}) igr) = a_1\varphi_1(\elem{v}) + \dots + a_k\varphi_k(\elem{v}), so \psi = a_1\varphi_1 + \dots + a_k\varphi_k. Note that V was arbitrary; only F^k needed to be finite-dimensional. (b) (\Leftarrow) If the intersection is \{\elem{0}\}, it lies in \ker\psi for every \psi \in V^{*}, so every \psi is in the span by (a). (\Rightarrow) Suppose the \varphi_i span V^{*}, and let \elem{v} lie in every \ker\varphi_i. Every \psi \in V^{*} is a combination \sum c_i\varphi_i, so \psi(\elem{v}) = \sum c_i\varphi_i(\elem{v}) = 0. By @thm-functionals-separate-points (b), \elem{v} = \elem{0}. [C3: Evaluations as a dual basis] Let n \in 
N. 1. Let x_0, \dots, x_n \in F be distinct. Prove that the evaluations (\varepsilon_{x_0}, \dots, \varepsilon_{x_n}) form a basis of F[x]_{\le n}^{*}, and that they are the dual basis of some basis of F[x]_{\le n}. 2. Over 
F_2 with n = 2, show that the evaluations at the elements of 
F_2 do not span 
F_2[x]_{\le 2}^{*}. Hint: for (a), use @thm-interpolation-unique to build the basis first. (a) For each j, @thm-interpolation-unique gives \ell_j \in F[x]_{\le n} with \ell_j(x_i) = \delta_{ij} for i = 0, \dots, n, because the x_i are distinct. If \sum_j c_j\ell_j = 0, evaluating at x_i gives c_i = 0. So (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_n) is independent of length n + 1 = \dim F[x]_{\le n}, hence a basis by @thm-right-size-basis. The evaluations are linear (@exm-linear-functionals) and \varepsilon_{x_i}(\ell_j) = \delta_{ij}, so by the uniqueness in @thm-dual-basis (a) they are the dual basis of (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_n), and by @thm-dual-basis (b) a basis of F[x]_{\le n}^{*}. (b) 
F_2 = \{0, 1\} has only two elements, so only \varepsilon_0 and \varepsilon_1 are available, and \dim 
F_2[x]_{\le 2}^{*} = 3 by @cor-dimension-dual-space. Two functionals cannot span a 3-dimensional space (@thm-size-bounds). Concretely, p = x^2 + x is nonzero but p(0) = 0 and p(1) = 1 + 1 = 0; the coefficient functional of x^2 takes the value 1 on p, so it is not a combination of \varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_1. The hypothesis “distinct points” in (a) needs n + 1 distinct elements of F, which a small field may not have. [C4: How large is F\lbrack xbrack^{*}?] Let F^{
N} be the space of sequences with entries in F. 1. Prove that \Phi \colon F[x]^{*} 	o F^{
N}, \varphi \mapsto (\varphi(1), \varphi(x), \varphi(x^2), \dots), is an isomorphism. 2. Identify \Phi(\varphi_k) for the coordinate functionals \varphi_k of @prp-coordinate-functionals-do-not-span, and \Phi(\varepsilon_1). Explain how @prp-coordinate-functionals-do-not-span matches @exm-sequence-standard-vectors. Hint: for surjectivity, remember that a polynomial has only finitely many nonzero coefficients. (a) Linear. The k-th entry of \Phi(c\varphi + \psi) is (c\varphi + \psi)(x^k) = c\varphi(x^k) + \psi(x^k), by the pointwise operations of @def-dual-space. Injective. If \Phi(\varphi) = \elem{0}, then \varphi vanishes on the basis \{x^k\} of @exm-basis-of-polynomials. Every polynomial is a finite combination of the x^k, so \varphi = 0 by @thm-linear-combination; hence \Phi is injective by @thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel. Surjective. Given (a_0, a_1, \dots) \in F^{
N}, define \varphi(b_0 + b_1x + \dots + b_Nx^N) \coloneqq a_0b_0 + \dots + a_Nb_N. This is a finite sum, it is well defined because coefficients are unique, and it is linear because coefficients add and scale; it is the linear map with \varphi(x^k) = a_k given by @thm-linear-map-from-any-basis. Then \Phi(\varphi) = (a_0, a_1, \dots). By @thm-inverse-is-linear, \Phi is an isomorphism. (b) \Phi(\varphi_k) = (\delta_{k0}, \delta_{k1}, \dots) = \elem{e}_k, and \Phi(\varepsilon_1) = (1, 1, 1, \dots). An isomorphism carries spans to spans, so \varepsilon_1 \in \Span\{\varphi_k\} would give (1, 1, 1, \dots) \in \Span\{\elem{e}_k\}. @exm-sequence-standard-vectors showed this is false, because finite combinations of the \elem{e}_k have only finitely many nonzero entries. So F[x], with its basis \{x^k\} indexed by 
N, has a dual as large as the whole sequence space F^{
N}.

title: 5.2 Annihilators
content:
Annihilators Section 1 built the dual space V^{*}, the space of linear measurements on V. Now we connect subspaces of V with subspaces of V^{*}. A plane in 
R^3 can be described by a spanning list or by an equation, and an equation is a functional. This section collects all the equations that a set of vectors satisfies into one subspace of V^{*}, the annihilator, counts its dimension, and shows that it turns sums into intersections and intersections into sums. The equations a subspace satisfies Every object comes with its subobjects. The dual space V^{*} has subspaces of its own, and the question is which of them are attached to subspaces of V. The standard example shows the way. Let U = \Span((1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1)), a plane in 
R^3. The functional \varphi(x, y, z) = x + y - z vanishes on both spanning vectors, so by linearity it vanishes on all of U: the plane satisfies the equation x + y - z = 0. The annihilator of a set of vectors is the space of all linear equations that every one of those vectors satisfies. [Annihilator] Let V be a vector space over F, and let S \subseteq V be any subset. The annihilator of S is S^{0} \coloneqq \{ \varphi \in V^{*} : \varphi(\elem{s}) = 0 	ext{ for all } \elem{s} \in S \}. In words: S^{0} is a subset of the dual space V^{*}, not of V. A functional belongs to it when it vanishes at every vector of S; a single nonzero value disqualifies it. The set S needs no structure: it may be a subspace, a finite list of vectors, or even empty. The superscript 0 recalls the value that the functionals take on S. Well-definedness. The definition makes sense for every subset.
