eq 0. For a finite field F = \{c_1, \dots, c_q\}, let g = (x - c_1)\cdots(x - c_q) + 1. It has degree q \ge 2 (@thm-degree-of-product), and g(c_i) = 0 + 1 = 1 
eq 0 for every i by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations. So g is a nonconstant polynomial without a root in F. 2. Over 
R, x^2 + 1 has no root, since c^2 + 1 \ge 1. Over 
Q, x^2 - 2 has no root, since \sqrt2 is irrational (@thm-sqrt2-irrational) and the only real roots are \pm\sqrt2. 3. For x^2 + 1 over 
R, growth holds, and c \mapsto \lvert c^2 + 1 vert attains its minimum 1 at c = 0. The step that breaks is d’Alembert’s lemma (@lem-dalembert): at z_0 = 0 we have b_0 = 1, k = 2, b_2 = 1, and we need u with u^2 = -1, which does not exist in 
R. 4. Suppose r_0 \in 
Q satisfies \lvert r_0^2 - 2 vert \le \lvert r^2 - 2 vert for every r \in 
Q. Put m = \lvert r_0^2 - 2 vert; then m > 0 by (b). Case 1: r_0^2 \le 	frac25. Then m = 2 - r_0^2 \ge 	frac85 > 1 = \lvert 1^2 - 2 vert, contradicting minimality at r = 1. Case 2: r_0^2 > 	frac25. Then r_0 
eq 0, and r_1 = (r_0^2 + 2)/(2r_0) \in 
Q. Expanding, r_1^2 - 2 =  rac{(r_0^2 + 2)^2 - 8r_0^2}{4r_0^2} =  rac{(r_0^2 - 2)^2}{4r_0^2}, \qquad 	ext{so} \qquad \lvert r_1^2 - 2 vert = m \cdot  rac{m}{4r_0^2} . We claim m < 4r_0^2. If r_0^2 \ge 2, then m = r_0^2 - 2 < 4r_0^2. If 	frac25 < r_0^2 < 2, then m = 2 - r_0^2 < 	frac85 < 4r_0^2. Hence \lvert r_1^2 - 2 vert < m, contradicting minimality. So there is no minimum. The step of the proof that breaks is @lem-minimum-modulus-attained, which rests on the extreme value theorem (A2). That fact is about the completeness of 
R, and 
Q is not complete: the values \lvert r^2 - 2 vert get arbitrarily close to 0 without reaching it. [C2: Sums of two squares] Let f \in 
R[x] be monic with no real root. 1. Prove that \deg f is even and that f(c) > 0 for every c \in 
R. 2. Prove that f = g^2 + h^2 for some g, h \in 
R[x]. Hint for (b): each irreducible factor of f is (x - z)(x - \conj{z}). Collect one root from each pair into a complex polynomial G, and split G into real and imaginary parts. 1. By @cor-real-factorization, f = (x - c_1)\cdots(x - c_r)\,q_1\cdots q_s, with leading coefficient 1 since f is monic. A factor x - c_1 would give the real root c_1, so r = 0 and \deg f = 2s is even. (If s = 0, then f = 1 and the claims hold.) Each q_j = x^2 +  eta x + \gamma has no real root, so by the remark after @cor-real-irreducibles,  eta^2 < 4\gamma. For real c, q_j(c) = \Bigl(c +  rac{ eta}{2}\Bigr)^2 +  rac{4\gamma -  eta^2}{4} > 0 . By @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, f(c) = q_1(c)\cdots q_s(c) is a product of positive reals, so f(c) > 0. 2. For each j, q_j is nonconstant, so by @thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra it has a root z_j \in 
C, not real. As in @exr-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra-b3 (a), q_j = (x - z_j)(x - \conj{z_j}). Let G = (x - z_1)\cdots(x - z_s) \in 
C[x]. By the product rule for conjugate polynomials proved in @thm-real-roots-conjugate-pairs, \conj{G} = (x - \conj{z_1})\cdots(x - \conj{z_s}), so f = G\,\conj{G} (commutativity, @thm-polynomial-ring-laws). Write each coefficient of G as \alpha_k + i eta_k with \alpha_k,  eta_k \in 
R, and put g = \sum_k \alpha_kx^k and h = \sum_k  eta_kx^k in 
R[x]. Then G = g + ih and \conj{G} = g - ih, so f = (g + ih)(g - ih) = g^2 - i^2h^2 + (ihg - igh) = g^2 + h^2 . For example, for x^4 + 1 take z_1 = e^{i\pi/4} and z_2 = e^{3i\pi/4} from @exm-factor-x4-plus-1. Then z_1 + z_2 = i\sqrt2 and z_1z_2 = e^{i\pi} = -1, so G = x^2 - i\sqrt2\,x - 1, g = x^2 - 1, h = -\sqrt2\,x, and x^4 + 1 = (x^2 - 1)^2 + 2x^2.

title: 6.6 Interpolation and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content:
Interpolation and the Chinese Remainder Theorem Chapter 3 proved that through n + 1 points with distinct x-values there passes exactly one polynomial of degree at most n (@thm-interpolation-unique). The proof went through an invertible matrix, and it never wrote the polynomial down. This section gives the formula. Then it reads interpolation in the arithmetic of this chapter: “p(c) = y” says that p leaves remainder y on division by x - c. Prescribing remainders modulo several pairwise coprime polynomials at once is the Chinese Remainder Theorem. We prove it twice, once with Bézout’s identity, which gives a formula, and once by counting dimensions in the quotient spaces F[x]/\langle m angle. The Lagrange basis Suppose we want the polynomial of degree at most n taking prescribed values y_0, \dots, y_n at distinct points c_0, \dots, c_n. The problem is linear in the data: if p fits the values (y_i) and q fits (y_i'), then p + q fits (y_i + y_i'), by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations. So it is enough to solve the simplest data sets, a single 1 and zeros everywhere else, and add up. The polynomial that vanishes at every c_j with j 
e i is easy to write: \prod_{j 
e i}(x - c_j). At c_i it takes the value \prod_{j 
e i}(c_i - c_j), which is a product of nonzero scalars, so we can divide by it. In @exm-dual-basis-polynomials we met these polynomials for the three points -1, 0, 1. Here is the general case. The i-th Lagrange polynomial is the polynomial of degree n that is 1 at the i-th node and 0 at every other node. [Lagrange Basis] Let n \in 
N, and let c_0, c_1, \dots, c_n \in F be distinct. For i = 0, \dots, n, the i-th Lagrange polynomial for these nodes is \ell_i(x) \coloneqq \prod_{\substack{j = 0 \ j 
e i}}^{n}  rac{x - c_j}{c_i - c_j} \in F[x]. The list (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_n) is the Lagrange basis for the nodes c_0, \dots, c_n. In words: the numerator makes \ell_i vanish at every node except c_i, and the denominator rescales so that the value at c_i is exactly 1. The points c_i are called nodes. Well-definedness. Each denominator c_i - c_j with j 
e i is nonzero because the nodes are distinct, so the quotients exist in F. The product has n linear factors, each with leading coefficient (c_i - c_j)^{-1} 
e 0, so \deg \ell_i = n by @thm-degree-of-product. The name “basis” is justified by the theorem below. Examples. - One node. For n = 0 the product is empty, so \ell_0 = 1. The degenerate case is consistent: a polynomial of degree at most 0 with value y_0 at c_0 is the constant y_0 = y_0\ell_0. - Two nodes. For c_0 = 0, c_1 = 1 we get \ell_0 =  rac{x - 1}{0 - 1} = 1 - x and \ell_1 =  rac{x - 0}{1 - 0} = x. The line through (0, y_0) and (1, y_1) is y_0(1 - x) + y_1x. - Three nodes. For -1, 0, 1, \ell_{-1} =  rac{x(x - 1)}{(-1)(-2)} = 	frac12x(x - 1), \ell_0 =  rac{(x + 1)(x - 1)}{(1)(-1)} = 1 - x^2, and \ell_1 = 	frac12x(x + 1), the polynomials of @exm-dual-basis-polynomials. (Here we index the nodes by their values.) Nonexample by minimal change. Take the nodes 0, 1, 1. The numerator of \ell_1 is still defined, (x - 0)(x - 1), but the denominator contains c_1 - c_2 = 0, which has no inverse. No rescaling helps: a polynomial that vanishes at c_2 = 1 cannot take the value 1 at c_1 = 1. The clause that fails is “distinct”. Everything about the Lagrange polynomials follows from one table of values, the Kronecker delta \ell_i(c_j) = \delta_{ij}. [Lagrange Interpolation] Let n \in 
N, let c_0, \dots, c_n \in F be distinct, and let (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_n) be the Lagrange basis for these nodes. 1. \ell_i(c_j) = \delta_{ij} for all i, j \in \{0, \dots, n\}. 2. (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_n) is a basis of F[x]_{\le n}, and every p \in F[x]_{\le n} satisfies p = \sum_{i=0}^{n} p(c_i)\,\ell_i . 3. For all y_0, \dots, y_n \in F, the unique p \in F[x]_{\le n} with p(c_i) = y_i for every i is p = \sum_{i=0}^{n} y_i\,\ell_i . ① The delta table is a direct evaluation. ② Evaluating a vanishing combination \sum a_i\ell_i at c_j kills every term but a_j, so the list is independent, and it has the right length, so we count instead of checking spanning. ③ The expansion of p and the interpolation formula are the same computation: both sides of a candidate identity are polynomials of degree at most n with the same values at n + 1 nodes. (a) By @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, \ell_i(c_j) = \prod_{k 
e i}  rac{c_j - c_k}{c_i - c_k}. If j = i, every factor is 1, so \ell_i(c_i) = 1. If j 
e i, the factor with k = j is 0, so \ell_i(c_j) = 0. (b) Each \ell_i has degree n, so it lies in F[x]_{\le n}. Let a_0\ell_0 + \dots + a_n\ell_n = 0. Evaluating at c_j and using (a) gives 0 = \sum_i a_i\delta_{ij} = a_j for each j. Hence the list is linearly independent. It has length n + 1 = \dim F[x]_{\le n} (@exm-standard-bases), so it is a basis by @thm-right-size-basis (a). Now let p \in F[x]_{\le n}, and put q = p - \sum_i p(c_i)\ell_i \in F[x]_{\le n}. By (a), q(c_j) = p(c_j) - p(c_j) = 0 for every j. So q has the n + 1 distinct roots c_0, \dots, c_n and degree at most n. By @cor-root-bound-general, q = 0, which is the expansion of p. (c) By (a),  igl(\sum_i y_i\ell_i igr)(c_j) = \sum_i y_i\delta_{ij} = y_j, so \sum_i y_i\ell_i has the required values, and it lies in F[x]_{\le n}. By @thm-interpolation-unique, it is the only such polynomial. This proves the theorem. So Chapter 3’s existence statement now comes with a formula, and the uniqueness half of (c) is the expansion in (b) read backwards: a polynomial of degree at most n is determined by its values at the nodes, because those values are its coordinates in the Lagrange basis. [The Chapter 3 Cubic by Lagrange’s Formula] Use @thm-lagrange-interpolation to find the p \in 
Q[x]_{\le 3} with p(-1) = 2, p(0) = 1, p(1) = 2, and p(2) = 11, and compare with @exm-interpolation-cubic. The nodes -1, 0, 1, 2 are distinct. Write \ell_{-1}, \ell_0, \ell_1, \ell_2 for the Lagrange polynomials, indexed by the node. The denominators are \prod_{j 
e i}(c_i - c_j):  egin{aligned} \ell_{-1} &=  rac{x(x - 1)(x - 2)}{(-1)(-2)(-3)} = -	frac16x(x - 1)(x - 2), \ \ell_0 &=  rac{(x + 1)(x - 1)(x - 2)}{(1)(-1)(-2)} = 	frac12(x + 1)(x - 1)(x - 2), \end{aligned}  egin{aligned} \ell_1 &=  rac{(x + 1)x(x - 2)}{(2)(1)(-1)} = -	frac12(x + 1)x(x - 2), \ \ell_2 &=  rac{(x + 1)x(x - 1)}{(3)(2)(1)} = 	frac16(x + 1)x(x - 1). \end{aligned} Expanding,  egin{aligned} \ell_{-1} &= -	frac16x^3 + 	frac12x^2 - 	frac13x, \ \ell_0 &= 	frac12x^3 - x^2 - 	frac12x + 1, \ \ell_1 &= -	frac12x^3 + 	frac12x^2 + x, \ \ell_2 &= 	frac16x^3 - 	frac16x . \end{aligned} By @thm-lagrange-interpolation (c), p = 2\ell_{-1} + \ell_0 + 2\ell_1 + 11\ell_2. Collecting coefficients:  egin{aligned} x^3 &\colon\ -	frac13 + 	frac12 - 1 + 	frac{11}{6} = 1, \ x^2 &\colon\ 1 - 1 + 1 + 0 = 1, \ x &\colon\ -	frac23 - 	frac12 + 2 - 	frac{11}{6} = -1, \ 1 &\colon\ 1 . \end{aligned} Hence p = x^3 + x^2 - x + 1, the polynomial found by elimination in @exm-interpolation-cubic, as uniqueness demands. The elimination solved a 4 	imes 4 system for these particular values. The Lagrange polynomials were computed once, and would serve for any other values at the same nodes. The interpolant has degree at most n, not exactly n. Through the three points (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2) the formula gives 0 \cdot \ell_0 + 1 \cdot \ell_1 + 2\ell_2, where \ell_1 = -x(x - 2) and \ell_2 = 	frac12x(x - 1); this is -x^2 + 2x + x^2 - x = x. The degree-2 terms cancel, because the points lie on a line. Each \ell_i has degree exactly n, but a combination of them need not. Let n \ge 1 and let (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_n) be the Lagrange basis for distinct nodes c_0, \dots, c_n. What is \sum_{i=0}^{n} c_i\ell_i? It is the polynomial x. Indeed x \in F[x]_{\le n} since n \ge 1, and its values at the nodes are c_0, \dots, c_n, so @thm-lagrange-interpolation (b) gives x = \sum_i c_i\ell_i. Evaluations are the dual basis The delta table \ell_i(c_j) = \delta_{ij} can be read the other way round. For c \in F, evaluation at c is the linear functional \varepsilon_c \colon p \mapsto p(c) (@exm-linear-functionals), which we restrict to F[x]_{\le n}. Then the table says \varepsilon_{c_j}(\ell_i) = \delta_{ji}: the evaluations at the nodes behave on the Lagrange basis exactly as a dual basis must (@thm-dual-basis). @exr-linear-functionals-c3 proved from @thm-interpolation-unique that the evaluations form the dual basis of some basis. We can now name that basis. [Evaluations Are Dual to the Lagrange Basis] Let c_0, \dots, c_n \in F be distinct, with Lagrange basis (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_n). Then (\varepsilon_{c_0}, \dots, \varepsilon_{c_n}) is the dual basis of (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_n) in F[x]_{\le n}^{*}. In particular, every linear functional \varphi on F[x]_{\le n} is a combination of evaluations at the nodes: \varphi = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \varphi(\ell_i)\,\varepsilon_{c_i} . The evaluations are linear (@exm-linear-functionals), and \varepsilon_{c_i}(\ell_j) = \ell_j(c_i) = \delta_{ij} by @thm-lagrange-interpolation (a). Since (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_n) is a basis (@thm-lagrange-interpolation (b)), the uniqueness in @thm-dual-basis (a) shows that the evaluations are its dual basis. The formula for \varphi is the second formula of @thm-dual-basis (c). The first formula of @thm-dual-basis (c), p = \sum_i \varepsilon_{c_i}(p)\,\ell_i, is the expansion in @thm-lagrange-interpolation (b). So Lagrange’s formula is the statement “a vector is recovered from its dual-basis coordinates”, for the space F[x]_{\le n} and the measurements “value at c_i”. The formula for \varphi has a practical reading: any linear measurement of a polynomial of degree at most n can be computed from n + 1 of its values, with weights \varphi(\ell_i) that do not depend on the polynomial. [Integrals and Slopes from Values] 1. Find w_0, w_1, w_2 \in 
R such that \int_0^1 p(t)\,\dd t = w_0\,p(0) + w_1\,p(	frac12) + w_2\,p(1) for every p \in 
R[x]_{\le 2}. 2. Express p \mapsto p'(0) on 
R[x]_{\le 2} as a combination of \varepsilon_{-1}, \varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_1. (a) Integration over [0, 1] is a linear functional on 
R[x]_{\le 2} (@exm-linear-functionals). For the nodes 0, 	frac12, 1,  egin{aligned} \ell_0 &=  rac{(x -  rac12)(x - 1)}{(- rac12)(-1)} = 2x^2 - 3x + 1, \ \ell_{1/2} &=  rac{x(x - 1)}{( rac12)(- rac12)} = -4x^2 + 4x, \ \ell_1 &=  rac{x(x -  rac12)}{(1)( rac12)} = 2x^2 - x . \end{aligned} Their integrals are 	frac23 - 	frac32 + 1 = 	frac16, -	frac43 + 2 = 	frac23, and 	frac23 - 	frac12 = 	frac16. By @cor-evaluations-dual-to-lagrange, \int_0^1 p(t)\,\dd t = 	frac16\,p(0) + 	frac23\,p(	frac12) + 	frac16\,p(1) \qquad 	ext{for all } p \in 
R[x]_{\le 2}. Check with p = x^2: the right side is 	frac23 \cdot 	frac14 + 	frac16 = 	frac13 = \int_0^1 t^2\,\dd t. This is Simpson’s rule, which here is exact rather than approximate because p has degree at most 2. (b) With \ell_{-1} = 	frac12x(x - 1), \ell_0 = 1 - x^2, and \ell_1 = 	frac12x(x + 1), the derivatives at 0 are -	frac12, 0, and 	frac12. Hence p'(0) = 	frac12 igl(p(1) - p(-1) igr) for every p \in 
R[x]_{\le 2}, the symmetric difference quotient, exact on quadratics. Congruences and the Chinese Remainder Theorem Now we change the point of view. By @thm-remainder-theorem, the remainder of p on division by x - c is p(c). So the interpolation conditions p(c_i) = y_i say that p leaves the remainder y_i on division by x - c_i, for each i. Nothing in this reformulation needs the divisors to be linear. What happens if we prescribe the remainders modulo arbitrary polynomials m_1, \dots, m_k? The integers faced the same question long ago, which explains the name of the answer. We first need the language of congruences, copied from 
Z. [Congruence Modulo a Polynomial] Let m \in F[x]. Two polynomials f, g \in F[x] are congruent modulo m, written f \equiv g \pmod{m}, if m \mid f - g. For example, x^2 \equiv -1 \pmod{x^2 + 1}, and f \equiv f(c) \pmod{x - c} for every f, by @thm-remainder-theorem. Congruence modulo m is an equivalence relation, and it respects sums and products: if f \equiv f' and g \equiv g' \pmod m, then f + g - (f' + g') = (f - f') + (g - g') and fg - f'g' = f(g - g') + (f - f')g' are divisible by m. By @thm-polynomial-division, if m 
e 0, every f is congruent modulo m to exactly one polynomial of degree less than \deg m, its remainder: f = qm + r gives f \equiv r, and if f \equiv r \equiv r' with both degrees below \deg m, then m \mid r - r' with \deg(r - r') < \deg m, which forces r - r' = 0. Interpolation needed distinct nodes. The general condition is that the moduli share no factor, and the proof needs a way to pass from “coprime in pairs” to “coprime to the product”. [Coprime to Each, Coprime to the Product] 1. Let p, q_1, \dots, q_s \in F[x]. If p is coprime to each q_j, then there are a, b \in F[x] with ap + b\,q_1 \cdots q_s = 1, and p is coprime to q_1 \cdots q_s. 2. Let m_1, \dots, m_k \in F[x] be nonzero and pairwise coprime, that is, \gcd(m_i, m_j) = 1 whenever i 
e j. If m_i \mid h for every i, then m_1 \cdots m_k \mid h. (a) By @cor-bezout-polynomials, for each j there are a_j, b_j with a_jp + b_jq_j = 1. Multiplying these s identities, 1 = \prod_{j=1}^{s} (a_jp + b_jq_j) = ap + (b_1 \cdots b_s)\,q_1 \cdots q_s for some a \in F[x], because every term of the expanded product except (b_1q_1) \cdots (b_sq_s) contains a factor a_jp. Let d = \gcd(p, q_1 \cdots q_s). By @thm-gcd-properties, d divides p and q_1 \cdots q_s, hence divides ap + b\,q_1 \cdots q_s = 1, where b = b_1 \cdots b_s. So d is a nonzero constant by @thm-degree-of-product, and being monic, d = 1. Hence p and q_1 \cdots q_s are coprime (@def-coprime). (b) We use induction on k. For k = 1 there is nothing to prove. Let k \ge 2. The moduli m_1, \dots, m_{k-1} are pairwise coprime and each divides h, so by the induction hypothesis M \coloneqq m_1 \cdots m_{k-1} divides h, say h = Mg. Since m_k \mid h = Mg, and m_k is coprime to M by (a), @thm-coprime-divides-product gives m_k \mid g, say g = m_kg'. Then h = m_1 \cdots m_k\,g', as claimed. [Chinese Remainder Theorem for Polynomials] Let m_1, \dots, m_k \in F[x] be nonzero and pairwise coprime, and put m = m_1 \cdots m_k. For all r_1, \dots, r_k \in F[x]: 1. there is f \in F[x] with f \equiv r_i \pmod{m_i} for every i; 2. if f and g both satisfy (a), then f \equiv g \pmod{m}; 3. there is exactly one such f with \deg f < \deg m. Copy Lagrange. There, \ell_i was 1 at c_i and 0 at the other nodes; in the new language, \ell_i \equiv 1 \pmod{x - c_i} and \ell_i \equiv 0 \pmod{x - c_j}. So we look for e_i with e_i \equiv 1 \pmod{m_i} and e_i \equiv 0 \pmod{m_j} for j 
e i, and then f = \sum_i r_ie_i works. To be 0 modulo every other m_j, e_i should be a multiple of M_i = \prod_{j 
e i} m_j; to be 1 modulo m_i, it should be 1 - a\,m_i. Bézout’s identity a\,m_i + b\,M_i = 1 provides exactly such an element: e_i = b\,M_i. (a) Fix i, and let M_i = \prod_{j 
e i} m_j. Since m_i is coprime to each m_j with j 
e i, @lem-coprime-product (a) gives a_i, b_i \in F[x] with a_im_i + b_iM_i = 1. Put e_i = b_iM_i. Then e_i - 1 = -a_im_i, so e_i \equiv 1 \pmod{m_i}, and m_j \mid M_i \mid e_i for j 
e i, so e_i \equiv 0 \pmod{m_j}. Let f = r_1e_1 + \dots + r_ke_k. Since congruence modulo m_j respects sums and products, f \equiv r_1 \cdot 0 + \dots + r_j \cdot 1 + \dots + r_k \cdot 0 = r_j \pmod{m_j} for each j. (b) If f and g satisfy (a), then f - g \equiv r_i - r_i = 0 \pmod{m_i}, that is, m_i \mid f - g, for every i. By @lem-coprime-product (b), m \mid f - g. (c) Since each m_i 
e 0, m 
e 0 (@thm-degree-of-product). Let f be as in (a), and let f_0 be its remainder on division by m (@thm-polynomial-division). Then m_i \mid m \mid f - f_0, so f_0 \equiv f \equiv r_i \pmod{m_i} for each i, and \deg f_0 < \deg m. If g is another solution with \deg g < \deg m, then m \mid f_0 - g by (b), and \deg(f_0 - g) < \deg m, so f_0 = g. This proves the theorem. Lagrange is the case m_i = x - c_i. For distinct nodes, (x - c_j) - (x - c_i) = c_i - c_j is a nonzero constant, so  rac{1}{c_i - c_j}(x - c_j) -  rac{1}{c_i - c_j}(x - c_i) = 1, and any common divisor of x - c_i and x - c_j divides 1: the moduli are pairwise coprime. The congruence f \equiv y_i \pmod{x - c_i} means f(c_i) = y_i by @thm-remainder-theorem, and \deg m = n + 1. So part (c) is @thm-interpolation-unique. The element e_i has degree less than n + 1 after reduction modulo m, is 1 at c_i and 0 at the other nodes, so after reduction it is \ell_i. [A Linear and a Quadratic Modulus] Find the polynomial f \in 
Q[x] of degree less than 3 with f \equiv 1 \pmod{x - 2}, \qquad f \equiv 2x - 1 \pmod{x^2 + 1}. Bézout. Divide x^2 + 1 by x - 2: x^2 + 1 = (x + 2)(x - 2) + 5. Hence 	frac15(x^2 + 1) - 	frac15(x + 2)(x - 2) = 1, and the moduli are coprime, since any common divisor divides 1. The elements e_i. Put e_1 = 	frac15(x^2 + 1) and e_2 = -	frac15(x + 2)(x - 2) = 1 - e_1. Then e_1 is a multiple of x^2 + 1 and e_1 = 1 + 	frac15(x + 2)(x - 2) \equiv 1 \pmod{x - 2}; symmetrically, e_2 \equiv 0 \pmod{x - 2} and e_2 \equiv 1 \pmod{x^2 + 1}. Combine and reduce. By the proof of @thm-crt-polynomials, f \equiv 1 \cdot e_1 + (2x - 1)e_2 \pmod{(x - 2)(x^2 + 1)}. Expanding, e_1 + (2x - 1)e_2 = 	frac15(x^2 + 1) - 	frac15(2x - 1)(x^2 - 4) = 	frac15 igl(-2x^3 + 2x^2 + 8x - 3 igr). Dividing by m = (x - 2)(x^2 + 1) = x^3 - 2x^2 + x - 2 gives quotient -	frac25 and remainder f = 	frac15 igl(-2x^2 + 10x - 7 igr). Check. f(2) = 	frac15(-8 + 20 - 7) = 1, so f \equiv 1 \pmod{x - 2}. Modulo x^2 + 1, x^2 \equiv -1, so f \equiv 	frac15(2 + 10x - 7) = 2x - 1. The moduli must be coprime in pairs; coprime as a whole family is not enough. Without coprimality a system can be unsolvable: with m_1 = x and m_2 = x^2, the system f \equiv 0 \pmod{x}, f \equiv 1 \pmod{x^2} has no solution: the first condition says f(0) = 0, the second says f = 1 + x^2q, so f(0) = 1. For three moduli, x, x - 1, and x(x - 1) have no common factor, yet the first and third share x, and f \equiv 0 \pmod x, f \equiv 1 \pmod{x(x - 1)} is again impossible. [Values and Slopes by CRT] 1. Let c, a, b \in F and f \in F[x]. Show that f \equiv a + b(x - c) \pmod{(x - c)^2} if and only if f(c) = a and f'(c) = b. 2. Find the p \in 
Q[x]_{\le 3} with p(0) = 2, p'(0) = -1, p(1) = 1, and p'(1) = 3. (a) Divide by (x - c)^2: f = q(x - c)^2 + r with \deg r \le 1 (@thm-polynomial-division). Writing r = r_0 + r_1(x - c), which is possible because (1, x - c) is a basis of F[x]_{\le 1} by @thm-distinct-degrees-independent and @thm-right-size-basis, the uniqueness of the remainder says f \equiv a + b(x - c) exactly when r_0 = a and r_1 = b. Now f(c) = r_0. By @thm-formal-derivative-rules, f' = q'(x - c)^2 + 2q(x - c) + r_1, so f'(c) = r_1. Hence the congruence holds if and only if f(c) = a and f'(c) = b. (b) By (a), the conditions are p \equiv 2 - x \pmod{x^2} and p \equiv 1 + 3(x - 1) \pmod{(x - 1)^2}. The moduli are coprime, since (2x + 1)(x - 1)^2 - (2x - 3)x^2 = (2x^3 - 3x^2 + 1) - (2x^3 - 3x^2) = 1 . So e_0 = (2x + 1)(x - 1)^2 is \equiv 0 \pmod{(x - 1)^2} and \equiv 1 \pmod{x^2}, while e_1 = -(2x - 3)x^2 = 3x^2 - 2x^3 is \equiv 0 \pmod{x^2} and \equiv 1 \pmod{(x - 1)^2}. The polynomial e_1 is the smooth step 3x^2 - 2x^3 of @exm-hermite-existence: value 0 and slope 0 at 0, value 1 and slope 0 at 1. By @thm-crt-polynomials, p is the remainder of (2 - x)e_0 + (3x - 2)e_1 = -8x^4 + 20x^3 - 12x^2 - x + 2 on division by x^2(x - 1)^2 = x^4 - 2x^3 + x^2. Adding 8(x^4 - 2x^3 + x^2) gives p = 4x^3 - 4x^2 - x + 2 . Check. p(0) = 2; p' = 12x^2 - 8x - 1, so p'(0) = -1; p(1) = 4 - 4 - 1 + 2 = 1; p'(1) = 12 - 8 - 1 = 3. The same recipe handles any finite set of nodes c_i with multiplicities k_i: the moduli (x - c_i)^{k_i} are pairwise coprime for distinct nodes, by @lem-coprime-product (a) applied twice: first x - c_i is coprime to (x - c_j)^{k_j}, and then (x - c_j)^{k_j} is coprime to (x - c_i)^{k_i}. So for any prescribed remainders modulo (x - c_i)^{k_i}, there is exactly one polynomial of degree less than k_1 + \dots + k_s with those remainders. In characteristic 0, the Taylor expansion of @thm-polynomial-taylor translates “the remainder modulo (x - c)^k” into the values f(c), f'(c), \dots, f^{(k-1)}(c), and this is Hermite interpolation. The quotient space F[x]/\langle m angle Congruence modulo m is equality of cosets. The ideal \langle m angle is a subspace of F[x]: it is nonempty and closed under addition and under multiplication by constant polynomials (@def-ideal-polynomials). So the quotient space F[x]/\langle m angle of @def-quotient-space exists, and by @lem-coset-equality (b), f + \langle m angle = g + \langle m angle \iff f - g \in \langle m angle \iff f \equiv g \pmod{m} . An element of F[x]/\langle m angle is a polynomial “known only modulo m”. We cannot quote @thm-dimension-quotient for its dimension, because F[x] is infinite-dimensional (@thm-polynomials-infinite-dimensional). The remainder does the job instead. [Dimension of F[x]/\langle m angle] Let m \in F[x] be nonzero of degree d. Then F[x]/\langle m angle is finite-dimensional with \dim F[x]/\langle m angle = \deg m = d . If d \ge 1, the cosets (1 + \langle m angle, x + \langle m angle, \dots, x^{d-1} + \langle m angle) form a basis. If d = 0, then m is a nonzero constant, and every f = (m^{-1}f)m lies in \langle m angle. So \langle m angle = F[x] and the quotient is the zero space, of dimension 0. Let d \ge 1, and define ho \colon F[x] 	o F[x]_{\le d-1} by letting ho(f) be the remainder of f on division by m (@thm-polynomial-division). Linear. If f = q_1m + ho(f) and g = q_2m + ho(g), then for c \in F, cf + g = (cq_1 + q_2)m +  igl(cho(f) + ho(g) igr), and \deg(cho(f) + ho(g)) < d by @thm-degree-of-sum. By the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-division, ho(cf + g) = cho(f) + ho(g). Surjective. If \deg r < d, then r = 0 \cdot m + r, so ho(r) = r. Kernel. ho(f) = 0 exactly when f = qm for some q, that is, f \in \langle m angle. By the First Isomorphism Theorem (@thm-first-isomorphism),  arho \colon F[x]/\langle m angle 	o F[x]_{\le d-1}, f + \langle m angle \mapsto ho(f), is a well-defined injective linear map with image \im ho = F[x]_{\le d-1}, so it is an isomorphism. Since  arho(x^j + \langle m angle) = x^j for j < d, and (1, x, \dots, x^{d-1}) is a basis of F[x]_{\le d-1} (@exm-standard-bases), the inverse isomorphism  arho^{-1} carries it to the basis (x^j + \langle m angle)_{j < d} (@thm-isomorphism-preserves-bases). Hence \dim F[x]/\langle m angle = d. For example, 
R[x]/\langle x^2 + 1 angle has basis (1 + \langle x^2 + 1 angle, x + \langle x^2 + 1 angle), so each element is a + bx + \langle x^2 + 1 angle for unique a, b \in 
R. Cosets can also be multiplied: (f + \langle m angle)(g + \langle m angle) \coloneqq fg + \langle m angle is well defined, because congruence modulo m respects products. In 
R[x]/\langle x^2 + 1 angle, x \cdot x = x^2 \equiv -1, so the coset of x squares to minus the coset of 1, and (a + bx)(a' + b'x) \equiv (aa' - bb') + (ab' + a'b)x: this is multiplication in 
C, with the coset of x playing the role of i. The Chinese Remainder Theorem now becomes a statement about linear maps. Reducing a polynomial modulo each m_i records its k remainders; the theorem says that this record, taken modulo m, is a perfect dictionary. Recall from @def-product-of-spaces that V_1 	imes \dots 	imes V_k is the space of lists with entrywise operations. [CRT as an Isomorphism] Let m_1, \dots, m_k \in F[x] be nonzero and pairwise coprime, and put m = m_1 \cdots m_k. Then  egin{aligned} &\Phi \colon F[x]/\langle m angle 	o F[x]/\langle m_1 angle 	imes \dots 	imes F[x]/\langle m_k angle, \ &\qquad f + \langle m angle \mapsto  igl(f + \langle m_1 angle, \dots, f + \langle m_k angle igr), \end{aligned} is a well-defined isomorphism of vector spaces. The map that does not care about well-definedness is \Psi \colon f \mapsto (f + \langle m_i angle)_i on F[x] itself. Its kernel is the set of polynomials divisible by every m_i, which is \langle m angle by @lem-coprime-product. So the First Isomorphism Theorem makes \Phi well defined and injective in one stroke. For surjectivity we do not construct a preimage. We count: both sides have dimension \deg m, because degrees add under products. Let \Psi \colon F[x] 	o F[x]/\langle m_1 angle 	imes \dots 	imes F[x]/\langle m_k angle, \Psi(f) = (f + \langle m_1 angle, \dots, f + \langle m_k angle). Each entry is a quotient map, which is linear by @thm-quotient-space-operations-well-defined (c), and the operations in the product are entrywise, so \Psi is linear. By @lem-coset-equality (b), \Psi(f) = \elem{0} if and only if m_i \mid f for every i. If m \mid f, then m_i \mid f for all i, since m_i \mid m; conversely, if every m_i \mid f, then m \mid f by @lem-coprime-product (b). Hence \ker \Psi = \langle m angle. By the First Isomorphism Theorem (@thm-first-isomorphism), the rule f + \langle m angle \mapsto \Psi(f) is a well-defined injective linear map; this is \Phi. By @thm-dimension-polynomial-quotient, @thm-degree-of-product, and @thm-dimension-of-product,  egin{aligned} \dim F[x]/\langle m angle &= \deg m = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \deg m_i = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \dim F[x]/\langle m_i angle \ &= \dim\Bigl(F[x]/\langle m_1 angle 	imes \dots 	imes F[x]/\langle m_k angle\Bigr). \end{aligned} Since \Phi is injective between spaces of the same finite dimension, it is bijective by @cor-rank-nullity-consequences (e), hence an isomorphism (@def-isomorphism). Surjectivity of \Phi is the existence part of @thm-crt-polynomials, and injectivity is the uniqueness part. So the count has given a second proof of the Chinese Remainder Theorem, one that never uses Bézout’s identity for existence. It is the same trade as in @exm-interpolation-by-counting: counting proves that a solution exists, and the Bézout construction says what it is. By the remark above, \Phi also respects products of cosets, since reduction modulo each m_i does. In Chapter 9 this splitting of F[x]/\langle m angle into pieces, one for each coprime factor of m, reappears as a splitting of a space on which an operator acts. The next section begins that story. What is \dim 
Q[x]/\langle x^3 - x angle? Into which three spaces does @thm-crt-isomorphism split it, and what does \Phi do to the coset of x^2? By @thm-dimension-polynomial-quotient, the dimension is 3. Since x^3 - x = x(x - 1)(x + 1) with distinct linear factors, which are pairwise coprime, \Phi maps it isomorphically onto 
Q[x]/\langle x angle 	imes 
Q[x]/\langle x - 1 angle 	imes 
Q[x]/\langle x + 1 angle, a product of three one-dimensional spaces. Modulo x - c, a polynomial is congruent to its value at c, so \Phi(x^2 + \langle x^3 - x angle) is the list of cosets of the constants 0, 1, 1: the values of x^2 at 0, 1, -1. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the Lagrange basis for distinct nodes c_0, \dots, c_n, and state the value of \ell_i at c_j. 2. True or false: for four distinct nodes, the polynomial of degree at most 3 through the four points always has degree exactly 3. Justify your answer. 3. State the Chinese Remainder Theorem for polynomials, with all hypotheses. 4. True or false: if \gcd(m_1, m_2, m_3) = 1, then every system f \equiv r_i \pmod{m_i}, i = 1, 2, 3, has a solution. Justify your answer. 5. What is \dim_{
R} 
R[x]/\langle x^4 + 1 angle? Give a basis. 6. Which functional on F[x]_{\le n} is the i-th vector of the dual basis (@thm-dual-basis) of the Lagrange basis? (a) For distinct c_0, \dots, c_n \in F, \ell_i = \prod_{j 
e i}  rac{x - c_j}{c_i - c_j} (@def-lagrange-basis), and \ell_i(c_j) = \delta_{ij} (@thm-lagrange-interpolation (a)). (b) False. The points (0, 0), (1, 0), (2, 0), (3, 0) are fitted by the zero polynomial, of degree -\infty; by uniqueness (@thm-interpolation-unique), that is the interpolant. (c) If m_1, \dots, m_k \in F[x] are nonzero and pairwise coprime and m = m_1 \cdots m_k, then for all r_1, \dots, r_k \in F[x] there is f with f \equiv r_i \pmod{m_i} for each i, unique modulo m, and exactly one such f has \deg f < \deg m (@thm-crt-polynomials). (d) False. x, x - 1, x(x - 1) have gcd 1 as a family, but f \equiv 0 \pmod x, f \equiv 0 \pmod{x - 1}, f \equiv 1 \pmod{x(x - 1)} has no solution: the last condition gives f(0) = 1, contradicting the first. (e) 4, with basis (1, x, x^2, x^3) of cosets modulo \langle x^4 + 1 angle, by @thm-dimension-polynomial-quotient. (f) Evaluation at the i-th node, \varepsilon_{c_i} \colon p \mapsto p(c_i) (@cor-evaluations-dual-to-lagrange). B. Practice [B1: A Lagrange interpolant] Let c_0, c_1, c_2, c_3 = 0, 1, 2, 3. Write down the Lagrange basis for these nodes in factored form, and use it to find the p \in 
Q[x]_{\le 3} with p(0) = 1, p(1) = 0, p(2) = 1, and p(3) = 10. Hence compute p(4). The denominators \prod_{j 
e i}(c_i - c_j) are (-1)(-2)(-3) = -6, (1)(-1)(-2) = 2, (2)(1)(-1) = -2, and (3)(2)(1) = 6. So  egin{aligned} \ell_0 &= -	frac16(x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3), \ \ell_1 &= 	frac12x(x - 2)(x - 3), \ \ell_2 &= -	frac12x(x - 1)(x - 3), \ \ell_3 &= 	frac16x(x - 1)(x - 2). \end{aligned} By @thm-lagrange-interpolation (c), p = \ell_0 + 0 \cdot \ell_1 + \ell_2 + 10\ell_3. Expanding each needed term,  egin{aligned} \ell_0 &= -	frac16(x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6), \ \ell_2 &= -	frac12(x^3 - 4x^2 + 3x), \ 10\ell_3 &= 	frac53(x^3 - 3x^2 + 2x). \end{aligned} The coefficient of x^3 is -	frac16 - 	frac12 + 	frac53 = 1; of x^2, 1 + 2 - 5 = -2; of x, -	frac{11}{6} - 	frac32 + 	frac{10}{3} = 0; the constant is 1. Hence p = x^3 - 2x^2 + 1 . Check: p(0) = 1, p(1) = 0, p(2) = 8 - 8 + 1 = 1, p(3) = 27 - 18 + 1 = 10. Hence p(4) = 64 - 32 + 1 = 33. [B2: A CRT system] Find the polynomial f \in 
Q[x] of degree less than 3 with f \equiv 2 \pmod{x - 1} and f \equiv x \pmod{x^2 + 1}. Hence describe all g \in 
Q[x] satisfying both congruences. Bézout. x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)(x - 1) + 2, so 	frac12(x^2 + 1) - 	frac12(x + 1)(x - 1) = 1, and the moduli are coprime. The elements e_i. e_1 = 	frac12(x^2 + 1) is a multiple of x^2 + 1 and e_1 = 1 + 	frac12(x + 1)(x - 1) \equiv 1 \pmod{x - 1}. And e_2 = 1 - e_1 = -	frac12(x + 1)(x - 1) is a multiple of x - 1 with e_2 \equiv 1 \pmod{x^2 + 1}. Combine and reduce. By the proof of @thm-crt-polynomials, f \equiv 2e_1 + xe_2 = (x^2 + 1) - 	frac12x(x^2 - 1) = -	frac12x^3 + x^2 + 	frac12x + 1. Modulo m = (x - 1)(x^2 + 1) = x^3 - x^2 + x - 1, add 	frac12m: f = -	frac12x^3 + x^2 + 	frac12x + 1 + 	frac12(x^3 - x^2 + x - 1) = 	frac12x^2 + x + 	frac12 = 	frac12(x + 1)^2 . Check. f(1) = 2. Modulo x^2 + 1, f \equiv 	frac12(-1) + x + 	frac12 = x. By @thm-crt-polynomials (b), and since every g \equiv f \pmod m satisfies both congruences (because x - 1 and x^2 + 1 divide m), the solutions are exactly g = 	frac12(x + 1)^2 + h\,(x - 1)(x^2 + 1) with h \in 
Q[x]. [B3: The Lagrange basis sums to one] Let c_0, \dots, c_n \in F be distinct with Lagrange basis (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_n). 1. Prove that \ell_0 + \ell_1 + \dots + \ell_n = 1. 2. Prove more generally that \sum_{i=0}^{n} c_i^{\,k}\,\ell_i = x^k for k = 0, 1, \dots, n (with c^0 = 1). 3. For n = 2 and nodes 0, 1, 2, verify (a) by expanding. (a) This is (b) with k = 0. (b) Let 0 \le k \le n. Then x^k \in F[x]_{\le n}, and its value at c_i is c_i^{\,k} (@def-polynomial-evaluation). By @thm-lagrange-interpolation (b), x^k = \sum_i c_i^{\,k}\ell_i. (c) \ell_0 =  rac{(x - 1)(x - 2)}{2} = 	frac12x^2 - 	frac32x + 1, \ell_1 =  rac{x(x - 2)}{-1} = -x^2 + 2x, \ell_2 =  rac{x(x - 1)}{2} = 	frac12x^2 - 	frac12x. Adding: x^2 has coefficient 	frac12 - 1 + 	frac12 = 0, x has -	frac32 + 2 - 	frac12 = 0, and the constant is 1. So the sum is 1. C. Going deeper [C1: Interpolation over a finite field] Let p be a prime and F = 
F_p. 1. Explain why @thm-lagrange-interpolation cannot be applied with more than p nodes. 2. Let E \colon 
F_p[x]_{\le p} 	o 
F_p^{\,p}, E(f) = (f(0), f(1), \dots, f(p - 1)). Prove that E is linear and surjective but not injective, and find a nonzero polynomial in \ker E. 3. Deduce that every function 
F_p 	o 
F_p is the polynomial function of exactly one polynomial of degree at most p - 1, but of more than one polynomial of degree at most p. (a) The theorem needs distinct nodes, and 
F_p has only p elements, so there are no p + 1 distinct nodes. (b) Linear. Each entry f \mapsto f(c) is linear by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations. Surjective. The p elements 0, 1, \dots, p - 1 of 
F_p are distinct nodes, so for every (y_0, \dots, y_{p-1}), @thm-lagrange-interpolation (c) with n = p - 1 gives f = \sum_i y_i\ell_i \in 
F_p[x]_{\le p - 1} \subseteq 
F_p[x]_{\le p} with E(f) = (y_0, \dots, y_{p-1}). Not injective. \dim 
F_p[x]_{\le p} = p + 1 > p = \dim 
F_p^{\,p}, so E is not injective by @cor-rank-nullity-consequences (c). Concretely, g = \prod_{c \in 
F_p}(x - c) is monic of degree p, hence nonzero, and g(c) = 0 for every c \in 
F_p, because one factor vanishes (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations). (c) A function 
F_p 	o 
F_p is the same as its list of values (y_0, \dots, y_{p-1}). By (b), the restriction of E to 
F_p[x]_{\le p-1} is surjective, and it is injective because a polynomial of degree at most p - 1 vanishing at p distinct points is 0 (@cor-root-bound-general). So exactly one polynomial of degree at most p - 1 has the given values. In degree at most p, if f has the given values, so does f + g 
e f, with g from (b). Unlike over 
R, a polynomial over 
F_p is not determined by its function. [C2: Newton’s form of the interpolant] Let c_0, \dots, c_n \in F be distinct. Put N_0 = 1 and N_k = (x - c_0)(x - c_1) \cdots (x - c_{k-1}) for 1 \le k \le n + 1. 1. Prove that (N_0, \dots, N_n) is a basis of F[x]_{\le n}. 2. Let p = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_kN_k. Show that p(c_i) = \sum_{k=0}^{i} a_kN_k(c_i) and N_i(c_i) 
e 0. Explain why the coefficients a_0, a_1, \dots of the interpolant can be found one at a time, and show that a_0 = y_0 and a_1 =  rac{y_1 - y_0}{c_1 - c_0}. 3. Let p_n \in F[x]_{\le n} interpolate y_0, \dots, y_n at c_0, \dots, c_n, and let c_{n+1} be a further node, distinct from the others, with a value y_{n+1}. Prove that the interpolant p_{n+1} \in F[x]_{\le n+1} is p_{n+1} = p_n +  rac{y_{n+1} - p_n(c_{n+1})}{N_{n+1}(c_{n+1})}\,N_{n+1} . 4. Find the Newton form of the interpolant of @exr-interpolation-and-crt-b1, and then the interpolant after adding the point (4, 0). Why is this more economical than recomputing with Lagrange’s formula? Hint: for (c), check the values of the right-hand side at all n + 2 nodes. (a) N_k is a product of k monic linear factors, so it is monic of degree k (@thm-degree-of-product). The polynomials N_0, \dots, N_n are nonzero with pairwise distinct degrees, hence linearly independent by @thm-distinct-degrees-independent. The list has length n + 1 = \dim F[x]_{\le n}, so it is a basis by @thm-right-size-basis (a). (b) For k > i, N_k contains the factor x - c_i, so N_k(c_i) = 0; this gives the formula for p(c_i). And N_i(c_i) = \prod_{j < i}(c_i - c_j) is a product of nonzero scalars, since the nodes are distinct, so it is nonzero. The conditions p(c_i) = y_i therefore form a lower triangular system: the i-th equation involves only a_0, \dots, a_i, with coefficient N_i(c_i) 
e 0 on a_i. Solving in the order i = 0, 1, \dots, n determines each a_i from the earlier ones. For i = 0: p(c_0) = a_0, so a_0 = y_0. For i = 1: y_1 = a_0 + a_1(c_1 - c_0), so a_1 =  rac{y_1 - y_0}{c_1 - c_0}, the slope of the chord, the first “divided difference”. (c) Let q be the right-hand side; the division is legal because N_{n+1}(c_{n+1}) 
e 0 by (b). Then \deg q \le n + 1. For i \le n, N_{n+1}(c_i) = 0, so q(c_i) = p_n(c_i) = y_i. At c_{n+1}, q(c_{n+1}) = p_n(c_{n+1}) + y_{n+1} - p_n(c_{n+1}) = y_{n+1}. By @thm-interpolation-unique, q = p_{n+1}. (d) With nodes 0, 1, 2, 3: N_1 = x, N_2 = x(x - 1), N_3 = x(x - 1)(x - 2). Forward substitution: a_0 = p(0) = 1; 0 = p(1) = 1 + a_1, so a_1 = -1; 1 = p(2) = 1 - 2 + 2a_2, so a_2 = 1; 10 = p(3) = 1 - 3 + 6 + 6a_3, so a_3 = 1. Thus p_3 = 1 - x + x(x - 1) + x(x - 1)(x - 2) = x^3 - 2x^2 + 1, agreeing with @exr-interpolation-and-crt-b1. Adding (4, 0): p_3(4) = 33 and N_4(4) = 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 24, so by (c)  egin{aligned} p_4 &= x^3 - 2x^2 + 1 - 	frac{33}{24}\,x(x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3) \ &= x^3 - 2x^2 + 1 - 	frac{11}{8}\,x(x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3). \end{aligned} One checks p_4(4) = 33 - 	frac{11}{8} \cdot 24 = 0. Adding a node changes every Lagrange polynomial, since each \ell_i acquires a new factor; in Newton’s form the old coefficients a_0, \dots, a_n survive and only one new coefficient is computed.

title: 6.7 Polynomials of an Operator
content:
Polynomials of an Operator Chapter 2 taught us to substitute an operator into a polynomial: for T \in \cL(V) and p \in F[x], the operator p(T) replaces each x^k by T^k (@def-polynomial-of-operator). That section used the idea for a few examples. With the arithmetic of this chapter in hand, the idea becomes a method. Divisibility, ideals, and Bézout’s identity in F[x] turn into statements about T: every operator on a finite-dimensional space satisfies a polynomial equation, the polynomials it satisfies form an ideal, and a factorization of such a polynomial into coprime pieces splits the space. The last statement, the kernel splitting lemma, is the engine that Chapter 9 will run to take operators apart. The new point of view is to treat “substitute T” as a single map from F[x] to \cL(V), and to ask what it preserves. Both sides are vector spaces, and both have a multiplication. It is multiplicative and sends 1 to \id_V: (pq)(T) = p(T)\,q(T) and 1(T) = \id_V. 3. title: Determinants
content: Determinants A square matrix is invertible or it is not, and so far deciding which has meant row reducing it. The determinant packages that decision into a single number. The same number measures how the linear map scales areas and volumes, and its sign records whether the map preserves or reverses orientation. It also produces the characteristic polynomial, the gateway to eigenvalues in Chapter 9. This chapter does not start from a formula. It starts from what a signed volume must do. Scaling one edge scales the volume. Sliding one edge along another does not change it. The unit cube has volume 1. We prove that exactly one function has these properties, write it down, and then derive every property of the determinant from that uniqueness: multiplicativity, the transpose rule, cofactor expansion, the inverse formula, and Cramer’s rule. Nothing is assumed, and no formula is used before it is proved. What you need. From Chapter 0, permutations and transpositions (@thm-transpositions-generate) and the characteristic of a field (@def-characteristic). From Chapter 1, linear independence and the Linear Dependence Lemma (@def-linear-independence, @thm-linear-dependence-lemma). From Chapter 3, elementary matrices and the invertible matrix theorem (@def-elementary-matrix, @thm-invertible-tfae). From Chapter 2, the matrix of a linear map and similarity (@def-matrix-of-linear-map, @thm-similar-iff-same-operator). From Chapter 5, only the word linear functional (@def-linear-functional), which §02 borrows to say what a multilinear form is in each argument separately; no result of that chapter is used in a proof here. From Chapter 6, the root bound for polynomials (@cor-root-bound-general). Roadmap - Signed area and volume. Three rules that any reasonable notion of signed volume obeys, and the formula ad - bc forced by them. - Multilinear alternating forms. The rules made precise for functions of n vectors, and their first consequences. - Permutations and sign. Counting inversions, and why the parity of a permutation is well defined. - Existence and uniqueness of the determinant. Exactly one alternating form takes the value 1 on the identity; the Leibniz formula. - Row operations and multiplicativity. Computing determinants by elimination, \det(\A\B) = \det \A \det \B, and the determinant of an operator. - Cofactor expansion, the adjugate, and Cramer’s rule. Expanding along a row or column, and a formula for the inverse. - Minors, rank, and Cauchy–Binet. Rank read off from minors, and the determinant of a product of rectangular matrices. - Special determinants. Vandermonde, tridiagonal, and block triangular matrices, and rank-one updates. - Orientation and volume. The determinant as a volume scaling factor, and the two orientations of \nR^n. - The characteristic polynomial. \det(x\I - \A), its coefficients, and why similar matrices share it. Named moves - Derive from the rules, not the formula. Prove determinant facts from multilinearity, alternation and normalization, so no property is assumed before it is proved. - Uniqueness does the work. To prove two expressions agree, show both are alternating multilinear in the columns and agree on the identity. - Build from elementary matrices. Check a claim for elementary matrices, then extend it to products. - Look-alike matrices. A matrix with two equal rows has determinant zero; expanding such a matrix proves the adjugate identity. - Induct on size. Expand along a row or column to reduce an n \times n determinant to smaller ones.

title: 7.1 Signed Area and Volume
content:
Signed Area and Volume In Chapter 0 a single number, ad - bc, decided whether a 2 	imes 2 matrix is invertible (@thm-two-by-two-inverse). For an n 	imes n matrix, Chapter 3 answered the same question by row reduction, which is a procedure, not a number. Is there one number for every square matrix that does the job of ad - bc? This section does not define it yet. Instead it asks what such a number should mean, finds the answer in area and volume, and extracts a short list of rules. From the rules alone, ad - bc comes out, with no other choice possible. Area as a function of two vectors Take two vectors \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \in 
R^2 and the parallelogram they span, P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = \{ s\cvec{u} + t\cvec{v} : 0 \le s \le 1,\ 0 \le t \le 1 \}. Its corners are \cvec{0}, \cvec{u}, \cvec{v}, and \cvec{u} + \cvec{v}. We want to understand its area as a function of the two vectors, without drawing a coordinate grid and counting squares. Four features are visible without any formula. Scaling a side scales the area. Replacing \cvec{v} by 2\cvec{v} stacks two copies of P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) on top of each other, so the area doubles. Replacing \cvec{v} by 3\cvec{v} triples it, and replacing \cvec{v} by  rac12\cvec{v} halves it. Shearing does not change the area. Replace \cvec{v} by \cvec{v} + c\cvec{u}. The top edge slides along its own line, parallel to the base \cvec{u}. The base stays the same, and so does the height, so the area stays the same. The picture shows c = 1: the triangle cut off on the left of P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) reappears, moved by \cvec{u}, on the right of P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} + \cvec{u}). The solid outline is P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) and the dashed one completes P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} + \cvec{u}). Both consist of the unshaded middle triangle plus a shaded triangle, and the two shaded triangles T and T + \cvec{u} are translates of each other. Equal sides give area zero. P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{u}) is a segment, which has no area. More generally, if \cvec{v} is a multiple of \cvec{u}, the parallelogram is flat. The unit square has area one. P(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) is the unit square. This fixes the unit of measurement. Why the area needs a sign The first feature is not quite right as stated. Replacing \cvec{v} by -\cvec{v} moves the parallelogram to the other side of the line of \cvec{u} (the point reflection \cvec{x} \mapsto \cvec{u} - \cvec{x} carries P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) onto P(\cvec{u}, -\cvec{v})) and does not change its area, so ordinary area satisfies \operatorname{area}(\cvec{u}, c\cvec{v}) = \lvert c vert \operatorname{area}(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}), with an absolute value. That absolute value spoils a second, very useful property. Fix the base \cvec{u} and let the second vector vary. The area is base times height, and heights along a fixed direction add up: if \cvec{v} reaches height 1 above the line of \cvec{u} and \cvec{w} reaches height 1.5, then \cvec{v} + \cvec{w} reaches height 2.5. So we expect \operatorname{area}(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} + \cvec{w}) = \operatorname{area}(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) + \operatorname{area}(\cvec{u}, \cvec{w}). The picture shows it: P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{w}), moved up by \cvec{v}, sits exactly on top of P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}), and the two together have the same base and total height as P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} + \cvec{w}) (dashed). Now take \cvec{w} = -\cvec{v}. Then \cvec{v} + \cvec{w} = \cvec{0} and the left side is \operatorname{area}(\cvec{u}, \cvec{0}) = 0, while the right side is 2 \operatorname{area}(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}), which is positive. Additivity fails, because -\cvec{v} points below the line of \cvec{u} and its height should count as negative. The repair is to give area a sign. Signed area is ordinary area, counted positive when the second vector lies on the counterclockwise side of the first, and negative when it lies on the clockwise side. So P(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) has signed area +1, because \cvec{e}_2 is a quarter turn counterclockwise from \cvec{e}_1, and P(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1) has signed area -1. With the sign in place, scaling holds with c instead of \lvert c vert, and heights add with their signs, so additivity holds for all \cvec{v}, \cvec{w}. Write D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) for the signed area. The pictures suggest that D \colon 
R^2 	imes 
R^2 	o 
R obeys the following rules, for all \cvec{u}, \cvec{v}, \cvec{w} \in 
R^2 and all c \in 
R: 1. (Scaling) D(c\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = cD(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) and D(\cvec{u}, c\cvec{v}) = cD(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}). 2. (Shear) D(\cvec{u} + c\cvec{v}, \cvec{v}) = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) and D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} + c\cvec{u}) = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}). 3. (Equal sides) D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{u}) = 0. 4. (Normalization) D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = 1. 5. (Additivity) D(\cvec{u} + \cvec{w}, \cvec{v}) = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) + D(\cvec{w}, \cvec{v}) and D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} + \cvec{w}) = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) + D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{w}). These are rules read off from pictures, not yet a definition. The question is what they force. The rules force ad - bc A 2 	imes 2 matrix \A =  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{pmatrix} has columns \cvec{u} = (a, c) and \cvec{v} = (b, d), and P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) is the image of the unit square under \cvec{x} \mapsto \A\cvec{x}. We now show that the first four rules leave no freedom at all. The method is the column version of elimination: use shears to clear entries until the parallelogram becomes a rectangle. [ad - bc from the Rules] Let D \colon 
R^2 	imes 
R^2 	o 
R be any function satisfying (R1)–(R4). Show that D((a, c), (b, d)) = ad - bc for all a, b, c, d \in 
R. Write \cvec{u} = (a, c) and \cvec{v} = (b, d). Two consequences of (R1) come first. Taking the scalar 0 in (R1) gives D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{0}) = D(\cvec{u}, 0\cvec{v}) = 0 \cdot D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = 0, and likewise D(\cvec{0}, \cvec{v}) = 0. Using (R1) twice and then (R4),  egin{aligned} D((p, 0), (0, q)) &= D(p\cvec{e}_1, q\cvec{e}_2) = pq\,D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) \ &= pq \qquad 	ext{for all } p, q \in 
R. \end{aligned} 	ag{$\ast$} Case 1: a 
eq 0. By the second shear rule with scalar -b/a, D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = D igl(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} - 	frac{b}{a}\cvec{u} igr) = D igl(\cvec{u}, (0, d') igr), \qquad 	ext{where } d' = d - 	frac{bc}{a}. If d' = 0, this is D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{0}) = 0 = ad'. If d' 
eq 0, the first shear rule with scalar -c/d' clears the second entry of \cvec{u}: D igl(\cvec{u}, (0, d') igr) = D igl(\cvec{u} - 	frac{c}{d'}(0, d'), (0, d') igr) = D igl((a, 0), (0, d') igr) = ad' by (\ast). In both sub-cases D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = ad' = ad - bc. Case 2: a = 0 and b 
eq 0. By the first shear rule with scalar 1, D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = D(\cvec{u} + \cvec{v}, \cvec{v}), and \cvec{u} + \cvec{v} = (b, c + d) has first entry b 
eq 0. Case 1, applied to the columns (b, c + d) and (b, d), gives D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = bd - b(c + d) = -bc = ad - bc, since a = 0. Case 3: a = b = 0. If c = 0, then \cvec{u} = \cvec{0} and D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = 0. If c 
eq 0, the second shear rule with scalar -d/c gives D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} - 	frac{d}{c}\cvec{u}) = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{0}) = 0. In both sub-cases D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = 0 = ad - bc. The three cases cover all a, b, c, d, so D((a, c), (b, d)) = ad - bc, as claimed. So at most one function obeys (R1)–(R4). Conversely, (a, c), (b, d) \mapsto ad - bc obeys all five rules; for instance, for the second shear rule, replacing (b, d) by (b + ta, d + tc) gives a(d + tc) - (b + ta)c = ad - bc. The other checks are just as short. Hence exactly one function satisfies (R1)–(R4), and it satisfies (R5) as well. Two things in this computation are worth noticing. First, (R3) was never used. It follows from the others: D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{u}) = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{u} - \cvec{u}) = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{0}) = 0, by a shear and then scaling by 0. Second, the argument used only addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by nonzero numbers. So over any field F, exactly one function F^2 	imes F^2 	o F satisfies (R1)–(R4), namely ad - bc. The picture needs 
R; the algebra does not. There is also a shorter route, if we allow additivity. Expanding \cvec{u} = a\cvec{e}_1 + c\cvec{e}_2 and \cvec{v} = b\cvec{e}_1 + d\cvec{e}_2 with (R5) and (R1) gives four terms: D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = ab\,D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1) + ad\,D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) + cb\,D(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1) + cd\,D(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_2). The first and last vanish by (R3), D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = 1 by (R4), and D(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1) = -1 (see the Quick check below). This expansion is the route that generalizes to n vectors later in the chapter, while the elimination route of @exm-two-by-two-from-rules becomes the practical way to compute. Using only (R1) and (R2), show that D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = -D(\cvec{v}, \cvec{u}) for all \cvec{u}, \cvec{v}. Deduce D(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1). Apply shears and one scaling:  egin{aligned} D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) &\overset{	ext{(R2)}}{=} D(\cvec{u} + \cvec{v}, \cvec{v}) \ &\overset{	ext{(R2)}}{=} D igl(\cvec{u} + \cvec{v}, \cvec{v} - (\cvec{u} + \cvec{v}) igr) = D(\cvec{u} + \cvec{v}, -\cvec{u}) \ &\overset{	ext{(R2)}}{=} D igl((\cvec{u} + \cvec{v}) + (-\cvec{u}), -\cvec{u} igr) = D(\cvec{v}, -\cvec{u}) \ &\overset{	ext{(R1)}}{=} -D(\cvec{v}, \cvec{u}). \end{aligned} With \cvec{u} = \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_2, and (R4), D(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1) = -D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = -1. This agrees with ad - bc = 0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1 for the columns (0, 1), (1, 0). Now compare with Chapter 0. By @thm-two-by-two-inverse, \A is invertible if and only if ad - bc 
eq 0. In the language of this section: \A is invertible exactly when the parallelogram spanned by its columns is not flat, that is, when the columns do not lie on a common line through the origin. The number that decides invertibility and the signed area of the image of the unit square are the same number. Drag the images of \cvec{e}_1 and \cvec{e}_2 below and watch the signed area pass through 0 exactly when the two columns line up. The unit square (dashed) and its image under \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, a parallelogram of signed area 2 \cdot 3 - 1 \cdot 1 = 5. The second column lies counterclockwise from the first, so the sign is positive. Volume in three dimensions The same story plays out one dimension up. Three vectors \cvec{u}, \cvec{v}, \cvec{w} \in 
R^3 span a parallelepiped P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}, \cvec{w}) = \{ r\cvec{u} + s\cvec{v} + t\cvec{w} : 0 \le r, s, t \le 1 \}, a slanted box whose faces are parallelograms. Its volume is the area of the base P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) (shaded) times the height of \cvec{w} above the plane of the base. Each feature from the plane has a counterpart: - scaling one edge scales the volume; - replacing \cvec{w} by \cvec{w} + a\cvec{u} + b\cvec{v} slides the top face within its own plane, so the base and height, hence the volume, are unchanged, and similarly for shears of \cvec{u} or \cvec{v}; - if two edges are equal, the box is flat and the volume is 0; - the unit cube P(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3) has volume 1; - with a sign attached, heights add, so the signed volume is additive in each edge. The sign in three dimensions records whether (\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}, \cvec{w}) is arranged like (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3), the right-hand rule. We make this precise as orientation later in the chapter. For now the point is that the rules are the same rules, now for a function D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}, \cvec{w}) of three vectors. The Quick check above also carries over word for word: shearing and scaling two of the arguments while the third stays fixed shows that swapping two arguments changes the sign. What we will prove Here is the goal for the next three sections. Let F be a field and n \ge 1. There is exactly one function D of n vectors in F^n that is linear in each argument separately, is 0 whenever two arguments are equal, and takes the value 1 at (\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n). Its value on the columns of a matrix \A will be the determinant \det \A. The plan follows the shorter route for n = 2. Expanding every argument in the standard basis gives n^n terms. The rule for equal arguments kills every term with a repeated basis vector, which leaves one term for each rearrangement (\cvec{e}_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, \cvec{e}_{\sigma(n)}) of the standard basis. Each surviving value is \pm 1, reached from D(\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n) = 1 by swaps, with one sign change per swap. That creates two tasks: 1. Name and study functions of several vectors with these rules. This is the next section, on multilinear alternating forms. 2. Make sure the sign of a rearrangement is well defined, even though it can be reached by different sequences of swaps. This is the section on permutations and sign. The existence and uniqueness theorem itself comes after both. Sarrus’s rule is a 3 	imes 3 coincidence. For a 3 	imes 3 matrix, the “diagonals” shortcut (add the three products along the down-right diagonals of the array with its first two columns copied to the right, subtract the three along the up-right diagonals) gives the correct six terms, because there are exactly 3! = 6 rearrangements. The same picture for 4 	imes 4 gives 4 + 4 = 8 products, while the expansion above has 4! = 24 terms. It fails already for the matrix with columns \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_3, \cvec{e}_4: every one of the eight wrapped diagonals passes through a zero entry, so the shortcut returns 0, but the swap rule gives D(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_3, \cvec{e}_4) = -D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3, \cvec{e}_4) = -1. Never use Sarrus’s rule beyond 3 	imes 3, and never use it as a proof tool. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the four rules (R1)–(R4) for signed area. 2. True or false: ordinary (unsigned) area satisfies \operatorname{area}(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} + \cvec{w}) = \operatorname{area}(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) + \operatorname{area}(\cvec{u}, \cvec{w}) for all \cvec{u}, \cvec{v}, \cvec{w} \in 
R^2. Justify your answer. 3. Find the signed area of P((1, 3), (2, 4)). Is  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} invertible? 4. Explain why any D satisfying (R1) and (R2) has D(\cvec{u}, 5\cvec{u}) = 0. 5. How many terms does the full expansion for 4 	imes 4 matrices have, and how many products does the 4 	imes 4 analogue of Sarrus’s rule use? (a) For all \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \in 
R^2 and c \in 
R: D(c\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = cD(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = D(\cvec{u}, c\cvec{v}); D(\cvec{u} + c\cvec{v}, \cvec{v}) = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} + c\cvec{u}); D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{u}) = 0; D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = 1. (b) False. Take \cvec{u} = \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{w} = -\cvec{e}_2. The left side is the area of P(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{0}), which is 0; the right side is 1 + 1 = 2. (c) With a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, d = 4, the signed area is ad - bc = 4 - 6 = -2. Since -2 
eq 0, the matrix is invertible by @thm-two-by-two-inverse. (d) By the second shear rule with scalar -5, D(\cvec{u}, 5\cvec{u}) = D(\cvec{u}, 5\cvec{u} - 5\cvec{u}) = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{0}), and D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{0}) = D(\cvec{u}, 0 \cdot \cvec{u}) = 0 \cdot D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{u}) = 0 by (R1). (e) The expansion has 4! = 24 terms, one for each rearrangement of \cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_4. The Sarrus-type diagram has only 8 products, so it must miss 16 of them. B. Practice [B1: Signed Areas from the Rules] Using only (R1)–(R4), in the manner of @exm-two-by-two-from-rules, compute the following. Then check each answer against ad - bc. 1. D((2, 1), (4, 5)). 2. D((1, 2), (3, 6)). 3. D((0, 3), (2, 0)). (a) By the second shear rule with scalar -2, D((2, 1), (4, 5)) = D((2, 1), (4, 5) - 2(2, 1)) = D((2, 1), (0, 3)). By the first shear rule with scalar -	frac13, this equals D((2, 1) - 	frac13(0, 3), (0, 3)) = D((2, 0), (0, 3)). By (R1) twice and (R4), D(2\cvec{e}_1, 3\cvec{e}_2) = 6D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = 6. Check: 2 \cdot 5 - 4 \cdot 1 = 6. (b) By the second shear rule with scalar -3, D((1, 2), (3, 6)) = D((1, 2), (0, 0)), and D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{0}) = D(\cvec{u}, 0 \cdot \cvec{u}) = 0 by (R1). So the value is 0. Check: 1 \cdot 6 - 3 \cdot 2 = 0. The columns lie on one line, and the parallelogram is flat. (c) By (R1) twice, D(3\cvec{e}_2, 2\cvec{e}_1) = 6D(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1). By the Quick check (which uses only (R1) and (R2)), D(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1) = -D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = -1 by (R4). So the value is -6. Check: with columns (0, 3) and (2, 0), a = 0, b = 2, c = 3, d = 0, and ad - bc = -6. The sign is negative because (2, 0) lies clockwise from (0, 3). [B2: Equal Sides Force the Swap Rule] Let D \colon 
R^2 	imes 
R^2 	o 
R satisfy (R1), (R3) and (R5), but not necessarily (R2). 1. Prove that D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = -D(\cvec{v}, \cvec{u}) for all \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \in 
R^2. 2. Suppose moreover that (R4) holds. Deduce that D((a, c), (b, d)) = ad - bc. Hint: expand D(\cvec{u} + \cvec{v}, \cvec{u} + \cvec{v}). (a) Let \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \in 
R^2. By (R3), D(\cvec{u} + \cvec{v}, \cvec{u} + \cvec{v}) = 0. Expanding with (R5) in the first argument and then in the second, 0 = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{u}) + D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) + D(\cvec{v}, \cvec{u}) + D(\cvec{v}, \cvec{v}) = D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) + D(\cvec{v}, \cvec{u}), where the second equality uses (R3) twice. Hence D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = -D(\cvec{v}, \cvec{u}). (b) Write (a, c) = a\cvec{e}_1 + c\cvec{e}_2 and (b, d) = b\cvec{e}_1 + d\cvec{e}_2. By (R5) and (R1) in each argument, D((a, c), (b, d)) = ab\,D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1) + ad\,D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) + cb\,D(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1) + cd\,D(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_2). By (R3) the first and last terms are 0. By (R4), D(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = 1, and by (a), D(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1) = -1. Hence D((a, c), (b, d)) = ad - bc. C. Going deeper [C1: Area of a Triangle] Let \cvec{p}, \cvec{q}, \cvec{r} \in 
R^2. 1. Explain why the triangle with vertices \cvec{p}, \cvec{q}, \cvec{r} has area 	frac12 \lvert D(\cvec{q} - \cvec{p}, \cvec{r} - \cvec{p}) vert, where D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) is the signed area. 2. Find the area of the triangle with vertices (1, 2), (4, 3), (2, 6). 3. Hence decide whether the points (0, 1), (2, 4), (6, 10) lie on a line. Justify your answer. (a) Translating by -\cvec{p} does not change areas, so the triangle has the same area as the triangle with vertices \cvec{0}, \cvec{u} = \cvec{q} - \cvec{p}, \cvec{v} = \cvec{r} - \cvec{p}. That triangle is half of the parallelogram P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}): the diagonal from \cvec{u} to \cvec{v} cuts P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) into the triangle with vertices \cvec{0}, \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} and the triangle with vertices \cvec{u} + \cvec{v}, \cvec{v}, \cvec{u}, and the point reflection \cvec{x} \mapsto \cvec{u} + \cvec{v} - \cvec{x} maps the first onto the second, so they have equal area. The area of P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) is \lvert D(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) vert, since the signed area differs from the area only by its sign. Hence the triangle has area 	frac12 \lvert D(\cvec{q} - \cvec{p}, \cvec{r} - \cvec{p}) vert. (b) Here \cvec{q} - \cvec{p} = (3, 1) and \cvec{r} - \cvec{p} = (1, 4), so D = 3 \cdot 4 - 1 \cdot 1 = 11 and the area is 	frac{11}{2}. (c) With \cvec{p} = (0, 1), \cvec{q} - \cvec{p} = (2, 3) and \cvec{r} - \cvec{p} = (6, 9), so D = 2 \cdot 9 - 6 \cdot 3 = 0 and the “triangle” has area 0. Indeed (6, 9) = 3(2, 3), so \cvec{r} - \cvec{p} is a multiple of \cvec{q} - \cvec{p}, and all three points lie on the line through (0, 1) with direction (2, 3). Yes, they are collinear. [C2: The 1 	imes 1 Case] For n = 1, the rules ask for a function f \colon F 	o F of one vector in F^1 = F. 1. Explain why the rule “zero whenever two arguments are equal” imposes no condition when n = 1. 2. Prove that the only function f \colon F 	o F that is linear with f(1) = 1 is f(a) = a. Hence the determinant of a 1 	imes 1 matrix (a) must be a. (a) The rule speaks about two different positions i 
eq j holding equal vectors. With one argument there is no pair of positions, so the condition is vacuously true (@exm-vacuous-truth). (b) Let f be linear with f(1) = 1, and let a \in F. Since a = a \cdot 1, homogeneity gives f(a) = f(a \cdot 1) = a f(1) = a. Conversely, a \mapsto a is linear and sends 1 to 1. Hence f(a) = a is the only such function.

title: 7.2 Multilinear Alternating Forms
content:
Multilinear Alternating Forms The previous section found that signed area obeys a few rules: it is linear in each side separately, it vanishes when two sides are equal, and swapping the sides changes its sign. This section gives these rules names for functions of k vectors in an arbitrary vector space, and derives everything that follows from them before any formula exists. The main result is that “zero on equal arguments” already implies the swap rule, the shear rule, and vanishing on dependent lists. The swap rule, in turn, gives back “zero on equal arguments” only when 1 + 1 
eq 0 in the field. Throughout, V is a vector space over a field F, k \ge 1 is an integer, and V^k = V 	imes \cdots 	imes V is the set of k-tuples of vectors (@def-n-tuple). Multilinear forms Signed area is not a linear function of the pair (\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}): doubling both sides multiplies the area by four, not by two. What it does have is linearity in \cvec{u} when \cvec{v} is held fixed, and linearity in \cvec{v} when \cvec{u} is held fixed. This “one slot at a time” linearity recurs throughout the book: in the dot product, later in inner products and bilinear forms, and in the determinant. So we give it a name. A multilinear form is a function of several vectors that is linear in each vector while the others are held fixed. [Multilinear Form] A function f \colon V^k 	o F is k-linear, or a multilinear form on V, if for every position i \in \{1, \dots, k\} and every choice of \elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_{i-1}, \elem{v}_{i+1}, \dots, \elem{v}_k \in V, the function V 	o F, \qquad \elem{x} \mapsto f(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_{i-1}, \elem{x}, \elem{v}_{i+1}, \dots, \elem{v}_k) is linear. A 2-linear form is called bilinear. In words: fix all arguments except the one in position i. What remains is a function of one vector, and it must be a linear functional (@def-linear-functional). Written out, for all \elem{x}, \elem{y} \in V and c \in F,  egin{aligned} f(\dots, \elem{x} + \elem{y}, \dots) &= f(\dots, \elem{x}, \dots) + f(\dots, \elem{y}, \dots), \ f(\dots, c\elem{x}, \dots) &= c\,f(\dots, \elem{x}, \dots), \end{aligned} where the dots stand for the same fixed vectors on both sides. The condition is imposed for every position i, one at a time. Some examples: - Signed area. On F^2, f(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = u_1v_2 - u_2v_1 is bilinear. For fixed \cvec{v}, the map \cvec{u} \mapsto v_2u_1 - v_1u_2 is a linear functional on F^2, and for fixed \cvec{u}, so is \cvec{v} \mapsto u_1v_2 - u_2v_1. - The dot product. On F^n, (\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) \mapsto u_1v_1 + \dots + u_nv_n is bilinear, by the same one-slot check. - Products of functionals. For \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_k \in V^{*}, f(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) = \varphi_1(\elem{v}_1)\varphi_2(\elem{v}_2) \cdots \varphi_k(\elem{v}_k) is k-linear: in position i it is the linear functional \varphi_i multiplied by the fixed scalar \prod_{j 
eq i} \varphi_j(\elem{v}_j). For instance, on F[x], (p, q) \mapsto p(0)q(1) is bilinear, since evaluation at a point is linear (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations). - The degenerate case k = 1. A 1-linear form is exactly a linear functional on V. So multilinear forms generalize the dual space of Chapter 5. Multilinear is not linear. A bilinear form is not a linear function of the pair. For the signed area f(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = u_1v_2 - u_2v_1 on 
R^2, scaling both arguments by 2 gives f(2\cvec{e}_1, 2\cvec{e}_2) = 4, not 2f(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = 2. Adding in both slots at once is not allowed either: f(\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2) = f(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2) = 1, while f(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1) + f(\cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_2) = 0. Pull out scalars and split sums one slot at a time. Alternating and skew-symmetric forms The second rule of signed area was geometric: if two edges coincide, the parallelogram or box is flat. There are two natural ways to put this into algebra. One says the value is zero when two arguments are equal. The other says the value changes sign when two arguments are swapped. They look like two phrasings of one idea, but they are not the same, and we must choose. An alternating form vanishes as soon as two of its arguments coincide. [Alternating Form] A k-linear form f \colon V^k 	o F is alternating if f(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) = 0 whenever \elem{v}_i = \elem{v}_j for some pair of positions i 
eq j. [Skew-Symmetric Form] A k-linear form f \colon V^k 	o F is skew-symmetric if, for all \elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k \in V and all positions i < j, swapping the arguments in positions i and j multiplies the value by -1: f(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_j, \dots, \elem{v}_i, \dots, \elem{v}_k) = -f(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_i, \dots, \elem{v}_j, \dots, \elem{v}_k), where on the left \elem{v}_j sits in position i, \elem{v}_i sits in position j, and all other positions are unchanged. In words: “alternating” asks for the value 0 as soon as any two positions, adjacent or not, hold the same vector, whatever the remaining arguments are. It is a condition on the inputs where two entries coincide, and says nothing directly about other inputs. “Skew-symmetric” is a condition on every input: it compares the value at a list with the value at the list with two entries exchanged. We chose “zero when two arguments are equal” as the basic notion, and in the form “any two positions”. There are two reasons. Consequences of the alternating condition Everything that elimination does to a determinant will come from the following theorem. Its four parts are the column operations of Chapter 3 seen through a form: swap two arguments, add a multiple of one to another, scale one, and the extreme case of a dependent list. [Properties of Alternating Forms] Let f \colon V^k 	o F be an alternating k-linear form, let \elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k \in V, and let i 
eq j be positions in \{1, \dots, k\}. 1. (Swap) Exchanging the arguments in positions i and j multiplies f(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) by -1. In particular, f is skew-symmetric. 2. (Shear) For every c \in F, replacing \elem{v}_i by \elem{v}_i + c\elem{v}_j does not change f(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k). 3. (Scaling) For every c \in F, replacing \elem{v}_i by c\elem{v}_i multiplies f(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) by c. 4. (Dependence) If the list (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) is linearly dependent, then f(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) = 0. In particular, f(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) = 0 if some \elem{v}_i = \elem{0}. Parts (a)–(c) involve at most the two slots i and j, so freeze the other k - 2 arguments. What is left is a bilinear form g(\elem{x}, \elem{y}) with g(\elem{x}, \elem{x}) = 0, and the k-argument statements become two-argument statements about g. For the swap, the move is to feed g a sum in both slots, g(\elem{x} + \elem{y}, \elem{x} + \elem{y}) = 0, and expand: the two “square” terms die and the two cross terms must cancel. The zero function is k-linear, since in each position it is the zero functional, and it is alternating, since all its values are 0. Let f and g be k-linear and a \in F. For \elem{x}, \elem{y} \in V and c \in F, the pointwise definition and linearity of f and g in position i give  egin{aligned} (f + g)(\dots, \elem{x} + \elem{y}, \dots) &= f(\dots, \elem{x}, \dots) + f(\dots, \elem{y}, \dots) \ &\qquad + g(\dots, \elem{x}, \dots) + g(\dots, \elem{y}, \dots) \ &= (f + g)(\dots, \elem{x}, \dots) + (f + g)(\dots, \elem{y}, \dots) \end{aligned} and (f + g)(\dots, c\elem{x}, \dots) = c\,f(\dots, \elem{x}, \dots) + c\,g(\dots, \elem{x}, \dots) = c\,(f + g)(\dots, \elem{x}, \dots). So f + g is k-linear. In the same way (af)(\dots, \elem{x} + \elem{y}, \dots) = a f(\dots, \elem{x}, \dots) + a f(\dots, \elem{y}, \dots) and (af)(\dots, c\elem{x}, \dots) = c\,(af)(\dots, \elem{x}, \dots), using commutativity in F, so af is k-linear. (a) Expanding \cvec{u} = u_1\cvec{e}_1 + u_2\cvec{e}_2 and \cvec{v} = v_1\cvec{e}_1 + v_2\cvec{e}_2 by linearity in each argument gives f(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = \sum_{r, s} u_rv_s f(\cvec{e}_r, \cvec{e}_s) = \sum_{r, s} b_{rs}u_rv_s. Conversely, for any scalars b_{rs}, the function \sum_{r, s} b_{rs}u_rv_s is linear in \cvec{u} for fixed \cvec{v} (a combination of the coordinates u_r with coefficients \sum_s b_{rs}v_s) and similarly in \cvec{v}, and it takes the value b_{rs} at (\cvec{e}_r, \cvec{e}_s). So bilinear forms on F^2 correspond exactly to quadruples (b_{11}, b_{12}, b_{21}, b_{22}), and over 
F_2 there are 2^4 = 16. (b) In 
F_2, -a = a for every a, so f is skew-symmetric exactly when f(\cvec{v}, \cvec{u}) = f(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) for all \cvec{u}, \cvec{v}. (\Rightarrow) Taking \cvec{u} = \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_2 gives b_{21} = b_{12}. (\Leftarrow) If b_{12} = b_{21}, then b_{rs} = b_{sr} for all r, s, and f(\cvec{v}, \cvec{u}) = \sum_{r, s} b_{rs}v_ru_s = \sum_{r, s} b_{sr}u_sv_r = f(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}). The entries b_{11}, b_{22} and the common value b_{12} = b_{21} are free, so there are 2^3 = 8 skew-symmetric forms. (c) (\Rightarrow) If f is alternating, then b_{11} = f(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1) = 0 and b_{22} = 0, and 0 = f(\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2) = b_{11} + b_{12} + b_{21} + b_{22} = b_{12} + b_{21}, so b_{21} = -b_{12} = b_{12}. (\Leftarrow) With b_{11} = b_{22} = 0 and b_{12} = b_{21} = b, f(\cvec{u}, \cvec{u}) = b(u_1u_2 + u_2u_1) = (1 + 1)\,b\,u_1u_2 = 0. Only b \in \{0, 1\} is free, so there are 2 alternating forms. Hence 8 - 2 = 6 skew-symmetric forms over 
F_2 are not alternating; u_1v_1 (with b_{11} = 1, all others 0) is one of them, as in the warning. A brute-force check of all 16 forms against all pairs in 
F_2^2 gives the same counts, 8 and 2. (d) Over 
R the two sets are equal. Alternating forms are skew-symmetric by @thm-skew-symmetric-alternating (a), and since 
R has characteristic 0, skew-symmetric forms are alternating by part (b) of that theorem. Concretely, both conditions say b_{11} = b_{22} = 0 and b_{21} = -b_{12}.

title: 7.3 Permutations and Sign
content:
Permutations and Sign An alternating form changes sign when two of its arguments are swapped (@thm-alternating-properties). To compare f(\elem{v}_3, \elem{v}_1, \elem{v}_2) with f(\elem{v}_1, \elem{v}_2, \elem{v}_3), we reach one list from the other by swaps and collect a factor -1 per swap. But the same rearrangement can be reached by different sequences of swaps, and Chapter 0 showed that even their number is not unique. If one route used an even number of swaps and another an odd number, we would get f(\elem{v}_1, \elem{v}_2, \elem{v}_3) = -f(\elem{v}_1, \elem{v}_2, \elem{v}_3) for every alternating form, which is absurd for signed volume. This section rules that out. It attaches to each permutation a sign defined without any choices, proves that the sign is multiplicative, and deduces that the parity of the number of transpositions is well defined, as Chapter 0 promised. Permutations, recalled Recall from Chapter 0 that S_n is the group of bijections \{1, \dots, n\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}, with n! elements. A permutation can be written in two-line notation, with \sigma(i) below i, or as a product of cycles. The product \sigma	au is the composition \sigma \circ 	au: first 	au, then \sigma, so products of cycles are read from right to left (@exm-cycle-notation). A transposition (i\ j) swaps i and j and fixes everything else, and for n \ge 2 every permutation is a product of transpositions (@thm-transpositions-generate). The product is far from unique, since (1\ 2\ 3) = (1\ 3)(1\ 2) = (1\ 2)(2\ 3) = (1\ 3)(1\ 2)(1\ 2)(1\ 2). Here the numbers of transpositions are 2, 2, 4, all even. The goal is to show this is no accident. Why can we not simply define the sign of \sigma as (-1)^r, where \sigma is a product of r transpositions? Because that definition depends on a choice of product, and we would have to prove that every choice gives the same answer. That is the statement we are trying to prove. We need a definition that involves no choice at all. Inversions and the sign To measure how much a permutation scrambles 1, 2, \dots, n, look at the bottom row \sigma(1), \dots, \sigma(n) of its two-line notation and count the pairs of entries that are in the wrong order. A sorted row has none, and each swap of two neighboring entries changes the count by exactly one. So the count is a natural candidate for tracking the parity of swaps. The sign of a permutation records whether it puts an even or an odd number of pairs out of order. [Inversion] Let \sigma \in S_n. An inversion of \sigma is a pair (i, j) of positions with 1 \le i < j \le n and \sigma(i) > \sigma(j). We write \operatorname{inv}(\sigma) for the number of inversions of \sigma. [Sign of a Permutation] The sign of \sigma \in S_n is \sgn \sigma = (-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)} \in \{1, -1\}. The permutation \sigma is even if \sgn \sigma = 1 and odd if \sgn \sigma = -1. In words: an inversion is a pair of positions whose order \sigma reverses. The condition i < j makes each pair of positions count once, and \sigma(i) > \sigma(j) says the values come out in the opposite order. Since \operatorname{inv}(\sigma) is the size of a subset of the finite set of pairs i < j, it is a well-defined integer between 0 and n(n-1)/2, and there is nothing to choose. That is the whole reason for this definition. The identity. Its bottom row is sorted, so \operatorname{inv}(\id) = 0 and \id is even. In S_1 = \{\id\} this is the only permutation, with sign 1. The degenerate case matters: the identity is the empty product of transpositions, and its sign 1 = (-1)^0 is what a product of 0 swaps should give. All of S_3. Here is each permutation with its bottom row and inversions. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- \sigma \id (1\,2) (2\,3) (1\,3) (1\,2\,3) (1\,3\,2) ------------ ---------- ---------- ---------- --------------------- -------------- -------------- bottom row 1\,2\,3 2\,1\,3 1\,3\,2 3\,2\,1 2\,3\,1 3\,1\,2 inversions none (1,2) (2,3) (1,2), (1,3), (2,3) (1,3), (2,3) (1,2), (1,3) \sgn 1 -1 -1 -1 1 1 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- For (1\ 2\ 3), the bottom row is \sigma(1), \sigma(2), \sigma(3) = 2, 3, 1, and the out-of-order pairs of positions are (1, 3), since 2 > 1, and (2, 3), since 3 > 1. Two things stand out. The three transpositions are odd, although (1\ 3) has three inversions, not one. And the two 3-cycles are even, consistent with (1\ 2\ 3) = (1\ 3)(1\ 2) being a product of two transpositions. Why all pairs, not just neighbors. A tempting shortcut counts only adjacent positions (i, i + 1) with \sigma(i) > \sigma(i + 1). For (1\ 3), with bottom row 3, 2, 1, this count is 2, which would make (1\ 3) “even”.
