Prove that \det(\A + \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p) = \det \A\, ig(1 + \cvec{v}	p \A^{-1}\cvec{u} ig). 2. Deduce that \A + \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p is invertible if and only if \cvec{v}	p \A^{-1}\cvec{u} 
e -1. 3. Give an example over 
Q with n = 2 where \A is invertible, \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p 
e \O, and \A + \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p is not invertible. (a) Since \A is invertible, \A + \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p = \A(\I_n + \A^{-1}\cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p) = \A ig(\I_n + (\A^{-1}\cvec{u})\cvec{v}	p ig) by @thm-matrix-multiplication-properties. By @thm-det-multiplicative and @thm-matrix-determinant-lemma applied to the vectors \A^{-1}\cvec{u} and \cvec{v}, \det(\A + \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p) = \det \A\,(1 + \cvec{v}	p \A^{-1}\cvec{u}). (b) \det \A 
e 0 by @thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible, so \det(\A + \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p) 
e 0 exactly when 1 + \cvec{v}	p \A^{-1}\cvec{u} 
e 0. Apply @thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible again. (c) Take \A = \I_2, \cvec{u} = (-1, 0), \cvec{v} = (1, 0). Then \cvec{v}	p\cvec{u} = -1, and indeed \A + \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} is not invertible.

title: 7.9 Orientation and Volume
content:
Orientation and Volume The chapter began in §1 with a picture: the area of a parallelogram, with a sign attached, obeys a few simple rules, and those rules pinned down ad - bc. We have since built the determinant in every size from the same rules. It is time to return to geometry and say precisely what the determinant measures. There are two halves to the answer. Its absolute value measures volume, and its sign measures orientation, the difference between a left hand and a right hand. Both halves need care. “Volume” in 
R^7 has no meaning until someone defines it, and “orientation” has no meaning at all over 
C. Throughout this section the field is 
R. What should the volume of a parallelepiped be? For vectors \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n \in 
R^n, the parallelepiped they span is the set P(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) \coloneqq \{ t_1\cvec{a}_1 + \dots + t_n\cvec{a}_n : 0 \le t_i \le 1 	ext{ for every } i \}. For n = 2 it is the parallelogram with sides \cvec{a}_1, \cvec{a}_2 at the origin, and for n = 3 a slanted box. For n = 1 it is the segment from 0 to \cvec{a}_1. We would like to say “its volume is \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a}_1 & \cdots & \cvec{a}_n \end{pmatrix} vert”. But a theorem needs two sides, and one side is missing: we have no definition of the volume of a subset of 
R^n. School geometry supplies one for n = 2 and n = 3 through “base times height”, and the proper general notion, Lebesgue measure, belongs to a course in measure theory. So we proceed honestly in three steps. We define the volume of a parallelepiped by the determinant. We prove that this is the only function obeying the rules that any reasonable notion of volume must obey. And we state, without proof, that it agrees with Lebesgue measure. The volume of a parallelepiped is the size of the determinant of its edge vectors. [Volume of a Parallelepiped] Let n \ge 1 and \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n \in 
R^n. The (n-dimensional) volume of the parallelepiped spanned by \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n is \vol(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) \coloneqq  ig\lvert \det egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a}_1 & \cvec{a}_2 & \cdots & \cvec{a}_n \end{pmatrix}  igvert \ \ge 0 . In words: stack the n edge vectors as the columns of a square matrix, take its determinant, and forget the sign. There must be exactly n vectors in 
R^n, so that the matrix is square. Examples. - The unit cube P(\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n) has volume \lvert \det \I_n vert = 1. - A box with edges d_1\cvec{e}_1, \dots, d_n\cvec{e}_n has volume \lvert \det\diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) vert = \lvert d_1 \cdots d_n vert by @thm-det-triangular: the product of its side lengths, as it should be. - The parallelepiped spanned by (1, 2, 0), (0, 1, 1), (1, 0, 3) in 
R^3 has volume \left\lvert \det egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 2 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} ightvert = \lvert 1\cdot(3 - 0) - 0 + 1\cdot(2 - 0) vert = 5, expanding along the first row. - Degenerate case. If \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n are linearly dependent, the parallelepiped is flattened into a proper subspace, and its volume is 0 by @thm-alternating-properties. For n = 2, P((1, 2), (2, 4)) is the segment from (0, 0) to (3, 6), with area \lvert 4 - 4 vert = 0. This case matters: “volume zero” is the geometric face of “not invertible”. Nonexample by minimal change. Drop one vector: (1, 2, 0) and (0, 1, 1) span a genuine parallelogram in 
R^3, but the matrix  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} is 3 	imes 2 and has no determinant. The clause that fails is exactly n vectors in 
R^n. The 3-dimensional volume of that flat parallelogram would be 0, and its area needs a different formula (@exr-orientation-and-volume-c1). Why this definition. Reordering the vectors multiplies the determinant by a sign (@thm-alternating-properties), which the absolute value removes, so the volume does not depend on the order in which the edges are listed. The absolute value is also what makes volume nonnegative. The sign we threw away is not garbage: it is the orientation, the subject of the second half of this section. Volume is not linear. Scaling one edge by 2 doubles the volume, but scaling the whole parallelepiped by 2 multiplies it by 2^n: \vol(2\cvec{a}_1, \dots, 2\cvec{a}_n) = \lvert \det(2\A) vert = 2^n \vol(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n), where \A has columns \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n. A cube of side 2 in 
R^3 has volume 8, not 2; this failure persists even with the sign kept, since \det is linear in each edge separately, not in all edges at once. The absolute value also destroys additivity in a single edge: \vol(\cvec{a}_1 + \cvec{b}_1, \cvec{a}_2, \dots) is in general not \vol(\cvec{a}_1, \cvec{a}_2, \dots) + \vol(\cvec{b}_1, \cvec{a}_2, \dots): with \cvec{a}_1 = \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{b}_1 = -\cvec{e}_1 in 
R^2, and \cvec{a}_2 = \cvec{e}_2, the left side is 0 and the right side is 2. Volume is forced by its rules Why should anyone accept @def-parallelepiped-volume? Because of what any notion of volume of parallelepipeds must satisfy. The pictures in §1 showed three facts about area, and they have obvious n-dimensional versions: stretching one edge by a factor c multiplies the volume by \lvert c vert; sliding one edge parallel to another (a shear) does not change the volume; and the unit cube has volume 1. The next theorem says that these three rules alone determine the volume completely. So any definition that obeys them, whether from school geometry or from measure theory, must agree with ours. [Volume Is Determined by Its Rules] Let n \ge 1, and let g be a function assigning a real number g(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) to every list of n vectors in 
R^n. Suppose that for every list, every i 
e j, and every c \in 
R: 1. g(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, c\cvec{a}_i, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) = \lvert c vert\, g(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_i, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) (only slot i changes); 2. g(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_i + c\cvec{a}_j, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) = g(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_i, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) (only slot i changes); 3. g(\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n) = 1. Then g(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) = \vol(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) for every list. Moreover, \vol itself satisfies (V1)–(V3). Think of g as a function of the matrix \M with columns \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n. ① If the columns are dependent, shear one column to \cvec{0} and scale by 0: g = 0. ② Each elementary column operation changes g by the factor \lvert \det \E vert. Scaling and shearing are (V1) and (V2); a swap is not among the rules, but three shears and a sign change perform it. ③ An invertible \M is a product of elementary matrices, so peel them off one at a time until only \I is left. For \M \in M_n(
R) with columns \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n, write h(\M) = g(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n). Step 1: dependent columns give h(\M) = 0. Suppose the columns are linearly dependent. By @thm-linear-dependence-lemma, some \cvec{a}_i = c_1\cvec{a}_1 + \dots + c_{i-1}\cvec{a}_{i-1} (for i = 1, \cvec{a}_1 = \cvec{0}). Applying (V2) to slot i with the scalars -c_1, \dots, -c_{i-1}, one at a time, does not change g, and it replaces \cvec{a}_i by \cvec{0} while the other slots stay fixed. Then (V1) with c = 0 gives g(\dots, \cvec{0}, \dots) = g(\dots, 0 \cdot \cvec{0}, \dots) = 0 \cdot g(\dots, \cvec{0}, \dots) = 0. Hence h(\M) = 0. Step 2: h(\M\E) = \lvert \det \E vert\, h(\M) for every elementary matrix \E. By @thm-row-op-is-left-multiplication and @thm-transpose-properties, \M\E = (\E	p \M	p)	p, and \E	p is the elementary matrix \P_{ij}, \D_i(c), or \I + c\E_{ji} when \E is \P_{ij}, \D_i(c), or \I + c\E_{ij}. So right multiplication by \E performs a column operation: swap columns i and j; multiply column i by c 
e 0; or add c times column i to column j. The determinants are \det \P_{ij} = -1, \det \D_i(c) = c, and \det(\I + c\E_{ij}) = 1 by @thm-det-row-operations. - For \E = \I + c\E_{ij}, (V2) gives h(\M\E) = h(\M) = \lvert 1 vert\, h(\M). - For \E = \D_i(c), (V1) gives h(\M\E) = \lvert c vert\, h(\M). - For \E = \P_{ij}, watch only slots i and j, holding \cvec{x} and \cvec{y}. By (V2) three times, (\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) 	o (\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}, \cvec{y}) 	o (\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}, -\cvec{x}) 	o (\cvec{y}, -\cvec{x}) leaves g unchanged, where the second step subtracts slot i from slot j and the third adds slot j to slot i. By (V1) with c = -1 on slot j, g at (\cvec{y}, \cvec{x}) equals \lvert -1 vert times g at (\cvec{y}, -\cvec{x}). Hence h(\M\P_{ij}) = h(\M) = \lvert -1 vert\, h(\M). Step 3: conclusion. If the columns of \M are dependent, then h(\M) = 0 by Step 1 and \det \M = 0 by @thm-alternating-properties, so h(\M) = \lvert \det \M vert. Otherwise \M is invertible by @thm-invertible-tfae, hence \M = \E_1\E_2\cdots \E_k is a product of elementary matrices by the same theorem. Applying Step 2 k times, starting from \I, and then (V3), h(\M) = h(\I\E_1\cdots \E_k) = \lvert \det \E_1 vert \cdots \lvert \det \E_k vert\, h(\I) = \lvert \det(\E_1\cdots \E_k) vert = \lvert \det \M vert, where the third equality uses @thm-det-multiplicative and \lvert xy vert = \lvert x vert \lvert y vert. This proves g = \vol. Finally, \vol satisfies (V1) because the determinant is linear in each column (@thm-leibniz-formula-alternating) and \lvert c\,d vert = \lvert c vert \lvert d vert; (V2) by @thm-alternating-properties; and (V3) because \det \I_n = 1. Agreement with area and volume from school. For n = 2, let g(\cvec{a}_1, \cvec{a}_2) be the area of the parallelogram P(\cvec{a}_1, \cvec{a}_2) in the sense of school geometry, base times height. The pictures of §1 are exactly (V1)–(V3) for this g: stretching a side by c stretches the base or the height by \lvert c vert; a shear \cvec{a}_1 \mapsto \cvec{a}_1 + c\cvec{a}_2 slides the opposite side along a line parallel to the base \cvec{a}_2, keeping base and height; and the unit square has area 1. Hence, by @thm-volume-characterization, school area equals \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a}_1 & \cvec{a}_2 \end{pmatrix} vert. For n = 3 the same argument works with “area of base times height”. What the theorem cannot supply is the geometric input itself: it takes the three rules as given. Agreement with Lebesgue measure. In measure theory, every reasonable subset S \subseteq 
R^n has an n-dimensional volume, its Lebesgue measure. One can prove that the Lebesgue measure of P(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) satisfies (V1)–(V3), and hence equals \vol(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n). We state this without proof; nothing in this book depends on it. Which of the rules (V1)–(V3) does the function g(\cvec{a}_1, \cvec{a}_2) = \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a}_1 & \cvec{a}_2 \end{pmatrix} vert^2 on 
R^2 break? It satisfies (V2), since shears do not change the determinant, and (V3), since 1^2 = 1. It breaks (V1): g(2\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = 4, while \lvert 2 vert\, g(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = 2. So the theorem does not apply, and indeed g 
e \vol. Linear maps scale volume Applying a linear map to a parallelepiped gives another parallelepiped: by linearity, T ig(\sum t_i\cvec{a}_i ig) = \sum t_iT\cvec{a}_i, so T(P(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n)) = P(T\cvec{a}_1, \dots, T\cvec{a}_n). How does the volume change? Multiplicativity answers this in one line, and the answer does not depend on the parallelepiped. [Linear Maps Scale Volume by \lvert \det vert] Let T \in \cL(
R^n) and \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n \in 
R^n. Then \vol(T\cvec{a}_1, \dots, T\cvec{a}_n) = \lvert \det T vert \cdot \vol(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n). In particular, the image of the unit cube under T has volume \lvert \det T vert. Let \B be the matrix of T in the standard basis, so T\cvec{x} = \B\cvec{x} for all \cvec{x} (@thm-matrix-of-map-coordinates) and \det T = \det \B (@def-det-operator). Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a}_1 & \cdots & \cvec{a}_n \end{pmatrix}. By @thm-three-views-of-product, \B\A =  egin{pmatrix} \B\cvec{a}_1 & \cdots & \B\cvec{a}_n \end{pmatrix}. By @thm-det-multiplicative, \vol(T\cvec{a}_1, \dots, T\cvec{a}_n) = \lvert \det(\B\A) vert = \lvert \det \B vert\,\lvert \det \A vert = \lvert \det T vert\,\vol(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n). For the unit cube take \cvec{a}_i = \cvec{e}_i, with \vol(\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n) = 1. This is the meaning of the determinant of a real operator: the factor by which it scales every volume. An operator with \det T = 0 squashes 
R^n into a lower-dimensional subspace, where n-dimensional volume is 0. In multivariable calculus the same fact, applied to the linear approximation of a smooth map, becomes the Jacobian factor \lvert \det \J vert in the change-of-variables formula for integrals. [Area of an Image] Let T \colon 
R^2 	o 
R^2 be T(x, y) = (3x + y,\ x + 2y). Find the area of the image of the unit square, and of the image of the parallelogram P((1, 1), (-1, 2)). The standard matrix is \B =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, with \det T = 6 - 1 = 5. By @thm-det-volume-scaling the image of the unit square, the parallelogram spanned by (3, 1) and (1, 2), has area 5. The parallelogram P((1, 1), (-1, 2)) has area \lvert 2 + 1 vert = 3, so its image has area 5 \cdot 3 = 15. Check directly: T(1, 1) = (4, 3) and T(-1, 2) = (-1, 3), and \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} 4 & -1 \ 3 & 3 \end{pmatrix} vert = \lvert 12 + 3 vert = 15. Orientation Now the sign. In 
R^2, the ordered basis (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) turns counterclockwise from its first vector to its second, while (\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1) turns clockwise. No rotation carries one arrangement to the other: a rotation of the plane keeps counterclockwise turns counterclockwise. The determinant sees the difference: \det egin{pmatrix} \cvec{e}_1 & \cvec{e}_2 \end{pmatrix} = 1 > 0 and \det egin{pmatrix} \cvec{e}_2 & \cvec{e}_1 \end{pmatrix} = -1 < 0. To compare two bases of an arbitrary real space, we compare them with each other rather than with a fixed standard basis, using the change-of-coordinates matrix of Chapter 4. Two bases have the same orientation when the matrix converting one into the other has positive determinant. Orientation Let V be a vector space over 
R with \dim V = n \ge 1, and let \sB and \sC be ordered bases of V. We say \sB and \sC have the same orientation if \det \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} > 0, and opposite orientations if \det\mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} < 0. In words: write each vector of \sB in coordinates with respect to \sC, put the coordinate columns side by side (@def-change-of-coordinates-matrix), and look at the sign of the determinant. Exactly one of the two cases occurs, because \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} is invertible (@thm-change-of-coordinates (c)), so its determinant is nonzero (@thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible), and a nonzero real number is either positive or negative. The bases must be ordered: reordering a basis can change the answer. For V = 
R^n there is a shortcut. If \B and \C are the matrices whose columns are the vectors of \sB and \sC, then \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sE} = \B and \mtx{\id}{\sC}{\sE} = \C for the standard basis \sE. By @thm-change-of-coordinates (b) and (c), \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} = \C^{-1}\B. Since \det \C\,\det \C^{-1} = \det \I = 1 (@thm-det-multiplicative), \det\mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} = \det \B / \det \C. So \sB and \sC have the same orientation if and only if \det \B and \det \C have the same sign. Examples. - In 
R^2, (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) and (\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1) have opposite orientations: \det \I_2 = 1 and \det egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = -1. - In 
R^3, (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3) and (\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3, \cvec{e}_1) have the same orientation. The second matrix is the permutation matrix of a 3-cycle, whose sign is (-1)^{3-1} = 1. A cyclic shift of three vectors is two swaps. - In V = 
R[x]_{\le 1}, the bases \sB = (1, x) and \sC = (x, 1 + x) have 1 = -x + (1 + x) and x = x + 0 \cdot (1 + x), so \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, with determinant -1. They have opposite orientations. Orientation makes sense in any real space, with no picture at all. - Degenerate case, n = 1. Bases of 
R are single nonzero numbers (a), and \mtx{\id}{(a)}{(b)} = (a/b). So (a) and (b) have the same orientation exactly when a and b have the same sign. The two orientations of a line are its two directions. Nonexample by minimal change. In 
R^2, (-\cvec{e}_1, -\cvec{e}_2) has the same orientation as (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2): \det(-\I_2) = 1, and indeed it is the rotation of (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) by a half-turn. Change only one sign, to (\cvec{e}_1, -\cvec{e}_2): the determinant becomes -1, and the orientation flips. What changed is the sign of the determinant, which is the whole content of the definition. In 
R^3, by contrast, -\I_3 has determinant -1: negating all three vectors reverses orientation. Why this definition. Using the change-of-coordinates matrix, rather than the matrices \B and \C above, makes the definition work in every real space, including spaces like 
R[x]_{\le 1} that have no standard picture. Requiring \det > 0 rather than \det = 1 is what gives a coarse, two-valued answer: rescaling a basis vector by a positive number should not change its handedness. The payoff is that “same orientation” really sorts all bases into two families, as the pictures suggest. [There Are Exactly Two Orientations] Let V be a vector space over 
R with \dim V = n \ge 1. 1. “Having the same orientation” is an equivalence relation on the set of ordered bases of V. 2. It has exactly two equivalence classes. If \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n), then \sB^- = (-\elem{v}_1, \elem{v}_2, \dots, \elem{v}_n) lies in the class not containing \sB. The three axioms are three facts about change-of-coordinates matrices: \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sB} = \I; the matrix back is the inverse; and matrices compose along a chain \sB 	o \sC 	o \sD. Determinants turn these into 1 > 0, 1/	ext{positive} > 0, and 	ext{positive} \cdot 	ext{positive} > 0. For “exactly two”, flipping one vector gives a second class, and “negative times negative is positive” shows there is no third. Write d(\sB, \sC) = \det\mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC}. By @thm-change-of-coordinates (b) and @thm-det-multiplicative, for bases \sB, \sC, \sD, d(\sB, \sD) = d(\sC, \sD)\, d(\sB, \sC). 	ag{$\ast$} (a) Reflexive: \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sB} = \I_n, so d(\sB, \sB) = 1 > 0. Symmetric: by (\ast) with \sD = \sB, d(\sC, \sB)\,d(\sB, \sC) = d(\sB, \sB) = 1, so d(\sC, \sB) = 1/d(\sB, \sC), which is positive when d(\sB, \sC) is. Transitive: if d(\sB, \sC) > 0 and d(\sC, \sD) > 0, then d(\sB, \sD) > 0 by (\ast), since a product of positive reals is positive. By @def-equivalence-relation, this is an equivalence relation. (b) At least two classes. \sB^- is a basis, and \mtx{\id}{\sB^-}{\sB} = \diag(-1, 1, \dots, 1), because -\elem{v}_1 = (-1)\elem{v}_1 and \elem{v}_j = 1 \cdot \elem{v}_j. Its determinant is -1 by @thm-det-triangular. So d(\sB^-, \sB) < 0, and \sB^- and \sB lie in different classes. At most two classes. Let \sC and \sD be bases, neither of which has the same orientation as \sB. Then d(\sC, \sB) < 0 and d(\sD, \sB) < 0, and by symmetry d(\sB, \sD) < 0 as well. By (\ast), d(\sC, \sD) = d(\sB, \sD)\,d(\sC, \sB) is a product of two negative reals, hence positive. So all bases outside the class of \sB lie in one class, and there are exactly two classes. Choosing one of the two classes is called orienting V; its bases are then called positively oriented, and the others negatively oriented. On 
R^n the standard choice is the class of (\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n). By the shortcut above, (\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) is positively oriented if and only if \det egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a}_1 & \cdots & \cvec{a}_n \end{pmatrix} > 0. So the determinant of a real square matrix carries two independent pieces of information: its absolute value is a volume, and its sign is an orientation. Orientation needs 
R. The proof used two facts about the reals: every nonzero number is positive or negative, and products and inverses of positive numbers are positive. Over 
C there is no such splitting. Suppose we tried “\sB and \sC have the same orientation if d(\sB, \sC) has positive real part”. In 
C^1, with z = e^{i\pi/3}, the bases (\cvec{e}_1), (z\cvec{e}_1), (z^2\cvec{e}_1) give d((\cvec{e}_1), (z\cvec{e}_1)) = z^{-1} and d((z\cvec{e}_1), (z^2\cvec{e}_1)) = z^{-1}, both with real part  rac12 > 0, but d((\cvec{e}_1), (z^2\cvec{e}_1)) = z^{-2} has real part - rac12: transitivity fails. Over 
F_2, -1 = 1, so the second basis \sB^- of the proof is \sB itself. The theorem holds verbatim over any field with a compatible order, such as 
Q, but not over 
C or a finite field. Do ((1, 2), (3, 4)) and ((3, 4), (1, 2)) have the same orientation? Does ((1, 2), (3, 4)) have the standard orientation of 
R^2? \det egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} = 4 - 6 = -2 and \det egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = 6 - 4 = 2. The signs differ, so the two bases have opposite orientations. The first has negative determinant, so it is negatively oriented: it is not in the class of (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2). The right-hand rule In 
R^3, the standard orientation is the one described by the right hand: curl the fingers of the right hand from the first basis vector toward the second, and the thumb points along the third. For (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3) with the usual picture of the axes, this is the familiar arrangement below. The cross product of \cvec{a} = (a_1, a_2, a_3) and \cvec{b} = (b_1, b_2, b_3) in 
R^3 is \cvec{a} 	imes \cvec{b} \coloneqq (a_2b_3 - a_3b_2,\ a_3b_1 - a_1b_3,\ a_1b_2 - a_2b_1). Physics defines it by the right-hand rule. Here is the linear-algebra reason the two descriptions match: (\cvec{a}, \cvec{b}, \cvec{a} 	imes \cvec{b}) is always positively oriented. Expand \det egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a} & \cvec{b} & \cvec{a} 	imes \cvec{b} \end{pmatrix} along its third column (@thm-laplace-expansion). The cofactors of that column are C_{13} = a_2b_3 - a_3b_2, C_{23} = -(a_1b_3 - a_3b_1) and C_{33} = a_1b_2 - a_2b_1, which are exactly the three components of \cvec{a} 	imes \cvec{b}. Hence \det egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a} & \cvec{b} & \cvec{a} 	imes \cvec{b} \end{pmatrix} = (a_2b_3 - a_3b_2)^2 + (a_3b_1 - a_1b_3)^2 + (a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)^2 \ \ge\ 0 . If \cvec{a} and \cvec{b} are linearly independent, the 3 	imes 2 matrix  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a} & \cvec{b} \end{pmatrix} has rank 2, so one of its 2 	imes 2 minors, which are \pm the components of \cvec{a} 	imes \cvec{b}, is nonzero (@thm-rank-via-minors). Then the determinant is strictly positive, so (\cvec{a}, \cvec{b}, \cvec{a} 	imes \cvec{b}) is a basis (@thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible) with the standard orientation. For example, \cvec{e}_1 	imes \cvec{e}_2 = (0, 0, 1) = \cvec{e}_3, matching the picture. Orientation-preserving maps An invertible operator carries each basis to a basis. Does it keep the orientation? The answer is the same for every basis and depends only on the sign of \det T. [Determinant Sign and Orientation] Let V be a vector space over 
R with \dim V = n \ge 1, let T \in \cL(V) be invertible, and let \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) be any basis of V. Then T\sB = (T\elem{v}_1, \dots, T\elem{v}_n) is a basis of V, and \mtx{\id}{T\sB}{\sB} = \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}. Hence \sB and T\sB have the same orientation if and only if \det T > 0, and this does not depend on \sB. Since T is invertible, it is an isomorphism, so T\sB is a basis by @thm-isomorphism-preserves-bases. By @def-change-of-coordinates-matrix, column j of \mtx{\id}{T\sB}{\sB} is \coord{T\elem{v}_j}{\sB}, which is column j of \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} by @def-matrix-of-linear-map. Hence the two matrices are equal, and by @def-det-operator, \det\mtx{\id}{T\sB}{\sB} = \det T. By @def-orientation and the symmetry in @thm-two-orientations (a), \sB and T\sB have the same orientation exactly when \det T > 0. An invertible operator with \det T > 0 is orientation-preserving, and one with \det T < 0 is orientation-reversing. Rotations of the plane preserve orientation and reflections reverse it (@exr-orientation-and-volume-c2). In 
R^3, the map \cvec{x} \mapsto -\cvec{x} reverses orientation, since \det(-\I_3) = -1: a right hand, pushed through the origin, becomes a left hand. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the definition of the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n \in 
R^n, and say what it is when the vectors are dependent. 2. True or false: \vol(\cvec{a}_1 + \cvec{b}, \cvec{a}_2, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) = \vol(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) + \vol(\cvec{b}, \cvec{a}_2, \dots, \cvec{a}_n). Justify your answer. 3. Which three rules characterize volume in @thm-volume-characterization? 4. True or false: if \det T = -2, then T doubles every volume. Justify your answer. 5. Define “same orientation” for two ordered bases of a real vector space. 6. True or false: for every n \ge 1, the map \cvec{x} \mapsto -\cvec{x} on 
R^n reverses orientation. Justify your answer. (a) \vol(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n) = \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a}_1 & \cdots & \cvec{a}_n \end{pmatrix} vert (@def-parallelepiped-volume). For dependent vectors it is 0, by @thm-alternating-properties. (b) False. With n = 2, \cvec{a}_1 = \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{b} = -\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{a}_2 = \cvec{e}_2: the left side is \vol(\cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_2) = 0, the right side is 1 + 1 = 2. The absolute value destroys additivity. (c) (V1) scaling one vector by c scales the volume by \lvert c vert; (V2) adding a multiple of one vector to another does not change it; (V3) the unit cube has volume 1. (d) True. By @thm-det-volume-scaling, \vol(T\cvec{a}_1, \dots, T\cvec{a}_n) = \lvert -2 vert \vol(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n). The sign only affects orientation. (e) \sB and \sC have the same orientation if \det\mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} > 0 (@def-orientation). (f) False. \det(-\I_n) = (-1)^n, so by @prp-orientation-preserving the map reverses orientation for odd n and preserves it for even n. In 
R^2 it is the rotation by a half-turn. B. Practice [B1: Volume of a parallelepiped] Find the volume of the parallelepiped in 
R^3 spanned by (2, 1, 0), (1, 3, 1), and (0, 1, 1). Hence find the volume of its image under the map T(x, y, z) = (x + y,\ y + z,\ 2z). Expanding along the first row, \det egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 3 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = 2(3 - 1) - 1\cdot(1 - 0) + 0 = 3, so the volume is 3. The standard matrix of T is  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, upper triangular with determinant 2 (@thm-det-triangular). By @thm-det-volume-scaling the image has volume 2 \cdot 3 = 6. [B2: Comparing orientations] In 
R^3, let  egin{aligned} \sB &= ((1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1), (1, 0, 1)), \ \sC &= ((0, 1, 0), (1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 1)), \ \sD &= ((1, 0, 1), (1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1)). \end{aligned} Determine which pairs have the same orientation, and which are positively oriented. Justify your answer. By the shortcut after @def-orientation, compare signs of the determinants of the matrices with these columns. Expanding along the first row: \det egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = 1\cdot(1 - 0) - 0 + 1\cdot(1 - 0) = 2, \qquad \det egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = -1, the second by expanding along the last row: 1 \cdot \det egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = -1. The list \sD is \sB shifted cyclically, (\cvec{b}_3, \cvec{b}_1, \cvec{b}_2); moving the last column to the front takes two column swaps, so by @thm-alternating-properties its determinant is (-1)^2 \cdot 2 = 2. Hence \sB and \sD are positively oriented and have the same orientation; \sC is negatively oriented, opposite to both. [B3: Areas of images] Let T(x, y) = (2x + y,\ -x + 3y) on 
R^2. 1. Find the area of the image of the unit square under T. 2. Find the area of the image of the parallelogram P((1, 0), (1, 2)), first by @thm-det-volume-scaling and then directly. 3. Is T orientation-preserving? (a) The standard matrix  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} has determinant 6 + 1 = 7, so the image of the unit square has area 7. (b) \vol((1, 0), (1, 2)) = \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} vert = 2, so the image has area 7 \cdot 2 = 14. Directly, T(1, 0) = (2, -1) and T(1, 2) = (4, 5), and \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \ -1 & 5 \end{pmatrix} vert = \lvert 10 + 4 vert = 14. (c) Yes: \det T = 7 > 0, so by @prp-orientation-preserving T preserves orientation. C. Going deeper [C1: Area of a triangle in space] For \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \in 
R^3, let \A =  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{u} & \cvec{v} \end{pmatrix} \in M_{3 	imes 2}(
R). We define the area of the parallelogram P(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) \subseteq 
R^3 to be \sqrt{\det(\A	p \A)}; Chapter 13 justifies this with inner products, where \det(\A	p\A) is recognized as a Gram determinant. 1. Show that \det(\A	p \A) \ge 0, so the square root exists, and that \det(\A	p \A) = (u_2v_3 - u_3v_2)^2 + (u_3v_1 - u_1v_3)^2 + (u_1v_2 - u_2v_1)^2. 2. Show that if \cvec{u} and \cvec{v} lie in the plane z = 0, this area equals the area \vol((u_1, u_2), (v_1, v_2)) of @def-parallelepiped-volume in 
R^2. 3. Find the area of the triangle with vertices (1, 0, 0), (0, 2, 0), (0, 0, 3). Hint: apply @cor-gram-determinant-nonnegative to \A	p. (a) \A	p \in M_{2 	imes 3}(
R) and (\A	p)	p = \A, so by @cor-gram-determinant-nonnegative applied to \A	p, \det(\A	p \A) = \sum_{|S| = 2} (\det (\A	p)_{[2],S})^2 \ge 0. The 2 	imes 2 minors of \A	p =  egin{pmatrix} u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \end{pmatrix} are u_1v_2 - u_2v_1, u_1v_3 - u_3v_1, u_2v_3 - u_3v_2 for S = \{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{2,3\}; squaring removes the signs, giving the stated sum. (b) If u_3 = v_3 = 0, two of the three squares vanish, and \det(\A	p \A) = (u_1v_2 - u_2v_1)^2. Hence \sqrt{\det(\A	p \A)} = \lvert u_1v_2 - u_2v_1 vert = \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} u_1 & v_1 \ u_2 & v_2 \end{pmatrix} vert, which is \vol((u_1, u_2), (v_1, v_2)). (c) The triangle is half of the parallelogram spanned by \cvec{u} = (0, 2, 0) - (1, 0, 0) = (-1, 2, 0) and \cvec{v} = (0, 0, 3) - (1, 0, 0) = (-1, 0, 3). By (a), \det(\A	p \A) = (6 - 0)^2 + (0 + 3)^2 + (0 + 2)^2 = 36 + 9 + 4 = 49. As a check, \A	p \A =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 1 \ 1 & 10 \end{pmatrix} has determinant 50 - 1 = 49. So the parallelogram has area 7, and the triangle has area  rac72. [C2: Rotations and reflections] For 	heta \in 
R, let \R_	heta =  egin{pmatrix} \cos	heta & -\sin	heta \ \sin	heta & \cos	heta \end{pmatrix} (rotation by 	heta) and \S_	heta =  egin{pmatrix} \cos 2	heta & \sin 2	heta \ \sin 2	heta & -\cos 2	heta \end{pmatrix} (reflection in the line through 0 at angle 	heta). 1. Show that every rotation preserves orientation and area, and every reflection reverses orientation and preserves area. 2. Show that \S_	heta \S_\varphi is orientation-preserving for all 	heta, \varphi. (It is in fact a rotation, but you need not show this.) 3. Prove that no \M \in M_2(
R) satisfies \M^2 = \S_0 = \diag(1, -1). Does the same argument rule out \M^2 = -\I_2? (a) \det \R_	heta = \cos^2	heta + \sin^2	heta = 1 > 0 and \det \S_	heta = -\cos^2 2	heta - \sin^2 2	heta = -1 < 0. By @prp-orientation-preserving, rotations preserve and reflections reverse orientation. Both have \lvert \det vert = 1, so both preserve area by @thm-det-volume-scaling. (b) By @thm-det-multiplicative, \det(\S_	heta \S_\varphi) = (-1)(-1) = 1 > 0. (c) If \M^2 = \S_0, then (\det \M)^2 = \det \S_0 = -1 by @thm-det-multiplicative, impossible for a real number \det \M. The argument says nothing about -\I_2, since \det(-\I_2) = 1; and indeed \R_{\pi/2}^2 = \R_{\pi/2}\R_{\pi/2} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}^2 = -\I_2. An orientation-reversing map can never be the square of a real map, since the square of anything preserves orientation.

title: 7.10 The Characteristic Polynomial
content:
The Characteristic Polynomial For a square matrix \A over F and a scalar c \in F, when is c\I - \A invertible? The question matters: c\I - \A fails to be invertible exactly when \A\cvec{v} = c\cvec{v} for some nonzero vector \cvec{v}, the situation Chapter 9 is built around. The determinant answers the question for each single c. This section lets c vary. Replacing the number c by a variable x turns \det(c\I - \A) into a polynomial, the characteristic polynomial, and the scalars we are looking for become its roots. The price is that x\I - \A is a matrix of polynomials, not of field elements, so we must check which determinant facts survive there. The remarks at the ends of §4, §5, and §6 did exactly that bookkeeping, and here we cash them in. From a number to a variable Take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
Q). For each c \in 
Q, \det(c\I - \A) = \det egin{pmatrix} c - 1 & -2 \ -3 & c - 4 \end{pmatrix} = (c - 1)(c - 4) - 6 = c^2 - 5c - 2 . The same expression c^2 - 5c - 2 appears whatever c is. It is the value at c of one polynomial, and that polynomial deserves a name. To define it directly, without first choosing c, we put the variable x into the matrix and take the determinant of x\I - \A =  egin{pmatrix} x - 1 & -2 \ -3 & x - 4 \end{pmatrix}, a matrix whose entries lie in F[x]. Is that allowed? F[x] is not a field, but it is a commutative ring in the sense of the remark in §4: all the field axioms hold except the existence of inverses (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws). The Leibniz formula of @def-determinant uses only sums, differences and products of entries, so it defines \det \M \in F[x] for every \M \in M_n(F[x]). The characteristic polynomial of \A is the determinant of x\I - \A, computed with polynomial entries. [Characteristic Polynomial] Let n \ge 1 and \A = (a_{ij}) \in M_n(F). The characteristic polynomial of \A is p_{\A}(x) \coloneqq \det(x\I_n - \A) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \prod_{j=1}^{n}  ig(x\,\delta_{\sigma(j)j} - a_{\sigma(j)j} ig) \ \in F[x], where \delta_{ij} = 1 if i = j and 0 otherwise, so that x\delta_{ij} - a_{ij} is the (i, j)-entry of x\I_n - \A. The determinant is the Leibniz sum of @def-determinant, computed in the commutative ring F[x]. In words: subtract \A from x times the identity, so that x appears only on the diagonal; then take the determinant exactly as for a matrix of numbers, multiplying and adding polynomials instead of scalars. The result is one polynomial, not a number. Well-definedness. Each term of the Leibniz sum is a product of n polynomials, and the sum is finite, so p_{\A} is a polynomial. It depends only on \A. How to compute it. By the remarks in §4, §5, and §6, the following results were proved without dividing, and so hold for matrices over F[x]: @thm-det-transpose and @thm-det-triangular (§4), @thm-det-multiplicative by its first proof (§5), @thm-laplace-expansion (§6), and @thm-det-block-triangular (§8). So we may expand \det(x\I - \A) along any row or column, and read it off from triangular or block triangular shape. What we may not do is row reduce x\I - \A by dividing by a polynomial entry, as the warning below explains. Examples. - 1 	imes 1. For \A = (a), p_{\A}(x) = x - a. - 2 	imes 2. For \A =  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{pmatrix},  egin{aligned} p_{\A}(x) &= (x - a)(x - d) - bc = x^2 - (a + d)x + (ad - bc) \ &= x^2 - (	r \A)\,x + \det \A . \end{aligned} For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} this is x^2 - 5x - 2, as above. - Triangular. If \A is upper or lower triangular, so is x\I - \A, with diagonal entries x - a_{ii}. By @thm-det-triangular over F[x], p_{\A}(x) = (x - a_{11})(x - a_{22})\cdots(x - a_{nn}). - Degenerate cases. The zero matrix has p_{\O}(x) = x^n, and the identity has p_{\I_n}(x) = (x - 1)^n; both are triangular. These two polynomials are different, although both matrices are as simple as possible, which already shows that p_{\A} records something about \A. [A 3 	imes 3 Characteristic Polynomial] Find p_{\A} for \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 3 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(
Q). We have x\I - \A =  egin{pmatrix} x - 2 & 0 & -1 \ -1 & x - 3 & -1 \ -1 & 0 & x - 2 \end{pmatrix}. Column 2 has a single nonzero entry, x - 3 in position (2, 2). Expanding along it (@thm-laplace-expansion over F[x]),  egin{aligned} p_{\A}(x) &= (x - 3)\,(-1)^{2+2}\det egin{pmatrix} x - 2 & -1 \ -1 & x - 2 \end{pmatrix} \ &= (x - 3) ig((x - 2)^2 - 1 ig) = (x - 1)(x - 3)^2 . \end{aligned} Multiplied out, p_{\A}(x) = x^3 - 7x^2 + 15x - 9. Compare with 	r \A = 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 and \det \A = 9 (expand \A along column 2: 3(4 - 1) = 9). A companion-type example. Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 6 \ 1 & 0 & -11 \ 0 & 1 & 6 \end{pmatrix}, with ones just below the diagonal, a last column (6, -11, 6), and zeros elsewhere. Expanding x\I - \A =  egin{pmatrix} x & 0 & -6 \ -1 & x & 11 \ 0 & -1 & x - 6 \end{pmatrix} along the first row (@thm-laplace-expansion over F[x]),  egin{aligned} p_{\A}(x) &= x\det egin{pmatrix} x & 11 \ -1 & x - 6 \end{pmatrix} + (-6)\det egin{pmatrix} -1 & x \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \ &= x(x^2 - 6x + 11) - 6 = x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 , \end{aligned} which factors as (x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3). The last column of \A lists the coefficients -6, 11, -6 of 1, x, x^2 in p_{\A}, with their signs changed. This is no accident: @exr-characteristic-polynomial-c1 shows that the same pattern works in every size. Nonexample by minimal change. Swap the order of subtraction: \det(\A - x\I). Each of the n columns of \A - x\I is -1 times the corresponding column of x\I - \A, so by multilinearity \det(\A - x\I) = (-1)^n p_{\A}(x). For \A = (a) this is a - x, whose leading coefficient is -1. What still works: the roots are the same. What fails: the result is not monic when n is odd. Why this definition. Some books use \det(\A - x\I). We use x\I - \A so that the characteristic polynomial is always monic (@thm-charpoly-coefficients below), which makes statements like “p_{\A} = (x - 1)(x - 3)^2” true without sign bookkeeping. The name comes from the fact that the roots of this polynomial are the “characteristic values” of \A, which Chapter 9 calls eigenvalues. Do not row reduce x\I - \A by dividing by polynomials. Over a field, a matrix with nonzero determinant is invertible (@thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible), but that proof runs through elimination, which divides by pivots, and it fails over F[x]. For \A = \O_1 \in M_1(F), the matrix x\I - \A = (x) has determinant x 
e 0, yet it has no inverse in M_1(F[x]): if x\,q(x) = 1 for a polynomial q, then q 
e 0, and 1 + \deg q = \deg 1 = 0 by @thm-degree-of-product, which is impossible since \deg q \ge 0. Likewise, “divide row 1 of x\I - \A by x - 1” produces entries that are not polynomials and that make no sense at x = 1. Compute p_{\A} by expansion, by triangular or block shape, or by the Leibniz formula. Before looking at the coefficients, we record the fact that makes p_{\A} useful: evaluating it at a scalar c gives the same result as putting c in place of x before taking the determinant. [Evaluating the Characteristic Polynomial] Let \A \in M_n(F) and c \in F. Then p_{\A}(c) = \det(c\I_n - \A). By @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, evaluation at c turns sums of polynomials into sums and products into products, and sends a constant a to a. Applying it to the Leibniz sum in @def-characteristic-polynomial term by term, p_{\A}(c) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma)\prod_{j=1}^{n} ig(c\,\delta_{\sigma(j)j} - a_{\sigma(j)j} ig), and c\,\delta_{ij} - a_{ij} is the (i, j)-entry of c\I_n - \A. By @def-determinant, the right side is \det(c\I_n - \A). The shape of the characteristic polynomial The 2 	imes 2 example suggests a pattern: the leading coefficient is 1, the next coefficient is minus the trace, and the constant term is the determinant up to sign. The same holds in every size. [Coefficients of the Characteristic Polynomial] Let n \ge 1 and \A \in M_n(F). Then p_{\A} is monic of degree n, and p_{\A}(x) = x^n - (	r \A)\,x^{n-1} + \dots + (-1)^n\det \A, that is, the coefficient of x^{n-1} is -	r \A and the constant term is (-1)^n\det \A. (For n = 1 these two statements concern the same coefficient, and both say it is -a_{11}.) Look at the Leibniz sum term by term and count powers of x. A factor x\delta_{\sigma(j)j} - a_{\sigma(j)j} contains x only if \sigma(j) = j. A permutation other than the identity moves at least two indices, so its term has degree at most n - 2 and cannot affect the top two coefficients. The identity contributes \prod_j(x - a_{jj}), whose top two coefficients are 1 and -\sum_j a_{jj}. For the constant term, set x = 0. Write m_{ij} = x\delta_{ij} - a_{ij} for the entries of x\I - \A. By @def-characteristic-polynomial, p_{\A} = \sum_{\sigma} t_\sigma with t_\sigma = \sgn(\sigma)\prod_{j} m_{\sigma(j)j}. Terms with \sigma 
e \id. If \sigma(j) 
e j for some j, then \sigma(\sigma(j)) 
e \sigma(j), because \sigma is injective. So \sigma moves at least two indices, and at most n - 2 indices are fixed. For a moved index j, m_{\sigma(j)j} = -a_{\sigma(j)j} has degree at most 0; for a fixed index it has degree at most 1. By @thm-degree-of-product, \deg t_\sigma \le n - 2. The term \sigma = \id. We show by induction on k \ge 1 that \prod_{j=1}^{k}(x - a_{jj}) = x^k - s_kx^{k-1} + r_k with s_k = a_{11} + \dots + a_{kk} and \deg r_k \le k - 2. For k = 1, take r_1 = 0. If it holds for k, then with a = a_{k+1,k+1}, (x^k - s_kx^{k-1} + r_k)(x - a) = x^{k+1} - (s_k + a)x^k +  ig(s_kax^{k-1} + r_kx - ar_k ig), and the bracket has degree at most k - 1 by @thm-degree-of-sum and @thm-degree-of-product. This completes the induction. Since \sgn(\id) = 1, t_{\id} = x^n - (	r \A)\,x^{n-1} + r_n with \deg r_n \le n - 2. Adding, p_{\A} = x^n - (	r \A)\,x^{n-1} +  ig(r_n + \sum_{\sigma 
e \id} t_\sigma ig), and the bracket has degree at most n - 2 by @thm-degree-of-sum. Hence p_{\A} is monic of degree n, with coefficient -	r \A at x^{n-1} (@def-trace). Constant term. The constant term of a polynomial is its value at 0 (@def-polynomial-evaluation). By @lem-charpoly-evaluation with c = 0, p_{\A}(0) = \det(-\A). The matrix -\A is obtained from \A by multiplying each of its n columns by -1, so \det(-\A) = (-1)^n\det \A by @thm-det-row-operations (d). This proves the theorem. So the characteristic polynomial packages two invariants we already know, the trace and the determinant, and adds n - 2 more coefficients in between. For n = 2 nothing is in between, which is why p_{\A}(x) = x^2 - (	r \A)x + \det \A for every 2 	imes 2 matrix. Without expanding any determinant, find the coefficient of x^2 and the constant term of p_{\A} for \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, given that \det \A = 2. By @thm-charpoly-coefficients, the coefficient of x^2 is -	r \A = 0, and the constant term is (-1)^3\det \A = -2. (In full, p_{\A}(x) = x^3 - 3x - 2 = (x - 2)(x + 1)^2.) Similar matrices, same polynomial Similar matrices describe the same operator in different bases (@thm-similar-iff-same-operator), so everything intrinsic to the operator should agree for them. The trace and determinant do (@thm-trace-similarity-invariant, @cor-det-similarity-invariant). The characteristic polynomial, which contains both, does too, and the proof is the proof for the determinant, run over F[x]. [Similar Matrices Have the Same Characteristic Polynomial] If \A, \B \in M_n(F) are similar, then p_{\A} = p_{\B}. Let \B = \P^{-1}\A\P with \P \in M_n(F) invertible. Regard \P, \P^{-1}, \A, and \I as matrices over F[x] whose entries happen to be constants. The laws of matrix arithmetic in @thm-matrix-multiplication-properties are proved from the ring axioms alone, so they hold in M_n(F[x]). Hence \P^{-1}(x\I - \A)\P = x\,\P^{-1}\P - \P^{-1}\A\P = x\I - \B . By @thm-det-multiplicative, valid over F[x] by the remark in §5,  egin{aligned} p_{\B} &= \det ig(\P^{-1}(x\I - \A)\P ig) = \det(\P^{-1})\,\det(x\I - \A)\,\det \P \ &= \det(\P^{-1})\det(\P)\; p_{\A} , \end{aligned} using commutativity of F[x] in the last step. Finally \det(\P^{-1})\det \P = \det(\P^{-1}\P) = \det \I = 1 by @thm-det-multiplicative over F. Hence p_{\B} = p_{\A}. This is exactly the case singled out in the remark in §5: the proof of @cor-det-similarity-invariant survives over F[x] because \P is invertible already over F. The theorem lets us attach a characteristic polynomial to an operator. [Characteristic Polynomial of an Operator] Let V be a vector space over F with \dim V = n \ge 1, and let T \in \cL(V). The characteristic polynomial of T is p_T(x) \coloneqq p_{\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}}(x) = \det ig(x\I_n - \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} ig), where \sB is any basis of V. This does not depend on \sB: for bases \sB and \sC, the matrices \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} and \mtx{T}{\sC}{\sC} are similar by @thm-similar-iff-same-operator (a), so they have the same characteristic polynomial by @thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant. By @thm-charpoly-coefficients, p_T is monic of degree \dim V, with coefficient -	r T at x^{n-1} and constant term (-1)^n\det T (@def-trace-operator, @def-det-operator). [Characteristic Polynomials of Two Operators] On V = 
R[x]_{\le 2}, find the characteristic polynomials of differentiation D(q) = q' and of the shift S(q)(x) = q(x + 1). Use the basis \sB = (1, x, x^2). Since D(1) = 0, D(x) = 1, D(x^2) = 2x, and S(1) = 1, S(x) = 1 + x, S(x^2) = 1 + 2x + x^2, \mtx{D}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mtx{S}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Both are upper triangular, so p_D(t) = t^3 and p_S(t) = (t - 1)^3. (We name the variable t here, since x is already the variable of the polynomials in V.) As a check, 	r S = 3 and \det S = 1, matching the coefficient -3 of t^2 and the constant term (-1)^3 \cdot 1. Equal characteristic polynomials do not make matrices similar. The converse of @thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant is false. Recall the pair from the warning in Chapter 4, §02: \I_2 and \J =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} both have characteristic polynomial (x - 1)^2, since both are triangular with diagonal 1, 1. But \I_2 is similar only to itself, so \J 
ot\sim \I_2. In particular the characteristic polynomial does not determine the matrix, not even up to similarity. Deciding similarity needs finer invariants; Chapter 10 finds a complete set. Roots and singular matrices We can now answer the opening question. The determinant tests invertibility of c\I - \A for one c at a time; the characteristic polynomial tests all c at once, and the answer is a finite set. [Roots of the Characteristic Polynomial] Let \A \in M_n(F) with n \ge 1, and let c \in F. 1. The following are equivalent: (i) p_{\A}(c) = 0; (ii) c\I - \A is not invertible; (iii) there is a nonzero \cvec{v} \in F^n with \A\cvec{v} = c\cvec{v}. 2. There are at most n scalars c \in F with these properties. (a) By @lem-charpoly-evaluation, p_{\A}(c) = \det(c\I - \A), which is a determinant of a matrix over the field F. By @thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible, it is zero if and only if c\I - \A is not invertible; this is (i) \Leftrightarrow (ii). By @thm-invertible-tfae, c\I - \A is not invertible if and only if (c\I - \A)\cvec{v} = \cvec{0} for some \cvec{v} 
e \cvec{0}, and (c\I - \A)\cvec{v} = c\cvec{v} - \A\cvec{v} by @thm-matrix-multiplication-properties; this is (ii) \Leftrightarrow (iii). (b) By @thm-charpoly-coefficients, p_{\A} is monic of degree n, in particular nonzero. By @cor-root-bound-general, it has at most n distinct roots in F, and by (a) these are exactly the scalars in question. Notice where the evaluation happens: first substitute c, getting a matrix over the field F, then use the invertibility test, which is valid over fields. That order is what the warning about F[x] above requires. The same holds for an operator T on V with \dim V = n \ge 1: p_T(c) = 0 if and only if c\,\id_V - T is not invertible, by (a) applied to \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} together with @thm-rank-map-equals-rank-matrix (b), since \mtx{c\,\id_V - T}{\sB}{\sB} = c\I - \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}. The scalars c of this theorem are the eigenvalues of \A, and the vectors \cvec{v} in (iii) its eigenvectors. They are the subject of Chapter 9, which starts from this theorem. Examples. - For \A in @exm-charpoly-small, p_{\A} = (x - 1)(x - 3)^2, so c\I - \A is singular exactly for c = 1 and c = 3. For instance 3\I - \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \ -1 & 0 & -1 \ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has a zero column, and \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_2 satisfies \A\cvec{e}_2 = 3\cvec{e}_2. - The rotation \R =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has p_{\R} = x^2 + 1. Over 
R this has no root, so c\I - \R is invertible for every real c: no nonzero real vector is merely stretched by a quarter-turn. Over 
C, the roots \pm i appear, and for example \R(1, -i) = (i, 1) = i\,(1, -i). The field matters. For which c \in 
Q is c\I - \A invertible, where \A =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & -2 \ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}? p_{\A}(x) = x^2 - (	r \A)x + \det \A = x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3). By @thm-charpoly-root-iff-singular, c\I - \A is invertible exactly for c 
e 2, 3. A tempting false proof Here is a statement that is true, and important: every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial, p_{\A}(\A) = \O. This is the Cayley–Hamilton Theorem, proved in Chapter 9. Here p_{\A}(\A) means substituting the matrix \A into the polynomial p_{\A}, replacing each x^k by \A^k and the constant term a_0 by a_0\I (@def-polynomial-of-matrix). For a 2 	imes 2 matrix it says \A^2 - (	r \A)\A + (\det \A)\I = \O, which you can check by multiplying out. A one-line “proof” suggests itself, and it is wrong. The fake proof of Cayley–Hamilton. “Since p_{\A}(x) = \det(x\I - \A), put x = \A: p_{\A}(\A) = \det(\A\I - \A) = \det(\O) = 0.” This is invalid for two reasons. First, the two sides are different kinds of object: p_{\A}(\A) is an n 	imes n matrix, while \det(\cdots) is a scalar, so “= 0” compares a matrix with a number. Second, @lem-charpoly-evaluation lets us substitute only a scalar c \in F into the entries of x\I - \A. Substituting a matrix for x inside the entries would produce a matrix whose entries are matrices, and “\A\I - \A” silently treats the x in the entry x - a_{11} as if the entry became \A - a_{11}, which is not what substitution into a polynomial means. The same “argument” proves false statements, which shows it is not a proof. Replace \det by 	r: let q(x) = 	r(x\I - \A) = nx - 	r \A. The fake reasoning gives “q(\A) = 	r(\A\I - \A) = 	r \O = 0”. But for \A = \diag(1, 0), q(x) = 2x - 1 and q(\A) = 2\A - \I = \diag(1, -1) 
e \O. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the characteristic polynomial of \A \in M_n(F), and say in which ring its determinant is computed. 2. State the degree, leading coefficient, coefficient of x^{n-1}, and constant term of p_{\A}. 3. True or false: \det(\A - x\I) = p_{\A}(x) for every \A \in M_3(F). Justify your answer. 4. True or false: if p_{\A} = p_{\B}, then \A \sim \B. Justify your answer. 5. What does p_{\A}(c) = 0 say about the matrix c\I - \A? About vectors? 6. Explain in one sentence why “p_{\A}(\A) = \det(\A\I - \A) = 0” is not a proof. (a) p_{\A}(x) = \det(x\I_n - \A), the Leibniz sum computed in the commutative ring F[x] (@def-characteristic-polynomial). (b) Degree n, leading coefficient 1, coefficient -	r \A at x^{n-1}, constant term (-1)^n\det \A (@thm-charpoly-coefficients). (c) False. \det(\A - x\I) = (-1)^3p_{\A}(x) = -p_{\A}(x), since each of the three columns changes sign. For \A = \O, \det(-x\I_3) = -x^3 
e x^3 = p_{\A}(x). (d) False. \I_2 and  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} both have p = (x - 1)^2 but are not similar. (e) c\I - \A is not invertible; equivalently there is a nonzero \cvec{v} with \A\cvec{v} = c\cvec{v} (@thm-charpoly-root-iff-singular). (f) p_{\A}(\A) is a matrix obtained by substituting \A into a polynomial, while \det(\A\I - \A) is a scalar, and substitution into the entries of x\I - \A is only justified for scalars (@lem-charpoly-evaluation). B. Practice [B1: Computing characteristic polynomials] Find the characteristic polynomial of each matrix over 
Q, factor it as far as possible over 
Q, and check the trace and determinant against @thm-charpoly-coefficients. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. Hence list the c \in 
Q for which c\I - \A, respectively c\I - \B, is not invertible. For \A. Expanding x\I - \A =  egin{pmatrix} x - 1 & -1 & 0 \ 0 & x - 1 & -1 \ -1 & 0 & x - 1 \end{pmatrix} along the first row (@thm-laplace-expansion over F[x]),  egin{aligned} p_{\A}(x) &= (x - 1) ig((x - 1)^2 - 0 ig) - (-1) ig(0 - 1 ig) + 0 \ &= (x - 1)^3 - 1 = x^3 - 3x^2 + 3x - 2 . \end{aligned} Check: -	r \A = -3; \det \A = 1\cdot(1 - 0) - 1\cdot(0 - 1) + 0 = 2, and (-1)^3 \cdot 2 = -2. Since p_{\A}(2) = 1 - 1 = 0, divide by x - 2: p_{\A} = (x - 2)(x^2 - x + 1). The quadratic has discriminant 1 - 4 = -3 < 0, so no rational (indeed no real) root. By @thm-charpoly-root-iff-singular, c\I - \A is singular only for c = 2. For \B. x\I - \B is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks x\I -  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} and x\I -  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. By @thm-det-block-triangular over F[x] and the 2 	imes 2 formula, p_{\B}(x) = (x - 2)^2\, ig(x^2 - 0\cdot x + (-1 - 3) ig) = (x - 2)^2(x^2 - 4) = (x - 2)^3(x + 2) . Multiplied out, p_{\B} = x^4 - 4x^3 + 16x - 16. Check: -	r \B = -(2 + 2 + 1 - 1) = -4; \det \B = 4 \cdot (-4) = -16 by @thm-det-block-triangular, and (-1)^4(-16) = -16. So c\I - \B is singular exactly for c = 2 and c = -2. [B2: Transpose] Prove that p_{\A	p} = p_{\A} for every \A \in M_n(F). Hence show that c\I - \A is invertible if and only if c\I - \A	p is. By @thm-transpose-properties, (x\I - \A)	p = x\I	p - \A	p = x\I - \A	p; these rules are proved entrywise from the ring axioms, so they hold over F[x]. By @thm-det-transpose, which holds over F[x] by the remark in §4, p_{\A	p} = \det(x\I - \A	p) = \det ig((x\I - \A)	p ig) = \det(x\I - \A) = p_{\A} . By @thm-charpoly-root-iff-singular, c\I - \A is not invertible exactly when p_{\A}(c) = 0, which is exactly when p_{\A	p}(c) = 0, that is, when c\I - \A	p is not invertible. [B3: \A\B and \B\A] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) with \A invertible. 1. Show that \B\A = \A^{-1}(\A\B)\A, and deduce p_{\A\B} = p_{\B\A}. 2. Deduce that 	r(\A\B) = 	r(\B\A) and \det(\A\B) = \det(\B\A) in this case. 3. Check (a) for \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, and note that \A\B 
e \B\A. (Chapter 9 removes the hypothesis that \A is invertible.) (a) By associativity, \A^{-1}(\A\B)\A = (\A^{-1}\A)(\B\A) = \B\A. So \B\A \sim \A\B (@def-similar-matrices, with \P = \A), and p_{\A\B} = p_{\B\A} by @thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant. (b) By @thm-charpoly-coefficients, the coefficient of x^{n-1} is -	r(\A\B) in p_{\A\B} and -	r(\B\A) in p_{\B\A}; the constant terms are (-1)^n\det(\A\B) and (-1)^n\det(\B\A). Equal polynomials have equal coefficients. (c) \A\B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \B\A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, so \A\B 
e \B\A. Both have trace 1 and determinant 0, so both characteristic polynomials are x^2 - x = x(x - 1). C. Going deeper [C1: Companion matrices] Let n \ge 2 and p(x) = x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + a_1x + a_0 \in F[x]. The companion matrix of p is the matrix \C(p) \in M_n(F) with 1 in each position (i + 1, i) just below the diagonal, last column (-a_0, -a_1, \dots, -a_{n-1}), and 0 elsewhere: \C(p) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & -a_0 \ 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & -a_1 \ 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & -a_2 \ \vdots & & \ddots & & \vdots \ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 & -a_{n-1} \end{pmatrix}. (The matrix \C of @exr-polynomials-of-operators-b2 is \C(x^3 - 2x^2 + x - 2).) 1. Let \M = x\I - \C(p). For each i, show that deleting row i and column n of \M leaves a block diagonal matrix whose blocks are an (i - 1) 	imes (i - 1) lower triangular matrix with diagonal x, \dots, x and an (n - i) 	imes (n - i) upper triangular matrix with diagonal -1, \dots, -1 (either block may be absent when i = 1 or i = n). Deduce that the cofactor C_{in} of \M equals x^{i-1}. 2. Deduce, by expanding along the last column, that p_{\C(p)} = p. 3. Verify (b) for p = x^4 + x^3 - 2x + 3 by writing \C(p) and checking the coefficients predicted by @thm-charpoly-coefficients. 4. Deduce that every monic polynomial of degree n \ge 1 over F is the characteristic polynomial of some n 	imes n matrix over F. (a) The entries of \M are: x at (j, j) for j < n; -1 at (j + 1, j); a_{j-1} at (j, n) for j < n; x + a_{n-1} at (n, n); 0 elsewhere. Delete row i and column n. In the remaining matrix, rows 1, \dots, i - 1 have nonzero entries only in columns j - 1 and j for row j, all at most i - 1; and rows i + 1, \dots, n have nonzero entries only in columns j - 1 and j \le n - 1, all at least i. So the matrix is block diagonal with blocks on rows and columns \{1, \dots, i-1\} and on rows \{i + 1, \dots, n\}, columns \{i, \dots, n - 1\}. The first block has x on its diagonal and -1 just below it, so it is lower triangular. In the second block, row j of \M (for j > i) has -1 in column j - 1, which is the diagonal position of the block, and x in column j, one step to the right; so it is upper triangular with diagonal -1, \dots, -1. By @thm-det-block-triangular and @thm-det-triangular over F[x] (both division-free), the minor is M_{in} = x^{i-1}(-1)^{n-i}, where an absent block contributes the factor 1 (for i = 1 or i = n the matrix is a single triangular block). Hence C_{in} = (-1)^{i+n}(-1)^{n-i}x^{i-1} = (-1)^{2n}x^{i-1} = x^{i-1}. (b) By @thm-laplace-expansion along column n, valid over F[x],  egin{aligned} p_{\C(p)} &= \det \M = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} a_{i-1}\,x^{i-1} + (x + a_{n-1})\,x^{n-1} \ &= a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + x^n = p . \end{aligned} (c) Here a_3 = 1, a_2 = 0, a_1 = -2, a_0 = 3, so \C(p) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & -3 \ 1 & 0 & 0 & 2 \ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. Its trace is -1, so @thm-charpoly-coefficients predicts the coefficient 1 = a_3 at x^3, as in p. Its determinant, expanding along the first row, whose only nonzero entry is -3 in position (1, 4), is (-3)(-1)^{1+4}\det \I_3 = 3, since deleting row 1 and column 4 leaves \I_3. So the predicted constant term is (-1)^4 \cdot 3 = 3 = a_0. (d) For n \ge 2, take \C(p) and use (b). For n = 1, p = x + a_0 is p_{(-a_0)}. [C2: Nilpotent 2 	imes 2 matrices] Let \A \in M_2(F) satisfy \A^k = \O for some k \ge 1. 1. Show that the constant term of p_{\A} is 0. 2. By multiplying out, verify that \A^2 - (	r \A)\A + (\det \A)\I = \O for every \A \in M_2(F). 3. Deduce that 	r \A = 0, and hence p_{\A} = x^2 and \A^2 = \O. 4. Give an example showing that \A^2 = \O does not force \A = \O. (a) By @thm-det-multiplicative, (\det \A)^k = \det(\A^k) = \det \O = 0, so \det \A = 0 because a field has no zero divisors (@thm-field-basic-properties). The constant term is (-1)^2\det \A = 0 by @thm-charpoly-coefficients. (b) Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{pmatrix}. Then \A^2 =  egin{pmatrix} a^2 + bc & ab + bd \ ca + dc & bc + d^2 \end{pmatrix} and (a + d)\A =  egin{pmatrix} a^2 + ad & ab + bd \ ac + dc & ad + d^2 \end{pmatrix}. The difference is  egin{pmatrix} bc - ad & 0 \ 0 & bc - ad \end{pmatrix} = -(\det \A)\I, as claimed. (c) By (a) and (b), \A^2 = (	r \A)\A. By induction, \A^m = (	r \A)^{m-1}\A for all m \ge 1: if it holds for m, then \A^{m+1} = (	r \A)^{m-1}\A^2 = (	r \A)^m\A. If \A = \O, then 	r \A = 0. If \A 
e \O, then \O = \A^k = (	r \A)^{k-1}\A forces (	r \A)^{k-1} = 0, since a nonzero matrix times a scalar is zero only if the scalar is zero; here k \ge 2, because k = 1 would give \A = \O. Hence 	r \A = 0 by @thm-field-basic-properties (f), applied repeatedly. So p_{\A} = x^2 - 0\cdot x + 0 = x^2, and \A^2 = (	r \A)\A = \O. (d) \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has \A^2 = \O and \A 
e \O. [C3: Odd size over the reals] Let n be odd and \A \in M_n(
R). 1. Prove that there is c \in 
R and a nonzero \cvec{v} \in 
R^n with \A\cvec{v} = c\cvec{v}. 2. Show by an example that (a) fails for n = 2. 3. Show that (a) holds for every \A \in M_n(
C) and every n \ge 1. (a) By @thm-charpoly-coefficients, p_{\A} \in 
R[x] has odd degree n. By @cor-odd-degree-real-root, it has a real root c. By @thm-charpoly-root-iff-singular, there is a nonzero \cvec{v} \in 
R^n with \A\cvec{v} = c\cvec{v}. (b) The rotation \R =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has p_{\R} = x^2 + 1, with no real root; by @thm-charpoly-root-iff-singular no real c and nonzero real \cvec{v} satisfy \R\cvec{v} = c\cvec{v}. (c) p_{\A} \in 
C[x] has degree n \ge 1, so it has a root c \in 
C by @thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra. Apply @thm-charpoly-root-iff-singular over F = 
C.

title: Block Matrices
content: Block Matrices A large matrix often has structure that its entries hide. Split it into blocks, smaller matrices arranged in a grid, and the structure shows. A direct sum of subspaces becomes a block-diagonal matrix. A subspace that an operator maps into itself becomes a block of zeros in the corner. A system of equations that splits into two groups becomes a two-by-two system whose “entries” are matrices. This chapter makes block arithmetic rigorous and then puts it to work. Multiplying block by block, eliminating a whole block at once, and taking the Schur complement \D - \C \A^{-1}\B turn statements about big matrices into statements about small ones: ranks, determinants, and inverses. The Kronecker product rewrites matrix equations such as \A \X + \X \B = \C as ordinary linear systems. The chapter ends with a question that looks like it needs heavy machinery but does not: which matrices can be written as a commutator \X \Y - \Y \X? What you need. From Chapter 0, matrix multiplication (@def-matrix-multiplication) and polynomials without zero divisors (@cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors). From Chapter 1, subspaces, spans, and bases with the dimension formula for a sum (@thm-span-subspace, @thm-basis-extension, @thm-size-bounds, @thm-subspace-dimension, @prp-sum-of-spans, @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim), the unique representation of a vector in a basis (@thm-unique-representation, @thm-independence-unique-combination), and the direct sum criteria (@thm-direct-sum-k-criteria), which is what §01 reads off a block decomposition; §05 also uses the standard bases and the trace-free matrices as examples (@exm-standard-bases, @exm-trace-free-matrices, @thm-zero-product). From Chapter 3, rank (@def-rank-matrix). From Chapter 2, the matrix of a linear map and change of basis (@def-matrix-of-linear-map, @thm-change-of-basis-maps), quotient spaces (@def-quotient-space), the rank inequalities (@thm-sylvester-rank-inequality), and the trace (@def-trace-operator). From Chapter 7, determinants of block triangular matrices and the characteristic polynomial (@thm-det-block-triangular, @thm-charpoly-coefficients). Roadmap - Partitions and block multiplication. Multiplying matrices block by block, and what block-diagonal and block-triangular shapes say about a linear map. - Rank and block matrices. Rank inequalities proved by clearing blocks, including Frobenius’s inequality. - Schur complements. The Schur complement, the determinant, rank, and inverse of a block matrix, the Woodbury formula, and determinants with commuting blocks over any field. - The Kronecker product. A product of matrices of different sizes, and matrix equations turned into linear systems. - Commutators and trace-zero matrices. Every trace-zero matrix over a field of characteristic zero is a commutator. Named moves - Partition to match the structure. Choose the blocks so that the zeros you know about sit in whole blocks. - Eliminate a block. Multiply by an invertible block triangular matrix to clear a block, just as a row operation clears an entry. - Pass to the Schur complement. Reduce a question about \begin{pmatrix} \A & \B \\ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} with \A invertible to a question about \A and \D - \C \A^{-1}\B. - Vectorize. Turn a linear equation in an unknown matrix \X into a linear system in the entries of \X. - Adjoin an indeterminate. To remove an invertibility hypothesis, replace \D by \D + x\I, work over F[x], and set x = 0 at the end.

title: 8.1 Partitions and Block Multiplication
content:
Partitions and Block Multiplication A large matrix often has structure that its individual entries hide: a corner of zeros, a copy of the identity, a smaller matrix repeated. Chapter 7 already met one such shape, the block triangular matrix, and computed its determinant from two smaller determinants. This section makes the idea systematic. We cut matrices into rectangular pieces, prove that products can be computed piece by piece, and use the pieces to read off structure: direct sums become block diagonal matrices, and a subspace that an operator maps into itself becomes a zero block in the corner. Rows, columns, and outer products The finest and coarsest partitions turn @thm-block-multiplication into facts we already know, and one mixed choice gives something new. Partition \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) trivially (one block) and \B \in M_{n 	imes p}(F) into columns (row partition n, column partition 1, \dots, 1). These are conformable, and the theorem says that the k-th block of \A \B, its k-th column, is \A\cvec{b}_k. That is the column view of @thm-three-views-of-product. Partitioning \A into rows and \B trivially gives the row view in the same way. Now cut \A into columns and \B into rows. Both middle partitions are 1, 1, \dots, 1 (with n ones), so they are conformable, and the product has a single block. [Outer Product Expansion] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) have columns \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n \in F^m, and let \B \in M_{n 	imes p}(F) have rows \cvec{r}_1, \dots, \cvec{r}_n \in M_{1 	imes p}(F). Then \A \B = \cvec{a}_1\cvec{r}_1 + \cvec{a}_2\cvec{r}_2 + \dots + \cvec{a}_n\cvec{r}_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \cvec{a}_k\cvec{r}_k , where each \cvec{a}_k\cvec{r}_k \in M_{m 	imes p}(F) is column k of \A times row k of \B. Give \A the row partition m and the column partition 1, \dots, 1, so that its blocks are \A_{1k} = \cvec{a}_k; give \B the row partition 1, \dots, 1 and the column partition p, so that \B_{k1} = \cvec{r}_k. The partitions are conformable, and by @thm-block-multiplication the single block of \A \B is \sum_{k} \A_{1k}\B_{k1} = \sum_k \cvec{a}_k\cvec{r}_k. Each term \cvec{a}_k\cvec{r}_k is a column times a row, an outer product, and it has rank at most 1: its columns are the multiples r_{kj}\cvec{a}_k of the single vector \cvec{a}_k. Block diagonal matrices Diagonal matrices are the easiest matrices to compute with: they multiply, power, and invert entry by entry along the diagonal. Replace the diagonal entries by square blocks and all of this survives, one block at a time. A block diagonal matrix is several square matrices placed corner to corner along the diagonal, with zeros everywhere else. e j. A square matrix is block diagonal with respect to the partition k_1, \dots, k_r if it has this form. For two blocks, \A \oplus \B =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \B \end{pmatrix}. In words: the same partition is used for rows and columns, so the diagonal blocks are square; the blocks on the diagonal may be anything; every block off the diagonal is zero.
