e \O. The least such j is 3. Explicitly, \M =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \M^2 = \E_{13}.

title: 8.2 Rank and Block Matrices
content:
Rank and Block Matrices Rank is the most robust number attached to a matrix, and Chapters 3 and 4 found several inequalities for it: the rank of a product is at most the rank of each factor, and Sylvester’s inequality bounds it from below. Those proofs worked with subspaces. This section proves rank inequalities by a different and very mechanical method. We place the matrices we care about as blocks of one bigger matrix, and then change that matrix by block row and column operations, which never change the rank, until its rank can be read off. The method gives short proofs of the Frobenius inequality and of identities such as ank(\I_m - \A \B) + n = ank(\I_n - \B \A) + m, which are awkward to reach with subspaces alone. Three basic inequalities We start with what the shape of a block matrix alone says about its rank. Write  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \end{pmatrix} for the matrix obtained by placing \B to the right of \A (same number of rows), and  egin{pmatrix} \A \ \C \end{pmatrix} for \C below \A (same number of columns). In these results the blocks need not be square. [Rank Inequalities for Block Matrices] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes k}(F), \B \in M_{m 	imes l}(F), \C \in M_{p 	imes k}(F), and \D \in M_{p 	imes l}(F). 1. \max(ank \A, ank \B) \le ank egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \end{pmatrix} \le ank \A + ank \B, and \max(ank \A, ank \C) \le ank egin{pmatrix} \A \ \C \end{pmatrix} \le ank \A + ank \C. 2. ank egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix} = ank \A + ank \D. 3. ank egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix} \ge ank \A + ank \D and ank egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} \ge ank \A + ank \D. Rank is the dimension of the column space, so look at columns. In (a) the columns of  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \end{pmatrix} are those of \A together with those of \B, and dimensions of sums are at most sums of dimensions. In (b) the columns coming from \A and from \D live in two subspaces that meet only in \cvec{0}. In (c) we cannot use the column space of \B, which is unknown, so instead we pick independent columns of \A and of \D and show that the columns of the big matrix standing above them are still independent: the zero block lets us peel off the \D-part first. For \cvec{y} \in F^m and \cvec{z} \in F^p, write  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{y} \ \cvec{z} \end{pmatrix} \in F^{m+p} for the stacked vector. (a) The columns of  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \end{pmatrix} are the columns of \A followed by the columns of \B, so its column space is \col(\A) + \col(\B) by @prp-sum-of-spans. It contains \col(\A) and \col(\B), which gives the lower bound by @thm-subspace-dimension, and by @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim ank egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \end{pmatrix} = ank \A + ank \B - \dim(\col \A \cap \col \B) \le ank \A + ank \B . For the stacked matrix, @prp-block-transpose gives  egin{pmatrix} \A \ \C \end{pmatrix}	p =  egin{pmatrix} \A	p & \C	p \end{pmatrix}, and a matrix and its transpose have the same rank (@thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank). Apply the first part to \A	p and \C	p. (b) Let \M =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix}. Its first k columns are  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a}_j \ \cvec{0} \end{pmatrix} and its last l columns are  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{0} \ \cvec{d}_q \end{pmatrix}, where \cvec{a}_j, \cvec{d}_q are the columns of \A, \D. So \col(\M) = Y + Z with Y = \{  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{y} \ \cvec{0} \end{pmatrix} : \cvec{y} \in \col \A \} and Z = \{  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{0} \ \cvec{z} \end{pmatrix} : \cvec{z} \in \col \D \}. A vector in Y \cap Z has both parts zero, so Y \cap Z = \{\cvec{0}\}. The map \cvec{y} \mapsto  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{y} \ \cvec{0} \end{pmatrix} is linear and injective from \col \A onto Y, so \dim Y = ank \A (@thm-isomorphic-iff-same-dimension); likewise \dim Z = ank \D. By @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim, ank \M = ank \A + ank \D - 0. (c) Let \M =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix}, r = ank \A, and s = ank \D. By @thm-basis-column-space there are columns \cvec{a}_{j_1}, \dots, \cvec{a}_{j_r} of \A that are linearly independent, and columns \cvec{d}_{q_1}, \dots, \cvec{d}_{q_s} of \D that are linearly independent. The corresponding columns of \M are  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a}_{j_i} \ \cvec{0} \end{pmatrix} and  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{b}_{q_i} \ \cvec{d}_{q_i} \end{pmatrix}, where \cvec{b}_q is column q of \B. Let \sum_{i=1}^{r} \alpha_i  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{a}_{j_i} \ \cvec{0} \end{pmatrix} + \sum_{i=1}^{s}  eta_i  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{b}_{q_i} \ \cvec{d}_{q_i} \end{pmatrix} = \cvec{0} . The last p entries give \sum_i  eta_i\cvec{d}_{q_i} = \cvec{0}, so all  eta_i = 0. The first m entries then give \sum_i \alpha_i\cvec{a}_{j_i} = \cvec{0}, so all \alpha_i = 0. Hence \col(\M) contains r + s linearly independent vectors, and ank \M \ge r + s by @thm-size-bounds. For the lower triangular shape,  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix}	p =  egin{pmatrix} \A	p & \C	p \ \O & \D	p \end{pmatrix} by @prp-block-transpose; apply the first case and @thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank. All three inequalities, the two in (a) and the one in (c), can be strict, and small witnesses show it. For \A = \B = (1), ank egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = 1 < 2: the two column spaces overlap. For \A = \cvec{e}_1 and \B = \cvec{e}_2 in F^2, ank egin{pmatrix} \cvec{e}_1 & \cvec{e}_2 \end{pmatrix} = ank \I_2 = 2 > \max(1, 1): each block adds something the other lacks. For \A = \D = \O_1 and \B = (1), ank egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = 1 > 0 + 0: the off-diagonal block contributes rank of its own. The proof of (a) says exactly when the upper bound is attained: ank egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \end{pmatrix} = ank \A + ank \B if and only if \col \A \cap \col \B = \{\cvec{0}\}. The ranks of the four blocks do not determine the rank of the whole. Over 
Q,  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} have all four 1 	imes 1 blocks of rank 1, but ranks 1 and 2. Only special shapes, like the zero blocks in (b) and (c), turn block ranks into information about the whole matrix. Without computing, find ank egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 0 \ 2 & 4 & 0 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \end{pmatrix}. With row partition 2, 2 and column partition 2, 3, the matrix is  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix} with \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} of rank 1 (the second row is twice the first) and \D =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 3 \ 0 & 1 & 5 \end{pmatrix} of rank 2 (the first two columns are \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2). By @thm-block-rank-inequalities (b), the rank is 1 + 2 = 3. Block elimination Gaussian elimination changes a matrix by row operations, which are multiplications by invertible matrices on the left, and the rank never changes. The same is true when the “rows” are whole block rows and the multipliers are matrices. The matrices that do this are the block triangular matrices with identity blocks on the diagonal from @thm-block-triangular-inverse, together with block swaps. Fix a partition of \M =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} \in M_{(m+p) 	imes (k+l)}(F) with \A \in M_{m 	imes k}(F). For matrices \X \in M_{m 	imes p}(F) and \Y \in M_{k 	imes l}(F), @thm-block-multiplication gives  egin{aligned}  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \X \ \O & \I_p \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} &=  egin{pmatrix} \A + \X \C & \B + \X \D \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix}, \  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \Y \ \O & \I_l \end{pmatrix} &=  egin{pmatrix} \A & \A \Y + \B \ \C & \C \Y + \D \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} In words: multiplying on the left adds \X times block row 2 to block row 1, with \X on the left of the row; multiplying on the right adds block column 1 times \Y to block column 2, with \Y on the right of the column. The lower triangular multipliers  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \O \ \X' & \I_p \end{pmatrix} and  egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \O \ \Y' & \I_l \end{pmatrix} act the same way in the other direction. Sides matter: the multiplier sits on the side of the product where the matrix operation happens. [Block Elimination Preserves Rank] Let \M =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} be as above. 1. For all \X \in M_{m 	imes p}(F), \X' \in M_{p 	imes m}(F), \Y \in M_{k 	imes l}(F), and \Y' \in M_{l 	imes k}(F), the matrices  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \X \ \O & \I_p \end{pmatrix}, \quad  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \O \ \X' & \I_p \end{pmatrix}, \quad  egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \Y \ \O & \I_l \end{pmatrix}, \quad  egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \O \ \Y' & \I_l \end{pmatrix} are invertible, and so are the block swaps  egin{pmatrix} \O & \I_p \ \I_m & \O \end{pmatrix} \in M_{m+p}(F) and  egin{pmatrix} \O & \I_k \ \I_l & \O \end{pmatrix} \in M_{k+l}(F). Hence multiplying \M on the left or right by any product of such matrices does not change its rank. The swaps give  egin{pmatrix} \O & \I_p \ \I_m & \O \end{pmatrix}\M =  egin{pmatrix} \C & \D \ \A & \B \end{pmatrix} and \M egin{pmatrix} \O & \I_k \ \I_l & \O \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \B & \A \ \D & \C \end{pmatrix}. 2. If \col(\B) \subseteq \col(\A), or if ow(\B) \subseteq ow(\D), then ank egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix} = ank \A + ank \D. (a) By @thm-block-triangular-inverse (c), with identity blocks on the diagonal,  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \X \ \O & \I_p \end{pmatrix} has inverse  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & -\X \ \O & \I_p \end{pmatrix}; the lower triangular case follows by transposing (@prp-block-transpose, @thm-inverse-matrix-properties). In the swap \S =  egin{pmatrix} \O & \I_p \ \I_m & \O \end{pmatrix} the row partition is p, m and the column partition is m, p. Let \S' =  egin{pmatrix} \O & \I_m \ \I_p & \O \end{pmatrix}, with row partition m, p and column partition p, m. These are conformable, and @thm-block-multiplication gives \S'\S =  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \O \ \O & \I_p \end{pmatrix} = \I_{m+p}, so \S is invertible by @thm-one-sided-inverse; the other swap is the same with k, l in place of m, p. The two displayed products are @thm-block-multiplication. Rank is unchanged by invertible factors on either side (@thm-rank-product-inequality). (b) Suppose \col(\B) \subseteq \col(\A). Each column \cvec{b}_q of \B is then \A\cvec{y}_q for some \cvec{y}_q \in F^k (@def-column-space, @thm-matrix-times-vector-columns). Let \Y \in M_{k 	imes l}(F) have columns \cvec{y}_q, so that \A \Y = \B by @thm-three-views-of-product. By the computation before the theorem,  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \I_k & -\Y \ \O & \I_l \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \A & -\A \Y + \B \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix}, and (a) together with @thm-block-rank-inequalities (b) gives the claim. If ow(\B) \subseteq ow(\D), the same argument applied to rows gives \B = \X \D for some \X \in M_{m 	imes p}(F), and  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & -\X \ \O & \I_p \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix}. Part (b) is the typical use of (a): a block that is a multiple of a neighboring block can be cleared, exactly as an entry below a pivot is cleared in Gaussian elimination. The zero block of @thm-block-rank-inequalities (c) is what lets the cleared matrix fall apart into a direct sum. Frobenius’s inequality by blocks Recall Sylvester’s rank inequality (@thm-sylvester-rank-inequality): for \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \B \in M_{n 	imes p}(F), ank(\A \B) \ge ank \A + ank \B - n. In @exr-rank-factorization-c1 we met a stronger statement, Frobenius’s inequality, and proved it by comparing intersections of subspaces with a null space. Here is a proof in which nothing is chosen: we write down one block matrix whose rank we know, and eliminate. [Frobenius’s Rank Inequality] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), \B \in M_{n 	imes p}(F), and \C \in M_{p 	imes q}(F). Then ank(\A \B \C) + ank \B \ge ank(\A \B) + ank(\B \C) . The left side is the rank of  egin{pmatrix} \A \B \C & \O \ \O & \B \end{pmatrix}, by @thm-block-rank-inequalities (b). The right side is a lower bound for any block triangular matrix with diagonal blocks \A \B and \B \C, by part (c). So we want to turn the first matrix into the second by block elimination. Found backwards: \A times the second block row puts \A \B into the top-right corner; then the second block column times \C cancels \A \B \C and puts \B \C into the bottom-left corner. A swap of the two block columns finishes the job. Let \P =  egin{pmatrix} \A \B \C & \O \ \O & \B \end{pmatrix}, with row partition m, n and column partition q, p. By @thm-block-rank-inequalities (b), ank \P = ank(\A \B \C) + ank \B. By @thm-block-multiplication,  egin{aligned}  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \A \ \O & \I_n \end{pmatrix} \P &=  egin{pmatrix} \A \B \C & \A \B \ \O & \B \end{pmatrix}, \  egin{pmatrix} \A \B \C & \A \B \ \O & \B \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \I_q & \O \ -\C & \I_p \end{pmatrix} &=  egin{pmatrix} \A \B \C - \A \B \C & \A \B \ -\B \C & \B \end{pmatrix} \ &=  egin{pmatrix} \O & \A \B \ -\B \C & \B \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} Multiplying on the right by the block swap  egin{pmatrix} \O & \I_q \ \I_p & \O \end{pmatrix} exchanges the two block columns and gives \Q =  egin{pmatrix} \A \B & \O \ \B & -\B \C \end{pmatrix}. By @thm-block-elimination-rank (a), ank \Q = ank \P. By @thm-block-rank-inequalities (c), ank \Q \ge ank(\A \B) + ank(-\B \C) = ank(\A \B) + ank(\B \C), where ank(-\B \C) = ank(\B \C) because -\B \C and \B \C have the same column space. Hence ank(\A \B \C) + ank \B \ge ank(\A \B) + ank(\B \C). Taking \B = \I_n gives ank(\A \C) + n \ge ank \A + ank \C for \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \C \in M_{n 	imes q}(F), which is Sylvester’s inequality again. Taking \A = \I_n or \C = \I_p gives an equality and no information, as it should. The inequality says that multiplying by \A on the left loses at least as much rank from \B \C as from \B: the rank lost is ank(\B \C) - ank(\A \B \C) \le ank \B - ank(\A \B). A smaller column space has less to lose. A worked example: \I - \A \B and \I - \B \A Products in the two orders, \A \B and \B \A, are different matrices of possibly different sizes, and Chapter 4 showed that even their ranks can differ. Yet \I - \A \B and \I - \B \A are tightly linked. The block matrix that links them contains \I_m, \A, \B, and \I_n, and each identity block can be used as a pivot to clear its neighbors. [Rank of \I - \A \B versus \I - \B \A] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \B \in M_{n 	imes m}(F). 1. Prove that ank(\I_m - \A \B) + n = ank(\I_n - \B \A) + m. 2. Deduce that for m = n, ank(\I_n - \A \B) = ank(\I_n - \B \A), and \I_n - \A \B is invertible if and only if \I_n - \B \A is. 3. Check (a) for \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} over 
Q. (a) Let \M =  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \A \ \B & \I_n \end{pmatrix} \in M_{m+n}(F), with partition m, n for rows and columns. We eliminate in two different ways. Using \I_m as the pivot. Subtract \B times block row 1 from block row 2, then subtract block column 1 times \A from block column 2. By @thm-block-multiplication,  egin{aligned}  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \O \ -\B & \I_n \end{pmatrix} \M &=  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \A \ \O & \I_n - \B \A \end{pmatrix}, \  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \A \ \O & \I_n - \B \A \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \I_m & -\A \ \O & \I_n \end{pmatrix} &=  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \O \ \O & \I_n - \B \A \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} By @thm-block-elimination-rank (a) and @thm-block-rank-inequalities (b), ank \M = m + ank(\I_n - \B \A). Using \I_n as the pivot. Subtract \A times block row 2 from block row 1, then subtract block column 2 times \B from block column 1:  egin{aligned}  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & -\A \ \O & \I_n \end{pmatrix} \M &=  egin{pmatrix} \I_m - \A \B & \O \ \B & \I_n \end{pmatrix}, \  egin{pmatrix} \I_m - \A \B & \O \ \B & \I_n \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \O \ -\B & \I_n \end{pmatrix} &=  egin{pmatrix} \I_m - \A \B & \O \ \O & \I_n \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} So ank \M = ank(\I_m - \A \B) + n in the same way. Comparing the two expressions for ank \M proves (a). (b) For m = n the two added terms are equal and cancel. A square matrix is invertible exactly when its rank is n (@thm-invertible-tfae-det (d)), so \I_n - \A \B is invertible if and only if \I_n - \B \A is. (c) Here \A \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \I_2, so ank(\I_2 - \A \B) = 0, and \B \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \I_3 - \B \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, which has rank 1. Indeed 0 + 3 = 1 + 2. So \A \B = \I_2 while \B \A 
e \I_3, and the identity accounts for the difference exactly: \I_3 - \B \A has rank 3 - 2 = 1. The trick is worth naming. To compare two expressions, find one block matrix from which both can be obtained by elimination, and compute its rank twice. Section 3 does the same with determinants and inverses, and the pair \I - \A \B, \I - \B \A returns there as Sylvester’s determinant identity. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the three inequalities of @thm-block-rank-inequalities. 2. True or false: ank egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix} = ank \A + ank \D for all blocks of compatible sizes. Justify your answer. 3. Which matrix do you multiply  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} by, and on which side, to replace \C by \C - \X \A? 4. True or false: ank egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \end{pmatrix} = ank \A + ank \B whenever \A and \B have the same number of rows. Justify your answer. 5. State Frobenius’s inequality, and explain how Sylvester’s inequality follows from it. (a) \max(ank \A, ank \B) \le ank egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \end{pmatrix} \le ank \A + ank \B (and the same for stacked blocks); ank egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix} = ank \A + ank \D; and both block triangular shapes have rank at least ank \A + ank \D. (b) False.  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} with 1 	imes 1 blocks has rank 1, but ank(0) + ank(0) = 0. Only \ge holds in general. (c) Multiply on the left by  egin{pmatrix} \I & \O \ -\X & \I \end{pmatrix}: block row 2 becomes  egin{pmatrix} \C - \X \A & \D - \X \B \end{pmatrix} by @thm-block-multiplication. The rank does not change (@thm-block-elimination-rank). (d) False.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has rank 1, not 1 + 1. Equality holds exactly when \col \A \cap \col \B = \{\cvec{0}\}. (e) ank(\A \B \C) + ank \B \ge ank(\A \B) + ank(\B \C) for matrices of compatible sizes. With \B = \I_n it reads ank(\A \C) + n \ge ank \A + ank \C, which is Sylvester’s inequality. B. Practice [B1: Ranks of block matrices] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} and \D =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} in M_2(
Q). Find the rank of each 4 	imes 4 matrix, citing the result you use. In which case is the lower bound of @thm-block-rank-inequalities (c) strict? 1. \M_1 =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix}. 2. \M_2 =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix} with \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}. 3. \M_3 =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \I_2 \ \O & \O \end{pmatrix}. ank \A = 1, since the second row is twice the first and \A 
e \O; ank \D = 2, since \det \D = 1 
e 0. (a) By @thm-block-rank-inequalities (b), ank \M_1 = 1 + 2 = 3. (b) The columns of \B are (1, 2) and (3, 6) = 3(1, 2), and (1, 2) is the first column of \A. So \col \B \subseteq \col \A, and by @thm-block-elimination-rank (b), ank \M_2 = 1 + 2 = 3. (Explicitly \B = \A \Y with \Y =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.) (c) The lower bound is ank \A + ank \O = 1. But the last two columns of \M_3 are \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, and every column lies in \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2), so ank \M_3 = 2. This is the strict case: the block \I_2 is not a multiple of \A or of the zero block. [B2: Shifted products] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), \B \in M_{n 	imes m}(F), and c \in F with c 
e 0. 1. By adapting @exm-rank-i-minus-ab, prove that ank(c\I_m - \A \B) + n = ank(c\I_n - \B \A) + m. 2. Check (a) over 
Q for c = 2, \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, and \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. 3. Show by an example with m = 1, n = 2 that (a) can fail for c = 0. (a) Since c 
e 0, put \A' = c^{-1}\A. Then c\I_m - \A \B = c(\I_m - \A'\B) and c\I_n - \B \A = c(\I_n - \B \A'). Multiplying a matrix by the nonzero scalar c does not change its column space, hence not its rank. By @exm-rank-i-minus-ab (a) applied to \A' and \B,  egin{aligned} ank(c\I_m - \A \B) + n &= ank(\I_m - \A'\B) + n \ &= ank(\I_n - \B \A') + m \ &= ank(c\I_n - \B \A) + m . \end{aligned} (b) Here m = 3, n = 2, and 2\I_3 - \A \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & -1 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad 2\I_2 - \B \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, since \A \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and \B \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. In the first matrix, row 1 equals -(	ext{row } 2) - (	ext{row } 3), and rows 2 and 3 are not multiples of each other, so its rank is 2 (@thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank). The second has rank 1. Indeed 2 + 2 = 1 + 3. (c) For c = 0 the identity would say ank(\A \B) + n = ank(\B \A) + m. Take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{pmatrix}: \A \B = (1) has rank 1, and \B \A = \E_{11} \in M_2(F) has rank 1, but 1 + 2 
e 1 + 1. [B3: Idempotents by blocks] Let \A \in M_n(F). 1. Starting from  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \I_n - \A \end{pmatrix}, use block elimination to prove ank \A + ank(\I_n - \A) = n + ank(\A - \A^2) . 2. Deduce that \A^2 = \A if and only if ank \A + ank(\I_n - \A) = n. 3. Compare (b) with what Chapter 4 says about projections. Hint: first add block row 1 to block row 2, then add block column 2 to block column 1. (a) Write \I = \I_n. By @thm-block-multiplication, each step being multiplication by one of the matrices of @thm-block-elimination-rank (a):  egin{aligned}  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \I - \A \end{pmatrix} &\xrightarrow{\ 	ext{row}_2 + 	ext{row}_1\ }  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \A & \I - \A \end{pmatrix} \ &\xrightarrow{\ 	ext{col}_1 + 	ext{col}_2\ }  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \I & \I - \A \end{pmatrix} \ &\xrightarrow{\ 	ext{row}_1 - \A\,	ext{row}_2\ }  egin{pmatrix} \O & \A^2 - \A \ \I & \I - \A \end{pmatrix} \ &\xrightarrow{\ 	ext{col}_2 - 	ext{col}_1(\I - \A)\ }  egin{pmatrix} \O & \A^2 - \A \ \I & \O \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} The multipliers are, in order,  egin{pmatrix} \I & \O \ \I & \I \end{pmatrix} on the left,  egin{pmatrix} \I & \O \ \I & \I \end{pmatrix} on the right,  egin{pmatrix} \I & -\A \ \O & \I \end{pmatrix} on the left, and  egin{pmatrix} \I & -(\I - \A) \ \O & \I \end{pmatrix} on the right. In the third step the top row becomes  egin{pmatrix} \A - \A \I & \O - \A(\I - \A) \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \O & \A^2 - \A \end{pmatrix}, and in the fourth the bottom-right block becomes (\I - \A) - \I(\I - \A) = \O. Swapping the block columns (@thm-block-elimination-rank (a)) gives  egin{pmatrix} \A^2 - \A & \O \ \O & \I \end{pmatrix}, of rank ank(\A^2 - \A) + n by @thm-block-rank-inequalities (b). The first matrix has rank ank \A + ank(\I - \A), and rank is unchanged throughout. Since \A^2 - \A = -(\A - \A^2) has the same rank as \A - \A^2, (a) follows. (b) By (a), ank \A + ank(\I - \A) = n if and only if ank(\A - \A^2) = 0, that is, \A - \A^2 = \O. (c) If \A^2 = \A, then T_{\A} is a projection (@def-projection-operator), so F^n = \im T_{\A} \oplus \ker T_{\A} by @thm-projection-direct-sum, with \ker T_{\A} = \col(\I - \A) (a vector \cvec{v} with \A\cvec{v} = \cvec{0} equals (\I - \A)\cvec{v}, and conversely \A(\I - \A) = \A - \A^2 = \O). So ank \A + ank(\I - \A) = \dim\im T_{\A} + \dim\ker T_{\A} = n, which is the forward direction of (b). The block argument also gives the converse, and it never mentions subspaces. C. Going deeper [C1: The rank of \A - \A \B \A] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \B \in M_{n 	imes m}(F). 1. Verify, by block multiplication, the following chain, in which each arrow is multiplication by an invertible block triangular matrix:  egin{aligned}  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \I_n - \B \A \end{pmatrix} &	o  egin{pmatrix} \A & \A \ \O & \I_n - \B \A \end{pmatrix} 	o  egin{pmatrix} \A & \A \ \B \A & \I_n \end{pmatrix} \ &	o  egin{pmatrix} \A - \A \B \A & \A \ \O & \I_n \end{pmatrix} 	o  egin{pmatrix} \A - \A \B \A & \O \ \O & \I_n \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} Name each multiplier and the side it acts on. 2. Deduce that ank(\A - \A \B \A) = ank \A + ank(\I_n - \B \A) - n. 3. Suppose \A \B \A = \A. Show that \B \A is idempotent and that ank(\B \A) = ank \A. Hint for (c): use (b), then @exr-rank-of-block-matrices-b3. (a) The partitions are m, n for rows and n, n for columns. By @thm-block-multiplication: 1. Right multiplication by  egin{pmatrix} \I_n & \I_n \ \O & \I_n \end{pmatrix} adds block column 1 to block column 2:  egin{pmatrix} \A & \A + \O \ \O & \O + (\I_n - \B \A) \end{pmatrix}. 2. Left multiplication by  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \O \ \B & \I_n \end{pmatrix} adds \B times block row 1 to block row 2: the new row is  egin{pmatrix} \B \A & \B \A + \I_n - \B \A \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \B \A & \I_n \end{pmatrix}. 3. Right multiplication by  egin{pmatrix} \I_n & \O \ -\B \A & \I_n \end{pmatrix} subtracts block column 2 times \B \A from block column 1: the new column is  egin{pmatrix} \A - \A \B \A \ \B \A - \I_n\B \A \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \A - \A \B \A \ \O \end{pmatrix}. 4. Left multiplication by  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & -\A \ \O & \I_n \end{pmatrix} subtracts \A times block row 2 from block row 1: the new row is  egin{pmatrix} \A - \A \B \A - \A\cdot \O & \A - \A \I_n \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \A - \A \B \A & \O \end{pmatrix}. All four multipliers are invertible by @thm-block-elimination-rank (a). (b) By @thm-block-elimination-rank (a) the first and last matrices have the same rank, and by @thm-block-rank-inequalities (b) these ranks are ank \A + ank(\I_n - \B \A) and ank(\A - \A \B \A) + n. Rearranging gives the formula. (c) (\B \A)^2 = \B(\A \B \A) = \B \A, so \B \A is idempotent. By (b), 0 = ank(\A - \A \B \A) = ank \A + ank(\I_n - \B \A) - n, so ank(\I_n - \B \A) = n - ank \A. By @exr-rank-of-block-matrices-b3 (b) applied to the idempotent \B \A, ank(\B \A) = n - ank(\I_n - \B \A) = ank \A. [C2: Involutions and the field] Let \A \in M_n(F). 1. Suppose the characteristic of F is not 2. Starting from  egin{pmatrix} \A - \I_n & \O \ \O & \A + \I_n \end{pmatrix}, prove that ank(\A - \I_n) + ank(\A + \I_n) = n + ank(\A^2 - \I_n) . 2. Deduce that if \A^2 = \I_n (and \operatorname{char} F 
e 2), then ank(\A - \I_n) + ank(\A + \I_n) = n. 3. Show that (b) fails over 
F_2, and point to the step of (a) that breaks. Hint for (a): add block column 2 to block column 1, and subtract block row 2 from block row 1; then -2\I_n is an invertible pivot. (a) Write \I = \I_n and \P = \A + \I. Since \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, 2 
e 0 in F, so  rac12 exists and -2\I is invertible. By @thm-block-multiplication, with each multiplier from @thm-block-elimination-rank (a):  egin{aligned}  egin{pmatrix} \A - \I & \O \ \O & \P \end{pmatrix} &\xrightarrow{\ 	ext{col}_1 + 	ext{col}_2\ }  egin{pmatrix} \A - \I & \O \ \P & \P \end{pmatrix} \xrightarrow{\ 	ext{row}_1 - 	ext{row}_2\ }  egin{pmatrix} -2\I & -\P \ \P & \P \end{pmatrix} \ &\xrightarrow{\ 	ext{col}_2 - 	ext{col}_1 \cdot  rac12 \P\ }  egin{pmatrix} -2\I & \O \ \P & \P -  rac12 \P^2 \end{pmatrix} \ &\xrightarrow{\ 	ext{row}_2 +  rac12 \P\,	ext{row}_1\ }  egin{pmatrix} -2\I & \O \ \O & \P -  rac12 \P^2 \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} In the second step (\A - \I) - \P = -2\I; in the third, -\P - (-2\I)	frac12 \P = \O and \P - \P\cdot rac12 \P = \P -  rac12\P^2; in the fourth, \P +  rac12\P(-2\I) = \O. Finally \P - 	frac12\P^2 = 	frac12 \P(2\I - \P) = 	frac12(\A + \I)(\I - \A) = 	frac12(\I - \A^2), where the product (\A + \I)(\I - \A) = \I - \A + \A - \A^2 expands by distributivity. The first matrix has rank ank(\A - \I) + ank(\A + \I) and the last has rank n + ank(	frac12(\I - \A^2)) = n + ank(\A^2 - \I) by @thm-block-rank-inequalities (b), nonzero scalar multiples having the same column space. Rank is unchanged throughout. (b) If \A^2 = \I_n, then ank(\A^2 - \I_n) = 0. (c) Over 
F_2, take \A = \I_n. Then \A^2 = \I_n, but \A - \I_n = \O and \A + \I_n = 2\I_n = \O, so the left side is 0 
e n. The step that breaks is the pivot: -2\I_n = \O is not invertible, and  rac12 does not exist. (Chapter 2’s decomposition of an involution into \pm 1 parts, @thm-involution-decomposition, needs the same hypothesis.)

title: 8.3 Schur Complements
content:
Schur Complements Section 1 inverted block triangular matrices, and Section 2 cleared blocks without changing the rank. A general block matrix  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} has no zero block to help, but when one diagonal block is invertible, a single step of block elimination creates one. What is left in the opposite corner is a new matrix, the Schur complement, and it carries everything that the invertible block does not: the determinant, the rank, and the inverse of the whole matrix can all be read off from the block and its complement. This section introduces it, derives these formulas, uses the two complements of one matrix to prove the Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury formula, and ends with the determinant of a block matrix whose lower blocks commute, over every field. Eliminating a block Suppose we must solve a linear system whose unknowns come in two groups, \cvec{x} \in F^k and \cvec{y} \in F^l:  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \cvec{x} \ \cvec{y} \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{f} \ \cvec{g} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad	ext{that is,}\qquad  egin{aligned} \A\cvec{x} + \B\cvec{y} &= \cvec{f}, \ \C\cvec{x} + \D\cvec{y} &= \cvec{g}, \end{aligned} with \A \in M_k(F) invertible. Do what we would do for two equations in two numbers: solve the first equation for \cvec{x}, and substitute. The first equation gives \cvec{x} = \A^{-1}(\cvec{f} - \B\cvec{y}). Substituting into the second, \C \A^{-1}\cvec{f} - \C \A^{-1}\B\cvec{y} + \D\cvec{y} = \cvec{g}, \qquad	ext{so}\qquad (\D - \C \A^{-1}\B)\,\cvec{y} = \cvec{g} - \C \A^{-1}\cvec{f} . The unknown \cvec{x} has disappeared, and \cvec{y} solves a smaller system whose matrix is \D - \C \A^{-1}\B. Once \cvec{y} is known, \cvec{x} = \A^{-1}(\cvec{f} - \B\cvec{y}). So the big system is solvable for every right-hand side exactly when the small matrix \D - \C \A^{-1}\B allows it, and this matrix will keep appearing. For k = l = 1 we have met it before: d - cb/a = (ad - bc)/a is the determinant divided by the pivot a, which is what Gaussian elimination leaves in the corner after clearing the entry c. The Schur complement of an invertible block is what remains in the opposite corner after that block has been used to eliminate its row and column. [Schur Complement] Let \M =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} \in M_{(k+p) 	imes (k+l)}(F) be a block matrix with \A \in M_k(F), \B \in M_{k 	imes l}(F), \C \in M_{p 	imes k}(F), and \D \in M_{p 	imes l}(F), where k, p, l \ge 1. 1. If \A is invertible, the Schur complement of \A in \M is \M/\A \coloneqq \D - \C \A^{-1}\B \in M_{p 	imes l}(F) . 2. Symmetrically, if \M =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} with \D \in M_l(F) invertible, \A \in M_{m 	imes k}(F), \B \in M_{m 	imes l}(F), and \C \in M_{l 	imes k}(F), the Schur complement of \D in \M is \M/\D \coloneqq \A - \B \D^{-1}\C \in M_{m 	imes k}(F). In words, clause by clause. The block whose complement we take must be square and invertible, since its inverse appears in the formula; the other blocks may be rectangular. The complement has the size of the opposite corner: \M/\A has the shape of \D, and \M/\D has the shape of \A. In \C \A^{-1}\B the factors come in the only order the sizes allow: \C is p 	imes k, \A^{-1} is k 	imes k, \B is k 	imes l. A way to remember it: go from the corner \D to \A along its row (\C), invert, and come back along its column (\B). Well-definedness. \M/\A depends on \M and on the chosen partition, which says which corner is \A. The inverse \A^{-1} is unique (@thm-inverse-matrix-properties), so there is no other choice to make. Examples. - Scalars. For \M =  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{pmatrix} with a 
e 0, \M/a = d - ca^{-1}b = (ad - bc)/a. In particular a \cdot (\M/a) = \det \M. - An identity corner. If \A = \I_k, then \M/\I_k = \D - \C \B. No inversion is needed at all. - Block triangular. If \C = \O, then \M/\A = \D: nothing needs to be eliminated. - A 3 	imes 3 example. For \M = \left( egin{array}{cc|c} 2 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \ \hline 3 & 1 & 4 \end{array}ight) over 
Q, \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has \A^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, and \C \A^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\A^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, so \M/\A = 4 -  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{pmatrix} = (2). This 1 	imes 1 complement is the last pivot of Gaussian elimination on \M: subtracting  rac12 row 1 from row 2 and  rac32 row 1 from row 3 gives the rows (0,  rac12, - rac12) and (0, - rac12,  rac52), and adding the first of these to the second gives (0, 0, 2). Nonexample by minimal change. For \M =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \M/(1) = 0 - 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = (-1). Change the corner entry 1 to 0: \M' =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. The blocks \B, \C, \D, and the partition are unchanged, and \M' is still invertible, but \M'/\O_1 is not defined, because the clause “\A is invertible” fails. Here \M'/\D is not defined either, since \D = \O_1. Why this definition. The formula is read off from the elimination in the hook, so the question is only about the name and the hypotheses. “Complement” refers to position: \M/\A sits in the corner complementary to \A. The quotient notation \M/\A is suggested by the first example, \det(\M/a) = \det \M / \det a, and the determinant formula below shows that this holds for blocks of every size. Invertibility of \A cannot be dropped, since \A^{-1} is in the formula; the price is that some invertible matrices, like \M', have no Schur complement for a given partition. \M can be invertible while \A is not. For \M' =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, neither corner is invertible, so neither Schur complement exists for the partition 1, 1. Before using a formula below, check that the block you invert is invertible. If it is not, try the other corner (\M/\D), a different partition, or first permute rows:  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\M' = \I_2. The same issue appears in Gaussian elimination as a zero pivot. Let \M = \left( egin{array}{c|cc} 2 & 4 & 2 \ \hline 1 & 3 & 5 \ 3 & 1 & 0 \end{array}ight) with partition 1, 2. Compute \M/(2). Here \A = (2), \B =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 3 \end{pmatrix}, \D =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 5 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Then \C \A^{-1}\B =  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \ 12 & 6 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 6 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, so \M/(2) =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \ -5 & -3 \end{pmatrix}. These are exactly the entries left in rows 2, 3 after clearing column 1 with the pivot 2. The block LDU factorization The elimination of the hook, written with matrices, factors \M into a lower block triangular matrix, a block diagonal matrix, and an upper block triangular matrix. Everything else in this section follows from this factorization. [Block LDU Factorization] Let \M =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} be partitioned as in @def-schur-complement. 1. If \A \in M_k(F) is invertible, then \M =  egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \O \ \C \A^{-1} & \I_p \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \M/\A \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \A^{-1}\B \ \O & \I_l \end{pmatrix}. 2. If \D \in M_l(F) is invertible, then \M =  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \B \D^{-1} \ \O & \I_l \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \M/\D & \O \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \O \ \D^{-1}\C & \I_l \end{pmatrix}. The left factor in (a) records the row operation “subtract \C \A^{-1} times block row 1 from block row 2”, which turns \C into \O and \D into \M/\A. The right factor records the column operation “subtract block column 1 times \A^{-1}\B from block column 2”, which turns \B into \O. Undoing both operations gives the factorization. To prove it we need not retrace the elimination: multiplying out is enough. (a) Write \S = \M/\A = \D - \C \A^{-1}\B. The sizes are conformable throughout. By @thm-block-multiplication,  egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \S \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \A^{-1}\B \ \O & \I_l \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \A \A^{-1}\B \ \O & \S \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \O & \S \end{pmatrix}, and then  egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \O \ \C \A^{-1} & \I_p \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \O & \S \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C \A^{-1}\A & \C \A^{-1}\B + \S \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix}, since \C \A^{-1}\A = \C and \C \A^{-1}\B + (\D - \C \A^{-1}\B) = \D. By associativity (@thm-matrix-multiplication-properties) the triple product equals \M. (b) Write \S' = \M/\D = \A - \B \D^{-1}\C. By @thm-block-multiplication,  egin{aligned}  egin{pmatrix} \S' & \O \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \O \ \D^{-1}\C & \I_l \end{pmatrix} &=  egin{pmatrix} \S' & \O \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix}, \  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \B \D^{-1} \ \O & \I_l \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \S' & \O \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} &=  egin{pmatrix} \S' + \B \D^{-1}\C & \B \D^{-1}\D \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} = \M . \end{aligned} The outer factors are block triangular with identity blocks on the diagonal. They are invertible, with inverses obtained by changing the sign of the off-diagonal block (@thm-block-triangular-inverse), and they have determinant 1. So, up to these harmless factors, \M is the block diagonal matrix \A \oplus (\M/\A) when \A and \D are square. Determinant, rank, and invertibility cannot tell the difference. Determinant and rank The outer factors of @thm-block-ldu do not change the determinant or the rank, so both can be read off from the middle factor. [Schur Determinant Formula] Let \M =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} \in M_{k+l}(F) with \A \in M_k(F), \D \in M_l(F), and k, l \ge 1. 1. If \A is invertible, then \det \M = \det \A \cdot \det(\M/\A). 2. If \D is invertible, then \det \M = \det \D \cdot \det(\M/\D). (a) By @thm-block-ldu (a), \M = \L\,(\A \oplus (\M/\A))\,\U with \L =  egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \O \ \C \A^{-1} & \I_l \end{pmatrix} and \U =  egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \A^{-1}\B \ \O & \I_l \end{pmatrix}. Here p = l because \M is square, so \M/\A \in M_l(F). By @thm-det-block-triangular, \det \L = \det \I_k\det \I_l = 1, \det \U = 1, and \det(\A \oplus (\M/\A)) = \det \A\det(\M/\A). By @thm-det-multiplicative, \det \M = \det \L \cdot \det \A\det(\M/\A) \cdot \det \U = \det \A\det(\M/\A) . (b) The same argument with @thm-block-ldu (b), where \M/\D \in M_k(F) because \M is square. This is the correct replacement for the false rule \det \M = \det(\A \D - \B \C) of Section 1: the determinant of \M is that of \A times that of the complement. For k = l = 1 it is a ig(d - ca^{-1}b ig) = ad - bc. Chapter 7 promised this, and it relies on @thm-det-block-triangular in exactly the form proved there, with square diagonal blocks. [Schur Rank Formula] Let \M =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} be partitioned as in @def-schur-complement. If \A \in M_k(F) is invertible, then ank \M = k + ank(\M/\A) . Symmetrically, if \D \in M_l(F) is invertible, then ank \M = l + ank(\M/\D). By @thm-block-ldu (a), \M = \L egin{pmatrix} \A & \O \ \O & \M/\A \end{pmatrix}\U, where \L and \U are invertible by @thm-block-elimination-rank (a). By @thm-rank-product-inequality, ank \M equals the rank of the middle factor, which is ank \A + ank(\M/\A) = k + ank(\M/\A) by @thm-block-rank-inequalities (b) and @thm-invertible-tfae. The second statement follows in the same way from @thm-block-ldu (b). In words: an invertible block of size k contributes exactly k to the rank, and all the remaining rank sits in its complement. For example, in @exm-rank-i-minus-ab the matrix  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \A \ \B & \I_n \end{pmatrix} has the two complements \I_n - \B \A and \I_m - \A \B, and the theorem gives both expressions for its rank at once. Inverting a block matrix Since \A \oplus (\M/\A) is invertible exactly when \M/\A is, the factorization also inverts \M: invert the three factors and multiply them in the reverse order. [Block Inverse Formula] Let \M =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} \in M_{k+l}(F) with \A \in M_k(F) and \D \in M_l(F). 1. Suppose \A is invertible, and let \S = \M/\A. Then \M is invertible if and only if \S is invertible, and in that case \M^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} \A^{-1} + \A^{-1}\B \S^{-1}\C \A^{-1} & -\A^{-1}\B \S^{-1} \ -\S^{-1}\C \A^{-1} & \S^{-1} \end{pmatrix}. Then \cvec{v}	p \A^{-1}\cvec{u} = 1 -  rac12 +  rac12 = 1, so 1 + \cvec{v}	p \A^{-1}\cvec{u} = 2 
e 0. By @cor-sherman-morrison, \A + \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p is invertible, \det(\A + \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p) = 8 \cdot 2 = 16, and  egin{aligned} (\A + \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p)^{-1} &= \diag ig(1, 	frac12, 	frac14 ig) -  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 \  rac12 \  rac14 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 1 & - rac12 &  rac12 \end{pmatrix} \ &=  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 &  rac12 & 0 \ 0 & 0 &  rac14 \end{pmatrix} -  egin{pmatrix}  rac12 & - rac14 &  rac14 \  rac14 & - rac18 &  rac18 \  rac18 & - rac1{16} &  rac1{16} \end{pmatrix} \ &=  egin{pmatrix}  rac12 &  rac14 & - rac14 \ - rac14 &  rac58 & - rac18 \ - rac18 &  rac1{16} &  rac3{16} \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} Check: \A + \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 2 \ 1 & 1 & 2 \ 1 & -1 & 6 \end{pmatrix}, and its row 1 times column 1 of the answer is 1 +  rac14 -  rac14 = 1, times column 2 is  rac12 -  rac58 +  rac18 = 0. [B3: Identity corners] Let \B \in M_{k 	imes l}(F), \C \in M_{l 	imes k}(F), and \M =  egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \B \ \C & \I_l \end{pmatrix}. 1. Show that \M is invertible if and only if \S = \I_l - \C \B is, and write down \M^{-1} in terms of \S^{-1}. 2. Deduce the inverse of  egin{pmatrix} \I_k & \B \ \O & \I_l \end{pmatrix}. 3. For \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 2 \end{pmatrix} and \C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} over 
Q, compute \M^{-1}. (a) The block \I_k is invertible and \M/\I_k = \I_l - \C \I_k^{-1}\B = \I_l - \C \B. By @thm-block-inverse-formula (a), \M is invertible if and only if \I_l - \C \B is, and then, with \A^{-1} = \I_k, \M^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} \I_k + \B \S^{-1}\C & -\B \S^{-1} \ -\S^{-1}\C & \S^{-1} \end{pmatrix}. (b) With \C = \O, \S = \I_l - \C \B = \I_l and \S^{-1} = \I_l, so the inverse is  egin{pmatrix} \I_k & -\B \ \O & \I_l \end{pmatrix}, in agreement with @thm-block-triangular-inverse. (c) \C \B = (3), so \S = \I_1 - \C \B = (-2) and \S^{-1} = (- rac12). Then \B \S^{-1}\C = - rac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, -\B \S^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix}  rac12 \ 1 \end{pmatrix}, and -\S^{-1}\C =  egin{pmatrix}  rac12 &  rac12 \end{pmatrix}, so \M^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix}  rac12 & - rac12 &  rac12 \ -1 & 0 & 1 \  rac12 &  rac12 & - rac12 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \M =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 2 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Check: row 3 of \M times column 3 of \M^{-1} is  rac12 + 1 -  rac12 = 1, and times column 1 is  rac12 - 1 +  rac12 = 0. C. Going deeper [C1: Sylvester’s determinant identity] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \B \in M_{n 	imes m}(F) with m, n \ge 1. 1. Compute both Schur complements of the identity blocks in \M =  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & -\A \ \B & \I_n \end{pmatrix}, and deduce \det(\I_m + \A \B) = \det(\I_n + \B \A) . 2. Deduce that for every nonzero c \in F, \det(c\I_m - \A \B) = c^{m-n}\det(c\I_n - \B \A). 3. Deduce @thm-matrix-determinant-lemma from (a). (a) Both identity blocks are invertible. By @def-schur-complement,  egin{aligned} \M/\I_m &= \I_n - \B \I_m^{-1}(-\A) = \I_n + \B \A, \ \M/\I_n &= \I_m - (-\A)\I_n^{-1}\B = \I_m + \A \B . \end{aligned} By @thm-schur-determinant (a) and (b), \det \M = \det \I_m\det(\I_n + \B \A) and \det \M = \det \I_n\det(\I_m + \A \B). Hence \det(\I_m + \A \B) = \det(\I_n + \B \A). (b) Let \A' = -c^{-1}\A. Then c\I_m - \A \B = c(\I_m + \A'\B) and c\I_n - \B \A = c(\I_n + \B \A'). Multiplying an m 	imes m matrix by c multiplies each of its m rows by c, so it multiplies the determinant by c^m (@thm-det-row-operations). By (a) applied to \A' and \B,  egin{aligned} \det(c\I_m - \A \B) &= c^m\det(\I_m + \A'\B) = c^m\det(\I_n + \B \A') \ &= c^m c^{-n}\det(c\I_n - \B \A) = c^{m-n}\det(c\I_n - \B \A) . \end{aligned} (c) Let \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \in F^n, and apply (a) with the sizes m, n there replaced by n, 1: \A = \cvec{u} \in M_{n 	imes 1}(F) and \B = \cvec{v}	p \in M_{1 	imes n}(F). Then \det(\I_n + \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p) = \det(\I_1 + \cvec{v}	p\cvec{u}) = 1 + \cvec{v}	p\cvec{u}, because the determinant of a 1 	imes 1 matrix is its entry. [C2: Pivots as Schur complements] Let \A \in M_n(F), and for 1 \le k \le n let \A_k be its leading principal submatrix (the top-left k 	imes k corner), as in @exr-lu-factorization-c1. 1. Suppose \A_{k-1} is invertible, where 2 \le k \le n, and write \A_k =  egin{pmatrix} \A_{k-1} & \cvec{b} \ \cvec{c}	p & d \end{pmatrix}. Show that s_k \coloneqq \A_k/\A_{k-1} is the scalar d - \cvec{c}	p \A_{k-1}^{-1}\cvec{b}, and that \det \A_k = \det \A_{k-1}\cdot s_k. 2. Suppose \A_1, \dots, \A_n are all invertible, and put s_1 = a_{11}. Prove that \det \A_k = s_1s_2\cdots s_k for every k, and that every s_k is nonzero. 3. Keep the hypothesis of (b). In the proof of @exr-lu-factorization-c1 (c), the last pivot is z = d - \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y} with \cvec{y} = \L'^{-1}\cvec{b} and \cvec{x}	p = \cvec{c}	p \U'^{-1}. Show that z = \A_n/\A_{n-1}. Deduce that the diagonal entries of \U in the LU factorization are u_{kk} = \det \A_k / \det \A_{k-1}, with \det \A_0 \coloneqq 1. 4. Check (c) for \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \ 4 & 3 & 3 \ 8 & 7 & 9 \end{pmatrix} over 
Q. (a) With the partition k - 1, 1, @def-schur-complement gives the 1 	imes 1 matrix \A_k/\A_{k-1} = d - \cvec{c}	p \A_{k-1}^{-1}\cvec{b}, which we identify with its entry. By @thm-schur-determinant (a), \det \A_k = \det \A_{k-1}\det(s_k) = \det \A_{k-1}\cdot s_k. (b) By induction on k. For k = 1, \det \A_1 = a_{11} = s_1. If \det \A_{k-1} = s_1\cdots s_{k-1}, then by (a), which applies since \A_{k-1} is invertible, \det \A_k = s_1\cdots s_{k-1}s_k. Since \A_k is invertible, \det \A_k 
e 0 (@thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible), so no factor s_k is zero (@thm-field-basic-properties (d)). (c) \A_{n-1} = \L'\U' with both factors invertible, so \A_{n-1}^{-1} = \U'^{-1}\L'^{-1} (@thm-inverse-matrix-properties (3)) and \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y} = \cvec{c}	p \U'^{-1}\L'^{-1}\cvec{b} = \cvec{c}	p \A_{n-1}^{-1}\cvec{b}. Hence z = d - \cvec{c}	p \A_{n-1}^{-1}\cvec{b} = \A_n/\A_{n-1} = s_n by (a). The same construction applied to \A_k (whose LU factors are the top-left corners \L_k, \U_k of \L, \U, by @exr-lu-factorization-c1 (a) and @thm-lu-unique) shows u_{kk} = s_k for every k. By (a) and (b), s_k = \det \A_k/\det \A_{k-1}, with s_1 = \det \A_1/1. (d) \det \A_1 = 2, \det \A_2 = 6 - 4 = 2, and expanding, \det \A_3 = 2(27 - 21) - 1(36 - 24) + 1(28 - 24) = 12 - 12 + 4 = 4. The predicted pivots are 2, 2/2 = 1, 4/2 = 2. Elimination gives \L =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 2 & 1 & 0 \ 4 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and \U =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}: subtract 2 and 4 times row 1 to get rows (0, 1, 1) and (0, 3, 5), then 3 times the new row 2 to get (0, 0, 2). The diagonal of \U is 2, 1, 2, as predicted. [C3: When \A and \C commute] Let n \ge 1 and \A, \B, \C, \D \in M_n(F) with \A \C = \C \A, and \M =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix}. 1. Assume \A is invertible. Use @thm-schur-determinant to prove \det \M = \det(\A \D - \C \B). 2. Remove the assumption that \A is invertible, over any field, by adapting the proof of @thm-det-commuting-blocks with \A_x = \A + x\I_n. 3. For \A = \I_2, \B = \E_{12}, \C = \E_{21}, \D = \E_{11} in M_2(
Q), check that \A \C = \C \A, and compare \det \M, \det(\A \D - \C \B), and \det(\A \D - \B \C). Hint for (b): multiply \M_x on the left by a block matrix that clears the lower-left block. (a) By @thm-schur-determinant (a) and @thm-det-multiplicative,  egin{aligned} \det \M &= \det \A\det(\D - \C \A^{-1}\B) \ &= \det ig(\A(\D - \C \A^{-1}\B) ig) = \det(\A \D - \A \C \A^{-1}\B) . \end{aligned} Since \A \C = \C \A, \A \C \A^{-1} = \C \A \A^{-1} = \C, so \det \M = \det(\A \D - \C \B). (b) Let \A_x = \A + x\I_n over F[x]. Then \A_x\C = \A \C + x\C = \C \A + x\C = \C \A_x. Let \M_x =  egin{pmatrix} \A_x & \B \ \C & \D \end{pmatrix} and \L =  egin{pmatrix} \I_n & \O \ -\C & \A_x \end{pmatrix}. By @thm-block-multiplication over F[x], \L \M_x =  egin{pmatrix} \A_x & \B \ -\C \A_x + \A_x\C & -\C \B + \A_x\D \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \A_x & \B \ \O & \A_x\D - \C \B \end{pmatrix}. By @thm-det-multiplicative and @thm-det-block-triangular over F[x] (Chapter 7 §5 and §8), \det \A_x\det \M_x = \det \A_x\det(\A_x\D - \C \B), using \det \L = \det \I_n\det \A_x. As in the proof of @thm-det-commuting-blocks, \det \A_x = p_{-\A}(x) is monic, hence nonzero, and @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors (2) gives \det \M_x = \det(\A_x\D - \C \B). Evaluating at x = 0 with @lem-evaluate-polynomial-matrix gives \det \M = \det(\A \D - \C \B). (c) \A \C = \C = \C \A, since \A = \I_2. As computed in Section 1, \det \M = -1. Also \A \D - \C \B = \E_{11} - \E_{21}\E_{12} = \E_{11} - \E_{22} = \diag(1, -1), with determinant -1, in agreement with (b). But \A \D - \B \C = \E_{11} - \E_{12}\E_{21} = \E_{11} - \E_{11} = \O, with determinant 0. So with \A \C = \C \A the product must be taken as \C \B, not \B \C; here \C \D = \E_{21} 
e \O = \D \C, so @thm-det-commuting-blocks does not apply.

title: 8.4 The Kronecker Product
content:
The Kronecker Product So far the unknown in a matrix equation has been a vector: \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}. Many natural questions have a matrix as the unknown instead. Which matrices commute with a given \A? Which \X solve \A \X + \X \B = \C? Such an equation is still linear in the entries of \X, so in principle it is an ordinary linear system. The trouble is bookkeeping: we need to know what the coefficient matrix of that system is. This section builds it from \A and \B with one operation, the Kronecker product, and turns matrix equations into systems we already know how to solve. From a matrix equation to a linear system Take \A, \B \in M_2(F) and an unknown \X = (x_{ij}) \in M_2(F), and look at the equation \A \X \B = \C. By @def-matrix-multiplication, applied twice, (\A \X \B)_{rs} = \sum_{i=1}^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{2} a_{ri}\,x_{ij}\,b_{js} . So each entry of \A \X \B is a linear combination of the four unknowns x_{11}, x_{21}, x_{12}, x_{22}, and the coefficient of x_{ij} in entry (r, s) is the product b_{js}a_{ri}: an entry of \B times an entry of \A. Writing the four equations as a 4 	imes 4 system, every coefficient is such a product. For instance, if we list the unknowns column by column as (x_{11}, x_{21}, x_{12}, x_{22}) and the equations in the same order, the first row of the coefficient matrix is  egin{pmatrix} b_{11}a_{11} & b_{11}a_{12} & b_{21}a_{11} & b_{21}a_{12} \end{pmatrix}. The left half of this row is b_{11} times row 1 of \A, and the right half is b_{21} times row 1 of \A. That is a recurring pattern: a big matrix whose entries are all the products of the entries of two small matrices, arranged in blocks. It deserves a name. The Kronecker product The Kronecker product of \A and \B is the block matrix obtained by replacing each entry a_{ij} of \A by the block a_{ij}\B. [Kronecker product] Let \A = (a_{ij}) \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \B = (b_{kl}) \in M_{p 	imes q}(F), of any sizes. The Kronecker product of \A and \B is the mp 	imes nq block matrix \A \otimes \B \coloneqq  egin{pmatrix} a_{11}\B & a_{12}\B & \cdots & a_{1n}\B \ a_{21}\B & a_{22}\B & \cdots & a_{2n}\B \ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \ a_{m1}\B & a_{m2}\B & \cdots & a_{mn}\B \end{pmatrix} \in M_{mp 	imes nq}(F), with m rows and n columns of blocks, each block of size p 	imes q (@def-block-partition). In words: the outer layout is the layout of \A, and the inner pattern of every block is \B. The sizes multiply, rows with rows and columns with columns. No condition on the sizes is needed, unlike for an ordinary product. To work with single entries we need to know where each product a_{ij}b_{kl} sits. Block (i, j) occupies rows (i-1)p + 1, \dots, ip and columns (j-1)q + 1, \dots, jq. Inside it, entry (k, l) is a_{ij}b_{kl}. So  egin{aligned} &(\A \otimes \B)_{(i-1)p+k,\ (j-1)q+l} = a_{ij}\,b_{kl} \ &\qquad (1 \le i \le m,\ 1 \le j \le n,\ 1 \le k \le p,\ 1 \le l \le q). \end{aligned} 	ag{$\ast$} Every entry is reached exactly once. Division with remainder writes each row index r \in \{1, \dots, mp\} uniquely as r = (i-1)p + k with 1 \le i \le m and 1 \le k \le p (divide r - 1 by p), and likewise for columns. So (\ast) is a complete description of \A \otimes \B, and it is the formula we use in proofs. In words, the rows of \A \otimes \B are labeled by pairs (row of \A, row of \B) in dictionary order, and the columns by pairs (column of \A, column of \B) in dictionary order. Examples. 1. A 2 	imes 2 example. With \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} and \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \A \otimes \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1\B & 2\B \ 3\B & 4\B \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 & 2 \ 1 & 0 & 2 & 0 \ 0 & 3 & 0 & 4 \ 3 & 0 & 4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Check one entry against (\ast): row 3 = (2-1)\cdot 2 + 1 and column 2 = (1-1)\cdot 2 + 2 give a_{21}b_{12} = 3 \cdot 1 = 3, as displayed. 2. Vectors. For column vectors \cvec{u} \in F^m and \cvec{v} \in F^p (so n = q = 1), \cvec{u} \otimes \cvec{v} \in F^{mp} lists all products u_iv_k in dictionary order. In particular, for standard basis vectors, \cvec{e}_i \otimes \cvec{e}_k = \cvec{e}_{(i-1)p+k} \in F^{mp}: the only nonzero product is 1 \cdot 1 in position (i-1)p + k. For a column \cvec{u} \in F^m and a row \cvec{v}	p, \cvec{u} \otimes \cvec{v}	p is the m 	imes p matrix with entries u_iv_k, which is the outer product \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p of @cor-outer-product-expansion. 3. Identity blocks. \I_n \otimes \B has \B in each diagonal block and zero blocks elsewhere, so it is the block diagonal matrix \B \oplus \dots \oplus \B with n copies of \B (@def-block-diagonal). By contrast, \A \otimes \I_m replaces each entry a_{ij} by the m 	imes m block a_{ij}\I_m. Taking both, \I_n \otimes \I_m = \I_{nm}: by (\ast) its entries are \delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}, which is 1 exactly when the row and column labels (i, k) and (j, l) agree. 4. The degenerate case 1 	imes 1. If \A = (a) is 1 	imes 1, then \A \otimes \B = a\B; if \B = (b), then \A \otimes \B = b\A. So a 1 	imes 1 factor behaves like a scalar, and (1) \otimes \B = \B. This case is worth keeping in mind: it shows that the Kronecker product extends scalar multiplication, which is why it is bilinear below. Nonexample by minimal change. Swap the two factors of Example 1: \B \otimes \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0\A & 1\A \ 1\A & 0\A \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 3 & 4 \ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \ 3 & 4 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. It has the same size and the same multiset of entries, since both list all products a_{ij}b_{kl}. What fails is the position formula (\ast): in \B \otimes \A the outer layout comes from \B, so the products sit in different places. For instance, the (1, 2)-entry is a_{11}b_{12} = 1 in \A \otimes \B but b_{11}a_{12} = 0 in \B \otimes \A. Why this definition. The dictionary order in (\ast) is a convention, and the other order would simply give \B \otimes \A. We fix it because it makes the block picture true: the Kronecker product is literally “\A with entries replaced by blocks”, so block multiplication (@thm-block-multiplication) applies to it directly. The symbol \otimes anticipates the tensor product of Chapter 15, of which this is the matrix version. The Kronecker product is not commutative, and it is not the ordinary product. The two matrices in Example 1 and the nonexample differ, so \A \otimes \B 
e \B \otimes \A in general, even for square matrices of the same size. Also do not confuse \A \otimes \B with \A \B: for \A, \B \in M_2(F), \A \B is 2 	imes 2 while \A \otimes \B is 4 	imes 4, and \A \otimes \B is defined for all sizes. We will see below that \A \otimes \B and \B \otimes \A are always similar when \A and \B are square, so they share rank, trace, and determinant, but they are not equal. Algebraic properties The Kronecker product interacts well with every operation we have. The most useful rule is the one connecting it to ordinary multiplication: multiply the two left factors together and the two right factors together. [Properties of the Kronecker Product] Let c \in F. Whenever the sizes make each side defined: 1. (Bilinearity) (\A + \A') \otimes \B = \A \otimes \B + \A' \otimes \B, \A \otimes (\B + \B') = \A \otimes \B + \A \otimes \B', and (c\A) \otimes \B = c(\A \otimes \B) = \A \otimes (c\B). 2. (Associativity) (\A \otimes \B) \otimes \C = \A \otimes (\B \otimes \C) for all \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), \B \in M_{p 	imes q}(F), \C \in M_{r 	imes s}(F). 3. (Mixed product rule) For \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), \C \in M_{n 	imes t}(F), \B \in M_{p 	imes q}(F), and \D \in M_{q 	imes u}(F), (\A \otimes \B)(\C \otimes \D) = (\A \C) \otimes (\B \D) . 4. (Transpose) (\A \otimes \B)	p = \A	p \otimes \B	p. 5. (Inverse) If \A \in M_n(F) and \B \in M_m(F) are invertible, then \A \otimes \B is invertible and (\A \otimes \B)^{-1} = \A^{-1} \otimes \B^{-1}. Parts (a), (b), and (d) are entry checks with (\ast). For (c), both factors on the left are block matrices, and the columns of blocks of \A \otimes \B (n of them, each q wide) match the rows of blocks of \C \otimes \D (n of them, each q tall). So we may multiply blockwise, and each block of the product is a sum \sum_j (a_{ij}\B)(c_{jk}\D) in which the scalars come out. Part (e) is (c) with \C = \A^{-1}, \D = \B^{-1}. (a) By (\ast), the entry of (\A + \A') \otimes \B in position ((i-1)p + k, (j-1)q + l) is (a_{ij} + a'_{ij})b_{kl} = a_{ij}b_{kl} + a'_{ij}b_{kl}, which is the entry of \A \otimes \B + \A' \otimes \B in the same position. The other identities are checked the same way, using (ca_{ij})b_{kl} = c(a_{ij}b_{kl}) = a_{ij}(cb_{kl}). (b) Both sides are mpr 	imes nqs. Let 1 \le i \le m, 1 \le k \le p, 1 \le t \le r, and similarly j, l, u for columns. Applying (\ast) twice, the entry of (\A \otimes \B) \otimes \C in row  ig((i-1)p + k - 1 ig)r + t and column  ig((j-1)q + l - 1 ig)s + u is (\A \otimes \B)_{(i-1)p+k,\,(j-1)q+l}\;c_{tu} = a_{ij}b_{kl}c_{tu}. Likewise the entry of \A \otimes (\B \otimes \C) in row (i-1)pr + (k-1)r + t and column (j-1)qs + (l-1)s + u is a_{ij}(\B \otimes \C)_{(k-1)r+t,\,(l-1)s+u} = a_{ij}b_{kl}c_{tu}. Since  ig((i-1)p + k - 1 ig)r + t = (i-1)pr + (k-1)r + t, and similarly for columns, the two matrices have the same entry in every position; every position arises from exactly one choice of indices, by division with remainder. Hence they are equal. (c) Partition \A \otimes \B into m rows and n columns of blocks as in @def-kronecker-product, each block p 	imes q, and \C \otimes \D into n rows and t columns of blocks, each q 	imes u. The column partition of the first matrix (n parts of size q) equals the row partition of the second, so the partitions are conformable, and by @thm-block-multiplication the (i, k) block of the product is \sum_{j=1}^{n} (a_{ij}\B)(c_{jk}\D) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij}c_{jk}\,\B \D = (\A \C)_{ik}\,\B \D, where the first equality uses @thm-matrix-multiplication-properties (4) and the second uses @def-matrix-multiplication. This is the (i, k) block of (\A \C) \otimes (\B \D), a matrix partitioned into m rows and t columns of p 	imes u blocks. So the two matrices agree block by block, hence entry by entry. (d) (\A \otimes \B)	p is nq 	imes mp. By @def-transpose and (\ast), its entry in row (j-1)q + l and column (i-1)p + k is (\A \otimes \B)_{(i-1)p+k,\,(j-1)q+l} = a_{ij}b_{kl} = (\A	p)_{ji}(\B	p)_{lk}, which by (\ast) is the entry of \A	p \otimes \B	p in the same position. (e) By (c) and Example 3, (\A \otimes \B)(\A^{-1} \otimes \B^{-1}) = (\A \A^{-1}) \otimes (\B \B^{-1}) = \I_n \otimes \I_m = \I_{nm}, and similarly (\A^{-1} \otimes \B^{-1})(\A \otimes \B) = \I_{nm}.
