By @thm-exponential-properties (b), \cvec{x}'(t) = \A e^{t\A}\cvec{x}_0 = \A\cvec{x}(t). And \cvec{x}(0) = e^{\O}\cvec{x}_0 = \cvec{x}_0 by @thm-exponential-properties (a). Uniqueness. Let \cvec{y} \colon 
R 	o 
C^{n} be differentiable with \cvec{y}' = \A\cvec{y} and \cvec{y}(0) = \cvec{x}_0. Put \cvec{z}(t) = e^{-t\A}\cvec{y}(t). By the product rule (A3) and @thm-exponential-properties (b) applied to -\A, \cvec{z}'(t) =  igl(-\A e^{-t\A} igr)\cvec{y}(t) + e^{-t\A}\cvec{y}'(t) = -\A e^{-t\A}\cvec{y}(t) + e^{-t\A}\A\cvec{y}(t) = \cvec{0} , where the last step uses e^{-t\A}\A = \A e^{-t\A} from @thm-exponential-properties (b). By (A4) each entry of \cvec{z} is constant, so \cvec{z}(t) = \cvec{z}(0) = \cvec{x}_0 for all t. Multiplying by e^{t\A} and using @thm-exponential-properties (c), \cvec{y}(t) = e^{t\A}\cvec{z}(t) = e^{t\A}\cvec{x}_0 = \cvec{x}(t) . This proves the theorem. The formula is only as useful as our ability to compute e^{t\A}, and the Jordan form does that. Two shapes of answer occur, and they are worth seeing side by side. [Two Two-Dimensional Systems] Solve \cvec{x}' = \A\cvec{x} with \cvec{x}(0) = (1, 0) for 1. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 \ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix} (complex eigenvalues); 2. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} (one eigenvalue, one block of size 2). (a) p_{\A} = (x-1)^2 + 4, with roots \lambda = 1 \pm 2i, distinct, so \A is diagonalizable over 
C and every block has size 1. Solving (\A - (1+2i)\I)\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}: the first row reads -2ix_1 - 2x_2 = 0, so x_2 = -ix_1 and (1, -i) is an eigenvector; (1, i) is one for 1 - 2i. With \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ -i & i\end{pmatrix} we get \det \P = 2i and \P^{-1} = 	frac{1}{2i} egin{pmatrix} i & -1 \ i & 1\end{pmatrix} = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ 1 & -i \end{pmatrix}, so \P^{-1}\A \P = \diag(1+2i, 1-2i). By @cor-exponential-of-jordan-block,  egin{aligned} e^{t\A} &= \P\diag igl(e^{(1+2i)t},\, e^{(1-2i)t} igr)\P^{-1} \ &= 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} e^{(1+2i)t} + e^{(1-2i)t} & i igl(e^{(1+2i)t} - e^{(1-2i)t} igr) \ -i igl(e^{(1+2i)t} - e^{(1-2i)t} igr) & e^{(1+2i)t} + e^{(1-2i)t}\end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} By (A1), e^{(1 \pm 2i)t} = e^{t}(\cos 2t \pm i\sin 2t), so e^{(1+2i)t} + e^{(1-2i)t} = 2e^{t}\cos 2t and e^{(1+2i)t} - e^{(1-2i)t} = 2ie^{t}\sin 2t. Substituting, and using i \cdot 2i = -2, e^{t\A} = e^{t} egin{pmatrix} \cos 2t & -\sin 2t \ \sin 2t & \cos 2t \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{x}(t) = e^{t\A} egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{pmatrix} = e^{t} egin{pmatrix} \cos 2t \ \sin 2t\end{pmatrix}. The solution spirals outwards: rotation at angular speed 2, growth at rate 1. The entries are real, as they must be for a real \A and a real \cvec{x}_0. Check. \cvec{x}'(t) = e^{t}(\cos 2t - 2\sin 2t,\ \sin 2t + 2\cos 2t), and \A\cvec{x}(t) = e^{t}(\cos 2t - 2\sin 2t,\ 2\cos 2t + \sin 2t). They agree, and \cvec{x}(0) = (1,0). (b) \A = \J_2(2) is its own Jordan form. Writing \A = 2\I + \M with \M =  egin{pmatrix} 0&1\0&0\end{pmatrix}, the two summands commute and \M^2 = \O, so @cor-exponential-of-jordan-block with k = 2 gives e^{t\A} = e^{2t} igl(\I + t\M igr) = e^{2t} egin{pmatrix} 1 & t \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}. So \cvec{x}(t) = e^{2t}(1, 0). A different initial vector shows the new phenomenon: \cvec{x}(0) = (0,1) gives \cvec{x}(t) = e^{2t}(t, 1), whose first entry is te^{2t}. A repeated eigenvalue with a block of size k produces solutions containing t^{j}e^{\lambda t} for j < k. This is the same t^{j}\lambda^{m} pattern that Chapter 9 met for recurrences with repeated roots, now in continuous time. A scalar equation of higher order is a system in disguise, and the translation is the companion matrix of Section 5. [A Second-Order Equation with a Repeated Root] Solve y'' - 4y' + 4y = 0 with y(0) = 1 and y'(0) = 3. Make it a system. Put \cvec{u} = (y, y'). Then \cvec{u}' = (y', y'') = (y', 4y' - 4y), so \cvec{u}' = \M\cvec{u} with \M =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -4 & 4\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{u}(0) = (1, 3). Note that p_{\M} = x(x - 4) + 4 = x^2 - 4x + 4 is the polynomial of the equation, and that \M = \C(p_{\M})	p for the companion matrix \C(p_{\M}) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -4 \ 1 & 4\end{pmatrix} of @def-companion-matrix; by @cor-a-similar-to-transpose the two are similar, so which of them one uses is immaterial. Exponentiate. p_{\M} = (x-2)^2. Put \N = \M - 2\I =  egin{pmatrix} -2 & 1 \ -4 & 2\end{pmatrix}; then \N^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 4 - 4 & -2+2 \ 8-8 & -4+4\end{pmatrix} = \O, so 2\I and \N commute and @thm-exponential-properties (d) gives, as in the previous example, e^{t\M} = e^{2t}(\I + t\N) = e^{2t} egin{pmatrix} 1 - 2t & t \ -4t & 1 + 2t\end{pmatrix}. (No basis change was needed: \M is a scalar plus a nilpotent matrix on the nose.) Read off the answer. \cvec{u}(t) = e^{t\M} egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 3\end{pmatrix} = e^{2t} egin{pmatrix} (1 - 2t) + 3t \ -4t + 3(1 + 2t)\end{pmatrix} = e^{2t} egin{pmatrix} 1 + t \ 3 + 2t \end{pmatrix}, so y(t) = (1+t)e^{2t}. Check. y' = e^{2t} + 2(1+t)e^{2t} = (3 + 2t)e^{2t}, which is the second entry of \cvec{u}, as it should be, and y'(0) = 3. Then y'' = 2e^{2t} + 2(3+2t)e^{2t} = (8 + 4t)e^{2t}, and y'' - 4y' + 4y =  igl[(8 + 4t) - 4(3 + 2t) + 4(1 + t) igr]e^{2t} = 0 . The repeated root 2 produces the term te^{2t}, exactly as the size-2 block predicts. Chapter 16 will return to e^{\A} with norms available, which give quantitative bounds instead of exact formulas. The next section stays with exact formulas and asks the discrete-time question: what happens to \A^{m}? Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the formula for p(\J_k(\lambda)) and say where the factorials come from. 2. Define f(\A) for \A \in M_n(
C) with a given Jordan form, and list the two choices whose irrelevance has to be checked. 3. Which values of f and its derivatives does f(\A) depend on? How many numbers is that? 4. State the five properties of e^{\A} proved in @thm-exponential-properties, with their hypotheses. 5. True or false: e^{\A+\B} = e^{\A}e^{\B} for all \A, \B \in M_n(
C). Justify your answer. 6. True or false: e^{\A} can be singular. Justify your answer. (a) p(\J_k(\lambda)) is upper triangular with p^{(j)}(\lambda)/j! in every position (r, r+j) (@lem-polynomial-of-jordan-block). The factorials come from the Taylor expansion p = \sum_j  rac{p^{(j)}(\lambda)}{j!}(x-\lambda)^j (@thm-polynomial-taylor), whose j-th term contributes \J_k(0)^{j}, the matrix with ones on the j-th superdiagonal. (b) f(\A) = \P igl( igoplus_i f(\J_{k_i}(\lambda_i)) igr)\P^{-1} with f(\J_k(\lambda)) as in (a) (@def-matrix-function-jordan). The choices are the matrix \P and the order in which the blocks are listed; both are irrelevant because f(\A) = p(\A) for the Hermite interpolating polynomial p (@thm-matrix-function-hermite). (c) On f^{(j)}(\mu) for each eigenvalue \mu and each j < s_\mu, where s_\mu is the exponent of x - \mu in m_{\A}, that is, the largest \mu-block size. The total number is \sum_\mu s_\mu = \deg m_{\A} (@thm-matrix-function-hermite). (d) e^{\P^{-1}\A \P} = \P^{-1}e^{\A}\P for invertible \P;  rac{d}{dt}e^{t\A} = \A e^{t\A} = e^{t\A}\A; (e^{\A})^{-1} = e^{-\A}; e^{\A+\B} = e^{\A}e^{\B} provided \A \B = \B \A; and \det e^{\A} = e^{	r \A} with no hypothesis. (e) False. With \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0&1\0&0\end{pmatrix} and \B = \A	p, the matrices e^{\A}e^{\B} and e^{\B}e^{\A} differ, so the identity cannot hold for both orders; see the warning after @thm-exponential-properties. (f) False. \det e^{\A} = e^{	r \A} 
e 0 by @thm-exponential-properties (e) and (A1), so e^{\A} is always invertible (@thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible). B. Practice [B1: Computing exponentials] Compute e^{t\A} for each of the following. 1. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 3 & 1\end{pmatrix}. 2. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 1 \ 0 & 5\end{pmatrix}. 3. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 3 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 3\end{pmatrix} = \J_3(3). (a) p_{\A} = (x-1)^2 - 9, with roots 4 and -2. Eigenvectors: (\A - 4\I)\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} gives \Span((1,1)); (\A + 2\I)\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} gives \Span((1,-1)). With \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix} we have \det \P = -2, \P^{-1} = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}, and \P^{-1}\A \P = \diag(4, -2), so by @cor-exponential-of-jordan-block e^{t\A} = \P\diag(e^{4t}, e^{-2t})\P^{-1} = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} e^{4t} + e^{-2t} & e^{4t} - e^{-2t} \ e^{4t} - e^{-2t} & e^{4t} + e^{-2t}\end{pmatrix}. Check at t = 0: both diagonal entries give 1 and both off-diagonal ones 0, so e^{\O} = \I. (b) \A = \J_2(5), so @cor-exponential-of-jordan-block with k = 2 gives e^{t\A} = e^{5t}(\I + t\M) = e^{5t} egin{pmatrix} 1 & t \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}. (c) By @cor-exponential-of-jordan-block with k = 3 and \lambda = 3, or directly from \A = 3\I + \M with \M = \J_3(0) and \M^3 = \O, giving e^{t\A} = e^{3t} igl(\I + t\M + 	frac{t^2}{2}\M^2 igr): e^{t\A} = e^{3t} egin{pmatrix} 1 & t & 	frac{t^2}{2} \ 0 & 1 & t \ 0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}. This is @def-matrix-function-jordan for f(x) = e^{tx}: the j-th superdiagonal carries f^{(j)}(3)/j! = t^{j}e^{3t}/j!. [B2: Solving systems] Solve each initial value problem, and verify your answer by differentiating. 1. x' = x + 3y, y' = 3x + y, with x(0) = 2, y(0) = 0. 2. \cvec{x}' =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -3 \ 3 & 0\end{pmatrix}\cvec{x} with \cvec{x}(0) = (0, 1). 3. y''' = 0 with y(0) = 1, y'(0) = 0, y''(0) = 2, by turning it into a system. (a) This is \cvec{x}' = \A\cvec{x} for the matrix of @exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-b1 (a). By @thm-linear-ode-solution, \cvec{x}(t) = e^{t\A} egin{pmatrix} 2 \ 0\end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} e^{4t} + e^{-2t} \ e^{4t} - e^{-2t}\end{pmatrix}, that is, x = e^{4t} + e^{-2t} and y = e^{4t} - e^{-2t}. Check. x' = 4e^{4t} - 2e^{-2t} and x + 3y = e^{4t} + e^{-2t} + 3e^{4t} - 3e^{-2t} = 4e^{4t} - 2e^{-2t}; similarly for y'. And x(0) = 2, y(0) = 0. (b) Write \A = 3\R with \R =  egin{pmatrix} 0&-1\1&0\end{pmatrix}, whose eigenvalues are \pm i (@exm-complex-eigenvalues-real-matrix), so those of \A are \pm 3i, distinct. Repeating the computation of @exm-ode-oscillation-and-resonance (a) with 1 \pm 2i replaced by \pm 3i — eigenvectors (1, -i) for 3i and (1, i) for -3i — gives e^{t\A} =  egin{pmatrix} \cos 3t & -\sin 3t \ \sin 3t & \cos 3t\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{x}(t) =  egin{pmatrix} -\sin 3t \ \cos 3t\end{pmatrix}. Check. \cvec{x}'(t) = (-3\cos 3t, -3\sin 3t) and \A\cvec{x}(t) = (-3\cos 3t, -3\sin 3t); and \cvec{x}(0) = (0,1). The solution runs around the unit circle: no growth, since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary. (c) Put \cvec{u} = (y, y', y''). Then \cvec{u}' = (y', y'', 0) = \M\cvec{u} with \M = \J_3(0), and \cvec{u}(0) = (1, 0, 2). By @cor-exponential-of-jordan-block with \lambda = 0 and k = 3, e^{t\M} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & t & t^2/2 \ 0 & 1 & t \ 0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{u}(t) = e^{t\M} egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 0 \ 2\end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 + t^2 \ 2t \ 2\end{pmatrix}. So y(t) = 1 + t^2. Check. y' = 2t, y'' = 2, y''' = 0, and the three initial values are 1, 0, 2. The eigenvalue 0 with one block of size 3 gives polynomial solutions t^{j}e^{0t} = t^{j} for j < 3. [B3: A square root and a logarithm] 1. Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}. Compute f(\A) for f(x) = \sqrt x (positive branch) and verify that f(\A)^2 = \A. 2. Let \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Compute f(\B) for f(x) = \log x with \log 1 = 0, and verify that e^{f(\B)} = \B. 3. Explain why the same method produces no square root of  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. (a) p_{\A} = (x-2)^2 - 1 = (x-1)(x-3), eigenvalues 1, 3. Eigenvectors (1,-1) for 1 and (1,1) for 3. With \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix} and \P^{-1} = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}, f(\A) = \P\diag(1, \sqrt3)\P^{-1} = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 + \sqrt3 & -1 + \sqrt3 \ -1 + \sqrt3 & 1 + \sqrt3\end{pmatrix}. Squaring, the diagonal entry is 	frac14 igl[(1+\sqrt3)^2 + (\sqrt3 - 1)^2 igr] = 	frac14(4 + 2\sqrt3 + 4 - 2\sqrt3) = 2, and the off-diagonal entry is 	frac14\cdot 2(1+\sqrt3)(\sqrt3-1) = 	frac12(3 - 1) = 1. So f(\A)^2 = \A. (b) Here m_{\B} = (x-1)^2, since (\B - \I)^2 = \O 
e \B - \I, so by @thm-matrix-function-hermite the answer is p(\B) for the polynomial of degree < 2 with p(1) = f(1) = 0 and p'(1) = f'(1) = 1, namely p = x - 1. Hence f(\B) = \B - \I =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Its square is \O, so e^{f(\B)} = \I + f(\B) =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \B. The Jordan route gives the same thing: with \Q = \diag(2, 1) we get \Q^{-1}\B \Q = \J_2(1), and f(\J_2(1)) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}, so f(\B) = \Q f(\J_2(1))\Q^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}. (c) The matrix is \J_2(0), with the single eigenvalue 0 and a block of size 2. @def-matrix-function-jordan needs f and f' at 0, and f(x) = \sqrt x is not differentiable at 0 — the entry f'(0) does not exist. In fact \J_2(0) has no square root at all: if \X^2 = \J_2(0), then \X^4 = \J_2(0)^2 = \O, so \X is nilpotent, so \X^2 = \O by @prp-nilpotent-basic (a) with n = 2, contradicting \X^2 = \J_2(0) 
e \O. C. Going deeper [C1: How badly the exponential law fails] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} and \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} in M_2(
R). 1. Compute e^{\A}, e^{\B}, e^{\A}e^{\B}, and e^{\B}e^{\A}. 2. Compute e^{\A+\B} in closed form. Hint: (\A+\B)^2 = \I, so split the series into even and odd terms. 3. Verify \det e^{\A+\B} = e^{	r(\A+\B)} and \det(e^{\A}e^{\B}) = e^{	r \A}e^{	r \B}, and explain why equal determinants do not rescue the identity. 4. Show that e^{\A}e^{\B} = e^{\C} for some \C \in M_2(
R), and find 	r \C. (a) \A^2 = \B^2 = \O, so e^{\A} = \I + \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} and e^{\B} = \I + \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}. Then e^{\A}e^{\B} =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad e^{\B}e^{\A} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}. (b) Let \K = \A + \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0&1\1&0\end{pmatrix}. Then \K^2 = \I, so \K^{2l} = \I and \K^{2l+1} = \K. Splitting the partial sums by parity, which is legitimate because each entry sequence is a sum of two convergent sequences (A3),  egin{aligned} e^{\K} &= \Bigl(\sum_{l \ge 0} rac{1}{(2l)!}\Bigr)\I + \Bigl(\sum_{l \ge 0} rac{1}{(2l+1)!}\Bigr)\K \ &=  rac{e + e^{-1}}{2}\I +  rac{e - e^{-1}}{2}\K =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac{e+e^{-1}}{2} & 	frac{e - e^{-1}}{2} \ 	frac{e-e^{-1}}{2} & 	frac{e+e^{-1}}{2}\end{pmatrix}, \end{aligned} where the two scalar sums were identified by adding and subtracting the series for e^{1} and e^{-1} term by term (A1). Numerically the diagonal entries are about 1.543, not 2, so e^{\A+\B} 
e e^{\A}e^{\B}. (c) 	r(\A+\B) = 0 and \det e^{\A+\B} =  igl(	frac{e+e^{-1}}{2} igr)^2 -  igl(	frac{e-e^{-1}}{2} igr)^2 = 	frac14 igl[(e+e^{-1})^2 - (e - e^{-1})^2 igr] = 	frac14\cdot 4 = 1 = e^{0}. Also \det(e^{\A}e^{\B}) = 2 - 1 = 1 = e^{0}e^{0}. The determinants agree because both matrices are products of exponentials of trace-zero matrices; a determinant is one number and cannot distinguish two matrices, so it gives no information about the identity either way. The entries do. (d) \X = e^{\A}e^{\B} =  egin{pmatrix} 2&1\1&1\end{pmatrix} is symmetric with \det \X = 1 and 	r \X = 3, so p_{\X} = x^2 - 3x + 1, whose roots 	frac{3 \pm \sqrt5}{2} are real, distinct, and positive. So \X = \P\diag(\alpha,  eta)\P^{-1} with \alpha eta = 1, \alpha,  eta > 0. Put \C = \P\diag(\log\alpha, \log eta)\P^{-1}, a real matrix because \P can be taken real (the eigenvalues are real) and the logarithms are real. By @def-matrix-function-jordan applied to f = \exp, e^{\C} = \P\diag(\alpha,  eta)\P^{-1} = \X. Finally 	r \C = \log\alpha + \log eta = \log(\alpha eta) = \log 1 = 0, as @thm-exponential-properties (e) requires, since \det \X = 1. [C2: When does every solution die out?] Let \A \in M_n(
C). Prove that the following are equivalent: 1. every solution of \cvec{x}' = \A\cvec{x} satisfies \cvec{x}(t) 	o \cvec{0} entrywise as t 	o \infty; 2. every eigenvalue \lambda of \A has \operatorname{Re}\lambda < 0. Hint: compute the entries of e^{t\J_k(\lambda)} and use (A5). For the failing direction, an eigenvector gives a solution you can write down. (ii) \Rightarrow (i). By @thm-linear-ode-solution every solution is \cvec{x}(t) = e^{t\A}\cvec{x}_0, so it suffices to show e^{t\A} 	o \O entrywise. Write \A = \P \J \P^{-1} with \J =  igoplus_i \J_{k_i}(\lambda_i) (@thm-jordan-canonical-form). Each entry of e^{t\A} = \P e^{t\J}\P^{-1} is a fixed linear combination of entries of e^{t\J}, so by (A3) it is enough that e^{t\J} 	o \O. By @cor-exponential-of-jordan-block, the nonzero entries of e^{t\J_k(\lambda)} are  rac{t^{j}e^{\lambda t}}{j!} \qquad (0 \le j \le k-1). Writing \lambda = c + i\omega with c = \operatorname{Re}\lambda < 0, we get |t^{j}e^{\lambda t}| = t^{j}e^{ct}|e^{i\omega t}| = t^{j}e^{ct} for t \ge 0, since |e^{i\omega t}| = |\cos\omega t + i\sin\omega t| = 1 by (A1). By (A5) this tends to 0, and a complex sequence tends to 0 exactly when its moduli do. Hence e^{t\J} 	o \O. (iii) \Rightarrow (ii). Suppose some eigenvalue \lambda has \operatorname{Re}\lambda = c \ge 0, and let \cvec{v} 
e \cvec{0} be an eigenvector. Then \cvec{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t}\cvec{v} is a solution: it is differentiable with \cvec{x}'(t) = \lambda e^{\lambda t}\cvec{v} = e^{\lambda t}\A\cvec{v} = \A\cvec{x}(t), and \cvec{x}(0) = \cvec{v}. Pick a coordinate with v_r 
e 0; then  igl|x_r(t) igr| =  igl|e^{\lambda t} igr|\,|v_r| = e^{ct}|v_r| \ge |v_r| > 0 for every t \ge 0, because e^{ct} \ge 1 when c \ge 0. So x_r(t) does not tend to 0, and (i) fails. This proves the equivalence.

title: 10.10 Convergent and Power-Bounded Matrices
content:
Convergent and Power-Bounded Matrices Chapter 9 asked what happens to \A^{m} as m grows, and could answer only for diagonalizable matrices: the powers of \A behave like the powers of its eigenvalues. For a Markov chain that left a gap, because a transition matrix need not be diagonalizable. The Jordan form closes the gap completely. This section characterizes, in terms of the eigenvalues and the block sizes alone, when \A^{m} tends to zero, when it stays bounded, when it converges, and when the geometric series \I + \A + \A^{2} + \cdots converges. Convergence here means what it meant in Chapter 9: entrywise. No notion of the size of a matrix is used. Chapter 16 introduces norms and re-proves several of these results in a way that also gives numerical bounds; the price of doing without them is that we must look at one entry at a time, and the Jordan form is what makes that possible. Entrywise limits and bounds [Entrywise Convergence and Boundedness] Let \M_1, \M_2, \dots be matrices in M_{p 	imes q}(
C) and \M \in M_{p 	imes q}(
C). 1. The sequence (\M_m) converges to \M, written \M_m 	o \M, if for every position (r, s) the sequence of complex numbers (\M_m)_{rs} converges to \M_{rs}. We then write \M = \lim_m \M_m. 2. The sequence (\M_m) is bounded if there is a real c \ge 0 with \lvert (\M_m)_{rs}vert \le c for all m and all positions (r, s). 3. A series \sum_{k \ge 0} \M_k converges to \M if its sequence of partial sums \sum_{k=0}^{K}\M_k converges to \M. In words: nothing new is happening. Each of the pq positions is watched separately, and the words mean for matrices exactly what they mean for the finitely many number sequences at those positions. title: Inner Product Spaces
content:
Inner Product Spaces Nine chapters have described vector spaces without measuring anything in them. We can say that a list spans, that a subspace has dimension four, that two matrices are similar; we cannot say that a vector has length 3, that two vectors are perpendicular, or that one vector is the closest point of a plane to another. Every picture in the book so far has secretly used lengths and angles that the theory did not supply. This chapter supplies them, with a single piece of extra structure: an inner product, abstracted from the dot product on 
R^n by keeping exactly the properties that make the law of cosines work. The gain is out of all proportion to the cost. Length gives the Cauchy–Schwarz and triangle inequalities. Perpendicularity gives orthonormal bases, in which coordinates are read off by a single inner product and Gram–Schmidt produces one from any basis at all. Splitting a space into a subspace and its orthogonal complement gives the nearest point of a subspace to a given vector, and with it least squares, the standard answer to an inconsistent system. The Riesz representation theorem pays off a debt from Chapter 5: an inner product is precisely the extra data that makes V and V^{*} the same space. From Riesz comes the adjoint T^{*}, which turns the four fundamental subspaces into two orthogonal decompositions, and the isometries, which are the maps that preserve the whole geometry. The chapter ends with the computational and classical faces of the same ideas: the QR factorization, Fourier series, and orthogonal polynomials. Throughout, the field is 
R or 
C, because the construction needs both an ordering, so that a length squared can be positive, and complex conjugation, so that it can be real. What you need. From Chapter 0, the complex conjugate and modulus with their arithmetic (@def-conjugate-modulus, @thm-conjugate-properties) and the trace (@def-trace, @thm-trace-properties). From Chapter 1, independence, bases, dimension, basis extension, and direct sums (@def-linear-independence, @thm-right-size-basis, @thm-basis-extension, @thm-direct-sum-criteria). From Chapter 2, the coordinate isomorphism and Rank–Nullity (@cor-coordinate-isomorphism, @thm-rank-nullity). From Chapter 3, the Invertible Matrix Theorem (@thm-invertible-tfae). From Chapter 4, the matrix of a linear map (@def-matrix-of-linear-map). From Chapter 5, the dual space, the annihilator, and the dual map, together with the warning that an isomorphism V \cong V^{*} needs a choice (@def-dual-space, @def-annihilator, @def-dual-map, @thm-matrix-of-dual-map). From Chapter 6, the root bound and Lagrange interpolation (@cor-root-bound-general, @thm-lagrange-interpolation). From Chapter 7, multiplicativity of the determinant and the nonnegativity of Gram determinants (@thm-det-multiplicative, @cor-gram-determinant-nonnegative). From Chapter 8 §01, one fact, used four times in §08: a product of partitioned matrices multiplies blockwise (@thm-block-multiplication). Chapter 9 is used only in examples and in one classification (@def-eigenvalue); nothing before Section 7 needs an eigenvalue. Roadmap - Inner products and norms. The axioms, abstracted from the dot product; length, orthogonality, Pythagoras, Cauchy–Schwarz, and the triangle inequality. - Orthonormal bases and Gram–Schmidt. Coordinates that cost one inner product each, the process that builds such a basis from any basis, and Gram matrices. - Orthogonal complements and projections. The splitting V = U \oplus U^{\perp}, the projection P_U, and the fact that P_U\elem{v} is the point of U nearest to \elem{v}. - Least squares and minimum-norm solutions. What to do with an inconsistent system: the normal equations, and the smallest solution of an underdetermined one. - The Riesz representation theorem. Every linear functional is an inner product with one fixed vector, which is the chosen isomorphism V \cong V^{*} that Chapter 5 could not supply. - The adjoint. Moving an operator to the other side of an inner product, the matrix \A^{*}, and the four fundamental subspaces in orthogonal form. - Isometries and unitary maps. The maps that preserve all lengths, their many equivalent descriptions, the Frobenius norm and its blindness to unitary factors, and the classification of \Orth(2). - QR, Householder, and Hessenberg. Gram–Schmidt as a matrix factorization, reflections that do the same job more robustly, and the first step of a serious eigenvalue algorithm. - Bessel, Parseval, and Fourier series. What an orthonormal list captures of a vector, and the classical Fourier coefficients as an instance. - Orthogonal polynomials. Gram–Schmidt on 1, x, x^2, \dots, the three-term recurrence, real roots, and Gaussian quadrature. Named moves - To show a vector is zero, pair it with itself. Only \elem{0} has \inner{\elem{z}}{\elem{z}} = 0, so an identity of that form ends the argument. - To move T across an inner product, pay with T^{*}. The adjoint is the price of the transfer, and most proofs about special operators compute one inner product in two ways. - Work with the norm squared, then expand. Square roots do not expand; 
orm{\elem{u} + \elem{v}}^2 = \inner{\elem{u} + \elem{v}}{\elem{u} + \elem{v}} does. - Fix an orthonormal basis. In its coordinates every inner product becomes the dot product, and an abstract statement becomes a matrix statement. - Project, then subtract. The same move orthogonalizes a list (Gram–Schmidt), finds the nearest point of a subspace, and solves a least-squares problem.

title: 11.1 Inner Products and Norms
content:
Inner Products and Norms Nine chapters, and we have not measured anything. We can say that a list is independent, that a subspace has dimension four, that an operator is diagonalizable. We cannot yet say that a vector has length 3, or that two vectors meet at a right angle. Geometry has appeared only in pictures, never in the theory. This section puts it into the theory, by abstracting the one operation in 
R^n that already computes lengths and angles: the dot product. The field for this chapter Throughout Chapter 11 the field F is 
R or 
C. This is not laziness; two features of these fields are used on every page, and no other field has both. The first is positivity. The point of the whole construction is that \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} should be the square of a length, so it must be a number we can compare with 0. Over 
F_p there is no ordering compatible with the arithmetic at all: in 
F_5, adding 1 to itself five times returns to 0, so no nonzero element can be called “positive” in any useful sense. Over 
Q there is an ordering, but lengths would not exist, since \sqrt{2} 
otin 
Q. Over 
R every sum of squares is \ge 0 and every nonnegative number has a square root, and that is exactly what we need. The second is conjugation. Over 
C the naive sum of squares fails immediately: 1^2 + i^2 = 0, so “z_1^2 + z_2^2” is not a length for (1, i) 
e \cvec{0}. The repair is to use z\conj{z} = \lvert z vert^2 instead of z^2 (@thm-conjugate-properties (c)), and this needs the complex conjugate. We write \conj{a} for the conjugate of a \in F, with the convention that \conj{a} = a when F = 
R; every formula below then reads correctly over both fields at once. From the dot product to the axioms In 
R^n the dot product is \cvec{x} \cdot \cvec{y} = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n . It computes lengths, because \cvec{x} \cdot \cvec{x} = x_1^2 + \dots + x_n^2 is the square of the Euclidean length by Pythagoras. It computes angles too. For nonzero \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^2 at an angle 	heta, the law of cosines applied to the triangle with sides \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}, and \cvec{x} - \cvec{y} says \lVert \cvec{x} - \cvec{y} Vert^2 = \lVert \cvec{x} Vert^2 + \lVert \cvec{y} Vert^2 - 2\lVert \cvec{x} Vert \lVert \cvec{y} Vert \cos	heta , while expanding the left side entry by entry gives \lVert \cvec{x} Vert^2 + \lVert \cvec{y} Vert^2 - 2(\cvec{x} \cdot \cvec{y}). Comparing the two, \cvec{x} \cdot \cvec{y} = \lVert \cvec{x} Vert \lVert \cvec{y} Vert \cos	heta. So one bilinear expression carries both length and angle, and perpendicularity is the single equation \cvec{x} \cdot \cvec{y} = 0. Which properties of the dot product did that argument use? Only three: it is linear in each slot separately, it is symmetric, and \cvec{x} \cdot \cvec{x} > 0 for \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}. Those three we can demand of an abstract space. Over 
C, as we saw, symmetry has to be weakened to conjugate symmetry, and the price is small: a conjugate bar in the second slot. An inner product is a way of multiplying two vectors into a scalar so that a vector paired with itself has positive “length squared”. [Inner Product] Let F be 
R or 
C, and let V be a vector space over F. An inner product on V is a map \inner{\cdot}{\cdot} \colon V 	imes V 	o F such that for all \elem{u}, \elem{v}, \elem{w} \in V and all a, b \in F: 1. \inner{a\elem{u} + b\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} = a\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} + b\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} (linear in the first slot); 2. \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{u}} = \conj{\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}}} (conjugate symmetry); 3. \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} > 0 for every nonzero \elem{v} \in V (positive definiteness). A vector space equipped with an inner product is an inner product space. When F = 
R it is a real inner product space, when F = 
C a complex one. In words, clause by clause. (IP1) says that if we freeze the second slot, what is left is a linear functional on V: the inner product distributes over sums and lets scalars out of the first argument untouched. (IP2) says that swapping the two arguments conjugates the answer; over 
R it is plain symmetry, \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{u}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}}. (IP3) says that a nonzero vector pairs with itself to give a strictly positive number. For the inequality in (IP3) to mean anything, \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} must be a real number; it is, and the reason is (IP2), as the next result shows. Note also what (IP3) does not say: it says nothing about \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} for \elem{u}

[First Properties of an Inner Product] Let V be an inner product space over F. title: 11.2 Orthonormal Bases and Gram–Schmidt
content:
Orthonormal Bases and Gram–Schmidt A basis lets us write every vector in coordinates, but finding those coordinates costs work: in @def-coordinates the scalars a_1, \dots, a_n come from solving a linear system. In an inner product space one kind of basis makes that cost disappear. If the basis vectors are mutually orthogonal unit vectors, then the i-th coordinate of \elem{v} is just \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}, one inner product, computed without reference to the others. This section defines such bases, shows that every finite-dimensional inner product space has one, and gives the algorithm that produces them. Orthonormal lists The standard basis of 
R^n has two features beyond being a basis: distinct vectors are orthogonal, and each has length 1. The two conditions can be packed into a single formula using the Kronecker delta \delta_{ij}, which is 1 when i = j and 0 otherwise. An orthonormal list is a list of unit vectors that are pairwise perpendicular. [Orthonormal List] Let V be an inner product space. A list (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k) of vectors of V is orthonormal if \inner{\elem{e}_i}{\elem{e}_j} = \delta_{ij} \qquad 	ext{for all } i, j \in \{1, \dots, k\}, that is, if \inner{\elem{e}_i}{\elem{e}_j} = 0 whenever i 
e j (orthogonal) and 
orm{\elem{e}_i} = 1 for every i (normalized). In words: the single equation \inner{\elem{e}_i}{\elem{e}_j} = \delta_{ij} carries two conditions at once, because the case i 
e j says the vectors are orthogonal and the case i = j says 
orm{\elem{e}_i}^2 = 1. The list must be ordered, as every list in this book is, but nothing in the definition depends on the order. Note that no vector of an orthonormal list is \elem{0}, since 
orm{\elem{0}} = 0 
e 1; so by @thm-orthogonal-independent, every orthonormal list is linearly independent. That single sentence is why orthonormality is so useful: independence, which normally takes an argument, comes for free. [Orthonormal Basis] An orthonormal basis of an inner product space V is an orthonormal list that is a basis of V. Examples. - The standard basis. In F^n with the standard inner product, \inner{\cvec{e}_i}{\cvec{e}_j} = \delta_{ij} by inspection. This is the model, and the notation \cvec{e}_i is deliberately reused for orthonormal vectors in a general space. - A rotated basis of

An isomorphism with this property is an isometric isomorphism, so every n-dimensional inner product space over F is isometrically isomorphic to F^n. By @thm-gram-schmidt, V has an orthonormal basis \sE = (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n). Hence the standard inner product of T\elem{u} and T\elem{v} in F^n is \sum_i \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{e}_i}\conj{\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}}, which equals \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} by @thm-orthonormal-coordinates (b). So dimension is a complete invariant of finite-dimensional inner product spaces over a fixed field: there is nothing to classify. This should be compared with @thm-isomorphic-iff-same-dimension, which said the same for vector spaces; adding an inner product adds no new invariant. If \sum_j x_j\elem{v}_j = \elem{0}, then for each i, (\G\cvec{x})_i = \sum_j \inner{\elem{v}_j}{\elem{v}_i}x_j = \inner{\sum_j x_j\elem{v}_j}{\elem{v}_i} = 0 by (IP1), so \G\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}. Conversely, if \G\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}, then \cvec{x}^{*}\G\cvec{x} = 0, so \lVert\sum_j x_j\elem{v}_jVert = 0 by (b) and hence \sum_j x_j\elem{v}_j = \elem{0} by @thm-norm-properties (a). Now \G is invertible if and only if \G\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} forces \cvec{x} = \cvec{0} (@thm-invertible-tfae, (a) \Leftrightarrow (b)), which by the displayed equality of sets says exactly that the only dependence relation among the \elem{v}_j is the trivial one. (d) Let U = \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k), let r = \dim U, and let (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_r) be an orthonormal basis of U, which exists by @thm-gram-schmidt. Let \A \in M_{r 	imes k}(F) have as its j-th column the coordinate vector of \elem{v}_j, so that \elem{v}_j = \sum_p a_{pj}\elem{e}_p. By @thm-orthonormal-coordinates (b), (\G)_{ij} = \inner{\elem{v}_j}{\elem{v}_i} = \sum_{p=1}^{r} a_{pj}\conj{a_{pi}} = (\A^{*}\A)_{ij}, so \G = \A^{*}\A. If the list is dependent, then \G is singular by (c) and \det \G = 0. If it is independent, then r = k and \A is square. By @thm-det-transpose, \det(\A^{*}) = \det(\conj{\A}), and \det(\conj{\A}) = \conj{\det \A}, because by the Leibniz formula (@thm-leibniz-formula-alternating) the determinant is a sum of products of entries and conjugation preserves sums and products (@thm-conjugate-properties). Hence, by @thm-det-multiplicative, \det \G = \det(\A^{*})\det(\A) = \conj{\det\A}\,\det\A = \lvert\det\Avert^2 . This is real and \ge 0, and it is > 0 because \A is the matrix of an isomorphism onto its coordinates, hence invertible with \det \A 
e 0 (@thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible). Over 
R, with V = 
R^n and the dot product, part (d) is the statement Chapter 7 reached from Cauchy–Binet: @cor-gram-determinant-nonnegative says that \det(\A\A	p) \ge 0 for a real \A, with equality exactly when the rows of \A are dependent. Taking the rows of \A to be \cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_k makes \A\A	p the Gram matrix, so that corollary is the special case of (d) in which the ambient space is 
R^n. The pointer left there is now paid: a Gram matrix is exactly a matrix of pairwise inner products, and its determinant is nonnegative for that reason. [Deciding Independence with a Gram Matrix] Decide whether ((1,1,0), (1,0,1), (0,1,-1)) is independent in 
R^3, using its Gram matrix. The pairwise dot products give \G =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & -1 \ 1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, and expanding along the first row, \det \G = 2(4 - 1) - 1(2 + 1) + 1(-1 - 2) = 6 - 3 - 3 = 0. By @thm-gram-matrix-properties (d) the list is dependent. Indeed \G\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} for \cvec{x} = (1, -1, -1), and @thm-gram-matrix-properties (c) says this is a dependence relation: (1,1,0) - (1,0,1) - (0,1,-1) = \cvec{0}. Two features of this method are worth noting. It never needs coordinates in the ambient space, so it works verbatim for polynomials and functions, where writing the vectors as columns is not an option. And the answer comes with a witness: a null vector of \G is a dependence relation, ready to read off. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define an orthonormal list, using the Kronecker delta, and say what an orthonormal basis is. 2. Why is every orthonormal list linearly independent? Name the result used. 3. Write down the coordinates of \elem{v} in an orthonormal basis (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n), and state Parseval’s identity. 4. True or false: the Gram–Schmidt process (@thm-gram-schmidt) applied to a list and to the same list in reverse order produces the same orthonormal list. Justify your answer. 5. State the criterion for linear independence in terms of the Gram matrix. 6. True or false: every 3-dimensional real inner product space is isometrically isomorphic to 
R^3 with the dot product. Justify your answer. (a) A list (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k) with \inner{\elem{e}_i}{\elem{e}_j} = \delta_{ij} for all i, j (@def-orthonormal-list); an orthonormal basis is such a list that is also a basis (@def-orthonormal-basis). (b) Its vectors are pairwise orthogonal and nonzero (each has norm 1), so @thm-orthogonal-independent applies. (c) \elem{v} = \sum_i \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}\elem{e}_i, and 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 = \sum_i \lvert\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}vert^2 (@thm-orthonormal-coordinates). (d) False. On ((0,1),(1,1)) the process returns ((0,1),(1,0)), while on ((1,1),(0,1)) it returns  ig(	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1), 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(-1,1) ig). (e) The list is independent if and only if its Gram matrix is invertible, if and only if \det \G > 0 (@thm-gram-matrix-properties (c), (d)). (f) True. By @cor-inner-product-spaces-isomorphic, the coordinate map with respect to any orthonormal basis is an isometric isomorphism onto 
R^3. B. Practice [B1: Gram–Schmidt with numbers] Apply the Gram–Schmidt process of @thm-gram-schmidt to each list, with the dot product. 1. ((1,0,1), (1,1,0), (0,1,1)) in 
R^3. 2. ((1,1,0,0), (1,0,1,0), (0,0,1,1)) in 
R^4. (a) 
orm{(1,0,1)}^2 = 2, so \cvec{e}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,0,1). Next \inner{(1,1,0)}{\cvec{e}_1} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}, so \cvec{w}_2 = (1,1,0) - 	frac12(1,0,1) = 	frac12(1, 2, -1), with 
orm{\cvec{w}_2}^2 = 	frac14 \cdot 6 = 	frac32, giving \cvec{e}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt6}(1, 2, -1). Finally \inner{(0,1,1)}{\cvec{e}_1} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} and \inner{(0,1,1)}{\cvec{e}_2} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt6}, so \cvec{w}_3 = (0,1,1) - 	frac12(1,0,1) - 	frac16(1,2,-1) = 	frac23(-1, 1, 1), with 
orm{\cvec{w}_3}^2 = 	frac49 \cdot 3 = 	frac43, giving \cvec{e}_3 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt3}(-1, 1, 1). (b) \cvec{e}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1,0,0). Then \inner{(1,0,1,0)}{\cvec{e}_1} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}, so \cvec{w}_2 = (1,0,1,0) - 	frac12(1,1,0,0) = 	frac12(1,-1,2,0), with 
orm{\cvec{w}_2}^2 = 	frac14 \cdot 6 = 	frac32 and \cvec{e}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt6}(1,-1,2,0). Finally \inner{(0,0,1,1)}{\cvec{e}_1} = 0 and \inner{(0,0,1,1)}{\cvec{e}_2} = 	frac{2}{\sqrt6}, so \cvec{w}_3 = (0,0,1,1) - 	frac13(1,-1,2,0) = 	frac13(-1,1,1,3), with 
orm{\cvec{w}_3}^2 = 	frac19 \cdot 12 = 	frac43 and \cvec{e}_3 = 	frac{1}{2\sqrt3}(-1,1,1,3). [B2: Gram–Schmidt on polynomials] In 
R[x]_{\le 2} with \inner{p}{q} = \int_{0}^{1} p(t)q(t)\,\dd t, apply the Gram–Schmidt process of @thm-gram-schmidt to (1, x, x^2). Compare the monic outputs with those of @exm-gram-schmidt-legendre and explain the difference. 
orm{1}^2 = 1, so \elem{e}_1 = 1. Then \inner{x}{1} = \int_0^1 t\,\dd t = 	frac12, so \elem{w}_2 = x - 	frac12 and 
orm{\elem{w}_2}^2 = \int_0^1 \Big(t - 	frac12\Big)^2\,\dd t = 	frac13 - 	frac12 + 	frac14 = 	frac{1}{12}, giving \elem{e}_2 = \sqrt3\,(2x - 1). Next \inner{x^2}{\elem{e}_1} = 	frac13 and \inner{x^2}{\elem{e}_2} = \sqrt3\int_0^1 (2t^3 - t^2)\,\dd t = \sqrt3\Big(	frac12 - 	frac13\Big) = 	frac{\sqrt3}{6}, so \elem{w}_3 = x^2 - 	frac13 - 	frac{\sqrt3}{6}\cdot\sqrt3(2x - 1) = x^2 - x + 	frac16. Its squared norm is \int_0^1\Big(t^2 - t + 	frac16\Big)^2\,\dd t = 	frac{1}{180}, so \elem{e}_3 = \sqrt5\,(6x^2 - 6x + 1). The monic outputs are 1, x - 	frac12, x^2 - x + 	frac16, whereas on [-1, 1] they were 1, x, x^2 - 	frac13. Orthogonality is a property of the inner product, not of the polynomials: changing the interval changes which polynomials are orthogonal. These are the shifted Legendre polynomials, and the substitution t \mapsto 2t - 1 carries one family to the other. [B3: Coordinates without solving a system] Let \cvec{e}_1 = 	frac13(1,2,2), \cvec{e}_2 = 	frac13(2,1,-2), \cvec{e}_3 = 	frac13(2,-2,1) in 
R^3. 1. Write \cvec{v} = (1, -1, 4) in this basis. 2. Compute 
orm{\cvec{v}}^2 in two ways, and state which theorem says the answers agree. 3. Compute \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{u}} for \cvec{u} = (3, 0, 3) from the coordinates of \cvec{v} and \cvec{u}, using @exm-orthonormal-coordinates-r3 for \cvec{u}. (a) \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{e}_1} = 	frac13(1 - 2 + 8) = 	frac73, \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{e}_2} = 	frac13(2 - 1 - 8) = -	frac73, \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{e}_3} = 	frac13(2 + 2 + 4) = 	frac83. So \cvec{v} = 	frac73\cvec{e}_1 - 	frac73\cvec{e}_2 + 	frac83\cvec{e}_3. (b) Directly, 
orm{\cvec{v}}^2 = 1 + 1 + 16 = 18. From the coordinates, 	frac{49}{9} + 	frac{49}{9} + 	frac{64}{9} = 	frac{162}{9} = 18. They agree by @thm-orthonormal-coordinates (c). (c) The coordinates of \cvec{u} are (3, 0, 3) by @exm-orthonormal-coordinates-r3, so by @thm-orthonormal-coordinates (b), \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{u}} = 	frac73 \cdot 3 +  ig(-	frac73 ig)\cdot 0 + 	frac83 \cdot 3 = 7 + 8 = 15 . Directly, \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{u}} = 3 + 0 + 12 = 15. [B4: Gram matrices] For each list, write down the Gram matrix and use it to decide whether the list is independent. 1. ((1,1,0), (1,0,1), (0,1,1)) in 
R^3 with the dot product. 2. ((1, i), (i, 1)) in 
C^2 with the standard inner product. 3. (1, x, x^2 - 	frac13) in 
R[x]_{\le 2} with \inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1} pq. (a) \G =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, and expanding along the first row, \det \G = 2(4 - 1) - 1(2 - 1) + 1(1 - 2) = 6 - 1 - 1 = 4 > 0. By @thm-gram-matrix-properties (d) the list is independent. (b) \inner{(1,i)}{(1,i)} = 1 + 1 = 2 and \inner{(i,1)}{(1,i)} = i\conj{1} + 1\conj{i} = i - i = 0, so \G = 2\I_2 by @thm-gram-matrix-properties (a). Then \det \G = 4 > 0 and the list is independent; in fact it is orthogonal, so @thm-orthogonal-independent already gives the answer. (c) These are the monic outputs of @exm-gram-schmidt-legendre, so they are pairwise orthogonal, and \G = \diag(2, 	frac23, 	frac{8}{45}). Its determinant is 2 \cdot 	frac23 \cdot 	frac{8}{45} = 	frac{32}{135} > 0, so the list is independent. A Gram matrix is diagonal exactly when the list is orthogonal. C. Going deeper [C1: The Gram matrix determines the list] Let (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) be a list in an inner product space V and (\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_k) a list in an inner product space W, both over F, with the same Gram matrix: \inner{\elem{v}_j}{\elem{v}_i} = \inner{\elem{w}_j}{\elem{w}_i} for all i, j. 1. Prove that \sum_j x_j\elem{v}_j = \elem{0} if and only if \sum_j x_j\elem{w}_j = \elem{0}, for every \cvec{x} \in F^k. 2. Deduce that there is an isomorphism T \colon \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) 	o \Span(\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_k), well defined by T\elem{v}_j = \elem{w}_j for every j. 3. Prove that T is an isometric isomorphism, that is, \inner{T\elem{u}}{T\elem{u}'} = \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{u}'} for all \elem{u}, \elem{u}' in the domain. (a) Let \G be the common Gram matrix. By @thm-gram-matrix-properties (b),  ig\lVert\sum_j x_j\elem{v}_j igVert^2 = \cvec{x}^{*}\G\cvec{x} =  ig\lVert\sum_j x_j\elem{w}_j igVert^2. By @thm-norm-properties (a), one side is 0 if and only if the other is, and a norm is 0 only at the zero vector. (b) Every element of U = \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) is \sum_j x_j\elem{v}_j for some \cvec{x}. Define T ig(\sum_j x_j\elem{v}_j ig) = \sum_j x_j\elem{w}_j. This is well defined: if \sum_j x_j\elem{v}_j = \sum_j y_j\elem{v}_j, then \sum_j (x_j - y_j)\elem{v}_j = \elem{0}, so \sum_j (x_j - y_j)\elem{w}_j = \elem{0} by (a), that is \sum_j x_j\elem{w}_j = \sum_j y_j\elem{w}_j. It is linear because the formula is linear in \cvec{x}, it is surjective onto \Span(\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_k) by construction, and it is injective: if T(\sum x_j\elem{v}_j) = \elem{0}, then \sum x_j\elem{w}_j = \elem{0}, so \sum x_j\elem{v}_j = \elem{0} by (a). (c) Let \elem{u} = \sum_j x_j\elem{v}_j and \elem{u}' = \sum_i y_i\elem{v}_i. Expanding by (IP1) and @thm-inner-product-basic-properties (b), \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{u}'} = \sum_{i}\sum_{j} x_j\conj{y_i}\inner{\elem{v}_j}{\elem{v}_i} , and the same computation in W gives \inner{T\elem{u}}{T\elem{u}'} = \sum_i\sum_j x_j\conj{y_i}\inner{\elem{w}_j}{\elem{w}_i}. The two sums are equal term by term, since the Gram matrices agree. [C2: Gram–Schmidt on a dependent list] Let (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_m) be a list in an inner product space, not assumed independent, and run the recursion of @thm-gram-schmidt. 1. Let k be the smallest index with \elem{v}_k \in \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_{k-1}). Prove that the recursion is defined up to \elem{e}_{k-1} and that \elem{w}_k = \elem{0}, so the step \elem{e}_k = \elem{w}_k/
orm{\elem{w}_k} fails. 2. Repair the process: show that if, whenever \elem{w}_k = \elem{0}, we discard \elem{v}_k and continue with \elem{v}_{k+1}, the output is an orthonormal basis of \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_m). 3. Run the repaired process on ((1,1,0), (2,2,0), (1,0,1)) in 
R^3. (a) The list (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_{k-1}) is independent, since a dependence among its members would, by @thm-linear-dependence-lemma, put some \elem{v}_j with j < k in the span of its predecessors, contradicting the minimality of k. So @thm-gram-schmidt applies to it and produces \elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_{k-1} with \Span(\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_{k-1}) = \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_{k-1}) =: U. Since \elem{v}_k \in U, @thm-orthonormal-coordinates (a) applied inside U gives \elem{v}_k = \sum_{i<k}\inner{\elem{v}_k}{\elem{e}_i}\elem{e}_i, which is precisely the vector subtracted, so \elem{w}_k = \elem{0}. Dividing by 
orm{\elem{w}_k} = 0 is impossible. (b) Let \elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_s be the vectors that the repaired process outputs. The proof of @thm-gram-schmidt shows, unchanged, that after processing \elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k the accumulated list is orthonormal and spans \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k): the only step that used independence was the claim \elem{w}_k 
e \elem{0}, and in the repaired process a step with \elem{w}_k = \elem{0} discards a \elem{v}_k that lies in the span already built, so the span does not change. Taking k = m, the output is an orthonormal list spanning \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_m), hence an orthonormal basis of it. (c) \cvec{e}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1,0). For \cvec{v}_2 = (2,2,0): \inner{\cvec{v}_2}{\cvec{e}_1} = 	frac{4}{\sqrt2} = 2\sqrt2, so \cvec{w}_2 = (2,2,0) - 2\sqrt2 \cdot 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1,0) = \cvec{0}, and \cvec{v}_2 is discarded. For \cvec{v}_3 = (1,0,1): \inner{\cvec{v}_3}{\cvec{e}_1} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}, so \cvec{w}_3 = (1,0,1) - 	frac12(1,1,0) = 	frac12(1,-1,2), with 
orm{\cvec{w}_3}^2 = 	frac64 = 	frac32 and \cvec{e}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt6}(1,-1,2). The output  ig(	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1,0), 	frac{1}{\sqrt6}(1,-1,2) ig) is an orthonormal basis of the plane spanned by the three given vectors.

title: 11.3 Orthogonal Complements and Projections
content:
Orthogonal Complements and Projections Chapter 1 proved that every subspace of a finite-dimensional space has a complement, and then warned that it has many: the x-axis in 
R^2 is complemented by every other line through the origin. An inner product breaks the tie. Among all the complements of U there is now one built from U alone, the set of vectors perpendicular to everything in U, and the projection onto U along it turns out to solve an approximation problem: it finds the vector of U closest to a given \elem{v}. This section constructs that complement, that projection, and that answer. Throughout, V is an inner product space over F = 
R or F = 
C, with inner product \inner{\cdot}{\cdot} (@def-inner-product) and induced norm 
orm{\cdot} (@def-induced-norm). We do not assume V is finite-dimensional; what we assume, each time, is that the subspace we project onto is. Orthogonal complements In 
R^3, a plane U through the origin has a distinguished line attached to it: the normal line, the set of vectors perpendicular to the whole plane. Nothing about the plane had to be chosen to produce it. That construction is available in any inner product space, and it is available for any subset, not only for subspaces. The orthogonal complement of U collects every vector that is perpendicular to all of U at once. [Orthogonal complement] Let V be an inner product space over F and let S \subseteq V be any subset. The orthogonal complement of S is S^{\perp} = \{\, \elem{v} \in V : \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{s}} = 0 	ext{ for every } \elem{s} \in S \,\}, read “S perp”. In words: \elem{v} belongs to S^{\perp} when \elem{v} is orthogonal (@def-orthogonal) to every single element of S, not merely to some of them. The quantifier is what makes the definition useful, and it is also what makes S^{\perp} a subspace even when S is not. Note that the condition could equally be written \inner{\elem{s}}{\elem{v}} = 0 for every \elem{s} \in S, since \inner{\elem{s}}{\elem{v}} = \conj{\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{s}}} and a complex number vanishes exactly when its conjugate does. We will use whichever slot is convenient. [Perp is always a subspace] For every subset S of an inner product space V, the set S^{\perp} is a subspace of V. Moreover S^{\perp} = \Span(S)^{\perp}. We apply the Subspace Test (@thm-subspace-test). First, \inner{\elem{0}}{\elem{s}} = 0 for every \elem{s}, because \inner{\cdot}{\elem{s}} is linear in the first slot and a linear map sends \elem{0} to 0 (@thm-zero-maps-to-zero); so \elem{0} \in S^{\perp}. Next, let \elem{v}, \elem{w} \in S^{\perp} and a \in F. For every \elem{s} \in S, \inner{\elem{v} + \elem{w}}{\elem{s}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{s}} + \inner{\elem{w}}{\elem{s}} = 0, \qquad \inner{a\elem{v}}{\elem{s}} = a\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{s}} = 0, both by linearity in the first slot. Hence \elem{v} + \elem{w} \in S^{\perp} and a\elem{v} \in S^{\perp}. For the second claim, S \subseteq \Span(S) gives \Span(S)^{\perp} \subseteq S^{\perp}. Conversely let \elem{v} \in S^{\perp} and let \elem{u} = a_1\elem{s}_1 + \dots + a_k\elem{s}_k with \elem{s}_i \in S. Then \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = a_1\inner{\elem{s}_1}{\elem{v}} + \dots + a_k\inner{\elem{s}_k}{\elem{v}} = 0, since each \inner{\elem{s}_i}{\elem{v}} = \conj{\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{s}_i}} = 0. So \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{u}} = \conj{\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}}} = 0, and \elem{v} \in \Span(S)^{\perp}. The second half is what makes computation possible: to test membership in U^{\perp} it is enough to test against a spanning list of U, not against all of U. Examples. - The extremes. \{\elem{0}\}^{\perp} = V, since \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{0}} = 0 always. And V^{\perp} = \{\elem{0}\}: if \elem{v} \in V^{\perp}, then in particular \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0, and positive definiteness forces \elem{v} = \elem{0}. This is the “pair it with itself” move, and it is the shape in which positivity almost always enters; it is the only place where positivity is used; we will use it again and again. - A plane in 
R^3. Let U = \{ (x, y, z) : x + y + z = 0 \} with the dot product. The condition x + y + z = 0 says exactly \inner{(x, y, z)}{(1, 1, 1)} = 0, so U = \{(1,1,1)\}^{\perp}. The Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem below will give the converse, U^{\perp} = \Span((1, 1, 1)). - A subset that is not a subspace. In 
R^3, take S = \{ (1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0) \}, two vectors and nothing else. Then S^{\perp} = \{ (x, y, z) : x = 0,\ x + y = 0 \} = \Span((0, 0, 1)), a subspace, as @prp-orthogonal-complement-subspace promises. It equals \Span(S)^{\perp}, the perp of the xy-plane. - Polynomials. On 
R[x]_{\le 2} with \inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1} p(t)q(t)\,\dd t, let U = \Span(1) be the constants. Then p \in U^{\perp} means \int_{-1}^{1} p(t)\,\dd t = 0: the polynomials of average value zero. For instance x and x^2 - 	frac13 lie in U^{\perp}, and they span it, since the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem below gives \dim U^{\perp} = 3 - 1 = 2. Nonexample by minimal change. Weaken “for every \cvec{s} \in S” to “for some \cvec{s} \in S”. With S = \{\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2\} in 
R^2, the weakened set is \{ \cvec{v} : \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{e}_1} = 0 	ext{ or } \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{e}_2} = 0 \}, the union of the two axes. Closure under scalars still holds, and \cvec{0} still belongs; what fails is closure under addition, since (1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1) lies on neither axis. This is the union of @exm-union-axes again, in new clothing. The universal quantifier is doing real work. Why this definition. One could try to define “the” complement of U by choosing a basis of U, extending it, and spanning the new vectors, which is what @thm-complement-exists does. That answer depends on every choice made along the way. The definition above depends only on U and on the inner product, and the next theorem shows that it really is a complement. The orthogonal decomposition Here is the theorem that makes U^{\perp} more than a definition. Note the hypothesis: U must be finite-dimensional, but V need not be. The reason is that the proof needs an orthonormal basis of U, and Gram–Schmidt supplies one only for a finite list. [Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem] Let V be an inner product space over F and let U be a finite-dimensional subspace of V. Then: 1. V = U \oplus U^{\perp}; 2. (U^{\perp})^{\perp} = U; 3. if in addition V is finite-dimensional, then \dim U^{\perp} = \dim V - \dim U. For (a) we must produce, from an arbitrary \elem{v}, a piece inside U and a piece perpendicular to U. Fix an orthonormal basis of U. @thm-orthonormal-coordinates says that a vector of U is the sum of its coordinates against that basis; so for a \elem{v} that is not in U, the same sum is the natural guess for the U-piece. Then we subtract and check. That is the move of Gram–Schmidt — project, then subtract — used once instead of repeatedly. Uniqueness of the splitting is the “pair with itself” move.
