By @cor-projection-orthogonal-basis, P_U(x^4) =  rac{2/5}{2}\cdot 1 +  rac{16/105}{8/45}\Bigl(x^2 - 	frac13\Bigr) = 	frac15 + 	frac67\Bigl(x^2 - 	frac13\Bigr) = 	frac67 x^2 - 	frac{3}{35}. For the distance, @thm-pythagoras applied to x^4 = P_U(x^4) + (x^4 - P_U(x^4)) gives d^2 = 
orm{x^4}^2 - 
orm{P_U(x^4)}^2. Here 
orm{x^4}^2 = \int_{-1}^1 t^8\,\dd t = 	frac29 and, the basis being orthogonal, 
orm{P_U(x^4)}^2 = \Bigl(	frac15\Bigr)^2 \cdot 2 + \Bigl(	frac67\Bigr)^2\cdot	frac{8}{45} = 	frac{2}{25} + 	frac{32}{245} = 	frac{258}{1225}. Hence d^2 = 	frac29 - 	frac{258}{1225} = 	frac{2450 - 2322}{11025} = 	frac{128}{11025} and d(x^4, U) = 	frac{8\sqrt2}{105} \approx 0.108. C. Going deeper [C1: Perp turns sums into intersections] Let U and W be subspaces of an inner product space V. 1. Prove that (U + W)^{\perp} = U^{\perp} \cap W^{\perp}. (No finiteness is needed.) 2. Assume now that V is finite-dimensional. Deduce that (U \cap W)^{\perp} = U^{\perp} + W^{\perp}. (a) (\subseteq) Let \elem{v} \in (U + W)^{\perp}. Since U \subseteq U + W (@thm-subspace-sum), \elem{v} is orthogonal to every element of U, so \elem{v} \in U^{\perp}; likewise \elem{v} \in W^{\perp}. (\supseteq) Let \elem{v} \in U^{\perp} \cap W^{\perp} and let \elem{u} + \elem{w} \in U + W with \elem{u} \in U, \elem{w} \in W. Then \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{u} + \elem{w}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{u}} + \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} = 0, using additivity in the second slot. Hence \elem{v} \in (U + W)^{\perp}. (b) Apply (a) to the subspaces U^{\perp} and W^{\perp}:  igl(U^{\perp} + W^{\perp} igr)^{\perp} = (U^{\perp})^{\perp} \cap (W^{\perp})^{\perp} = U \cap W, where the second equality is @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (b), available because V is finite-dimensional, so all subspaces are (@thm-subspace-dimension). Now take \perp of both ends and use @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (b) once more, this time on the subspace U^{\perp} + W^{\perp}: U^{\perp} + W^{\perp} = \Bigl( igl(U^{\perp} + W^{\perp} igr)^{\perp}\Bigr)^{\perp} = (U \cap W)^{\perp}. This proves the second identity. [C2: A subspace with no orthogonal complement] Let V = 
R[x], with the coefficient inner product \inner{p}{q} = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_kb_k \quad 	ext{for } p = \sum_k a_kx^k,\ q = \sum_k b_kx^k, a finite sum, since a polynomial has only finitely many nonzero coefficients. Let U = \{\, p \in V : p(1) = 0 \,\}. 1. Verify that \inner{\cdot}{\cdot} is an inner product on V and that U is a subspace with U 
eq V. 2. Prove that U^{\perp} = \{0\}. Conclude that U \oplus U^{\perp} 
eq V, so @thm-orthogonal-decomposition fails without the hypothesis that U is finite-dimensional. 3. Explain what goes wrong geometrically by exhibiting, for each m \ge 1, an element p_m \in U with 
orm{p_m - 1} = 1/\sqrt{m}. (a) The form is symmetric and bilinear over 
R because each term a_kb_k is, and \inner{p}{p} = \sum_k a_k^2 > 0 whenever some a_k 
eq 0, that is whenever p 
eq 0. So it is an inner product. The map \varepsilon \colon p \mapsto p(1) is linear (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), so U = \ker\varepsilon is a subspace (@thm-prop-kernel). It is proper, since the constant polynomial 1 has \varepsilon(1) = 1 
eq 0. (b) Note first that x^i - x^j \in U for all i, j \ge 0, since 1 - 1 = 0. Let q = \sum_k b_kx^k \in U^{\perp}. Pairing with x^i - x^j gives b_i - b_j = 0, so all the coefficients of q are equal, say to c. But only finitely many of them are nonzero, and there are infinitely many indices, so c = 0 and q = 0. Hence U^{\perp} = \{0\} and U + U^{\perp} = U 
eq V. (c) Take p_m = 1 - 	frac1m(x + x^2 + \dots + x^m). Then p_m(1) = 1 - m \cdot 	frac1m = 0, so p_m \in U, while 
orm{p_m - 1}^2 = \Bigl\|	frac1m(x + \dots + x^m)\Bigr\|^2 = m \cdot  rac{1}{m^2} =  rac1m . So the polynomial 1 
otin U has elements of U arbitrarily close to it: U leaves no room outside itself for a perpendicular direction, and the best approximation to 1 from U does not exist (the distances 
orm{1 - p} get arbitrarily close to 0 without reaching it). The obstruction is not the dimension of V as such but the fact that U is not closed: filling in the missing limits is exactly what the theory of Hilbert spaces does, and there @thm-orthogonal-decomposition is recovered for closed subspaces. That is analysis, not linear algebra, and we do not pursue it. [C3: Which projections are orthogonal] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space and let P \in \cL(V) satisfy P^2 = P. Prove that the following are equivalent: 1. P = P_U for some subspace U; 2. \inner{P\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{P\elem{v}} for all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V; 3. \ker P = (\im P)^{\perp}. Hint: for (b) \Rightarrow (c), pair a vector of \ker P with P\elem{v}. (a) \Rightarrow (b) is @thm-projection-formula (b). (b) \Rightarrow (c). (\subseteq) Let \elem{x} \in \ker P and let P\elem{v} \in \im P be arbitrary. Then \inner{\elem{x}}{P\elem{v}} = \conj{\inner{P\elem{v}}{\elem{x}}} = \conj{\inner{\elem{v}}{P\elem{x}}} = \conj{\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{0}}} = 0, using (b) in the second equality. So \elem{x} \in (\im P)^{\perp}. (\supseteq) Let \elem{x} \in (\im P)^{\perp}. Then \inner{P\elem{x}}{P\elem{x}} = \inner{\elem{x}}{P(P\elem{x})} = \inner{\elem{x}}{P\elem{x}} = 0, the first equality by (b), the second by P^2 = P, and the third because P\elem{x} \in \im P while \elem{x} \in (\im P)^{\perp}. Positive definiteness gives P\elem{x} = \elem{0}, so \elem{x} \in \ker P. (c) \Rightarrow (a). Put U = \im P. By @thm-projection-direct-sum (a), V = \im P \oplus \ker P = U \oplus U^{\perp}, and P is the identity on U and zero on \ker P = U^{\perp}. By the uniqueness clause of @thm-projection-direct-sum (b), P is the projection onto U along U^{\perp}, which is P_U by @def-orthogonal-projection.

title: 11.4 Least Squares and Minimum-Norm Solutions
content:
Least Squares and Minimum-Norm Solutions Chapter 3 taught us to decide whether \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} has a solution, and to find them all when it does. Real data rarely cooperates. Measure a quantity that depends linearly on two unknowns, take ten measurements, and you have ten equations in two unknowns; each measurement carries a little error, and the ten equations are almost certainly inconsistent. Refusing to answer is not useful. This section replaces the question “which \cvec{x} solves \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}?” with “which \cvec{x} comes closest?”, and shows that the new question always has an answer, computed by solving a square system. The other half of the section handles the opposite complaint. When a system is consistent but underdetermined, there are too many solutions, and we want a canonical one. Orthogonality picks it: exactly one solution is perpendicular to the kernel, and it is the shortest. Throughout, F = 
R or F = 
C, and F^n and F^m carry the standard inner product \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \sum_i x_i\conj{y_i}, with 
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 = \sum_i |x_i|^2. The residual, and a piece of notation Given \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \cvec{b} \in F^m, write \cvec{r} = \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x} for the residual of a candidate \cvec{x}. The system is consistent exactly when some \cvec{x} makes \cvec{r} = \cvec{0}. When none does, we ask for the \cvec{x} making \cvec{r} as short as possible, that is, minimizing 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{m}  igl| (\A\cvec{x})_i - b_i  igr|^2 , a sum of squares; hence the name least squares. Two observations turn this into geometry. First, as \cvec{x} ranges over F^n, the vector \A\cvec{x} ranges over exactly the column space \col(\A) \subseteq F^m (@thm-matrix-times-vector-columns), a finite-dimensional subspace. Second, minimizing 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}} over all \cvec{x} is therefore the same as finding the point of \col(\A) nearest to \cvec{b}. We already know that point: it is P_{\col(\A)}\cvec{b}, by @thm-best-approximation. All that remains is to turn “the residual is perpendicular to \col(\A)” into equations, and for that we need one piece of notation. Recall the conjugate transpose \A^{*} \in M_{n 	imes m}(F) of @def-conjugate-transpose: the matrix with entries (\A^{*})_{ij} = \conj{a_{ji}}, obtained by transposing and then conjugating every entry, so that \A^{*} = \A	p over 
R. Comparing entries and using @thm-transpose-properties together with the rules for conjugation (@thm-conjugate-properties) gives (\A + \B)^{*} = \A^{*} + \B^{*}, \quad (c\A)^{*} = \conj{c}\,\A^{*}, \quad (\A\B)^{*} = \B^{*}\A^{*}, \quad \A^{**} = \A , whenever the sizes match. The third is the one worth seeing done: ((\A\B)^{*})_{ij} = \conj{(\A\B)_{ji}} = \conj{\sum_k a_{jk}b_{ki}} = \sum_k \conj{b_{ki}}\,\conj{a_{jk}} = \sum_k (\B^{*})_{ik}(\A^{*})_{kj} = (\B^{*}\A^{*})_{ij}, which is where the order reverses. The one consequence we really use is the following. [Moving a matrix across the inner product] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). Then for all \cvec{x} \in F^n and \cvec{y} \in F^m, \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\A^{*}\cvec{y}}, \qquad \inner{\cvec{y}}{\A\cvec{x}} = \inner{\A^{*}\cvec{y}}{\cvec{x}} . Regarding vectors as columns, \inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}} = \cvec{w}^{*}\cvec{u}, a 1 	imes 1 matrix identified with its entry. Hence \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \cvec{y}^{*}(\A\cvec{x}) = (\cvec{y}^{*}\A)\cvec{x} =  igl((\A^{*}\cvec{y})^{*} igr)\cvec{x} = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\A^{*}\cvec{y}}, where the third equality uses (\A^{*}\cvec{y})^{*} = \cvec{y}^{*}\A^{**} = \cvec{y}^{*}\A. The second identity follows by conjugating the first, since \inner{\cvec{y}}{\A\cvec{x}} = \conj{\inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}}} and \conj{\inner{\cvec{x}}{\A^{*}\cvec{y}}} = \inner{\A^{*}\cvec{y}}{\cvec{x}}. The lemma is the matrix case of a general principle: to move a map across an inner product, pay with its adjoint. Section 6 develops that principle for linear maps between abstract inner product spaces; here the two lines above are all we need. The normal equations [Least Squares Theorem] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \cvec{b} \in F^m, and write U = \col(\A). For \cvec{x} \in F^n, the following are equivalent: 1. 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}} \le 
orm{\A\cvec{z} - \cvec{b}} for every \cvec{z} \in F^n; 2. \A\cvec{x} = P_U\cvec{b}; 3. \A^{*}\A\cvec{x} = \A^{*}\cvec{b}. Moreover such an \cvec{x} always exists. A vector satisfying these conditions is called a least-squares solution of \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}, and the equations in (c) are the normal equations. Condition (a) is a minimization over \cvec{x}; condition (b) is the same minimization rewritten in F^m, where @thm-best-approximation has already solved it. So (a) \Leftrightarrow (b) is a translation, not an argument. The content is (b) \Leftrightarrow (c): saying \A\cvec{x} = P_U\cvec{b} is the same as saying the residual is perpendicular to U, and “perpendicular to every column of \A” is what \A^{*}(\cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x}) = \cvec{0} says. Existence is free, because P_U\cvec{b} lies in U = \col(\A) and so is \A\cvec{x} for some \cvec{x}. Since \{ \A\cvec{z} : \cvec{z} \in F^n \} = \col(\A) = U (@thm-matrix-times-vector-columns), condition (a) says that \A\cvec{x} is a vector of U at least as close to \cvec{b} as every other vector of U. By @thm-best-approximation the unique such vector is P_U\cvec{b}. Hence (a) \Leftrightarrow (b). (b) \Leftrightarrow (c). Write \cvec{b} = P_U\cvec{b} + (\cvec{b} - P_U\cvec{b}), the splitting of @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (a) with \cvec{b} - P_U\cvec{b} \in U^{\perp}. For \cvec{x} \in F^n we have \A\cvec{x} \in U, so \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x} \in U^{\perp} holds if and only if \A\cvec{x} is the U-part of \cvec{b}, that is, if and only if \A\cvec{x} = P_U\cvec{b}. It remains to see that \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x} \in U^{\perp} \iff \A^{*}\A\cvec{x} = \A^{*}\cvec{b} . Put \cvec{r} = \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x}. By @prp-orthogonal-complement-subspace, \cvec{r} \in U^{\perp} if and only if \cvec{r} is orthogonal to every \A\cvec{z}, and by @lem-conjugate-transpose-pairing, \inner{\cvec{r}}{\A\cvec{z}} = \inner{\A^{*}\cvec{r}}{\cvec{z}} \qquad 	ext{for every } \cvec{z} \in F^n . If \A^{*}\cvec{r} = \cvec{0}, all these vanish. Conversely, if all vanish, take \cvec{z} = \A^{*}\cvec{r} to get \inner{\A^{*}\cvec{r}}{\A^{*}\cvec{r}} = 0, hence \A^{*}\cvec{r} = \cvec{0} by positive definiteness. So \cvec{r} \in U^{\perp} if and only if \A^{*}\cvec{r} = \cvec{0}, which rearranges to \A^{*}\A\cvec{x} = \A^{*}\cvec{b}. Existence. P_U\cvec{b} \in U = \col(\A), so P_U\cvec{b} = \A\cvec{x} for some \cvec{x} \in F^n, and that \cvec{x} satisfies (b). Three things are worth extracting. The normal equations are a square n 	imes n system, whatever the shape of \A. They are always consistent, by the existence clause, even when \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} is not. And the minimizing value \A\cvec{x} is unique — it is P_U\cvec{b} — even if the minimizing \cvec{x} is not. “Closest” is measured by the inner product, so the answer moves when the inner product does. Least squares is not a coordinate-free notion: it minimizes 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}} for a particular norm on F^m, and rescaling one coordinate — reporting one measurement in centimeters instead of meters, say — is a change of inner product. Concretely, for the data (0, 2), (1, 1), (2, 8) the least-squares line is y = 	frac23 + 3t; if the middle point is trusted twice as much, so that the second coordinate of F^3 is weighted by 2, the best line becomes y = 3t. Both are correct answers to their own question, and Exercise C1 works the general case out. Before fitting, decide which errors count equally. The system \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} may have no solution at all, yet the normal equations \A^{*}\A\cvec{x} = \A^{*}\cvec{b} always have one. Where does the proof arrange that, and what stops the same argument from solving \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} itself? The existence clause uses that P_U\cvec{b} lies in U = \col(\A), and every vector of \col(\A) is \A\cvec{x} for some \cvec{x}. So the normal equations ask \A\cvec{x} to hit P_U\cvec{b}, a target that is inside the column space by construction. The original system asks \A\cvec{x} to hit \cvec{b}, which need not be in \col(\A) at all. Projecting first is exactly the step that moves the target into reach; what is given up is the requirement \cvec{r} = \cvec{0}, which becomes \cvec{r} \perp \col(\A). When is the least-squares solution unique? The minimizers of 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}} are the solutions of the normal equations, so they form the solution set of a linear system: a coset \cvec{x}_0 + 
ul(\A^{*}\A) (@thm-general-solution-structure). To read off uniqueness we therefore need 
ul(\A^{*}\A), and the following small lemma computes it. [The null space of \A^{*}\A] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). Then 
ul(\A^{*}\A) = 
ul(\A). (\supseteq) If \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}, then \A^{*}\A\cvec{x} = \A^{*}\cvec{0} = \cvec{0}. (\subseteq) Suppose \A^{*}\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}. Pair with \cvec{x} and move \A^{*} across using @lem-conjugate-transpose-pairing: 0 = \inner{\A^{*}(\A\cvec{x})}{\cvec{x}} = \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\A\cvec{x}} = 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}^2 . Hence \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} by positive definiteness. This proves the lemma. This is the “pair it with itself” move once more, and it is the whole reason the normal equations behave well. It will return in Section 6 in the form \ker(T^{*}T) = \ker T for a linear map T between inner product spaces, with the same two-line proof; the matrix statement above is the case we need now. [Uniqueness of the least-squares solution] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \cvec{b} \in F^m. The following are equivalent: 1. \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} has exactly one least-squares solution (for one, equivalently for every, \cvec{b}); 2. the columns of \A are linearly independent, that is ank \A = n; 3. \A^{*}\A is invertible. In that case the least-squares solution is \cvec{x} = (\A^{*}\A)^{-1}\A^{*}\cvec{b}. By @thm-least-squares the least-squares solutions are the solutions of \A^{*}\A\cvec{x} = \A^{*}\cvec{b}, a consistent system; by @thm-general-solution-structure its solution set is a coset of 
ul(\A^{*}\A), which is 
ul(\A) by @lem-kernel-normal-equations. So the solution is unique, for one \cvec{b} or for all, exactly when 
ul(\A) = \{\cvec{0}\}. Now 
ul(\A) = \{\cvec{0}\} says precisely that the only vanishing linear combination of the columns of \A is the trivial one, that is, that the columns are independent; and by @thm-rank-nullity-matrix this is the same as ank\A = n. This proves (a) \Leftrightarrow (b). (b) \Leftrightarrow (c). The matrix \A^{*}\A is n 	imes n, so it is invertible if and only if 
ul(\A^{*}\A) = \{\cvec{0}\} (@thm-invertible-tfae). By @lem-kernel-normal-equations this happens exactly when 
ul(\A) = \{\cvec{0}\}. Finally, if \A^{*}\A is invertible, multiplying the normal equations on the left by (\A^{*}\A)^{-1} gives the stated formula. (\A^{*}\A)^{-1} is not \A^{-1}(\A^{*})^{-1}. The rule (\B\C)^{-1} = \C^{-1}\B^{-1} needs \B and \C to be invertible, and in least squares \A is usually not even square. Take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad (\A	p\A)^{-1} =  rac13 egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. The left side exists; the symbols \A^{-1} and (\A	p)^{-1} do not exist at all, since \A is 3 	imes 2. The formula \cvec{x} = (\A^{*}\A)^{-1}\A^{*}\cvec{b} must be read as one object (\A^{*}\A)^{-1} applied to \A^{*}\cvec{b}, never simplified. Fitting a line and a parabola [The least-squares line through four points] Find the line y = c + dt that minimizes the sum of the squared vertical errors at the four data points (1, 3), \quad (2, 1), \quad (3, 5), \quad (4, 5). Compute the residual and the minimum value of the sum of squares. Asking for c + dt_i = y_i at the four points is the system \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} with \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \ 1 & 3 \ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{x} =  egin{pmatrix} c \ d \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{b} =  egin{pmatrix} 3 \ 1 \ 5 \ 5 \end{pmatrix}, and 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}}^2 is exactly the sum of the squared vertical errors. The columns of \A are independent (they are not multiples of each other), so @cor-least-squares-unique gives a unique answer. Over 
R, \A^{*} = \A	p, and \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 10 \ 10 & 30 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A	p\cvec{b} =  egin{pmatrix} 3 + 1 + 5 + 5 \ 3 + 2 + 15 + 20 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 14 \ 40 \end{pmatrix}. The normal equations 4c + 10d = 14, 10c + 30d = 40 simplify to 2c + 5d = 7 and c + 3d = 4; subtracting twice the second from the first gives -d = -1, so d = 1 and c = 1. The least-squares line is y = 1 + t . Its values at t = 1, 2, 3, 4 are 2, 3, 4, 5, so the residual is \cvec{r} = \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x} = (3, 1, 5, 5) - (2, 3, 4, 5) = (1, -2, 1, 0), and the minimum sum of squares is 
orm{\cvec{r}}^2 = 1 + 4 + 1 + 0 = 6. Check. The residual must be orthogonal to both columns of \A: 1 - 2 + 1 + 0 = 0 and 1 - 4 + 3 + 0 = 0. Both hold, which confirms the normal equations. The same machinery fits any linear combination of prescribed functions; only the columns of \A change. “Linear” refers to the unknown coefficients, not to the shape of the curve. [The least-squares parabola] Find the quadratic y = a + bt + ct^2 minimizing the sum of squared errors at (-2, 7), \quad (-1, 6), \quad (0, 2), \quad (1, 0), \quad (2, 5). Now \A has columns (1, 1, 1, 1, 1), (t_i) and (t_i^2): \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 4 \ 1 & -1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{b} =  egin{pmatrix} 7 \ 6 \ 2 \ 0 \ 5 \end{pmatrix}. Because the nodes are symmetric about 0, every odd power sums to zero: \sum t_i = 0 and \sum t_i^3 = 0. With \sum t_i^2 = 10 and \sum t_i^4 = 34, \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 & 10 \ 0 & 10 & 0 \ 10 & 0 & 34 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A	p\cvec{b} =  egin{pmatrix} 20 \ -10 \ 54 \end{pmatrix}. The middle equation decouples: 10b = -10, so b = -1. The outer two are 5a + 10c = 20 and 10a + 34c = 54; the first gives a = 4 - 2c, and substituting gives 40 + 14c = 54, so c = 1 and a = 2. The least-squares parabola is y = 2 - t + t^2 . Its values at the nodes are 8, 4, 2, 2, 4, so \cvec{r} = (-1, 2, 0, -2, 1) and the minimum sum of squares is 
orm{\cvec{r}}^2 = 1 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 1 = 10. Check. \sum r_i = 0, \sum t_ir_i = 2 - 2 + 0 - 2 + 2 = 0, and \sum t_i^2r_i = -4 + 2 + 0 - 2 + 4 = 0: the residual is orthogonal to all three columns. Two practical remarks. Choosing the nodes symmetrically, as above, made \A	p\A nearly diagonal and the arithmetic painless; the same trick appears again in Section 9 when the columns are trigonometric functions. And although the normal equations are the right way to understand least squares, they are not always the right way to compute it: Section 8 solves the same problem through a QR factorization, which avoids forming \A^{*}\A at all. The minimum-norm solution Now the opposite situation: \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} is consistent, but \A has a nontrivial null space, so the solutions form an infinite family \cvec{x}_0 + 
ul(\A) (@thm-general-solution-structure). Which one should we report? Orthogonality answers. [Minimum-Norm Solution] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and let \cvec{b} \in F^m be such that \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} is consistent. Write K = 
ul(\A). Then: 1. exactly one solution \cvec{x}_{\min} of \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} lies in K^{\perp}; 2. 
orm{\cvec{x}_{\min}} < 
orm{\cvec{x}} for every other solution \cvec{x}. We call \cvec{x}_{\min} the minimum-norm solution. The solution set is a coset \cvec{x}_0 + K, and F^n = K \oplus K^{\perp}. Throwing away the K-part of \cvec{x}_0 keeps it a solution, because that part is in the kernel, and lands it in K^{\perp}. Once there, Pythagoras compares it with every other solution: the others differ from it by a kernel vector, which is perpendicular to it and only adds length. (a) Existence. Let \cvec{x}_0 be any solution. Since K is a subspace of the finite-dimensional space F^n, @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (a) gives F^n = K \oplus K^{\perp}; write \cvec{x}_0 = \cvec{k} + \cvec{x}_{\min} with \cvec{k} \in K and \cvec{x}_{\min} \in K^{\perp}. Then \A\cvec{x}_{\min} = \A\cvec{x}_0 - \A\cvec{k} = \cvec{b} - \cvec{0} = \cvec{b}, so \cvec{x}_{\min} is a solution lying in K^{\perp}. Uniqueness. If \cvec{x}_{\min} and \cvec{y} are solutions in K^{\perp}, then \A(\cvec{x}_{\min} - \cvec{y}) = \cvec{0}, so \cvec{x}_{\min} - \cvec{y} \in K \cap K^{\perp} = \{\cvec{0}\} by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (a). (b) Every solution has the form \cvec{x} = \cvec{x}_{\min} + \cvec{k} with \cvec{k} \in K, by @thm-general-solution-structure. Since \cvec{x}_{\min} \in K^{\perp} and \cvec{k} \in K, the two are orthogonal, and @thm-pythagoras gives 
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 = 
orm{\cvec{x}_{\min}}^2 + 
orm{\cvec{k}}^2 . If \cvec{x} 
eq \cvec{x}_{\min}, then \cvec{k} 
eq \cvec{0}, so 
orm{\cvec{k}}^2 > 0 and 
orm{\cvec{x}} > 
orm{\cvec{x}_{\min}}. This proves the theorem. The subspace K^{\perp} has a matrix description that makes \cvec{x}_{\min} computable. For \cvec{x} \in F^n,  egin{aligned} \cvec{x} \in \col(\A^{*})^{\perp} &\iff \inner{\cvec{x}}{\A^{*}\cvec{y}} = 0 \ 	ext{ for all } \cvec{y} \in F^m \ &\iff \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = 0 \ 	ext{ for all } \cvec{y} \in F^m \ &\iff \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}, \end{aligned} where the first step is @def-orthogonal-complement together with \col(\A^{*}) = \{\A^{*}\cvec{y} : \cvec{y} \in F^m\} (@thm-matrix-times-vector-columns), the second is @lem-conjugate-transpose-pairing, and the last uses the choice \cvec{y} = \A\cvec{x} with positive definiteness. So 
ul(\A) = \col(\A^{*})^{\perp}, and applying \perp once more (@thm-orthogonal-decomposition (b)) gives  igl(
ul(\A) igr)^{\perp} = \col(\A^{*}) . In words: the minimum-norm solution is the unique solution that is a combination of the columns of \A^{*}, that is, of the conjugated rows of \A. Section 6 proves the same statement for linear maps, together with the three companion identities that make up the four fundamental subspaces. [A minimum-norm solution] Find the solution of smallest norm of  egin{cases} x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 3, \ x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 7. \end{cases} Here \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. Subtracting the first equation from the second gives x_2 + 2x_3 = 4, so x_2 = 4 - 2x_3 and then x_1 = 3 - x_2 - x_3 = x_3 - 1. With t = x_3 the solutions are \cvec{x}(t) = (-1, 4, 0) + t(1, -2, 1), \qquad t \in 
R , so K = 
ul(\A) = \Span((1, -2, 1)). By @thm-minimum-norm-solution the answer is the unique t with \cvec{x}(t) \perp (1, -2, 1): \inner{\cvec{x}(t)}{(1, -2, 1)} = (-1 + t) - 2(4 - 2t) + t = 6t - 9 = 0, \qquad t = 	frac32 . Hence \cvec{x}_{\min} =  igl(	frac12, 1, 	frac32 igr), with 
orm{\cvec{x}_{\min}}^2 = 	frac14 + 1 + 	frac94 = 	frac72. Check. It is a solution, since 	frac12 + 1 + 	frac32 = 3 and 	frac12 + 2 + 	frac92 = 7, and it is orthogonal to the kernel, since 	frac12 - 2 + 	frac32 = 0. By the identity (
ul\A)^{\perp} = \col(\A	p) above it must also be a combination of the rows of \A, and it is: \cvec{x}_{\min} = 	frac12(1, 2, 3), half the second row. Finally, the solution \cvec{x}(0) = (-1, 4, 0) has 
orm{\cvec{x}(0)}^2 = 17 > 	frac72, as @thm-minimum-norm-solution (b) requires. The two answers of this section — the least-squares solution and the minimum-norm solution — are usually wanted together: given any \A and \cvec{b}, first minimize 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}}, then among the minimizers take the shortest. Chapter 13 packages the combined answer as a single matrix, the pseudoinverse \A^{+}, with \cvec{x} = \A^{+}\cvec{b} in all cases at once. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define a least-squares solution of \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}, and write down the normal equations. 2. True or false: if \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} is consistent, then its solutions are exactly its least-squares solutions. Justify your answer. 3. Explain in one sentence why the normal equations are always consistent. 4. Give a condition on the columns of \A equivalent to uniqueness of the least-squares solution. 5. Where does the minimum-norm solution of a consistent system live, and why is it unique there? 6. True or false: (\A^{*}\A)^{-1} = \A^{-1}(\A^{*})^{-1}. Justify your answer. (a) A vector \cvec{x} \in F^n with 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}} \le 
orm{\A\cvec{z} - \cvec{b}} for every \cvec{z} \in F^n. The normal equations are \A^{*}\A\cvec{x} = \A^{*}\cvec{b} (@thm-least-squares). (b) True. If \A\cvec{x}_0 = \cvec{b} then 
orm{\A\cvec{x}_0 - \cvec{b}} = 0, which is the smallest possible value, so \cvec{x}_0 is a least-squares solution; conversely a least-squares solution \cvec{x} has 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}} \le 0, hence \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}. Least squares extends the notion of a solution without changing it when solutions exist. (c) Because the target P_{\col(\A)}\cvec{b} lies in \col(\A) by construction, so \A\cvec{x} = P_{\col(\A)}\cvec{b} is solvable (@thm-least-squares, existence). (d) The columns are linearly independent, equivalently ank\A = n, equivalently \A^{*}\A is invertible (@cor-least-squares-unique). (e) In (
ul \A)^{\perp} = \col(\A^{*}). Two solutions there would differ by an element of 
ul(\A) \cap (
ul\A)^{\perp} = \{\cvec{0}\} (@thm-minimum-norm-solution). (f) False, and usually meaningless: \A need not be square, so \A^{-1} need not exist, while (\A^{*}\A)^{-1} can exist perfectly well — see the 3 	imes 2 example in the warning after @cor-least-squares-unique. B. Practice [B1: A least-squares line] Find the least-squares line y = c + dt for the data (0, 3), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 6). Compute the residual, verify that it is orthogonal to both columns of \A, and give the minimum sum of squares. With \A having columns (1,1,1,1) and (0,1,2,3) and \cvec{b} = (3, 2, 3, 6), \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 6 \ 6 & 14 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A	p\cvec{b} =  egin{pmatrix} 14 \ 0 + 2 + 6 + 18 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 14 \ 26 \end{pmatrix}. The normal equations are 2c + 3d = 7 and 3c + 7d = 13. Multiplying the first by 3 and the second by 2 and subtracting gives 9d - 14d = 21 - 26, so d = 1, and then c = 2. The line is y = 2 + t. Its values at t = 0, 1, 2, 3 are 2, 3, 4, 5, so \cvec{r} = (1, -1, -1, 1). Orthogonality: 1 - 1 - 1 + 1 = 0 against the first column and 0 - 1 - 2 + 3 = 0 against the second. The minimum sum of squares is 
orm{\cvec{r}}^2 = 4. [B2: A least-squares parabola] Find the least-squares quadratic y = a + bt + ct^2 for the data (-1, 2), (0, 8), (1, 6), (2, 16), and the minimum sum of squares. Hint: write down \A	p\A from the power sums \sum t_i^k, k = 0, \dots, 4. The power sums are \sum 1 = 4, \sum t_i = 2, \sum t_i^2 = 6, \sum t_i^3 = 8, \sum t_i^4 = 18, so \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 & 6 \ 2 & 6 & 8 \ 6 & 8 & 18 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A	p\cvec{b} =  egin{pmatrix} 2 + 8 + 6 + 16 \ -2 + 0 + 6 + 32 \ 2 + 0 + 6 + 64 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 32 \ 36 \ 72 \end{pmatrix}. Solving: from the first two equations, 2a + b + 3c = 16 and a + 3b + 4c = 18; eliminating a gives 5b + 5c = 20, so b + c = 4. The third equation is 3a + 4b + 9c = 36. Substituting b = 4 - c into 2a + b + 3c = 16 gives 2a + 2c = 12, so a = 6 - c; then 3(6 - c) + 4(4 - c) + 9c = 36 becomes 34 + 2c = 36, so c = 1, b = 3, a = 5. The parabola is y = 5 + 3t + t^2 . Its values at t = -1, 0, 1, 2 are 3, 5, 9, 15, so \cvec{r} = (-1, 3, -3, 1) and the minimum sum of squares is 1 + 9 + 9 + 1 = 20. Check: \sum r_i = 0, \sum t_ir_i = 1 + 0 - 3 + 2 = 0, \sum t_i^2r_i = -1 + 0 - 3 + 4 = 0. [B3: A minimum-norm solution] Find the minimum-norm solution of  egin{cases} x_1 + x_3 = 2, \ x_2 + x_3 = 3, \end{cases} and verify that it is orthogonal to 
ul(\A). With x_3 = t the solutions are \cvec{x}(t) = (2 - t,\ 3 - t,\ t) = (2, 3, 0) + t(-1, -1, 1), so 
ul(\A) = \Span((-1, -1, 1)). By @thm-minimum-norm-solution we need \inner{\cvec{x}(t)}{(-1,-1,1)} = 0: -(2 - t) - (3 - t) + t = 3t - 5 = 0, \qquad t = 	frac53 . So \cvec{x}_{\min} =  igl(	frac13, 	frac43, 	frac53 igr), with 
orm{\cvec{x}_{\min}}^2 = 	frac{1 + 16 + 25}{9} = 	frac{14}{3}. It solves the system, since 	frac13 + 	frac53 = 2 and 	frac43 + 	frac53 = 3, and -	frac13 - 	frac43 + 	frac53 = 0 confirms the orthogonality. For comparison, 
orm{(2, 3, 0)}^2 = 13 > 	frac{14}{3}. C. Going deeper [C1: Weighted least squares] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R), \cvec{b} \in 
R^m, and let w_1, \dots, w_m > 0 be weights, with \W = \diag(w_1, \dots, w_m). 1. Show that \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}}_{\W} = \cvec{y}	p\W\cvec{x} is an inner product on 
R^m. 2. Prove that the minimizers of \sum_{i=1}^{m} w_i igl((\A\cvec{x})_i - b_i igr)^2 are exactly the solutions of \A	p\W\A\cvec{x} = \A	p\W\cvec{b}. 3. For the data (0, 2), (1, 1), (2, 8) with weights (1, 2, 1), find the weighted least-squares line, and compare it with the unweighted one. (a) It is bilinear and symmetric because \cvec{y}	p\W\cvec{x} = \sum_i w_ix_iy_i, and \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}}_{\W} = \sum_i w_ix_i^2 > 0 whenever some x_i 
eq 0, because every w_i > 0. (This is where positivity of the weights is used; a zero weight would destroy definiteness.) (b) Write 
orm{\cdot}_{\W} for the norm induced by \inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\W}. The quantity to minimize is exactly 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}}_{\W}^2. The proof of @thm-least-squares used nothing about the inner product except its axioms, so it applies verbatim with \inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\W} in place of the standard one: the minimizers are the \cvec{x} for which \A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b} is \inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\W}-orthogonal to \col(\A), that is, for which \inner{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}}{\A\cvec{z}}_{\W} = 0 for all \cvec{z} \in 
R^n. Now \inner{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}}{\A\cvec{z}}_{\W} = (\A\cvec{z})	p\W(\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}) = \cvec{z}	p igl(\A	p\W\A\cvec{x} - \A	p\W\cvec{b} igr), and this vanishes for all \cvec{z} \in 
R^n exactly when \A	p\W\A\cvec{x} - \A	p\W\cvec{b} = \cvec{0}, by taking \cvec{z} equal to that vector. (c) With \A having columns (1,1,1) and (0,1,2), \cvec{b} = (2, 1, 8) and \W = \diag(1,2,1), \A	p\W\A =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 4 \ 4 & 6 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A	p\W\cvec{b} =  egin{pmatrix} 2 + 2 + 8 \ 0 + 2 + 16 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 12 \ 18 \end{pmatrix}, so 4c + 4d = 12 and 4c + 6d = 18, giving d = 3 and c = 0: the weighted line is y = 3t. Unweighted, \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 3 \ 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix} and \A	p\cvec{b} = (11, 17), giving 3c + 3d = 11, 3c + 5d = 17, so d = 3 and c = 	frac23: the unweighted line is y = 	frac23 + 3t. The middle point is trusted twice as much in the weighted fit, and the line moves down to pass closer to it. The weighted fit has weighted error 4 + 2 \cdot 4 + 4 = 16, smaller than the weighted error 	frac{160}{9} of the unweighted line, while the unweighted fit has plain error 	frac{32}{3}, smaller than the plain error 12 of the weighted line: each line wins the contest it was designed for. [C2: The residual, two ways] Let \cvec{x} be a least-squares solution of \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} and let \cvec{r} = \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x}. 1. Prove that 
orm{\cvec{r}}^2 = 
orm{\cvec{b}}^2 - 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}^2, and also that 
orm{\cvec{r}}^2 = \inner{\cvec{b}}{\cvec{r}} = 
orm{\cvec{b}}^2 - \inner{\A^{*}\cvec{b}}{\cvec{x}}. 2. Use the second formula to recompute the minimum sum of squares in @exm-least-squares-line without finding the residual vector. (a) By @thm-least-squares, \A\cvec{x} = P_U\cvec{b} with U = \col(\A), so \cvec{r} = \cvec{b} - P_U\cvec{b} \in U^{\perp} while \A\cvec{x} \in U. The two are orthogonal, and \cvec{b} = \A\cvec{x} + \cvec{r}, so @thm-pythagoras gives 
orm{\cvec{b}}^2 = 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}^2 + 
orm{\cvec{r}}^2, which is the first identity. For the second, \inner{\cvec{b}}{\cvec{r}} = \inner{\A\cvec{x} + \cvec{r}}{\cvec{r}} = \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{r}} + 
orm{\cvec{r}}^2 = 
orm{\cvec{r}}^2, since \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{r}} = \conj{\inner{\cvec{r}}{\A\cvec{x}}} = 0 by orthogonality. Expanding the other way, and using @lem-conjugate-transpose-pairing, \inner{\cvec{b}}{\cvec{r}} = \inner{\cvec{b}}{\cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x}} = 
orm{\cvec{b}}^2 - \inner{\cvec{b}}{\A\cvec{x}} = 
orm{\cvec{b}}^2 - \inner{\A^{*}\cvec{b}}{\cvec{x}} . (b) In @exm-least-squares-line, 
orm{\cvec{b}}^2 = 9 + 1 + 25 + 25 = 60, \A	p\cvec{b} = (14, 40) and \cvec{x} = (1, 1), so 
orm{\cvec{r}}^2 = 60 - \inner{(14, 40)}{(1, 1)} = 60 - 54 = 6, matching the value found there. Only the data already assembled for the normal equations is needed. [C3: A rank-deficient least-squares problem] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{b} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 2 \ 0 \end{pmatrix}. 1. Show that \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} is inconsistent and that ank\A = 2. 2. Describe all least-squares solutions. 3. Find the one of smallest norm, and the minimum sum of squares. (a) The third column is the sum of the first two, so the columns are dependent and ank\A \le 2; the first two columns are independent, so ank\A = 2 and \col(\A) = \Span igl((1,0,1), (0,1,1) igr). A vector (b_1, b_2, b_3) lies in \col(\A) exactly when b_3 = b_1 + b_2; here 0 
eq 1 + 2, so \cvec{b} 
otin \col(\A) and the system is inconsistent. (b) By @thm-least-squares the least-squares solutions solve \A	p\A\cvec{x} = \A	p\cvec{b}. Here \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \ 1 & 2 & 3 \ 3 & 3 & 6 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A	p\cvec{b} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 2 \ 3 \end{pmatrix}. Row reducing, the third row is the sum of the first two, and subtracting suitable multiples gives x_1 + x_3 = 0 and x_2 + x_3 = 1. Hence \cvec{x}(t) = (0, 1, 0) + t(-1, -1, 1), \qquad t \in 
R , a coset of 
ul(\A) = \Span((-1,-1,1)) = 
ul(\A	p\A), as @lem-kernel-normal-equations predicts. (c) The minimizers form a coset of 
ul(\A), so the argument of @thm-minimum-norm-solution applies to it verbatim: the shortest is the one orthogonal to (-1, -1, 1). From -(-t) - (1 - t) + t = 3t - 1 = 0 we get t = 	frac13 and \cvec{x}_{\min} = \Bigl(-	frac13, 	frac23, 	frac13\Bigr), \qquad 
orm{\cvec{x}_{\min}}^2 = 	frac{1 + 4 + 1}{9} = 	frac23 . Every minimizer gives the same \A\cvec{x} = (0, 1, 1) = P_{\col(\A)}\cvec{b}, with residual \cvec{r} = (1, 1, -1) and minimum sum of squares

title: 11.5 The Riesz Representation Theorem
content:
The Riesz Representation Theorem Chapter 5 built the dual space V^{*} of all linear functionals on V, proved that \dim V^{*} = \dim V in finite dimension, and then delivered a warning: the resulting isomorphism V \cong V^{*} is not canonical. Every basis of V gives one, different bases give different ones, and no argument singles out a preferred choice (@cor-dimension-dual-space, and the contrast with the natural map \ev_V \colon V 	o V^{**} of @thm-evaluation-natural). The chapter closed by promising that an inner product would supply the missing ingredient. This section keeps the promise. The mechanism is simple to state. Fix \elem{w} \in V and let \varphi_{\elem{w}}(\elem{v}) = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}}. Because the inner product is linear in the first slot, \varphi_{\elem{w}} is a linear functional. The Riesz Representation Theorem says that in finite dimension there are no others. Throughout, V is a finite-dimensional inner product space over F = 
R or F = 
C, unless the text says otherwise. Every functional is an inner product In F^n, @thm-functionals-on-fn already told us that every functional has the form \cvec{x} \mapsto a_1x_1 + \dots + a_nx_n for a unique row of coefficients. With the standard inner product \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \sum_i x_i\conj{y_i}, that reads \varphi(\cvec{x}) = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{w}} with \cvec{w} = (\conj{a_1}, \dots, \conj{a_n}). So in coordinates the theorem is a restatement of a fact we already have; the content is that it survives the removal of coordinates. [Riesz Representation Theorem] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F and let \varphi \in V^{*}. Then there is a unique \elem{w} \in V such that \varphi(\elem{v}) = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} \qquad 	ext{for every } \elem{v} \in V . If (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n) is any orthonormal basis of V, then \elem{w} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \conj{\varphi(\elem{e}_i)}\,\elem{e}_i. Fix an orthonormal basis. Then a linear functional is determined by the n numbers \varphi(\elem{e}_i), and a vector is determined by its n coordinates, which @thm-orthonormal-coordinates reads off as inner products. Matching the two lists tells us what \elem{w} must be, and the only care needed is the conjugate: \elem{w} sits in the second slot, so its coordinates come out conjugated. Uniqueness is the standard move — if two vectors pair identically with everything, subtract and pair the difference with itself. Existence. Let (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n) be an orthonormal basis of V, which exists by @thm-gram-schmidt, and put \elem{w} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \conj{\varphi(\elem{e}_i)}\,\elem{e}_i . For each j, conjugate-linearity in the second slot and \inner{\elem{e}_j}{\elem{e}_i} = \delta_{ij} give \inner{\elem{e}_j}{\elem{w}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \conj{\conj{\varphi(\elem{e}_i)}}\,\inner{\elem{e}_j}{\elem{e}_i} = \varphi(\elem{e}_j). So the two linear functionals \elem{v} \mapsto \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} and \varphi agree on a basis, hence are equal by @thm-linear-transform-basis. (The first is linear because the inner product is linear in the first slot.) Uniqueness. Suppose \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}'} for every \elem{v}. Then \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w} - \elem{w}'} = 0 for every \elem{v}, by additivity in the second slot. Taking \elem{v} = \elem{w} - \elem{w}' gives 
orm{\elem{w} - \elem{w}'}^2 = 0, so \elem{w} = \elem{w}' by positive definiteness. Call \elem{w} the Riesz vector of \varphi. The formula is worth reading twice: the coordinates of \elem{w} in an orthonormal basis are the conjugates of the values of \varphi on that basis. Over 
R the conjugation is invisible, which is why real textbooks can omit it and complex ones cannot. [Two Riesz vectors] 1. On V = 
R[x]_{\le 1} with \inner{p}{q} = \int_{0}^{1} p(t)q(t)\,\dd t, find the Riesz vector of \varphi(p) = p(0). 2. On V = M_n(
C) with the Frobenius inner product \inner{\A}{\B} = 	r(\B^{*}\A), find the Riesz vector of \varphi(\A) = 	r\A. (a) We look for w = a + bx with \inner{p}{w} = p(0) for all p. By linearity it is enough to impose this on the basis (1, x): \int_{0}^{1}(a + bt)\,\dd t = a + 	frac{b}{2} = 1, \qquad \int_{0}^{1} t(a + bt)\,\dd t = 	frac{a}{2} + 	frac{b}{3} = 0 . The second equation gives a = -	frac23 b; substituting into the first gives -	frac23 b + 	frac12 b = -	frac16 b = 1, so b = -6 and a = 4. Hence w = 4 - 6x. Check. \int_0^1 (4 - 6t)\,\dd t = 4 - 3 = 1 and \int_0^1 t(4 - 6t)\,\dd t = 2 - 2 = 0, as required; and for a general p = c + dx the pairing gives c\cdot 1 + d\cdot 0 = c = p(0). Note how little w resembles “evaluation at 0”: the Riesz vector is manufactured by the inner product, not by the point 0. (b) We look for \W with 	r(\W^{*}\A) = 	r\A for every \A. Taking \W = \I_n works, since \I_n^{*} = \I_n and 	r(\I_n\A) = 	r\A. By uniqueness, \W = \I_n is the answer. (This example was not solved by the basis formula, but by guessing and then invoking uniqueness — a legitimate and often faster route.) The Riesz map, and the data Chapter 5 was missing Uniqueness in @thm-riesz-representation lets us read the theorem as a statement about a map. [The Riesz map] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F. Define \Phi \colon V 	o V^{*}, \qquad \Phi(\elem{w}) = \inner{\cdot}{\elem{w}} . Then \Phi is a bijection, and for all \elem{w}, \elem{w}' \in V and c \in F, \Phi(\elem{w} + \elem{w}') = \Phi(\elem{w}) + \Phi(\elem{w}'), \qquad \Phi(c\elem{w}) = \conj{c}\,\Phi(\elem{w}). In particular \Phi is an isomorphism of vector spaces when F = 
R, and is conjugate-linear when F = 
C. Each \Phi(\elem{w}) lies in V^{*} because the inner product is linear in the first slot. Surjectivity is the existence half of @thm-riesz-representation and injectivity is the uniqueness half (if \Phi(\elem{w}) = \Phi(\elem{w}'), then \elem{w} = \elem{w}'). For the two rules, evaluate at an arbitrary \elem{v}: additivity in the second slot gives \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w} + \elem{w}'} = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} + \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}'}, and conjugate-homogeneity in the second slot gives \inner{\elem{v}}{c\elem{w}} = \conj{c}\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}}. Over 
R we have \conj{c} = c, so \Phi is linear, and a linear bijection is an isomorphism (@thm-bijective-iff-invertible). This is the payoff Chapter 5 promised. There, V \cong V^{*} was proved by choosing a basis \sB and sending \elem{v}_i \mapsto \varphi_i, and the warning was that the isomorphism changes when \sB does: a vector does not come with “its” functional. Here \Phi is written down with no basis at all. It is not free of choices — it depends on \inner{\cdot}{\cdot} — but the choice has been made once, in advance, and it is a choice of geometry rather than of coordinates. The inner product is exactly the extra data that turns V \cong V^{*} from a counting fact into a formula. The two descriptions fit together neatly. Let \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) be an orthonormal basis of V, with dual basis (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n) (@thm-dual-basis). Then \Phi(\elem{v}_i) is the functional \elem{v} \mapsto \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}_i}, which sends \elem{v}_j to \delta_{ij}; that is, \Phi(\elem{v}_i) = \varphi_i \qquad (i = 1, \dots, n), over either field. Over 
R, where \Phi is linear, this says that \Phi is Chapter 5’s basis-dependent isomorphism \elem{v}_i \mapsto \varphi_i, for the inner product that declares \sB orthonormal. Choosing a basis and choosing an inner product are two ways of supplying the same missing data. Let \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) be an orthonormal basis of a complex inner product space and let (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n) be its dual basis. What is the Riesz vector of i\varphi_1? By the identity \Phi(\elem{v}_i) = \varphi_i above, which holds over 
C as well, \varphi_1 has Riesz vector \elem{v}_1. For i\varphi_1, use conjugate-homogeneity in reverse: \Phi(-i\elem{v}_1) = \conj{(-i)}\Phi(\elem{v}_1) = i\varphi_1. So the Riesz vector of i\varphi_1 is -i\elem{v}_1, not i\elem{v}_1. Alternatively, apply the formula of @thm-riesz-representation: the coordinates of the Riesz vector are \conj{(i\varphi_1)(\elem{v}_j)} = \conj{i\delta_{1j}} = -i\delta_{1j}. Over 
C, the Riesz map is not linear, so it is not an isomorphism of complex vector spaces. It is a bijection, and it is linear over 
R, but \Phi(i\elem{w}) = -i\Phi(\elem{w}). Complex spaces V and V^{*} are still isomorphic — they have the same dimension — but the isomorphism produced by an inner product is the conjugate-linear \Phi. Most of what we do with \Phi (Section 6 builds the adjoint from it) is unaffected, because the conjugation cancels when \Phi is used twice. The Riesz vector depends on the inner product, not on \varphi alone. On 
R^2 let \varphi(\cvec{x}) = x_1 + x_2. With the dot product, \varphi(\cvec{x}) = \inner{\cvec{x}}{(1, 1)}, so \cvec{w} = (1, 1). With the weighted inner product \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = 2x_1y_1 + x_2y_2, we need 2w_1 = 1 and w_2 = 1, so \cvec{w} =  igl(	frac12, 1 igr). Same functional, different representing vector. Whenever two inner products are in play, the notation must say which \Phi is meant. Annihilators become orthogonal complements Section 3 warned that the annihilator U^{0} \subseteq V^{*} and the orthogonal complement U^{\perp} \subseteq V are different objects that happen to have the same dimension. The Riesz map explains the coincidence: it carries one onto the other. [Perp corresponds to the annihilator] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F, let U be a subspace, and let \Phi be the Riesz map. Then \Phi(U^{\perp}) = U^{0} . Equivalently, a functional \varphi \in V^{*} annihilates U if and only if its Riesz vector lies in U^{\perp}. Let \elem{w} \in V. Then \Phi(\elem{w}) \in U^{0} \iff \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} = 0 	ext{ for every } \elem{u} \in U \iff \elem{w} \in U^{\perp}, the first equivalence being the definition of the annihilator (@def-annihilator) applied to the functional \Phi(\elem{w}) = \inner{\cdot}{\elem{w}}, and the second the definition of the orthogonal complement (@def-orthogonal-complement). Since \Phi is a bijection (@cor-riesz-isomorphism), the set \Phi(U^{\perp}) is therefore exactly U^{0}. The dimension count now has a reason rather than a coincidence: \dim U^{0} = \dim V - \dim U (@thm-dimension-annihilator) and \dim U^{\perp} = \dim V - \dim U (@thm-orthogonal-decomposition (c)) agree because the two spaces correspond under a bijection. (Over 
C the bijection is only conjugate-linear, but a conjugate-linear bijection still carries subspaces to subspaces of the same dimension, since c\Phi(\elem{w}) = \Phi(\conj{c}\elem{w}).) Here is the correspondence in 
R^3. Let U = \Span((1, 2, 0)) with the dot product. Then U^{\perp} = \{ (a, b, c) : a + 2b = 0 \} = \Span igl((2, -1, 0), (0, 0, 1) igr), and U^{0} consists of the functionals \cvec{x} \mapsto \alpha x_1 +  eta x_2 + \gamma x_3 with \alpha + 2 eta = 0, spanned by 2x_1 - x_2 and x_3. These are precisely \Phi((2, -1, 0)) and \Phi((0, 0, 1)). Section 6 uses @thm-annihilator-vs-orthogonal-complement in the same way for maps: the dual map T' \colon W^{*} 	o V^{*} of Chapter 5 and the adjoint T^{*} \colon W 	o V are the same map, read through the two Riesz maps. What happens in infinite dimension The proof used an orthonormal basis of the whole of V, so finite dimension was essential, and the theorem genuinely fails without it. [A functional with no Riesz vector] Let V = 
R[x] with the coefficient inner product \inner{p}{q} = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_kb_k for p = \sum_k a_kx^k and q = \sum_k b_kx^k (a finite sum, and an inner product by @exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projections-c2 (a)). Show that \varphi(p) = p(1) has no Riesz vector. Suppose w = \sum_{k} b_kx^k satisfied \inner{p}{w} = p(1) for every p \in V. Taking p = x^i gives b_i = \inner{x^i}{w} = \varphi(x^i) = 1^i = 1 \qquad 	ext{for every } i \ge 0 . So every coefficient of w equals 1. But a polynomial has only finitely many nonzero coefficients, so no such w exists. What fails is not “infinite dimension” as a slogan. Two things are missing at once, and the same example shows both. First, V has gaps: @exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projections-c2 exhibits polynomials p_m \in \ker\varphi with 
orm{p_m - 1} = 1/\sqrt m, so the vectors p_m crowd around the polynomial 1 without any limit being forced to lie in \ker\varphi. Second, \varphi is wildly discontinuous with respect to 
orm{\cdot}: along the same sequence, \varphi(p_m) = 0 for every m, while \varphi(1) = 1. Repairing both defects — completing the space, and restricting attention to functionals \varphi with |\varphi(\elem{v})| \le C
orm{\elem{v}} — restores the theorem. That statement is the Riesz representation theorem for Hilbert spaces, and it belongs to analysis, not to linear algebra; we record its existence and go no further. What survives here with no hypotheses at all is the easy direction: for every \elem{w} \in V, the map \inner{\cdot}{\elem{w}} is a linear functional. Only the converse needs finite dimension. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the Riesz Representation Theorem, including every hypothesis. 2. Write down the formula for the Riesz vector of \varphi in terms of an orthonormal basis, and say where the conjugate comes from. 3. True or false: over 
C, the Riesz map \Phi \colon V 	o V^{*} is a linear isomorphism. Justify your answer. 4. In what sense does an inner product answer the question Chapter 5 left open about V \cong V^{*}? 5. Under \Phi, which subspace of V^{*} corresponds to U^{\perp}? 6. Give an example showing that the theorem fails in infinite dimension. (a) If V is a finite-dimensional inner product space over 
R or 
C and \varphi \in V^{*}, then there is a unique \elem{w} \in V with \varphi(\elem{v}) = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} for all \elem{v} \in V (@thm-riesz-representation). (b) \elem{w} = \sum_i \conj{\varphi(\elem{e}_i)}\elem{e}_i for any orthonormal basis (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n). The conjugate appears because \elem{w} occupies the second slot, where scalars come out conjugated: to make \inner{\elem{e}_j}{\elem{w}} equal \varphi(\elem{e}_j), the coefficient of \elem{e}_j in \elem{w} must be \conj{\varphi(\elem{e}_j)}. (c) False. \Phi is a bijection, but \Phi(c\elem{w}) = \conj{c}\Phi(\elem{w}), so it is conjugate-linear and not 
C-linear (@cor-riesz-isomorphism). It is linear over 
R, and over 
R it is an isomorphism. (d) Chapter 5 showed V \cong V^{*} by counting dimensions, with an isomorphism depending on a chosen basis and no preferred choice available (@cor-dimension-dual-space). An inner product supplies a specific map \Phi(\elem{w}) = \inner{\cdot}{\elem{w}}, written without reference to any basis. The inner product is the extra data; picking an orthonormal basis and picking an inner product that makes a given basis orthonormal are the same act. (e) U^{0}, the annihilator of U (@thm-annihilator-vs-orthogonal-complement). (f) On 
R[x] with the coefficient inner product, \varphi(p) = p(1) has no Riesz vector: such a vector would need every coefficient equal to 1 (@exm-functional-with-no-riesz-vector). B. Practice [B1: Riesz vectors for evaluation] On V = 
R[x]_{\le 2} use the node inner product \inner{p}{q} = p(-1)q(-1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1). Find the Riesz vectors of \varphi(p) = p(0) and of \psi(p) = p(1). Since -1, 0, 1 are three distinct nodes and \dim V = 3, a polynomial of V is determined by its values there (@thm-interpolation-unique). Writing w for a candidate Riesz vector of \varphi, the requirement \inner{p}{w} = p(0) reads p(-1)w(-1) + p(0)w(0) + p(1)w(1) = p(0) \qquad 	ext{for all } p \in V . Taking for p the three Lagrange polynomials at the nodes, which have value 1 at one node and 0 at the others (@def-lagrange-basis), the three equations become w(-1) = 0, w(0) = 1, w(1) = 0. The unique quadratic with those values is w = 1 - x^2. For \psi the same argument gives w(-1) = 0, w(0) = 0, w(1) = 1, whose interpolant is w = 	frac12 x(x + 1). Check. For p = 3 + 2x - x^2 we get p(-1) = 0, p(0) = 3, p(1) = 4. Pairing with 1 - x^2, whose values are 0, 1, 0, gives 3 = p(0); pairing with 	frac12x(x+1), whose values are 0, 0, 1, gives 4 = p(1). [B2: Riesz vectors on matrices] On M_n(
C) with the Frobenius inner product \inner{\A}{\B} = 	r(\B^{*}\A), find the Riesz vector of: 1. \varphi(\A) = a_{12} (assume n \ge 2); 2. \varphi_{\C}(\A) = 	r(\C\A), for a fixed \C \in M_n(
C). (a) Let \E_{12} be the matrix unit with a 1 in position (1, 2) and zeros elsewhere. Then \E_{12}^{*} = \E_{21}, and (\E_{21}\A)_{kk} = \sum_j (\E_{21})_{kj}a_{jk}, which is 0 unless k = 2, where it equals a_{12}. Hence 	r(\E_{12}^{*}\A) = a_{12} = \varphi(\A), and by uniqueness in @thm-riesz-representation the Riesz vector is \E_{12}. (b) We need \W with 	r(\W^{*}\A) = 	r(\C\A) for all \A. Taking \W^{*} = \C, that is \W = \C^{*}, works. By uniqueness it is the only answer. Part (a) is the case \C = \E_{21}, and the example in the text is the case \C = \I_n. [B3: The correspondence in 
R^4] In 
R^4 with the dot product, let U = \Span igl((1, 0, 1, 0), (0, 1, 0, 1) igr). Find a basis of U^{\perp} and a basis of U^{0}, and verify that \Phi carries the first to the second. A vector (a, b, c, d) lies in U^{\perp} exactly when a + c = 0 and b + d = 0 (@prp-orthogonal-complement-subspace, testing against the two spanning vectors). So U^{\perp} = \Span igl((1, 0, -1, 0),\ (0, 1, 0, -1) igr), of dimension 2 = 4 - 2. A functional \varphi(\cvec{x}) = \alpha x_1 +  eta x_2 + \gamma x_3 + \delta x_4 lies in U^{0} exactly when it kills both spanning vectors, that is, when \alpha + \gamma = 0 and  eta + \delta = 0. So U^{0} = \Span(\varphi_1, \varphi_2) with \varphi_1(\cvec{x}) = x_1 - x_3, \qquad \varphi_2(\cvec{x}) = x_2 - x_4 . Over 
R, \Phi(\cvec{w})(\cvec{x}) = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{w}} = \sum_i x_iw_i, so \Phi((1,0,-1,0)) = \varphi_1 and \Phi((0,1,0,-1)) = \varphi_2. Since \Phi is linear over 
R and bijective, it carries the span of the two vectors onto the span of the two functionals, confirming @thm-annihilator-vs-orthogonal-complement. C. Going deeper [C1: Riesz without an orthonormal basis] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space and let \varphi \in V^{*} be nonzero. Write K = \ker\varphi. 1. Prove that \dim K^{\perp} = 1. 2. Let \elem{u} span K^{\perp} with 
orm{\elem{u}} = 1. Prove that \elem{w} = \conj{\varphi(\elem{u})}\,\elem{u} satisfies \varphi(\elem{v}) = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} for all \elem{v} \in V. 3. Deduce @thm-riesz-representation, including the case \varphi = 0. Hint for (b): split \elem{v} using V = K \oplus K^{\perp}. (a) Since \varphi 
eq 0, its image is a nonzero subspace of the 1-dimensional space F, so \im\varphi = F and ank\varphi = 1. By @thm-rank-nullity, \dim K = \dim V - 1, and by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (c), \dim K^{\perp} = \dim V - \dim K = 1. (b) By @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (a), V = K \oplus K^{\perp}, so each \elem{v} \in V is \elem{v} = \elem{k} + c\elem{u} with \elem{k} \in K and c \in F. Then \varphi(\elem{v}) = \varphi(\elem{k}) + c\varphi(\elem{u}) = c\varphi(\elem{u}). On the other side, \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} = \inner{\elem{k} + c\elem{u}}{\conj{\varphi(\elem{u})}\elem{u}} = \varphi(\elem{u}) igl(\inner{\elem{k}}{\elem{u}} + c\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{u}} igr) = \varphi(\elem{u})\,c, using conjugate-homogeneity in the second slot (which conjugates \conj{\varphi(\elem{u})} back to \varphi(\elem{u})), then \inner{\elem{k}}{\elem{u}} = 0 because \elem{u} \in K^{\perp} and \elem{k} \in K, and \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{u}} = 
orm{\elem{u}}^2 = 1. The two sides agree. (c) If \varphi = 0, then \elem{w} = \elem{0} represents it. If \varphi 
eq 0, part (a) supplies a unit vector \elem{u} spanning the line K^{\perp} — any nonzero vector of that line divided by its norm — and part (b) supplies \elem{w}. Uniqueness is unchanged: if \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}'} for all \elem{v}, take \elem{v} = \elem{w} - \elem{w}' to get 
orm{\elem{w} - \elem{w}'}^2 = 0. Note that this proof never mentions a basis of V; it uses only the orthogonal decomposition along the hyperplane \ker\varphi. [C2: Evaluation at 0 is not represented] Let V = 
R[x] with \inner{p}{q} = \int_{0}^{1}p(t)q(t)\,\dd t, and let \varphi(p) = p(0). Suppose, for a contradiction, that w = \sum_{j=0}^{d} c_jx^j satisfied \inner{p}{w} = p(0) for every p \in V. 1. Show that \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{d}  rac{c_j}{k + j + 1} = 0 for every integer k \ge 1, and that the same sum equals 1 for k = 0. 2. Let N(s) = \sum_{j=0}^{d} c_j \prod_{i 
eq j}(s + i + 1), the product running over i \in \{0, \dots, d\}\setminus\{j\}. Show that N(k) = 0 for every integer k \ge 1, and deduce that N is the zero polynomial. 3. Deduce that every c_j = 0, and hence a contradiction. (a) Take p = x^k. Then p(0) = 0 for k \ge 1 and p(0) = 1 for k = 0, while \inner{x^k}{w} = \int_{0}^{1} t^k\sum_{j=0}^{d}c_jt^j\,\dd t = \sum_{j=0}^{d} c_j\int_0^1 t^{k+j}\,\dd t = \sum_{j=0}^{d} rac{c_j}{k + j + 1}. (b) For an integer k \ge 1, multiply the identity of (a) by \prod_{i=0}^{d}(k + i + 1), a nonzero number. Each term c_j/(k + j + 1) becomes c_j\prod_{i 
eq j}(k + i + 1), so the result is exactly N(k) = 0. Thus the polynomial N, of degree at most d, has the infinitely many distinct roots 1, 2, 3, \dots. A nonzero polynomial of degree d has at most d distinct roots (@cor-root-bound-general), so N = 0. (c) Evaluate N at s = -(j_0 + 1) for a fixed j_0 \in \{0, \dots, d\}. Every product \prod_{i 
eq j}(s + i + 1) with j 
eq j_0 contains the factor s + j_0 + 1 = 0 and so vanishes; the term j = j_0 contributes c_{j_0}\prod_{i 
eq j_0}(i - j_0), and that product is nonzero because the factors i - j_0 are nonzero integers. Since N = 0, we get c_{j_0} = 0. This holds for every j_0, so w = 0. But then the case k = 0 of (a) reads 0 = 1, a contradiction. Hence no Riesz vector exists. The moral matches @exm-functional-with-no-riesz-vector: point evaluation is a perfectly good linear functional, but on an infinite-dimensional space it is not represented by any vector, whichever of these two inner products we use.

title: 11.6 The Adjoint
content:
The Adjoint Chapter 5 attached to every linear map T \colon V 	o W a dual map T' \colon W^{*} 	o V^{*} running backwards between the dual spaces (@def-dual-map). An inner product puts a copy of the dual space back inside the space itself, by the Riesz correspondence of @thm-riesz-representation. Composing the two turns the backward map on functionals into a backward map on vectors, W 	o V. That map is the adjoint T^{*}, and it is the single most useful construction in this chapter. This section builds it, computes its matrix, uses it to split both V and W into orthogonal pieces, and names the two classes of operators it singles out. Throughout, F is 
R or 
C, every inner product is linear in the first slot and conjugate-linear in the second, and every inner product space is finite-dimensional over F unless we say otherwise. Paying to cross the inner product Here is the situation the adjoint answers. We have a linear map T and an inner product, and an expression like \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} in which T sits in the first slot. Very often the argument needs T out of the way: we know something about \elem{w}, or about the second slot, and the T is in the wrong place. Can we move it across? For matrices the answer is already on the table. @lem-conjugate-transpose-pairing, proved in Section 4, says that for \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), \cvec{x} \in F^n and \cvec{y} \in F^m, \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\A^{*}\cvec{y}}, with \A^{*} the conjugate transpose of @def-conjugate-transpose. The one-line reason is worth repeating, because it is the model for the whole section: writing \cvec{y}^{*} for the row vector \conj{\cvec{y}}	p, the standard inner product is the matrix product \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x}, so \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = (\cvec{y}^{*}\A)\cvec{x} = (\A^{*}\cvec{y})^{*}\cvec{x} = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\A^{*}\cvec{y}}. So a matrix does cross the inner product, and the price is a conjugate transpose. Over 
R the price is a transpose; over 
C a transpose and a conjugation. To move a map from the first slot to the second slot, you pay with a new map going the other way. That statement is about matrices and the standard inner product. The next theorem says the same map exists for every linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces, with no coordinates at all. Riesz does the work: the expression \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}}, read as a function of \elem{v} with \elem{w} frozen, is a linear functional on V, and @thm-riesz-representation says that every such functional is pairing against one fixed vector. [Existence and Uniqueness of the Adjoint] Let V and W be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F, and let T \in \cL(V, W). Then there is exactly one map T^{*} \colon W 	o V such that \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}}_W = \inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}\elem{w}}_V \qquad 	ext{for all } \elem{v} \in V,\ \elem{w} \in W, and this T^{*} is linear. Freeze \elem{w}. Then \elem{v} \mapsto \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} is a functional on V, so Riesz hands us one vector that represents it; call it T^{*}\elem{w}. That is the whole of existence, and it also gives uniqueness, since the Riesz vector is unique. Linearity is not part of the construction and has to be checked, and the way to check an identity between vectors is the signature move of this chapter: show the difference pairs to zero with everything, then pair it with itself. Existence. Fix \elem{w} \in W and define \varphi_{\elem{w}} \colon V 	o F by \varphi_{\elem{w}}(\elem{v}) \coloneqq \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}}. It is linear: for \elem{v}_1, \elem{v}_2 \in V and c \in F, \varphi_{\elem{w}}(\elem{v}_1 + c\elem{v}_2) = \inner{T\elem{v}_1 + cT\elem{v}_2}{\elem{w}} = \inner{T\elem{v}_1}{\elem{w}} + c\inner{T\elem{v}_2}{\elem{w}}, using the linearity of T and linearity in the first slot (@def-inner-product). Since V is finite-dimensional, @thm-riesz-representation gives a unique \elem{u} \in V with \varphi_{\elem{w}}(\elem{v}) = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{u}} for all \elem{v} \in V. Define T^{*}\elem{w} \coloneqq \elem{u}. By construction \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}\elem{w}} for all \elem{v}, which is the required identity. Uniqueness. Suppose S \colon W 	o V also satisfies \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{S\elem{w}} for all \elem{v}, \elem{w}. Fix \elem{w}. Then \inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}\elem{w} - S\elem{w}} = 0 for every \elem{v} \in V, by conjugate-additivity in the second slot. Taking \elem{v} = T^{*}\elem{w} - S\elem{w} gives 
orm{T^{*}\elem{w} - S\elem{w}}^2 = 0, so T^{*}\elem{w} = S\elem{w} by positive definiteness (@def-inner-product). As \elem{w} was arbitrary, S = T^{*}. Linearity. Let \elem{w}_1, \elem{w}_2 \in W and c \in F. For every \elem{v} \in V,  egin{aligned} \inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}(\elem{w}_1 + c\elem{w}_2)} &= \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}_1 + c\elem{w}_2} = \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}_1} + \conj{c}\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}_2} \ &= \inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}\elem{w}_1} + \conj{c}\inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}\elem{w}_2} = \inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}\elem{w}_1 + cT^{*}\elem{w}_2}, \end{aligned} where the second and the last equalities use conjugate-linearity in the second slot. Hence \inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}(\elem{w}_1 + c\elem{w}_2) - T^{*}\elem{w}_1 - cT^{*}\elem{w}_2} = 0 for every \elem{v}, and pairing the right-hand vector with itself makes it \elem{0}. So T^{*} is linear. This proves the theorem. Notice where the two conjugations went. The scalar c came out of the second slot as \conj{c} and went back in as c; the two conjugations cancel, which is exactly why T^{*} is linear and not conjugate-linear. Notice also that only V had to be finite-dimensional: the proof never uses a basis of W. We keep both spaces finite-dimensional because the rest of the section does need it. The adjoint The theorem produced an object attached to T and to the two inner products, and it is unique, so it deserves a name and a notation. The adjoint of T is the map you must apply on the other side of the inner product to leave the value unchanged. [Adjoint] Let V and W be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F and let T \in \cL(V, W). The adjoint of T is the unique linear map T^{*} \in \cL(W, V) satisfying \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}\elem{w}} \qquad 	ext{for all } \elem{v} \in V 	ext{ and all } \elem{w} \in W . In words, clause by clause: - T^{*} goes backwards: its domain is the codomain of T. If T \colon V 	o W then T^{*} \colon W 	o V, like the dual map and unlike anything else we have attached to T. - The defining equation is an identity in two variables, and it must hold for all \elem{v} and all \elem{w}. By linearity in the first slot and conjugate-linearity in the second, it is enough to check it when \elem{v} and \elem{w} range over bases of V and of W, and that is usually how T^{*} gets computed. - The left inner product lives in W, the right one in V. They are different inner products; only the notation hides it. - The definition mentions no basis, but it does mention the two inner products. Change an inner product and T^{*} changes. [Four Adjoints] Compute the adjoint in each case. In (a) and (b) the spaces carry the standard inner product; in (c) and (d), V and W are arbitrary finite-dimensional inner product spaces. 1. T_{\A} \colon 
C^3 	o 
C^2 for \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 + i & 0 & 2 \ i & 1 & -i \end{pmatrix}. 2. The forward shift S \colon F^3 	o F^3, S(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (0, x_1, x_2). 3. \id_V and the zero map V 	o W. 4. The orthogonal projection P_U \colon V 	o V onto a subspace U \subseteq V. (a) By @lem-conjugate-transpose-pairing, \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\A^{*}\cvec{y}} for all \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}, which is the defining identity of the adjoint; so (T_{\A})^{*} = T_{\A^{*}} for every matrix, by uniqueness in @thm-adjoint-exists. Here \A^{*} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 - i & -i \ 0 & 1 \ 2 & i \end{pmatrix}, so T_{\A}^{*}(y_1, y_2) =  igl((1 - i)y_1 - iy_2,\ y_2,\ 2y_1 + iy_2 igr).
