Repair it by dividing each column of \Q by \sqrt2 and multiplying the matching row of \R by \sqrt2: \Q = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \R =  egin{pmatrix} \sqrt2 & 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} \ 0 & 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}\end{pmatrix}. (c) No. The identity is correct and the columns of \Q = \I_2 are orthonormal, but r_{11} = -1 < 0, so clause (b) fails. Repair it by moving the sign across: \Q = \diag(-1, 1), whose columns are still orthonormal, and \R = \I_2, whose diagonal is positive. This is the move described in @exr-qr-and-householder-c1 with \D = \diag(-1,1). C. Going deeper [C1: All the QR factorizations of a matrix] Let \A \in M_{m	imes n}(F) have independent columns, with QR factorization \A = \Q\R as in @thm-qr-factorization. 1. Prove that an upper triangular \S \in M_n(F) with \S^{*}\S = \I_n is diagonal, with diagonal entries of modulus 1. 2. Deduce that the pairs (\Q_1, \R_1) with \Q_1^{*}\Q_1 = \I_n, \R_1 upper triangular and invertible, and \A = \Q_1\R_1, are exactly the pairs (\Q\D^{-1}, \D\R) for \D = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) with \lvert d_kvert = 1. 3. Hence give a second proof of the uniqueness statement of @thm-qr-factorization. (a) Let \cvec{s}_1, \dots, \cvec{s}_n be the columns of \S; as in the proof of @thm-qr-factorization, \S^{*}\S = \I_n says \inner{\cvec{s}_j}{\cvec{s}_i} = \delta_{ij}. We show \cvec{s}_j = s_{jj}\cvec{e}_j with \lvert s_{jj}vert = 1, by induction on j. Suppose this holds for every i < j. For such i, 0 = \inner{\cvec{s}_j}{\cvec{s}_i} = \conj{s_{ii}}\inner{\cvec{s}_j}{\cvec{e}_i} = \conj{s_{ii}}\,s_{ij}, and s_{ii} 
e 0, so s_{ij} = 0. Together with upper triangularity this gives \cvec{s}_j = s_{jj}\cvec{e}_j, and 
orm{\cvec{s}_j} = 1 gives \lvert s_{jj}vert = 1. (b) (\Leftarrow) If \lvert d_kvert = 1 for all k, then \D^{*}\D = \I_n, so (\Q\D^{-1})^{*}(\Q\D^{-1}) = (\D^{-1})^{*}\Q^{*}\Q\D^{-1} = (\D\D^{*})^{-1} = \I_n; the matrix \D\R is upper triangular and invertible; and (\Q\D^{-1})(\D\R) = \Q\R = \A. (\Rightarrow) Suppose \A = \Q_1\R_1 as stated. Exactly as in the proof of @thm-qr-factorization, \R_1^{*}\R_1 = \A^{*}\A = \R^{*}\R, and \S = \R_1\R^{-1} is upper triangular with \S^{*}\S = \I_n. By (a), \S = \D is diagonal with \lvert d_kvert = 1. Then \R_1 = \D\R and \Q_1 = \A\R_1^{-1} = \Q\R\R^{-1}\D^{-1} = \Q\D^{-1}. (c) If in addition both \R and \R_1 = \D\R have positive real diagonal entries, then d_k = (\R_1)_{kk}/(\R)_{kk} is a positive real number of modulus 1, so d_k = 1 for every k. Hence \D = \I_n, \R_1 = \R, and \Q_1 = \Q. [C2: Reflections do not mind dependence] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1 & 3 \ 2 & 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, whose third column is the sum of the first two. 1. Run the Gram–Schmidt process of @thm-gram-schmidt on the columns of \A and say precisely which step fails. 2. Carry out the Householder reduction of @thm-qr-householder on \A and exhibit \R. 3. Explain, using @thm-qr-factorization, why no factorization \A = \Q\R with \Q^{*}\Q = \I_3 and \R upper triangular with positive diagonal can exist. (a) Steps 1 and 2 go through: \cvec{q}_1 = 	frac13(1,2,2) and, since \inner{\cvec{a}_2}{\cvec{q}_1} = 	frac13(1 + 2 + 6) = 3, \cvec{w}_2 = (1,1,3) - (1,2,2) = (0,-1,1) and \cvec{q}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(0,-1,1). At step 3, \cvec{a}_3 = \cvec{a}_1 + \cvec{a}_2 lies in \Span(\cvec{a}_1,\cvec{a}_2) = \Span(\cvec{q}_1,\cvec{q}_2), so by @thm-orthonormal-coordinates (a) the vector subtracted from \cvec{a}_3 is \cvec{a}_3 itself and \cvec{w}_3 = \cvec{0}. The normalization \cvec{q}_3 = \cvec{w}_3/
orm{\cvec{w}_3} divides by 0 and fails. This is the situation of @exr-orthonormal-bases-c2. (b) The first column is (1,2,2), so as in @exr-qr-and-householder-b2 we take \cvec{w}_1 = (4,2,2) with 
orm{\cvec{w}_1}^2 = 24, and \H_1\cvec{v} = \cvec{v} - 	frac{1}{12}\inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{w}_1}\cvec{w}_1. The inner products of the three columns with \cvec{w}_1 are 12, 12, and 24, so \H_1\A =  egin{pmatrix} -3 & -3 & -6 \ 0 & -1 & -1 \ 0 & 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}. The trailing vector of column 2 is (-1,1), which by @exr-qr-and-householder-b2 (b) the second reflection sends to \sqrt2\,\cvec{e}_1; it sends the trailing vector of column 3, which is the same vector (-1,1), to the same place. Hence \R =  egin{pmatrix} -3 & -3 & -6 \ 0 & \sqrt2 & \sqrt2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, upper triangular, with a zero in position (3,3) exactly where the dependence sits. No step of the algorithm divided by zero. (c) Such an \R would be invertible by @lem-triangular-invertible, so ank\A = ank(\Q\R) = ank\Q = 3. But \cvec{a}_3 = \cvec{a}_1 + \cvec{a}_2, so the columns are dependent and ank\A \le 2, a contradiction. The positive-diagonal factorization exists precisely for matrices of full column rank. [C3: Triangularizing with rotations] 1. Let (a, b) \in 
R^2 be nonzero and r = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}. Verify that the Givens rotation \G of @def-givens-rotation with c = a/r and s = b/r satisfies \G(a,b) = (r, 0), and that \G \in \SO(2). 2. Use (a) to write \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 4 & 2\end{pmatrix} as \Q\R with \Q \in \SO(2) and \R upper triangular with positive diagonal. 3. How many Givens rotations does it take to triangularize a general 3	imes3 real matrix, and which entries does each one kill? Compare with the number of Householder reflections. (a) \G(a,b) = (ca + sb,\ -sa + cb) =  ig((a^2+b^2)/r,\ (-ab+ab)/r ig) = (r, 0). Also c^2 + s^2 = 1, so the columns of \G are orthonormal and \det\G = c^2 + s^2 = 1; hence \G \in \SO(2). (b) The first column is (3,4), so r = 5, c = 	frac35, s = 	frac45, and \G = 	frac15 egin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \ -4 & 3\end{pmatrix}. Then \G\A = 	frac15 egin{pmatrix} 9 + 16 & 3 + 8 \ -12 + 12 & -4 + 6 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 	frac{11}{5} \ 0 & 	frac25 \end{pmatrix} =: \R , whose diagonal entries 5 and 	frac25 are positive. Since \G^{-1} = \G	p \in \SO(2), we get \A = \Q\R with \Q = \G	p = 	frac15 egin{pmatrix} 3 & -4 \ 4 & 3\end{pmatrix}. As a check, \det\A = 2 = 5 \cdot 	frac25 = \det\R. (c) Three: one for a_{21} (rows 1, 2), one for a_{31} (rows 1, 3), and one for the new (3,2)-entry (rows 2, 3). The last acts on rows 2 and 3, which by then have zeros in column 1, so it does not undo the earlier work. Householder needs two reflections, one per column, since each clears a whole column at once.

title: 11.9 Bessel, Parseval, and Fourier Series
content:
Bessel, Parseval, and Fourier Series Section 3 measured a vector against a finite-dimensional subspace and produced the nearest point in it. Read that answer coefficient by coefficient and it becomes an inequality: the numbers \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i} collected against an orthonormal list can never carry more squared length than \elem{v} itself has. That is Bessel’s inequality. It costs nothing in dimension, it holds in spaces far too large for Chapter 1’s machinery, and its equality case is Parseval’s identity. This section proves both, applies them to the sines and cosines, and then stops at the exact place where linear algebra stops and analysis begins. Throughout, V is an inner product space over F = 
R or F = 
C, with inner product \inner{\cdot}{\cdot} (@def-inner-product) and induced norm 
orm{\cdot} (@def-induced-norm). We do not assume that V is finite-dimensional. What we assume each time is that the list we compute against is finite. Coefficients against an orthonormal list In @thm-orthonormal-coordinates the list was an orthonormal basis, and the coefficients \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i} recovered \elem{v} exactly. Suppose now the list is only a list: too short to be a basis, or sitting inside a space that has no finite basis at all, like the continuous functions on an interval. The numbers \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i} are still there. What can be said about them when they no longer determine \elem{v}? Against a shorter list you can only lose length, never gain it. [Fourier Coefficients With Respect to an Orthonormal List] Let (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k) be an orthonormal list in an inner product space V and let \elem{v} \in V. The scalars \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_1},\ \dots,\ \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_k} \in F are the Fourier coefficients of \elem{v} with respect to the list. The name is borrowed from the classical case below, where the \elem{e}_i are sines and cosines; nothing in the definition mentions trigonometry. When the list happens to be a basis, these are exactly the coordinates of \elem{v}, by @thm-orthonormal-coordinates (a). When it is not, they are the coordinates of a shadow of \elem{v}, and the next theorem measures that shadow. [Bessel’s Inequality] Let V be an inner product space over F, not assumed finite-dimensional, and let (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k) be an orthonormal list in V. Then for every \elem{v} \in V, \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lvert \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i} vert^2 \;\le\; 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 . The left-hand side is not a quantity out of nowhere. Let U be the span of the list. By the projection formula, P_U\elem{v} is exactly \sum_i \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}\elem{e}_i, and its summands are pairwise orthogonal, so Pythagoras turns its squared length into precisely that sum. The inequality then says no more than “a shadow is no longer than what casts it”, which we already proved. The one point needing care is that V may be infinite-dimensional; it does not matter, because Section 3 only ever asked the subspace to be finite-dimensional. Put U = \Span(\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k). The vectors \elem{e}_i are orthogonal and nonzero, so the list is linearly independent by @thm-orthogonal-independent; being a spanning list of U as well, it is an orthonormal basis of U, and \dim U = k is finite. Hence @thm-projection-formula applies to U even though V need not be finite-dimensional, and part (a) of it gives P_U\elem{v} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}\,\elem{e}_i . The summands \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}\elem{e}_i are pairwise orthogonal, since \elem{e}_i \perp \elem{e}_j for i 
e j and scalars come out of both slots. So @thm-pythagoras and @thm-norm-properties (b) give 
orm{P_U\elem{v}}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lvert \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i} vert^2 
orm{\elem{e}_i}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lvert \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i} vert^2 , using 
orm{\elem{e}_i} = 1. By @thm-projection-formula (c), 
orm{P_U\elem{v}} \le 
orm{\elem{v}}. Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring preserves the inequality, and this proves the theorem. The proof gives more than the inequality, and the surplus is worth recording. The vector \elem{v} - P_U\elem{v} lies in U^{\perp} by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition, so it is orthogonal to P_U\elem{v} \in U, and @thm-pythagoras turns \elem{v} = P_U\elem{v} + (\elem{v} - P_U\elem{v}) into 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 = 
orm{P_U\elem{v}}^2 + 
orm{\elem{v} - P_U\elem{v}}^2. Rearranging, and substituting 
orm{P_U\elem{v}}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\lvert\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}vert^2 from the proof above, 
orm{\elem{v} - P_U\elem{v}}^2 = 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lvert \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i} vert^2 . 	ag{$\ast$} In words: the deficit in Bessel’s inequality is the squared distance from \elem{v} to the span of the list (@def-distance-to-subspace). An inequality with a known defect is much more useful than an inequality, and we will read (\ast) from both sides. For an infinite orthonormal list (\elem{e}_1, \elem{e}_2, \elem{e}_3, \dots), apply the theorem to the first k terms for each k. The partial sums \sum_{i \le k}\lvert\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}vert^2 increase with k and are all bounded above by 
orm{\elem{v}}^2, so they converge, and \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\lvert\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}vert^2 \le 
orm{\elem{v}}^2. This is the only fact from analysis used in the present paragraph: a bounded increasing sequence of real numbers converges. Now the equality case, which is where the word basis returns. [Parseval’s Identity] Let (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k) be an orthonormal list in an inner product space V and let \elem{v} \in V. Then \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lvert \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i} vert^2 = 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 \quad	ext{if and only if}\quad \elem{v} \in \Span(\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k) . In particular, if (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k) is an orthonormal basis of V, the identity holds for every \elem{v} \in V. Keep the notation of the proof of @thm-bessel-inequality, where we showed \sum_i \lvert\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}vert^2 = 
orm{P_U\elem{v}}^2 with U = \Span(\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k). So the stated equality says 
orm{P_U\elem{v}} = 
orm{\elem{v}}, and by @thm-projection-formula (c) this holds if and only if \elem{v} \in U. If the list is a basis of V, then U = V and every \elem{v} \in V lies in U. For an orthonormal basis of a finite-dimensional space this is @thm-orthonormal-coordinates (c) again; what is new is the equality case, which identifies exactly the vectors for which no length is lost. Keep the two statements apart: - Bessel is about an orthonormal list, in any inner product space, and it is an inequality. - Parseval is the equality, and it holds exactly for the vectors the list already spans. The whole difference is whether the list reaches \elem{v}. An orthonormal list is not an orthonormal basis, and the deficit in Bessel can be everything. In C[-\pi, \pi] below, the list (\cos x, \sin x) is orthonormal, and for the constant function f = 1 both coefficients are 0, so the left-hand side of Bessel is 0 while 
orm{f}^2 = 2. Nothing at all is captured. A short orthonormal list is not a bad basis; it is not a basis. In 
R^4 with the dot product, let \cvec{e}_1 = 	frac12(1, 1, 1, 1) and \cvec{e}_2 = 	frac12(1, 1, -1, -1), and let \cvec{v} = (1, 2, 3, 4). Check that (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) is orthonormal, compute both sides of Bessel’s inequality, and say what the deficit equals. Each has norm 	frac12\sqrt{4} = 1, and \inner{\cvec{e}_1}{\cvec{e}_2} = 	frac14(1 + 1 - 1 - 1) = 0, so the list is orthonormal. The coefficients are \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{e}_1} = 	frac12(1 + 2 + 3 + 4) = 5 and \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{e}_2} = 	frac12(1 + 2 - 3 - 4) = -2, so the left-hand side is 25 + 4 = 29, while 
orm{\cvec{v}}^2 = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30. The inequality is strict, and by (\ast) the deficit 1 is the squared distance from \cvec{v} to \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2). Indeed P_U\cvec{v} = 5\cvec{e}_1 - 2\cvec{e}_2 =  ig(	frac32, 	frac32, 	frac72, 	frac72 ig) and \cvec{v} - P_U\cvec{v} = 	frac12(-1, 1, -1, 1), whose squared norm is 4 \cdot 	frac14 = 1. The trigonometric system The classical home of these two statements is a space of functions, and the first thing to fix is the inner product, constant included. Let V = C[-\pi, \pi] be the space of continuous functions f \colon [-\pi, \pi] 	o 
R, a real vector space, and define \inner{f}{g} =  rac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(t)\,g(t)\,\dd t . This is the continuous-function inner product of @def-inner-product on a different interval and rescaled by the positive constant 1/\pi; rescaling by a positive constant preserves all three axioms, and positive definiteness is the argument given there. The constant is chosen for one reason only: it makes the sines and cosines unit vectors. With 1/(2\pi) in front they would have norm 1/\sqrt2, and with no constant at all, norm \sqrt{\pi}. Always state the normalizing constant before computing. Formulas for Fourier coefficients differ between books by exactly such a factor, and a misplaced \pi or 2 changes every number below. In this section \inner{f}{g} =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg, and every coefficient, norm, and inequality is written for that choice. Here are the facts we assume. From calculus: the integral of a finite sum is the sum of the integrals; \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \dd t = 2\pi; \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin(mt)\,\dd t = 0 for every integer m and \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos(mt)\,\dd t = 0 for every nonzero integer m (for m 
eq 0 evaluate the antiderivative -\cos(mt)/m, respectively \sin(mt)/m, each of which takes the same value at t = -\pi as at t = \pi; for m = 0 the sine integrand is 0); integration by parts, and the substitution t \mapsto -t, both of which we use later in the section when computing particular Fourier coefficients. From trigonometry: the product-to-sum identities. No theorem about convergence is used anywhere in this section; every integral we compute is the integral of a finite sum of sines and cosines. [The Trigonometric System Is Orthonormal] Fix n \ge 1. Show that the list of 2n + 1 functions  rac{1}{\sqrt2},\ \cos x,\ \sin x,\ \cos 2x,\ \sin 2x,\ \dots,\ \cos nx,\ \sin nx is orthonormal in V = C[-\pi, \pi] with \inner{f}{g} =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg. There are five kinds of pair. Write j, k for indices in \{1, \dots, n\}. The constant with itself. 
orm{1/\sqrt2}^2 =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}	frac12\,\dd t =  rac1\pi \cdot \pi = 1. Constant against \cos kx or \sin kx. These are  rac{1}{\pi\sqrt2}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos(kt)\,\dd t = 0 and  rac{1}{\pi\sqrt2}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin(kt)\,\dd t = 0, since k 
e 0. Two cosines. By \cos A\cos B = 	frac12[\cos(A - B) + \cos(A + B)], \inner{\cos jx}{\cos kx} =  rac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\! ig[\cos((j - k)t) + \cos((j + k)t) ig]\dd t . If j 
e k, both j - k and j + k are nonzero integers, so both integrals vanish and the value is 0. If j = k, the first integrand is the constant 1 and the second has nonzero frequency 2k, so the value is  rac{1}{2\pi}(2\pi + 0) = 1. Two sines. By \sin A\sin B = 	frac12[\cos(A - B) - \cos(A + B)], the same two integrals appear with a minus sign, giving 0 for j 
e k and  rac{1}{2\pi}(2\pi - 0) = 1 for j = k. A sine against a cosine. By \sin A\cos B = 	frac12[\sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B)], \inner{\sin jx}{\cos kx} =  rac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\! ig[\sin((j + k)t) + \sin((j - k)t) ig]\dd t = 0 , because every integral of a sine over [-\pi, \pi] vanishes, including the case j = k where the second integrand is \sin 0 = 0. So each of the 2n + 1 functions is a unit vector and distinct ones are orthogonal, which is @def-orthonormal-list. Write W_n = \Span(1, \cos x, \sin x, \dots, \cos nx, \sin nx), the space of trigonometric polynomials of degree at most n. The list above is an orthonormal list, hence independent (@thm-orthogonal-independent), and it spans W_n, since 1 = \sqrt2 \cdot 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}. So it is an orthonormal basis of W_n and \dim W_n = 2n + 1. For f \in V the classical Fourier coefficients of f are a_k =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(t)\cos(kt)\,\dd t, \qquad b_k =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(t)\sin(kt)\,\dd t , for k \ge 0 and k \ge 1 respectively. Comparing with the inner product, a_k = \inner{f}{\cos kx} and b_k = \inner{f}{\sin kx}, while the coefficient against the constant of the orthonormal list is \inner{f}{1/\sqrt2} = a_0/\sqrt2. These are exactly the Fourier coefficients of @def-fourier-coefficients for this list. [Fourier Partial Sums Are Best Approximations] Let f \in C[-\pi, \pi], let n \ge 1, and let a_k, b_k be the Fourier coefficients of f. Put S_nf =  rac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{n} ig(a_k\cos kx + b_k\sin kx ig) . Then, with \inner{f}{g} =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg: 1. S_nf = P_{W_n}f; 2. 
orm{f - S_nf} \le 
orm{f - g} for every g \in W_n, with equality only for g = S_nf; 3. \displaystyle  rac{a_0^2}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{n} ig(a_k^2 + b_k^2 ig) \le  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(t)^2\,\dd t. Nothing new happens here. The subspace W_n is finite-dimensional and we have an orthonormal basis of it, so Section 3 answers the approximation question and @thm-bessel-inequality answers the coefficient question; the work is only to match the classical notation to ours. The one thing to watch is the factor 	frac12 in front of a_0: it is not a convention pulled from the air, it is what \inner{f}{1/\sqrt2} \cdot 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} equals. (a) By @exm-trigonometric-orthonormal the list  ig(	frac{1}{\sqrt2}, \cos x, \sin x, \dots, \cos nx, \sin nx ig) is an orthonormal basis of W_n. By @thm-projection-formula (a), P_{W_n}f = \Big\langle f, 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} \Bigangle 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} + \sum_{k=1}^{n} ig(\inner{f}{\cos kx}\cos kx + \inner{f}{\sin kx}\sin kx ig). The first term is  rac{a_0}{\sqrt2}\cdot rac{1}{\sqrt2} =  rac{a_0}{2}, and the remaining terms are a_k\cos kx + b_k\sin kx. Hence P_{W_n}f = S_nf. (b) This is @thm-best-approximation applied to the subspace U = W_n, which is legitimate because \dim W_n = 2n + 1 is finite, together with (a). (c) This is @thm-bessel-inequality for the same orthonormal list, since \lvert\inner{f}{1/\sqrt2}vert^2 = a_0^2/2 and 
orm{f}^2 =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f^2. So the Fourier partial sum is not a guess at f that happens to work: it is the orthogonal projection of f onto the trigonometric polynomials of degree at most n, and by @thm-best-approximation it is the unique trigonometric polynomial of that degree closest to f in this norm. The mysterious a_0/2 of the classical formula is an artifact of normalizing the constant function. A worked computation [The Fourier Coefficients of f(x) = x] In C[-\pi, \pi] with \inner{f}{g} =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg, let f(x) = x. Find all a_k and b_k, write down S_nf, and say what @thm-fourier-best-approximation (c) gives. We use one further calculus fact: a continuous odd function integrates to 0 over [-\pi, \pi], and a continuous even one integrates to twice its integral over [0, \pi]. Both come from the substitution t \mapsto -t. The cosine coefficients. For every k \ge 0 the function t\cos(kt) is odd, so a_k = 0. In particular a_0 = 0. The sine coefficients. The function t\sin(kt) is even, so for k \ge 1, b_k =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} t\sin(kt)\,\dd t =  rac2\pi\int_{0}^{\pi} t\sin(kt)\,\dd t . Integrating by parts, with \dd(-\cos(kt)/k) = \sin(kt)\,\dd t, \int_{0}^{\pi} t\sin(kt)\,\dd t = \Big[ rac{-t\cos(kt)}{k}\Big]_0^{\pi} +  rac1k\int_0^{\pi}\cos(kt)\,\dd t =  rac{-\pi\cos(k\pi)}{k} , since the last integral is [\sin(kt)/k^2]_0^\pi = 0. As \cos(k\pi) = (-1)^k, this equals \pi(-1)^{k+1}/k, and therefore b_k =  rac{2(-1)^{k+1}}{k} . The partial sums. Hence S_nf = \sum_{k=1}^{n} rac{2(-1)^{k+1}}{k}\sin kx = 2\sin x - \sin 2x + 	frac23\sin 3x - \dots , and by @thm-fourier-best-approximation (b) this is the closest trigonometric polynomial of degree at most n to the function x in this norm. What Bessel’s inequality (@thm-bessel-inequality) gives. First 
orm{f}^2 =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} t^2\,\dd t =  rac1\pi\cdot rac{2\pi^3}{3} =  rac{2\pi^2}{3}. Since a_k = 0 and b_k^2 = 4/k^2, part (c) of @thm-fourier-best-approximation reads \sum_{k=1}^{n} rac{4}{k^2} \le  rac{2\pi^2}{3}, \qquad	ext{that is}\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{n} rac{1}{k^2} \le  rac{\pi^2}{6} for every n. The partial sums on the left increase and are bounded above, so they converge, and \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 1/k^2 \le \pi^2/6. That bound is sharp: the true value of the sum is \pi^2/6. But sharpness is not something Bessel can deliver. By @thm-parseval-identity, equality for a fixed finite list holds only when f lies in the span of that list, and the function x lies in no W_n — it is not a trigonometric polynomial, since every element of W_n takes the same value at -\pi and at \pi. Getting the equality requires a statement about the infinite system, and that statement is an input from analysis; @exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-c1 carries it out and flags it. Let g(x) = \cos^2 x in C[-\pi, \pi]. Using \cos^2 x = 	frac12 + 	frac12\cos 2x, write down all Fourier coefficients of g, find S_1g, and compute the deficit in Bessel’s inequality for n = 1. The right-hand side 	frac12 + 	frac12\cos 2x already lies in W_2, and coefficients against an orthonormal basis are unique (@thm-orthonormal-coordinates (a)), so, applying that result inside W_2 and reading the coefficients off: a_0 = 1, a_2 = 	frac12, and all other a_k and all b_k are 0. Hence S_1g = a_0/2 = 	frac12, a constant. For the deficit, 
orm{g}^2 =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^4 t\,\dd t =  rac1\pi\cdot rac{3\pi}{4} = 	frac34, while the Bessel sum for n = 1 is a_0^2/2 = 	frac12. The deficit is 	frac14, and by (\ast) it should be 
orm{g - S_1g}^2 =  ig\lVert	frac12\cos 2x igVert^2 = 	frac14\cdot 1 = 	frac14. It is. What best approximation does and does not say It is worth being exact about the boundary here, because it is easy to read more into @thm-fourier-best-approximation than it contains. Identity (\ast) applied to U = W_n says 
orm{f - S_nf}^2 = 
orm{f}^2 -  rac{a_0^2}{2} - \sum_{k=1}^{n} ig(a_k^2 + b_k^2 ig) . The subtracted sum never decreases as n grows, so the numbers 
orm{f - S_nf}^2 never increase, and they are bounded below by 0. Hence they converge to some limit L \ge 0. Everything up to this sentence is linear algebra plus one fact about monotone bounded sequences. Whether L = 0 is a different kind of question. It asks whether the trigonometric polynomials come arbitrarily close, in this norm, to every continuous function, and no argument in this book decides it. The statement is true, and it is the analytic content of the theory of Fourier series; it is what makes the infinite trigonometric system behave like an orthonormal basis even though it is not a basis in the sense of Chapter 1. And even L = 0 would not be a statement about individual points. Our norm averages the error over the whole interval, so it tolerates a large error on a short interval. The function f(x) = x shows this at once: S_nf(\pi) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} rac{2(-1)^{k+1}}{k}\sin(k\pi) = 0 for every n, while f(\pi) = \pi. The error at the single point x = \pi never shrinks at all. Mean-square best approximation is not pointwise approximation. @thm-fourier-best-approximation says that S_nf minimizes \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}(f - g)^2 over g \in W_n. It does not say that S_nf(x) is close to f(x) for a given x, and for f(x) = x at x = \pi it is not. Whether a Fourier series converges at a point is a question in analysis with a delicate answer; it is not decided by anything in this chapter, and a projection theorem cannot decide it. Legendre and Chebyshev Two families of orthogonal polynomials show the same two theorems at work with a different weight. Legendre. @exm-gram-schmidt-legendre ran Gram–Schmidt on (1, x, x^2) in 
R[x]_{\le 2} with \inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1} pq, producing the orthogonal list 1,\ x,\ x^2 - 	frac13 and, after normalizing, the orthonormal basis \elem{e}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}, \qquad \elem{e}_2 = \sqrt{3/2}\,x, \qquad \elem{e}_3 = 	frac{\sqrt{10}}{4} ig(3x^2 - 1 ig). Inside 
R[x]_{\le 2} this is a basis, so @thm-parseval-identity gives 
orm{p}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{3}\lvert\inner{p}{\elem{e}_i}vert^2 for every quadratic p. Viewed inside the larger space C[-1, 1] of continuous functions, the same three vectors are only a list, and for an f outside 
R[x]_{\le 2} @thm-bessel-inequality is strict, the deficit being the squared distance from f to 
R[x]_{\le 2} by (\ast). That deficit is what @exm-best-quadratic-approximation computed for f = x^3. One list, two readings, and which reading applies depends on the ambient space, not on the list. In practice one projects with the orthogonal list 1,\ x,\ x^2 - 	frac13 through @cor-projection-orthogonal-basis and avoids the square roots entirely. Chebyshev. Change the weight. On 
R[x] define \inner{p}{q}_w = \int_{-1}^{1} rac{p(t)\,q(t)}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}}\,\dd t . The integrand is unbounded at t = \pm 1, so this is an improper integral; it converges for polynomials, because \lvert pq vert is bounded on [-1, 1] and \int_{-1}^{1}\dd t/\sqrt{1 - t^2} = \pi. The three axioms are checked as in @def-inner-product, positivity because 1/\sqrt{1 - t^2} > 0 on (-1, 1). The Chebyshev polynomials are defined by the requirement T_n(\cos	heta) = \cos n	heta \qquad 	ext{for all } 	heta, which does determine a polynomial of degree n, and determines it uniquely, since \cos	heta runs over the whole of [-1, 1] and two polynomials agreeing on an infinite set are equal (@cor-root-bound-general). The first few are T_0 = 1, T_1 = x, T_2 = 2x^2 - 1 (from \cos 2	heta = 2\cos^2	heta - 1), and @exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-c2 handles the general case. They are orthogonal for \inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_w: \inner{T_m}{T_n}_w = 0 \quad (m 
e n), \qquad \inner{T_n}{T_n}_w =  egin{cases} \pi, & n = 0, \ \pi/2, & n \ge 1. \end{cases} For m, n \le 2 this can be checked by hand, using \int_{-1}^{1}\dd t/\sqrt{1 - t^2} = \pi and \int_{-1}^{1} t^2\,\dd t/\sqrt{1 - t^2} = \pi/2 (both come from t = \cos	heta). The pairs (T_0, T_1) and (T_1, T_2) have odd integrands on a symmetric interval, so those integrals are 0 by the substitution t \mapsto -t. For the remaining pair, \inner{T_0}{T_2}_w = \int_{-1}^{1} rac{2t^2 - 1}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}}\,\dd t = 2\cdot rac{\pi}{2} - \pi = 0 . Why should such a weight produce orthogonality? Because it is the trigonometric system in disguise. Substituting t = \cos	heta turns \inner{p}{q}_w into \int_0^{\pi} p(\cos	heta)q(\cos	heta)\,\dd	heta, and on the Chebyshev polynomials that integrand is \cos m	heta\cos n	heta — the very product whose integral we computed in @exm-trigonometric-orthonormal. @exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-c2 asks for this in full. Since the T_n are orthogonal but not normalized, projections onto their span are computed with @cor-projection-orthogonal-basis rather than @thm-projection-formula. Section 10 of this chapter takes up orthogonal polynomials as a subject in their own right, including the recurrence that generates the T_n and the quadrature rules they produce. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State Bessel’s inequality, saying exactly what is assumed about the space and what is assumed about the list. 2. State Parseval’s identity, including the condition under which equality holds for a given vector. 3. True or false: Bessel’s inequality requires the ambient space to be finite-dimensional. Justify your answer. 4. Write down the inner product used on C[-\pi, \pi] in this section, including its normalizing constant, and say what the constant is for. 5. State what @thm-fourier-best-approximation gives about S_nf, and name one thing it does not give. 6. True or false: if (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k) is an orthonormal list and \sum_i\lvert\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}vert^2 = 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 for one particular \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}, then the list is an orthonormal basis of V. Justify your answer. (a) If (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k) is an orthonormal list in an inner product space V over 
R or 
C, then \sum_{i=1}^{k}\lvert\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}vert^2 \le 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 for every \elem{v} \in V (@thm-bessel-inequality). The list is assumed finite and orthonormal; the space is assumed only to be an inner product space, with no dimension hypothesis. (b) Equality \sum_i\lvert\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}vert^2 = 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 holds if and only if \elem{v} \in \Span(\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k); in particular it holds for every \elem{v} when the list is an orthonormal basis of V (@thm-parseval-identity). (c) False. Only the span of the list has to be finite-dimensional, and it automatically is, being spanned by k vectors. The proof uses @thm-projection-formula, whose hypothesis is that the subspace projected onto is finite-dimensional. The application to C[-\pi, \pi] is exactly a case where V is not finite-dimensional. (d) \inner{f}{g} =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(t)g(t)\,\dd t. The constant 1/\pi makes \cos kx and \sin kx unit vectors for every k \ge 1; without it their norms would be \sqrt{\pi}. (e) It gives that S_nf is the orthogonal projection of f onto W_n, hence the unique element of W_n minimizing 
orm{f - g}, and it gives Bessel’s inequality for the coefficients. It does not give that S_nf(x) 	o f(x) at any particular x, nor even that 
orm{f - S_nf} 	o 0. (f) False. Equality for one \elem{v} says only that \elem{v} \in \Span(\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k) (@thm-parseval-identity). In 
R^3 take the list (\cvec{e}_1) and \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_1: equality holds, and the list is not a basis. B. Practice [B1: Fourier coefficients] Work in C[-\pi, \pi] with \inner{f}{g} =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg. Find all Fourier coefficients a_k and b_k of each of the following, and in each case write down S_2f. 1. f(x) = \lvert x vert. 2. f(x) = x^2. 3. f(x) = 3 - 2\sin x + \sin 3x. (a) \lvert t vert \sin(kt) is odd, so b_k = 0 for all k. For the cosines, \lvert t vert\cos(kt) is even, so a_k =  rac2\pi\int_0^{\pi} t\cos(kt)\,\dd t. For k = 0 this is  rac2\pi\cdot rac{\pi^2}{2} = \pi. For k \ge 1, integrating by parts, \int_0^{\pi} t\cos(kt)\,\dd t = \Big[ rac{t\sin(kt)}{k}\Big]_0^{\pi} -  rac1k\int_0^{\pi}\sin(kt)\,\dd t =  rac{(-1)^k - 1}{k^2}, since the bracket vanishes and \int_0^\pi \sin(kt)\,\dd t = (1 - (-1)^k)/k. Hence a_k =  rac{2 ig((-1)^k - 1 ig)}{\pi k^2} =  egin{cases} -\dfrac{4}{\pi k^2}, & k 	ext{ odd},\[2pt] 0, & k 	ext{ even},\end{cases} and S_2f = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{4}{\pi}\cos x. (b) t^2\sin(kt) is odd, so b_k = 0. Also a_0 =  rac2\pi\int_0^\pi t^2\,\dd t =  rac{2\pi^2}{3}. For k \ge 1, integrating by parts twice gives \int_0^{\pi} t^2\cos(kt)\,\dd t = \Big[ rac{t^2\sin(kt)}{k}\Big]_0^\pi -  rac2k\int_0^\pi t\sin(kt)\,\dd t =  rac{2\pi(-1)^{k}}{k^2}, using \int_0^\pi t\sin(kt)\,\dd t = \pi(-1)^{k+1}/k from @exm-fourier-of-x. Hence a_k =  rac2\pi\cdot rac{2\pi(-1)^k}{k^2} =  rac{4(-1)^k}{k^2}, so a_1 = -4, a_2 = 1, and S_2f =  rac{\pi^2}{3} - 4\cos x + \cos 2x . (c) The function already lies in W_3. Coefficients against an orthonormal basis are unique (@thm-orthonormal-coordinates (a)), so, applying that result inside W_3, we may read them off: a_0/2 = 3, that is a_0 = 6, together with b_1 = -2 and b_3 = 1; every other coefficient is 0. Hence S_2f = 3 - 2\sin x, which is not f: the term \sin 3x lies outside W_2 and is discarded by the projection. (From n = 3 on, S_nf = f, as @thm-projection-formula (a) predicts, since f \in W_3 and a projection fixes its own subspace.) [B2: Verifying Bessel for a truncation] 1. In 
R^4 with the dot product let \cvec{e}_1 = 	frac12(1, 1, 1, 1), \cvec{e}_2 = 	frac12(1, -1, 1, -1) and \cvec{v} = (2, 0, 0, 2). Verify @thm-bessel-inequality for \cvec{v} and this list, compute the deficit, and check against (\ast) by computing 
orm{\cvec{v} - P_U\cvec{v}} directly, where U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2). 2. For f(x) = \lvert x vert and n = 1, write out both sides of @thm-fourier-best-approximation (c) using @exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-b1 (a), and show that the resulting inequality is equivalent to 96 \le \pi^4. (a) Both vectors have norm 	frac12\sqrt4 = 1 and \inner{\cvec{e}_1}{\cvec{e}_2} = 	frac14(1 - 1 + 1 - 1) = 0, so the list is orthonormal. The coefficients are \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{e}_1} = 	frac12(2 + 0 + 0 + 2) = 2 and \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{e}_2} = 	frac12(2 - 0 + 0 - 2) = 0, so the left-hand side of Bessel is 4, while 
orm{\cvec{v}}^2 = 4 + 4 = 8. The inequality 4 \le 8 holds, with deficit 4. By @thm-projection-formula (a), P_U\cvec{v} = 2\cvec{e}_1 = (1, 1, 1, 1), so \cvec{v} - P_U\cvec{v} = (1, -1, -1, 1) and 
orm{\cvec{v} - P_U\cvec{v}}^2 = 4, matching (\ast). (b) With a_0 = \pi and a_1 = -4/\pi, and b_1 = 0, the left-hand side of (c) for n = 1 is  rac{a_0^2}{2} + a_1^2 =  rac{\pi^2}{2} +  rac{16}{\pi^2} . The right-hand side is 
orm{f}^2 =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} t^2\,\dd t =  rac{2\pi^2}{3}. So the inequality reads  rac{\pi^2}{2} +  rac{16}{\pi^2} \le  rac{2\pi^2}{3} , that is 16/\pi^2 \le 2\pi^2/3 - \pi^2/2 = \pi^2/6, that is 96 \le \pi^4. Since \pi > 3.14 and 3.14^4 > 97, the inequality is true, and it is tight: the deficit is \pi^2/6 - 16/\pi^2 \approx 0.024, so the single cosine \cos x already captures almost all of \lvert x vert. [B3: The best approximation by \Span(1, \cos x)] In C[-\pi, \pi] with \inner{f}{g} =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg, let U = \Span(1, \cos x) and f(x) = x^2. Find P_Uf and d(f, U)^2. Hint: the list (1, \cos x) is orthogonal but not orthonormal. The two functions are orthogonal, since \inner{1}{\cos x} =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos t\,\dd t = 0, and both are nonzero, with \inner{1}{1} = 2 and \inner{\cos x}{\cos x} = 1 by @exm-trigonometric-orthonormal. So (1, \cos x) is an orthogonal basis of U, and @cor-projection-orthogonal-basis gives P_Uf =  rac{\inner{f}{1}}{2}\cdot 1 +  rac{\inner{f}{\cos x}}{1}\cdot\cos x . By @exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-b1 (b), \inner{f}{1} = a_0 = 2\pi^2/3 and \inner{f}{\cos x} = a_1 = -4. Hence P_Uf =  rac{\pi^2}{3} - 4\cos x . For the distance, normalize: (1/\sqrt2,\ \cos x) is an orthonormal basis of the same U, with coefficients \inner{f}{1/\sqrt2} = a_0/\sqrt2 and \inner{f}{\cos x} = a_1. Now 
orm{f}^2 =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} t^4\,\dd t =  rac1\pi\cdot rac{2\pi^5}{5} =  rac{2\pi^4}{5} and the Bessel sum is a_0^2/2 + a_1^2 = 2\pi^4/9 + 16, so (\ast) gives d(f, U)^2 =  rac{2\pi^4}{5} -  rac{2\pi^4}{9} - 16 =  rac{8\pi^4}{45} - 16 \approx 1.32 . It is positive, as it must be, since x^2 
otin U. C. Going deeper [C1: Parseval for the full trigonometric system] This exercise uses an input from analysis that this book does not prove: the trigonometric system is complete in C[-\pi, \pi], meaning that for every f \in C[-\pi, \pi],  rac{a_0^2}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} ig(a_k^2 + b_k^2 ig) =  rac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(t)^2\,\dd t . 1. Apply this to f(x) = x and deduce that \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 1/k^2 = \pi^2/6. 2. Hence deduce that \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 1/(2k - 1)^2 = \pi^2/8. 3. Say precisely which step used the analysis input, and explain why no result of this section can supply it. (a) By @exm-fourier-of-x, a_k = 0 for all k and b_k = 2(-1)^{k+1}/k, so b_k^2 = 4/k^2; and 
orm{f}^2 = 2\pi^2/3. The stated identity becomes \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} rac{4}{k^2} =  rac{2\pi^2}{3}, so \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 1/k^2 = \pi^2/6. (b) All terms are positive and the series converges, so it may be split into its even-index and odd-index parts. The even part is \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} rac{1}{(2j)^2} =  rac14\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} rac{1}{j^2} =  rac{\pi^2}{24}. Hence the odd part is \pi^2/6 - \pi^2/24 = (4\pi^2 - \pi^2)/24 = \pi^2/8, which is the claim. (c) The analysis input is used exactly once, at the equality sign in (a). This section proves only the inequality \sum_{k\le n} 4/k^2 \le 2\pi^2/3 for each n (@thm-bessel-inequality), and @thm-parseval-identity turns that inequality into an equality only when f lies in the span of the finitely many functions used. The function x lies in no W_n, since every element of W_n takes equal values at -\pi and \pi while f(-\pi) = -\pi 
e \pi = f(\pi). Passing to the infinite system is a statement about a limit of functions, and nothing in this book proves such a statement. Remark. The classical route to \sum 1/(2k-1)^2 = \pi^2/8 applies the same identity to the square wave, the function equal to -1 on [-\pi, 0) and 1 on [0, \pi], whose coefficients are b_k = 4/(\pi k) for odd k and 0 otherwise. That function is not continuous, so it does not live in the space C[-\pi, \pi] of this section, and enlarging the space to all integrable functions destroys positive definiteness, as the third nonexample of Section 1 shows. Working with f(x) = x keeps everything inside a genuine inner product space. [C2: Chebyshev orthogonality by substitution] Let \inner{p}{q}_w = \int_{-1}^{1} p(t)q(t)(1 - t^2)^{-1/2}\,\dd t on 
R[x], the Chebyshev inner product of the text. 1. Prove that for every n \ge 0 there is a polynomial T_n of degree n with T_n(\cos	heta) = \cos n	heta for all 	heta, and find T_0, T_1, T_2, T_3. 2. Prove that \inner{p}{q}_w = \int_0^{\pi} p(\cos	heta)\,q(\cos	heta)\,\dd	heta for all polynomials p, q. 3. Deduce that \inner{T_m}{T_n}_w = 0 for m 
e n, and compute \inner{T_n}{T_n}_w. Hint for (a): the identity \cos((n+1)	heta) + \cos((n-1)	heta) = 2\cos	heta\cos n	heta. (a) Induction on n. Take T_0 = 1 and T_1 = x, which satisfy T_0(\cos	heta) = 1 = \cos 0	heta and T_1(\cos	heta) = \cos	heta, of degrees 0 and 1. Suppose T_{n-1} and T_n exist, of degrees n - 1 and n. Put T_{n+1} = 2xT_n - T_{n-1}. Then for every 	heta, T_{n+1}(\cos	heta) = 2\cos	heta\cos n	heta - \cos((n-1)	heta) = \cos((n+1)	heta) by the stated identity. Its degree is n + 1, since the leading term of 2xT_n has degree n + 1 and T_{n-1} has degree n - 1. This completes the induction, and the recurrence gives T_2 = 2x^2 - 1 and T_3 = 2x(2x^2 - 1) - x = 4x^3 - 3x. (b) The integral is improper at both endpoints, so it means the limit as \delta 	o 0^{+} of the integrals over [-1 + \delta,\ 1 - \delta]. On each such interval the integrand is continuous, and t = \cos	heta is a continuously differentiable bijection from the corresponding 	heta-interval, so the change-of-variables rule applies there. With t = \cos	heta, 	heta running from \pi down to 0, we have \dd t = -\sin	heta\,\dd	heta and \sqrt{1 - t^2} = \sin	heta, which is \ge 0 on [0, \pi]. The two minus signs cancel when the limits are reversed, and letting \delta 	o 0^{+}, \int_{-1}^{1} rac{p(t)q(t)}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}}\,\dd t = \int_{0}^{\pi} p(\cos	heta)\,q(\cos	heta)\,\dd	heta . The right-hand side is a proper integral of a continuous function, so both sides converge, and the limits agree. (c) By (a) and (b), \inner{T_m}{T_n}_w = \int_0^{\pi}\cos m	heta\cos n	heta\,\dd	heta. Using \cos A\cos B = 	frac12[\cos(A-B) + \cos(A+B)] and \int_0^{\pi}\cos(p	heta)\,\dd	heta = [\sin(p	heta)/p]_0^{\pi} = 0 for every nonzero integer p: if m 
e n, then m - n 
e 0, and m + n \ge 1 because the two indices differ, so both integrals vanish and the value is 0; if m = n \ge 1, the value is 	frac12 ig(\int_0^\pi 1\,\dd	heta + 0 ig) = \pi/2; if m = n = 0, the integrand is 1 and the value is \pi. So the T_n are orthogonal for \inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_w, with \inner{T_0}{T_0}_w = \pi and \inner{T_n}{T_n}_w = \pi/2 for n \ge 1. Consequently  ig(T_0/\sqrt{\pi},\ T_1\sqrt{2/\pi},\ \dots,\ T_n\sqrt{2/\pi} ig) is an orthonormal list, and @thm-bessel-inequality applies to it verbatim.

title: 11.10 Orthogonal Polynomials
content:
Orthogonal Polynomials Section 2 ran Gram–Schmidt on (1, x, x^2) with \inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1} pq, and stopped at degree 2 only because the space did (@exm-gram-schmidt-legendre). Nothing in the process cared. Feed it (1, x, x^2, x^3, \dots) and it returns an infinite orthogonal sequence, one polynomial of each degree. Three things make such sequences worth a section. Each member is computable from the two before it. Each member of degree k has k distinct real roots inside the interval. And those roots are the best possible points at which to sample a function to estimate its integral. The first fact rests on one small identity; the other two rest on the first. Throughout this section the field is 
R. Two ways to make an inner product on polynomials Both constructions we need appeared in Section 1. From a weight. Fix an interval with endpoints -\infty \le a < b \le \infty and a weight w: a function continuous and strictly positive on the open interval (a, b), with \int_a^b \lvert t vert^k w(t)\,\dd t finite for every k \in 
N. Define \inner{p}{q} = \int_a^b p(t)\,q(t)\,w(t)\,\dd t . Finiteness of the moments makes this a real number for all p, q \in 
R[x], and bilinearity and symmetry come from linearity of the integral. For positivity, let p 
e 0. Then p^2w is continuous and \ge 0 on (a, b), and > 0 off the finitely many roots of p (@cor-root-bound-general), so \inner{p}{p} > 0. That last step is the one calculus fact this section leans on: a continuous nonnegative function on an interval whose integral is 0 vanishes identically. As in @def-inner-product it follows from the local fact that a continuous function nonzero at a point stays bounded away from 0 on a small interval around it, which then contributes a positive amount to the integral. From nodes. Fix distinct c_0 < \dots < c_n in 
R and put \inner{p}{q} = \sum_{i=0}^{n} p(c_i)q(c_i). Section 1 checked that this is an inner product on 
R[x]_{\le n}, positivity coming from the root bound. It is not one on 
R[x]: the polynomial (x - c_0)\cdots(x - c_n) is nonzero and pairs with itself to give 0. So in the node case everything below stops at degree n. The two constructions share one property, and it is the engine of the section. [Multiplication by x is symmetric] Let \inner{\cdot}{\cdot} be an inner product on 
R[x] coming from a weight, or the node inner product on 
R[x]_{\le n}. Then \inner{xp}{q} = \inner{p}{xq} for all polynomials p, q in the space (in the node case, for all p, q of degree at most n - 1, so that xp and xq still lie in it). In the weight case both sides equal \int_a^b t\,p(t)q(t)w(t)\,\dd t, and in the node case both sides equal \sum_{i=0}^{n} c_i\,p(c_i)q(c_i). The proof is one line, but the statement is not a triviality: multiplication by x moves from one slot to the other for free. That is exactly the identity \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{T\elem{v}} defining a self-adjoint operator (@def-self-adjoint), and it is the reason the recurrence below has three terms instead of k + 2. Multiplication by x is not an operator on

e k (@def-orthogonal-polynomial-sequence). (b) With p_{-1} = 0, p_0 = 1, and p_1 = x - a_0, one has p_{k+1} = (x - a_k)p_k - b_kp_{k-1} for k \ge 1, where a_k = \inner{xp_k}{p_k}/\inner{p_k}{p_k} and b_k = \inner{p_k}{p_k}/\inner{p_{k-1}}{p_{k-1}} (@thm-three-term-recurrence). (c) True. Both \inner{p_k}{p_k} = 
orm{p_k}^2 and \inner{p_{k-1}}{p_{k-1}} = 
orm{p_{k-1}}^2 are strictly positive, since p_k and p_{k-1} are nonzero and the inner product is positive definite. (d) Seven roots, all real, all distinct, all in the open interval (-1, 1) (@thm-orthogonal-polynomial-roots). In particular p_7 has no complex roots and no repeated ones. (e) False. Take the coefficient inner product \inner{p}{q} = \sum_k u_kv_k on 
R[x], where p = \sum_k u_kx^k and q = \sum_k v_kx^k (@exm-functional-with-no-riesz-vector). Then \inner{x\cdot 1}{x} = \inner{x}{x} = 1, while \inner{1}{x\cdot x} = \inner{1}{x^2} = 0. The identity is a property of the weight and node constructions (@prp-multiplication-by-x-symmetric), not of inner products in general. (f) Six. A k-point rule is exact up to degree 2k - 1, and 2\cdot 6 - 1 = 11. B. Practice [B1: A weighted interval] On 
R[x] put \inner{p}{q} = \int_0^1 p(t)q(t)\,t\,\dd t. Compute the monic p_0, p_1, and p_2, and verify directly that p_2 \perp 
R[x]_{\le 1}. The moments are \inner{x^k}{1} = \int_0^1 t^{k+1}\dd t = 1/(k+2), so 	frac12, 	frac13, 	frac14, 	frac15 for k = 0, 1, 2, 3. p_0 = 1. Then a_0 = \inner{x}{1}/\inner{1}{1} = (1/3)/(1/2) = 	frac23, so p_1 = x - 	frac23, and \inner{p_1}{p_1} = 	frac14 - 	frac43\cdot	frac13 + 	frac49\cdot	frac12 = 	frac14 - 	frac29 = 	frac{1}{36}. Next \inner{xp_1}{p_1} = \int_0^1 (t^4 - 	frac43t^3 + 	frac49t^2)\dd t = 	frac15 - 	frac13 + 	frac{4}{27} = 	frac{2}{135}, so a_1 =  rac{2/135}{1/36} =  rac{8}{15}, \qquad b_1 =  rac{1/36}{1/2} =  rac{1}{18}, and @thm-three-term-recurrence gives p_2 = \Big(x - 	frac{8}{15}\Big)\Big(x - 	frac23\Big) - 	frac{1}{18} = x^2 - 	frac65 x + 	frac{3}{10}. Verification. \inner{p_2}{1} = \int_0^1 (t^3 - 	frac65t^2 + 	frac{3}{10}t)\dd t = 	frac14 - 	frac25 + 	frac{3}{20} = 0, and \inner{p_2}{x} = \int_0^1 (t^4 - 	frac65t^3 + 	frac{3}{10}t^2)\dd t = 	frac15 - 	frac{3}{10} + 	frac{1}{10} = 0. Since (1, x) spans 
R[x]_{\le 1}, this is the whole check. [B2: Two rows of the table] Verify the degree-1 and degree-2 entries of the table for two of the classical families. 1. Chebyshev: w(t) = (1 - t^2)^{-1/2} on (-1, 1). You may use, without proof, that \int_{-1}^{1} (1 - t^2)^{-1/2}\dd t = \pi and \int_{-1}^{1} t^2(1 - t^2)^{-1/2}\dd t = \pi/2. 2. Laguerre: w(t) = e^{-t} on (0, \infty). You may use, without proof, that \int_0^\infty t^ke^{-t}\,\dd t = k!. (a) The weight is even, so \inner{x^j}{x^i} = 0 whenever i + j is odd. Hence \inner{x}{1} = 0, and x is monic of degree 1 and orthogonal to 
R[x]_{\le 0}, so p_1 = x by @prp-monic-orthogonal-sequence. Write p_2 = x^2 +  eta x + \gamma. Then \inner{p_2}{x} = \inner{x^2}{x} +  eta\inner{x}{x} + \gamma\inner{1}{x} = 0 +  eta\cdot	frac{\pi}{2} + 0, forcing  eta = 0; and \inner{p_2}{1} = 	frac{\pi}{2} + 0 + \gamma\pi = 0, forcing \gamma = -	frac12. So p_2 = x^2 - 	frac12. (b) The moments are \inner{x^k}{1} = k!, so 1, 1, 2, 6 for k = 0, 1, 2, 3. For p_1 = x +  eta: \inner{p_1}{1} = 1 +  eta = 0, so p_1 = x - 1. For p_2 = x^2 +  eta x + \gamma, the two conditions \inner{p_2}{1} = 0 and \inner{p_2}{x} = 0 read 2 +  eta + \gamma = 0, \qquad 6 + 2 eta + \gamma = 0 . Subtracting gives  eta = -4, then \gamma = 2. So p_2 = x^2 - 4x + 2, whose roots 2 \pm \sqrt2 we already located in the Quick check above. [B3: One more Legendre polynomial] Continue @exm-legendre-recurrence: compute \inner{p_3}{p_3} for p_3 = x^3 - 	frac35 x, then use @thm-three-term-recurrence to find p_4. Verify that \inner{p_4}{1} = \inner{p_4}{x^2} = 0. \inner{p_3}{p_3} = \int_{-1}^{1}\Big(t^6 - 	frac65 t^4 + 	frac{9}{25}t^2\Big)\dd t = 	frac27 - 	frac65\cdot	frac25 + 	frac{9}{25}\cdot	frac23 = 	frac27 - 	frac{6}{25} = 	frac{8}{175}. Since the weight is even, a_3 = 0, and b_3 = \inner{p_3}{p_3}/\inner{p_2}{p_2} = (8/175)/(8/45) = 	frac{9}{35}. Hence p_4 = x\Big(x^3 - 	frac35 x\Big) - 	frac{9}{35}\Big(x^2 - 	frac13\Big) = x^4 - 	frac67 x^2 + 	frac{3}{35}. Verification. \inner{p_4}{1} = 	frac25 - 	frac67\cdot	frac23 + 	frac{3}{35}\cdot 2 = 	frac{14 - 20 + 6}{35} = 0, and \inner{p_4}{x^2} = 	frac27 - 	frac67\cdot	frac25 + 	frac{3}{35}\cdot	frac23 = 	frac{10 - 12 + 2}{35} = 0 . Orthogonality to x and x^3 is automatic by parity. [B4: A two-point rule on the unit interval] Work on (0, 1) with w = 1. Exercise B2 of Section 2 (@exr-orthonormal-bases-b2) found the monic orthogonal polynomials 1, x - 	frac12, x^2 - x + 	frac16. 1. Write down the two-point Gaussian rule for \int_0^1 f. 2. Check it on f = x^3, and show that it fails on f = x^4. (a) The nodes are the roots of x^2 - x + 	frac16, namely t_{1,2} = 	frac12 \mp 	frac{\sqrt3}{6}, \qquad t_2 - t_1 = 	frac{\sqrt3}{3}, both in (0, 1), as @thm-orthogonal-polynomial-roots promises. With \ell_1 = (x - t_2)/(t_1 - t_2) and \int_0^1 t\,\dd t = 	frac12, \alpha_1 =  rac{	frac12 - t_2}{t_1 - t_2} =  rac{-\sqrt3/6}{-\sqrt3/3} = 	frac12, and \alpha_2 = 	frac12 likewise. So \int_0^1 f = 	frac12 ig(f(t_1) + f(t_2) ig) for f \in 
R[x]_{\le 3}. (b) Write t_{1,2} = 	frac12 \mp u with u = \sqrt3/6, so u^2 = 	frac{1}{12}. The odd powers of u cancel in a sum over t_1 and t_2, so t_1^3 + t_2^3 = 2\Big(	frac18 + 3\cdot	frac12\cdot	frac{1}{12}\Big) = 2\cdot	frac14 = 	frac12, and half of that is 	frac14 = \int_0^1 t^3\,\dd t. For the quartic, t_1^4 + t_2^4 = 2\Big(	frac{1}{16} + 6\cdot	frac14\cdot	frac{1}{12} + 	frac{1}{144}\Big) = 2\cdot	frac{28}{144} = 	frac{7}{18}, so the rule returns 	frac{7}{36}, whereas \int_0^1 t^4\,\dd t = 	frac15. The rule is exact to degree 3 = 2k - 1 and no further. C. Going deeper [C1: Interlacing roots] Let w be a weight on (a, b) and let (p_k) be its monic orthogonal polynomial sequence. The roots of p_k are said to interlace those of p_{k+1} when exactly one root of p_k lies strictly between each pair of consecutive roots of p_{k+1}. This is true for every k; prove the first two cases by hand. 1. Let r be the root of p_1 and s_1 < s_2 the roots of p_2. Prove that s_1 < r < s_2. 2. Let u_1 < u_2 < u_3 be the roots of p_3. Prove that u_1 < s_1 < u_2 < s_2 < u_3. Hint: evaluate the three-term recurrence at a root. (a) By @thm-three-term-recurrence with k = 1, p_2 = (x - a_1)p_1 - b_1p_0 = (x - a_1)(x - r) - b_1. Evaluating at r gives p_2(r) = -b_1 < 0, since b_1 > 0. By @thm-orthogonal-polynomial-roots, p_2 = (x - s_1)(x - s_2) with s_1 < s_2 real, and this product is negative exactly on (s_1, s_2). Hence s_1 < r < s_2. (b) By @thm-three-term-recurrence with k = 2, p_3 = (x - a_2)p_2 - b_2p_1. At a root of p_2 the first term dies, so p_3(s_i) = -b_2\,p_1(s_i) = -b_2(s_i - r) \qquad (i = 1, 2). By (a), s_1 - r < 0 and s_2 - r > 0, and b_2 > 0, so p_3(s_1) > 0 and p_3(s_2) < 0. By @thm-orthogonal-polynomial-roots, p_3 = (x - u_1)(x - u_2)(x - u_3) with u_1 < u_2 < u_3. Such a product is negative on (-\infty, u_1), positive on (u_1, u_2), negative on (u_2, u_3), and positive on (u_3, \infty). So p_3(s_1) > 0 puts s_1 in (u_1, u_2) or in (u_3, \infty), and p_3(s_2) < 0 puts s_2 in (-\infty, u_1) or in (u_2, u_3). The option s_1 > u_3 is impossible: it would give s_2 > s_1 > u_3, where p_3 is positive, contradicting p_3(s_2) < 0. The option s_2 < u_1 is impossible too: it would give s_1 < s_2 < u_1, where p_3 is negative, contradicting p_3(s_1) > 0. Hence u_1 < s_1 < u_2 and u_2 < s_2 < u_3, which is the assertion. The general case is not proved this way. The coefficients a_k and b_k assemble into a symmetric tridiagonal matrix whose characteristic polynomial is p_k, and the interlacing then follows from the interlacing theorem for the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix and its leading submatrices, which is Chapter 17’s business. [C2: The ceiling is 2k − 1] Let w be a weight on (a, b) and let k \ge 1. 1. Let t_1, \dots, t_k be any k distinct real numbers and \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k any real numbers. Prove that there is an f \in 
R[x]_{\le 2k} with \int_a^b fw 
e \sum_i \alpha_i f(t_i). 2. Hence deduce that the Gaussian rule of @thm-gaussian-quadrature is exact on 
R[x]_{\le 2k-1} and on no larger space 
R[x]_{\le d}. (a) Put g = (x - t_1)\cdots(x - t_k) and f = g^2, a polynomial of degree 2k. Every node is a root of g, so f(t_i) = 0 for every i and the right-hand side is 0, whatever the \alpha_i are. The left-hand side is \int_a^b g^2w = \inner{g}{g}, and g 
e 0, so \inner{g}{g} > 0 by positive definiteness. The two sides differ. (b) Exactness on 
R[x]_{\le 2k-1} is @thm-gaussian-quadrature. Suppose the rule were exact on 
R[x]_{\le d} for some d \ge 2k. Since 
R[x]_{\le 2k} \subseteq 
R[x]_{\le d}, it would then be exact on every polynomial of degree at most 2k. But its nodes are k distinct real numbers (@thm-orthogonal-polynomial-roots), so (a) supplies a polynomial of degree 2k on which it is not. Hence no such d exists, and 2k - 1 is the largest degree for which the rule is exact. The concrete instance k = 2, f = x^4 is the failure computed in @exm-two-point-gauss-legendre.

title: Spectral Theory
content:
Spectral Theory Take the unit circle of 
R^2 and push it through a linear map. What comes out is an ellipse. The ellipse has two axes, at right angles to each other, and it is natural to ask whether those axes sit along directions that the map merely stretches — whether, in other words, the map’s eigenvectors are perpendicular. Usually they are not. Chapter 9 found eigenvectors and asked only that they be independent; a basis of eigenvectors can be as skewed as it likes, and for a matrix like  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} it is. Perpendicular eigenvectors are a strictly stronger demand, and it is the demand that matters in practice: coordinates in an orthonormal basis are read off by one inner product each, the change of basis is an isometry, and nothing is distorted along the way. This chapter answers the question completely. There is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors exactly when the operator commutes with its adjoint over 
C, and exactly when it equals its adjoint over 
R. Those two statements are the spectral theorems, and they are the most used theorems in applied linear algebra. Everything else here grows out of them: the triangular form that every complex matrix has in an orthonormal basis (Schur), the shape of a rotation in three dimensions, several commuting operators diagonalized at once, functions of an operator computed on its spectrum, the discrete Fourier transform as one instance of the whole picture, and finally a number that measures how far a matrix is from being normal. The field is 
R or 
C throughout, as in Chapter 11, and every statement says which one it needs. The difference between the two is not cosmetic: the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra hands 
C an eigenvalue for free, and over 
R each eigenvalue has to be earned. What you need. From Chapter 6, the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra and the splitting it gives (@thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra, @cor-complex-polynomial-splits), together with Lagrange interpolation (@thm-lagrange-interpolation). From Chapter 9, eigenvalues and eigenspaces, the characteristic polynomial and multiplicities, the existence of an eigenvalue over 
C (@def-eigenvalue, @thm-eigenvalue-characterizations, @thm-complex-operator-has-eigenvalue), triangularization and what its diagonal records (@thm-triangularization, @cor-complex-triangularizable, @thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form, @thm-trace-det-eigenvalues), the conjugate-pair behavior of real matrices (@thm-real-matrix-complex-eigenvalues), and the two results on commuting operators (@thm-commuting-common-eigenvector, @thm-simultaneous-diagonalization). From Chapter 1, the complexification of a real vector space (@def-complexification, @thm-complexification-basis). From Chapter 0, the trace with its cyclic invariance, the transpose, polynomials of a matrix, and the roots of unity that §09’s Fourier matrix is built from (@thm-trace-properties, @thm-transpose-properties, @thm-polynomial-of-matrix-properties, @exm-roots-of-unity). From Chapter 2, the bookkeeping every proof here does silently: a linear map is free on a basis (@thm-linear-transform-basis), polynomials of an operator (@def-polynomial-of-operator), and invertibility (@thm-invertible-operator-tfae). From Chapter 3, permutation matrices (@lem-permutation-matrices) and the Invertible Matrix Theorem (@thm-invertible-tfae). From Chapter 4, the matrix of a map and of a composition with the isomorphism onto matrices (@def-matrix-of-linear-map, @thm-matrix-of-composition, @thm-linear-maps-isomorphic-to-matrices), and change of coordinates with similarity (@def-change-of-coordinates-matrix, @thm-change-of-basis-maps, @thm-similar-iff-same-operator). From Chapter 7, determinants: the triangular and block triangular rules, multiplicativity, the invertibility criterion, and the characteristic polynomial with its similarity invariance (@thm-det-triangular, @thm-det-block-triangular, @thm-det-multiplicative, @thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible, @cor-det-similarity-invariant, @def-charpoly-operator, @thm-charpoly-coefficients, @thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant). From Chapter 10, the Jordan form and the rotation-scaling block (@thm-jordan-canonical-form, @def-real-jordan-block). From Chapter 8, the Kronecker product and the vec operator (@def-kronecker-product, @thm-kronecker-properties, @def-vec-operator, @thm-vec-identity). Above all, from Chapter 11: orthonormal bases and Gram–Schmidt (@thm-gram-schmidt, @cor-extend-orthonormal-basis, @thm-orthonormal-coordinates), orthogonal complements and projections (@thm-orthogonal-decomposition, @def-orthogonal-projection, @thm-projection-formula), the adjoint with its arithmetic and its matrix (@def-adjoint, @thm-adjoint-properties, @thm-matrix-of-adjoint, @thm-four-subspaces-orthogonal), the two classes of operators it singles out (@def-self-adjoint, @def-normal-operator, @prp-self-adjoint-immediate), and isometries (@def-isometry, @thm-isometry-characterizations, @def-unitary-orthogonal, @def-unitary-orthogonal-groups). Roadmap - Schur’s unitary triangularization. Every complex matrix is upper triangular in some orthonormal basis; the workhorse the rest of the chapter runs on, and the real block version alongside it. - Self-adjoint operators. Real eigenvalues over both fields, orthogonal eigenspaces, invariant complements, and the test \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0 that forces T = 0. - Normal operators. The weakest hypothesis that works over 
C: four equivalent descriptions, \ker T = \ker T^{*}, and why a normal operator has no Jordan blocks. - The complex spectral theorem. Normal is exactly the same as having an orthonormal eigenbasis; Schur plus one entry-by-entry computation. - The real spectral theorem. Self-adjoint is exactly the same as having an orthonormal eigenbasis over 
R; the principal axis theorem, and the rotation that shows why “normal” is not enough here. - The shape of an orthogonal matrix. Blocks [1], [-1], and plane rotations; every element of \SO(3) is a turn about an axis, and reflections generate. - Commuting families. One orthonormal basis that diagonalizes every member of a commuting family of normal operators at once. - Spectral resolutions and functions of a normal operator. Writing T = \sum \lambda_i P_i with orthogonal projections, and defining f(T) by applying f to the spectrum. - Circulants and the discrete Fourier transform. One unitary matrix diagonalizes every circulant, and multiplication becomes convolution. - The Sylvester equation and block diagonalization. When \X \mapsto \A\X - \X\B is invertible, and what that buys for block triangular matrices. - How far from normal? Schur’s inequality turns normality from a yes-or-no property into a measurement. Named moves - Take one eigenvector, then pass to its orthogonal complement. As soon as the operator is normal or self-adjoint, that complement is invariant, so the induction on dimension runs inside the space instead of in a quotient. This replaces Chapter 9’s “extend a basis and pass to the quotient”. - Compute \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} two ways. Once with the eigenvalue equation, once by moving T across to T^{*}. Comparing the two is almost the whole of the elementary theory. - Work with 
orm{T\elem{v}}^2 = \inner{T^{*}T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}. A statement about lengths becomes a statement about the single operator T^{*}T, and a difference of two such operators is tested by the zero test. - Triangular plus normal forces diagonal. Compare one diagonal entry of \A^{*}\A with the same entry of \A\A^{*}, and a row of off-diagonal entries has to vanish. - Split into real and imaginary parts. Write T = A + iB with A and B self-adjoint; then T is normal exactly when A and B commute, and questions about T become questions about a commuting pair. - Diagonalize, then read the answer off the diagonal. Powers, square roots, exponentials, and the whole functional calculus are one line once an orthonormal eigenbasis is in hand.

title: 12.1 Schur Triangularization
content:
Schur Triangularization Chapter 9 proved that every operator on a nonzero complex vector space has an upper triangular matrix in some basis (@cor-complex-triangularizable). That basis was built by extending an eigenvector and passing to a quotient, and it came out as skewed as the operator happened to be. Now we have lengths and angles, so we can be fussier and ask for an orthonormal basis. The remarkable thing is that the answer is still yes, at no extra cost in hypotheses, and the proof is the same induction run inside an orthogonal complement rather than in a quotient. This section proves it, reads off the first consequences, and gives the real version, where a conjugate pair of eigenvalues costs one 2 	imes 2 block. Throughout, V is a finite-dimensional inner product space over F = 
R or F = 
C, and every matrix statement uses the standard inner product on F^n. Why the obvious route fails Here is the natural first attempt, and it is worth watching it fail, because the repair is the whole idea of the proof. We want an orthonormal basis \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) with \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} upper triangular, that is, with T\elem{v}_j \in \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_j) \qquad 	ext{for every } j . For j = 1 this says \elem{v}_1 is an eigenvector of T, and over 
C one exists (@thm-complex-operator-has-eigenvalue). Normalize it, set U = (\Span(\elem{v}_1))^{\perp}, and try to finish by induction on U. The attempt stops at once: to speak of T restricted to U we need U to be T-invariant, and it need not be. [An Eigenline Whose Complement Is Not Invariant] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} act on 
C^2. Check that \cvec{e}_1 is an eigenvector and decide whether (\Span(\cvec{e}_1))^{\perp} is invariant. \A\cvec{e}_1 = (1, 0) = \cvec{e}_1, so \cvec{e}_1 is an eigenvector for the eigenvalue 1. The orthogonal complement of \Span(\cvec{e}_1) is \Span(\cvec{e}_2), and \A\cvec{e}_2 = (1, 2), which is not a multiple of \cvec{e}_2. So (\Span(\cvec{e}_1))^{\perp} is not invariant, and the induction has nothing to run on. So the first basis vector is the wrong end to start from. Look at the target instead. Suppose \sB is orthonormal and \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} = \T is upper triangular. By @thm-matrix-of-adjoint the matrix of T^{*} in the same basis is \T^{*}, which is lower triangular; and the last column of a lower triangular matrix has only its bottom entry. Reading that column off, T^{*}\elem{v}_n = \conj{t_{nn}}\,\elem{v}_n . In the basis we are trying to build, the last vector is an eigenvector of T^{*} — not of T. That is the vector to produce first, and it is exactly the one whose orthogonal complement behaves. [Eigenvectors of the Adjoint Cut Out Invariant Subspaces] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F, let T \in \cL(V), and let W \subseteq V be a T^{*}-invariant subspace. Then W^{\perp} is T-invariant. Let \elem{u} \in W^{\perp} and \elem{w} \in W. Since W is T^{*}-invariant, T^{*}\elem{w} \in W, so by @def-adjoint \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{T^{*}\elem{w}} = 0 . As \elem{w} \in W was arbitrary, T\elem{u} \in W^{\perp}. Hence T(W^{\perp}) \subseteq W^{\perp}. The special case we need is W = \Span(\elem{v}) with T^{*}\elem{v} = \mu\elem{v}: one vector, one line, and an invariant complement of dimension n - 1 to recurse into. And over 
C such a \elem{v} always exists, because T^{*} is an operator on a nonzero complex space and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra gives it an eigenvalue. That is where the field enters, and it is the only place it enters. The theorem [Schur’s Unitary Triangularization] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over 
C with \dim V = n \ge 1, and let T \in \cL(V). 1. There is an orthonormal basis \sB of V such that \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} is upper triangular. 2. More precisely, let \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n be the eigenvalues of T, each listed as often as its algebraic multiplicity, in any order we please. Then \sB can be chosen so that the i-th diagonal entry of \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} is \lambda_i. Induction on \dim V, building the basis from its last vector backwards. ① Pick the eigenvalue \lambda_n we want in the bottom-right corner; the conjugate \conj{\lambda_n} is then an eigenvalue of T^{*}, because starring turns a noninvertible operator into a noninvertible operator. ② Take a unit eigenvector \elem{e} of T^{*} for \conj{\lambda_n} and put U = (\Span(\elem{e}))^{\perp}; by @lem-adjoint-eigenline-complement it is T-invariant, so T|_U exists and lives on a space of dimension n - 1. ③ Check that the characteristic polynomial of T|_U is p_T with the factor x - \lambda_n removed, so the inductive hypothesis may be applied with the shortened list. ④ Append \elem{e} to the basis it returns. We induct on n = \dim V. Since 
C is algebraically closed, p_T splits (@cor-complex-polynomial-splits), so a list \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n as in (b) exists and p_T = (x - \lambda_1)\cdots(x - \lambda_n); proving (b) proves (a). For n = 1, any unit vector \elem{v}_1 is a basis, every 1 	imes 1 matrix is upper triangular, and its single entry is the single eigenvalue \lambda_1. Let n \ge 2 and assume the statement for all inner product spaces of dimension n - 1. Fix a list \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n as in (b). \conj{\lambda_n} is an eigenvalue of T^{*}. Since \lambda_n is an eigenvalue of T, the operator T - \lambda_n\,\id_V is not invertible (@thm-eigenvalue-characterizations). By @thm-adjoint-properties (a), (b), and (d), its adjoint is T^{*} - \conj{\lambda_n}\,\id_V, and the adjoint of that is T - \lambda_n\,\id_V again. If T^{*} - \conj{\lambda_n}\,\id_V were invertible, then @thm-adjoint-properties (e) would make its adjoint T - \lambda_n\,\id_V invertible too. So T^{*} - \conj{\lambda_n}\,\id_V is not invertible, and \conj{\lambda_n} \in \spec(T^{*}). Choose an eigenvector of T^{*} for \conj{\lambda_n}; it is nonzero, so dividing by its norm gives a unit vector \elem{e} with T^{*}\elem{e} = \conj{\lambda_n}\elem{e}. Put U = (\Span(\elem{e}))^{\perp}. By @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (c), \dim U = n - 1 \ge 1, and U is T-invariant by @lem-adjoint-eigenline-complement. Write S = T|_U \in \cL(U), where U carries the inner product of V. The bottom-right entry is \lambda_n. R) is similar to \A, so p_{\T} = p_{\A} (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant); but p_{\T} = (x - t_{11})(x - t_{22}) has the real roots t_{11}, t_{22}, while p_{\A} has none. Contradiction. (c) Since \A has no real eigenvalue, the real Schur form of \A is a single 2 	imes 2 diagonal block; \Q = \I_2 and \T = \A already work. There is nothing to simplify: over 
R this matrix is as reduced as it gets. C. Going deeper [C1: Cayley–Hamilton from the triangular factors] Let \T \in M_n(
C) be upper triangular with diagonal entries \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, and set \N_k = (\T - \lambda_1\I)(\T - \lambda_2\I)\cdots(\T - \lambda_k\I) for 1 \le k \le n. 1. Prove by induction on k that the first k columns of \N_k are zero. 2. Deduce that p_{\T}(\T) = \O. 3. Deduce the Cayley–Hamilton Theorem (@thm-cayley-hamilton) for every \A \in M_n(
C), using @cor-schur-matrix. Hint for (a): the j-th column of \T - \lambda_j\I has its only possibly nonzero entries in rows 1, \dots, j - 1. (a) For k = 1: the first column of \T - \lambda_1\I is (\lambda_1 - \lambda_1, 0, \dots, 0) = \cvec{0}, since \T is upper triangular. Assume the first k - 1 columns of \N_{k-1} are zero, where 2 \le k \le n. Then \N_k = \N_{k-1}(\T - \lambda_k\I), so the j-th column of \N_k is \N_{k-1}\cvec{c}_j with \cvec{c}_j the j-th column of \T - \lambda_k\I. For j \le k - 1 we get \N_k\cvec{e}_j = \N_{k-1}(\T - \lambda_k\I)\cvec{e}_j, and since (\T - \lambda_k\I)\cvec{e}_j \in \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_j) by upper triangularity, this is a combination of the first j \le k - 1 columns of \N_{k-1}, all zero. For j = k the column \cvec{c}_k of \T - \lambda_k\I has its (k, k) entry equal to \lambda_k - \lambda_k = 0 and zeros below, so \cvec{c}_k \in \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_{k-1}), and \N_{k-1}\cvec{c}_k is a combination of the first k - 1 columns of \N_{k-1}, again zero. So all of the first k columns of \N_k vanish. (b) By @thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form (a), p_{\T} = (x - \lambda_1)\cdots(x - \lambda_n), so p_{\T}(\T) = \N_n. By (a) with k = n, all n columns of \N_n are zero, that is p_{\T}(\T) = \O. (c) Write \A = \U\T\U^{*} by @cor-schur-matrix. Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant), so p_{\A} = p_{\T}, and \A^k = \U\T^k\U^{*} for every k \ge 0 because the inner factors \U^{*}\U cancel. Hence p_{\A}(\A) = \U\,p_{\T}(\T)\,\U^{*} = \U\,\O\,\U^{*} = \O . Chapter 9 reached the same conclusion from the flag of invariant subspaces (@exr-triangularization-c1); here the whole argument happens inside one matrix product. [C2: The Frobenius norm is unitarily invariant] Chapter 11 §07 introduced the Frobenius norm 
orm{\A}_F =  igl(\sum_{i, j} \lvert a_{ij} vert^2 igr)^{1/2} and proved (a) and (b) below as @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant. Prove them again here without looking, since the argument is two lines and (c) is what this section is for. 1. Prove that 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 	r(\A^{*}\A). 2. Prove that 
orm{\U\A}_F = 
orm{\A}_F = 
orm{\A\V}_F whenever \U \in M_m(
C) and \V \in M_n(
C) are unitary. 3. Deduce that if \A = \U\T\U^{*} is a Schur factorization (@cor-schur-matrix), then 
orm{\A}_F = 
orm{\T}_F. (a) The (j, j) entry of \A^{*}\A is \sum_{i} \conj{a_{ij}}a_{ij} = \sum_i \lvert a_{ij} vert^2. Summing over j gives 	r(\A^{*}\A) = \sum_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij}vert^2 = 
orm{\A}_F^2. (b) By (a) and \U^{*}\U = \I_m, 
orm{\U\A}_F^2 = 	r igl((\U\A)^{*}(\U\A) igr) = 	r(\A^{*}\U^{*}\U\A) = 	r(\A^{*}\A) = 
orm{\A}_F^2 . For the other side, use 	r(\B\C) = 	r(\C\B) (@thm-trace-properties (3)) and \V\V^{*} = \I_n: 
orm{\A\V}_F^2 = 	r(\V^{*}\A^{*}\A\V) = 	r(\A^{*}\A\V\V^{*}) = 	r(\A^{*}\A) = 
orm{\A}_F^2 . Norms are nonnegative, so the squares being equal gives the norms equal. (c) Apply (b) twice: 
orm{\A}_F = 
orm{\U\T\U^{*}}_F = 
orm{\T\U^{*}}_F = 
orm{\T}_F, using that \U^{*} is unitary as well. So a Schur factorization redistributes the size of \A between the diagonal and the strictly upper triangle without changing the total. Section 11 turns that observation into a measurement. [C3: Distinct eigenvalues are dense, but not over the reals] 1. Sharpen @cor-schur-normal-matrix-nearby: prove that for every \A \in M_n(
C) and every \varepsilon > 0 there is \A' with n distinct eigenvalues and \lvert a_{ij} - a'_{ij} vert < \varepsilon for all i, j. 2. Show that the analogous statement fails over 
R: for \R =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} there is an \varepsilon > 0 such that no real matrix within \varepsilon of \R, entry by entry, has a real eigenvalue at all. Hint for (b): a real 2 	imes 2 matrix with entries a, b, c, d has real eigenvalues exactly when (a - d)^2 + 4bc \ge 0. (a) This is exactly what the proof of @cor-schur-normal-matrix-nearby produced, before the conclusion was weakened. There the \delta_k were chosen so that the diagonal entries of \T + \D are pairwise distinct, and by @thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form (b) those n distinct numbers are the eigenvalues of \T + \D, hence of the similar matrix \A' = \U(\T + \D)\U^{*}. The entrywise estimate is unchanged. (b) The characteristic polynomial of  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{pmatrix} is x^2 - (a + d)x + (ad - bc), whose discriminant is (a + d)^2 - 4(ad - bc) = (a - d)^2 + 4bc, so the eigenvalues are real exactly when this is \ge 0. Take \varepsilon = 	frac14 and let \A' have entries within \varepsilon of those of \R, so \lvert a vert, \lvert d vert \le 	frac14, b \in [-	frac54, -	frac34], and c \in [	frac34, 	frac54]. Then (a - d)^2 \le 	frac14 and bc \le -	frac9{16}, so (a - d)^2 + 4bc \le 	frac14 - 	frac94 = -2 < 0 . Hence \A' has no real eigenvalue, let alone two distinct ones. The reason is the one this section keeps meeting: over 
C the eigenvalues move continuously and can always be separated, while over 
R a conjugate pair cannot be pushed onto the real line by a small change.

title: 12.2 Self-Adjoint Operators
content:
Self-Adjoint Operators Among complex numbers, the real ones are those fixed by conjugation: \conj{z} = z. Among operators on an inner product space, conjugation is replaced by the adjoint, and the operators fixed by it are the self-adjoint ones, T^{*} = T. The analogy is not decoration. Self-adjoint operators have real eigenvalues, they come with a real-valued quantity \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} attached to every vector, they can be compared and ordered, and over 
R they are exactly the operators the spectral theorem applies to. This section collects everything about them that does not need a spectral theorem, and in doing so assembles every ingredient the real spectral theorem of Section 5 will use. Throughout, V is a finite-dimensional inner product space over F = 
R or F = 
C, and T \in \cL(V). The operators fixed by starring Chapter 11 already made the definition, so we only recall it: T \in \cL(V) is self-adjoint when T^{*} = T, equivalently when \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{T\elem{v}} \qquad 	ext{for all } \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V (@def-self-adjoint). In an orthonormal basis this says the matrix is Hermitian, \A^{*} = \A, which over 
R is symmetric, \A	p = \A (@thm-matrix-of-adjoint). Three facts were proved there and will be used without further comment: \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} is real for every \elem{v}, even over 
C; the diagonal entries of the matrix in an orthonormal basis are real; and every self-adjoint operator is normal (@prp-self-adjoint-immediate). Deciding self-adjointness is always the same job — compute T^{*}, or check the displayed identity on a basis — but the traps differ by example. [Four Tests] Determine which of the following are self-adjoint. Justify your answer; for those that are not, name the failing pair of vectors. 1. T_{\A} on 
C^2 with the standard inner product, \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 - i \ 1 + i & 3 \end{pmatrix}. 2. T_{\B} on 
C^2 with the standard inner product, \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ i & 1 \end{pmatrix}. 3. Differentiation D on V = 
R[x]_{\le 2} with \inner{p}{q} = \int_0^1 pq. 4. The orthogonal projection P_U onto a subspace U of any V. (a) Self-adjoint. Transposing swaps the off-diagonal entries and conjugating swaps them back, while the diagonal entries 2 and 3 are real; so \A^{*} = \A. The standard basis of 
C^2 is orthonormal, so @thm-matrix-of-adjoint turns this into T_{\A}^{*} = T_{\A}. (b) Not self-adjoint. It is symmetric, \B	p = \B, but \B^{*} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -i \ -i & 1 \end{pmatrix} 
e \B. The failing pair is \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2: \inner{\B\cvec{e}_1}{\cvec{e}_2} = i, while \inner{\cvec{e}_1}{\B\cvec{e}_2} = \conj{i} = -i. (c) Not self-adjoint. Take p = x and q = 1. Then Dp = 1 and Dq = 0, so \inner{Dp}{q} = \int_0^1 1 \, \dd x = 1, \qquad \inner{p}{Dq} = 0 . The obstruction is visible in general: integration by parts gives \inner{Dp}{q} + \inner{p}{Dq} = p(1)q(1) - p(0)q(0), so D is as far from self-adjoint as it could be — the two sides add up rather than agreeing, apart from boundary terms. (d) Self-adjoint, for every U. By @thm-projection-formula (b), \inner{P_U\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{P_U\elem{v}} for all \elem{u}, \elem{v}, which is the displayed identity. Over 
C, symmetric is not the right notion; Hermitian is. Part (b) above is symmetric and its eigenvalues are not even real: 	r\B = 2 and \det\B = 1 - i^2 = 2, so p_{\B} = x^2 - 2x + 2 and the eigenvalues are 1 + i and 1 - i. Every theorem in this section would fail for it. The word “symmetric matrix” belongs to the real case, where conjugation does nothing and \A^{*} = \A	p; over 
C always write, and check, \A^{*} = \A. Eigenvalues are real The first theorem is the operator version of “a number equal to its own conjugate is real”, and its proof is the move that runs this whole chapter: compute one inner product two different ways. [Self-adjoint Operators Have Real Eigenvalues] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F = 
R or F = 
C and let T \in \cL(V) be self-adjoint. Then every eigenvalue of T is real. Take T\elem{v} = \lambda\elem{v} with \elem{v} 
e \elem{0} and pair it with \elem{v}. Computing \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} straight off the eigenvalue equation produces \lambda; computing it by pushing T into the second slot produces \conj\lambda, because a scalar leaving the second slot picks up a conjugate. The two answers must agree, and 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 
e 0 lets us cancel. Let \lambda be an eigenvalue of T, with eigenvector \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}. On one side, \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\lambda\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \lambda
orm{\elem{v}}^2 , by linearity in the first slot. On the other, using @def-self-adjoint and then conjugate-linearity in the second slot, \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{T\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{\lambda\elem{v}} = \conj{\lambda}
orm{\elem{v}}^2 . So \lambda
orm{\elem{v}}^2 = \conj{\lambda}
orm{\elem{v}}^2. Since \elem{v} 
e \elem{0} we have 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 
e 0 by positive definiteness (@def-inner-product), and dividing gives \lambda = \conj{\lambda}. A scalar equal to its own conjugate is real. Chapter 11 already proved this, in the remark after @prp-self-adjoint-immediate. It is promoted to a theorem here because Sections 3 to 5 lean on it constantly, and a result cited that often should have a number. Over 
R the conclusion sounds empty, because the eigenvalues of a real operator are real by definition. What is not empty over 
R is the corresponding statement about the roots of the characteristic polynomial, and that is the next theorem: it says the roots do not escape into
