C, which is exactly what guarantees that a real self-adjoint operator has an eigenvector at all. Existence over the real numbers Over 
C an eigenvalue is free (@thm-complex-operator-has-eigenvalue). Over 
R it is not, and the rotation of 
R^2 by a quarter turn has none. Self-adjointness is what rules that out. [Real Self-adjoint Operators Have an Eigenvalue] Let V 
e \{\elem{0}\} be a finite-dimensional inner product space over 
R and let T \in \cL(V) be self-adjoint. Then: 1. every root of p_T in 
C is real, so p_T splits over 
R; 2. T has an eigenvalue. There is no complex number in sight, so we put one there. Fix an orthonormal basis; the matrix \A of T is real symmetric. The same array of numbers, read as a complex matrix, is Hermitian, and it acts on 
C^n, which is the complexification of 
R^n (@def-complexification, @exm-complexification-rn) — the arena Chapter 1 built, and Chapter 9 put to work, precisely so that a real matrix could borrow complex eigenvalues. Over 
C an eigenvalue exists, and @thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues says it is real. A real root of p_T is an eigenvalue of T itself, and we are back where we started, one eigenvalue richer. Let n = \dim V \ge 1. By @thm-gram-schmidt, V has an orthonormal basis \sB; put \A = \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} \in M_n(
R). By @thm-matrix-of-adjoint and @def-self-adjoint, \A^{*} = \A, and since \A is real this says \A	p = \A. Now read \A as an element of M_n(
C), acting on 
C^n with the standard inner product; this is the extension of the real map T_{\A} to the complexification (
R^n)_{
C} = 
C^n, which acts on \cvec{x} + i\cvec{y} by \A\cvec{x} + i\A\cvec{y} (Chapter 9, Section 2). Because \A is real and symmetric, \A^{*} = \conj{\A}	p = \A	p = \A, so T_{\A} is self-adjoint as an operator on 
C^n (@thm-matrix-of-adjoint again, the standard basis of 
C^n being orthonormal). (a) By @def-charpoly-operator, p_T = p_{\A}, and the entries of x\I - \A are real, so this is the same polynomial whether the determinant is expanded over 
R or over 
C; it lies in 
R[x] \subseteq 
C[x]. Let \lambda \in 
C be a root of p_{\A}. By @thm-eigenvalue-characterizations, \lambda is an eigenvalue of \A over 
C, and \A is self-adjoint there, so \lambda \in 
R by @thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues. Since every root of p_T in 
C lies in 
R, and p_T splits over 
C by @cor-complex-polynomial-splits, it splits over 
R. (b) p_T is monic of degree n \ge 1 (@thm-charpoly-coefficients), so by (a) it has a root \lambda \in 
R. By @thm-eigenvalue-characterizations ((e) \Rightarrow (a)), \lambda is an eigenvalue of T. This proves the theorem. There is a second, very different route to (b): the function \elem{v} \mapsto \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} is real-valued and continuous on the unit sphere of V, which is closed and bounded, so it attains a maximum, and a vector where it does so turns out to be an eigenvector for the largest eigenvalue. That argument is shorter to state but it is analysis, not algebra, and it appeals to the extreme value theorem directly. We keep to the algebraic route, which reaches that theorem only at one remove: the proof just given rests on @cor-complex-polynomial-splits, hence on the fundamental theorem of algebra (@thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra), and the proof of that in Chapter 6 uses the extreme value theorem on a closed disc. The maximization picture returns in Chapter 17, where the Rayleigh quotient and the Courant–Fischer theorem describe every eigenvalue of a self-adjoint operator by optimization. The rotation \R =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} on 
R^2 has no eigenvalue, and over 
C its eigenvalues \pm i are not real. Which hypothesis of @thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue does it fail, and how do you see it in one line? Self-adjointness. In the standard orthonormal basis the matrix of \R^{*} is \R	p =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = -\R, which is not \R. So \R is skew-adjoint, not self-adjoint, and neither theorem applies. (It is, however, normal, since \R	p\R = \R\R	p = \I — which is why Section 5 has to insist on self-adjoint rather than normal over 
R.) Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal The second theorem is the same move with two vectors instead of one, and it is the geometric half of the spectral theorem: the eigenspaces are not merely independent, as in Chapter 9, but perpendicular. [Distinct Eigenvalues Give Orthogonal Eigenvectors] Let T \in \cL(V) be self-adjoint, and let \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V satisfy T\elem{u} = \lambda\elem{u} and T\elem{v} = \mu\elem{v} with \lambda 
e \mu. Then \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = 0. Consequently E_\lambda(T) \perp E_\mu(T) for distinct eigenvalues \lambda, \mu. Compute \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} two ways. First, \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\lambda\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \lambda\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}}. Second, by @def-self-adjoint and conjugate-linearity in the second slot, \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{T\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{\mu\elem{v}} = \conj{\mu}\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \mu\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}}, the last step because \mu is real by @thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues. Subtracting, (\lambda - \mu)\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = 0, and \lambda - \mu 
e 0, so \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = 0. Since every element of E_\lambda(T) is such a \elem{u} and every element of E_\mu(T) such a \elem{v}, the two eigenspaces are orthogonal. Note where the previous theorem was spent: it made \conj{\mu} = \mu, so that the conjugation which appears on the way out of the second slot does no damage. Without real eigenvalues the computation would end at \lambda\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \conj{\mu}\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}}, which says nothing when \lambda = \conj{\mu}. [A Hermitian Two-by-Two] For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 - i \ 1 + i & 3 \end{pmatrix} on 
C^2, find the eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each, and verify that the two eigenvectors are orthogonal. Here 	r\A = 5 and \det\A = 6 - (1 - i)(1 + i) = 6 - 2 = 4, so p_{\A} = x^2 - 5x + 4 = (x - 1)(x - 4) . Both eigenvalues are real, as @thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues promised. For \lambda = 1: \A - \I =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 - i \ 1 + i & 2 \end{pmatrix}, and the first row gives x + (1 - i)y = 0, so \cvec{u} = (-1 + i, 1). Check the second row: (1 + i)(-1 + i) + 2 = (-1 + i - i + i^2) + 2 = -2 + 2 = 0. For \lambda = 4: \A - 4\I =  egin{pmatrix} -2 & 1 - i \ 1 + i & -1 \end{pmatrix}, and the first row gives -2x + (1 - i)y = 0, so \cvec{v} = (1 - i, 2). Finally \inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{v}} = (-1 + i)\conj{(1 - i)} + 1 \cdot \conj{2} = (-1 + i)(1 + i) + 2 = -2 + 2 = 0 , so \cvec{u} \perp \cvec{v}, as @thm-self-adjoint-orthogonal-eigenspaces requires. Normalizing, 
orm{\cvec{u}}^2 = 2 + 1 = 3 and 
orm{\cvec{v}}^2 = 2 + 4 = 6, so \Bigl(	frac1{\sqrt3}(-1 + i, 1),\ 	frac1{\sqrt6}(1 - i, 2)\Bigr) is an orthonormal basis of 
C^2 consisting of eigenvectors of \A. Section 4 proves that this always happens, for exactly the operators it happens for. Invariant complements Section 5 will prove the real spectral theorem by the move named at the front of the chapter: find one eigenvector, pass to its orthogonal complement, induct. For that to work the complement must be invariant, and the restriction must again be self-adjoint so that the induction can be applied to it. Both hold, and neither needs an eigenvector — the statement is about any invariant subspace. [Self-adjointness Passes to Orthogonal Complements] Let T \in \cL(V) be self-adjoint and let U \subseteq V be a T-invariant subspace. Then: 1. U^{\perp} is T-invariant; 2. T|_U \in \cL(U) and T|_{U^{\perp}} \in \cL(U^{\perp}) are self-adjoint, for the inner products inherited from V. (a) Since T is self-adjoint, T^{*} = T, so U is T^{*}-invariant. By @lem-adjoint-eigenline-complement, U^{\perp} is T-invariant. (b) U is T-invariant, so T|_U maps U to U and is an operator on U. For \elem{u}_1, \elem{u}_2 \in U, \inner{T|_U\elem{u}_1}{\elem{u}_2} = \inner{T\elem{u}_1}{\elem{u}_2} = \inner{\elem{u}_1}{T\elem{u}_2} = \inner{\elem{u}_1}{T|_U\elem{u}_2} , where the inner products are those of V, which is what U inherits. By @def-self-adjoint, T|_U is self-adjoint. The same three equalities with U^{\perp} in place of U give the second claim, using (a) to know that T|_{U^{\perp}} is an operator on U^{\perp}. So the pair (U, U^{\perp}) splits a self-adjoint operator into two self-adjoint operators on smaller spaces, and nothing is lost: V = U \oplus U^{\perp} by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (a). Combined with @thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue, which guarantees that a nonzero space always offers an eigenvector to start from, this is a complete induction, and Section 5 will do no more than write it out. Two zero tests, and the gap between the fields An operator carries the function \elem{v} \mapsto \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}, sometimes called its quadratic form. How much of T does that one function remember? The answer depends on the field, and the difference is the sharpest illustration in this book of why 
C is the easier place to work. [The Zero Test for Self-adjoint Operators] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F = 
R or F = 
C and let T \in \cL(V) be self-adjoint. If \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0 for every \elem{v} \in V, then T = 0. The hypothesis only ever feeds T one vector, while the conclusion is about \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} for two. So manufacture two out of one: apply the hypothesis to \elem{u} + \elem{w} and expand. The diagonal terms die by hypothesis and what is left is a statement about the cross terms, which self-adjointness turns into a statement about \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} alone. Let \elem{u}, \elem{w} \in V. Expanding \inner{T(\elem{u} + \elem{w})}{\elem{u} + \elem{w}} in both slots,  egin{aligned} 0 &= \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{u}} + \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} + \inner{T\elem{w}}{\elem{u}} + \inner{T\elem{w}}{\elem{w}} \ &= \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} + \inner{T\elem{w}}{\elem{u}}, \end{aligned} the two outer terms vanishing by hypothesis. Since T is self-adjoint, \inner{T\elem{w}}{\elem{u}} = \inner{\elem{w}}{T\elem{u}} = \conj{\inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}}} by conjugate symmetry. Writing z = \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}}, the display says z + \conj{z} = 0, that is \operatorname{Re}\inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} = 0 \qquad 	ext{for all } \elem{u}, \elem{w} \in V . 	ag{$\ast$} If F = 
R this already says \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} = 0 for all \elem{u}, \elem{w}. If F = 
C, apply (\ast) with i\elem{w} in place of \elem{w}: since \inner{T\elem{u}}{i\elem{w}} = \conj{i}\,z = -iz and \operatorname{Re}(-iz) = \operatorname{Im}(z), we also get \operatorname{Im}\inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} = 0. Either way \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} = 0 for all \elem{u}, \elem{w}. Taking \elem{w} = T\elem{u} gives 
orm{T\elem{u}}^2 = 0, so T\elem{u} = \elem{0} for every \elem{u}, that is T = 0. This proves the theorem. Now drop the hypothesis. Over 
C nothing is lost. [The Zero Test over the Complex Numbers] Let V be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let T \in \cL(V) be any operator. If \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0 for every \elem{v} \in V, then T = 0. The previous proof used self-adjointness in exactly one place: to convert \inner{T\elem{w}}{\elem{u}} into \conj{\inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}}}, which gave the real part only. Without it we must extract the imaginary part some other way, and over 
C there is another way — substitute \elem{u} + i\elem{w} as well as \elem{u} + \elem{w}, and take a combination of the two identities. There is no third substitution available over 
R, which is precisely why the real statement is false. Let \elem{u}, \elem{w} \in V. Applying the hypothesis to \elem{u} + \elem{w} and expanding as before, \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} + \inner{T\elem{w}}{\elem{u}} = 0 . 	ag{1} Applying it to \elem{u} + i\elem{w} and using \inner{T\elem{u}}{i\elem{w}} = -i\inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}}, \inner{T(i\elem{w})}{\elem{u}} = i\inner{T\elem{w}}{\elem{u}}, and \inner{T(i\elem{w})}{i\elem{w}} = i\conj{i}\inner{T\elem{w}}{\elem{w}} = 0, -i\inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} + i\inner{T\elem{w}}{\elem{u}} = 0 . Multiplying that by i gives \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} - \inner{T\elem{w}}{\elem{u}} = 0 . 	ag{2} Adding (1) and (2), 2\inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} = 0, so \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} = 0 for all \elem{u}, \elem{w}. Taking \elem{w} = T\elem{u} gives 
orm{T\elem{u}}^2 = 0, hence T = 0. This statement appeared once already, as @exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-c2 (b), where it was an exercise in the arithmetic of complex inner products. It is restated and proved here because Section 3 needs to cite it as a theorem: the four characterizations of a normal operator all come from applying it to T^{*}T - TT^{*}. The proof is the same one; what is new is the company it now keeps. Over 
R, the quadratic form does not determine the operator. Let T be the quarter turn of 
R^2, T(x_1, x_2) = (-x_2, x_1). Then \inner{T\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = -x_2x_1 + x_1x_2 = 0 \qquad 	ext{for every } \cvec{x} \in 
R^2 , and yet T 
e 0. So @thm-complex-zero-test genuinely fails over 
R, and @thm-self-adjoint-zero-test genuinely needs its hypothesis: this T is not self-adjoint, since T^{*} = -T. The general real statement is that \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0 for all \elem{v} forces T^{*} = -T and no more — @exr-self-adjoint-operators-c3. Over 
C, suppose \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} is real for every \elem{v} \in V. Must T be self-adjoint? Yes. Put S = T - T^{*}. For every \elem{v}, \inner{T^{*}\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{T\elem{v}} = \conj{\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}} = \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}, the last step because the number is real. Hence \inner{S\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0 for all \elem{v}, and @thm-complex-zero-test gives S = 0, that is T^{*} = T. Combined with @prp-self-adjoint-immediate (a), this says that over 
C “self-adjoint” and “\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} always real” are the same condition. Over 
R the criterion is useless, since \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} is automatically real for every operator. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State what it means for T \in \cL(V) to be self-adjoint, in terms of T^{*} and in terms of inner products, and say what the matrix condition is and in which bases it may be used. 2. True or false: a symmetric matrix in M_2(
C) has real eigenvalues. Justify your answer. 3. Which field does @thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue concern, and which earlier theorem supplies the eigenvalue it borrows? 4. True or false: if T is self-adjoint and U is any subspace, then U^{\perp} is T-invariant. Justify your answer. 5. State the difference between @thm-self-adjoint-zero-test and @thm-complex-zero-test, and give the standard example showing the second has no real analogue. 6. Give a normal operator on 
R^2 that is not self-adjoint. (a) T^{*} = T; equivalently \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{T\elem{v}} for all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V (@def-self-adjoint). The matrix condition is \A^{*} = \A, and by @thm-matrix-of-adjoint it may be used only in an orthonormal basis. (b) False. \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ i & 1 \end{pmatrix} is symmetric with eigenvalues 1 \pm i (@exm-self-adjoint-tests (b) and the warning after it). Over 
C the relevant condition is \A^{*} = \A, not \A	p = \A. (c) The real field: it says a self-adjoint operator on a nonzero real inner product space has an eigenvalue. The eigenvalue is borrowed from @thm-complex-operator-has-eigenvalue, applied to the matrix read as a complex matrix on the complexification 
C^n of 
R^n, and is then shown to be real by @thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues. (d) False as stated: U must be T-invariant (@thm-self-adjoint-invariant-complement). For example, T = T_{\A} on 
R^2 with \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is self-adjoint, and U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1) has U^{\perp} = \Span(\cvec{e}_2) with T\cvec{e}_2 = \cvec{e}_1 
otin U^{\perp}. Here U was not invariant either, since T\cvec{e}_1 = \cvec{e}_2. (e) @thm-self-adjoint-zero-test holds over 
R and 
C but assumes T self-adjoint; @thm-complex-zero-test drops that assumption but holds only over 
C. The quarter turn T(x_1, x_2) = (-x_2, x_1) of 
R^2 satisfies \inner{T\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = 0 for every \cvec{x} and is not zero. (f) The same quarter turn: T^{*} = -T, so T^{*}T = TT^{*} = \id and T is normal, while T^{*} 
e T. B. Practice [B1: Determine which are self-adjoint] Determine which of the following operators are self-adjoint. Justify your answer; for those that are not, exhibit a pair \elem{u}, \elem{v} with \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} 
e \inner{\elem{u}}{T\elem{v}}, or compute T^{*}. 1. T_{\A} on 
C^2, \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 + i \ 2 - i & -5 \end{pmatrix}, standard inner product. 2. T_{\B} on 
C^2, \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, standard inner product. 3. T_{\C} on 
R^3, \C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \ 2 & 1 & 3 \ 0 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, standard inner product. 4. S^{*}S, for an arbitrary S \in \cL(V, W) between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. 5. P_U - P_{U^{\perp}}, for a subspace U of a finite-dimensional V. 6. T(x_1, x_2) = (x_2, x_1) on 
R^2 with the standard inner product, whose matrix in the basis \sC = ((1, 0), (1, 2)) is  egin{pmatrix} -	frac12 & 	frac32 \ 	frac12 & 	frac12 \end{pmatrix}, which is not symmetric. (a) Self-adjoint. The diagonal entries 1 and -5 are real and the off-diagonal pair 2 + i, 2 - i are conjugates, so \A^{*} = \A; the standard basis is orthonormal, so @thm-matrix-of-adjoint applies. (b) Not self-adjoint. \B^{*} = \B	p =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = -\B, so T_{\B} is skew-adjoint. Concretely \inner{\B\cvec{e}_1}{\cvec{e}_2} = -1 while \inner{\cvec{e}_1}{\B\cvec{e}_2} = 1. (c) Self-adjoint. \C is real and \C	p = \C, and the standard basis of 
R^3 is orthonormal. (d) Self-adjoint, for every S. By @thm-adjoint-properties (c) and (d), (S^{*}S)^{*} = S^{*}S^{**} = S^{*}S. (e) Self-adjoint. Each of P_U and P_{U^{\perp}} is self-adjoint (@exm-self-adjoint-tests (d)), and by @thm-adjoint-properties (a) and (b) the difference of self-adjoint operators is self-adjoint: (P_U - P_{U^{\perp}})^{*} = P_U^{*} - P_{U^{\perp}}^{*} = P_U - P_{U^{\perp}}. (f) Self-adjoint, in spite of the nonsymmetric matrix. The basis \sC is not orthonormal — \inner{(1,0)}{(1,2)} = 1 
e 0 — so @thm-matrix-of-adjoint does not apply to it, and the shape of \mtx{T}{\sC}{\sC} says nothing either way. Test the definition instead: for \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^2, \inner{T\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = x_2y_1 + x_1y_2 = \inner{\cvec{x}}{T\cvec{y}} , so T^{*} = T. In the standard basis, which is orthonormal, the matrix is  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, symmetric as it must be. The moral is the one Chapter 11, Section 6 closes with: self-adjointness is a property of the operator and the inner product, never of a matrix taken on its own. [B2: Eigenvalues and orthogonality] 1. For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \ i & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
C), check that \A is Hermitian, find its eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each, and verify that the eigenvectors are orthogonal. 2. For \S =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 3 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(
R), find the eigenvalues with their multiplicities and bases of the eigenspaces, and verify that the two eigenspaces are orthogonal. 3. Hence write down an orthonormal basis of 
R^3 consisting of eigenvectors of \S. (a) \A^{*} = \conj{\A}	p =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \ i & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \A, so \A is Hermitian. Then 	r\A = 0 and \det\A = 0 - (-i)(i) = -1, so p_{\A} = x^2 - 1 and the eigenvalues are 1 and -1, both real. \A(1, i) = (-i \cdot i,\; i \cdot 1) = (1, i), so \cvec{u} = (1, i) works for \lambda = 1. \A(1, -i) = (-1,\; i) = -(1, -i), so \cvec{v} = (1, -i) works for \lambda = -1. Finally \inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{v}} = 1 \cdot \conj{1} + i\,\conj{(-i)} = 1 + i \cdot i = 0 . (b) Expanding the determinant gives p_{\S} = (x - 5)(x - 2)^2, so \spec(\S) = \{5, 2\} with algebraic multiplicities 1 and 2. The eigenspaces are read off from \S = 2\I + \J, where \J is the all-ones matrix: since \J(1, 1, 1) = (3, 3, 3) and \J\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} exactly when x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0, E_5(\S) = \Span igl((1, 1, 1) igr), \quad E_2(\S) = \Span igl((1, -1, 0), (1, 0, -1) igr), of dimensions 1 and 2. Orthogonality: (1, 1, 1) \cdot (1, -1, 0) = 0 and (1, 1, 1) \cdot (1, 0, -1) = 0, so E_5(\S) \perp E_2(\S), as @thm-self-adjoint-orthogonal-eigenspaces requires. (c) The two vectors spanning E_2(\S) are not orthogonal to each other, so run Gram–Schmidt inside that eigenspace (@thm-gram-schmidt). With \cvec{w}_1 = (1, -1, 0), (1, 0, -1) - 	frac{1}{2}(1, -1, 0) = 	frac12(1, 1, -2) . Normalizing all three vectors gives the orthonormal eigenbasis 	frac1{\sqrt3}(1, 1, 1), \quad 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0), \quad 	frac1{\sqrt6}(1, 1, -2) . The eigenvalues are 5, 2, 2 in that order. [B3: A self-adjoint square root of zero] Let T \in \cL(V) be self-adjoint with T^2 = 0. Prove that T = 0. Deduce that a self-adjoint T with T^k = 0 for some k \ge 1 is zero. For every \elem{v} \in V, by @def-self-adjoint, 
orm{T\elem{v}}^2 = \inner{T\elem{v}}{T\elem{v}} = \inner{T^2\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{0}}{\elem{v}} = 0 , so T\elem{v} = \elem{0}. As \elem{v} was arbitrary, T = 0. For the deduction, use strong induction on k (@thm-strong-induction). If k = 1 there is nothing to prove. Let k \ge 2 with T^k = 0, and put m = \lceil k/2 ceil, so that 1 \le m < k and 2m \ge k. Then (T^m)^2 = T^{2m} = T^{2m-k}T^k = 0, and T^m is self-adjoint, since (T^m)^{*} = (T^{*})^m = T^m by @thm-adjoint-properties (c). By the first part, T^m = 0, and the inductive hypothesis applied to the exponent m gives T = 0. C. Going deeper [C1: The operator S^{*}S] Let S \in \cL(V, W) between finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F, and set T = S^{*}S \in \cL(V). 1. Prove that T is self-adjoint and that \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} \ge 0 for every \elem{v} \in V, with equality if and only if S\elem{v} = \elem{0}. 2. Deduce that every eigenvalue of T is a nonnegative real number. 3. Prove that T is invertible if and only if S is injective. Hint for (a): the quantity \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} is a norm squared in disguise. (a) T^{*} = (S^{*}S)^{*} = S^{*}S^{**} = S^{*}S = T, by @thm-adjoint-properties (c) and (d). For the second claim, use conjugate symmetry and then @def-adjoint: \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \conj{\inner{\elem{v}}{S^{*}S\elem{v}}} = \conj{\inner{S\elem{v}}{S\elem{v}}} = 
orm{S\elem{v}}^2 , the last step because a norm squared is a nonnegative real number and is its own conjugate. So \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} \ge 0, with equality exactly when 
orm{S\elem{v}} = 0, that is S\elem{v} = \elem{0} (@def-inner-product). (b) Let T\elem{v} = \lambda\elem{v} with \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}. By @thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues, \lambda \in 
R. By (a), 0 \le \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \lambda
orm{\elem{v}}^2, and 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 > 0, so \lambda \ge 0. (c) (\Rightarrow) If S\elem{v} = \elem{0} then T\elem{v} = \elem{0}, so injectivity of T forces \elem{v} = \elem{0}; and an invertible operator is injective. (\Leftarrow) If S is injective and T\elem{v} = \elem{0}, then by (a) 
orm{S\elem{v}}^2 = \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0, so S\elem{v} = \elem{0} and \elem{v} = \elem{0}. Thus \ker T = \{\elem{0}\}, so T is injective, hence bijective by @cor-rank-nullity-consequences (e). This is @cor-rank-adjoint (b) again, seen from the quadratic form. Operators with the property in (a) are called positive, and they are the subject of Chapter 13; part (b) is the first half of the characterization proved there. [C2: Sums and products] Let S, T \in \cL(V) be self-adjoint. 1. Prove that S + T and cT are self-adjoint for every real scalar c, and show by example that cT need not be self-adjoint for c \in 
C. 2. Prove that ST is self-adjoint if and only if ST = TS. 3. Give self-adjoint S, T \in \cL(
C^2) with ST not self-adjoint. (a) By @thm-adjoint-properties (a), (S + T)^{*} = S^{*} + T^{*} = S + T. By (b) of the same theorem, (cT)^{*} = \conj{c}\,T^{*} = \conj{c}\,T, which equals cT exactly when \conj{c} = c or T = 0. For a complex counterexample take T = \id on 
C^2 and c = i: then (i\,\id)^{*} = -i\,\id 
e i\,\id. (b) By @thm-adjoint-properties (c), (ST)^{*} = T^{*}S^{*} = TS. So (ST)^{*} = ST if and only if TS = ST. (c) Take S = T_{\A} and T = T_{\B} on 
C^2 with \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . Both are Hermitian. But \A\B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \B\A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, which differ, so by (b) the product is not self-adjoint. Indeed (\A\B)^{*} = \B\A 
e \A\B. [C3: What the real quadratic form does determine] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over 
R and T \in \cL(V). Call T skew-adjoint if T^{*} = -T. 1. Prove that \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0 for every \elem{v} \in V if and only if T is skew-adjoint. 2. Deduce that every T \in \cL(V) can be written uniquely as T = A + B with A self-adjoint and B skew-adjoint, and that \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{A\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} for every \elem{v}. 3. Conclude that over 
R the function \elem{v} \mapsto \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} determines A and nothing about B. Contrast this with the complex case. (a) (\Leftarrow) If T^{*} = -T, then for every \elem{v}, \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}\elem{v}} = -\inner{\elem{v}}{T\elem{v}} = -\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}, the last step by symmetry of a real inner product. A real number equal to its own negative is 0. (\Rightarrow) Suppose \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0 for all \elem{v}. Expanding \inner{T(\elem{u} + \elem{w})}{\elem{u} + \elem{w}} = 0 and canceling the two diagonal terms, \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} + \inner{T\elem{w}}{\elem{u}} = 0 . Over 
R, \inner{T\elem{w}}{\elem{u}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{T\elem{w}}, so \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{-T\elem{w}} for all \elem{u}, \elem{w}. By the uniqueness in @thm-adjoint-exists, T^{*} = -T. (b) Put A = 	frac12(T + T^{*}) and B = 	frac12(T - T^{*}). Then A + B = T, and by @thm-adjoint-properties (a), (b), and (d), A^{*} = A and B^{*} = -B. For uniqueness, if T = A' + B' is another such splitting, then T^{*} = A' - B', so A' = 	frac12(T + T^{*}) = A and B' = B. Finally \inner{B\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0 for every \elem{v} by (a), so \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{A\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} + \inner{B\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{A\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}. (c) By (b), two operators T and T' with the same self-adjoint part have the same quadratic form; and conversely, if \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{T'\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} for all \elem{v}, then A - A' is self-adjoint with vanishing quadratic form, so A = A' by @thm-self-adjoint-zero-test. So the quadratic form sees exactly A. The skew part is invisible: the quarter turn of 
R^2 is skew-adjoint, and adding it to any T changes nothing. Over 
C, by contrast, @thm-complex-zero-test says the quadratic form determines T completely — there is no invisible part at all, which is why the complex theory is the easier one.

title: 12.3 Normal Operators
content:
Normal Operators Section 2 collected everything a self-adjoint operator gives us: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenspaces, an invariant orthogonal complement. That is exactly the equipment an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors needs. But over 
C the hypothesis is too heavy, and this section finds the lighter one that still carries the load. It is a condition already met in Chapter 11, and the rest of the chapter runs on it. As throughout, F is 
R or 
C, inner products are linear in the first slot, and every inner product space is finite-dimensional unless we say otherwise. The hypothesis that self-adjointness overshoots Take the operator on 
C^2 whose matrix in the standard basis is \D = \diag(1, i). The standard basis is orthonormal and consists of eigenvectors of \D, so this operator has everything the spectral theorem promises. Yet it is not self-adjoint: one of its eigenvalues is i, and a self-adjoint operator has only real eigenvalues (@thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues). So over 
C self-adjointness cannot be the condition we are looking for. It is sufficient and not necessary, and we are throwing away every operator with a nonreal eigenvalue — including every unitary operator other than the trivial ones. What survives? Compare the two computations. For a self-adjoint T we have T^{*}T = TT = TT^{*}. For \D = \diag(1, i) we have \D^{*} = \diag(1, -i), which is a different matrix, but \D^{*}\D = \diag(1, 1) = \D\D^{*} . Neither operator equals its adjoint; both commute with their adjoints. That is the common feature, and Chapter 11 already gave it a name. A normal operator is one that never gets in its adjoint’s way: the two may be applied in either order. Recall @def-normal-operator: an operator T \in \cL(V) is normal when T^{*}T = TT^{*}. That is a single equation between two operators, with no vectors and no quantifiers in it, and it is strictly weaker than T^{*} = T. Section 6 of Chapter 11 checked the definition on self-adjoint operators, on unitary ones, on i\I, and on diagonal matrices, and found the 2 	imes 2 Jordan block \J_2(0) failing it. We take those for granted and go one step further: normality is best understood as a statement about lengths, and that is the content of the first theorem below. Before it, a wider catalog, since the class is larger than Chapter 11’s four examples suggest. [Which of these are normal?] Decide which of the following matrices are normal, with the standard inner product on 
C^n or 
R^n. For those that are, say which familiar family they belong to. 1. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 + i \ 1 - i & 3 \end{pmatrix} over 
C. 2. \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ -2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} over 
R. 3. \U = 	frac1{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ i & 1 \end{pmatrix} over 
C. 4. \C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \ 3 & 1 & 2 \ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} over 
C. 5. \M =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} over 
R. 6. \N =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} over 
R. (a) Normal. \A^{*} = \A, since transposing swaps the off-diagonal entries and conjugating swaps them back, so \A is Hermitian and both products equal \A^2. Every self-adjoint operator is normal. (b) Normal. \B	p = -\B, so \B	p\B = -\B^2 = \B\B	p. An operator with T^{*} = -T is called skew-adjoint, and the same one-line computation makes every such operator normal. (c) Normal. \U^{*}\U = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & -i \ -i & 1 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ i & 1 \end{pmatrix} = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \I, so \U is unitary (@def-unitary-orthogonal), and then \U^{*}\U = \I = \U\U^{*}. (d) Normal. Each row of \C is the previous one shifted cyclically to the right; such a matrix is called a circulant. Writing out the products, \C	p\C = \C\C	p =  egin{pmatrix} 14 & 11 & 11 \ 11 & 14 & 11 \ 11 & 11 & 14 \end{pmatrix} . Both entries in position (i, j) are the dot product of two rows of \C, or of two columns, and cyclic shifting makes those two lists of dot products agree. Section 9 explains circulants properly and diagonalizes all of them at once. (e) Normal, and in none of the families above: \M	p 
eq \pm\M and \M	p\M = 5\I 
eq \I. Still, \M	p\M = \M\M	p =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \ 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix} . This is \sqrt5 times a rotation of the plane, which is the rotation-scaling block \vLambda(2 + i) transposed (@def-real-jordan-block). Normality is genuinely wider than “self-adjoint or unitary”. (f) Not normal: \N	p\N =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \N\N	p =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} . The (1,1) entries already disagree, 1 
eq 2. This matrix is diagonalizable, with eigenvalues 1 and 2; Section 4 shows what it costs to be diagonalizable and not normal. Normality is a statement about lengths The definition compares two operators. The next theorem turns it into a comparison of two numbers, one vector at a time, and that is the form every later proof uses. The engine is the zero test of Section 2: a self-adjoint operator S with \inner{S\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0 for all \elem{v} is zero. [Characterizations of Normality] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F and let T \in \cL(V). The following are equivalent. 1. T is normal. 2. 
orm{T\elem{v}} = 
orm{T^{*}\elem{v}} for every \elem{v} \in V. 3. \inner{T\elem{u}}{T\elem{v}} = \inner{T^{*}\elem{u}}{T^{*}\elem{v}} for all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V. Suppose in addition that F = 
C, and set A = 	frac12(T + T^{*}), \qquad B = 	frac1{2i}(T - T^{*}), so that A and B are self-adjoint and T = A + iB. Then (a)–(c) are further equivalent to 4. AB = BA. Condition (a) says that the operator S = T^{*}T - TT^{*} is zero. That operator is self-adjoint, so by the zero test of @thm-self-adjoint-zero-test it is enough to know \inner{S\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0 for every \elem{v} — and \inner{S\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} is exactly 
orm{T\elem{v}}^2 - 
orm{T^{*}\elem{v}}^2. So (a) and (b) are the same statement read at two different levels of resolution. Condition (c) is (b) with the two slots unglued, and it costs nothing in one direction and a specialization in the other. Condition (d) is the operator version of writing a complex number as a + bi; that decomposition appeared in @exr-adjoints-c2 (c), and multiplying out TT^{*} - T^{*}T in terms of A and B leaves only the commutator. (a) \Rightarrow (c). For all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V, by @def-adjoint and T^{**} = T (@thm-adjoint-properties (d)), \inner{T\elem{u}}{T\elem{v}} = \inner{T^{*}T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}}, \qquad \inner{T^{*}\elem{u}}{T^{*}\elem{v}} = \inner{TT^{*}\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} . Since T^{*}T = TT^{*}, the two right-hand sides agree. (b) \Rightarrow (b). Take \elem{u} = \elem{v}. Then 
orm{T\elem{v}}^2 = 
orm{T^{*}\elem{v}}^2, and both norms are nonnegative reals, so they are equal. (c) \Rightarrow (a). Put S = T^{*}T - TT^{*}. Then S is self-adjoint: by @thm-adjoint-properties (a), (c), and (d), S^{*} = (T^{*}T)^{*} - (TT^{*})^{*} = T^{*}T^{**} - T^{**}T^{*} = T^{*}T - TT^{*} = S . For any \elem{v} \in V, using @def-adjoint twice,  egin{aligned} \inner{S\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} &= \inner{T^{*}T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} - \inner{TT^{*}\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} \ &= \inner{T\elem{v}}{T\elem{v}} - \inner{T^{*}\elem{v}}{T^{*}\elem{v}} \ &= 
orm{T\elem{v}}^2 - 
orm{T^{*}\elem{v}}^2 = 0 \end{aligned} by (b). Since S is self-adjoint, @thm-self-adjoint-zero-test gives S = 0, that is T^{*}T = TT^{*}. Now let F = 
C. By @thm-adjoint-properties (a), (b), and (d),  egin{aligned} A^{*} &= 	frac12(T^{*} + T) = A, \ B^{*} &= \conj{\Bigl(	frac1{2i}\Bigr)}(T^{*} - T) = 	frac1{2i}(T - T^{*}) = B, \end{aligned} so both are self-adjoint, and A + iB = 	frac12(T + T^{*}) + 	frac12(T - T^{*}) = T; this is the decomposition of @exr-adjoints-c2 (c). Expanding T = A + iB and T^{*} = A - iB,  egin{aligned} TT^{*} &= (A + iB)(A - iB) = A^2 + B^2 + i(BA - AB), \ T^{*}T &= (A - iB)(A + iB) = A^2 + B^2 + i(AB - BA) . \end{aligned} Subtracting, TT^{*} - T^{*}T = 2i(BA - AB). So T is normal exactly when AB = BA, which is (a) \Leftrightarrow (d). This proves the theorem. Condition (b) is the one to remember. It says that T and T^{*} stretch every single vector by the same amount, even though they need not move it in the same direction. Everything in the next three sections is squeezed out of that sentence. Condition (d) records that normality over 
C is the operator analogue of the fact that any two real numbers commute: split T into a “real part” and an “imaginary part”, and normality is precisely the failure of those two parts to interfere. The symmetric matrix  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and the skew-symmetric matrix  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} are both normal, the first being self-adjoint and the second skew-adjoint. Is their sum normal? No. The sum is  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = 2\J_2(0), which is twice the standard nonnormal example: it kills \cvec{e}_1 and sends \cvec{e}_2 to a vector of length 2, while its transpose does the opposite, so condition (b) fails at \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_1. The normal operators do not form a subspace of \cL(V), and they are not closed under composition either. What normality buys Four consequences, all short, all obtained by turning some statement about T into the same statement about T^{*}. [Kernel, Image, and an Orthogonal Splitting] Let T \in \cL(V) be normal on a finite-dimensional inner product space V. Then: 1. \ker T = \ker T^{*}; 2. \im T = \im T^{*}; 3. V = \ker T \oplus \im T, and the two summands are orthogonal to each other. (a) For \elem{v} \in V, @thm-normal-characterizations (b) gives 
orm{T\elem{v}} = 
orm{T^{*}\elem{v}}. So T\elem{v} = \elem{0} if and only if 
orm{T\elem{v}} = 0, if and only if 
orm{T^{*}\elem{v}} = 0, if and only if T^{*}\elem{v} = \elem{0}. (b) By @thm-four-subspaces-orthogonal (b) applied to T^{*} in place of T, and using T^{**} = T (@thm-adjoint-properties (d)), \im T = \im T^{**} = (\ker T^{*})^{\perp} = (\ker T)^{\perp} = \im T^{*}, where the third equality is (a) and the fourth is @thm-four-subspaces-orthogonal (b) for T. (c) By (b), \im T = (\ker T)^{\perp}, and V = \ker T \oplus (\ker T)^{\perp} by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (a). Orthogonality of the summands is the definition of the orthogonal complement. Part (c) fails badly without normality, and the failure is not subtle: for a general operator \ker T and \im T can be equal. Take T with matrix \J_2(0) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} on 
C^2. Then T\cvec{e}_1 = \cvec{0} and T\cvec{e}_2 = \cvec{e}_1, so \ker T = \Span(\cvec{e}_1) = \im T . The sum \ker T + \im T is one-dimensional, so it is neither direct nor all of 
C^2. Normality is exactly what rules this out. [An Eigenvector of a Normal Operator Is an Eigenvector of Its Adjoint] Let T \in \cL(V) be normal, let \lambda \in F, and let \elem{v} \in V. Then T\elem{v} = \lambda\elem{v} \quad 	ext{if and only if} \quad T^{*}\elem{v} = \conj{\lambda}\,\elem{v} . In particular E_{\lambda}(T) = E_{\conj{\lambda}}(T^{*}), and \lambda \in \spec(T) if and only if \conj{\lambda} \in \spec(T^{*}). Both sides say that \elem{v} lies in a kernel: the left in \ker(T - \lambda\,\id_V), the right in \ker(T^{*} - \conj{\lambda}\,\id_V). Those two operators are adjoint to each other, so @cor-normal-kernel (a) closes the gap — provided T - \lambda\,\id_V is itself normal, which is the only thing to check. Write S = T - \lambda\,\id_V. By @thm-adjoint-properties (a), (b), and (d), S^{*} = T^{*} - \conj{\lambda}\,\id_V. Since T^{*}T = TT^{*} and \id_V commutes with everything,  egin{aligned} S^{*}S &= T^{*}T - \conj{\lambda}T - \lambda T^{*} + \lvert\lambdavert^2\,\id_V \ &= TT^{*} - \lambda T^{*} - \conj{\lambda}T + \lvert\lambdavert^2\,\id_V = SS^{*} , \end{aligned} so S is normal. By @cor-normal-kernel (a), \ker S = \ker S^{*}. Now T\elem{v} = \lambda\elem{v} says \elem{v} \in \ker S, and T^{*}\elem{v} = \conj{\lambda}\elem{v} says \elem{v} \in \ker S^{*}, so the two conditions agree. The statement about eigenspaces is the equality \ker S = \ker S^{*} rewritten, and the statement about spectra follows because an eigenspace is nonzero exactly when the scalar is an eigenvalue (@thm-eigenvalue-characterizations). The theorem is the reason normal operators are so easy to handle: T and T^{*} have the same eigenvectors, with conjugate eigenvalues. The proof of the next corollary is the classical self-adjoint argument (@thm-self-adjoint-orthogonal-eigenspaces) with one conjugate bar inserted, and that bar is exactly what @thm-normal-eigenvector-shared supplies. [Eigenvectors for Distinct Eigenvalues Are Orthogonal] Let T \in \cL(V) be normal, let \lambda 
eq \mu be eigenvalues of T, and let T\elem{u} = \lambda\elem{u} and T\elem{v} = \mu\elem{v}. Then \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = 0. Hence E_{\lambda}(T) \perp E_{\mu}(T) whenever \lambda 
eq \mu. Compute \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} in two ways. First, \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\lambda\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \lambda\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}}. Second, by @def-adjoint and then @thm-normal-eigenvector-shared applied to \elem{v}, \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{T^{*}\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{\conj{\mu}\,\elem{v}} = \mu\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}}, the last step because a scalar leaves the second slot conjugated. Subtracting, (\lambda - \mu)\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = 0, and \lambda - \mu 
eq 0, so \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = 0. Every vector of E_{\lambda}(T) is orthogonal to every vector of E_{\mu}(T) by the same computation. [A Normal Operator Has No Hidden Kernel] Let T \in \cL(V) be normal. Then \ker T^{k} = \ker T for every integer k \ge 1. In particular, if T^{k} = 0 for some k \ge 1 — that is, if T is nilpotent (@def-nilpotent) — then T = 0. The inclusion \ker T \subseteq \ker T^2 is free, and the whole content is the reverse one. If T^2\elem{v} = \elem{0}, then the vector \elem{w} = T\elem{v} lies in \ker T, hence also in \ker T^{*} by @cor-normal-kernel; and a vector that is killed by T^{*} and is itself in the image of T must be \elem{0}, because pairing it with itself moves T across the inner product and hits the T^{*}. First take k = 2. The inclusion \ker T \subseteq \ker T^2 holds for every operator. Conversely, suppose T^2\elem{v} = \elem{0} and put \elem{w} = T\elem{v}. Then T\elem{w} = \elem{0}, so T^{*}\elem{w} = \elem{0} by @cor-normal-kernel (a). Therefore, by @def-adjoint,  egin{aligned} 
orm{\elem{w}}^2 &= \inner{\elem{w}}{\elem{w}} = \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} \ &= \inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}\elem{w}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{0}} = 0 , \end{aligned} so \elem{w} = T\elem{v} = \elem{0} and \elem{v} \in \ker T. Hence \ker T^2 = \ker T. Now induct on k. The cases k = 1, 2 are done. Let k \ge 2 and assume \ker T^{k} = \ker T. If T^{k+1}\elem{v} = \elem{0}, then T^{2} igl(T^{k-1}\elem{v} igr) = \elem{0}, so T^{k}\elem{v} = T igl(T^{k-1}\elem{v} igr) = \elem{0} by the case k = 2, and then T\elem{v} = \elem{0} by the inductive hypothesis. So \ker T^{k+1} \subseteq \ker T, and the reverse inclusion is again free. Finally, if T^{k} = 0 for some k \ge 1, then \ker T = \ker T^{k} = V, so T = 0. This is the sentence that explains why normal operators never produce Jordan blocks. Over 
C, a Jordan block of size m \ge 2 for the eigenvalue \lambda contributes a vector killed by (T - \lambda\,\id_V)^{m} but not by T - \lambda\,\id_V (@def-jordan-chain). For a normal T the operator T - \lambda\,\id_V is normal, as the proof of @thm-normal-eigenvector-shared showed, so @thm-normal-powers forbids such a vector. Every block in the Jordan form of a normal operator therefore has size 1, and a normal operator on a complex space is diagonalizable (@thm-jordan-canonical-form, @def-diagonalizable). That is diagonalizable, not yet orthogonally diagonalizable. The eigenspaces of distinct eigenvalues are already mutually orthogonal by @cor-normal-orthogonal-eigenspaces, so all that is missing is an orthonormal basis inside each eigenspace, which Gram–Schmidt supplies (@thm-gram-schmidt). Section 4 proves the whole statement in one stroke instead, from Schur’s theorem, because that proof also delivers the converse and works without Chapter 10. Two converses are worth flagging now, so that you know they are coming and do not try to prove them here. A normal operator whose eigenvalues are all real is self-adjoint, and a normal operator whose eigenvalues all have modulus 1 is unitary. Both are false without normality, and neither can be reached with the tools of this section: they need an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, which is the business of Section 4. Before the warning, one structural fact deserves to be stated where later sections can lean on it. It is the reason a normal operator can be taken apart orthogonally at all. [An Invariant Subspace of a Normal Operator Is Reducing] Let T \in \cL(V) be normal on a finite-dimensional inner product space, and let U \subseteq V be T-invariant. Then U is T^{*}-invariant, U^{\perp} is T-invariant, and T|_U is a normal operator on U. Write the matrix in an orthonormal basis adapted to U. Invariance kills the block below the diagonal, and normality, read on the top-left block alone, kills the block above it. The trace is what converts “these two blocks agree” into “that block is zero”. Choose an orthonormal basis \sB_U = (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_r) of U and extend it to an orthonormal basis \sB of V (@cor-extend-orthonormal-basis). Since T\elem{e}_j \in U for j \le r, the first r columns of \A = \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} have zeros below row r, so \A =  egin{pmatrix} \B & \C \ \O & \D \end{pmatrix}, with \B of size r 	imes r. Because \sB is orthonormal, \mtx{T^{*}}{\sB}{\sB} = \A^{*} (@thm-matrix-of-adjoint), and T normal means \A^{*}\A = \A\A^{*}. Comparing the (1,1) blocks (@thm-block-multiplication), (\A^{*}\A)_{11} = \B^{*}\B, \qquad (\A\A^{*})_{11} = \B\B^{*} + \C\C^{*} . Taking traces and using 	r(\B^{*}\B) = 	r(\B\B^{*}) (@thm-trace-properties (3)) gives 	r(\C\C^{*}) = 0. But 	r(\C\C^{*}) = \sum_{i,j}\lvert c_{ij}vert^2, a sum of nonnegative reals, so \C = \O. Hence \A = \B \oplus \D. Reading the last n - r columns, T\elem{e}_j \in U^{\perp} for j > r, so U^{\perp} is T-invariant; reading the first r columns of \A^{*}, U is T^{*}-invariant. Finally \mtx{T|_U}{\sB_U}{\sB_U} = \B and the (1,1) blocks above now read \B^{*}\B = \B\B^{*}, so T|_U is normal. This shows all three claims. Normality cannot be read off a corner. A principal submatrix of a normal matrix need not be normal. The 3 	imes 3 cyclic shift \S =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is a permutation matrix, hence orthogonal (@exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-b3), hence normal; but deleting its last row and column leaves  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, the transpose of \J_2(0), which is not normal. Equivalently: the operator that \S compresses to \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) is not normal, because that subspace is not \S-invariant. What is true is that an invariant subspace of a normal operator is automatically invariant under the adjoint too, and the restriction there is normal; that is @prp-normal-invariant-reducing, proved just above. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the definition of a normal operator, and state one equivalent condition phrased in terms of norms. 2. True or false: every self-adjoint operator is normal, and every normal operator is self-adjoint. Justify both halves. 3. Let T be normal with T\elem{v} = 3\elem{v}. What is T^{*}\elem{v}? What if T\elem{v} = 3i\elem{v}? 4. Give a normal operator on 
R^2 that is neither self-adjoint nor unitary. 5. True or false: if S and T are normal then S + T is normal. Justify your answer. 6. Explain in one sentence why a normal operator cannot be nilpotent unless it is zero. (a) T is normal when T^{*}T = TT^{*} (@def-normal-operator). Equivalently, 
orm{T\elem{v}} = 
orm{T^{*}\elem{v}} for every \elem{v} \in V (@thm-normal-characterizations (b)). (b) The first half is true: if T^{*} = T then both products are T^2. The second half is false: \diag(1, i) on 
C^2 is normal and has a nonreal eigenvalue, so it is not self-adjoint (@thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues). (c) T^{*}\elem{v} = 3\elem{v} in the first case and T^{*}\elem{v} = -3i\elem{v} in the second, by @thm-normal-eigenvector-shared: the adjoint has the conjugate eigenvalue on the same eigenvector. (d)  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} works (@exm-normal-catalog (e)): it is not symmetric, and \M	p\M = 5\I 
eq \I. Any \vLambda(\lambda) with \lvert\lambdavert 
eq 1 and \operatorname{Im}\lambda 
eq 0 does. (e) False.  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} +  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is a sum of two normal matrices and is not normal. (f) If T^{k} = 0 then \ker T = \ker T^{k} = V by @thm-normal-powers, so T = 0. B. Practice [B1: Determine which are normal] Determine which of the following matrices are normal, with the standard inner product. Justify your answer; for those that are not, exhibit a vector \cvec{v} with 
orm{\A\cvec{v}} 
eq 
orm{\A^{*}\cvec{v}}. 1.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} over 
R. 2.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} over 
R. 3.  egin{pmatrix} 0 & i \ i & 0 \end{pmatrix} over 
C. 4.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} over 
R. 5.  egin{pmatrix} i & 1 \ 0 & i \end{pmatrix} over 
C. (a) Normal: the matrix is symmetric, so it is self-adjoint over 
R, and self-adjoint implies normal. (b) Not normal. \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} and \A\A	p =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. With \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_1, 
orm{\A\cvec{e}_1} = 
orm{(1,0)} = 1 while 
orm{\A	p\cvec{e}_1} = 
orm{(1,1)} = \sqrt2. (c) Normal. \A^{*} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \ -i & 0 \end{pmatrix} = -\A, so \A is skew-adjoint and \A^{*}\A = -\A^2 = \A\A^{*}. (Concretely both products are \I.) (d) Normal: the matrix is (1) \oplus \vLambda(i), a direct sum of a 1 	imes 1 block and a rotation by a quarter turn, and its columns are orthonormal, so it is orthogonal (@thm-isometry-characterizations (f)). (e) Not normal. \A^{*}\A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -i \ i & 2 \end{pmatrix} and \A\A^{*} =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -i \ i & 1 \end{pmatrix}; with \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_1 we get 
orm{\A\cvec{e}_1} = \lvert ivert = 1 and 
orm{\A^{*}\cvec{e}_1} = 
orm{(-i, 1)} = \sqrt2. Adding i\I to a nonnormal matrix does not repair it: \A = i\I + \J_2(0) and i\I is normal, but sums of normal matrices need not be normal. [B2: The splitting of a singular normal operator] Let \C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & -1 \ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(
R), and let T = T_{\C} be the operator it defines on 
R^3. 1. Verify that T is normal. 2. Compute \ker T and \ker T^{*} and check that they agree. 3. Compute \im T, and verify directly that 
R^3 = \ker T \oplus \im T with the two summands orthogonal, as @cor-normal-kernel (c) predicts. (a) Each row of \C is the previous one shifted cyclically, so \C is a circulant. Explicitly, \C	p\C = \C\C	p =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & -1 \ -1 & 2 & -1 \ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, so T is normal. (b) \C\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} reads x_1 = x_2 = x_3, because the first two rows give x_1 = x_2 and x_2 = x_3. So \ker T = \Span igl((1,1,1) igr). The transpose \C	p has rows (1, 0, -1), (-1, 1, 0), (0, -1, 1), and \C	p\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} again reads x_1 = x_3 and x_1 = x_2. The two kernels agree, as @cor-normal-kernel (a) requires. (c) The rank is 3 - 1 = 2 by @thm-rank-nullity, and the first two columns (1, 0, -1) and (-1, 1, 0) are independent, so \im T = \Span igl((1,0,-1),\ (-1,1,0) igr) . Both spanning vectors have coordinate sum 0, hence are orthogonal to (1,1,1), so \im T \perp \ker T. Since \dim\ker T + \dim\im T = 1 + 2 = 3 and the two subspaces meet only in \cvec{0} (being orthogonal), 
R^3 = \ker T \oplus \im T. Indeed \im T = \{\cvec{x} : x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0\} = (\ker T)^{\perp}. [B3: Triangular and normal, by hand] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ 0 & d \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
C). 1. Compute the (1,1) entries of \A^{*}\A and of \A\A^{*}. 2. Hence prove that \A is normal if and only if b = 0, that is, if and only if \A is diagonal. 3. Which upper triangular matrices in M_2(
C) are unitary? Hint: for (a), you only need one entry of each product. (a) The (1,1) entry of \A^{*}\A is the squared norm of the first column of \A, namely \lvert avert^2. The (1,1) entry of \A\A^{*} is the squared norm of the first row, namely \lvert avert^2 + \lvert bvert^2. In full,  egin{aligned} \A^{*}\A &=  egin{pmatrix} \lvert avert^2 & \conj{a}b \ a\conj{b} & \lvert bvert^2 + \lvert dvert^2 \end{pmatrix}, \[4pt] \A\A^{*} &=  egin{pmatrix} \lvert avert^2 + \lvert bvert^2 & b\conj{d} \ \conj{b}d & \lvert dvert^2 \end{pmatrix} . \end{aligned} (b) (\Rightarrow) If \A is normal, comparing the (1,1) entries gives \lvert avert^2 = \lvert avert^2 + \lvert bvert^2, so \lvert bvert^2 = 0 and b = 0. (\Leftarrow) A diagonal matrix is normal, since \D^{*}\D = \D\D^{*} = \diag(\lvert avert^2, \lvert dvert^2). (c) A unitary matrix is normal, so by (b) it must be diagonal, \diag(a, d), and then \A^{*}\A = \diag(\lvert avert^2, \lvert dvert^2) = \I forces \lvert avert = \lvert dvert = 1. Conversely every such matrix is unitary. So the upper triangular unitary matrices are exactly \diag(a, d) with \lvert avert = \lvert dvert = 1. C. Going deeper [C1: A normal operator with no proper invariant subspace] Let V be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space with V 
eq \{\elem{0}\}, and let T \in \cL(V) be normal. Suppose the only T-invariant subspaces of V are \{\elem{0}\} and V. 1. Show that \dim V = 1. 2. Show that the conclusion fails over 
R, by exhibiting a normal operator on 
R^2 whose only invariant subspaces are \{\cvec{0}\} and 
R^2. 3. Where exactly does the argument of (a) use that the field is 
C? Hint: an eigenvector spans an invariant subspace. (a) Since V 
eq \{\elem{0}\} and the field is 
C, T has an eigenvector \elem{v} 
e \elem{0} (@thm-complex-operator-has-eigenvalue). Then \Span(\elem{v}) is T-invariant and nonzero, so by hypothesis \Span(\elem{v}) = V and \dim V = 1. Normality is not needed for this direction. (b) The quarter turn \R_{\pi/2} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} is orthogonal, hence normal. A 1-dimensional invariant subspace would be spanned by a real eigenvector, and \R_{\pi/2} has none: its characteristic polynomial is x^2 + 1, with no real root. So its only invariant subspaces are \{\cvec{0}\} and 
R^2, while \dim 
R^2 = 2. (c) Only in the existence of an eigenvector. Over 
C that is the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (@thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra) reaching the characteristic polynomial; over 
R the polynomial may have no root, which is exactly what (b) exploits. Note that @prp-normal-invariant-reducing still holds over 
R — it says nothing about invariant subspaces existing. [C2: Arithmetic of normal operators] Let S, T \in \cL(V) be normal. 1. Prove that T^{*} is normal and that cT is normal for every c \in F. 2. Prove that p(T) is normal for every polynomial p \in F[x]. 3. Give a concrete S and T, both normal, with ST not normal. (Part (b) shows that this cannot happen when S is a polynomial in T.) (a) (T^{*})^{*}T^{*} = TT^{*} = T^{*}T = T^{*}(T^{*})^{*}, using T^{**} = T (@thm-adjoint-properties (d)). For cT, by @thm-adjoint-properties (b) we have (cT)^{*} = \conj{c}T^{*}, so (cT)^{*}(cT) = \conj{c}c\,T^{*}T = \lvert cvert^2\,TT^{*} = (cT)(cT)^{*} . (b) Write p(x) = \sum_{k} a_kx^{k}. Then p(T)^{*} = \sum_k \conj{a_k}(T^{*})^{k} by @thm-adjoint-properties (a), (b), and (c). Every power of T commutes with every power of T^{*}: from TT^{*} = T^{*}T one moves a T^{*} past one T at a time. Hence p(T) and p(T)^{*}, being sums of products of such powers, commute, and p(T) is normal. (c) Take S =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} and T =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, both symmetric and hence normal. Then  egin{aligned} ST &=  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \[4pt] (ST)	p(ST) &=  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad (ST)(ST)	p =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, \end{aligned} so ST is not normal. [C3: Normality depends on the inner product] Normality is a property of T together with an inner product, not of T alone. Work on V = 
R^2 with the operator T whose standard matrix is \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. 1. Verify that T is normal for the standard inner product. 2. Now use \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}}_{\G} = \cvec{y}	p\G\cvec{x} with \G = \diag(1, 2), which is an inner product on 
R^2. Using the rule \mtx{T^{*}}{\sE}{\sE} = \G^{-1}\A	p\G in the standard basis \sE (@exr-adjoints-c3), compute the matrix of the adjoint of T for this inner product. 3. Show that T is not normal for \inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\G}, and reconcile this with (a). (a) \A	p\A = \A\A	p = \I, so T is even orthogonal, hence normal. (b) \G^{-1} = \diag(1, 	frac12), so  egin{aligned} \G^{-1}\A	p\G &=  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 	frac12 \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \[4pt] &=  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ -	frac12 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . \end{aligned} Call this matrix \A^{\star}. (c) Computing both products, \A\A^{\star} =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac12 & 0 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A^{\star}\A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & 	frac12 \end{pmatrix}, which differ, so T is not normal for \inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\G}. There is no contradiction: the adjoint is built from the inner product (@def-adjoint), so changing the inner product changes T^{*}, and with it the equation T^{*}T = TT^{*}. The standard basis is orthonormal for the first inner product and not for the second, which is exactly the hypothesis @thm-matrix-of-adjoint needs.

title: 12.4 The Complex Spectral Theorem
content:
The Complex Spectral Theorem Two things are now on the table. Section 1 put every complex operator into upper triangular form in an orthonormal basis, and Section 3 identified the operators that commute with their adjoints. Put them together and the chapter’s main theorem falls out in a few lines: a triangular matrix that is normal has nothing above the diagonal. This section proves that, reads off the consequences, and says exactly how much of the resulting picture is unique. The field is 
C throughout this section, and every inner product space is finite-dimensional. The reason for insisting on 
C is Schur’s theorem, and behind it the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (@thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra): over 
R an operator can fail to have a single eigenvector, and Section 5 shows what has to change. Triangular plus normal forces diagonal Start with the smallest case, where the mechanism is visible at a glance. Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ 0 & d \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
C) be upper triangular. The (1,1) entry of \A^{*}\A is the squared length of the first column of \A, and the (1,1) entry of \A\A^{*} is the squared length of the first row: (\A^{*}\A)_{11} = \lvert avert^2, \qquad (\A\A^{*})_{11} = \lvert avert^2 + \lvert bvert^2 . If \A is normal these are equal, so \lvert bvert^2 = 0 and b = 0. One entry of one product did all the work. (This is @exr-normal-operators-b3, which you may already have done.) The general case is the same comparison run down the diagonal, one row at a time. Nothing is clever; the only care needed is to use, at step j, the zeros that steps 1, \dots, j-1 have already produced. [A Normal Triangular Matrix Is Diagonal] Let \T = (t_{ij}) \in M_n(
C) be upper triangular and normal. Then \T is diagonal. For any square matrix, the j-th diagonal entry of \T^{*}\T is the squared length of column j, and the j-th diagonal entry of \T\T^{*} is the squared length of row j. Normality says those two lengths agree for every j. For an upper triangular matrix, column j reaches only down to the diagonal and row j only rightwards from it, so the equation compares “what sits above t_{jj}” with “what sits to the right of t_{jj}”. Row 1 has nothing above it, so the right side must be empty too; that clears row 1, which empties the column sums one step further down, and the argument walks down the diagonal. For each j, computing the (j, j) entries of the two products entry by entry, (\T^{*}\T)_{jj} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \conj{t_{ij}}\,t_{ij} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert t_{ij}vert^2, \qquad (\T\T^{*})_{jj} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \lvert t_{jk}vert^2 . Since \T is upper triangular, t_{ij} = 0 whenever i > j, and t_{jk} = 0 whenever k < j. So normality of \T says \sum_{i \le j} \lvert t_{ij}vert^2 = \sum_{k \ge j} \lvert t_{jk}vert^2 \qquad (j = 1, \dots, n). {#eq-normal-row-column} We prove by induction on j that t_{jk} = 0 for every k > j. Base case j = 1. The left-hand side of @eq-normal-row-column has the single term \lvert t_{11}vert^2, so \lvert t_{11}vert^2 = \lvert t_{11}vert^2 + \sum_{k > 1} \lvert t_{1k}vert^2 . Hence \sum_{k>1}\lvert t_{1k}vert^2 = 0, a sum of nonnegative reals, so t_{1k} = 0 for every k > 1. Inductive step. Let 1 < j \le n and suppose t_{mk} = 0 whenever m < j and k > m. In the left-hand side of @eq-normal-row-column, every term with i < j is \lvert t_{ij}vert^2 with i < j, hence with j > i; by the inductive hypothesis, taking m = i and k = j, each such t_{ij} is 0. So the left-hand side reduces to \lvert t_{jj}vert^2 and @eq-normal-row-column becomes \lvert t_{jj}vert^2 = \lvert t_{jj}vert^2 + \sum_{k > j} \lvert t_{jk}vert^2 , whence t_{jk} = 0 for every k > j, again because a sum of nonnegative reals vanishes only when every term does. By induction, every entry strictly above the diagonal is zero. Every entry strictly below it is zero because \T is upper triangular. So \T is diagonal, as claimed. Note what the proof did not need: no eigenvector was chosen, no dimension was inducted on, no subspace was split off. The whole argument is an identity between two lists of nonnegative numbers. That is why it also survives, unchanged in spirit, into the block version used in Section 5 and the quantitative version in Section 11. The theorem [Complex Spectral Theorem] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over 
C and let T \in \cL(V). The following are equivalent. 1. T is normal. 2. V has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of T. (\Leftarrow) is a one-line check: in such a basis the matrix of T is diagonal, the matrix of T^{*} is its conjugate transpose, and two diagonal matrices commute. (\Rightarrow) is Schur plus the lemma: take an orthonormal basis making the matrix triangular, observe that normality of T is normality of that matrix because the basis is orthonormal, and apply @lem-triangular-normal-diagonal. A diagonal matrix in the basis \sB says precisely that each vector of \sB is an eigenvector. (\Leftarrow) Suppose \sB = (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n) is an orthonormal basis with T\elem{e}_j = \lambda_j\elem{e}_j for each j. Then \D \coloneqq \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n), and since \sB is orthonormal, \mtx{T^{*}}{\sB}{\sB} = \D^{*} = \diag(\conj{\lambda_1}, \dots, \conj{\lambda_n}) by @thm-matrix-of-adjoint. Both products are the same diagonal matrix: \D^{*}\D = \D\D^{*} = \diag igl(\lvert\lambda_1vert^2, \dots, \lvert\lambda_nvert^2 igr) . Taking the matrix of an operator in a fixed basis turns composition into matrix multiplication and is injective (@thm-matrix-of-composition, @thm-linear-maps-isomorphic-to-matrices), so T^{*}T = TT^{*}. (\Rightarrow) Suppose T is normal. By Schur’s theorem (@thm-schur-triangularization) there is an orthonormal basis \sB = (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n) of V in which \T \coloneqq \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} is upper triangular. Because \sB is orthonormal, @thm-matrix-of-adjoint gives \mtx{T^{*}}{\sB}{\sB} = \T^{*}, so the equation T^{*}T = TT^{*} reads \T^{*}\T = \T\T^{*}: the matrix \T is normal. By @lem-triangular-normal-diagonal, \T is diagonal, say \T = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n). Reading off the j-th column (@def-matrix-of-linear-map), T\elem{e}_j = \lambda_j\elem{e}_j, and \elem{e}_j 
eq \elem{0} because 
orm{\elem{e}_j} = 1. So \sB is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of T. This proves the theorem. [Unitary Diagonalization] Let \A \in M_n(
C). Then \A is normal if and only if there exist a unitary \U \in \Unit(n) and a diagonal \D \in M_n(
C) with \A = \U\D\U^{*} . A matrix admitting such a factorization is called unitarily diagonalizable. The diagonal of \D is the list of eigenvalues of \A with multiplicity, in an order that may be prescribed in advance, and the columns of \U are a corresponding orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Apply @thm-spectral-complex to the operator T_{\A} on 
C^n with its standard inner product, for which the standard basis is orthonormal. (\Rightarrow) Let (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_n) be an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, \A\cvec{u}_j = \lambda_j\cvec{u}_j, and let \U be the matrix with these columns; it is unitary because its columns are orthonormal (@thm-isometry-characterizations (f)). Then \A\U has j-th column \lambda_j\cvec{u}_j, which is the j-th column of \U\D for \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n). So \A\U = \U\D and \A = \U\D\U^{-1} = \U\D\U^{*}. (\Leftarrow) If \A = \U\D\U^{*} then \A^{*} = \U\D^{*}\U^{*}, and \A^{*}\A = \U\D^{*}\D\U^{*} = \U\D\D^{*}\U^{*} = \A\A^{*}, using \U^{*}\U = \I twice and the fact that diagonal matrices commute. Finally, \A is similar to \D, so they have the same characteristic polynomial (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant), and the roots of \det(x\I - \D) = \prod_j (x - \lambda_j) are the diagonal entries with multiplicity. Reordering the eigenvectors reorders the columns of \U and the diagonal of \D in the same way, so any order may be prescribed. [Unitarily diagonalizing a Hermitian matrix] Find a unitary \U and a diagonal \D with \U^{*}\A\U = \D, for \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 - i \ 1 + i & 3 \end{pmatrix} . \A^{*} = \A, so \A is Hermitian, hence normal, and @cor-spectral-complex-matrix applies. Its characteristic polynomial is  egin{aligned} x^2 - (	r \A)x + \det \A &= x^2 - 5x +  igl(6 - (1-i)(1+i) igr) \ &= x^2 - 5x + 4, \end{aligned} since (1-i)(1+i) = 1 - i^2 = 2. So the eigenvalues are 4 and 1, both real as @thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues promises. For \lambda = 4, the first row of \A - 4\I =  egin{pmatrix} -2 & 1-i \ 1+i & -1 \end{pmatrix} gives -2z_1 + (1-i)z_2 = 0; taking z_2 = 2 gives \cvec{u} = (1 - i,\, 2), with 
orm{\cvec{u}}^2 = 2 + 4 = 6. For \lambda = 1, the first row of \A - \I =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1-i \ 1+i & 2 \end{pmatrix} gives z_1 = -(1-i)z_2; taking z_2 = 1 gives \cvec{w} = (-1 + i,\, 1), with 
orm{\cvec{w}}^2 = 2 + 1 = 3. The two are orthogonal, as @cor-normal-orthogonal-eigenspaces predicts:  egin{aligned} \inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}} &= (1-i)\conj{(-1+i)} + 2 \cdot \conj{1} \ &= (1-i)(-1-i) + 2 = -2 + 2 = 0 . \end{aligned} Normalizing and using them as columns, \U =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac{1-i}{\sqrt6} & 	frac{-1+i}{\sqrt3} \[2pt] 	frac{2}{\sqrt6} & 	frac{1}{\sqrt3} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \D =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, and \U^{*}\U = \I, \U^{*}\A\U = \D. As a check on the arithmetic, 	r \D = 5 = 	r \A and \det \D = 4 = \det \A. Reading the class off the spectrum Once the eigenvalues sit on a diagonal, every question about T that is invariant under a unitary change of basis becomes a question about a list of complex numbers. Here are three answers. [The Spectrum Decides] Let T \in \cL(V) be normal on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space. 1. T is self-adjoint if and only if every eigenvalue of T is real. 2. T is unitary if and only if every eigenvalue of T has modulus 1. 3. \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} is a nonnegative real number for every \elem{v} \in V if and only if every eigenvalue of T is a nonnegative real. By @thm-spectral-complex there is an orthonormal basis (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n) with T\elem{e}_j = \lambda_j\elem{e}_j, and then T^{*}\elem{e}_j = \conj{\lambda_j}\elem{e}_j by @thm-normal-eigenvector-shared. Two operators that agree on a basis are equal, so each of the three conditions can be tested one basis vector at a time, where it becomes a statement about the single number \lambda_j. Fix an orthonormal basis (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n) of eigenvectors, T\elem{e}_j = \lambda_j\elem{e}_j (@thm-spectral-complex), and recall T^{*}\elem{e}_j = \conj{\lambda_j}\elem{e}_j (@thm-normal-eigenvector-shared). Every eigenvalue of T occurs among \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, because \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n) is the matrix of T and its characteristic polynomial is \prod_j (x - \lambda_j). (a) T = T^{*} holds if and only if T\elem{e}_j = T^{*}\elem{e}_j for every j (@thm-linear-transform-basis), that is \lambda_j\elem{e}_j = \conj{\lambda_j}\elem{e}_j, that is \lambda_j = \conj{\lambda_j} since \elem{e}_j 
eq \elem{0}. A complex number equals its conjugate exactly when it is real. (b) T^{*}T\elem{e}_j = T^{*}(\lambda_j\elem{e}_j) = \lambda_j\conj{\lambda_j}\elem{e}_j = \lvert\lambda_jvert^2\elem{e}_j, so T^{*}T = \id_V if and only if \lvert\lambda_jvert^2 = 1 for every j. That is what it means for T to be unitary (@def-unitary-orthogonal): the equation T^{*}T = \id_V makes T injective, hence invertible on a finite-dimensional space (@thm-invertible-operator-tfae), with T^{-1} = T^{*} and therefore TT^{*} = \id_V as well. (c) Write \elem{v} = \sum_j c_j\elem{e}_j. Expanding both slots and using \inner{\elem{e}_j}{\elem{e}_i} = \delta_{ij}, \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \Bigl\langle \sum_j c_j\lambda_j\elem{e}_j, \sum_i c_i\elem{e}_i \Bigrangle = \sum_j \lambda_j\lvert c_jvert^2 . (\Leftarrow) If every \lambda_j is a nonnegative real, this is a sum of nonnegative reals. (\Rightarrow) Taking \elem{v} = \elem{e}_j gives \inner{T\elem{e}_j}{\elem{e}_j} = \lambda_j, which is then a nonnegative real by hypothesis. Part (c) names a class that Chapter 13 takes as its subject: the positive operators. Over 
C the hypothesis of normality is not really needed in (c), because \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} real for every \elem{v} already forces T = T^{*}: apply @thm-complex-zero-test to the operator T - T^{*}, for which \inner{(T - T^{*})\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} - \conj{\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}} = 0. Over 
R that shortcut is unavailable, and Section 5 shows the quarter turn defeating it. The next corollary is a small shock. The adjoint is defined through the inner product and has nothing to do with polynomials. For a normal operator it is one anyway. [The Adjoint of a Normal Operator Is a Polynomial in It] Let T \in \cL(V) be normal on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, with distinct eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k. Then there is a polynomial p \in 
C[x] of degree less than k with T^{*} = p(T). The scalars \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k are distinct, so by Lagrange interpolation (@thm-lagrange-interpolation) there is a polynomial p \in 
C[x] of degree less than k with p(\lambda_i) = \conj{\lambda_i} \qquad (i = 1, \dots, k) . Let (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n) be an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors (@thm-spectral-complex), with T\elem{e}_j = \mu_j\elem{e}_j where each \mu_j is one of the \lambda_i. Then p(T)\elem{e}_j = p(\mu_j)\elem{e}_j = \conj{\mu_j}\elem{e}_j = T^{*}\elem{e}_j, the first equality because T^{i}\elem{e}_j = \mu_j^{i}\elem{e}_j for every i \ge 0, by induction from T\elem{e}_j = \mu_j\elem{e}_j, and the last by @thm-normal-eigenvector-shared. The operators p(T) and T^{*} agree on a basis, hence are equal (@thm-linear-transform-basis). One consequence is worth stating on its own. Any operator S that commutes with T also commutes with every polynomial in T, hence with T^{*}. So for normal operators the apparently stronger requirement “commutes with T and with T^{*}” is no requirement at all, and Section 7 will use this to diagonalize whole commuting families at once. The polynomial depends on T and not only on its size: for T = \id_V one may take the constant p = 1, while for the matrix \diag(1, i) the conditions p(1) = 1 and p(i) = -i are met by p(x) = ix + (1 - i), as one checks by substituting x = 1 and x = i. Exactly what is unique The factorization \A = \U\D\U^{*} is not unique, and it is worth being precise about which parts of it are. Unique: the set of eigenvalues \spec(T), and for each \lambda \in \spec(T) the eigenspace E_{\lambda}(T) with its dimension. These are defined from T alone, without any choice. Consequently the diagonal of \D is unique as a list with multiplicities up to reordering: each \lambda appears exactly \dim E_{\lambda}(T) times. Not unique: the order of the diagonal, and the matrix \U. Two freedoms create all the others. First, permuting the eigenvectors permutes the columns of \U and the diagonal of \D in step. Second, within a single eigenspace E_{\lambda}(T) of dimension m, any orthonormal basis of that eigenspace will do, and there are many when m \ge 2: the choices are related by the unitary maps of E_{\lambda}(T). For \A = \I_n, for instance, every unitary \U satisfies \U^{*}\A\U = \I_n. What no freedom can change is that eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues stay orthogonal (@cor-normal-orthogonal-eigenspaces), so the decomposition V = E_{\lambda_1}(T) \oplus \dots \oplus E_{\lambda_k}(T) into mutually orthogonal eigenspaces is itself unique. Section 8 turns that decomposition into the spectral resolution and shows it determines T completely. The matrix \A = \diag(1, 1, 2) is normal. Write down two different unitary matrices \U with \U^{*}\A\U = \A, and explain why, for \diag(1, 2, 3) with the order of the diagonal fixed, the freedom shrinks to a single unit-modulus scalar on each column. Take \U_1 = \I_3 and \U_2 =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}; more generally \R \oplus (1) works for any \R \in \Unit(2), because \A = \I_2 \oplus (2) and \R^{*}\I_2\R = \I_2. The freedom comes from the two-dimensional eigenspace E_1(\A) = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2), inside which every orthonormal basis is as good as any other. For \diag(1,2,3) each eigenspace is a line, and a line has exactly two unit vectors over 
R and a circle of them over 
C; the residual freedom is only the scalar factor of modulus 1 in each column, which changes \U but not the decomposition into eigenspaces. “Diagonalizable” and “unitarily diagonalizable” are different conditions. Every unitarily diagonalizable matrix is diagonalizable, because \U is in particular invertible. The converse fails, and it fails for matrices as small and as ordinary as  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Having n distinct eigenvalues guarantees diagonalizability (@cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable) and guarantees nothing about orthogonality. [Diagonalizable, and no orthonormal eigenbasis] For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
R), find an invertible \P with \P^{-1}\A\P diagonal, and show that no orthogonal \Q makes \Q	p\A\Q diagonal. The matrix is upper triangular, so its eigenvalues are the diagonal entries 1 and 2 (@thm-det-triangular). For \lambda = 1, \A - \I =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has kernel spanned by (1, 0). For \lambda = 2, \A - 2\I =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has kernel spanned by (1, 1). Two distinct eigenvalues in dimension 2 give a basis of eigenvectors (@cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable), so with \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad	ext{we get}\quad \P^{-1}\A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Now suppose \Q	p\A\Q = \D were diagonal with \Q orthogonal. Then \A = \Q\D\Q	p would be normal by @cor-spectral-complex-matrix. But \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 5 \end{pmatrix} 
eq  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} = \A\A	p , so \A is not normal and no such \Q exists. The obstruction is visible without any theory: the eigenvectors are (1,0) and (1,1), the eigenspaces are lines and therefore the only candidates for eigenvector directions, and (1,0)\cdot(1,1) = 1 
eq 0. There simply is no orthogonal pair of eigenvectors to build \Q from. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the complex spectral theorem, including every hypothesis, and state its matrix form. 2. What goes wrong with the proof if the field is 
R? Name the exact step. 3. True or false: a matrix in M_n(
C) with n distinct eigenvalues is unitarily diagonalizable. Justify your answer. 4. Let \A \in M_3(
C) be normal with \spec(\A) = \{2, 2, -1\} as a list with multiplicity. Is the unitary \U in \A = \U\D\U^{*} determined by \A and the order of \D? What is determined? 5. A normal operator T satisfies T^{*} = T^{3}. What can you say about its eigenvalues? 6. Explain why @lem-triangular-normal-diagonal cannot be weakened to “a normal matrix with some of its below-diagonal entries zero is diagonal”. (a) For a finite-dimensional inner product space V over 
C and T \in \cL(V): T is normal if and only if V has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of T (@thm-spectral-complex). Matrix form: \A \in M_n(
C) is normal if and only if \A = \U\D\U^{*} with \U unitary and \D diagonal (@cor-spectral-complex-matrix). (b) Schur’s theorem. It needs an eigenvalue at every stage of its induction, which over 
C comes from @thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra; over 
R an operator may have none at all, and then there is no triangular form to start from. (c) False.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} has the distinct eigenvalues 1 and 2 and is not normal, hence is not unitarily diagonalizable (@exm-diagonalizable-not-normal). (d) No. The eigenspace E_2(\A) is two-dimensional, and replacing its orthonormal basis by any other one changes \U while leaving \D alone. What is determined: \spec(\A) = \{2, -1\}, the eigenspaces E_2(\A) and E_{-1}(\A), their dimensions 2 and 1, and their mutual orthogonality. (e) By @thm-normal-eigenvector-shared, T\elem{v} = \lambda\elem{v} gives T^{*}\elem{v} = \conj{\lambda}\elem{v}, while T^{*} = T^3 gives T^{*}\elem{v} = \lambda^3\elem{v}. Hence \conj{\lambda} = \lambda^3. Taking moduli, \lvert\lambdavert = \lvert\lambdavert^3, so \lvert\lambdavert is 0 or 1. If \lambda 
eq 0, multiplying \conj{\lambda} = \lambda^3 by \lambda gives \lvert\lambdavert^2 = \lambda^4, that is \lambda^4 = 1. So every eigenvalue lies in \{0, 1, -1, i, -i\}. (f) The lemma uses triangularity at every index, not at a few places: the comparison of row and column lengths at step j is informative only because the whole of column j below the diagonal is already known to vanish. Zeros in some of those positions buy nothing. The circulant  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} is normal and has zeros in positions (2,1) and (3,2), two of the three places below its diagonal, and it is not diagonal. B. Practice [B1: Unitarily diagonalize] For each matrix, find a unitary \U and a diagonal \D with \U^{*}\A\U = \D. 1. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & -i \ i & 3 \end{pmatrix}. 2. \A = 	frac1{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ i & 1 \end{pmatrix}. (a) \A^{*} = \A, so \A is Hermitian and normal. Its characteristic polynomial is x^2 - 6x + (9 - (-i)(i)) = x^2 - 6x + 8, with roots 4 and 2. For \lambda = 4: \A - 4\I =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & -i \ i & -1 \end{pmatrix}, and the first row gives z_1 = -iz_2; take \cvec{u} = (-i, 1), 
orm{\cvec{u}}^2 = 2. For \lambda = 2: \A - 2\I =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -i \ i & 1 \end{pmatrix}, and the first row gives z_1 = iz_2; take \cvec{w} = (i, 1), 
orm{\cvec{w}}^2 = 2. They are orthogonal: \inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}} = (-i)\conj{i} + 1 = (-i)(-i) + 1 = -1 + 1 = 0. Hence \U = 	frac1{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} -i & i \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \D =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. (b) \A is unitary (@exm-normal-catalog (c)), hence normal. Here 	r \A = \sqrt2 and \det \A = 	frac12(1 - i^2) = 1, so the characteristic polynomial is x^2 - \sqrt2 x + 1, with roots x =  rac{\sqrt2 \pm \sqrt{2 - 4}}{2} =  rac{1 \pm i}{\sqrt2}, both of modulus 1, as @cor-normal-spectral-corollaries (b) requires. For \lambda = (1+i)/\sqrt2, the equation \A\cvec{z} = \lambda\cvec{z} reads 	frac1{\sqrt2}(z_1 + iz_2) = 	frac{1+i}{\sqrt2}z_1, that is iz_2 = iz_1, so \cvec{u} = (1, 1). For \lambda = (1-i)/\sqrt2 the same line gives iz_2 = -iz_1, so \cvec{w} = (1, -1). These are orthogonal, so \U = 	frac1{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \D = 	frac1{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 + i & 0 \ 0 & 1 - i \end{pmatrix} . Here \U is real orthogonal even though \A is not real. [B2: A circulant, diagonalized] Let \omega = e^{2\pi i/3}, so \omega^3 = 1 and 1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0, and let \C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(
