C) . 1. Verify that \C is normal. 2. Show that \cvec{f}_j = 	frac1{\sqrt3}(1, \omega^{j}, \omega^{2j}) is an eigenvector of \C for j = 0, 1, 2, and find the eigenvalue. 3. Deduce a unitary \F with \F^{*}\C\F diagonal, and write down the diagonal explicitly. (a) Both products are the same matrix: \C^{*}\C = \C\C^{*} =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} . (The entries are dot products of pairs of rows, respectively columns, of \C; cyclic shifting makes the two lists agree.) (b) Write \cvec{f} = (1, \omega^{j}, \omega^{2j}) before normalizing. Then \C\cvec{f} =  igl(1 + \omega^{j},\ \omega^{j} + \omega^{2j},\ 1 + \omega^{2j} igr) . Using \omega^{3j} = 1, the second entry is \omega^{j}(1 + \omega^{j}) and the third is \omega^{2j}(\omega^{-2j} + 1) = \omega^{2j}(\omega^{j} + 1), since \omega^{-2j} = \omega^{j}. So \C\cvec{f} = (1 + \omega^{j})\cvec{f}, and the eigenvalue is 1 + \omega^{j}. (c) The three vectors \cvec{f}_0, \cvec{f}_1, \cvec{f}_2 are orthonormal: each has norm 	frac1{\sqrt3}\sqrt{3} = 1, and for j 
eq l, \inner{\cvec{f}_j}{\cvec{f}_l} = 	frac13\sum_{m=0}^{2} \omega^{mj}\conj{\omega^{ml}} = 	frac13\sum_{m=0}^{2}  igl(\omega^{j-l} igr)^{m} = 0, because \omega^{j-l} 
eq 1 is a cube root of unity and 1 + z + z^2 = 0 for such z. Taking \F with columns \cvec{f}_0, \cvec{f}_1, \cvec{f}_2,  egin{aligned} \F^{*}\C\F &= \diag igl(2,\ 1 + \omega,\ 1 + \omega^2 igr) \ &= \diag\Bigl(2,\ 	frac12 + 	frac{\sqrt3}{2}i,\ 	frac12 - 	frac{\sqrt3}{2}i\Bigr), \end{aligned} using \omega = -	frac12 + 	frac{\sqrt3}{2}i. Section 9 shows that this one matrix \F diagonalizes every 3 	imes 3 circulant. [B3: Decide unitary diagonalizability] Determine which of the following matrices are unitarily diagonalizable over 
C, and which are merely diagonalizable. Justify your answer. 1.  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. 2.  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. 3.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. 4.  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. (a) Unitarily diagonalizable: the matrix is skew-symmetric, hence skew-adjoint over 
C and normal, so @cor-spectral-complex-matrix applies. (Its eigenvalues are \pm i.) (b) Neither. Comparing (1,1) entries, (\A^{*}\A)_{11} = 4 and (\A\A^{*})_{11} = 4 + 9 = 13, so \A is not normal. It is not even diagonalizable: the only eigenvalue is 2 and \A - 2\I = 3\J_2(0) 
eq \O has rank 1, so \dim E_2(\A) = 1 < 2 (@thm-diagonalization). (c) Diagonalizable but not unitarily: the eigenvalues 1 and 3 are distinct (@cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable), while (\A^{*}\A)_{11} = 1 
eq 5 = (\A\A^{*})_{11}, so \A is not normal. (d) Unitarily diagonalizable: the matrix is a permutation matrix, so its columns are orthonormal and it is unitary, hence normal. (Its eigenvalues are the cube roots of unity.) C. Going deeper [C1: Operators of finite order] Let T \in \cL(V) be normal on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, and suppose T^{k} = \id_V for some integer k \ge 1. 1. Prove that every eigenvalue of T is a k-th root of unity. 2. Deduce that T is unitary and unitarily diagonalizable. 3. Show that the hypothesis “normal” cannot be dropped from (b) by exhibiting a T with T^{2} = \id_V that is not unitary. (a) If T\elem{v} = \lambda\elem{v} with \elem{v} 
eq \elem{0}, then T^{k}\elem{v} = \lambda^{k}\elem{v} (@exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-b3 (a)) and T^{k}\elem{v} = \elem{v}, so (\lambda^{k} - 1)\elem{v} = \elem{0} and \lambda^{k} = 1. (b) Every k-th root of unity has modulus 1, so T is unitary by @cor-normal-spectral-corollaries (b), and it is unitarily diagonalizable by @thm-spectral-complex because it is normal. (c) On 
C^2 take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. Then \A^2 = \I, so T_{\A} has order 2; but its second column (1, -1) has norm \sqrt2 
eq 1, so \A is not unitary (@thm-isometry-characterizations (f)). It is still diagonalizable, with eigenvalues 1 and -1; what fails is only the orthogonality of the eigenvectors. [C2: Same spectrum, same multiplicities] Let \A, \B \in M_n(
C) be normal, and suppose they have the same eigenvalues with the same multiplicities, that is, the same characteristic polynomial. 1. Prove that there is a unitary \W with \B = \W\A\W^{*} (one says \A and \B are unitarily similar). 2. Give two matrices in M_2(
C) with the same characteristic polynomial that are not unitarily similar, and say which hypothesis of (a) they violate. 3. Deduce that two normal matrices are unitarily similar if and only if they are similar. (a) By @cor-spectral-complex-matrix write \A = \U\D\U^{*} and \B = \V\D'\V^{*} with \U, \V unitary and \D, \D' diagonal. The diagonals of \D and \D' are the eigenvalue lists of \A and \B with multiplicity, which agree as multisets; and the order on the diagonal may be prescribed, so we may choose the eigenvector orderings to make \D' = \D. Then \B = \V\D\V^{*} = \V\U^{*}\A\U\V^{*} = \W\A\W^{*} \quad	ext{with}\quad \W = \V\U^{*}, and \W is unitary because \Unit(n) is closed under products and inverses (@prp-orthogonal-group-properties). (b) \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \B = \O both have characteristic polynomial x^2; they are not even similar, since similar matrices have equal rank. A pair that is similar but not unitarily similar:  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} and \diag(1, 2). In both cases the violated hypothesis is normality of one of the two matrices. (c) (\Rightarrow) A unitary similarity is a similarity. (\Leftarrow) Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant), so if both are normal, (a) upgrades the similarity to a unitary one. [C3: Normality cannot be dropped] @cor-normal-spectral-corollaries reads the class of a normal operator off its spectrum. This exercise shows that each part fails without that hypothesis. 1. Give \A \in M_2(
C) with both eigenvalues real that is not Hermitian. 2. Give \A \in M_2(
C) with both eigenvalues of modulus 1 that is not unitary. 3. Over 
R, give \A \in M_2(
R) with \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} \ge 0 for every \cvec{x} \in 
R^2 whose eigenvalues are not nonnegative reals. Why does no such example exist over 
C? (a) \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} has eigenvalues 1 and 2 and is not Hermitian, since \A^{*} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} 
eq \A. It is not normal (@exm-diagonalizable-not-normal). (b) \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has 1 as its only eigenvalue, of modulus 1, and is not unitary: its second column has norm \sqrt2. Again it is not normal, the (1,1) entries of \A^{*}\A and \A\A^{*} being 1 and 2. (c) Take the quarter turn \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. For every \cvec{x} = (x_1, x_2) \in 
R^2, \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = -x_2x_1 + x_1x_2 = 0 \ge 0, yet \A has no real eigenvalue at all; over 
C its eigenvalues are \pm i, which are not nonnegative reals. Over 
C no such example exists: if \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0 for every \elem{v} then T = 0 by @thm-complex-zero-test, and more generally \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} real for every \elem{v} forces T to be self-adjoint, hence normal, by applying @thm-complex-zero-test to T - T^{*}. Real scalars are not enough to detect an operator over 
R, and they are over 
C.

title: 12.5 The Real Spectral Theorem
content:
The Real Spectral Theorem Over 
C the answer was clean: an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors exists exactly for the normal operators. Over 
R the same question has a different answer, and a smaller one. The class shrinks from normal to self-adjoint, and the reason is a single example that we have met since Chapter 9 and can finally name as the obstruction: a rotation of the plane is as normal as an operator can be and has no eigenvector at all. This section proves the real theorem, examines that obstruction, and then rescues what can be rescued for real normal operators. It ends with the application that made the theorem famous outside linear algebra: the axes of a conic. Throughout, V is a finite-dimensional inner product space over 
R unless stated otherwise, and “symmetric” means \A	p = \A. One eigenvector, then its orthogonal complement The proof is the signature move of the chapter, run as an induction. Section 2 did all the work: it produced an eigenvector, and it showed that the orthogonal complement of an invariant subspace is again invariant with a self-adjoint restriction. Those two facts fit together into an induction on dimension with nothing left over. [Real Spectral Theorem] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over 
R and let T \in \cL(V). The following are equivalent. 1. T is self-adjoint. 2. V has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of T. (\Leftarrow) In such a basis the matrix is diagonal, and a real diagonal matrix is its own transpose. (\Rightarrow) Induct on \dim V. Peel off one unit eigenvector \elem{e}_1, which exists by @thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue; the line U = \Span(\elem{e}_1) is invariant, so @thm-self-adjoint-invariant-complement makes U^{\perp} invariant with a self-adjoint restriction. That restriction lives on a space of dimension \dim V - 1, so the inductive hypothesis applies to it, and the basis it returns is already orthogonal to \elem{e}_1. (\Leftarrow) Let \sB be an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, so \D \coloneqq \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} is diagonal with real entries. Since \sB is orthonormal, \mtx{T^{*}}{\sB}{\sB} = \D^{*} = \D	p = \D by @thm-matrix-of-adjoint, the last equality because a diagonal matrix equals its transpose. Two operators with the same matrix in one basis are equal (@thm-linear-maps-isomorphic-to-matrices), so T^{*} = T. (\Rightarrow) Induct on n = \dim V. If n = 0 the empty list is an orthonormal basis and there is nothing to prove. Let n \ge 1 and suppose the statement holds for every real inner product space of dimension n - 1. Since V 
eq \{\elem{0}\} and T is self-adjoint, T has an eigenvalue \lambda \in 
R by @thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue, say T\elem{v} = \lambda\elem{v} with \elem{v} 
eq \elem{0}. Put \elem{e}_1 = \elem{v}/
orm{\elem{v}}, a unit eigenvector, and U = \Span(\elem{e}_1). Then U is T-invariant, because T(c\elem{e}_1) = c\lambda\elem{e}_1 \in U. By @thm-self-adjoint-invariant-complement, U^{\perp} is T-invariant and the restriction T|_{U^{\perp}} is a self-adjoint operator on U^{\perp}, which is an inner product space in its own right under the restricted inner product. Its dimension is n - 1 by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (c). By the inductive hypothesis, U^{\perp} has an orthonormal basis (\elem{e}_2, \dots, \elem{e}_n) of eigenvectors of T|_{U^{\perp}}; each \elem{e}_j satisfies T\elem{e}_j = \mu_j\elem{e}_j in V as well, since the restriction is the same map. Finally (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n) is orthonormal: the last n-1 vectors are orthonormal among themselves and each lies in U^{\perp}, hence is orthogonal to \elem{e}_1, which has norm 1. An orthonormal list is linearly independent (@thm-orthogonal-independent), and it has n = \dim V members, so it is a basis (@thm-right-size-basis). Every member is an eigenvector of T. This proves the theorem. No complexification appears anywhere in that induction, which is worth noticing: the argument is entirely real. The one place where complex numbers were needed is inside @thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue, whose proof complexifies once to borrow an eigenvalue from the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (@thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra) and then observes that the eigenvalue is real. So 
C is used exactly once, to start the machine, and never again. [Orthogonal Diagonalization] Let \A \in M_n(
R). Then \A is symmetric if and only if there are an orthogonal \Q \in \Orth(n) and a real diagonal \D with \A = \Q\D\Q	p . The diagonal of \D is the eigenvalue list of \A with multiplicity, in any prescribed order, and the columns of \Q are a corresponding orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Apply @thm-spectral-real to T_{\A} on 
R^n with the standard inner product, for which the standard basis is orthonormal, so that \A	p = \A is exactly self-adjointness (@thm-matrix-of-adjoint). (\Rightarrow) Let (\cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_n) be an orthonormal basis with \A\cvec{q}_j = \lambda_j\cvec{q}_j, and let \Q have these columns; it is orthogonal by @thm-isometry-characterizations (f). Column j of \A\Q is \lambda_j\cvec{q}_j, which is column j of \Q\D for \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n). So \A\Q = \Q\D and \A = \Q\D\Q^{-1} = \Q\D\Q	p. The eigenvalues are real because \A is self-adjoint (@thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues), so \D is a real matrix. (\Leftarrow) If \A = \Q\D\Q	p with \D real diagonal, then \A	p = (\Q\D\Q	p)	p = \Q\D	p\Q	p = \Q\D\Q	p = \A . The claims about the order and the columns are as in @cor-spectral-complex-matrix. The negative result: normal is not enough over the reals Over 
C the class with an orthonormal eigenbasis was the normal operators. Over 
R @thm-spectral-real says it is the self-adjoint ones, which is a strictly smaller class: every self-adjoint operator is normal, and the converse now fails. It is worth seeing exactly how it fails, because the failure is not a technicality about multiplicities or about a badly chosen basis. It is the complete absence of an eigenvector. [A normal real operator with no eigenvector] Let T \in \cL(
R^2) be the quarter turn, with matrix \R =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} in the standard basis. Show that T is normal, and that T has no eigenvalue and no eigenvector in 
R^2. Normality: \R	p\R = \R\R	p = \I, so T is even orthogonal, hence normal. (One may also read it off the shape: \R = \vLambda(i) is the rotation-scaling block of @def-real-jordan-block.) No eigenvalue: p_{\R}(x) = x^2 + 1, which has no root in 
R. So \R - \lambda\I is invertible for every real \lambda, and \ker(T - \lambda\,\id) = \{\cvec{0}\} (@thm-eigenvalue-characterizations). Geometrically, T turns every nonzero vector by a right angle, so T\cvec{v} is never a real multiple of \cvec{v}; the operator maps no line to itself. That example rules out every possible improvement of @thm-spectral-real to normal operators over 
R, and not by a narrow margin. An orthonormal basis of eigenvectors needs n eigenvectors; the quarter turn supplies none. So the two spectral theorems are not two versions of one statement with a technical difference: the real one has a genuinely smaller hypothesis, and the only reason it is not smaller still is @thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue, which manufactures the eigenvector that the rotation lacks. Two further remarks keep the picture honest. First, the quarter turn is not exceptional. Over 
R, every normal operator that is not self-adjoint fails to have an orthonormal eigenbasis, because @thm-spectral-real is an equivalence: having such a basis and being self-adjoint are the same condition. Second, nothing is wrong with the operator; what is missing is the field. Regard \R as a complex matrix and it is unitarily diagonalizable, with eigenvalues \pm i and eigenvectors (1, \mp i) in 
C^2 (the sign of the eigenvalue and of the entry being opposite). The complex spectral theorem never fails; it simply answers a question about 
C^n. Is \R =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} orthogonally diagonalizable over 
R? Is it unitarily diagonalizable over 
C? Are the two answers consistent? Not over 
R: an orthogonal diagonalization \R = \Q\D\Q	p would make \R symmetric by @cor-spectral-real-matrix, and \R	p = -\R 
eq \R. Over 
C it is unitarily diagonalizable, because it is normal (@cor-spectral-complex-matrix); explicitly \U^{*}\R\U = \diag(i, -i) for \U = 	frac1{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ -i & i \end{pmatrix}. There is no conflict: the two statements concern different spaces, 
R^2 and 
C^2, and the diagonalizing basis of the second one is not real. What a real normal operator does look like The rotation is not a defect to be apologized for; it is a building block. Chapter 10 already promoted it to one when it built the real Jordan form, and the same 2 	imes 2 block returns here as the only thing that can obstruct a real diagonalization of a normal operator. [Real Normal Form of a Normal Operator] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over 
R and let T \in \cL(V) be normal. Then V has an orthonormal basis in which the matrix of T is block diagonal, (c_1) \oplus \dots \oplus (c_p) \oplus \vLambda(\lambda_1) \oplus \dots \oplus \vLambda(\lambda_q), with c_1, \dots, c_p \in 
R and, for each j, \lambda_j = a_j + b_ji with b_j > 0 and \vLambda(\lambda_j) =  egin{pmatrix} a_j & -b_j \ b_j & a_j \end{pmatrix} the rotation-scaling block of @def-real-jordan-block. In matrix form: \A \in M_n(
R) is normal if and only if \A = \Q\B\Q	p with \Q \in \Orth(n) and \B of the displayed shape. The real Schur form of Section 1 gets us to a block triangular matrix with 1 	imes 1 and 2 	imes 2 diagonal blocks, and the corner blocks above the diagonal are the only obstruction left. The argument that killed them in the complex case, comparing a diagonal entry of \T	p\T with the same entry of \T\T	p, works verbatim on blocks once “entry” is replaced by “trace of a block”: the identity 	r(\X\X	p) = \sum_{i,j} x_{ij}^2 turns the comparison into a sum of squares that has to vanish. What remains is to see what a 2 	imes 2 real normal matrix can be, and there are exactly two answers: symmetric, which splits further, or a rotation-scaling block. Fix an orthonormal basis of V and let \A \in M_n(
R) be the matrix of T in it; then \A	p is the matrix of T^{*} (@thm-matrix-of-adjoint), and T normal means \A	p\A = \A\A	p. Every orthogonal change of orthonormal basis replaces \A by \Q	p\A\Q, which is again normal: (\Q	p\A\Q)	p(\Q	p\A\Q) = \Q	p\A	p\A\Q = \Q	p\A\A	p\Q, and the same computation in the other order gives (\Q	p\A\Q)(\Q	p\A\Q)	p. So we may replace \A by any orthogonally similar matrix at will. Step 1: a block triangular form. By the real Schur form (@thm-real-schur) there is \Q_1 \in \Orth(n) with \T = \Q_1	p\A\Q_1 block upper triangular, its diagonal blocks of size 1 	imes 1 and 2 	imes 2. Write the block partition as \T = (\T_{kl})_{1 \le k, l \le m} with \T_{kl} = \O for k > l. By the previous paragraph \T is normal. Step 2: the corners vanish. A normal, block upper triangular real matrix is block diagonal. Induct on the number m of diagonal blocks; m = 1 is trivial. Comparing the (1,1) blocks of the two products (@thm-block-multiplication) and using \T_{k1} = \O for k > 1,  egin{aligned} (\T	p\T)_{11} &= \T_{11}	p\T_{11}, \ (\T\T	p)_{11} &= \T_{11}\T_{11}	p + \sum_{l > 1} \T_{1l}\T_{1l}	p . \end{aligned} Take traces. Since 	r(\X\Y) = 	r(\Y\X) (@thm-trace-properties), the two terms 	r(\T_{11}	p\T_{11}) and 	r(\T_{11}\T_{11}	p) are equal and cancel, leaving \sum_{l > 1} 	r igl(\T_{1l}\T_{1l}	p igr) = 0 . For a real matrix \X, 	r(\X\X	p) = \sum_{i,j} x_{ij}^2 \ge 0, with equality only for \X = \O. So \T_{1l} = \O for every l > 1: the first block row is clear, and \T = \T_{11} \oplus \T' where \T' is the trailing block upper triangular matrix with m - 1 diagonal blocks. Then \T	p\T = \T_{11}	p\T_{11} \oplus {\T'}	p\T', \qquad \T\T	p = \T_{11}\T_{11}	p \oplus \T'{\T'}	p, so normality of \T gives normality of \T', and the inductive hypothesis applies. So after Step 2 the matrix is \D_1 \oplus \dots \oplus \D_m with each \D_k of size 1 or 2. Both products are now computed blockwise, so normality of the whole reads \D_k	p\D_k = \D_k\D_k	p for each k: every diagonal block is normal. Step 3: the shape of a 2 	imes 2 real normal block. Let \D =  egin{pmatrix} p & q \ r & s \end{pmatrix} be real and normal. Expanding both products, \D\D	p - \D	p\D =  egin{pmatrix} q^2 - r^2 & (r - q)(p - s) \ (r - q)(p - s) & r^2 - q^2 \end{pmatrix}, so normality says q^2 = r^2 and (r - q)(p - s) = 0. The first equation gives q = r or q = -r, and when q = -r = 0 both hold, so the following two cases are exhaustive. Case 1: q = r. Then \D is symmetric, and @cor-spectral-real-matrix supplies an orthogonal 2 	imes 2 matrix turning it into a real diagonal matrix, which is two 1 	imes 1 blocks. Case 2: q = -r and q 
eq 0. Then r - q = -2q 
eq 0, so p = s and \D =  egin{pmatrix} p & q \ -q & p \end{pmatrix} . If q < 0, this is \vLambda(p - qi) with -q > 0, as required. If q > 0, conjugate by the orthogonal matrix \diag(1, -1):  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} p & q \ -q & p \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} p & -q \ q & p \end{pmatrix}, which is \vLambda(p + qi) with q > 0. Step 4: assembling. Apply Step 3 inside each diagonal block, using the direct sum \Q_2 of the resulting 1 	imes 1 and 2 	imes 2 orthogonal matrices, which is orthogonal because its columns are orthonormal. Then \Q = \Q_1\Q_2 is orthogonal and \Q	p\A\Q has the stated shape; reordering the blocks by a permutation matrix, itself orthogonal, puts the 1 	imes 1 blocks first. The columns of \Q are the required orthonormal basis. For the converse, a block diagonal matrix \B of the displayed shape is normal, since \B	p\B and \B\B	p are computed blockwise and every block is normal: (c)	p(c) = (c^2) = (c)(c)	p, and \vLambda(\lambda)	p\vLambda(\lambda) = \lvert\lambdavert^2\I_2 = \vLambda(\lambda)\vLambda(\lambda)	p. Then \A = \Q\B\Q	p is normal by the first paragraph. This proves the theorem. The two theorems now fit together. A real normal operator is self-adjoint exactly when no \vLambda block occurs, and then @thm-real-normal-form is @thm-spectral-real. The eigenvalues of \A are the numbers c_i together with the conjugate pairs \lambda_j, \conj{\lambda_j}, so the \vLambda blocks are precisely the nonreal part of the spectrum, packaged two real dimensions at a time. Section 6 specializes this to orthogonal operators, where \lvert\lambdavert = 1 forces every 2 	imes 2 block to be a plane rotation. A symmetric matrix as a sum of projections Writing \A = \Q\D\Q	p and expanding the product column by column turns the diagonalization into a sum of very simple matrices. [Spectral Decomposition of a Symmetric Matrix] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be symmetric, and let (\cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_n) be an orthonormal basis of 
R^n with \A\cvec{q}_i = \lambda_i\cvec{q}_i. Then \A = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i\,\cvec{q}_i\cvec{q}_i	p , and each \cvec{q}_i\cvec{q}_i	p is the matrix of the orthogonal projection of 
R^n onto the line \Span(\cvec{q}_i). Let \Q have columns \cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_n and \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n), so \A = \Q\D\Q	p by @cor-spectral-real-matrix. The columns of \Q\D are \lambda_i\cvec{q}_i, and the rows of \Q	p are \cvec{q}_i	p, so the column-times-row expansion of the product (@cor-outer-product-expansion) gives \A = \sum_i (\lambda_i\cvec{q}_i)\cvec{q}_i	p, which is the stated sum. For the second claim, \cvec{q}_i is a unit vector, so the orthogonal projection onto \Span(\cvec{q}_i) is \cvec{x} \mapsto \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{q}_i}\cvec{q}_i by @thm-projection-formula. Since \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{q}_i} = \cvec{q}_i	p\cvec{x} is a scalar, \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{q}_i}\cvec{q}_i = \cvec{q}_i(\cvec{q}_i	p\cvec{x}) = (\cvec{q}_i\cvec{q}_i	p)\cvec{x}. [Orthogonally diagonalizing a 3 by 3 matrix] Orthogonally diagonalize \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 3 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, and write it as a sum of rank-one orthogonal projections. The rows all sum to 5, so \A(1,1,1) = 5(1,1,1) and 5 is an eigenvalue. Also \A = 2\I + \J where \J is the all-ones matrix, and \J\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} exactly when x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0; on that plane \A\cvec{x} = 2\cvec{x}. So E_5(\A) = \Span igl((1,1,1) igr), \qquad E_2(\A) = \{\cvec{x} : x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0\}, of dimensions 1 and 2, which already account for all of 
R^3. The two eigenspaces are orthogonal, as @thm-self-adjoint-orthogonal-eigenspaces requires. Inside E_2(\A) any orthonormal basis will do. Start from the independent pair (1,-1,0) and (1,0,-1), both in the plane, and run one step of Gram–Schmidt (@thm-gram-schmidt): the second vector minus its component along the first is (1,0,-1) - 	frac12(1,-1,0) = 	frac12(1,1,-2), a multiple of (1,1,-2). Normalizing all three, \cvec{q}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1,1,1), \quad \cvec{q}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1,0), \quad \cvec{q}_3 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt6}(1,1,-2). With \Q = (\cvec{q}_1 \mid \cvec{q}_2 \mid \cvec{q}_3) we get \Q	p\Q = \I and \Q	p\A\Q = \diag(5, 2, 2). By @cor-symmetric-rank-one-sum, \A = 5\,\cvec{q}_1\cvec{q}_1	p + 2\,\cvec{q}_2\cvec{q}_2	p + 2\,\cvec{q}_3\cvec{q}_3	p . As a check, \cvec{q}_2\cvec{q}_2	p + \cvec{q}_3\cvec{q}_3	p = \I - \cvec{q}_1\cvec{q}_1	p because the three projections sum to the identity, so the right-hand side is 2\I + 3\,\cvec{q}_1\cvec{q}_1	p = 2\I + \J, which is \A. Notice that \cvec{q}_2 and \cvec{q}_3 were not forced on us, while the two projections \cvec{q}_1\cvec{q}_1	p and \cvec{q}_2\cvec{q}_2	p + \cvec{q}_3\cvec{q}_3	p were: they are the projections onto the two eigenspaces. Section 8 makes that observation into a theorem. The principal axis theorem Here is the application. A quadratic form on 
R^n is a function q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}x_ix_j for some \A \in M_n(
R). Only the symmetric part of \A matters, since \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{x}	p\A	p\cvec{x} for a 1 	imes 1 matrix, so we always take \A symmetric; then \A is determined by q, with a_{ii} the coefficient of x_i^2 and a_{ij} half the coefficient of x_ix_j for i 
eq j. Chapter 14 studies such forms in their own right. [Principal Axis Theorem] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be symmetric, let q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x}, and let \Q \in \Orth(n) with \Q	p\A\Q = \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n), the columns \cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_n of \Q being an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Substituting \cvec{x} = \Q\cvec{y}, that is, taking y_i = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{q}_i} to be the coordinates of \cvec{x} in that basis, q(\cvec{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i y_i^2 . In particular, for n = 2 with \lambda_1, \lambda_2 > 0, the level set \{q = 1\} is an ellipse whose axes lie along \cvec{q}_1 and \cvec{q}_2, with half-lengths 1/\sqrt{\lambda_1} and 1/\sqrt{\lambda_2}. Since \Q is invertible, \cvec{x} = \Q\cvec{y} sets up a bijection between \cvec{x} and \cvec{y} = \Q^{-1}\cvec{x} = \Q	p\cvec{x}, whose i-th entry is \cvec{q}_i	p\cvec{x} = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{q}_i}. Substituting, q(\Q\cvec{y}) = (\Q\cvec{y})	p\A(\Q\cvec{y}) = \cvec{y}	p(\Q	p\A\Q)\cvec{y} = \cvec{y}	p\D\cvec{y} = \sum_i \lambda_iy_i^2 , using (\Q\cvec{y})	p = \cvec{y}	p\Q	p (@thm-transpose-properties). For n = 2 with both \lambda_i > 0, the condition q(\cvec{x}) = 1 becomes \lambda_1y_1^2 + \lambda_2y_2^2 = 1, the standard equation of an ellipse in the \cvec{y} coordinates, meeting the y_1-axis where y_1 = \pm 1/\sqrt{\lambda_1} and the y_2-axis where y_2 = \pm 1/\sqrt{\lambda_2}. Those axes are the lines \Span(\cvec{q}_1) and \Span(\cvec{q}_2) of the original picture, because \cvec{y} = \cvec{e}_1 corresponds to \cvec{x} = \Q\cvec{e}_1 = \cvec{q}_1. Since \Q is orthogonal, it preserves lengths (@thm-isometry-characterizations), so the half-lengths are unchanged by the substitution. [Finding the axes of a conic] Identify the curve 3x^2 - 2xy + 3y^2 = 1 in 
R^2, and find its axes and their half-lengths. The symmetric matrix of the form is \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, the off-diagonal entries being half of -2. Its characteristic polynomial is x^2 - 6x + 8, so the eigenvalues are 2 and 4. For \lambda = 2, \A - 2\I =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} gives x = y and the unit eigenvector \cvec{q}_1 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1). For \lambda = 4, \A - 4\I =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & -1 \ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} gives x = -y and \cvec{q}_2 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1). In the coordinates y_1 = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{q}_1}, y_2 = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{q}_2}, the equation is 2y_1^2 + 4y_2^2 = 1. Both eigenvalues are positive, so the curve is an ellipse. Its major axis lies along \cvec{q}_1, the line y = x, with half-length 1/\sqrt2; its minor axis lies along \cvec{q}_2, the line y = -x, with half-length 1/2. The check is that 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1) scaled to length 1/\sqrt2 is the point (	frac12, 	frac12), and 3\cdot	frac14 - 2\cdot	frac14 + 3\cdot	frac14 = 1. Two features of the picture are worth naming. The axes are orthogonal because the eigenvectors are, and that is the whole content of the theorem; a nonsymmetric matrix in the same role would produce a pair of distinguished directions that need not be perpendicular. And the bigger eigenvalue gives the shorter axis, since the half-length is 1/\sqrt{\lambda}: a large \lambda makes q reach the value 1 sooner. Chapter 14 will diagonalize quadratic forms again, but by congruence: replacing \A by \P	p\A\P for an arbitrary invertible \P, not necessarily orthogonal. That is a weaker relation, and it destroys the eigenvalues while preserving only their signs, which is Sylvester’s law of inertia. What makes the present theorem special is that \Q	p = \Q^{-1}, so \Q	p\A\Q = \Q^{-1}\A\Q and the two relations coincide: an orthogonal change of variables is a similarity and a congruence, so it keeps the eigenvalues and the geometry at once. The theorem needs 
R, and symmetry is not the same as having real eigenvalues. The matrix  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is symmetric with rational entries, but its eigenvalues are (1 \pm \sqrt5)/2, which are irrational; over 
Q there is no eigenvector at all, and no version of @thm-spectral-real survives. Conversely  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} has the real eigenvalues 1 and 2 and is not symmetric; real eigenvalues alone buy nothing, since they do not make the eigenvectors orthogonal. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the real spectral theorem and its matrix form, with every hypothesis. 2. Which two results from Section 2 does the induction use, and what does each one supply? 3. True or false: a normal operator on a real inner product space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Justify your answer. 4. What are the possible diagonal blocks in the real normal form of a normal operator, and what does the condition b > 0 rule out? 5. Given a symmetric \A with orthonormal eigenvectors \cvec{q}_1, \cvec{q}_2 and eigenvalues 9 and 1, describe the curve \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = 1. 6. True or false: a real matrix with real eigenvalues is symmetric. Justify your answer. (a) For a finite-dimensional real inner product space V and T \in \cL(V): T is self-adjoint if and only if V has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors (@thm-spectral-real). Matrix form: \A \in M_n(
R) is symmetric if and only if \A = \Q\D\Q	p with \Q orthogonal and \D real diagonal (@cor-spectral-real-matrix). (b) @thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue supplies one eigenvector to peel off, and @thm-self-adjoint-invariant-complement supplies the smaller object to induct on, namely the self-adjoint restriction to the orthogonal complement. (c) False. The quarter turn of 
R^2 is normal and has no eigenvector at all (@exm-rotation-normal-no-real-eigenvector). (d) Blocks (c) with c \in 
R, and 2 	imes 2 blocks \vLambda(\lambda) =  egin{pmatrix} a & -b \ b & a \end{pmatrix} with b > 0 (@thm-real-normal-form). The condition b > 0 rules out the transposed block \vLambda(\conj\lambda), which is orthogonally similar to it via \diag(1, -1); fixing the sign is what makes the list of blocks well defined. (e) An ellipse with axes along \cvec{q}_1 and \cvec{q}_2, of half-lengths 1/3 and 1 (@thm-principal-axes). The longer axis is along \cvec{q}_2, the eigenvector for the smaller eigenvalue. (f) False.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} has eigenvalues 1, 2 and is not symmetric. The correct statement is the converse: a symmetric real matrix has real eigenvalues. B. Practice [B1: Orthogonally diagonalize] For each symmetric matrix, find an orthogonal \Q and a diagonal \D with \Q	p\A\Q = \D. 1. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. 2. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 2 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}. (a) p_{\A}(x) = x^2 - 2x - 3 = (x-3)(x+1), so the eigenvalues are 3 and -1. For \lambda = 3, \A - 3\I =  egin{pmatrix} -2 & 2 \ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} gives x_1 = x_2 and \cvec{q}_1 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1); for \lambda = -1, \cvec{q}_2 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1). Hence \Q = 	frac1{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \D =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} . (b) The second coordinate is untouched: \A\cvec{e}_2 = 2\cvec{e}_2. On \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_3) the matrix acts as  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, with eigenvalues 5 and 3 and eigenvectors (1,1) and (1,-1) there. Lifting back, \cvec{q}_1 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,0,1), \quad \cvec{q}_2 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(-1,0,1), \quad \cvec{q}_3 = (0,1,0), with eigenvalues 5, 3, 2. These are orthonormal, so \Q = (\cvec{q}_1 \mid \cvec{q}_2 \mid \cvec{q}_3) is orthogonal and \Q	p\A\Q = \diag(5, 3, 2). As a check, 5 + 3 + 2 = 10 = 	r \A. [B2: Identify the conic] Identify the curve 5x^2 + 4xy + 5y^2 = 1: say what kind of conic it is, find its axes, and find their half-lengths. The symmetric matrix of the form is \A =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, the off-diagonal entries being half of 4. Its characteristic polynomial is x^2 - 10x + 21 = (x-7)(x-3), so the eigenvalues are 7 and 3. For \lambda = 7, \A - 7\I =  egin{pmatrix} -2 & 2 \ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} gives \cvec{q}_1 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1); for \lambda = 3, \cvec{q}_2 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1). By @thm-principal-axes the equation becomes 7y_1^2 + 3y_2^2 = 1. Both eigenvalues are positive, so the curve is an ellipse. Its axes are the lines y = x and y = -x, with half-lengths 1/\sqrt7 along \cvec{q}_1 and 1/\sqrt3 along \cvec{q}_2; the major axis is the second one. Check: the point 	frac1{\sqrt3}\cvec{q}_2 = 	frac1{\sqrt6}(1,-1) gives 	frac56 - 	frac46 + 	frac56 = 1. [B3: A sum of rank-one projections] Using your answer to @exr-spectral-theorem-real-b1 (b), write \A =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 2 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix} as \sum_i \lambda_i\cvec{q}_i\cvec{q}_i	p, with the three matrices \cvec{q}_i\cvec{q}_i	p written out, and verify the identity by adding them. With \cvec{q}_1 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,0,1), \cvec{q}_2 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(-1,0,1), \cvec{q}_3 = (0,1,0), and \lambda = 5, 3, 2, \cvec{q}_1\cvec{q}_1	p = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{q}_2\cvec{q}_2	p = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, and \cvec{q}_3\cvec{q}_3	p is the matrix with a single 1 in position (2,2). Then 5\,\cvec{q}_1\cvec{q}_1	p + 3\,\cvec{q}_2\cvec{q}_2	p =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, since 	frac12(5+3) = 4 on the diagonal and 	frac12(5-3) = 1 off it. Adding 2\,\cvec{q}_3\cvec{q}_3	p inserts the 2 in position (2,2) and gives \A, as @cor-symmetric-rank-one-sum requires. C. Going deeper [C1: One eigenvalue only] 1. Let \A \in M_n(
R) be symmetric with every eigenvalue equal to \lambda. Prove that \A = \lambda\I. 2. Show that (a) fails without symmetry, by exhibiting a matrix in M_2(
R) whose only eigenvalue is 0 and which is not \O. 3. Deduce that a symmetric \A with \A^2 = \A is the matrix of an orthogonal projection. (a) By @cor-spectral-real-matrix, \A = \Q\D\Q	p with \D diagonal carrying the eigenvalues, so \D = \lambda\I. Hence \A = \Q(\lambda\I)\Q	p = \lambda\Q\Q	p = \lambda\I. (b) \J_2(0) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has characteristic polynomial x^2, so 0 is its only eigenvalue, and it is not the zero matrix. It is of course not symmetric. (c) If \A^2 = \A and \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} with \cvec{x} 
eq \cvec{0}, then \lambda^2\cvec{x} = \A^2\cvec{x} = \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x}, so \lambda^2 = \lambda and \lambda \in \{0, 1\}. By @cor-spectral-real-matrix, \A = \Q\D\Q	p with \D diagonal of zeros and ones, so \A = \sum_{i \in S}\cvec{q}_i\cvec{q}_i	p where S indexes the eigenvalue 1 (@cor-symmetric-rank-one-sum). That is the sum of the projections onto an orthonormal basis of U = E_1(\A), which is the orthogonal projection P_U by @thm-projection-formula. [C2: Diagonalizing two matrices at once] Let \A, \B \in M_n(
R) be symmetric with \A\B = \B\A. 1. Prove that each eigenspace E_{\lambda}(\A) is \B-invariant, and that the restriction of T_{\B} to it is self-adjoint. 2. Prove that there is a single \Q \in \Orth(n) with \Q	p\A\Q and \Q	p\B\Q both diagonal. 3. Show that the conclusion fails without commutativity, using  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Hint for (b): apply @thm-spectral-real inside each eigenspace of \A. (a) Invariance is @thm-commuting-preserves-eigenspaces: if \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} then \A(\B\cvec{x}) = \B(\A\cvec{x}) = \lambda\B\cvec{x}. For self-adjointness of the restriction, take \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \in E_{\lambda}(\A); then \inner{\B\cvec{u}}{\cvec{v}} = \inner{\cvec{u}}{\B\cvec{v}} because \B is symmetric on all of 
R^n, and both \B\cvec{u} and \B\cvec{v} lie in E_{\lambda}(\A) by the first part, so the identity holds inside the subspace with its restricted inner product. (b) Let \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k be the distinct eigenvalues of \A. By @thm-spectral-real, 
R^n is the direct sum of the eigenspaces E_{\lambda_i}(\A), and these are mutually orthogonal (@thm-self-adjoint-orthogonal-eigenspaces). By (a) and @thm-spectral-real applied to the self-adjoint operator T_{\B}|_{E_{\lambda_i}(\A)}, each E_{\lambda_i}(\A) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of \B. Every vector of E_{\lambda_i}(\A) is an eigenvector of \A, so these basis vectors are common eigenvectors. Stringing the k bases together gives an orthonormal basis of 
R^n, orthonormal across the blocks because distinct eigenspaces of \A are orthogonal. Let \Q have those vectors as columns; then \Q \in \Orth(n) and both \Q	p\A\Q and \Q	p\B\Q are diagonal. (c) These two do not commute: \A\B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} while \B\A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. And no common eigenbasis exists: the eigenvectors of \A are the multiples of \cvec{e}_1 and of \cvec{e}_2, while \B\cvec{e}_1 = \cvec{e}_2 is not a multiple of \cvec{e}_1. Commutativity is necessary as well as sufficient, since two simultaneously diagonalized matrices commute. [C3: A rotation-scaling in normal form] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \ -4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
R). 1. Verify that \A is normal and not symmetric, and find its complex eigenvalues. 2. Find an orthogonal \Q with \Q	p\A\Q = \vLambda(\lambda) for the eigenvalue \lambda with positive imaginary part. 3. Explain why no orthogonal \Q makes \Q	p\A\Q diagonal, and why this does not contradict @thm-spectral-complex. (a) \A	p\A = \A\A	p = 25\I, so \A is normal; \A	p 
eq \A since 4 
eq -4. Its characteristic polynomial is x^2 - 6x + 25 = (x-3)^2 + 16, with roots 3 \pm 4i. (b) The eigenvalue with positive imaginary part is \lambda = 3 + 4i, so \vLambda(\lambda) =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & -4 \ 4 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. Take \Q = \diag(1, -1), which is orthogonal. Then \Q	p\A\Q =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \ -4 & 3 \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & -4 \ 4 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, which is \vLambda(3 + 4i). This is Case 2 of the proof of @thm-real-normal-form with p = 3 and q = 4. (c) If \Q	p\A\Q were diagonal for some \Q \in \Orth(2), then \A = \Q\D\Q	p would be symmetric by @cor-spectral-real-matrix, and it is not. There is no contradiction with @thm-spectral-complex, which concerns a complex inner product space: over 
C^2 the matrix \A is indeed unitarily diagonalizable, to \diag(3+4i, 3-4i), but the diagonalizing basis 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1, \pm i) is not real, so it is unavailable inside 
R^2.

title: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content:
The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix An orthogonal matrix is normal, so the real normal form of the previous section applies to it — and the extra information that an orthogonal matrix carries, that every eigenvalue has modulus 1, collapses that form into something very small. What comes out is a complete description of the rigid motions of 
R^n fixing the origin: a few axes reversed, and the rest of the space turned in independent two-dimensional planes. In dimension 3 this is the statement that every rotation has an axis, and we push it as far as an explicit formula for the rotation matrix in terms of its axis and angle. Throughout, 
R^n carries the standard inner product, and \Q is a real matrix. From the real normal form to the canonical form Two pieces of notation, both recalled. For 	heta \in 
R, Chapter 11 wrote \R_{	heta} =  egin{pmatrix} \cos	heta & -\sin	heta \ \sin	heta & \cos	heta \end{pmatrix} for the matrix that rotates the plane by 	heta (@thm-orthogonal-2x2). It is exactly the rotation-scaling block of Chapter 10 for a complex number on the unit circle: \R_{	heta} = \vLambda(e^{i	heta}) in the notation of @def-real-jordan-block, since e^{i	heta} = \cos	heta + i\sin	heta. And \A \oplus \B is the block diagonal matrix with diagonal blocks \A and \B. Now the observation that starts everything. If \Q \in \Orth(n) then \Q	p\Q = \I_n = \Q\Q	p, so \Q commutes with its own adjoint: every orthogonal matrix is normal. So @thm-real-normal-form applies. All that remains is to say what the blocks can be, and for that we use the one thing an orthogonal matrix has that a general normal matrix does not. [Canonical Form of an Orthogonal Matrix] Let \Q \in \Orth(n). Then there are integers p, q, m \ge 0 with p + q + 2m = n, and angles 	heta_1, \dots, 	heta_m with 0 < 	heta_j < \pi, and a matrix \P \in \Orth(n), such that \P	p\Q\P = \I_p \oplus (-\I_q) \oplus \R_{	heta_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus \R_{	heta_m} . Moreover \det \Q = (-1)^q, and p, q, and the multiset \{	heta_1, \dots, 	heta_m\} are determined by \Q. \Q is normal, so @thm-real-normal-form already hands us a block diagonal matrix with 1 	imes 1 blocks [a] and 2 	imes 2 blocks \vLambda(\lambda). The blocks are unconstrained for a general normal matrix; here they are not, because the eigenvalues of an isometry lie on the unit circle. A real eigenvalue on the unit circle is \pm 1, and a conjugate pair on the unit circle is e^{\pm i	heta}, which turns the scaling block into a pure rotation. Then sort the \pm 1s to the front. The operator T_{\Q} on 
R^n satisfies T_{\Q}^{*} = T_{\Q	p} by @thm-matrix-of-adjoint, since the standard basis is orthonormal, so T_{\Q}^{*}T_{\Q} = T_{\Q	p\Q} = \id and likewise in the other order. Hence T_{\Q} is normal (@def-normal-operator), and by @thm-real-normal-form there is an orthonormal basis \sB of 
R^n in which \mtx{T_{\Q}}{\sB}{\sB} = [a_1] \oplus \cdots \oplus [a_r] \oplus \vLambda(\lambda_1) \oplus \cdots \oplus \vLambda(\lambda_m), where a_i \in 
R and \lambda_j = c_j + d_ji with d_j > 0. Let \P be the matrix whose columns are the vectors of \sB. Its columns are orthonormal, so \P \in \Orth(n) by @thm-isometry-characterizations (f), and \P	p\Q\P = \P^{-1}\Q\P = \mtx{T_{\Q}}{\sB}{\sB} by @thm-change-of-basis-maps. The blocks. A block diagonal matrix is triangular by blocks, so the eigenvalues of \mtx{T_{\Q}}{\sB}{\sB} over 
C are the a_i together with the roots of each \det(x\I_2 - \vLambda(\lambda_j)) = (x - c_j)^2 + d_j^2, namely \lambda_j and \conj{\lambda_j}. Now \Orth(n) = \Unit(n) \cap M_n(
R) by @prp-orthogonal-group-properties (a), so \Q is unitary, and every complex eigenvalue \lambda of \Q satisfies \lvert\lambdavert = 1 by @prp-isometry-eigenvalues-modulus-one applied to T_{\Q} on 
C^n. Therefore a_i = \pm 1 for each i, and c_j^2 + d_j^2 = 1 for each j. Since c_j^2 + d_j^2 = 1 and d_j > 0, there is a unique 	heta_j \in (0, \pi) with c_j = \cos	heta_j and d_j = \sin	heta_j, and then \vLambda(\lambda_j) = \R_{	heta_j}. Sorting. Let p be the number of i with a_i = 1 and q the number with a_i = -1, so p + q + 2m = n. Reordering the vectors of \sB so that the +1 blocks come first, then the -1 blocks, then the rotation blocks in pairs, leaves the basis orthonormal and permutes the diagonal blocks; the new \P is the old one with its columns permuted, still orthogonal. This gives the displayed form. The determinant and uniqueness. By @thm-det-multiplicative and @cor-det-similarity-invariant, \det \Q = \det(\P	p\Q\P), and the determinant of a block diagonal matrix is the product of the determinants of its blocks (@thm-det-block-triangular), which are 1, -1, and \det\R_{	heta_j} = \cos^2	heta_j + \sin^2	heta_j = 1. Hence \det\Q = (-1)^q. Finally, similar matrices have the same eigenvalues with the same multiplicities, and reading the eigenvalues off the displayed form gives 1 with multiplicity p, -1 with multiplicity q, and the pairs e^{\pm i	heta_j}; so p, q, and the 	heta_j are recovered from \Q alone. This proves the theorem. So an orthogonal matrix is, up to an orthogonal change of coordinates, nothing but a list of angles together with a count of reversed axes. The number q of reversed axes is not itself an invariant of the geometry — a -1 block and a -1 block together make -\I_2 = \R_{\pi}, a rotation by \pi — which is why the theorem demands 	heta_j 
eq \pi and keeps the -1s separate. What the determinant sees is only the parity of q. What is the canonical form of a \Q \in \Orth(2) with \det\Q = -1? Compare with @thm-orthogonal-2x2. Here p + q + 2m = 2 and (-1)^q = -1, so q is odd, forcing q = 1, p = 1, m = 0. The canonical form is \I_1 \oplus (-\I_1) = \diag(1, -1). Chapter 11 found that such a \Q is the reflection \M_{	heta} in a line L, fixing L and negating L^{\perp}; in the orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of @thm-orthogonal-2x2 (b) its matrix is exactly \diag(1, -1). Note what the canonical form drops: the angle of the mirror. All reflections of the plane are orthogonally similar to one another, and @exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-c1 makes this comparison precise. Rotations of space In dimension 3 the arithmetic p + q + 2m = 3 leaves very few possibilities, and they all look the same. [Orthogonal Matrices in Dimension Three] Let \Q \in \Orth(3). Then there are an orthonormal basis (\cvec{u}, \cvec{w}_1, \cvec{w}_2) of 
R^3 and an angle 	heta \in [0, \pi] such that, in that basis, the matrix of T_{\Q} is [1] \oplus \R_{	heta} \quad	ext{if } \det\Q = 1, \qquad [-1] \oplus \R_{	heta} \quad	ext{if } \det\Q = -1 . In particular every \Q \in \SO(3) fixes the line \Span(\cvec{u}) pointwise and rotates the plane \Span(\cvec{u})^{\perp} by 	heta. Write the canonical form of @thm-orthogonal-canonical-form, with p + q + 2m = 3 and \det\Q = (-1)^q. Case \det\Q = 1. Then q is even, so q \in \{0, 2\}. If q = 0 then p + 2m = 3, giving (p, m) = (3, 0) or (1, 1); if q = 2 then p = 1 and m = 0. The three forms are \I_3 = [1] \oplus \R_0, \qquad [1] \oplus \R_{	heta_1}, \qquad [1] \oplus (-\I_2) = [1] \oplus \R_{\pi}, and in every case p \ge 1, so the form is [1] \oplus \R_{	heta} with 	heta \in [0, \pi]. Case \det\Q = -1. Then q is odd, so q \in \{1, 3\}. If q = 1 then p + 2m = 2, giving (p, m) = (2, 0) or (0, 1); if q = 3 then p = m = 0. The three forms are [-1] \oplus \I_2 = [-1] \oplus \R_0, then [-1] \oplus \R_{	heta_1}, and -\I_3 = [-1] \oplus \R_{\pi}. In both cases the first basis vector \cvec{u} spans the \pm 1 eigenline and (\cvec{w}_1, \cvec{w}_2) is an orthonormal basis of \Span(\cvec{u})^{\perp}, which is what the last sentence asserts when \det\Q = 1. Chapter 11 proved the \SO(3) statement directly, as @thm-so3-rotation, by producing a real eigenvalue from the odd degree of the characteristic polynomial and then invoking the classification of \Orth(2). We do not repeat that argument: the point here is that the same conclusion falls out of the canonical form with no work at all, and that the same three lines also settle \det\Q = -1. An orthogonal matrix of determinant -1 in dimension 3 is a rotatory reflection: a rotation about an axis followed by the reflection in the plane perpendicular to it. Its two extreme cases are the plane reflection (	heta = 0) and the antipodal map -\I_3 (	heta = \pi). Composing rotations Two rotations of the plane about the origin compose into a rotation, and the angles add: \R_{\alpha}\R_{ eta} = \R_{\alpha+ eta}, so \SO(2) is abelian (Chapter 11). In dimension 3 the picture changes completely, because there is an axis to move as well as an angle to add.
