The invertible matrix theorem grows Chapter 2 collected the conditions equivalent to invertibility for an operator (@thm-invertible-operator-tfae); Chapter 3 gave the eight matrix conditions of the Invertible Matrix Theorem (@thm-invertible-tfae); Chapter 7 added the determinant (@thm-invertible-tfae-det) and Chapter 9 the eigenvalue 0 (@thm-invertible-tfae-eigen). Positivity adds a pair, and they are the ones used whenever a square system is attacked through least squares. [Invertible Matrix Theorem, with Positive Definiteness] Let \A \in M_n(F) with F = 
R or F = 
C. The following are equivalent, and each is equivalent to each of the conditions of @thm-invertible-tfae, @thm-invertible-tfae-det, and @thm-invertible-tfae-eigen. 1. \A is invertible. 2. \A^{*}\A \succ \O. 3. \A\A^{*} \succ \O. For a general \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), one always has \A^{*}\A \succeq \O, with \A^{*}\A \succ \O if and only if the columns of \A are linearly independent. Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). Then \A^{*}\A is positive semidefinite by @thm-psd-characterizations ((c) \Rightarrow (a)). Whether it is definite is decided by the identity \inner{\A^{*}\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{x}^{*}\A^{*}\A\cvec{x} = 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}^2, computed in the proof of @thm-psd-characterizations ((c) \Rightarrow (a)) and recorded in operator form in @exr-self-adjoint-operators-c1 (a): the left side is > 0 for every \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0} exactly when \A\cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0} for every \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}, that is, exactly when 
ul(\A) = \{\cvec{0}\}, that is, exactly when the columns of \A are linearly independent. The same conclusion comes from @lem-kernel-normal-equations, which says 
ul(\A^{*}\A) = 
ul(\A) and so lets one read the condition off \A directly. Now let \A be square. Then “
ul(\A) = \{\cvec{0}\}” is item (b) of @thm-invertible-tfae, which gives (a) \Leftrightarrow (b). Also \A is invertible if and only if \A^{*} is, since (\A^{-1})^{*} is a two-sided inverse of \A^{*} and conversely; applying (a) \Leftrightarrow (b) to \A^{*} therefore gives (a) \Leftrightarrow (c). The two new items look like a detour — why test \A^{*}\A when \A itself is available? Because \A^{*}\A is Hermitian and positive, and everything in this chapter applies to it. Chapter 11 already used it once, in the normal equations of least squares; Section 9 will use it again, to build the singular value decomposition of a matrix that is not even square, and that decomposition supplies the last item of the list: a square matrix is invertible exactly when none of its singular values is zero. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the definition of \A \succeq \O and of \A \succ \O, including every quantifier and the field. 2. Explain why clause (P1) cannot be dropped from the real definition, with a concrete matrix. 3. True or false: if \A is Hermitian and every leading principal minor of \A is \ge 0, then \A \succeq \O. Justify your answer. 4. Write down the three conditions of the 2 	imes 2 test for \A \succeq \O. 5. Name the item of @thm-psd-characterizations that says every positive semidefinite matrix is a Gram matrix. (a) \A \in M_n(F) with F = 
R or 
C is positive semidefinite if \A^{*} = \A and \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} \ge 0 for every \cvec{x} \in F^n; positive definite if \A^{*} = \A and \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} > 0 for every nonzero \cvec{x} \in F^n (@def-positive-semidefinite). (b) Because over 
R the quadratic form does not see the skew part. The quarter turn  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} has \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = 0 for every \cvec{x} \in 
R^2 and is not symmetric. (c) False. \diag(0, -1) has leading principal minors 0 and 0, and \inner{\A\cvec{e}_2}{\cvec{e}_2} = -1. All principal minors are needed (@thm-psd-characterizations (e)). (d) With \A =  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ \conj b & d\end{pmatrix} Hermitian: a \ge 0, d \ge 0, and ad - \lvert bvert^2 \ge 0. (e) Item (c): \A = \B^{*}\B, and \B^{*}\B is the Gram matrix of the columns of \B. B. Practice [B1: Determine the definiteness] For each matrix below, determine whether it is positive definite, positive semidefinite but not positive definite, or neither. Justify your answer. 1.  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix} over 
R. 2.  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix} over 
R. 3.  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \ -1 & 2 & -1 \ 0 & -1 & 2\end{pmatrix} over 
R. 4. The all-ones matrix \J \in M_3(
R). 5.  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix} over 
R. 6.  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1+i \ 1-i & 1\end{pmatrix} over 
C. (a) Positive definite. Symmetric, with leading principal minors 2 and 4 - 1 = 3, both positive (@thm-pd-characterizations (d)). (b) Neither. The leading principal minors are 0 and 0, which tempts one into “semidefinite”, but the principal minor \det \A_{\{2\},\{2\}} = -1 is negative, and \inner{\A\cvec{e}_2}{\cvec{e}_2} = -1 < 0. (c) Positive definite. Symmetric, with leading principal minors 2, 4 - 1 = 3, and 2\cdot 3 - (-1)(-2) = 4, all positive. (d) Positive semidefinite, not positive definite. \J = \1\1	p, which is @exm-psd-first-examples (b) with \cvec{x} = \1; so \inner{\J\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = \lvert\inner{\cvec{x}}{\1}vert^2 \ge 0. It vanishes at the nonzero \cvec{x} = (1, -1, 0), so it is not definite. (Equivalently, \det \J = 0.) (e) Neither: it is not symmetric, so (P1) fails and it is not in the class at all. Its quadratic form is identically 0, which shows how little the form sees over 
R. (f) Positive semidefinite, not positive definite. Hermitian, with a = 2 \ge 0, d = 1 \ge 0, and ad - \lvert bvert^2 = 2 - 2 = 0. The determinant is 0, so definiteness fails; indeed \A(1+i, -2) = \cvec{0}. [B2: A parameter] For which t \in 
R is \A(t) =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & t & 0 \ t & 2 & t \ 0 & t & 3 \end{pmatrix} positive definite? Justify your answer. \A(t) is symmetric for every real t, so Sylvester’s criterion applies (@thm-pd-characterizations (d)). The leading principal minors are \det \A_1 = 1, \qquad \det \A_2 = 2 - t^2, \qquad \det \A_3 = 6 - 4t^2 , the last by expansion along the first row: 1\cdot(6 - t^2) - t\cdot(3t - 0) = 6 - 4t^2. All three are positive exactly when t^2 < 2 and t^2 < 3/2, that is when t^2 < 3/2. Hence \A(t) \succ \O if and only if \lvert tvert < \sqrt{6}/2. At t = \sqrt{6}/2 the matrix is positive semidefinite but singular, and for \lvert tvert > \sqrt{6}/2 the determinant is negative, so \A(t) has an odd number of negative eigenvalues and is not even semidefinite. [B3: The inverse of a positive definite matrix] Let \A \in M_n(F) with \A \succ \O. Prove that \A is invertible and that \A^{-1} \succ \O. By @thm-pd-characterizations (b), every eigenvalue of \A is positive, so 0 
otin \spec(\A) and \A is invertible (@thm-invertible-tfae-eigen). Then (\A^{-1})^{*} = (\A^{*})^{-1} = \A^{-1}, so \A^{-1} is Hermitian. Apply @prp-congruence-positivity (b) with \S = \A^{-1}, which is invertible: \S^{*}\A\S = \A^{-1}\A\A^{-1} = \A^{-1} \succ \O . (Alternatively: the eigenvalues of \A^{-1} are the reciprocals 1/\lambda_i of those of \A, hence positive, and @thm-pd-characterizations (b) applies again.) C. Going deeper [C1: Zero trace forces zero] Let \A \in M_n(F) with \A \succeq \O. 1. Prove that a_{ii} \ge 0 for every i, and that 	r \A \ge 0. 2. Prove that if 	r \A = 0 then \A = \O. 3. Deduce that if \A \succeq \O and -\A \succeq \O, then \A = \O. (a) a_{ii} = \cvec{e}_i^{*}\A\cvec{e}_i = \inner{\A\cvec{e}_i}{\cvec{e}_i} \ge 0 by (P2). Summing, 	r \A = \sum_i a_{ii} \ge 0. (b) Write \A = \U\D\U^{*} with \U unitary and \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n) the eigenvalues (@cor-spectral-complex-matrix, @cor-spectral-real-matrix). Then 	r \A = 	r(\D\U^{*}\U) = 	r \D = \sum_i\lambda_i by @thm-trace-properties, and each \lambda_i \ge 0 by @thm-psd-characterizations (b). A sum of nonnegative reals is 0 only if every term is 0, so \D = \O and hence \A = \O. Alternatively, without eigenvalues: by (a) each a_{ii} \ge 0, so 	r \A = 0 forces every a_{ii} = 0. Writing \A = \B^{*}\B (@thm-psd-characterizations (c)), the i-th diagonal entry is 
orm{\cvec{b}_i}^2 for the i-th column \cvec{b}_i of \B; so every column of \B is \cvec{0}, that is \B = \O and \A = \O. (c) If both \A \succeq \O and -\A \succeq \O, then by (a) 	r \A \ge 0 and 	r(-\A) = -	r \A \ge 0, so 	r \A = 0 and (b) gives \A = \O. [C2: The cone of positive matrices] Let \cP_n \subseteq M_n(F) be the set of positive semidefinite matrices. 1. Prove that if \A, \B \in \cP_n and c \ge 0 is real, then \A + \B \in \cP_n and c\A \in \cP_n. (A set with these two properties is a convex cone: it contains (1-t)\A + t\B for 0 \le t \le 1 as well.) 2. Prove that \cP_n contains no line through \O: if \A \in \cP_n and -\A \in \cP_n then \A = \O. 3. Prove that \cP_n is closed under congruence: if \A \in \cP_n and \S \in M_n(F), then \S^{*}\A\S \in \cP_n. Give an example showing that \cP_n is not closed under multiplication. Hint for (c): for the example, two positive semidefinite matrices whose product is not even Hermitian will do. (a) Sums and real multiples of Hermitian matrices are Hermitian. For every \cvec{x}, \inner{(\A + \B)\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} + \inner{\B\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} \ge 0 , and \inner{c\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = c\inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} \ge 0 since c \ge 0. Convexity follows by taking c = 1 - t and c = t and adding. (b) This is @exr-positive-definite-matrices-c1 (c). (c) Immediate from @prp-congruence-positivity (a). For the failure of multiplicativity, take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} , both positive semidefinite (\A = \cvec{e}_1\cvec{e}_1	p and \B = \1\1	p). Then \A\B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} , which is not symmetric, so it is not positive semidefinite — it fails (P1), never mind (P2). Section 2 shows what does survive: 	r(\A\B) \ge 0, and \A\B \succeq \O whenever \A and \B commute. [C3: The largest entry sits on the diagonal] Let \A \in M_n(F) with \A \succeq \O. 1. Prove that \lvert a_{ij}vert^2 \le a_{ii}a_{jj} for all i, j. 2. Deduce that if a_{ii} = 0 for some i, then the whole i-th row and i-th column of \A are zero. 3. Deduce that \max_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij}vert = \max_i a_{ii}. Hint for (a): look at a 2 	imes 2 principal submatrix. (a) For i = j the claim is a_{ii}^2 \le a_{ii}^2. For i 
e j, take I = \{i, j\}. By the proof of @thm-psd-characterizations ((a) \Rightarrow (e)), \A_{I,I} \succeq \O, and @exm-two-by-two-criterion gives a_{ii}a_{jj} - \lvert a_{ij}vert^2 = \det \A_{I,I} \ge 0. (b) If a_{ii} = 0, then (a) gives \lvert a_{ij}vert^2 \le 0 \cdot a_{jj} = 0 for every j, so a_{ij} = 0; and a_{ji} = \conj{a_{ij}} = 0 since \A is Hermitian. (c) Let M = \max_i a_{ii}, a maximum of nonnegative reals by @exr-positive-definite-matrices-c1 (a). By (a), \lvert a_{ij}vert \le \sqrt{a_{ii}a_{jj}} \le M for all i, j, so \max_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij}vert \le M. The reverse inequality holds because the diagonal entries are among the entries. Hence the two maxima are equal.

title: 13.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content:
Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization A nonnegative real number has exactly one nonnegative square root, and it is the reason “nonnegative” is a useful class of numbers at all: it lets us take lengths, define standard deviations, and undo a squaring. Section 1 produced the matrix analogue as one clause of a theorem. This section makes it an object with a name, adds the one property the clause did not mention — that the square root is a polynomial in the matrix — and then turns the same idea into the triangular factorization that elimination discovers, the one Chapter 3 promised and could not yet explain. Throughout, F = 
R or F = 
C, and all matrices are over F. The positive square root @thm-psd-characterizations (d) already says that a positive semidefinite \A has exactly one positive semidefinite square root. That is an existence-and-uniqueness statement, so by the usual convention it deserves a notation. The square root of a positive matrix is what you get by taking square roots of its eigenvalues and leaving the eigenvectors alone. The Positive Square Root Let \A \in M_n(F) with \A \succeq \O. Then there is exactly one \C \in M_n(F) with \C \succeq \O and \C^2 = \A. We write \C = \A^{1/2}, also \sqrt{\A}. Moreover: 1. \A^{1/2} = p(\A) for some polynomial p with real coefficients (the nodes \lambda_i and the values \sqrt{\lambda_i} are real, so the interpolation of @thm-lagrange-interpolation may be run over 
R, and 
R[x] \subseteq 
C[x]); 2. \A^{1/2}\B = \B\A^{1/2} for every \B \in M_n(F) with \A\B = \B\A; 3. 
ul(\A^{1/2}) = 
ul(\A) and ank \A^{1/2} = ank \A; in particular \A^{1/2} is invertible if and only if \A is. The eigenvalues of \A^{1/2} are the nonnegative square roots of those of \A, with the same eigenvectors. Existence and uniqueness are Section 1. What is new is (a), and it is the reason (b) is free. On the spectrum, the square root is just a function \lambda \mapsto \sqrt\lambda defined at finitely many points, and a function defined at finitely many points is a polynomial — that is Lagrange interpolation from Chapter 6. The functional calculus of Chapter 12 says that applying a polynomial to \A and applying the corresponding function to the spectrum are the same operation, so the interpolating polynomial evaluated at \A is the square root. Once \A^{1/2} is a polynomial in \A, anything commuting with \A commutes with it, with no further work. Existence and uniqueness are @thm-psd-characterizations (d). (a) Let \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k be the distinct eigenvalues of \A and let \A = \sum_i\lambda_i\P_i be its spectral resolution (@def-spectral-resolution, @thm-spectral-resolution), which exists because a Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Every \lambda_i is a nonnegative real number by @thm-psd-characterizations (b), so the numbers \sqrt{\lambda_i} are defined and real. Let f(\lambda) = \sqrt{\lambda} on \spec(\A). By @thm-functional-calculus-properties (b) and (a), f(\A)^2 = (f^2)(\A) = \A , and by (c) and (d), f(\A) is Hermitian with spectrum \{\sqrt{\lambda_1}, \dots, \sqrt{\lambda_k}\} \subseteq [0, \infty), so f(\A) \succeq \O by @thm-psd-characterizations (b). Uniqueness gives f(\A) = \A^{1/2}. The numbers \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k are distinct, so by Lagrange interpolation (@thm-lagrange-interpolation) there is a polynomial p of degree at most k - 1, with real coefficients, such that p(\lambda_i) = \sqrt{\lambda_i} for every i. By @thm-functional-calculus-properties (a), p(\A) = \sum_i p(\lambda_i)\P_i = f(\A) = \A^{1/2}. (b) Suppose \A\B = \B\A. Then \B commutes with every power of \A, hence with every polynomial in \A, hence with p(\A) = \A^{1/2}. (c) If \A^{1/2}\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} then \A\cvec{x} = \A^{1/2}(\A^{1/2}\cvec{x}) = \cvec{0}. Conversely, if \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}, then since \A^{1/2} is Hermitian, 
orm{\A^{1/2}\cvec{x}}^2 = \inner{\A^{1/2}\cvec{x}}{\A^{1/2}\cvec{x}} = \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = 0 , so \A^{1/2}\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}. Hence the two null spaces agree, and the ranks agree by @thm-rank-nullity-matrix. Invertibility is the case 
ul = \{\cvec{0}\} (@thm-invertible-tfae). The last sentence is the spectral mapping statement of @thm-functional-calculus-properties (d) for f = \sqrt{\ }. Two routes to the same matrix, then, and both are worth practicing: assemble \sum_i\sqrt{\lambda_i}\P_i from the projections, or find one interpolating polynomial and substitute. [Two Square Roots] Compute \A^{1/2} for 1. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 13 & 12 \ 12 & 13\end{pmatrix}; 2. \B =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}, in each case by the spectral resolution and by a polynomial. (a) \A is symmetric. Since \A(1,1) = (25, 25) and \A(1,-1) = (1,-1), the eigenvalues are 25 and 1, with eigenlines spanned by (1,1) and (1,-1). Both are positive, so \A \succ \O. The orthogonal projections onto the two eigenlines are \P_1 = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \P_2 = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}, so \A = 25\P_1 + \P_2 and \A^{1/2} = 5\P_1 + 1\cdot\P_2 =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix} . By the polynomial route: we need p with p(25) = 5 and p(1) = 1. The line through the two points is p(x) = 	frac16 x + 	frac56, and 	frac16\A + 	frac56\I = 	frac16 egin{pmatrix} 18 & 12 \ 12 & 18\end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix} . Check:  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 13 & 12 \ 12 & 13\end{pmatrix}. (b) Here \B = \I + \J with \J the all-ones matrix. Since \J\1 = 3\1 and \J\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} for every \cvec{x} with entries summing to 0, the eigenvalues of \J are 3 and 0, so those of \B are 4 and 1; both are positive, so \B \succ \O. We need p with p(4) = 2 and p(1) = 1, namely p(x) = 	frac13x + 	frac23, giving \B^{1/2} = 	frac13\B + 	frac23\I = 	frac13 egin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 4 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 4\end{pmatrix} . Check by squaring: the diagonal entry of the square is 	frac19(16 + 1 + 1) = 2 and an off-diagonal entry is 	frac19(4 + 4 + 1) = 1, which reproduces \B. Only two distinct eigenvalues appear, so a polynomial of degree 1 suffices even though \B is 3 	imes 3. \A^{1/2} is not the entrywise square root, and it is not the only square root. For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 13 & 12 \ 12 & 13\end{pmatrix} the entrywise roots  egin{pmatrix} \sqrt{13} & \sqrt{12} \ \sqrt{12} & \sqrt{13}\end{pmatrix} form a matrix whose square is not \A. And \A has other square roots: -\A^{1/2} is one, and 5\P_1 - \P_2 =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \ 3 & 2\end{pmatrix} is another symmetric one. The word positive in “positive square root” is what makes the object unique; drop it and this \A, whose two eigenvalues are distinct and positive, has four symmetric square roots, one for each choice of sign on each eigenline. When an eigenvalue repeats there are infinitely many, symmetric ones included: every reflection  egin{psmallmatrix} \cos	heta & \sin	heta \ \sin	heta & -\cos	heta\end{psmallmatrix} is a symmetric square root of \I_2. Let \A \succeq \O and let \U be unitary. What is (\U^{*}\A\U)^{1/2}? \U^{*}\A^{1/2}\U. It is positive semidefinite by @prp-congruence-positivity (a), since \A^{1/2} \succeq \O, and its square is \U^{*}\A^{1/2}\U\U^{*}\A^{1/2}\U = \U^{*}\A\U because \U\U^{*} = \I. Uniqueness in @thm-psd-square-root does the rest. In words: the square root does not care which orthonormal coordinates we use, which is exactly what one wants of an operation defined on the spectrum. The absolute value of a matrix A complex number has a modulus \lvert zvert = \sqrt{\conj{z}z}, and the polar form z = e^{i	heta}\lvert zvert splits it into a rotation and a nonnegative stretch. Section 10 will split a matrix the same way, and the stretching factor it needs is built now. For any matrix, square or not, \A^{*}\A is positive semidefinite (@thm-invertible-tfae-positive), so it has a square root. [Absolute Value of a Matrix] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). The absolute value of \A is \lvert\Avert \coloneqq (\A^{*}\A)^{1/2} \in M_n(F) , the unique positive semidefinite square root of \A^{*}\A. Note the size: \lvert\Avert is n 	imes n, not m 	imes n, because \A^{*}\A acts on the domain of \A. It is well defined because \A^{*}\A \succeq \O and @thm-psd-square-root gives exactly one root. [What the absolute value preserves] Let \A \in M_{m	imes n}(F). Then for every \cvec{x} \in F^n, 
orm{\lvert\Avert\cvec{x}} = 
orm{\A\cvec{x}} . Consequently 
ul\lvert\Avert = 
ul \A and ank\lvert\Avert = ank \A. Since \lvert\Avert is Hermitian and \lvert\Avert^2 = \A^{*}\A, 
orm{\lvert\Avert\cvec{x}}^2 = \inner{\lvert\Avert^2\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = \inner{\A^{*}\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}^2 , using @lem-conjugate-transpose-pairing twice. Both sides are nonnegative reals, so the norms agree. Hence \lvert\Avert\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} if and only if \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}, and the rank statement follows by @thm-rank-nullity-matrix. So \lvert\Avert does exactly what \A does to lengths, and nothing else. That single identity is the whole engine of the polar decomposition: the map \lvert\Avert\cvec{x} \mapsto \A\cvec{x} preserves norms, so it extends to a unitary matrix, and \A = \W\lvert\Avert follows. [Two Absolute Values] Compute \lvert\Avert for \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} and for \B =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 4 & 0\end{pmatrix}, both over 
R. For the quarter turn, \A	p\A = \I, so \lvert\Avert = \I^{1/2} = \I. This is right: a rotation changes no length, so the matrix that does the same thing to lengths and nothing else is the identity. For \B, \B	p\B =  egin{pmatrix} 25 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}, whose positive square root is \lvert\Bvert =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}. Check @prp-absolute-value-properties: 
orm{\B\cvec{x}} = 
orm{(3x_1, 4x_1)} = 5\lvert x_1vert = 
orm{\lvert\Bvert\cvec{x}}. Both have rank 1 and null space \Span(\cvec{e}_2). \lvert\Avert is not the entrywise absolute value, and \lvert\A\Bvert 
e \lvert\Avert\lvert\Bvert. For the quarter turn above, the entrywise absolute value is  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}, while \lvert\Avert = \I. For the product rule, take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} . Then \A\B = \O, so \lvert\A\Bvert = \O, while \lvert\Avert = \A and \lvert\Bvert = 	frac1{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}, giving \lvert\Avert\lvert\Bvert = 	frac1{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} 
e \O . That product is not even Hermitian, so it could not be the absolute value of anything. The modulus of a product of numbers is the product of the moduli because numbers commute; matrices do not. Cholesky: elimination on a positive definite matrix Chapter 3 ran elimination on a symmetric matrix and found that the two triangular factors are secretly the same one: \A = \L\D\L	p (@thm-ldlt). It then observed that when every entry of \D is positive one can split \D = \D^{1/2}\D^{1/2} and write \A = (\L\D^{1/2})(\L\D^{1/2})	p, called this the Cholesky factorization, and promised that Chapter 13 would connect it with positive definite matrices. Here is the connection, and it is the best kind: the hypothesis “every entry of \D is positive” is not an extra assumption at all. It holds exactly when \A is positive definite, and it can be checked while the elimination runs. [Cholesky Factorization] Let \A \in M_n(F) be Hermitian. Then \A \succ \O if and only if \A = \L\L^{*} for some lower triangular \L \in M_n(F) whose diagonal entries are real and strictly positive. In that case \L is unique. (\Leftarrow) is one line: such an \L is invertible, and \L\L^{*} = (\L^{*})^{*}\L^{*} is @thm-pd-characterizations (c) with \B = \L^{*}. (\Rightarrow) is Chapter 3’s elimination with its hypothesis supplied, run symmetrically. One pass clears the first column and the first row at once and leaves a smaller matrix that is again positive definite, so an induction produces \A = \M\D\M^{*} with \M unit lower triangular and every pivot d_k > 0. Absorbing \D^{1/2} into \M finishes it. For uniqueness, strip the positive diagonal off each candidate \L; what is left is an LU factorization of \A, and Chapter 3 already proved those unique. (\Leftarrow) Suppose \A = \L\L^{*} with \L lower triangular and every \ell_{kk} > 0. Then \L is invertible by @lem-triangular-invertible, hence so is \L^{*}, and \A = (\L^{*})^{*}\L^{*} is positive definite by @thm-pd-characterizations ((c) \Rightarrow (a)). (\Rightarrow) Suppose \A \succ \O. There are a unit lower triangular \M \in M_n(F) and a diagonal \D = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) whose entries are real and strictly positive, with \A = \M\D\M^{*}. Induction on n. For n = 1, the single entry is a_{11} = \inner{\A\cvec{e}_1}{\cvec{e}_1} > 0 by (P2) of @def-positive-semidefinite in its strict form, so \M = (1) and \D = (a_{11}) will do. Let n \ge 2. Since \A^{*} = \A, we may write \A =  egin{pmatrix} \alpha & \cvec{c}^{*} \ \cvec{c} & \A' \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \alpha = a_{11},\quad \cvec{c} \in F^{n-1},\quad \A' \in M_{n-1}(F)\ 	ext{Hermitian} . Here \alpha = \inner{\A\cvec{e}_1}{\cvec{e}_1} > 0, so \alpha^{-1} exists and is a positive real number. Put \S \coloneqq \A' - \alpha^{-1}\cvec{c}\cvec{c}^{*} , which is Hermitian, since (\cvec{c}\cvec{c}^{*})^{*} = \cvec{c}\cvec{c}^{*} and \alpha is real. The smaller matrix is again positive definite. Let \cvec{y} \in F^{n-1} with \cvec{y} 
e \cvec{0}, set t = -\alpha^{-1}\cvec{c}^{*}\cvec{y} and \cvec{x} = (t, \cvec{y}) \in F^n, which is nonzero because \cvec{y} is. Multiplying out in blocks (@thm-block-multiplication), \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x} = \alpha\lvert tvert^2 + \conj{t}\,\cvec{c}^{*}\cvec{y} + \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{c}\,t + \cvec{y}^{*}\A'\cvec{y} . With \cvec{c}^{*}\cvec{y} = -\alpha t and \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{c} = \conj{\cvec{c}^{*}\cvec{y}} = -\alpha\conj{t}, the first three terms are \alpha\lvert tvert^2 - \alpha\lvert tvert^2 - \alpha\lvert tvert^2 = -\alpha\lvert tvert^2 = -\alpha^{-1}\lvert \cvec{c}^{*}\cvec{y}vert^2 , so \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{y}^{*} igl(\A' - \alpha^{-1}\cvec{c}\cvec{c}^{*} igr)\cvec{y} = \inner{\S\cvec{y}}{\cvec{y}}. The left side is > 0 because \A \succ \O and \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}. Hence \S \succ \O. The induction step. By the induction hypothesis, \S = \M'\D'(\M')^{*} with \M' \in M_{n-1}(F) unit lower triangular and \D' = \diag(d_2, \dots, d_n) real with positive entries. Put \M =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & \cvec{0}	p \ \alpha^{-1}\cvec{c} & \M' \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \D =  egin{pmatrix} \alpha & \cvec{0}	p \ \cvec{0} & \D' \end{pmatrix} . Then \M is unit lower triangular and \D is diagonal with the positive real entries \alpha, d_2, \dots, d_n. Block multiplication (@thm-block-multiplication) gives \M\D\M^{*} =  egin{pmatrix} \alpha & \cvec{0}	p \ \cvec{c} & \M'\D' \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} 1 & \alpha^{-1}\cvec{c}^{*} \ \cvec{0} & (\M')^{*} \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \alpha & \cvec{c}^{*} \ \cvec{c} & \alpha^{-1}\cvec{c}\cvec{c}^{*} + \M'\D'(\M')^{*} \end{pmatrix} , and \alpha^{-1}\cvec{c}\cvec{c}^{*} + \M'\D'(\M')^{*} = \alpha^{-1}\cvec{c}\cvec{c}^{*} + \S = \A'. So \M\D\M^{*} = \A, which proves the claim. The claim is one pass of elimination performed symmetrically, and d_1 = \alpha, d_2, \dots, d_n are its pivots. Over 
R it is the \L\D\L	p factorization of @thm-ldlt with the hypothesis that makes every pivot positive. Write d_1, \dots, d_n for the diagonal entries of \D, all of them positive real numbers. Then \D^{1/2} \coloneqq \diag(\sqrt{d_1}, \dots, \sqrt{d_n}) is a real matrix, and putting \L = \M\D^{1/2} gives a lower triangular matrix — its (i, j)-entry is m_{ij}\sqrt{d_j}, which vanishes for i < j — whose k-th diagonal entry is \sqrt{d_k} > 0, and \L\L^{*} = \M\D^{1/2}(\D^{1/2})^{*}\M^{*} = \M\D\M^{*} = \A . Uniqueness. Suppose \A = \L_1\L_1^{*} = \L_2\L_2^{*}, with each \L_i lower triangular with positive diagonal entries. Split off the diagonal: write \vDelta_i = \diag((\L_i)_{11}, \dots, (\L_i)_{nn}), a real diagonal matrix with positive entries, and \M_i = \L_i\vDelta_i^{-1}, which is lower triangular with every diagonal entry 1. Then \L_i = \M_i\vDelta_i and \A = \M_i\vDelta_i^2\M_i^{*} = \M_i igl(\vDelta_i^2\M_i^{*} igr) . The second factor is upper triangular, its (k, l)-entry being (\vDelta_i^2)_{kk}\conj{(\M_i)_{lk}}, which vanishes for k > l. So for i = 1 and i = 2 this displays an LU factorization of \A, which is invertible: \L_1 is triangular with nonzero diagonal, hence invertible by @lem-triangular-invertible, and \A = \L_1\L_1^{*} is a product of two invertible matrices. By @thm-lu-unique the two agree: \M_1 = \M_2 \qquad	ext{and}\qquad \vDelta_1^2\M_1^{*} = \vDelta_2^2\M_2^{*} . Canceling the invertible \M_1^{*} = \M_2^{*} gives \vDelta_1^2 = \vDelta_2^2, and since both have positive diagonal entries, \vDelta_1 = \vDelta_2. Hence \L_1 = \M_1\vDelta_1 = \M_2\vDelta_2 = \L_2. This proves the theorem. The pivots are determinant ratios. For i, j \le k, a term of (\M\D\M^{*})_{ij} = \sum_l m_{il}(\D\M^{*})_{lj} with l > k has l > i and so m_{il} = 0; the sum therefore stops at l = k, which says that the leading principal submatrices multiply: \A_k = \M_k\D_k(\M^{*})_k = \M_k\D_k\M_k^{*}. Taking determinants with @thm-det-multiplicative and @thm-det-triangular gives \det \A_k = d_1\cdots d_k, so d_1 = \det \A_1 and d_k = \det \A_k/\det \A_{k-1} for k \ge 2. Read the other way, this is Sylvester’s criterion (@thm-pd-characterizations (d)) appearing inside the elimination: the leading minors are positive exactly when the pivots are. Reading the equation \A = \L\L^{*} entry by entry turns it into a recipe, and the recipe is the standard way to factor by hand. Comparing the (j, j) entry of both sides gives a_{jj} = \sum_{k \le j}\lvert \ell_{jk}vert^2, and comparing the (i, j) entry for i > j gives a_{ij} = \sum_{k \le j}\ell_{ik}\conj{\ell_{jk}}. Solving each for its one new unknown, column by column:  egin{aligned} \ell_{jj} &= \Bigl(a_{jj} - 	extstyle\sum_{k < j}\lvert \ell_{jk}vert^2\Bigr)^{1/2}, \ \ell_{ij} &= \Bigl(a_{ij} - 	extstyle\sum_{k < j}\ell_{ik}\conj{\ell_{jk}}\Bigr) ig/\ell_{jj} \qquad (i > j). \end{aligned} [A Cholesky Factorization, and One That Fails] Factor \A =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & -2 & 6 \ -2 & 5 & -1 \ 6 & -1 & 26 \end{pmatrix} as \L\L	p, and run the same algorithm on the matrix \A' obtained from \A by changing the (3,3) entry to 9. Column 1. \ell_{11} = \sqrt{4} = 2; then \ell_{21} = -2/2 = -1 and \ell_{31} = 6/2 = 3. Column 2. \ell_{22} = \sqrt{5 - (-1)^2} = \sqrt4 = 2; then \ell_{32} =  rac{a_{32} - \ell_{31}\ell_{21}}{\ell_{22}} =  rac{-1 - 3(-1)}{2} = 1 . Column 3. \ell_{33} = \sqrt{26 - 3^2 - 1^2} = \sqrt{16} = 4. So \L =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \ -1 & 2 & 0 \ 3 & 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, and multiplying back confirms \L\L	p = \A. The diagonal entries 2, 2, 4 are positive, so \A \succ \O by @thm-cholesky; their squares 4, 4, 16 are the pivots d_k = \det\A_k/\det\A_{k-1}, consistent with \det \A_1 = 4, \det\A_2 = 16, \det \A = 256. The failure. For \A', columns 1 and 2 are unchanged, and the last step asks for \ell_{33} = \sqrt{9 - 3^2 - 1^2} = \sqrt{-1} , which is not a positive real number. The algorithm stops, and by @thm-cholesky its stopping is a proof: \A' is not positive definite. Indeed \det \A' = -16 < 0, so Sylvester’s criterion fails at k = 3. The example shows the practical point. The algorithm is the test. To decide whether a numerical Hermitian matrix is positive definite, one does not compute eigenvalues and one does not compute n determinants; one starts the Cholesky recursion and watches whether every quantity under a square root stays positive. Sylvester’s criterion guarantees that this verdict is correct, because d_1\cdots d_k = \det \A_k. Two remarks on cost, both of which belong properly to Chapter 24. First, Cholesky does about half the arithmetic of a general LU factorization, because it computes only \L and never the second triangular factor. Second, and less obvious, it needs no pivoting: the recursion above never divides by something that positive definiteness allows to be zero, so the row swaps that Chapter 3 introduced for stability are simply not required here. Positive definiteness is the one structural hypothesis under which elimination is unconditionally safe. Cholesky needs definiteness, not just semidefiniteness, for uniqueness. The matrix \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} is positive semidefinite and does factor as \L\L	p, for instance with \L = \A. But the diagonal entry \ell_{11} = 0 is not positive, so @thm-cholesky does not apply — and indeed uniqueness fails, since  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} and  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix} are two different lower triangular matrices \L with \L\L	p = \A. Also note that the \L of Cholesky is not the \L of Chapter 3’s LU factorization: the latter is unit lower triangular, and the two differ by the factor \D^{1/2}. Let \A \succ \O with Cholesky factor \L. What is \det \A in terms of \L, and what is the Cholesky factor of \A^{-1}? \det \A = \det\L\,\det\L^{*} = \lvert\ell_{11}\cdots\ell_{nn}vert^2 = (\ell_{11}\cdots\ell_{nn})^2, by @thm-det-multiplicative and @thm-det-triangular, the last step because the \ell_{kk} are positive reals. For the inverse, \A^{-1} = (\L\L^{*})^{-1} = (\L^{*})^{-1}\L^{-1} = \M\M^{*} with \M = (\L^{*})^{-1}, which is upper triangular; so this is not itself a Cholesky factorization. The Cholesky factor of \A^{-1} is a different matrix, which is why solving \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} is done by two triangular substitutions with \L rather than by inverting anything. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State what \A^{1/2} is, including the two conditions that pin it down. 2. Define \lvert\Avert for \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and say what size it is. 3. State the Cholesky factorization theorem. 4. True or false: every Hermitian matrix has exactly one Hermitian square root. Justify your answer. 5. Explain in one sentence why the Cholesky algorithm is a test for positive definiteness. (a) For \A \succeq \O, \A^{1/2} is the unique matrix \C with \C \succeq \O and \C^2 = \A (@thm-psd-square-root). Both conditions are needed: positivity, and squaring to \A. (b) \lvert\Avert = (\A^{*}\A)^{1/2}, which is n 	imes n, the size of the domain of \A (@def-matrix-absolute-value). (c) A Hermitian \A is positive definite if and only if \A = \L\L^{*} with \L lower triangular with positive real diagonal entries, and then \L is unique (@thm-cholesky). (d) False, twice over. A Hermitian matrix with a negative eigenvalue has no Hermitian square root at all, since \C^2 \succeq \O always. And a positive semidefinite \A with two distinct eigenvalues has at least two Hermitian square roots, \pm\A^{1/2}. Uniqueness needs the root itself to be positive semidefinite. (e) Because the algorithm computes \ell_{jj}^2 = \det\A_j/\det\A_{j-1} one step at a time, so it produces a positive real \ell_{jj} at every step exactly when Sylvester’s criterion holds. B. Practice [B1: Square roots] Compute \A^{1/2} for each of the following, and in each case give a polynomial p with p(\A) = \A^{1/2}. 1. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \ 4 & 5\end{pmatrix}. 2. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 10 & -6 \ -6 & 10\end{pmatrix}. (a) \A(1,1) = (9,9) and \A(1,-1) = (1,-1), so the eigenvalues are 9 and 1 with eigenlines \Span((1,1)) and \Span((1,-1)); both positive, so \A \succ \O. With \P_1, \P_2 the projections onto those lines, \A^{1/2} = 3\P_1 + \P_2 =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix} . For the polynomial, solve p(9) = 3, p(1) = 1: p(x) = 	frac14x + 	frac34, and 	frac14\A + 	frac34\I =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}. Check:  egin{pmatrix} 2&1\1&2\end{pmatrix}^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 5&4\4&5\end{pmatrix}. (b) \A(1,-1) = (16,-16) and \A(1,1) = (4,4), so the eigenvalues are 16 and 4. Then \A^{1/2} = 4\cdot	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix} + 2\cdot	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \ -1 & 3\end{pmatrix} . For the polynomial, p(16) = 4 and p(4) = 2 give p(x) = 	frac16x + 	frac43, and 	frac16\A + 	frac43\I =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \ -1 & 3\end{pmatrix}. Check:  egin{pmatrix} 3&-1\-1&3\end{pmatrix}^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 10&-6\-6&10\end{pmatrix}. [B2: Cholesky, and a planted failure] 1. Find the Cholesky factor of \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \ 2 & 5 & 1 \ -1 & 1 & 14\end{pmatrix}, and hence write down \det \A. 2. Run the same algorithm on \A' =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \ 2 & 5 & 1 \ -1 & 1 & 9\end{pmatrix} and say what the outcome proves. (a) \ell_{11} = \sqrt1 = 1, \ell_{21} = 2, \ell_{31} = -1. Then \ell_{22} = \sqrt{5 - 4} = 1 and \ell_{32} =  rac{1 - (-1)(2)}{1} = 3 . Finally \ell_{33} = \sqrt{14 - 1 - 9} = \sqrt4 = 2. So \L =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 2 & 1 & 0 \ -1 & 3 & 2\end{pmatrix}, and \L\L	p = \A. All diagonal entries are positive, so \A \succ \O. By the Quick check above, \det \A = (1\cdot 1\cdot 2)^2 = 4. (b) Columns 1 and 2 are identical, and the last step asks for \ell_{33} = \sqrt{9 - 1 - 9} = \sqrt{-1}. The algorithm fails, so \A' is not positive definite (@thm-cholesky). Confirming by Sylvester: \det \A'_1 = 1, \det \A'_2 = 1, and \det \A' = 1\cdot 44 - 2\cdot 19 - 7 = -1 < 0. [B3: An absolute value] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
R). Compute \lvert\Avert, verify 
orm{\lvert\Avert\cvec{x}} = 
orm{\A\cvec{x}} directly, and determine whether \lvert\Avert = \A. \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}, whose eigenvalues are 4 and 0 with eigenlines \Span((1,1)) and \Span((1,-1)). Hence \lvert\Avert = 2\cdot	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} + \O =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \A . Directly: \A\cvec{x} = (x_1 + x_2)(1,1), so 
orm{\A\cvec{x}} = \sqrt2\,\lvert x_1 + x_2vert, and the same computation applies to \lvert\Avert = \A. The equality \lvert\Avert = \A is no accident: \A \succeq \O here, and for a positive semidefinite \A one has \A^{*}\A = \A^2, so \lvert\Avert = (\A^2)^{1/2} = \A by uniqueness in @thm-psd-square-root. C. Going deeper [C1: The trace of a product of positive matrices] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) with \A \succeq \O and \B \succeq \O. 1. Prove that 	r(\A\B) = 	r(\A^{1/2}\B\A^{1/2}), and deduce that 	r(\A\B) \ge 0. 2. Prove that 	r(\A\B) = 0 if and only if \A\B = \O. Hint for (b): a positive semidefinite matrix of trace 0 is \O. (a) By @thm-trace-properties, 	r(\X\Y) = 	r(\Y\X). With \X = \A^{1/2} and \Y = \A^{1/2}\B, 	r(\A\B) = 	r(\A^{1/2}\A^{1/2}\B) = 	r(\A^{1/2}\B\A^{1/2}) . Now \A^{1/2}\B\A^{1/2} = (\A^{1/2})^{*}\B\A^{1/2} \succeq \O by @prp-congruence-positivity (a), since \A^{1/2} is Hermitian. The trace of a positive semidefinite matrix is \ge 0 by @exr-positive-definite-matrices-c1 (a). Hence 	r(\A\B) \ge 0. (b) (\Leftarrow) is clear. (\Rightarrow) Suppose 	r(\A\B) = 0. By (a), \C \coloneqq \A^{1/2}\B\A^{1/2} \succeq \O and 	r \C = 0, so \C = \O by @exr-positive-definite-matrices-c1 (b). Put \M = \B^{1/2}\A^{1/2}. Then \M^{*}\M = \A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}\B^{1/2}\A^{1/2} = \A^{1/2}\B\A^{1/2} = \C = \O , so \M = \O by @lem-kernel-normal-equations (its null space is all of F^n, hence so is 
ul \M). Therefore \A\B = \A^{1/2}(\A^{1/2}\B^{1/2})\B^{1/2} = \A^{1/2}\M^{*}\B^{1/2} = \O . [C2: Commuting positive matrices] Let \A \in M_n(F) with \A \succeq \O. 1. Prove without using @thm-psd-square-root (a) that if \B\A = \A\B, then \B\A^{1/2} = \A^{1/2}\B. Hint: show that \B maps each eigenspace of \A into itself. 2. Let \B \succeq \O with \A\B = \B\A. Prove that \A\B \succeq \O and that (\A\B)^{1/2} = \A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}. (a) Let \lambda \in \spec(\A) and \A\cvec{v} = \lambda\cvec{v}. Then \A(\B\cvec{v}) = \B(\A\cvec{v}) = \lambda\B\cvec{v}, so \B maps E_\lambda(\A) into itself. Since \A \succeq \O, its distinct eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k are nonnegative reals, and \A^{1/2} = \sum_i\sqrt{\lambda_i}\,\P_i with \P_i the orthogonal projection onto E_{\lambda_i}(\A) (proof of @thm-psd-square-root). For \cvec{v} \in E_{\lambda_j}(\A) we have \P_i\cvec{v} = \cvec{0} for i 
e j and \P_j\cvec{v} = \cvec{v}, so \A^{1/2}\cvec{v} = \sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\cvec{v}. Now F^n = E_{\lambda_1}(\A) \oplus \dots \oplus E_{\lambda_k}(\A) (@thm-spectral-resolution), so it suffices to check \B\A^{1/2}\cvec{v} = \A^{1/2}\B\cvec{v} for \cvec{v} \in E_{\lambda_j}(\A). The left side is \sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\B\cvec{v}; the right side is \A^{1/2}(\B\cvec{v}) = \sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\B\cvec{v} as well, because \B\cvec{v} \in E_{\lambda_j}(\A) by the first sentence. Hence \B\A^{1/2} = \A^{1/2}\B. (b) By (a), \A^{1/2} commutes with \B. Applying (a) once more, this time to \B \succeq \O with the commuting matrix \A^{1/2}, gives that \A^{1/2} commutes with \B^{1/2}. Put \C = \A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}. Then \C^{*} = (\B^{1/2})^{*}(\A^{1/2})^{*} = \B^{1/2}\A^{1/2} = \C , so \C is Hermitian, and \C^2 = \A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}\A^{1/2}\B^{1/2} = \A\B after one commutation. It remains to see \C \succeq \O. The matrices \A^{1/2} and \B^{1/2} are commuting Hermitian matrices, so by @cor-simultaneous-unitary-matrix (over 
C) or @cor-simultaneous-orthogonal-real (over 
R) there is a unitary \U with \U^{*}\A^{1/2}\U = \diag(\alpha_i) and \U^{*}\B^{1/2}\U = \diag( eta_i), all \alpha_i,  eta_i \ge 0. Then \U^{*}\C\U = \diag(\alpha_i eta_i) \succeq \O, so \C \succeq \O by @prp-congruence-positivity (a). Hence \A\B = \C^2 \succeq \O and, by uniqueness in @thm-psd-square-root, (\A\B)^{1/2} = \C = \A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}. [C3: Why definiteness is needed] 1. Give a positive semidefinite \A \in M_2(
R), not positive definite, together with two different lower triangular \L satisfying \A = \L\L	p. Which hypothesis of @thm-cholesky fails? 2. Prove that if \A \succeq \O then \A + t\I \succ \O for every real t > 0, and hence that every positive semidefinite matrix is a limit of positive definite ones in the entrywise sense. (a) Take \A = \diag(0, 1). Then \L_1 = \diag(0, 1) and \L_2 = \diag(0, -1) are both lower triangular with \L_i\L_i	p = \A. The hypothesis that fails is that the diagonal entries of \L be strictly positive: \ell_{11} = 0 here, which is exactly the first pivot vanishing. Uniqueness in @thm-cholesky is not available without it. (b) \A + t\I is Hermitian, and for \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}, \inner{(\A + t\I)\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} + t
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 \ge t
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 > 0 , so \A + t\I \succ \O. Each entry of \A + t\I differs from the corresponding entry of \A by t or by 0, so letting t decrease to 0 recovers \A entry by entry. This is the standard device for extending a statement from positive definite to positive semidefinite matrices whenever the statement survives taking limits; @thm-psd-characterizations already used it in the form \det(\A + t\I) > 0.

title: 13.3 Gram Matrices
content:
Gram Matrices Chapter 11 attached to every list of vectors the matrix of its pairwise inner products and read three facts off it: it is Hermitian, its quadratic form is a squared length, and it is invertible exactly when the list is independent (@def-gram-matrix, @thm-gram-matrix-properties). One question was left standing. Given a square matrix, is it the Gram matrix of something? The answer is the shortest possible one: exactly when it is positive semidefinite. This section proves that, and then spends it twice — the determinant of a Gram matrix is a squared volume, and a ratio of two Gram determinants is a distance to a subspace. Throughout, F = 
R or F = 
C and all inner product spaces are over F. When the list must be named we write \G(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) for its Gram matrix, whose entries are \inner{\elem{v}_j}{\elem{v}_i} as in @def-gram-matrix. Which matrices are Gram matrices? Half of the answer is already proved. By @thm-gram-matrix-properties (a) and (b), a Gram matrix \G is Hermitian and satisfies \cvec{x}^{*}\G\cvec{x} = \Big\lVert \sum_{j} x_j\elem{v}_j \BigVert^2 \ \ge\ 0 for every \cvec{x} \in F^k. That is word for word the definition of positive semidefiniteness (@def-positive-semidefinite). So being positive semidefinite is necessary. The content of the next theorem is that nothing else is needed, and this is where the chapter’s second signature move earns its keep: a positive semidefinite matrix factors as \B^{*}\B, and the columns of \B are then the list we were looking for. [Gram Matrices Are Exactly the Positive Semidefinite Matrices] Let \G \in M_k(F).
