Note that the eigenvalues of \A \circ \B have nothing to do with those of \A and \B, and that \det(\A \circ \B) = 40 is much larger than \det \A\det \B = 4 \cdot 2 = 8. The next theorem explains part of that: it forces \det(\A \circ \B) \ge \det\A \prod_i b_{ii} = 24. Getting down to the product \det\A\det\B needs Hadamard’s inequality (@thm-hadamard-inequality) as well, which is @exr-schur-product-theorem-c2. Let \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} and \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & -1 \ -1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}. Compute \A \circ \B and decide whether it is positive definite. Does this contradict @thm-schur-product (b)? \A \circ \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & -1 \ -1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}, with leading principal minors 2 and 3, so it is positive definite. There is no contradiction: @thm-schur-product (b) is an implication, not an equivalence. Here \A is only positive semidefinite (\A = \1\1	p, so \det \A = 0), and the theorem’s hypothesis fails — but the conclusion happens to hold anyway. Part (a) is what applies, and it correctly predicts \A \circ \B \succeq \O. Oppenheim’s inequality Hadamard’s inequality of Section 7 compared \det \A with the product of the diagonal entries of \A. Oppenheim’s inequality does the same for a Hadamard product, and it contains Hadamard’s as the special case \B = \I. Oppenheim’s Inequality Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) with \A \succeq \O and \B \succeq \O. Then \det(\A \circ \B) \ \ge \ \det \A \cdot b_{11}b_{22}\cdots b_{nn} . Induct on n, taking both matrices positive definite first. Split off the (1,1) entry of each: the Schur complements \A/\alpha and \B/ eta are positive definite of size n - 1, and a short computation, whose only real step is @lem-hadamard-rank-one again, shows that the Schur complement of the corner in \A \circ \B is (\A \circ \B)/(\alpha eta) = (\A/\alpha) \circ \B' + 	frac1\alpha\,(\cvec{a}\cvec{a}^{*}) \circ (\B/ eta) , a positive definite matrix plus a positive semidefinite one. So its determinant is at least that of the first term, by @lem-det-psd-increment, and the inductive hypothesis handles that. The semidefinite case follows by replacing \A and \B with \A + t\I and \B + t\I and letting t shrink to 0. Case 1: \A \succ \O and \B \succ \O. Induct on n. For n = 1 both sides are a_{11}b_{11}. Let n \ge 2, and split both matrices with a 1 	imes (n-1) partition: \A =  egin{pmatrix} \alpha & \cvec{a}^{*} \ \cvec{a} & \A' \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix}  eta & \cvec{b}^{*} \ \cvec{b} & \B' \end{pmatrix}, with \alpha = a_{11} > 0,  eta = b_{11} > 0, and \cvec{a}, \cvec{b} \in F^{n-1}. The Schur complements are \A/\alpha = \A' - 	frac1\alpha\,\cvec{a}\cvec{a}^{*}, \qquad \B/ eta = \B' - 	frac1 eta\,\cvec{b}\cvec{b}^{*} , and both are positive definite by @thm-block-psd-schur (b). Since conjugation acts entrywise, \cvec{a}^{*} \circ \cvec{b}^{*} = (\cvec{a} \circ \cvec{b})^{*}, so \A \circ \B =  egin{pmatrix} \alpha eta & (\cvec{a} \circ \cvec{b})^{*} \ \cvec{a} \circ \cvec{b} & \A' \circ \B' \end{pmatrix} , and \alpha eta > 0, so this matrix too has a Schur complement at its corner: (\A \circ \B)/(\alpha eta) = \A' \circ \B' - 	frac1{\alpha eta}\,(\cvec{a} \circ \cvec{b})(\cvec{a} \circ \cvec{b})^{*} . By @lem-hadamard-rank-one the subtracted term is 	frac1{\alpha eta}(\cvec{a}\cvec{a}^{*}) \circ (\cvec{b}\cvec{b}^{*}). Substituting \A' = \A/\alpha + 	frac1\alpha\cvec{a}\cvec{a}^{*} and expanding by bilinearity,  egin{aligned} \A' \circ \B' &= (\A/\alpha) \circ \B' + 	frac1\alpha\,(\cvec{a}\cvec{a}^{*}) \circ \B' \ &= (\A/\alpha) \circ \B' + 	frac1\alpha\,(\cvec{a}\cvec{a}^{*}) \circ \Bigl(\B/ eta + 	frac1 eta\cvec{b}\cvec{b}^{*}\Bigr) , \end{aligned} and the last term of this is exactly 	frac1{\alpha eta}(\cvec{a}\cvec{a}^{*}) \circ (\cvec{b}\cvec{b}^{*}). It therefore cancels, leaving (\A \circ \B)/(\alpha eta) = \underbrace{(\A/\alpha) \circ \B'}_{	extstyle \succ \O} \;+\; \underbrace{	frac1\alpha\,(\cvec{a}\cvec{a}^{*}) \circ (\B/ eta)}_{	extstyle \succeq \O} . 	ag{$\ast$} The first term is positive definite by @thm-schur-product (b), since \A/\alpha \succ \O and \B' \succ \O (the latter by @thm-block-psd-schur (a) applied to \B). The second is positive semidefinite by @thm-schur-product (a), since \cvec{a}\cvec{a}^{*} \succeq \O by @exm-psd-first-examples (b) and \B/ eta \succ \O, and 1/\alpha > 0. Now compute. By @thm-schur-determinant applied to \A \circ \B, then (\ast) with @lem-det-psd-increment, then the inductive hypothesis applied to the pair \A/\alpha and \B':  egin{aligned} \det(\A \circ \B) &= \alpha eta\cdot\det igl[(\A \circ \B)/(\alpha eta) igr] \ &\ge \alpha eta\cdot\det igl[(\A/\alpha) \circ \B' igr] \ &\ge \alpha eta\cdot\det(\A/\alpha)\cdot b_{22}\cdots b_{nn} . \end{aligned} By @thm-schur-determinant again, now for \A, we have \det(\A/\alpha) = \det \A/\alpha. Substituting and canceling \alpha, \det(\A \circ \B) \ \ge \  eta\,\det \A\cdot b_{22}\cdots b_{nn} = \det \A\cdot b_{11}b_{22}\cdots b_{nn} , which completes the induction. Case 2: \A \succeq \O and \B \succeq \O. For real t > 0, the matrices \A + t\I and \B + t\I are positive definite, as in the proof of @cor-fischer-inequality. Case 1 gives \det igl[(\A + t\I) \circ (\B + t\I) igr] \ \ge \ \det(\A + t\I)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{n}(b_{ii} + t) . Every entry of (\A + t\I) \circ (\B + t\I) is a polynomial in t, so both sides are polynomial, hence continuous, functions of t (@thm-leibniz-formula-alternating). Letting t decrease to 0 preserves the inequality and gives the statement. This proves the theorem. Taking \B = \I recovers Hadamard’s inequality. Indeed \A \circ \I = \diag(a_{11}, \dots, a_{nn}) and \prod_i b_{ii} = 1, so the conclusion reads a_{11}\cdots a_{nn} \ge \det \A, which is @thm-hadamard-inequality (a). Swapping the roles of \A and \B gives the companion bound \det(\A \circ \B) \ge \det \B\cdot\prod_i a_{ii}, and combining either one with Hadamard’s inequality gives \det(\A \circ \B) \ge \det \A\det \B; that last consequence is @exr-schur-product-theorem-c2. Where this gets used The natural home of the Hadamard product is data. A covariance matrix is a Gram matrix (@thm-gram-matrix-properties), hence positive semidefinite, and rescaling each variable to unit variance turns it into a correlation matrix: positive semidefinite with every diagonal entry equal to 1. The Schur product theorem says that the entrywise product of two correlation matrices is another one — the diagonal entries stay 1 \cdot 1 = 1 — so one can damp the correlations of one model by those of another and still have a legitimate covariance structure. Nothing in the definition of “positive semidefinite” makes that obvious, and it is the reason the theorem is quoted far outside linear algebra. Entrywise products preserve positivity; entrywise inverses do not. Let \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}, which is positive definite, with leading principal minors 2 and 3. Replacing each entry by its reciprocal gives  egin{psmallmatrix} 1/2 & 1 \ 1 & 1/2\end{psmallmatrix}, whose determinant is 	frac14 - 1 = -	frac34 < 0: not positive semidefinite. The entrywise reciprocal is not the Hadamard inverse of anything useful, and the matrix inverse \A^{-1}, which is positive definite (@exr-positive-definite-matrices-b3), has nothing to do with it. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define \A \circ \B, and say what shapes the two factors must have. 2. What is \A \circ \I? What is \A \circ \J? 3. State the Schur product theorem. 4. True or false: if \A \succ \O, then the matrix with entries 1/a_{ij} (assuming no entry is 0) is positive definite. Justify your answer. 5. What does Oppenheim’s inequality say when \B = \I? (a) For \A, \B \in M_{m	imes n}(F) of the same shape, (\A \circ \B)_{ij} = a_{ij}b_{ij}, and \A \circ \B has that same shape (@def-hadamard-product). (b) \A \circ \I = \diag(a_{11}, \dots, a_{nn}), and \A \circ \J = \A, since \J has every entry 1. (c) If \A \succeq \O and \B \succeq \O, then \A \circ \B \succeq \O; if both are positive definite, so is \A \circ \B (@thm-schur-product). (d) False. For \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} \succ \O, the entrywise reciprocal is  egin{psmallmatrix} 1/2 & 1 \ 1 & 1/2\end{psmallmatrix}, with determinant -3/4 < 0. (e) By @thm-oppenheim it says \det(\A \circ \I) \ge \det \A \cdot 1, that is a_{11}\cdots a_{nn} \ge \det \A: Hadamard’s inequality, @thm-hadamard-inequality (a). B. Practice [B1: Compute and decide] For each pair below, compute \A \circ \B and determine whether it is positive definite, positive semidefinite but not definite, or neither. Say in each case whether @thm-schur-product applies. 1. \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}, \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}. 2. \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}, \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}. 3. \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}, \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 3 & -1 \ -1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}. (a) \A \circ \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}. Both factors are \1\1	p \succeq \O (@exm-psd-first-examples (b)), so @thm-schur-product (a) applies and predicts \succeq \O. The product has determinant 0, so it is positive semidefinite but not definite. (b) \A \circ \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}, whose determinant is 1 - 4 = -3 < 0: neither. The theorem does not apply, since \B is not positive semidefinite (its determinant is -3). This is what the hypothesis is for. (c) \A \succ \O (minors 2, 3) and \B \succ \O (minors 3, 2), so @thm-schur-product (b) applies. Indeed \A \circ \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 6 & -1 \ -1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}, with minors 6 and 11, is positive definite. @thm-oppenheim also checks out: 11 \ge \det \A\cdot b_{11}b_{22} = 3 \cdot 3 = 9. [B2: Entrywise squares] Let \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 2 \ 1 & 2 & 3\end{psmallmatrix}. 1. Show that \A \succ \O. 2. Compute \A \circ \A, the matrix of squared entries, and verify that it is positive definite. 3. Explain why (b) needed no computation. (a) The leading principal minors are 1, 2 - 1 = 1 and, expanding along the first row, 1(6-4) - 1(3-2) + 1(2-2) = 1. All positive, so \A \succ \O by @thm-pd-characterizations (d). (b) \A \circ \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 4 & 4 \ 1 & 4 & 9\end{psmallmatrix}, with leading principal minors 1, 4 - 1 = 3, and 1(36 - 16) - 1(9 - 4) + 1(4 - 4) = 20 - 5 = 15. All positive, so it is positive definite. (c) @thm-schur-product (b) with \B = \A gives \A \circ \A \succ \O immediately. C. Going deeper [C1: Polynomials applied entrywise] Let \A \in M_n(F) with \A \succeq \O. 1. Prove that the entrywise power \A^{\circ m}, with (i, j) entry a_{ij}^{\,m}, is positive semidefinite for every integer m \ge 1. 2. Let p(x) = c_0 + c_1x + \dots + c_dx^d have nonnegative real coefficients. Prove that the matrix p^{\circ}(\A) with (i, j) entry p(a_{ij}) is positive semidefinite. 3. Give an example of \A \succeq \O and a polynomial p with a negative coefficient for which p^{\circ}(\A) is not positive semidefinite. (a) Induct on m. For m = 1 the claim is the hypothesis. If \A^{\circ m} \succeq \O, then \A^{\circ(m+1)} = \A^{\circ m} \circ \A \succeq \O by @thm-schur-product (a). (b) By definition of the entries, p^{\circ}(\A) = c_0\J + c_1\A + c_2\A^{\circ 2} + \dots + c_d\A^{\circ d}, since each side has (i, j) entry \sum_k c_ka_{ij}^{\,k} (with a_{ij}^0 = 1, which is the (i,j) entry of \J). Now \J = \1\1	p \succeq \O by @exm-psd-first-examples (b), each \A^{\circ k} \succeq \O by (a), and each c_k \ge 0. A nonnegative combination of positive semidefinite matrices is positive semidefinite (@exr-positive-definite-matrices-c2 (a)). (c) Take \A = \J \in M_2(
R), which is positive semidefinite, and p(x) = x - 2. Then p^{\circ}(\A) has every entry -1, that is p^{\circ}(\A) = -\J, and \inner{-\J\cvec{e}_1}{\cvec{e}_1} = -1 < 0. So the hypothesis on the coefficients cannot be dropped. [C2: The product of the determinants] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) with \A \succeq \O and \B \succeq \O. Prove that \det(\A \circ \B) \ \ge \ \det \A \cdot \det \B . Is the inequality ever an equality with both matrices positive definite? By @thm-oppenheim, \det(\A \circ \B) \ge \det \A\cdot\prod_i b_{ii}. By @thm-hadamard-inequality (a) applied to \B \succeq \O, \prod_i b_{ii} \ge \det \B. Both \det \A \ge 0 and \prod_i b_{ii} \ge 0 (the diagonal entries of a positive semidefinite matrix are \ge 0 by @exr-positive-definite-matrices-c1 (a)), so multiplying the second inequality by \det \A \ge 0 and chaining, \det(\A \circ \B) \ \ge\ \det \A\prod_i b_{ii} \ \ge\ \det \A\det \B . Yes, equality can occur: take \A = \B = \I_n, so that \A \circ \B = \I_n and all three quantities are 1. More generally, take \A \succ \O diagonal and \B = \I_n. [C3: The rank of an entrywise product] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) with \A \succeq \O and \B \succeq \O, of ranks r and s. Prove that ank(\A \circ \B) \le rs . Hint: how many terms in the proof of @thm-schur-product (a) are actually nonzero? Write \A = \sum_i\lambda_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{u}_i^{*} and \B = \sum_j\mu_j\cvec{w}_j\cvec{w}_j^{*} as in the proof of @thm-schur-product (a). The number of nonzero eigenvalues of \A is ank \A = r: diagonalizing, \A = \U\D\U^{*} with \U invertible, so ank \A = ank \D by @thm-rank-product-inequality, and ank \D counts the nonzero \lambda_i. Likewise exactly s of the \mu_j are nonzero. Dropping the vanishing terms, \A \circ \B = \sum_{\lambda_i 
e 0}\ \sum_{\mu_j 
e 0} \lambda_i\mu_j\,\cvec{z}_{ij}\cvec{z}_{ij}^{*}, \qquad \cvec{z}_{ij} = \cvec{u}_i \circ \cvec{w}_j , a sum of rs matrices, each of rank at most 1, since every column of \cvec{z}_{ij}\cvec{z}_{ij}^{*} lies in \Span(\cvec{z}_{ij}). The rank of a sum of two matrices is at most the sum of their ranks (@exr-rank-c1); applying that repeatedly to the rs summands gives ank(\A \circ \B) \le rs.

title: 13.9 The Singular Value Decomposition
content:
The Singular Value Decomposition Chapter 12 answered one question completely: an operator has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors exactly when it is normal. That answer is useless for a 3 	imes 5 matrix, which has no eigenvalues at all — the equation \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} is not even type-correct, because \A\cvec{x} and \cvec{x} live in different spaces. This section shows that every matrix, of every shape, still admits an orthonormal-to-orthogonal description, and that the numbers in it are the eigenvalues of a positive semidefinite matrix we already understand. It is the most-used factorization in applied linear algebra, and the whole of it comes from applying the spectral theorem to \A^{*}\A. Throughout, F is 
R or 
C, \A^{*} is the conjugate transpose (the transpose when F = 
R), and unitary means unitary over 
C and orthogonal over 
R, as in @def-unitary-orthogonal. Both F^m and F^n carry their standard inner products. Where to look when there are no eigenvalues Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). There is exactly one square matrix that can be built from \A at no cost, and Chapter 11 has already used it twice: the n 	imes n matrix \A^{*}\A of the normal equations. It is self-adjoint, since (\A^{*}\A)^{*} = \A^{*}\A^{**} = \A^{*}\A, and it is positive semidefinite for the reason that makes every argument in this chapter work: \inner{\A^{*}\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\A\cvec{x}} = 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}^2 \ge 0 . {#eq-svd-psd} So \A^{*}\A \succeq \O, and @thm-psd-characterizations says its eigenvalues are nonnegative real numbers, while the spectral theorem supplies an orthonormal basis of F^n consisting of its eigenvectors. Those eigenvalues are attached to \A, they exist for every shape of \A, and @eq-svd-psd says what they measure: how much \A stretches. A rectangular matrix has no eigenvalues of its own, but \A^{*}\A does, and their square roots are the stretching factors of \A. [Singular Values] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and put p = \min(m, n). Let \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n \ge 0 be the eigenvalues of \A^{*}\A \in M_n(F), listed with multiplicity in decreasing order. The singular values of \A are \sigma_i(\A) \coloneqq \sqrt{\lambda_i} \qquad (i = 1, \dots, p), so that \sigma_1(\A) \ge \sigma_2(\A) \ge \dots \ge \sigma_p(\A) \ge 0. We write \sigma_i when \A is clear. Clause by clause. The list has exactly p = \min(m, n) entries, not n: when n > m the matrix \A^{*}\A has rank ank \A \le m < n by @cor-rank-adjoint (b), so \lambda_{m+1} = \dots = \lambda_n = 0 and the discarded eigenvalues are all zero. The square root is the ordinary nonnegative real square root, available because every \lambda_i \ge 0. The ordering is decreasing, matching the book’s convention \lambda_1(\A) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(\A) for the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix, and it is part of the definition: “the second singular value” means a definite number. Finally, the singular values are attached to \A itself, with no choices made, because the eigenvalue list of \A^{*}\A is. Four examples, simplest first. 1. The identity. \A = \I_n gives \A^{*}\A = \I_n, so every \sigma_i = 1. More generally a unitary \U \in M_n(F) has \U^{*}\U = \I, so all its singular values are 1. A unitary matrix stretches nothing in any direction, and the list of singular values says exactly that. 2. A rectangular diagonal matrix. If \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) has a_{ii} = d_i for i \le p and all other entries 0, then \A^{*}\A = \diag(\lvert d_1vert^2, \dots) and the singular values are \lvert d_1 vert, \dots, \lvert d_p vert sorted downwards. The absolute value matters: the singular values of \diag(1, -2) are 2, 1. 3. A positive semidefinite matrix. If \A \succeq \O then \A^{*}\A = \A^2, whose eigenvalues are \lambda_i(\A)^2 with \lambda_i(\A) \ge 0, so \sigma_i(\A) = \lambda_i(\A). For the matrices this chapter started with, singular values and eigenvalues coincide. 4. A single row. For \A = \cvec{a}^{*} \in M_{1 	imes n}(F) with \cvec{a} 
e \cvec{0}, p = 1 and \A^{*}\A = \cvec{a}\cvec{a}^{*}, whose nonzero eigenvalue is 
orm{\cvec{a}}^2. So \sigma_1 = 
orm{\cvec{a}}. The degenerate case \A = \O has every \sigma_i = 0, and it matters: it is the only matrix with \sigma_1 = 0, since \sigma_1 = 0 forces \A^{*}\A = \O and then 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}^2 = 0 for every \cvec{x} by @eq-svd-psd. Now the nonexample, by minimal change. Replace “square roots of the eigenvalues of \A^{*}\A” by “absolute values of the eigenvalues of \A”. For \A \succeq \O, and more generally for any normal \A, the two agree (@exr-singular-value-decomposition-c3). But the second recipe is undefined for a nonsquare matrix, and for \N =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} it returns 0, 0, while \N^{*}\N = \diag(0, 1) gives the singular values 1, 0. The clause that fails is the one that does all the work: \A^{*}\A is positive semidefinite for every \A, whereas \A itself may have no useful spectrum. Singular values are not eigenvalues. The matrix \N above has both eigenvalues equal to 0 and largest singular value 1: it annihilates \cvec{e}_1 but sends \cvec{e}_2 to a unit vector, so calling it “small” because its spectrum is \{0\} is wrong. Singular values are always real and nonnegative; eigenvalues need not be either. The two lists agree, after taking absolute values, exactly for normal matrices — this is @exr-singular-value-decomposition-c3, and Chapter 12’s Schur inequality is what makes the converse true. What are the singular values of an orthogonal projection \P \in M_n(F) onto an r-dimensional subspace? \P^{*}\P = \P^2 = \P, because an orthogonal projection is self-adjoint and idempotent. So the eigenvalues of \P^{*}\P are those of \P, namely 1 with multiplicity r and 0 with multiplicity n - r. Sorted downwards, the singular values are \sigma_1 = \dots = \sigma_r = 1 and \sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_n = 0. This is also Example 3 above, since \P \succeq \O. The theorem Here is the payoff. The eigenvectors of \A^{*}\A are an orthonormal basis of the domain; the claim is that \A carries them to an orthogonal list in the codomain, whose lengths are the singular values. [Singular Value Decomposition] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), let p = \min(m, n), and let \sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_p \ge 0 be its singular values. Then there are unitary matrices \U \in M_m(F) and \V \in M_n(F) such that \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} , where \vSigma \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R) has (\vSigma)_{ii} = \sigma_i for i = 1, \dots, p and every other entry 0. Moreover the number of nonzero \sigma_i equals ank \A. Picture the 2 	imes 2 real case. A matrix carries the unit circle to an ellipse, and an ellipse has two perpendicular axes; the theorem says that the two unit vectors sent to the ends of those axes are themselves perpendicular. That is exactly what Chapter 12’s principal axis theorem (@thm-principal-axes) said about the level curves of a quadratic form, and the link is that 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}^2 = \cvec{x}^{*}(\A^{*}\A)\cvec{x} is a quadratic form, with matrix \A^{*}\A. So the plan is: ① diagonalize \A^{*}\A by the spectral theorem, getting an orthonormal basis \cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n with \A^{*}\A\cvec{v}_i = \sigma_i^2\cvec{v}_i; ② compute \inner{\A\cvec{v}_i}{\A\cvec{v}_j} and watch the eigenvalue equation force it to be \sigma_i^2\delta_{ij}, so the images are already orthogonal; ③ normalize the nonzero ones to unit vectors \cvec{u}_i, and, if there are fewer than m of them, pad the list out to an orthonormal basis of F^m; ④ read \A\V = \U\vSigma off column by column. Step 1: diagonalize \A^{*}\A. The matrix \A^{*}\A \in M_n(F) is self-adjoint, and @eq-svd-psd makes it positive semidefinite in the sense of @def-positive-semidefinite. By the spectral theorem in matrix form — @cor-spectral-real-matrix when F = 
R, @cor-spectral-complex-matrix when F = 
C, each of which allows the eigenvalues to be listed in a prescribed order — there is a unitary \V \in M_n(F) with columns \cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n such that \A^{*}\A\,\cvec{v}_i = \lambda_i\cvec{v}_i, \qquad \lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n \ge 0 , the eigenvalues being nonnegative by @thm-psd-characterizations. Set \sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i} for all i \le n; for i \le p these are the singular values of @def-singular-values. Step 2: the images are orthogonal. For all i, j, using \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x} and the eigenvalue equation, \inner{\A\cvec{v}_i}{\A\cvec{v}_j} = \inner{\A^{*}\A\cvec{v}_i}{\cvec{v}_j} = \lambda_i\inner{\cvec{v}_i}{\cvec{v}_j} = \lambda_i\delta_{ij} , the first equality by @def-adjoint and the last because \V is unitary, so its columns are orthonormal (@thm-isometry-characterizations (f)). In particular 
orm{\A\cvec{v}_i}^2 = \lambda_i = \sigma_i^2, so \A\cvec{v}_i = \cvec{0} \iff \sigma_i = 0 . {#eq-svd-kernel-test} Step 3: normalize, and count. Let r be the number of indices with \sigma_i > 0; since the \sigma_i decrease, these are i = 1, \dots, r. For i \le r put \cvec{u}_i \coloneqq  rac{1}{\sigma_i}\A\cvec{v}_i , which is legitimate because \sigma_i 
eq 0. By Step 2, \inner{\cvec{u}_i}{\cvec{u}_j} = \lambda_i\delta_{ij}/(\sigma_i\sigma_j) = \delta_{ij} for i, j \le r, so (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_r) is an orthonormal list in F^m. We claim r = ank \A. Any \cvec{x} \in F^n is \cvec{x} = \sum_i c_i\cvec{v}_i since (\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n) is a basis, and then \A\cvec{x} = \sum_{i \le r} c_i\sigma_i\cvec{u}_i by @eq-svd-kernel-test. Hence \im \A = \Span(\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_r), and the \cvec{u}_i are orthonormal, hence independent (@thm-orthogonal-independent), so ank \A = r. In particular r \le \min(m, n) = p, so every index i with \sigma_i > 0 satisfies i \le p, and the nonzero singular values are exactly \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_r. Step 4: pad the list. If r = m the list (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_r) is already an orthonormal basis of F^m, and we set \U = (\cvec{u}_1 \mid \dots \mid \cvec{u}_m). If r < m, apply @cor-extend-orthonormal-basis to the orthonormal list (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_r) in F^m: there are \cvec{u}_{r+1}, \dots, \cvec{u}_m making (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_m) an orthonormal basis of F^m. Either way let \U \in M_m(F) have these columns; it is unitary because its columns are orthonormal (@thm-isometry-characterizations (f)). Note that the padding vectors are not determined by \A, and nothing below uses any property of them beyond orthonormality. Step 5: read off the columns. Let \vSigma \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R) be as in the statement. Column i of \U\vSigma is \U times column i of \vSigma, which is \sigma_i\cvec{e}_i for i \le p and \cvec{0} for i > p; so column i of \U\vSigma is \sigma_i\cvec{u}_i for i \le p and \cvec{0} for i > p. Column i of \A\V is \A\cvec{v}_i. Compare: - for i \le r, \A\cvec{v}_i = \sigma_i\cvec{u}_i by the definition of \cvec{u}_i; - for r < i \le p, \sigma_i = 0, so both columns are \cvec{0} by @eq-svd-kernel-test; - for i > p (possible only when n > m), we have i > p \ge r, so \sigma_i = 0 and \A\cvec{v}_i = \cvec{0}, and both columns are \cvec{0}. Hence \A\V = \U\vSigma. Since \V is unitary, \V^{-1} = \V^{*}, so \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*}. This proves the theorem. A factorization \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} as in the theorem is called a singular value decomposition of \A, the columns \cvec{u}_i of \U are left singular vectors and the columns \cvec{v}_i of \V are right singular vectors. The two equations to keep in mind are the ones the proof produced, \A\cvec{v}_i = \sigma_i\cvec{u}_i, \qquad \A^{*}\cvec{u}_i = \sigma_i\cvec{v}_i \qquad (i \le r), {#eq-singular-vector-pairing} the second obtained by applying \A^{*} to the first and using \A^{*}\A\cvec{v}_i = \sigma_i^2\cvec{v}_i. In words: \A matches up two orthonormal bases, one in each space, stretching the i-th direction by \sigma_i, and \A^{*} runs the same correspondence backwards with the same factors. The last item on the invertibility list. For a square \A \in M_n(F), the count at the end of the theorem says that all n singular values are nonzero exactly when ank \A = n, which is invertibility (@thm-invertible-tfae-det (d)). This is the item Chapter 3 promised when it began the list (@thm-invertible-tfae), later grown in @thm-invertible-tfae-det, @thm-invertible-tfae-eigen, and @thm-invertible-tfae-positive, and it is the last one the book adds. Here is the picture the Idea described, in the real 2 	imes 2 case. Compare the principal axes figure of Chapter 12 §05. There the ellipse was a level curve \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = 1 of a quadratic form and the axes lay along the eigenvectors of a symmetric \A; here the ellipse is the image of the unit circle under an arbitrary \A. The two pictures are the same picture, because 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}^2 = \cvec{x}^{*}(\A^{*}\A)\cvec{x} is a quadratic form with matrix \A^{*}\A, and the right singular vectors of \A are its principal axes. A large \sigma_i now means a long semi-axis, whereas in @thm-principal-axes a large \lambda_i meant a short one; the reason is that the two pictures are related by taking reciprocals of square roots. What is unique and what is not The singular values were defined before the theorem, so they cannot depend on any choice. What needs saying is the converse: any factorization of the stated shape recovers them. [The Singular Values Are Determined] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and suppose \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} with \U, \V unitary and \vSigma \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R) of the shape in @thm-svd, with diagonal entries s_1 \ge \dots \ge s_p \ge 0. Then s_i = \sigma_i(\A) for every i. Moreover: 1. the columns of \V are forced to be an orthonormal basis of F^n consisting of eigenvectors of \A^{*}\A, with \A^{*}\A\cvec{v}_i = \sigma_i^2\cvec{v}_i for every i \le n, where \sigma_i \coloneqq 0 for p < i \le n; and any such basis occurs; 2. once \V is chosen, \cvec{u}_i = \A\cvec{v}_i/\sigma_i is forced for every i \le r = ank\A, while \cvec{u}_{r+1}, \dots, \cvec{u}_m may be any orthonormal basis of (\im\A)^{\perp}. From \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} and \U^{*}\U = \I_m, \A^{*}\A = \V\vSigma^{*}\U^{*}\U\vSigma\V^{*} = \V(\vSigma^{*}\vSigma)\V^{*} , and \vSigma^{*}\vSigma \in M_n(
R) is the diagonal matrix with entries s_1^2, \dots, s_p^2 followed by zeros. So \A^{*}\A is unitarily diagonalized with this diagonal, and its eigenvalue list in decreasing order is therefore s_1^2 \ge \dots \ge s_p^2 \ge 0 \ge \dots — already sorted, since the s_i are. Comparing with @def-singular-values gives s_i^2 = \sigma_i(\A)^2, hence s_i = \sigma_i(\A) because both are nonnegative. (a) The displayed equation says the i-th column of \V satisfies \A^{*}\A\cvec{v}_i = \sigma_i^2\cvec{v}_i, and the columns of a unitary matrix are orthonormal. Conversely, given any orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of \A^{*}\A ordered by decreasing eigenvalue, Steps 2–5 of the proof of @thm-svd build a factorization from it. (b) For i \le r we have \sigma_i 
eq 0, and comparing column i of \A\V = \U\vSigma gives \A\cvec{v}_i = \sigma_i\cvec{u}_i, so \cvec{u}_i = \A\cvec{v}_i/\sigma_i. For i > r the corresponding column of \vSigma is zero, so \cvec{u}_i is unconstrained by the equation \A\V = \U\vSigma; the only constraint left is that (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_m) be orthonormal, which says exactly that (\cvec{u}_{r+1}, \dots, \cvec{u}_m) is an orthonormal basis of \Span(\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_r)^{\perp} = (\im\A)^{\perp}. So \vSigma is unique and \U, \V are not. The freedom is of two kinds, and both are visible in small cases. If \A^{*}\A has a repeated eigenvalue, any orthonormal basis of that eigenspace may be used: \A = \I_2 has \vSigma = \I_2 and \I_2 = \U\I_2\U^{*} for every unitary \U, with \V = \U. If the eigenvalues are distinct, each \cvec{v}_i is still free up to a scalar of modulus 1, and replacing \cvec{v}_i by c\cvec{v}_i replaces \cvec{u}_i by c\cvec{u}_i, leaving \sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*} unchanged because c\conj{c} = 1. That last observation is why the factorization is worth having even though it is not unique: the products \sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*} are what later sections use, and those are unchanged by the phase freedom. Section 12 will define the pseudoinverse through a singular value decomposition and will have to check exactly this. The compact form, and the four subspaces Steps 3 and 5 of the proof produced more than the statement recorded: they located \im\A and \ker\A inside the two bases. Writing the factorization so that only the nonzero singular values appear makes this visible. [Compact Singular Value Decomposition] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) have rank r and let \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} be as in @thm-svd, with columns \cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_m and \cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n. Then \A = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i\,\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*} , a sum of r matrices of rank 1. Equivalently \A = \U_r\vSigma_r\V_r^{*}, where \U_r \in M_{m 	imes r}(F) and \V_r \in M_{n 	imes r}(F) hold the first r columns of \U and \V, and \vSigma_r = \diag(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_r) is square and invertible. Write \A = (\U\vSigma)\V^{*}. The columns of \U\vSigma are \sigma_1\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \sigma_p\cvec{u}_p followed by zero columns, as computed in Step 5 of @thm-svd, and the rows of \V^{*} are \cvec{v}_1^{*}, \dots, \cvec{v}_n^{*}. By the outer product expansion of a matrix product (@cor-outer-product-expansion), \A = \sum_{i=1}^{p} (\sigma_i\cvec{u}_i)\cvec{v}_i^{*} = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i\,\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*} , the terms with i > r vanishing because \sigma_i = 0 there. Each \cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*} is nonzero with all columns multiples of \cvec{u}_i, hence of rank 1. The same computation with the truncated matrices gives \U_r\vSigma_r\V_r^{*} = \sum_{i \le r}\sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*}, and \vSigma_r is invertible because its diagonal entries \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_r are nonzero. [The Four Fundamental Subspaces from the Compact Form] With the notation of @thm-compact-svd: 1. (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_r) is an orthonormal basis of \im\A = \col(\A); 2. (\cvec{u}_{r+1}, \dots, \cvec{u}_m) is an orthonormal basis of \ker\A^{*}; 3. (\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_r) is an orthonormal basis of \im\A^{*}; 4. (\cvec{v}_{r+1}, \dots, \cvec{v}_n) is an orthonormal basis of \ker\A. Two of the four were proved on the way to @thm-svd. The other two come for free by applying the same statements to \A^{*}, whose singular value decomposition is \A^{*} = \V\vSigma^{*}\U^{*} — the roles of \cvec{u} and \cvec{v} simply swap. Part (a). Step 3 of @thm-svd showed \im\A = \Span(\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_r), and these r vectors are orthonormal. Part (d). By @eq-svd-kernel-test, \A\cvec{v}_i = \cvec{0} exactly for i > r, and for \cvec{x} = \sum_i c_i\cvec{v}_i we computed \A\cvec{x} = \sum_{i \le r} c_i\sigma_i\cvec{u}_i. Since the \cvec{u}_i are independent and the \sigma_i nonzero for i \le r, \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} if and only if c_1 = \dots = c_r = 0, that is, \cvec{x} \in \Span(\cvec{v}_{r+1}, \dots, \cvec{v}_n). Parts (b) and (c). Taking conjugate transposes, \A^{*} = \V\vSigma^{*}\U^{*}, and \vSigma^{*} \in M_{n 	imes m}(
R) has the same diagonal \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_p. So this is a singular value decomposition of \A^{*}, with the columns of \V as left singular vectors and those of \U as right singular vectors, and ank\A^{*} = ank\A = r by @cor-rank-adjoint (a). Now the two parts just proved, applied to \A^{*} instead of \A, give exactly (c) and (b). This is the cleanest possible form of @thm-four-subspaces-orthogonal. That theorem said the four subspaces come in two orthogonal pairs, F^n = \ker\A \oplus \im\A^{*} and F^m = \im\A \oplus \ker\A^{*}. The corollary hands over orthonormal bases of all four at once, out of two matrices, and adds the missing piece of information: how \A maps one pair to the other. Restricted to \im\A^{*}, the map \A is a bijection onto \im\A, and in the bases (\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_r) and (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_r) its matrix is the diagonal \vSigma_r. Every matrix, after an orthonormal change of basis on each side, is a positive diagonal matrix padded with zeros. Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) have rank r. Using @cor-svd-four-subspaces, what is \dim\ker\A^{*}, and why does the answer not depend on which singular value decomposition was used? The list (\cvec{u}_{r+1}, \dots, \cvec{u}_m) has m - r members, so \dim\ker\A^{*} = m - r. It cannot depend on the factorization because r = ank\A is determined by \A (@thm-singular-values-unique), and in any case the answer agrees with \dim(\im\A)^{\perp} = m - ank\A from @thm-four-subspaces-orthogonal and @thm-orthogonal-decomposition. Two computations and one comparison The Frobenius norm. From 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 	r(\A^{*}\A) and \A^{*}\A = \V(\vSigma^{*}\vSigma)\V^{*}, or directly from @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant, 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 
orm{\U\vSigma\V^{*}}_F^2 = 
orm{\vSigma}_F^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{p} \sigma_i^2 . So the Frobenius norm is the Euclidean length of the singular value list. Section 11 turns this one identity into the best low-rank approximation theorem. The largest stretch. Let \cvec{x} = \sum_i c_i\cvec{v}_i be a unit vector, so \sum_i \lvert c_ivert^2 = 1 by @thm-parseval-identity. Then \A\cvec{x} = \sum_{i \le r} c_i\sigma_i\cvec{u}_i, and since the \cvec{u}_i are orthonormal, Pythagoras (@thm-pythagoras) gives 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}^2 = \sum_{i \le r} \sigma_i^2\lvert c_ivert^2 \le \sigma_1^2\sum_i \lvert c_ivert^2 = \sigma_1^2 , with equality at \cvec{x} = \cvec{v}_1. So \sigma_1 = \max\{
orm{\A\cvec{x}} : 
orm{\cvec{x}} = 1\}: the largest singular value is the largest factor by which \A can lengthen a vector. Chapter 16 gives that quantity a name, the operator norm 
orm{\A}_2, and this computation is why 
orm{\A}_2 = \sigma_1. Against the eigenvalues. For a normal \A \in M_n(
C), write \A = \U\D\U^{*} with \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n) by @cor-spectral-complex-matrix. Then \A^{*}\A = \U\D^{*}\D\U^{*} = \U\diag igl(\lvert\lambda_1vert^2, \dots, \lvert\lambda_nvert^2 igr)\U^{*} , so the singular values of \A are the moduli \lvert\lambda_ivert, sorted downwards. For a general matrix there is no relation at all in one direction — \N =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has spectrum \{0\} and \sigma_1 = 1 — and only the crude bound \lvert\lambdavert \le \sigma_1 in the other, since \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} with 
orm{\cvec{x}} = 1 gives \lvert\lambdavert = 
orm{\A\cvec{x}} \le \sigma_1. [A singular value decomposition of a 2 by 3 matrix] Find a singular value decomposition of \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_{2 	imes 3}(
R), and read off orthonormal bases of its four fundamental subspaces. Here m = 2, n = 3, p = 2. The proof asks for the eigenvectors of the 3 	imes 3 matrix \A	p\A, but there is a shortcut worth taking whenever m < n: run the proof on \A	p instead. It produces \A	p = \V\vSigma	p\U	p, and transposing that equation gives \A = \U\vSigma\V	p, which is what we want. The eigenvalue computation then lives in the smaller matrix \A\A	p =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Step 1. The characteristic polynomial of \A\A	p is x^2 - 4x + 3 = (x-1)(x-3), so the eigenvalues are 3 and 1 and the singular values are \sigma_1 = \sqrt3, \sigma_2 = 1. For \lambda = 3, \A\A	p - 3\I =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & -1 \ -1 & -1\end{pmatrix} gives x_1 = -x_2, and for \lambda = 1 we get x_1 = x_2. Normalizing, \cvec{u}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1), \qquad \cvec{u}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1). Both singular values are nonzero, so r = ank\A = 2. Steps 2–4. The roles of \cvec{u} and \cvec{v} are swapped along with the roles of \A and \A	p, so here \cvec{v}_i = \A	p\cvec{u}_i/\sigma_i: \cvec{v}_1 = 	frac{\A	p(1,-1)}{\sqrt2\,\sqrt3} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt6}(1,-1,2), \qquad \cvec{v}_2 = 	frac{\A	p(1,1)}{\sqrt2} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1,0). This time the padding step is needed, since r = 2 < 3: a unit vector orthogonal to both is \cvec{v}_3 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt3}(-1,1,1). Step 5. Assembling, \U = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \vSigma =  egin{pmatrix} \sqrt3 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \V =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac{1}{\sqrt6} & 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} & -	frac{1}{\sqrt3} \[3pt] -	frac{1}{\sqrt6} & 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} & 	frac{1}{\sqrt3} \[3pt] 	frac{2}{\sqrt6} & 0 & 	frac{1}{\sqrt3} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A = \U\vSigma\V	p . As a check, 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 4 and \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 = 3 + 1 = 4. The four subspaces (@cor-svd-four-subspaces), with r = 2: \col(\A) has the orthonormal basis \cvec{u}_1, \cvec{u}_2, which is all of 
R^2, so 
ul(\A	p) = \{\cvec{0}\}; ow(\A) = \col(\A	p) has the orthonormal basis \cvec{v}_1, \cvec{v}_2; and 
ul(\A) = \Span(\cvec{v}_3) is the line through (-1,1,1). The last is easy to verify directly: \A(-1,1,1) = (-1+1, 1-1) = \cvec{0}. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the singular values of a matrix \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). How many are there? 2. State the singular value decomposition, with the size and the defining property of each factor. 3. True or false: the singular values of \A are the absolute values of its eigenvalues. Justify your answer. 4. How many nonzero singular values does \A have, and why? 5. Given a compact singular value decomposition \A = \sum_{i \le r}\sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*}, write down orthonormal bases of all four fundamental subspaces of \A. 6. True or false: in \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} the three factors are determined by \A. Justify your answer. (a) They are \sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i} for i = 1, \dots, \min(m,n), where \lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n \ge 0 are the eigenvalues of \A^{*}\A with multiplicity (@def-singular-values). There are \min(m, n) of them. (b) @thm-svd: \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} with \U \in M_m(F) unitary, \V \in M_n(F) unitary, and \vSigma \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R) having \sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_p \ge 0 in positions (i,i) and zeros elsewhere. (c) False. \N =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has both eigenvalues 0 and singular values 1, 0. The statement is true for normal matrices (@exr-singular-value-decomposition-c3), and for a nonsquare matrix it does not even make sense. (d) Exactly ank\A, by @thm-svd. The reason is that \A\cvec{v}_i = \cvec{0} precisely when \sigma_i = 0, so the \cvec{v}_i with \sigma_i = 0 span \ker\A. (e) (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_r) for \im\A; (\cvec{u}_{r+1}, \dots, \cvec{u}_m) for \ker\A^{*}; (\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_r) for \im\A^{*}; (\cvec{v}_{r+1}, \dots, \cvec{v}_n) for \ker\A (@cor-svd-four-subspaces). (f) False for \U and \V, true for \vSigma (@thm-singular-values-unique). For instance \I_2 = \U\I_2\U^{*} for every unitary \U. The freedom is: any orthonormal eigenbasis of \A^{*}\A may be used for \V, and the last m - r columns of \U may be any orthonormal basis of (\im\A)^{\perp}. B. Practice [B1: A 2 by 2 decomposition] Find a singular value decomposition \A = \U\vSigma\V	p of \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
R), and compare the singular values with the eigenvalues of \A. \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 25 & 20 \ 20 & 25 \end{pmatrix}, with characteristic polynomial x^2 - 50x + (625 - 400) = x^2 - 50x + 225, whose roots are 45 and 5. So \sigma_1 = 3\sqrt5 and \sigma_2 = \sqrt5. For \lambda = 45 the equation -20x_1 + 20x_2 = 0 gives \cvec{v}_1 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1); for \lambda = 5, \cvec{v}_2 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1). Then \cvec{u}_1 =  rac{\A\cvec{v}_1}{3\sqrt5} =  rac{(3,9)}{3\sqrt{10}} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(1,3), \qquad \cvec{u}_2 =  rac{\A\cvec{v}_2}{\sqrt5} =  rac{(3,-1)}{\sqrt{10}} . Hence \U = 	frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 3 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \vSigma =  egin{pmatrix} 3\sqrt5 & 0 \ 0 & \sqrt5 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \V = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, and \U\vSigma\V	p = \A. Check: \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 = 45 + 5 = 50 = 9 + 16 + 25 = 
orm{\A}_F^2. The eigenvalues of \A are 3 and 5, the diagonal entries of a triangular matrix. They are not the singular values, not even after reordering: \A is not normal, since \A	p\A 
eq \A\A	p =  egin{pmatrix} 9 & 12 \ 12 & 41 \end{pmatrix}. Note, however, that \sigma_1\sigma_2 = 15 = \lvert\det\Avert, as @exr-singular-value-decomposition-c2 explains. [B2: When the left singular vectors must be padded] Find a singular value decomposition of \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in M_{3 	imes 2}(
R), saying explicitly where the padding step of @thm-svd is used. \A	p\A = \diag(2, 1), already diagonal with decreasing diagonal, so \V = \I_2, \cvec{v}_1 = \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{v}_2 = \cvec{e}_2, and \sigma_1 = \sqrt2, \sigma_2 = 1. Both are nonzero, so r = 2. Then \cvec{u}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}\A\cvec{e}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,0,1), \qquad \cvec{u}_2 = \A\cvec{e}_2 = (0,1,0). Here r = 2 < 3 = m, so Step 4 of @thm-svd applies: extend (\cvec{u}_1, \cvec{u}_2) to an orthonormal basis of 
R^3. A vector orthogonal to both is (1,0,-1), so take \cvec{u}_3 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,0,-1). Then \U =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} & 0 & 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} \[3pt] 0 & 1 & 0 \[3pt] 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} & 0 & -	frac{1}{\sqrt2} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \vSigma =  egin{pmatrix} \sqrt2 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \V = \I_2 , and \U\vSigma\V	p = \U\vSigma = \A. The vector \cvec{u}_3 is not determined by \A beyond its line: -\cvec{u}_3 would do just as well. By @cor-svd-four-subspaces, 
ul(\A	p) = \Span(\cvec{u}_3), which is confirmed by \A	p(1,0,-1) = (1 - 1, 0) = \cvec{0}. [B3: Compact form and the four subspaces] For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 1 & 1 \ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in M_{3 	imes 2}(
R), find the compact singular value decomposition \A = \sum_{i \le r}\sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i	p, and hence orthonormal bases of all four fundamental subspaces. \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 9 & 9 \ 9 & 9 \end{pmatrix}, with eigenvalues 18 and 0, so \sigma_1 = 3\sqrt2, \sigma_2 = 0, and r = 1. An eigenvector for 18 is \cvec{v}_1 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1), and for 0 it is \cvec{v}_2 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1). Then \cvec{u}_1 =  rac{\A\cvec{v}_1}{3\sqrt2} =  rac{(4,2,4)}{\sqrt2 \cdot 3\sqrt2} = 	frac13(2,1,2), a unit vector since 4 + 1 + 4 = 9. The compact form is \A = 3\sqrt2\,\cvec{u}_1\cvec{v}_1	p, and multiplying out gives back \A. Four subspaces: \col(\A) = \Span igl(	frac13(2,1,2) igr) and ow(\A) = \Span igl(	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1) igr), both one-dimensional; 
ul(\A) = \Span igl(	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1) igr); and 
ul(\A	p) is the plane \{\cvec{y} : 2y_1 + y_2 + 2y_3 = 0\}, for which an orthonormal basis is 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,0,-1) and 	frac1{3\sqrt2}(1,-4,1). (Any orthonormal basis of that plane is a legitimate (\cvec{u}_2, \cvec{u}_3), which is the freedom described in @thm-singular-values-unique (b).) [B4: Determine whether] Determine which of the following statements are correct. For those that are correct, prove them; for those that are not, give a counterexample. 1. If every eigenvalue of \A \in M_n(
C) is 0, then every singular value of \A is 0. 2. \sigma_i(c\A) = \lvert cvert\,\sigma_i(\A) for every scalar c. 3. \sigma_i(\A^2) = \sigma_i(\A)^2 for every square \A. 4. \A is invertible if and only if n = m and every singular value of \A is nonzero. (a) Incorrect. \N =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has spectrum \{0\}, while \N^{*}\N = \diag(0,1) gives \sigma_1 = 1. (b) Correct. (c\A)^{*}(c\A) = \conj{c}c\,\A^{*}\A = \lvert cvert^2\A^{*}\A, whose eigenvalues are \lvert cvert^2\lambda_i; taking square roots and noting that multiplying by \lvert cvert^2 \ge 0 preserves the decreasing order gives the claim. (c) Incorrect, with the same \N: \N^2 = \O has both singular values 0, while \sigma_1(\N)^2 = 1. (It is correct for \A \succeq \O, and more generally for normal \A, because then the singular values are the moduli of the eigenvalues and \A^2 has eigenvalues \lambda_i^2.) (d) Correct. If \A \in M_n(F) then, by @thm-svd, the number of nonzero singular values is ank\A, and \A is invertible exactly when ank\A = n (@thm-invertible-tfae-det (d)). A nonsquare matrix is never invertible. C. Going deeper [C1: The Frobenius norm and the largest singular value] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) with singular values \sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_p. 1. The text obtained 
orm{\A}_F^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{p}\sigma_i^2 from unitary invariance. Prove it a second way, directly from 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 	r(\A^{*}\A) and the eigenvalues of \A^{*}\A, without invoking @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant. 2. Deduce that \sigma_1 \le 
orm{\A}_F, and determine exactly when equality holds. (a) Take a singular value decomposition \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} (@thm-svd). By @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant, applied once on each side, 
orm{\A}_F = 
orm{\U\vSigma\V^{*}}_F = 
orm{\vSigma}_F. The only nonzero entries of \vSigma are \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_p on the diagonal, so 
orm{\vSigma}_F^2 = \sum_i \sigma_i^2. (b) Every term of \sum_i\sigma_i^2 is nonnegative, so \sigma_1^2 \le \sum_i\sigma_i^2 = 
orm{\A}_F^2, and taking nonnegative square roots gives \sigma_1 \le 
orm{\A}_F. Equality holds if and only if \sigma_2 = \dots = \sigma_p = 0, that is, if and only if ank\A \le 1 (@thm-svd). [C2: The adjoint and the determinant] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). 1. Prove that \A and \A^{*} have the same nonzero singular values, with the same multiplicities. 2. Suppose m = n. Prove that \lvert\det\Avert = \sigma_1\sigma_2\cdots\sigma_n. 3. Hence give a formula for \lvert\det\Avert in terms of \A^{*}\A only, and check it on \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}. (a) If \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} is a singular value decomposition, then \A^{*} = \V\vSigma^{*}\U^{*} with \V, \U unitary and \vSigma^{*} \in M_{n 	imes m}(
R) carrying the same diagonal entries \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_p. By @thm-singular-values-unique this is a singular value decomposition of \A^{*}, so the singular value list of \A^{*} is \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_p as well. (The two lists have the same length p = \min(m,n), so they are in fact equal, not merely equal in their nonzero parts.) (b) Take determinants in \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*}. By @thm-det-multiplicative, \det\A = \det\U \cdot \det\vSigma \cdot \det\V^{*}. A unitary \U has \lvert\det\Uvert = 1, since \det(\U^{*})\det(\U) = \det(\I) = 1 and \det(\U^{*}) = \conj{\det\U}, so \lvert\det\Uvert^2 = 1. The same holds for \V^{*}. And \det\vSigma = \sigma_1\cdots\sigma_n by @thm-det-triangular. Taking absolute values gives \lvert\det\Avert = \sigma_1\cdots\sigma_n. (c) Squaring, \lvert\det\Avert^2 = \prod_i\sigma_i^2 = \det(\A^{*}\A), so \lvert\det\Avert = \sqrt{\det(\A^{*}\A)}. For the given \A, \det\A = 15 and \det(\A	p\A) = 625 - 400 = 225 = 15^2. [C3: Singular values equal to eigenvalue moduli] Let \A \in M_n(
C) have eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n listed with algebraic multiplicity and ordered so that \lvert\lambda_1vert \ge \dots \ge \lvert\lambda_nvert. 1. Prove that if \A is normal, then \sigma_i(\A) = \lvert\lambda_ivert for every i. 2. Prove the converse: if \sigma_i(\A) = \lvert\lambda_ivert for every i, then \A is normal. Hint for (b): compare two expressions for 
orm{\A}_F^2. (a) Suppose \A is normal. By @cor-spectral-complex-matrix, \A = \U\D\U^{*} with \U unitary and \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n). Then \A^{*}\A = \U\D^{*}\U^{*}\U\D\U^{*} = \U\,\diag igl(\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 igr)\,\U^{*} , so the eigenvalues of \A^{*}\A are \lvert\lambda_1vert^2, \dots, \lvert\lambda_nvert^2 with multiplicity. These are already in decreasing order by hypothesis, so \sigma_i(\A) = \lvert\lambda_ivert for every i by @def-singular-values. (b) Suppose \sigma_i(\A) = \lvert\lambda_ivert for every i. By @exr-singular-value-decomposition-c1 (a), \sum_{i=1}^{n}\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_i^2 = 
orm{\A}_F^2 . Schur’s inequality (@thm-schur-inequality) says \sum_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 \le 
orm{\A}_F^2 with equality if and only if \A is normal. We have equality, so \A is normal.

title: 13.10 Polar Decomposition and Takagi's Factorization
content:
Polar Decomposition and Takagi’s Factorization Every nonzero complex number is a rotation times a stretch, z = e^{i	heta}r with r = \lvert zvert > 0. Section 9 has put the matrix version within reach: if \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*}, then inserting \V^{*}\V = \I in the middle splits the factorization into a unitary part and a positive semidefinite part. This section carries that out, proves that the unitary part is the closest unitary matrix to \A, and then treats a factorization that looks like the singular value decomposition but is not: Takagi’s, for complex symmetric matrices. The field is 
C unless stated otherwise, and \lvert\Avert = (\A^{*}\A)^{1/2} is the matrix absolute value of @def-matrix-absolute-value. Rotation times stretch [Polar Decomposition] Let \A \in M_n(
C). Then there is a unitary \W \in M_n(
