(d) False in general, true exactly for normal \A. For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 25 & 20 \ 20 & 25 \end{pmatrix} 
e  egin{pmatrix} 9 & 12 \ 12 & 41 \end{pmatrix} = \A\A	p, so the two square roots differ. (e) @thm-takagi: a symmetric \A \in M_n(
C) is \U\vSigma\U	p with \U unitary and \vSigma the diagonal matrix of singular values. Against the singular value decomposition: the right factor is not free but forced to be \conj{\U}. Against the spectral theorem: the hypothesis is symmetry rather than normality, the operation is the congruence \X \mapsto \U\X\U	p rather than a similarity, and the diagonal carries singular values rather than eigenvalues. (f) False. \N =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ i & -1 \end{pmatrix} is symmetric and nonzero with \N^2 = \O, so its minimal polynomial is x^2, which has a repeated root; it is not diagonalizable. B. Practice [B1: A polar decomposition by hand] Find both polar decompositions \A = \W\lvert\Avert = \lvert\A^{*}vert\W of \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, and say what \W is geometrically. \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 9 & 0 \ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, which is diagonal with nonnegative entries, so \lvert\Avert = \diag(3, 2): this is positive semidefinite and squares to \A	p\A, which by @thm-psd-square-root identifies it. Since \A is invertible, \W = \A\lvert\Avert^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 	frac13 & 0 \ 0 & 	frac12 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, the quarter turn of 
R^2. Check: \W	p\W = \I and \W\lvert\Avert = \A. For the right-handed form, \A\A	p = \diag(4, 9), so \lvert\A^{*}vert = \diag(2,3), and indeed \lvert\A^{*}vert\W =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \A . The two absolute values are different, which is consistent with \A not being normal. In words: \A stretches by 3 horizontally and 2 vertically, then rotates by a quarter turn; equivalently it rotates first and then stretches by 2 horizontally and 3 vertically. [B2: The nearest unitary matrix] Let \A = \diag(2, -3) \in M_2(
R). Find the unitary matrix nearest to \A in the Frobenius norm, compute the distance, and verify the value against the formula of @cor-unitary-nearest. \A^{*}\A = \diag(4, 9), so \lvert\Avert = \diag(2, 3) and \W = \A\lvert\Avert^{-1} = \diag(1, -1), which is unitary. By @cor-unitary-nearest, \W is the nearest unitary matrix, and it is the only one since \A is invertible. Directly, \A - \W = \diag(1, -2), \qquad 
orm{\A - \W}_F^2 = 1 + 4 = 5 . The formula gives 
orm{\A}_F^2 + n - 2(\sigma_1 + \sigma_2) = 13 + 2 - 2(3 + 2) = 5, the same. So the distance is \sqrt5. [B3: A Takagi factorization] Find a Takagi factorization of \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, and explain why no real \U can work. \A is symmetric and \A^{*}\A = \A^2 = \I, so \sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = 1 and \vSigma = \I. We need a unitary \U with \U\U	p = \A. Diagonalize \A over 
R: its eigenvalues are 1 and -1, with unit eigenvectors 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1) and 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1), so \A = \Q\diag(1,-1)\Q	p with \Q = 	frac1{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. Following Step 3 of @thm-takagi, take square roots 1 and i of the diagonal entries: \U = \Q\diag(1, i) = 	frac1{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ 1 & -i \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \U\U	p = \Q\diag(1,-1)\Q	p = \A . \U is unitary, and \U\vSigma\U	p = \U\U	p = \A. No real \U works: a real \U with \U^{*}\U = \I is orthogonal, and then \U\vSigma\U	p = \U\U	p = \I 
e \A. C. Going deeper [C1: The positive factor is forced] Let \A \in M_n(
C). 1. Suppose \A = \Q\P with \Q unitary and \P \succeq \O. Prove that \P = \lvert\Avert. (Invertibility is not assumed.) 2. Deduce that \A is unitary if and only if \lvert\Avert = \I. (a) From \A = \Q\P we get \A^{*}\A = \P^{*}\Q^{*}\Q\P = \P^{*}\P = \P^2, using \Q^{*}\Q = \I and \P^{*} = \P. So \P is a positive semidefinite square root of \A^{*}\A. Such a square root is unique (@thm-psd-square-root), and \lvert\Avert is one by definition (@def-matrix-absolute-value). Hence \P = \lvert\Avert. (b) (\Rightarrow) If \A is unitary then \A^{*}\A = \I, and \I \succeq \O with \I^2 = \I, so \lvert\Avert = \I by uniqueness. (\Leftarrow) If \lvert\Avert = \I then \A^{*}\A = \lvert\Avert^2 = \I, which for a square matrix says \A is unitary (@def-unitary-orthogonal). [C2: Normality through the polar factors] Let \A \in M_n(
C) be invertible with polar decomposition \A = \W\lvert\Avert. Prove that the following are equivalent. 1. \A is normal. 2. \lvert\Avert = \lvert\A^{*}vert. 3. \W\lvert\Avert = \lvert\Avert\W. (a) \Rightarrow (b). If \A^{*}\A = \A\A^{*}, then \lvert\Avert and \lvert\A^{*}vert are positive semidefinite square roots of the same matrix, hence equal by @thm-psd-square-root. (b) \Rightarrow (c). By @thm-polar-decomposition, \lvert\A^{*}vert = \W\lvert\Avert\W^{*}. If this equals \lvert\Avert, multiply on the right by \W to get \lvert\Avert\W = \W\lvert\Avert. (c) \Rightarrow (a). Write \P = \lvert\Avert, so \A = \W\P = \P\W. Then \A\A^{*} = \W\P\P^{*}\W^{*} = \W\P^2\W^{*} = \P^2\W\W^{*} = \P^2 , using \P^{*} = \P, then \W\P^2 = \P^2\W (which follows from \W\P = \P\W), then \W\W^{*} = \I. And \A^{*}\A = \P^{*}\W^{*}\W\P = \P^2. So \A\A^{*} = \A^{*}\A. [C3: Complex symmetric matrices are transposed squares] Let \A \in M_n(
C) be symmetric and invertible. 1. Using @thm-takagi, prove that \A = \B	p\B for some invertible \B \in M_n(
C). 2. Show that over 
R the analogous statement is false unless \A is positive definite, and give a 1 	imes 1 witness. 3. Explain in one sentence why (a) and (b) do not contradict each other. (a) By @thm-takagi, \A = \U\vSigma\U	p with \U unitary and \vSigma = \diag(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n), where every \sigma_i > 0 because \A is invertible (@thm-svd). Let \vSigma^{1/2} = \diag(\sqrt{\sigma_1}, \dots, \sqrt{\sigma_n}) and put \B \coloneqq \vSigma^{1/2}\U	p, which is invertible as a product of invertible matrices. Then \B	p\B = \U\,\vSigma^{1/2}\vSigma^{1/2}\,\U	p = \U\vSigma\U	p = \A , using (\vSigma^{1/2})	p = \vSigma^{1/2} and (\U	p)	p = \U. (b) Over 
R, if \A = \B	p\B with \B \in M_n(
R) then \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = 
orm{\B\cvec{x}}^2 \ge 0 for every \cvec{x}, so \A \succeq \O, and \A \succ \O when \B is invertible. So no real \A with a negative eigenvalue is of this form: for n = 1, \A = (-1) is symmetric and invertible but b^2 = -1 has no real solution. (c) The factor \B produced in (a) is complex, and over 
C the quantity \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} is not a sum of squared lengths — the transpose carries no conjugation, so \B	p\B says nothing about positivity. Indeed b = i solves b^2 = -1.

title: 13.11 Low-Rank Approximation
content:
Low-Rank Approximation The compact singular value decomposition writes a matrix as a sum of rank-one pieces arranged in decreasing order of size. A sum can be cut short. This section shows that cutting it short after k terms produces the best approximation to \A by a matrix of rank k, measured in the Frobenius norm, and that the error it leaves is a quantity we can write down before doing any work. One theorem answers three questions at once: how to compress a matrix, which k-dimensional subspace best fits a cloud of data, and how far a given matrix is from being singular. Throughout, F = 
R or F = 
C, \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), p = \min(m, n), r = ank\A, and \sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_p \ge 0 are the singular values of \A (@def-singular-values), so that \sigma_i > 0 exactly for i \le r. We fix a singular value decomposition \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} (@thm-svd) and write \cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_m for the columns of \U and \cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n for the columns of \V. Cutting the sum short Multiplying out \U\vSigma\V^{*} column by column gives the rank-one expansion \A = \sum_{i=1}^{p} \sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*} = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*} , the second equality because the terms with i > r have \sigma_i = 0; this is the compact form @thm-compact-svd. Each summand is a matrix of rank one, and the coefficients decrease. The natural thing to do with such a sum is to keep the large terms and discard the small ones. Keep the first k rank-one pieces and throw the rest away. [Truncated singular value decomposition] For 0 \le k \le p, the rank-k truncation of \A relative to the chosen singular value decomposition \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} (@thm-svd) is \A_k \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*} , with \A_0 = \O; for k \ge p we set \A_k = \A. Two clauses need comment. The subscript counts terms kept, not rows and columns: \A_k is the same size as \A, not a submatrix of it. (Section 1 used \A_k for the top-left k 	imes k corner; that meaning is gone for the rest of this section.) And the definition says “relative to the chosen decomposition”, because @thm-singular-values-unique leaves the unitary factors some freedom, and different choices can give different truncations. Everything proved below holds for every choice; the warning at the end of the section shows that the dependence is real. The rank of \A_k is exactly \min(k, r): the vectors \cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_k are orthonormal, hence independent, so the columns of \A_k span \Span(\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_{\min(k,r)}) once the vanishing terms are dropped. [Truncating a diagonal matrix] Let \A = \diag(5, 3, 1) \in M_3(
R). Write down \A_1 and \A_2. A diagonal matrix with positive decreasing entries is already in the form \U\vSigma\V^{*} with \U = \V = \I_3, so \sigma_i = 5, 3, 1 and \cvec{u}_i = \cvec{v}_i = \cvec{e}_i. Hence \A_1 = 5\cvec{e}_1\cvec{e}_1^{*} = \diag(5, 0, 0), \qquad \A_2 = \diag(5, 3, 0) . Truncation of a diagonal matrix is just deleting its smallest diagonal entries. Everything in this section is this statement, conjugated by two unitary matrices. The first thing to compute is how much was thrown away. [The Frobenius norm counts singular values] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) have singular values \sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_p. Then (the first identity is the one Section 9 already obtained, recorded here with a label because the proof of the main theorem uses it repeatedly) 
orm{\A}_F^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{p} \sigma_i^2 , \qquad 
orm{\A - \A_k}_F^2 = \sum_{i > k} \sigma_i^2 for every 0 \le k \le p. The Frobenius norm does not see unitary factors (@lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant), so from \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*}, 
orm{\A}_F = 
orm{\vSigma\V^{*}}_F = 
orm{\vSigma}_F . The only nonzero entries of \vSigma are \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_p on the diagonal, so 
orm{\vSigma}_F^2 = \sum_i \sigma_i^2. For the second identity, subtract the first k terms of the rank-one expansion: \A - \A_k = \sum_{i > k} \sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*} = \U\vSigma^{(k)}\V^{*} , where \vSigma^{(k)} is \vSigma with its first k diagonal entries replaced by 0. Applying the first identity to this matrix — the display is a singular value decomposition of it in the sense of @thm-svd, up to reordering the diagonal — gives 
orm{\A - \A_k}_F^2 = \sum_{i > k}\sigma_i^2. So the truncation error is decided in advance by the singular values, and it is small exactly when the discarded \sigma_i are small. The content of the section is that no other matrix of rank k does better. A matrix has singular values 5, 4, 3. What is the smallest k for which the relative error 
orm{\A - \A_k}_F/
orm{\A}_F is at most 	frac12? By @lem-frobenius-sum-of-squares, 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 25 + 16 + 9 = 50. For k = 1 the error squared is 16 + 9 = 25, so the relative error is \sqrt{25/50} = 1/\sqrt2 \approx 0.71, too big. For k = 2 the error squared is 9, and \sqrt{9/50} \approx 0.42 \le 	frac12. So k = 2. Note that the test is on the squares: halving the error means keeping three quarters of \sum\sigma_i^2. How much a subspace can hold The proof of the theorem needs one inequality, and it is the only place where any work happens. The question it answers is: if we are allowed to keep only an s-dimensional subspace of F^m, how much of \A can we capture? The answer is \sigma_1^2 + \dots + \sigma_s^2, and the best subspace is the span of the leading left singular vectors. [An orthonormal list captures at most the leading singular values] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) with singular values \sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_p, extended by \sigma_i = 0 for p < i \le m. Let \cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_s be an orthonormal list in F^m, so that s \le m. Then \sum_{j=1}^{s} 
orm{\A^{*}\cvec{q}_j}^2 \ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^{s} \sigma_i^2 . Write each \cvec{q}_j in the orthonormal basis (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_m). The quantity 
orm{\A^{*}\cvec{q}_j}^2 then becomes \sum_i \sigma_i^2\lvert c_{ji}vert^2, so the total is \sum_i \sigma_i^2 t_i with weights t_i = \sum_j \lvert c_{ji}vert^2. Two facts pin the weights down: each t_i \le 1, because the \cvec{q}_j are orthonormal and Bessel’s inequality applies to \cvec{u}_i; and \sum_i t_i = s, because each \cvec{q}_j is a unit vector. A weighted sum of a decreasing sequence with weights in [0, 1] that sum to s is largest when the first s weights are 1 — which is the last display of the proof. If s = 0 both sides are empty sums, so assume s \ge 1. Fix j and put c_{ji} = \inner{\cvec{q}_j}{\cvec{u}_i} for 1 \le i \le m, so that the i-th entry of \U^{*}\cvec{q}_j is c_{ji}. Since \A^{*} = \V\vSigma^{*}\U^{*} and \V is unitary, hence an isometry (@def-unitary-orthogonal, @thm-isometry-characterizations), 
orm{\A^{*}\cvec{q}_j}^2 = 
orm{\vSigma^{*}\U^{*}\cvec{q}_j}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sigma_i^2\lvert c_{ji}vert^2 , because \vSigma^{*} multiplies the i-th entry by \sigma_i and discards the entries beyond the p-th, which is the same as using \sigma_i = 0 there. Summing over j and exchanging the two finite sums, \sum_{j=1}^{s} 
orm{\A^{*}\cvec{q}_j}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sigma_i^2 t_i , \qquad t_i \coloneqq \sum_{j=1}^{s} \lvert c_{ji}vert^2 . Now bound the weights. Since \lvert c_{ji}vert = \lvert\inner{\cvec{u}_i}{\cvec{q}_j}vert and (\cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_s) is an orthonormal list, Bessel’s inequality (@thm-bessel-inequality) applied to the vector \cvec{u}_i gives t_i = \sum_{j=1}^{s} \lvert \inner{\cvec{u}_i}{\cvec{q}_j}vert^2 \ \le\ 
orm{\cvec{u}_i}^2 = 1 . Since (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_m) is an orthonormal basis of F^m, Parseval’s identity (@thm-parseval-identity) gives \sum_{i=1}^m \lvert c_{ji}vert^2 = 
orm{\cvec{q}_j}^2 = 1 for each j, and therefore \sum_{i=1}^{m} t_i = \sum_{j=1}^{s} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \lvert c_{ji}vert^2 = s . Finally, using \sigma_i^2 \ge \sigma_s^2 together with t_i - 1 \le 0 for i \le s, and \sigma_i^2 \le \sigma_s^2 together with t_i \ge 0 for i > s,  egin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sigma_i^2 t_i - \sum_{i=1}^{s} \sigma_i^2 &= \sum_{i \le s} \sigma_i^2(t_i - 1) + \sum_{i > s} \sigma_i^2 t_i \ &\le \sigma_s^2\Bigl(\sum_{i \le s}(t_i - 1) + \sum_{i > s} t_i\Bigr) \ &= \sigma_s^2\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{m} t_i - s\Bigr) = 0 . \end{aligned} This is the stated inequality. Equality is attainable: take \cvec{q}_j = \cvec{u}_j for j \le s. Then \A^{*}\cvec{u}_j = \sigma_j\cvec{v}_j by the rank-one expansion, so 
orm{\A^{*}\cvec{u}_j}^2 = \sigma_j^2 and the two sides agree. The lemma is the extreme case of a family of statements about sums of the largest eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix; Chapter 17 develops the family through the Courant–Fischer min–max theorem, of which the inequality above is the crudest and most useful consequence. The Eckart–Young theorem Now the theorem. Read it as a statement about a minimization problem: over the set of matrices of rank at most k — which is not a subspace, so no earlier optimization theorem applies to it directly — the minimum of 
orm{\A - \B}_F exists, is attained at a matrix we can write down, and has a value we already computed. [Eckart–Young Theorem, Frobenius case] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) with singular values \sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_p, and let 0 \le k \le p. Then for every \B \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) with ank\B \le k, 
orm{\A - \B}_F \ \ge\ \Bigl(\sum_{i > k}\sigma_i^2\Bigr)^{1/2} , and equality holds for \B = \A_k. In words: the truncation \A_k minimizes 
orm{\A - \B}_F over all matrices of rank at most k, and the minimum value is  igl(\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 igr)^{1/2}. The difficulty is that \B is an arbitrary matrix of rank \le k, and there is no formula for such a thing. The rescue is to stop looking at \B and look only at its column space S, a subspace of dimension s \le k. ① Every column of \B lies in S, so column by column the Best Approximation Theorem says \B cannot beat P_S\A, the matrix obtained by projecting every column of \A onto S. So it suffices to minimize over subspaces. ② For a subspace, Pythagoras splits the error into “all of \A” minus “the part S captures”, and the captured part is exactly the quantity @lem-orthonormal-capture-bound bounds. ③ The bound is \sigma_1^2 + \dots + \sigma_k^2, and subtracting it from 
orm{\A}_F^2 = \sum_i\sigma_i^2 leaves \sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2, which @lem-frobenius-sum-of-squares says is exactly what \A_k achieves. Step 1: reduce to a projection. Let \B have rank \le k and put S = \col(\B), so s \coloneqq \dim S = ank\B \le k. Write \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n and \cvec{b}_1, \dots, \cvec{b}_n for the columns of \A and of \B. By the definition of the Frobenius norm, summing squares of entries column by column, 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{n} 
orm{\cvec{a}_j - \cvec{b}_j}^2 . Each \cvec{b}_j lies in S, so @thm-best-approximation gives 
orm{\cvec{a}_j - \cvec{b}_j} \ge 
orm{\cvec{a}_j - P_S\cvec{a}_j} for every j, where P_S is the orthogonal projection onto S (@def-orthogonal-projection), identified throughout with its matrix in the standard basis of F^m. Hence 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 \ \ge\ \sum_{j=1}^{n} 
orm{\cvec{a}_j - P_S\cvec{a}_j}^2 = 
orm{\A - P_S\A}_F^2 , the last equality because the j-th column of P_S\A is P_S\cvec{a}_j. Step 2: what a subspace captures. Choose an orthonormal basis (\cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_s) of S. For each j, the vectors \cvec{a}_j - P_S\cvec{a}_j and P_S\cvec{a}_j are orthogonal, so @thm-pythagoras gives 
orm{\cvec{a}_j - P_S\cvec{a}_j}^2 = 
orm{\cvec{a}_j}^2 - 
orm{P_S\cvec{a}_j}^2, and summing over j, 
orm{\A - P_S\A}_F^2 = 
orm{\A}_F^2 - 
orm{P_S\A}_F^2 . By @thm-projection-formula (a), P_S\cvec{a}_j = \sum_{l \le s}\inner{\cvec{a}_j}{\cvec{q}_l}\cvec{q}_l, whose summands are pairwise orthogonal, so @thm-pythagoras gives 
orm{P_S\cvec{a}_j}^2 = \sum_{l=1}^{s}\lvert\inner{\cvec{a}_j}{\cvec{q}_l}vert^2. Exchanging the sums, 
orm{P_S\A}_F^2 = \sum_{l=1}^{s} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \lvert\inner{\cvec{a}_j}{\cvec{q}_l}vert^2 = \sum_{l=1}^{s} 
orm{\A^{*}\cvec{q}_l}^2 , where the last equality holds because \inner{\cvec{a}_j}{\cvec{q}_l} = \cvec{q}_l^{*}\cvec{a}_j is the j-th entry of the row vector \cvec{q}_l^{*}\A, whose entries are the conjugates of those of \A^{*}\cvec{q}_l. Step 3: apply the bound. By @lem-orthonormal-capture-bound and s \le k, and since all \sigma_i^2 \ge 0, 
orm{P_S\A}_F^2 \ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^{s} \sigma_i^2 \ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i^2 . Combining the three steps with 
orm{\A}_F^2 = \sum_{i}\sigma_i^2 (@lem-frobenius-sum-of-squares), 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 \ \ge\ 
orm{\A}_F^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_i^2 = \sum_{i > k}\sigma_i^2 . Equality. The matrix \A_k has rank \min(k, r) \le k, and 
orm{\A - \A_k}_F^2 = \sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 by @lem-frobenius-sum-of-squares. So the lower bound is attained, and it is the minimum. This proves the theorem. Three remarks are worth extracting. First, the theorem is a genuine minimum, not an infimum: the minimizing matrix is exhibited. Second, the minimum value depends on \A only through its singular values, so it is unchanged if \A is replaced by \U'\A\V' with \U', \V' unitary. Third, the case k = r - 1 reads: the Frobenius distance from \A to the matrices of rank < r is \sigma_r, the smallest nonzero singular value. Exercise C1 turns that into a statement about how far an invertible matrix is from being singular. The same matrix \A_k is also optimal in the spectral norm 
orm{\cdot}_2, where the minimum value is \sigma_{k+1} rather than  igl(\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 igr)^{1/2}. We cannot state that here, because the spectral norm is defined only in Chapter 16. In fact both statements are instances of one theorem: \A_k is a best rank-k approximation in every unitarily invariant norm. Chapter 21 proves that, and the proof is genuinely different from the one above — it needs inequalities between the singular values of \A and of \A - \B, not a projection argument. A worked example [The best rank-one approximation of a 3 × 2 matrix] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_{3 	imes 2}(
R) . Find the best rank-one approximation of \A in the Frobenius norm, and compute the error in two ways. Singular values and vectors. Since \A has more rows than columns, work with the 2 	imes 2 matrix \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, whose eigenvalues are 3 and 1 with orthonormal eigenvectors \cvec{v}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1), \qquad \cvec{v}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1) . Hence \sigma_1 = \sqrt3 and \sigma_2 = 1, and the left singular vectors are \cvec{u}_i = \A\cvec{v}_i/\sigma_i: \cvec{u}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt6}(1, 1, 2), \qquad \cvec{u}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0) . (Both are unit vectors, as they must be: 1 + 1 + 4 = 6 and 1 + 1 = 2.) The approximation. By @thm-eckart-young the answer is \A_1 = \sigma_1\cvec{u}_1\cvec{v}_1	p. The scalar in front is \sqrt3/(\sqrt6\sqrt2) = \sqrt3/\sqrt{12} = 	frac12, so \A_1 =  rac12  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} . It has rank one, its two columns being equal and nonzero. The error, twice. Directly, \A - \A_1 =  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad 
orm{\A - \A_1}_F^2 = 4 \cdot 	frac14 = 1 . From the theorem, the error squared is \sigma_2^2 = 1. The two agree. As a further check, 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 and \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 = 3 + 1 = 4, as @lem-frobenius-sum-of-squares requires; the relative error of the rank-one approximation is \sqrt{1/4} = 	frac12. Best-fitting subspaces Step 1 of the proof did more than its job. It showed that the optimal \B may be taken of the form P_S\A, and Steps 2 and 3 identified the best S. That identification is a theorem in its own right, and it is the statement people mean when they speak of fitting a low-dimensional structure to data. [The best-fitting subspace] Let \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n \in F^m be the columns of \A, and let 1 \le k \le p. Among all subspaces S \subseteq F^m with \dim S \le k, the total squared distance D(S) \coloneqq \sum_{j=1}^{n} d(\cvec{a}_j, S)^2 is smallest for S = \Span(\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_k), and its smallest value is \sum_{i > k}\sigma_i^2. By @def-distance-to-subspace, d(\cvec{a}_j, S) = 
orm{\cvec{a}_j - P_S\cvec{a}_j}, so D(S) = 
orm{\A - P_S\A}_F^2 as in Step 1 of @thm-eckart-young. Since ank(P_S\A) \le \dim S \le k, the theorem gives D(S) \ge \sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2. For S_0 = \Span(\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_k) the columns \cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_k are orthonormal, so @thm-projection-formula (a) gives P_{S_0}\A = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \cvec{u}_i\cvec{u}_i^{*}\A = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*} = \A_k , using \cvec{u}_i^{*}\A = \sigma_i\cvec{v}_i^{*}, which is the rank-one expansion read one row at a time. Hence D(S_0) = 
orm{\A - \A_k}_F^2 = \sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2. What this is used for, honestly. Two applications are within reach of what we have proved, and a third is not. The first is compression. Storing \A costs mn numbers; storing \A_k as \sigma_1, \cvec{u}_1, \cvec{v}_1, \dots, \sigma_k, \cvec{u}_k, \cvec{v}_k costs k(m + n + 1). When k is much smaller than m and n that is a large saving, and @thm-eckart-young says no other rank-k object stored the same way is closer to \A in the Frobenius norm. The relative error is  igl(\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 / \sum_i\sigma_i^2 igr)^{1/2}, computable before choosing k. Whether that error is acceptable is not a mathematical question. The second is principal components. Take n data points in 
R^m and place them as the columns of \A. Then @cor-best-fitting-subspace says: the k-dimensional subspace through the origin that minimizes the total squared distance to the data is spanned by \cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_k, the leading left singular vectors. These directions are the principal components of the data, and the numbers \sigma_i^2 measure how much of \sum_j
orm{\cvec{a}_j}^2 each one accounts for. That is a theorem of linear algebra, and it is the whole of what this book has proved. What is not proved here is the statistics. The usual procedure subtracts the mean of the data first, so that 	frac{1}{n}\A\A	p becomes a sample covariance matrix, and then interprets \sigma_i^2/\sum_l\sigma_l^2 as a fraction of variance explained. Those steps need a probabilistic model, a reason to prefer squared error, and an argument that the sample answer says something about a larger population. Chapter 24 §10 supplies the first two — the model for the finite population of the data themselves, where expectation is an average and no measure theory is needed, and three reasons to prefer squared error — and says plainly that the third belongs to probability and statistics, which this book does not develop. It also says why a singular value decomposition is never computed by forming \A^{*}\A and finding its eigenvalues, the route taken in every hand computation in this chapter; the algorithm that replaces it is assembled nowhere in this book. The truncation is optimal for this norm, and low rank does not mean small. Two mistakes to avoid. Other measures of error give other answers. Let \A = \diag(2, 1), so \sigma_1 = 2, \sigma_2 = 1, and \A_1 = \diag(2, 0), whose error matrix \diag(0, 1) has a largest entry of modulus 1. The rank-one matrix \B =  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 3 & \sqrt3 \ \sqrt3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A - \B =  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & -\sqrt3 \ -\sqrt3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, has \det\B = 	frac34 - 	frac34 = 0, so ank\B = 1, and every entry of \A - \B has modulus at most \sqrt3/2 \approx 0.87 < 1. So \B beats \A_1 if the error is measured entrywise. It loses in the Frobenius norm, as it must: 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = 2 > 1 = 
orm{\A - \A_1}_F^2. Small rank and small size are unrelated. The n 	imes n all-ones matrix \J has rank 1 and 
orm{\J}_F = n, while \varepsilon\I_n has rank n and 
orm{\varepsilon\I_n}_F = \varepsilon\sqrt n, as small as we like. “Approximating by a matrix of low rank” is a statement about structure, never about magnitude. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the Eckart–Young Theorem, including the value of the minimum. 2. Express 
orm{\A}_F in terms of the singular values of \A. 3. Let ank\A = r. What is \A_k for k \ge r, and what is the minimum of 
orm{\A - \B}_F over ank\B \le k in that case? 4. True or false: the truncation \A_k is the unique matrix of rank at most k nearest to \A in the Frobenius norm. Justify your answer. 5. A matrix of rank 1 is close to \O in the Frobenius norm. True or false? Justify your answer. (a) For \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) with singular values \sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_p and 0 \le k \le p: every \B with ank\B \le k satisfies 
orm{\A - \B}_F \ge  igl(\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 igr)^{1/2}, with equality for \B = \A_k = \sum_{i \le k}\sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*}. (b) 
orm{\A}_F =  igl(\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sigma_i^2 igr)^{1/2} (@lem-frobenius-sum-of-squares). (c) \A_k = \A, since the terms with i > r are zero; the minimum is 0, attained at \B = \A itself, which has rank r \le k. (d) False in general. Take \A = \I_2, so \sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = 1. Both \B_1 = \diag(1, 0) and \B_2 = 	frac12 egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} have rank 1, and 
orm{\I_2 - \B_1}_F^2 = 1 = 
orm{\I_2 - \B_2}_F^2, which is the minimum \sigma_2^2. (Both are truncations of \I_2, for two different singular value decompositions.) (e) False. Rank is unrelated to size: the all-ones matrix \J \in M_n(
R) has rank 1 and 
orm{\J}_F = n. B. Practice [B1: Errors from the singular values alone] A matrix \A has singular values 6, 3, 2, 1. 1. Compute 
orm{\A}_F and the minimum of 
orm{\A - \B}_F over matrices \B of rank at most k, for k = 1, 2, 3. 2. Find the smallest k for which the relative error 
orm{\A - \A_k}_F/
orm{\A}_F is at most 0.3. (a) 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 36 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 50, so 
orm{\A}_F = \sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt2. By @thm-eckart-young the minima are \sqrt{9 + 4 + 1} = \sqrt{14}, \qquad \sqrt{4 + 1} = \sqrt5, \qquad \sqrt{1} = 1 for k = 1, 2, 3. (b) The condition is \sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 \le 0.09 \cdot 50 = 4.5. For k = 2 the left side is 5 > 4.5; for k = 3 it is 1 \le 4.5. So k = 3. [B2: A best rank-one approximation] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
R). Find the singular values of \A, the best rank-one approximation \A_1 in the Frobenius norm, and the error, computed both directly and from the theorem. \A is symmetric with eigenvalues 4 and 2 (trace 6, determinant 8) and orthonormal eigenvectors \cvec{q}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1), \cvec{q}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1). Both eigenvalues are positive, so \A \succ \O, and \A	p\A = \A^2 has eigenvalues 16 and 4; hence \sigma_1 = 4, \sigma_2 = 2, with \cvec{u}_i = \cvec{v}_i = \cvec{q}_i. Therefore \A_1 = 4\cvec{q}_1\cvec{q}_1	p = 4 \cdot  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, which has rank one. Directly, \A - \A_1 =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad 
orm{\A - \A_1}_F^2 = 4 . From @thm-eckart-young the error squared is \sigma_2^2 = 4. The two agree, and 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 9 + 1 + 1 + 9 = 20 = 16 + 4 checks @lem-frobenius-sum-of-squares. [B3: Pythagoras for the truncation] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and 0 \le k \le p. Prove that 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 
orm{\A_k}_F^2 + 
orm{\A - \A_k}_F^2 , and deduce that k \mapsto 
orm{\A - \A_k}_F is nonincreasing. By @lem-frobenius-sum-of-squares applied to \A and to \A - \A_k, and by the same lemma applied to \A_k, whose singular values are \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_k followed by zeros (it equals \U\vSigma'\V^{*} with \vSigma' the matrix keeping only the first k diagonal entries of \vSigma), 
orm{\A_k}_F^2 + 
orm{\A - \A_k}_F^2 = \sum_{i \le k}\sigma_i^2 + \sum_{i > k}\sigma_i^2 = 
orm{\A}_F^2 . Since 
orm{\A - \A_k}_F^2 = \sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 and the \sigma_i^2 are nonnegative, increasing k by one removes a nonnegative term, so the sequence is nonincreasing. This proves both claims. C. Going deeper [C1: How far is a matrix from being singular?] Let \A \in M_n(F) be invertible, with singular values \sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_n > 0. 1. Prove that 
orm{\A - \B}_F \ge \sigma_n for every singular \B \in M_n(F). 2. Exhibit a singular \B with 
orm{\A - \B}_F = \sigma_n. 3. Deduce that the distance from \A to the set of singular matrices, measured in the Frobenius norm, is exactly \sigma_n, and illustrate this with \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}. (a) A singular \B \in M_n(F) has ank\B \le n - 1 (@thm-invertible-tfae-det (d)). By @thm-eckart-young with k = n - 1, 
orm{\A - \B}_F \ \ge\ \Bigl(\sum_{i > n-1}\sigma_i^2\Bigr)^{1/2} = \sigma_n . (b) Take \B = \A_{n-1} = \sum_{i \le n-1}\sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*}. Its rank is n - 1 < n, so it is singular, and 
orm{\A - \B}_F = \sigma_n by @lem-frobenius-sum-of-squares. (c) By (a) the distance is at least \sigma_n and by (b) it is at most \sigma_n, so it equals \sigma_n; in particular the minimum is attained. For the given \A, Exercise B2 found \sigma_2 = 2 and \A_1 =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}, which is singular and at Frobenius distance 2. So no singular matrix is closer to \A than 2. The smallest singular value is therefore a quantitative version of invertibility: \A is invertible exactly when \sigma_n > 0, and it is far from singular exactly when \sigma_n is large. [C2: The best line through a cloud of points] The four points (1, 1), (2, 2), (1, -1) and (0, 0) of 
R^2 are to be fitted by a line through the origin, minimizing the total squared distance from the points to the line. 1. Write the points as the columns of a matrix \A and compute \A\A	p and the singular values of \A. 2. Use @cor-best-fitting-subspace to find the best line and the minimum total squared distance. 3. Verify the answer by computing the four distances directly. (a) With the points as columns, \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A\A	p =  egin{pmatrix} 6 & 4 \ 4 & 6 \end{pmatrix} . The eigenvalues of \A\A	p are 10 and 2 (trace 12, determinant 20), with orthonormal eigenvectors \cvec{u}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1) and \cvec{u}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1). The eigenvalues of \A\A	p are the squares of the singular values, since \A\A	p = \U\vSigma\vSigma^{*}\U^{*}; hence \sigma_1 = \sqrt{10} and \sigma_2 = \sqrt2. (b) By @cor-best-fitting-subspace with k = 1, the best line is S_0 = \Span(\cvec{u}_1), the line y = x, and the minimum total squared distance is \sigma_2^2 = 2. (c) The points (1, 1), (2, 2) and (0, 0) lie on y = x, contributing 0. For (1, -1), the projection onto \Span igl((1,1) igr) is 	frac{1 - 1}{2}(1, 1) = (0, 0), so the distance squared is 1 + 1 = 2. The total is 2, as predicted. (The point (0, 0) contributes nothing to any subspace through the origin; it is there as a reminder that the corollary counts all columns, including zero ones.) [C3: Truncation respects unitaries but not sums] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), and let \Q \in M_m(F) and \R \in M_n(F) be unitary (orthogonal, when F = 
R). 1. Prove that \Q\A_k\R^{*} is a best rank-k approximation of \Q\A\R^{*} in the Frobenius norm. 2. Deduce that the function \A \mapsto \min\{
orm{\A - \B}_F : ank\B \le k\} is unchanged by \A \mapsto \Q\A\R^{*}. 3. Give \A, \B \in M_2(
R) with (\A + \B)_1 
e \A_1 + \B_1 for every choice of the truncations involved. Hint: two rank-one matrices whose sum is a multiple of the identity. (a) If \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} is a singular value decomposition (@thm-svd), then \Q\A\R^{*} = (\Q\U)\vSigma(\R\V)^{*} is one as well, since a product of unitary matrices is unitary (@prp-orthogonal-group-properties (a)) and \vSigma is unchanged. Its left and right singular vectors are \Q\cvec{u}_i and \R\cvec{v}_i, so its rank-k truncation for this decomposition is \sum_{i \le k}\sigma_i(\Q\cvec{u}_i)(\R\cvec{v}_i)^{*} = \Q\Bigl(\sum_{i \le k}\sigma_i\cvec{u}_i\cvec{v}_i^{*}\Bigr)\R^{*} = \Q\A_k\R^{*} . By @thm-eckart-young applied to \Q\A\R^{*}, this is a best rank-k approximation. (b) The two matrices have the same singular values, so by @thm-eckart-young both minima equal  igl(\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 igr)^{1/2}. (c) Take \A = \diag(1, 0) and \B = \diag(0, 1). Each has rank one, so \A_1 = \A and \B_1 = \B for every singular value decomposition, and \A_1 + \B_1 = \I_2. But \A + \B = \I_2, whose rank-one truncations all have rank one, hence are never \I_2. So (\A + \B)_1 
e \A_1 + \B_1. Truncation is not a linear operation, which is why “keep the biggest pieces” cannot be analyzed one summand at a time.

title: 13.12 The Moore–Penrose Pseudoinverse
content:
The Moore–Penrose Pseudoinverse Chapter 11 solved \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} twice over: when there is no solution it produced a least-squares solution, and when there are too many it produced the shortest one. It then left an IOU. The two answers “are usually wanted together: given any \A and \cvec{b}, first minimize 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}}, then among the minimizers take the shortest. Chapter 13 packages the combined answer as a single matrix, the pseudoinverse \A^{+}, with \cvec{x} = \A^{+}\cvec{b} in all cases at once.” This section builds that matrix and pays the debt. Throughout, F = 
R or F = 
C, \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), p = \min(m, n), and r = ank\A, with singular values \sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_p \ge 0 (@def-singular-values), so \sigma_i > 0 exactly for i \le r. One matrix instead of three formulas Here is the state of play at the end of Chapter 11. To answer “what is the best \cvec{x}?” we had three different recipes, and choosing between them required knowing something about \A first. - If \A is square and invertible, \cvec{x} = \A^{-1}\cvec{b}. - If the columns of \A are independent, \cvec{x} = (\A^{*}\A)^{-1}\A^{*}\cvec{b} (@cor-least-squares-unique). - If \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} is consistent but \A has a kernel, \cvec{x} = \cvec{x}_{\min}, the unique solution orthogonal to 
ul(\A) (@thm-minimum-norm-solution). Three recipes, three hypotheses, and a gap: when \A has both a kernel and a column space missing \cvec{b}, none of them applies. That is not an exotic case. It is what happens whenever a large table of measurements has both redundant columns and noise. The goal, stated before we know how to reach it, is a single matrix \A^{+}, depending on \A alone, for which \cvec{x} = \A^{+}\cvec{b} is the right answer in every case. Reading the goal backwards tells us what \A^{+} must do, and the singular value decomposition tells us how to build it. Inverting what can be inverted Why is there no inverse in general? Two obstructions, and they are the two halves of @thm-four-subspaces-orthogonal. The map \cvec{x} \mapsto \A\cvec{x} may fail to be injective, because 
ul(\A) 
e \{\cvec{0}\}; and it may fail to be surjective, because \col(\A) 
e F^m. Neither obstruction is fatal if we are willing to sacrifice part of the domain and part of the codomain. Restrict the map to \col(\A^{*}) = 
ul(\A)^{\perp}, which throws away the kernel. What is left is a bijection onto \col(\A), and a bijection has an inverse. Extend that inverse to all of F^m by declaring it \cvec{0} on \col(\A)^{\perp}, where nothing in the image can tell us anything. That is the whole construction, and it is the same trick that turns \sin into \arcsin: shrink the domain until the function is injective, shrink the codomain until it is surjective, invert, and say clearly what was given up. Invert what can be inverted, and send the rest to zero. The singular value decomposition performs all three operations at once, because it presents \A as a diagonal matrix in orthonormal coordinates, and a diagonal matrix is inverted one entry at a time. [Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and let \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} be a singular value decomposition (@thm-svd), so that \U \in M_m(F) and \V \in M_n(F) are unitary and \vSigma \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) has the singular values \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_p on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Let \vSigma^{+} \in M_{n 	imes m}(F) be the matrix with (\vSigma^{+})_{ii} =  egin{cases} \sigma_i^{-1}, & \sigma_i > 0, \ 0, & \sigma_i = 0, \end{cases} for 1 \le i \le p, and all other entries 0. The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of \A is \A^{+} \coloneqq \V\vSigma^{+}\U^{*} \in M_{n 	imes m}(F) . Clause by clause. The matrix \vSigma^{+} is \vSigma transposed and then inverted where inversion is legal: the shape flips from m 	imes n to n 	imes m, each nonzero diagonal entry is replaced by its reciprocal, and each zero diagonal entry is left alone — not replaced by anything, since 0^{-1} does not exist. The outer factors are exchanged and starred, exactly as they would be in (\U\vSigma\V^{*})^{-1} = \V\vSigma^{-1}\U^{*} if \vSigma were invertible. And the result is n 	imes m, the shape an inverse of \A would have to be. Well-definedness is a real question here, not a formality. The singular values are determined by \A, but the unitary factors are not (@thm-singular-values-unique), so the recipe above is applied to a choice, and nothing so far says that two choices give the same answer. They do. [The pseudoinverse does not depend on the decomposition] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and let \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} be any singular value decomposition (@thm-svd). Then \X = \V\vSigma^{+}\U^{*} is the unique matrix in M_{n 	imes m}(F) such that 1. for every \cvec{y} \in \col(\A), \X\cvec{y} is the unique vector of \col(\A^{*}) that \A sends to \cvec{y}; 2. \X\cvec{y} = \cvec{0} for every \cvec{y} \in \col(\A)^{\perp}. In particular \A^{+} depends on \A alone. Conditions (i) and (ii) mention only \A, so if one matrix satisfies them, that matrix is determined by \A. The work is to check that they can be satisfied at all — which is the “restrict, invert, extend” story of the previous page written out — and that the matrix built from an arbitrary decomposition is the one that satisfies them. For the second part, the singular vectors are orthonormal bases of the subspaces involved, so both conditions can be checked on basis vectors. The conditions determine at most one matrix. First, \A maps \col(\A^{*}) bijectively onto \col(\A). Injectivity: if \cvec{x} \in \col(\A^{*}) and \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}, then \cvec{x} \in 
ul(\A) \cap 
ul(\A)^{\perp} = \{\cvec{0}\}, since \col(\A^{*}) = 
ul(\A)^{\perp} by @thm-four-subspaces-orthogonal (b). Surjectivity: the image is contained in \col(\A), and by injectivity it has dimension \dim\col(\A^{*}) = ank\A^{*} = ank\A = \dim\col(\A), the middle equality by @cor-rank-adjoint (a) applied to \cvec{x} \mapsto \A\cvec{x}. So (i) prescribes \X on \col(\A) and (ii) prescribes it on \col(\A)^{\perp}; since F^m = \col(\A) \oplus \col(\A)^{\perp} by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (a), a linear map is determined by the two prescriptions. The matrix \X = \V\vSigma^{+}\U^{*} satisfies them. Write \cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_m and \cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n for the columns of \U and \V. Since rank is unchanged by invertible factors (@thm-rank-product-inequality), r = ank\A = ank\vSigma is the number of nonzero \sigma_i. By @cor-svd-four-subspaces, (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_r) is an orthonormal basis of \col(\A), the remaining \cvec{u}_j are an orthonormal basis of \col(\A)^{\perp}, and (\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_r) is an orthonormal basis of \col(\A^{*}). Multiplying out the definition, \X = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i^{-1}\cvec{v}_i\cvec{u}_i^{*} , so \X\cvec{u}_i = \sigma_i^{-1}\cvec{v}_i for i \le r and \X\cvec{u}_j = \cvec{0} for j > r. The second statement gives (ii) by linearity. For (i), let \cvec{y} = \sum_{i \le r}c_i\cvec{u}_i \in \col(\A). Then \X\cvec{y} = \sum_{i \le r}c_i\sigma_i^{-1}\cvec{v}_i \in \col(\A^{*}), and since \A\cvec{v}_i = \sigma_i\cvec{u}_i (the rank-one expansion of @thm-compact-svd read one column at a time), \A(\X\cvec{y}) = \sum_{i \le r} c_i\sigma_i^{-1}\sigma_i\cvec{u}_i = \cvec{y} . By the injectivity proved above, \X\cvec{y} is the unique vector of \col(\A^{*}) with this property. This proves (i), and with it the proposition. So \A^{+} is an honest function of \A. Five examples, simplest first. [Five pseudoinverses] 1. \A invertible. Then m = n = r, \vSigma is invertible and \vSigma^{+} = \vSigma^{-1}, so \A^{+} = \V\vSigma^{-1}\U^{*} = (\U\vSigma\V^{*})^{-1} = \A^{-1}. The pseudoinverse extends the inverse, which is the first thing it had to do. 2. \A = \O \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). Every singular value is 0, so \vSigma^{+} = \O and \A^{+} = \O \in M_{n 	imes m}(F). The degenerate case is worth keeping in mind: the pseudoinverse of the worst possible matrix is not undefined, it is zero, which is what “invert nothing, kill everything” means. 3. Diagonal. \diag(2, 0, 5)^{+} = \diag igl(	frac12, 0, 	frac15 igr). The zero is left where it is. 4. A single nonzero column \cvec{a} \in M_{n 	imes 1}(F). Here \sigma_1 = 
orm{\cvec{a}}, \cvec{u}_1 = \cvec{a}/
orm{\cvec{a}}, and \cvec{v}_1 = 1, so \cvec{a}^{+} = \cvec{a}^{*}/
orm{\cvec{a}}^2, a row vector. Then \cvec{a}^{+}\cvec{a} = 1 but \cvec{a}\cvec{a}^{+} = \cvec{a}\cvec{a}^{*}/
orm{\cvec{a}}^2 is the orthogonal projection onto \Span(\cvec{a}). 5. \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}. This is \sigma_1\cvec{u}_1\cvec{v}_1^{*} with \sigma_1 = 2 and \cvec{u}_1 = \cvec{v}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1), since 2\cvec{u}_1\cvec{v}_1^{*} = 2 \cdot 	frac12 egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} = \A. Hence \A^{+} = 	frac12\cvec{v}_1\cvec{u}_1^{*} =  rac14 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . A nonexample by minimal change. Item (a) of the list is often written \A^{+} = (\A^{*}\A)^{-1}\A^{*}, and @thm-pseudoinverse-properties below confirms that formula whenever the columns of \A are independent. (c) \A\A^{+} = P_{\col(\A)} and \A^{+}\A = P_{\col(\A^{*})} (@thm-pseudoinverse-properties (a)). The second is \I_n exactly when \col(\A^{*}) = F^n, that is when ank\A = n, that is when the columns of \A are independent. (d) \O^{+} = \O \in M_{n 	imes m}(F); \A^{+} = \A^{-1} when \A is invertible. (e) False. With \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} and \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} the two sides are  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} and 	frac12 egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, as computed in the warning above. R); 2. \A = (1, 2, 2)	p \in M_{3 	imes 1}(

R); 4. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_{2 	imes 3}(
R). (a) A diagonal matrix is its own singular value decomposition (@thm-svd) up to ordering, so invert the nonzero entries in place: \A^{+} = \diag igl(	frac13, 0, 0, 	frac14 igr). (b) A single nonzero column, so @exm-pseudoinverse-first-examples (d) applies with 
orm{\A}^2 = 1 + 4 + 4 = 9: \A^{+} = 	frac19(1, 2, 2) \in M_{1 	imes 3}(
R) . (c) Rank one: \A = \cvec{u}\cvec{v}	p with \cvec{u} = (1, 2) and \cvec{v} = (1, 2). Then \sigma_1 = 
orm{\cvec{u}}\,
orm{\cvec{v}} = 5 with \cvec{u}_1 = \cvec{u}/\sqrt5 and \cvec{v}_1 = \cvec{v}/\sqrt5, so \A^{+} = 	frac15\cvec{v}_1\cvec{u}_1	p = 	frac{1}{25} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} . (Check: \A\A^{+} = 	frac{1}{25} egin{psmallmatrix} 5 & 10 \ 10 & 20\end{psmallmatrix} is Hermitian and idempotent, and \A\A^{+}\A = \A.) (d) The rows are independent, so ank\A = 2 = m and @thm-pseudoinverse-properties (e) gives \A^{+} = \A	p(\A\A	p)^{-1}. And \A\cvec{x}_{\min} = \cvec{u} igl(\cvec{v}	p\cvec{x}_{\min} igr) = \cvec{u} igl(	frac13 + 	frac43 igr) = 	frac53\cvec{u}. They agree. Shortest. [B3: Checking a candidate] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and \X = \dfrac13 egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \ -1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Verify the four Penrose conditions for \X, and hence find the minimum-norm least-squares solution of \A\cvec{x} = (1, 2, 3). Compute the two products first: \X\A =  rac13 egin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \I_2, \qquad \A\X =  rac13 egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \ -1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} . (P4): \X\A = \I_2 is Hermitian. (P3): \A\X is visibly symmetric. (P1): \A\X\A = \A(\X\A) = \A\I_2 = \A. (P2): \X\A\X = \I_2\X = \X. All four hold, so \X = \A^{+} by @thm-penrose-conditions. Then \cvec{x}_{\min} = \X(1, 2, 3) =  rac13(2 + 2 - 3,\ -1 + 2 + 6) = \Bigl(	frac13, 	frac73\Bigr) . (The columns of \A are independent, so this is also (\A	p\A)^{-1}\A	p\cvec{b}, and it is the unique least-squares solution; the normal equations  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}\cvec{x} = (3, 5) confirm it.) C. Going deeper [C1: Pseudoinverses of \A^{*}\A] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). 1. Prove that (\A^{*}\A)^{+} = \A^{+}(\A^{+})^{*}. 2. Deduce that \A^{+} = (\A^{*}\A)^{+}\A^{*}, the formula (\A^{*}\A)^{-1}\A^{*} with the inverse replaced by the pseudoinverse. Hint: use a singular value decomposition and reduce each identity to an identity between diagonal matrices. Write \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*}. (a) Then \A^{*}\A = \V\vSigma^{*}\vSigma\V^{*}, and \vSigma^{*}\vSigma \in M_n(F) is diagonal with entries \sigma_1^2, \dots, \sigma_p^2 followed by zeros. That display is a singular value decomposition of \A^{*}\A in the sense of @thm-svd (both outer factors are \V, which is unitary, and the middle factor is diagonal with nonnegative entries), so (\A^{*}\A)^{+} = \V(\vSigma^{*}\vSigma)^{+}\V^{*}, where (\vSigma^{*}\vSigma)^{+} is diagonal with entries \sigma_i^{-2} for i \le r and 0 elsewhere. On the other side, (\A^{+})^{*} = (\V\vSigma^{+}\U^{*})^{*} = \U(\vSigma^{+})^{*}\V^{*}, so \A^{+}(\A^{+})^{*} = \V\vSigma^{+}\U^{*}\U(\vSigma^{+})^{*}\V^{*} = \V\vSigma^{+}(\vSigma^{+})^{*}\V^{*} . The middle factor \vSigma^{+}(\vSigma^{+})^{*} is diagonal with entries \sigma_i^{-1}\sigma_i^{-1} = \sigma_i^{-2} for i \le r and 0 elsewhere, which is (\vSigma^{*}\vSigma)^{+}. Hence the two sides agree. (b) Using (a) and \A^{*} = \V\vSigma^{*}\U^{*}, (\A^{*}\A)^{+}\A^{*} = \V\vSigma^{+}(\vSigma^{+})^{*}\vSigma^{*}\U^{*} . Now (\vSigma^{+})^{*}\vSigma^{*} = (\vSigma\vSigma^{+})^{*} = \vSigma\vSigma^{+}, which is the m 	imes m diagonal matrix with r ones and then zeros; and \vSigma^{+} multiplied by it on the right is \vSigma^{+}, since \vSigma^{+} has nonzero entries only in the first r columns. So the right-hand side is \V\vSigma^{+}\U^{*} = \A^{+}. [C2: When the reversal rule does hold] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) with ank\A = n and \B \in M_{n 	imes q}(F) with ank\B = n. Prove that (\A\B)^{+} = \B^{+}\A^{+} . Hint: write both pseudoinverses with the formulas of @thm-pseudoinverse-properties (e) and verify the Penrose conditions for the product. By @thm-pseudoinverse-properties (e), \A^{+} = (\A^{*}\A)^{-1}\A^{*} and \B^{+} = \B^{*}(\B\B^{*})^{-1}, the two inverses existing because ank\A = n and ank\B^{*} = n. Put \X = \B^{+}\A^{+} = \B^{*}(\B\B^{*})^{-1}(\A^{*}\A)^{-1}\A^{*} . Throughout we use \A^{+}\A = \I_n and \B\B^{+} = \I_n, which the two formulas give at once. (P1): (\A\B)\X(\A\B) = \A(\B\B^{+})(\A^{+}\A)\B = \A\I_n\I_n\B = \A\B. (P2): \X(\A\B)\X = \B^{+}(\A^{+}\A)(\B\B^{+})\A^{+} = \B^{+}\A^{+} = \X. (P3): (\A\B)\X = \A(\B\B^{+})\A^{+} = \A\A^{+} = \A(\A^{*}\A)^{-1}\A^{*}, which equals its own conjugate transpose, since \A^{*}\A is Hermitian and so is its inverse. (P4): \X(\A\B) = \B^{+}(\A^{+}\A)\B = \B^{+}\B = \B^{*}(\B\B^{*})^{-1}\B, Hermitian for the same reason. All four hold, so \X = (\A\B)^{+} by @thm-penrose-conditions. [C3: When the pseudoinverse is the adjoint] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). 1. Prove that \A^{+} = \A^{*} if and only if \A\A^{*}\A = \A. 2. Deduce that \A^{+} = \A^{*} if and only if every nonzero singular value of \A equals 1. 3. Give an example of such an \A in M_2(
R) which is neither unitary nor an orthogonal projection. (a) (\Rightarrow) If \A^{+} = \A^{*}, then (P1) reads \A\A^{*}\A = \A. (\Leftarrow) Suppose \A\A^{*}\A = \A and put \X = \A^{*}. Then (P1) is the hypothesis; (P2) is \A^{*}\A\A^{*} = (\A\A^{*}\A)^{*} = \A^{*}; (P3) is (\A\A^{*})^{*} = \A\A^{*}, true for every \A; and (P4) is (\A^{*}\A)^{*} = \A^{*}\A, likewise. By @thm-penrose-conditions, \A^{+} = \A^{*}. (b) With \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*} we have \A^{*} = \V\vSigma^{*}\U^{*} and \A^{+} = \V\vSigma^{+}\U^{*}. Since \U and \V are invertible, \A^{+} = \A^{*} if and only if \vSigma^{+} = \vSigma^{*}, that is if and only if \sigma_i^{-1} = \sigma_i for every i \le r, that is if and only if every nonzero singular value is 1 (the equation \sigma^2 = 1 with \sigma > 0 forces \sigma = 1). (c) Take \A =  rac{1}{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . Then \A\A	p =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, so \A\A	p\A = \A and (a) applies. Its singular values are 1 and 0, matching (b). It is not unitary, since it is singular, and not an orthogonal projection, since \A	p 
e \A. Such a matrix maps \col(\A^{*}) isometrically onto \col(\A) and sends 
ul(\A) to \cvec{0}: a unitary matrix on the part of the space where it is invertible, and nothing at all elsewhere.

title: 13.13 Projections Revisited
content:
Projections Revisited Chapter 4 built projections out of nothing but a direct sum: given V = U \oplus W, the operator that keeps the U-piece and discards the W-piece satisfies P^2 = P, and every operator satisfying P^2 = P arises this way. Chapter 11 built a second kind by taking W = U^{\perp}, the orthogonal projection P_U. The second is a special case of the first, and Chapter 4 left the comparison open, saying only that its projections “are often called oblique projections, to distinguish them from the orthogonal projections met later, in the chapters on inner product spaces”. This section makes the distinction exact, measures how far an oblique projection is from being orthogonal, and closes Part III. Throughout, V is a finite-dimensional inner product space over F = 
R or 
C, and n = \dim V. Which projections are orthogonal? Two recollections, because the section is about the gap between them. From Chapter 2: an operator P \in \cL(V) with P^2 = P is a projection, also called an idempotent (@def-projection-operator); it satisfies V = \im P \oplus \ker P, it is the identity on \im P and zero on \ker P, and each splitting V = U \oplus W has exactly one projection with image U and kernel W (@thm-projection-direct-sum). No inner product appears there, and the field was arbitrary. From Chapter 11: the splitting V = U \oplus U^{\perp} of @thm-orthogonal-decomposition is one of the many available, and P_U is the projection belonging to it (@def-orthogonal-projection). Chapter 4 warned that a subspace is the image of infinitely many projections, one per complement. Which one does the inner product pick out, and how is it recognized without being told the kernel? A projection is orthogonal exactly when it throws away perpendicularly — and that is the same as costing nothing to move across the inner product. [Orthogonal Projections Among the Idempotents] Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F and let P \in \cL(V) satisfy P^2 = P. The following are equivalent. 1. P is the orthogonal projection onto its image: P = P_U with U = \im P. 2. \ker P = (\im P)^{\perp}. 3. P^{*} = P. 4. P is normal. 5. 
orm{P\elem{v}} \le 
orm{\elem{v}} for every \elem{v} \in V. Conditions (a) and (b) say one thing twice, once about the operator and once about its two subspaces. Going from (b) to (c) is a computation Chapter 11 has already done for P_U. Coming back from (c) is the four-subspaces theorem: \ker P^{*} is always (\im P)^{\perp}, so once P^{*} = P the kernel is forced; normality is the same remark with \ker P^{*} replaced by \ker P. The one direction with work in it is (e) \Rightarrow (b), where a bound on lengths has to become a statement about angles. Feed P a vector \elem{u} + t\elem{w} with \elem{u} \in \im P and \elem{w} \in \ker P: its image is \elem{u} whatever t is, so choosing t to make 
orm{\elem{u} + t\elem{w}} as small as possible squeezes \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} to zero. (a) \Leftrightarrow (b). Write U = \im P. (\Rightarrow) If P = P_U, then \ker P = \ker P_U = U^{\perp}, since P_U is the projection onto U along U^{\perp} (@def-orthogonal-projection and @thm-projection-direct-sum (b)). (\Leftarrow) If \ker P = U^{\perp}, then P is a projection with image U and kernel U^{\perp}, and so is P_U; by the uniqueness in @thm-projection-direct-sum (b), applied to V = U \oplus U^{\perp}, the two are equal. (b) \Rightarrow (c). By the equivalence just proved, P = P_U with U = \im P. By @thm-projection-formula (b), \inner{P\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{P\elem{v}} for all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V. That is the defining identity of the adjoint, so P^{*} = P by the uniqueness in @def-adjoint. (c) \Rightarrow (d). If P^{*} = P then P^{*}P = P^2 = PP^{*}, which is @def-normal-operator. (d) \Rightarrow (b). Since P is normal, \ker P = \ker P^{*} by @cor-normal-kernel (a). By @thm-four-subspaces-orthogonal (a), \ker P^{*} = (\im P)^{\perp}. Combining the two gives (b). (b) \Rightarrow (e). Let \elem{v} \in V and split it as \elem{v} = P\elem{v} + (\elem{v} - P\elem{v}). The first piece lies in \im P, and the second lies in \ker P, because P(\elem{v} - P\elem{v}) = P\elem{v} - P^2\elem{v} = \elem{0}. By (b) the two pieces are orthogonal, so @thm-pythagoras gives 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 = 
orm{P\elem{v}}^2 + 
orm{\elem{v} - P\elem{v}}^2 \ge 
orm{P\elem{v}}^2 , and taking nonnegative square roots gives 
orm{P\elem{v}} \le 
orm{\elem{v}}. (e) \Rightarrow (b). We first show \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} = 0 for every \elem{u} \in \im P and every \elem{w} \in \ker P. There is nothing to prove when \elem{w} = \elem{0}, so assume \elem{w} 
e \elem{0}, write z = \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{w}}, and put t = - rac{z}{
orm{\elem{w}}^2}, \qquad \elem{v} = \elem{u} + t\elem{w} , which is legitimate because 
orm{\elem{w}} 
e 0. Then P\elem{v} = P\elem{u} + tP\elem{w} = \elem{u}, since P is the identity on \im P and zero on \ker P (@thm-projection-direct-sum (a)). Expanding the norm squared and using conjugate symmetry,  egin{aligned} 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 &= 
orm{\elem{u}}^2 + \conj{t}\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} + t\inner{\elem{w}}{\elem{u}} + \lvert tvert^2
orm{\elem{w}}^2 \ &= 
orm{\elem{u}}^2 -  rac{\lvert zvert^2}{
orm{\elem{w}}^2} -  rac{\lvert zvert^2}{
orm{\elem{w}}^2} +  rac{\lvert zvert^2}{
orm{\elem{w}}^2} = 
orm{\elem{u}}^2 -  rac{\lvert zvert^2}{
orm{\elem{w}}^2} . \end{aligned} Now (e) applied to this \elem{v} says 
orm{\elem{u}}^2 = 
orm{P\elem{v}}^2 \le 
orm{\elem{v}}^2, which forces \lvert zvert^2 \le 0 and hence z = 0. So \ker P \subseteq (\im P)^{\perp}. The two subspaces have the same dimension: \dim\ker P = n - ank P by @thm-rank-nullity, and \dim(\im P)^{\perp} = n - \dim\im P = n - ank P by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (c). A subspace contained in another of the same finite dimension equals it (@thm-dim-impl-eq), so \ker P = (\im P)^{\perp}. This closes the cycle and proves the theorem. The theorem is the promised comparison. Every projection of Chapter 4 that is not self-adjoint is oblique, and now “oblique” has a precise meaning: its kernel is a complement of its image that is not the perpendicular one. Chapter 12 has already met a pair of such projections, in @exm-oblique-projections, and the Quick check after @thm-spectral-resolution-unique traced exactly what their obliqueness cost. Clause (c) also settles Chapter 4’s warning that “projection onto U” is incomplete information. [One Orthogonal Projection per Subspace] Let U be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space V. Among the projections of V with image U — one for each complement of U, by @thm-projection-direct-sum — exactly one is self-adjoint, namely P_U. P_U has image U and is self-adjoint by @thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoint, (a) \Rightarrow (c). Conversely, let P be a self-adjoint projection with \im P = U. By the same theorem, (c) \Rightarrow (b), \ker P = U^{\perp}, which is also \ker P_U. Two projections with the same image and the same kernel are equal, by the uniqueness in @thm-projection-direct-sum (b). Chapter 4’s own example is now decided by inspection. On 
R^2 with the dot product, P(x, y) = (x, 0) and P'(x, y) = (x - y, 0) are both projections onto the x-axis, with standard matrices \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \P' =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . The standard basis is orthonormal, so @thm-matrix-of-adjoint says self-adjointness is symmetry of these matrices. The first is symmetric, so P = P_U for the x-axis U. The second is not, so P' is oblique — as the picture in Chapter 4 showed, it slides along the line y = x rather than straight down. Clause (e) fails visibly at \cvec{v} = (1, -1): there P'\cvec{v} = (2, 0), and 
orm{P'\cvec{v}} = 2 while 
orm{\cvec{v}} = \sqrt2. Does \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} act on 
R^2 as a projection? If so, is it an orthogonal projection? \A^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \A, so yes, it is a projection. Its image is the span of its columns, \Span((1, 1)), and its kernel is \Span(\cvec{e}_2). Since \inner{(1, 1)}{\cvec{e}_2} = 1 
e 0, the kernel is not (\im \A)^{\perp}, so the projection is oblique by @thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoint (b). The quickest route is clause (c): \A	p 
e \A. Clause (e) is a statement about every vector, and one vector proves nothing. For the oblique \P' above, 
orm{\P'\cvec{e}_1} = 1 = 
orm{\cvec{e}_1} and 
orm{\P'(1, 1)} = 0 \le \sqrt2; both are consistent with the bound, and both are worthless as evidence. The bound fails only in the direction (1, -1). If you want to certify a projection as orthogonal by hand, check \P^{*} = \P in an orthonormal basis, not the length of one image. An orthogonal projection is almost never an orthogonal matrix. If \P is unitary and idempotent, it is invertible, so multiplying \P^2 = \P by \P^{-1} gives \P = \I. Apart from the identity, every orthogonal projection is singular. “Orthogonal” in P_U names the direction of the discarding, not membership in \Orth(n). The block that measures obliqueness Chapter 2 already knows the shape of a projection up to a change of basis: with a basis of \im P followed by a basis of \ker P, the matrix is \diag(1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots, 0) with ank P ones (@cor-projection-matrix). That basis is built to fit P and is usually not orthonormal, so the normal form erases exactly the information we now want. Insisting on an orthonormal basis costs one extra block, and that block is the answer. [Canonical Form of an Idempotent in an Orthonormal Basis] Let V be an n-dimensional inner product space over F and let P \in \cL(V) be a projection of rank r. Let (\elem{f}_1, \dots, \elem{f}_r) be any orthonormal basis of \im P and (\elem{f}_{r+1}, \dots, \elem{f}_n) any orthonormal basis of (\im P)^{\perp}. Then \sB = (\elem{f}_1, \dots, \elem{f}_n) is an orthonormal basis of V, and \mtx{P}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} \I_r & \X \ \O & \O \end{pmatrix} for some \X \in M_{r 	imes (n - r)}(F). Moreover P is an orthogonal projection if and only if \X = \O. Only two facts are used, and both are already proved. First, P fixes its image, so the first r columns are forced to be \cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_r. Second, every output of P lies in \im P, so the last n - r columns have nothing below row r. What sits above row r in those columns is unconstrained, and that is \X: it records where P sends the directions perpendicular to its image, which an orthogonal projection would send to \elem{0}. Write U = \im P, so \dim U = r and \dim U^{\perp} = n - r by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (c). Each \elem{f}_i with i \le r is orthogonal to each \elem{f}_j with j > r, since the first lies in U and the second in U^{\perp}; so \sB is an orthonormal list of n vectors, hence an orthonormal basis of V (@thm-orthogonal-independent). For i \le r we have \elem{f}_i \in \im P, so P\elem{f}_i = \elem{f}_i by @thm-projection-direct-sum (a), and column i of \mtx{P}{\sB}{\sB} is \cvec{e}_i. For j > r we have P\elem{f}_j \in \im P = U = \Span(\elem{f}_1, \dots, \elem{f}_r), so P\elem{f}_j = \sum_{i \le r} x_{ij}\elem{f}_i for scalars x_{ij} \in F, and column j has zeros in rows r + 1, \dots, n. Collecting the x_{ij} into \X gives the displayed shape. For the last claim, \sB is orthonormal, so \mtx{P^{*}}{\sB}{\sB} = (\mtx{P}{\sB}{\sB})^{*} by @thm-matrix-of-adjoint, and (\mtx{P}{\sB}{\sB})^{*} =  egin{pmatrix} \I_r & \O \ \X^{*} & \O \end{pmatrix} . The two matrices agree if and only if \X = \O. Since an operator is determined by its matrix in a basis, P^{*} = P if and only if \X = \O, and P^{*} = P says P is an orthogonal projection by @thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoint. The block \X is not unique, because the two orthonormal bases were not. Replacing them changes \X into \A^{*}\X\B for some unitary \A \in M_r(F) and \B \in M_{n-r}(F), and that leaves the singular values of \X alone: since (\A^{*}\X\B)^{*}(\A^{*}\X\B) = \B^{*}(\X^{*}\X)\B , the two matrices (\A^{*}\X\B)^{*}(\A^{*}\X\B) and \X^{*}\X are unitarily similar, so they have the same eigenvalues, and @def-singular-values reads the singular values off those. So the list \sigma_1(\X) \ge \sigma_2(\X) \ge \dots belongs to P itself, and P is an orthogonal projection exactly when that list is all zeros. The two-dimensional case, in full Take n = 2 and r = 1, so that \X is a single scalar x \in F, and \mtx{P}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & x \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \sB = (\elem{f}_1, \elem{f}_2), with \elem{f}_1 spanning the line \im P and \elem{f}_2 spanning the perpendicular line (\im P)^{\perp}. Everything about P can be read off this one number. The kernel. P(a\elem{f}_1 + b\elem{f}_2) = (a + xb)\elem{f}_1, which is \elem{0} exactly when a = -xb. So \ker P = \Span(-x\elem{f}_1 + \elem{f}_2) , a line that meets (\im P)^{\perp} = \Span(\elem{f}_2) only at \elem{0} unless x = 0. The angle. Suppose F = 
R. The two lines \im P and \ker P are distinct, since their intersection is \{\elem{0}\}; let 	heta \in (0, \pi/2] be the angle between them, meaning the angle of @def-angle between \elem{f}_1 and whichever of \pm(-x\elem{f}_1 + \elem{f}_2) makes it acute. With \elem{k} = -x\elem{f}_1 + \elem{f}_2 we have 
orm{\elem{k}} = \sqrt{1 + x^2} and \inner{\elem{f}_1}{\elem{k}} = -x, so \cos	heta =  rac{\lvert xvert}{\sqrt{1 + x^2}}, \qquad \sin	heta =  rac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^2}}, \qquad \lvert x vert = \cot	heta . The dictionary is complete: x = 0 is 	heta = \pi/2, the orthogonal case; and as the kernel tips toward the image, 	heta 	o 0 and \lvert xvert 	o \infty. The single entry x is the obliqueness, in the units of a cotangent. The stretching. For a unit vector \elem{v} = a\elem{f}_1 + b\elem{f}_2, we have 
orm{P\elem{v}} = \lvert a + xbvert = \lvert\inner{(a, b)}{(1, \conj{x})}vert in F^2 with the standard inner product, so @thm-cauchy-schwarz gives 
orm{P\elem{v}} \le \sqrt{1 + \lvert xvert^2} , with equality exactly when (a, b) is a multiple of (1, \conj{x}), for instance (a, b) = (1, \conj{x})/\sqrt{1 + \lvert xvert^2}. So the largest value of 
orm{P\elem{v}} over unit vectors \elem{v} is \sqrt{1 + \lvert xvert^2}, which over 
R is 1/\sin	heta. Chapter 16 will give this number a name, the operator norm 
orm{P}; here it is enough to say that an orthogonal projection never lengthens a vector, while an oblique one lengthens some vector by 1/\sin	heta, a factor that is unbounded as the kernel closes in on the image. [Two Oblique Projections, Measured] For each of \P' =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Q =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \ 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix} on 
R^2, verify that it is a projection, put it in the form of @thm-idempotent-canonical-form, and find the angle between its image and its kernel and the largest length of an image of a unit vector. The matrix \P'. (\P')^2 = \P' by direct multiplication, and \im\P' = \Span(\cvec{e}_1), \ker\P' = \Span((1, 1)). Here \cvec{f}_1 = \cvec{e}_1 already spans the image and \cvec{f}_2 = \cvec{e}_2 spans its perpendicular, and the standard basis is orthonormal, so the given matrix is the canonical form, with x = -1. Hence \cot	heta = 1, that is 	heta = \pi/4, and the largest value of 
orm{\P'\cvec{v}} on the unit circle is \sqrt{1 + 1} = \sqrt2, attained at \cvec{v} = (1, -1)/\sqrt2. Both readings match Chapter 4’s figure, where \P' projects along the line y = x. The matrix \Q. \Q^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 4 - 2 & -2 + 1 \ 4 - 2 & -2 + 1\end{pmatrix} = \Q, so \Q is a projection, of rank 1. Its image is \Span((1, 1)) and its kernel is \Span((1, 2)), since \Q(1, 2) = (0, 0). Take \cvec{f}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1), \qquad \cvec{f}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1), an orthonormal basis of \im\Q and of (\im\Q)^{\perp} respectively. Then \Q\cvec{f}_1 = \cvec{f}_1 and \Q\cvec{f}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(3, 3) = 3\cvec{f}_1, so x = 3 and \mtx{T_{\Q}}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . Hence \cot	heta = 3. Checking against the two lines directly: the angle between (1, 1) and (1, 2) has \cos	heta = 3/\sqrt{10} and \sin	heta = 1/\sqrt{10}, so \cot	heta = 3, and the largest value of 
orm{\Q\cvec{v}} on the unit circle is \sqrt{1 + 9} = \sqrt{10} = 1/\sin	heta. The two routes agree. In higher rank the same block \X does the same job, and @exr-projections-revisited-c3 turns its largest singular value into the largest value of 
orm{P\elem{v}} over unit \elem{v}, by the argument that just ran in the 2 	imes 2 case. The reason the singular values appear is the one this chapter has used throughout: \X is a rectangular matrix, so its eigenvalues do not exist, and @thm-svd is what measures it instead. Looking back at Part III Part III added one piece of structure to the vector spaces of Parts I and II, and spent three chapters finding out what it buys. Chapter 11 added the inner product, and with it length, orthogonality, and angle. Orthonormal bases made coordinates free, orthogonal complements split every space canonically, and projection onto a subspace solved the nearest-point problem, hence least squares. Its deepest construction was the adjoint, the price of moving an operator from one slot of the inner product to the other; the adjoint is what turned the kernel and the image into two orthogonal pairs of subspaces. Chapter 12 asked which operators the inner product can diagonalize, and the adjoint answered: over 
C the normal ones, over 
R the self-adjoint ones. Written without bases, the spectral theorem says T = \sum_i\lambda_iP_i with the P_i orthogonal projections onto the eigenspaces — which is why the present section had to exist, and why @thm-spectral-resolution needed clause (b) at all. Once a matrix is diagonal in an orthonormal basis, anything can be done to its eigenvalues and undone afterwards, and that is the functional calculus. Chapter 13 asked which self-adjoint operators behave like nonnegative numbers, collected the equivalent answers in @thm-psd-characterizations, and used them twice: to build the square root and the absolute value \lvert\Avert = (\A^{*}\A)^{1/2} of @def-matrix-absolute-value, and then to get past the restriction that had hung over the whole part. The spectral theorem needs a square operator, and most matrices are not square — but \A^{*}\A always is square, self-adjoint, and positive semidefinite, whatever \A is. Applying the spectral theorem to it and reading the result back through \A gives @thm-svd, and with it orthonormal bases of all four fundamental subspaces (@cor-svd-four-subspaces), the polar decomposition of @thm-polar-decomposition, the best low-rank approximation, and the pseudoinverse. A rectangular matrix has no eigenvalues; it has singular values, and they do the work. So the part is one chain, each link an application of the last: inner product 	o adjoint 	o spectral theorem 	o singular value decomposition. Its named moves travel. To show a vector is zero, pair it with itself. To move an operator across the inner product, pay with the adjoint. Work with the norm squared. Fix an orthonormal basis. Project, then subtract. Test positivity with the single scalar \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}}, and factor a positive matrix as \B^{*}\B. Diagonalize, work on the eigenvalues, come back. When the matrix is not square, apply the spectral theorem to \A^{*}\A. And when the answer is a sum ordered by size, truncate it. What comes next takes the quadratic form \cvec{x} \mapsto \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}}, which was only a test in this chapter, and makes it the object of study: Chapter 14 classifies forms up to congruence, by inertia, over 
R and over 
C. Chapter 16 gives the operator norm promised twice above, and Chapter 17 characterizes the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix as maxima and minima of \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} — at which point the test becomes the theory. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define what it means for P \in \cL(V) to be a projection, and what it means for it to be the orthogonal projection onto a subspace U. Which of the two definitions needs an inner product? 2. State three conditions on a projection P, each equivalent to “P is an orthogonal projection”. 3. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if 
orm{P\elem{v}} \le 
orm{\elem{v}} for some nonzero \elem{v}, then the projection P is orthogonal. 4. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: every projection of rank r on an n-dimensional inner product space has matrix \I_r \oplus \O in some orthonormal basis. (a) P is a projection when P^2 = P (@def-projection-operator); P is the orthogonal projection onto U when it is the projection onto U along U^{\perp} (@def-orthogonal-projection). Only the second needs an inner product, since U^{\perp} is undefined without one. (b) By @thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoint: \ker P = (\im P)^{\perp}; P^{*} = P; P is normal; 
orm{P\elem{v}} \le 
orm{\elem{v}} for every \elem{v}. Any three of these will do. (c) Incorrect. Take \P' =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} on 
R^2 and \cvec{v} = (1, 1). Then \P'\cvec{v} = \cvec{0}, so 
orm{\P'\cvec{v}} = 0 \le \sqrt2, yet \P' is oblique because (\P')	p 
e \P'. Clause (e) of @thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoint quantifies over every \cvec{v}. (d) Incorrect in general, and correct exactly for the orthogonal projections. By @thm-idempotent-canonical-form the matrix in a suitable orthonormal basis is  egin{psmallmatrix} \I_r & \X \ \O & \O\end{psmallmatrix}, and it is \I_r \oplus \O only when \X = \O. If some orthonormal basis gave \I_r \oplus \O, that matrix would be Hermitian, so P would be self-adjoint by @thm-matrix-of-adjoint. The matrix \P' of part (c) is a counterexample. (In a basis that is merely a basis, \I_r \oplus \O is always attainable: that is @cor-projection-matrix.) B. Practice [B1: Which are orthogonal projections?] Determine which of the following matrices are projections, and among those, which are orthogonal projections. Justify your answer. For the oblique ones over 
R, find the angle between image and kernel. 1. \A =  rac{1}{5} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} on 
R^2. 2. \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ -2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} on 
R^2. 3. \C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} on 
R^2. 4. \D =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} on 
C^2. (a) \A^2 =  rac{1}{25} egin{psmallmatrix} 5 & 10 \ 10 & 20\end{psmallmatrix} = \A, so \A is a projection, and \A	p = \A. By @thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoint it is the orthogonal projection onto \im\A = \Span((1, 2)). (b) \B^2 = \B, so \B is a projection, but \B	p 
e \B, so it is oblique. Its image is \Span((1, -2)) and its kernel is \Span(\cvec{e}_2). The angle between these lines has \cos	heta = \lvert\inner{(1, -2)}{(0, 1)}vert/(\sqrt5 \cdot 1) = 2/\sqrt5, so \sin	heta = 1/\sqrt5 and \cot	heta = 2; that is 	heta = \arctan(1/2), about 26.6^{\circ}. (c) \C^2 =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} = 2\C 
e \C, so \C is not a projection at all, although it is symmetric. Symmetry alone is not idempotence;  rac12\C is the orthogonal projection onto \Span((1, 1)). (d) \D^2 = \D, so \D is a projection, and \D^{*} =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ -i & 0\end{psmallmatrix} 
e \D, so it is oblique. It is already in the canonical form of @thm-idempotent-canonical-form, with x = i. There is no angle over 
C (@def-angle is stated for real spaces), but \lvert xvert = 1, and the largest value of 
orm{\D\cvec{v}} over unit \cvec{v} is \sqrt{1 + 1} = \sqrt2, the same number the real matrix \P' produced. [B2: Putting a projection in canonical form] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} act on 
R^3 with the dot product. 1. Verify that \A is a projection and find \im\A and \ker\A. 2. Find an orthonormal basis \sB of 
R^3 as in @thm-idempotent-canonical-form and write down \mtx{T_{\A}}{\sB}{\sB}. 3. Hence determine whether \A is an orthogonal projection, and find ank\A without row reducing. (a) \A^2 = \A, by multiplying out: the second column of \A^2 is \A(1, 1, 0) = (1, 1, 0), and the first and third columns are \cvec{0} and \cvec{e}_3, unchanged. The columns of \A span \im\A = \Span((1, 1, 0), \cvec{e}_3), which is 2-dimensional. And \A\cvec{x} = (x_2, x_2, x_3) is \cvec{0} exactly when x_2 = x_3 = 0, so \ker\A = \Span(\cvec{e}_1). (b) \im\A has the orthonormal basis \cvec{f}_1 =  rac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1, 0), \cvec{f}_2 = \cvec{e}_3, and (\im\A)^{\perp} = \Span((1, -1, 0)) has the orthonormal basis \cvec{f}_3 =  rac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0). Now \A\cvec{f}_1 = \cvec{f}_1 and \A\cvec{f}_2 = \cvec{f}_2, while \A\cvec{f}_3 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(-1, -1, 0) = -\cvec{f}_1 . Hence \mtx{T_{\A}}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \X =  egin{pmatrix} -1 \ 0 \end{pmatrix} . (c) \X 
e \O, so \A is oblique by @thm-idempotent-canonical-form; indeed \ker\A = \Span(\cvec{e}_1) is not (\im\A)^{\perp} = \Span((1, -1, 0)). The rank is the number of ones in the canonical form, namely 2; equivalently ank\A = 	r\A = 0 + 1 + 1 = 2 by @thm-rank-equals-trace-projection. [B3: The complementary projection] Let P \in \cL(V) be a projection on a finite-dimensional inner product space, with U = \im P. 1. Prove that P is an orthogonal projection if and only if \id_V - P is. 2. Prove that in that case \id_V - P = P_{U^{\perp}}. Hint: @exr-projections-and-trace-b2 identifies the image and the kernel of \id_V - P. (a) By @exr-projections-and-trace-b2 (a), \id_V - P is a projection. By @thm-adjoint-properties (a), (b) and (d), (\id_V - P)^{*} = \id_V - P^{*}. Hence (\id_V - P)^{*} = \id_V - P if and only if P^{*} = P, and @thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoint converts each side into the corresponding statement about orthogonal projections. (b) Suppose P is an orthogonal projection. By @exr-projections-and-trace-b2 (b), \im(\id_V - P) = \ker P, which is U^{\perp} by @thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoint (b). By (a), \id_V - P is an orthogonal projection, so by clause (a) of that theorem it is the orthogonal projection onto its own image, that is P_{U^{\perp}}. C. Going deeper [C1: Products of orthogonal projections] Let P and Q be orthogonal projections on a finite-dimensional inner product space V, with images U and W. 1. Prove that PQ is an orthogonal projection if and only if PQ = QP. 2. Suppose PQ = QP. Prove that PQ = P_{U \cap W}. 3. Give an explicit example of two orthogonal projections on 
R^2 whose product is not a projection. (a) (\Leftarrow) Suppose PQ = QP. Then (PQ)^2 = P(QP)Q = P(PQ)Q = P^2Q^2 = PQ, so PQ is a projection, and (PQ)^{*} = Q^{*}P^{*} = QP = PQ by @thm-adjoint-properties (c) and self-adjointness of P and Q. By @thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoint, PQ is an orthogonal projection. (\Rightarrow) Suppose PQ is an orthogonal projection. Then PQ = (PQ)^{*} = Q^{*}P^{*} = QP. (b) Assume PQ = QP, so PQ is an orthogonal projection by (a), and by clause (a) of @thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoint it equals P_{\im(PQ)}. It remains to show \im(PQ) = U \cap W. (\subseteq) Every value PQ\elem{v} lies in \im P = U; and PQ\elem{v} = QP\elem{v} lies in \im Q = W. (\supseteq) If \elem{v} \in U \cap W, then Q\elem{v} = \elem{v} and P\elem{v} = \elem{v}, since a projection fixes its image (@thm-projection-direct-sum (a)), so PQ\elem{v} = \elem{v} and \elem{v} \in \im(PQ). (c) Project onto the x-axis and onto the line y = x, with standard matrices \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Q = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} . Both are symmetric and idempotent, hence orthogonal projections. But \P\Q =  rac12 egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} and (\P\Q)^2 =  rac14 egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} 
e \P\Q, so the product is not even a projection. Consistently with (a), \Q\P =  rac12 egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} 
e \P\Q. [C2: The Frobenius norm detects obliqueness] Let \P \in M_n(F) be idempotent, of rank r. 1. Prove that 
orm{\P}_F^2 \ge r. 2. Prove that equality holds if and only if \P is an orthogonal projection. Hint: the canonical form of @thm-idempotent-canonical-form, together with the invariance of the Frobenius norm under a unitary change of orthonormal basis. Apply @thm-idempotent-canonical-form to the operator \cvec{x} \mapsto \P\cvec{x} on F^n, and let \U be the matrix whose columns are the vectors of the orthonormal basis it produces.
