Then \U is unitary (@thm-isometry-characterizations (f)), and the change-of-basis formula gives \U^{*}\P\U = \U^{-1}\P\U =  egin{pmatrix} \I_r & \X \ \O & \O \end{pmatrix} . By @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant, 
orm{\P}_F = 
orm{\U^{*}\P\U}_F. (a) Summing the squared moduli of the entries of the block matrix, 
orm{\P}_F^2 = 
orm{\I_r}_F^2 + 
orm{\X}_F^2 = r + 
orm{\X}_F^2 \ge r , since 
orm{\X}_F^2 \ge 0. (b) Equality holds if and only if 
orm{\X}_F = 0, that is \X = \O, which by @thm-idempotent-canonical-form is exactly the condition that \P be an orthogonal projection. (Note that r = ank\P = 	r\P by @thm-rank-equals-trace-projection, so the criterion may also be written 	r(\P^{*}\P) = 	r\P.) [C3: How far an oblique projection can stretch] Let P be a projection of rank r on an n-dimensional inner product space V over F, with 0 < r < n, and let \X be the block of @thm-idempotent-canonical-form, with largest singular value \sigma_1 = \sigma_1(\X). 1. Prove that 
orm{\X\cvec{z}} \le \sigma_1
orm{\cvec{z}} for every \cvec{z} \in F^{\,n-r}, with equality for some \cvec{z} 
e \cvec{0}. 2. Prove that the largest value of 
orm{P\elem{v}} over unit vectors \elem{v} \in V is \sqrt{1 + \sigma_1^2}. 3. Deduce the two-dimensional formula \sqrt{1 + \lvert xvert^2} of the text, and state what the answer becomes when P is an orthogonal projection. (a) Write \X = \U\vSigma\V^{*} as in @thm-svd, with \U, \V unitary, and let p be the length of the list of singular values. For \cvec{z} \in F^{\,n-r} put \cvec{w} = \V^{*}\cvec{z}, so that 
orm{\cvec{w}} = 
orm{\cvec{z}} and 
orm{\X\cvec{z}} = 
orm{\vSigma\cvec{w}}, a unitary matrix preserving norms (@thm-isometry-characterizations). The vector \vSigma\cvec{w} has entries \sigma_i w_i for i \le p and 0 beyond, so 
orm{\vSigma\cvec{w}}^2 = \sum_{i \le p} \sigma_i^2\lvert w_ivert^2 \le \sigma_1^2\sum_{i \le p}\lvert w_ivert^2 \le \sigma_1^2
orm{\cvec{w}}^2 = \sigma_1^2
orm{\cvec{z}}^2 , since \sigma_1 is the largest of the \sigma_i. Taking \cvec{z} = \V\cvec{e}_1, a unit vector, gives \cvec{w} = \cvec{e}_1 and 
orm{\X\cvec{z}} = \sigma_1, so the bound is attained. (b) Use the orthonormal basis \sB of @thm-idempotent-canonical-form and write a vector of V by its coordinate vector (\cvec{y}, \cvec{z}) with \cvec{y} \in F^r and \cvec{z} \in F^{\,n-r}; since \sB is orthonormal, @thm-orthonormal-coordinates (c) gives 
orm{\elem{v}}^2 = 
orm{\cvec{y}}^2 + 
orm{\cvec{z}}^2, and P\elem{v} has coordinates (\cvec{y} + \X\cvec{z}, \cvec{0}). By @cor-triangle-inequality, then (a), then @thm-cauchy-schwarz in 
R^2 applied to (
orm{\cvec{y}}, 
orm{\cvec{z}}) and (1, \sigma_1),  egin{aligned} 
orm{P\elem{v}} = 
orm{\cvec{y} + \X\cvec{z}} &\le 
orm{\cvec{y}} + \sigma_1
orm{\cvec{z}} \ &\le \sqrt{1 + \sigma_1^2}\,\sqrt{
orm{\cvec{y}}^2 + 
orm{\cvec{z}}^2} = \sqrt{1 + \sigma_1^2}\,
orm{\elem{v}} . \end{aligned} For equality, let \cvec{z}_0 be the unit vector of (a), so \X\cvec{z}_0 = \sigma_1\cvec{u}_0 with 
orm{\cvec{u}_0} = 1 (take \cvec{u}_0 = \X\cvec{z}_0/\sigma_1 if \sigma_1 > 0; if \sigma_1 = 0 take any unit \cvec{u}_0). Put \cvec{y} =  rac{\cvec{u}_0}{\sqrt{1 + \sigma_1^2}}, \qquad \cvec{z} =  rac{\sigma_1\cvec{z}_0}{\sqrt{1 + \sigma_1^2}} . Then 
orm{\cvec{y}}^2 + 
orm{\cvec{z}}^2 = 1 and \cvec{y} + \X\cvec{z} = (1 + \sigma_1^2)\cvec{u}_0/\sqrt{1 + \sigma_1^2}, whose norm is \sqrt{1 + \sigma_1^2}. (c) When n = 2 and r = 1, \X is the 1 	imes 1 matrix (x), whose only singular value is \lvert xvert; the formula becomes \sqrt{1 + \lvert xvert^2}. When P is an orthogonal projection, \X = \O, so \sigma_1 = 0 and the largest value is 1 — an orthogonal projection never lengthens a vector, which is clause (e) of @thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoint with the sharpest constant.

title: Bilinear and Quadratic Forms
content:
Bilinear and Quadratic Forms An inner product does two jobs at once. It pairs two vectors and returns a scalar, linearly in each of them; and it measures, because \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} is a positive number whenever \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}. Chapters 11 to 13 leaned on the second job constantly: lengths, angles, orthonormal bases, least squares, positive definiteness, and the singular value decomposition are all consequences of positivity. This chapter keeps the pairing and throws the measuring away. What is left is a bilinear form, a function  eta \colon V 	imes V 	o F linear in each slot, with no sign condition, no symmetry required, and no field restriction. The question of the chapter is what survives. A surprising amount does. Forms still have matrices, and the matrices still change by a rule when the basis changes — but the rule is \A \mapsto \P	p\A\P, not \A \mapsto \P^{-1}\A\P. The organizing relation is therefore congruence, not similarity, and the two are genuinely different: congruent matrices need not share a single eigenvalue. What they do share is a rank, a symmetry type, and — over 
R — a triple of signs, which is Sylvester’s law of inertia and the central classification theorem of the chapter. Beyond 
R the classification depends on the arithmetic of the field, and beyond symmetry there is a second world, the alternating forms, where every nondegenerate example looks like every other of the same size. Along the way we meet vectors on which a form vanishes without being zero, the groups that preserve a form, the geometry that physics runs on, and one algebra built to make a quadratic form into a square. The field is a general F here. Since Chapter 10 the book has worked over 
R or 
C, because inner products need them; this chapter opens the field back up, and that is the point rather than an afterthought. Chapters 11 to 13 turn out to have been the positive definite special case of one line of this theory. Two consequences of the general setting are worth flagging in advance. First, “positive” has no meaning over a field with no order, so the definiteness arguments of Chapter 13 simply cannot be run; what replaces them is either a square-class computation or nothing at all. Second, when 1 + 1 = 0 — characteristic 2, @def-characteristic — the identity  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) = 	frac12 igl(q(\elem{u}+\elem{v}) - q(\elem{u}) - q(\elem{v}) igr) is unavailable, and symmetric and alternating forms stop being complementary. Every statement below that needs a characteristic hypothesis carries one, and every statement without one holds over every field. What you need. From Chapter 7, multilinearity and alternation, which this chapter reuses rather than redefines (@def-multilinear-form, @def-alternating-form, @def-skew-symmetric-form, @thm-alternating-properties, @thm-skew-symmetric-alternating), together with the determinant and its multiplicativity (@def-determinant, @thm-det-multiplicative, @thm-det-transpose). From Chapter 2, the rank of a linear map (@def-rank). From Chapter 4, the matrix of a map, change of coordinates, and similarity (@def-matrix-of-linear-map, @thm-matrix-of-map-coordinates, @def-change-of-coordinates-matrix, @thm-change-of-coordinates, @thm-change-of-basis-maps, @def-similar-matrices), together with equivalence of matrices and the rank normal form (@def-equivalent-matrices, @thm-rank-normal-form). From Chapter 5, the dual space and its bases (@def-linear-functional, @def-dual-space, @thm-dual-basis, @cor-dimension-dual-space, @thm-dual-of-subspace, @thm-double-dual-isomorphism). From Chapter 0, fields and characteristic (@def-field, @def-characteristic, @thm-characteristic-prime), the transpose and symmetry (@def-transpose, @def-symmetric-matrix, @thm-transpose-properties), and groups (@def-group, @def-subgroup). From Chapter 1, the dimension counting that every classification here ends with: direct sums and complements (@thm-direct-sum-criteria, @thm-direct-sum-k-criteria, @thm-complement-exists), the dimension formula for a sum of subspaces (@thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim), and the step from an inclusion to an equality (@thm-dim-impl-eq). From Chapter 3, the \L\D\L	p factorization (@thm-ldlt). From Chapters 11 to 13, everything used for the real and complex specializations: the orthogonal and unitary groups (@def-unitary-orthogonal, @def-unitary-orthogonal-groups), the real spectral theorem and principal axes (@thm-spectral-real, @cor-spectral-real-matrix, @thm-principal-axes), the orthogonal group in low dimension (@prp-orthogonal-group-properties, @thm-orthogonal-canonical-form), and positivity (@def-positive-semidefinite, @thm-psd-characterizations, @thm-pd-characterizations, @prp-congruence-positivity, @thm-simultaneous-congruence). Those last results are used only where the field is 
R or 
C; they are never hypotheses of the general theory. Roadmap - Bilinear forms and their matrices. What a form is, the Gram matrix that records it, the bijection between forms and matrices, and the form’s companion map V 	o V^{*}, whose kernel is the radical and whose invertibility is nondegeneracy. - Congruence. Changing the basis replaces \A by \P	p\A\P. What that relation preserves — rank, symmetry type, nondegeneracy, the square class of the determinant — and what it destroys, starting with the eigenvalues. - Three kinds of form. Symmetric, alternating, skew-symmetric, and Hermitian; why the middle two coincide exactly when the characteristic is not 2; polarization, and the quadratic form. - Completing the square. Over any field of characteristic 
e 2, every symmetric form has an orthogonal basis. The proof is an induction, and the algorithm is symmetric row-and-column elimination. - Inertia. Over 
R the number of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries does not depend on the diagonalization. This classifies real symmetric matrices up to congruence and reconciles congruence with the spectral theorem. - Definiteness revisited. Chapter 13’s tests, restated as statements about signatures, and the second-derivative test they decide. - Where the form vanishes. Isotropic vectors, totally isotropic subspaces, hyperbolic planes, and the Witt decomposition of a nondegenerate space. - Witt’s theorems. An isometry between subspaces extends to the whole space; one summand of an orthogonal sum may be canceled from both sides. - Symplectic forms. A nondegenerate alternating form lives only in even dimension and has exactly one shape, over every field, with no characteristic hypothesis anywhere. - The classical groups. \Orth(n), \Orth(p,q), \Unit(n), and the symplectic group, all read off one equation \P	p\A\P = \A. - Minkowski space. The signature (1,3) form, the light cone, hyperbolic rotations, and the triangle inequality running backwards. - A first look at Clifford algebras. Making a quadratic form into a square, and how 
C and the quaternions come out of it. Named moves - Polarize. A symmetric form and its quadratic function q(\elem{v}) =  eta(\elem{v},\elem{v}) carry the same information, because  eta can be recovered from q by expanding q(\elem{u} + \elem{v}) and dividing by 2. That division is the whole reason characteristic 2 is excluded whenever it is excluded. - Complete the square. Every diagonalization theorem for symmetric forms in this chapter is this one manipulation, applied by induction on the dimension: isolate a variable that actually appears, absorb its cross terms into a perfect square, and recurse on what is left. - Split off a hyperbolic plane. For indefinite forms this replaces “peel off an eigenvector”. A single nonzero isotropic vector forces a two-dimensional piece of standard shape to split off orthogonally, and the induction runs on the rest. - Count signs, not values. The numbers on a diagonalized form are not invariants; their signs are. Whenever a quantity refuses to be an invariant, ask whether some coarser feature of it is. - Congruence, not similarity. At every theorem, ask which relation is in play. If the matrix is eaten twice by the same vector, the relation is congruence and eigenvalues are not available; if it is eaten once and returns a vector, the relation is similarity and they are.

title: 14.1 Bilinear Forms and Their Matrices
content:
Bilinear Forms and Their Matrices Chapter 7 needed a function of several vectors that was linear in each of them separately, and called it a multilinear form (@def-multilinear-form). Chapter 11 needed a function of two vectors that was linear in the first, conjugate-linear in the second, and positive on the diagonal, and called it an inner product. This section takes the common skeleton of the two — two slots, linear in each, nothing else assumed — and studies it on its own. The payoff is immediate: such a function is recorded by a square matrix, exactly as a linear map is, and the whole rest of the chapter is about how that matrix behaves. Throughout, V is a vector space over a field F. From the second subsection on, V is finite-dimensional with \dim V = n \ge 1, and \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) is an ordered basis of V. No hypothesis on the characteristic of F is used anywhere in this section, and none is used in the next one either. Pairing without measuring The dot product on F^n is a machine with two inputs and one scalar output. Over 
R it does two different jobs. It pairs: it takes \cvec{x} and \cvec{y} and returns \sum_i x_iy_i, linearly in each of them. And it measures: \cvec{x} \cdot \cvec{x} is a sum of squares, so it is positive unless \cvec{x} = \cvec{0}, and from that one fact Chapter 11 extracted lengths, angles, orthonormal bases, and everything built on them. Measuring is the fragile half. It needs an order on F, so it is meaningless over 
C without a conjugation and meaningless over 
F_5 altogether. Pairing needs nothing: \sum_i x_iy_i makes sense over every field, and so do plenty of other two-slot expressions, such as x_1y_2 - x_2y_1 or x_1y_1 - x_2y_2. Chapter 7 already met the first of these as the signed area, and met the general notion as the case k = 2 of a multilinear form. We give that case its own name, because from here on it is the object of study rather than a step toward the determinant. A bilinear form pairs two vectors of the same space into a scalar, linearly in each slot separately. [Bilinear Form] Let V be a vector space over a field F. A bilinear form on V is a function  eta \colon V 	imes V 	o F that is linear in each argument when the other is held fixed: for all \elem{u}, \elem{u}', \elem{v}, \elem{v}' \in V and all c \in F, 1.  eta(\elem{u} + \elem{u}', \elem{v}) =  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) +  eta(\elem{u}', \elem{v}) and  eta(c\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = c\, eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}); 2.  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v} + \elem{v}') =  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) +  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}') and  eta(\elem{u}, c\elem{v}) = c\, eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}). Equivalently,  eta is a 2-linear form on V in the sense of @def-multilinear-form. In words: (B1) says that for each fixed \elem{v}, the function \elem{u} \mapsto  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) is a linear functional on V (@def-linear-functional), and (B2) says the same for \elem{v} \mapsto  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) with \elem{u} fixed. The word fixed is the whole content. Nothing is assumed about how the two slots compare:  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) and  eta(\elem{v}, \elem{u}) may be unrelated, and  eta(\elem{v}, \elem{v}) may be any scalar at all, including 0 for a nonzero \elem{v}. Two consequences come free from linearity in one slot. Taking c = 0 in (B1) gives  eta(\elem{0}, \elem{v}) = 0 for every \elem{v}, and likewise  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{0}) = 0. And by induction on the number of terms,  eta\Bigl(\sum_i a_i\elem{u}_i,\ \sum_j b_j\elem{v}_j\Bigr) = \sum_{i,j} a_ib_j\, eta(\elem{u}_i, \elem{v}_j), which is the identity everything in this section rests on: a bilinear form is determined by its values on pairs drawn from a spanning set. [Six two-slot functions] Decide which of the following are bilinear forms on the given space over the given field. 1. The dot product on F^n:  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n. 2. On F^n, for a fixed \A \in M_n(F):  eta_{\A}(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}. 3. On F^2:  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_2 - x_2y_1. 4. On 
R[x]_{\le 2}:  eta(f, g) = \int_0^1 f(t)g(t)\,\dd t. 5. On any V: the zero function  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = 0. 6. On 
R^n:  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = 
orm{\cvec{x}}\,
orm{\cvec{y}}, the product of the Euclidean lengths. (a) Fix \cvec{y}. Then \cvec{x} \mapsto \sum_i x_iy_i is a linear functional on F^n, since it is a fixed linear combination of the coordinate functionals (@thm-functionals-on-fn). Fixing \cvec{x} gives the same statement in \cvec{y}. So (B1) and (B2) hold and the dot product is bilinear. (b) With \A = \I_n this is (a). In general, write out the entries: \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}x_iy_j. For fixed \cvec{y} this is \sum_i  igl(\sum_j a_{ij}y_j igr)x_i, a fixed linear combination of the coordinates of \cvec{x}, hence a linear functional; symmetrically in \cvec{y}. So  eta_{\A} is bilinear for every \A, symmetric or not. Part (c) below is the case \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}. (c) This is the signed area of Chapter 7, and it is bilinear by @exm-alternating-forms (a). It is worth noticing what it does on the diagonal:  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{x}) = x_1x_2 - x_2x_1 = 0 for every \cvec{x}. A bilinear form may vanish identically on the diagonal without being the zero form. (d) For fixed g, the map f \mapsto \int_0^1 fg is linear, because the integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals and constants come out. Symmetrically in g. So  eta is bilinear. Here  eta(f, f) = \int_0^1 f^2 \ge 0, so over 
R this form does measure: it is the inner product of Chapter 11. (e) Both clauses read 0 = 0 + 0 and 0 = c \cdot 0. The zero form is bilinear on every space over every field. It is the degenerate case, and it matters: it shows that a bilinear form can carry no information whatsoever, and it is the form whose matrix below is the zero matrix. (f) Not bilinear. Fix \cvec{y} = \cvec{e}_1. Then  eta(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1) +  eta(-\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1) = 1 + 1 = 2, while  eta(\cvec{e}_1 + (-\cvec{e}_1), \cvec{e}_1) =  eta(\cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_1) = 0. Additivity in the first slot fails, so (B1) fails. The homogeneity half of (B1) also fails, since  eta(-\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1) = 1 
e - eta(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1). Item (f) is the nonexample by minimal change worth remembering: the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality says that \lvert\cvec{x} \cdot \cvec{y}vert \le 
orm{\cvec{x}}
orm{\cvec{y}}, so 
orm{\cvec{x}}
orm{\cvec{y}} sits right next to the dot product numerically, and yet it is not a form at all, because the absolute value hidden in the norm destroys additivity. A second minimal change makes the same point more cheaply:  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + 1 fails (B1) because  eta(\cvec{0}, \cvec{0}) = 1 
e 0. Bilinear is not linear. A bilinear form is not a linear function of the pair (\elem{u}, \elem{v}), and the two properties are not even compatible in general. For the dot product on 
R^2, doubling both arguments multiplies the value by 4:  eta(2\cvec{e}_1, 2\cvec{e}_1) = 4, not 2 eta(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1) = 2. Sums may only be split one slot at a time, with the other slot held frozen. Chapter 7 gave this warning for multilinear forms in general; it is repeated here because it is the mistake readers make most often when a form is written with the familiar-looking symbol \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}. The same definition with two different spaces,  eta \colon V 	imes W 	o F linear in each slot, is called a bilinear pairing of V and W. The basic example is the evaluation pairing V^{*} 	imes V 	o F, (\varphi, \elem{v}) \mapsto \varphi(\elem{v}), which is linear in \varphi by the definition of the operations on V^{*} (@def-dual-space) and linear in \elem{v} because \varphi is. We insist on V = W in @def-bilinear-form because the questions of this chapter — is  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) equal to  eta(\elem{v},\elem{u}), what is  eta(\elem{v},\elem{v}), which vectors are orthogonal to which — only make sense when both slots hold vectors of the same space. The matrix of a form The displayed expansion above says that a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional space is determined by finitely many numbers: the values  eta(\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j) on pairs of basis vectors. There are n^2 of them, they are indexed by a row and a column, and that is a matrix. Chapter 2 recorded a linear map by a matrix in exactly the same spirit (@def-matrix-of-linear-map), and the only difference is where the bases sit. There the two bases belonged to the input space and the output space. A form has no output space to speak of, but it has two slots, and each slot has to be fed a basis before the table can be written down. Throughout this chapter both slots hold vectors of the same V and we feed them the same basis, so the two choices coincide; the notation still records both, with the subscript naming the basis used on the first slot and the superscript the basis used on the second. The matrix of a form is its table of values on pairs of basis vectors. [Matrix of a Bilinear Form] Let  eta be a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional V with ordered basis \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n). The matrix of  eta with respect to \sB, also called its Gram matrix, is the matrix \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} \in M_n(F) with entries  igl(\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} igr)_{ij} \coloneqq  eta(\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j) . In words: the entry in row i and column j is the value of  eta with the i-th basis vector in the left slot and the j-th in the right slot. The subscript is the basis read into the left slot and the superscript the basis read into the right one; here they are the same \sB, and the notation writes it twice rather than leaving a slot empty. The order matters, because  eta(\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j) and  eta(\elem{v}_j, \elem{v}_i) need not agree; the convention chosen here is the one that makes the recovery formula below carry no transpose on the matrix. Chapter 11 also called a matrix of pairings a Gram matrix, and the two conventions differ, so it is worth saying how. @def-gram-matrix set (\G)_{ij} = \inner{\elem{v}_j}{\elem{v}_i}, with the indices crossed, because an inner product is conjugate-linear in its second slot and the crossing is what makes \G Hermitian and \cvec{x}^{*}\G\cvec{x} come out as a squared norm. A bilinear form has no conjugation to accommodate, so here the natural order is the uncrossed one, which is what makes the recovery formula below free of transposes. For a real symmetric form the two agree; in general each is the transpose of the other. Nothing needs checking for well-definedness: once \sB is fixed, each entry is a single value of a function. What does need saying is that no information is lost. [Forms and Matrices Correspond] Let V be an n-dimensional vector space over F with ordered basis \sB, and let  eta be a bilinear form on V with \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}. 1. For all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V,  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = \coord{\elem{u}}{\sB}	p\,\A\,\coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} . 2. \A is the only matrix in M_n(F) with this property. 3. The assignment  eta \mapsto \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} is a bijection from the set of bilinear forms on V onto M_n(F), and it respects sums and scalar multiples: \mtx{ eta + \gamma}{\sB}{\sB} = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} + \mtx{\gamma}{\sB}{\sB} and \mtx{c eta}{\sB}{\sB} = c\,\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}. Part (a) is the expansion  eta(\sum a_i\elem{v}_i, \sum b_j\elem{v}_j) = \sum_{i,j}a_ib_j eta(\elem{v}_i,\elem{v}_j) with the double sum recognized as a matrix product. For (b), feed the property a pair of basis vectors and watch it return a single entry. For (c), (b) gives injectivity, and surjectivity is @exm-bilinear-forms-first (b) transported to V through coordinates. (a) Write \coord{\elem{u}}{\sB} = (a_1, \dots, a_n) and \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} = (b_1, \dots, b_n), so that \elem{u} = \sum_i a_i\elem{v}_i and \elem{v} = \sum_j b_j\elem{v}_j. Expanding one slot at a time, by (B1) and then (B2),  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_ib_j\, eta(\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j) = \sum_{i,j} a_i\,a_{ij}\,b_j , writing a_{ij} =  eta(\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j) for the entries of \A. The last sum is the 1 	imes 1 matrix product \coord{\elem{u}}{\sB}	p\A\coord{\elem{v}}{\sB}, by the definition of matrix multiplication (@def-matrix-multiplication). (b) Suppose \M \in M_n(F) also satisfies  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = \coord{\elem{u}}{\sB}	p\M\coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} for all \elem{u}, \elem{v}. Take \elem{u} = \elem{v}_i and \elem{v} = \elem{v}_j. Then \coord{\elem{v}_i}{\sB} = \cvec{e}_i and \coord{\elem{v}_j}{\sB} = \cvec{e}_j, so the right-hand side is \cvec{e}_i	p\M\cvec{e}_j = m_{ij}, while the left-hand side is  eta(\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j) = a_{ij}. Hence m_{ij} = a_{ij} for all i, j, that is, \M = \A. (c) Injective. If \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} = \mtx{\gamma}{\sB}{\sB}, then by (a) the two forms agree at every pair (\elem{u}, \elem{v}), so  eta = \gamma. Surjective. Given \M \in M_n(F), define \gamma(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) \coloneqq \coord{\elem{u}}{\sB}	p\M\coord{\elem{v}}{\sB}. The coordinate map \elem{v} \mapsto \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} is linear (@cor-coordinate-isomorphism), and (\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) \mapsto \cvec{x}	p\M\cvec{y} is bilinear on F^n by @exm-bilinear-forms-first (b); composing a bilinear form with a linear map in each slot leaves it bilinear, so \gamma is a bilinear form on V. By (b) its matrix is \M. Linear. The forms  eta + \gamma and c eta are defined pointwise, so their values at (\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j) are  eta(\elem{v}_i,\elem{v}_j) + \gamma(\elem{v}_i,\elem{v}_j) and c\, eta(\elem{v}_i,\elem{v}_j). These are the entries of \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} + \mtx{\gamma}{\sB}{\sB} and of c\,\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}. This proves the theorem. So bilinear forms on an n-dimensional space are the same thing as n 	imes n matrices, once a basis is fixed — and in particular they form a vector space of dimension n^2. The qualification “once a basis is fixed” is not decoration; the next section is entirely about what happens when the basis is changed. [Four Gram matrices] Compute \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} in each case. 1. The dot product on F^n, with \sB = \sE the standard basis. 2.  eta_{\A}(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} on F^n, with \sB = \sE. 3. The signed area  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_2 - x_2y_1 on F^2, with \sB = \sE. 4.  eta(f, g) = \int_0^1 fg on 
R[x]_{\le 2}, with \sB = (1, x, x^2). (a)  eta(\cvec{e}_i, \cvec{e}_j) = \delta_{ij}, so \mtx{ eta}{\sE}{\sE} = \I_n. The dot product is the form whose matrix is the identity. (b)  eta_{\A}(\cvec{e}_i, \cvec{e}_j) = \cvec{e}_i	p\A\cvec{e}_j = a_{ij}, so \mtx{ eta_{\A}}{\sE}{\sE} = \A. Together with @thm-form-matrix-determines (c) this says that on F^n with the standard basis, “form” and “matrix” are two words for the same data, and \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} is the general form. (c)  eta(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1) = 0,  eta(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = 1,  eta(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1) = -1,  eta(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_2) = 0, so \mtx{ eta}{\sE}{\sE} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. The matrix is not symmetric, and its diagonal is zero — the two features that will separate this form from the dot product throughout the chapter. (d) With \sB = (1, x, x^2) the (i,j) entry is \int_0^1 t^{\,i-1}t^{\,j-1}\dd t = 1/(i + j - 1), so \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 	frac12 & 	frac13 \[2pt] 	frac12 & 	frac13 & 	frac14 \[2pt] 	frac13 & 	frac14 & 	frac15 \end{pmatrix}. This matrix is symmetric, as it must be, since  eta(f, g) =  eta(g, f). Its determinant is 1/2160, so it is invertible; what that means for  eta is the subject of the last part of this section. A bilinear form  eta on F^2 satisfies  eta(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1) = 2,  eta(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = -1,  eta(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1) = 3, and  eta(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_2) = 0. What is  eta igl((1,1), (1,-1) igr)? The matrix is \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & -1 \ 3 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, and by @thm-form-matrix-determines (a),  eta igl((1,1),(1,-1) igr) =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \ 3 & 0\end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ -1\end{pmatrix} = 6 . Expanding by hand gives the same. The pair is (\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2,\ \cvec{e}_1 - \cvec{e}_2), so the four terms are  eta(\cvec{e}_1,\cvec{e}_1) -  eta(\cvec{e}_1,\cvec{e}_2) +  eta(\cvec{e}_2,\cvec{e}_1) -  eta(\cvec{e}_2,\cvec{e}_2), which is 2 - (-1) + 3 - 0 = 6. Note that the two off-diagonal values enter with opposite roles:  eta(\cvec{e}_1,\cvec{e}_2) comes from the minus sign in the right slot,  eta(\cvec{e}_2,\cvec{e}_1) from the plus sign in the left one. Since  eta(\cvec{e}_1,\cvec{e}_2) 
e  eta(\cvec{e}_2,\cvec{e}_1) here, swapping them would change the answer. Now the warning that the rest of the chapter exists to manage. The matrix of a form and the matrix of a map are different objects with the same name. Both are square arrays attached to V and a basis, both are written \A, and both change when the basis changes — by different rules. If \P is the change-of-coordinates matrix between the old and the new basis, then 	ext{a map: } \A \mapsto \P^{-1}\A\P, \qquad 	ext{a form: } \A \mapsto \P	p\A\P . The first is @thm-change-of-basis-maps; the second is proved in the next section. They agree only when \P	p = \P^{-1}. Concretely, take \A = \diag(1,2) and \P =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}. Then \P^{-1}\A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \P	p\A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix} . The first still has eigenvalues 1 and 2; the second has eigenvalues 2 \pm \sqrt2. Same \A, same \P, two answers with nothing in common. Before writing \A down, ask what it eats: a map eats one vector and returns a vector, so \A\cvec{x} is meaningful; a form eats two vectors and returns a scalar, so \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} is meaningful and \A\cvec{x} is a meaningless intermediate. Almost every error in this chapter is this confusion. The form as a map into the dual space Fixing the right slot of  eta leaves a function of the left slot, and clause (B1) says that function is a linear functional. So each \elem{v} \in V produces an element of V^{*} (@def-dual-space), and clause (B2) says the production is itself linear. That is a linear map V 	o V^{*}, and it is the cleanest way to say what it means for a form to be nondegenerate. Write R_ eta \colon V 	o V^{*} for the map sending \elem{v} to the functional  eta(\cdot, \elem{v}), that is,  igl(R_ eta(\elem{v}) igr)(\elem{u}) =  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) \qquad (\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V). The letter is local to this section and the subscript names the form; R is for the right slot, the one that is fixed. That R_ eta(\elem{v}) lies in V^{*} is (B1), and that R_ eta is linear is (B2). Its kernel has a name. [Radical of a Form] Let  eta be a bilinear form on V. The radical of  eta is \operatorname{rad}( eta) \coloneqq \{\, \elem{v} \in V :  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = 0 	ext{ for every } \elem{u} \in V \,\} = \ker R_ eta , a subspace of V. Its elements are the vectors that every vector is orthogonal to. [Nondegenerate Form] A bilinear form  eta on V is nondegenerate if \operatorname{rad}( eta) = \{\elem{0}\}, that is, if for every nonzero \elem{v} \in V there exists \elem{u} \in V with  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) 
e 0. Otherwise  eta is degenerate. In words: nondegeneracy says that no nonzero vector is invisible to the form. It does not say that  eta(\elem{v},\elem{v}) 
e 0, and it does not say that  eta is positive in any sense; it only says that a vector which the form cannot distinguish from \elem{0} must be \elem{0}. On a finite-dimensional space it is a rank condition. [Nondegeneracy is invertibility of the Gram matrix] Let  eta be a bilinear form on an n-dimensional V with ordered basis \sB, and put \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}. Then: 1. \A is the matrix of R_ eta from the basis \sB to the dual basis \sB^{*}; that is, \A = \mtx{R_ eta}{\sB}{\sB^{*}}. 2. \dim\operatorname{rad}( eta) = n - ank\A. 3. The following are equivalent:  eta is nondegenerate; \A is invertible; R_ eta is an isomorphism V 	o V^{*}. Only (a) has content, and it is one line once the right formula is recalled: the coordinates of a functional in the dual basis are its values on \sB (@thm-dual-basis (c)), and the values of R_ eta(\elem{v}_j) on \sB are the entries of the j-th column of \A. Parts (b) and (c) are then Rank–Nullity and the invertible matrix theorem, applied to a map we now know the matrix of. (a) By @def-matrix-of-linear-map, the j-th column of \mtx{R_ eta}{\sB}{\sB^{*}} is \coord{R_ eta(\elem{v}_j)}{\sB^{*}}. By @thm-dual-basis (c), a functional \varphi \in V^{*} has \varphi = \sum_i \varphi(\elem{v}_i)\varphi_i in the dual basis \sB^{*} = (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n), so the i-th coordinate of R_ eta(\elem{v}_j) is  igl(R_ eta(\elem{v}_j) igr)(\elem{v}_i) =  eta(\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j) = a_{ij}. Hence the (i,j) entry of \mtx{R_ eta}{\sB}{\sB^{*}} is a_{ij}, as claimed. (b) By (a) and @thm-rank-map-equals-rank-matrix, ank R_ eta = ank\A. Since \operatorname{rad}( eta) = \ker R_ eta, Rank–Nullity (@thm-rank-nullity) gives \dim\operatorname{rad}( eta) = n - ank\A. (c) By (b), \operatorname{rad}( eta) = \{\elem{0}\} if and only if ank\A = n, which by @thm-invertible-tfae is exactly invertibility of \A. Since \dim V^{*} = n = \dim V (@cor-dimension-dual-space), the map R_ eta is an isomorphism if and only if it is injective (@cor-rank-nullity-consequences (e)), that is, if and only if its kernel is \{\elem{0}\} (@thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel). This proves the proposition. Freezing the left slot instead gives a second map \elem{u} \mapsto  eta(\elem{u}, \cdot), whose kernel is the left radical \{\elem{u} :  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) = 0 	ext{ for all } \elem{v}\}. The same computation shows its matrix is \A	p, so by @thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank and @thm-rank-nullity the two radicals have the same dimension — although, as @exr-bilinear-forms-b3 shows, they need not be the same subspace. In particular “nondegenerate” means the same thing read from either side, and for the symmetric forms that occupy most of this chapter the two radicals coincide. [Three radicals] Find \operatorname{rad}( eta) and decide degeneracy. 1.  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 on F^2. 2.  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 - x_2y_2 on 
R^2. 3. The zero form on any V 
e \{\elem{0}\}. (a) \mtx{ eta}{\sE}{\sE} =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, of rank 1, so the radical is one-dimensional by @prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible (b). Explicitly,  eta(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) = u_1v_1 vanishes for all \cvec{u} exactly when v_1 = 0, so \operatorname{rad}( eta) = \Span(\cvec{e}_2). Degenerate. (b) \mtx{ eta}{\sE}{\sE} = \diag(1, -1), invertible, so  eta is nondegenerate. Yet  eta igl((1,1),(1,1) igr) = 1 - 1 = 0: a nonzero vector on which the form vanishes when paired with itself. Nondegeneracy forbids a vector orthogonal to everything; it says nothing about a vector orthogonal to itself. This form is the one this chapter returns to twice, in the sections on isotropic vectors and on Minkowski space. (c) The matrix is 0, of rank 0, and \operatorname{rad}( eta) = V. This is the extreme degenerate case: every vector is invisible. Nondegenerate does not mean definite, and the radical is not the set where  eta(\elem{v},\elem{v}) = 0. Example (b) above is nondegenerate, and the set \{\cvec{v} :  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) = 0\} is the pair of lines x_2 = \pm x_1 — not a subspace, and not the radical, which is \{\cvec{0}\}. Example (c) of @exm-bilinear-forms-first has  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) = 0 for every \cvec{v} and is still nondegenerate, since its matrix  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} is invertible. An inner-product-trained reader expects “ eta(\elem{v},\elem{v}) = 0 \Rightarrow \elem{v} = \elem{0}”, and that expectation is a theorem about positive definite forms over 
R, not about forms. Let  eta be a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional V, and let U = \operatorname{rad}( eta). Is  eta nondegenerate on the subspace U? No, unless U = \{\elem{0}\} — and then only for a silly reason. The restriction of  eta to U 	imes U is the zero form, since  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = 0 already for \elem{u} \in V and \elem{v} \in U. The zero form on a nonzero space is degenerate, so the restriction is nondegenerate exactly when U = \{\elem{0}\}, that is, exactly when  eta was nondegenerate to begin with. The point of the question is that “nondegenerate” is a property of a form on a specified space, and restricting changes the space. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define what it means for  eta \colon V 	imes V 	o F to be a bilinear form, stating both clauses in full. 2. Define the matrix \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} of a bilinear form with respect to an ordered basis \sB, and state how  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) is recovered from it. 3. Determine whether the following is correct, with a reason: every bilinear form on F^n is  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} for exactly one \A \in M_n(F). 4. Define the radical of  eta and state what it means for  eta to be nondegenerate. 5. Determine whether the following is correct, with a reason: if  eta(\elem{v}, \elem{v}) = 0 for some \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}, then  eta is degenerate. (a) @def-bilinear-form: linearity in the left slot for each fixed right argument, (B1), and linearity in the right slot for each fixed left argument, (B2). (b) @def-form-matrix:  igl(\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} igr)_{ij} =  eta(\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j). Recovery is @thm-form-matrix-determines (a):  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) = \coord{\elem{u}}{\sB}	p\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}\coord{\elem{v}}{\sB}. (c) Correct. Existence and uniqueness are @thm-form-matrix-determines (c) and (b) with \sB = \sE, for which \coord{\cvec{x}}{\sE} = \cvec{x}. (d) @def-radical and @def-nondegenerate: \operatorname{rad}( eta) = \{\elem{v} :  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) = 0 	ext{ for all } \elem{u}\}, and  eta is nondegenerate when this is \{\elem{0}\}. (e) Incorrect. The two conditions are unrelated. The signed area on F^2 has  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) = 0 for every \cvec{v} and is nondegenerate, since its matrix  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} is invertible (@prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible). B. Practice [B1: Which are forms?] Determine which of the following are bilinear forms on the given space. Justify your answer; for those that fail, name the clause that fails and give a witness. 1. On 
R^2:  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + 2x_1y_2 - 3x_2y_1. 2. On 
R^2:  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + 1. 3. On 
R[x]_{\le 2}:  eta(f, g) = f(1)g(2) - f(0)g(0). 4. On 
R^2:  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1^2y_1. 5. On M_2(
R):  eta(\X, \Y) = 	r(\X	p\Y). (a) Bilinear: it is \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} with \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 \ -3 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, so @exm-bilinear-forms-first (b) applies. (b) Not bilinear. Clause (B1) fails:  eta(\cvec{0}, \cvec{0}) = 1, whereas homogeneity with c = 0 forces  eta(\cvec{0}, \cvec{y}) = 0 for any bilinear form. (c) Bilinear. Evaluation at a point is linear (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), so for fixed g the map f \mapsto g(2)f(1) - g(0)f(0) is a linear combination of two linear functionals, hence linear; symmetrically in g. (d) Not bilinear. Clause (B1) fails in the additive half: with \cvec{y} = \cvec{e}_1,  eta(\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1) = 4 while  eta(\cvec{e}_1,\cvec{e}_1) +  eta(\cvec{e}_1,\cvec{e}_1) = 2. The homogeneity half fails too, since  eta(c\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = c^2x_1^2y_1. (e) Bilinear. By @thm-transpose-properties and linearity of the trace (@thm-trace-properties), for fixed \Y the map \X \mapsto 	r(\X	p\Y) is linear, and for fixed \X the map \Y \mapsto 	r(\X	p\Y) is linear. This is the Frobenius inner product of Chapter 11, seen as a form. [B2: A Gram matrix from sample values] On V = 
R[x]_{\le 2}, define  eta(f, g) = f(0)g(0) + f(1)g(1) + f(2)g(2). 1. Verify that  eta is a bilinear form and compute \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} for \sB = (1, x, x^2). 2. Compute  eta(1 + x,\ x^2 - 1) directly from the definition, and again from the matrix. Check that the answers agree. 3. Hence decide whether  eta is nondegenerate. (a) Each of the three terms is a product of two evaluations, hence bilinear as in @exr-bilinear-forms-b1 (c), and a sum of bilinear forms is bilinear by @thm-form-matrix-determines (c). Numbering rows and columns 1, 2, 3 for 1, x, x^2, the (i,j) entry is \sum_{t \in \{0,1,2\}} t^{\,i-1}t^{\,j-1}, with 0^0 = 1. So \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 3 & 5 \ 3 & 5 & 9 \ 5 & 9 & 17 \end{pmatrix}. (b) Directly: f = 1 + x takes the values 1, 2, 3 at 0, 1, 2, and g = x^2 - 1 takes the values -1, 0, 3. So  eta(f, g) = 1(-1) + 2 \cdot 0 + 3 \cdot 3 = 8. From the matrix, \coord{f}{\sB} = (1,1,0) and \coord{g}{\sB} = (-1,0,1), and \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}\coord{g}{\sB} = (2, 6, 12), \qquad (1,1,0) \cdot (2,6,12) = 8 . (c) Let \M be the matrix with rows (1, t, t^2) for t = 0, 1, 2. Then \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} = \M	p\M, and \det\M = 2 by the Vandermonde formula (@thm-vandermonde-determinant), so \det\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} = 4 
e 0 by @thm-det-multiplicative and @thm-det-transpose. By @prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible,  eta is nondegenerate. [B3: Two radicals] On F^3, let  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} with \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \ 2 & 4 & 6 \ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. Find \operatorname{rad}( eta) and the left radical, give a basis of each, and decide whether they are equal. Every row of \A is a multiple of (1, 2, 3), so ank\A = 1 and both radicals have dimension 3 - 1 = 2, by @prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible (b) and the remark following it. The radical is 
ul(\A) = \{\cvec{y} : y_1 + 2y_2 + 3y_3 = 0\}, with basis (-2, 1, 0) and (-3, 0, 1). The left radical is 
ul(\A	p). Every row of \A	p is a multiple of (1, 2, 1), so it is \{\cvec{x} : x_1 + 2x_2 + x_3 = 0\}, with basis (-2, 1, 0) and (-1, 0, 1). They are not equal: (-3, 0, 1) lies in the radical but -3 + 0 + 1 = -2 
e 0, so it is not in the left radical. Equal dimensions, different subspaces. In particular  eta is degenerate. C. Going deeper [C1: Over 
F_2] Let  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 on V = 
F_2^2. 1. Write down \mtx{ eta}{\sE}{\sE} and prove that  eta is nondegenerate. 2. Find every \cvec{v} \in V with  eta(\cvec{v}, \cvec{v}) = 0. 3. Hence explain why the argument “ eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) = 0 only for \cvec{v} = \cvec{0}” cannot be used to prove nondegeneracy over a general field, even for the dot product. (a) \mtx{ eta}{\sE}{\sE} = \I_2, which is invertible, so  eta is nondegenerate by @prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible. (b)  eta(\cvec{v}, \cvec{v}) = v_1^2 + v_2^2. In 
F_2 every element satisfies t^2 = t, so this is v_1 + v_2, which vanishes for \cvec{v} = (0,0) and \cvec{v} = (1,1). So the nonzero vector (1,1) satisfies  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) = 0. (c) Over 
R,  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) = v_1^2 + v_2^2 is a sum of squares and vanishes only at \cvec{0}, so the implication holds there; the proof uses that a sum of nonnegative reals is zero only when each term is. Over 
F_2 there is no order, nothing is nonnegative, and the conclusion is false for (1,1) even though the form is the dot product and is nondegenerate. Nondegeneracy is a statement about the rank of a matrix and survives the change of field; the diagonal statement is a statement about positivity and does not. [C2: Orthogonal complements for a form] Let  eta be a bilinear form on a vector space V with \dim V = n, and for a subspace U \subseteq V put U^{\perp_ eta} \coloneqq \{\, \elem{v} \in V :  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = 0 	ext{ for every } \elem{u} \in U \,\}. 1. Prove that U^{\perp_ eta} is a subspace and that \dim U^{\perp_ eta} \ge n - \dim U. 2. Prove that equality holds when  eta is nondegenerate. 3. Give an example with \dim U = 1 in which the inequality in (a) is strict. Hint: consider the map V 	o U^{*} that sends \elem{v} to the restriction of  eta(\cdot, \elem{v}) to U. (a) Let ho \colon V^{*} 	o U^{*} be the restriction map and S = ho R_ eta \colon V 	o U^{*}, so S(\elem{v}) =  eta(\cdot, \elem{v}) ig|_U. Both factors are linear, so S is linear, and U^{\perp_ eta} = \ker S by the definition of S; hence U^{\perp_ eta} is a subspace. By Rank–Nullity (@thm-rank-nullity), \dim U^{\perp_ eta} = n - ank S \ge n - \dim U^{*} = n - \dim U , using \im S \subseteq U^{*} and \dim U^{*} = \dim U (@cor-dimension-dual-space). (b) If  eta is nondegenerate then R_ eta is an isomorphism (@prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible (c)), and ho is surjective (@thm-dual-of-subspace). So S = ho R_ eta is surjective, ank S = \dim U, and the inequality in (a) is an equality. (c) Take  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 on F^2 and U = \Span(\cvec{e}_2). Then  eta(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{v}) = 0 for every \cvec{v}, so U^{\perp_ eta} = F^2 has dimension 2, while n - \dim U = 1. The form is degenerate, as (b) requires it to be. [C3: The evaluation pairing] Let V be finite-dimensional and let W = V^{*} 	imes V. Define  eta on W by  eta igl((\varphi, \elem{v}), (\psi, \elem{w}) igr) \coloneqq \psi(\elem{v}) + \varphi(\elem{w}). 1. Prove that  eta is a bilinear form on W. 2. Prove that  eta is nondegenerate. Hint: the two summands of an element of the radical can be killed separately. 3. Deduce that if \elem{v} \in V satisfies \varphi(\elem{v}) = 0 for every \varphi \in V^{*}, then \elem{v} = \elem{0}, and name the result of Chapter 5 this recovers. (a) Fix (\psi, \elem{w}). The map (\varphi, \elem{v}) \mapsto \psi(\elem{v}) + \varphi(\elem{w}) is the sum of (\varphi,\elem{v}) \mapsto \psi(\elem{v}), which is linear because \psi is and because projection onto the second summand is linear, and (\varphi, \elem{v}) \mapsto \varphi(\elem{w}) = \ev_{\elem{w}}(\varphi), which is linear because \ev_{\elem{w}} \in V^{**} (@thm-evaluation-map-linear-injective). So clause (B1) holds. Clause (B2) follows by the same argument with the roles of the two arguments exchanged, since the defining expression is symmetric in them. (b) Suppose (\psi, \elem{w}) \in \operatorname{rad}( eta), so \psi(\elem{v}) + \varphi(\elem{w}) = 0 for all \varphi \in V^{*} and all \elem{v} \in V. Taking \varphi = 0 gives \psi(\elem{v}) = 0 for every \elem{v}, so \psi = 0. Taking \elem{v} = \elem{0} then gives \varphi(\elem{w}) = 0 for every \varphi \in V^{*}, so \ev_{\elem{w}} = 0 in V^{**}, and \elem{w} = \elem{0} because \ev_V is injective (@thm-evaluation-map-linear-injective). Hence the radical is \{\elem{0}\}. (c) The second half of (b) is exactly that statement: \varphi(\elem{v}) = 0 for all \varphi \in V^{*} forces \elem{v} = \elem{0}. It recovers the injectivity of the evaluation map \ev_V \colon V 	o V^{**} of @thm-evaluation-map-linear-injective, which is the first half of @thm-double-dual-isomorphism. So the nondegeneracy of this form is the statement that functionals separate points (@thm-functionals-separate-points).

title: 14.2 Congruence
content:
Congruence The matrix of a form in @def-form-matrix depends on a basis, and a basis is a choice. As with linear maps in Chapter 4, the useful question is therefore not “what is the matrix?” but “which matrices arise from the same form?”. The answer here is \P	p\A\P rather than \P^{-1}\A\P, and one symbol’s difference changes the whole theory: the new relation keeps the rank and the symmetry type of a matrix and throws its eigenvalues away. This section proves the change-of-basis rule, names the relation, sorts the invariants from the casualties, and settles the debt Chapters 12 and 13 ran up when they kept postponing all of this. Throughout, V is a vector space over an arbitrary field F with \dim V = n \ge 1, and  eta is a bilinear form on V. No hypothesis on the characteristic of F is needed in this section. The change-of-basis rule for a form Two bases \sB and \sB' of V give two matrices for one form. The link between them is the change-of-coordinates matrix of @def-change-of-coordinates-matrix, and the computation is three lines, because @thm-form-matrix-determines (a) already expresses the form through coordinates. [Change of Basis for a Form] Let  eta be a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional V, let \sB and \sB' be ordered bases of V, and let \P = \mtx{\id}{\sB'}{\sB} be the change-of-coordinates matrix from \sB' to \sB. Then \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{\sB'} = \P	p\,\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}\,\P . There is nothing to discover: write the form in \sB-coordinates, substitute \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} = \P\coord{\elem{v}}{\sB'} in both slots, and read off the matrix that appears between the two coordinate vectors. The uniqueness clause of @thm-form-matrix-determines then says that matrix is the one we want, with no further checking. Write \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}. By @thm-change-of-coordinates (a), \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} = \P\coord{\elem{v}}{\sB'} for every \elem{v} \in V. So for all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V, using @thm-form-matrix-determines (a) and then @thm-transpose-properties (part 4),  egin{aligned}  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) &= \coord{\elem{u}}{\sB}	p\,\A\,\coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} \ &=  igl(\P\coord{\elem{u}}{\sB'} igr)	p\A\, igl(\P\coord{\elem{v}}{\sB'} igr) \ &= \coord{\elem{u}}{\sB'}	p\, igl(\P	p\A\P igr)\,\coord{\elem{v}}{\sB'} . \end{aligned} Thus \P	p\A\P is a matrix with the property that characterizes \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{\sB'}, and by the uniqueness in @thm-form-matrix-determines (b) it is \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{\sB'}. This proves the theorem. Notice that \P is the same matrix as in @thm-change-of-basis-maps: the change-of-coordinates matrix from the new basis to the old one, whose columns are the new basis vectors written in old coordinates. Only the way it acts has changed, from \P^{-1}\A\P to \P	p\A\P. [Killing the cross term] On 
R^2, let  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + 2x_1y_2 + 2x_2y_1 + x_2y_2, so that \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sE}{\sE} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Compute \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{\sB'} for \sB' =  igl((1, 0),\ (-2, 1) igr), both by @thm-change-of-basis-form and directly from @def-form-matrix. The columns of \P = \mtx{\id}{\sB'}{\sE} are the vectors of \sB' in standard coordinates, so \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & -3 \end{pmatrix}, and therefore \P	p\A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & -3 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -3 \end{pmatrix}. Directly: with \cvec{v}'_1 = (1,0) and \cvec{v}'_2 = (-2,1), the four values are  eta(\cvec{v}'_1, \cvec{v}'_1) = 1,  eta(\cvec{v}'_1, \cvec{v}'_2) =  eta(\cvec{v}'_2, \cvec{v}'_1) = 0, and  eta(\cvec{v}'_2, \cvec{v}'_2) = -3. The two computations agree. The new basis was not guessed. In coordinates the form reads q(\cvec{x}) = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 + x_2^2 = (x_1 + 2x_2)^2 - 3x_2^2, a perfect square plus a leftover, and the substitution y_1 = x_1 + 2x_2, y_2 = x_2 — that is, \cvec{x} = \P\cvec{y} — is what completing the square asks for. A later section turns this into a theorem and an algorithm. Congruent matrices Every invertible \P is a change-of-coordinates matrix between some pair of bases (@prp-invertible-matrix-change-of-basis), so @thm-change-of-basis-form says exactly this: the matrices of one form, over all bases, are the matrices \P	p\A\P with \P invertible. That set deserves a name, and the name is the organizing idea of the chapter. Two matrices are congruent when they record the same form in two bases. Congruent Matrices Let \A, \B \in M_n(F). We say \A is congruent to \B, written \A \simeq \B, if there exists an invertible \P \in M_n(F) such that \B = \P	p\A\P . In words: congruence allows one matrix to be sandwiched by an invertible matrix and its transpose. The word invertible is essential; without it, \A \mapsto \P	p\A\P with \P = \O would relate everything to \O. The transpose, not the inverse, is what distinguishes the relation from similarity (@def-similar-matrices), and the symbol \simeq is chosen to sit near \sim without being it. Three immediate readings. First, by @thm-change-of-basis-form, \A \simeq \B if and only if \A and \B are the matrices of a single bilinear form in two bases. Second, in the language of quadratic expressions on F^n, \A \simeq \B says that the substitution \cvec{x} = \P\cvec{y} turns \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} into \cvec{y}	p\B\cvec{y}: congruence is invertible change of variables in a quadratic expression. Third, over 
R it is the relation \A \mapsto \S^{*}\A\S of Chapter 13, because there the star is the transpose. [Congruences and a noncongruence] 1. \I_2 \simeq  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} over any field. 2. \I_2 \simeq \diag(4, 1) over 
Q. 3. \A \simeq \A for every \A. 4. \I_2 
ot\simeq  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} over any field. (a) Take \P =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}, which is invertible with determinant 1. Then \P	p\I_2\P = \P	p\P =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}. (b) Take \P = \diag(2, 1), invertible over 
Q. Then \P	p\I_2\P = \diag(4, 1). Scaling a basis vector by c scales the corresponding diagonal entry by c^2, which is the single most useful congruence to have in mind. (c) Take \P = \I_n. (d) Suppose  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} = \P	p\I_2\P = \P	p\P for some \P. Then, by @thm-transpose-properties, (\P	p\P)	p = \P	p\P, so the matrix would be symmetric; it is not. This is the nonexample by minimal change: one entry of  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} in (a) is altered, and congruence to \I_2 is lost — not for a subtle reason, but because the altered matrix is not the matrix of a symmetric form in any basis. The general statement is @prp-congruence-preserves-symmetry below. Before using the word “congruent” in both directions, we owe the usual check. [Congruence is an equivalence relation] Congruence is an equivalence relation on M_n(F) (@def-equivalence-relation). Reflexive: \A = \I_n	p\A\I_n. Symmetric: suppose \B = \P	p\A\P with \P invertible, and put \Q = \P^{-1}, which is invertible. By @thm-transpose-properties (part 4), \Q	p\P	p = (\P\Q)	p = \I_n	p = \I_n, so \Q	p\B\Q =  igl(\Q	p\P	p igr)\A igl(\P\Q igr) = \I_n\A\I_n = \A . Transitive: if \B = \P	p\A\P and \C = \Q	p\B\Q with \P, \Q invertible, then \P\Q is invertible and \C = \Q	p\P	p\A\P\Q = (\P\Q)	p\A(\P\Q). This proves the proposition. So the matrices in M_n(F) fall into congruence classes, and the classification problem of this chapter is to describe them. The rest of the section collects the tools for telling classes apart. What congruence preserves Three invariants come out of the definition with almost no work. The first is the rank, which we already know is the co-dimension of the radical (@prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible). [Congruence preserves rank] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) with \A \simeq \B. Then ank\A = ank\B. Consequently, whether the associated form is nondegenerate is a property of the congruence class, and it is legitimate to speak of the rank of a bilinear form, meaning the rank of its matrix in any basis. Write \B = \P	p\A\P with \P invertible. Then \P	p is invertible, with inverse (\P^{-1})	p (@thm-transpose-properties). Multiplying by invertible matrices on either side does not change the rank (@thm-rank-product-inequality), so ank\B = ank(\A\P) = ank\A. Nondegeneracy is the condition ank\A = n by @prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible (c), so it too depends only on the class. The last sentence follows because, by @thm-change-of-basis-form, any two matrices of one form are congruent. The second invariant is the symmetry type. Here “alternating” is used in the matrix sense that @def-alternating-form suggests: a zero diagonal on top of skew-symmetry. The next section separates the three conditions carefully; for now we only need that congruence respects each of them. [Congruence preserves the symmetry type] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) with \B = \P	p\A\P for an invertible \P. 1. If \A	p = \A, then \B	p = \B. 2. If \A	p = -\A, then \B	p = -\B. 3. If \A	p = -\A and every diagonal entry of \A is 0, the same holds for \B. Each implication is an equivalence, since congruence is symmetric (@prp-congruence-equivalence). By @thm-transpose-properties, \B	p = (\P	p\A\P)	p = \P	p\A	p\P. (a) If \A	p = \A, this is \P	p\A\P = \B. (b) If \A	p = -\A, it is \P	p(-\A)\P = -\B. (c) Assume the hypothesis of (c). Then \B is skew-symmetric by (b), so only the diagonal is left to check. For any \cvec{x} \in F^n, grouping the terms of the double sum in pairs, \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = \sum_{i<j}(a_{ij} + a_{ji})x_ix_j + \sum_i a_{ii}x_i^2 = 0 , since a_{ij} + a_{ji} = 0 by skew-symmetry and a_{ii} = 0 by hypothesis. Writing \cvec{p}_1, \dots, \cvec{p}_n for the columns of \P, the i-th diagonal entry of \B = \P	p\A\P is b_{ii} = \cvec{e}_i	p\P	p\A\P\cvec{e}_i = \cvec{p}_i	p\A\cvec{p}_i, which is 0 by the display. This proves the proposition. The third invariant is the determinant, but only in a weakened sense: congruence multiplies it by a square. [Congruence changes the determinant by a square] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) with \B = \P	p\A\P for an invertible \P. Then \det\B = (\det\P)^2\,\det\A , with \det\P 
e 0. In particular \det\A = 0 if and only if \det\B = 0, and when they are nonzero, \det\B = c^2\det\A for some c \in F \setminus\{0\}. By @thm-det-multiplicative and @thm-det-transpose, \det\B = \det(\P	p)\det\A\det\P = (\det\P)^2\det\A . Since \P is invertible, \det\P 
e 0 (@thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible), so (\det\P)^2 
e 0 and the two determinants vanish together. Taking c = \det\P gives the last claim. The determinant itself is therefore not a congruence invariant — @exm-congruence-first (b) moved it from 1 to 4. What is invariant is the determinant read modulo squares. Write F^{	imes} = F \setminus\{0\}, and for a, b \in F^{	imes} declare a and b equivalent when a = c^2b for some c \in F^{	imes}. This is an equivalence relation on F^{	imes} (@def-equivalence-relation): it is reflexive with c = 1, symmetric with c^{-1}, and transitive by multiplying the two scalars. Its classes are called square classes, and the set of them is commonly written F^{	imes}/(F^{	imes})^2. [Discriminant] Let  eta be a nondegenerate bilinear form on an n-dimensional V. The discriminant of  eta is the square class of \det\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} in F^{	imes}, for any ordered basis \sB of V. This is well defined by @thm-congruence-determinant-class and @thm-change-of-basis-form: another basis changes the determinant by the square (\det\P)^2, hence not its class. The discriminant is coarse but genuinely useful, and how much it sees depends entirely on the field. Over 
C every nonzero number is a square, so there is only one class and the discriminant says nothing. Over 
R there are two, \{t > 0\} and \{t < 0\}, so the discriminant records one bit: the sign of the determinant. Over 
Q there are infinitely many, and the discriminant is a strong invariant. Over 
R, are \diag(1, 1) and \diag(-1, -1) distinguished by their discriminants? No. Both determinants equal 1, so the discriminants agree. And yet the two matrices are not congruent over 
R. Suppose \diag(-1,-1) = \P	p\I_2\P = \P	p\P for an invertible \P. Evaluating both sides on \cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_1 gives -1 = \cvec{e}_1	p\diag(-1,-1)\cvec{e}_1 = \cvec{e}_1	p\P	p\P\cvec{e}_1 = 
orm{\P\cvec{e}_1}^2 \ge 0 , a contradiction. So the discriminant is not a complete invariant, even over 
R and even for 2 	imes 2 matrices. Proving that the full “sign pattern” is an invariant, and that it is the complete one over 
R, is the law of inertia, proved later in this chapter. What congruence destroys Now the negative result of the section, and the reason the previous three chapters could not have been this one. [Congruent, with no eigenvalue in common] 1. \I_2 \simeq  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} by @exm-congruence-first (a). Compare their eigenvalues. 2.  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} \simeq \diag(1, -3) by @exm-form-in-a-new-basis. Compare their eigenvalues. (a) \I_2 has the single eigenvalue 1, twice. The characteristic polynomial of  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} is x^2 - 3x + 1, whose roots are (3 \pm \sqrt5)/2, that is, approximately 2.618 and 0.382. The two matrices share no eigenvalue. They do share a rank, 2; a symmetry type, symmetric; and a discriminant, since \det = 1 for both. (b) The characteristic polynomial of  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} is x^2 - 2x - 3 = (x-3)(x+1), so its eigenvalues are 3 and -1. Those of \diag(1,-3) are 1 and -3. Again no eigenvalue in common — but this time one positive and one negative on each side, and the determinants are -3 both times. The signs survived; the numbers did not. That is the pattern the law of inertia will explain. Chapter 13 introduced this operation twice and both times deferred it to here. Section 1 of that chapter wrote that “the operation \A \mapsto \S^{*}\A\S is called congruence, and Chapter 14 studies it for its own sake”, keeping only that it preserves the sign of a positive form (@prp-congruence-positivity). Section 4 repeated the promise in fuller form: “Chapter 14 studies congruence in its own right, including what it does preserve; for now, note that it certainly does not preserve eigenvalues, since \S^{*}\I\S = \S^{*}\S can be any positive definite matrix at all.” Both debts are now paid, and it is worth saying the answer in one place. What congruence preserves: the rank (@thm-congruence-preserves-rank), and with it nondegeneracy and the dimension of the radical; the symmetry type (@prp-congruence-preserves-symmetry); and the square class of the determinant when that is nonzero (@thm-congruence-determinant-class), the discriminant. Over 
R it preserves one thing more, the triple of signs, and that is the deepest of the four; it is proved in the section on inertia. What congruence destroys: the eigenvalues, and therefore the characteristic polynomial, the trace, and the determinant itself. Not every similarity invariant is lost — rank and invertibility, parts (a) and (b) of @prp-similarity-invariants, survive both relations — but every invariant that reads the eigenvalues is. Chapter 13’s parenthetical remark is exactly right and can be made sharper: taking \A = \I_n in @def-congruent, the congruence class of \I_n over 
R is the set of all matrices \P	p\P with \P invertible, which by @thm-pd-characterizations (c) is the set of all positive definite matrices. One class, every spectrum with all eigenvalues positive. Congruent and similar are different relations, and neither implies the other. By @exm-congruent-different-eigenvalues (a), \I_2 \simeq  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}, while the only matrix similar to \I_2 is \I_2 itself, since \P^{-1}\I_2\P = \I_2 for every invertible \P. In the other direction, \diag(1,2) is similar to  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 0 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} — conjugate by  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} — but not congruent to it, because \diag(1,2) is symmetric and the other matrix is not (@prp-congruence-preserves-symmetry). So do not carry any habit across. In particular, “diagonalizable” means two different things in this chapter, and a matrix that is diagonalizable by congruence need not be diagonalizable by similarity, nor conversely. Where the two relations meet There is exactly one situation in which the confusion is harmless: when the change-of-basis matrix satisfies \P	p = \P^{-1}, that is, when \P is orthogonal (@def-unitary-orthogonal-groups). [An orthogonal change of basis is both] Let \A \in M_n(
R) and \Q \in \Orth(n). Then \Q	p\A\Q = \Q^{-1}\A\Q, so this matrix is at once congruent and similar to \A. Consequently, if \A is symmetric, then \A is congruent to the diagonal matrix \D of its eigenvalues, listed with multiplicity in any prescribed order. The first statement is the definition of an orthogonal matrix, \Q	p\Q = \I_n, which gives \Q	p = \Q^{-1}; the matrix \Q	p\A\Q is then congruent to \A by @def-congruent, since \Q is invertible, and similar to \A by @def-similar-matrices. For the second statement, let \A be symmetric. By @cor-spectral-real-matrix there are \Q \in \Orth(n) and a real diagonal \D, carrying the eigenvalues of \A in any prescribed order, with \A = \Q\D\Q	p. Multiplying on the left by \Q	p and on the right by \Q gives \D = \Q	p\A\Q, which is a congruence. This proves the proposition. This is why the real spectral theorem is so strong, and it is what Chapter 12 meant when it said, of the principal axis theorem, that “an orthogonal change of variables is a similarity and a congruence, so it keeps the eigenvalues and the geometry at once”. The general theory of this chapter has no orthogonal matrices to call on — a general field has no inner product, hence no orthogonal group in that sense — so the two relations part company and only congruence remains. What @prp-orthogonal-congruence-similarity gives over 
R is a bridge: it says that every real symmetric matrix is congruent to a diagonal matrix, and it identifies the diagonal entries as eigenvalues. The section on inertia will show that the entries are free to move but their signs are not, which is how the two pictures are finally reconciled. Over 
R, which matrices are congruent to \I_n? Exactly the positive definite symmetric matrices. If \B = \P	p\I_n\P = \P	p\P with \P invertible, then \B is symmetric and \cvec{x}	p\B\cvec{x} = 
orm{\P\cvec{x}}^2 > 0 for \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}, since \P\cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}. Conversely every positive definite \B is \P	p\P for an invertible \P by @thm-pd-characterizations. Compare the similarity class of \I_n, which contains \I_n alone: one relation collapses this class to a point, the other spreads it over every positive definite matrix there is. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the change-of-basis rule for the matrix of a bilinear form, saying which matrix \P appears. 2. Define what it means for \A, \B \in M_n(F) to be congruent. 3. For each of rank, symmetry, determinant, eigenvalues, and the square class of a nonzero determinant, say whether it is a congruence invariant. 4. Determine whether the following is correct, with a reason: congruent matrices are similar. 5. State the one circumstance in which a change of basis is simultaneously a similarity and a congruence. (a) @thm-change-of-basis-form: \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{\sB'} = \P	p\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}\P, where \P = \mtx{\id}{\sB'}{\sB} is the change-of-coordinates matrix from the new basis to the old one. (b) @def-congruent: \B = \P	p\A\P for some invertible \P \in M_n(F). (c) Invariant: rank (@thm-congruence-preserves-rank); symmetry (@prp-congruence-preserves-symmetry); the square class of a nonzero determinant (@thm-congruence-determinant-class). Not invariant: the determinant itself, and the eigenvalues (@exm-congruent-different-eigenvalues). (d) Incorrect. \I_2 \simeq  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}, but the only matrix similar to \I_2 is \I_2. (e) When the change-of-coordinates matrix \P satisfies \P	p = \P^{-1}, that is, when \P is orthogonal (@prp-orthogonal-congruence-similarity). B. Practice [B1: A congruence in 
Q] Let \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} and \P =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix}, both over 
Q. 1. Compute \P	p\A\P, and hence write down a matrix congruent to \A that is diagonal. 2. Find the eigenvalues of both matrices and compare them. 3. Compute the discriminant of the form \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} and check that it agrees for the two matrices. (a) \P is invertible, with \det\P = -2 
e 0. Then \A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \P	p\A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & -2\end{pmatrix}. So \A \simeq \diag(2, -2) over 
Q. (b) The characteristic polynomial of \A is x^2 - 1, so its eigenvalues are 1 and -1; those of \diag(2,-2) are 2 and -2. No eigenvalue is shared, and each matrix has one positive and one negative eigenvalue. (c) \det\A = -1 and \det\diag(2,-2) = -4 = (-2)^2 \cdot (-1), which is the relation \det\B = (\det\P)^2\det\A of @thm-congruence-determinant-class. The two determinants differ by the square 4, so they lie in the same square class of 
Q^{	imes} and the discriminants agree, as @def-discriminant requires. [B2: A noncongruence over 
Q] 1. Prove that \diag(1,1) and \diag(1,2) are not congruent over 
Q. 2. Prove that they are congruent over 
R, by exhibiting \P. 3. Explain in one sentence why (a) and (b) are consistent. (a) Suppose \diag(1,2) = \P	p\diag(1,1)\P with \P \in M_2(
Q) invertible. By @thm-congruence-determinant-class, 2 = (\det\P)^2 \cdot 1, so \det\P \in 
Q would satisfy (\det\P)^2 = 2. No rational number squares to 2 (@thm-sqrt2-irrational), a contradiction. Hence the two are not congruent over 
Q. (b) Take \P = \diag(1, 1/\sqrt2), which is invertible over 
R. Then \P	p\diag(1,2)\P = \diag(1, 1), and congruence is symmetric (@prp-congruence-equivalence). (c) Congruence is a relation over a specified field: the matrix \P is required to have entries in that field, and 1/\sqrt2 is available in 
R but not in 
Q. Equivalently, 2 is a square in 
R^{	imes} and not in 
Q^{	imes}, so the discriminant separates the two matrices over 
Q and not over 
R. [B3: Completing the square, again] On 
R^2, let  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 - x_1y_2 - x_2y_1 + 2x_2y_2. 1. Write down \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sE}{\sE} and expand q(\cvec{x}) =  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{x}) as a polynomial in x_1, x_2. 2. Complete the square to find a basis \sB' with \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{\sB'} = \I_2. Verify by computing \P	p\A\P. 3. Hence find the eigenvalues of \A and compare them with those of \I_2. (a) \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}, and q(\cvec{x}) = x_1^2 - 2x_1x_2 + 2x_2^2. (b) q(\cvec{x}) = (x_1 - x_2)^2 + x_2^2. So the substitution y_1 = x_1 - x_2, y_2 = x_2, that is x_1 = y_1 + y_2 and x_2 = y_2, makes q = y_1^2 + y_2^2. This is \cvec{x} = \P\cvec{y} with \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \P	p\A\P = \I_2 . By @thm-change-of-basis-form the basis is \sB' =  igl((1,0),\ (1,1) igr), the columns of \P. (c) The characteristic polynomial of \A is x^2 - 3x + 1, with roots (3 \pm \sqrt5)/2; \I_2 has the eigenvalue 1 twice. The two matrices are congruent with no eigenvalue in common. What they share is that all eigenvalues are positive on both sides, which by the check above is no accident: the congruence class of \I_2 over 
R consists of exactly the positive definite matrices. C. Going deeper [C1: Congruence versus equivalence] 1. Prove that if \A \simeq \B then \A and \B are equivalent in the sense of @def-equivalent-matrices. 2. Give two matrices in M_2(
Q) that are equivalent but not congruent, and justify your example. 3. Hence explain what “the congruence classes refine the equivalence classes” means, and say what extra information a congruence class carries that a rank does not. (a) If \B = \P	p\A\P with \P invertible, then \P	p is invertible (@thm-transpose-properties), so \B = \Q\A\P with \Q = \P	p and \P both invertible, which is @def-equivalent-matrices. (b) Take \diag(1,1) and \diag(1,2). Both have rank 2, so they are equivalent by @thm-rank-normal-form (c). They are not congruent over 
Q by @exr-congruence-b2 (a). (c) By (a), each congruence class lies inside a single equivalence class, and by (b) an equivalence class may split into more than one congruence class; that is what “refine” means. An equivalence class is named by the rank alone (@thm-rank-normal-form (c)). A congruence class remembers the rank, and in addition the symmetry type and the discriminant — and over 
R, the signs. Equivalence allows two independent changes of basis, one in each slot; congruence allows only one, used twice, and the extra invariants are the price of that constraint. [C2: Orthogonal congruence] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be symmetric with eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, listed with multiplicity. 1. Prove that \A \simeq \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n). 2. Deduce that if every \lambda_i is nonzero, then \A is congruent to a diagonal matrix all of whose entries are \pm1. 3. Give two real symmetric 2 	imes 2 matrices that are congruent and have no eigenvalue in common. Hint for (b): recall from @exm-congruence-first (b) what scaling a basis vector does to a diagonal entry. (a) This is @prp-orthogonal-congruence-similarity: by @cor-spectral-real-matrix there is \Q \in \Orth(n) with \Q	p\A\Q = \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n), and \Q is invertible, so \A \simeq \D. (b) Let \S = \diag(c_1, \dots, c_n) with c_i = 1/\sqrt{\lvert\lambda_ivert}, which is defined and nonzero because \lambda_i 
e 0. Then \S is invertible and \S	p\D\S = \diag(c_1^2\lambda_1, \dots, c_n^2\lambda_n), whose i-th entry is \lambda_i/\lvert\lambda_ivert = \pm1 according to the sign of \lambda_i. By (a) and transitivity (@prp-congruence-equivalence), \A is congruent to that matrix. (c) By (b), \diag(1, -3) and \diag(2, -1) are both congruent to \diag(1,-1), hence to each other by @prp-congruence-equivalence; explicitly, \P = \diag(\sqrt2, 1/\sqrt3) gives \P	p\diag(1,-3)\P = \diag(2,-1). Their eigenvalues are \{1, -3\} and \{2, -1\}, which are disjoint. Note that the signs match, one positive and one negative on each side; part (b) is the reason, and the law of inertia will say it is forced. [C3: How much the discriminant sees] 1. Show that 
C^{	imes} has exactly one square class, and that 
R^{	imes} has exactly two. 2. List the squares in 
F_5^{	imes} and show that 
F_5^{	imes} has exactly two square classes. 3. Hence determine, for each of 
C, 
R, and 
F_5, the largest number of pairwise noncongruent invertible matrices in M_n that the discriminant alone can distinguish. (a) Over 
C, every a 
e 0 has a square root (@exm-complex-square-root), so a = c^2 \cdot 1 and every element is equivalent to 1: one class. Over 
R, squares of nonzero reals are exactly the positive reals, so a and b are equivalent precisely when a/b > 0, which happens exactly when they have the same sign. The classes are the positive reals and the negative reals: two classes, and they are distinct since 1 and -1 are not related. (b) The squares are 1^2 = 1, 2^2 = 4, 3^2 = 4, 4^2 = 1, so the set of nonzero squares is \{1, 4\}. Multiplying \{1,4\} by 2 gives \{2, 3\}, so the classes are \{1, 4\} and \{2, 3\}: two classes, each of size 2, covering all four elements of 
F_5^{	imes}. (c) The discriminant takes one value per square class, so it can separate at most as many classes as there are square classes: one over 
C, two over 
R, and two over 
F_5. Over 
C it is therefore useless, and over 
R and 
F_5 it sorts invertible matrices into at most two piles. By @exr-congruence-c2 (b), over 
R every invertible symmetric matrix is congruent to one of the n + 1 matrices \I_p \oplus -\I_{n-p}, whose determinant is (-1)^{n-p}; so the discriminant sees only the parity of n - p, and for n \ge 2 it cannot separate, say, \I_2 from -\I_2. That the n+1 matrices really are pairwise noncongruent is the law of inertia, not anything the discriminant can deliver.

title: 14.3 Three Kinds of Form
content:
Three Kinds of Form A bilinear form has two slots, and so far nothing has related them. Almost every form that occurs in practice does relate them: the dot product does not care which vector goes first, while the determinant of a 2 	imes 2 matrix changes sign when its columns are swapped. This section names the three symmetry conditions the rest of the chapter runs on, shows that two of them are the same condition exactly when 1 + 1 
e 0 in the field, and extracts from a symmetric form the single-variable function q(\elem{v}) =  eta(\elem{v}, \elem{v}) that carries all of its information. Throughout, V is a finite-dimensional vector space over a field F, and  eta is a bilinear form on V (@def-bilinear-form). The characteristic hypothesis is stated wherever it is needed and nowhere else. Symmetric forms The dot product on F^n satisfies \cvec{x} \cdot \cvec{y} = \cvec{y} \cdot \cvec{x}, and so does every integral pairing \int_0^1 fg, and so does \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} whenever \A happens to satisfy \A	p = \A. The condition recurs, so it gets a name. A symmetric form cannot tell its two arguments apart. [Symmetric Bilinear Form] A bilinear form  eta \colon V 	imes V 	o F is symmetric if  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) =  eta(\elem{v}, \elem{u}) for all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V. In words: the value is unchanged by swapping the two inputs. The condition is imposed for every pair, not just for pairs of basis vectors — although, as the next result shows, checking it on basis vectors is enough. Three examples and one nonexample. - The dot product on F^n,  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n. Each product x_iy_i is unchanged by the swap because multiplication in F is commutative. - A symmetric matrix,  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} with \A	p = \A (@def-symmetric-matrix). Here \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} is a 1 	imes 1 matrix, so it equals its own transpose \cvec{y}	p\A	p\cvec{x} = \cvec{y}	p\A\cvec{x} by @thm-transpose-properties. - Evaluation pairings. On F[x]_{\le n}, fix scalars t_1, \dots, t_k \in F and set  eta(p, q) = \sum_i p(t_i)q(t_i). Symmetry is again commutativity of F. - A nonexample by minimal change. On F^2 put  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_2. It is bilinear, by the one-slot check of @def-multilinear-form. But  eta(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) = 1 and  eta(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1) = 0, so the symmetry clause fails at that one pair. Exactly one clause has been broken: bilinearity survives untouched. The matrix of a form (@def-form-matrix) turns the condition into a matrix condition, and turns “for all \elem{u}, \elem{v}” into a finite check. [Symmetry Is Visible in the Matrix] Let \sB be a basis of V and \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}. Then  eta is symmetric if and only if \A	p = \A. (\Rightarrow) Suppose  eta is symmetric. Writing \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n), the entries of \A are a_{ij} =  eta(\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j), so a_{ij} =  eta(\elem{v}_j, \elem{v}_i) = a_{ji}, which is @def-symmetric-matrix.
