Write down the matrix \A in the standard basis in each case and apply @prp-form-symmetry-matrix and @prp-alternating-form-matrix. (a) \A = \diag(1,-1), which satisfies \A	p = \A: symmetric. Not skew-symmetric, since \A	p = -\A would need 1 = -1 in 
Q. Not alternating, since  eta(\cvec{e}_1,\cvec{e}_1) = 1. (b) \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 3 \ -3 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, with \A	p = -\A and zero diagonal: skew-symmetric and alternating. Not symmetric, since 3 
e -3. (c) \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 2 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}. Symmetry would need 1 = 2 and skewness would need 1 = -2, both false in 
Q; so it is neither, and it is not alternating either, since an alternating form is skew-symmetric. (Its diagonal entries do vanish, so  eta(\cvec{e}_i,\cvec{e}_i) = 0 for the two basis vectors — but  eta(\1,\1) = 1 + 2 = 3 
e 0. Checking the basis vectors alone is not enough.) (d) The zero form is symmetric, skew-symmetric, and alternating at once; its matrix is \O, which satisfies every condition. By the Quick check above it is the only form that is both symmetric and alternating over 
Q. [B2: Polarizing a quadratic form] Over 
R, let q(x_1,x_2,x_3) = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 - 2x_2x_3 + 5x_3^2. 1. Find the symmetric matrix \A with q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x}. 2. Compute  eta(\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3) directly from \A, and again from the polarization formula 	frac12(q(\cvec{u}+\cvec{v}) - q(\cvec{u}) - q(\cvec{v})). (a) The squared terms give a_{11} = 1, a_{22} = 0, a_{33} = 5; the cross terms give a_{12} = a_{21} = 2, a_{23} = a_{32} = -1, a_{13} = a_{31} = 0. So \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \ 2 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & -1 & 5 \end{pmatrix}. (b) Put \cvec{u} = (1,1,0) and \cvec{v} = (0,0,1). Directly, \A\cvec{v} = (0,-1,5) and \cvec{u}	p(\A\cvec{v}) = 0 - 1 = -1. By polarization, q(\cvec{u}) = 1 + 4 = 5 and q(\cvec{v}) = 5, while \cvec{u} + \cvec{v} = (1,1,1) gives q(\cvec{u}+\cvec{v}) = 1 + 4 - 2 + 5 = 8. Hence 	frac12(8 - 5 - 5) = -1. The two agree, as @thm-polarization-forms says they must. [B3: Splitting a form] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 5 \ -1 & 4 \end{pmatrix} over 
Q, and let  eta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}. Write  eta =  eta_s +  eta_a as in @thm-symmetric-alternating-decomposition, giving the matrix of each part, and verify that  eta and  eta_s have the same quadratic form. We have \A	p =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 5 & 4\end{psmallmatrix}, so 	frac12(\A + \A	p) =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad 	frac12(\A - \A	p) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 3 \ -3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. The first is symmetric and the second is alternating, and they sum to \A. For the quadratic forms, \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = x_1^2 + 5x_1x_2 - x_2x_1 + 4x_2^2 = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 + 4x_2^2, and the symmetric part gives x_1^2 + 2x_1x_2 + 2x_2x_1 + 4x_2^2, the same polynomial. The alternating part contributes 3x_1x_2 - 3x_2x_1 = 0. C. Going deeper [C1: Is this still true over 
F_2?] Let V be a vector space over 
F_2 with \dim V = n \ge 1. 1. Prove that every alternating bilinear form on V is symmetric. 2. Prove that the alternating forms on V form a subspace of the space of all bilinear forms, and compute its dimension. 3. Deduce that for n = 2 there is exactly one nonzero alternating form on V, and write down its matrix. Hint: for (b), use @prp-alternating-form-matrix. (a) Let  eta be alternating. By @thm-alternating-vs-skew (a),  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) = - eta(\elem{v},\elem{u}). Over 
F_2 we have -1 = 1, so - eta(\elem{v},\elem{u}) =  eta(\elem{v},\elem{u}) and  eta is symmetric. (b) Fix a basis \sB. The map  eta \mapsto \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} is a linear bijection from bilinear forms to M_n(
F_2) (@thm-form-matrix-determines). By @prp-alternating-form-matrix (b),  eta is alternating exactly when its matrix satisfies \A	p = -\A with zero diagonal; over 
F_2 the first condition is \A	p = \A, so the image is the set of symmetric matrices with zero diagonal. Such a matrix is determined freely by its entries a_{ij} with i < j, of which there are  inom{n}{2}. These conditions are linear, so the set of alternating forms is a subspace, of dimension n(n-1)/2. (c) For n = 2 the dimension is 1, so the space of alternating forms is \{\elem{0},  eta\} for a single nonzero  eta, whose matrix must be  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} — the only symmetric 
F_2-matrix with zero diagonal other than \O. Concretely  eta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = x_1y_2 + x_2y_1, and indeed  eta(\cvec{x},\cvec{x}) = 2x_1x_2 = 0. [C2: How much of a form does q see?] Let \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 and let  eta be any bilinear form on V, with q(\elem{v}) =  eta(\elem{v},\elem{v}). 1. Prove that two bilinear forms have the same quadratic form if and only if their difference is alternating. 2. Deduce that the set of bilinear forms with a given quadratic form q contains exactly one symmetric form. 3. For \dim V = n, how many bilinear forms share a given quadratic form when F = 
F_3? (a) (\Rightarrow) Suppose  eta_1(\elem{v},\elem{v}) =  eta_2(\elem{v},\elem{v}) for all \elem{v}. Then \delta =  eta_1 -  eta_2 is bilinear with \delta(\elem{v},\elem{v}) = 0 for all \elem{v}, which is @def-alternating-form at k = 2. (\Leftarrow) If \delta =  eta_1 -  eta_2 is alternating then  eta_1(\elem{v},\elem{v}) -  eta_2(\elem{v},\elem{v}) = \delta(\elem{v},\elem{v}) = 0 for every \elem{v}. (b) Existence: by @thm-symmetric-alternating-decomposition write  eta =  eta_s +  eta_a; then  eta_s is symmetric with the same quadratic form, since  eta_a(\elem{v},\elem{v}) = 0. Uniqueness: two symmetric forms with the same q are equal by @thm-polarization-forms. (c) By (a), the forms sharing q are exactly  eta_s +  eta_a with  eta_a alternating, so there are as many as there are alternating forms. Over a field with 3 elements, an alternating form corresponds by @prp-alternating-form-matrix (b) to a matrix with \A	p = -\A and zero diagonal, which is determined freely by the  inom{n}{2} entries above the diagonal. So there are 3^{n(n-1)/2} of them. [C3: A Hermitian form is a real symmetric form in disguise] Let  eta be a Hermitian form on 
C^n with matrix \A = \A^{*} as in @prp-hermitian-form-matrix, and regard 
C^n as a real vector space of dimension 2n by forgetting multiplication by i. 1. Prove that 	au(\cvec{u},\cvec{v}) = \operatorname{Re} eta(\cvec{u},\cvec{v}) is a symmetric 
R-bilinear form on that real space, with 	au(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) =  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}). 2. Prove that \omega(\cvec{u},\cvec{v}) = \operatorname{Im} eta(\cvec{u},\cvec{v}) is an alternating 
R-bilinear form. 3. For n = 1 and \A = (1), write both 	au and \omega as explicit forms on 
R^2. (a) Taking real parts of an 
R-linear identity is 
R-linear, and  eta is additive in each slot and commutes with real scalars in each slot (conjugation fixes 
R), so 	au is 
R-bilinear. Symmetry:  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{u}) = \conj{ eta(\cvec{u},\cvec{v})}, and conjugate numbers have equal real parts, so 	au(\cvec{v},\cvec{u}) = 	au(\cvec{u},\cvec{v}). Finally  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) is real, as noted after @def-hermitian-form, so 	au(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) =  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}). (b) 
R-bilinearity is the same argument with imaginary parts. Conjugate numbers have opposite imaginary parts, so \omega(\cvec{v},\cvec{u}) = -\omega(\cvec{u},\cvec{v}): \omega is skew-symmetric, and since \operatorname{char}
R = 0 
e 2, @thm-alternating-vs-skew (b) makes it alternating. (Directly:  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) is real, so its imaginary part is 0.) (c) Here  eta(u,v) = u\conj{v} for u, v \in 
C. Writing u = x_1 + ix_2 and v = y_1 + iy_2, we get u\conj{v} = (x_1y_1 + x_2y_2) + i(x_2y_1 - x_1y_2). So 	au is the dot product on 
R^2 and \omega(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = x_2y_1 - x_1y_2, the negative of the signed area.

title: 14.4 Completing the Square
content:
Completing the Square Every symmetric matrix over 
R can be diagonalized by an orthogonal matrix, which is Chapter 12’s spectral theorem. That theorem needs 
R, an inner product, and the existence of eigenvalues. This section proves a weaker conclusion under far weaker hypotheses: over any field of characteristic 
e 2, with no inner product, no order, and no eigenvalues available, every symmetric form still becomes diagonal after a change of basis — provided we ask only for congruence, not for similarity. The proof is one algebraic manipulation, completing the square, run by induction; and the induction has a case that a careless proof loses. Throughout, F is a field with \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 (@def-characteristic), V is a finite-dimensional vector space over F,  eta is a symmetric bilinear form on V (@def-symmetric-form), and q(\elem{v}) =  eta(\elem{v},\elem{v}) is its quadratic form (@def-quadratic-form). Orthogonality without an inner product Chapter 11 called two vectors orthogonal when their inner product vanished. The word survives the loss of positivity unchanged, because only the vanishing was ever used. [Orthogonal Basis for a Form] Let  eta be a bilinear form on V. Vectors \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V are orthogonal with respect to  eta if  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) = 0. An ordered basis \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) of V is an orthogonal basis for  eta if  eta(\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j) = 0 \qquad 	ext{whenever } i 
e j . The definition is engineered to say exactly one thing about matrices: by @def-form-matrix, \sB is an orthogonal basis for  eta precisely when \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} is a diagonal matrix, with q(\elem{v}_1), \dots, q(\elem{v}_n) down the diagonal. Two warnings come free. The vectors of such a basis are not required to satisfy q(\elem{v}_i) = 1, and over a general field they usually cannot be rescaled to. And a vector may be orthogonal to itself: q(\elem{v}_i) = 0 is allowed, and for a degenerate form it is unavoidable. What an orthogonal basis buys is that q becomes a sum of squares with no cross terms. If \elem{v} = c_1\elem{v}_1 + \dots + c_n\elem{v}_n and d_i = q(\elem{v}_i), then expanding by bilinearity and deleting the i 
e j terms, q(\elem{v}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i\,c_i^2 . {#eq-diagonal-quadratic-form} That is the “sum of squares” a reader has met when completing the square in two variables, and @eq-diagonal-quadratic-form is the reason the whole section is called what it is. The theorem, and the case that breaks it Here is the naive argument, and it is worth seeing it fail. To make q(\cvec{v}) = ax_1^2 + 2bx_1x_2 + cx_2^2 into a sum of squares, write q = a\Bigl(x_1 +  rac{b}{a}x_2\Bigr)^{2} + \Bigl(c -  rac{b^2}{a}\Bigr)x_2^2 , which is exactly a change of variable. The step divides by a = q(\cvec{e}_1). If a = 0 there is nothing to complete, and one may hope to start with x_2 instead — but q(\cvec{x}) = 2x_1x_2 has q(\cvec{e}_1) = q(\cvec{e}_2) = 0, and neither variable offers a foothold. The repair is to change the vector, not the variable: q(\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2) = 2 
e 0. That repair is a lemma, and it is where \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 is spent. [A Non-Zero Form Is Non-Zero Somewhere on the Diagonal] Let \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 and let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on V with  eta 
e 0. Then there exists \elem{v} \in V with q(\elem{v}) 
e 0. Since  eta 
e 0, there are \elem{u}, \elem{w} \in V with a =  eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) 
e 0. If q(\elem{u}) 
e 0 or q(\elem{w}) 
e 0 we are done. So suppose q(\elem{u}) = q(\elem{w}) = 0. Expanding by bilinearity and using symmetry, q(\elem{u} + \elem{w}) = q(\elem{u}) + 2 eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) + q(\elem{w}) = (1+1)a . Since \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, the element 1 + 1 is nonzero, and a product of two nonzero elements of a field is nonzero, so q(\elem{u}+\elem{w}) 
e 0. This proves the lemma. Contrapositively: if q vanishes identically then  eta = 0. That is the case the induction must handle separately, and the lemma is what lets it be handled in one line. [Diagonalization of a Symmetric Form] Let F be a field with \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, and let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on V. Then V has an orthogonal basis for  eta. Equivalently: every symmetric \A \in M_n(F) is congruent to a diagonal matrix, that is, there is an invertible \P \in M_n(F) with \P	p\A\P diagonal. Induction on \dim V. The step wants to peel off one basis vector and recurse on a complement, exactly as “peel off an eigenvector” does in Chapter 9 — but the complement here is the set of vectors orthogonal to the chosen one, not an invariant subspace, and it is available only if the chosen \elem{v}_1 has q(\elem{v}_1) 
e 0. So the proof splits into two steps: ① if q vanishes everywhere, the form is zero and every basis is orthogonal; ② otherwise @lem-anisotropic-vector-exists supplies a \elem{v}_1 with q(\elem{v}_1) 
e 0, the linear functional \elem{w} \mapsto  eta(\elem{v}_1,\elem{w}) is nonzero, its kernel W is a hyperplane meeting \Span(\elem{v}_1) trivially, and the induction hypothesis applies to  eta restricted to W. Step ① is not a formality: without it the argument has no base for the recursion when the form degenerates, and the word “equivalently” in the statement would be unearned. We induct on n = \dim V. If n = 0 the empty basis is orthogonal, vacuously; if n = 1 any basis (\elem{v}_1) is orthogonal, since there is no pair i 
e j. Let n \ge 2 and suppose the result holds for all spaces of dimension n - 1 over F. Step 1: the form vanishes on the diagonal. Suppose q(\elem{v}) = 0 for every \elem{v} \in V. By @lem-anisotropic-vector-exists, read contrapositively,  eta = 0. Then  eta(\elem{v}_i,\elem{v}_j) = 0 for every pair of vectors whatsoever, so any basis of V is an orthogonal basis for  eta, and its matrix is \O, which is diagonal. Step 2: the form does not vanish on the diagonal. Otherwise there is \elem{v}_1 \in V with c = q(\elem{v}_1) 
e 0; in particular \elem{v}_1 
e \elem{0}. Define \varphi \colon V 	o F, \qquad \varphi(\elem{w}) =  eta(\elem{v}_1, \elem{w}) . Then \varphi is linear, because  eta is linear in its second argument, and \varphi(\elem{v}_1) = c 
e 0, so \varphi 
e 0. A nonzero functional is surjective onto F (@prp-nonzero-functional-surjective), so ank\varphi = 1 and, by the Rank–Nullity Theorem (@thm-rank-nullity), W = \ker\varphi has \dim W = n - 1. Moreover \Span(\elem{v}_1) \cap W = \{\elem{0}\}: if a\elem{v}_1 \in W then 0 = \varphi(a\elem{v}_1) = ac, and c 
e 0 forces a = 0. So the sum \Span(\elem{v}_1) + W is direct, and \dim(\Span(\elem{v}_1) + W) = 1 + (n-1) = n, both by @thm-direct-sum-criteria. A subspace of V of dimension \dim V is all of V (@thm-dim-impl-eq), so V = \Span(\elem{v}_1) \oplus W . The restriction of  eta to W 	imes W is a bilinear form on W, and it is symmetric because  eta is. As \dim W = n - 1, the induction hypothesis provides an orthogonal basis (\elem{v}_2, \dots, \elem{v}_n) of W for that restriction. Concatenating bases of the summands of a direct sum gives a basis of it (@thm-direct-sum-k-criteria, (a) \Leftrightarrow (d)), so \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \elem{v}_2, \dots, \elem{v}_n) is a basis of V. It is orthogonal for  eta: for j \ge 2 we have \elem{v}_j \in W = \ker\varphi, so  eta(\elem{v}_1, \elem{v}_j) = \varphi(\elem{v}_j) = 0, and  eta(\elem{v}_j, \elem{v}_1) = 0 by symmetry; and for 2 \le i 
e j the value  eta(\elem{v}_i,\elem{v}_j) is 0 by the choice of the basis of W. This completes the induction. For the matrix statement, let \A \in M_n(F) be symmetric and let  eta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} on V = F^n, which is symmetric by @prp-form-symmetry-matrix and has \mtx{ eta}{\sE}{\sE} = \A in the standard basis \sE. Take an orthogonal basis \sB as above and let \P = \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sE}, the matrix whose columns are the vectors of \sB, which is invertible. By @thm-change-of-basis-form, \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} = \P	p\A\P, and this matrix is diagonal. This proves the theorem. Two hypotheses did visible work. Symmetry was used twice: to make  eta(\elem{v}_j,\elem{v}_1) vanish along with  eta(\elem{v}_1,\elem{v}_j), and to keep the restriction to W symmetric so the induction could run. The characteristic hypothesis was used exactly once, inside @lem-anisotropic-vector-exists — and that single use is essential: Exercise C2 below exhibits a symmetric matrix over 
F_2 that is congruent to no diagonal matrix at all. Diagonal does not mean “the diagonal entries are eigenvalues”. The matrix \P	p\A\P of @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable is congruent to \A, not similar to it, and its entries are the values q(\elem{v}_i) at whatever basis the algorithm happened to produce. Over 
R they can be scaled at will: replacing \elem{v}_i by t\elem{v}_i replaces d_i by t^2d_i. There is no canonical list of numbers here. The next section finds what there is. In @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable, how many of the diagonal entries d_i are zero? Exactly n - ank\A of them. A diagonal matrix has rank equal to its number of nonzero entries, and congruence preserves rank (@thm-congruence-preserves-rank), so the count is the same for every orthogonal basis even though the individual d_i are not. In the language of Section 1, those \elem{v}_i with d_i = 0 span the radical \operatorname{rad}( eta) of @def-radical, since in an orthogonal basis such a \elem{v}_i pairs to zero with every basis vector; and  eta is nondegenerate (@def-nondegenerate) exactly when no d_i is zero. The algorithm: symmetric row and column operations The proof is constructive, but running it by hand means chasing kernels of functionals. There is a bookkeeping device that does the same work on the matrix directly, and it is the practical content of this section. The key observation is that a congruence by an elementary matrix is a pair of operations. Let \E be an elementary matrix (@def-elementary-matrix). Right multiplication \A\E performs a column operation, and left multiplication \E	p\A performs the corresponding row operation. So \A \mapsto \E	p\A\E performs both, and the result is congruent to \A and again symmetric. Doing the operations in pairs is exactly what keeps the matrix symmetric, and that is the whole idea. To diagonalize a symmetric \A \in M_n(F) by congruence, write \A and \I_n side by side and repeat, for i = 1, 2, \dots, n in turn: - If a_{ii} = 0 but some a_{jj} 
e 0 with j > i, swap rows i, j and then columns i, j. - If a_{ii} = 0 and every a_{jj} = 0 for j \ge i, look for an entry a_{ij} 
e 0 with j > i. If there is none, then row i and column i are already zero in every position, so move on to i + 1. If there is one, add row j to row i, then column j to column i; the new a_{ii} is 2a_{ij} 
e 0. - Now a_{ii} 
e 0. For each j > i with a_{ij} 
e 0, subtract (a_{ij}/a_{ii}) times row i from row j, then (a_{ij}/a_{ii}) times column i from column j. Over a field where division is inconvenient — 
Q or 
Z-valued data by hand — the clearing step may instead be done as 	ext{row } j \mapsto a_{ii}\,	ext{row } j - a_{ij}\,	ext{row } i, with the matching column operation. That is the same move composed with scaling row and column j by a_{ii} 
e 0, which is itself a congruence, so it is legitimate; it keeps the entries integral and changes the diagonal result only by square factors. The worked example below takes this route. Perform only the column half of each operation on the matrix standing to the right. When \A has become diagonal, that matrix is \P, and \P	p\A\P is the diagonal result. The second bullet is @lem-anisotropic-vector-exists made mechanical, and the factor 2 = 1 + 1 in it is where the algorithm would stop in characteristic 2. The right-hand matrix works because applying the column operations \E_1, \E_2, \dots, \E_k in order turns \I into \E_1\E_2\cdots\E_k, which is the product whose transpose and self sandwich \A. [Diagonalizing a symmetric matrix with zero diagonal] Over 
Q, diagonalize \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} by congruence, producing an invertible \P with \P	p\A\P diagonal. The form is q(\cvec{x}) = 2x_1x_2 + 2x_1x_3 + 2x_2x_3: every diagonal entry is 0, so there is no square to complete yet, and the second bullet applies. Step 1 (create a pivot). Add row 2 to row 1, then column 2 to column 1. The matrix becomes  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \ \longrightarrow\  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 2 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ 2 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, the left matrix after the row operation and the right one after the matching column operation. The new corner entry is q(\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2) = 2. Step 2 (clear the first row and column, in two paired moves). Rather than divide by 2, use the operation “row 2 \mapsto 2\cdot	ext{row } 2 - 	ext{row } 1”, which is a scaling followed by an addition, hence a congruence by a product of two elementary matrices, and legitimate because 2 
e 0 in 
Q. Apply it and its column partner. This keeps every entry an integer:  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 2 \ 0 & -1 & 0 \ 2 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \ \longrightarrow\  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 2 \ 0 & -2 & 0 \ 2 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Then “row 3 \mapsto 	ext{row } 3 - 	ext{row } 1” and its column partner:  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 2 \ 0 & -2 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \ \longrightarrow\  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & -2 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}. The transforming matrix. Applying the three column operations to \I_3 in the same order gives \I_3 	o  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} 	o  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} 	o  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & -1 \ 1 & 1 & -1 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \P . Here \det\P = 2 
e 0, so \P is invertible, and \P	p\A\P = \diag(2, -2, -2). The check is one column at a time: with \cvec{p}_1 = (1,1,0), \cvec{p}_2 = (-1,1,0), and \cvec{p}_3 = (-1,-1,1), we get q(\cvec{p}_1) = 2, q(\cvec{p}_2) = -2, and q(\cvec{p}_3) = 2 - 2 - 2 = -2, while  eta(\cvec{p}_1,\cvec{p}_2) = \cvec{p}_1	p\A\cvec{p}_2 = (1,1,0)\cdot(1,-1,0) = 0 and similarly for the other two pairs. Two observations about that example. The determinants are \det\A = 2 and \det(\P	p\A\P) = 8, and they differ by (\det\P)^2 = 4: a congruence multiplies the determinant by a square, which is the discriminant statement of Section 2. And the eigenvalues of \A are 2, -1, -1, whose signs are +, -, - — the same pattern of signs as 2, -2, -2, with none of the same numbers. That coincidence is Section 5. Over the complex numbers, and over a general field The diagonal entries produced by the algorithm are not canonical, but there is a precise statement of how much freedom remains. [Diagonal Entries Are Defined Only up to Squares] Let \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) be an orthogonal basis for  eta with d_i = q(\elem{v}_i), and let t_1, \dots, t_n \in F be nonzero. Then (t_1\elem{v}_1, \dots, t_n\elem{v}_n) is again an orthogonal basis for  eta, with diagonal entries t_i^2d_i. Scaling basis vectors by nonzero scalars again gives a basis. For i 
e j, bilinearity gives  eta(t_i\elem{v}_i, t_j\elem{v}_j) = t_it_j eta(\elem{v}_i,\elem{v}_j) = 0, so the new basis is orthogonal; and q(t_i\elem{v}_i) = t_i^2q(\elem{v}_i) = t_i^2d_i. So each nonzero d_i can be changed to any other element of its coset in the group F^{	imes}/(F^{	imes})^2 of square classes, and no further, by this move. How much that costs depends entirely on the arithmetic of F: - Over 
C, every element is a square, so there is exactly one nonzero square class and every nonzero d_i can be turned into 1. - Over 
R, the squares are the positive numbers, so there are two classes and every nonzero d_i can be turned into 1 or -1, according to its sign — the subject of the next section. - Over 
Q there are infinitely many classes (2, 3, 5, \dots are pairwise inequivalent), so the 1-dimensional forms q(x) = x^2 and q(x) = 2x^2 are already noncongruent. - Over 
F_p with p odd there are exactly two classes, as for 
R, but “which class” is not a matter of sign. The complex case collapses completely. [Classification of Complex Symmetric Matrices by Rank] Let \A \in M_n(
C) be symmetric of rank r. Then \A is congruent to \I_r \oplus \O_{n-r} = \diag(\underbrace{1, \dots, 1}_{r}, 0, \dots, 0). Consequently two symmetric matrices in M_n(
C) are congruent if and only if they have the same rank, and there are exactly n + 1 congruence classes. By @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable (with \operatorname{char}
C = 0) there is an invertible \P_1 with \P_1	p\A\P_1 = \D = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) diagonal. Congruence preserves rank (@thm-congruence-preserves-rank), and the rank of a diagonal matrix is its number of nonzero entries, so exactly r of the d_i are nonzero. Permuting the basis vectors is a congruence by a permutation matrix \P_2, so we may assume d_1, \dots, d_r 
e 0 and d_{r+1} = \dots = d_n = 0. Every nonzero complex number has a square root, so choose s_i \in 
C with s_i^2 = d_i for i \le r, and set t_i = 1/s_i for i \le r and t_i = 1 otherwise. By @prp-diagonal-entries-square-classes the congruence by \P_3 = \diag(t_1, \dots, t_n) replaces d_i by t_i^2d_i, which is 1 for i \le r and 0 otherwise. So \P	p\A\P = \I_r \oplus \O_{n-r} with \P = \P_1\P_2\P_3. For the classification: congruent matrices have equal rank by @thm-congruence-preserves-rank, and matrices of equal rank are both congruent to the same normal form, hence to each other by @prp-congruence-equivalence. The possible ranks are 0, 1, \dots, n, giving n+1 classes. This proves the corollary. Contrast this with similarity, where complex symmetric matrices are not classified by anything so simple: the matrix  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & i \ i & -1\end{psmallmatrix} is symmetric, nonzero, and satisfies \A^2 = \O, so it is not even diagonalizable as an operator. Congruence is a coarser relation than similarity on symmetric matrices, and over 
C it is coarse enough to be finite. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define what it means for an ordered basis to be an orthogonal basis for a bilinear form  eta, and say what that means about \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}. 2. State @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable with all of its hypotheses. 3. Which step of the proof uses \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, and what exactly is divided by? 4. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if \P	p\A\P = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n), then the d_i are the eigenvalues of \A. 5. Describe the pair of operations that a congruence by an elementary matrix performs. (a) \sB = (\elem{v}_1,\dots,\elem{v}_n) is orthogonal for  eta if  eta(\elem{v}_i,\elem{v}_j) = 0 whenever i 
e j. Equivalently \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} is diagonal, with entries q(\elem{v}_i). (b) If \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, V is finite-dimensional over F and  eta is a symmetric bilinear form on V, then V has an orthogonal basis for  eta; equivalently every symmetric \A \in M_n(F) is congruent to a diagonal matrix. (c) @lem-anisotropic-vector-exists, inside Step 2 of the proof. It produces q(\elem{u}+\elem{w}) = (1+1) eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) and needs 1 + 1 
e 0 to conclude that this is nonzero. Equivalently, the algorithm’s repair move multiplies by 2, so it needs 2 
e 0. (d) Incorrect. The relation is congruence, not similarity. In @exm-symmetric-elimination-3x3 the diagonal entries are 2, -2, -2 while the eigenvalues are 2, -1, -1. Only the signs matched there, and Section 5 explains why. (e) A column operation and the matching row operation: \A \mapsto \E	p\A\E. Performing both keeps the matrix symmetric and keeps it in the same congruence class. B. Practice [B1: Symmetric elimination] Over 
Q, let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \ 2 & 1 & 3 \ 0 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Diagonalize \A by paired row and column operations, exhibiting \P and \P	p\A\P. Here a_{11} = 1 
e 0, so the pivot is already available. Clear the first row and column. Subtract 2 	imes row 1 from row 2, then 2 	imes column 1 from column 2. The entry a_{13} is already 0, so nothing else is needed in this round:  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \ 0 & -3 & 3 \ 0 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \ \longrightarrow\  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & -3 & 3 \ 0 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Clear the second row and column. The pivot is -3, and a_{23} = 3, so add row 2 to row 3 and then column 2 to column 3:  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & -3 & 3 \ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \ \longrightarrow\  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & -3 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}. The transforming matrix. Applying the two column operations to \I_3 gives \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & -2 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \P	p\A\P = \diag(1, -3, 4). As a check, \det\P = 1 and \det\A = -12 = \det\diag(1,-3,4). [B2: No pivot on the diagonal] Over 
Q, let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and q(\cvec{x}) = 2x_1x_2. 1. Find a vector \cvec{v} with q(\cvec{v}) 
e 0, as in @lem-anisotropic-vector-exists. 2. Diagonalize \A by paired operations and exhibit \P. 3. Write q as a difference of two squares in the new coordinates. (a) Both \cvec{e}_1 and \cvec{e}_2 give q = 0, so take \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2: q(\cvec{v}) = 2 
e 0. (b) Add row 2 to row 1, then column 2 to column 1, reaching  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}. Then apply “row 2 \mapsto 2\cdot	ext{row } 2 - 	ext{row } 1” and its column partner, reaching \diag(2,-2). Applying the same two column operations to \I_2 gives \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \P	p\A\P = \diag(2,-2). Check directly: \P	p\A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1\end{psmallmatrix} and multiplying by \P gives  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & -2\end{psmallmatrix}. (c) With \cvec{x} = \P\cvec{y}, that is x_1 = y_1 - y_2 and x_2 = y_1 + y_2, we get q = 2(y_1-y_2)(y_1+y_2) = 2y_1^2 - 2y_2^2. This is the familiar identity ab =  igl(	frac{a+b}{2} igr)^2 -  igl(	frac{a-b}{2} igr)^2 read as a change of variable, and it needs 2 to be invertible. [B3: Reading off the rank] Let \A \in M_4(
C) be symmetric with ank\A = 3. Write down the normal form of \A under congruence, and say how many congruence classes of symmetric matrices there are in M_4(
C). By @cor-complex-symmetric-classification, \A is congruent to \I_3 \oplus \O_1 = \diag(1,1,1,0). Since rank is a complete invariant there, the classes correspond to the possible ranks 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, so there are 5 of them. C. Going deeper [C1: Square classes over a finite field] Work over 
F_5, whose nonzero squares are 1 and 4. 1. Prove that the 1 	imes 1 matrices (1) and (2) are not congruent over 
F_5. 2. Prove that \I_2 and 2\I_2 are congruent over 
F_5, by exhibiting a \P. 3. Explain why (a) and (b) are consistent with @prp-diagonal-entries-square-classes. Hint: for (b), look for two vectors \cvec{p}_1, \cvec{p}_2 with \cvec{p}_i \cdot \cvec{p}_i = 2 and \cvec{p}_1 \cdot \cvec{p}_2 = 0. (a) A congruence of 1 	imes 1 matrices is (a) \mapsto (p^2a) with p 
e 0. So (1) and (2) are congruent exactly when 2 = p^2 for some p \in 
F_5^{	imes}. The squares of 1, 2, 3, 4 are 1, 4, 4, 1, so 2 is not a square and the two are not congruent. (b) Take \cvec{p}_1 = (1,1) and \cvec{p}_2 = (1,4). Then \cvec{p}_1 \cdot \cvec{p}_1 = 2, \cvec{p}_2 \cdot \cvec{p}_2 = 1 + 16 = 17 = 2, and \cvec{p}_1 \cdot \cvec{p}_2 = 1 + 4 = 5 = 0 in 
F_5. With \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det\P = 4 - 1 = 3 
e 0, we get \P	p\I_2\P = \P	p\P = \diag(2,2) = 2\I_2. (c) @prp-diagonal-entries-square-classes only says what rescaling a single basis vector can do, and that move cannot change a square class. Part (b) does not contradict it, because the congruence there is not diagonal: it mixes the two coordinates, and both diagonal entries change square class at once. What is invariant is the class of their product, the determinant: \det\I_2 = 1 and \det(2\I_2) = 4 differ by 4 = 2^2, a square. [C2: Is this still true over 
F_2?] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} over 
F_2, and let  eta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} on 
F_2^2. 1. Prove that  eta is alternating. 2. Prove that if \P \in M_2(
F_2) is invertible, then every diagonal entry of \P	p\A\P is 0. 3. Deduce that \A is congruent to no diagonal matrix except the zero matrix, and hence that @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable fails over 
F_2. (a) By @prp-alternating-form-matrix (b): over 
F_2 we have -\A = \A, so \A	p = \A = -\A, and the diagonal entries of \A are 0. (Directly:  eta(\cvec{x},\cvec{x}) = 2x_1x_2 = 0.) (b) The i-th diagonal entry of \P	p\A\P is \cvec{p}_i	p\A\cvec{p}_i = q(\cvec{p}_i), where \cvec{p}_i is the i-th column of \P. By (a), q vanishes identically, so every diagonal entry is 0. (c) A diagonal matrix congruent to \A has all diagonal entries 0 by (b), hence is the zero matrix. But congruence preserves rank (@thm-congruence-preserves-rank) and ank\A = 2 
e 0 = ank\O. So no diagonal matrix is congruent to \A. Since \A is symmetric over 
F_2, the conclusion of @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable fails there, and the hypothesis \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 cannot be dropped. [C3: Diagonalizing the restriction] Let \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on V, and let U \subseteq V be a subspace. 1. Prove that U has an orthogonal basis for the restriction of  eta to U. 2. Give an example, with \dim V = 2, in which  eta is nondegenerate but its restriction to some 1-dimensional U is the zero form. 3. Deduce that an orthogonal basis of U cannot always be extended to an orthogonal basis of V by adding vectors of U alone, and say in one sentence what @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable does guarantee instead. (a) The restriction  eta|_{U 	imes U} is bilinear, since it is the same function on a smaller domain, and symmetric for the same reason. U is finite-dimensional, being a subspace of a finite-dimensional space (@thm-subspace-dimension). So @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable applies to (U,  eta|_{U	imes U}) directly. (b) Over 
Q take  eta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = x_1y_2 + x_2y_1 on 
Q^2, with matrix  egin{psmallmatrix} 0&1\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}, which is invertible, so  eta is nondegenerate. Put U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1). Then  eta(a\cvec{e}_1, b\cvec{e}_1) = 0 for all a, b, so the restriction is the zero form even though  eta is not. (c) In (b) the single vector \cvec{e}_1 is an orthogonal basis of U, but no vector of U can be added to it, and any orthogonal basis of V for this  eta must consist of vectors \cvec{v} with q(\cvec{v}) 
e 0 (its matrix is diagonal and invertible), so \cvec{e}_1 belongs to none of them. What the theorem guarantees is only the existence of some orthogonal basis of V, built from scratch; it promises nothing about extending a given orthogonal list, and Section 8 is where a correct extension statement finally appears.

title: 14.5 Sylvester's Law of Inertia
content:
Sylvester’s Law of Inertia The previous section produced a diagonal matrix and then took it away again: the diagonal entries are not invariants, because rescaling the i-th basis vector by t multiplies the i-th entry by t^2. Over 
R the squares are exactly the positive numbers, so rescaling can change the size of an entry but never its sign. This section proves that the signs are all that survives, and that they survive completely: the number of positive, negative, and zero entries is the same for every diagonalization. That is the classification of real symmetric matrices up to congruence, and it is also the missing link between congruence and the spectral theorem. Throughout this section the field is 
R. Every form is a symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space V, and every matrix is a real symmetric matrix. The words “positive” and “negative” have no meaning over a general field, and almost nothing in this section survives the move to one; @cor-complex-symmetric-classification already showed that over 
C the answer is different, since rank alone classifies there. Normalizing the diagonal Start from @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable, which applies because \operatorname{char}
R = 0. It gives an orthogonal basis (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) for  eta, with q(\elem{v}_i) = d_i. Over 
R we may go one step further and scale. By @prp-diagonal-entries-square-classes, replacing \elem{v}_i by t_i\elem{v}_i replaces d_i by t_i^2d_i. Choosing t_i = 1/\sqrt{\lvert d_ivert} when d_i 
e 0, and t_i = 1 when d_i = 0, turns every diagonal entry into 1, -1, or 0. A permutation of the basis then sorts them, so after a further congruence by a permutation matrix the matrix of  eta is \I_{n_+} \oplus (-\I_{n_-}) \oplus \O_{n_0}, {#eq-real-canonical-form} where n_+ counts the positive d_i, n_- the negative ones and n_0 the zeros, and n_+ + n_- + n_0 = n. Nothing yet says that these three counts do not depend on the orthogonal basis we started from. That is the theorem. One of the three counts is already known to be an invariant, by a result of Section 2. Which one, and why? The count n_0. A diagonal matrix has rank equal to its number of nonzero entries, so n_+ + n_- = ank\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}, and congruence preserves rank (@thm-congruence-preserves-rank). Hence n_+ + n_- is the same for every orthogonal basis, and so is n_0 = n - (n_+ + n_-). What is not yet known is how that total splits into positives and negatives — which is exactly the work left for the theorem below. The law of inertia Sylvester’s Law of Inertia Let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space V with \dim V = n, and let \sB and \sB' be two orthogonal bases for  eta. Let (n_+, n_-, n_0) be the numbers of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries of \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB}, and (n_+', n_-', n_0') the corresponding numbers for \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{\sB'}. Then n_+ = n_+', \qquad n_- = n_-', \qquad n_0 = n_0' . Rank has already delivered n_+ + n_- = n_+' + n_-', so it is enough to prove n_+ = n_+', and for that we may suppose n_+ > n_+' and look for a disaster. The two bases carve out two subspaces with incompatible behavior: on U = \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_{n_+}) the form is strictly positive away from \elem{0}, because @eq-diagonal-quadratic-form has only positive coefficients there; on U' = \Span(\elem{v}_{n_+'+1}', \dots, \elem{v}_n') it is \le 0 everywhere, because there the coefficients are all \le 0. A nonzero vector in both would have q(\elem{v}) > 0 and q(\elem{v}) \le 0 at once, so the two subspaces meet only in \elem{0}. But their dimensions add up to more than n, and two such subspaces of an n-dimensional space cannot meet only in \elem{0}. Contradiction plus a dimension count. Write \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) and \sB' = (\elem{v}_1', \dots, \elem{v}_n'), and order each so that the positive entries come first, then the negative ones, then the zeros; reordering a basis does not change the three counts. Put d_i = q(\elem{v}_i) and d_j' = q(\elem{v}_j'), so that d_1, \dots, d_{n_+} > 0, \qquad d_{n_+'+1}', \dots, d_n' \le 0 . As in the Quick check, n_+ + n_- = ank\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} = ank\mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{\sB'} = n_+' + n_-' by @thm-congruence-preserves-rank, and n_0 = n - (n_+ + n_-). So it suffices to prove n_+ = n_+'; the other two equalities then follow. Suppose not. Swapping the names of the two bases if necessary, we may assume n_+ > n_+'. Put U = \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_{n_+}), \qquad U' = \Span(\elem{v}_{n_+'+1}', \dots, \elem{v}_n') , so that \dim U = n_+ and \dim U' = n - n_+'. Claim: U \cap U' = \{\elem{0}\}. Let \elem{v} \in U \cap U' with \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}. Writing \elem{v} = \sum_{i \le n_+} c_i\elem{v}_i and using @eq-diagonal-quadratic-form for the basis \sB, whose later coordinates of \elem{v} are zero, q(\elem{v}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n_+} d_i c_i^2 > 0 , because every d_i with i \le n_+ is positive, every c_i^2 \ge 0, and at least one c_i 
e 0 since \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}. Writing instead \elem{v} = \sum_{j > n_+'} b_j\elem{v}_j' and using @eq-diagonal-quadratic-form for \sB', q(\elem{v}) = \sum_{j = n_+'+1}^{n} d_j' b_j^2 \le 0 , because every d_j' with j > n_+' is \le 0 and every b_j^2 \ge 0. A real number cannot be both > 0 and \le 0, so no such \elem{v} exists, which proves the claim. On the other hand, U + U' is a subspace of V, so \dim(U + U') \le n, and the dimension formula (@thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim) gives  egin{aligned} \dim(U \cap U') &= \dim U + \dim U' - \dim(U + U') \ &\ge n_+ + (n - n_+') - n \ &= n_+ - n_+' > 0 . \end{aligned} So U \cap U' contains a nonzero vector, contradicting the claim. Therefore n_+ = n_+', and with it n_- = n_-' and n_0 = n_0'. This proves the theorem. The name comes from mechanics, where the form is an inertia tensor and the theorem says that a change of coordinates cannot turn a direction of positive inertia into one of negative inertia. The invariant has a name of its own. [Inertia and Signature] Let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space V of dimension n, diagonalized in some orthogonal basis. The triple (n_+, n_-, n_0) of numbers of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries is the inertia of  eta, and it is well defined by @thm-sylvester-inertia. The pair (n_+, n_-) is the signature of  eta, and n_+ + n_- = ank eta while n_0 = n - ank eta. The same words are used for a real symmetric matrix \A, through the form  eta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}, and we write n_+(\A), n_-(\A), n_0(\A). Two conventions are in circulation and both are called the signature: the pair (n_+, n_-), used here, and the single integer n_+ - n_-. They carry the same information once the rank is known, and the difference is only ever notational; where a source writes “signature 2” it means n_+ - n_- = 2. The triple (n_+, n_-, n_0) is the safest thing to quote, since it also records the degeneracy. The classification over the reals [Classification of Real Symmetric Matrices by Signature] Let \A, \B \in M_n(
R) be symmetric. Then: 1. \A is congruent to \I_{n_+} \oplus (-\I_{n_-}) \oplus \O_{n_0}, where (n_+, n_-, n_0) is the inertia of \A, and to no other matrix of this shape; 2. \A \simeq \B if and only if \A and \B have the same inertia; 3. the number of congruence classes of symmetric matrices in M_n(
R) is 	frac12(n+1)(n+2). (a) The congruence to \I_{n_+} \oplus (-\I_{n_-}) \oplus \O_{n_0} is @eq-real-canonical-form, obtained from @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable followed by the scaling and sorting described above. That matrix is itself diagonal with inertia (n_+, n_-, n_0), so by @thm-sylvester-inertia no matrix of the same shape with a different triple can be congruent to \A. (b) (\Rightarrow) A congruence \B = \P	p\A\P with \P invertible is a change of basis for the form (@thm-change-of-basis-form), so an orthogonal basis diagonalizing \B yields one diagonalizing \A with the same diagonal, and @thm-sylvester-inertia makes the inertia equal. (\Leftarrow) If \A and \B have the same inertia, each is congruent to the same matrix \I_{n_+} \oplus (-\I_{n_-}) \oplus \O_{n_0} by (a), hence to each other, since congruence is an equivalence relation (@prp-congruence-equivalence). (c) By (b) the classes correspond to the triples (n_+, n_-, n_0) of nonnegative integers summing to n, equivalently to the pairs (n_+, n_-) with n_+ + n_- \le n. For each value k = n_+ + n_- \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\} there are k + 1 choices of n_+, so the total is 1 + 2 + \dots + (n+1) = 	frac12(n+1)(n+2). This proves the corollary. So congruence over 
R has a complete and finite list of invariants, in sharp contrast to similarity, where even 2 	imes 2 real symmetric matrices fall into infinitely many classes (one for each unordered pair of eigenvalues). Congruence forgets a great deal; the point of the law of inertia is that what it forgets is precisely everything except the signs. Reconciling congruence with the spectral theorem Chapter 12 diagonalized a real symmetric matrix a different way, by an orthogonal \Q, and got the eigenvalues on the diagonal. Chapter 12 also pointed out why that theorem is special: because \Q	p = \Q^{-1}, the one equation \Q	p\A\Q = \D can be read twice, and “an orthogonal change of variables is a similarity and a congruence, so it keeps the eigenvalues and the geometry at once”. Reading the same equation twice is all that is needed to identify the inertia. [Inertia Is the Sign Pattern of the Spectrum] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be symmetric. Then n_+(\A) is the number of positive eigenvalues of \A, counted with multiplicity, n_-(\A) the number of negative ones, and n_0(\A) the multiplicity of 0. By @cor-spectral-real-matrix there is an orthogonal \Q \in \Orth(n) and a real diagonal \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n) with \A = \Q\D\Q	p, where \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n is the eigenvalue list of \A with multiplicity. Equivalently \D = \Q	p\A\Q. Read as a similarity: \Q	p = \Q^{-1}, so \D = \Q^{-1}\A\Q and the diagonal entries of \D are the eigenvalues of \A. Read as a congruence: \Q is invertible, so \D = \Q	p\A\Q exhibits \D as congruent to \A (@def-congruent). Being diagonal, \D is the matrix of the form of \A in an orthogonal basis, namely the columns of \Q. By @thm-sylvester-inertia its numbers of positive, negative, and zero entries are the inertia of \A. The same list of numbers is being counted both times, so the counts agree. This proves the theorem. This is what Chapter 13 promised when, having diagonalized a pencil and found \S	p\B\S = \diag(-1, 3) while the eigenvalues of \B were 3 \pm 3\sqrt2, it observed that the signs (-, +) “match the signs of the eigenvalues of \B itself” and said that Chapter 14 would show this is no coincidence. It is not: the congruence \S	p\B\S has the inertia of \B by @thm-sylvester-inertia, and that inertia is the sign pattern of the spectrum by @thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues. Here 3 + 3\sqrt2 > 0 and 3 - 3\sqrt2 < 0 — since 3\sqrt2 > 4 — so the inertia of \B is (1, 1, 0), and any congruent diagonal matrix must show exactly one positive and one negative entry, as \diag(-1,3) does. The same reading settles the definiteness tests of Chapter 13 in one line: \A \succ \O means \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} > 0 for all \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}, which by @thm-pd-characterizations is the statement that every eigenvalue is positive, which by @thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues is the statement that the inertia is (n, 0, 0). Section 6 takes that dictionary further. Congruent matrices have the same inertia and unrelated eigenvalues. Take \A = \diag(1, -1) and \P = \diag(2, 3). Then \P	p\A\P = \diag(4, -9), so \A \simeq \diag(4,-9), yet the eigenvalues have moved from 1, -1 to 4, -9. Nothing about their sizes, their ratios, their sum, or their product is preserved — 	r goes from 0 to -5, \det from -1 to -36 — and only the pattern (+, -) survives. For a second witness with no scaling in sight, \I_2 is congruent to \S	p\S =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} with \S =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}; the eigenvalues change from 1, 1 to (3 \pm \sqrt5)/2, and the inertia stays (2,0,0). Computing a signature @thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues gives a method — find the eigenvalues and count signs — but it is the expensive one, since it needs the roots of a degree-n polynomial. The cheap method is the algorithm of the previous section, which needs only arithmetic: diagonalize by paired row and column operations and read off the signs. The eigenvalues are never computed and never needed. [A signature by symmetric elimination] Find the inertia of \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \ 1 & 2 & 3 \ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, and say whether the form q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} is positive definite. The corner entry is 1, so no repair move is needed. Clear the first row and column. Subtract row 1 from row 2 and 2	imes row 1 from row 3, then do the same two operations on columns:  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & -3 \end{pmatrix} \ \longrightarrow\  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & -3 \end{pmatrix}. Clear the second row and column. The pivot is 1 and a_{23} = 1, so subtract row 2 from row 3 and then column 2 from column 3:  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & -4 \end{pmatrix} \ \longrightarrow\ \diag(1, 1, -4). So the inertia is (2, 1, 0) and the signature is (2,1). The form is not positive definite: it is negative at the third basis vector of the new basis, namely the third column of \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & -1 \ 0 & 1 & -1 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, which is \cvec{p}_3 = (-1,-1,1). Checking directly, \A\cvec{p}_3 = (0, 0, -4) and \cvec{p}_3 \cdot (0,0,-4) = -4 < 0. The eigenvalue route would have to factor \det(x\I - \A) = x^3 - 4x^2 - 9x + 4, whose roots are irrational; the elimination never met them. As a partial check on the arithmetic, \det\A = -4 and \det\diag(1,1,-4) = -4, consistent with \det\P = 1. Over 
R, then, a symmetric matrix carries exactly two pieces of congruence data, and both are cheap: its rank and how that rank splits into positive and negative directions. The next section reads the same two numbers as a statement about definiteness, and uses them to decide maxima and minima. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the inertia and the signature of a real symmetric matrix. 2. State @thm-sylvester-inertia, with all hypotheses. 3. Which part of the inertia is already an invariant before the law of inertia is proved, and by which earlier result? 4. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: congruent real symmetric matrices have the same trace. 5. Explain in one sentence why an orthogonal change of basis lets the spectral theorem compute an inertia. (a) Diagonalize the associated form in an orthogonal basis. The inertia is the triple (n_+, n_-, n_0) of numbers of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries, and the signature is the pair (n_+, n_-). (b) If  eta is a symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space and \sB, \sB' are two orthogonal bases for  eta, then the two matrices \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} and \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{\sB'} have the same numbers of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries. (c) The count n_0, equivalently the sum n_+ + n_-, because that sum is the rank and congruence preserves rank (@thm-congruence-preserves-rank). (d) Incorrect. \diag(1,-1) and \diag(4,-9) are congruent, by the congruence with \P = \diag(2,3), and their traces are 0 and -5. Trace is a similarity invariant (@thm-trace-similarity-invariant), not a congruence invariant. (e) For an orthogonal \Q we have \Q	p = \Q^{-1}, so the single equation \Q	p\A\Q = \D is simultaneously a similarity, which puts the eigenvalues on the diagonal, and a congruence, which makes that diagonal compute the inertia. B. Practice [B1: Signatures by elimination] Find the inertia of each of the following real symmetric matrices by paired row and column operations. Do not compute any eigenvalues. 1. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \ 2 & 1 & 3 \ 0 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. 2. \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. 3. \C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}. (a) By @exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-b1, \A is congruent to \diag(1,-3,4). Inertia (2,1,0). (b) By @exm-symmetric-elimination-3x3, \B is congruent to \diag(2,-2,-2). Inertia (1,2,0). (c) Subtract 2	imes row 1 from row 2, then 2	imes column 1 from column 2:  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \ \longrightarrow\  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Inertia (1,0,1): the form q(\cvec{x}) = (x_1 + 2x_2)^2 is degenerate, vanishing on the line x_1 = -2x_2. [B2: Which of these are congruent?] Sort the following real symmetric matrices into congruence classes, justifying each answer. \A_1 = \diag(1, 1, -1), \quad \A_2 = \diag(5, 2, -7), \quad \A_3 = \diag(1, -1, -1), \A_4 =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A_5 =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & -3 \end{pmatrix}. Compute each inertia and apply @cor-real-symmetric-classification (b). \A_1: (2,1,0). \A_2: (2,1,0). \A_3: (1,2,0). \A_5: (1,1,1). For \A_4, the top-left 2	imes2 block is the form 2x_1x_2, which @exr-diagonalizing-symmetric-forms-b2 diagonalizes to \diag(2,-2); so \A_4 is congruent to \diag(2,-2,1), with inertia (2,1,0). Therefore the classes are \{\A_1, \A_2, \A_4\}, \{\A_3\}, and \{\A_5\}. Note that \A_1 and \A_3 have the same rank and are still not congruent, so rank alone does not classify over 
R — unlike over 
C (@cor-complex-symmetric-classification). [B3: Inertia from a characteristic polynomial] Let \A \in M_3(
R) be symmetric with \det(x\I - \A) = x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6. 1. Find the inertia of \A. 2. Is \A congruent to \diag(1, 1, -1)? Is it similar to it? (a) The polynomial factors as (x-1)(x+2)(x-3), since 1 is a root and dividing gives x^2 - x - 6. The eigenvalues are 1, 3, -2, so by @thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues the inertia is (2, 1, 0). (b) Congruent: yes, since \diag(1,1,-1) also has inertia (2,1,0) and @cor-real-symmetric-classification (b) applies. Similar: no, because similar matrices have equal characteristic polynomials, and \diag(1,1,-1) has (x-1)^2(x+1) 
e (x-1)(x-3)(x+2). C. Going deeper [C1: An intrinsic description of n_+] Let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space V of dimension n, with quadratic form q. Call a subspace U \subseteq V positive if q(\elem{v}) > 0 for every \elem{v} \in U with \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}. 1. Prove that n_+ is the largest dimension of a positive subspace of V. 2. Deduce @thm-sylvester-inertia again from (a), in two lines. 3. State and prove the corresponding description of n_-. Hint: for (a), use an orthogonal basis to produce one positive subspace of dimension n_+, and the dimension formula to rule out a larger one. (a) Fix an orthogonal basis (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) ordered so that d_1, \dots, d_{n_+} > 0 and d_j \le 0 for j > n_+. A positive subspace of dimension n_+. Put U = \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_{n_+}). For \elem{v} = \sum_{i \le n_+} c_i\elem{v}_i nonzero, @eq-diagonal-quadratic-form gives q(\elem{v}) = \sum_{i \le n_+} d_ic_i^2 > 0, since all d_i > 0 and some c_i 
e 0. So U is positive and \dim U = n_+. No larger one. Let X be positive with \dim X = k, and put W = \Span(\elem{v}_{n_++1}, \dots, \elem{v}_n), of dimension n - n_+. Every \elem{w} \in W has q(\elem{w}) = \sum_{j > n_+} d_jc_j^2 \le 0. If k > n_+ then by @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim, \dim(X \cap W) \ge k + (n - n_+) - n = k - n_+ > 0, so there is a nonzero \elem{v} \in X \cap W with q(\elem{v}) > 0 and q(\elem{v}) \le 0, which is impossible. Hence k \le n_+, and the maximum is n_+. (b) The right-hand side of (a) — the largest dimension of a positive subspace — is defined from  eta alone and mentions no basis. So the number n_+ computed from any orthogonal basis equals that basis-free quantity, hence is the same for all of them. Then n_+ + n_- = ank eta is basis-free too (@thm-congruence-preserves-rank), so n_- and n_0 are determined as well. (c) n_- is the largest dimension of a negative subspace, one on which q(\elem{v}) < 0 for every \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}. Apply (a) to the form - eta, whose diagonal entries in any orthogonal basis are the negatives of those of  eta, so that n_+(- eta) = n_-( eta), and whose positive subspaces are exactly the negative subspaces of  eta. [C2: Congruence cannot be read off the eigenvalues, and inertia can] 1. Give two real symmetric 2	imes2 matrices that are congruent but have no eigenvalue in common. 2. Prove that if \A and \B are real symmetric and similar, then they are congruent. 3. Give two real symmetric 2	imes2 matrices that are congruent but not similar, so that the converse of (b) fails. (a) \diag(1,-1) and \diag(4,-9), congruent by \P = \diag(2,3). Their spectra are \{1,-1\} and \{4,-9\}, which are disjoint. (b) Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant), hence the same eigenvalues with multiplicity. By @thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues they then have the same inertia, and by @cor-real-symmetric-classification (b) they are congruent. (Alternatively and more directly: by @cor-spectral-real-matrix each is orthogonally congruent to the diagonal matrix of its eigenvalues, and those diagonal matrices agree up to a permutation.) (c) The pair in (a) again: \diag(1,-1) and \diag(4,-9) are congruent, but their characteristic polynomials are x^2 - 1 and x^2 + 5x - 36, so they are not similar (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant). Congruence is strictly coarser than similarity on real symmetric matrices. [C3: Inertia of a block matrix] Let \A \in M_m(
R) and \B \in M_k(
R) be symmetric. Let also \D \in M_n(
R) be symmetric and invertible, let \cvec{b} \in 
R^n, let c \in 
R, and put \M =  egin{pmatrix} \D & \cvec{b} \ \cvec{b}	p & c \end{pmatrix} \in M_{n+1}(
R). 1. Prove that the inertia of \A \oplus \B is the entrywise sum of the inertias of \A and \B. 2. Prove that \M is congruent to \D \oplus (c - \cvec{b}	p\D^{-1}\cvec{b}). 3. Hence find the inertia of \M when \D = \diag(1,-1), \cvec{b} = (1,1), and c = 0. Hint: for (b), the congruence is the block elimination of Chapter 8, and the leftover scalar is a Schur complement. (a) Let \P	p\A\P and \Q	p\B\Q be the canonical forms of @cor-real-symmetric-classification (a). Then \P \oplus \Q is invertible and (\P\oplus\Q)	p(\A\oplus\B)(\P\oplus\Q) = (\P	p\A\P)\oplus(\Q	p\B\Q), a diagonal matrix whose positive, negative, and zero entries are those of the two blocks together. By @thm-sylvester-inertia those counts are the inertia of \A\oplus\B. (b) Put \S =  egin{pmatrix} \I_n & -\D^{-1}\cvec{b} \ \cvec{0}	p & 1 \end{pmatrix}, which is invertible, being unit upper triangular. Multiplying, the first block row of \M\S is (\D \mid \D(-\D^{-1}\cvec{b}) + \cvec{b}) = (\D \mid \cvec{0}), and then \S	p\M\S =  egin{pmatrix} \D & \cvec{0} \ \cvec{0}	p & c - \cvec{b}	p\D^{-1}\cvec{b} \end{pmatrix}, using \D	p = \D. This is \D \oplus (c - \cvec{b}	p\D^{-1}\cvec{b}), the Schur complement \M/\D sitting in the corner. (c) Here \D^{-1} = \diag(1,-1), so \cvec{b}	p\D^{-1}\cvec{b} = 1 - 1 = 0 and the leftover scalar is c - 0 = 0. By (b) and (a), the inertia of \M is the inertia of \diag(1,-1) plus that of the 1	imes1 zero matrix, namely (1,1,0) + (0,0,1) = (1,1,1). In particular \M is singular.

title: 14.6 Definiteness and Second Derivatives
content:
Definiteness and Second Derivatives Chapter 13 studied positive definite matrices at length, and the previous section showed that the signature is what congruence remembers. Putting the two together costs almost nothing and buys two things: a vocabulary that covers the forms Chapter 13 had no name for, the indefinite and the semidefinite ones, and the classical application that made quadratic forms worth studying in the first place. Nothing from Chapter 13 is reproved here. The field is 
R throughout, since none of the five words below means anything without an order. Throughout, V is a finite-dimensional real vector space,  eta is a symmetric bilinear form on V (@def-symmetric-form), q(\elem{v}) =  eta(\elem{v},\elem{v}) is its quadratic form (@def-quadratic-form), and \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} is its matrix in a basis \sB (@def-form-matrix), a real symmetric matrix. Five words for the sign of a form Chapter 13 named two of the possible behaviors of q: never negative, and always positive away from \cvec{0}. There are three more, and the missing ones are not exotic. The form q(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 - x_2^2 is positive at \cvec{e}_1, negative at \cvec{e}_2, and nothing in Chapter 13’s vocabulary describes it. A form is definite when q has one strict sign, semidefinite when it has one sign but is allowed to vanish, and indefinite when it has both signs. [Definiteness of a Real Symmetric Form] Let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space V, with quadratic form q. Then  eta is: 1. positive definite if q(\elem{v}) > 0 for every nonzero \elem{v} \in V; 2. positive semidefinite if q(\elem{v}) \ge 0 for every \elem{v} \in V; 3. negative definite if q(\elem{v}) < 0 for every nonzero \elem{v} \in V; 4. negative semidefinite if q(\elem{v}) \le 0 for every \elem{v} \in V; 5. indefinite if there exist \elem{u}, \elem{w} \in V with q(\elem{u}) > 0 and q(\elem{w}) < 0. The same five words apply to a real symmetric matrix \A, through the form  eta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} on 
R^n. The small words carry the weight. In (a) and (c) the inequality is strict and the vector must be nonzero; in (b) and (d) it is weak and \elem{v} = \elem{0} is allowed, where q(\elem{0}) = 0 makes the condition automatic. Definite implies semidefinite of the same sign. Clause (e) is not the negation of (b): q(x_1,x_2) = -x_1^2 is neither positive semidefinite nor indefinite. For matrices, (a) and (b) are @def-positive-semidefinite restricted to F = 
R, so \A \succ \O and \A \succeq \O keep their meanings, and the negative versions are the positive ones for -\A. Four examples on 
R^2, all diagonal so that q can be read off @eq-diagonal-quadratic-form: x_1^2 + x_2^2 is positive definite; x_1^2 is positive semidefinite but not definite, since it vanishes at \cvec{e}_2 
e \cvec{0}; -x_1^2 - x_2^2 is negative definite; x_1^2 - x_2^2 is indefinite. The zero form is the degenerate case, satisfying (b) and (d) and nothing else — which is why the five classes overlap rather than partition. Changing one sign in the third gives the nonexample -x_1^2 + x_2^2: it is no longer negative semidefinite, and the clause that fails is (d) at \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_2, where q = 1 > 0. Now the reading through the signature, which makes all five conditions into statements about three integers. [Definiteness Is the Signature] Let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space V of dimension n, with inertia (n_+, n_-, n_0) (@def-signature). Then: 1.  eta is positive definite \iff (n_+, n_-, n_0) = (n, 0, 0); 2.  eta is positive semidefinite \iff n_- = 0; 3.  eta is negative definite \iff (n_+, n_-, n_0) = (0, n, 0); 4.  eta is negative semidefinite \iff n_+ = 0; 5.  eta is indefinite \iff n_+ > 0 and n_- > 0. Fix an orthogonal basis. Then q is \sum_i d_i c_i^2 with no cross terms, and each of the five conditions becomes a visible condition on the signs of the d_i: plugging in a basis vector reads off one d_i, and a general \elem{v} mixes the d_i with nonnegative weights. Sylvester’s law is what lets us fix one basis and still be talking about  eta. By @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable there is an orthogonal basis \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) for  eta; put d_i = q(\elem{v}_i). By @thm-sylvester-inertia the numbers of positive, negative, and zero d_i are n_+, n_-, and n_0, whichever orthogonal basis is used. For \elem{v} = \sum_i c_i\elem{v}_i, @eq-diagonal-quadratic-form gives q(\elem{v}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i c_i^2 . (b) (\Rightarrow) If some d_j < 0 then q(\elem{v}_j) = d_j < 0, so  eta is not positive semidefinite. (\Leftarrow) If no d_i is negative then every term d_ic_i^2 is \ge 0, so q(\elem{v}) \ge 0. (c) (\Rightarrow) A positive definite  eta is positive semidefinite, so n_- = 0 by (b); and if some d_j = 0 then q(\elem{v}_j) = 0 with \elem{v}_j 
e \elem{0}, a contradiction. Hence n_0 = 0 and n_+ = n. (\Leftarrow) If every d_i > 0 and \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}, some c_j 
e 0, so q(\elem{v}) \ge d_jc_j^2 > 0, the other terms being \ge 0. (d) and (d) follow by applying (a) and (b) to - eta, whose diagonal entries are -d_i and whose inertia is therefore (n_-, n_+, n_0). (e) (\Rightarrow) Suppose q(\elem{u}) > 0 and q(\elem{w}) < 0. Then  eta is neither positive semidefinite nor negative semidefinite, so n_- > 0 by (b) and n_+ > 0 by (d). (\Leftarrow) If n_+ > 0 and n_- > 0, some d_i > 0 and some d_j < 0, and the basis vectors \elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j are the required \elem{u}, \elem{w}. This proves the theorem. So the five words sort the 	frac12(n+1)(n+2) congruence classes of @cor-real-symmetric-classification into named families, and every one of them is decided by counting signs. Two of these five verdicts were already settled in Chapter 13 by other means, and it is worth putting the tests side by side. [Chapter 13’s Tests, in the Language of Forms] Let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on an n-dimensional real vector space, \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} its matrix in any basis, and \A_k the top-left k 	imes k corner of \A. Then: 1.  eta is positive definite \iff every eigenvalue of \A is positive \iff \det \A_k > 0 for k = 1, \dots, n; 2.  eta is negative definite \iff every eigenvalue of \A is negative \iff (-1)^k\det \A_k > 0 for k = 1, \dots, n. (a) By @def-form-matrix and @thm-form-matrix-determines, q(\elem{v}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} where \cvec{x} = \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB}, and \elem{v} 
e \elem{0} exactly when \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}. So  eta is positive definite exactly when \A \succ \O, and the two stated tests are @thm-pd-characterizations (b) and (d), the second being Sylvester’s criterion. (b) Apply (a) to - eta, whose matrix is -\A. The eigenvalues of -\A are the negatives of those of \A, and (-\A)_k = -\A_k has \det(-\A_k) = (-1)^k\det\A_k, since scaling each of the k rows by -1 multiplies the determinant by -1 once per row (@thm-det-row-operations (b)). This proves the proposition. The eigenvalue test is the one to think with, the minor test the one to compute with; cheapest of all is the symmetric elimination of Section 4, which returns the whole signature rather than a verdict. Nothing is said about the semidefinite cases on purpose: Sylvester’s criterion has no weak version, as Chapter 13 showed with \diag(0,-1), whose leading minors are both 0. A real symmetric \A \in M_3(
R) has \det \A_1 = -2, \det \A_2 = 5, \det \A_3 = -1. What is its definiteness? Negative definite. The signs alternate from a negative one, so (-1)^k\det\A_k > 0 for k = 1, 2, 3: indeed (-1)(-2) = 2 > 0, (+1)(5) = 5 > 0, (-1)(-1) = 1 > 0. By @prp-definiteness-tests-for-forms (b) the form is negative definite, and by @thm-definiteness-by-signature (c) its inertia is (0, 3, 0). Note that \det \A_3 = \det\A < 0 on its own would have been no evidence at all. The second-derivative test Here is the use. A differentiable function f \colon 
R^n 	o 
R is constant to first order at a critical point, so whether the point is a minimum, a maximum, or neither is decided — usually — by the second-order behavior. That behavior is a quadratic form, and @thm-definiteness-by-signature decides it. The linear algebra is the whole content; what has to be imported is one theorem of analysis, and we state it rather than hide it. [Hessian] Let f be a real-valued function on an open set U \subseteq 
R^n, twice continuously differentiable on U, and let \cvec{a} \in U. The Hessian of f at \cvec{a} is the matrix \H_f(\cvec{a}) \in M_n(
R), \qquad  igl(\H_f(\cvec{a}) igr)_{ij} =  rac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i\,\partial x_j}(\cvec{a}) . A point \cvec{a} \in U with 
abla f(\cvec{a}) = \cvec{0} is a critical point of f. Two facts about \H_f(\cvec{a}) are needed, and neither is linear algebra. They are exactly the analysis this book imports, so we set them out as assumptions rather than let them pass unnoticed. Let f be twice continuously differentiable on an open U \subseteq 
R^n and let \cvec{a} \in U. 1. (Symmetry of the second derivatives.) The mixed partial derivatives satisfy \partial^2f/\partial x_i\partial x_j = \partial^2f/\partial x_j\partial x_i on U, so \H_f(\cvec{a}) is a symmetric matrix. 2. (Taylor’s theorem with a second-order remainder.) For every \cvec{h} small enough that \cvec{a} + \cvec{h} \in U, f(\cvec{a} + \cvec{h}) = f(\cvec{a}) + 
abla f(\cvec{a})\cdot\cvec{h} + 	frac12\,\cvec{h}	p\H_f(\cvec{a})\cvec{h} + r(\cvec{h}), where the remainder satisfies r(\cvec{h})/
orm{\cvec{h}}^2 	o 0 as \cvec{h} 	o \cvec{0}. These are two standard theorems of multivariable calculus. This book proves neither. They are quoted so that the theorem below has hypotheses to stand on, and Chapter 18 quotes them again for its second-derivative test of convexity, exactly as the theorem of Abel and Ruffini was quoted in Chapter 11. Everything after them is linear algebra. By (A1) the Hessian is a real symmetric matrix, so it has an inertia, and by @thm-definiteness-by-signature that inertia decides the definiteness of the quadratic form \cvec{h} \mapsto \cvec{h}	p\H_f(\cvec{a})\cvec{h}. One small lemma converts definiteness into a quantitative bound, and it is the only place where a real number is needed rather than a sign. [A Positive Definite Form Is Bounded Below by a Multiple of the Norm Squared] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be symmetric and positive definite, and let \lambda be its smallest eigenvalue. Then \lambda > 0 and \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} \ \ge\ \lambda
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 \qquad 	ext{for every } \cvec{x} \in 
R^n . By @cor-spectral-real-matrix there are an orthogonal \Q \in \Orth(n) and a diagonal \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n) listing the eigenvalues of \A with \A = \Q\D\Q	p. By @thm-pd-characterizations (b) every \lambda_i > 0, so \lambda = \min_i \lambda_i > 0. Put \cvec{y} = \Q	p\cvec{x}. Then \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{y}	p\D\cvec{y} = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i y_i^2 \ \ge\ \lambda\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2 = \lambda
orm{\cvec{y}}^2 , using \lambda_i \ge \lambda and y_i^2 \ge 0 termwise. Finally \Q\Q	p = \I, so 
orm{\cvec{y}}^2 = \cvec{x}	p\Q\Q	p\cvec{x} = 
orm{\cvec{x}}^2. This proves the lemma. The Second-Derivative Test Let f be a real-valued function, twice continuously differentiable on an open set U \subseteq 
R^n, let \cvec{a} \in U be a critical point of f, and let (n_+, n_-, n_0) be the inertia of \H_f(\cvec{a}). Then: 1. if \H_f(\cvec{a}) is positive definite, that is (n_+, n_-, n_0) = (n, 0, 0), then \cvec{a} is a strict local minimum of f; 2. if \H_f(\cvec{a}) is negative definite, that is (n_+, n_-, n_0) = (0, n, 0), then \cvec{a} is a strict local maximum of f; 3. if \H_f(\cvec{a}) is indefinite, that is n_+ > 0 and n_- > 0, then \cvec{a} is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum: every neighborhood of \cvec{a} contains points where f > f(\cvec{a}) and points where f < f(\cvec{a}). Such an \cvec{a} is a saddle point. If n_0 > 0 and \cvec{a} is not covered by (a)–(c), the test gives no information. Taylor says f(\cvec{a}+\cvec{h}) - f(\cvec{a}) is 	frac12 q(\cvec{h}) plus a remainder that is smaller than 
orm{\cvec{h}}^2 near \cvec{0}, where q(\cvec{h}) = \cvec{h}	p\H_f(\cvec{a})\cvec{h}. For (a) the quadratic term is at least 	frac12\lambda
orm{\cvec{h}}^2 by @lem-definite-form-bounded-below, which beats a remainder eventually smaller than 	frac14\lambda
orm{\cvec{h}}^2; so the difference is positive. For (c) there is no bound in every direction, and none is needed: walk along a single line \cvec{h} = t\cvec{u} where q(\cvec{u}) > 0, and the whole thing is t^2 times something tending to 	frac12q(\cvec{u}) > 0. One direction up, one direction down, and no extremum. Write \H = \H_f(\cvec{a}) and q(\cvec{h}) = \cvec{h}	p\H\cvec{h}. Since \cvec{a} is critical, 
abla f(\cvec{a}) = \cvec{0}, so (A2) reads f(\cvec{a}+\cvec{h}) - f(\cvec{a}) = 	frac12 q(\cvec{h}) + r(\cvec{h}), \qquad  rac{r(\cvec{h})}{
orm{\cvec{h}}^2} 	o 0 . 	ag{$\ast$} (a) Let \lambda > 0 be the smallest eigenvalue of \H, so that q(\cvec{h}) \ge \lambda

(b) The Hessian of -f at \cvec{a} is -\H, whose inertia is (n, 0, 0) because that of \H is (0, n, 0); so -\H is positive definite by @thm-definiteness-by-signature (a). Part (a) applied to -f makes \cvec{a} a strict local minimum of -f, that is a strict local maximum of f. (c) By @thm-definiteness-by-signature (e) there are \cvec{u}, \cvec{w} \in
