e 0. Every neighborhood of \cvec{a} contains points of both kinds, so \cvec{a} is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum. This proves the theorem. Cases (a)–(c) exhaust the nondegenerate ones: if n_0 = 0 then n_+ + n_- = n, so either n_+ = n, or n_- = n, or both are positive. What is left undecided is exactly n_0 > 0, and there the test is silent because it has to be. [Two critical points of a cubic surface] Find the critical points of f(x,y) = x^3 - 3xy + y^3 on 
R^2 and classify each one. The partial derivatives are f_x = 3x^2 - 3y and f_y = -3x + 3y^2. Setting both to zero gives y = x^2 and x = y^2, hence x = x^4, so x(x^3 - 1) = 0 and x \in \{0, 1\}. The real critical points are (0,0) and (1,1). Differentiating again, \H_f(x,y) =  egin{pmatrix} 6x & -3 \ -3 & 6y\end{pmatrix} . At (0,0) the Hessian is  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & -3 \ -3 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, with \det = -9 < 0. A 2 	imes 2 symmetric matrix with negative determinant has eigenvalue product -9, hence one eigenvalue of each sign, so its inertia is (1,1,0) by @thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues and the form is indefinite. By @thm-second-derivative-test (c), (0,0) is a saddle point. Concretely f(t,t) = 2t^3 - 3t^2 < 0 and f(t,-t) = 3t^2 > 0 for small t > 0. At (1,1) the Hessian is  egin{psmallmatrix} 6 & -3 \ -3 & 6\end{psmallmatrix}, whose leading principal minors are 6 > 0 and 36 - 9 = 27 > 0. By @prp-definiteness-tests-for-forms (a) it is positive definite, so (1,1) is a strict local minimum, with value f(1,1) = -1. [One Hessian, three answers] The three functions g_1 = x^2 + y^4, \qquad g_2 = x^2 - y^4, \qquad g_3 = x^2 all have 
abla g_i(0,0) = \cvec{0} and the same Hessian at the origin. What is that Hessian, and what happens at the origin in each case? Every second derivative of y^4 vanishes at y = 0, so all three have \H_{g_i}(0,0) =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}, with inertia (1, 0, 1): positive semidefinite, not definite, not indefinite. The test is silent, and it must be, because the three answers differ. For g_1 the origin is a strict local minimum, since x^2 + y^4 > 0 away from \cvec{0}. For g_2 it is a saddle: g_2(t,0) = t^2 > 0 and g_2(0,t) = -t^4 < 0 for t 
e 0. For g_3 it is a minimum but not a strict one, since g_3 vanishes along the whole y-axis. The quadratic term decided nothing here; the quartic term decided everything. The test reads the signature, not the determinant. In two variables the familiar rule is “\det \H > 0 and f_{xx} > 0 means a minimum”, and the second half is not decoration: \diag(-1,-1) has \det = 1 > 0, and -x^2-y^2 has a strict local maximum at the origin. All \det\H > 0 says in two variables is that n_0 = 0 and n_- is even — definite, of a sign the determinant cannot see. In three variables it says even less: \diag(1,-1,-1) has \det = 1 > 0 and is indefinite. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define what it means for a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space to be indefinite. 2. State the signature condition equivalent to negative semidefiniteness, and the one equivalent to positive definiteness. 3. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: a symmetric form that is not positive semidefinite is indefinite. 4. Name the two results of analysis that @thm-second-derivative-test assumes, and say which part of its proof uses each. 5. A critical point has n_0 = 2 and n_- = 0. What does @thm-second-derivative-test conclude? (a)  eta is indefinite if there exist \elem{u} and \elem{w} in V with q(\elem{u}) > 0 and q(\elem{w}) < 0, where q(\elem{v}) =  eta(\elem{v},\elem{v}). (b) Negative semidefinite \iff n_+ = 0; positive definite \iff (n_+, n_-, n_0) = (n, 0, 0), equivalently n_+ = n. Both are @thm-definiteness-by-signature. (c) Incorrect. The form q(x_1,x_2) = -x_1^2 has inertia (0,1,1); it is not positive semidefinite, since q(\cvec{e}_1) = -1, and not indefinite, since q is never positive. Failing (b) of @def-definiteness-of-a-form means only n_- > 0; being indefinite needs n_+ > 0 as well. (d) Symmetry of the mixed second partial derivatives, which makes the Hessian symmetric so that it has an inertia at all; and Taylor’s theorem with a second-order remainder, which is the identity (\ast) that every part of the proof manipulates. (e) Nothing. Here n_+ = n - 2 and n_- = 0, so the Hessian is positive semidefinite but not definite and not indefinite, and none of (a), (b), (c) applies. @exm-degenerate-hessian shows that all of “strict minimum”, “nonstrict minimum”, and “saddle” really do occur in this situation. B. Practice [B1: Classify by the signature] Determine the definiteness of each of the following real symmetric matrices, and give the inertia of each. Justify your answers. \A_1 =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix},\quad \A_2 =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 \ 2 & -5\end{pmatrix},\quad \A_3 =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}. For \A_1: \det(\A_1)_1 = 2 > 0 and \det \A_1 = 4 - 1 = 3 > 0, so \A_1 is positive definite by @prp-definiteness-tests-for-forms (a), with inertia (2,0,0). For \A_2: (-1)^1\det(\A_2)_1 = 1 > 0 and (-1)^2\det\A_2 = 5 - 4 = 1 > 0, so \A_2 is negative definite by @prp-definiteness-tests-for-forms (b), with inertia (0,2,0). For \A_3: \det\A_3 = 1 - 4 = -3 < 0, so the two eigenvalues have product -3 and hence opposite signs. The inertia is (1,1,0) by @thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues, and \A_3 is indefinite by @thm-definiteness-by-signature (e). Explicitly q(1,1) = 6 > 0 and q(1,-1) = -2 < 0. [B2: Critical points of a quartic] Find all critical points of f(x,y) = x^4 + y^4 - 4xy and classify each with @thm-second-derivative-test. f_x = 4x^3 - 4y and f_y = 4y^3 - 4x, so y = x^3 and x = y^3 = x^9. Then x(x^8 - 1) = 0, so x \in \{0, 1, -1\} and the critical points are (0,0), (1,1), (-1,-1). The Hessian is \H_f(x,y) =  egin{pmatrix} 12x^2 & -4 \ -4 & 12y^2\end{pmatrix}. At (0,0) it is  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & -4 \ -4 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, with determinant -16 < 0, hence inertia (1,1,0) and a saddle point. At (\pm1,\pm1) it is  egin{psmallmatrix} 12 & -4 \ -4 & 12\end{psmallmatrix}, with leading minors 12 > 0 and 144 - 16 = 128 > 0, hence positive definite: both are strict local minima, each of value f = 1 + 1 - 4 = -2. C. Going deeper [C1: The signature measures positive subspaces] Let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space V of dimension n, with inertia (n_+, n_-, n_0). Call a subspace U \subseteq V positive if q(\elem{v}) > 0 for every nonzero \elem{v} \in U. 1. Prove that V has a positive subspace of dimension n_+. 2. Prove that every positive subspace has dimension at most n_+. Hint: consider a subspace on which q \le 0 of the largest available dimension. 3. Hence deduce that n_+ equals the largest dimension of a positive subspace, and that this gives a second proof that n_+ does not depend on the orthogonal basis. Fix an orthogonal basis \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) for  eta, ordered so that d_i = q(\elem{v}_i) > 0 for i \le n_+, then negative, then zero. (a) Put U = \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_{n_+}). For a nonzero \elem{v} = \sum_{i \le n_+} c_i\elem{v}_i, @eq-diagonal-quadratic-form gives q(\elem{v}) = \sum_{i\le n_+} d_ic_i^2 > 0, since every d_i > 0 and some c_i 
e 0. So U is positive of dimension n_+. (b) Put U' = \Span(\elem{v}_{n_++1}, \dots, \elem{v}_n), of dimension n - n_+. For \elem{v} \in U', @eq-diagonal-quadratic-form gives q(\elem{v}) = \sum_{i > n_+} d_ic_i^2 \le 0, every d_i there being \le 0. Let W be any positive subspace. Then W \cap U' = \{\elem{0}\}, since a nonzero vector in the intersection would have q > 0 and q \le 0. By the dimension formula (@thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim), \dim W + (n - n_+) = \dim(W + U') \le n , so \dim W \le n_+. (c) By (a) and (b) the largest dimension of a positive subspace is exactly n_+. That description mentions only  eta and V, no basis, so n_+ is an invariant of  eta. Together with the invariance of ank eta = n_+ + n_- under congruence (@thm-congruence-preserves-rank) this recovers @thm-sylvester-inertia. [C2: A saddle the determinant hides] Let f(x,y,z) = x^2 - y^2 - z^2 + xyz. 1. Verify that the origin is a critical point and compute \H_f(\cvec{0}) and its determinant. 2. Classify the origin, and explain why the sign of \det \H_f(\cvec{0}) alone would have been useless. 3. Prove that no twice continuously differentiable g \colon 
R^3 	o 
R has a strict local maximum at a critical point \cvec{0} with \det\H_g(\cvec{0}) > 0, and give a g \colon 
R^2 	o 
R that does. Which feature of the dimension is responsible? (a) f_x = 2x + yz, f_y = -2y + xz, f_z = -2z + xy, all zero at \cvec{0}. The second derivatives at \cvec{0} are f_{xx} = 2, f_{yy} = f_{zz} = -2, and f_{xy} = z, f_{xz} = y, f_{yz} = x, all zero at \cvec{0}. So \H_f(\cvec{0}) = \diag(2,-2,-2), with \det = 8 > 0. (b) The inertia is (1,2,0), so the Hessian is indefinite and \cvec{0} is a saddle point by @thm-second-derivative-test (c). The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues (@cor-det-product-eigenvalues-again) and therefore records only the parity of n_-; here \det > 0 says n_- is even, which is equally true of the negative definite \diag(-2,-2,-2) and of the positive definite \I_3. It cannot distinguish them. (c) Suppose \cvec{0} is a local maximum of g and write q(\cvec{h}) = \cvec{h}	p\H_g(\cvec{0})\cvec{h}. If q(\cvec{u}) > 0 for some \cvec{u}, the computation in the proof of @thm-second-derivative-test (c) gives g(t\cvec{u}) > g(\cvec{0}) for all small t 
e 0, contradicting the maximum. So q(\cvec{u}) \le 0 for every \cvec{u}, that is \H_g(\cvec{0}) is negative semidefinite and n_+ = 0 by @thm-definiteness-by-signature (d). If moreover \det \H_g(\cvec{0}) > 0 then 0 is not an eigenvalue, so n_0 = 0 and the inertia is (0,3,0). But then \det\H_g(\cvec{0}) = \lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3 is a product of three negative numbers, hence negative — a contradiction. On 
R^2 there is no obstruction: g(x,y) = -x^2 - y^2 has \H_g(\cvec{0}) = -2\I_2, determinant 4 > 0, and a strict local maximum at \cvec{0}. The responsible feature is the parity of the dimension: the determinant is the product of n eigenvalues, so a negative definite Hessian has \det of sign (-1)^n.

title: 14.7 Where the Form Vanishes
content:
Where the Form Vanishes Sections 4 and 5 diagonalized a symmetric form and counted the signs on the diagonal. Over 
R that is the whole story, but it hides the feature that makes indefinite forms geometrically different from inner products: there are nonzero vectors on which the form vanishes. This section takes those vectors seriously. They are not defects to be quarantined; they organize the space, because each one forces a two-dimensional piece of completely standard shape to split off. The result is a decomposition of any nondegenerate space into a pile of identical planes plus a remainder on which the form vanishes nowhere. Throughout, F is a field with \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 (@def-characteristic), V is a finite-dimensional vector space over F with \dim V = n, and  eta is a symmetric bilinear form on V (@def-symmetric-form) with quadratic form q(\elem{v}) =  eta(\elem{v},\elem{v}) (@def-quadratic-form). Two vectors are orthogonal when  eta pairs them to 0 (@def-orthogonal-basis-form). For a subspace U \subseteq V we write, as in @exr-bilinear-forms-c2, U^{\perp_ eta} = \{\, \elem{v} \in V :  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) = 0 	ext{ for every } \elem{u} \in U \,\}, and we write V = U \perp W to say that V = U \oplus W with every vector of U orthogonal to every vector of W — an orthogonal direct sum. The subscript  eta is dropped when only one form is in play. An intuition to give up Thirteen chapters have trained one reflex above all others: \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0 forces \elem{v} = \elem{0}. It is how we proved that an isometry is injective, that an orthogonal list is independent, that a Gram matrix determines its vectors. It is also the first thing that goes. Take V = 
R^2 with q(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 - x_2^2, \qquad \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}. The vector \cvec{v} = (1,1) has q(\cvec{v}) = 1 - 1 = 0. It is not \cvec{0}, and the form is not defective: \det \A = -1 
e 0, so  eta is nondegenerate (@prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible). Indeed  eta(\cvec{v}, (1,-1)) = 1 - (1)(-1) = 2 
e 0, so \cvec{v} is perfectly visible to  eta — it is only invisible to itself. The line \Span(\cvec{v}) is a line of “length zero” inside a space where length is otherwise perfectly well behaved. It gets worse, and the worse case is the one worth internalizing. Take V = 
R^4 with q(\cvec{x}) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 - x_3^2 - x_4^2 , of signature (2,2) and therefore nondegenerate. Let W = \Span(\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_3,\ \cvec{e}_2 + \cvec{e}_4), a plane. For \cvec{w} = a(\cvec{e}_1+\cvec{e}_3) + b(\cvec{e}_2+\cvec{e}_4), q(\cvec{w}) = a^2 + b^2 - a^2 - b^2 = 0 , and in fact  eta vanishes on every pair from W, since  eta(\cvec{e}_1+\cvec{e}_3, \cvec{e}_2+\cvec{e}_4) = 0 too. So  eta restricted to W is the zero form on a two-dimensional subspace of a four-dimensional space on which  eta is nondegenerate. Say that again, because it is the sentence an inner-product-trained reader will refuse. A nondegenerate form can vanish identically on a subspace of half the dimension of the whole space. Nondegeneracy is a statement about V; it says that no vector is orthogonal to everything. It says nothing whatsoever about what  eta does inside a subspace. The vectors of W above are orthogonal to each other and to themselves; they are not orthogonal to \cvec{e}_1 - \cvec{e}_3, and that is all nondegeneracy ever promised. Once that is accepted, the rest of the section is straightforward. The vanishing vectors get a name, and then a structure theorem. Isotropic vectors and totally isotropic subspaces An isotropic vector is a nonzero vector that the form cannot tell from zero when it looks at it twice. [Isotropic and Anisotropic] Let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on V with quadratic form q. 1. A vector \elem{v} \in V is isotropic if \elem{v} 
e \elem{0} and q(\elem{v}) = 0, and anisotropic if q(\elem{v}) 
e 0. 2. The form  eta is anisotropic if it has no isotropic vectors: that is, if q(\elem{v}) = 0 implies \elem{v} = \elem{0}. Otherwise  eta is isotropic. Both clauses hinge on small words. In (a) the vector is required to be nonzero, so \elem{0} is neither isotropic nor anisotropic; the zero vector always has q(\elem{0}) = 0 and carries no information. In (b), “anisotropic” is a property of the form on a particular space. Anisotropy passes down to subspaces, since a subspace has fewer vectors to test; isotropy does not, and a form isotropic on V is very often anisotropic on a subspace. The word comes from iso (equal) and tropos (direction): a vector along which the form does not distinguish one direction from another. Examples, over several fields. - A positive definite form has no isotropic vectors. If q(\elem{v}) > 0 for \elem{v} 
e \elem{0} then q(\elem{v}) = 0 forces \elem{v} = \elem{0}. So every inner product is anisotropic, which is exactly the reflex described above. The same holds for negative definite forms. - Over 
R, signature (1,1). For q = x_1^2 - x_2^2 the isotropic vectors are the nonzero multiples of (1,1) and of (1,-1), since q = (x_1-x_2)(x_1+x_2). Two lines, and nothing else. - Over 
C. For q = x_1^2 + x_2^2 on 
C^2 the factorization q = (x_1 + ix_2)(x_1 - ix_2) is available, so (1, i) and (1,-i) are isotropic. Over 
R the same q is positive definite. Isotropy depends on the field, not only on the polynomial. - Over 
F_3 and 
F_5. For q = x_1^2 + x_2^2 the squares in 
F_3 are 0 and 1, so q(\cvec{x}) = 0 needs x_1 = x_2 = 0 and the form is anisotropic. In 
F_5, however, 1^2 + 2^2 = 5 = 0, so (1,2) is isotropic. The same formula, two finite fields, two answers. - The degenerate case. Every nonzero vector of the radical is isotropic, since \elem{v} \in \operatorname{rad}( eta) gives  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) = 0 for every \elem{u}, in particular for \elem{u} = \elem{v}. So a degenerate form is automatically isotropic. The converse fails, and the 
R^2 example above is the witness. When a whole subspace consists of isotropic vectors, more is true than the definition says, and it deserves its own name. [Totally Isotropic Subspace] A subspace W \subseteq V is totally isotropic for  eta if  eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) = 0 for all \elem{u}, \elem{w} \in W; equivalently, if W \subseteq W^{\perp_ eta}. The zero subspace is totally isotropic, trivially. The two formulations agree because W \subseteq W^{\perp_ eta} says exactly that every \elem{w} \in W is orthogonal to every \elem{u} \in W. A third formulation is available in characteristic 
e 2 and is the one to use in practice: W is totally isotropic if and only if q(\elem{w}) = 0 for every \elem{w} \in W. One direction is immediate; the other is @thm-polarization-forms applied to the restricted form, which recovers  eta on W from q on W and so makes it zero. In the 
R^4 example above we checked exactly this: q vanished on W, and therefore so did  eta. Before the first theorem, one dimension count has to be on the table, because almost everything in this section and the next is a step away from it. @exr-bilinear-forms-c2 set it as an exercise in Section 1; here it is with a proof, so that the results below rest on it rather than on the exercise. [Dimension of an Orthogonal Complement] Let  eta be a nondegenerate bilinear form on V with \dim V = n, and let U \subseteq V be a subspace. Then U^{\perp_ eta} is a subspace of V, and \dim U^{\perp_ eta} = n - \dim U . Freezing the second slot of  eta turns it into a map V 	o V^{*}, and restricting a functional to U turns V^{*} into U^{*}. The composite has kernel exactly U^{\perp_ eta}, and nondegeneracy makes both maps surjective, so Rank–Nullity converts “onto U^{*}” into the count. Let R \colon V 	o V^{*} send \elem{v} to the functional  eta(\cdot, \elem{v}) — the map called R_ eta in Section 1 — and let ho \colon V^{*} 	o U^{*} be restriction to U. Both are linear, so S \coloneqq ho \circ R \colon V 	o U^{*} is linear, and S(\elem{v}) =  eta(\cdot, \elem{v}) ig|_U. By the definition of U^{\perp_ eta}, a vector \elem{v} lies in U^{\perp_ eta} exactly when  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = 0 for every \elem{u} \in U, that is, exactly when S(\elem{v}) = 0. Hence U^{\perp_ eta} = \ker S, which is a subspace. Since  eta is nondegenerate, R is an isomorphism (@prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible (c)), and ho is surjective (@thm-dual-of-subspace). A composite of two surjections is a surjection, so ank S = \dim U^{*} = \dim U (@cor-dimension-dual-space). By Rank–Nullity (@thm-rank-nullity), \dim U^{\perp_ eta} = \dim\ker S = n - ank S = n - \dim U , as claimed. Totally isotropic subspaces cannot be too large. [Half the Dimension, at Most] Let  eta be a nondegenerate symmetric form on V with \dim V = n, and let W \subseteq V be totally isotropic. Then \dim W \le n/2. Since  eta is nondegenerate, \dim W^{\perp_ eta} = n - \dim W by @lem-perp-dimension. Since W is totally isotropic, W \subseteq W^{\perp_ eta}, so \dim W \le n - \dim W, which is the claim. An isotropic vector is not a zero vector, and a form that vanishes on a subspace need not be degenerate. These are two different errors and both are common. The first confuses q(\elem{v}) = 0 with \elem{v} = \elem{0}; over 
R^{2} with q = x_1^2 - x_2^2 the vector (1,1) separates them. The second confuses “ eta vanishes on W 	imes W” with “ eta vanishes on \{\elem{v}\} 	imes V”. Degeneracy is about the second: the radical consists of vectors killed by pairing with everything. The plane W of the 
R^4 example carries the zero form and contains no radical vector at all. Is the plane \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) \subseteq 
R^4 totally isotropic for q(\cvec{x}) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 - x_3^2 - x_4^2? What about \Span(\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_3, \cvec{e}_1 - \cvec{e}_3)? No to both. On \Span(\cvec{e}_1,\cvec{e}_2) the form restricts to x_1^2 + x_2^2, which is positive definite, so that plane is as far from totally isotropic as possible: it is anisotropic. The second plane is \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_3), on which q restricts to x_1^2 - x_3^2; its two spanning vectors \cvec{e}_1 \pm \cvec{e}_3 are indeed isotropic, but  eta(\cvec{e}_1+\cvec{e}_3, \cvec{e}_1-\cvec{e}_3) = 1 - (-1) = 2 
e 0, so the plane is not totally isotropic. Containing isotropic vectors is not the same as being totally isotropic. Splitting off a nondegenerate piece Everything below rests on one mechanism: if a subspace carries a nondegenerate restriction, it splits off orthogonally and the rest of the space is again nondegenerate. That is the analogue of “restrict to an invariant complement”, and it is what makes induction possible. [A Nondegenerate Subspace Splits Off] Let  eta be a nondegenerate symmetric form on V with \dim V = n, and let U \subseteq V be a subspace such that  eta|_{U 	imes U} is nondegenerate. Then V = U \perp U^{\perp_ eta} , and  eta restricted to U^{\perp_ eta} is nondegenerate. Two things to check and one dimension count. The intersection U \cap U^{\perp_ eta} is precisely the radical of the restricted form, which the hypothesis kills; the dimension of U^{\perp_ eta} is n - \dim U because the global form is nondegenerate; and a vector of U^{\perp_ eta} orthogonal to U^{\perp_ eta} is orthogonal to all of V, hence zero. Write U^{\perp} = U^{\perp_ eta}. A vector \elem{v} \in U \cap U^{\perp} lies in U and satisfies  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) = 0 for every \elem{u} \in U, so \elem{v} \in \operatorname{rad}( eta|_{U	imes U}), which is \{\elem{0}\} by hypothesis (@def-nondegenerate). Hence U \cap U^{\perp} = \{\elem{0}\} and the sum U + U^{\perp} is direct (@thm-direct-sum-criteria). Since  eta is nondegenerate on V, @lem-perp-dimension gives \dim U^{\perp} = n - \dim U. So \dim(U \oplus U^{\perp}) = n, and a subspace of V of dimension n is V (@thm-dim-impl-eq). F_3 are 0^2 = 0, 1^2 = 1, 2^2 = 1, so the values of x_1^2 + x_2^2 are 0, 1, 2 — which is all of 
F_3, so (b) gives nothing directly. Argue instead from the definition: q(\cvec{x}) = 0 needs x_1^2 = -x_2^2 = 2x_2^2. If x_2 
e 0 then x_2^2 = 1, so x_1^2 = 2, which is not a square in 
F_3; hence x_2 = 0 and then x_1 = 0. The form is anisotropic, its Witt index is 0, and the Gram matrix \I_2 shows it is nondegenerate. Over 
F_5 the same form is isotropic, since 1^2 + 2^2 = 0. [C2: A maximal totally isotropic subspace and its complement] Let  eta be nondegenerate symmetric on V with \dim V = n, and let W \subseteq V be totally isotropic with \dim W = \operatorname{ind}( eta) = m. 1. Prove that \dim W^{\perp_ eta} = n - m and W \subseteq W^{\perp_ eta}. 2. Prove that the form induced by  eta on the quotient W^{\perp_ eta}/W is well defined and anisotropic. Hint: a coset with an isotropic representative would enlarge W. 3. Deduce that n - 2m = \dim(W^{\perp_ eta}/W) agrees with the dimension of the anisotropic part in @thm-witt-decomposition. (a) The dimension is @lem-perp-dimension, using nondegeneracy, and the inclusion is @def-totally-isotropic-subspace. (b) For \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in W^{\perp_ eta} and \elem{w}, \elem{w}' \in W,  eta(\elem{u} + \elem{w}, \elem{v} + \elem{w}') =  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) , because each of the three remaining terms pairs a vector of W with a vector of W^{\perp_ eta} \supseteq W, hence vanishes. So  ar eta(\elem{u} + W, \elem{v} + W) \coloneqq  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) is well defined, and it is bilinear and symmetric. Suppose  ar q(\elem{u} + W) = 0 with \elem{u} 
otin W, that is q(\elem{u}) = 0 with \elem{u} \in W^{\perp_ eta}\setminus W. Then W + \Span(\elem{u}) is totally isotropic: it is spanned by isotropic vectors,  eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) = 0 for \elem{w} \in W because \elem{u} \in W^{\perp_ eta}, and  eta vanishes on W 	imes W. Its dimension is m + 1 > \operatorname{ind}( eta), a contradiction. So  ar eta is anisotropic. (c) By (a), \dim(W^{\perp_ eta}/W) = (n-m) - m = n - 2m. By @prp-witt-index-counts-planes the anisotropic part V_0 of a Witt decomposition also has dimension n - 2m, since the index is m. (That the two anisotropic forms agree, and not merely their dimensions, is proved in the next section.) [C3: Where characteristic 2 breaks] Work over 
F_2 and let  eta be the dot product on 
F_2^2, with Gram matrix \I_2. 1. Verify that  eta is symmetric and nondegenerate, and find all \cvec{v} with q(\cvec{v}) = 0. 2. Show that  eta has a vector with q(\cvec{v}) = 0 and \cvec{v} 
e \cvec{0} that lies in no hyperbolic plane, and identify which line of the proof of @lem-isotropic-extends-to-hyperbolic fails. 3. Explain in one sentence why the third description of “totally isotropic” given after @def-totally-isotropic-subspace is unavailable here. (a) The Gram matrix \I_2 is symmetric and invertible, so  eta is symmetric and nondegenerate (@prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible). Here q(\cvec{x}) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 = (x_1+x_2)^2 over 
F_2, which vanishes exactly when x_1 = x_2. So q(\cvec{v}) = 0 for \cvec{v} = \cvec{0} and for \cvec{v} = (1,1). (b) Take \cvec{v} = (1,1). A hyperbolic plane containing it would need \cvec{f} with q(\cvec{f}) = 0 and  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{f}) = 1. The only nonzero vector with q = 0 is \cvec{v} itself, and  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) = q(\cvec{v}) = 0 
e 1. The step that fails is the correction \cvec{f} = \cvec{u} - 	frac12 q(\cvec{u})\cvec{e}: the element 2 = 1 + 1 is 0 in 
F_2 and is not invertible, so 	frac12 does not exist. (c) Because it is @thm-polarization-forms, which needs \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 to divide by 2; over 
F_2 the line \Span((1,1)) has q \equiv 0 on it and is indeed totally isotropic here, but the implication “q vanishes on W implies  eta vanishes on W 	imes W” is not available in general.

title: 14.8 Witt's Extension and Cancellation Theorems
content:
Witt’s Extension and Cancellation Theorems The previous section left one question open. A nondegenerate space splits as hyperbolic planes plus an anisotropic remainder, and the number of planes is pinned down by the Witt index — but the remainder is a subspace chosen along the way, and different choices give different subspaces. What should be true is that they all carry the same form. Proving it needs a theorem with a much wider reach: any isometry between two subspaces of a nondegenerate space is the restriction of an isometry of the whole space. That theorem is the longest proof of the chapter, and the cancellation statement that finishes Section 7 falls out of it in four lines. Throughout, F is a field with \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 (@def-characteristic), all spaces are finite-dimensional over F, and all forms are symmetric bilinear forms (@def-symmetric-form). Orthogonal complements U^{\perp_ eta}, orthogonal direct sums U \perp W, and isotropic and hyperbolic vocabulary are as in Section 7. Isometries of forms Chapter 11 called a linear map an isometry when it preserved the inner product (@def-isometry). The same word works here, with the form in place of the inner product and with no positivity anywhere. An isometry is a change of variables that the form does not notice. [Isometry of Bilinear Spaces] Let  eta be a bilinear form on V and  eta' one on V'. An isometry from (V, eta) to (V', eta') is a linear bijection \sigma \colon V 	o V' with  eta' igl(\sigma(\elem{u}), \sigma(\elem{v}) igr) =  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) \qquad 	ext{for all } \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V . The two spaces are isometric, written (V, eta) \cong (V', eta') or just V \cong V', if such a \sigma exists. An isometry of (V, eta) with itself is an isometry of V. When U \subseteq V and U' \subseteq V' are subspaces, “an isometry U 	o U'” always means an isometry for the restricted forms  eta|_{U	imes U} and  eta'|_{U'	imes U'}. Two clauses need pointing at. The map must be a bijection, so that the inverse is again an isometry; and the identity must hold for all pairs, though by bilinearity it is enough to check it on a pair of bases. The symbol \cong is the one used for isomorphism throughout the book, and no confusion arises: an isometry is an isomorphism that also respects the form, and within this chapter \cong between spaces carrying forms always means isometric. Three readings make the notion concrete. - Isometry is congruence in disguise. If \sB is a basis of V and \sB' one of V', then \sigma is an isometry exactly when the Gram matrices satisfy \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} = \P	p\,\mtx{ eta'}{\sB'}{\sB'}\,\P with \P = \mtx{\sigma}{\sB}{\sB'}. So (V, eta) \cong (V', eta') if and only if their Gram matrices are congruent (@def-congruent). Every classification theorem of this chapter is therefore a classification up to isometry. - Over 
R. Two real spaces with nondegenerate symmetric forms are isometric exactly when they have the same signature, by @cor-real-symmetric-classification. So, writing 
R^{p,q} for 
R^{p+q} carrying the form of signature (p,q), we have 
R^{2,1} 
ot\cong 
R^{1,2} even though both are three-dimensional and both nondegenerate. - The degenerate case. An isometry carries \operatorname{rad}( eta) onto \operatorname{rad}( eta'), because  eta'(\sigma\elem{u}, \sigma\elem{v}) =  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) and \sigma is surjective. In particular isometric spaces have radicals of equal dimension. The isometries of a fixed (V, eta) form a group under composition; Section 10 names the classical examples. For now only two kinds are needed, and the second is built from the first. Reflections Chapter 11 §08 built Householder reflections out of an inner product, to clear a column. The same formula works for any symmetric form, provided the vector we reflect in is anisotropic, and it is the only explicit isometry this section needs. [Reflection in an Anisotropic Vector] Let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on V and let \elem{w} \in V be anisotropic, that is q(\elem{w}) 
e 0. The reflection in \elem{w} is the map 	au_{\elem{w}} \colon V 	o V, \qquad 	au_{\elem{w}}(\elem{v}) = \elem{v} -  rac{2 eta(\elem{v},\elem{w})}{q(\elem{w})}\,\elem{w} . The formula is @def-householder-reflection with \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} replaced by  eta(\elem{v},\elem{w}) and 
orm{\elem{w}}^2 by q(\elem{w}); the division is legitimate precisely because \elem{w} is anisotropic. [Reflections Are Involutive Isometries] Let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on V and \elem{w} \in V anisotropic. Then 	au_{\elem{w}} is linear, and: 1. 	au_{\elem{w}}(\elem{w}) = -\elem{w}, and 	au_{\elem{w}}(\elem{v}) = \elem{v} for every \elem{v} with  eta(\elem{v},\elem{w}) = 0; 2. 	au_{\elem{w}} \circ 	au_{\elem{w}} = \id_V; in particular 	au_{\elem{w}} is bijective; 3.  eta(	au_{\elem{w}}\elem{u}, 	au_{\elem{w}}\elem{v}) =  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) for all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V. Hence 	au_{\elem{w}} is an isometry of V. Linearity holds because \elem{v} \mapsto  eta(\elem{v},\elem{w}) is linear and q(\elem{w}) is a fixed nonzero scalar. Write c(\elem{v}) = 2 eta(\elem{v},\elem{w})/q(\elem{w}). (a) c(\elem{w}) = 2q(\elem{w})/q(\elem{w}) = 2, so 	au_{\elem{w}}(\elem{w}) = \elem{w} - 2\elem{w} = -\elem{w}. If  eta(\elem{v},\elem{w}) = 0 then c(\elem{v}) = 0 and 	au_{\elem{w}}(\elem{v}) = \elem{v}. (b) By (a) and linearity,  eta(	au_{\elem{w}}\elem{v}, \elem{w}) =  eta(\elem{v},\elem{w}) - c(\elem{v})q(\elem{w}) = - eta(\elem{v},\elem{w}), so c(	au_{\elem{w}}\elem{v}) = -c(\elem{v}) and 	au_{\elem{w}}(	au_{\elem{w}}\elem{v}) =  igl(\elem{v} - c(\elem{v})\elem{w} igr) + c(\elem{v})\elem{w} = \elem{v} . (c) Expanding by bilinearity and using symmetry,  egin{aligned}  eta(	au_{\elem{w}}\elem{u},	au_{\elem{w}}\elem{v}) &=  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) - c(\elem{v}) eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) - c(\elem{u}) eta(\elem{w},\elem{v}) \ &\qquad + c(\elem{u})c(\elem{v})q(\elem{w}) . \end{aligned} Now c(\elem{u})c(\elem{v})q(\elem{w}) = 4 eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) eta(\elem{v},\elem{w})/q(\elem{w}), while the two middle terms together contribute -4 eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) eta(\elem{v},\elem{w})/q(\elem{w}). They cancel, leaving  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}). Together with (b) this makes 	au_{\elem{w}} a bijective linear map preserving  eta, that is an isometry. The use of reflections is that they move one anisotropic vector to any other of the same value — the one explicit construction the long proof below will need. [Moving One Anisotropic Vector to Another] Let \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, let  eta be a symmetric bilinear form on V, and let \elem{u}, \elem{u}' \in V satisfy q(\elem{u}) = q(\elem{u}') 
e 0 . Then there is an isometry ho of V with ho(\elem{u}) = \elem{u}', and ho may be taken to be a reflection or a product of two reflections. The reflection in \elem{u} - \elem{u}' is the natural candidate, and it works whenever \elem{u} - \elem{u}' is anisotropic. It need not be — but \elem{u} + \elem{u}' then is, because the two values q(\elem{u}-\elem{u}') and q(\elem{u}+\elem{u}') add up to 4q(\elem{u}) 
e 0 and so cannot both vanish. Reflecting in \elem{u} + \elem{u}' overshoots to -\elem{u}', and one more reflection, in \elem{u}' itself, brings it back. Expanding both by bilinearity and adding, q(\elem{u}-\elem{u}') + q(\elem{u}+\elem{u}') = 2q(\elem{u}) + 2q(\elem{u}') = 4q(\elem{u}) 
e 0 , where the last step uses q(\elem{u}) = q(\elem{u}') 
e 0. So at least one of q(\elem{u}-\elem{u}') and q(\elem{u}+\elem{u}') is nonzero. Case 1: q(\elem{u} - \elem{u}') 
e 0. Put \elem{w} = \elem{u} - \elem{u}'. Then q(\elem{w}) = q(\elem{u}) - 2 eta(\elem{u},\elem{u}') + q(\elem{u}') = 2 igl(q(\elem{u}) -  eta(\elem{u},\elem{u}') igr), while  eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) = q(\elem{u}) -  eta(\elem{u},\elem{u}'). Hence 2 eta(\elem{u},\elem{w})/q(\elem{w}) = 1, and 	au_{\elem{w}}(\elem{u}) = \elem{u} - \elem{w} = \elem{u}' . Take ho = 	au_{\elem{w}}. Case 2: q(\elem{u}-\elem{u}') = 0. Then q(\elem{u}+\elem{u}') = 4q(\elem{u}) 
e 0; put \elem{w} = \elem{u} + \elem{u}'. The same computation with -\elem{u}' in place of \elem{u}' gives q(\elem{w}) = 2(q(\elem{u}) +  eta(\elem{u},\elem{u}')) and  eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) = q(\elem{u}) +  eta(\elem{u},\elem{u}'), so again 2 eta(\elem{u},\elem{w})/q(\elem{w}) = 1 and 	au_{\elem{w}}(\elem{u}) = \elem{u} - \elem{w} = -\elem{u}' . Since q(\elem{u}') 
e 0, the reflection 	au_{\elem{u}'} is defined, and 	au_{\elem{u}'}(-\elem{u}') = \elem{u}' by @prp-form-reflection-properties (a). Take ho = 	au_{\elem{u}'}\circ	au_{\elem{w}}, a composition of two isometries and hence an isometry. This proves the lemma. In 
R^3 with q(\cvec{x}) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 - x_3^2, find a reflection carrying \cvec{e}_1 to \cvec{e}_2. Both have q = 1 
e 0, so @lem-reflection-moves-anisotropic applies. Case 1 works: \cvec{w} = \cvec{e}_1 - \cvec{e}_2 has q(\cvec{w}) = 1 + 1 = 2 
e 0, so 	au_{\cvec{w}}(\cvec{v}) = \cvec{v} -  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{w})\,\cvec{w}, since 2/q(\cvec{w}) = 1. Then  eta(\cvec{e}_1,\cvec{w}) = 1 and 	au_{\cvec{w}}(\cvec{e}_1) = \cvec{e}_1 - (\cvec{e}_1 - \cvec{e}_2) = \cvec{e}_2, as required. The reflection fixes \cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2 and \cvec{e}_3, which are the vectors orthogonal to \cvec{w}. Witt’s extension theorem Here is the chapter’s long theorem. Read the statement carefully: the two subspaces live in the same space V, and the form on V is required to be nondegenerate, but nothing at all is assumed about the restrictions to U and U' — they may be degenerate, they may be zero. Witt’s Extension Theorem Let F be a field with \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, and let  eta be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on V. Let U, U' \subseteq V be subspaces and let \sigma \colon U 	o U' be an isometry for the restricted forms. Then there is an isometry \varphi of V with \varphi|_U = \sigma. Induction, but on what? Two different moves are available, and each improves a different number. ① If  eta|_U is nondegenerate, then U contains an anisotropic vector \elem{u}_1. A reflection moves \sigma(\elem{u}_1) back to \elem{u}_1, so we may assume \sigma fixes \elem{u}_1; then everything of U orthogonal to \elem{u}_1 stays inside the hyperplane \elem{u}_1^{\perp}, which is again nondegenerate and one dimension smaller. Recurse there and glue. ② If  eta|_U is degenerate, pick a nonzero \elem{z} in its radical. Nondegeneracy of  eta on V produces a partner \elem{w} making (\elem{z},\elem{w}) a hyperbolic pair orthogonal to the rest of U, and \sigma extends to U \oplus F\elem{w} by sending \elem{w} to the matching partner on the other side. The subspace has grown, but its radical has shrunk by one. So the induction runs on the pair (\dim V,\ \dim\operatorname{rad}( eta|_U)) read lexicographically: ① lowers the first entry, ② keeps it and lowers the second. Step 0 disposes of U = \{\elem{0}\}. We prove the statement for every triple (V, U, \sigma) satisfying the hypotheses, by induction on the pair  igl(\dim V,\ \dim\operatorname{rad}( eta|_{U	imes U}) igr) ordered lexicographically: one pair precedes another if its first entry is smaller, or the first entries agree and the second is smaller. This order on pairs of nonnegative integers has no infinite descending chain, so the induction is legitimate. Write R = \operatorname{rad}( eta|_{U	imes U}) = U \cap U^{\perp_ eta}. Step 0: U = \{\elem{0}\}. Then U' = \{\elem{0}\} and \varphi = \id_V works. Step 1: U 
e \{\elem{0}\} and R = \{\elem{0}\}. Since  eta|_U is nondegenerate and U 
e \{\elem{0}\}, the form  eta|_U is not the zero form. By @lem-anisotropic-vector-exists, applied to  eta|_U on U and using \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, there is \elem{u}_1 \in U with q(\elem{u}_1) 
e 0. We may assume \sigma(\elem{u}_1) = \elem{u}_1. Put \elem{u}_1' = \sigma(\elem{u}_1). Then q(\elem{u}_1') =  eta(\sigma\elem{u}_1,\sigma\elem{u}_1) = q(\elem{u}_1) 
e 0, so @lem-reflection-moves-anisotropic gives an isometry ho of V with ho(\elem{u}_1) = \elem{u}_1'. The composite 	au = ho^{-1}\circ\sigma is an isometry from U onto ho^{-1}(U') with 	au(\elem{u}_1) = \elem{u}_1, and if \varphi_0 is an isometry of V extending 	au, then ho\circ\varphi_0 is an isometry of V extending \sigma. So it suffices to treat 	au. Assume then that \sigma(\elem{u}_1) = \elem{u}_1. The map \elem{u} \mapsto  eta(\elem{u}_1,\elem{u}) is a linear functional on U taking the nonzero value q(\elem{u}_1) at \elem{u}_1, so its kernel U_1 = \{\, \elem{u} \in U :  eta(\elem{u}_1,\elem{u}) = 0 \,\} has \dim U_1 = \dim U - 1 by Rank–Nullity (@thm-rank-nullity), and U = \Span(\elem{u}_1) \oplus U_1, since a\elem{u}_1 \in U_1 forces a\,q(\elem{u}_1) = 0 and hence a = 0. Because q(\elem{u}_1) 
e 0, the form restricted to \Span(\elem{u}_1) is nondegenerate, so @prp-nondegenerate-restriction-splits gives V = \Span(\elem{u}_1) \perp W, \qquad W = \Span(\elem{u}_1)^{\perp_ eta}, with  eta|_W nondegenerate and \dim W = \dim V - 1. Now U_1 \subseteq W by definition, and \sigma(U_1) \subseteq W as well: for \elem{u} \in U_1,  eta(\elem{u}_1, \sigma\elem{u}) =  eta(\sigma\elem{u}_1, \sigma\elem{u}) =  eta(\elem{u}_1,\elem{u}) = 0 . So \sigma|_{U_1} \colon U_1 	o \sigma(U_1) is an isometry between two subspaces of W, and (W,  eta|_W) satisfies the hypotheses of the theorem with \dim W < \dim V. By the induction hypothesis there is an isometry 	heta of W with 	heta|_{U_1} = \sigma|_{U_1}. Define \varphi \colon V 	o V by \varphi(a\elem{u}_1 + \elem{x}) = a\elem{u}_1 + 	heta(\elem{x}) \qquad (a \in F,\ \elem{x} \in W), which is well defined and linear because V = \Span(\elem{u}_1)\oplus W, and bijective because 	heta is. It is an isometry: using the orthogonality of \Span(\elem{u}_1) and W on both sides,  egin{aligned}  eta igl(\varphi(a\elem{u}_1+\elem{x}), \varphi(b\elem{u}_1+\elem{y}) igr) &= ab\,q(\elem{u}_1) +  eta(	heta\elem{x},	heta\elem{y}) \ &= ab\,q(\elem{u}_1) +  eta(\elem{x},\elem{y}) \ &=  eta(a\elem{u}_1+\elem{x},\ b\elem{u}_1+\elem{y}) . \end{aligned} Finally \varphi extends \sigma: a vector \elem{u} \in U is a\elem{u}_1 + \elem{x} with \elem{x} \in U_1 \subseteq W, and \varphi(\elem{u}) = a\elem{u}_1 + 	heta(\elem{x}) = a\sigma(\elem{u}_1) + \sigma(\elem{x}) = \sigma(\elem{u}) . Step 2: R 
e \{\elem{0}\}. Choose \elem{z} \in R with \elem{z} 
e \elem{0} and a complement U_0 of \Span(\elem{z}) in U, so that U = \Span(\elem{z}) \oplus U_0 (@thm-complement-exists). Since \sigma is an isometry of U onto U', it carries R onto \operatorname{rad}( eta|_{U'}); write \elem{z}' = \sigma(\elem{z}) and U_0' = \sigma(U_0), so that U' = \Span(\elem{z}')\oplus U_0' and \elem{z}' lies in the radical of  eta|_{U'}. Note q(\elem{z}) = 0, because \elem{z} pairs to zero with everything in U, in particular with itself; likewise q(\elem{z}') = 0. There is \elem{w} \in V with q(\elem{w}) = 0,  eta(\elem{z},\elem{w}) = 1, and  eta(\elem{u}_0,\elem{w}) = 0 for every \elem{u}_0 \in U_0. Consider the linear map S \colon V 	o U^{*} sending \elem{v} to the restriction of  eta(\cdot,\elem{v}) to U. Its kernel is U^{\perp_ eta}, which has dimension \dim V - \dim U by @lem-perp-dimension, since  eta is nondegenerate. By Rank–Nullity (@thm-rank-nullity), ank S = \dim U = \dim U^{*}, so S is surjective. Let \psi_{\elem{z}} \in U^{*} be the functional with \psi_{\elem{z}}(\elem{z}) = 1 and \psi_{\elem{z}}(U_0) = 0, which exists because U = \Span(\elem{z})\oplus U_0. Pick \elem{w}_0 \in V with S(\elem{w}_0) = \psi_{\elem{z}}, that is  eta(\elem{z},\elem{w}_0) = 1 and  eta(\elem{u}_0,\elem{w}_0) = 0 for \elem{u}_0 \in U_0. Put \elem{w} = \elem{w}_0 - 	frac12 q(\elem{w}_0)\,\elem{z}, which uses \operatorname{char} F 
e 2. Since q(\elem{z}) = 0 and  eta(\elem{u},\elem{z}) = 0 for every \elem{u} \in U,  eta(\elem{z},\elem{w}) = 1 - 	frac12q(\elem{w}_0)q(\elem{z}) = 1, \qquad  eta(\elem{u}_0,\elem{w}) = 0 , and q(\elem{w}) = q(\elem{w}_0) - q(\elem{w}_0) eta(\elem{w}_0,\elem{z}) + 	frac14q(\elem{w}_0)^2q(\elem{z}) = 0 , using  eta(\elem{w}_0,\elem{z}) =  eta(\elem{z},\elem{w}_0) = 1. Apply the claim on both sides: it gives \elem{w} for (\elem{z}, U_0) and, by the same argument with \elem{z}' and U_0', a vector \elem{w}' with q(\elem{w}') = 0,  eta(\elem{z}',\elem{w}') = 1, and  eta(U_0',\elem{w}') = 0. The vector \elem{w} is not in U, since  eta(\elem{z},\elem{w}) = 1 while  eta(\elem{z},\elem{u}) = 0 for every \elem{u} \in U; likewise \elem{w}' 
otin U'. So \widetilde U = U \oplus F\elem{w}, \qquad \widetilde U' = U' \oplus F\elem{w}' are subspaces of V of dimension \dim U + 1. Define \widetilde\sigma(\elem{u} + c\elem{w}) = \sigma(\elem{u}) + c\elem{w}', a linear bijection \widetilde U 	o \widetilde U'. It is an isometry: for \elem{u} = a\elem{z} + \elem{u}_0 \in U we have  eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) = a eta(\elem{z},\elem{w}) +  eta(\elem{u}_0,\elem{w}) = a , and \sigma(\elem{u}) = a\elem{z}' + \sigma(\elem{u}_0) with \sigma(\elem{u}_0) \in U_0', so  eta(\sigma\elem{u}, \elem{w}') = a as well. Hence, expanding by bilinearity and using q(\elem{w}) = q(\elem{w}') = 0,  egin{aligned}  eta igl(\widetilde\sigma(\elem{u} + c\elem{w}),\, \widetilde\sigma(\elem{y} + d\elem{w}) igr) &=  eta(\sigma\elem{u},\sigma\elem{y}) + d\, eta(\sigma\elem{u},\elem{w}') + c\, eta(\sigma\elem{y},\elem{w}') \ &=  eta(\elem{u},\elem{y}) + d\, eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) + c\, eta(\elem{y},\elem{w}) \ &=  eta(\elem{u} + c\elem{w},\ \elem{y} + d\elem{w}) . \end{aligned} \operatorname{rad}( eta|_{\widetilde U}) = R \cap U_0, and its dimension is \dim R - 1. Let \elem{x} = a\elem{z} + \elem{u}_0 + c\elem{w} lie in \operatorname{rad}( eta|_{\widetilde U}), with a, c \in F and \elem{u}_0 \in U_0. Pairing \elem{x} with \elem{w} gives a eta(\elem{z},\elem{w}) +  eta(\elem{u}_0,\elem{w}) + c\,q(\elem{w}) = a, so a = 0. Pairing \elem{x} with \elem{z} gives  eta(\elem{u}_0,\elem{z}) + c\, eta(\elem{w},\elem{z}) = c, since \elem{z} \in R kills \elem{u}_0; so c = 0. Hence \elem{x} = \elem{u}_0 \in U_0, and \elem{x} pairs to zero with all of U \subseteq \widetilde U, so \elem{x} \in R\cap U_0. Conversely a vector of R \cap U_0 pairs to zero with U and with \elem{w}, hence with \widetilde U. For the dimension: every \elem{r} \in R \subseteq U is a\elem{z} + \elem{u}_0, and \elem{u}_0 = \elem{r} - a\elem{z} \in R because \elem{z} \in R; so R = \Span(\elem{z})\oplus(R\cap U_0) and \dim(R\cap U_0) = \dim R - 1. The pair attached to the triple (V, \widetilde U, \widetilde\sigma) is therefore (\dim V, \dim R - 1), which precedes (\dim V, \dim R) in the lexicographic order. By the induction hypothesis there is an isometry \varphi of V with \varphi|_{\widetilde U} = \widetilde\sigma. Since U \subseteq \widetilde U and \widetilde\sigma|_U = \sigma, this \varphi extends \sigma. Steps 0, 1, and 2 cover every case, so the induction is complete and the theorem is proved. Three places earned their hypotheses. Nondegeneracy of  eta on V was used twice, once through @prp-nondegenerate-restriction-splits in Step 1 and once through the surjectivity of S in Step 2. Characteristic 
e 2 was used twice as well, in @lem-anisotropic-vector-exists and in the correction \elem{w} = \elem{w}_0 - 	frac12 q(\elem{w}_0)\elem{z}, which is the same correction that built a hyperbolic pair in @lem-isotropic-extends-to-hyperbolic. And symmetry is everywhere: without it, “the” radical and “the” orthogonal complement would each split into a left and a right version. Cancellation The corollary is what the theorem is usually used for, and it is where a careless statement goes wrong. Witt cancellation removes a summand from an orthogonal decomposition of two spaces that are already known to be isometric, and what it produces is an isometry of the complements. [Witt’s Cancellation Theorem] Let \operatorname{char} F 
e 2. 1. Let  eta be a nondegenerate symmetric form on V, and let U, U' \subseteq V be isometric subspaces. Then U^{\perp_ eta} \cong U'^{\perp_ eta}. 2. Let (V, eta) and (V', eta') be finite-dimensional spaces with nondegenerate symmetric forms, and suppose V = U \perp W, \qquad V' = U' \perp W' . If V \cong V' and U \cong U', then W \cong W'. For (a), extend the isometry U 	o U' to the whole of V and watch where the complement goes: an isometry of V carrying U onto U' has no choice but to carry U^{\perp} onto U'^{\perp}. For (b), transport everything into the single space V along an isometry V 	o V', and apply (a). (a) Let \sigma \colon U 	o U' be an isometry. By @thm-witt-extension there is an isometry \varphi of V with \varphi|_U = \sigma; in particular \varphi(U) = U'. If \elem{x} \in U^{\perp_ eta} and \elem{u}' \in U', write \elem{u}' = \varphi(\elem{u}) with \elem{u} \in U; then  eta(\elem{u}', \varphi\elem{x}) =  eta(\varphi\elem{u}, \varphi\elem{x}) =  eta(\elem{u},\elem{x}) = 0 , so \varphi(U^{\perp_ eta}) \subseteq U'^{\perp_ eta}. Both subspaces have dimension \dim V - \dim U by @lem-perp-dimension, using \dim U = \dim U', and \varphi is injective, so the inclusion is an equality. Restricting \varphi gives an isometry U^{\perp_ eta} 	o U'^{\perp_ eta}. (b) First, W = U^{\perp_ eta}: the orthogonality in V = U \perp W gives W \subseteq U^{\perp_ eta}, and both have dimension \dim V - \dim U, so they are equal (@thm-dim-impl-eq). Likewise W' = U'^{\perp_{ eta'}}. Let \psi \colon V 	o V' be an isometry. Then \psi^{-1}(U') is a subspace of V isometric to U', hence isometric to U. Moreover \psi^{-1} igl(U'^{\perp_{ eta'}} igr) =  igl(\psi^{-1}(U') igr)^{\perp_ eta}, because \psi preserves the forms and is surjective. Applying (a) inside V to the isometric subspaces U and \psi^{-1}(U'), W = U^{\perp_ eta} \cong  igl(\psi^{-1}(U') igr)^{\perp_ eta} = \psi^{-1}(W') \cong W' , the last isometry being the restriction of \psi. This proves the corollary. Cancellation needs the whole spaces to be isometric, and the sums to be orthogonal. Neither hypothesis can be dropped. Drop the first: inside 
R^2 with q = x_1^2 + x_2^2 and inside 
R^2 with q' = x_1^2 - x_2^2, the lines \Span(\cvec{e}_1) are isometric, each carrying the form \langle 1angle. Their complements are \Span(\cvec{e}_2) with q = x_2^2 and \Span(\cvec{e}_2) with q' = -x_2^2, which are not isometric: one is positive definite, the other negative definite. Isometric subspaces of different ambient spaces say nothing about complements. Drop the second: in 
R^2 with q = x_1^2 - x_2^2, both V = \Span(\cvec{e}_1) \oplus \Span(\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2) \quad	ext{and}\quad V = \Span(\cvec{e}_1) \oplus \Span(\cvec{e}_2) are direct sums with the same first summand. The second summands carry q(\cvec{e}_1+\cvec{e}_2) = 0 and q(\cvec{e}_2) = -1, so they are not isometric. The first decomposition is not orthogonal, since  eta(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1+\cvec{e}_2) = 1 
e 0, and that is exactly what breaks. The Witt decomposition is unique We can now close the question Section 7 left open. [The Anisotropic Part Is Determined] Let \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, let  eta be a nondegenerate symmetric form on a finite-dimensional V, and let V = H_1 \perp \dots \perp H_m \perp V_0 = H_1' \perp \dots \perp H_{m'}' \perp V_0' be two decompositions as in @thm-witt-decomposition. Then m = m' = \operatorname{ind}( eta) and V_0 \cong V_0'. That m = m' = \operatorname{ind}( eta) is @prp-witt-index-counts-planes. Put U = H_1\perp\dots\perp H_m and U' = H_1'\perp\dots\perp H_m'. Choosing a hyperbolic basis of each plane gives bases of U and of U' in which both Gram matrices are the same block diagonal matrix, namely m copies of  egin{psmallmatrix} 0&1\1&0\end{psmallmatrix} down the diagonal. The linear bijection U 	o U' matching these bases in order is therefore an isometry. Both V_0 and V_0' are complements: V_0 \subseteq U^{\perp_ eta} by orthogonality, and the dimensions agree, so V_0 = U^{\perp_ eta} (@thm-dim-impl-eq), and likewise V_0' = U'^{\perp_ eta}. By @cor-witt-cancellation (a), V_0 \cong V_0'. This proves the corollary. So a nondegenerate symmetric form is completely described by two pieces of data: an integer, the Witt index, and an anisotropic form, determined up to isometry. Classifying all forms over a field F therefore reduces to classifying the anisotropic ones, which is where the arithmetic of F enters and where the subject stops being linear algebra. Over 
R the anisotropic forms are the definite ones, so the data (\operatorname{ind}, V_0) is just the signature again. Over 
C the anisotropic forms have dimension 0 or 1, so the index and the parity of n are everything. Over 
Q the classification is a theorem of number theory and is not in this book. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State Witt’s extension theorem, with all its hypotheses. 2. Define the reflection 	au_{\elem{w}} and say which vectors it fixes. 3. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if U \subseteq V and U' \subseteq V' are isometric subspaces of nondegenerate spaces, then U^{\perp} and U'^{\perp} are isometric. 4. Where is \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 used in the proof of @thm-witt-extension? 5. Two real nondegenerate forms of dimension 6 both have Witt index 2. Must they be isometric? (a) Let \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, let  eta be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional V over F, let U, U' \subseteq V be subspaces and \sigma \colon U 	o U' an isometry for the restricted forms. Then \sigma extends to an isometry of V. (b) 	au_{\elem{w}}(\elem{v}) = \elem{v} -  igl(2 eta(\elem{v},\elem{w})/q(\elem{w}) igr)\elem{w}, defined for anisotropic \elem{w}. It fixes every \elem{v} with  eta(\elem{v},\elem{w}) = 0 and sends \elem{w} to -\elem{w}. (c) Incorrect. The warning after @cor-witt-cancellation gives the witness: the line \Span(\cvec{e}_1) inside (
R^2, x_1^2+x_2^2) and inside (
R^2, x_1^2-x_2^2) are isometric, with complements of opposite definiteness. Cancellation requires the ambient spaces to be isometric too. (d) Twice. In Step 1, through @lem-anisotropic-vector-exists, which produces an anisotropic vector in a nonzero subspace where the form is not zero. In Step 2, through the correction \elem{w} = \elem{w}_0 - 	frac12q(\elem{w}_0)\elem{z}, which divides by 2. (e) No. By @cor-witt-decomposition-unique each is two hyperbolic planes orthogonal to an anisotropic part of dimension 6 - 4 = 2, and over 
R an anisotropic form is definite, so that part has signature (2,0) or (0,2). The two possibilities give signatures (4,2) and (2,4) for the whole space, which are different, so the forms need not be isometric. What @cor-witt-decomposition-unique says is that the anisotropic part is determined by the form, not that the index determines the form. B. Practice [B1: Extend an isometry by hand] Let V = 
R^3 with q(\cvec{x}) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 - x_3^2, let U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1), U' = \Span(\cvec{e}_2), and let \sigma(\cvec{e}_1) = \cvec{e}_2. 1. Verify that \sigma is an isometry of U onto U'. 2. Extend \sigma to an isometry of V, and write down its matrix in the standard basis. 3. Determine U^{\perp_ eta} and U'^{\perp_ eta} and exhibit the isometry between them produced by your extension. (a)  eta(a\cvec{e}_1, b\cvec{e}_1) = ab and  eta(\sigma(a\cvec{e}_1),\sigma(b\cvec{e}_1)) =  eta(a\cvec{e}_2,b\cvec{e}_2) = ab, and \sigma is a linear bijection U 	o U'. (b) Use the Quick check: \cvec{w} = \cvec{e}_1 - \cvec{e}_2 has q(\cvec{w}) = 2, and 	au_{\cvec{w}}(\cvec{v}) = \cvec{v} -  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{w})\cvec{w} sends \cvec{e}_1 to \cvec{e}_2. In coordinates  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{w}) = v_1 - v_2, so 	au_{\cvec{w}}(\cvec{v}) = (v_2,\ v_1,\ v_3), \qquad \P =  egin{pmatrix} 0&1&0\ 1&0&0\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}. This swaps the first two coordinates and indeed satisfies \P	p\diag(1,1,-1)\P = \diag(1,1,-1). (c) U^{\perp_ eta} = \{\cvec{v} : v_1 = 0\} = \Span(\cvec{e}_2,\cvec{e}_3) and U'^{\perp_ eta} = \Span(\cvec{e}_1,\cvec{e}_3). The extension maps \cvec{e}_2 \mapsto \cvec{e}_1 and \cvec{e}_3\mapsto\cvec{e}_3, an isometry between them; both carry the form \diag(1,-1), as @cor-witt-cancellation (a) predicts. [B2: Cancel a hyperbolic plane] Let H denote a hyperbolic plane over 
R, and let A and B be nondegenerate real spaces with forms, with \dim A = \dim B = 3. Suppose H \perp A \cong H \perp B. 1. Prove that A \cong B. 2. If A has signature (2,1), what is the signature of B? 3. Does A \perp B \cong A \perp B with A \cong A allow us to conclude B \cong B? Say which part of @cor-witt-cancellation is being used and why the statement is not vacuous. (a) Put V = H \perp A and V' = H \perp B, both nondegenerate. The two copies of H are isometric, and V \cong V' by hypothesis, so @cor-witt-cancellation (b) gives A \cong B. (b) By (a), B \cong A, so B has signature (2,1) as well; isometric real spaces have equal signatures by @cor-real-symmetric-classification. (c) It uses (b) of @cor-witt-cancellation with U = U' = A and W = W' = B; the conclusion B \cong B is true but empty. The content of (b) appears only when the two decompositions are genuinely different, as in (a) above, where the hypothesis V \cong V' is an assumption about the whole spaces and not about A and B. [B3: Reflections in an indefinite space] In 
R^2 with q(\cvec{x}) = x_1^2 - x_2^2: 1. Compute the matrix of 	au_{\cvec{e}_1} and of 	au_{\cvec{e}_2} in the standard basis, and check each satisfies \P	p\A\P = \A with \A = \diag(1,-1). 2. Explain why 	au_{\cvec{v}} is undefined for \cvec{v} = (1,1), and say what fails. 3. Find an isometry carrying (1,0) to (-1,0) and one carrying (2,\sqrt3) to (-2,\sqrt3). (Check the values of q first.) (a) q(\cvec{e}_1) = 1 and  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{e}_1) = v_1, so 	au_{\cvec{e}_1}(\cvec{v}) = \cvec{v} - 2v_1\cvec{e}_1 = (-v_1, v_2), with matrix \diag(-1,1). Similarly q(\cvec{e}_2) = -1 and  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{e}_2) = -v_2, so the coefficient is 2(-v_2)/(-1) = 2v_2 and 	au_{\cvec{e}_2}(\cvec{v}) = \cvec{v} - 2v_2\cvec{e}_2 = (v_1,-v_2), with matrix \diag(1,-1). Both matrices \P are diagonal with entries \pm1, so \P	p\A\P = \P\A\P = \A, as each sign is squared. (b) q(1,1) = 1 - 1 = 0, so (1,1) is isotropic and the denominator q(\cvec{w}) in @def-form-reflection is zero. The formula divides by 0; there is no reflection in an isotropic vector. (c) Both (1,0) and (-1,0) have q = 1 
e 0. Here \cvec{u} - \cvec{u}' = (2,0) with q = 4 
e 0, so Case 1 of @lem-reflection-moves-anisotropic applies: 	au_{(2,0)} = 	au_{\cvec{e}_1} works, and indeed 	au_{\cvec{e}_1}(1,0) = (-1,0). For the second pair, q(2,\sqrt3) = 4 - 3 = 1 = q(-2,\sqrt3). Now \cvec{u} - \cvec{u}' = (4,0), with q = 16 
e 0, so 	au_{\cvec{e}_1} again works: it negates the first coordinate and fixes the second. C. Going deeper [C1: Inertia from cancellation] Work over 
R and let V be an n-dimensional space with a nondegenerate symmetric form. 1. Prove that if 
R^{p,q} denotes 
R^{p+q} with the form x_1^2 + \dots + x_p^2 - x_{p+1}^2 - \dots - x_{p+q}^2, then 
R^{p,q} \cong 
R^{p',q'} forces p = p' and q = q', using only @cor-witt-cancellation and @prp-witt-index-real-complex. 2. Explain in one sentence how this compares with the proof of @thm-sylvester-inertia in Section 5. (a) Suppose 
R^{p,q} \cong 
R^{p',q'}. Equal dimension gives p + q = p' + q' = n. By @prp-witt-index-real-complex (a) the Witt index is an isometry invariant, so \min(p,q) = \min(p',q') = k. By @cor-witt-decomposition-unique each space is k hyperbolic planes orthogonal to an anisotropic part, and those anisotropic parts are isometric. The anisotropic part of 
R^{p,q} is positive definite of dimension p - q when p \ge q and negative definite of dimension q - p when q > p. A positive definite form is never isometric to a negative definite one of the same dimension, since q > 0 on one and q < 0 on the other away from \elem{0} — unless both dimensions are 0. So the two anisotropic parts have the same dimension and the same sign, giving p - q = p' - q'. With p + q = p' + q' this forces p = p' and q = q'. (b) Section 5 proved this directly, by producing a positive subspace and a nonpositive subspace whose dimensions are too large to intersect trivially; the route here instead invokes the whole Witt machinery, so it is longer but shows that inertia is the real instance of a statement that holds over every field of characteristic 
e 2. [C2: The isometry group acts transitively] Let  eta be a nondegenerate symmetric form on V, with \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, and let G be the group of isometries of V. 1. Prove that if q(\elem{u}) = q(\elem{u}') 
e 0 then some \varphi \in G has \varphi(\elem{u}) = \elem{u}'. 2. Prove that if \elem{u} and \elem{u}' are both isotropic and nonzero, then some \varphi \in G has \varphi(\elem{u}) = \elem{u}'. Hint: an isotropic line is a one-dimensional subspace on which the form is zero. 3. Deduce that G acts transitively on each “level set” \{\elem{v} 
e \elem{0} : q(\elem{v}) = c\} for c 
e 0, and on the set of nonzero isotropic vectors. (a) This is @lem-reflection-moves-anisotropic, which already produces such an isometry as a product of at most two reflections. Alternatively, \Span(\elem{u}) 	o \Span(\elem{u}'), \elem{u} \mapsto \elem{u}', is an isometry of one-dimensional subspaces because q(\elem{u}) = q(\elem{u}'), so @thm-witt-extension extends it. (b) The map \sigma \colon \Span(\elem{u}) 	o \Span(\elem{u}') with \sigma(a\elem{u}) = a\elem{u}' is a linear bijection, and  eta(\sigma(a\elem{u}),\sigma(b\elem{u})) = ab\,q(\elem{u}') = 0 = ab\,q(\elem{u}) =  eta(a\elem{u},b\elem{u}), so it is an isometry of the restricted forms — both of which are zero. By @thm-witt-extension it extends to \varphi \in G. Note the restricted forms here are degenerate, which is exactly the case Step 2 of the proof was built for. (c) Immediate from (a) and (b): any two members of such a set are carried to one another by some \varphi \in G. In particular, over 
R^{1,3} the isometry group moves any nonzero null vector to any other, which is the statement that the light cone has no distinguished direction. [C3: What extension does not say] 1. Give an example of a nondegenerate (V, eta) and subspaces U, U' of the same dimension that are not isometric, and say why @thm-witt-extension does not apply. 2. Let  eta be nondegenerate on V and let U \subseteq V be totally isotropic with \dim U = \operatorname{ind}( eta). Prove that any two such U are carried onto one another by an isometry of V. 3. Deduce that all maximal totally isotropic subspaces of a nondegenerate space have the same dimension, and compare with @prp-totally-isotropic-bound. (a) Take V = 
R^2 with q = x_1^2 - x_2^2, U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1), and U' = \Span(\cvec{e}_2). Both are lines, but q is positive on U\setminus\{\cvec{0}\} and negative on U'\setminus\{\cvec{0}\}, so no linear bijection can preserve the form. @thm-witt-extension has nothing to extend: its hypothesis is that an isometry U 	o U' is given, and here none exists. (b) Let U and U' be totally isotropic of the same dimension k. Any linear bijection \sigma \colon U 	o U' is an isometry, since both restricted forms are identically zero, so  eta(\sigma\elem{u},\sigma\elem{v}) = 0 =  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) for all \elem{u},\elem{v} \in U. By @thm-witt-extension, \sigma extends to an isometry \varphi of V, and \varphi(U) = U'. (c) Let U be maximal among totally isotropic subspaces, and let U_1 be one of the largest dimension m = \operatorname{ind}( eta). If \dim U < m, choose any k-dimensional subspace U_2 \subseteq U_1 with k = \dim U; it is totally isotropic, so by (b) there is an isometry \varphi of V with \varphi(U) = U_2. Then \varphi^{-1}(U_1) is totally isotropic of dimension m > k and contains \varphi^{-1}(U_2) = U, contradicting maximality. So \dim U = m for every maximal U. @prp-totally-isotropic-bound says only m \le n/2; the present statement is sharper, since it says that no totally isotropic subspace can be maximal below the top dimension.

title: 14.9 Alternating Forms and Darboux Bases
content:
Alternating Forms and Darboux Bases Almost every classification theorem so far in this chapter has carried the same asterisk — the exceptions being the crude invariants of Section 2, rank and the square class of the determinant, which need nothing of the field. Diagonalize a symmetric form: characteristic 
e 2. Split a form into a symmetric and an alternating half: characteristic 
e 2. Recover a form from its quadratic form: characteristic 
e 2. This section has no asterisk. Alternating forms admit a complete classification over every field, with no hypothesis on the characteristic at all, and the classification is as clean as a classification gets: one congruence class for each even rank. Throughout, F is an arbitrary field, V is a finite-dimensional vector space over F, and  eta is an alternating bilinear form on V (@def-alternating-form), meaning  eta(\elem{v}, \elem{v}) = 0 for every \elem{v} \in V. Two facts from Section 3 are used constantly. First,  eta is then skew-symmetric,  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = - eta(\elem{v}, \elem{u}), by @thm-alternating-vs-skew (a) — and that direction needs no hypothesis on F. Second, by @prp-alternating-form-matrix (b) the matrix of  eta in any basis is skew-symmetric with zero diagonal, and we call such a matrix alternating. Symmetry of the situation is worth noting once: since  eta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) = 0 if and only if  eta(\elem{v},\elem{u}) = 0, “orthogonal” needs no left or right, and the radical \operatorname{rad}( eta) of @def-radical is what one would want it to be from either side. The two-dimensional model A symmetric form has a one-dimensional model to build from: on a line \Span(\elem{v}) it is q(c\elem{v}) = c^2 q(\elem{v}), a scalar multiple of the squaring function, and Section 4 assembled a general symmetric form out of such lines. An alternating form offers nothing on a line at all. For any \elem{v} and any scalars c, d,  eta(c\elem{v}, d\elem{v}) = cd\, eta(\elem{v}, \elem{v}) = 0 , so  eta restricted to any line is zero. The one-dimensional pieces are all identical and all trivial. The smallest place where an alternating form has something to say is a plane, and there is essentially only one thing it can say there. [Alternating Forms on a Plane] Describe all alternating bilinear forms on F^2, and decide which are nondegenerate. An alternating 2 	imes 2 matrix has zero diagonal and a_{21} = -a_{12}, so it is \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & a \ -a & 0 \end{pmatrix} for a single scalar a \in F, and every such matrix is alternating. By @thm-form-matrix-determines the corresponding form is  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = a(x_1y_2 - x_2y_1). Its determinant is a^2, so by @prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible the form is nondegenerate exactly when a 
e 0. When a 
e 0, replacing the basis vector \cvec{e}_2 by a^{-1}\cvec{e}_2 replaces a by 1. So up to a change of basis there are exactly two alternating forms on F^2: the zero form and the one with matrix  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, whatever the field. That last matrix is the atom of the theory, and the pair of vectors producing it deserves a name. It is the alternating counterpart of the hyperbolic plane of Section 7: a two-dimensional space carrying a nondegenerate form on which the associated quadratic function vanishes identically. Here the vanishing is automatic, because every alternating form vanishes on the diagonal, so the whole content is in the pairing. A hyperbolic pair is two vectors that pair to 1 and to nothing else. [Hyperbolic Pair] Let  eta be an alternating form on V. A hyperbolic pair for  eta is an ordered pair (\elem{u}, \elem{w}) of vectors of V with  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{w}) = 1 . Its span H = \Span(\elem{u}, \elem{w}) is called a hyperbolic plane for  eta. The definition looks as though it asks for one condition, but it quietly supplies three more. Alternation already gives  eta(\elem{u},\elem{u}) =  eta(\elem{w},\elem{w}) = 0, and skewness gives  eta(\elem{w}, \elem{u}) = -1. So the matrix of  eta restricted to H in the ordered basis (\elem{u}, \elem{w}) is exactly  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}. Also, \elem{u} and \elem{w} are automatically linearly independent: if \elem{w} = c\elem{u} then  eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) = c\, eta(\elem{u},\elem{u}) = 0 
e 1, and \elem{u} 
e \elem{0} for the same reason. So H really is a plane, \dim H = 2, and  eta restricted to H is nondegenerate. An alternating form is never diagonalizable, except when it is zero. Section 4 found an orthogonal basis for every symmetric form in characteristic 
e 2; no such basis exists here. If \sB is any basis and \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} is diagonal, then its off-diagonal entries vanish by assumption and its diagonal entries vanish because  eta is alternating, so \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{\sB} = \O and  eta = 0. The standard form below is a block form, and it has to be: the 2 	imes 2 block is irreducible. Splitting off a hyperbolic pair The move that drives the whole section is the one Section 7 used for isotropic vectors: find a small nondegenerate piece, and cut the space along it. Here the small piece is a hyperbolic plane, and it can always be found as soon as  eta is not identically zero. [Peeling Off a Hyperbolic Plane] Let  eta be an alternating form on a finite-dimensional V, and suppose  eta 
e 0. 1. There is a hyperbolic pair (\elem{u}, \elem{w}) for  eta. 2. For any such pair, with H = \Span(\elem{u}, \elem{w}) and H^{\perp_ eta} = \{\, \elem{v} \in V :  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) =  eta(\elem{w}, \elem{v}) = 0 \,\} , we have V = H \oplus H^{\perp_ eta} and \dim H^{\perp_ eta} = \dim V - 2. 3. \operatorname{rad}( eta) = \operatorname{rad} igl( eta|_{H^{\perp_ eta}} igr). In particular, if  eta is nondegenerate then so is its restriction to H^{\perp_ eta}. For (a), the hypothesis  eta 
e 0 hands us two vectors pairing to something nonzero; divide one of them by that scalar. For (b), the two conditions cutting out H^{\perp_ eta} are two linear conditions, so the count should be \dim V - 2, and Rank–Nullity will say so once we check that the two conditions are independent — which is exactly what  eta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) = 1 provides. So \B\cvec{v}_4 = (0,-1,0,0)	p and  eta(\cvec{v}_2, \cvec{v}_4) = \cvec{v}_2	p(\B\cvec{v}_4) = (-2)\cdot 0 + 1\cdot(-1) = -1 . This is nonzero but not 1, so rescale: replace \cvec{v}_4 by \cvec{w}_2 \coloneqq -\cvec{v}_4 = (0,0,1,-1), giving  eta(\cvec{v}_2, \cvec{w}_2) = 1. Set \cvec{u}_2 = \cvec{v}_2. The answer. e 0. [B2: Pfaffians and determinants] For each matrix below, compute the Pfaffian using the formula of @exm-pfaffian-small, and verify that its square is the determinant. \A_1 =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 \ -2 & 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 & 0 & 3 \ -1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A_2 =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \ -1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \ -1 & -1 & 0 & 1 \ -1 & -1 & -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . Hence write down, for each, an invertible matrix congruence class in the sense of @cor-alternating-even-rank. For \A_1: a = 2, b = 0, c = 1, d = 1, e = 0, f = 3, so \operatorname{Pf}(\A_1) = af - be + cd = 6 - 0 + 1 = 7 and \det\A_1 = 49. Expanding the determinant along the first row confirms 49. For \A_2: a = b = c = d = e = f = 1, so \operatorname{Pf}(\A_2) = 1 - 1 + 1 = 1 and \det\A_2 = 1. Both determinants are nonzero, so both matrices have rank 4, and by @cor-alternating-even-rank (b) both lie in the single congruence class of invertible alternating matrices in M_4(
Q): each is congruent to \vOmega_4, and therefore \A_1 \simeq \A_2. Note that the two have different determinants, 49 and 1; congruence changes the determinant by a square (@thm-congruence-determinant-class), and 49 = 7^2. [B3: Determine which of the following] Determine which of the following matrices are alternating, and for those that are, give the rank and the standard form \vOmega_{2m}\oplus\O_{n-2m} it is congruent to. Justify your answer. 1.  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 5 \ -5 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} over 
Q. 2.  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} over 
Q. 3.  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} over 
F_2. 4. The 5	imes 5 matrix with a_{ij} = j - i over 
Q. (a) Alternating: zero diagonal and a_{21} = -a_{12}. Its determinant is 25 
e 0, so the rank is 2 and it is congruent to \vOmega_2. (Explicitly, scaling the second basis vector by 1/5 does it.) (b) Not alternating. It is symmetric with a_{12} = 1 
e -1 = -a_{21}, so it is not even skew-symmetric over 
Q. (c) Alternating. Over 
F_2 we have 1 = -1, so the matrix is skew-symmetric, and its diagonal is zero. Its determinant is -1 = 1 
e 0, so the rank is 2 and it is congruent to \vOmega_2 =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} — it is \vOmega_2, since -1 = 1. Comparing (b) and (c): the same array of symbols is alternating over one field and not over another. (d) Alternating: a_{ii} = 0 and a_{ji} = i - j = -a_{ij}. Its rank is even by @cor-alternating-even-rank (a), and it is not zero, so the rank is 2 or 4. Every row is a combination of (1,2,3,4,5) and (1,1,1,1,1): indeed row i is (j - i)_j = (1,2,3,4,5) - i(1,1,1,1,1). So the row space has dimension at most 2, and rows 1 and 2 are independent, giving rank exactly 2. Hence the matrix is congruent to \vOmega_2 \oplus \O_3. In particular it is singular, as @cor-alternating-even-rank (d) requires for odd size. C. Going deeper [C1: Lagrangian subspaces] Let  eta be a symplectic form on V with \dim V = 2m (@def-darboux-basis), and call a subspace U \subseteq V totally isotropic if  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{u}') = 0 for all \elem{u}, \elem{u}' \in U. 1. Prove that \Span(\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_m) is totally isotropic, for any symplectic basis. 2. Prove that every totally isotropic subspace satisfies \dim U \le m. 3. Deduce that a symplectic form on a space of dimension 2m has a totally isotropic subspace of dimension exactly m, and no larger one. (These are the Lagrangian subspaces.) Hint for (b): compare U with U^{\perp_ eta} of @exr-bilinear-forms-c2. (a) By @thm-symplectic-standard-form,  eta(\elem{u}_i, \elem{u}_j) = 0 for all i, j. A general pair of elements of the span is \sum_i c_i\elem{u}_i and \sum_j d_j\elem{u}_j, and bilinearity gives \sum_{i,j} c_id_j eta(\elem{u}_i,\elem{u}_j) = 0. (b) Let U be totally isotropic. By definition  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = 0 for all \elem{u} \in U and all \elem{v} \in U, so U \subseteq U^{\perp_ eta}. Since  eta is nondegenerate, \dim U^{\perp_ eta} = 2m - \dim U by @exr-bilinear-forms-c2 (b). Therefore \dim U \le 2m - \dim U , that is 2\dim U \le 2m. Both sides are integers, so \dim U \le m. (No division by 2 inside the field occurs here: the inequality is between integers, not field elements, so the argument is valid in every characteristic.) (c) The subspace of (a) has dimension m, since the \elem{u}_i are part of a basis, and it is totally isotropic; by (b) no totally isotropic subspace has dimension greater than m. [C2: The inverse of an alternating matrix] Let F be any field. 1. Prove that every alternating matrix of odd size over F is singular, without using determinants. 2. Let \A \in M_n(F) be alternating and invertible. Prove that \A^{-1} is alternating. Hint for (b): the adjugate. The (i,i) entry of \adj\A is a minor of \A of size n - 1. (a) This is @cor-alternating-even-rank (d): by @thm-symplectic-standard-form the rank is even, and an even number that is at most an odd n is at most n - 1, so the matrix is not invertible. The proof of the standard form uses no determinants. (b) Since \A is invertible, @thm-adjugate-identity gives \A^{-1} = (\det\A)^{-1}\adj\A. First, skewness: (\A^{-1})	p = (\A	p)^{-1} = (-\A)^{-1} = -\A^{-1}, using @thm-transpose-properties and the fact that inversion turns -\A = (-1)\A into (-1)^{-1}\A^{-1} = -\A^{-1}. Now the diagonal. By @def-adjugate the (i,i) entry of \adj\A is the cofactor C_{ii} = (-1)^{2i}M_{ii} = M_{ii}, the determinant of the matrix obtained from \A by deleting row i and column i. Deleting a row and the matching column of an alternating matrix leaves an alternating matrix, since the surviving entries keep their positions relative to the diagonal. Its size is n - 1, and n is even by @cor-alternating-even-rank (a) applied to the invertible \A; so n - 1 is odd and M_{ii} = 0 by (a). Hence every diagonal entry of \A^{-1} is 0, and with skewness this makes \A^{-1} alternating. [C3: Counting over a finite field] Let q be a power of an odd prime. 1. How many alternating bilinear forms are there on 
F_q^{2m}? How many symmetric ones? 2. How many of the alternating forms on 
F_q^{2} are nondegenerate, and how many congruence classes do they fall into? 3. How many of the symmetric forms on 
F_q^{1} are nondegenerate, and how many congruence classes do they fall into? Hint: the squaring map 
F_q^{	imes} 	o 
F_q^{	imes} has kernel \{1, -1\}. 4. Explain in one or two sentences why the answers to (b) and (c) differ, in terms of what a change of basis can do to the single free parameter in each case. (a) By @thm-form-matrix-determines (c), forms correspond bijectively to matrices, so we count matrices. An alternating matrix of size n = 2m is determined freely by its entries above the diagonal, of which there are  inom{n}{2} = m(2m-1); so there are q^{m(2m-1)} alternating forms. A symmetric matrix is determined freely by its entries on and above the diagonal,  inom{n}{2} + n = m(2m+1) of them, giving q^{m(2m+1)}. (b) The alternating forms on 
F_q^2 have matrices  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & a \ -a & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, so there are q of them, and the nondegenerate ones are those with a 
e 0, of which there are q - 1. By @cor-alternating-even-rank (b) all of these have rank 2 and so lie in a single congruence class. (c) A symmetric form on 
F_q^{1} has matrix [d] and is nondegenerate exactly when d 
e 0, so there are q - 1 of them. Congruence in size 1 replaces d by p^2 d with p 
e 0 (@def-congruent), so the classes are the cosets of the subgroup of squares in 
F_q^{	imes}. The squaring homomorphism

ot\simeq [2]. (d) In the alternating case a change of basis may replace a by ca for any c 
e 0, because the two slots of  eta(\elem{u}, \elem{w}) hold different basis vectors and only one of them need be rescaled. In the symmetric case the parameter sits in  eta(\elem{v},\elem{v}), where both slots hold the same vector, so rescaling changes d to c^2d — by a square only.
