Compute the six values  eta(\cvec{e}_i, \cvec{f}_j), where (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) and (\cvec{f}_1, \cvec{f}_2, \cvec{f}_3) are the standard bases. 3. Write  eta in the basis \{E^{r}_{(i,j)}\} of @thm-multilinear-maps-dimension, and say how many of the 12 coefficients are nonzero. (a) Freeze \cvec{y}. Each output coordinate is a fixed linear combination of x_1 and x_2, hence a linear functional of \cvec{x} (@thm-functionals-on-fn), and a map into F^2 whose coordinates are linear is linear. Freeze \cvec{x}: each output coordinate is a fixed linear combination of y_1, y_2, y_3, and the same argument applies. So  eta is bilinear. (b) Substituting the standard basis vectors:  egin{aligned}  eta(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{f}_1) &= (1, 0), &  eta(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{f}_2) &= (0, 1), &  eta(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{f}_3) &= (0, 0), \  eta(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{f}_1) &= (0, 1), &  eta(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{f}_2) &= (0, 0), &  eta(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{f}_3) &= (-2, 0). \end{aligned} (c) Reading the coordinates off, c_{(1,1),1} = 1, c_{(1,2),2} = 1, c_{(2,1),2} = 1, and c_{(2,3),1} = -2, all others zero. Hence  eta = E^{1}_{(1,1)} + E^{2}_{(1,2)} + E^{2}_{(2,1)} - 2\,E^{1}_{(2,3)}, so 4 of the 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 12 coefficients are nonzero. C. Going deeper [C1: Bilinear forms on coordinate spaces are matrices] Let m, n \ge 1. 1. Prove that for every bilinear  eta \colon F^m 	imes F^n 	o F there is a unique \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) with  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} for all \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}. 2. Hence deduce that \dim \cM(F^m, F^n; F) = mn, and check that this agrees with @eq-multilinear-dimension. Hint for (a): the entries of \A can only be the values of  eta on pairs of standard basis vectors. (a) Existence. Put a_{ij} \coloneqq  eta(\cvec{e}_i, \cvec{f}_j), where (\cvec{e}_i) and (\cvec{f}_j) are the standard bases of F^m and F^n, and let \A = (a_{ij}). For \cvec{x} = \sum_i x_i\cvec{e}_i and \cvec{y} = \sum_j y_j\cvec{f}_j, expanding one slot at a time by @def-multilinear-map gives  eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = \sum_{i, j} x_iy_j\, eta(\cvec{e}_i, \cvec{f}_j) = \sum_{i,j} x_ia_{ij}y_j = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} . Uniqueness. If \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} = \cvec{x}	p\A'\cvec{y} for all \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}, take \cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_i and \cvec{y} = \cvec{f}_j: the left side is a_{ij} and the right side is a'_{ij}. Hence \A = \A'. (b) By (a) the map \cM(F^m, F^n; F) 	o M_{m 	imes n}(F),  eta \mapsto \A, is a bijection, and it is linear because the entries  eta(\cvec{e}_i, \cvec{f}_j) depend linearly on  eta by the definition of the pointwise operations. So it is an isomorphism, and \dim \cM(F^m, F^n; F) = \dim M_{m	imes n}(F) = mn by @thm-isomorphic-iff-same-dimension. @eq-multilinear-dimension gives 1 \cdot m \cdot n = mn, the same value. [C2: Linear and bilinear at once] Let V, W, Z be vector spaces over F and let  eta \colon V 	imes W 	o Z be a function. 1. Prove that if  eta is both bilinear and linear as a map on the product space V 	imes W, then  eta is the zero map. 2. Give an example, with V = W = Z = F, of a nonzero bilinear map and a nonzero linear map on the product, and say which property each one fails. 3. Does (a) still hold when V = \{\elem{0}\}? Explain what the statement says in that case. (a) Let \elem{v} \in V and \elem{w} \in W. In the product space, (\elem{v}, \elem{w}) = (\elem{v}, \elem{0}) + (\elem{0}, \elem{w}). Since  eta is linear on the product,  eta(\elem{v}, \elem{w}) =  eta(\elem{v}, \elem{0}) +  eta(\elem{0}, \elem{w}). Since  eta is bilinear, freezing the first slot at \elem{v} makes \elem{y} \mapsto  eta(\elem{v}, \elem{y}) linear, so  eta(\elem{v}, \elem{0}) = \elem{0} by @thm-zero-maps-to-zero; freezing the second slot at \elem{w} gives  eta(\elem{0}, \elem{w}) = \elem{0} likewise. Therefore  eta(\elem{v}, \elem{w}) = \elem{0} for all \elem{v}, \elem{w}, that is,  eta = 0. (b) The product \mu(a, b) = ab is bilinear and fails linearity on the product, since \mu(2 \cdot (1,1)) = 4 
e 2\mu(1,1). The sum \sigma(a, b) = a + b is linear on the product and fails bilinearity, since \sigma(0, 1) = 1

(c) Yes, but it says nothing: if V = \{\elem{0}\} then \elem{v} = \elem{0} always, and the only function \{\elem{0}\} 	imes W 	o Z that is bilinear is already the zero map, since  eta(\elem{0}, \elem{w}) = \elem{0}. The content of (a) appears only when both V and W are nonzero and Z

title: 15.2 The Tensor Product
content: The Tensor Product The previous section ended with a wish: a space through which every bilinear map out of V \times W becomes a linear map. This section grants it. The object is called the tensor product, and building it is the main technical work of the chapter — but the way we go about it matters more than the object itself, because the same three moves recur four more times, for the tensor algebra, the symmetric powers, the exterior powers and the Clifford algebra. The three moves are: state what the object must do, in the form of a property of the maps out of it; prove that any two objects doing it are isomorphic by a unique isomorphism, using nothing but that property; and only then construct one, to know that the definition is not empty. The middle move is what licenses the word “the”. @thm-tensor-unique below is written out at full length and is the template for the rest of the chapter, so it is worth reading twice. Throughout, F is a field and all vector spaces are over F. No finite-dimensionality is assumed until we reach bases, where it is stated. What the object has to do Here is the goal, stated before its terms are defined. We want a space X and a bilinear map \tau \colon V \times W \to X such that every bilinear map \beta out of V \times W can be pushed through \tau, and what comes out the other side is linear. Two demands hide in that sentence. There must be at least one way to push \beta through, or the property is useless; and at most one, or we cannot recover \beta from its linear shadow. So we ask for existence and uniqueness together. A tensor product is the most efficient bilinear map out of V \times W: every other one is it, followed by a single linear map. [Tensor Product] Let V and W be vector spaces over F. A tensor product of V and W is a pair (X, \tau), where X is a vector space over F and \tau \colon V \times W \to X is a bilinear map, satisfying: 1. (universal property) For every vector space Z over F and every bilinear map \beta \colon V \times W \to Z, there is a unique linear map \bar\beta \colon X \to Z with \bar\beta \circ \tau = \beta. In words, clause by clause. For every Z: the property is a demand about all targets at once, not about one favorite target. Every bilinear \beta: the arbitrary bilinear map is the input; nothing is assumed about it beyond @def-multilinear-map with k = 2. There is a unique linear \bar\beta: exactly one, so both existence and uniqueness are being asserted. With \bar\beta \circ \tau = \beta: this is an equality of functions on V \times W, namely \bar\beta(\tau(\elem{v}, \elem{w})) = \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{w}) for all \elem{v}, \elem{w}. We say \beta factors through \tau, and picture it as a triangle: the two routes from V \times W to Z, one direct and one through X, give the same answer. Notice what the definition does not say. It says nothing about the elements of X, nothing about a formula, and nothing about a basis: it is a statement purely about maps. That is deliberate, since a definition naming elements would depend on a construction, and there are several. The definition does not say that every element of X has the form \tau(\elem{v}, \elem{w}). It says that the values \tau(\elem{v}, \elem{w}) are enough to determine a linear map on X — which, as we prove below, means they span X, not that they exhaust it. Sums of them are generally not of that form. This is the single most common misreading of the tensor product, and we return to it with a proof at the end of the section. Any two tensor products are the same Before building anything, we settle the word “the”. If two pairs both satisfy (T1), each one’s property produces a map to the other, and the composites have no choice but to be identities. This is the argument Chapter 14 used for the Clifford algebra (@prp-clifford-uniqueness), and it is the argument we will use in four more sections. [Uniqueness of the Tensor Product] Let V and W be vector spaces over F, and let (X, \tau) and (X', \tau') both be tensor products of V and W. Then there is a unique isomorphism \varphi \colon X \to X' with \varphi \circ \tau = \tau'. Three steps. ① Each pair’s universal property, applied with the other pair’s bilinear map as input, produces a linear map; so we get \varphi \colon X \to X' and \psi \colon X' \to X at once, for free. ② Compose them. The composite \psi\varphi is a linear self-map of X that does nothing to \tau — and so is the identity. ③ The uniqueness half of (T1), applied with Z = X and \beta = \tau, says there is only one linear self-map doing nothing to \tau. So the two coincide. The uniqueness half is the engine; without it the argument produces two maps and no reason for them to be inverse. Step 1. The map \tau' \colon V \times W \to X' is bilinear. Apply (T1) for (X, \tau) with Z = X' and \beta = \tau': there is a unique linear \varphi \colon X \to X' with \varphi \circ \tau = \tau'. Symmetrically, applying (T1) for (X', \tau') with Z = X and \beta = \tau gives a unique linear \psi \colon X' \to X with \psi \circ \tau' = \tau. Step 2. The composite \psi\varphi \colon X \to X is linear (@thm-composition-linear (a)), and (\psi\varphi) \circ \tau = \psi \circ (\varphi \circ \tau) = \psi \circ \tau' = \tau . The identity \id_X is also linear and satisfies \id_X \circ \tau = \tau. Step 3. Apply (T1) for (X, \tau) with Z = X and \beta = \tau, which is bilinear by hypothesis. It says there is exactly one linear map X \to X whose composite with \tau is \tau. Both \psi\varphi and \id_X are such maps. Hence \psi\varphi = \id_X. Swapping the roles of (X, \tau) and (X', \tau') gives \varphi\psi = \id_{X'}. So \varphi has a two-sided inverse and is a bijection, hence an isomorphism (@thm-inverse-is-linear). It is the unique isomorphism with \varphi \circ \tau = \tau', because (T1) already produced it as the unique linear map with that property, and an isomorphism is in particular linear. This proves the theorem. Aftermath, and the template. Read the proof again with the names removed. It says: an object defined by a universal property is determined up to a unique isomorphism compatible with its structure map, because each object’s property hands you a comparison map, and the uniqueness clause forces the composites to be identities. Nothing in it used bilinearity, or vector spaces, or two factors. Sections 06, 07, 08, and 10 define the tensor algebra, the symmetric power, the exterior power, and the Clifford algebra by universal properties of exactly this shape, and each time the uniqueness proof is these three steps with different letters. When you meet them, do not reread the argument; recognize it. Because of @thm-tensor-unique we may now speak of the tensor product and fix notation. [Notation for Tensors] When a tensor product of V and W exists, we write it V \otimes W, write \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} for \tau(\elem{v}, \elem{w}), and call an element of the form \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} a simple tensor (also called a pure or decomposable tensor). The defining property then reads: every bilinear \beta \colon V \times W \to Z has a unique linear \bar\beta \colon V \otimes W \to Z with \bar\beta(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{w}). Bilinearity of \tau, rewritten in this notation, gives the rules we compute with: \begin{aligned} (\elem{v} + \elem{v}') \otimes \elem{w} &= \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} + \elem{v}' \otimes \elem{w}, \\ \elem{v} \otimes (\elem{w} + \elem{w}') &= \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} + \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}', \\ (c\elem{v}) \otimes \elem{w} = c(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) &= \elem{v} \otimes (c\elem{w}) . \end{aligned} The third line is the one to remember: a scalar moves freely across the \otimes sign. That is the whole reason \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} does not determine \elem{v} and \elem{w}. Building one: a free space modulo relations Uniqueness is worthless if nothing satisfies (T1), so we construct a tensor product. The strategy is the one named in the chapter introduction: take a space in which the symbols \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} are completely unrelated, then divide out exactly the relations bilinearity demands. Both halves need a tool. The first tool is a space with a basis indexed by an arbitrary set. It is the space of finitely supported functions, which Chapter 1 met for S = \nN (@exr-infinite-dimensional-b1). [Free Vector Space on a Set] Let S be a set and F a field. The free vector space on S over F is F^{(S)} \coloneqq \{\, f \colon S \to F \ :\ f(s) = 0 \text{ for all but finitely many } s \,\}, a subset of the space F^{S} of all functions S \to F (@exm-vector-spaces (d)), with the pointwise operations. For s \in S, let \delta_s \in F^{(S)} be the function with \delta_s(s) = 1 and \delta_s(t) = 0 for t \ne s. [Universal Property of the Free Vector Space] Let S be a set and F a field. 1. F^{(S)} is a subspace of F^{S}, and \{\delta_s : s \in S\} is a basis of it. 2. For every vector space Z over F and every function g \colon S \to Z — no structure on g is assumed, since S is only a set — there is exactly one linear map \bar g \colon F^{(S)} \to Z with \bar g(\delta_s) = g(s) for all s \in S. (a) We use @thm-subspace-test. The zero function vanishes everywhere, so it lies in F^{(S)}. If f, h \in F^{(S)} vanish outside the finite sets A and B, then f + h vanishes outside A \cup B, which is finite, and cf vanishes outside A. So F^{(S)} is a subspace. Each \delta_s lies in F^{(S)}. Spanning: if f \in F^{(S)} is nonzero exactly on the finite set \{s_1, \dots, s_r\}, then f and \sum_{i} f(s_i)\delta_{s_i} take the same value at every point of S, hence are equal. Independence: if \sum_{i} a_i\delta_{s_i} = 0 for distinct s_1, \dots, s_r, evaluate at s_j to get a_j = 0. By @def-basis, \{\delta_s\} is a basis, possibly infinite in the sense of @thm-basis-extension-general. (b) Immediate from (a) and @thm-linear-map-from-any-basis, which prescribes a linear map arbitrarily on a basis, in one and only one way. In words: a function on a set becomes a linear map on the free space, for free. That is the point of the construction, and the whole of it: F^{(S)} imposes no relations among the \delta_s, so nothing can obstruct a prescription. The second tool is the quotient. Chapter 2 recorded exactly the statement we need: a linear map that kills a subspace U passes, in exactly one way, to a linear map on V/U (@thm-quotient-universal-property (a)). We use it in the form “to define a map out of a quotient, define it upstairs and check it kills the relations”. [Existence of the Tensor Product] For every pair of vector spaces V, W over F, a tensor product (X, \tau) of V and W exists. Write down the symbols \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} as a basis of a huge space P, one basis vector for each pair of vectors — so at this stage \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} has no properties at all. The four bilinearity rules are then four families of elements of P that we want to be zero, so divide by the subspace they span. A bilinear \beta becomes a linear map on P by @lem-free-vector-space, kills each relation because it is bilinear, and therefore passes to the quotient by @thm-quotient-universal-property. Uniqueness of the induced map is spanning: the cosets of the basis vectors span the quotient. Let S = V \times W, regarded as a set, and let P = F^{(S)} be the free vector space on it (@def-free-vector-space), with basis \{\delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w})}\}. Let R \subseteq P be the span of all elements of the four forms \begin{aligned} &\delta_{(\elem{v} + \elem{v}',\, \elem{w})} - \delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w})} - \delta_{(\elem{v}', \elem{w})}, \qquad \delta_{(\elem{v},\, \elem{w} + \elem{w}')} - \delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w})} - \delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w}')}, \\ &\delta_{(c\elem{v},\, \elem{w})} - c\,\delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w})}, \qquad\qquad\qquad\ \ \delta_{(\elem{v},\, c\elem{w})} - c\,\delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w})}, \end{aligned} taken over all \elem{v}, \elem{v}' \in V, all \elem{w}, \elem{w}' \in W, and all c \in F. A span is a subspace, so R is one. Put X \coloneqq P/R, \qquad \tau(\elem{v}, \elem{w}) \coloneqq \pi\bigl(\delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w})}\bigr), where \pi \colon P \to P/R is the quotient map, which is linear with kernel R (@thm-quotient-space-operations-well-defined). \tau is bilinear. The element \delta_{(\elem{v} + \elem{v}', \elem{w})} - \delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w})} - \delta_{(\elem{v}', \elem{w})} lies in R = \ker \pi, so applying \pi and using its linearity gives \tau(\elem{v} + \elem{v}', \elem{w}) - \tau(\elem{v}, \elem{w}) - \tau(\elem{v}', \elem{w}) = \elem{0}. The other three families give, in the same way, additivity in the second slot and the two scalar rules. These are the clauses of @def-multilinear-map for k = 2. (T1), existence. Let Z be a vector space and \beta \colon V \times W \to Z bilinear. Regarding \beta as a function on the set S, @lem-free-vector-space (b) gives a unique linear b \colon P \to Z with b(\delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w})}) = \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{w}). It kills every generator of R: for instance b\bigl(\delta_{(\elem{v} + \elem{v}', \elem{w})} - \delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w})} - \delta_{(\elem{v}', \elem{w})}\bigr) = \beta(\elem{v} + \elem{v}', \elem{w}) - \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{w}) - \beta(\elem{v}', \elem{w}) = \elem{0} because \beta is linear in its first slot, and the other three families vanish by the other three clauses of bilinearity. Since b is linear and vanishes on a spanning set of R, it vanishes on R (@thm-linear-combination); that is, R \subseteq \ker b. By @thm-quotient-universal-property (a) there is exactly one linear \bar\beta \colon X \to Z with \bar\beta \circ \pi = b, and then \bar\beta(\tau(\elem{v}, \elem{w})) = \bar\beta\bigl(\pi(\delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w})})\bigr) = b\bigl(\delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w})}\bigr) = \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{w}), so \bar\beta \circ \tau = \beta. (T1), uniqueness. Suppose L \colon X \to Z is linear with L \circ \tau = \beta. Since \pi is surjective and the \delta_{(\elem{v}, \elem{w})} span P, the elements \tau(\elem{v}, \elem{w}) = \pi(\delta_{(\elem{v},\elem{w})}) span X. On each of them, L and \bar\beta agree, both giving \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{w}). Two linear maps that agree on a spanning set agree everywhere, by @thm-linear-combination. Hence L = \bar\beta. So (X, \tau) satisfies (T1), which proves the theorem. Aftermath. The construction is ugly and the object is not. That is normal for a universal property: the model is a scaffolding, and after this proof we never open it again. Every later fact about V \otimes W in this book is derived from (T1), never from cosets of formal sums — which is also why the identification F^m \otimes F^n \cong M_{m \times n}(F) below is legitimate as an alternative model, and much more pleasant to compute in. One property is worth extracting at once, because we will use it constantly and because it is the second appearance of the self-map trick. [Simple Tensors Span] Let (V \otimes W, \tau) be a tensor product. Then V \otimes W = \Span\{\, \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} : \elem{v} \in V, \ \elem{w} \in W \,\}. Let Y = \Span\{\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}\}, a subspace of V \otimes W, and let j \colon Y \to V \otimes W be the inclusion, which is linear. Restricting the codomain of \tau gives a bilinear map \tau_Y \colon V \times W \to Y, (\elem{v}, \elem{w}) \mapsto \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}; it is bilinear because \tau is and because Y is a subspace, so the identities hold already in Y. By (T1) with Z = Y there is a linear L \colon V \otimes W \to Y with L \circ \tau = \tau_Y. Then jL is a linear self-map of V \otimes W with jL\tau = j\tau_Y = \tau, and so is \id. By the uniqueness clause of (T1) with Z = V \otimes W and \beta = \tau, we get jL = \id. Hence j is surjective, so Y = V \otimes W. That proof used no basis, no construction, and no finite dimension — only (T1). It is the same three lines as Step 1 of @prp-clifford-spanning’s proof in Chapter 14, where the generated subalgebra was shown to be everything. Once you see “a subobject that receives the structure map must be the whole thing”, you can reuse it verbatim. A basis and a dimension Now we can count. The prediction at the end of the previous section was \dim(V \otimes W) = (\dim V)(\dim W), and here it is, with a basis attached. [Basis of a Tensor Product] Let V and W be finite-dimensional, with bases (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) of V and (\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_m) of W. Then the nm simple tensors \elem{v}_i \otimes \elem{w}_j, \qquad 1 \le i \le n, \quad 1 \le j \le m, form a basis of V \otimes W. In particular \dim(V \otimes W) = (\dim V)(\dim W). Spanning is bilinearity: expand both slots of a simple tensor and use @prp-simple-tensors-span. Independence needs linear functionals on V \otimes W that pick out one coefficient — and (T1) manufactures functionals out of bilinear forms, while @thm-dual-basis supplies all the bilinear forms we could want, namely (\elem{x}, \elem{y}) \mapsto \varphi_p(\elem{x})\psi_q(\elem{y}). Spanning. By @prp-simple-tensors-span it suffices to write each simple tensor in terms of the listed ones. Let \elem{v} = \sum_i a_i\elem{v}_i and \elem{w} = \sum_j b_j\elem{w}_j. Expanding one slot at a time by the rules following @def-tensor-notation, \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} = \Bigl(\sum_i a_i \elem{v}_i\Bigr) \otimes \Bigl(\sum_j b_j\elem{w}_j\Bigr) = \sum_{i,j} a_ib_j\,(\elem{v}_i \otimes \elem{w}_j). Independence. Let (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n) and (\psi_1, \dots, \psi_m) be the bases of V^{*} and W^{*} dual to the given ones, so \varphi_p(\elem{v}_i) = \delta_{pi} and \psi_q(\elem{w}_j) = \delta_{qj} (@thm-dual-basis). Fix p and q. The function \beta_{pq} \colon V \times W \to F, \qquad \beta_{pq}(\elem{x}, \elem{y}) = \varphi_p(\elem{x})\,\psi_q(\elem{y}), is bilinear: freezing \elem{y} leaves \psi_q(\elem{y})\varphi_p, a scalar multiple of a linear functional, and symmetrically. By (T1) there is a linear f_{pq} \colon V \otimes W \to F with f_{pq}(\elem{x} \otimes \elem{y}) = \varphi_p(\elem{x})\psi_q(\elem{y}); in particular f_{pq}(\elem{v}_i \otimes \elem{w}_j) = \delta_{pi}\delta_{qj}. Now suppose \sum_{i,j} c_{ij}\,(\elem{v}_i \otimes \elem{w}_j) = \elem{0}. Apply f_{pq}. By linearity the left side becomes \sum_{i,j} c_{ij}\delta_{pi}\delta_{qj} = c_{pq}, and the right side is 0. Hence c_{pq} = 0. Since p and q were arbitrary, all coefficients vanish. So the nm listed tensors form a basis, and \dim(V \otimes W) = nm. This proves the theorem. Aftermath: the count agrees. We found \dim \cM(V, W; Z) = (\dim Z)(\dim V)(\dim W) in @thm-multilinear-maps-dimension, and we argued that a universal object X would have to satisfy \dim \cL(X, Z) = \dim \cM(V, W; Z), forcing \dim X = (\dim V)(\dim W). @thm-tensor-basis delivers exactly that number, and the agreement is not a coincidence — it is the universal property, counted. Here is the statement behind it. [Bilinear Maps Are Linear Maps on the Tensor Product] Let V, W, Z be vector spaces over F. The map \Xi \colon \cL(V \otimes W, Z) \to \cM(V, W; Z), \qquad L \mapsto L \circ \tau, is an isomorphism of vector spaces. When V, W, and Z are finite-dimensional, both sides have dimension (\dim Z)(\dim V)(\dim W). \Xi lands where claimed: L \circ \tau is bilinear, since freezing one slot of \tau gives a linear map and composing with the linear L keeps it linear (@thm-composition-linear (a)). It is linear in L by @thm-composition-linear (d), which gives (L_1 + L_2) \circ \tau = L_1\tau + L_2\tau and (cL)\circ\tau = c(L\tau). It is surjective by the existence half of (T1) and injective by the uniqueness half: if L\tau = 0, then both L and the zero map are linear maps composing with \tau to give the zero bilinear map, so L = 0, and @thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel applies. The dimension count is @thm-multilinear-maps-dimension on one side and @thm-linear-maps-isomorphic-to-matrices together with @thm-tensor-basis on the other. What is V \otimes W when W = F, viewed as a one-dimensional space over itself? What is it when W = \{\elem{0}\}? For W = F: \dim(V \otimes F) = (\dim V) \cdot 1 = \dim V by @thm-tensor-basis, and indeed \elem{v} \mapsto \elem{v} \otimes 1 is an isomorphism V \to V \otimes F, since it carries a basis (\elem{v}_i) to the basis (\elem{v}_i \otimes 1). For W = \{\elem{0}\}: the dimension is 0, so V \otimes \{\elem{0}\} = \{\elem{0}\}. Both are the degenerate cases one should be able to predict from the product formula, and both come out right. Coordinates: the tensor product of coordinate spaces An abstract object is easier to trust once it has a concrete model. For coordinate spaces there is a very good one: F^m \otimes F^n is the space of m \times n matrices, with the simple tensor \cvec{x} \otimes \cvec{y} corresponding to the outer product \cvec{x}\cvec{y}\tp. [F^m \otimes F^n \cong M_{m \times n}(F)] Let m, n \ge 1. There is a unique linear map \Theta \colon F^m \otimes F^n \to M_{m \times n}(F), \qquad \Theta(\cvec{x} \otimes \cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}\cvec{y}\tp, and it is an isomorphism, carrying \cvec{e}_i \otimes \cvec{f}_j to the matrix unit \E_{ij}. Under \Theta, the simple tensors correspond exactly to the matrices of rank at most 1. The map (\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) \mapsto \cvec{x}\cvec{y}\tp is bilinear: its (i, j) entry is x_iy_j, and with \cvec{y} frozen, (\cvec{x} + \cvec{x}')\cvec{y}\tp = \cvec{x}\cvec{y}\tp + \cvec{x}'\cvec{y}\tp and (c\cvec{x})\cvec{y}\tp = c(\cvec{x}\cvec{y}\tp) by @thm-matrix-multiplication-properties (2) and (4); freezing \cvec{x} is the same computation (@exr-multilinear-maps-b1 (c)). By (T1) there is a unique linear \Theta with \Theta(\cvec{x} \otimes \cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}\cvec{y}\tp. On standard basis vectors, \cvec{e}_i\cvec{f}_j\tp has a single 1 in position (i, j), so \Theta(\cvec{e}_i \otimes \cvec{f}_j) = \E_{ij}. By @thm-tensor-basis the mn tensors \cvec{e}_i \otimes \cvec{f}_j form a basis of F^m \otimes F^n, and the mn matrix units form a basis of M_{m \times n}(F) (@exm-standard-bases (c)). By @thm-linear-transform-basis there is a linear \Psi \colon M_{m \times n}(F) \to F^m \otimes F^n with \Psi(\E_{ij}) = \cvec{e}_i \otimes \cvec{f}_j. Then \Psi\Theta and \Theta\Psi are linear maps fixing a basis, hence are the identities by the uniqueness half of @thm-linear-transform-basis. So \Theta is an isomorphism. For the last claim, a nonzero \cvec{x}\cvec{y}\tp is a product of an m \times 1 and a 1 \times n matrix, so it has rank 1 by @prp-rank-minimal-factorization; and \cvec{x}\cvec{y}\tp = \O when \cvec{x} = \cvec{0} or \cvec{y} = \cvec{0}, of rank 0. Conversely, a matrix \A of rank 1 factors as \A = \cvec{x}\cvec{y}\tp with \cvec{x} \in F^m and \cvec{y}\tp \in M_{1 \times n}(F), again by @prp-rank-minimal-factorization, and the zero matrix is \cvec{0} \otimes \cvec{0}. This proves the theorem. [Computing in F^2 \otimes F^3] Work in F^2 \otimes F^3 with standard bases (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) and (\cvec{f}_1, \cvec{f}_2, \cvec{f}_3). 1. Expand (\cvec{e}_1 + 2\cvec{e}_2) \otimes (3\cvec{f}_1 - \cvec{f}_2) in the basis of @thm-tensor-basis, and write the corresponding matrix. 2. Decide whether t = \cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{f}_1 + 2\,\cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{f}_2 + 3\,\cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{f}_1 + 6\,\cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{f}_2 is a simple tensor, and if so write it as one. 3. Decide whether u = \cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{f}_1 + \cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{f}_2 is a simple tensor. (a) Expanding one slot at a time, (\cvec{e}_1 + 2\cvec{e}_2) \otimes (3\cvec{f}_1 - \cvec{f}_2) = 3\,\cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{f}_1 - \cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{f}_2 + 6\,\cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{f}_1 - 2\,\cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{f}_2 . The coefficient of \cvec{e}_i \otimes \cvec{f}_j is the (i, j) entry of the matrix, so \Theta sends it to \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 6 & -2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, which is the outer product predicted by @thm-tensor-fn-matrices. (b) The coefficients give \Theta(t) = \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}. Its second row is 3 times its first, so every 2 \times 2 minor vanishes and the rank is 1 (@thm-rank-via-minors). By @thm-tensor-fn-matrices, t is simple. Factoring, \Theta(t) = (1, 3)\tp(1, 2, 0), so t = (\cvec{e}_1 + 3\cvec{e}_2) \otimes (\cvec{f}_1 + 2\cvec{f}_2), which expands back to t. (c) Here \Theta(u) = \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, whose first two columns are independent, so its rank is 2. By @thm-tensor-fn-matrices, u is not simple. No amount of rewriting will turn it into a single \cvec{v} \otimes \cvec{w}. Three things a tensor is not Part (c) above is not a curiosity; it is the central negative fact about tensor products, and the first of three misreadings worth naming before they happen. Not every tensor is simple [A tensor that is not simple] In F^2 \otimes F^2, the element u = \cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{e}_2 is not a simple tensor, for any field F. Two routes, and both are worth having. The quick one: \Theta(u) = \I_2, of rank 2, while simple tensors have rank at most 1. The portable one: suppose u = \cvec{v} \otimes \cvec{w}, hit it with the four coordinate functionals f_{pq} built in the proof of @thm-tensor-basis, and read off four scalar equations that cannot all hold. Suppose u = \cvec{v} \otimes \cvec{w} for some \cvec{v}, \cvec{w} \in F^2. Let (\varphi_1, \varphi_2) be the basis of (F^2)^{*} dual to (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2), and for p, q \in \{1, 2\} let f_{pq} \colon F^2 \otimes F^2 \to F be the linear map with f_{pq}(\cvec{x} \otimes \cvec{y}) = \varphi_p(\cvec{x})\varphi_q(\cvec{y}), supplied by (T1) as in the proof of @thm-tensor-basis. Applying f_{pq} to both sides of u = \cvec{v} \otimes \cvec{w} gives v_pw_q = f_{pq}(u) = \delta_{p1}\delta_{q1} + \delta_{p2}\delta_{q2}, that is, v_1w_1 = 1, v_2w_2 = 1, v_1w_2 = 0, and v_2w_1 = 0. From v_1w_1 = 1 we get v_1 \ne 0, so v_1w_2 = 0 forces w_2 = 0 — and then v_2w_2 = 0 \ne 1. This contradiction shows that no such \cvec{v}, \cvec{w} exist, so u is not simple. A general element of V \otimes W is a sum of simple tensors, not a simple tensor. @prp-simple-tensors-span says the simple tensors span; @exm-non-simple-tensor says they do not exhaust. A statement proved only for simple tensors is therefore proved for nothing until you extend it by linearity — which is legitimate precisely when the statement is about a linear map, and illegitimate when it is about, say, ranks or products. Whenever you want to define something on V \otimes W, do not write “define it on \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} and extend”: use (T1), which is that move done correctly. The smallest number of simple tensors needed to write a given tensor is a genuine invariant, and for coordinate spaces @thm-tensor-fn-matrices identifies it: it is the rank of the corresponding matrix. So “not simple” means “rank at least 2”. A later section meets the same failure for elements of \Lambda^2 V that are not wedges of two vectors, and the closing section meets it again under the name entanglement. A simple tensor vanishes only for an obvious reason [When a Simple Tensor Is Zero] Let V and W be finite-dimensional, \elem{v} \in V and \elem{w} \in W. Then \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} = \elem{0} if and only if \elem{v} = \elem{0} or \elem{w} = \elem{0}. (\Leftarrow) If \elem{v} = \elem{0}, then \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} = (0 \cdot \elem{0}) \otimes \elem{w} = 0(\elem{0} \otimes \elem{w}) = \elem{0}, using that a scalar passes across \otimes. The case \elem{w} = \elem{0} is the same with the slots swapped. (\Rightarrow) Suppose \elem{v} \ne \elem{0} and \elem{w} \ne \elem{0}. By @thm-functionals-separate-points (a) there are \varphi \in V^{*} and \psi \in W^{*} with \varphi(\elem{v}) = 1 and \psi(\elem{w}) = 1. The map (\elem{x}, \elem{y}) \mapsto \varphi(\elem{x})\psi(\elem{y}) is bilinear, so (T1) gives a linear f \colon V \otimes W \to F with f(\elem{x} \otimes \elem{y}) = \varphi(\elem{x})\psi(\elem{y}). Then f(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = 1 \ne 0, while f(\elem{0}) = 0. Hence \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} \ne \elem{0}. This proves the proposition. A product of nonzero things can be zero in many algebraic settings, but not here. It is tempting to expect V \otimes W to behave like a ring with zero divisors, so that some \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} vanishes accidentally. It does not: @prp-simple-tensor-zero says the only way to get \elem{0} is to feed in \elem{0}. The zero divisors appear one level later — in the algebras of the following sections, where products of nonzero sums of simple tensors can vanish. A simple tensor does not remember its factors [When Two Simple Tensors Agree] Let V and W be finite-dimensional, and let \elem{v}, \elem{v}' \in V and \elem{w}, \elem{w}' \in W with \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} \ne \elem{0}. Then \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} = \elem{v}' \otimes \elem{w}' if and only if there is a scalar c \ne 0 with \elem{v}' = c\elem{v} and \elem{w}' = c^{-1}\elem{w}. The “if” half is the scalar rule. For “only if”, the danger is that \elem{v}' points somewhere new. Suppose it does; then (\elem{v}, \elem{v}') is independent, so there is a functional killing \elem{v} and not \elem{v}', and the corresponding f on V \otimes W separates the two sides. (\Leftarrow) If \elem{v}' = c\elem{v} and \elem{w}' = c^{-1}\elem{w}, then \elem{v}' \otimes \elem{w}' = (c\elem{v}) \otimes (c^{-1}\elem{w}) = c c^{-1}(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}, moving each scalar across \otimes. (\Rightarrow) Suppose \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} = \elem{v}' \otimes \elem{w}' \ne \elem{0}. By @prp-simple-tensor-zero all four vectors are nonzero. Suppose, for a contradiction, that \elem{v}' \notin \Span(\elem{v}). Then (\elem{v}, \elem{v}') is linearly independent, so it extends to a basis of V (@thm-basis-extension), and the dual basis (@thm-dual-basis) provides \varphi \in V^{*} with \varphi(\elem{v}) = 0 and \varphi(\elem{v}') = 1. Since \elem{w}' \ne \elem{0}, @thm-functionals-separate-points (a) provides \psi \in W^{*} with \psi(\elem{w}') = 1. By (T1) there is a linear f \colon V \otimes W \to F with f(\elem{x} \otimes \elem{y}) = \varphi(\elem{x})\psi(\elem{y}). Evaluating both sides of \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} = \elem{v}' \otimes \elem{w}', 0 = \varphi(\elem{v})\psi(\elem{w}) = f(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = f(\elem{v}' \otimes \elem{w}') = \varphi(\elem{v}')\psi(\elem{w}') = 1, which is absurd. Hence \elem{v}' = c\elem{v} for some c \in F, and c \ne 0 because \elem{v}' \ne \elem{0}. Then \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} = (c\elem{v}) \otimes \elem{w}' = \elem{v} \otimes (c\elem{w}'), so \elem{v} \otimes (\elem{w} - c\elem{w}') = \elem{0} by bilinearity. Since \elem{v} \ne \elem{0}, @prp-simple-tensor-zero forces \elem{w} - c\elem{w}' = \elem{0}, that is, \elem{w}' = c^{-1}\elem{w}. This proves the proposition. \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} = \elem{v}' \otimes \elem{w}' does not mean \elem{v} = \elem{v}' and \elem{w} = \elem{w}'. Already 2\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} = \elem{v} \otimes 2\elem{w}, with different factors on the two sides. So “the first factor of a simple tensor” is not a well-defined function: writing t = \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} and then speaking of “the \elem{v} of t” is an error. What @prp-simple-tensor-equality salvages is that the lines \Span(\elem{v}) and \Span(\elem{w}) are determined, which is exactly the information carried by a rank-one matrix: its column space and its row space. In \nR^2 \otimes \nR^2, is \cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{e}_2 + \cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{e}_1 a simple tensor? No. Its matrix under \Theta is \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, of determinant -1 \ne 0, hence of rank 2 (@thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible). By @thm-tensor-fn-matrices a simple tensor would have rank at most 1. Note how little the symmetry of the expression helps: being a sum of two simple tensors is the generic situation, not a special one. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. (b) That any two tensor products of V and W are isomorphic by a unique isomorphism commuting with the two structure maps. The uniqueness clause: it says there is only one linear self-map X \to X composing with \tau to give \tau, and since both \psi\varphi and \id_X are such maps, they are equal. (c) (\dim V)(\dim W), with basis (\elem{v}_i \otimes \elem{w}_j) for bases (\elem{v}_i) of V and (\elem{w}_j) of W (@thm-tensor-basis). (d) False. In F^2 \otimes F^2, \cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{e}_2 is not simple (@exm-non-simple-tensor). (a) The map V \times W \to W \otimes V, (\elem{v}, \elem{w}) \mapsto \elem{w} \otimes \elem{v}, is bilinear, because \otimes is bilinear and swapping the slots exchanges the two clauses of @def-multilinear-map. By (T1) for V \otimes W there is a unique linear \sigma with \sigma(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = \elem{w} \otimes \elem{v}. Symmetrically, (T1) for W \otimes V gives a unique linear \sigma' \colon W \otimes V \to V \otimes W with \sigma'(\elem{w} \otimes \elem{v}) = \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}. Then \sigma'\sigma is a linear self-map of V \otimes W with (\sigma'\sigma)(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}, and so is the identity; by the uniqueness clause of (T1) applied with Z = V \otimes W and \beta = \tau, the two agree, so \sigma'\sigma = \id. Symmetrically \sigma\sigma' = \id. Hence \sigma is an isomorphism (@thm-inverse-is-linear). (b) With V = W, part (a) gives \sigma' = \sigma, since both are the unique linear map sending \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} to \elem{w} \otimes \elem{v}. Hence \sigma^2 = \sigma'\sigma = \id. (c) Every step used only (T1) and the bilinearity of \otimes. So the argument works for infinite-dimensional spaces, where @thm-tensor-basis is unavailable, and it produces a canonical isomorphism, whereas a basis-dependent construction would give one isomorphism per basis and no reason to prefer any of them. [C2: Recovering the factors from a simple tensor] Let V and W be finite-dimensional and let t = \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} \ne \elem{0}. 1. Prove that the subspace \Span(\elem{v}) \subseteq V depends only on t, not on the chosen factorization. 2. Prove the corresponding statement for \Span(\elem{w}) \subseteq W. 3. For V = F^m and W = F^n, identify these two subspaces in terms of the matrix \Theta(t) of @thm-tensor-fn-matrices, and say why (a) and (b) are then statements you already knew. (a) Suppose t = \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} = \elem{v}' \otimes \elem{w}' with t \ne \elem{0}. By @prp-simple-tensor-equality there is c \ne 0 with \elem{v}' = c\elem{v}. A nonzero scalar multiple spans the same subspace, so \Span(\elem{v}') = \Span(\elem{v}). Hence the line is determined by t alone. (b) The same proposition gives \elem{w}' = c^{-1}\elem{w} with c^{-1} \ne 0, so \Span(\elem{w}') = \Span(\elem{w}). (c) Under \Theta, t corresponds to \A = \cvec{v}\cvec{w}\tp, a matrix of rank 1 (@thm-tensor-fn-matrices). Every column of \A is a scalar multiple of \cvec{v}, and \A is nonzero, so \col(\A) = \Span(\cvec{v}); every row is a multiple of \cvec{w}\tp, so \row(\A) = \Span(\cvec{w}\tp). Thus (a) and (b) say that a matrix has a well-defined column space and row space, which Chapter 2 established long ago. The tensor language adds nothing here except the reason the statement looks surprising: it is surprising only if one expects \cvec{v} itself, rather than its line, to be recoverable.

title: 15.3 Tensor Products of Maps
content: Tensor Products of Maps Section 02 built the space V \otimes W. A construction on spaces is worth little until it acts on maps as well: the philosophy of the whole book has been objects first, then the maps between them. So given S \colon V \to V' and T \colon W \to W', we want a single map V \otimes W \to V' \otimes W' built from the two. This section builds it, computes its matrix, and discovers that the matrix is the Kronecker product of Chapter 8 — which pays both of the debts that Chapter 8 §04 left open. It ends with the identification V^{*} \otimes W \cong \cL(V, W), which every later section of the chapter uses. A map on each factor gives a map on the product The definition writes itself, and that is the danger. We want a map that sends \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} to S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w}, so the temptation is to write “Define (S \otimes T)(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) \coloneqq S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w}, and extend linearly.” Nothing in that sentence is a definition. Simple tensors span V \otimes W (@prp-simple-tensors-span), but they do not exhaust it, and worse, the expression of an element as a combination of them is wildly nonunique: \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} = (2\elem{v}) \otimes (\tfrac12\elem{w}), and \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} + \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}' = \elem{v} \otimes (\elem{w} + \elem{w}'). A formula prescribed on simple tensors may therefore assign two different values to one element, and then it defines nothing at all. Here is a formula that really does fail. Try to define g \colon V \otimes W \to V by g(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) \coloneqq \elem{v}. Taking \elem{w} = \elem{0} gives \elem{v} \otimes \elem{0} = \elem{0} (@prp-simple-tensor-zero), so g would have to send \elem{0} to every \elem{v} at once. To build a map out of V \otimes W, never write a formula on simple tensors: write down a bilinear map and let the universal property produce the linear one. That is the discipline of this chapter, and applied here it costs three lines. [Tensor Product of Two Linear Maps] Let V, V', W, W' be vector spaces over F, and let S \in \cL(V, V') and T \in \cL(W, W'). Then there is exactly one linear map f \colon V \otimes W \to V' \otimes W' with f(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} for all \elem{v} \in V and \elem{w} \in W. The assignment (\elem{v}, \elem{w}) \mapsto S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} is bilinear, because S and T are linear and \otimes is bilinear in its two slots. A bilinear map out of V \times W is exactly what the universal property consumes, and what it returns is a unique linear map out of V \otimes W. There is nothing else to check. Define \beta \colon V \times W \to V' \otimes W' by \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{w}) \coloneqq S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w}. Fix \elem{w} \in W. The map \elem{v} \mapsto S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} is the composite of S, which is linear, with the map \elem{u} \mapsto \elem{u} \otimes T\elem{w}, which is linear because the map \otimes \colon V' \times W' \to V' \otimes W' of @def-tensor-product is bilinear, hence linear in its first slot with the second slot held fixed. A composite of linear maps is linear (@thm-composition-linear), so \beta is linear in its first argument. Fixing \elem{v} instead and swapping the roles of the two slots gives linearity in the second. Hence \beta is bilinear. By the universal property in @def-tensor-product there is a unique linear f \colon V \otimes W \to V' \otimes W' with f(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{w}) = S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} for all \elem{v}, \elem{w}. This proves both existence and uniqueness. Uniqueness is what licenses a name. [Tensor product of linear maps] Let S \in \cL(V, V') and T \in \cL(W, W'). The tensor product of S and T is the unique linear map S \otimes T \colon V \otimes W \to V' \otimes W' of @thm-tensor-of-maps-well-defined, characterized by (S \otimes T)(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} \quad (\elem{v} \in V,\ \elem{w} \in W). The symbol \otimes now has three jobs — a space, a vector, a map — and they agree: S \otimes T applied to \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} is S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w}, which is the only thing the notation could mean. Examples. 1. The identity. \id_V \otimes \id_W sends \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} to \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}, and so does \id_{V \otimes W}. Both are linear and both are the factorization of the same bilinear map, so \id_V \otimes \id_W = \id_{V \otimes W} by the uniqueness clause. Degenerate, and used in almost every proof below. 2. Acting on one slot. S \otimes \id_W sends \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} to S\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}: it does S in the first slot and leaves the second alone. If V = W = F[x] and S = D is differentiation, D \otimes \id is “differentiate the first factor”. 3. Scalars. For c, d \in F, (c\,\id_V) \otimes (d\,\id_W) sends \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} to c\elem{v} \otimes d\elem{w} = cd\,(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}), so it is cd\,\id_{V \otimes W}. In particular a scalar may be moved from one slot to the other, which is the map-level shadow of c\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} = \elem{v} \otimes c\elem{w}. 4. Zero. If S = 0, then (S \otimes T)(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = \elem{0} \otimes T\elem{w} = \elem{0}, so S \otimes T = 0. The converse also holds; see @exr-tensor-products-of-maps-c1. Nonexample by minimal change. Keep S and T linear, but try to send \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} to S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} + \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}. This one is legitimate: the assignment (\elem{v}, \elem{w}) \mapsto S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} + \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} is a sum of two bilinear maps, hence bilinear, and the universal property applies. What is not legitimate is (\elem{v}, \elem{w}) \mapsto S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} + \elem{u}_0 for a fixed nonzero \elem{u}_0 \in V' \otimes W': the added constant destroys linearity in each slot, so no linear map on V \otimes W does this, and indeed the prescription contradicts itself at \elem{w} = \elem{0}. The exact clause that fails is bilinearity, and it fails for the same reason as in the map g above. We will lean repeatedly on the following consequence of the uniqueness clause. It replaces the phrase “and extend linearly”, which we are not allowed to use. [Simple Tensors Determine a Map] Let Z be a vector space over F and let f, g \colon V \otimes W \to Z be linear. If f(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = g(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) for all \elem{v} \in V and \elem{w} \in W, then f = g. Put \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{w}) \coloneqq f(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}). Since \otimes is bilinear and f is linear, \beta is bilinear. By hypothesis \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{w}) = g(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) as well, so f and g are both linear maps factoring \beta through \otimes. The universal property of @def-tensor-product says there is only one such map. Hence f = g. No finite-dimensionality is needed, and no basis is chosen. With it, the algebra of \otimes on maps is a formality. [Algebra of Tensor Products of Maps] Let S, S_1, S_2 \in \cL(V, V'), T, T_1, T_2 \in \cL(W, W'), and c \in F. Let also R \in \cL(V', V'') and U \in \cL(W', W''). Then: 1. (S_1 + S_2) \otimes T = S_1 \otimes T + S_2 \otimes T and S \otimes (T_1 + T_2) = S \otimes T_1 + S \otimes T_2; 2. (cS) \otimes T = c(S \otimes T) = S \otimes (cT); 3. (R \otimes U)(S \otimes T) = RS \otimes UT; 4. \id_V \otimes \id_W = \id_{V \otimes W}. In each part both sides are linear maps out of V \otimes W, so by @lem-determined-by-simple-tensors it suffices to compare their values at a simple tensor \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}. (a) The left side gives (S_1 + S_2)\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} = (S_1\elem{v} + S_2\elem{v}) \otimes T\elem{w}, which equals S_1\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} + S_2\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} because \otimes is additive in its first slot. That is the value of the right side. The second identity is the same argument in the other slot. (b) (cS)\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} = (c\,S\elem{v}) \otimes T\elem{w} = c(S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w}) = S\elem{v} \otimes (c\,T\elem{w}), where both outer equalities use bilinearity of \otimes. (c) (R \otimes U)\big((S \otimes T)(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w})\big) = (R \otimes U)(S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w}) = RS\elem{v} \otimes UT\elem{w}, which is the value of RS \otimes UT. (d) Done in Example 1. Part (c) is the statement that \otimes respects composition: it is functoriality, and we will see in a moment that it is the mixed product rule of @thm-kronecker-properties in disguise. Two more structural facts are needed before §04 can speak of tensors with several slots. The first extends the universal property from two factors to any number, and the second says that the brackets do not matter. For k \ge 2 define the iterated tensor product by V_1 \otimes \dots \otimes V_k \coloneqq (V_1 \otimes \dots \otimes V_{k-1}) \otimes V_k , starting from V_1 itself when k = 1, and write \elem{v}_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \elem{v}_k for (\elem{v}_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \elem{v}_{k-1}) \otimes \elem{v}_k. Multilinear maps of k arguments were defined in @def-multilinear-map. [Universal Property for k Factors] Let V_1, \dots, V_k and Z be vector spaces over F, and let \beta \colon V_1 \times \dots \times V_k \to Z be multilinear. Then there is exactly one linear map \bar\beta \colon V_1 \otimes \dots \otimes V_k \to Z with \bar\beta(\elem{v}_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \elem{v}_k) = \beta(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) for all \elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k. Moreover the tensors \elem{v}_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \elem{v}_k span V_1 \otimes \dots \otimes V_k. Induction on k, freezing the last argument. With \elem{v}_k held fixed, \beta is multilinear in the first k-1 arguments, so the inductive hypothesis converts it into a linear map on X = V_1 \otimes \dots \otimes V_{k-1}. Letting \elem{v}_k move again gives a bilinear map on X \times V_k, and (T1) finishes. The spanning claim is the same induction. For k = 1 take \bar\beta = \beta, which is linear, and the claim is trivial; for k = 2 the statement is @def-tensor-product together with @prp-simple-tensors-span. Let k \ge 3 and assume the lemma for k - 1. Put X \coloneqq V_1 \otimes \dots \otimes V_{k-1}. Fix \elem{v}_k \in V_k. The map (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_{k-1}) \mapsto \beta(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) is multilinear, so the inductive hypothesis gives a unique linear g_{\elem{v}_k} \colon X \to Z with g_{\elem{v}_k}(\elem{v}_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \elem{v}_{k-1}) = \beta(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k). The map X \times V_k \to Z, (x, \elem{v}_k) \mapsto g_{\elem{v}_k}(x), is bilinear. It is linear in x because each g_{\elem{v}_k} is. For linearity in \elem{v}_k, fix \elem{v}_k, \elem{v}'_k \in V_k and c \in F: the linear maps g_{\elem{v}_k + c\elem{v}'_k} and g_{\elem{v}_k} + c\,g_{\elem{v}'_k} agree at every \elem{v}_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \elem{v}_{k-1}, because \beta is linear in its last argument, and those tensors span X by the inductive hypothesis; so the two maps are equal. By @def-tensor-product there is a unique linear \bar\beta on X \otimes V_k = V_1 \otimes \dots \otimes V_k with \bar\beta(x \otimes \elem{v}_k) = g_{\elem{v}_k}(x); taking x = \elem{v}_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \elem{v}_{k-1} gives \bar\beta(\elem{v}_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \elem{v}_k) = \beta(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k). Finally, X \otimes V_k is spanned by the simple tensors x \otimes \elem{v}_k (@prp-simple-tensors-span), each x is a combination of \elem{v}_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \elem{v}_{k-1} by the inductive hypothesis, and \otimes is linear in its first slot; so the k-fold tensors span. A linear map is determined by its values on a spanning set, which gives uniqueness of \bar\beta. [Associativity of the Tensor Product] Let U, V, W be vector spaces over F. There is a unique isomorphism \alpha \colon (U \otimes V) \otimes W \to U \otimes (V \otimes W) with \alpha\big((\elem{u} \otimes \elem{v}) \otimes \elem{w}\big) = \elem{u} \otimes (\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) for all \elem{u}, \elem{v}, \elem{w}. The map (\elem{u}, \elem{v}, \elem{w}) \mapsto \elem{u} \otimes (\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) is trilinear, since \otimes is bilinear in each of its two uses. By @lem-multilinear-universal with k = 3 there is a unique linear \alpha on (U \otimes V) \otimes W with the stated values. Symmetrically, freezing the first argument instead and running the two-factor property twice produces a linear \alpha' \colon U \otimes (V \otimes W) \to (U \otimes V) \otimes W with \alpha'(\elem{u} \otimes (\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w})) = (\elem{u} \otimes \elem{v}) \otimes \elem{w}. The composite \alpha'\alpha fixes every (\elem{u} \otimes \elem{v}) \otimes \elem{w}, and those span by @lem-multilinear-universal, so \alpha'\alpha = \id; symmetrically \alpha\alpha' = \id. Hence \alpha is an isomorphism. From now on we drop the brackets and write U \otimes V \otimes W, with \elem{u} \otimes \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w} for the element that both ways of bracketing name, and likewise for any number of factors. The matrix of a tensor product of maps Now we compute. A matrix needs ordered bases, and V \otimes W has a basis indexed by pairs (i, k), so the whole content of the computation is which order we put the pairs in. Order the basis \elem{v}_i \otimes \elem{w}_k by dictionary order on the pair (i, k): the index of the first factor changes slowly, the index of the second factor runs fastest. [The product basis, ordered] Let \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) be an ordered basis of V and \sC = (\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_q) an ordered basis of W. Write \sB \otimes \sC for the basis (\elem{v}_i \otimes \elem{w}_k) of V \otimes W given by @thm-tensor-basis, ordered so that \elem{v}_i \otimes \elem{w}_k occupies position (i - 1)q + k \qquad (1 \le i \le n,\ 1 \le k \le q), that is, in the order \elem{v}_1 \otimes \elem{w}_1,\ \dots,\ \elem{v}_1 \otimes \elem{w}_q,\ \elem{v}_2 \otimes \elem{w}_1,\ \dots,\ \elem{v}_n \otimes \elem{w}_q . Division with remainder writes every position 1, \dots, nq as (i-1)q + k for exactly one pair, so this really is an ordering of the whole basis. It is the dictionary order on pairs, and it is the same rule that Chapter 8 used to label the rows and columns of a Kronecker product in the formula (\ast) after @def-kronecker-product. That is not a coincidence, and the next theorem says why. [The Kronecker Product Is the Matrix of a Tensor Product of Maps] Let V, V', W, W' be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F with ordered bases \begin{aligned} \sB &= (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) \text{ of } V, &\quad \sB' &= (\elem{v}'_1, \dots, \elem{v}'_m) \text{ of } V', \\ \sC &= (\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_q) \text{ of } W, &\quad \sC' &= (\elem{w}'_1, \dots, \elem{w}'_p) \text{ of } W' . \end{aligned} Let S \in \cL(V, V') and T \in \cL(W, W'). Then, with the orderings of @def-tensor-basis-ordering on both sides, \mtx{S \otimes T}{\sB \otimes \sC}{\sB' \otimes \sC'} = \mtx{S}{\sB}{\sB'} \otimes \mtx{T}{\sC}{\sC'} , the Kronecker product of @def-kronecker-product. A matrix is read off column by column, and column (j, l) of the left side holds the coordinates of (S \otimes T)(\elem{v}_j \otimes \elem{w}_l) = S\elem{v}_j \otimes T\elem{w}_l. Expanding S\elem{v}_j and T\elem{w}_l in their bases and multiplying out by bilinearity produces the coefficient a_{ij}b_{kl} on \elem{v}'_i \otimes \elem{w}'_k — a product of one entry of each matrix. The entry formula (\ast) of Chapter 8 says the Kronecker product puts exactly that number in exactly that place, provided the pairs are read in dictionary order. So the theorem is the entry formula and bilinearity, nothing more. Write \A = (a_{ij}) = \mtx{S}{\sB}{\sB'} \in M_{m \times n}(F) and \B = (b_{kl}) = \mtx{T}{\sC}{\sC'} \in M_{p \times q}(F), so that by @def-matrix-of-linear-map S\elem{v}_j = \sum_{i=1}^{m} a_{ij}\elem{v}'_i, \qquad T\elem{w}_l = \sum_{k=1}^{p} b_{kl}\elem{w}'_k . Fix j and l. Using @def-tensor-of-maps and then bilinearity of \otimes in each slot, \begin{aligned} (S \otimes T)(\elem{v}_j \otimes \elem{w}_l) &= S\elem{v}_j \otimes T\elem{w}_l \\ &= \Big(\sum_{i} a_{ij}\elem{v}'_i\Big) \otimes \Big(\sum_{k} b_{kl}\elem{w}'_k\Big) \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{k=1}^{p} a_{ij}b_{kl}\,(\elem{v}'_i \otimes \elem{w}'_k) . \end{aligned} By @def-tensor-basis-ordering, \elem{v}_j \otimes \elem{w}_l is the basis vector in position (j-1)q + l of \sB \otimes \sC, and \elem{v}'_i \otimes \elem{w}'_k is the basis vector in position (i-1)p + k of \sB' \otimes \sC'. So the displayed expansion says that the entry of \mtx{S \otimes T}{\sB \otimes \sC}{\sB' \otimes \sC'} in row (i-1)p + k and column (j-1)q + l is a_{ij}b_{kl}. By the entry formula (\ast) accompanying @def-kronecker-product, that is exactly the entry of \A \otimes \B in the same position. Every row index of an mp \times nq matrix is (i-1)p + k for exactly one pair (i, k), and every column index is (j-1)q + l for exactly one pair (j, l), so the two matrices agree in every position. This proves the theorem. The ordering is the whole content, so it is worth being exact about it. Suppose we had ordered the product basis the other way, putting \elem{v}_i \otimes \elem{w}_k in position (k-1)n + i, so that the second index changes slowly. Running the proof again, the entry in row (k-1)m + i and column (l-1)n + j is still a_{ij}b_{kl}, which by (\ast) is the entry of \B \otimes \A in that position. So the other ordering gives \mtx{T}{\sC}{\sC'} \otimes \mtx{S}{\sB}{\sB'} , the Kronecker product with the factors swapped — not the transpose, and not the same matrix. For square factors the two answers are related exactly as @prp-kronecker-swap-similar says, by conjugating with the permutation matrix that relabels dictionary order into its reverse — which is precisely the change-of-coordinates matrix between the two orderings of the product basis. In the rectangular setting of @thm-kronecker-is-tensor the relation is not a conjugation at all: the row and column relabelings are different permutations, so \B \otimes \A = \P_\sigma\tp(\A \otimes \B)\P_\tau with two matrices, as Chapter 8 notes just after that proposition’s proof. Do not reverse the two factors of the basis ordering. The theorem needs the index of the first tensor factor to be the slow one, matching Chapter 8’s dictionary order in (\ast). With the fast and slow indices exchanged the matrix of S \otimes T is [T] \otimes [S]. For \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} and \B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} these two differ in the (1,2) entry, which is a_{11}b_{12} = 1 in the first and b_{11}a_{12} = 0 in the second (the nonexample after @def-kronecker-product). Chapter 8’s two promises, paid. At @def-kronecker-product, Chapter 8 wrote that the symbol \otimes “anticipates the tensor product of Chapter 15, of which this is the matrix version”. @thm-kronecker-is-tensor is that statement, made precise and proved: the Kronecker product of two matrices is the matrix of the tensor product of the two maps they represent, taken in the product bases. At the end of the same section, Chapter 8 wrote that the Kronecker product is “the coordinate shadow of a basis-free construction: the tensor product of linear maps, in Chapter 15, whose matrix in suitable bases is exactly \A \otimes \B”, and promised that “the dictionary order in (\ast) will reappear there as an ordering of a basis \elem{v}_i \otimes \elem{w}_k”. The suitable bases are \sB \otimes \sC and \sB' \otimes \sC'; the dictionary order has reappeared, as @def-tensor-basis-ordering; and the shadow is cast by S \otimes T. The second promise gets a sharper payment at the end of this section, where the vec identity turns out to be this same theorem applied to a space of matrices. [Computing with a tensor product of maps] Let S \colon F^2 \to F^2 and T \colon F^3 \to F^2 have matrices, in the standard bases, \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Compute (S \otimes T)(\cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{f}_2 + \cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{f}_3) directly from @def-tensor-of-maps, and again from the matrix of @thm-kronecker-is-tensor. Here (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) is the standard basis of F^2 and (\cvec{f}_1, \cvec{f}_2, \cvec{f}_3) that of F^3. Directly. Columns of \A and \B give S\cvec{e}_1 = 2\cvec{e}_1, S\cvec{e}_2 = \cvec{e}_1 + 3\cvec{e}_2, T\cvec{f}_2 = \cvec{e}_2, and T\cvec{f}_3 = -\cvec{e}_1. Hence \begin{aligned} (S \otimes T)(\cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{f}_2 + \cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{f}_3) &= 2\cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{e}_2 + (\cvec{e}_1 + 3\cvec{e}_2) \otimes (-\cvec{e}_1) \\ &= -\,\cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{e}_1 + 2\,\cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{e}_2 - 3\,\cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{e}_1 , \end{aligned} using bilinearity of \otimes in both slots. By matrix. The domain basis, ordered as in @def-tensor-basis-ordering, is (\cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{f}_1, \cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{f}_2, \cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{f}_3, \cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{f}_1, \cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{f}_2, \cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{f}_3), so the input has coordinate column (0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1). By @thm-kronecker-is-tensor the matrix of S \otimes T is \A \otimes \B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & -2 & 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 4 & 2 & 0 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 6 & 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, and multiplying it by that column gives (-1, 2, -3, 0). In the codomain basis (\cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{e}_2) this is the same element as before. What Chapter 8 was computing Every property of the Kronecker product proved by entry-chasing in Chapter 8 is now a property of maps, and several of them become one-liners. We record the three that the rest of the chapter uses. The mixed product rule comes first, because it is the one Chapter 8 called “the engine of everything that follows”. [The Mixed Product Rule Is Functoriality] Let \A \in M_{m \times n}(F), \C \in M_{n \times t}(F), \B \in M_{p \times q}(F), and \D \in M_{q \times u}(F). Then (\A \otimes \B)(\C \otimes \D) = (\A \C) \otimes (\B \D) . Let S, R, T, U be the linear maps with matrices \A, \C, \B, \D in the standard bases of the relevant spaces F^k. By @thm-kronecker-is-tensor, with all product bases ordered as in @def-tensor-basis-ordering, \A \otimes \B and \C \otimes \D are the matrices of S \otimes T and R \otimes U. By @thm-matrix-of-composition the product of the matrices is the matrix of the composite (S \otimes T)(R \otimes U), which is SR \otimes TU by @prp-tensor-of-maps-algebra (c). Applying @thm-kronecker-is-tensor once more, and @thm-matrix-of-composition again to each factor, the matrix of SR \otimes TU is (\A \C) \otimes (\B \D). This is @thm-kronecker-properties (c), which Chapter 8 proved by partitioning both matrices into conformable blocks and multiplying blockwise. The proof above says what the identity means: doing two things one after the other in each slot separately is the same as doing them one after the other in both slots at once. In the same way, the bilinearity of @thm-kronecker-properties (a) is parts (a) and (b) of @prp-tensor-of-maps-algebra, its associativity (b) is @prp-tensor-associative, and its inverse rule (e) is parts (c) and (d) together with invertibility of a composite. Next, the numerical invariants. [Rank, Determinant, and Trace of a Tensor Product of Maps] Let V, V', W, W' be finite-dimensional over F, S \in \cL(V, V'), T \in \cL(W, W'). Then \rank(S \otimes T) = \rank S \cdot \rank T . If moreover V = V' and W = W', with n = \dim V \ge 1 and m = \dim W \ge 1, then \det(S \otimes T) = (\det S)^{m}(\det T)^{n}, \qquad \tr(S \otimes T) = \tr S \cdot \tr T . For the rank, choose bases adapted to the two kernels: then S \otimes T kills most product basis vectors and sends the remaining \rank S \cdot \rank T of them to independent vectors. For the determinant, split S \otimes T = (S \otimes \id)(\id \otimes T). The factor \id_V \otimes T preserves each of the n subspaces \elem{v}_i \otimes W and acts on each as T; the factor S \otimes \id_W preserves each of the m subspaces V \otimes \elem{w}_k and acts as S. So each factor is block diagonal with repeated blocks, and the exponents count the other space’s dimension, which is where the exponents come from. The trace we take from the matrix. Rank. Let r = \rank S and s = \rank T. Choose a basis (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) of V whose last n - r vectors form a basis of \ker S; this is possible by @thm-basis-extension-general applied to a basis of \ker S, after reordering. Then S\elem{v}_1, \dots, S\elem{v}_r span \im S by @thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images, and being r = \rank S spanning vectors of an r-dimensional space they form a basis of \im S (@thm-right-size-basis). Choose a basis (\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_m) of W the same way, so that T\elem{w}_1, \dots, T\elem{w}_s is a basis of \im T and T\elem{w}_l = \elem{0} for l > s. By @thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images, \im(S \otimes T) is spanned by the vectors S\elem{v}_j \otimes T\elem{w}_l, and those with j > r or l > s are \elem{0}. Extend (S\elem{v}_1, \dots, S\elem{v}_r) to a basis of V' and (T\elem{w}_1, \dots, T\elem{w}_s) to a basis of W' (@thm-basis-extension-general). By @thm-tensor-basis the products of these basis vectors form a basis of V' \otimes W'; in particular the rs vectors S\elem{v}_j \otimes T\elem{w}_l with j \le r, l \le s are linearly independent. They therefore form a basis of \im(S \otimes T), and \rank(S \otimes T) = rs. Determinant. By @prp-tensor-of-maps-algebra (c) and (d), S \otimes T = (S \otimes \id_W)(\id_V \otimes T), so \det(S \otimes T) = \det(S \otimes \id_W)\det(\id_V \otimes T) by @thm-det-operator-properties. Fix bases \sB of V and \sC of W and use the ordering of @def-tensor-basis-ordering. For each i, the subspace \elem{v}_i \otimes W \coloneqq \Span(\elem{v}_i \otimes \elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_i \otimes \elem{w}_m) is carried into itself by \id_V \otimes T, which acts on it as T does on W; and V \otimes W is the direct sum of these n subspaces, because their bases together form the basis \sB \otimes \sC. Consecutive blocks of the ordering are exactly these subspaces, so \mtx{\id_V \otimes T}{\sB \otimes \sC}{\sB \otimes \sC} = \underbrace{\mtx{T}{\sC}{\sC} \oplus \dots \oplus \mtx{T}{\sC}{\sC}}_{n \text{ blocks}}, whose determinant is (\det T)^{n} by @thm-block-diagonal-arithmetic (d) and induction on the number of blocks. The same argument for S \otimes \id_W, using instead the m subspaces V \otimes \elem{w}_k, gives \det(S \otimes \id_W) = (\det S)^{m}. (This time the relevant basis vectors are not consecutive in the ordering of @def-tensor-basis-ordering, so reorder the basis to make them so; matrices of one operator in two bases are similar, by @thm-change-of-basis-maps, hence have the same determinant, by @cor-det-similarity-invariant.) Multiplying the two gives the formula. Trace. By @thm-kronecker-is-tensor the matrix of S \otimes T in \sB \otimes \sC is \mtx{S}{\sB}{\sB} \otimes \mtx{T}{\sC}{\sC}, so by @def-trace-operator and @thm-kronecker-rank-trace-det (b), \tr(S \otimes T) = \tr S \cdot \tr T. These are parts (a), (c), and (b) of @thm-kronecker-rank-trace-det, transported to operators. Two remarks on what has changed. First, the exponents in the determinant formula are no longer something to memorize: \det S appears to the power \dim W because S \otimes \id_W runs S once on each of the \dim W copies of V inside V \otimes W. Second, the proof of the trace formula above is still a computation in a basis. There is a genuinely basis-free reason, and §04 gives it. The determinant, too, has a basis-free explanation, which has to wait for the top exterior power in §09. Most operators on V \otimes W are not of the form S \otimes T. The operators that are of this form are heavily constrained: by @cor-tensor-map-invariants their rank is a product rs with r \le \dim V and s \le \dim W. Take V = W = F^2, so \dim(V \otimes W) = 4, and let P be any operator on V \otimes W of rank 3, for instance the projection onto the span of the first three basis vectors of @def-tensor-basis-ordering. Then 3 = rs with r, s \in \{0, 1, 2\} is impossible, so P \ne S \otimes T for every S and T. The maps S \otimes T do span \cL(V \otimes W), which is a different and weaker statement; this is the same distinction as between simple tensors and general tensors in §02. Let S \in \cL(V) and T \in \cL(W) with \dim V = 3 and \dim W = 2, and suppose \det S = 2 and \det T = -1. What are \det(S \otimes T) and \det(T \otimes S), where the second is an operator on W \otimes V? By @cor-tensor-map-invariants, \det(S \otimes T) = (\det S)^{\dim W}(\det T)^{\dim V} = 2^{2}(-1)^{3} = -4. For T \otimes S the roles swap, giving (\det T)^{\dim V}(\det S)^{\dim W} = (-1)^{3}2^{2} = -4 as well. The two agree, as they must: a determinant is a product of scalars, and the exponent always belongs to the other factor’s dimension. The tempting wrong answer, (\det S)^{3}(\det T)^{2} = 8, puts each map’s own dimension in its exponent. Maps as tensors We come to the identification that the rest of the chapter runs on. A functional \varphi \in V^{*} and a vector \elem{w} \in W together determine a linear map V \to W: measure with \varphi, then scale \elem{w} by the answer. That recipe is bilinear in (\varphi, \elem{w}), which is now a reflex: it must come from a linear map on V^{*} \otimes W. [Tensors Are Maps] Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F. There is a unique linear map \Theta \colon V^{*} \otimes W \to \cL(V, W), \qquad \Theta(\varphi \otimes \elem{w})(\elem{v}) = \varphi(\elem{v})\,\elem{w} , and it is an isomorphism. Moreover, for R \in \cL(V_0, V) and U \in \cL(W, W_0) with V_0, W_0 finite-dimensional, \Theta\big((R' \otimes U)(\xi)\big) = U\,\Theta(\xi)\,R \qquad (\xi \in V^{*} \otimes W), where R' \colon V^{*} \to V_0^{*} is the dual map of @def-dual-map and the \Theta on the left is the one for the pair (V_0, W_0). Existence is the universal property again. For bijectivity, count: both sides have dimension \dim V \cdot \dim W, so it is enough to see that \Theta carries a basis onto a basis. It carries \varphi_j \otimes \elem{w}_i to the map whose matrix is the matrix unit \E_{ij}, and the matrix units are a basis. The last formula is the statement that \Theta turns the tensor product of maps into composition on the two sides; it is checked on simple tensors. Existence and uniqueness. For fixed \varphi and \elem{w}, the assignment \elem{v} \mapsto \varphi(\elem{v})\elem{w} is linear, so it is an element \varphi \cdot \elem{w} of \cL(V, W). The map (\varphi, \elem{w}) \mapsto \varphi \cdot \elem{w} is bilinear: for every \elem{v}, \begin{aligned} (\varphi + \psi)(\elem{v})\elem{w} &= \varphi(\elem{v})\elem{w} + \psi(\elem{v})\elem{w}, \\ \varphi(\elem{v})(\elem{w} + \elem{w}') &= \varphi(\elem{v})\elem{w} + \varphi(\elem{v})\elem{w}', \\ (c\varphi)(\elem{v})\elem{w} &= c\,\varphi(\elem{v})\elem{w} = \varphi(\elem{v})(c\elem{w}), \end{aligned} and two maps agreeing at every \elem{v} are equal. By @def-tensor-product there is a unique linear \Theta with \Theta(\varphi \otimes \elem{w}) = \varphi \cdot \elem{w}. Bijectivity. Let \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) be a basis of V with dual basis \sB^{*} = (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n) (@def-dual-basis), and \sC = (\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_m) a basis of W. By @thm-tensor-basis the products \varphi_j \otimes \elem{w}_i form a basis of V^{*} \otimes W, of size nm. Now \Theta(\varphi_j \otimes \elem{w}_i) sends \elem{v}_k to \varphi_j(\elem{v}_k)\elem{w}_i = \delta_{jk}\elem{w}_i, so it sends \elem{v}_j to \elem{w}_i and every other basis vector to \elem{0}. By @def-matrix-of-linear-map its matrix is the matrix unit \E_{ij}. The matrix units form a basis of M_{m \times n}(F) (@exm-standard-bases) and T \mapsto \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sC} is an isomorphism (@thm-linear-maps-isomorphic-to-matrices), so the nm maps \Theta(\varphi_j \otimes \elem{w}_i) form a basis of \cL(V, W). Hence \im \Theta contains a basis of \cL(V, W), so \Theta is surjective (@thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images). Since \dim(V^{*} \otimes W) = nm = \dim \cL(V, W), @thm-rank-nullity gives \nullity \Theta = 0, so \Theta is injective (@thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel). Therefore \Theta is an isomorphism. Naturality. Both \xi \mapsto \Theta((R' \otimes U)\xi) and \xi \mapsto U\,\Theta(\xi)\,R are linear in \xi, so by @lem-determined-by-simple-tensors it suffices to check them at \xi = \varphi \otimes \elem{w}. On the left, (R' \otimes U)(\varphi \otimes \elem{w}) = R'\varphi \otimes U\elem{w}, and for \elem{v} \in V_0, \Theta(R'\varphi \otimes U\elem{w})(\elem{v}) = (R'\varphi)(\elem{v})\,U\elem{w} = \varphi(R\elem{v})\,U\elem{w} , using @def-dual-map. On the right, \big(U\,\Theta(\varphi \otimes \elem{w})\,R\big)(\elem{v}) = U\big(\varphi(R\elem{v})\elem{w}\big) = \varphi(R\elem{v})\,U\elem{w} by linearity of U. The two agree. Finite dimension is a hypothesis, not decoration. The map \Theta is defined and injective for any V and W, but it is surjective only onto the maps of finite rank: \Theta(\sum_{t=1}^{N} \varphi_t \otimes \elem{w}_t) has image inside \Span(\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_N), so its rank is at most N. On V = W = F[x], the identity map has infinite rank and is therefore not \Theta(\xi) for any \xi \in V^{*} \otimes V. Everything below uses the finite-dimensional statement. The letter \Theta is deliberate: taking V = F^n and W = F^m and using the dual basis to identify (F^n)^{*} with F^n, this \Theta is the isomorphism F^m \otimes F^n \cong M_{m \times n}(F) of @thm-tensor-fn-matrices, with the two factors written in the order that makes the source a space of maps rather than of matrices. Section 02’s model was the special case; this is the general statement. Two uses of the theorem, immediately. First, it names the matrix units: under \Theta, the map with matrix \E_{ij} is the tensor \varphi_j \otimes \elem{w}_i, so a matrix is a sum \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}\,\varphi_j \otimes \elem{w}_i. Note the index order — the functional carries the column index, the vector the row index — and compare it with Chapter 8’s vectorization, which stacks columns. Second, the naturality formula is the vec identity. [The vec identity, read as a tensor product of maps] Let \A \in M_{k \times m}(F) and \B \in M_{n \times l}(F), and let \Psi \colon M_{m \times n}(F) \to M_{k \times l}(F), \qquad \X \mapsto \A\X\B , which is linear. Identify M_{m \times n}(F) with \cL(F^n, F^m) and M_{k \times l}(F) with \cL(F^l, F^k). Explain why @thm-vec-identity, \vecop(\A\X\B) = (\B\tp \otimes \A)\vecop\X, is @thm-kronecker-is-tensor applied to \Psi. Let R \colon F^l \to F^n and U \colon F^m \to F^k be the maps with matrices \B and \A in the standard bases. Under the identification, \Psi becomes the map \cL(F^n, F^m) \to \cL(F^l, F^k) sending T to UTR, so by the naturality clause of @thm-tensor-hom-iso it corresponds, through \Theta, to R' \otimes U \colon (F^n)^{*} \otimes F^m \to (F^l)^{*} \otimes F^k . Order the basis of (F^n)^{*} \otimes F^m as in @def-tensor-basis-ordering, using the dual standard basis (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n) first and the standard basis (\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_m) second. Then \varphi_j \otimes \cvec{e}_i sits in position (j-1)m + i, and \Theta(\varphi_j \otimes \cvec{e}_i) = \E_{ij}. By @def-vec-operator, \vecop \E_{ij} = \cvec{e}_{(j-1)m+i}. So \vecop is the coordinate map of this ordered basis: the dictionary order with the column index slow is exactly the order in which vectorization stacks the columns. Now apply @thm-kronecker-is-tensor. The matrix of R' in the dual standard bases is \B\tp, because the matrix of a dual map is the transpose (@thm-matrix-of-dual-map), and the matrix of U is \A. Hence the matrix of R' \otimes U in the product bases above is \B\tp \otimes \A. Reading that equality of matrices through the coordinate map \vecop gives \vecop(\A\X\B) = (\B\tp \otimes \A)\vecop\X, which is @thm-vec-identity. For a numerical check, take \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and \B = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. Writing the four images \A\E_{ij}\B in the order \E_{11}, \E_{21}, \E_{12}, \E_{22} and stacking the four columns \vecop(\A\E_{ij}\B) side by side gives \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 6 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, which is \B\tp \otimes \A written out. So the transpose in the vec identity, which Chapter 8 had to warn readers not to get wrong, is not a bookkeeping accident: it is there because \Psi multiplies \X on the right by \B, and right multiplication is precomposition, which reverses arrows. The dual map is what reverses them, and the matrix of a dual map is a transpose. That is the sharper form of Chapter 8’s second promise, and it is why the wrong guesses \A \otimes \B\tp and \B \otimes \A are wrong. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the defining property of S \otimes T, and say why writing “(S \otimes T)(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w}, extended linearly” is not by itself a definition. 2. Let \dim V = 3, \dim W = 4, \dim V' = 2, \dim W' = 5. What are the sizes of \mtx{S}{\sB}{\sB'}, \mtx{T}{\sC}{\sC'}, and \mtx{S \otimes T}{\sB \otimes \sC}{\sB' \otimes \sC'}? 3. In the ordering of @def-tensor-basis-ordering with \dim V = 3 and \dim W = 4, which basis vector of V \otimes W sits in position 7? 4. True or false: every operator on V \otimes W is of the form S \otimes T. Justify your answer. 5. State @thm-tensor-hom-iso, including its hypothesis, and say what \Theta(\varphi \otimes \elem{w}) does to a vector \elem{v}. (a) S \otimes T is the unique linear map V \otimes W \to V' \otimes W' with (S \otimes T)(\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}) = S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} for all \elem{v}, \elem{w} (@def-tensor-of-maps). The quoted phrase is not a definition because a general element of V \otimes W is a sum of simple tensors in many different ways, so a prescription on simple tensors may be inconsistent; \elem{v} \otimes \elem{0} = \elem{0} already forces consistency conditions. What makes it work is that (\elem{v}, \elem{w}) \mapsto S\elem{v} \otimes T\elem{w} is bilinear, so @def-tensor-product supplies the map. (b) 2 \times 3, 5 \times 4, and 10 \times 12 (@thm-kronecker-is-tensor: an m \times n and a p \times q matrix give an mp \times nq one). (c) With q = 4, position 7 = (i-1)\cdot 4 + k forces i = 2, k = 3. So it is \elem{v}_2 \otimes \elem{w}_3. (d) False. By @cor-tensor-map-invariants, \rank(S \otimes T) = \rank S \cdot \rank T. With \dim V = \dim W = 2, an operator of rank 3 on the 4-dimensional space V \otimes W cannot have its rank factored as a product of two integers each at most 2. (e) For V, W finite-dimensional, there is a unique linear \Theta \colon V^{*} \otimes W \to \cL(V, W) with \Theta(\varphi \otimes \elem{w})(\elem{v}) = \varphi(\elem{v})\elem{w}, and it is an isomorphism. So \Theta(\varphi \otimes \elem{w}) measures \elem{v} with \varphi and scales \elem{w} by the result. B. Practice [B1: A tensor product of maps, two ways] Let S \colon \nQ^2 \to \nQ^2 and T \colon \nQ^2 \to \nQ^3 have matrices, in the standard bases, \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. 1. Write down \mtx{S \otimes T}{\sB \otimes \sC}{\sB' \otimes \sC'} for the standard bases, ordered as in @def-tensor-basis-ordering. 2. Compute (S \otimes T)(\cvec{e}_1 \otimes \cvec{e}_2 - \cvec{e}_2 \otimes \cvec{e}_1) directly from @def-tensor-of-maps. 3. Check (b) against (a) by multiplying the matrix by the coordinate column of the input. (a) By @thm-kronecker-is-tensor the matrix is \A \otimes \B, of size 6 \times 4: \A \otimes \B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
