e \elem{0} (@thm-wedge-nonzero-iff-independent), comparing coefficients gives the stated formula. This is @thm-laplace-expansion (a). The row version follows from it by @thm-det-transpose, exactly as in Chapter 7. The gain is again structural rather than practical: the sign (-1)^{i+j}, which in Chapter 7 arrived from a careful count of row and column moves, is here the price of two reversals, j-1 in one direction and i-1 in the other. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the defining property of \Lambda^kT, and say why a rule given on wedges needs an argument before it defines a map. 2. State @thm-det-is-top-exterior. 3. Name one thing this section’s construction of the determinant adds to Chapter 7’s, and one thing it does not. 4. True or false: for every T \in \cL(V) and every k, the map \Lambda^kT is multiplication by a scalar. Justify your answer. 5. What are the coordinates of \cvec{v}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \cvec{v}_k in \Lambda^kF^n, in the basis (\elem{e}_I)? (a) \Lambda^kT is the unique linear map \Lambda^kV 	o \Lambda^kW with \Lambda^kT(\elem{v}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{v}_k) = T\elem{v}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge T\elem{v}_k (@def-exterior-power-of-map). An element of \Lambda^kV has many expressions as a sum of wedges, so a rule stated on wedges might assign two different values to one element; the universal property of @def-exterior-power removes the danger by producing the map from an alternating multilinear map upstairs. (b) If \dim V = n \ge 1 and T \in \cL(V), then \dim \Lambda^nV = 1 and \Lambda^nT(\omega) = (\det T)\omega for every \omega \in \Lambda^nV. (c) It adds that the determinant is the induced map on a line, so that no basis and no similarity-invariance argument is needed to define \det T, and multiplicativity becomes @thm-exterior-power-functorial. It does not add a new value, a new method of computation, or any improvement to \det \A	p = \det \A. (d) False. It is true when k = n = \dim V, and when k > n for the trivial reason that \Lambda^kV = \{\elem{0}\}. For 1 \le k < n it usually fails: see @exm-lambda-two-of-a-three-by-three, where \Lambda^2T has matrix with rows (8, 2, -11), (-1, -13, -5), (-20, -5, 2), not a scalar matrix. (e) The k 	imes k minors of the matrix whose columns are \cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_k: the coordinate at \elem{e}_I is \det \A_{I,[k]} (@thm-wedge-coordinates-are-minors). B. Practice [B1: A second exterior power] Let T \colon 
Q^3 	o 
Q^3 have standard matrix \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 3 \ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Find the matrix of \Lambda^2T in the basis (\cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_3, \cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_3). Hence verify that \det(\Lambda^2T) = (\det T)^2. By @def-exterior-power-of-map and @thm-wedge-coordinates-are-minors, the entry of [\Lambda^2T] in row I and column J is \det \A_{I,J}, with rows and columns indexed by \{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{2,3\} in that order. Computing the nine 2 	imes 2 minors, [\Lambda^2T] =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 & 6 \ -4 & 1 & 2 \ -2 & -6 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Its determinant is 169. Expanding \det \A along the first column (@thm-laplace-expansion) gives 1 \cdot (1 - 0) + 2 \cdot (6 - 0) = 13, and 13^2 = 169. [B2: Independence by minors] In 
Q^4, let \cvec{v}_1 = (1, 2, 0, 1), \cvec{v}_2 = (0, 1, 1, 1), and \cvec{v}_3 = (1, 0, -2, -1). Compute the coordinates of \cvec{v}_1 \wedge \cvec{v}_2 \wedge \cvec{v}_3 in \Lambda^3
Q^4, and hence determine whether the list is linearly independent. Justify your answer. Let \A \in M_{4 	imes 3}(
Q) have these columns. By @thm-wedge-coordinates-are-minors the four coordinates are the 3 	imes 3 minors on the row sets \{1,2,3\}, \{1,2,4\}, \{1,3,4\}, \{2,3,4\}. Computing them, \det \A_{\{1,2,3\}} = \det  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 2 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix} = 0 , and the same for the other three: \det \A_{\{1,2,4\}} = \det \A_{\{1,3,4\}} = \det \A_{\{2,3,4\}} = 0. So \cvec{v}_1 \wedge \cvec{v}_2 \wedge \cvec{v}_3 = \elem{0}, and by @thm-wedge-nonzero-iff-independent the list is dependent. Indeed \cvec{v}_3 = \cvec{v}_1 - 2\cvec{v}_2. [B3: Determinant of an inverse] Let \dim V = n \ge 1 and let T \in \cL(V) be invertible. Using @thm-exterior-power-functorial and @thm-det-is-top-exterior, and no formula for the determinant, prove that \Lambda^nT is invertible and that \det(T^{-1}) = (\det T)^{-1}. By @thm-exterior-power-functorial, (\Lambda^nT)(\Lambda^n T^{-1}) = \Lambda^n(TT^{-1}) = \Lambda^n(\id_V) = \id, and symmetrically in the other order. So \Lambda^nT is invertible with inverse \Lambda^nT^{-1}. By @thm-det-is-top-exterior these two maps are multiplication by \det T and by \det(T^{-1}) on the line \Lambda^nV, and their composite is multiplication by \det T \cdot \det(T^{-1}), which equals \id. Since \Lambda^nV 
e \{\elem{0}\}, this forces \det T \cdot \det(T^{-1}) = 1. In particular \det T 
e 0, and \det(T^{-1}) = (\det T)^{-1}. C. Going deeper [C1: The trace of an exterior power] Let \A \in M_n(F) and 1 \le k \le n, and let T \colon F^n 	o F^n be \cvec{x} \mapsto \A\cvec{x}. 1. Prove that the matrix of \Lambda^kT in the basis (\elem{e}_I) has (I, J)-entry \det \A_{I,J}. 2. Deduce that 	r(\Lambda^kT) is the sum of the  inom{n}{k} principal k 	imes k minors of \A, those with I = J. 3. Compute 	r(\Lambda^2T) for the matrix \A of @exm-lambda-two-of-a-three-by-three, and check it against the matrix found there. (a) Column J = \{j_1 < \dots < j_k\} of the matrix is the coordinate vector of \Lambda^kT(\elem{e}_J) = \cvec{a}_{j_1} \wedge \dots \wedge \cvec{a}_{j_k}, where \cvec{a}_j = T\cvec{e}_j is the j-th column of \A (@def-exterior-power-of-map). By @thm-wedge-coordinates-are-minors applied to the n 	imes k matrix with columns \cvec{a}_{j_1}, \dots, \cvec{a}_{j_k}, the coordinate at \elem{e}_I is the determinant of its submatrix on rows I, which is \det \A_{I,J} (@def-submatrix-minor). (b) The trace is the sum of the diagonal entries, that is, of the entries with I = J, and by (a) those are the principal minors \det \A_{I,I}. (c) The three principal 2 	imes 2 minors of \A are \det  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 0 & 4\end{psmallmatrix} = 8, \det  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 3 \ 5 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} = -13, and \det  egin{psmallmatrix} 4 & 1 \ 2 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} = 2. Their sum is -3, which is the sum of the diagonal entries 8, -13, 2 of the matrix computed in @exm-lambda-two-of-a-three-by-three. [C2: Cauchy–Binet from a wedge] Let m \le n, let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \B \in M_{n 	imes m}(F), and let T_{\A} \colon F^n 	o F^m and T_{\B} \colon F^m 	o F^n be the associated maps. 1. Show that \Lambda^m T_{\B}(\cvec{e}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \cvec{e}_m) = \sum_{J} (\det \B_{J,[m]})\, \elem{e}_J, the sum over m-element subsets J \subseteq [n]. 2. Show that \Lambda^m T_{\A}(\elem{e}_J) = (\det \A_{[m],J})\, \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \cvec{e}_m for each such J. 3. Hence deduce the Cauchy–Binet formula \det(\A\B) = \sum_{J} \det \A_{[m],J} \det \B_{J,[m]} (@thm-cauchy-binet). (a) \Lambda^mT_{\B}(\cvec{e}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \cvec{e}_m) = \B\cvec{e}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \B\cvec{e}_m by @def-exterior-power-of-map, and the columns of \B are \B\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \B\cvec{e}_m. Apply @thm-wedge-coordinates-are-minors in F^n with k = m. (b) Writing J = \{j_1 < \dots < j_m\}, we get \Lambda^mT_{\A}(\elem{e}_J) = \A\cvec{e}_{j_1} \wedge \dots \wedge \A\cvec{e}_{j_m}, a wedge of m vectors of F^m. By @thm-wedge-coordinates-are-minors with k = m = n there is only one index set, [m] itself, and the coefficient is the determinant of the matrix with those columns, which is \A_{[m],J}. (c) By @thm-exterior-power-functorial, \Lambda^m(T_{\A}T_{\B}) = (\Lambda^mT_{\A})(\Lambda^mT_{\B}). The map T_{\A}T_{\B} is the operator on F^m with matrix \A\B, so by @thm-det-is-top-exterior the left side sends \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \cvec{e}_m to \det(\A\B)\,\cvec{e}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \cvec{e}_m. By (a) and then (b), the right side sends it to \sum_J \det \B_{J,[m]} \det \A_{[m],J}\, \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \cvec{e}_m. Comparing coefficients on the basis vector \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \cvec{e}_m 
e \elem{0} gives the formula. [C3: Exterior powers of an injection] Let T \colon V 	o W be an injective linear map between finite-dimensional spaces and let 1 \le k \le \dim V. Prove that \Lambda^kT is injective. Is the analogous statement true with “injective” replaced by “surjective”? Hint: choose a basis of V and use @thm-exterior-power-basis in both spaces. Let (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_m) be a basis of V. Since T is injective, (T\elem{v}_1, \dots, T\elem{v}_m) is linearly independent in W, so it extends to a basis (T\elem{v}_1, \dots, T\elem{v}_m, \elem{w}_{m+1}, \dots) of W (@thm-basis-extension). By @thm-exterior-power-basis, the wedges \elem{v}_{i_1} \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{v}_{i_k} over increasing tuples form a basis of \Lambda^kV, and \Lambda^kT sends each of them to T\elem{v}_{i_1} \wedge \dots \wedge T\elem{v}_{i_k}, which is one of the basis vectors of \Lambda^kW provided by the extended basis. So \Lambda^kT carries a basis to a linearly independent list, hence is injective. Yes for surjective as well, and more cheaply: if T is surjective then every \elem{w}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{w}_k equals T\elem{v}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge T\elem{v}_k for preimages \elem{v}_i, so the image of \Lambda^kT contains a spanning set of \Lambda^kW (@thm-exterior-power-basis) and is therefore all of it.

title: 15.10 The Exterior Algebra, and Clifford at Last
content:
The Exterior Algebra, and Clifford at Last The exterior powers have so far been used one degree at a time, and the wedge of two of them has had nowhere to live: \Lambda^2V and \Lambda^3V are different spaces, and until now nothing said what (\elem{u} \wedge \elem{w}) \wedge \elem{x} means as an operation. Stacking them fixes that, exactly as stacking the tensor powers produced the tensor algebra (@def-tensor-algebra) and stacking the symmetric powers produced the symmetric algebra (@def-symmetric-algebra). The result is a 2^n-dimensional algebra, and it is the last object this chapter needs. With it we can finally pay the debt Chapter 14 recorded in writing: a Clifford algebra of (V, q) exists, and its dimension is 2^n. Throughout, F is a field and V is a vector space over F with \dim V = n. From the subsection on decomposability on, \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, because @def-clifford-algebra assumes it. We use the exterior powers of @def-exterior-power with their universal property for alternating maps, their bases of increasing wedges (@thm-exterior-power-basis), the test @thm-wedge-nonzero-iff-independent, and the reordering rule @lem-alternating-map-properties (b) of the previous section. Stacking the exterior powers The pieces are already in place; only the multiplication is missing. The pattern is the one @prp-symmetric-product-well-defined used for symmetric powers: a product of a k-fold wedge and an l-fold wedge ought to be the (k+l)-fold wedge of all the vectors, and the only thing to check is that this depends on the two factors and not on the way each was written. [The Wedge of Two Exterior Powers] Let k, l \ge 1. There is a unique bilinear map \Lambda^{k}V 	imes \Lambda^{l}V 	o \Lambda^{k+l}V, \qquad (\omega, \eta) \mapsto \omega \wedge \eta , such that for all \elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k, \elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_l \in V, (\elem{u}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{u}_k) \wedge (\elem{w}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{w}_l) = \elem{u}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{u}_k \wedge \elem{w}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{w}_l . Freeze the second factor’s vectors and use the universal property once, in the first k slots; that turns the left-hand factor into an element of \Lambda^kV. Then let the second factor’s vectors vary: what we have built depends on them l-linearly, and vanishes as soon as two of them coincide, with values in a space of linear maps, so the universal property applies a second time. Fix \elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_l \in V. The map V^k 	o \Lambda^{k+l}V given by (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k) \mapsto \elem{u}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{u}_k \wedge \elem{w}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{w}_l is k-linear, since the wedge of k + l vectors is linear in each slot and the last l are frozen, and alternating, since a repeat among the first k arguments is a repeat among all k+l. By @def-exterior-power it induces a unique linear map R(\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_l) \colon \Lambda^{k}V 	o \Lambda^{k+l}V with R(\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_l)(\elem{u}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{u}_k) equal to the displayed wedge. Now let the \elem{w}’s vary. The assignment (\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_l) \mapsto R(\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_l), with values in the vector space \cL(\Lambda^kV, \Lambda^{k+l}V), is l-linear and alternating: two linear maps on \Lambda^kV are equal as soon as they agree on the wedges \elem{u}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{u}_k, which span \Lambda^kV (@thm-exterior-power-basis), and on those the required identities are the linearity and the alternation of the wedge of k+l vectors in its last l slots. So @def-exterior-power applies again and gives a unique linear map \Lambda^{l}V 	o \cL(\Lambda^{k}V, \Lambda^{k+l}V), \qquad \elem{w}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{w}_l \mapsto R(\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_l) . Reading a linear map into a space of linear maps as a bilinear map gives the required product, with the stated values. It is unique because the wedges span both factors and a bilinear map is determined on a pair of spanning sets. This proves the proposition. With the product in hand, the algebra assembles itself. The exterior algebra is all the exterior powers at once, multiplied by wedging. [Exterior Algebra] Let V be a vector space over F, with \Lambda^{0}V = F and \Lambda^{1}V = V as in @def-exterior-power. The exterior algebra, or Grassmann algebra, of V is the vector space \Lambda V \coloneqq  igoplus_{k \ge 0} \Lambda^{k}V, whose elements are the sequences x = (x_0, x_1, \dots) with x_k \in \Lambda^kV and only finitely many x_k nonzero, with componentwise operations, and whose multiplication is (x \wedge y)_m = \sum_{k + l = m} x_k \wedge y_l , where \wedge on the right is @prp-wedge-product-well-defined for k, l \ge 1, and is scalar multiplication when k = 0 or l = 0. We identify each \Lambda^kV with the sequences supported in position k, so that F and V are subspaces of \Lambda V, and call an element of \Lambda^kV \subseteq \Lambda V homogeneous of degree k. In words: an element of \Lambda V is a finite sum x_0 + x_1 + \dots + x_N of pieces of different degrees, the scalars sit inside as the degree-0 piece, and the product adds degrees. The finiteness clause is automatic here, since \Lambda^kV = \{\elem{0}\} once k > n (@thm-exterior-power-basis). [Structure of the Exterior Algebra] Let \dim V = n with basis (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n). For a subset S = \{i_1 < \dots < i_k\} \subseteq [n] write \elem{e}_S = \elem{e}_{i_1} \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{e}_{i_k}, with \elem{e}_\emptyset = 1. Then 1. \Lambda V is an associative unital F-algebra with identity 1 \in \Lambda^0V = F, and \Lambda^kV \wedge \Lambda^lV \subseteq \Lambda^{k+l}V. 2. The 2^n elements \elem{e}_S, one for each subset S \subseteq [n], form a basis of \Lambda V. In particular \dim_F \Lambda V = 2^n. 3. \Lambda V is generated as an algebra by 1 and V. (a) Bilinearity of the product holds componentwise, by @prp-wedge-product-well-defined. For associativity, both (x \wedge y) \wedge z and x \wedge (y \wedge z) are trilinear in (x, y, z), so it is enough to compare them on homogeneous elements, and then on the wedges of vectors, which span each \Lambda^kV for k \ge 1 (@thm-exterior-power-basis) while \Lambda^0V is spanned by 1. On those both sides are the single wedge of all the listed vectors in order, by the defining identity of @prp-wedge-product-well-defined applied twice. The scalar 1 acts on each \Lambda^kV as multiplication by 1, hence as the identity. The grading statement is built into the definition of the product. (b) By @thm-exterior-power-basis the \elem{e}_S with \lvert S vert = k form a basis of \Lambda^kV, and \Lambda^kV = \{\elem{0}\} for k > n. A basis of a direct sum is the union of bases of the summands, so the \elem{e}_S over all S \subseteq [n] form a basis of \Lambda V. Their number is \sum_{k=0}^{n} inom{n}{k} = 2^n, by the binomial theorem applied to (1+1)^n. (c) Each \elem{e}_S is a product of elements of V by the defining identity of the product, and the \elem{e}_S span by (b). The one structural fact that is not inherited from the tensor algebra is how the order of a product matters. [Graded Commutativity] Let \omega \in \Lambda^kV and \eta \in \Lambda^lV. Then \omega \wedge \eta = (-1)^{kl}\, \eta \wedge \omega . In particular \omega \wedge \omega = \elem{0} whenever k is odd, over every field. Count the swaps. To turn \elem{w}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{w}_l \wedge \elem{u}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{u}_k into \elem{u}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{u}_k \wedge \elem{w}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{w}_l, each of the k vectors \elem{u}_i must cross each of the l vectors \elem{w}_j, and every crossing costs a sign. Both sides are bilinear in (\omega, \eta), so by @thm-exterior-power-basis it suffices to take \omega = \elem{u}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{u}_k and \eta = \elem{w}_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \elem{w}_l, and the cases k = 0 or l = 0 are scalar multiplication and are clear. The permutation of \{1, \dots, k+l\} carrying the list (\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_l, \elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k) to (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k, \elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_l) has exactly kl inversions, one for each pair consisting of a \elem{u} and a \elem{w}, so its sign is (-1)^{kl} (@def-sign-permutation). By @lem-alternating-map-properties (b) the two wedges differ by that factor, which is the claim. For the last sentence let k be odd and \omega \in \Lambda^kV. Write \omega = \sum_S c_S\,\elem{e}_S in the basis of @thm-exterior-algebra-structure, the sum over the S with \lvert S vert = k. Then \omega \wedge \omega = \sum_{S}\sum_{T} c_Sc_T\,\elem{e}_S \wedge \elem{e}_T . A term with S = T has a repeated vector, so \elem{e}_S \wedge \elem{e}_S = \elem{0}. A pair S 
e T occurs twice, and the two occurrences are c_Sc_T\,\elem{e}_S \wedge \elem{e}_T and c_Tc_S\,\elem{e}_T \wedge \elem{e}_S = -c_Sc_T\,\elem{e}_S \wedge \elem{e}_T, since (-1)^{kl} = (-1)^{k^2} = -1 for odd k. So the two cancel, and nothing divides by 2 anywhere. Graded commutative is not commutative. In \Lambda F^2 we have \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_2 = -\cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_1, and these are different elements unless \operatorname{char} F = 2. What is true in all degrees is only the signed rule. And the sign is +1 as soon as one of the degrees is even, so an element of \Lambda^2V commutes with everything, while two elements of \Lambda^1V = V anticommute. \omega \wedge \omega need not be zero. The identity \elem{v} \wedge \elem{v} = \elem{0} is a statement about degree 1. For \omega = \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_2 + \cvec{e}_3 \wedge \cvec{e}_4 in \Lambda F^4, a direct expansion gives \omega \wedge \omega = 2\,\cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_3 \wedge \cvec{e}_4, which is nonzero whenever \operatorname{char} F 
e 2. Squaring to zero is the privilege of odd degree. [The exterior algebra of a three-dimensional space] Describe \Lambda F^3 completely, and compute (\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_3) \wedge (\cvec{e}_2 + \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_3). By @thm-exterior-algebra-structure it has dimension 2^3 = 8, with basis 1; \quad \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3; \quad \elem{e}_{12}, \elem{e}_{13}, \elem{e}_{23}; \quad \elem{e}_{123}, writing \elem{e}_{ij} for \cvec{e}_i \wedge \cvec{e}_j and \elem{e}_{123} for \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_3. The degrees have dimensions 1, 3, 3, 1. Every product of two elements of degree \ge 2 lands in degree \ge 4, hence is \elem{0}. For the computation, expand by bilinearity into four products:  egin{aligned} \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_2 &= \elem{e}_{12}, \ \cvec{e}_1 \wedge (\cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_3) &= \elem{0} \quad (	ext{repeated } \cvec{e}_1), \ (\cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_3) \wedge \cvec{e}_2 &= \elem{0} \quad (	ext{repeated } \cvec{e}_2), \ (\cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_3) \wedge (\cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_3) &= \elem{0} \quad (	ext{degree } 4). \end{aligned} So the product is \elem{e}_{12}, while the reversed product is -\elem{e}_{12} plus the same three zeros. In \Lambda F^4, what is (\cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_2) \wedge (\cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_3), and what is (\cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_2) \wedge (\cvec{e}_3 \wedge \cvec{e}_4)? The first is \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_3 = \elem{0}, since \cvec{e}_2 is repeated. The second is \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_3 \wedge \cvec{e}_4, a basis vector of \Lambda^4F^4, so it is nonzero. Wedging two 2-vectors gives zero exactly when the four vectors involved are dependent. The algebra of dimension 2^n that settled the matter is the exterior algebra, but it is not the Clifford algebra: it is only a space that \operatorname{Cl}(q) acts on, and independence came from the action rather than from an identification. Chapter 14 also guessed that “\operatorname{Cl}(q) is assembled from the exterior powers \Lambda^kV, one for each k”, and \Phi is that assembly, matching the sorted product on S with the wedge \elem{e}_S. \operatorname{Cl}(q) and \Lambda V are the same size, not the same algebra. The map \Phi above is an isomorphism of vector spaces only. It is not multiplicative, and no other map is either, unless q = 0: in \Lambda V the square of a vector is \elem{0}, while in \operatorname{Cl}(q) it is q(\elem{v})1. Writing an element of \operatorname{Cl}(q) as a sum of wedges is a choice of coordinates, not a description of the multiplication. That warning deserves a proof rather than a slogan. Then j(\elem{v})^2 = \elem{v} \wedge \elem{v} = \elem{0} = q(\elem{v})1, so (C1) holds for j. e 0 and put x = \varphi(\iota(\elem{v})). Then x \wedge x = \varphi igl(\iota(\elem{v})^2 igr) = \varphi igl(q(\elem{v})1 igr) = q(\elem{v})\cdot 1 , a nonzero scalar, so x \in F\cdot 1 by the claim, say x = c\cdot 1 = \varphi(c\,1_{\operatorname{Cl}(q)}). If A is generated as an algebra by 1_A and \iota_A(V), then (A, \iota_A) is a Clifford algebra of (V, q). Let (C, \iota) be the Clifford algebra of @thm-clifford-exists. By its universal property there is an algebra homomorphism \psi \colon C 	o A with \psi\iota = \iota_A. Its image is a subalgebra of A containing 1_A and \iota_A(V), hence is all of A by the generation hypothesis. So \psi is surjective, and \dim_F C = 2^n = \dim_F A by @thm-clifford-dimension-proved, so \psi is an isomorphism. It remains to transport (C2). Let f \colon V 	o B be linear with f(\elem{v})^2 = q(\elem{v})1_B. Then  ar f\psi^{-1} \colon A 	o B is an algebra homomorphism with  ar f\psi^{-1}\iota_A =  ar f\iota = f, where  ar f \colon C 	o B comes from (C2) for C; and if g \colon A 	o B is another one, then g\psi \colon C 	o B satisfies g\psi\iota = g\iota_A = f, so g\psi =  ar f by uniqueness for C, whence g =  ar f\psi^{-1}. R) \cong M_2(

With that, Chapter 14’s last open statement is closed and the construction side of this chapter is complete. The final section spends the machinery on one application, where the failure of decomposability proved above reappears under another name. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. (b) \omega \wedge \eta = (-1)^{kl}\eta \wedge \omega for \omega \in \Lambda^kV, \eta \in \Lambda^lV (@thm-exterior-algebra-graded-commutative). They are isomorphic as vector spaces, and as algebras exactly when q = 0 (@prp-clifford-versus-exterior). B. Practice [B1: Multiplying in the exterior algebra] In \Lambda F^4 with F =

(a) Expanding into four products:  egin{aligned} \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_2 &= \elem{e}_{12}, & \cvec{e}_1 \wedge (\cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_4) &= \elem{0}, \ (\cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_3) \wedge \cvec{e}_2 &= \elem{0}, & (\cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_3) \wedge (\cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_4) &= \elem{e}_{1234} . \end{aligned} The last one sorts as \cvec{e}_2 \wedge \cvec{e}_3 \wedge \cvec{e}_1 \wedge \cvec{e}_4 = \elem{e}_{1234}, since moving \cvec{e}_1 two places to the left costs (-1)^2. Put \elem{u} = c_{12}\elem{e}_1 - c_{23}\elem{e}_3 - c_{24}\elem{e}_4, \qquad \elem{w} = \elem{e}_2 + 	frac{c_{13}}{c_{12}}\elem{e}_3 + 	frac{c_{14}}{c_{12}}\elem{e}_4 . The last comes from (-c_{23}\elem{e}_3 - c_{24}\elem{e}_4) \wedge \Bigl(	frac{c_{13}}{c_{12}}\elem{e}_3 + 	frac{c_{14}}{c_{12}}\elem{e}_4\Bigr) = 	frac{c_{13}c_{24} - c_{14}c_{23}}{c_{12}}\,\elem{e}_{34} . By hypothesis c_{13}c_{24} - c_{14}c_{23} = c_{12}c_{34}, so that coefficient is c_{34} and \elem{u} \wedge \elem{w} = \omega. Hence \omega is decomposable. [C2: Characteristic two] Let F = 
F_2 and \dim V = 4 with basis (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_4). 1. Prove that \omega \wedge \omega = \elem{0} for every \omega \in \Lambda^2V. 2. e T rather than by dividing. Over

e 2, \dim V = n \ge 1, and let (C, \iota) be a Clifford algebra of (V, q), and let (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n) be an orthogonal basis of V for  eta. otin C^{-}, and C^{-}C^{-} \subseteq C^{+} by the same parity count, so C^{-} fails to be closed as soon as it holds an element with nonzero square, such as \iota(\elem{e}_i) with q(\elem{e}_i) 
e 0.

title: 15.11 Tensors in Quantum Mechanics
content:
Tensors in Quantum Mechanics The chapter ends outside mathematics, and the arrangement is the one Chapter 14 used for Minkowski space and for the second derivative test: physics supplies a modeling assumption, the book quotes it and proves nothing about it, and everything after it is linear algebra. The assumption is that a composite quantum system is the tensor product of its parts. Two things follow. One is a phenomenon, entanglement, which turns out to be nothing but §02’s observation that not every element of V \otimes W is a simple tensor. The other is a theorem, the Schmidt decomposition, which turns out to be Chapter 13’s singular value decomposition wearing different notation. The second is the real payoff, and it is why this section closes Part IV: it joins the two halves of the book’s later chapters at a single point. What is quoted and what is proved Quantum mechanics, as a physical theory, is not derived here and cannot be. What we take from it is a short list of modeling conventions, stated once so that the reader can see exactly where the mathematics starts. 1. The states of a quantum system are the unit vectors of a complex inner product space V, where two unit vectors differing by a scalar of modulus 1 describe the same state. 2. If a system A has state space V and a system B has state space W, then the composite system “A together with B” has state space V \otimes W. 3. If A is in the state \elem{v} and B is in the state \elem{w}, then the composite is in the state \elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}. None of (Q1)–(Q3) is a theorem, and this book does not argue for any of them. They are quoted exactly as Taylor’s theorem was quoted in Chapter 14 §06 — as hypotheses that give the mathematics below something to stand on. Everything proved in this section is a statement about finite-dimensional complex inner product spaces, true whether or not (Q1)–(Q3) describe the world. Two remarks make the list less arbitrary. First, \otimes rather than \oplus is visible in a dimension count: a spin has a two-dimensional state space, a qubit, and two spins together have a four-dimensional one, not a three-dimensional one. Of the two standard constructions, only \otimes produces the observed count, since \dim(V \otimes W) = \dim V \cdot \dim W by @thm-tensor-basis. Second, (Q3) very nearly forces (Q2): the assignment (\elem{v}, \elem{w}) \mapsto 	ext{(joint state)} is required to be bilinear, and by @def-tensor-product every bilinear map out of V 	imes W factors uniquely through V \otimes W. The universal property is the precise statement that the joint state depends on the parts bilinearly and in no other way. Genuine quantum mechanics uses infinite-dimensional spaces with a completeness condition. Everything below is finite-dimensional, which is where this book lives, and where qubits live too. Before states can be unit vectors, V \otimes W needs an inner product. There is only one reasonable candidate, and it exists. [The Inner Product on a Tensor Product] Let V and W be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F = 
C (or over 
R). Then there is exactly one inner product on V \otimes W satisfying \inner{\elem{v} \otimes \elem{w}}{\elem{v}' \otimes \elem{w}'} = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}'}\,\inner{\elem{w}}{\elem{w}'} for all \elem{v}, \elem{v}' \in V and \elem{w}, \elem{w}' \in W. Moreover, if \sE and \sF are orthonormal bases of V and W, then (\elem{e}_i \otimes \elem{f}_j) is an orthonormal basis of V \otimes W. Uniqueness. The simple tensors span V \otimes W (@prp-simple-tensors-span), and an inner product is additive in the first slot and conjugate-additive in the second, so its values on all pairs of vectors are determined by its values on pairs of simple tensors. Looking back at Part IV Part IV asked one question in two ways. Chapter 14 took a single bilinear form and asked what it is up to a change of basis; Chapter 15 asked what all multilinear maps have in common, and answered by building the space that turns every one of them into a linear map. The two chapters answer each other. Chapter 14 worked one form at a time and classified: congruence rather than similarity, complete the square, split off a hyperbolic plane, count signs rather than values. Every invariant it produced — the inertia of @thm-sylvester-inertia, the Witt index of @def-witt-index, the discriminant of @def-discriminant — was a number attached to a form that survives a change of basis, and every classification theorem said that a short list of such numbers is all there is. Chapter 15 worked with all forms at once and constructed: define by universal property and then build a model, impose relations by a quotient, define a map out of a quotient upstairs first, and count a basis by counting index tuples. Where Chapter 14 diagonalized a symmetric form by completing the square, Chapter 15 produced the space \Sym^2 V on which that form is a single linear functional; where Chapter 14 proved that alternating is the characteristic-free strengthening of skew, Chapter 15 built \Lambda^k V by killing \elem{v}\otimes\elem{v} for exactly that reason; and where Chapter 14 could only say that a Clifford algebra is unique if it exists, Chapter 15 built one out of T(V) and settled its dimension. This last section adds a third connection, backwards rather than sideways. The Schmidt decomposition is not a new theorem; it is @thm-compact-svd with V \otimes W written in place of M_{m	imes n}. Part III spent a chapter on what a matrix does to two orthonormal bases, one in each of two spaces; Part IV spent a chapter on the space in which a pair of vectors, one from each of two spaces, becomes a single object. Those are the same statement read in two directions, and @thm-tensor-hom-iso is the sentence that says so. Asked years from now what the tensor product is for, a reader may answer that it is where a bilinear map becomes linear; the shortest true answer is that V \otimes W is where the two sides of a matrix live. The number r and the \sigma_k are unique; the lists are not. (d) The Schmidt rank is that r (@def-schmidt-rank). By @cor-schmidt-rank-one-separable, \elem{z} is entangled exactly when r \ge 2. (e) False. The Schmidt rank is at most 3, but need not equal 3: the warning after @def-entangled displays a four-term sum whose Schmidt rank is 1. (f) It is @thm-compact-svd, the compact form of the Singular Value Decomposition @thm-svd. The translation is licensed by @thm-tensor-hom-iso, which identifies a tensor with a linear map and hence, in bases, with a matrix. B. Practice [B1: Determine which are entangled] Work in 
C^2\otimes
C^2 with the standard orthonormal bases. Determine which of the following unit vectors are entangled. Justify your answer, and for each product state exhibit the two factors. 1. 	frac12(\elem{e}_1\otimes\elem{f}_1 + \elem{e}_1\otimes\elem{f}_2 + \elem{e}_2\otimes\elem{f}_1 + \elem{e}_2\otimes\elem{f}_2) 2. 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\elem{e}_1\otimes\elem{f}_2 - \elem{e}_2\otimes\elem{f}_1) 3. 	frac{1}{\sqrt3}(\elem{e}_1\otimes\elem{f}_1 + \elem{e}_1\otimes\elem{f}_2 + \elem{e}_2\otimes\elem{f}_2) 4. 	frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(\elem{e}_1\otimes\elem{f}_1 + 2\elem{e}_1\otimes\elem{f}_2 - \elem{e}_2\otimes\elem{f}_1 - 2\elem{e}_2\otimes\elem{f}_2) By @cor-schmidt-rank-one-separable and the identification of the Schmidt rank with the rank of the coefficient matrix, it suffices to compute ank\C in each case, and for a 2	imes2 matrix that is decided by the determinant. (a) \C = 	frac12 egin{psmallmatrix}1&1\1&1\end{psmallmatrix}, with \det\C = 0 and \C 
e \O, so ank\C = 1: a product state. Indeed it equals 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\elem{e}_1+\elem{e}_2) \otimes 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\elem{f}_1+\elem{f}_2). (b) \C = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} egin{psmallmatrix}0&1\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}, with \det\C = 	frac12

e 0, so ank\C = 2: entangled. (d) \C = 	frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} egin{psmallmatrix}1&2\-1&-2\end{psmallmatrix}, with \det\C = 0 and \C 
e \O, so ank\C = 1: a product state, equal to 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\elem{e}_1-\elem{e}_2) \otimes 	frac{1}{\sqrt5}(\elem{f}_1+2\elem{f}_2). [B2: A Schmidt decomposition] In 
C^2\otimes
C^2, let \elem{z} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} igl(\elem{e}_1\otimes\elem{f}_1 + 2\elem{e}_1\otimes\elem{f}_2 + 2\elem{e}_2\otimes\elem{f}_1 + \elem{e}_2\otimes\elem{f}_2 igr). The coefficient matrix is \C = 	frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} egin{psmallmatrix}1&2\2&1\end{psmallmatrix}, which is real symmetric. Then \C\C	p = 	frac{1}{10} egin{pmatrix}5&4\4&5\end{pmatrix}, with characteristic polynomial x^2 - x + 	frac{9}{100} and eigenvalues 	frac{9}{10} and 	frac1{10}. So the Schmidt coefficients are \sigma_1 = 	frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} and \sigma_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}, the Schmidt rank is 2, and \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 = 	frac9{10} + 	frac1{10} = 1. Eigenvectors of \C\C	p are \cvec{u}_1 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1) for 	frac9{10} and \cvec{u}_2 = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1) for 	frac1{10}. Then \cvec{v}_1 = 	frac{\C	p\cvec{u}_1}{\sigma_1} = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1), \qquad \cvec{v}_2 = 	frac{\C	p\cvec{u}_2}{\sigma_2} = 	frac1{\sqrt2}(-1,1). All entries are real, so reading the columns back as in Step 3 of @thm-schmidt-decomposition,  egin{aligned} \elem{x}_1 &= 	frac{\elem{e}_1+\elem{e}_2}{\sqrt2}, & \elem{y}_1 &= 	frac{\elem{f}_1+\elem{f}_2}{\sqrt2}, \ \elem{x}_2 &= 	frac{\elem{e}_1-\elem{e}_2}{\sqrt2}, & \elem{y}_2 &= 	frac{-\elem{f}_1+\elem{f}_2}{\sqrt2}, \end{aligned} and \elem{z} = 	frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\,\elem{x}_1\otimes\elem{y}_1 + 	frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\,\elem{x}_2\otimes\elem{y}_2. Expanding the two terms gives 	frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}(3 - 1)\elem{e}_1\otimes\elem{f}_1 and similarly for the other three coefficients, recovering \elem{z}. [B3: How large can the Schmidt rank be?] Let V and W be complex inner product spaces with \dim V = m and \dim W = n. 1. Prove that every nonzero \elem{z} \in V \otimes W has Schmidt rank at most \min(m, n). 2. Give, for each r with 1 \le r \le \min(m,n), a unit vector of Schmidt rank exactly r. (a) Fix orthonormal bases and let \C \in M_{m	imes n}(
C) be the coefficient matrix of \elem{z}. By @thm-schmidt-decomposition the Schmidt rank is ank\C, and the rank of an m 	imes n matrix is at most \min(m,n) because ank\C = \dim\col(\C) \le m and ank\C = \dimow(\C) \le n. (b) Take \elem{z}_r = 	frac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_{k=1}^{r}\elem{e}_k\otimes\elem{f}_k. The lists (\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_r) and (\elem{f}_1, \dots, \elem{f}_r) are orthonormal and every coefficient 1/\sqrt r is positive, so this is already an expression of the shape @eq-schmidt; by the uniqueness clause the Schmidt rank is r. It is a unit vector since r \cdot (1/\sqrt r)^2 = 1. C. Going deeper [C1: Acting on one part at a time] Let S \in \cL(V) and T \in \cL(W) be unitary, and let \elem{z} \in V \otimes W be nonzero. 1. Prove that (S \otimes T)(\elem{z}) has the same Schmidt coefficients, and hence the same Schmidt rank, as \elem{z}. 2. Hence deduce that no operator of the form S \otimes T with S, T unitary carries the Bell state \elem{z}_0 of @exm-bell-state to a product state. Hint for (a): apply S \otimes T to a Schmidt decomposition. (a) Write \elem{z} = \sum_{k=1}^{r}\sigma_k\,\elem{x}_k\otimes\elem{y}_k as in @thm-schmidt-decomposition. By @def-tensor-of-maps, (S\otimes T)(\elem{x}_k\otimes\elem{y}_k) = S\elem{x}_k\otimes T\elem{y}_k, so by linearity (S\otimes T)(\elem{z}) = \sum_{k=1}^{r}\sigma_k\,(S\elem{x}_k)\otimes(T\elem{y}_k). A unitary operator preserves inner products (@thm-isometry-characterizations), so \inner{S\elem{x}_k}{S\elem{x}_l} = \inner{\elem{x}_k}{\elem{x}_l} = \delta_{kl} and likewise for T. Both lists are therefore orthonormal, the \sigma_k are still positive and decreasing, and the display is an expression of the shape @eq-schmidt for (S\otimes T)(\elem{z}). By the uniqueness clause of @thm-schmidt-decomposition, its Schmidt coefficients are \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_r and its Schmidt rank is r. (b) The Schmidt rank of \elem{z}_0 is 2, as computed in the warning after @cor-schmidt-rank-one-separable. By (a), (S\otimes T)(\elem{z}_0) also has Schmidt rank 2, and by @cor-schmidt-rank-one-separable a product state has Schmidt rank 1. So (S \otimes T)(\elem{z}_0) is entangled. [C2: Best approximation by a state of small Schmidt rank] Let \elem{z} \in V \otimes W be nonzero with Schmidt decomposition \elem{z} = \sum_{k=1}^{r}\sigma_k\,\elem{x}_k\otimes\elem{y}_k, and let 0 \le k \le r. Put \elem{z}_{(k)} = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_i\,\elem{x}_i\otimes\elem{y}_i. 1. Fix orthonormal bases of V and W and let \C be the coefficient matrix of \elem{z}. Prove that

orm{\elem{z} - \elem{z}'} \ \ge\ \Bigl(\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2\Bigr)^{1/2}, with equality for \elem{z}' = \elem{z}_{(k)}. (a) By @prp-tensor-inner-product the basis (\elem{e}_i\otimes\elem{f}_j) of V\otimes W is orthonormal, so 
orm{\elem{z}}^2 = \sum_{i,j}\lvert c_{ij}vert^2 by @thm-parseval-identity, and that sum is

For the second claim, Step 2 of @thm-schmidt-decomposition produced the Schmidt coefficients as the nonzero singular values of \C, and @thm-svd says there are ank\C of them. (b) The map \elem{z} \mapsto \C is the coordinate isomorphism attached to the basis (\elem{e}_i\otimes\elem{f}_j) (@cor-coordinate-isomorphism), with the mn coordinates arranged in a rectangle, so it is linear and bijective; and by (a) it carries

[C3: Does the field matter?] Let V and W be real inner product spaces of dimensions m and n, with orthonormal bases \sE and \sF, and let \elem{z} \in V\otimes W have coefficient matrix \C \in M_{m	imes n}(
R). Let \elem{z}_{

C^m \otimes

R, with orthonormal lists of real vectors. 2. Prove that \elem{z} and \elem{z}_{

R. @thm-gram-schmidt, @thm-tensor-basis, @thm-compact-svd, @thm-orthonormal-coordinates, and @thm-orthogonal-decomposition are all stated for F =

title: Norms and Matrix Analysis
content:
Norms and Matrix Analysis Nine chapters have been writing promissory notes. Chapter 9 asked what happens to \A^{m} and Chapter 10 §10 answered exactly, entry by entry, with no number attached to the answer: @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero says whether the powers die out, never how fast. Chapter 10 §09 built e^{\A} out of a series (@def-matrix-exponential) and promised that the estimates would come once there was something to estimate with. Chapter 11 solved the least-squares problem (@thm-least-squares) and then, at @thm-qr-factorization, recommended one algorithm over another for a reason it could not yet state. Chapter 12 §01 proved that every matrix has a diagonalizable matrix arbitrarily close to it (@cor-schur-normal-matrix-nearby) and left the word “close” doing work no definition supported. Chapter 13 §09 met a number, the largest stretching factor of a matrix, and said that this chapter would give it a name. Every one of those debts is the same debt: the book has had no way to say how big a vector or a matrix is, except through one particular inner product. A norm is that way. It keeps exactly what measurement needs — a length is zero only for the zero vector, it scales with the scalar, and a detour is never shorter than the direct route — and it throws away the inner product that Chapter 11 used to produce it. There are many norms, and the first surprise is that in finite dimension it does not matter which one you pick: any two of them are trapped between constant multiples of each other, so they agree about every limit, every bounded set, and every continuous function. The second surprise is that the constants cannot be made independent of the dimension, and that the whole theorem collapses in infinite dimension. From there the chapter measures matrices, and then uses the measurements: the spectral radius as the infimum of all the norms, a geometric series that inverts \I - \A, quantitative bounds for the exponential, the continuity of eigenvalues, and finally the condition number, which is the exact constant in the sentence “a small change in the data produces a small change in the answer”. The field in this chapter is 
R or 
C. A norm returns a real number and its homogeneity clause uses \lvert c vert, so the scalars must have an absolute value; no other field in this book has one. This is the same restriction Chapters 11 to 13 worked under, and for the same reason. The analysis this chapter imports This chapter leans on analysis harder than any before it, and the book’s practice is to name what it borrows rather than let it pass unnoticed — as Chapter 14 §06 did with Taylor’s theorem, and Chapter 11 with the theorem of Abel and Ruffini. Here is the complete list. Each item is standard, each is quoted without proof, and each is named again at the point where it is used. 1. (Completeness.) Every nonempty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound; equivalently, every Cauchy sequence of real or complex numbers converges. One standard consequence is used as well: every real number is the limit of a sequence of rational numbers. 2. (Monotone convergence.) An increasing sequence of real numbers that is bounded above converges, and its limit is its least upper bound. 3. (Compactness of the closed unit ball.) In 
R^{n} and in 
C^{n} with the Euclidean norm, every sequence lying in a closed bounded set has a subsequence converging to a point of that set. In particular the closed unit ball and the unit sphere are compact. 4. (Extreme value theorem.) A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact set attains a maximum value and a minimum value; the bounds are not merely approached, they are reached. 5. (Intermediate value theorem.) A continuous real-valued function on an interval takes every value between any two of its values. 6. (Mean value theorem.) A real-valued function differentiable on an interval satisfies f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b-a) for some c strictly between a and b. Two consequences are used: a function with negative derivative throughout an interval is strictly decreasing there, and a function whose derivative is positive to the left of a point and negative to its right attains its maximum at that point. Alongside these, the elementary algebra of limits is used throughout without further comment: limits respect sums, products, and quotients with nonvanishing denominator; sums, products, and composites of continuous functions are continuous; and a nonstrict inequality survives a limit, so that a_k \le M for every k forces \lim a_k \le M. Chapter 10 §09 quoted the same package as its fact (A3). What the list above records is everything beyond that. Several of these speak of continuity, which the book has not needed until now, so fix the meaning here. A function f defined on a subset of a normed space is continuous at \elem{x} when 
orm{\elem{x}_k - \elem{x}} 	o 0 forces f(\elem{x}_k) 	o f(\elem{x}) for every sequence (\elem{x}_k) in its domain, and continuous when it is continuous at every point of its domain. This is the sequential form, matching the way (A3) is stated. Every continuity claim in this chapter is established the same cheap way: by exhibiting a constant M with \lvert f(\elem{x}) - f(\elem{y})vert \le M
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}}, which gives the implication at once. §02 proves the first such bound. Nothing else analytic enters silently. Where a section needs a fact outside this list — the differentiability of the entries of a matrix-valued function, or the continuous dependence of the roots of a polynomial on its coefficients — it is recorded as an assumption in the same manner, with a counterexample proved where one is available, and never used as a step in a proof that pretends to be self-contained. What you need The chapter is built on results the book already has. Gathered by source, so that a reader can go back to one place at a time: - Chapter 0 §06 and §09 — two small facts, each used once: the triangle inequality for complex numbers, which §07 needs before it can bound a sum of moduli, and the cyclic invariance of the trace, which §06 uses on the Frobenius inner product: @thm-complex-triangle-inequality, @thm-trace-properties. - Chapter 2, with Chapter 1 for the words — bases, dimension, and coordinates: @def-basis, @def-dimension, @def-coordinates, @thm-coordinates-linear, @cor-coordinate-isomorphism. What the proofs cite is the coordinate isomorphism; basis and dimension are vocabulary the chapter assumes rather than results it leans on. - Chapter 11 §01 and §07 — the inner product and the norm it induces, with their three properties and the two inequalities that follow: @def-inner-product, @def-induced-norm, @thm-norm-properties, @thm-cauchy-schwarz, @cor-triangle-inequality, together with the two exercises that recover an inner product from its norm, @exr-inner-products-c1 and @exr-inner-products-c2; and, from §07, the Frobenius norm and its unitary invariance, @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant. - Chapter 11 §04 and §08 — least squares and the \Q\R factorization whose stability claim was deferred: @thm-least-squares, @cor-least-squares-unique, @thm-qr-factorization. - Chapter 10 §10 — the whole convergence apparatus that this chapter re-proves with numbers attached: @def-entrywise-convergence, @lem-powers-transfer-along-similarity, @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero, @thm-matrix-powers-bounded, @thm-matrix-powers-converge, @thm-neumann-series-spectral, @cor-markov-powers-converge. - Chapter 10 §09 and §03 — the matrix exponential and the Jordan form: @def-matrix-exponential, @thm-exponential-series-converges, @thm-exponential-properties, @thm-jordan-canonical-form. - Chapter 7 — determinants, and only in §§06 and 07: the Leibniz formula, minors and cofactors, Laplace expansion, and the adjugate identity, which between them make the entries of an inverse polynomial in the entries of the matrix; and the characteristic polynomial: @thm-leibniz-formula-alternating, @def-minor-cofactor, @thm-laplace-expansion, @def-adjugate, @thm-adjugate-identity, @thm-charpoly-coefficients, @thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant. - Chapter 9 — where the spectral radius comes from: the characterizations of an eigenvalue and the algebraic multiplicity, the eigenvalues on the diagonal of a triangular form, and the spectral mapping theorem: @thm-eigenvalue-characterizations, @def-algebraic-multiplicity, @thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form, @thm-spectral-mapping. - Chapter 12 — Schur triangularization with its density corollary, and the defect the Frobenius norm measures: @thm-schur-triangularization, @cor-schur-normal-matrix-nearby, @thm-schur-inequality, @def-departure-from-normality. - Chapter 13 — the singular value decomposition and the two constructions built on it: @thm-svd, @def-singular-values, @def-pseudoinverse. Roadmap - Norms. The three axioms, the 1-, 2-, and \infty-norms with their unit balls drawn, and the test that decides which norms come from an inner product: the parallelogram law. This pays off a promise made in Chapter 11 §01. - All norms agree. On a finite-dimensional space any two norms are trapped between constant multiples of each other. Compactness enters the book here, and the payoff is that Chapter 10 §10’s entrywise convergence is simply the convergence, whatever norm one prefers. - Measuring a matrix. Submultiplicativity, and the operator norm 
orm{\A} = \max\{
orm{\A\cvec{x}} : 
orm{\cvec{x}} = 1\} induced by a vector norm. Its formulas for p = 1, 2, \infty, including 
orm{\A}_2 = \sigma_1(\A), which is the name Chapter 13 §09 asked for. - The spectral radius. ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A} for every matrix norm, a norm that comes within \varepsilon of ho(\A), and Gelfand’s formula ho(\A) = \lim 
orm{\A^{k}}^{1/k}. - Inverting a perturbation of the identity. The Neumann series, the openness of the invertible matrices, and the first perturbation estimate. - The exponential, with bounds; and derivatives. 
orm{e^{\A}} \le e^{
orm{\A}}, decay when the spectrum sits in the left half plane, and the derivatives of the determinant and of the inverse. - Eigenvalues move continuously. Continuously as a multiset, and no better: a Jordan block’s eigenvalues move like \varepsilon^{1/k}. - How wrong can the answer be? The condition number \kappa(\A) = 
orm{\A}
orm{\A^{-1}}, what it predicts about solving \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}, and why the normal equations square it. Named moves - Compactness turns “for all unit vectors” into a maximum. A supremum over the unit sphere is hard to control; a maximum is attained at a vector you can name and feed back into the argument. Both the equivalence of norms and the very existence of the operator norm are this one move. - Ask for submultiplicativity. A matrix is a vector, so a matrix norm is a vector norm; what makes it useful is the extra clause 
orm{\A\B} \le 
orm{\A}
orm{\B}, which is the only reason a bound on 
orm{\A} says anything about \A^{k}. Test every candidate against it, and expect natural-looking candidates to fail. - Bound the tail of a series. Neumann, the exponential, and Gelfand all reduce to estimating \sum_{k \ge K}
orm{\A}^{k} or \sum_{k \ge K}
orm{\A}^{k}/k! by something that visibly tends to zero. - Perturb and compare. Replace \A by \A + \E, subtract the two conclusions, and read the result as a bound on the relative change in the answer by a constant times the relative change in the data. The constant is the condition number. - Reduce to the 2-norm. Equivalence of norms means any single norm may be used as the hub: prove the estimate for the Euclidean norm, where the inner product and the singular value decomposition are available, and transfer.

title: 16.1 Norms
content:
Norms Chapter 11 measured vectors, and measured them in exactly one way: 
orm{\elem{v}} = \sqrt{\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}}. Every length in Chapters 11 to 13 came out of that formula. This section keeps the measuring and throws the inner product away. The reason is not economy. The quantities this part of the book owes — how fast a sequence of matrices settles down, how far a solution moves when the data moves — are often measured most naturally by a size that no inner product produces, and the arguments that use them turn out to need only three properties of a length. The field here is 
R or 
C, as it is throughout the chapter. A length is a real number, and the scaling rule below multiplies it by \lvert c vert; so the scalars must carry an absolute value, and these are the only fields in this book that do. What measurement actually needs Look back at how 
orm{\cdot} was used after Chapter 11 defined it. Cauchy–Schwarz needed the inner product. So did Pythagoras, orthogonality, and the adjoint. But a long list of arguments did not: that a convergent sequence is bounded, that 
orm{\A\cvec{x}} is small when \cvec{x} is small, that a limit of unit vectors is a unit vector, that 
orm{\elem{u} - \elem{w}} \le 
orm{\elem{u} - \elem{v}} + 
orm{\elem{v} - \elem{w}}. Every one of those used only that 
orm{\elem{v}} vanishes just for \elem{v} = \elem{0}, that 
orm{c\elem{v}} = \lvert c vert
orm{\elem{v}}, and the triangle inequality of @cor-triangle-inequality. Three properties, used over and over. Following the book’s habit, we give the three of them a name and see what else satisfies them. A norm is a length: zero only at the zero vector, scaling with the scalar, and never rewarding a detour. [Norm] Let F be 
R or 
C and let V be a vector space over F. A norm on V is a function 
orm{\cdot} \colon V 	o 
R such that for all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V and all c \in F: 1. 
orm{\elem{v}} \ge 0, and 
orm{\elem{v}} = 0 only for \elem{v} = \elem{0} (positive definiteness); 2. 
orm{c\elem{v}} = \lvert c vert\,
orm{\elem{v}} (absolute homogeneity); 3. 
orm{\elem{u} + \elem{v}} \le 
orm{\elem{u}} + 
orm{\elem{v}} (the triangle inequality). A vector space carrying a norm is a normed space. A vector with 
orm{\elem{v}} = 1 is a unit vector, and replacing a nonzero \elem{v} by \elem{v}/
orm{\elem{v}} is normalizing it. In words, clause by clause. (N1) says the output is a genuine nonnegative size, and that only the zero vector has size zero; the word only is the whole content, since the reverse implication is free (take c = 0 in (N2) to get 
orm{\elem{0}} = 0\cdot
orm{\elem{0}} = 0). (N2) says that stretching a vector by c stretches its length by \lvert c vert — the absolute value of c, so that 
orm{-\elem{v}} = 
orm{\elem{v}} and, over 
C, 
orm{i\elem{v}} = 
orm{\elem{v}}. (N3) says that going from \elem{0} to \elem{u} + \elem{v} directly is at most as long as going by way of \elem{u}. Note what the definition does not mention: no second vector is paired with the first, no angle appears, and there is no inner product anywhere. Two remarks on the shape of the definition. First, the codomain is 
R even when F = 
C: a length is never complex. Second, the three clauses are not independent of the arithmetic of 
R — (N3) is an inequality, and inequalities are why the field had to be restricted. [The 1-, 2-, and \infty-norms on F^n] For \cvec{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in F^n put  egin{aligned} 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 &= \lvert x_1vert + \dots + \lvert x_nvert , \

A norm either obeys it, and then it is secretly an inner product with an inner product’s entire apparatus of angles, orthogonality, and adjoints; or it violates it once, and then no inner product will ever produce it. Neither 
orm{\cdot}_1 nor 
orm{\cdot}_\infty comes from an inner product. Test (\ast) on \cvec{u} = \cvec{e}_1 and \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_2 in F^2. Both \cvec{u} + \cvec{v} = (1,1) and \cvec{u} - \cvec{v} = (1,-1) have 
orm{\cdot}_1 = 2, so the left side of (\ast) is 4 + 4 = 8, while the right side is 2 + 2 = 4. For 
orm{\cdot}_\infty both have norm 1, so the left side is 2 and the right side is again 4. One failing pair is enough, and there is no repair: by @thm-parallelogram-characterization no inner product whatsoever induces these norms, in any dimension \ge 2. The same two vectors f(t) = t and g(t) = 1 - t in C[0,1] refute it for the sup norm, since 
orm{f}_\infty = 
orm{g}_\infty = 
orm{f+g}_\infty = 
orm{f-g}_\infty = 1. The function N(\cvec{x}) =  igl(x_1^2 + 4x_2^2 igr)^{1/2} is a norm on 
R^2, and it is lopsided: N(\cvec{e}_1) = 1 while N(\cvec{e}_2) = 2. Does it come from an inner product? Yes. It is the norm induced by \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = x_1y_1 + 4x_2y_2, which satisfies (IP1) and (IP2) by inspection and (IP3) because x_1^2 + 4x_2^2 > 0 for \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}. One may also check (\ast) directly: both sides expand to 2x_1^2 + 8x_2^2 + 2y_1^2 + 8y_2^2. The lesson is that a norm can be visibly lopsided — its unit ball here is an ellipse, not a circle — and still be an inner-product norm. What matters is not roundness but the parallelogram law. So the norms of this book split in two. On one side sit 
orm{\cdot}_2, the Frobenius norm, and every weighted Euclidean norm, where Chapters 11 to 13 apply in full. On the other sit 
orm{\cdot}_1, 
orm{\cdot}_\infty, and the sup norm, where there is no orthogonality and no adjoint, and the only tools are the three axioms. The next section shows that for questions about convergence the split does not matter at all. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the three clauses of @def-norm, and say which one fails for N(\cvec{x}) = \lvert x_1vert on F^2. 2. Deduce 
orm{\elem{0}} = 0 from (N2) alone, and explain why (N1) is therefore stated with the word only. 3. True or false: a function satisfying (N1) and (N3) but not (N2) cannot exist. It is the weighted norm of @exm-induced-and-weighted-norms (b) in its 1-norm form: (N1) because both terms are \ge 0 and both vanish only for \cvec{x} = \cvec{0}; (N2) because \lvert cx_ivert = \lvert cvert\lvert x_ivert; (N3) coordinatewise, exactly as for 
orm{\cdot}_1. (b) Not a norm. (N2) and (N3) hold, inherited from \lvert\cdotvert on 
R. (N1) fails: N igl((1,1) igr) = 0 with (1,1)

(N3) fails: with \cvec{u} = (1,1) and \cvec{v} = (1,-1) we get N(\cvec{u}) = N(\cvec{v}) = 1 - 	frac14 = 	frac34, while \cvec{u} + \cvec{v} = (2,0) has N(\cvec{u} + \cvec{v}) = 2 - 0 = 2 > 	frac32. e \cvec{0}. Compare (c): there the subtracted term was large enough to break (N3), here it is not, and the way to tell is to rewrite the formula rather than to guess. [B3: Which of these come from an inner product?] For each norm, determine whether it is induced by an inner product. Justify your answer, using @thm-parallelogram-characterization in each case. 1.

It is bilinear and symmetric by inspection, and \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = x_1^2 + x_1x_2 + x_2^2 = (x_1 + 	frac12x_2)^2 + 	frac34x_2^2, which is > 0 unless x_2 = 0 and x_1 = 0; so (IP3) holds and the induced norm is the given one. Then \A \pm \B has entries 1 and \pm 1 in the first row and zeros elsewhere, so N(\A + \B) = N(\A - \B) = 1 and the left side of (\ast) is 2, while the right side is 2 \cdot 1 + 2\cdot 1 = 4. R^n gives

C as a one-dimensional complex vector space, and also as 
R^2 by z = a + bi \leftrightarrow (a,b). Define N(z) = 2\lvert avert + \lvert bvert. 1. Prove that N is a norm on 
R^2. 2. Prove that N is not a norm on 
C as a complex vector space, and name the exact clause that fails. 3. Prove that if

(b) (N2) fails for the complex scalar c = i. Indeed N(1) = 2 and N(i) = 1, while (N2) would demand N(i\cdot 1) = \lvert ivert N(1) = 2. (c) Restricting the scalars from 
C to 
R leaves the vectors, the addition, and the zero vector unchanged, so (N1) and (N3) are the same statements. (N2) for real c is a special case of (N2) for complex c, the absolute value of a real number being the same in 
R and in 
C. There is no contradiction with (b) because the implication runs one way only: (N2) over

orm{\elem{v}} \le t if and only if \elem{v}/t lies in the closed unit ball of 
orm{\cdot}. 2. Hence prove that 
orm{\elem{v}} = N(\elem{v}) for every \elem{v} \in V. 3. Give two different norms on 
R^2 whose closed unit balls have the same area, and say why (b) does not apply to them. (a) Since t > 0, (N2) gives 
orm{\elem{v}/t} = 
orm{\elem{v}}/t. So \elem{v}/t lies in the ball exactly when 
orm{\elem{v}}/t \le 1, that is, exactly when 
orm{\elem{v}} \le t. (b) For \elem{v} = \elem{0} both sides are 0 by (N1). Let \elem{v} 
e \elem{0} and put t = 
orm{\elem{v}} > 0. By (a), \elem{v}/t lies in the ball of 
orm{\cdot}, hence in the ball of N, hence N(\elem{v}) \le t = 
orm{\elem{v}} by (a) applied to N. Swapping the roles of 
orm{\cdot} and N gives 
orm{\elem{v}} \le N(\elem{v}). Therefore 
orm{\elem{v}} = N(\elem{v}). (c) Take 
orm{\cdot}_1, whose ball is the diamond with vertices \pm\cvec{e}_1 and \pm\cvec{e}_2, of area 2; and N(\cvec{x}) = 2\lvert x_1vert + 	frac12\lvert x_2vert, whose ball is the diamond with vertices \pm	frac12\cvec{e}_1 and \pm2\cvec{e}_2, also of area 2. title: 16.2 All Norms Agree
content:
All Norms Agree §01 left a worry. There are many norms on F^n, they give different answers, and every statement of the form “this quantity is small” now has to say small in which norm. This section removes the worry in finite dimension, in the strongest way available: any two norms on a finite-dimensional space are trapped between fixed multiples of each other, so they agree about every limit, every bounded set, and every continuous function. It also says what the theorem costs — constants that grow with the dimension — and where it stops being true. Trapped between multiples Look again at @prp-p-norm-inequalities. Its four inequalities say that on F^n, 	frac{1}{\sqrt n}\,
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 \ \le\ 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \ \le\ 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 , so 
orm{\cdot}_2 never differs from 
orm{\cdot}_1 by a factor worse than \sqrt n, in either direction. Whatever 
orm{\cdot}_1 calls small, 
orm{\cdot}_2 calls small too, at the cost of a fixed factor. That is a relation worth naming. Two norms are equivalent when each is sandwiched between two fixed multiples of the other, so that neither can be small while the other is large. [Equivalent Norms] Let V be a vector space over F = 
R or 
C, and let 
orm{\cdot}_a and 
orm{\cdot}_b be norms on V. They are equivalent if there exist real constants c, C > 0, not depending on the vector, such that c\,
orm{\elem{v}}_b \ \le\ 
orm{\elem{v}}_a \ \le\ C\,
orm{\elem{v}}_b \qquad 	ext{for every } \elem{v} \in V . In words. The two inequalities are read separately: the right one says 
orm{\cdot}_a is no larger than a fixed multiple of 
orm{\cdot}_b, and the left one says it is no smaller than a fixed positive multiple. The phrase not depending on the vector is the whole content, since for each individual \elem{v} 
e \elem{0} the ratio 
orm{\elem{v}}_a/
orm{\elem{v}}_b is some positive number and one could always take that number as the constant. What is being asked is that one pair of constants works for all \elem{v} at once. Note also that the definition says nothing about the two norms being close; c may be 10^{-6}. [The three p-norms, with best constants] On F^n, @prp-p-norm-inequalities gives  egin{aligned} 
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty &\le 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le \sqrt n\,

orm{\cvec{x}}_1 \le n\,
