orm{\cvec{x}}_1 &\le 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 , \end{aligned} so the three are pairwise equivalent. The middle line’s upper constant comes from 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 \le \sqrt n
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le \sqrt n\cdot\sqrt n\,
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty. Every constant shown is attained, so none of them can be improved. On the first two lines the lower constant is attained at \cvec{e}_1 and the upper one at \1. The third line runs the other way: at \1 the lower inequality reads 	frac{1}{\sqrt n}\cdot n = \sqrt n \le \sqrt n, and at \cvec{e}_1 the upper one reads 1 \le 1. Before the theorem, one small fact makes the proof strategy possible: it is enough to compare every norm with a single one of our choosing. [Equivalence of Norms Is an Equivalence Relation] On a fixed vector space V over F, the relation of @def-equivalent-norms is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Reflexive: take c = C = 1. Symmetric: if c
orm{\elem{v}}_b \le 
orm{\elem{v}}_a \le C
orm{\elem{v}}_b for all \elem{v}, then dividing through by the positive constants gives C^{-1}
orm{\elem{v}}_a \le 
orm{\elem{v}}_b \le c^{-1}
orm{\elem{v}}_a. Transitive: if in addition c'
orm{\elem{v}}_d \le 
orm{\elem{v}}_b \le C'
orm{\elem{v}}_d, then multiplying the first chain’s outer inequalities by the positive constants c and C gives cc'
orm{\elem{v}}_d \le c
orm{\elem{v}}_b \le 
orm{\elem{v}}_a \le C
orm{\elem{v}}_b \le CC'
orm{\elem{v}}_d , and cc', CC' > 0. This proves all three properties. So to prove that any two norms on V are equivalent, it suffices to prove that every norm is equivalent to one fixed reference norm. We take the reference to be the Euclidean norm of a chosen basis, because that is where compactness lives. Compactness enters the book [Equivalence of Norms in Finite Dimension] Let V be a vector space over F = 
R or 
C with \dim V = n < \infty. Then any two norms on V are equivalent. Explicitly, if \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) is a basis of V, if 
orm{\cdot}_2 denotes the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector, \Bigl\lVert \sum_i x_i\elem{v}_i \BigrVert_2 \coloneqq  igl(\lvert x_1vert^2 + \dots + \lvert x_nvert^2 igr)^{1/2} , and if N is any norm on V, then there are constants 0 < m \le M with m\,
orm{\elem{v}}_2 \ \le\ N(\elem{v}) \ \le\ M\,
orm{\elem{v}}_2 \qquad 	ext{for every } \elem{v} \in V . The two inequalities are not symmetric, and it is worth seeing why before starting. The upper bound is cheap: write \elem{v} in the basis, apply the triangle inequality once, and the constant M is built out of the numbers N(\elem{v}_i). The lower bound cannot be obtained the same way; there is no inequality running from N(\sum x_i\elem{v}_i) down to the individual coordinates, and the temptation to assume that the two norms are comparable on the basis and then “extend by linearity” is exactly the error the theorem exists to forbid — @exm-two-norms-agree-on-a-basis below shows two norms agreeing on a basis and differing by a factor of n elsewhere. The route is therefore ① upper bound by the triangle inequality; ② use that upper bound to show N is continuous as a function of the coordinates; ③ restrict N to the Euclidean unit sphere, which is compact, so N attains a minimum m there; ④ the minimum is positive because N vanishes only at \cvec{0}, which is not on the sphere; ⑤ scale back. Compactness is what turns the infimum over infinitely many unit vectors into a value attained at a particular unit vector, and a value attained at a vector can be tested for positivity one vector at a time. By @prp-equivalence-of-norms-relation it suffices to prove the displayed two-sided bound, since then any two norms N_1, N_2 are each equivalent to 
orm{\cdot}_2 and hence to each other. If n = 0 then V = \{\elem{0}\}, both norms are the zero function and m = M = 1 works; assume n \ge 1. The coordinate map \Phi \colon F^n 	o V, \cvec{x} \mapsto \sum_i x_i\elem{v}_i, is an isomorphism (@cor-coordinate-isomorphism), and by construction 
orm{\Phi(\cvec{x})}_2 = 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 is the Euclidean norm of @exm-p-norms. It is enough to prove the two bounds for \cvec{x} \in F^n with N replaced by f(\cvec{x}) \coloneqq N(\Phi(\cvec{x})). Step 1. The upper bound. Let M =  igl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} N(\elem{v}_i)^2 igr)^{1/2}. For \cvec{x} \in F^n, the triangle inequality (N3) applied n - 1 times and then (N2) give f(\cvec{x}) = N\Bigl(\sum_i x_i\elem{v}_i\Bigr) \le \sum_i \lvert x_ivert\,N(\elem{v}_i) , and @thm-cauchy-schwarz in 
R^n, applied to the vectors (\lvert x_1vert, \dots, \lvert x_nvert) and (N(\elem{v}_1), \dots, N(\elem{v}_n)), bounds the right-hand side by M
orm{\cvec{x}}_2. Hence f(\cvec{x}) \le M
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 for every \cvec{x}. Also M > 0, since N(\elem{v}_1) > 0 by (N1) and \elem{v}_1 
e \elem{0}. Step 2. f is continuous on F^n for the Euclidean norm. By @lem-reverse-triangle-norm applied to N, and then Step 1 applied to \cvec{x} - \cvec{y}, \lvert f(\cvec{x}) - f(\cvec{y})vert \le N igl(\Phi(\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}) igr) \le M\,
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}}_2 . So f changes by at most M times the distance moved: it is continuous, and the continuity was deduced from Step 1 rather than assumed. Step 3. The minimum on the unit sphere. Let S = \{\cvec{x} \in F^n : 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 = 1\} , which is nonempty because n \ge 1 (it contains \cvec{e}_1). It is bounded, and it is closed: if 
orm{\cvec{x}_k - \cvec{x}}_2 	o 0 with every 
orm{\cvec{x}_k}_2 = 1, then @lem-reverse-triangle-norm gives  igl\lvert 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 - 1 igrvert \le 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{x}_k}_2 	o 0, so 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 = 1 and \cvec{x} \in S. By the compactness of closed bounded sets in F^n, fact (A3) of the chapter introduction, S is compact; by the extreme value theorem, fact (A4), the continuous function f of Step 2 attains a minimum value on S. Say m = f(\cvec{x}_0) with \cvec{x}_0 \in S. Step 4. The minimum is positive. Since \cvec{x}_0 \in S we have 
orm{\cvec{x}_0}_2 = 1 
e 0, so \cvec{x}_0 
e \cvec{0} and hence \Phi(\cvec{x}_0) 
e \elem{0}, \Phi being injective. By (N1) for N, m = N(\Phi(\cvec{x}_0)) > 0. This is the step that needs a minimum rather than an infimum: an infimum of positive numbers can be 0, while a minimum is the value at an actual vector, and there (N1) can be applied. Step 5. Scaling back. Let \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}. Then \cvec{x}/
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \in S, so f(\cvec{x}/
orm{\cvec{x}}_2) \ge m, and (N2) for N gives f(\cvec{x}) \ge m
orm{\cvec{x}}_2. For \cvec{x} = \cvec{0} both sides are 0. Combining with Step 1, m\,
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \ \le\ f(\cvec{x}) \ \le\ M\,
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \qquad (\cvec{x} \in F^n), and transporting along \Phi gives the statement for V. Since m \le f(\cvec{x}_0) \le M
orm{\cvec{x}_0}_2 = M, the constants satisfy 0 < m \le M. This proves the theorem. The proof used the finite dimension twice, and it is worth saying where: once in Step 1, where the triangle inequality was applied finitely many times to a finite basis expansion, and once in Step 3, where F^n is the space in which closed bounded sets are compact. Remove either and the argument collapses, as the last part of this section shows. [Agreeing on a basis is not enough] On F^n, the norms 
orm{\cdot}_1 and 
orm{\cdot}_\infty both give every standard basis vector the value 1. Yet 
orm{\1}_1 = n and 
orm{\1}_\infty = 1. So the data “N_1(\elem{v}_i) = N_2(\elem{v}_i) for every basis vector” implies no inequality between N_1 and N_2 beyond what @thm-norm-equivalence gives for any pair at all. In Step 1 the constant was M =  igl(\sum_i N(\elem{v}_i)^2 igr)^{1/2}. Where would the proof break if we tried the symmetric guess m = \min_i N(\elem{v}_i) for the lower bound? It breaks immediately, and @exm-two-norms-agree-on-a-basis is the witness. Take V = F^2 with the basis (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2), N = 
orm{\cdot}_\infty, and 
orm{\cdot}_2 the Euclidean norm. Then \min_i N(\cvec{e}_i) = 1, and the guessed inequality 
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty \ge 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 fails at \cvec{x} = \1, where the two sides are 1 and \sqrt 2. The reason is that the triangle inequality only ever bounds N(\sum x_i\elem{v}_i) from above; there is no lower bound in the axioms, because a sum of long vectors can be short. Getting a lower bound needs a genuinely different mechanism, and compactness is that mechanism. What the theorem buys The point of the theorem is that whole sentences may now drop the words “in which norm”. [Convergence and Boundedness Do Not Depend on the Norm] Let V be finite-dimensional over 
R or 
C, let 
orm{\cdot}_a and 
orm{\cdot}_b be norms on V, and let (\elem{u}_k) be a sequence in V with \elem{u} \in V. Then: 1. 
orm{\elem{u}_k - \elem{u}}_a 	o 0 if and only if 
orm{\elem{u}_k - \elem{u}}_b 	o 0; 2. (\elem{u}_k) is bounded for 
orm{\cdot}_a if and only if it is bounded for 
orm{\cdot}_b; 3. (\elem{u}_k) is Cauchy for 
orm{\cdot}_a if and only if it is Cauchy for 
orm{\cdot}_b. By @thm-norm-equivalence there are c, C > 0 with c
orm{\elem{v}}_b \le 
orm{\elem{v}}_a \le C
orm{\elem{v}}_b for every \elem{v} \in V. For (a), apply this to \elem{v} = \elem{u}_k - \elem{u}: if 
orm{\elem{u}_k - \elem{u}}_b 	o 0 then 0 \le 
orm{\elem{u}_k - \elem{u}}_a \le C
orm{\elem{u}_k - \elem{u}}_b 	o 0, and conversely 
orm{\elem{u}_k - \elem{u}}_b \le c^{-1}
orm{\elem{u}_k - \elem{u}}_a 	o 0. For (b), a bound 
orm{\elem{u}_k}_b \le K for all k gives 
orm{\elem{u}_k}_a \le CK, and conversely with c^{-1}. For (c), apply the same two estimates to \elem{v} = \elem{u}_k - \elem{u}_l. This proves all three. Now the connection this chapter was built for. Chapter 10 §10 defined convergence of matrices entrywise (@def-entrywise-convergence) and said, in its opening paragraph, that no notion of the size of a matrix was used and that Chapter 16 would supply one. Here is the reconciliation. [Entrywise Convergence Is Convergence in Every Norm] Let \M_1, \M_2, \dots and \M lie in M_{p	imes q}(
C), and let 
orm{\cdot} be any norm on M_{p	imes q}(
C). Then \M_k 	o \M entrywise in the sense of @def-entrywise-convergence if and only if 
orm{\M_k - \M} 	o 0. Likewise (\M_k) is bounded in the sense of @def-entrywise-convergence if and only if  igl(
orm{\M_k} igr) is a bounded sequence of real numbers. Entrywise convergence is convergence in one particular norm, the entrywise maximum. @thm-norm-equivalence says every other norm is trapped between two multiples of it, and a quantity squeezed between two multiples of something tending to 0 tends to 0 as well. Both directions are that one sentence. The space M_{p	imes q}(
C) is a complex vector space of dimension pq, and N_\infty(\M) = \max_{r,s}\lvert m_{rs}vert is a norm on it: it is the \infty-norm of @exm-p-norms read on the list of entries, through the coordinate isomorphism of @cor-coordinate-isomorphism that sends a matrix to its pq entries. By @def-entrywise-convergence (a), \M_k 	o \M entrywise means (\M_k)_{rs} 	o \M_{rs} for each of the finitely many positions (r,s), and since a maximum of finitely many nonnegative sequences tends to 0 exactly when each of them does, this says precisely N_\infty(\M_k - \M) 	o 0. By @thm-norm-equivalence the norms N_\infty and 
orm{\cdot} are equivalent, so @cor-convergence-norm-independent (a) converts this into 
orm{\M_k - \M} 	o 0. The statement about boundedness is @def-entrywise-convergence (b) together with @cor-convergence-norm-independent (b), read the same way. [Watching one sequence converge] In M_2(
R) let \M_k =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac1k & 2 \[2pt] 0 & 1 - 	frac1k \end{pmatrix} , \qquad k \ge 1 . Entry by entry, 	frac1k 	o 0, 2 	o 2, 0 	o 0, and 1 - 	frac1k 	o 1, so \M_k 	o \M =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 2 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} in the sense of @def-entrywise-convergence. The corollary says this is convergence in every norm, and here one can see it directly: \M_k - \M = \diag(	frac1k, -	frac1k), so 
orm{\M_k - \M}_F = \sqrt{	frac{1}{k^2} + 	frac{1}{k^2}} =  rac{\sqrt2}{k} \longrightarrow 0 , and 
orm{\M_k - \M}_\infty, the largest absolute row sum, is 	frac1k. Different norms, different constants, the same verdict — which is the content of the corollary. So Chapter 10 §10 lost nothing by working entrywise. Its @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero, @thm-matrix-powers-bounded, @thm-matrix-powers-converge, and @thm-neumann-series-spectral are statements about the convergence of matrices, and every norm this chapter introduces — the Frobenius norm, the operator norms of §03, anything at all — measures the same thing. What the norms add is not a new notion of limit but a rate: a single number 
orm{\A^{k}} that can be bounded, compared, and summed, where an entrywise statement gives pq separate sequences and no way to combine them. One more corollary, which §03 will use to know that the operator norm exists at all. [Closed and Bounded Is Compact, in Every Norm] Let V be finite-dimensional over 
R or 
C. Call a subset K \subseteq V bounded for a norm if K \subseteq \{\elem{v} : 
orm{\elem{v}} \le R\} for some real R, and closed for that norm if whenever 
orm{\elem{u}_k - \elem{u}} 	o 0 with every \elem{u}_k \in K, also \elem{u} \in K. Then a subset that is closed and bounded for one norm is closed and bounded for every norm, and is compact: every sequence in it has a subsequence converging to a point of it. In particular, when V 
e \{\elem{0}\}, the unit sphere \{\elem{v} : 
orm{\elem{v}} = 1\} of any norm is nonempty and compact, and a continuous real-valued function on it attains a maximum and a minimum. Both words in “closed and bounded” are defined by a norm, so the first thing to check is that changing the norm changes neither. That is @thm-norm-equivalence again. Once the words are norm-free, the statement is @thm-norm-equivalence’s own compactness step read in a coordinate-free way: carry K to F^n by coordinates, apply (A3), and carry the limit back. Fix a basis and transport everything to F^n by the coordinate isomorphism (@cor-coordinate-isomorphism), as in the proof of @thm-norm-equivalence. Let 
orm{\cdot}_a and 
orm{\cdot}_b be norms, with c
orm{\cdot}_b \le 
orm{\cdot}_a \le C
orm{\cdot}_b from @thm-norm-equivalence. A set bounded for one is bounded for the other by the same two estimates as in @cor-convergence-norm-independent (b). A set closed for one is closed for the other, because by @cor-convergence-norm-independent (a) the two norms have the same convergent sequences with the same limits, and the notion of closed defined in the statement asks exactly that limits of convergent sequences stay in the set. For compactness, let K \subseteq F^n be closed and bounded for some norm; by the previous paragraph it is closed and bounded for 
orm{\cdot}_2. By the compactness of closed bounded sets in F^n, fact (A3) of the chapter introduction, every sequence in K has a subsequence converging in 
orm{\cdot}_2 to a point of K, and by @cor-convergence-norm-independent (a) that subsequence converges in every norm to the same point. The unit sphere of a norm N is bounded, and it is closed because \lvert N(\elem{v}) - N(\elem{u}_k)vert \le N(\elem{v} - \elem{u}_k) by @lem-reverse-triangle-norm, so a limit of vectors with N = 1 has N = 1; it is nonempty when V 
e \{\elem{0}\}, since N(\elem{v})^{-1}\elem{v} lies on it for any \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}. The last sentence is then the extreme value theorem, fact (A4), applied to that nonempty compact set. This proves the corollary. Two warnings, and where the theorem stops The theorem is not permission to forget which norm is in use. Here is the first reason. The constants depend on the dimension, and grow. @exm-norm-equivalence-constants gives 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 \le n
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty on F^n, and @exr-vector-norms-c1 shows the constant \sqrt n in 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 \le \sqrt n
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 is attained, hence best possible. So a statement such as “the error is at most 10^{-6} in the \infty-norm” translates into the 1-norm as “at most n \cdot 10^{-6}”, which is a different statement when n is a million. @thm-norm-equivalence says the two norms cannot disagree about whether something tends to zero; it says nothing about how fast, and every quantitative estimate in the rest of this chapter names its norm for that reason. The second reason is that the theorem is false without the finite dimension, and not by a narrow margin. [Two inequivalent norms on a space of polynomials] Let V = 
R[x], the real polynomials — equivalently, the sequences of real coefficients with only finitely many nonzero terms. For p = a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_dx^d put 
orm{p}_1 = \lvert a_0vert + \dots + \lvert a_dvert , \qquad 
orm{p}_\infty = \max_i \lvert a_ivert . Both are norms, by the same coordinatewise checks as in @exm-p-norms; the only difference is that the number of coordinates is unbounded. One inequality survives: 
orm{p}_\infty \le 
orm{p}_1 always. The other fails completely. Put p_k = 1 + x + x^2 + \dots + x^{k-1} . Then 
orm{p_k}_1 = k while 
orm{p_k}_\infty = 1, so a constant C with 
orm{p}_1 \le C
orm{p}_\infty for all p would have to satisfy C \ge k for every k. No such C exists, and the two norms are not equivalent. Look at what the sequence  igl(	frac1k p_k igr) does: it tends to 0 in 
orm{\cdot}_\infty, since 
orm{	frac1k p_k}_\infty = 1/k, while 
orm{	frac1k p_k}_1 = 1 for every k. So the two norms disagree about which sequences converge — not about the rate, about the fact. Everything in @cor-convergence-norm-independent and @cor-closed-bounded-compact fails here at once, and it fails because Step 3 of the proof of @thm-norm-equivalence has nothing to stand on. The general reason is recorded, and not proved, in the warning below. Infinite dimension is outside the scope of this book. The closed unit ball of a normed space is compact only when the space is finite-dimensional. That is a genuine theorem, due to Riesz, and it is recorded here, not proved: it lies outside the four imported facts of the chapter introduction, this book never uses it as a step in an argument, and it is stated only so that @exm-norms-not-equivalent-infinite-dimension is not mistaken for an accident of a badly chosen pair. Every result of this chapter carries the hypothesis \dim V < \infty, and on C[0,1] or 
R[x] none of them is available. The study of norms on infinite-dimensional spaces is functional analysis, and there the choice of norm is the main content rather than an irrelevance. On C[0,1], compare the sup norm 
orm{f}_\infty of @exm-induced-and-weighted-norms (c) with 
orm{f}_1 = \int_0^1\lvert fvert, which is a norm because a continuous f \ge 0 with \int_0^1 f = 0 is the zero function — the one fact from analysis that Chapter 11 §01 recorded when it put an inner product on C[0,1], quoted again here. Which of the two inequalities of @def-equivalent-norms holds, and which fails? The inequality 
orm{f}_1 \le 
orm{f}_\infty holds, since \int_0^1\lvert fvert \le \int_0^1
orm{f}_\infty = 
orm{f}_\infty. The other fails. Take f_k(t) = \max(0, 1 - kt) for k \ge 1, the spike that drops from 1 to 0 on [0, 1/k]. Then 
orm{f_k}_\infty = f_k(0) = 1, while 
orm{f_k}_1 = \int_0^{1/k}(1 - kt)\,\dd t =  rac{1}{2k} , the area of a triangle of base 1/k and height 1, so no integration theory is needed to evaluate it. A constant C with 
orm{f}_\infty \le C
orm{f}_1 would need C \ge 2k for every k. A tall thin spike has small integral and large maximum, and in infinite dimension nothing stops it from being arbitrarily thin. With the choice of norm made harmless in finite dimension, the next section can measure matrices without apologizing for which measurement it uses — and then, when the estimates start to matter, name the norm on purpose. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State @def-equivalent-norms, and explain why the phrase “not depending on the vector” cannot be dropped. 2. State @thm-norm-equivalence, including its hypothesis on V. 3. Which two of the four imported analysis facts does the proof of @thm-norm-equivalence use, and at which step is each used? 4. True or false: if two norms on 
R^n are equivalent, then some sequence converges in one and not the other. Justify your answer. 5. True or false: equivalent norms give the same value to every vector. Justify your answer. (a) Two norms 
orm{\cdot}_a, 
orm{\cdot}_b on V are equivalent if there are constants c, C > 0, independent of the vector, with c
orm{\elem{v}}_b \le 
orm{\elem{v}}_a \le C
orm{\elem{v}}_b for every \elem{v} \in V (@def-equivalent-norms). Without the phrase the condition is vacuous: for each \elem{v} 
e \elem{0} the number 
orm{\elem{v}}_a/
orm{\elem{v}}_b is positive and could be taken as both c and C at that one vector, so every pair of norms would qualify. (b) On a finite-dimensional vector space over 
R or 
C, any two norms are equivalent (@thm-norm-equivalence). Finite dimension is essential — see @exm-norms-not-equivalent-infinite-dimension. (c) Fact (A3), the compactness of closed bounded sets in F^n, at Step 3, to know the Euclidean unit sphere is compact; and fact (A4), the extreme value theorem, also at Step 3, to know that the continuous function f attains a minimum there rather than merely approaching an infimum. (d) False, and this is the content of @cor-convergence-norm-independent (a): equivalent norms have exactly the same convergent sequences with exactly the same limits. (e) False. 
orm{\cdot}_1 and 
orm{\cdot}_\infty on 
R^2 are equivalent by @exm-norm-equivalence-constants, yet 
orm{\1}_1 = 2 
e 1 = 
orm{\1}_\infty. Equivalence constrains ratios, not values. B. Practice [B1: Best constants for a weighted norm] On 
R^2 let N(\cvec{x}) =  igl(x_1^2 + 4x_2^2 igr)^{1/2}. Find the best constants c, C > 0 with c\,
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty \le N(\cvec{x}) \le C\,
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty \qquad (\cvec{x} \in 
R^2), and give a vector attaining each. Hence deduce that N and 
orm{\cdot}_\infty are equivalent. Write a = \lvert x_1vert, b = \lvert x_2vert, and M = \max(a,b) = 
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty. Then N(\cvec{x})^2 = a^2 + 4b^2. Upper: a^2 + 4b^2 \le M^2 + 4M^2 = 5M^2, so N(\cvec{x}) \le \sqrt5\,
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty. Equality needs a = b = M, and \cvec{x} = (1,1) gives N(\cvec{x}) = \sqrt5 and 
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty = 1. So C = \sqrt5 and it cannot be lowered. Lower: if M = a then a^2 + 4b^2 \ge a^2 = M^2, and if M = b then a^2 + 4b^2 \ge 4b^2 \ge M^2. Either way N(\cvec{x}) \ge 
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty, so c = 1 works, and \cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_1 gives N(\cvec{x}) = 
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty = 1, so it cannot be raised. Since 1 and \sqrt5 are positive constants independent of \cvec{x}, the two norms are equivalent by @def-equivalent-norms. [B2: Reading a convergence off the entries] In M_2(
R) let \M_k =  egin{pmatrix} 1 +  rac{1}{k} &  rac{(-1)^k}{k^2} \  rac{1}{2^k} & 3 -  rac{5}{k} \end{pmatrix} . Determine \lim_k \M_k in the sense of @def-entrywise-convergence, and compute 
orm{\M_k - \M}_F explicitly. Hence confirm @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence for this sequence and the Frobenius norm. Each entry converges: 1 + 1/k 	o 1, (-1)^k/k^2 	o 0, 2^{-k} 	o 0, 3 - 5/k 	o 3. So \M_k 	o \M =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 3\end{pmatrix} entrywise. Then 
orm{\M_k - \M}_F = \Bigl(	frac{1}{k^2} + 	frac{1}{k^4} + 	frac{1}{4^k} + 	frac{25}{k^2}\Bigr)^{1/2} , which is at most  igl(28/k^2 igr)^{1/2} = \sqrt{28}/k for k \ge 1, since 1/k^4 \le 1/k^2 and 4^{-k} \le 1/k^2 for k \ge 1. Hence 
orm{\M_k - \M}_F 	o 0, as @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence predicts. Note what the norm added: a single sequence \sqrt{28}/k bounding the whole matrix, where the entrywise statement gave four unrelated sequences. [B3: An equivalence with the constants written down] Let V = 
R[x]_{\le 2} with basis \sB = (1, x, x^2). For p \in V let 
orm{p}_{\sB} be the Euclidean norm of the coefficient vector, and let N(p) = \lvert p(0)vert + \lvert p(1)vert + \lvert p(-1)vert. 1. Prove that N is a norm on V. 2. Find an explicit M with N(p) \le M
orm{p}_{\sB}, following Step 1 of the proof of @thm-norm-equivalence. 3. Explain, without computing it, why a constant m > 0 with N(p) \ge m
orm{p}_{\sB} exists. (a) (N2) and (N3) are inherited pointwise from \lvert\cdotvert on 
R, exactly as for 
orm{\cdot}_1 in @exm-p-norms. For (N1): N(p) = 0 forces p(0) = p(1) = p(-1) = 0, so p has three distinct roots while \deg p \le 2, hence p = 0. This is the only clause with any content, and it is where \dim V = 3 and the three sample points match up. (b) Step 1 takes M =  igl(\sum_i N(\elem{v}_i)^2 igr)^{1/2} over the basis. Here N(1) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, N(x) = 0 + 1 + 1 = 2, and N(x^2) = 0 + 1 + 1 = 2, so M =  igl(9 + 4 + 4 igr)^{1/2} = \sqrt{17} . (c) V is finite-dimensional, so @thm-norm-equivalence applies to the pair N, 
orm{\cdot}_{\sB} and delivers both constants at once. Only the upper one is computable by hand from the basis; the lower one comes from compactness and the proof gives no formula for it. C. Going deeper [C1: Every linear map out of a finite-dimensional space is continuous] Let V be finite-dimensional over F with norm 
orm{\cdot}_V, let W be a normed space over F with norm 
orm{\cdot}_W, and let T \colon V 	o W be linear. Fix a basis \sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n) of V and write 
orm{\cdot}_1 for the 1-norm of the coordinate vector in the basis \sB. 1. Prove that 
orm{T\elem{v}}_W \le K
orm{\elem{v}}_1 for every \elem{v} \in V, where K = \max_i
orm{T\elem{v}_i}_W. 2. Hence prove that there is a constant L with 
orm{T\elem{u} - T\elem{v}}_W \le L
orm{\elem{u} - \elem{v}}_V for all \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V. 3. Explain why (b) may fail when V is infinite-dimensional, using @exm-norms-not-equivalent-infinite-dimension. (a) Write \elem{v} = \sum_i x_i\elem{v}_i. By linearity of T, then (N3) and (N2) in W, 
orm{T\elem{v}}_W = \Bigl\lVert \sum_i x_iT\elem{v}_i \BigrVert_W \le \sum_i \lvert x_ivert\,
orm{T\elem{v}_i}_W \le K
orm{\elem{v}}_1 . (b) The function 
orm{\cdot}_1 is a norm on V (it is 
orm{\cdot}_1 of @exm-p-norms transported by the coordinate isomorphism @cor-coordinate-isomorphism), and V is finite-dimensional, so by @thm-norm-equivalence there is C > 0 with 
orm{\elem{v}}_1 \le C
orm{\elem{v}}_V for all \elem{v}. Put L = KC. By linearity, T\elem{u} - T\elem{v} = T(\elem{u} - \elem{v}), so (a) gives 
orm{T\elem{u} - T\elem{v}}_W \le K
orm{\elem{u} - \elem{v}}_1 \le L
orm{\elem{u} - \elem{v}}_V . (c) Part (a) needs a finite basis expansion, and part (b) needs @thm-norm-equivalence, which is false in infinite dimension. Concretely, take V = 
R[x] with the coefficient norm 
orm{\cdot}_\infty of @exm-norms-not-equivalent-infinite-dimension, W = 
R with \lvert\cdotvert, and the linear functional T(p) = p(1), which adds up the coefficients. With p_k = 1 + x + \dots + x^{k-1} as there, the polynomials q_k = 	frac1k p_k satisfy 
orm{q_k}_\infty = 1/k 	o 0 while T(q_k) = 1 for every k. So T sends a sequence tending to 0 to a sequence that does not, and no constant L can exist. [C2: No dimension-free constants] For each n \ge 1 let c_n, C_n > 0 be the best constants with c_n
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty \le 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 \le C_n
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty \qquad (\cvec{x} \in F^n) . 1. Determine c_n and C_n, with a vector attaining each. 2. Deduce that there is no pair of constants c, C > 0 working simultaneously for every n. 3. A statement about 
R^n says “the error \cvec{e} satisfies 
orm{\cvec{e}}_\infty \le 10^{-6}”. What is the strongest bound on 
orm{\cvec{e}}_1 that follows, and for which n does it stop being informative if the entries of \cvec{e} are themselves of size about 10^{-6}? (a) c_n = 1 and C_n = n. Indeed 
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty = \lvert x_kvert for some k, and \lvert x_kvert \le \sum_i\lvert x_ivert = 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1, with equality at \cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_1; and 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 = \sum_i\lvert x_ivert \le n\max_i\lvert x_ivert = n
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty, with equality at \cvec{x} = \1. Both constants are therefore attained and cannot be improved. (b) A dimension-free C would need C \ge C_n = n for every n, which is impossible. (The constant c = 1 does happen to work for all n; it is the upper constant that blows up, and one blown-up constant is enough.) (c) The strongest bound is 
orm{\cvec{e}}_1 \le n\cdot 10^{-6}, by (a), and it is attained when all entries have modulus 10^{-6} — which is exactly the situation described. So for n = 10^{6} the bound reads 
orm{\cvec{e}}_1 \le 1, which says nothing useful about a quantity that is itself of order 1. The two norms agree that the error tends to 0 as the computation improves; they disagree, by a factor of n, about whether it is currently small. [C3: A finite-dimensional subspace is closed] Let W be a normed space over F with norm 
orm{\cdot}, and let U \subseteq W be a finite-dimensional subspace. Let (\elem{u}_k) be a sequence in U with 
orm{\elem{u}_k - \elem{w}} 	o 0 for some \elem{w} \in W. 1. Prove that (\elem{u}_k) is bounded in U for the restricted norm. 2. Using @cor-closed-bounded-compact, produce a subsequence (\elem{u}_{k_j}) converging to some \elem{u} \in U. 3. Deduce that \elem{w} = \elem{u}, so that U contains the limit of every convergent sequence of its own elements. Hint: the triangle inequality, through \elem{u}_{k_j}. (a) By @lem-reverse-triangle-norm,  igl\lvert
orm{\elem{u}_k} - 
orm{\elem{w}} igrvert \le 
orm{\elem{u}_k - \elem{w}}, and the right side tends to 0. So there is K with 
orm{\elem{u}_k - \elem{w}} \le 1 for k \ge K, whence 
orm{\elem{u}_k} \le 
orm{\elem{w}} + 1 for those k; the finitely many earlier terms are bounded by their maximum. Hence (\elem{u}_k) is bounded. (b) The restriction of 
orm{\cdot} to U is a norm on U, and U is finite-dimensional. The set K = \{\elem{u} \in U : 
orm{\elem{u}} \le R\}, with R the bound from (a), is closed and bounded in U, hence compact by @cor-closed-bounded-compact. The sequence (\elem{u}_k) lies in K, so some subsequence (\elem{u}_{k_j}) converges to a point \elem{u} \in K \subseteq U. (c) For every j, by (N3), 
orm{\elem{w} - \elem{u}} \le 
orm{\elem{w} - \elem{u}_{k_j}} + 
orm{\elem{u}_{k_j} - \elem{u}} . Both terms on the right tend to 0 as j 	o \infty: the first because (\elem{u}_k) converges to \elem{w} and a subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit, the second by (b). The left side does not depend on j, so 
orm{\elem{w} - \elem{u}} = 0, and (N1) gives \elem{w} = \elem{u} \in U. Hence U contains every such limit, which is what it means for U to be closed in W. Note that W itself was never assumed finite-dimensional; only U was, and that is exactly where @cor-closed-bounded-compact was applied.

title: 16.3 Measuring a Matrix
content:
Measuring a Matrix Chapter 12 §11 gave the Frobenius norm its own symbol and explained the subscript: a bare 
orm{\cdot} already meant the norm of a vector, and a matrix, it warned, would shortly be asked to carry both kinds of measurement. This is that moment. A matrix is a list of mn numbers, and it is also a map; measuring the list is easy, measuring the map is what we usually want, and the two answers are not the same number. This section builds the second measurement, computes it in the three cases anyone computes, and says exactly where the first one fails. Throughout, F is 
R or 
C, all spaces are finite-dimensional, and 
orm{\cdot} with no subscript is a norm in the sense of @def-norm. What a matrix norm has to do Chapter 10 §10 decided whether \A^{m} 	o \O by looking at one entry of one Jordan block at a time. A single number attached to \A would be a far better instrument — but only if it interacts with matrix multiplication, because the questions we want to answer are questions about products: \A^{m}, \sum_k \A^{k}, e^{\A}. A norm that satisfies 
orm{\A\B} \le 
orm{\A}\,
orm{\B} immediately gives

e 1 for n \ge 2, whereas every operator norm has 
orm{\I_n} = 1 by @thm-operator-norm-properties (c). (e) Incorrect; only \le holds, by @thm-operator-norm-properties (d). Take \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, for which 
orm{\A}_2 = 1 but \A^2 = \O, so 
orm{\A^2}_2 = 0. B. Practice [B1: Four numbers for one matrix] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
R). Compute 
orm{\A}_1, 
orm{\A}_{\infty}, 
orm{\A}_F, and 
orm{\A}_2, and verify that 
orm{\A}_2 \le 
orm{\A}_F. Absolute column sums: 2 + 2 = 4 and 1 + 2 = 3, so 
orm{\A}_1 = 4. Absolute row sums: 2 + 1 = 3 and 2 + 2 = 4, so 
orm{\A}_{\infty} = 4. Also 
orm{\A}_F = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4 + 4} = \sqrt{13}. For the spectral norm, \A	p\A =  egin{pmatrix} 8 & 2 \ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, with trace 13 and determinant 40 - 4 = 36, so its eigenvalues solve \lambda^2 - 13\lambda + 36 = 0, giving \lambda = 9 and \lambda = 4. Hence \sigma_1 = 3, \sigma_2 = 2, and 
orm{\A}_2 = 3 by @thm-operator-norm-formulas (c). Finally 3 \le \sqrt{13}, as @prp-spectral-vs-frobenius requires; the inequality is strict because ank\A = 2. [B2: A rank-one matrix] Let \cvec{u} \in F^m and \cvec{v} \in F^n be nonzero and put \A = \cvec{u}\cvec{v}^{*}. 1. Prove that 
orm{\A}_2 = 
orm{\cvec{u}}_2
orm{\cvec{v}}_2. 2. Verify the formula for \cvec{u} = (1, 2) and \cvec{v} = (2, -1) in 
R^2 by computing \sigma_1(\A) directly. (a) For \cvec{x} \in F^n we have \A\cvec{x} = (\cvec{v}^{*}\cvec{x})\cvec{u}, so 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}_2 = \lvert\cvec{v}^{*}\cvec{x}vert\,
orm{\cvec{u}}_2. By @thm-cauchy-schwarz, \lvert\cvec{v}^{*}\cvec{x}vert = \lvert\inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{v}}vert \le 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2
orm{\cvec{v}}_2, with equality when \cvec{x} = \cvec{v}/
orm{\cvec{v}}_2. Hence for unit \cvec{x} the quantity 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}_2 is at most 
orm{\cvec{u}}_2
orm{\cvec{v}}_2 and attains that value, so 
orm{\A}_2 = 
orm{\cvec{u}}_2
orm{\cvec{v}}_2. (b) Here \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & -1 \ 4 & -2 \end{psmallmatrix} and \A	p\A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 20 & -10 \ -10 & 5\end{psmallmatrix}, of trace 25 and determinant 100 - 100 = 0. So the eigenvalues are 25 and 0, giving \sigma_1 = 5. And 
orm{\cvec{u}}_2
orm{\cvec{v}}_2 = \sqrt5 \cdot \sqrt5 = 5, in agreement. Note also 
orm{\A}_F = 5 = 
orm{\A}_2, as @prp-spectral-vs-frobenius predicts for a rank-one matrix. [B3: The star trick] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). Prove that 
orm{\A^{*}\A}_2 = 
orm{\A}_2^2. Hint: the eigenvalues of \A^{*}\A. By @def-singular-values the eigenvalues of \A^{*}\A are \sigma_1^2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_n^2 \ge 0, where the \sigma_i are the singular values of \A padded with zeros if n > m. The matrix \A^{*}\A is positive semidefinite, hence Hermitian, so by @cor-spectral-complex-matrix it is \W\D\W^{*} with \W unitary and \D = \diag(\sigma_1^2, \dots, \sigma_n^2). Then (\A^{*}\A)^{*}(\A^{*}\A) = \W\D^2\W^{*}, whose eigenvalues are \sigma_i^4, so the singular values of \A^{*}\A are the \sigma_i^2 and its largest is \sigma_1^2. By @thm-operator-norm-formulas (c), applied to \A^{*}\A and then to \A, 
orm{\A^{*}\A}_2 = \sigma_1^2 = 
orm{\A}_2^2 . This proves the claim. Notice that it is an equality, whereas @thm-operator-norm-properties (d) alone would give only 
orm{\A^{*}\A}_2 \le 
orm{\A^{*}}_2
orm{\A}_2. C. Going deeper [C1: The spectral norm between the other two] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). 1. Prove that 
orm{\A}_2 \le \sqrt{
orm{\A}_1
orm{\A}_{\infty}}. 2. Check the inequality on the matrix of @exm-three-norms-of-a-matrix, and say how far it is from equality. Hint for (a): apply @thm-cauchy-schwarz to the splitting \lvert a_{ij}vert = \lvert a_{ij}vert^{1/2}\cdot\lvert a_{ij}vert^{1/2}\lvert x_jvert inside one row. (a) Write C = 
orm{\A}_1 and R = 
orm{\A}_{\infty} for the largest column and row sums (@thm-operator-norm-formulas). Let 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 = 1. For each i, @thm-cauchy-schwarz applied to the vectors with entries \lvert a_{ij}vert^{1/2} and \lvert a_{ij}vert^{1/2}\lvert x_jvert gives \Bigl\lvert\sum_j a_{ij}x_j\Bigrvert^2 \le \Bigl(\sum_j \lvert a_{ij}vert\Bigr) \Bigl(\sum_j \lvert a_{ij}vert\,\lvert x_jvert^2\Bigr) \le R\sum_j \lvert a_{ij}vert\,\lvert x_jvert^2 . Summing over i and exchanging the two finite sums, 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}_2^2 \le R\sum_j \lvert x_jvert^2\sum_i \lvert a_{ij}vert \le RC\sum_j\lvert x_jvert^2 = RC . Taking the maximum over unit \cvec{x} gives 
orm{\A}_2^2 \le RC, as claimed. (b) There 
orm{\A}_1 = 7 and 
orm{\A}_{\infty} = 9, so the bound is \sqrt{63} \approx 7.937, while 
orm{\A}_2 = 3\sqrt5 \approx 6.708. The bound overestimates by about 18 per cent. It is sharp in general: for \A = \I_n all three numbers are 1. [C2: Repairing the entrywise maximum] For \A \in M_n(F) let N(\A) = \max_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij}vert, as in @exm-entrywise-max-not-submultiplicative. 1. Prove that N(\A\B) \le nN(\A)N(\B), and deduce that \A \mapsto nN(\A) is a matrix norm. 2. Deduce that nN(\cdot) is not an operator norm for any n \ge 2. 3. Explain why (a) and (b) together show that submultiplicativity and 
orm{\I} = 1 are independent requirements. (a) For all i, j, \lvert(\A\B)_{ij}vert = \Bigl\lvert\sum_k a_{ik}b_{kj}\Bigrvert \le \sum_k \lvert a_{ik}vert\,\lvert b_{kj}vert \le n\,N(\A)N(\B), so N(\A\B) \le nN(\A)N(\B). Put 
orm{\A} = nN(\A). It is a norm, being a positive multiple of the norm N, and 
orm{\A\B} = nN(\A\B) \le n^2N(\A)N(\B) = 
orm{\A}\,
orm{\B} . (b) 
orm{\I_n} = nN(\I_n) = n 
e 1 for n \ge 2, while every operator norm gives the identity the value 1 (@thm-operator-norm-properties (c)). (c) N itself is a norm with N(\I_n) = 1 that is not submultiplicative; nN is submultiplicative with nN(\I_n) = n. So neither property implies the other, and an operator norm is precisely a matrix norm that also passes the identity test — a necessary condition which, as 
orm{\cdot}_F already showed, is still not sufficient on its own for n large. [C3: When is a bound an equality?] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) be nonzero. 1. Prove that 
orm{\A}_2 = 
orm{\A}_F if and only if ank\A = 1. 2. Give an example with m = n = 2 where 
orm{\A}_F = \sqrt2\,
orm{\A}_2, the worst case allowed by @prp-spectral-vs-frobenius. 3. Is there a nonzero \A with 
orm{\A}_F < 
orm{\A}_2? Justify your answer. (a) This is the equality case of @prp-spectral-vs-frobenius, proved there: 
orm{\A}_F^2 = \sum_i\sigma_i^2 and 
orm{\A}_2^2 = \sigma_1^2, so the two agree exactly when \sigma_i = 0 for every i \ge 2, which by @thm-svd says ank\A = 1. (b) Take \A = \I_2. Its singular values are 1, 1, so 
orm{\A}_2 = 1 and 
orm{\A}_F = \sqrt2. Any matrix with two equal nonzero singular values does the same, for instance any 2 	imes 2 unitary matrix. (c) No. 
orm{\A}_2 = \sigma_1 \le  igl(\sum_i \sigma_i^2 igr)^{1/2} = 
orm{\A}_F always, since every term of the sum is nonnegative. The Frobenius norm counts all the singular values and the spectral norm only the largest, so the Frobenius norm can never be the smaller of the two.

title: 16.4 The Spectral Radius
content:
The Spectral Radius Every criterion in Chapter 10 §10 began by looking at the largest modulus of an eigenvalue, and that section gave the number a name in passing — the spectral radius — without a numbered definition and without a single norm available to compare it with. It also left a note: “Chapter 16 measures matrices by norms, proves that the spectral radius never exceeds the norm of \A induced by any vector norm, and recovers ho(\A) as a limit built from the norms of the powers \A^{m}.” This section pays that note in full, and is careful about what is new when it does. Throughout, matrices are complex. A real matrix is read inside M_n(
C), exactly as Chapter 10 §10 read it when it counted eigenvalues; over 
R a matrix may have no eigenvalue at all, and then there is nothing to take the largest modulus of. The number Chapter 10 named The spectral radius is the radius of the smallest disk about the origin that holds the whole spectrum. [Spectral Radius] Let \A \in M_n(
C) with n \ge 1. The spectral radius of \A is ho(\A) \coloneqq \max\{\,\lvert\lambdavert : \lambda \in \spec(\A)\,\} . For an operator T on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex vector space, ho(T) is defined by the same formula with \spec(T) in place of \spec(\A). The maximum is over a finite nonempty set, so it exists with no analysis at all: \spec(\A) is the root set of the characteristic polynomial p_{\A}, which is nonempty by the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (@thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra) and has at most n elements. It is the largest modulus of an eigenvalue, not the largest eigenvalue: over 
C there is no order to take a largest in, and even for a real spectrum ho(\diag(-5, 1)) = 5, not 1. This is the number Chapter 10 §10 introduced in prose, now with a label so that later sections can cite it. Some values, simplest first. - Diagonal or triangular. The eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are its diagonal entries (@thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form (b)), so ho is the largest modulus on the diagonal. For \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) it is \max_i\lvert d_ivert. - Normal. If \A is normal then \A = \U\D\U^{*} with \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n) (@cor-spectral-complex-matrix), so \A^{*}\A = \U\diag(\lvert\lambda_ivert^2)\U^{*} and the singular values of \A are the moduli \lvert\lambda_ivert. Hence ho(\A) = \sigma_1(\A) = 
orm{\A}_2 by @thm-operator-norm-formulas (c). For a normal matrix the spectral radius is the spectral norm, which is where the second name comes from. - A rotation.  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} has eigenvalues \pm i, so ho = 1, although no real vector is left in place. - Nilpotent. \J_k(0) is triangular with zero diagonal, so by the first bullet ho(\J_k(0)) = 0. The matrix itself is not \O when k \ge 2. The last entry is the degenerate case, and it is the important one: it says at once that ho is not a norm. ho is not a norm, and it is neither subadditive nor submultiplicative. Take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . Both are nilpotent, so ho(\A) = ho(\B) = 0 although neither is the zero matrix. Their sum  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} has eigenvalues \pm 1 and their product \A\B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} has eigenvalues 1 and 0. So ho(\A + \B) = 1 > 0 = ho(\A) + ho(\B) and ho(\A\B) = 1 > 0 = ho(\A)ho(\B). So positive definiteness and subadditivity both fail, and so does submultiplicativity, all on the same small pair. Only absolute homogeneity survives, since ho(c\A) = \lvert cvertho(\A) for every scalar c. So ho is a genuinely different kind of measurement from the ones of the previous section. The relation between the two is the subject of the rest of this section, and it is one-sided. Every norm dominates the spectral radius [The Spectral Radius Is a Lower Bound for Every Norm] Let \A \in M_n(
C). 1. If 
orm{\cdot} is the operator norm on M_n(
C) induced by a norm on 
C^n (@def-operator-norm), then ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A}. 2. More generally, ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A} for every matrix norm 
orm{\cdot} on M_n(
C) (@def-matrix-norm). For (a) there is nothing to do but write down the eigenvalue equation: an eigenvector is a vector on which \A acts by multiplication by \lambda, so the stretching factor \lvert\lambdavert is one of the factors the maximum in @def-operator-norm ranges over. For (b) there is no vector to feed the norm, only matrices — so manufacture one: fill an n 	imes n matrix with copies of the eigenvector, and the eigenvalue equation becomes a matrix equation that submultiplicativity can be applied to. (a) Let \lambda \in \spec(\A) and let \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0} with \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x}. Then 
orm{\A\cvec{x}} = \lvert\lambdavert\,
orm{\cvec{x}} by homogeneity, while 
orm{\A\cvec{x}} \le 
orm{\A}
orm{\cvec{x}} by @thm-operator-norm-properties (a). Since \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0} we have 
orm{\cvec{x}} > 0 and may divide, giving \lvert\lambdavert \le 
orm{\A}. This holds for every eigenvalue, so it holds for the largest modulus. (b) Let \lambda and \cvec{x} be as above, and let \X \in M_n(
C) be the matrix all of whose n columns equal \cvec{x}. Then \X 
e \O, so 
orm{\X} > 0. Computing column by column, \A\X has every column equal to \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x}, that is, \A\X = \lambda\X . Taking norms and using homogeneity on the left and submultiplicativity on the right, \lvert\lambdavert\,
orm{\X} = 
orm{\A\X} \le 
orm{\A}\,
orm{\X} . Dividing by 
orm{\X} > 0 gives \lvert\lambdavert \le 
orm{\A}, and again the largest modulus obeys the same bound. This proves the theorem. This is the inequality Chapter 10 §10 promised: the spectral radius never exceeds the norm of \A induced by any vector norm. Part (b) says more than was promised, and costs one extra line. The immediate use is that every computable norm is a computable upper bound for every eigenvalue — and two of the three formulas of @thm-operator-norm-formulas need no arithmetic beyond adding up moduli. [Cheap Bounds on the Spectrum] Let \A \in M_n(
C). Then every eigenvalue \lambda of \A satisfies \lvert\lambdavert \le ho(\A) \le \min igl\{
orm{\A}_1,\ 
orm{\A}_{\infty},\ 
orm{\A}_F igr\} , that is, ho(\A) is at most the largest absolute column sum, at most the largest absolute row sum, and at most 
orm{\A}_F. The first two are operator norms (@thm-operator-norm-formulas (a), (b)), so @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm (a) applies; 
orm{\cdot}_F is a matrix norm (@exm-frobenius-is-a-matrix-norm), so @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm (b) applies. A minimum of upper bounds is an upper bound. The bound ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A}_2 = \sigma_1(\A) is the same crude inequality \lvert\lambdavert \le \sigma_1 that Chapter 13 §09 obtained directly from \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x}. It is now one instance of a general principle rather than an isolated computation, and @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm (a) is that computation with the norm left unnamed. [Bounding a spectrum without finding it] Let \A = 	frac{1}{10} egin{pmatrix} 2 & 5 & 1 \ 3 & 1 & 4 \ 1 & 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}. Show that ho(\A) \le 	frac45, and hence that \A^{m} 	o \O. Every row of \A sums to 	frac{8}{10} = 	frac45, so 
orm{\A}_{\infty} = 	frac45 by @thm-operator-norm-formulas (b), and ho(\A) \le 	frac45 by @cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound. Since 	frac45 < 1, every eigenvalue has modulus less than 1 and \A^{m} 	o \O by @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero. No characteristic polynomial was computed. The column sums are 	frac{6}{10}, 	frac{8}{10}, and 1, so 
orm{\A}_1 = 1 and the column bound gives nothing. It is worth computing both and keeping the smaller. In fact ho(\A) = 	frac45 exactly, because the constant row sums make \1 an eigenvector with eigenvalue 	frac45, so the row bound here is attained. @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm says ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A} for every matrix norm. Why does it not follow that ho is the smallest matrix norm? Because ho is not a matrix norm at all: ho vanishes on every nonzero nilpotent matrix, and it fails both subadditivity and submultiplicativity, as the warning above showed. The correct statement is that ho(\A) is a lower bound for the values 
orm{\A}, one matrix at a time, and the next theorem shows it is the greatest such lower bound. A norm as close to the spectral radius as we like @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm leaves open how large the gap can be. It can be enormous for a fixed norm: \J_2(0) has ho = 0 and 
orm{\J_2(0)}_2 = 1, and multiplying the corner entry by 10^6 leaves ho = 0 while the norm becomes 10^6. But the norm may be chosen after the matrix, and then the gap can be made as small as we please. [Norms Close to the Spectral Radius] Let \A \in M_n(
C) and let \varepsilon > 0. Then there is a norm 
orm{\cdot}_t on 
C^n whose induced operator norm satisfies ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A}_t \le ho(\A) + \varepsilon . Schur-triangularize and then squash. ① By @cor-schur-matrix, \A = \U\T\U^{*} with \T upper triangular carrying the eigenvalues on its diagonal; the row sums of \T are the diagonal entry plus the off-diagonal junk. ② Conjugating \T by \D_t = \diag(1, t, \dots, t^{n-1}) multiplies the entry in position (i,j) by t^{i-j}, which leaves the diagonal alone and, for large t, shrinks everything strictly above it, because i - j < 0 there. ③ Choose t so that every off-diagonal row sum is below \varepsilon; the largest row sum is then below ho(\A) + \varepsilon, and the largest row sum is a norm we can compute, by @thm-operator-norm-formulas (b). ④ Transport that norm back to 
C^n along the invertible matrix \D_t\U^{*}. By @cor-schur-matrix there are a unitary \U and an upper triangular \T = (t_{ij}) with \A = \U\T\U^{*} and t_{ii} = \lambda_i, the eigenvalues of \A. For t \ge 1 put \D_t = \diag(1, t, t^2, \dots, t^{n-1}), an invertible matrix, and \T_t = \D_t\T\D_t^{-1}. Multiplying out, (\T_t)_{ij} = t^{\,i-1}\,t_{ij}\,t^{-(j-1)} = t^{\,i-j}t_{ij} . So \T_t is again upper triangular with the same diagonal \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, while for i < j the entry is scaled by t^{i-j} \le t^{-1}, using t \ge 1 and j - i \ge 1. Let M = \max_{i<j}\lvert t_{ij}vert if n \ge 2, and M = 0 if n = 1. Then the i-th absolute row sum of \T_t is at most \lvert\lambda_ivert + \sum_{j > i}t^{-1}\lvert t_{ij}vert \le ho(\A) +  rac{(n-1)M}{t} . Choose t = \max igl(1,\ (n-1)M/\varepsilon igr). Then every absolute row sum of \T_t is at most ho(\A) + \varepsilon, so 
orm{\T_t}_{\infty} \le ho(\A) + \varepsilon by @thm-operator-norm-formulas (b). Now define, for \cvec{x} \in 
C^n, 
orm{\cvec{x}}_t \coloneqq 
orm{\D_t\U^{*}\cvec{x}}_{\infty} . This is a norm: it is nonnegative, homogeneous, and subadditive because 
orm{\cdot}_{\infty} is and \cvec{x} \mapsto \D_t\U^{*}\cvec{x} is linear, and it vanishes only at \cvec{x} = \cvec{0} because \D_t\U^{*} is invertible. It remains to compute the induced operator norm. Put \Q = \D_t\U^{*}, so 
orm{\cvec{x}}_t = 
orm{\Q\cvec{x}}_{\infty}. As \cvec{x} runs over \{
orm{\cvec{x}}_t = 1\}, the vector \cvec{y} = \Q\cvec{x} runs over \{
orm{\cvec{y}}_{\infty} = 1\}, since \Q is a bijection. Moreover \Q\A\Q^{-1} = \D_t\U^{*}\A\U\D_t^{-1} = \D_t\T\D_t^{-1} = \T_t, so 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}_t = 
orm{\Q\A\cvec{x}}_{\infty} = 
orm{\T_t\,\cvec{y}}_{\infty} . Taking maxima over the two matching sets gives 
orm{\A}_t = 
orm{\T_t}_{\infty} \le ho(\A) + \varepsilon. The lower bound ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A}_t is @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm (a). This proves the theorem. Read together, the last two theorems say ho(\A) = \inf\{
orm{\A} : 
orm{\cdot} 	ext{ an induced matrix norm}\} . The infimum need not be attained. If \A 
e \O is nilpotent then ho(\A) = 0 while 
orm{\A} > 0 for every norm, so no norm achieves the value. At the other extreme, for a normal \A the spectral norm achieves it exactly: 
orm{\A}_2 = ho(\A), as computed at the start of this section. The gap between ho and the norms is a measure of how far \A is from being normal, which is the theme Chapter 12 §11 opened with the departure from normality. Gelfand’s formula The infimum above is over norms, and to use it we must choose one. There is a second description of ho(\A) that needs no choice: fix any norm at all, and let the powers of \A tell you the answer. Gelfand’s Formula Let \A \in M_n(
C) and let 
orm{\cdot} be any matrix norm on M_n(
C). Then \lim_{k 	o \infty}\ 
orm{\A^{k}}^{1/k} = ho(\A) . In particular the limit exists and does not depend on which matrix norm is used. Two inequalities, one for each direction, and they come from opposite ends of the chapter. ① The lower bound ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A^k}^{1/k} is @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm applied to \A^{k}, once we know ho(\A^{k}) = ho(\A)^{k} — which is the Spectral Mapping Theorem. This holds for every k, with no limit taken. ② For the upper bound, scale \A down by a whisker more than ho(\A). The scaled matrix has spectral radius below 1, so Chapter 10 §10’s criterion makes its powers tend to \O, and once they are below 1 in norm the inequality we want has been written down. @thm-norm-close-to-spectral-radius says the same decay is geometric, which is what the corollary below extracts. Lower bound. Fix k \ge 1. By @thm-spectral-mapping applied to q(x) = x^{k}, \spec(\A^{k}) = \{\lambda^{k} : \lambda \in \spec(\A)\}, so ho(\A^{k}) = \max_{\lambda \in \spec(\A)}\lvert\lambdavert^{k} = ho(\A)^{k} . By @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm (b) applied to \A^{k}, ho(\A)^{k} = ho(\A^{k}) \le 
orm{\A^{k}}. Taking k-th roots of these nonnegative reals, ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A^{k}}^{1/k} \qquad 	ext{for every } k \ge 1 . Upper bound. Let \varepsilon > 0, put s = ho(\A) + \varepsilon > 0 and \B = s^{-1}\A. Every eigenvalue of \B is \lambda/s for some \lambda \in \spec(\A) (@thm-spectral-mapping with q(x) = x/s), so ho(\B) =  rac{ho(\A)}{ho(\A) + \varepsilon} < 1 . By @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero, \B^{k} 	o \O entrywise. Entrywise convergence of matrices is convergence in every norm on M_n(
C), by @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence, so 
orm{\B^{k}} 	o 0. A real sequence tending to 0 is eventually below 1: there is K with 
orm{\B^{k}} \le 1 for all k \ge K. Since \B^{k} = s^{-k}\A^{k}, homogeneity gives 
orm{\A^{k}} \le s^{k}, that is, 
orm{\A^{k}}^{1/k} \le ho(\A) + \varepsilon \qquad (k \ge K) . Conclusion. Combining, for every \varepsilon > 0 there is K with ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A^{k}}^{1/k} \le ho(\A) + \varepsilon \qquad (k \ge K), which is the definition of 
orm{\A^{k}}^{1/k} 	o ho(\A). The independence of the norm is automatic, since the limit equals ho(\A) whichever matrix norm was fixed at the start. This proves the theorem. Which analysis was used. The lower bound used none. The upper bound used @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero, which is a theorem of this book, and @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence, likewise; the only analysis is that a real sequence tending to 0 is eventually less than 1, and that a sequence trapped between ho(\A) and ho(\A) + \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0 converges to ho(\A). Neither is an extra import: both are the definition of a limit of a real sequence, read forwards and backwards. Nothing from the list (A1)–(A4) of the chapter introduction is needed here, and nothing outside it is used. The formula is a genuine computation rule as well as a theorem. For a fixed k the number 
orm{\A^{k}}^{1/k} is an upper estimate of ho(\A) — that is the lower bound above, read the other way — and the estimates improve as k grows. [Watching the limit converge] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 10 \ 0 & 1/3 \end{pmatrix}. Compute 
orm{\A^{k}}_{\infty} exactly and confirm Gelfand’s formula. \A is upper triangular, so ho(\A) = \max(	frac12, 	frac13) = 	frac12 and the powers are upper triangular with diagonal 2^{-k}, 3^{-k}. For the corner entry, induction on k gives (\A^{k})_{12} = 10\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}2^{-j}3^{-(k-1-j)} = 60 igl(2^{-k} - 3^{-k} igr), the last step by summing the geometric series with ratio 3/2. The two absolute row sums are 2^{-k} + 60(2^{-k} - 3^{-k}) and 3^{-k}, the first being the larger, so by @thm-operator-norm-formulas (b) 
orm{\A^{k}}_{\infty} = 61\cdot 2^{-k} - 60\cdot 3^{-k} . At k = 1 this is 10.5, which overestimates ho(\A) = 	frac12 by a factor of 21; the k-th roots run 10.5,\ 2.93,\ 1.75,\ 1.32,\ 1.11,\ 0.98, \dots and settle toward 	frac12, which is what @thm-gelfand guarantees. The convergence is slow, and it has to be: the single number 
orm{\A}_{\infty} cannot know that the entry 10 sits above the diagonal rather than on it. What is new, and what is not [Powers Tending to Zero, with a Rate] Let \A \in M_n(
C) and let 
orm{\cdot} be any matrix norm on M_n(
C). 1. \A^{k} 	o \O if and only if ho(\A) < 1, and this holds if and only if 
orm{\A^{k}} 	o 0. 2. If ho(\A) < 1, then for every q with ho(\A) < q < 1 there is a constant C \ge 1, depending on \A, on q, and on the norm, such that 
orm{\A^{k}} \le C\,q^{k} for every k \ge 0. Part (a) is @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero translated into norms by @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence; nothing is proved that was not proved in Chapter 10. Part (b) is the new content, and it is @thm-norm-close-to-spectral-radius doing what it was built for: choose a norm in which \A itself is already smaller than q, take powers there, and pay one fixed constant to return to the norm we were given. (a) The first equivalence is @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero, since ho(\A) < 1 says exactly that every eigenvalue has modulus less than 1. The second is @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence: entrywise convergence of matrices and convergence in the norm 
orm{\cdot} are the same thing. (b) Let \varepsilon = q - ho(\A) > 0. By @thm-norm-close-to-spectral-radius there is an induced matrix norm 
orm{\cdot}_t on M_n(
C) with 
orm{\A}_t \le ho(\A) + \varepsilon = q. Submultiplicativity (@thm-operator-norm-properties (d)) gives 
orm{\A^{k}}_t \le 
orm{\A}_t^{k} \le q^{k} for every k \ge 0. By @thm-norm-equivalence, applied to the two norms 
orm{\cdot} and 
orm{\cdot}_t on the finite-dimensional space M_n(
C), there is C_0 > 0 with 
orm{\M} \le C_0
orm{\M}_t for every \M. Taking C = \max(C_0, 1), 
orm{\A^{k}} \le C_0
orm{\A^{k}}_t \le C\,q^{k} . This proves the corollary. It is worth being exact about the accounting. Part (a) is not new. Chapter 10 §10 proved that \A^{m} 	o \O if and only if every eigenvalue has modulus less than 1, and it proved it with the Jordan form and no norms whatsoever; all that has happened here is that the conclusion has been restated in a language where “small” is a number. What is new is part (b): a rate. Chapter 10 could say that the powers die; it could not say how fast, because it had nothing to measure a matrix with. Now every decaying matrix comes with a geometric envelope Cq^{k} for every q above its spectral radius, and that envelope is what later sections integrate, sum, and differentiate. Two honest limitations of the envelope deserve saying out loud. ho(\A) < 1 promises eventual decay, not immediate decay. The constant C in @cor-powers-converge-iff-rho-lt-one (b) is generally larger than 1 and grows as q approaches ho(\A). For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 9/10 & 10 \ 0 & 9/10 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A^{k} =  egin{pmatrix} (9/10)^{k} & 10k(9/10)^{k-1} \ 0 & (9/10)^{k} \end{pmatrix}, we have ho(\A) = 9/10 < 1, yet 
orm{\A^{k}}_{\infty} = (9/10)^{k-1}(9/10 + 10k) rises from 10.9 at k = 1 to about 39.13 at k = 9 before beginning its decay, and does not fall below 1 until k = 63. A transient hump of this kind is invisible to the spectral radius and is exactly what the constant C is paying for. For which matrices can one take C = 1 and q = ho(\A) in the bound of @cor-powers-converge-iff-rho-lt-one (b), with the spectral norm? For normal \A, among others. If \A is normal then so is \A^{k} (its adjoint is (\A^{*})^{k}, and powers of commuting matrices commute), so 
orm{\A^{k}}_2 = ho(\A^{k}) = ho(\A)^{k} by the computation at the start of this section together with @thm-spectral-mapping. There is then no transient at all: the norm of the powers is exactly geometric. The hump in the warning is possible only because that matrix is far from normal, with departure from normality 10 in the sense of @def-departure-from-normality. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the spectral radius, and say why the maximum in the definition exists. 2. State @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm and @thm-gelfand. 3. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: ho is a matrix norm on M_n(
C). 4. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if ho(\A) < 1 then 
orm{\A}_2 < 1. 5. Chapter 10 §10 already proved that \A^{m} 	o \O exactly when ho(\A) < 1. What does @cor-powers-converge-iff-rho-lt-one add to that? (a) ho(\A) = \max\{\lvert\lambdavert : \lambda \in \spec(\A)\} (@def-spectral-radius). The set \spec(\A) is finite and nonempty — it is the root set of p_{\A}, nonempty by @thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra — so the maximum of the finitely many moduli exists. (b) For every matrix norm on M_n(
C), ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A}; and for every matrix norm, 
orm{\A^{k}}^{1/k} 	o ho(\A) as k 	o \infty. (c) Incorrect. ho vanishes on nonzero nilpotent matrices, so it is not even a norm, and it is neither subadditive nor submultiplicative: see the warning after @def-spectral-radius. (d) Incorrect. \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 10 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} has ho(\A) = 0 and 
orm{\A}_2 = 10. The correct statement is that some norm has 
orm{\A} < 1, by @thm-norm-close-to-spectral-radius. (e) Nothing about the criterion, which is @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero restated; what it adds is the quantitative envelope 
orm{\A^{k}} \le Cq^{k} for every q \in (ho(\A), 1), a rate of decay rather than the bare fact of it. B. Practice [B1: Four numbers again] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ 1/4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Compute ho(\A), 
orm{\A}_1, 
orm{\A}_{\infty}, and 
orm{\A}_2, and verify @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm in each case. p_{\A}(x) = x^2 - 	frac12, so \spec(\A) = \{\pm 1/\sqrt2\} and ho(\A) = 1/\sqrt2 \approx 0.707. The absolute column sums are 	frac14 and 2, so 
orm{\A}_1 = 2; the absolute row sums are 2 and 	frac14, so 
orm{\A}_{\infty} = 2. For the spectral norm, \A	p\A = \diag(	frac1{16}, 4), whose eigenvalues are 	frac1{16} and 4; hence \sigma_1 = 2 and 
orm{\A}_2 = 2 by @thm-operator-norm-formulas (c). So ho(\A) = 0.707\dots \le 2 in all three cases, and the gap is a factor of nearly 3 even though \A is a very small matrix. The reason is the mismatch between the two off-diagonal entries: \A is far from normal. [B2: Gelfand exactly] With \A as in @exr-spectral-radius-b1, compute \A^{k} for every k and evaluate \lim_k
orm{\A^{k}}_{\infty}^{1/k} directly. \A^2 = 	frac12\I, so by induction \A^{2l} = 2^{-l}\I and \A^{2l+1} = 2^{-l}\A. Hence 
orm{\A^{2l}}_{\infty} = 2^{-l}, \qquad 
orm{\A^{2l+1}}_{\infty} = 2^{-l}\cdot 2 = 2^{1-l} . For even k = 2l, 
orm{\A^{k}}_{\infty}^{1/k} = (2^{-l})^{1/(2l)} = 2^{-1/2}, exactly ho(\A) for every l. For odd k = 2l+1, 
orm{\A^{k}}_{\infty}^{1/k} = 2^{(1-l)/(2l+1)}, and (1-l)/(2l+1) 	o -	frac12, so this too tends to 2^{-1/2}. Both subsequences converge to 1/\sqrt2 = ho(\A), confirming @thm-gelfand. [B3: Deciding convergence without eigenvalues] For each matrix, decide whether \A^{m} 	o \O, using only @cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound and @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero. 1. \A = 	frac{1}{4} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. 2. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 3 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. (a) The absolute row sums are 	frac34, 	frac12, and 	frac34, so 
orm{\A}_{\infty} = 	frac34 and ho(\A) \le 	frac34 < 1. By @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero, \A^{m} 	o \O. (b) Here the row sums are 	frac72 and 2 and the column sums are 	frac12 and 5, so the bounds give only ho(\A) \le 	frac72 and decide nothing. But the bound is an upper bound, and here the matrix is triangular, so the eigenvalues are visible: 	frac12 and 2, giving ho(\A) = 2 > 1. By @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero the powers do not tend to \O. The moral is that @cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound can only ever certify convergence, never rule it out. C. Going deeper [C1: A norm that sees the decay] Let \A \in M_n(
C). 1. Prove that if 
orm{\A} < 1 for some matrix norm, then \A^{k} 	o \O. 2. Give a matrix with \A^{k} 	o \O and 
orm{\A}_2 > 1, so that the converse of (a) fails for a fixed norm. 3. Prove that the converse of (a) nevertheless holds if the norm is allowed to depend on \A. (a) Submultiplicativity gives 
orm{\A^{k}} \le 
orm{\A}^{k} by induction on k. With r = 
orm{\A} < 1 the right-hand side tends to 0, so 
orm{\A^{k}} 	o 0, and by @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence this is the same as \A^{k} 	o \O entrywise. (b) \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 10 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} satisfies \A^2 = \O, so certainly \A^{k} 	o \O; but 
orm{\A}_2 = 10 > 1. The same happens for  egin{psmallmatrix} 1/2 & 10 \ 0 & 1/2\end{psmallmatrix}, which is not even nilpotent. (c) Suppose \A^{k} 	o \O. By @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero, ho(\A) < 1. Apply @thm-norm-close-to-spectral-radius with \varepsilon = 	frac12(1 - ho(\A)) > 0: it produces an induced matrix norm 
orm{\cdot}_t with 
orm{\A}_t \le ho(\A) + \varepsilon = 	frac12 igl(1 + ho(\A) igr) < 1 . So a norm witnessing the decay always exists, though it must be chosen after \A. [C2: Spectral radius zero] Let \A \in M_n(
C). 1. Prove that ho(\A) = 0 if and only if \A is nilpotent. 2. Deduce that for a nilpotent \A and any matrix norm, 
orm{\A^{k}}^{1/k} 	o 0, and verify this directly for \A = \J_n(0). 3. Explain why (a) shows that no inequality of the form 
orm{\A} \le c\,ho(\A), with c depending only on n, can hold. (a) (\Rightarrow) If ho(\A) = 0 then every eigenvalue is 0, so p_{\A}(x) = x^{n} because p_{\A} is monic of degree n and splits over 
C with all roots 0 (@thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra). By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem (@thm-cayley-hamilton), \A^{n} = p_{\A}(\A) = \O, so \A is nilpotent (@def-nilpotent). (\Leftarrow) If \A^{d} = \O and \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} with \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}, then \cvec{0} = \A^{d}\cvec{x} = \lambda^{d}\cvec{x}, so \lambda^{d} = 0 and \lambda = 0. Hence \spec(\A) = \{0\} and ho(\A) = 0. (b) By @thm-gelfand the limit is ho(\A) = 0. Directly for \A = \J_n(0): \A^{k} = \O for k \ge n, so 
orm{\A^{k}}^{1/k} = 0 for all k \ge n, and the sequence is eventually constant at 0. (c) Such an inequality would force 
orm{\A} = 0, hence \A = \O, for every nilpotent \A. But \J_2(0) 
e \O is nilpotent. So the two quantities cannot be compared in that direction at all; @thm-norm-close-to-spectral-radius is the best available substitute, and it buys its conclusion by changing the norm. [C3: When the infimum is attained] Call \A \in M_n(
C) radius-attaining if 
orm{\A} = ho(\A) for some matrix norm. 1. Prove that every normal \A is radius-attaining. 2. Prove that a nonzero nilpotent \A is not. 3. Deduce that  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix} is not radius-attaining, even though it is invertible. Hint for (c): consider \A - \I. (a) Let \A be normal, so \A = \U\D\U^{*} with \U unitary and \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n) (@cor-spectral-complex-matrix). Then \A^{*}\A = \U\diag(\lvert\lambda_ivert^2)\U^{*}, so the singular values of \A are the \lvert\lambda_ivert in decreasing order and 
orm{\A}_2 = \sigma_1 = \max_i\lvert\lambda_ivert = ho(\A) by @thm-operator-norm-formulas (c). (b) If \A 
e \O is nilpotent then ho(\A) = 0 by @exr-spectral-radius-c2 (a), while 
orm{\A} > 0 for every norm, since a norm vanishes only at \O (@def-norm). So no norm can give 
orm{\A} = ho(\A). (c) Put \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}, whose only eigenvalue is 1, so ho(\A) = 1. Suppose some matrix norm had 
orm{\A} = 1. Then 
orm{\A^{k}} \le 
orm{\A}^{k} = 1 for every k, so the sequence (\A^{k}) is bounded in that norm, hence bounded entrywise by @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence, whose second sentence covers boundedness. But \A^{k} =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & k \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}, whose (1,2)-entry is unbounded. Contradiction. (The hint points at the same phenomenon: \A - \I is a nonzero nilpotent, so \A is a unipotent matrix, and it is the nilpotent part that the spectral radius cannot see.)

title: 16.5 Inverting a Perturbation of the Identity
content:
Inverting a Perturbation of the Identity Chapter 10 §10 summed the series \I + \A + \A^2 + \dots and identified its sum as (\I - \A)^{-1}, under the exact hypothesis that every eigenvalue of \A has modulus less than 1. What it could not say is how large that inverse is. This section reruns the argument with a norm in hand. The hypothesis becomes cruder — 
orm{\A} < 1 instead of ho(\A) < 1 — and the conclusion becomes quantitative, which is the trade this chapter keeps making. The payoff is immediate: the invertible matrices turn out to form an open set, inversion turns out to be continuous, and a first estimate appears for how far the solution of \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} moves when \A and \cvec{b} are disturbed. Throughout, 
orm{\cdot} is the operator norm on M_n(
C) induced by a norm on 
C^{n} (@def-operator-norm), so that 
orm{\I} = 1 and 
orm{\X\Y} \le 
orm{\X}
orm{\Y} by @thm-operator-norm-properties (c) and (d). Both properties are used in every proof below, and the first of them is not free: the closing warning shows what happens without it. The geometric series, with a number attached The scalar identity behind everything here is 1 + r + r^2 + \dots = 1/(1-r) for 0 \le r < 1. Chapter 10 §10 gave the matrix version of the identity. What a norm adds is the matrix version of the inequality \lvert 1 + r + \dotsvert \le 1/(1-r): a ceiling on the inverse, expressed in the data. [Neumann Series with a Bound] Let \A \in M_n(
C) with 
orm{\A} < 1, and write a = 
orm{\A}. Then: 1. \I - \A is invertible, and \sum_{k \ge 0}\A^{k} = (\I - \A)^{-1}; 2. \displaystyle 
orm{(\I - \A)^{-1}} \le  rac{1}{1 - a}; 3. for every K \ge 0, the partial sum \S_K = \sum_{k=0}^{K}\A^{k} satisfies 
orm{(\I - \A)^{-1} - \S_K} \le  rac{a^{K+1}}{1 - a} ; 4. \displaystyle 
orm{(\I - \A)^{-1}} \ge  rac{1}{1 + a}. Part (a) is not new work: 
orm{\A} < 1 forces ho(\A) < 1 by @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm, which is exactly the hypothesis of Chapter 10’s @thm-neumann-series-spectral. Everything else is the tail-bounding move. Submultiplicativity turns 
orm{\A^{k}} into a^{k}, so each partial sum is bounded by a scalar geometric sum; the bound then has to be carried across the limit, and what carries it is the fact that a norm is continuous. For (c), the tail of the series factors as \A^{K+1} times the whole series again, so (b) bounds it. For (d), read \I = (\I - \A)(\I - \A)^{-1} through submultiplicativity. (a) By @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm (a), ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A} = a < 1, so every eigenvalue of \A has modulus less than 1. That is the hypothesis of @thm-neumann-series-spectral, which gives both the invertibility of \I - \A and the value of the sum. (b) Submultiplicativity (@thm-operator-norm-properties (d)) gives 
orm{\A^{k}} \le a^{k} for every k \ge 1, by induction on k; and 
orm{\A^{0}} = 
orm{\I} = 1 = a^{0} by part (c) of the same theorem. Hence, by subadditivity applied K times, 
orm{\S_K} \le \sum_{k=0}^{K}
orm{\A^{k}} \le \sum_{k=0}^{K}a^{k} =  rac{1 - a^{K+1}}{1 - a} \le  rac{1}{1-a}, the last step because a^{K+1} \ge 0 and 1 - a > 0. By (a) the sequence (\S_K) converges entrywise to (\I - \A)^{-1}, so 
orm{\S_K - (\I-\A)^{-1}} 	o 0 by @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence. Then @lem-reverse-triangle-norm gives  igl\lvert\,
orm{\S_K} - 
orm{(\I-\A)^{-1}}\, igrvert \le 
orm{\S_K - (\I-\A)^{-1}} 	o 0, so 
orm{\S_K} 	o 
orm{(\I - \A)^{-1}}. A nonstrict inequality survives a limit, so a limit of numbers each at most 1/(1-a) is at most 1/(1-a), which proves (b). (c) Fix K. For every M \ge 1, multiplying out and canceling, \S_{K+M} - \S_K = \sum_{k=K+1}^{K+M}\A^{k} = \A^{K+1}\,\S_{M-1} . Let M 	o \infty. The left-hand side tends to (\I-\A)^{-1} - \S_K by (a). The right-hand side tends to \A^{K+1}(\I-\A)^{-1}, because 
orm{\A^{K+1}\S_{M-1} - \A^{K+1}(\I-\A)^{-1}} \le 
orm{\A^{K+1}}\,
orm{\S_{M-1} - (\I-\A)^{-1}} , which tends to 0 by (a) and @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence again. A sequence has at most one limit, so (\I - \A)^{-1} - \S_K = \A^{K+1}(\I - \A)^{-1} . Taking norms and using submultiplicativity together with (b), 
orm{(\I-\A)^{-1} - \S_K} \le 
orm{\A^{K+1}}\,
orm{(\I-\A)^{-1}} \le  rac{a^{K+1}}{1-a} . (d) 1 = 
orm{\I} = 
orm{(\I - \A)(\I-\A)^{-1}} \le 
orm{\I - \A}\,
orm{(\I-\A)^{-1}}, and 
orm{\I - \A} \le 
orm{\I} + 
orm{\A} = 1 + a by subadditivity. Since 1 + a > 0 we may divide, which proves (d). This proves the theorem. Parts (b) and (d) together pin the inverse between two numbers computed from a alone:  rac{1}{1+a} \le 
orm{(\I-\A)^{-1}} \le  rac{1}{1-a} . As a approaches 1 the upper bound escapes to infinity while the lower one stays near 	frac12, and the gap is real rather than an artifact of the proof: \A = a\I attains the upper bound, and \A = -a\I attains the lower one. [The bound and the truth] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1/2 \ 1/3 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . Using the \infty-norm, check the hypothesis, compute (\I - \A)^{-1} exactly, and compare it with the bound of @thm-neumann-series (b). Then compare \S_3 with the true inverse and with the tail bound of (c). The hypothesis. The absolute row sums are 	frac12 and 	frac13, so 
orm{\A}_{\infty} = 	frac12 < 1 by @thm-operator-norm-formulas (b). So @thm-neumann-series applies with a = 	frac12. The inverse. \I - \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1/2 \ -1/3 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} has determinant 1 - 	frac16 = 	frac56, so by @thm-two-by-two-inverse (\I - \A)^{-1} = 	frac65 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1/2 \ 1/3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 6/5 & 3/5 \ 2/5 & 6/5 \end{pmatrix}, whose largest absolute row sum is 	frac65 + 	frac35 = 	frac95 = 1.8. The bound is 1/(1 - 	frac12) = 2. So the estimate is correct and loses only ten percent. The partial sum. Here \A^{2} = 	frac16\I, so \A^{3} = 	frac16\A and \S_3 =  igl(1 + 	frac16 igr)(\I + \A) = 	frac76 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1/2 \ 1/3 & 1\end{pmatrix} . Hence (\I-\A)^{-1} - \S_3 =  igl(	frac65 - 	frac76 igr)(\I + \A) = 	frac1{30}(\I + \A), with \infty-norm 	frac1{30}\cdot	frac32 = 	frac1{20} = 0.05. The bound of (c) with K = 3 is (	frac12)^{4}/(1 - 	frac12) = 	frac18 = 0.125. Again correct, and this time loose by a factor of 2.5 — the price of replacing four matrices by four copies of one number. Which theorem is stronger The two Neumann theorems must be compared honestly, because neither contains the other. Chapter 10’s @thm-neumann-series-spectral assumes ho(\A) < 1 and concludes that the series converges, with sum (\I-\A)^{-1}; and its hypothesis is sharp, since the statement is an “if and only if”. @thm-neumann-series assumes 
orm{\A} < 1, which by @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm is a strictly stronger demand: ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A} always, and the inequality is often strict. For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} we have ho(\A) = 0, so Chapter 10’s theorem applies and returns \sum_k \A^{k} = \I + \A; but 
orm{\A} = 2 in each of the 1-, 2-, and \infty-norms, so this section’s theorem says nothing at all about it. In the other direction, when this section’s theorem does apply it says strictly more: a ceiling on the inverse, a rate at which the partial sums approach it, and a floor as well. Chapter 10 could not have stated any of the three, having no way to measure a matrix. There is a third thing to say, and it dissolves most of the apparent conflict. If ho(\A) < 1, then by @thm-norm-close-to-spectral-radius there is a norm 
orm{\cdot}_t with 
orm{\A}_t \le ho(\A) + \varepsilon < 1, and @thm-neumann-series applies in that norm. For the matrix above, taking \D = \diag(1, 4) and 
orm{\cvec{x}}_t = 
orm{\D\cvec{x}}_{\infty} gives 
orm{\A}_t = 
orm{\D\A\D^{-1}}_{\infty} = 	frac12, so the bound reads 
orm{(\I-\A)^{-1}}_t \le 2; and indeed \D(\I + \A)\D^{-1} =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1/2 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} has \infty-norm 	frac32 \le 2. So the quantitative theorem can always be brought to bear on a matrix Chapter 10 accepts — at the cost of changing the norm, and the bound it then produces is a bound in that new norm, which may be a strange unit of measurement. Both theorems need a hypothesis. Which of the two hypotheses, ho(\A) < 1 and 
orm{\A} < 1, can be checked by looking at the entries of \A and doing no linear algebra? The second, for a suitable norm: 
orm{\A}_1 and 
orm{\A}_{\infty} are the largest absolute column and row sums (@thm-operator-norm-formulas), read straight off the entries. Deciding ho(\A) < 1 requires the eigenvalues, that is, the roots of a degree-n polynomial. This is the practical reason the cruder hypothesis is worth having: it is the one a reader can verify at a glance, and @cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound is the same observation used in the other direction. The hypothesis 
orm{\A} < 1 is sufficient and never necessary. A matrix can be as far from \I as one likes and still have \I - \A invertible: \A = 5\I gives (\I - \A)^{-1} = -	frac14\I. What fails when 
orm{\A} \ge 1 is not the invertibility but the argument, and with it the bound. Read 
orm{\A} < 1 as “\A is a small perturbation”, not as a criterion. The invertible matrices form an open set The theorem above concerns perturbations of \I. Every invertible matrix can be moved to \I by multiplication, so the general statement follows at once, and it is the statement several earlier arguments wanted: a matrix near an invertible matrix is invertible, and its inverse is near. [Invertibility Is an Open Condition, and Inversion Is Continuous] Let \B \in M_n(
C) be invertible and let \E \in M_n(
C) satisfy 
orm{\E} <  rac{1}{
orm{\B^{-1}}} . Write r = 
orm{\B^{-1}}
orm{\E} < 1. Then: 1. \B + \E is invertible, and \displaystyle 
orm{(\B+\E)^{-1}} \le  rac{

title: 16.6 Bounds for the Exponential, and Two Derivatives
content:
Bounds for the Exponential, and Two Derivatives Chapter 10 §09 built e^{\A} out of a series and closed with a promise: “Chapter 16 will return to e^{\A} with norms available, which give quantitative bounds instead of exact formulas.” That is what this section does. It does not rebuild the exponential; @def-matrix-exponential and @thm-exponential-series-converges stand as they are, and the Jordan form is not touched. What is new is that the series now has a size, so its sum has a ceiling, its truncation has an error bound, and its behavior as t 	o \infty has a rate. The second half takes the other step Chapter 10 could not: it differentiates. The derivative of the determinant and the derivative of the inverse are both needed later in the book, and both require one fact from calculus that linear algebra does not supply. That fact is stated before it is used. Throughout, 
orm{\cdot} is the operator norm on M_n(
C) induced by a norm on 
C^{n} (@def-operator-norm), so 
orm{\I} = 1 and 
orm{\X\Y} \le 
orm{\X}
orm{\Y} (@thm-operator-norm-properties (c), (d)). How big is the exponential Chapter 10 §10’s criteria answered whether; the norm answers how much. The bound to aim at is the one the scalar case suggests: \lvert e^{z}vert \le e^{\lvert zvert}, because the series has nonnegative terms once every term is replaced by its modulus. The matrix proof is the same sentence with submultiplicativity in place of \lvert zwvert = \lvert zvert\lvert wvert. One scalar fact is needed and is not on the chapter’s list of imports. We name it here rather than let it in quietly. A quoted fact. For every real s \ge 0 the series \sum_{m \ge 0}s^{m}/m! converges, with sum e^{s}. This is fact (A1) of Chapter 10 §09, quoted there and quoted again here; this book does not prove it. Because its terms are nonnegative, its partial sums increase to e^{s}, so every partial sum is at most e^{s} — that last step is (A2), monotone convergence, from the list in this chapter’s introduction. [Bounds for the Exponential] Let \A \in M_n(
C) and write a = 
orm{\A}. Then 1. 
orm{e^{\A}} \le e^{a}; 2. 
orm{e^{\A} - \I} \le e^{a} - 1; 3. 
orm{e^{\A} - \I - \A} \le e^{a} - 1 - a \le \dfrac{a^{2}e^{a}}{2}. In particular 
orm{e^{t\A}} \le e^{\lvert tvert a} for every real t. All three are the same computation stopped at a different place: bound the norm of a partial sum by the corresponding partial sum of \sum s^{m}/m!, then let the partial sums converge. The only thing that needs care is the passage to the limit, and @lem-reverse-triangle-norm does it, exactly as in @thm-neumann-series. For the second inequality in (c), compare m! with 2\,(m-2)!. Write \S_M = \sum_{m=0}^{M}\A^{m}/m!. By @thm-exponential-series-converges the sequence (\S_M) converges entrywise to e^{\A}, hence 
orm{\S_M - e^{\A}} 	o 0 by @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence, hence 
orm{\S_M} 	o 
orm{e^{\A}} by @lem-reverse-triangle-norm. The same three steps apply to \S_M - \I and to \S_M - \I - \A. So in each part it suffices to bound the partial sums, uniformly in M. (a) Submultiplicativity gives 
orm{\A^{m}} \le a^{m} for m \ge 1, by induction, and 
orm{\A^{0}} =
