Where exactly is invertibility used, and what does the formula say at a t_0 where \det\A(t_0) = 0? Only in the last line, where \adj\A(t_0) is rewritten as \det\A(t_0)\A(t_0)^{-1}. The adjugate itself is defined for every square matrix (@def-adjugate), so the first form survives. At a t_0 with \det\A(t_0) = 0 it still gives a number: for \A(t) = \diag(t, t) at t_0 = 0 we get \adj\A(0) = \O, so the derivative of \det\A(t) = t^{2} is 0 there, which is correct. The second form would read “0 times something undefined”. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the three bounds of @thm-exponential-norm-bound, and say which property of the norm each one needs. 2. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if 
orm{\A}_2 is large then 
orm{e^{\A}}_2 is large. 3. State @thm-exponential-decay, and say what the constant C is paying for. 4. State Jacobi’s formula (@thm-derivative-of-det), and name the fact from calculus its proof quotes. 5. Write down the derivative of t \mapsto \A(t)^{-1} and explain in one sentence why it is not -\A^{-2}\A'. (a) 
orm{e^{\A}} \le e^{
orm{\A}}, 
orm{e^{\A} - \I} \le e^{
orm{\A}} - 1, and 
orm{e^{\A} - \I - \A} \le e^{
orm{\A}} - 1 - 
orm{\A} \le 
orm{\A}^{2}e^{
orm{\A}}/2. All three need subadditivity (to bound a sum term by term) and submultiplicativity (to get 
orm{\A^{m}} \le 
orm{\A}^{m}); the first also needs 
orm{\I} = 1, which is what makes the m = 0 term equal 1. (b) Incorrect. For \A = t egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} we have 
orm{\A}_2 = t, arbitrarily large, while e^{\A} is a rotation matrix and 
orm{e^{\A}}_2 = 1 (@exm-exponential-bound-sharp-and-not). (c) If \mu is the largest real part of an eigenvalue of \A and 
u > \mu, there is C \ge 1 with 
orm{e^{t\A}} \le Ce^{
u t} for all t \ge 0. The constant pays for the transient: 
orm{e^{t\A}} may first grow, as in @exm-decay-with-a-transient, and it also pays for the gap between 
u and \mu. (d)  rac{d}{dt}\det\A(t) = 	r(\adj\A(t)\,\A'(t)), for a matrix-valued \A differentiable at t. The quoted fact is (D1): the linearity of differentiation and the product rule for complex-valued functions of a real variable. (e) (\A^{-1})' = -\A^{-1}\A'\A^{-1}. The two copies of \A^{-1} sit on opposite sides of \A', and matrices do not commute, so they may not be collected into \A^{-2} unless \A' commutes with \A. B. Practice [B1: Bound against truth] For each matrix, compute 
orm{e^{\A}}_{\infty} exactly and compare with e^{
orm{\A}_{\infty}}. 1. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 3 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. 2. \A = \diag(1, -4). (a) \A^{2} = \O, so the series stops: e^{\A} = \I + \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}, with 
orm{e^{\A}}_{\infty} = 4. Also 
orm{\A}_{\infty} = 3, so the bound is e^{3} \approx 20.09. Correct, and loose by a factor of about 5. (b) e^{\A} = \diag(e, e^{-4}), so 
orm{e^{\A}}_{\infty} = e \approx 2.718. Here 
orm{\A}_{\infty} = 4 and the bound is e^{4} \approx 54.6. The bound is governed by the entry of largest modulus, -4, while the exponential is governed by the largest real part, 1. This is the discrepancy @thm-exponential-decay exists to remove. [B2: A rate for a stable matrix] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} -2 & 4 \ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}. 1. Compute \mu and e^{t\A}, and give 
orm{e^{t\A}}_{\infty} for t \ge 0. 2. Find the largest value of 
orm{e^{t\A}}_{\infty} on t \ge 0. 3. Find the smallest C that works in @thm-exponential-decay for 
u = -1. (a) \A is upper triangular with diagonal -2, -2, so \spec(\A) = \{-2\} (@thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form (b)) and \mu = -2. Writing \A = -2\I + 4\N with \N =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0&1\0&0\end{psmallmatrix}, the summands commute and \N^2 = \O, so by @cor-exponential-of-jordan-block e^{t\A} = e^{-2t} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 4t \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad 
orm{e^{t\A}}_{\infty} = e^{-2t}(1 + 4t) . (b) The derivative of e^{-2t}(1+4t) is e^{-2t}(4 - 2 - 8t) = e^{-2t}(2 - 8t), which is positive for t < 	frac14 and negative after, so by fact (A6) the maximum is at t = 	frac14. The value there is 2e^{-1/2} \approx 1.213. (c) We need the smallest C with e^{-2t}(1+4t) \le Ce^{-t}, that is, C = \max_{t \ge 0}(1+4t)e^{-t}. Its derivative is e^{-t}(4 - 1 - 4t) = e^{-t}(3 - 4t), positive for t < 	frac34 and negative after, so by fact (A6) the maximum is at t = 	frac34 and C = 4e^{-3/4} \approx 1.890. [B3: Two derivatives] Let \A(t) =  egin{pmatrix} \cos t & -\sin t \ \sin t & \cos t \end{pmatrix}. 1. Compute  rac{d}{dt}\det\A(t) by @thm-derivative-of-det and check it against the exact value of \det\A(t). 2. Compute (\A^{-1})'(t) by @thm-derivative-of-inverse and check it by differentiating \A(t)^{-1} directly. (a) \det\A(t) = \cos^{2}t + \sin^{2}t = 1, so the derivative is 0. By the formula: \adj\A(t) =  egin{psmallmatrix} \cos t & \sin t \ -\sin t & \cos t \end{psmallmatrix} and \A'(t) =  egin{psmallmatrix} -\sin t & -\cos t \ \cos t & -\sin t\end{psmallmatrix}, so \adj\A(t)\A'(t) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, whose trace is 0. The two agree. (The diagonal entries are -\cos t\sin t + \sin t\cos t and \sin t\cos t - \cos t\sin t, both zero.) (b) Since \det\A(t) = 1, \A(t)^{-1} = \adj\A(t) =  egin{psmallmatrix} \cos t & \sin t \ -\sin t & \cos t\end{psmallmatrix}, whose entrywise derivative is  egin{psmallmatrix} -\sin t & \cos t \ -\cos t & -\sin t\end{psmallmatrix}. By the formula, using the product \adj\A(t)\A'(t) computed in (a), -\A^{-1}\A'\A^{-1} = - egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \cos t & \sin t \ -\sin t & \cos t\end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} -\sin t & \cos t \ -\cos t & -\sin t \end{pmatrix} . The two agree. C. Going deeper [C1: The determinant of the exponential, again] Let \A \in M_n(
C) and put \varphi(t) = \det e^{t\A}. 1. Prove that \varphi is differentiable with \varphi'(t) = (	r\A)\varphi(t). 2. Hence deduce \det e^{\A} = e^{	r\A}, recovering @thm-exponential-properties (e). Hint for (b): consider \psi(t) = e^{-t	r\A}\varphi(t). (a) The function t \mapsto e^{t\A} is differentiable with derivative \A e^{t\A} (@thm-exponential-properties (b)), and e^{t\A} is invertible with inverse e^{-t\A} (@thm-exponential-properties (c)). So @thm-derivative-of-det applies in its second form: \varphi'(t) = \det(e^{t\A})\,	r igl(e^{-t\A}\A e^{t\A} igr) . By @thm-trace-properties (3) with the two factors e^{-t\A} and \A e^{t\A}, we get 	r(e^{-t\A}\A e^{t\A}) = 	r(\A e^{t\A}e^{-t\A}) = 	r\A, giving \varphi'(t) = (	r\A)\varphi(t). (b) Put c = 	r\A and \psi(t) = e^{-ct}\varphi(t). By the product rule (D1) and (a), \psi'(t) = -c\,e^{-ct}\varphi(t) + e^{-ct}c\,\varphi(t) = 0 for every t, where  rac{d}{dt}e^{-ct} = -ce^{-ct} is @thm-exponential-properties (b) in the case n = 1. A differentiable function with vanishing derivative is constant — fact (A4) of Chapter 10 §09 — so \psi(t) = \psi(0) = \det(e^{0}) = \det\I = 1. Hence \varphi(t) = e^{ct}, and t = 1 gives \det e^{\A} = e^{	r\A}. [C2: Comparing two exponentials] Let \A, \B \in M_n(
C) with \A\B = \B\A. 1. Prove that 
orm{e^{\A} - e^{\B}} \le e^{
orm{\B}} igl(e^{
orm{\A - \B}} - 1 igr). 2. Deduce that \M \mapsto e^{\M} is continuous at every \M that commutes with a neighborhood of itself, and identify those \M: they are exactly the scalar matrices c\I. 3. Say exactly where the commuting hypothesis is used, and why the argument cannot simply be dropped. (a) Since \A and \B commute, so do \B and \A - \B. By @thm-exponential-properties (d), e^{\A} = e^{\B + (\A - \B)} = e^{\B}e^{\A - \B}. Hence e^{\A} - e^{\B} = e^{\B} igl(e^{\A-\B} - \I igr) , and submultiplicativity with @thm-exponential-norm-bound (a) and (b) gives 
orm{e^{\A} - e^{\B}} \le 
orm{e^{\B}}\,
orm{e^{\A-\B} - \I} \le e^{
orm{\B}} igl(e^{
orm{\A-\B}} - 1 igr) . (b) Take \B = c\I, which commutes with every matrix. For \A with 
orm{\A - c\I} = \delta, part (a) gives 
orm{e^{\A} - e^{c}\I} \le e^{\lvert cvert}(e^{\delta} - 1), and e^{\delta} - 1 	o 0 as \delta 	o 0, because t \mapsto e^{t} is differentiable by fact (A2) of Chapter 10 §09 and so continuous at 0. So e^{\A} 	o e^{c\I} as \A 	o c\I. (c) Only in the first line, where e^{\B + (\A-\B)} is split as e^{\B}e^{\A-\B}; @thm-exponential-properties (d) has commutation as a hypothesis, and Chapter 10 §09 exhibits matrices with e^{\A+\B} 
e e^{\A}e^{\B}. Without it there is no factorization to take norms of, and a different argument is needed. (The inequality itself is in fact true in general, but proving it needs an integral representation of e^{\A} - e^{\B}, which this book does not have.) [C3: A quantity that measures the decay] Let \A, \X, \Q \in M_n(
C) with \X and \Q positive definite (@def-positive-semidefinite) and \A^{*}\X + \X\A = -\Q . Let \cvec{x} \colon 
R 	o 
C^{n} be differentiable with \cvec{x}' = \A\cvec{x}, and put V(t) = \cvec{x}(t)^{*}\X\cvec{x}(t). 1. Prove that V is real-valued and differentiable, with V'(t) = \cvec{x}(t)^{*}(\A^{*}\X + \X\A)\cvec{x}(t). 2. Deduce that if \cvec{x}(0) 
e \cvec{0}, then V is strictly decreasing. 3. Explain how this relates to the Lyapunov equation of @def-lyapunov-equation, whose unknown sits between \A and \A^{*} the other way round. Hint for (a): \cvec{x}^{*} is a 1 	imes n matrix-valued function, and \conj{f}' = \conj{f'} for a differentiable f \colon 
R 	o 
C. (a) V(t) is a 1 	imes 1 matrix, and V(t)^{*} = \cvec{x}^{*}\X^{*}\cvec{x} = \cvec{x}^{*}\X\cvec{x} = V(t) since \X is Hermitian, so V(t) is real. Each entry of t \mapsto \cvec{x}(t)^{*} is the conjugate of an entry of \cvec{x}, hence differentiable with (\cvec{x}^{*})' = (\cvec{x}')^{*} = (\A\cvec{x})^{*} = \cvec{x}^{*}\A^{*}. By @lem-matrix-product-rule, applied twice to the product \cvec{x}^{*}\cdot\X\cdot\cvec{x} and using \X' = \O, V'(t) = \cvec{x}^{*}\A^{*}\X\cvec{x} + \cvec{x}^{*}\X\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{x}^{*}(\A^{*}\X + \X\A)\cvec{x} . (b) By hypothesis V'(t) = -\cvec{x}(t)^{*}\Q\cvec{x}(t). If \cvec{x}(t_1) = \cvec{0} for some t_1, then by @thm-linear-ode-solution \cvec{x}(t) = e^{t\A}\cvec{x}(0) for every t, and e^{t_1\A} is invertible by @thm-exponential-properties (c), so \cvec{x}(0) = \cvec{0}, contradicting the hypothesis. So \cvec{x}(t) 
e \cvec{0} for every t, and \Q \succ \O gives \cvec{x}(t)^{*}\Q\cvec{x}(t) > 0, hence V'(t) < 0 for every t. A differentiable real function with everywhere negative derivative is strictly decreasing; that last step is the mean value theorem, one more fact of one-variable calculus quoted here and not proved. (c) @def-lyapunov-equation writes the equation as \A\X + \X\A^{*} = -\Q; the equation used here is that one for the pair (\A^{*}, \Q). The two are interchanged by replacing \A with \A^{*}, which changes nothing about stability, since the eigenvalues of \A^{*} are the complex conjugates of those of \A and conjugation preserves real parts. So the decay of V is exactly the statement Chapter 12 §10 pointed forward to, for whichever of the two conventions one adopts, and such an \X does exist: @thm-lyapunov applied to \A^{*} produces one.

title: 16.7 Eigenvalues Move Continuously
content:
Eigenvalues Move Continuously Chapter 12 §01 proved that every complex matrix has diagonalizable matrices arbitrarily close to it (@cor-schur-normal-matrix-nearby), then admitted that the word “close” was doing work no definition supported, and handed the repair to this chapter. The repair is now in place: a norm on M_n(
C) says how close two matrices are, and @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence says that it does not matter which norm. This section asks the question that could not even be posed before that point. If the matrix moves a little, how far do its eigenvalues move? The answer has two halves, and the second is the one worth remembering. The eigenvalues do move only a little — provided they are read as an unordered list, which is the only way they can be read. But “a little” is not proportional to the movement of the matrix, and for a matrix with a large Jordan block it is spectacularly larger. Throughout, matrices are complex, as in Section 4, so that an n 	imes n matrix always has exactly n eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity (@cor-complex-polynomial-splits). From matrices to polynomials The eigenvalues of \A are the roots of p_{\A} (@thm-eigenvalue-characterizations), with algebraic multiplicity meaning multiplicity as a root (@def-algebraic-multiplicity). So the question splits in two: do the coefficients of p_{\A} move a little when \A does, and do the roots of a polynomial move a little when its coefficients do? The first half is easy and we do it now; the whole difficulty is in the second. The reason the first half is easy is that everything in sight is a polynomial in the entries. It is worth isolating that observation once, because it will be used four times in this section. [Polynomial Maps of the Entries Are Continuous] Let \Phi \colon M_{p 	imes q}(
C) 	o M_{r 	imes s}(
C) be a map each of whose output entries is given by a fixed polynomial, with complex coefficients, in the pq entries of the input. Fix any norm on the source and any norm on the target. Then \Phi is continuous: whenever 
orm{\A_k - \A} 	o 0 we have 
orm{\Phi(\A_k) - \Phi(\A)} 	o 0, and equivalently, for every \A and every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that 
orm{\B - \A} < \delta forces 
orm{\Phi(\B) - \Phi(\A)} < \varepsilon. The same holds for a map into 
C. Two reductions and one piece of arithmetic. Convergence in any norm is entrywise convergence, by @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence, in the source and in the target alike; so the claim is about pq complex sequences producing rs complex sequences. That reduces it to the statement that a polynomial in finitely many complex variables respects limits, which is the algebra of limits. Suppose 
orm{\A_k - \A} 	o 0. By @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence, each entry (\A_k)_{ij} 	o a_{ij}. Sums and products of convergent complex sequences converge to the sum and the product of the limits: for sums this is @thm-complex-triangle-inequality, and for products it follows from \lvert z_kw_k - zw vert \le \lvert z_k vert\,\lvert w_k - w vert + \lvert w vert\,\lvert z_k - z vert together with the fact that a convergent sequence is bounded. A polynomial is built from its variables and constants by finitely many sums and products, so each entry of \Phi(\A_k) converges to the corresponding entry of \Phi(\A). Applying @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence in M_{r 	imes s}(
C) gives 
orm{\Phi(\A_k) - \Phi(\A)} 	o 0. For the equivalence of the two formulations, suppose the \varepsilon–\delta statement failed at some \A for some \varepsilon > 0. Then for each k \ge 1 the value \delta = 1/k is not good enough, so there is \B_k with 
orm{\B_k - \A} < 1/k and 
orm{\Phi(\B_k) - \Phi(\A)} \ge \varepsilon. The sequence (\B_k) contradicts the sequential statement just proved. This proves the lemma. Now the first half of the question is answered. Write p_{\A}(x) = x^n + c_{n-1}(\A)x^{n-1} + \dots + c_0(\A), which is legitimate because p_{\A} is monic of degree n (@thm-charpoly-coefficients). Each c_j is a polynomial in the entries of \A: the Leibniz sum of @def-characteristic-polynomial expresses \det(x\I - \A) as a signed sum of products of the entries of x\I - \A, each of which is x - a_{jj} or -a_{ij}, and collecting the powers of x leaves every coefficient a polynomial with integer coefficients in the a_{ij}. So \A \mapsto (c_0(\A), \dots, c_{n-1}(\A)) is continuous by @lem-entrywise-polynomial-continuous. That leaves the second half: roots against coefficients. Before stating what is true there, we settle what cannot be true. Why the answer must be about the multiset The statement a reader would write down first is “each eigenvalue is a continuous function of the matrix”. It is not merely unproved; it is meaningless as written, because the eigenvalues come with no numbering — and the natural repair, “there is a way of numbering them that makes each one continuous”, is false. One two-by-two family shows it, and the failure is the ordinary square root. [There Is No Continuous Choice of a Single Eigenvalue] For t \in 
C put \A(t) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ t & 0 \end{pmatrix}, so that p_{\A(t)}(x) = x^2 - t and the eigenvalues of \A(t) are the two square roots of t. Then there is no continuous function \lambda \colon D 	o 
C on the closed unit disc D = \{t \in 
C : \lvert tvert \le 1\} such that \lambda(t) is an eigenvalue of \A(t) for every t \in D. Consequently there is no continuous \Lambda \colon M_2(
C) 	o 
C with \Lambda(\B) \in \spec(\B) for every \B. Walk t once around the unit circle. The two roots \pm\sqrt{t} trade places on the way round, so a choice that is continuous along the walk comes home as the other root. The bookkeeping is done by dividing the chosen root by one fixed root, which turns the walk into a continuous function with only the two values 1 and -1; on an interval such a function cannot jump, and it must. The characteristic polynomial is \det egin{psmallmatrix} x & -1 \ -t & x\end{psmallmatrix} = x^2 - t, so \mu is an eigenvalue of \A(t) if and only if \mu^2 = t (@thm-eigenvalue-characterizations). Suppose such a \lambda exists, so \lambda(t)^2 = t for all \lvert t vert \le 1. Define g \colon [0, 2\pi] 	o 
C by g(	heta) = \lambda igl(e^{i	heta} igr)\,e^{-i	heta/2} . It is continuous, being a composite and a product of continuous functions — the elementary algebra of limits recorded in the chapter introduction, applied to 	heta \mapsto e^{i	heta}, to \lambda, and to 	heta \mapsto e^{-i	heta/2}. Squaring, g(	heta)^2 = \lambda igl(e^{i	heta} igr)^2 e^{-i	heta} = e^{i	heta}e^{-i	heta} = 1 , so g(	heta) \in \{1, -1\} for every 	heta. In particular g is real-valued, and a continuous real-valued function on an interval taking only the values 1 and -1 is constant: if it took both, the intermediate value theorem would produce a 	heta with g(	heta) = 0. Hence g(2\pi) = g(0). But e^{i \cdot 0} = e^{i \cdot 2\pi} = 1, so g(0) = \lambda(1) while g(2\pi) = \lambda(1)e^{-i\pi} = -\lambda(1). Therefore \lambda(1) = -\lambda(1), that is \lambda(1) = 0, contradicting \lambda(1)^2 = 1. So no such \lambda exists. For the last sentence, if \Lambda were such a function then t \mapsto \Lambda(\A(t)) would be continuous, because t \mapsto \A(t) is continuous by @lem-entrywise-polynomial-continuous, and it would select an eigenvalue of \A(t) for each t. This proves the proposition. The intermediate value theorem is quoted here, and it is the only place in this chapter that uses it; it is fact (A5) of the chapter introduction, borrowed and not proved. Two things are worth reading off the argument. First, the obstruction is not exotic: \A(0) = \J_2(0) is the standard nilpotent matrix, and the trouble happens exactly at the parameter where the two eigenvalues collide. Second, nothing is wrong with the pair \{\sqrt t, -\sqrt t\}, which shrinks to \{0, 0\} as t 	o 0 in any reasonable sense. It is only the attempt to call one of them “the first” that fails. This is why the correct statement speaks of the roots as a multiset: a list with multiplicities and no order. The imported fact Here is what is true. It is the one statement in this chapter that the chapter does not prove. [Continuous Dependence of the Roots on the Coefficients] Let n \ge 1 and let p(x) = x^n + c_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + c_1x + c_0 \in 
C[x] be monic, with roots \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n \in 
C listed with multiplicity (@cor-complex-polynomial-splits). Let \varepsilon > 0. Then there is \delta > 0 with the following property. If q(x) = x^n + b_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + b_1x + b_0 is monic of the same degree n and \lvert b_j - c_j vert < \delta for every j, then the roots 
u_1, \dots, 
u_n of q, listed with multiplicity, can be numbered so that \lvert 
u_i - \mu_i vert < \varepsilon \qquad (i = 1, \dots, n). This chapter quotes this theorem, and Chapter 20 proves it. The classical proof uses complex analysis: one encircles each root of p by a small circle on which p does not vanish, counts the roots inside by a contour integral, and observes that an integer-valued quantity depending continuously on the coefficients cannot change. The book never develops that machinery, and it does not need to: compactness, fact (A3), together with unique factorization in 
C[x], is enough, and Chapter 20 §03 gives that proof. It is postponed there because it belongs with the quantitative bounds on how far roots move. Until then the statement is recorded in the manner this book has used before — Chapter 14 §06 with Taylor’s theorem, Chapter 11 with the theorem of Abel and Ruffini: named at the point of use, never buried inside a proof that presents itself as self-contained, and never strengthened in passing. What can be proved with the tools at hand is that the numbering in the statement has to be chosen afresh for each q, and that was @prp-no-continuous-root-selection. Two clauses of the statement carry weight. Monic of the same degree is essential: the roots of \delta x^2 + x are 0 and -1/\delta, which runs off to infinity as \delta 	o 0, while the limit polynomial x has the single root 0. Allowing the leading coefficient to vanish destroys everything, and monic polynomials of a fixed degree are exactly the family where it cannot. And numbered so that is the multiset formulation: the permutation matching up the two lists depends on q, and @prp-no-continuous-root-selection says it must. Eigenvalues, and the spectral radius Now the two halves are assembled. [Eigenvalues Depend Continuously on the Matrix] Let \A \in M_n(
C) with eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n listed with algebraic multiplicity, let 
orm{\cdot} be any norm on M_n(
C), and let \varepsilon > 0. Then there is \delta > 0 such that every \B \in M_n(
C) with 
orm{\B - \A} < \delta has eigenvalues \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n, listed with algebraic multiplicity, which can be numbered so that \lvert \mu_i - \lambda_i vert < \varepsilon for every i. The characteristic polynomial’s coefficients are polynomials in the entries, so they move continuously with \A; the quoted root theorem then moves the roots. The only work is composing the two estimates, choosing the tolerance for the coefficients small enough that the roots come out within \varepsilon. By @thm-charpoly-coefficients the polynomials p_{\A} and p_{\B} are monic of degree n, and by @thm-eigenvalue-characterizations together with @def-algebraic-multiplicity their root lists with multiplicity are the eigenvalue lists with algebraic multiplicity. Let \delta' > 0 be the number supplied by @thm-roots-depend-continuously for p = p_{\A} and this \varepsilon. The map \B \mapsto (c_0(\B), \dots, c_{n-1}(\B)) is continuous by @lem-entrywise-polynomial-continuous, as noted after that lemma, so there is \delta > 0 such that 
orm{\B - \A} < \delta forces \lvert c_j(\B) - c_j(\A) vert < \delta' for every j. For such a \B, @thm-roots-depend-continuously applies to q = p_{\B}. This proves the corollary. The corollary says exactly as much as @thm-roots-depend-continuously and no more: the numbering is not canonical and depends on \B. Any quantity that ignores the numbering, however, inherits honest continuity, and the spectral radius of Section 4 is the first example. Does @cor-eigenvalues-continuous make ho \colon M_n(
C) 	o 
R continuous, given that no individual eigenvalue is a continuous function of \A? Yes. Let \varepsilon > 0 and take \delta from @cor-eigenvalues-continuous. If 
orm{\B - \A} < \delta, fix a numbering with \lvert \mu_i - \lambda_i vert < \varepsilon. Then \lvert \mu_i vert \le \lvert \lambda_i vert + \varepsilon \le ho(\A) + \varepsilon for each i by @def-spectral-radius, so ho(\B) \le ho(\A) + \varepsilon; the same numbering read the other way gives \lvert\lambda_ivert \le \lvert\mu_ivert + \varepsilon \le ho(\B) + \varepsilon for each i, hence ho(\A) \le ho(\B) + \varepsilon, so \lvert ho(\B) - ho(\A) vert \le \varepsilon. The argument never names an individual eigenvalue, which is why it survives: ho is a function of the multiset alone. The limit argument, made routine Chapter 12 §01 called @cor-schur-normal-matrix-nearby “the tool behind a standard strategy: prove it for diagonalizable matrices, then take a limit”, and said that this chapter, “where matrices acquire norms and limits can be spoken of properly, runs arguments of exactly this shape”. Here is the shape. It costs two corollaries, and afterwards the strategy is three lines every time. [Diagonalizable Matrices Are Dense] Let 
orm{\cdot} be any norm on M_n(
C). For every \A \in M_n(
C) and every \varepsilon > 0 there is a diagonalizable \A' \in M_n(
C) with 
orm{\A - \A'} < \varepsilon. Equivalently, every complex square matrix is the limit of a sequence of diagonalizable matrices, in every norm. Chapter 12 produced a diagonalizable matrix near \A with the entries close. “Close in every norm” is now the same thing, by @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence, so the only task is to convert one tolerance into the other. Let N_{\infty}(\M) = \max_{i,j}\lvert m_{ij} vert, which is a norm on M_n(
C): it is the \infty-norm of @exm-p-norms read on the list of n^2 entries. By @thm-norm-equivalence there is C > 0 with 
orm{\M} \le C\,N_{\infty}(\M) for every \M. Apply @cor-schur-normal-matrix-nearby with the tolerance \varepsilon/C: it supplies a diagonalizable \A' with \lvert a_{ij} - a'_{ij} vert < \varepsilon/C for all i, j, hence with N_{\infty}(\A - \A') < \varepsilon/C, a maximum of finitely many numbers each below that bound. Therefore 
orm{\A - \A'} \le C\,N_{\infty}(\A - \A') < \varepsilon. Taking \varepsilon = 1/k gives a sequence \A_k of diagonalizable matrices with 
orm{\A - \A_k} 	o 0. This proves the corollary. [Proving an Identity by Density] Let \Phi \colon M_n(
C) 	o M_{r 	imes s}(
C) be a map each of whose output entries is a polynomial in the entries of the input. If \Phi(\A) = \O for every diagonalizable \A \in M_n(
C), then \Phi(\A) = \O for every \A \in M_n(
C). Both sides of the identity are continuous in \A, and they agree on the diagonalizable matrices, which are dense. A continuous function is determined by its values on a dense set, so they agree everywhere. Fix \A and a norm on each side. By @cor-diagonalizable-dense-again choose diagonalizable \A_k with 
orm{\A - \A_k} 	o 0. By @lem-entrywise-polynomial-continuous, 
orm{\Phi(\A_k) - \Phi(\A)} 	o 0. Since \Phi(\A_k) = \O by hypothesis, that says 
orm{\Phi(\A)} 	o 0; but 
orm{\Phi(\A)} does not depend on k, so 
orm{\Phi(\A)} = 0 and \Phi(\A) = \O by the positivity clause of @def-norm. This proves the corollary. The hypothesis “each output entry is a polynomial in the input entries” is the one to check, and it is usually free: any expression built from \A by addition, multiplication, transposition, conjugate transposition of a real matrix, determinants, adjugates, traces, and the coefficients of p_{\A} qualifies. What does not qualify is anything built from an inverse, an eigenvector, or a choice of ordering. Here is the strategy in action, on the theorem that Chapter 9 proved the long way. [Cayley–Hamilton, by a limit] Prove that p_{\A}(\A) = \O for every \A \in M_n(
C), using density rather than the adjugate identity of @thm-adjugate-identity. Put \Phi(\A) = p_{\A}(\A). Each entry of \Phi(\A) is a polynomial in the entries of \A: the coefficients c_j(\A) are, as noted after @lem-entrywise-polynomial-continuous, and \Phi(\A) = \A^n + c_{n-1}(\A)\A^{n-1} + \dots + c_0(\A)\I is then built from them by products and sums. Let \A be diagonalizable, say \A = \P\D\P^{-1} with \D = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n). By @thm-powers-diagonalizable, p_{\A}(\A) = \P\,\diag igl(p_{\A}(d_1), \dots, p_{\A}(d_n) igr)\,\P^{-1}. Each d_i is an eigenvalue of \A, hence a root of p_{\A} (@thm-eigenvalue-characterizations), so every diagonal entry is 0 and \Phi(\A) = \O. By @cor-identity-by-density, \Phi(\A) = \O for every \A \in M_n(
C), which is @thm-cayley-hamilton over 
C. That is the whole strategy: check the identity where the matrix is diagonal in some basis, where everything is a scalar computation, and let density carry it to the rest. It proves nothing new here — @thm-cayley-hamilton holds over every field, and the density argument is confined to 
C — but the three lines at the end are the part to transfer. @exr-continuity-of-eigenvalues-c2 runs the same argument with a different dense set. The warning: continuous is not Lipschitz Everything so far has been qualitative. The quantitative question is whether there is a constant L with 	ext{(eigenvalue movement)} \;\le\; L\,
orm{\B - \A} , which is what “continuous” is usually imagined to mean and what a numerical analyst actually needs. There is not, and the failure is severe. [A Jordan block’s eigenvalues move like \varepsilon^{1/k}] Let k \ge 2, let \varepsilon > 0, and perturb the nilpotent Jordan block in its bottom left corner: \A = \J_k(0), \qquad \A_{\varepsilon} = \J_k(0) + \varepsilon\E_{k1} . Find the eigenvalues of \A_{\varepsilon} and compare their distance from \spec(\A) = \{0\} with 
orm{\A_{\varepsilon} - \A}. The characteristic polynomial is x^k - \varepsilon. Write \M = x\I - \A_{\varepsilon}, so \M has x on the diagonal, -1 on the superdiagonal, -\varepsilon in position (k, 1), and zeros elsewhere. Expand along the first column (@thm-laplace-expansion (a)), whose only nonzero entries are m_{11} = x and m_{k1} = -\varepsilon. Deleting row 1 and column 1 leaves the (k-1) 	imes (k-1) upper triangular matrix with x on the diagonal, of determinant x^{k-1} (@thm-det-triangular). Deleting row k and column 1 leaves the matrix with rows 1, \dots, k-1 and columns 2, \dots, k of \M; its (i, j) entry is m_{i, j+1}, which is -1 when j = i and x when i = j + 1, so it is lower triangular with -1 all along its diagonal and determinant (-1)^{k-1}. The cofactor signs are (-1)^{1+1} = 1 and (-1)^{k+1}, so \det\M = x \cdot x^{k-1} + (-\varepsilon)(-1)^{k+1}(-1)^{k-1} = x^{k} - \varepsilon , since (-1)^{k+1}(-1)^{k-1} = (-1)^{2k} = 1. The eigenvalues. They are the k-th roots of \varepsilon, namely \varepsilon^{1/k}e^{2\pi i j/k} for j = 0, \dots, k-1, each of modulus \varepsilon^{1/k}. For k = 2 this is the pair \pm\sqrt{\varepsilon}, and \A_{\varepsilon} is the matrix \A(\varepsilon) of @prp-no-continuous-root-selection. The comparison. The perturbation \E = \varepsilon\E_{k1} has a single nonzero entry, so its largest absolute row sum and largest absolute column sum are both \varepsilon, and \E^{*}\E = \varepsilon^2\E_{11} has largest eigenvalue \varepsilon^2; hence 
orm{\E}_1 = 
orm{\E}_{\infty} = 
orm{\E}_2 = \varepsilon by @thm-operator-norm-formulas. Every eigenvalue of \A is 0, so the eigenvalues have moved a distance \varepsilon^{1/k} while the matrix moved a distance \varepsilon. The ratio is  rac{\varepsilon^{1/k}}{\varepsilon} = \varepsilon^{-(k-1)/k} \xrightarrow[\;\varepsilon 	o 0^{+}\;]{} \infty . A by-product worth keeping. The k roots \varepsilon^{1/k}e^{2\pi ij/k} are distinct for every \varepsilon > 0, so \A_{\varepsilon} has k distinct eigenvalues and is diagonalizable by @cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable. A single nilpotent Jordan block, which is as far from diagonalizable as a matrix gets, therefore has diagonalizable matrices arbitrarily close to it, and here they are written down. That is @cor-diagonalizable-dense-again made concrete for one family. Put numbers on it. For k = 2 and \varepsilon = 10^{-6} the matrix moves by one part in a million and the eigenvalues move to \pm 10^{-3}: an amplification of a thousand. For k = 10 and \varepsilon = 10^{-10} the matrix moves by 10^{-10} and the eigenvalues land on the circle of radius 10^{-1}, an amplification of a billion. No constant L survives this, so the continuity of @cor-eigenvalues-continuous cannot be upgraded to a Lipschitz bound, and the \delta it produces genuinely depends on \A and not only on n. Continuous does not mean stable. @cor-eigenvalues-continuous guarantees that a small enough perturbation moves the eigenvalues a little, and says nothing whatever about how small “small enough” is. For \J_{10}(0) a perturbation of size 10^{-10} — the kind of change one would call negligible in data recorded to ten digits — scatters the eigenvalues over a circle of radius 0.1. Reading a printed eigenvalue of a matrix with a large Jordan block as a property of the matrix, rather than of the matrix plus whatever noise reached it, is the mistake this example exists to prevent. The opposite extreme is worth seeing beside it. Take the Hermitian \A = \diag(1, 2) and the Hermitian perturbation \E = \varepsilon(\E_{12} + \E_{21}), of norm 
orm{\E}_2 = \varepsilon. The matrix \A + \E =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & \varepsilon \ \varepsilon & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} has trace 3 and determinant 2 - \varepsilon^2, so its eigenvalues are  rac{3 \pm \sqrt{1 + 4\varepsilon^2}}{2} , and since \sqrt{1 + u} \le 1 + u/2 for u \ge 0, each of them lies within \varepsilon^2 of the corresponding eigenvalue of \A. Here the eigenvalues move less than the matrix does, by a whole order in \varepsilon. That is not an accident of the example: Chapter 17 proves that the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix move by at most 
orm{\E}_2 under a Hermitian perturbation, and Chapter 20 proves the theorem of Bauer and Fike, which bounds the movement for a diagonalizable matrix by 
orm{\E}_2 times a factor measuring how far its eigenvector basis is from orthonormal. So the exponent 1/k in @exm-jordan-block-perturbation is not about size; it is about shape. It is decided by the largest Jordan block at the eigenvalue (@thm-jordan-canonical-form), and block size is precisely what Chapter 12 §11 was measuring when @exm-defect-jordan-block computed \Delta(\J_k(\lambda)) = \sqrt{k - 1} for the departure from normality of @def-departure-from-normality. The two statements match at both ends: \Delta = 0 exactly for the normal matrices, whose eigenvalues are the stable ones, and \Delta grows with the block that makes them fragile. They do not match in between, and it would be wrong to read \Delta as a formula for the exponent — \Delta is one number for the whole matrix, so it cannot report which eigenvalue carries which block, and @exm-defect-jordan-block records that it does not depend on \lambda at all. What \Delta(\A) does is tell you whether the question needs asking at all. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State @thm-roots-depend-continuously, paying attention to the two hypotheses on q. 2. Explain in one sentence why the theorem is stated for the multiset of roots rather than for a list of n individual roots. 3. Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: “the function sending \A \in M_2(
C) to its eigenvalue of largest modulus is continuous”. 4. For the k 	imes k Jordan block, how far do the eigenvalues move under a perturbation of norm \varepsilon, and what does that say about a Lipschitz bound? (a) See @thm-roots-depend-continuously. The two hypotheses are that q is monic and of the same degree n as p; without them the roots can escape to infinity, as \delta x^2 + x shows. (b) Because no continuous choice of an individual root exists: @prp-no-continuous-root-selection shows that following one square root of t once around the unit circle returns the other one, so the matching numbering must be allowed to depend on q. (c) Incorrect as stated, because a matrix can have two eigenvalues of equal largest modulus and then the phrase does not name a number; and incorrect even where it does name a number, since \A(t) of @prp-no-continuous-root-selection has the two eigenvalues \pm\sqrt t of equal modulus for every t 
e 0. The modulus itself, that is ho, is continuous — see the Quick check. (d) They move a distance \varepsilon^{1/k} (@exm-jordan-block-perturbation), so the ratio of eigenvalue movement to matrix movement is \varepsilon^{-(k-1)/k}, which is unbounded as \varepsilon 	o 0^{+}. No Lipschitz constant exists. B. Practice [B1: Two perturbations of the same size] Let \varepsilon = 10^{-8}. Compute the eigenvalues of \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ \varepsilon & 0 \end{pmatrix} \qquad	ext{and}\qquad \C =  egin{pmatrix} \varepsilon & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, each of which differs from \J_2(0) by a matrix of 2-norm \varepsilon. Hence explain why the constant in @cor-eigenvalues-continuous cannot depend on 
orm{\B - \A} alone. For \B: p_{\B}(x) = x^2 - \varepsilon by @exm-jordan-block-perturbation with k = 2, so the eigenvalues are \pm 10^{-4}. For \C: the matrix is upper triangular, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries \varepsilon = 10^{-8} and 0 (@thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form (b)). Both perturbations have 2-norm \varepsilon = 10^{-8}, since each is \varepsilon times a single matrix unit. The eigenvalues of \B have moved 10^{-4} from \spec(\J_2(0)) = \{0\}, those of \C only 10^{-8}: a factor of 10^{4} between two perturbations of exactly the same size. So the movement is not a function of 
orm{\E}, and the \delta of @cor-eigenvalues-continuous cannot be computed from \varepsilon and n alone. [B2: A diagonalizable neighbor, explicitly] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} and let \varepsilon > 0. 1. Show that \A is not diagonalizable. 2. Exhibit a diagonalizable \A' with 
orm{\A - \A'}_2 < \varepsilon, and say which theorem certifies that your \A' is diagonalizable. 3. What are the eigenvalues of your \A', and how far have they moved? (a) The only eigenvalue is 2, with algebraic multiplicity 2 (@thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form (b)). But \A - 2\I =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} has rank 1, so g_{\A}(2) = 1 < 2 = a_{\A}(2) and \A is not diagonalizable by @thm-diagonalization (e). (b) Take \delta with 0 < \delta < \varepsilon and \A' =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 0 & 2 + \delta\end{psmallmatrix}. It is upper triangular with distinct diagonal entries 2 and 2 + \delta, hence has two distinct eigenvalues (@thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form (b)) and is diagonalizable by @cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable. And \A - \A' = -\delta\E_{22}, so 
orm{\A - \A'}_2 = \delta < \varepsilon by @thm-operator-norm-formulas (c). (c) They are 2 and 2 + \delta. One eigenvalue has not moved and the other has moved \delta, which is exactly 
orm{\A - \A'}_2: here the movement is Lipschitz with constant 1. The failure in @exm-jordan-block-perturbation needed a perturbation below the diagonal, which is the direction a triangular form cannot absorb. [B3: The determinant and the trace, by density] Let \A, \B \in M_n(
C). Use @cor-identity-by-density to prove that 	r(\A\B) = 	r(\B\A) — after first checking that the map in question satisfies the hypothesis of that corollary — and then explain why this is a bad way to prove it. Fix \B and put \Phi(\A) = 	r(\A\B) - 	r(\B\A), a 1 	imes 1 matrix whose single entry is \sum_{i,j}(a_{ij}b_{ji} - b_{ij}a_{ji}), a polynomial in the entries of \A; so the hypothesis of @cor-identity-by-density holds. Let \A = \P\D\P^{-1} be diagonalizable, \D = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n), and put \X = \P^{-1}\B\P. By @thm-trace-similarity-invariant, similar matrices have equal traces, and \A\B = \P(\D\X)\P^{-1} while \B\A = \P(\X\D)\P^{-1}, so 	r(\A\B) = 	r(\D\X) and 	r(\B\A) = 	r(\X\D). For a diagonal \D both of those are \sum_i d_ix_{ii}, by inspection of the diagonal entries of the two products. Hence \Phi(\A) = \O for every diagonalizable \A, and @cor-identity-by-density extends it to every \A. It is a bad way to prove it because the identity is a two-line computation from the definition, 	r(\A\B) = \sum_{i,j}a_{ij}b_{ji} = 	r(\B\A), valid over every field; the density argument needs 
C, an imported theorem, and two corollaries, and delivers less. A density argument earns its keep only when the diagonalizable case is genuinely easier, as in @exm-cayley-hamilton-by-density. C. Going deeper [C1: How close to singular a nearby eigenvalue forces you to be] Let \A \in M_n(
C), let 
orm{\cdot} be an operator norm on M_n(
C) (@def-operator-norm), and let \E \in M_n(
C) with \E 
eq \O. 1. Suppose \mu is an eigenvalue of \A + \E and \mu 
otin \spec(\A). Prove that 
orm{(\A - \mu\I)^{-1}} \ge  rac{1}{
orm{\E}} . 2. Deduce that if 
orm{(\A - z\I)^{-1}} \le M for every z with \lvert z - \lambdavert = r, then no eigenvalue of \A + \E lies on that circle as soon as 
orm{\E} < 1/M. Hint: for (a), factor \A + \E - \mu\I and use @thm-neumann-series. (a) Since \mu 
otin \spec(\A), the matrix \A - \mu\I is invertible (@thm-eigenvalue-characterizations). Write \A + \E - \mu\I = (\A - \mu\I) igl(\I + (\A - \mu\I)^{-1}\E igr) . The left side is singular, because \mu is an eigenvalue of \A + \E. The first factor on the right is invertible, so the second factor is singular: a product with an invertible left factor is invertible as soon as the right factor is. Put \X = -(\A - \mu\I)^{-1}\E, so \I - \X is singular. By @thm-neumann-series, 
orm{\X} < 1 would make \I - \X invertible; hence 
orm{\X} \ge 1. Submultiplicativity (@thm-operator-norm-properties) gives 1 \le 
orm{\X} \le 
orm{(\A - \mu\I)^{-1}}\,
orm{\E}, and dividing by 
orm{\E} > 0 gives the claim. (b) Suppose \mu is an eigenvalue of \A + \E with \lvert \mu - \lambda vert = r. Then 
orm{(\A - \mu\I)^{-1}} \le M by hypothesis, and in particular \A - \mu\I is invertible, so \mu 
otin \spec(\A) and part (a) applies: M \ge 1/
orm{\E}, that is 
orm{\E} \ge 1/M. Contrapositively, 
orm{\E} < 1/M leaves no eigenvalue of \A + \E on the circle. [C2: Density of the invertible matrices, and \A\B versus \B\A] 1. Prove that for every \A \in M_n(
C) and every \varepsilon > 0 there is an invertible \A' with 
orm{\A - \A'} < \varepsilon, in any norm. Hint: consider \A - t\I. 2. Prove a version of @cor-identity-by-density with “invertible” in place of “diagonalizable”. 3. Hence give a second proof that p_{\A\B} = p_{\B\A} for all \A, \B \in M_n(
C), a statement first proved in @thm-ab-ba-eigenvalues (b). (a) The matrix \A - t\I is singular exactly when t \in \spec(\A) (@thm-eigenvalue-characterizations), and \spec(\A) has at most n elements. Let N_{\infty} and C be as in the proof of @cor-diagonalizable-dense-again, so 
orm{\M} \le C\,N_{\infty}(\M). Choose t 
e 0 with \lvert t vert < \varepsilon/C and t 
otin \spec(\A), possible because the disc of radius \varepsilon/C is infinite and only finitely many of its points are forbidden. Then \A' = \A - t\I is invertible and N_{\infty}(\A - \A') = \lvert t vert, so 
orm{\A - \A'} < \varepsilon. (b) Verbatim the proof of @cor-identity-by-density, with the sequence of diagonalizable matrices replaced by the sequence of invertible matrices supplied by (a) with \varepsilon = 1/k. (c) Fix \B and set \Phi(\A) =  igl(c_0(\A\B) - c_0(\B\A), \dots, c_{n-1}(\A\B) - c_{n-1}(\B\A) igr), a row of n entries. Each entry of \A\B and of \B\A is a polynomial in the entries of \A, and each c_j is a polynomial in the entries of its argument, so \Phi satisfies the hypothesis of (b). For invertible \A we have \B\A = \A^{-1}(\A\B)\A, so \A\B and \B\A are similar and p_{\A\B} = p_{\B\A} by @thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant; that is exactly \Phi(\A) = \O, and it is @exr-characteristic-polynomial-b3 (a). By (b), \Phi(\A) = \O for every \A, and two monic polynomials of degree n with the same lower coefficients are equal. [C3: Distinct eigenvalues is an open condition] Let \A \in M_n(
C) have n distinct eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, and let 
orm{\cdot} be a norm on M_n(
C). 1. Prove that there is \delta > 0 such that every \B with 
orm{\B - \A} < \delta also has n distinct eigenvalues, and is therefore diagonalizable. 2. Deduce that the set of matrices in M_n(
C) with a repeated eigenvalue contains no ball, that is, that its complement is dense. 3. Is the set of diagonalizable matrices open? Justify your answer. (a) Put 2\varepsilon = \min_{i 
e j}\lvert \lambda_i - \lambda_j vert, which is positive because the \lambda_i are distinct and there are finitely many pairs. Let \delta be the number that @cor-eigenvalues-continuous supplies for this \varepsilon. If 
orm{\B - \A} < \delta, number the eigenvalues of \B so that \lvert \mu_i - \lambda_i vert < \varepsilon for every i. For i 
e j, @thm-complex-triangle-inequality gives \lvert \mu_i - \mu_j vert \ge \lvert \lambda_i - \lambda_j vert - \lvert \mu_i - \lambda_i vert - \lvert \mu_j - \lambda_j vert > 2\varepsilon - \varepsilon - \varepsilon = 0 , so the \mu_i are pairwise distinct. There are n of them, so \B is diagonalizable by @cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable. (b) Let \A be arbitrary and \varepsilon > 0. By @exr-schur-triangularization-c3 (a) there is \A' with n distinct eigenvalues and \lvert a_{ij} - a'_{ij}vert < \varepsilon/C for all i, j, with C as in the proof of @cor-diagonalizable-dense-again; hence 
orm{\A - \A'} < \varepsilon. So every ball meets the set of matrices with n distinct eigenvalues, and no ball is contained in its complement. (c) No. The zero matrix is diagonalizable, and in M_2(
C) every ball around it contains \varepsilon\J_2(0), whose only eigenvalue is 0, with eigenspace of dimension 1 and algebraic multiplicity 2; so it is not diagonalizable by @thm-diagonalization (e). Dense (@cor-diagonalizable-dense-again) and open are independent properties, and the diagonalizable matrices are the first without being the second.

title: 16.8 How Wrong Can the Answer Be
Variational Principles and Interlacing
content:
Variational Principles and Interlacing Since Chapter 13 the book has written \lambda_1(\A) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(\A) for the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix without ever saying what the middle ones are. The two at the ends have an answer. Chapter 11 observed that \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} is real for a self-adjoint operator, and Chapter 13 §05 turned that into @lem-extreme-eigenvalues-quadratic-form: on the unit sphere, \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} runs from \lambda_n(\A) up to \lambda_1(\A), and both ends are attained at eigenvectors. Everything between the ends was left blank, twice and deliberately. Chapter 13 §05 said it in one sentence: the intermediate eigenvalues “have no description as a plain maximum over the whole unit sphere”. Chapter 13 §13 said where the blank would be filled: “Chapter 17 characterizes the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix as maxima and minima of \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} — at which point the test becomes the theory.” This is that chapter, and the device that fills the blank is a min–max. One maximum over the unit sphere is not enough information to see \lambda_2; a maximum over a subspace, followed by a minimum over all subspaces of the right dimension, is exactly enough. That is the Courant–Fischer theorem, and its proof is one dimension count repeated: two subspaces of F^n whose dimensions add to more than n must share a nonzero vector. Once every eigenvalue is a maximum and a minimum of a quantity that does not mention an eigenvector, eigenvalues of different matrices become comparable, and the rest of the chapter is the harvest. How far the eigenvalues move when the matrix moves (Weyl). How they move when a row and its column are deleted, or a rank-one matrix is added (Cauchy interlacing, and the secular equation). What sums of the largest eigenvalues optimize (Poincaré, Ky Fan), and what arbitrary index sets do (Wielandt, Lidskii). What the diagonal of a Hermitian matrix can be, given its spectrum (Schur). The same theory for singular values, which finally proves the approximation theorem Chapter 13 §11 could only state. Inertia, re-proved without a basis and then made additive across a Schur complement. And a first look at which scalar functions respect the Loewner order. Every matrix whose eigenvalues are indexed in this chapter is Hermitian, and the field is 
R or 
C. This is not a convenience. The index i in \lambda_i(\A) presupposes that the eigenvalues are real and can be sorted, which is @thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues, and every eigenvalue inequality below is false without it — §04 exhibits a non-Hermitian matrix with a 1 	imes 1 principal submatrix lying outside the convex hull of the whole matrix’s spectrum. Each section states the hypothesis once and keeps it. Eigenvalues are indexed decreasingly, \lambda_1(\A) \ge \lambda_2(\A) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(\A), repeated according to multiplicity, as Chapter 13 §05 fixed it. Many sources index the min–max theorem the other way, and the two statements differ by i \leftrightarrow n+1-i; §02 gives the increasing form once, as a remark, so that a reader who meets it elsewhere is not lost. The analysis this chapter imports None that is new. Chapter 16 named everything it borrowed from analysis in a numbered list (A1)–(A6) in its introduction, and this chapter uses that list and nothing else, citing an item by the same name at the point of use — “by the extreme value theorem, fact (A4) of Chapter 16’s introduction”. Compactness of the unit sphere (A3) and the extreme value theorem (A4) are the two that a reader will expect to see, since a min–max is an optimization and optimizations need their extrema to exist. It is worth saying in advance that the expectation is not always met. In §§01–02, where the maxima and minima are first written down, no analytic fact is invoked: the spectral theorem is already available, and it hands over a maximizer explicitly, so the extreme value theorem is never called on to prove that one exists. That is not the same as saying no analysis lies underneath. The spectral theorem rests on the fundamental theorem of algebra, and Chapter 6 §05 proves that with the extreme value theorem on a closed disc; the analysis was paid for there, once, and is not paid again here. Chapter 12 §02 avoided that theorem on purpose and said so; §§01–02 below return to the remark and settle the account. Where a later section does need an item of the list, it names it. Nothing is added to the list. What you need - Chapter 0 §09 — the trace and its cyclic invariance, which §§05 and 06 compute with: @thm-trace-properties. - Chapter 1 §07 — the dimension formula \dim(U + W) = \dim U + \dim W - \dim(U \cap W), @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim. It is the engine of every min–max proof in the chapter, and §02 packages it as a lemma. - Chapter 3 §04 and §05 — permutation matrices, which §08 uses to put a spectrum in order, and Rank–Nullity for matrices, which §09 counts singular values with: @def-permutation-matrix, @lem-permutation-matrices, @thm-rank-nullity-matrix. - Chapter 2 — the coordinate isomorphism and what it preserves, and Rank–Nullity, which §§07 and 10 count with: @cor-coordinate-isomorphism, @thm-isomorphism-preserves-bases, @thm-rank-nullity. - Chapter 4 — the matrix of a map read through coordinates, which is how §02 passes between an operator and its matrix: @thm-matrix-of-map-coordinates. - Chapter 6 §01 — one fact, in §04: a nonzero polynomial of degree at most n has at most n roots, which is how the bordered-determinant identity passes from all but finitely many scalars to every scalar: @cor-root-bound-general. - Chapter 7 and Chapter 8 — principal submatrices (@def-submatrix-minor) and Schur complements: @def-schur-complement, @thm-schur-determinant, @thm-block-ldu, @cor-sherman-morrison. §§04, 05, and 10 lean on them. - Chapter 9 — the trace and determinant as sum and product of the eigenvalues, @thm-trace-det-eigenvalues. - Chapter 11 — inner products, orthonormal bases, and the adjoint: @def-inner-product, @def-induced-norm, @thm-cauchy-schwarz, @thm-orthonormal-coordinates, @def-orthogonal-complement, @thm-orthogonal-decomposition, @cor-extend-orthonormal-basis, @def-self-adjoint, @thm-matrix-of-adjoint, @prp-self-adjoint-immediate. - Chapter 12 — the spectral theorems, in both the operator and the matrix form: @thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues, @thm-spectral-complex, @cor-spectral-complex-matrix, @thm-spectral-real, @cor-spectral-real-matrix, @cor-symmetric-rank-one-sum, and the functional calculus @def-function-of-normal-operator, @thm-functional-calculus-properties. - Chapter 13 — positivity, the Loewner order, and the singular value decomposition: @def-positive-semidefinite, @thm-psd-characterizations, @thm-pd-characterizations, @thm-psd-square-root, @def-loewner-order, @prp-loewner-partial-order, @lem-extreme-eigenvalues-quadratic-form, @thm-loewner-basic, @prp-square-root-monotone, @def-singular-values, @thm-svd, @thm-compact-svd, @def-truncated-svd, @lem-orthonormal-capture-bound, @thm-eckart-young; from §04 the generalized eigenvalues (@def-generalized-eigenvalue, @thm-generalized-eigenvalues-real), and from §06 Hadamard’s inequality and the block criterion (@thm-hadamard-inequality, @thm-block-psd-schur), each of which gets a second proof here. - Chapter 14 §§02, 05 — congruence (@def-congruent), inertia, and signature: @thm-sylvester-inertia, @def-signature, @thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues. This one is a connection rather than a prerequisite: §10 gives Sylvester’s law a second proof and reworks its examples, and no proof in the chapter cites Chapter 14 — one worked example and two exercises of §10 do. - Chapter 16 — the way a matrix is measured, and the questions left open: @def-operator-norm, @thm-operator-norm-properties, and @thm-operator-norm-formulas, whose part (c) is the formula 
orm{\A}_2 = \sigma_1(\A); then @def-spectral-radius, @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm, @def-condition-number, and the imported-analysis list of the Chapter 16 introduction. Roadmap - The Rayleigh quotient. R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) = \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}}/\inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} promoted from a test to an object: its range is exactly [\lambda_n, \lambda_1], its critical points on the unit sphere are exactly the unit eigenvectors, and the first description of \lambda_k — maximize after deflating by the top eigenvectors — is correct but circular. - The min–max theorem. Courant–Fischer: \lambda_k is a minimum over subspaces of a maximum over vectors, and equally a maximum over subspaces of a minimum. No eigenvector is named, so two matrices can now be compared eigenvalue by eigenvalue. - How far eigenvalues move. Weyl’s inequalities, and the Lipschitz bound \lvert\lambda_i(\A + \E) - \lambda_i(\A)vert \le 
orm{\E}_2 that Chapter 16 §07 promised. - Deleting a row and a column. Cauchy interlacing: the spectrum of a principal submatrix is caught between consecutive eigenvalues of the whole matrix. When the interlacing is strict, which settles a promise of Chapter 11: the zeros of consecutive orthogonal polynomials interlace strictly. And why none of it survives without symmetry. - Adding a rank-one matrix. Interlacing again, the secular equation that locates the new eigenvalues between the old, and the shifts that add up to 	au
orm{\cvec{v}}^2. - Subspaces and sums. Poincaré’s separation theorem, and Ky Fan’s: the sum of the k largest eigenvalues is a maximum of a trace over orthonormal k-frames, hence a convex function of the matrix. Chapter 13’s capture bound turns out to be one case of it. - Arbitrary index sets. The Wielandt min–max over a flag of subspaces, and Lidskii’s inequality. It contains Ky Fan’s subadditivity and the Weyl inequalities with one index at an end — but not all of Weyl’s, which is worth seeing. - The diagonal and the spectrum. Majorization; Schur’s theorem and Horn’s converse, which together say that the diagonals of the Hermitian matrices with a given spectrum are exactly the vectors that spectrum majorizes. - The same theory for singular values. The min–max for \sigma_k, perturbation with no hypothesis on the perturbation at all, the spectral-norm form of Eckart–Young, interlacing when a row or column is deleted, and the distance from an invertible matrix to the nearest singular one — which is what Chapter 16’s condition number was measuring all along. - Inertia, again and additively. A second proof of Sylvester’s law with no basis in it, now over 
C as well; how far a rank-r perturbation can move the inertia; and Haynsworth’s additivity across a Schur complement. - Which functions respect the order. Operator monotone and operator convex functions, why the square root behaves and the square does not, and a statement of the classification that Chapter 21 proves. Named moves - Count dimensions to force an intersection. Two subspaces of an n-dimensional space whose dimensions add to more than n meet in a nonzero vector. This one line proves Courant–Fischer and Weyl directly, and Cauchy interlacing and Poincaré through Courant–Fischer. It is the chapter’s single technique, and everything else is bookkeeping around it. - Prove a min–max by two inequalities of different characters. One direction exhibits a witness subspace — usually a span of eigenvectors — and computes on it. The other takes an arbitrary subspace and intersects it with a span of eigenvectors from the other end. Neither half resembles the other, and recognizing which half is which is most of the work in reading any proof below. - Apply the result to -\A. The two halves of Courant–Fischer, the two families of Weyl inequalities, and the top- and bottom-k trace theorems are each other’s images under \A \mapsto -\A, which reverses the order and sends \lambda_i to -\lambda_{n+1-i}. Deriving the second statement this way is a genuine argument, not a wave of the hand, and it is written out each time. - Compress, then interlace. Restricting the quadratic form to a subspace produces a smaller Hermitian matrix whose eigenvalues are trapped by the original’s. Deleting rows and columns, adding a rank-one matrix, and cutting a singular value decomposition short are all this move. - Perturb and compare, eigenvalue by eigenvalue. Chapter 16’s move, now applied one index at a time rather than to the spectrum as a whole. - Reduce singular values to eigenvalues. Either through \A^{*}\A, which is shortest, or through the Hermitian dilation, which is symmetric in \A and \A^{*}. Both appear, and each section says which it uses and why. - Majorize. When the right comparison is between sums of the largest entries rather than individual ones, compare the partial sums of the decreasing rearrangements. The diagonal of a Hermitian matrix against its spectrum (§08), and the Ky Fan and Lidskii sums (§§06–07), are all of this type.

title: 17.1 The Rayleigh Quotient
17.2 The Min–Max Theorem
17.3 How Far Eigenvalues Move
content:
How Far Eigenvalues Move Chapter 16 §07 asked what happens to the eigenvalues of a matrix when the matrix is nudged, and came back with a discouraging answer: they move continuously, and nothing better. @exm-jordan-block-perturbation exhibits a perturbation of size \varepsilon that moves every eigenvalue a distance \varepsilon^{1/k}, so no Lipschitz constant survives. That section also promised that the Hermitian case is different, and left the proof here. The reason the Hermitian case is different is now available. @thm-courant-fischer describes \lambda_k(\A) as an optimization over subspaces, and an optimization over subspaces reacts to a change in \A the way any optimization reacts to a change in the objective: by at most the change in the objective. Turning that sentence into inequalities is the business of this section, and the inequalities are sharper than the sentence suggests, because the index may be shifted as well. Throughout this section the field is 
R or 
C, and every matrix whose eigenvalues are written down is Hermitian, that is, \A^{*} = \A with \A \in M_n(F) and n \ge 1. Its eigenvalues are real and are always indexed decreasingly, \lambda_1(\A) \ge \lambda_2(\A) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(\A), as they have been since Chapter 13. Sums of Hermitian matrices are Hermitian, so \A + \B is again a matrix this section may write \lambda_i of. Two small facts about eigenvalue lists One small fact is used in every proof below, and it is the reason the index bookkeeping works out. If a vector lies in the span of the bottom eigenvectors of \A, its Rayleigh quotient cannot exceed the largest eigenvalue in that span; if it lies in the span of the top ones, the quotient cannot fall below the smallest eigenvalue there. [The Quotient on a Span of Eigenvectors] Let \A \in M_n(F) be Hermitian and let (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_n) be an orthonormal basis of F^n with \A\cvec{u}_p = \lambda_p(\A)\cvec{u}_p for every p. Fix i with 1 \le i \le n. 1. If \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0} lies in \Span\{\cvec{u}_i, \cvec{u}_{i+1}, \dots, \cvec{u}_n\}, then R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) \le \lambda_i(\A). 2. If \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0} lies in \Span\{\cvec{u}_1, \cvec{u}_2, \dots, \cvec{u}_i\}, then R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) \ge \lambda_i(\A). Such a basis exists by the spectral theorem: @cor-spectral-complex-matrix over 
C, where a Hermitian matrix is normal and its eigenvalues may be listed in any prescribed order, and @cor-spectral-real-matrix over 
R, where Hermitian means symmetric. (a) Write \cvec{x} = \sum_{p \ge i}c_p\cvec{u}_p, with the c_p not all zero. Since the \cvec{u}_p are orthonormal,  egin{aligned} \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} &= \Bigl\langle \sum_{p \ge i}c_p\lambda_p(\A)\cvec{u}_p,\ \sum_{q \ge i}c_q\cvec{u}_q\Bigrangle = \sum_{p \ge i}\lambda_p(\A)\lvert c_pvert^2 , \ 
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 &= \sum_{p \ge i}\lvert c_pvert^2 . \end{aligned} Every index in these sums satisfies p \ge i, so \lambda_p(\A) \le \lambda_i(\A) by the decreasing indexing, and therefore \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} \le \lambda_i(\A)
orm{\cvec{x}}^2. Since \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0} we have 
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 > 0 and may divide, which gives R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) \le \lambda_i(\A) by @def-rayleigh-quotient. (b) The same computation with \cvec{x} = \sum_{p \le i}c_p\cvec{u}_p gives \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = \sum_{p \le i}\lambda_p(\A)\lvert c_pvert^2, and now every index satisfies p \le i, so \lambda_p(\A) \ge \lambda_i(\A) and the inequality reverses. This proves the lemma. The two halves are the two ways of using an eigenvector span: (a) caps a quotient from above, (b) props it up from below. The proof of Weyl’s inequalities needs only (a), applied to a single vector for two different matrices at once; (b) is the form in which the same fact enters the witness half of a min–max argument. A second small fact converts statements about the top of an eigenvalue list into statements about the bottom. Negating a matrix negates its eigenvalues, and negation reverses the order of real numbers. [Negation Reverses the List] Let \A \in M_n(F) be Hermitian. Then -\A is Hermitian and \lambda_p(-\A) = -\lambda_{n+1-p}(\A) \qquad (1 \le p \le n) . (-\A)^{*} = -\A^{*} = -\A, so -\A is Hermitian. By the spectral theorem quoted in the proof of @lem-rayleigh-on-eigenspan, \A = \U\D\U^{*} with \D = \diag(\lambda_1(\A), \dots, \lambda_n(\A)) and \U unitary, whence -\A = \U(-\D)\U^{*}. So the eigenvalue list of -\A, with multiplicity, is -\lambda_1(\A), \dots, -\lambda_n(\A). Multiplying by -1 reverses the order of real numbers, so listing these decreasingly gives -\lambda_n(\A) \ \ge\ -\lambda_{n-1}(\A) \ \ge\ \dots \ \ge\ -\lambda_1(\A) , whose p-th entry is -\lambda_{n+1-p}(\A). This proves the lemma. The two families of Weyl inequalities Here is the question. Given the eigenvalues of \A and the eigenvalues of \B, separately, what can be said about the eigenvalues of \A + \B? Nothing exact: \diag(1,0) and \diag(0,1) have the same eigenvalue list as \diag(1,0) and \diag(1,0), while the two sums \I and \diag(2,0) do not. But a great deal inexactly, and the shape of the answer is dictated by the index arithmetic. [Weyl’s Inequalities] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) be Hermitian and let 1 \le i, j \le n. 1. If i + j - 1 \le n, then \lambda_{i+j-1}(\A + \B) \ \le\ \lambda_i(\A) + \lambda_j(\B) . 2. If i + j - n \ge 1, then \lambda_{i+j-n}(\A + \B) \ \ge\ \lambda_i(\A) + \lambda_j(\B) . For (a), read \lambda_{i+j-1}(\A+\B) through the max–min half of @thm-courant-fischer: it is the best guaranteed value of R_{\A+\B} on a subspace of dimension i+j-1. So take an arbitrary such subspace W and find one bad vector inside it — a vector on which R_{\A} is capped by \lambda_i(\A) and R_{\B} is capped by \lambda_j(\B) simultaneously. The span of the bottom n-i+1 eigenvectors of \A is a subspace on which R_{\A} is capped by \lambda_i(\A), and the span of the bottom n-j+1 eigenvectors of \B is one on which R_{\B} is capped by \lambda_j(\B). (The set of all vectors capped by \lambda_i(\A) is larger and is not a subspace; the spans are what the dimension count can use.) Three subspaces must meet, and the dimensions have been chosen so that they do — twice, by @lem-subspace-intersection. Since R_{\A+\B} = R_{\A} + R_{\B}, that one vector finishes the argument. Part (b) is not a new proof. Negating a Hermitian matrix reverses its eigenvalue list (@lem-eigenvalues-of-negation), so (a) applied to -\A and -\B at the reflected indices n+1-i and n+1-j says exactly (b), once every index is translated back. (a) Put k = i + j - 1, so 1 \le k \le n. By the spectral theorem choose an orthonormal basis (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_n) of eigenvectors of \A with \A\cvec{u}_p = \lambda_p(\A)\cvec{u}_p, and an orthonormal basis (\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n) of eigenvectors of \B with \B\cvec{v}_q = \lambda_q(\B)\cvec{v}_q. Set U = \Span\{\cvec{u}_i, \dots, \cvec{u}_n\}, \qquad V = \Span\{\cvec{v}_j, \dots, \cvec{v}_n\} , so that \dim U = n - i + 1 and \dim V = n - j + 1, the two lists being independent as parts of a basis. Let W \le F^n be any subspace with \dim W = k. Then \dim W + \dim U = (i + j - 1) + (n - i + 1) = n + j > n , since j \ge 1, so W \cap U 
e \{\cvec{0}\} by @lem-subspace-intersection. More than that is needed, namely how large W \cap U is, and the dimension formula @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim supplies it: \dim(W \cap U) = \dim W + \dim U - \dim(W + U) \ \ge\ (n + j) - n = j , because W + U is a subspace of F^n. Therefore \dim(W \cap U) + \dim V \ \ge\ j + (n - j + 1) = n + 1 > n , and a second application of @lem-subspace-intersection, to the subspaces W \cap U and V, produces a vector \cvec{x} \in W \cap U \cap V, \qquad \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0} . Now evaluate. Since \cvec{x} \in U, part (a) of @lem-rayleigh-on-eigenspan gives R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) \le \lambda_i(\A); since \cvec{x} \in V, the same part applied to \B gives R_{\B}(\cvec{x}) \le \lambda_j(\B). The inner product is additive in its first slot, so \inner{(\A+\B)\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} + \inner{\B\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} and hence R_{\A+\B}(\cvec{x}) = R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) + R_{\B}(\cvec{x}). Since \cvec{x} is a nonzero vector of W, \min_{\cvec{0} 
e \cvec{y} \in W} R_{\A+\B}(\cvec{y}) \ \le\ R_{\A+\B}(\cvec{x}) \ \le\ \lambda_i(\A) + \lambda_j(\B) . The subspace W of dimension k was arbitrary, so the maximum of the left-hand side over all such W obeys the same bound; and that maximum is \lambda_k(\A+\B) by the max–min half of @thm-courant-fischer. This proves (a). (b) Suppose i + j - n \ge 1 and set i' = n + 1 - i, \qquad j' = n + 1 - j , both of which lie in \{1, \dots, n\}. Then i' + j' - 1 = 2n + 1 - i - j \le n precisely because i + j - n \ge 1, so part (a) applies to the Hermitian matrices -\A and -\B at the indices i', j': \lambda_{i'+j'-1}(-\A - \B) \ \le\ \lambda_{i'}(-\A) + \lambda_{j'}(-\B) . Translate each term with @lem-eigenvalues-of-negation. On the right, \lambda_{i'}(-\A) = -\lambda_{n+1-i'}(\A) = -\lambda_i(\A), and likewise \lambda_{j'}(-\B) = -\lambda_j(\B). On the left, -\A-\B = -(\A+\B) with \A + \B Hermitian, and i'+j'-1 = 2n+1-i-j, so \lambda_{i'+j'-1} igl(-(\A+\B) igr) = -\lambda_{n+1-(2n+1-i-j)}(\A+\B) = -\lambda_{i+j-n}(\A+\B) . The displayed inequality therefore reads -\lambda_{i+j-n}(\A+\B) \le -\lambda_i(\A) - \lambda_j(\B). Multiplying by -1 reverses it and gives (b). This proves the theorem. Two remarks on the bookkeeping, because it is the whole content. First, the index on the left is not i or j but i + j - 1, so a fixed eigenvalue \lambda_k(\A+\B) receives k upper bounds from (a), one for each way of splitting k = i + j - 1, and the best of them is their minimum. Second, (a) only ever bounds from above and (b) only from below. To trap one eigenvalue \lambda_i(\A+\B) from both sides with the index of \A unchanged, take j = 1 in (a) and j = n in (b); that is the next corollary. Take i = j = 1 in (a) and i = j = n in (b). What do the two inequalities say, and which earlier result are they? They say \lambda_1(\A+\B) \le \lambda_1(\A) + \lambda_1(\B) and \lambda_n(\A+\B) \ge \lambda_n(\A) + \lambda_n(\B). For i = j = n the index on the left of (b) is n + n - n = n, as required. These are the statements that the largest eigenvalue is subadditive and the smallest superadditive, which one can also read straight off @lem-extreme-eigenvalues-quadratic-form: \inner{(\A+\B)\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} + \inner{\B\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} \le \lambda_1(\A) + \lambda_1(\B) for every unit \cvec{x}. Weyl’s inequalities are what happens when this easy observation is run at every index instead of only at the two ends. The eigenvalues are not subadditive index by index. It is tempting to read Weyl as \lambda_i(\A+\B) \le \lambda_i(\A) + \lambda_i(\B), and that statement is false. Take \A = \diag(1, 0) and \B = \diag(0, 1), so that \lambda(\A) = \lambda(\B) = (1, 0) and \A + \B = \I_2 with \lambda(\A+\B) = (1, 1). At i = 2 the proposed inequality reads 1 \le 0 + 0. The reverse reading \lambda_i(\A+\B) \ge \lambda_i(\A) + \lambda_i(\B) fails on the same pair at i = 1, where it reads 1 \ge 2. Only the shifted indices i+j-1 and i+j-n are correct. Here is the theorem in full on one pair of matrices, so that the index arithmetic can be seen doing its work. [Both families on one pair] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \ 1 & 1 & 2 \ 2 & 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 & 0 \ 2 & 3 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . Find the eigenvalues of \A, \B, and \A + \B, and check every inequality of @thm-weyl-inequalities. All three matrices are real symmetric. Their characteristic polynomials factor over 
Z:  egin{aligned} p_{\A}(x) &= x(x-4)(x+2), \ p_{\B}(x) &= x(x-5)(x-1), \ p_{\A+\B}(x) &= (x-8)(x-1)(x+1) , \end{aligned} so, in decreasing order, \lambda(\A) = (4, 0, -2), \qquad \lambda(\B) = (5, 1, 0), \qquad \lambda(\A+\B) = (8, 1, -1) . For \A one can see the list without computing: the rows (1,1,2) and (1,1,2) are equal, so ank \A = 2 and 0 is an eigenvalue; 	r\A = 2 and 	r(\A^2) = 20 then force the other two to be 4 and -2. With n = 3, family (a) applies when i + j \le 4 and family (b) when i + j \ge 4. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (i,j) family (a): \lambda_{i+j-1}(\A+\B) \le \lambda_i(\A) + \lambda_j(\B) ----------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------- (1,1) 8 \le 4 + 5 = 9 (1,2) 1 \le 4 + 1 = 5 (2,1) 1 \le 0 + 5 = 5 (1,3) -1 \le 4 + 0 = 4 (2,2) -1 \le 0 + 1 = 1 (3,1) -1 \le -2 + 5 = 3 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (i,j) family (b): \lambda_{i+j-3}(\A+\B) \ge \lambda_i(\A) + \lambda_j(\B) ----------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------- (1,3) 8 \ge 4 + 0 = 4 (3,1) 8 \ge -2 + 5 = 3 (2,2) 8 \ge 0 + 1 = 1 (2,3) 1 \ge 0 + 0 = 0 (3,2) 1 \ge -2 + 1 = -1 (3,3) -1 \ge -2 + 0 = -2 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Every inequality holds, and every one of them is strict. At (1,1) one can see why. Equality there would mean a unit \cvec{x} with R_{\A+\B}(\cvec{x}) = \lambda_1(\A) + \lambda_1(\B); since R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) \le \lambda_1(\A) and R_{\B}(\cvec{x}) \le \lambda_1(\B) by @lem-rayleigh-on-eigenspan (a) at i = 1, both would have to be equalities, and the computation in that proof shows that equality in \sum_p \lambda_p\lvert c_pvert^2 \le \lambda_1\sum_p \lvert c_pvert^2 forces c_p = 0 at every p with \lambda_p < \lambda_1. So \cvec{x} would lie in the \lambda_1-eigenspace of \A and in that of \B. Those are the lines through (1,1,1) and through (1,1,0) — as \A(1,1,1) = 4(1,1,1) and \B(1,1,0) = 5(1,1,0), and both eigenvalues are simple — and two distinct lines meet only at \cvec{0}. Perturbing one matrix Setting j = 1 in family (a) and j = n in family (b) leaves the index on the left equal to i. That is the case in which Weyl becomes a statement about perturbation: one matrix, moved. [Perturbation, Two-Sided] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) be Hermitian. Then for every i, \lambda_i(\A) + \lambda_n(\B) \ \le\ \lambda_i(\A + \B) \ \le\ \lambda_i(\A) + \lambda_1(\B) . For the upper bound take j = 1 in @thm-weyl-inequalities (a): the hypothesis i + 1 - 1 = i \le n holds, and the conclusion is \lambda_i(\A+\B) \le \lambda_i(\A) + \lambda_1(\B). For the lower bound take j = n in @thm-weyl-inequalities (b): the hypothesis i + n - n = i \ge 1 holds, and the conclusion is \lambda_i(\A+\B) \ge \lambda_i(\A) + \lambda_n(\B). This proves the corollary. In words: adding \B shifts each eigenvalue of \A, in order, by an amount trapped between the smallest and the largest eigenvalue of \B. Taking \B \succeq \O, so that \lambda_n(\B) \ge 0 by @thm-psd-characterizations (b), the lower bound becomes \lambda_i(\A+\B) \ge \lambda_i(\A) — which is @cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone again, now as a special case of Weyl’s inequalities. To turn @cor-weyl-monotone into a bound of the kind Chapter 16 wanted, the two numbers \lambda_1(\B) and \lambda_n(\B) must be replaced by one, and the right one is a norm. [The Spectral Norm of a Hermitian Matrix] Let \E \in M_n(F) be Hermitian. Then 
orm{\E}_2 = \max_{1 \le i \le n}\lvert \lambda_i(\E)vert = \max igl(\lambda_1(\E),\ -\lambda_n(\E) igr) . By the spectral theorem, \E = \U\D\U^{*} with \U unitary and \D = \diag(\lambda_1(\E), \dots, \lambda_n(\E)) real. Then \E^{*}\E = \E^2 = \U\D^2\U^{*} , so the eigenvalues of \E^{*}\E are the numbers \lambda_i(\E)^2, and the singular values of \E, which are their nonnegative square roots listed decreasingly (@def-singular-values), are the numbers \lvert\lambda_i(\E)vert listed decreasingly. Hence \sigma_1(\E) = \max_i \lvert\lambda_i(\E)vert, and 
orm{\E}_2 = \sigma_1(\E) by @thm-operator-norm-formulas (c). For the second equality, \lambda_n(\E) \le \lambda_i(\E) \le \lambda_1(\E) for all i, so \lvert\lambda_i(\E)vert \le \max(\lvert\lambda_1(\E)vert, \lvert\lambda_n(\E)vert), so the maximum is attained at one end of the list. Now \lambda_1(\E) \le \lvert\lambda_1(\E)vert and -\lambda_n(\E) \le \lvert\lambda_n(\E)vert, which gives one inequality between the two expressions. Conversely, \lvert\lambda_1(\E)vert is either \lambda_1(\E) or -\lambda_1(\E) \le -\lambda_n(\E), and \lvert\lambda_n(\E)vert is either -\lambda_n(\E) or \lambda_n(\E) \le \lambda_1(\E); in every case it is at most \max(\lambda_1(\E), -\lambda_n(\E)). This proves the lemma. [Hermitian Eigenvalues Are 1-Lipschitz] Let \A, \E \in M_n(F) be Hermitian. Then \lvert \lambda_i(\A + \E) - \lambda_i(\A)vert \ \le\ 
orm{\E}_2 \qquad 	ext{for every } i = 1, \dots, n . By @cor-weyl-monotone applied with \B = \E, \lambda_n(\E) \ \le\ \lambda_i(\A+\E) - \lambda_i(\A) \ \le\ \lambda_1(\E) . By @lem-hermitian-spectral-norm, \lambda_1(\E) \le 
orm{\E}_2 and -\lambda_n(\E) \le 
orm{\E}_2, that is, -
orm{\E}_2 \le \lambda_n(\E). So the difference lies in [-
orm{\E}_2, 
orm{\E}_2], which is the assertion. This proves the corollary. This is the sentence Chapter 16 §07 promised: the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix move by at most 
orm{\E}_2 under a Hermitian perturbation. It is worth being precise about what it adds to @cor-eigenvalues-continuous, the continuity statement of that section, because the gain is not continuity — that was already had — but a constant. - @cor-eigenvalues-continuous says: for each \A and each \varepsilon > 0 there is a \delta > 0 such that every matrix within \delta of \A has eigenvalues that can be numbered to lie within \varepsilon of those of \A. The \delta depends on \A, and @exm-jordan-block-perturbation shows that it must. - @cor-weyl-perturbation says, for Hermitian \A and Hermitian perturbations measured in 
orm{\cdot}_2: \delta = \varepsilon works, for every \A at once, and the numbering is simply the decreasing order. The movement is bounded by the perturbation itself, with Lipschitz constant 1. The constant does not depend on the size n of the matrices, it does not depend on how ill-conditioned \A is, and it does not depend on how close together the eigenvalues of \A are — three quantities that every reader of Chapter 16 has learned to expect in an error bound. It also cannot be improved: \E = t\I with t \in 
R gives \lambda_i(\A + t\I) = \lambda_i(\A) + t for every i, while 
orm{t\I}_2 = \lvert tvert, so the inequality is an equality at every index. Finally, the eigenvalues are matched by index: the i-th of \A + \E is compared with the i-th of \A, not with whichever eigenvalue of \A happens to be nearest, and no search for a good numbering is needed. [The Hermitian Eigenvalue Problem Is Perfectly Conditioned in Absolute Terms] Let \A, \E \in M_n(F) be Hermitian and write \lambda(\A) = (\lambda_1(\A), \dots, \lambda_n(\A)) for the decreasing eigenvalue list. Then 
orm{\lambda(\A + \E) - \lambda(\A)}_{\infty} \ \le\ 
orm{\E}_2 , and the constant 1 is the smallest one for which this holds. The \infty-norm of a vector is the largest modulus of its entries, so the left-hand side is \max_i\lvert\lambda_i(\A+\E) - \lambda_i(\A)vert, and the inequality is @cor-weyl-perturbation read over all i at once. For the last clause, \E = t\I with t > 0 makes both sides equal to t, so no constant below 1 can work. This proves the corollary. Chapter 16 §08 measured a linear system by \kappa(\A) = 
orm{\A}
orm{\A^{-1}} (@def-condition-number), the worst factor by which \A magnifies a relative error in the data. The corollary above is the corresponding statement for a different problem — not “solve \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}” but “report the eigenvalues of \A” — and the factor there is 1, in absolute rather than relative terms. The difference between absolute and relative matters here, and it is worth being exact. \A = \diag(10^{6}, 10^{-6}) is Hermitian with \kappa_2(\A) = 10^{12}, so solving with it is a delicate business, and yet its eigenvalues move by at most 
orm{\E}_2 under any Hermitian \E, exactly as those of every other Hermitian matrix do. Ill-conditioning of the linear system says nothing about the absolute conditioning of the eigenvalues. In relative terms the two numbers meet again. The Hermitian perturbation \E = -10^{-6}\,\cvec{e}_2\cvec{e}_2	p has relative size 
orm{\E}_2/
orm{\A}_2 = 10^{-12} and sends the eigenvalue 10^{-6} to 0, a relative change of 100\%: an amplification of exactly 10^{12} = \kappa_2(\A). In general, for an invertible Hermitian \A, @cor-weyl-perturbation bounds the relative change of the eigenvalue of smallest modulus by 
orm{\E}_2/\sigma_n(\A), which is \kappa_2(\A) times the relative size of \E, and a rank-one \E along its eigenvector attains it. So for Hermitian matrices, \kappa_2 is the relative condition number of the smallest eigenvalue. The contrast that makes the corollary worth having is with @exm-jordan-block-perturbation. There \A = \J_k(0) and \E = \varepsilon\E_{k1}, and the eigenvalues move a distance \varepsilon^{1/k} while 
orm{\E}_2 = \varepsilon, an amplification of \varepsilon^{-(k-1)/k} that is unbounded as \varepsilon 	o 0^{+}.
