e 0, dividing gives \M_k/\M_{k-1} = d_k/d_{k-1}. (b) Induct on k. For k = 1, \M_1 = (d_1) is a nonzero real scalar (real because \M is Hermitian), and \operatorname{In}(\M_1) is (1,0,0) or (0,1,0) according to the sign of d_1/d_0 = d_1. For the step, \M_{k-1} is invertible, so @thm-haynsworth applies to \M_k with \A = \M_{k-1}: \operatorname{In}(\M_k) = \operatorname{In}(\M_{k-1}) + \operatorname{In}(d_k/d_{k-1}) , and the last term is (1,0,0) or (0,1,0) according to the sign of the ratio, which is nonzero. Summing from k = 1 to n, \operatorname{In}(\M) = \operatorname{In}(\M_n) =  igl(\#\{k : d_k/d_{k-1} > 0\},\ \#\{k : d_k/d_{k-1} < 0\},\ 0 igr) , and d_k/d_{k-1} < 0 says exactly that d_{k-1} and d_k have opposite signs. (Taking n_- = 0 here recovers the leading-minor criterion of @thm-pd-characterizations: all d_k > 0 if and only if \M \succ \O.) (c) For \M =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \ 1 & 2 & 3 \ 2 & 3 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} the leading minors are d_1 = 1, d_2 = 2 - 1 = 1, and d_3 = -4, all nonzero, so (b) applies. The sequence d_0, d_1, d_2, d_3 = 1, 1, 1, -4 has exactly one sign change, at the last step. Hence n_- = 1, n_+ = 2, and \operatorname{In}(\M) = (2,1,0), agreeing with @exm-haynsworth-3x3 and with @exm-inertia-by-elimination.

title: 17.11 Which Functions Respect the Order
content:
Which Functions Respect the Order Chapter 13 §05 ended on two facts that sit awkwardly together. If \A \succeq \B \succeq \O, then \A^{1/2} \succeq \B^{1/2} (@prp-square-root-monotone); but \A^2 \succeq \B^2 can fail (@exm-loewner-not-monotone). For numbers, both t \mapsto t^{1/2} and t \mapsto t^2 are increasing on [0, \infty), and both preserve inequalities. This section names the property that separates them and proves it for every function the book can reach. It then compares that property with what §02’s min–max theorem already gives for every increasing function, and states without proof the classification that settles the question. Since this is the last section of the chapter, it ends by summing up the chapter’s moves and listing the promises the chapter has paid. Throughout, F = 
R or F = 
C, and every matrix whose eigenvalues are indexed is Hermitian, with eigenvalues \lambda_1(\A) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(\A) indexed decreasingly and repeated according to multiplicity. The letter I denotes an interval of real numbers (open, closed, or half-open, bounded or not). It is plain italic, and it is not the bold identity matrix \I. A function f \colon I 	o 
R is increasing when s \le t implies f(s) \le f(t); strictness is not required. Every result below holds for either choice of F, with the same proof. No analysis is used anywhere in this section except in the last part, which states a theorem without proving it. Functions of a Hermitian matrix Chapter 12 §08 already applies a function to a matrix, and nothing needs rebuilding. Let \A \in M_n(F) be Hermitian. The operator \cvec{x} \mapsto \A\cvec{x} on F^n has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors (@cor-spectral-complex-matrix, @cor-spectral-real-matrix), so it has a spectral resolution \A = \mu_1\P_1 + \dots + \mu_k\P_k with \mu_1, \dots, \mu_k the distinct eigenvalues and \P_j the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace of \mu_j (@def-spectral-resolution, @thm-spectral-resolution). For any function f defined on \spec(\A), @def-function-of-normal-operator sets f(\A) \coloneqq f(\mu_1)\P_1 + \dots + f(\mu_k)\P_k . In this section f is always defined on an interval I containing \spec(\A), and f(\A) is formed from the restriction of f to the spectrum: the values of f off the spectrum play no part. Four facts from @thm-functional-calculus-properties are used constantly. - Polynomials give the expected answer (part (a)): t \mapsto \alpha +  eta t gives \alpha\I +  eta\A, and t \mapsto t^2 gives \A^2. - Sums and products go through (part (b)): (f + g)(\A) = f(\A) + g(\A), (cf)(\A) = c\,f(\A), and (fg)(\A) = f(\A)g(\A). - Real-valued f gives a Hermitian f(\A) (part (c)). This is what lets f(\A) be compared with anything in the Loewner order. - The eigenvectors do not change (part (d)): f(\A) has the same orthonormal eigenbasis as \A. Two instances have names already. If 0 
otin \spec(\A), then t \mapsto 1/t gives \A^{-1}, as Chapter 12 §08 records right after @def-function-of-normal-operator. If \A \succeq \O, then t \mapsto t^{1/2} gives the positive square root \A^{1/2} of @thm-psd-square-root, which Chapter 13 §02 constructed in exactly this way. Operator monotone and operator convex functions Chapter 13 §05 introduced the Loewner order \A \succeq \B, meaning \A - \B \succeq \O (@def-loewner-order). With the functional calculus available, the natural question is which functions f carry \A \succeq \B to f(\A) \succeq f(\B). The obvious guess is “the increasing ones”, since that is the answer for numbers. It is wrong. The function t \mapsto t^2 is increasing on [0, \infty), and @exm-loewner-not-monotone gives Hermitian 2 	imes 2 matrices \A \succeq \B \succeq \O with \A^2 
ot\succeq \B^2. So the property we want is stronger than being increasing, and it needs its own name. A function is operator monotone when applying it to Hermitian matrices never breaks the Loewner order, at every size at once. Operator Monotone and Operator Convex Functions Let I \subseteq 
R be an interval and let f \colon I 	o 
R. 1. f is operator monotone on I if, for every size n \ge 1 and every pair of Hermitian matrices \A, \B \in M_n(F) whose spectra lie in I, \A \succeq \B \quad \Longrightarrow \quad f(\A) \succeq f(\B) . 2. f is operator convex on I if, for every size n \ge 1, every pair of Hermitian matrices \A, \B \in M_n(F) whose spectra lie in I, and every 	heta \in [0, 1], f igl(	heta\A + (1 - 	heta)\B igr) \preceq 	heta f(\A) + (1 - 	heta)f(\B) . It is operator concave on I if -f is operator convex on I. Here f(\A) is the matrix of @def-function-of-normal-operator. In words: the first condition takes any two Hermitian matrices of the same size with spectra inside the domain of f. If the first dominates the second, applying f must preserve that. The second condition is the matrix version of “the chord lies above the graph”. Both are infinitely many conditions, one for each size n. A function that passes the test for 2 	imes 2 matrices has not yet passed it for 3 	imes 3 ones. The clause “for every n” is why the notion is hard, and also why it is interesting. Everything in the definition makes sense. Since \spec(\A) \subseteq I, the matrix f(\A) is defined, and it is Hermitian because f is real-valued (@thm-functional-calculus-properties (c)). So f(\A) \succeq f(\B) is a statement about two Hermitian matrices, as @def-loewner-order requires. In (b) one more thing needs checking: the spectrum of \C = 	heta\A + (1-	heta)\B must lie in I, or f(\C) would not be defined. The matrix \C is Hermitian. Let \cvec{x} be a unit eigenvector of \C for the eigenvalue \mu. Then \mu = \inner{\C\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = 	heta\inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} + (1 - 	heta)\inner{\B\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} . By @lem-extreme-eigenvalues-quadratic-form, \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} lies in [\lambda_n(\A), \lambda_1(\A)]. That interval is contained in I, because its endpoints are eigenvalues of \A and I is an interval. Likewise \inner{\B\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} \in I. So \mu is a convex combination of two points of the interval I, and it therefore lies in I. The smallest size already says something, and the proof is three lines. [Operator Monotone Functions Are Increasing] If f is operator monotone on I, then f is increasing on I. Let s \le t in I, and take n = 1, \A = (t), \B = (s). These are Hermitian, their spectra \{t\} and \{s\} lie in I, and \A - \B = (t - s) \succeq \O. Hence f(\A) \succeq f(\B), and since f(\A) = (f(t)) and f(\B) = (f(s)), this says f(t) - f(s) \ge 0. This shows that f is increasing. The converse is false, and the failure is the reason this section exists. Increasing is not enough. “Increasing” is exactly the case n = 1 of the definition, and sizes n \ge 2 are where all the new content lies. The function t \mapsto t^2 is increasing on [0, \infty) and is not operator monotone there. The 2 	imes 2 matrices \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} and \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} of @exm-loewner-not-monotone satisfy \A \succeq \B \succeq \O, yet \A^2 - \B^2 has negative determinant. Chapter 13 §05 traced the failure to noncommutativity: the number proof factors a^2 - b^2 as (a - b)(a + b), and for matrices that factorization needs \A\B = \B\A. Is t \mapsto t^3 operator monotone on 
R when only n = 1 is tested? What does the answer tell you about n = 2? For n = 1 the condition says only that f is increasing, as the proof of @prp-operator-monotone-increasing shows, and t \mapsto t^3 is increasing on 
R. So it passes at n = 1. That tells us nothing about n = 2, where the test is genuinely new. In fact t \mapsto t^3 fails at n = 2 (exercise C3). The examples we can prove Four families are within reach, and the first is the simplest. It includes a degenerate case, the constant functions, which respect every order because they flatten everything to one matrix. [Increasing Affine Functions] Let \alpha,  eta \in 
R with  eta \ge 0. Then f(t) = \alpha +  eta t is operator monotone on 
R. Moreover, every affine function t \mapsto \alpha +  eta t, with  eta of either sign, is both operator convex and operator concave on 
R. By @thm-functional-calculus-properties (a), f(\A) = \alpha\I +  eta\A for every Hermitian \A. Let \A \succeq \B be Hermitian of the same size. Then f(\A) - f(\B) =  eta(\A - \B), and for every \cvec{x}, \inner{ eta(\A - \B)\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} =  eta\inner{(\A - \B)\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} \ \ge\ 0 , a product of two nonnegative numbers. Hence f(\A) \succeq f(\B). For the second statement, with \C = 	heta\A + (1-	heta)\B,  egin{aligned} f(\C) &= \alpha\I +  eta	heta\A +  eta(1-	heta)\B \ &= 	heta(\alpha\I +  eta\A) + (1-	heta)(\alpha\I +  eta\B) = 	heta f(\A) + (1-	heta)f(\B) , \end{aligned} so the inequality in @def-operator-monotone (b) holds with equality, for f and for -f alike. The second example is the one that behaves like the square root: t \mapsto -1/t. For numbers, a \ge b > 0 gives -1/a \ge -1/b because one may divide by the product ab. For matrices that division is unavailable, since \A and \B need not commute. Chapter 13 §05 already found the way round. [The Negative Reciprocal Is Operator Monotone] The function t \mapsto -1/t is operator monotone on (0, \infty). Explicitly: if \A, \B \in M_n(F) are Hermitian with \A \succeq \B \succ \O, then \A \succ \O and -\A^{-1} \ \succeq\ -\B^{-1}, \qquad	ext{that is,}\qquad \B^{-1} \succeq \A^{-1} . A congruence removes the noncommutativity. Conjugating by \B^{-1/2} turns \B into \I and \A into \C = \B^{-1/2}\A\B^{-1/2} \succeq \I. Now one of the two matrices is the identity, which commutes with everything, so the argument for numbers applies to the eigenvalues of \C: they are all \ge 1, so those of \C^{-1} are all \le 1. Undoing the congruence carries \I \succeq \C^{-1} back to \B^{-1} \succeq \A^{-1}. That is exactly the proof of @thm-loewner-basic (d), so the proposition is that clause read as a statement about the function t \mapsto -1/t. Let \A \succeq \B be Hermitian with spectra in (0, \infty). By @thm-pd-characterizations (b), a Hermitian matrix whose eigenvalues are all positive is positive definite, so \B \succ \O. By @thm-loewner-basic (d), \A \succ \O and \B^{-1} \succeq \A^{-1}. Put f(t) = -1/t. By @def-function-of-normal-operator and the instance t \mapsto 1/t recalled above, f(\A) = -\A^{-1} and f(\B) = -\B^{-1}. Hence f(\A) - f(\B) = \B^{-1} - \A^{-1} \ \succeq\ \O , which is the assertion. The size n was arbitrary, so f is operator monotone on (0, \infty). Two things make the whitening work, and they are worth separating. First, once one of the two matrices is \I, the comparison \C \succeq \I can be settled eigenvalue by eigenvalue, because \I commutes with everything. Second, inversion gets along with congruence: (\S^{*}\M\S)^{-1} = \S^{-1}\M^{-1}(\S^{-1})^{*} is again a congruence, and that is what carries the conclusion back from \C to \A. For a general f there is no such identity, since f(\S^{*}\M\S) is usually not a congruence of f(\M), so the argument does not simply transfer to other functions. To build more examples out of these, one needs to know which ways of combining functions preserve the property. [Combining Operator Monotone Functions] Let f and g be operator monotone on I. 1. For every c \ge 0 and every \alpha \in 
R, the functions f + g and \alpha + cf are operator monotone on I. 2. For every s \in 
R, the translate t \mapsto f(t + s) is operator monotone on the interval I - s = \{ t - s : t \in I \}. (a) Let \A \succeq \B be Hermitian of the same size with spectra in I. By @thm-functional-calculus-properties (b), (f + g)(\A) - (f + g)(\B) =  igl(f(\A) - f(\B) igr) +  igl(g(\A) - g(\B) igr). Both brackets are \succeq \O by hypothesis, and for every \cvec{x} the quadratic form of the sum is the sum of the two nonnegative quadratic forms. So the sum is \succeq \O by @def-positive-semidefinite. Likewise, using (b) and (a) of the same theorem, (\alpha + cf)(\A) - (\alpha + cf)(\B) = c igl(f(\A) - f(\B) igr), whose quadratic form is c \ge 0 times a nonnegative one. (b) Let g(t) = f(t + s) on I - s, and let \A be Hermitian with spectrum in I - s, with spectral resolution \A = \sum_j\mu_j\P_j. By @thm-spectral-resolution (c) and (d), \A + s\I = \sum_j (\mu_j + s)\P_j , and the numbers \mu_j + s are distinct. The \P_j are nonzero self-adjoint idempotents with \P_i\P_j = \O for i 
e j and \sum_j\P_j = \I (@thm-spectral-resolution (b), (c)). So by @thm-spectral-resolution-unique this is the spectral resolution of \A + s\I, whose spectrum \{\mu_j + s\} lies in I. By @def-function-of-normal-operator, applied to each side, f(\A + s\I) = \sum_j f(\mu_j + s)\P_j = g(\A) . Now if \A \succeq \B with spectra in I - s, then (\A + s\I) - (\B + s\I) = \A - \B \succeq \O, and both shifted matrices have spectra in I. Hence g(\A) = f(\A + s\I) \succeq f(\B + s\I) = g(\B). Combining the last two propositions produces a whole one-parameter family. It will reappear in the final part of the section as the building block of every operator monotone function. [Shifted Reciprocals] For every s \ge 0, the function t \mapsto -1/(t + s) is operator monotone on (0, \infty). For every s > 0, so is t \longmapsto  rac{t}{t + s} = 1 -  rac{s}{t + s} . By @prp-inverse-operator-monotone and @prp-operator-monotone-cone (b), t \mapsto -1/(t + s) is operator monotone on (0, \infty) - s = (-s, \infty). Every Hermitian matrix with spectrum in (0, \infty) has spectrum in (-s, \infty), so it is in particular operator monotone on (0, \infty). For the second function, t/(t + s) = 1 + s\cdot igl(-1/(t + s) igr) with s > 0, so @prp-operator-monotone-cone (a) applies. The fourth example is the one that started the section, and it is already proved. By @prp-square-root-monotone, \A \succeq \B \succeq \O implies \A^{1/2} \succeq \B^{1/2}. A Hermitian matrix has spectrum in [0, \infty) exactly when it is \succeq \O (@thm-psd-characterizations (b)), and \A^{1/2} is f(\A) for f(t) = t^{1/2}. So Chapter 13 §05’s proposition says precisely that t \mapsto t^{1/2} is operator monotone on [0, \infty). It is not re-proved here. Its proof was a different kind of argument, an eigenvector of \A^{1/2} - \B^{1/2} pushed to a contradiction, and it too never needs \A and \B to commute. A nonexample by minimal change. The function t \mapsto t = t^1 is operator monotone on [0, \infty) by @prp-affine-operator-monotone. Raise the exponent from 1 to 2. The function is still increasing, still a polynomial, and still satisfies the case n = 1. What fails is the clause “for every n”, already at n = 2, with the witness of @exm-loewner-not-monotone. Lowering the exponent from 1 to 	frac12 instead keeps the property. Among the powers, then, the dividing line lies somewhere around the exponent 1. Chapter 13 §05 said where it lies exactly, and the last part of this section returns to that. Why “for every n”. Each size imposes its own condition, and the conditions differ. At n = 1, t \mapsto t^2 passes on [0, \infty) and at n = 2 it fails. A definition at one fixed size would admit functions that break at the next size, and it would not say what the functional calculus does to matrices in general. Requiring every size at once makes the class small enough to classify completely, which is what Loewner’s theorem at the end of this section does. The name comes from the same place as the name of the order: both are Loewner’s. Eigenvalues move monotonically for every increasing function Operator monotonicity is a strong requirement, and a weaker one comes for free. §02 proved that the whole ordered list of eigenvalues respects the Loewner order: by @cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone, \A \succeq \B implies \lambda_i(\A) \ge \lambda_i(\B) for every i. That paid the debt Chapter 13 §05 recorded after @thm-loewner-basic, and it holds with no hypothesis on commuting. Composing with an increasing f keeps it, once one knows what f does to the ordered list of eigenvalues. [The Eigenvalue List of an Increasing Function] Let \A \in M_n(F) be Hermitian with \spec(\A) \subseteq I, and let f \colon I 	o 
R be increasing. Then f(\A) is Hermitian and \lambda_i igl(f(\A) igr) = f igl(\lambda_i(\A) igr) \qquad (i = 1, \dots, n) . The matrix f(\A) is Hermitian by @thm-functional-calculus-properties (c). By @cor-spectral-complex-matrix (over 
C) or @cor-spectral-real-matrix (over 
R), there is an orthonormal basis (\cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_n) of F^n with \A\cvec{q}_i = \lambda_i(\A)\cvec{q}_i. Let \A = \sum_j\mu_j\P_j be the spectral resolution, and fix i. Exactly one of the distinct eigenvalues equals \lambda_i(\A); call it \mu_{j_0}. Then \cvec{q}_i lies in the eigenspace of \mu_{j_0}, which is the image of \P_{j_0}, so \P_{j_0}\cvec{q}_i = \cvec{q}_i. For j 
e j_0, the eigenspace of \mu_{j_0} is orthogonal to that of \mu_j (@thm-spectral-resolution (a)), so \P_j\cvec{q}_i = \cvec{0}. By @def-function-of-normal-operator, f(\A)\cvec{q}_i = \sum_j f(\mu_j)\P_j\cvec{q}_i = f(\mu_{j_0})\cvec{q}_i = f igl(\lambda_i(\A) igr)\cvec{q}_i . Thus (\cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_n) is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of f(\A), and f(\lambda_1(\A)), \dots, f(\lambda_n(\A)) is its list of eigenvalues with multiplicity. Since \lambda_1(\A) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(\A) and f is increasing, this list is already in decreasing order. A decreasing list of all the eigenvalues with multiplicity is the list \lambda_1(f(\A)) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(f(\A)), so the two agree term by term. The lemma needs f increasing only for the order of the list. For a general f, the numbers f(\lambda_i(\A)) are still the eigenvalues of f(\A), but they may have to be re-sorted. Two lines now give the eigenvalue-level statement. [Every Increasing Function Is Monotone on Eigenvalues] Let f \colon I 	o 
R be increasing, and let \A, \B \in M_n(F) be Hermitian with spectra in I and \A \succeq \B. Then \lambda_i igl(f(\A) igr) \ \ge\ \lambda_i igl(f(\B) igr) \qquad 	ext{for every } i = 1, \dots, n . By @cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone, \lambda_i(\A) \ge \lambda_i(\B) for every i. Since f is increasing, f(\lambda_i(\A)) \ge f(\lambda_i(\B)). By @lem-eigenvalues-of-a-function, applied to \A and to \B, the two sides are \lambda_i(f(\A)) and \lambda_i(f(\B)). So the squaring map, which is not operator monotone, is nevertheless monotone on eigenvalues. The Chapter 13 witness shows both at once. [The Squares Are Not Ordered, but Their Eigenvalues Are] Let \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} and \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}, the pair of @exm-loewner-not-monotone, for which \A \succeq \B \succeq \O and \A^2 
ot\succeq \B^2. Compute the eigenvalues of \A^2 and \B^2 and compare them index by index. From @exm-loewner-not-monotone, \A^2 =  egin{psmallmatrix} 5 & 3 \ 3 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} and \B^2 =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}. The first has trace 7 and determinant 10 - 9 = 1, so its eigenvalues are the roots of x^2 - 7x + 1: \lambda_1(\A^2) =  rac{7 + 3\sqrt5}{2} \approx 6.854, \qquad \lambda_2(\A^2) =  rac{7 - 3\sqrt5}{2} \approx 0.146 . The second has trace 4 and determinant 0, so \lambda_1(\B^2) = 4 and \lambda_2(\B^2) = 0. Index by index:  rac{7 + 3\sqrt5}{2} \ge 4 because 3\sqrt5 \ge 1, and  rac{7 - 3\sqrt5}{2} \ge 0 because 49 \ge 45. So \lambda_i(\A^2) \ge \lambda_i(\B^2) for i = 1, 2, as @prp-eigenvalue-monotone-increasing predicts for the increasing function t \mapsto t^2 on [0, \infty). Nevertheless \A^2 - \B^2 is not \succeq \O. So for every increasing f, the eigenvalues of f(\A) dominate those of f(\B) one index at a time. What operator monotonicity adds is that the matrices are ordered, and the example shows that this is strictly more. Eigenvalues in order do not make matrices in order. It is tempting to read @prp-eigenvalue-monotone-increasing as “almost” operator monotonicity. It is not, because \lambda_i(\M) \ge \lambda_i(\N) for every i does not imply \M \succeq \N. Take \M = \diag(1, 0) and \N = \diag(0, 1): they have the same eigenvalues 1 \ge 0, yet \M - \N = \diag(1, -1) is indefinite. The Loewner order sees the eigenvectors as well as the eigenvalues, and the eigenvalue list forgets them. Operator convexity, and where the two notions part Operator convexity is the second notion of @def-operator-monotone, and one might expect it to behave like operator monotonicity. It does not: the function that fails to be operator monotone turns out to be operator convex. [The Square Is Operator Convex] The function t \mapsto t^2 is operator convex on 
R. Explicitly: for Hermitian \A, \B \in M_n(F) and 	heta \in [0, 1],  egin{aligned} 	heta\A^2 + (1 - 	heta)\B^2 &-  igl(	heta\A + (1 - 	heta)\B igr)^2 \ &= 	heta(1 - 	heta)(\A - \B)^2 \ \succeq\ \O . \end{aligned} For numbers, 	heta a^2 + (1-	heta)b^2 - (	heta a + (1-	heta)b)^2 = 	heta(1-	heta)(a - b)^2, which is a variance. The matrix version of the expansion produces \A\B + \B\A where the number version has 2ab, and that is exactly the cross term of (\A - \B)^2 = \A^2 - \A\B - \B\A + \B^2. So this time noncommutativity cancels itself out and costs nothing. The square of a Hermitian matrix is \succeq \O, which finishes the proof. By @thm-functional-calculus-properties (a), the function t \mapsto t^2 sends a Hermitian matrix to its square, so the displayed identity is what @def-operator-monotone (b) requires. Expanding, and keeping the order of every product,  egin{aligned}  igl(	heta\A + (1-	heta)\B igr)^2 &= 	heta^2\A^2 + 	heta(1-	heta)(\A\B + \B\A) \ &\quad + (1-	heta)^2\B^2 . \end{aligned} Subtracting this from 	heta\A^2 + (1-	heta)\B^2, and using 	heta - 	heta^2 = 	heta(1-	heta) = (1-	heta) - (1-	heta)^2,  egin{aligned} 	heta\A^2 + (1-	heta)\B^2 -  igl(	heta\A + (1-	heta)\B igr)^2 &= 	heta(1-	heta) igl(\A^2 - \A\B - \B\A + \B^2 igr) \ &= 	heta(1-	heta)(\A - \B)^2 . \end{aligned} The matrix \D = \A - \B is Hermitian, so \D^2 = \D^{*}\D \succeq \O by @thm-psd-characterizations (c). Since 	heta(1-	heta) \ge 0, the quadratic form of 	heta(1-	heta)\D^2 is nonnegative, which proves the inequality. The contrast is now complete, and it runs both ways. - t \mapsto t^2 is operator convex but not operator monotone on [0, \infty): @prp-square-operator-convex and @exm-loewner-not-monotone. - t \mapsto -1/t is operator monotone but not operator convex on (0, \infty): @prp-inverse-operator-monotone, and at n = 1 the scalar function -1/t is not even convex, since with a = 1, b = 3, and 	heta = 	frac12 the value at the midpoint is -	frac12, above the chord’s -	frac23. So neither notion implies the other. Each implies its scalar version (increasing, convex) by taking n = 1, and they strengthen those versions in different directions. Exercise C2 adds that t \mapsto 1/t is operator convex on (0, \infty), so -1/t is operator monotone and operator concave there. What is not proved here The question the section opened with has a complete answer, and this chapter does not prove it. Here is the statement, so that the reader knows what the answer looks like and which of the facts above are pieces of it. [Loewner’s Theorem, Statement] Let f \colon (0, \infty) 	o 
R. The following are equivalent. 1. f is operator monotone on (0, \infty). 2. There are \alpha \in 
R,  eta \ge 0, and a positive measure 
u on [0, \infty) with \int_{[0,\infty)}  rac{\dd
u(s)}{1 + s^2} < \infty, such that for every t > 0  egin{aligned} f(t) &= \alpha +  eta t \ &\quad + \int_{[0, \infty)} \Bigl( rac{s}{1 + s^2} -  rac{1}{t + s}\Bigr)\, \dd
u(s) . \end{aligned} 3. f is the restriction to (0, \infty) of a function that is analytic on 
C \setminus (-\infty, 0] and sends every point of the upper half-plane \{ z : \operatorname{Im} z > 0 \} to a point with nonnegative imaginary part. We do not prove this theorem here. Its proof needs complex analysis and some measure theory, which lie outside Chapter 16’s list (A1)–(A6); Chapter 21 proves it. Nothing in this chapter depends on it. Read (ii) against what was proved above. The functions it superposes are t \mapsto -1/(t + s) for s \ge 0, the translates of -1/t that @cor-shifted-inverse-operator-monotone showed to be operator monotone. The constants s/(1 + s^2) do not depend on t and are there only to make the integral converge. The term \alpha +  eta t is @prp-affine-operator-monotone. So the theorem says that the examples of this section are, in a precise sense, all the examples there are: every operator monotone function on (0, \infty) is an increasing affine function plus a nonnegative superposition of shifted reciprocals. The easy direction, (ii) \Rightarrow (i), is essentially @prp-operator-monotone-cone applied to an integral rather than a finite sum. What this book lacks is the analysis that carries the Loewner order through an integral, which is not on the list (A1)–(A6) in Chapter 16’s introduction. The hard direction, (i) \Rightarrow (ii), is the classification itself. Condition (iii) answers the opening question in one line. For z in the upper half-plane, z^{1/2} (the branch that is positive on (0, \infty)) halves the argument of z, so its argument stays between 0 and \pi/2 and z^{1/2} stays in the upper half-plane. The square doubles the argument, which can pass \pi. The square root keeps the upper half-plane, and the square folds it over. Find a point z of the upper half-plane whose square has negative imaginary part. Take z = -1 + i, with \operatorname{Im} z = 1 > 0. Then z^2 = 1 - 2i + i^2 = -2i, with imaginary part -2 < 0. So z \mapsto z^2 fails condition (iii) of @thm-loewner-statement, consistently with @exm-loewner-not-monotone. The same test settles the powers t \mapsto t^p. For 0 < p < 1, the function z^p multiplies the argument by p and keeps the upper half-plane, and indeed for t > 0 (a standard integral, not proved here) t^p =  rac{\sin p\pi}{\pi}\int_0^\infty s^{p-1}\, rac{t}{t + s}\, \dd s , a positive superposition of the functions t/(t + s) of @cor-shifted-inverse-operator-monotone. For p > 1, the argument of z^p passes \pi for some z in the upper half-plane, and the test fails. This is the dividing line at exponent 1 that Chapter 13 §05 announced. Both halves, that t^p is operator monotone on (0, \infty) for every p \in (0, 1) and that it is not for any p > 1, are proved in Chapter 21, with Loewner’s theorem. What is proved so far is the case p = 	frac12 (@prp-square-root-monotone) and, by applying it repeatedly, the cases p = 1/2^k (exercise C1). Summary and transfer The chapter began with a list of eigenvalues that the book had been able to order since Chapter 13 without being able to describe. It ends with each eigenvalue described as an optimization, and with a set of comparison theorems that follow from that description. Five moves did the work, and each transfers beyond this chapter. - The dimension count. Two subspaces of an n-dimensional space whose dimensions add to more than n share a nonzero vector. This one line drives Courant–Fischer (@thm-courant-fischer) and Weyl’s inequalities (§03) directly, and through Courant–Fischer everything after them. Transfer: whenever an extremal problem over vectors has to be compared with a fixed subspace, count dimensions before computing anything. - Min–max. Describe a quantity as a minimum over subspaces of a maximum over vectors, and prove it with two inequalities of different characters: one exhibits a witness subspace and computes, and the other takes an arbitrary subspace and intersects it with a span of eigenvectors. Applying the result to -\A gives the dual form for free. Transfer: a description that names no eigenvector is what makes two different matrices comparable. The same shape describes singular values (§09) and inertia (§10). - Compress and interlace. Restricting a Hermitian form to a subspace gives a smaller Hermitian matrix whose eigenvalues are trapped by the original’s: compressing to a k-dimensional subspace puts \lambda_i of the piece between \lambda_i and \lambda_{i+n-k} of the whole, which are consecutive when k = n - 1. Deleting a row and column (§04), compressing to an orthonormal frame (§06) and deleting a row or a column of a rectangular matrix (§09) are all this move; adding a rank-one term (§05) reaches the same interlaced picture by a different route, the Loewner order together with Weyl’s rank bound. Transfer: to bound the spectrum of a piece, look for the whole of which it is a compression. - Perturb in order. Compare \lambda_i(\A + \E) with \lambda_i(\A) index by index, never “each eigenvalue with its nearest neighbor”. For Hermitian perturbations the Lipschitz constant is 1 in the spectral norm, independent of n, of the gaps, and of the eigenvectors (§03). For singular values it needs no hypothesis on \E at all (§09). Transfer: where the Jordan block of Chapter 16 §07 showed that eigenvalues of general matrices can move like \varepsilon^{1/k}, the Hermitian and singular-value problems are perfectly conditioned. Reduce a question to one of them whenever possible. - Majorize. When the right comparison is between sums of the largest entries rather than individual ones, compare partial sums of decreasing rearrangements. The diagonal of a Hermitian matrix is majorized by its spectrum, and by the Schur–Horn theorem majorization describes the possible diagonals exactly (§08); and the Ky Fan and Lidskii sums (§§06–07) are of the same type. Transfer: a family of partial-sum inequalities indexed by k, together with equality of the totals, is a majorization in disguise, and writing it as one lets the whole family be used at once. Two supporting moves recur under these five: apply the result to -\A, which turns every max–min into a min–max and every top-k statement into a bottom-k one, and reduce singular values to eigenvalues, through \A^{*}\A or the Hermitian dilation. This section also reused a move from Chapter 13 §05, whiten, then compare: use a congruence to make one of the two matrices \I. It works for t \mapsto -1/t because inversion turns a congruence into a congruence, and not for a general f. The chapter also paid a series of promises made in earlier chapters, some of them long ago. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The promise Made in Paid by ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ The maximization route to eigenvalues “returns in Chapter 17, where the Rayleigh quotient and the Courant–Fischer theorem describe every eigenvalue of a self-adjoint operator by optimization” Chapter 12 §02 §01 (The Rayleigh quotient) and §02 (The min–max theorem), @thm-courant-fischer “Chapter 17 characterizes the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix as maxima and minima of \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} — at which point the test becomes the theory” Chapter 13 §13 §01 and §02, @thm-courant-fischer \A \succeq \B gives \lambda_i(\A) \ge \lambda_i(\B) for every i, not only i = 1 and i = n as in @thm-loewner-basic (b) Chapter 13 §05 §02, @cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone “The eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix move by at most 
orm{\E}_2 under a Hermitian perturbation” Chapter 16 §07 §03 (How far eigenvalues move), Weyl’s perturbation bound @lem-orthonormal-capture-bound is “the extreme case of a family of statements about sums of the largest eigenvalues” Chapter 13 §11 §06 (Subspaces and Sums of Eigenvalues), Ky Fan’s theorem, of which it is a special case The second half of the approximation theorem, in the spectral norm Chapter 13 §11 and Chapter 16 §08 §09 (The same theory for singular values), Eckart–Young in the spectral norm Interlacing of the zeros of consecutive orthogonal polynomials, “Chapter 17’s business” Chapter 11 §10 §04 (Deleting a row and a column): strict interlacing, through the bordered-matrix criterion The operator monotone functions named in Chapter 13 §05 Chapter 13 §05 §11: definition and first examples; t^s, \log t, and Loewner’s theorem remain Chapter 21’s, as that section said -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Four earlier theorems also received second proofs from the variational side, each of which shows something the first proof did not. The positivity of principal submatrices of a positive semidefinite matrix now follows from interlacing (§04, Deleting a row and a column). Hadamard’s inequality @thm-hadamard-inequality follows from AM–GM after a diagonal scaling, with Schur’s theorem supplying the equal totals (§08, The diagonal and the spectrum). Sylvester’s law of inertia @thm-sylvester-inertia is now a statement about the dimensions of subspaces, with no basis in it (§10, Inertia, again and additively). And the block test @thm-block-psd-schur is now a consequence of inertia additivity (§10). Some things the chapter did not do. Bounds for the eigenvalues of non-Hermitian matrices under perturbation, beginning with Bauer–Fike, are Chapter 20’s. Chapter 21 has Loewner’s theorem with the powers t^p, Schur-concave functions, the strongest form of Lidskii’s inequality, and Eckart–Young in every unitarily invariant norm. The variational principle itself, though, is now a tool the book can use without comment: an eigenvalue of a Hermitian matrix is a min–max, and comparison theorems follow from that. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define “f is operator monotone on I”, and say what the clause “for every n” ranges over. 2. Explain why an operator monotone function is increasing, and name an increasing function that is not operator monotone. 3. Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if f \colon I 	o 
R is increasing and \A \succeq \B are Hermitian with spectra in I, then \lambda_i(f(\A)) \ge \lambda_i(f(\B)) for every i. 4. Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if \A, \B are Hermitian of the same size and \lambda_i(\A) \ge \lambda_i(\B) for every i, then \A \succeq \B. 5. Which of t \mapsto t^2 and t \mapsto -1/t is operator monotone on (0, \infty), and which is operator convex there? 6. What does this section prove about Loewner’s theorem? (a) For every n \ge 1 and all Hermitian \A, \B \in M_n(F) with spectra in I, \A \succeq \B implies f(\A) \succeq f(\B), where f(\A) is formed by @def-function-of-normal-operator (@def-operator-monotone (a)). The clause ranges over all matrix sizes: the implication must hold for 1 	imes 1, 2 	imes 2, 3 	imes 3, … matrices simultaneously. (b) Taking n = 1 gives f(t) \ge f(s) whenever t \ge s in I (@prp-operator-monotone-increasing). The function t \mapsto t^2 on [0, \infty) is increasing and is not operator monotone (@exm-loewner-not-monotone). (c) Correct. This is @prp-eigenvalue-monotone-increasing: @cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone orders the eigenvalues of \A and \B index by index, f preserves each inequality, and @lem-eigenvalues-of-a-function identifies f(\lambda_i(\A)) with \lambda_i(f(\A)). (d) Incorrect. \diag(1, 0) and \diag(0, 1) have the same eigenvalues, but their difference \diag(1, -1) is indefinite, so neither dominates the other. (e) t \mapsto -1/t is operator monotone on (0, \infty) (@prp-inverse-operator-monotone) and is not operator convex, since already the scalar function is not convex: at 1, 3, and their midpoint 2, -	frac12 > 	frac12(-1 - 	frac13) = -	frac23. t \mapsto t^2 is operator convex (@prp-square-operator-convex) and not operator monotone on (0, \infty). The witness of @exm-loewner-not-monotone has 0 in the spectrum of \B, but the pair \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} \succeq \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} \succ \O works: \A^2 - \B^2 =  egin{psmallmatrix} 5 & 1 \ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} has determinant -1. (f) Only the statement (@thm-loewner-statement) and the fact that its building blocks t \mapsto -1/(t + s) are operator monotone (@cor-shifted-inverse-operator-monotone). The theorem itself is proved in Chapter 21. B. Practice [B1: Which are operator monotone?] Determine which of the following functions are operator monotone on the interval given. Justify your answer. 1. f(t) = 5 + 4t on 
R. 2. f(t) = 3 - 2t on 
R. 3. f(t) = 2 - \dfrac{3}{t + 1} on (0, \infty). 4. f(t) = \dfrac{t}{t + 2} on (0, \infty). 5. f(t) = t^2 on [0, \infty). (i) Operator monotone, by @prp-affine-operator-monotone with  eta = 4 \ge 0. (ii) Not operator monotone. It is not increasing, since f(1) = 1 < 3 = f(0), so it fails at n = 1 with \A = (1) \succeq \B = \O_1; compare @prp-operator-monotone-increasing. (iii) Operator monotone. By @cor-shifted-inverse-operator-monotone with s = 1, t \mapsto -1/(t + 1) is operator monotone on (0, \infty), and f = 2 + 3\cdot igl(-1/(t + 1) igr) with 3 \ge 0, so @prp-operator-monotone-cone (a) applies. (iv) Operator monotone, by @cor-shifted-inverse-operator-monotone with s = 2 > 0. (v) Not operator monotone: @exm-loewner-not-monotone gives \A \succeq \B \succeq \O, with spectra \{(3\pm\sqrt5)/2\} and \{0, 2\} in [0, \infty), and \A^2 
ot\succeq \B^2. [B2: One pair, three functions] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . 1. Show that \A \succeq \B \succ \O. 2. Compute \A^{-1} and \B^{-1}, and verify directly that \B^{-1} \succeq \A^{-1}, as @prp-inverse-operator-monotone predicts. 3. Show that \A^2 
ot\succeq \B^2 by exhibiting a vector \cvec{x} with \cvec{x}	p(\A^2 - \B^2)\cvec{x} < 0. 4. Compute the eigenvalues of \A^2 and \B^2, and verify that \lambda_i(\A^2) \ge \lambda_i(\B^2) for i = 1, 2. Hence explain which result of this section (c) and (d) illustrate together. (a) \A - \B = \diag(1, 0), a diagonal matrix with nonnegative entries, so \A - \B \succeq \O and \A \succeq \B. The leading principal minors of \B are 2 and 2 - 1 = 1, both positive, so \B \succ \O by Sylvester’s criterion (@thm-pd-characterizations (d)). (b) \det\A = 2 and \det\B = 1, so \A^{-1} =  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B^{-1} - \A^{-1} =  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . For every \cvec{x} \in 
R^2, \cvec{x}	p(\B^{-1} - \A^{-1})\cvec{x} = 	frac12(x_1 - x_2)^2 \ge 0, so \B^{-1} \succeq \A^{-1}. (c) \A^2 =  egin{psmallmatrix} 10 & 4 \ 4 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} and \B^2 =  egin{psmallmatrix} 5 & 3 \ 3 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix}, so \A^2 - \B^2 =  egin{psmallmatrix} 5 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, with determinant -1 < 0. With \cvec{x} = (1, -3), \cvec{x}	p(\A^2 - \B^2)\cvec{x} = 5 + 2\cdot(1)(-3) + 0 = -1 < 0 . (d) \A^2 has trace 12 and determinant (\det\A)^2 = 4, so its eigenvalues are 6 \pm \sqrt{32} = 6 \pm 4\sqrt2, approximately 11.657 and 0.343. \B^2 has trace 7 and determinant 1, so its eigenvalues are (7 \pm 3\sqrt5)/2, approximately 6.854 and 0.146. For i = 1, 12 + 8\sqrt2 \ge 7 + 3\sqrt5 because 8\sqrt2 > 3\sqrt5. For i = 2, 12 - 8\sqrt2 \ge 7 - 3\sqrt5 is 5 + 3\sqrt5 \ge 8\sqrt2. Both sides are positive, and squaring gives 70 + 30\sqrt5 \ge 128, that is \sqrt5 \ge 	frac{29}{15}, which holds because 5 \ge 	frac{841}{225}. Hence (c) and (d) together illustrate @prp-eigenvalue-monotone-increasing and the warning after it: the increasing function t \mapsto t^2 orders the eigenvalues but not the matrices. [B3: The convexity identity in numbers] With \A and \B as in B2 and 	heta = 	frac12, compute \M = 	frac12\A^2 + 	frac12\B^2 -  igl(	frac12\A + 	frac12\B igr)^2 directly, confirm that \M = 	frac14(\A - \B)^2, and hence conclude that  igl(	frac12(\A + \B) igr)^2 \preceq 	frac12(\A^2 + \B^2). From B2, 	frac12\A^2 + 	frac12\B^2 = 	frac12 egin{psmallmatrix} 15 & 7 \ 7 & 4 \end{psmallmatrix} =  egin{psmallmatrix} 15/2 & 7/2 \ 7/2 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix}. Next 	frac12(\A + \B) =  egin{psmallmatrix} 5/2 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}, whose square is  egin{pmatrix} 	frac{25}{4} + 1 & 	frac52 + 1 \ 	frac52 + 1 & 1 + 1 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac{29}{4} & 	frac72 \ 	frac72 & 2 \end{pmatrix} . Hence \M =  egin{psmallmatrix} 15/2 - 29/4 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} = \diag(	frac14, 0). On the other side, \A - \B = \diag(1, 0), so 	frac14(\A - \B)^2 = \diag(	frac14, 0) = \M, as @prp-square-operator-convex says with 	heta(1 - 	heta) = 	frac14. Since \diag(	frac14, 0) is diagonal with nonnegative entries, \M \succeq \O, which is the displayed inequality. C. Going deeper [C1: Iterated square roots] 1. Let \A \succeq \B \succeq \O. Prove that \A^{1/4} \succeq \B^{1/4}, where \A^{1/4} is f(\A) for f(t) = t^{1/4} on [0, \infty). 2. Deduce that t \mapsto t^{1/2^k} is operator monotone on [0, \infty) for every integer k \ge 0. 3. Explain why the argument of (b) cannot reach t \mapsto t^{3/4}, and say where the operator monotonicity of t^p for every p \in (0, 1) is proved. Hint for (a): the positive square root is unique. (a) Let g(t) = t^{1/4} on [0, \infty). Since \A \succeq \O, its spectrum lies in [0, \infty) (@thm-psd-characterizations (b)), and g(\A) = \sum_j\mu_j^{1/4}\P_j is Hermitian with nonnegative eigenvalues by @thm-functional-calculus-properties (c) and (d), so g(\A) \succeq \O. By @thm-functional-calculus-properties (b), g(\A)^2 = (g^2)(\A), and g^2(t) = t^{1/2}, so g(\A)^2 = \A^{1/2}. By the uniqueness in @thm-psd-characterizations (d), applied to \A^{1/2} \succeq \O, g(\A) is the positive square root of \A^{1/2}: \A^{1/4} = (\A^{1/2})^{1/2}. The same holds for \B. Now @prp-square-root-monotone applied to \A \succeq \B \succeq \O gives \A^{1/2} \succeq \B^{1/2}, and \B^{1/2} \succeq \O by @thm-psd-square-root. Applying @prp-square-root-monotone again, to \A^{1/2} \succeq \B^{1/2} \succeq \O, gives (\A^{1/2})^{1/2} \succeq (\B^{1/2})^{1/2}, that is \A^{1/4} \succeq \B^{1/4}. (b) Induction on k. For k = 0 the function is t \mapsto t, operator monotone by @prp-affine-operator-monotone. Suppose \A^{1/2^k} \succeq \B^{1/2^k} whenever \A \succeq \B \succeq \O. The argument of (a), with t^{1/2^{k+1}} in place of t^{1/4} and t^{1/2^k} in place of t^{1/2}, shows that \A^{1/2^{k+1}} = (\A^{1/2^k})^{1/2}, and similarly for \B. Both \A^{1/2^k} and \B^{1/2^k} are \succeq \O, so @prp-square-root-monotone applied to \A^{1/2^k} \succeq \B^{1/2^k} \succeq \O gives \A^{1/2^{k+1}} \succeq \B^{1/2^{k+1}}. (c) Each step of (b) takes a square root, which halves the exponent. Starting from 1, the exponents reached are exactly 1, 	frac12, 	frac14, \dots, and 	frac34 is not among them. The operator monotonicity of t^p for every p \in (0, 1) needs a new idea, an integral representation of the kind in @thm-loewner-statement, and it is proved in Chapter 21. [C2: The reciprocal is operator convex] 1. Let \G \in M_n(F) with \G \succ \O. Prove that the 2n 	imes 2n matrix  egin{pmatrix} \G & \I_n \ \I_n & \G^{-1} \end{pmatrix} is Hermitian and \succeq \O. 2. Let \A, \B \succ \O be of the same size and 	heta \in [0, 1]. Prove that  igl(	heta\A + (1 - 	heta)\B igr)^{-1} \ \preceq\ 	heta\A^{-1} + (1 - 	heta)\B^{-1} , that is, t \mapsto 1/t is operator convex on (0, \infty). 3. Deduce that t \mapsto -1/t is both operator monotone and operator concave on (0, \infty). Hint: Schur complements. (a) \G is Hermitian, and so is \G^{-1}, since (\G^{-1})^{*} = (\G^{*})^{-1} = \G^{-1}. The off-diagonal blocks are \I_n and \I_n^{*} = \I_n, so the block matrix \M_{\G} is Hermitian. Its corner \G is \succ \O, and its Schur complement is \M_{\G}/\G = \G^{-1} - \I_n^{*}\G^{-1}\I_n = \O \succeq \O . By @thm-block-psd-schur (b), \M_{\G} \succeq \O. (b) Put \C = 	heta\A + (1 - 	heta)\B. For \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}, \inner{\C\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = 	heta\inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} + (1 - 	heta)\inner{\B\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}}. Both inner products are > 0, and 	heta and 1 - 	heta are \ge 0 and not both zero, so the sum is > 0. Thus \C \succ \O. By (a), \M_{\A} \succeq \O and \M_{\B} \succeq \O, so for every \cvec{y} \in F^{2n} the quadratic form of 	heta\M_{\A} + (1 - 	heta)\M_{\B} =  egin{pmatrix} \C & \I_n \ \I_n & 	heta\A^{-1} + (1 - 	heta)\B^{-1} \end{pmatrix} is 	heta\inner{\M_{\A}\cvec{y}}{\cvec{y}} + (1 - 	heta)\inner{\M_{\B}\cvec{y}}{\cvec{y}} \ge 0, and this block matrix is \succeq \O. Its corner \C is \succ \O, so @thm-block-psd-schur (b) gives 	heta\A^{-1} + (1 - 	heta)\B^{-1} - \C^{-1} \ \succeq\ \O , which is the claim. Since t \mapsto 1/t sends a positive definite matrix to its inverse (@def-function-of-normal-operator), and a Hermitian matrix has spectrum in (0, \infty) exactly when it is \succ \O (@thm-pd-characterizations (b)), this is @def-operator-monotone (b) for f(t) = 1/t. (c) Operator monotone by @prp-inverse-operator-monotone. Operator concave by definition, because its negative t \mapsto 1/t is operator convex by (b). [C3: The cube needs its own witness] 1. With \A and \B as in B2, show that \A^3 
ot\succeq \B^3. Conclude that t \mapsto t^3 is not operator monotone on [0, \infty). 2. One might hope to deduce (a) from the failure of t \mapsto t^2. Suppose t \mapsto t^3 were operator monotone on [0, \infty). Applying it and t \mapsto t^{1/2} (@prp-square-root-monotone) to both sides of \A \succeq \B \succeq \O, repeatedly and in any order, yields inequalities \A^q \succeq \B^q for certain exponents q. Show that every such q has the form 3^j/2^k with integers j, k \ge 0, and that 2 never has this form. Explain why this means (a) needed a witness of its own. (a) From B2, \A \succeq \B \succeq \O, with spectra in (0, \infty). Multiplying the squares of B2 once more, \A^3 =  egin{pmatrix} 34 & 14 \ 14 & 6 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B^3 =  egin{pmatrix} 13 & 8 \ 8 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A^3 - \B^3 =  egin{pmatrix} 21 & 6 \ 6 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . The determinant is 21 - 36 = -15 < 0, so the difference is indefinite. Explicitly, with \cvec{x} = (1, -5), \cvec{x}	p(\A^3 - \B^3)\cvec{x} = 21 + 2\cdot 6\cdot(-5) + 25 = -14 < 0 . By @thm-functional-calculus-properties (a), t \mapsto t^3 sends \A to \A^3, so it is not operator monotone on [0, \infty). (b) Start from \A = \A^{3^0/2^0}. Taking the square root of \A^{q} gives \A^{q/2}, and cubing it gives \A^{3q}, by @thm-functional-calculus-properties (b) and the uniqueness of the positive square root, as in C1 (a); likewise for \B. If q = 3^j/2^k, the results are 3^j/2^{k+1} and 3^{j+1}/2^k, of the same form. By induction on the number of steps, every exponent reached has the form 3^j/2^k. If 2 = 3^j/2^k, then 3^j = 2^{k+1}, and the left side is odd while the right side is even, since k + 1 \ge 1. So no exponent reached equals 2. The hypothetical operator monotonicity of the cube therefore cannot be converted, by these means, into that of the square. The failure of the square does not formally imply the failure of the cube, and (a) had to find a pair of matrices of its own.

title: Convexity
content:
Convexity Three chapters in a row have met convexity and moved on. Chapter 16 §01 drew the unit balls of three norms and remarked that each is convex, because the triangle inequality forces 
orm{t\elem{u} + (1-t)\elem{v}} \le 1 whenever 
orm{\elem{u}}, 
orm{\elem{v}} \le 1 (@def-unit-ball). Chapter 13 §01 set as an exercise that the positive semidefinite matrices are closed under sums and nonnegative multiples (@exr-positive-definite-matrices-c2). Chapter 17 §06 proved that the sum of the k largest eigenvalues is subadditive, and so a convex function of the matrix (@cor-ky-fan-subadditive), and said that this was only to be expected of a maximum of linear functions. And Chapter 17 §08 showed, again in an exercise, that the possible diagonals of the Hermitian matrices with a given spectrum contain the segment between any two of their points (@exr-majorization-and-schur-c3). Each time, convexity was checked on the spot and not studied. One debt is older still: Chapter 16’s plan listed dual norms, and Chapter 16 never defined one. This chapter studies convexity for its own sake. A set is convex when it contains the segment between any two of its points, and the theory built on that single condition has two faces. One face is combinatorial. Every point of a convex hull in dimension n is an average of at most n + 1 of the original points, and from that count follow the theorems of Radon and Helly on how convex sets intersect. The other face is geometric, and it carries most of the weight. A point outside a closed convex set can be separated from it by a hyperplane, and the hyperplane comes from the nearest point of the set, generalizing the orthogonal projection of Chapter 11. From separation come the rest: a convex set described by the half-spaces that contain it, the dual norm as the support function of the unit ball, Farkas’s lemma and the duality of linear programming, the minimax theorem for matrix games, and the fact that a compact convex set is the hull of its extreme points. The chapter ends with convex functions, which is where the Ky Fan observation of Chapter 17 belongs. The field is 
R throughout. Convexity asks for weights t with 0 \le t \le 1, and “between 0 and 1” needs an order on the scalars, which 
C does not have. A complex space is treated as a real one when it is needed, by allowing only real scalars: the Hermitian n 	imes n matrices, for instance, form a real vector space and not a complex one, and that is how positive semidefinite matrices and eigenvalue functions enter. Spaces are finite-dimensional, and each section says whether a result needs only the vector space, a norm, or an inner product. Most of the chapter works in 
R^n with the standard inner product. The analysis this chapter imports The list is Chapter 16’s, facts (A1)–(A6) of that chapter’s introduction, cited by the same name at the point of use: “by the extreme value theorem, fact (A4) of Chapter 16’s introduction”. This chapter needs chiefly two of them. (A3), the compactness of closed bounded sets, and (A4), the extreme value theorem, are what make a nearest point, a maximum over a hull, or an extreme point exist rather than merely be approached. §02 uses (A3) to prove that the hull of a compact set is compact, and the separation and extreme-point theorems of §§03 and 08 rest on both. (A1), completeness, gives the suprema that define gauges and support functions. For the second-derivative test of convexity in §10, the one-variable case uses (A6), the mean value theorem, and the several-variable case uses the symmetry and Taylor assumptions that Chapter 14 §06 recorded for its own second-derivative test. §11 builds the logarithm from the exponential of Chapter 10 §09 (that section’s facts (A1)–(A3)) and needs (A5), the intermediate value theorem, to show every positive number has one. The words closed and open are defined in §01, in the sequential form in which Chapter 16’s introduction defines continuity, and a closedness argument uses nothing but that definition and the elementary algebra of limits. A section that needs any analytic fact outside Chapter 16’s list says so where it uses it. What you need - Chapter 0 §06 and §09 — the triangle inequality for complex numbers, which §11 uses twice, and the trace, which §10 uses once: @thm-complex-triangle-inequality, @thm-trace-properties. - Chapter 1 — independence and dimension, used to count points: @def-linear-independence, @thm-size-bounds, @thm-span-subspace, @thm-basis-extension, and the dimension formula @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim. Zorn’s lemma (@thm-zorn) is mentioned once, to mark where the infinite-dimensional Hahn–Banach theorem would begin. - Chapter 2 — Rank–Nullity: @thm-rank-nullity. - Chapter 4 — cosets, which are the affine subspaces of this chapter: @def-coset, @lem-coset-equality. - Chapter 3 §04 and §05 — the Invertible Matrix Theorem and the rank facts §09 counts the vertices of a polyhedron with: @thm-invertible-tfae, @thm-rank-nullity-matrix, @thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank. - Chapter 5 — linear functionals and hyperplanes, the raw material of every separation argument: @def-linear-functional, @thm-functionals-on-fn, @def-hyperplane, @thm-hyperplane-kernel-functional, @prp-affine-subspace-intersection. This chapter is named for its language and not as a step in an argument: §§01, 03, 04, 05, and 09 cite it in the text, to say which abstract object a half-space or an affine hyperplane is, and two examples use it, but no proof here rests on it. Once V = 
R^n, what is worked with is the concrete \cvec{x} \mapsto \cvec{a}	p\cvec{x}. - Chapter 10 §09 — the exponential of a number, with that section’s imported facts (A1)–(A3), from which §11 builds the logarithm and real powers: @thm-exponential-properties. The reference sits in the text of §11 that sets the construction up, not inside a proof. - Chapter 11 — the inner product and the orthogonal projection, which §03 generalizes from subspaces to closed convex sets: @def-inner-product, @thm-cauchy-schwarz, @thm-orthogonal-decomposition, @def-orthogonal-projection, @thm-projection-formula, @thm-best-approximation. - Chapter 12 §05 — the real spectral theorem, which is how §08 finds the extreme points of the density matrices and of the interval \O \preceq \X \preceq \I: @cor-spectral-real-matrix. - Chapter 13 — positivity: @def-positive-semidefinite, @thm-psd-characterizations, @def-loewner-order. - Chapter 14 §06 — the Hessian and the second-derivative test, @def-hessian and @thm-second-derivative-test, with that section’s Taylor assumption. As with Chapter 10, §10 names these in the text, to say what it is generalizing and which imported facts it borrows; the proofs cite the assumptions, not the theorem. - Chapter 16 — norms, their unit balls and their equivalence, compactness, and the operator norm: @def-norm, @def-unit-ball, @prp-p-norm-inequalities, @lem-reverse-triangle-norm, @thm-norm-equivalence, @cor-convergence-norm-independent, @cor-closed-bounded-compact, @def-operator-norm, @thm-operator-norm-formulas. - Chapter 17 — the places where convexity was met: @thm-ky-fan and @cor-ky-fan-subadditive, @def-majorization and @thm-schur-horn, @lem-am-gm, @def-operator-monotone and @prp-square-operator-convex. Roadmap - Convex sets and hulls. The definition, the first examples (half-spaces, the balls of every norm, the standard simplex, the positive semidefinite matrices, the vectors majorized by a fixed vector), the operations that preserve convexity, and the convex hull as the set of all convex combinations. Affine hulls, which are Chapter 4’s cosets. Closed and open sets. - Carathéodory’s theorem. In dimension n, every point of a hull is a convex combination of at most n + 1 of the points, and no fewer will do in general. Hence the hull of a compact set is compact. Radon’s theorem, and Helly’s theorem on intersections. - Separating hyperplanes. The nearest point of a closed convex set, characterized by an obtuse-angle condition that becomes Chapter 11’s orthogonality when the set is a subspace. Strict separation of a point from a closed convex set, supporting hyperplanes, and the finite-dimensional Hahn–Banach theorem. Why two disjoint closed convex sets need not be strictly separated. - Gauges, support functions, dual norms. Every bounded, closed, symmetric convex set that contains a ball around \cvec{0} is the unit ball of a norm, which is the converse of Chapter 16’s convexity remark. The support function, the polar set, and the dual norm, with the proof that the dual of the dual norm is the original norm. This supplies the dual norms that Chapter 16 left out. - Cones and Farkas’s lemma. Convex cones and their duals; a finitely generated cone is closed, which is the subtle step; the alternative theorem of Farkas; and a closed cone with a nonclosed linear image, showing why finite generation matters. - Linear programming. Weak and strong duality from Farkas’s lemma, complementary slackness, and a worked problem solved together with its dual. This answers the remark in Chapter 3 §07 that flows with capacities are a problem about inequalities. - The minimax theorem. Matrix games, mixed strategies over the simplex, and von Neumann’s theorem, contrasted with the Courant–Fischer min–max of Chapter 17, whose proof is a dimension count rather than convexity. - Extreme points. A compact convex set is the convex hull of its extreme points (Minkowski’s theorem). The extreme points of the unit balls of the three norms, of the density matrices, and of the doubly stochastic matrices; for the last, Birkhoff’s theorem that the permutation matrices are all of them is stated and left to Chapter 19. A compact convex set whose extreme points do not form a closed set. - Polytopes. Hulls of finitely many points against bounded intersections of finitely many half-spaces, and the Minkowski–Weyl theorem that they are the same sets. Vertices as the basic feasible points of linear programming. - Convex functions. The epigraph, Jensen’s inequality, the second-derivative test, and continuity. A pointwise supremum of affine functions is convex, which accounts for Chapter 17’s Ky Fan sums. - Three classical inequalities. The logarithm and real powers, built from Chapter 10’s exponential; the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality as Jensen’s inequality for -\log; Young’s and Hölder’s inequalities; Minkowski’s inequality, so that every 
orm{\cdot}_p is a norm on F^n; and the dual of every p-norm, which completes §04. The chapter’s summary closes this section. Named moves - Count, then drop a point. Too many points in too few dimensions are dependent, affinely or linearly. Move the weights along the dependence until one of them reaches zero, and drop that point without leaving the hull. Carathéodory’s theorem, its version for cones, and Radon’s theorem are all this move. - Nearest point, then the normal direction. To separate a point from a closed convex set, take the nearest point of the set and use the vector from it to the outside point as the normal of the hyperplane. The separation theorems are the geometry of this one projection. - Dualize. A closed convex set is determined by the half-spaces containing it, and a closed convex cone by its dual cone. Every statement about the one side has a statement about the other: Farkas’s lemma is that move made into a theorem, and linear-programming duality is Farkas applied to one combined system. - A supremum of linear functions is convex. Support functions, dual norms, the largest eigenvalue, and the Ky Fan sums are all suprema of linear functions, and each inherits its convexity from that alone. - Lift, then eliminate. To see what a set looks like from fewer coordinates, eliminate one variable at a time: Fourier–Motzkin elimination pairs each upper bound with each lower bound, and is what proves the Minkowski–Weyl theorem of §09. - Compactness turns a supremum into a maximum. Chapter 16’s move, used again: once a hull or a set of weights is known to be compact, a maximum or a nearest point is attained at a point that can be named and fed back into the argument.

title: 18.1 Convex Sets and Hulls
content:
Convex Sets and Hulls Convexity has turned up in this book four times without being asked for: in the unit balls of Chapter 16, the positive semidefinite matrices of Chapter 13, and the Ky Fan sums and the possible diagonals of Chapter 17 (the chapter introduction lists the places). Each time the property was checked by hand and set aside. This section gives it a name, finds the smallest convex set containing a given set, and fixes the words closed and open that the rest of the chapter needs. The field is 
R, throughout the chapter. The definition below asks for a scalar t with 0 \le t \le 1, which needs an order on the scalars; 
C has none. A complex space is treated as a real one by allowing only real scalars. That is how the Hermitian matrices enter below: they form a vector space over 
R, and not over 
C, since i\A is not Hermitian when \A 
e \O is. Unless a statement says otherwise, V is a real vector space; where a result needs a finite dimension, a norm, or an inner product, it says so. Segments, and sets that contain them Chapter 16 §01 checked the convexity of a unit ball with one line: if 
orm{\elem{u}}, 
orm{\elem{v}} \le 1 and 0 \le t \le 1, then 
orm{t\elem{u} + (1-t)\elem{v}} \le 1. The expression t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y}, with t running over [0, 1], keeps recurring, so it deserves a name, and so does the property of containing all of it. Picture it first. At t = 1 the expression is \elem{x}, at t = 0 it is \elem{y}, and at t = 	frac12 it is the midpoint. Writing it as \elem{y} + t(\elem{x} - \elem{y}) shows the rest: we start at \elem{y} and travel the fraction t of the way to \elem{x}. As t runs over [0,1], the point runs along the straight segment from \elem{y} to \elem{x}, and nowhere else. A convex set is one that contains the whole straight segment between any two of its points. [Convex Set] Let V be a vector space over 
R. A subset C \subseteq V is convex if, for all \elem{x}, \elem{y} \in C and every real t with 0 \le t \le 1, t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} \in C . The set \{ t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} : 0 \le t \le 1 \} is the segment joining \elem{x} and \elem{y}, written [\elem{x}, \elem{y}]. In words: pick any two points of C, possibly equal; the segment joining them must lie inside C. The quantifier “for all \elem{x}, \elem{y}” is what makes this a property of the set rather than of a pair; one segment escaping C is enough to make it nonconvex. The restriction 0 \le t \le 1 is the other half of the content, and the end of this subsection shows what happens without it. There is nothing to check for well-definedness: a subset either has the property or it does not. [The first convex sets] Check each of the following against @def-convex-set. 1. The empty set, and a single point \{\elem{p}\}. 2. A subspace U of V, and a coset \elem{p} + U of it (@def-coset). 3. A closed half-space \{\elem{x} \in V : \varphi(\elem{x}) \le c\}, where \varphi is a nonzero linear functional on V (@def-linear-functional) and c \in 
R. 4. A closed ball \{\elem{x} \in V : 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}} \le r\} of any norm on V, with center \elem{p} and radius r \ge 0. 5. The set of positive semidefinite matrices (@def-positive-semidefinite) in the real vector space of n 	imes n Hermitian matrices. (a) The empty set has no two points, so the condition holds vacuously; for \{\elem{p}\}, t\elem{p} + (1-t)\elem{p} = \elem{p}. These degenerate cases matter because an intersection of convex sets, which we meet shortly, is often empty or a single point, and the statements below must allow for both. (b) Let \elem{x} = \elem{p} + \elem{u} and \elem{y} = \elem{p} + \elem{w} with \elem{u}, \elem{w} \in U. Then t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} = \elem{p} +  igl(t\elem{u} + (1-t)\elem{w} igr) , and t\elem{u} + (1-t)\elem{w} \in U because a subspace is closed under linear combinations. Taking \elem{p} = \elem{0} gives the subspace itself. Here the restriction on t was not used at all; we return to this below. (c) Let \varphi(\elem{x}) \le c and \varphi(\elem{y}) \le c. By linearity, \varphi igl(t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} igr) = t\varphi(\elem{x}) + (1-t)\varphi(\elem{y}) \le tc + (1-t)c = c , where the inequality multiplies the first hypothesis by t and the second by 1 - t. Multiplying an inequality by a number preserves it only when the number is \ge 0, so both t \ge 0 and 1 - t \ge 0 were used. In 
R^n every linear functional is \cvec{x} \mapsto \cvec{a}	p\cvec{x} for some \cvec{a} (@thm-functionals-on-fn), so the closed half-spaces of 
R^n are the sets \{\cvec{x} : \cvec{a}	p\cvec{x} \le c\} with \cvec{a} 
e \cvec{0}. The same computation shows that the open half-space \{\elem{x} : \varphi(\elem{x}) < c\} is convex, and that the affine hyperplane \{\elem{x} : \varphi(\elem{x}) = c\} is convex. (d) Let 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}} \le r and 
orm{\elem{y} - \elem{p}} \le r. Since t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} - \elem{p} = t(\elem{x} - \elem{p}) + (1-t)(\elem{y} - \elem{p}), (N3) and (N2) of @def-norm give 
orm{t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} - \elem{p}} \le t
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}} + (1-t)
orm{\elem{y} - \elem{p}} \le r , where homogeneity used \lvert t vert = t and \lvert 1 - tvert = 1 - t. With \elem{p} = \elem{0} and r = 1 this is the closed unit ball of @def-unit-ball, and the computation is the one Chapter 16 §01 made there. (e) The Hermitian matrices form a real vector space: a real linear combination of Hermitian matrices is Hermitian. Let \A \succeq \O and \B \succeq \O. Then t\A + (1-t)\B is Hermitian, and for every \cvec{x} \in 
C^n, \inner{(t\A + (1-t)\B)\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = t\inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} + (1-t)\inner{\B\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} \ge 0 , since both inner products on the right are \ge 0 by (P2) and both coefficients are \ge 0. So (P1) and (P2) hold, and t\A + (1-t)\B \succeq \O. The same computation with any s, t \ge 0 in place of t and 1 - t shows s\A + t\B \succeq \O, so the positive semidefinite matrices form a convex cone, in the sense of §05. (This is what @exr-positive-definite-matrices-c2 (a) asks.) The standard example of a convex set in coordinates gets its own name, because the rest of this section keeps returning to it. [Standard Simplex] For n \ge 1, the standard simplex in 
R^n is \Delta_n \coloneqq \Bigl\{ \cvec{t} = (t_1, \dots, t_n) \in 
R^n : t_i \ge 0 	ext{ for every } i,\ \ t_1 + \dots + t_n = 1 \Bigr\} . \Delta_1 = \{1\} is a point, \Delta_2 is the segment from (1, 0) to (0, 1), and \Delta_3 is the triangle with corners \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3. It is convex: it is the intersection of the n closed half-spaces \{t_i \ge 0\} with the affine hyperplane \{t_1 + \dots + t_n = 1\}, and each of these is convex by @exm-convex-first-examples (c). (That an intersection of convex sets is convex is the first item of @prp-convexity-operations below; it is also immediate here, because a point that lies in each set lies in their intersection.) An element of \Delta_n is a list of n weights: nonnegative, and adding up to 1. A nonexample by minimal change. Keep the closed unit ball B_2 of 
R^2 but take only its edge, the unit circle \{\cvec{x} : 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 = 1\}. Much survives: the circle is symmetric under \cvec{x} \mapsto -\cvec{x}, bounded, and as round as the disc. But the clause “for all \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}” fails at \cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{y} = -\cvec{e}_1, t = 	frac12: the midpoint is \cvec{0}, and 
orm{\cvec{0}}_2 = 0 
e 1. What was lost is exactly the inequality \le 1 that absorbed the triangle inequality in @exm-convex-first-examples (d); with an equality there is nothing to absorb it. Why this definition. Two variations are worth trying. - Let t range over all of 
R. Then C must contain the whole line through any two of its points. The subspaces and cosets of @exm-convex-first-examples meet this demand, which is why (b) never used 0 \le t \le 1; the half-spaces and balls do not. @exr-convex-sets-c3 shows that, apart from \emptyset, the sets meeting it are exactly the cosets. - Ask only for t = 	frac12. A set containing the midpoint of any two of its points is midpoint convex, which is genuinely weaker: 
Q^2 is midpoint convex, yet it misses 	frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\cvec{e}_1 \in [\cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_1]. @exr-convex-sets-c1 shows that the gap disappears for closed sets, defined at the end of this section. The name is the everyday word: a convex lens has no dents. A union of convex sets need not be convex. The two coordinate axes in 
R^2 are subspaces, hence convex, but their union contains \cvec{e}_1 and \cvec{e}_2 and not their midpoint (	frac12, 	frac12), which lies on neither axis. Even two points fail: \{\cvec{0}\} \cup \{\cvec{e}_1\} is a union of two convex sets and misses 	frac12\cvec{e}_1. The operation that does respect convexity is intersection (@prp-convexity-operations), and the convex replacement for a union is the hull of the union, defined below. Is \{(x, y) \in 
R^2 : y \ge \lvert xvert\} convex? Is \{(x, y) \in 
R^2 : y \le \lvert xvert\} convex? The first is convex. It is the set where both y - x \ge 0 and y + x \ge 0, an intersection of two closed half-spaces, and a point on a segment between two points of both half-spaces lies in both by @exm-convex-first-examples (c). The second is not: (1, 1) and (-1, 1) belong to it, since 1 \le 1, but their midpoint (0, 1) does not, since 1 \le 0 is false. The two sets differ only in the direction of the inequality, and the direction decides everything; a convex function such as \lvert x vert has a convex region above its graph (§10). Here is a payoff. Chapter 17 §08 met a set of vectors that it could describe exactly, but whose convexity it proved only in an exercise. Everything needed to prove it is now in place. [The vectors majorized by a fixed vector] Let \vlambda \in 
R^n. Prove that the set \{\cvec{d} \in 
R^n : \cvec{d} \prec \vlambda\} of vectors majorized by \vlambda (@def-majorization) is convex, and deduce that the diagonals of the Hermitian matrices with spectrum \vlambda form a convex set. For \cvec{x} \in 
R^n and 1 \le k \le n, write s_k(\cvec{x}) = x^{\downarrow}_1 + \dots + x^{\downarrow}_k, the sum of the k largest entries. Step 1: any k entries add up to at most s_k(\cvec{x}). List the entries x_i at a set I of k positions decreasingly as v_1 \ge \dots \ge v_k. Since \cvec{x} has j entries v_1, \dots, v_j \ge v_j, we get x^{\downarrow}_j \ge v_j for each j. Summing gives \sum_{i \in I} x_i \le s_k(\cvec{x}), with equality when I holds the positions of the k largest entries. Step 2: s_k respects averages. Let \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n and 0 \le t \le 1, and let I hold the positions of the k largest entries of \cvec{z} = t\cvec{x} + (1-t)\cvec{y}. By Step 1, used once with equality and twice as an inequality, s_k(\cvec{z}) = t\sum_{i \in I}x_i + (1-t)\sum_{i \in I}y_i \le t\,s_k(\cvec{x}) + (1-t)\,s_k(\cvec{y}) , where the inequality again needs t \ge 0 and 1 - t \ge 0. Step 3: convexity. Let \cvec{d} \prec \vlambda and \cvec{d}' \prec \vlambda, and put \cvec{z} = t\cvec{d} + (1-t)\cvec{d}'. For k \le n - 1, Step 2 and (M1) for both vectors give s_k(\cvec{z}) \le t\,s_k(\vlambda) + (1-t)\,s_k(\vlambda) = s_k(\vlambda). The total of \cvec{z} is t\sum_i\lambda_i + (1-t)\sum_i\lambda_i = \sum_i\lambda_i by (M2) for both. So \cvec{z} \prec \vlambda, and the set is convex. For the deduction, the Schur–Horn Theorem (@thm-schur-horn) says that the diagonals of the Hermitian matrices with eigenvalues \vlambda are exactly the vectors \cvec{d} \prec \vlambda. So the set of those diagonals is the set just shown to be convex. This is the statement of @exr-majorization-and-schur-c3, now with a proof in the text, and Step 2 is a first glimpse of §10’s convex functions: s_k satisfies s_k(t\cvec{x} + (1-t)\cvec{y}) \le t\,s_k(\cvec{x}) + (1-t)\,s_k(\cvec{y}) because it is a maximum of linear functions. Operations that preserve convexity Checking the definition directly is rarely the fastest route. Most convex sets are built from simpler ones by a few operations, and the following proposition lists those that preserve convexity. It needs one construction. For subsets A, B \subseteq V and a real c, the Minkowski sum and the scalar multiple are A + B \coloneqq \{\elem{a} + \elem{b} : \elem{a} \in A,\ \elem{b} \in B\} , \qquad cA \coloneqq \{c\elem{a} : \elem{a} \in A\} . A translate \elem{p} + A is the Minkowski sum \{\elem{p}\} + A; a coset (@def-coset) is a translate of a subspace. [Operations Preserving Convexity] Let V and W be real vector spaces. 1. The intersection of any family of convex subsets of V is convex. 2. If T \colon V 	o W is linear, C \subseteq V is convex and D \subseteq W is convex, then the image T(C) and the preimage T^{-1}(D) = \{\elem{v} \in V : T\elem{v} \in D\} are convex. 3. If A, B \subseteq V are convex and c \in 
R, then A + B, cA, and every translate \elem{p} + A are convex. Rewrite the point of the segment so that convexity of the given sets applies: linearity moves the weights through T, and a Minkowski sum regroups term by term. Throughout, let 0 \le t \le 1. (a) Let (C_\alpha) be a family of convex sets and \elem{x}, \elem{y} \in  igcap_\alpha C_\alpha. For each \alpha, both points lie in C_\alpha, so t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} \in C_\alpha by convexity of C_\alpha. Hence the point lies in every C_\alpha, that is, in the intersection. (The intersection of the empty family is V by convention, and V is convex.) (b) Let T\elem{x}, T\elem{y} \in T(C) with \elem{x}, \elem{y} \in C. By linearity, tT\elem{x} + (1-t)T\elem{y} = T igl(t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} igr), and t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} \in C by convexity; so the point lies in T(C). For the preimage, let T\elem{x}, T\elem{y} \in D. Then T igl(t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} igr) = tT\elem{x} + (1-t)T\elem{y} \in D by convexity of D, so t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} \in T^{-1}(D). (c) Let \elem{a} + \elem{b} and \elem{a}' + \elem{b}' lie in A + B. Rearranging, t(\elem{a} + \elem{b}) + (1-t)(\elem{a}' + \elem{b}') =  igl(t\elem{a} + (1-t)\elem{a}' igr) +  igl(t\elem{b} + (1-t)\elem{b}' igr) , and the two brackets lie in A and in B by convexity. So the point lies in A + B. The scalar multiple cA is the image of A under the linear map \elem{v} \mapsto c\elem{v}, and is convex by (b). A translate \elem{p} + A = \{\elem{p}\} + A is convex because a single point is convex (@exm-convex-first-examples (a)). This proves the proposition. The proposition turns many checks into one line. The solution set of a system of linear inequalities, \{\cvec{x} \in

Convex combinations and the convex hull A convex set contains the segment between any two of its points. Apply that twice: it contains \elem{x}_1, \elem{x}_2, and hence every point of [\elem{x}_1, \elem{x}_2], and then every point on a segment from such a point to \elem{x}_3. The points reached are the averages of \elem{x}_1, \elem{x}_2, \elem{x}_3 with nonnegative weights, and the pattern deserves a name. [Convex Combination] Let V be a real vector space and \elem{x}_1, \dots, \elem{x}_k \in V, with k \ge 1. A convex combination of \elem{x}_1, \dots, \elem{x}_k is a vector t_1\elem{x}_1 + t_2\elem{x}_2 + \dots + t_k\elem{x}_k \qquad	ext{with } (t_1, \dots, t_k) \in \Delta_k , that is, with every t_i \ge 0 and t_1 + \dots + t_k = 1. It is a linear combination with two restrictions on the coefficients, and each restriction has a job. Dropping “t_i \ge 0” gives the affine combinations of the next subsection; dropping “sum to 1” as well gives all linear combinations, and the span. A convex combination of two points is a point of the segment joining them, with (t, 1-t) as the weights. The weights may be read as masses placed at the points, and the combination is then their center of mass. The case k = 1 is included and is 1 \cdot \elem{x}_1 = \elem{x}_1. [Convex Sets Contain Their Convex Combinations] Let C be a convex subset of a real vector space. Then every convex combination of points of C lies in C. Peel off the last point. A convex combination of k points is a combination of two points, one of which is a convex combination of the first k - 1 points, rescaled so that its weights again add up to 1. Induction on k does the rest; the only care needed is not to divide by zero while rescaling. We use induction on the number k of points. For k = 1, the combination is \elem{x}_1 \in C. Let k \ge 2, suppose the statement holds for k - 1 points, and let \elem{x} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i\elem{x}_i with \elem{x}_i \in C and (t_1, \dots, t_k) \in \Delta_k. Case 1: t_k = 1. Then the other weights are nonnegative and add up to 0, so all of them are 0, and \elem{x} = \elem{x}_k \in C. Case 2: t_k < 1. Put s = 1 - t_k > 0 and \elem{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} (t_i/s)\elem{x}_i. The division is legal because s 
e 0. The coefficients t_i/s are \ge 0 and add up to (1 - t_k)/s = 1, so \elem{y} is a convex combination of k - 1 points of C, and \elem{y} \in C by the inductive hypothesis. Then \elem{x} = s\elem{y} + t_k\elem{x}_k = (1 - t_k)\elem{y} + t_k\elem{x}_k , which lies in C by @def-convex-set, applied to the points \elem{x}_k and \elem{y} of C with t = t_k \in [0, 1]. This completes the induction. A set that is not convex can be enlarged to one that is. We want the most economical enlargement: nothing added that convexity does not force. The convex hull of a set is the smallest convex set containing it. [Convex Hull] Let S be a subset of a real vector space V. The convex hull of S is the intersection of all convex subsets of V that contain S: \conv S \coloneqq  igcap\,\{ C \subseteq V : C 	ext{ is convex and } S \subseteq C \} . The family being intersected is never empty, because V itself is convex and contains S. By @prp-convexity-operations (a), \conv S is convex; it contains S, since each set in the family does; and it lies inside every convex set containing S, since it is the intersection of all of them. So “smallest” in the slogan is literal: \conv S is a convex set containing S and contained in every other one. In particular, \conv C = C exactly when C is convex. This description from outside is clean but gives no way to decide whether a given point lies in the hull. The next theorem gives the description from inside.
