Affine combinations and the affine hull Dropping the sign condition from a convex combination gives the other natural kind of average. It describes the flat pieces of V: lines, planes, and their analogues, not necessarily through \elem{0}. Chapter 4 §04 already has these objects, as cosets \elem{p} + U of subspaces, and the point of this subsection is to connect them with combinations. [Affine Combination, Affine Hull] Let V be a real vector space. 1. An affine combination of \elem{x}_1, \dots, \elem{x}_k \in V, k \ge 1, is a vector \sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i\elem{x}_i with real t_i satisfying t_1 + \dots + t_k = 1. No sign condition is imposed. 2. An affine subspace of V is a coset \elem{p} + U of a subspace U (@def-coset). Its dimension is \dim U. 3. The affine hull of S \subseteq V, written \operatorname{aff} S, is the set of all affine combinations of points of S. The dimension in (b) is well defined, because the coset determines its subspace: U = \{\elem{a} - \elem{b} : \elem{a}, \elem{b} \in \elem{p} + U\}. Indeed each such difference is (\elem{p} + \elem{u}) - (\elem{p} + \elem{w}) = \elem{u} - \elem{w} \in U, and each \elem{u} \in U is the difference (\elem{p} + \elem{u}) - \elem{p}. So a line in 
R^3 not through \cvec{0} is an affine subspace of dimension 1, and a single point \{\elem{p}\} = \elem{p} + \{\elem{0}\} is one of dimension 0. [The Affine Hull Is a Coset] Let S be a nonempty subset of a real vector space V, let \elem{x}_0 \in S, and put U = \Span\{\elem{x} - \elem{x}_0 : \elem{x} \in S\}. Then \operatorname{aff} S = \elem{x}_0 + U , and \operatorname{aff} S is contained in every affine subspace of V that contains S. In particular U does not depend on the choice of \elem{x}_0 \in S. Since the weights add up to 1, an affine combination is \elem{x}_0 plus a linear combination of the differences \elem{x}_i - \elem{x}_0; that identity, read in both directions, gives the equality, and minimality follows because an affine subspace through \elem{x}_0 is \elem{x}_0 plus a subspace. (\subseteq) Let \elem{x} = \sum_i t_i\elem{x}_i with \elem{x}_i \in S and \sum_i t_i = 1. Since the t_i add up to 1, \elem{x}_0 = \sum_i t_i\elem{x}_0, and therefore \elem{x} = \elem{x}_0 + \sum_i t_i(\elem{x}_i - \elem{x}_0) \in \elem{x}_0 + U . (\supseteq) An element of \elem{x}_0 + U is \elem{x}_0 + \sum_{j} c_j(\elem{y}_j - \elem{x}_0) for some \elem{y}_j \in S and real c_j, by @def-span. It equals \Bigl(1 - \sum_j c_j\Bigr)\elem{x}_0 + \sum_j c_j\elem{y}_j , a combination of points of S whose coefficients add up to 1, hence an affine combination. Now let \elem{p} + W be an affine subspace containing S. Since \elem{x}_0 \in \elem{p} + W, @lem-coset-equality (b) gives \elem{p} + W = \elem{x}_0 + W. Each \elem{x} \in S also lies in \elem{x}_0 + W, so \elem{x} - \elem{x}_0 \in W. Thus W is a subspace containing every \elem{x} - \elem{x}_0, and U \subseteq W by @thm-span-subspace. Hence \operatorname{aff} S = \elem{x}_0 + U \subseteq \elem{x}_0 + W. Finally, U is the subspace determined by the coset \operatorname{aff} S, by the remark after @def-affine-hull, and that coset does not mention \elem{x}_0. This proves the proposition. So the affine hull is to affine subspaces what the span is to subspaces, and what the convex hull is to convex sets: the smallest one containing S. It also gives every convex set a dimension. (e) By @thm-convex-hull-combinations, \conv S = \{t\cvec{e}_1 + (1-t)\cvec{e}_2 : 0 \le t \le 1\}, the segment from \cvec{e}_1 to \cvec{e}_2, which is \Delta_2. By @def-affine-hull, \operatorname{aff} S = \{t\cvec{e}_1 + (1-t)\cvec{e}_2 : t \in 
R\}, the whole line x_1 + x_2 = 1. (f) [0, 1) is neither (see the warning above).

Expanding, tx^2 + (1-t)x'^2 - x_t^2 = t(1-t)(x - x')^2 \ge 0 , so ty + (1-t)y' \ge tx^2 + (1-t)x'^2 \ge x_t^2. (b) Not convex. The points (1, 1) and (-1, -1) satisfy xy = 1, but their midpoint (0, 0) has xy = 0 < 1. (c) Not convex. \A = \diag(1, 0) and \B = \diag(0, -1) are symmetric with \det\A = \det\B = 0, but 	frac12(\A + \B) = \diag(	frac12, -	frac12) has determinant -	frac14 < 0. (d) Convex. It is the affine hyperplane \{\varphi = 4\} for the linear functional \varphi(\cvec{x}) = x_1 + 2x_2 - x_3, convex by @exm-convex-first-examples (c). It is also a coset of \ker\varphi, convex by @exm-convex-first-examples (b). [B2: Membership in a hull] Let \cvec{p}_1 = (0, 0), \cvec{p}_2 = (4, 1), \cvec{p}_3 = (1, 3) in

As in @exm-hull-membership, \cvec{z} lies in the hull exactly when the system t_1\cvec{p}_1 + t_2\cvec{p}_2 + t_3\cvec{p}_3 = \cvec{z}, t_1 + t_2 + t_3 = 1 has a solution with every t_i \ge 0. Its coefficient matrix  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 4 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 3 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has determinant 11

Check: 	frac4{11}(4, 1) + 	frac6{11}(1, 3) = (	frac{16 + 6}{11}, 	frac{4 + 18}{11}) = (2, 2), and 	frac{1 + 4 + 6}{11} = 1. All weights are \ge 0, so (2, 2) is in the hull. For \cvec{z} = (3, 3): \cvec{t} = (-	frac4{11}, 	frac6{11}, 	frac9{11}). Check: 	frac6{11}(4, 1) + 	frac9{11}(1, 3) = (	frac{24 + 9}{11}, 	frac{6 + 27}{11}) = (3, 3), and 	frac{-4 + 6 + 9}{11} = 1. The unique solution has t_1 < 0, so no convex combination equals (3, 3), and it is not in the hull. C. Going deeper [C1: Midpoint convexity] Let V be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a norm, and let C \subseteq V be midpoint convex: 	frac12(\elem{x} + \elem{y}) \in C whenever \elem{x}, \elem{y} \in C. 1. Prove by induction on m that t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} \in C for all \elem{x}, \elem{y} \in C and every dyadic t = j/2^m with 0 \le j \le 2^m. 2. Prove that if C is also closed, then C is convex. 3. Give a midpoint convex subset of

If j is even, t = (j/2)/2^m and the inductive hypothesis applies. If j is odd, then t = 	frac12(t_- + t_+) with t_\pm = (j \pm 1)/2^{m+1} = 	frac{(j \pm 1)/2}{2^m}, which are dyadic of level m and lie in [0, 1]. By the inductive hypothesis \elem{z}_\pm = t_\pm\elem{x} + (1 - t_\pm)\elem{y} \in C, and 	frac12(\elem{z}_- + \elem{z}_+) = 	frac12(t_- + t_+)\elem{x} +  igl(1 - 	frac12(t_- + t_+) igr)\elem{y} = t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} , which lies in C by midpoint convexity. (b) Let \elem{x}, \elem{y} \in C and t \in [0, 1]. Put t_m = \lfloor 2^m tfloor/2^m, a dyadic number in [0, 1] with 0 \le t - t_m < 2^{-m} (the floor exists and 2^{-m} 	o 0 by the completeness of 
R, fact (A1) of Chapter 16’s introduction). By (a), \elem{z}_m = t_m\elem{x} + (1 - t_m)\elem{y} \in C. Then 
orm{\elem{z}_m -  igl(t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} igr)} = \lvert t_m - tvert\,

R. The midpoint of two rationals is rational, but 0, 1 \in

Q for t = 1/\sqrt2. The set is not closed: the rationals \lfloor 10^k/\sqrt2floor/10^k converge to 1/\sqrt2 (the floor exists and 10^{-k} 	o 0 by the completeness of 
R, fact (A1) of Chapter 16’s introduction). [C3: Sets that contain lines] Let V be a real vector space and A \subseteq V a nonempty set containing t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} for all \elem{x}, \elem{y} \in A and every real t. 1. Fix \elem{a} \in A and put U = \{\elem{x} - \elem{a} : \elem{x} \in A\}. Prove that U is a subspace of V, so that A = \elem{a} + U is an affine subspace. 2. Hence prove that a nonempty S \subseteq V is an affine subspace if and only if S = \operatorname{aff} S. Hint for (a): for closure under addition, use a midpoint and then a scaling. (a) \elem{0} = \elem{a} - \elem{a} \in U. Scalars: let \elem{u} = \elem{x} - \elem{a} \in U and c \in 
R. The point c\elem{x} + (1-c)\elem{a} lies in A by hypothesis, and it equals \elem{a} + c\elem{u}; so c\elem{u} \in U. Sums: let \elem{u} = \elem{x} - \elem{a} and \elem{w} = \elem{y} - \elem{a} with \elem{x}, \elem{y} \in A. The midpoint \elem{m} = 	frac12\elem{x} + 	frac12\elem{y} \in A, so 	frac12(\elem{u} + \elem{w}) = \elem{m} - \elem{a} \in U, and by the scalar step with c = 2, \elem{u} + \elem{w} \in U. By @thm-subspace-test, U is a subspace, and A = \elem{a} + U by the definition of U. (b) (\Leftarrow) If S = \operatorname{aff} S, then S is a coset by @prp-affine-hull-coset. (\Rightarrow) If S = \elem{p} + W is an affine subspace, then \operatorname{aff} S \subseteq S by the minimality clause of @prp-affine-hull-coset, and S \subseteq \operatorname{aff} S because each \elem{x} \in S is the affine combination 1 \cdot \elem{x}. title: 18.2 Carathéodory's Theorem
content:
Carathéodory’s Theorem By @thm-convex-hull-combinations, the convex hull of a set S consists of the convex combinations of points of S, with any number of points allowed. For a hundred points in the plane, that description permits a single point of the hull to be an average of all hundred at once. A picture says that this is wasteful: the hundred points spread out into a polygon, the polygon can be cut into triangles with corners among the points, and every point of the polygon lies in one of those triangles, so three points always suffice. This section proves the general statement. In a space of dimension n, every point of a convex hull is a convex combination of at most n + 1 points of the set, and the bound cannot be lowered. Two consequences follow. The hull of a compact set is compact, which §08 uses. And from the same counting argument come Radon’s theorem and Helly’s theorem, which describe how convex sets in 
R^n can intersect. As in §01, all spaces are real. Carathéodory’s theorem needs a finite dimension and nothing else; the compactness corollary needs, in addition, a norm, and any norm will do. When there are too many points The proof we want has a simple plan. If a point is written as a convex combination of too many points, find a way to shift the weights so that the point stays where it is while one weight falls to zero. That point can then be dropped. Two things are needed: a precise meaning of “too many”, and a way to shift the weights without moving the point. Both come from one observation. If \sum_i \lambda_i\elem{x}_i = \elem{0} and \sum_i \lambda_i = 0, then for every real s, \sum_i (t_i - s\lambda_i)\elem{x}_i = \sum_i t_i\elem{x}_i \quad	ext{and}\quad \sum_i (t_i - s\lambda_i) = \sum_i t_i . So the weights t_i - s\lambda_i describe the same point, and they still add up to 1. A relation of this shape is what we need a word for. A list of points is affinely dependent when some combination with coefficients adding to zero, not all of them zero, cancels out. [Affine Independence] Let V be a real vector space and let (\elem{x}_0, \elem{x}_1, \dots, \elem{x}_m) be a list in V, m \ge 0. The list is affinely independent if, for all real \lambda_0, \dots, \lambda_m, \sum_{i=0}^{m} \lambda_i\elem{x}_i = \elem{0} \ 	ext{ and } \ \sum_{i=0}^{m} \lambda_i = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda_0 = \lambda_1 = \dots = \lambda_m = 0 . It is affinely dependent otherwise. A relation \sum_i \lambda_i\elem{x}_i = \elem{0} with \sum_i\lambda_i = 0 and the \lambda_i not all zero is an affine dependence. In words: this is linear independence (@def-linear-independence) with one extra hypothesis, that the coefficients add up to zero. The extra hypothesis makes the condition easier to satisfy, and it makes the notion blind to the choice of origin. Translating every point by \elem{p} changes \sum_i\lambda_i\elem{x}_i by  igl(\sum_i\lambda_i igr)\elem{p} = \elem{0}, so a translated list is affinely dependent exactly when the original is. Some small cases: - A single point (\elem{x}_0) is always affinely independent: \lambda_0 = 0 is forced by the sum condition alone. - Two points (\elem{x}_0, \elem{x}_1) are affinely dependent exactly when they are equal: the condition forces \lambda_1 = -\lambda_0, and then \lambda_0(\elem{x}_0 - \elem{x}_1) = \elem{0} has a solution \lambda_0 
e 0 if and only if \elem{x}_0 = \elem{x}_1. - Three collinear points are affinely dependent: (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2) satisfy 1 \cdot (0, 0) - 2 \cdot (1, 1) + 1 \cdot (2, 2) = \cvec{0}, with 1 - 2 + 1 = 0. A nonexample by minimal change. The list (\cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) in 
R^2 is affinely independent: the \cvec{e}_1- and \cvec{e}_2-coordinates of \lambda_0\cvec{0} + \lambda_1\cvec{e}_1 + \lambda_2\cvec{e}_2 = \cvec{0} give \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = 0, and then the sum condition gives \lambda_0 = 0. Move the third point to 2\cvec{e}_1. The list (\cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_1, 2\cvec{e}_1) still spans the same line as (\cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_1), but now 1\cdot\cvec{0} - 2\cvec{e}_1 + 1 \cdot (2\cvec{e}_1) = \cvec{0} with 1 - 2 + 1 = 0: the three points have fallen onto one line, and the implication in the definition fails. Affine independence is not linear independence. The list (\cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) in 
R^2 is linearly dependent, since it contains \cvec{0}, yet it was just shown to be affinely independent. A triangle is an affinely independent list of three points in a two-dimensional space, which linear independence would never allow. That is why the bound in this section is n + 1, and not n. The implication does run one way: a linearly independent list is affinely independent, since an affine dependence is in particular a linear relation with coefficients not all zero. The next lemma converts affine dependence into linear dependence of differences, which is what allows a dimension count. [Affine Dependence by Differences] Let V be a real vector space and \elem{x}_0, \dots, \elem{x}_m \in V. 1. The list (\elem{x}_0, \dots, \elem{x}_m) is affinely independent if and only if the list (\elem{x}_1 - \elem{x}_0, \dots, \elem{x}_m - \elem{x}_0) is linearly independent. 2. If \dim V = n, every affinely independent list in V has at most n + 1 entries. Equivalently, every list of n + 2 or more points of V is affinely dependent. The sum condition determines \lambda_0 from the other coefficients, and eliminating it turns an affine relation among the points into a linear relation among the differences, and back. (a) Suppose \sum_{i=0}^{m}\lambda_i\elem{x}_i = \elem{0} and \sum_{i=0}^{m}\lambda_i = 0. Then \lambda_0 = -\sum_{i \ge 1}\lambda_i, and substituting, \sum_{i=1}^{m} \lambda_i(\elem{x}_i - \elem{x}_0) = \sum_{i=0}^{m}\lambda_i\elem{x}_i = \elem{0} . Conversely, if \sum_{i=1}^{m} \lambda_i(\elem{x}_i - \elem{x}_0) = \elem{0}, then setting \lambda_0 = -\sum_{i \ge 1}\lambda_i gives an affine relation \sum_{i=0}^{m}\lambda_i\elem{x}_i = \elem{0} with \sum_{i=0}^{m}\lambda_i = 0. These two passages are inverse to each other, and (\lambda_0, \dots, \lambda_m) is not all zero exactly when (\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m) is not all zero, because \lambda_0 is determined by the others. So affine dependences of the points correspond to linear relations, not all zero, among the differences, and one exists exactly when the other does. (b) If (\elem{x}_0, \dots, \elem{x}_m) is affinely independent, then by (a) the m differences \elem{x}_i - \elem{x}_0 are linearly independent, so m \le n by @thm-size-bounds (a). The list has m + 1 \le n + 1 entries. The theorem Now the plan can be carried out. The statement is sharper than the count: the points can be taken affinely independent, and the count is a consequence. Carathéodory’s Theorem Let V be a real vector space with \dim V = n, and let S \subseteq V. Every point of \conv S is a convex combination of an affinely independent list of points of S. In particular, every point of \conv S is a convex combination of at most n + 1 points of S. Count, then drop a point. Write \elem{x} with as few points as possible, so that every weight is positive. If the points were affinely dependent, the weights t_i - s\lambda_i would describe the same \elem{x} for every s. Start at s = 0 and increase s. The weights with \lambda_i > 0 decrease, and there is at least one of these, because the \lambda_i add up to zero without all being zero. Stop at the first moment a weight reaches 0: all the weights are still \ge 0, and one point has become unnecessary. That contradicts minimality. Let \elem{x} \in \conv S. By @thm-convex-hull-combinations, \elem{x} is a convex combination of finitely many points of S. Among all ways of writing it so, choose one, \elem{x} = \sum_{i=0}^{m} t_i\elem{x}_i , \qquad \elem{x}_i \in S,\ \ (t_0, \dots, t_m) \in \Delta_{m+1} , with the number m + 1 of points as small as possible. Then every t_i > 0: a zero weight could be deleted, and the remaining weights would still be nonnegative and add up to 1, giving a shorter expression. Suppose, for a contradiction, that (\elem{x}_0, \dots, \elem{x}_m) is affinely dependent, and let \sum_i\lambda_i\elem{x}_i = \elem{0}, \sum_i\lambda_i = 0 be an affine dependence. The \lambda_i are not all zero and add up to 0, so at least one of them is positive. Put s = \min\Bigl\{  rac{t_i}{\lambda_i} : \lambda_i > 0 \Bigr\} , a minimum over a nonempty finite set, and let j be an index where it is attained; s > 0 since each t_i > 0. Define t_i' = t_i - s\lambda_i. Then: - t_i' \ge 0 for every i. If \lambda_i \le 0, then t_i' \ge t_i > 0, since s > 0. If \lambda_i > 0, then s \le t_i/\lambda_i by the choice of s, so s\lambda_i \le t_i. - t_j' = t_j - (t_j/\lambda_j)\lambda_j = 0. - \sum_i t_i' = \sum_i t_i - s\sum_i\lambda_i = 1 and \sum_i t_i'\elem{x}_i = \sum_i t_i\elem{x}_i - s\sum_i\lambda_i\elem{x}_i = \elem{x}. So \elem{x} is a convex combination of the m points \elem{x}_i, i 
e j, contradicting the minimality of m + 1. Hence (\elem{x}_0, \dots, \elem{x}_m) is affinely independent. By @lem-affine-dependence (b) it has at most n + 1 entries. This proves the theorem. In the plane, then, every point of the hull of any set S lies in a triangle whose corners are points of S, possibly a degenerate one (a segment or a single point). In 
R^3 it lies in a tetrahedron with corners in S. The proof is constructive: given any convex combination, it says how to shorten it, one point at a time. [Dropping a point in the plane] In 
R^2 let \cvec{x}_0 = (0, 0), \cvec{x}_1 = (3, 0), \cvec{x}_2 = (0, 3), \cvec{x}_3 = (2, 2), and let \cvec{x} = 	frac14(\cvec{x}_0 + \cvec{x}_1 + \cvec{x}_2 + \cvec{x}_3) = (	frac54, 	frac54). Write \cvec{x} as a convex combination of three of these points by the method of the proof. Four points in 
R^2 are affinely dependent by @lem-affine-dependence (b). To find a dependence, solve \sum_i \lambda_i\cvec{x}_i = \cvec{0} and \sum_i\lambda_i = 0: the two coordinate equations read 3\lambda_1 + 2\lambda_3 = 0 and 3\lambda_2 + 2\lambda_3 = 0. Taking \lambda_3 = 3 gives \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = -2, and then \lambda_0 = -(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3) = 1. Check: 1\cdot(0,0) - 2(3,0) - 2(0,3) + 3(2,2) = (-6 + 6, -6 + 6) = \cvec{0}, and 1 - 2 - 2 + 3 = 0. The positive coefficients are \lambda_0 = 1 and \lambda_3 = 3, with ratios t_0/\lambda_0 = 	frac14 and t_3/\lambda_3 = 	frac1{12}. So s = 	frac1{12}, attained at j = 3, and the new weights are \cvec{t}' =  igl(	frac14 - 	frac1{12},\ 	frac14 + 	frac2{12},\ 	frac14 + 	frac2{12},\ 	frac14 - 	frac3{12} igr) =  igl(	frac16,\ 	frac5{12},\ 	frac5{12},\ 0 igr) . Check: 	frac5{12}(3, 0) + 	frac5{12}(0, 3) = (	frac54, 	frac54) = \cvec{x}, and 	frac2{12} + 	frac5{12} + 	frac5{12} = 1. So \cvec{x} = 	frac16\cvec{x}_0 + 	frac5{12}\cvec{x}_1 + 	frac5{12}\cvec{x}_2 lies in the triangle with corners \cvec{x}_0, \cvec{x}_1, \cvec{x}_2, and \cvec{x}_3 has been dropped. The minimum matters. Using the other positive coefficient, s = 	frac14, would make the weight of \cvec{x}_3 equal to 	frac14 - 	frac34 = -	frac12 < 0: the point would still be described correctly, but not as a convex combination. The bound n + 1 cannot be improved, and the standard simplex shows it. [The bound is attained] In 
R^n, let S = \{\cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n\} and let \cvec{c} = 	frac{1}{n+1}(\cvec{0} + \cvec{e}_1 + \dots + \cvec{e}_n) = 	frac1{n+1}\1. Show that \cvec{c} \in \conv S is not a convex combination of any n points of S. The point \cvec{c} is a convex combination of the n + 1 points of S, each with weight 	frac1{n+1}. A convex combination of n of the points leaves one out. If it leaves out \cvec{e}_j, the combination is t_0\cvec{0} + \sum_{i 
e j} t_i\cvec{e}_i, whose j-th coordinate is 0, while c_j = 	frac1{n+1} 
e 0. If it leaves out \cvec{0}, the combination is \sum_i t_i\cvec{e}_i = (t_1, \dots, t_n), whose coordinates add up to 1, while those of \cvec{c} add up to 	frac{n}{n+1} 
e 1. Either way it is not \cvec{c}. The bound can be far from attained for a particular set, however, and it is worth seeing one. [Two points suffice for a circle] Let S = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^2 : 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 = 1\} be the unit circle. Show that \conv S is the closed unit disc B_2, and that every point of B_2 is a convex combination of two points of S. B_2 is convex (@exm-convex-first-examples (d)) and contains S, so \conv S \subseteq B_2 by @def-convex-hull. Conversely, let (a, b) \in B_2, so a^2 + b^2 \le 1, and put c = \sqrt{1 - a^2}, which is real since \lvert avert \le 1. The points (a, c) and (a, -c) lie on S, and \lvert bvert \le c because b^2 \le 1 - a^2. With t = 	frac{c + b}{2c} when c > 0, t(a, c) + (1-t)(a, -c) =  igl(a,\ (2t - 1)c igr) = (a, b) , and 0 \le t \le 1 because -c \le b \le c. When c = 0, we have a = \pm1 and b = 0, and (a, b) is itself a point of S. So every point of the disc lies on a vertical chord of the circle, and B_2 \subseteq \conv S by @thm-convex-hull-combinations. A point of 
R^3 is given as a convex combination of seven points of a set S. What is the smallest number of points of S that @thm-caratheodory guarantees will suffice? Can one always manage with three? Four, since n + 1 = 4 for n = 3. Three do not always suffice: by @exm-caratheodory-sharp with n = 3, the point 	frac14(1, 1, 1) is a convex combination of \cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3 and of no three of them. The only place the proof used \dim V = n was the final count, through @lem-affine-dependence (b), and all that count needs is a space containing the differences of the points. If S lies in an affine subspace of dimension d, then n + 1 can be replaced by d + 1; @exr-caratheodory-c1 carries this out. A set of points on a line in 
R^{100} needs only two at a time. The hull of a compact set The first use of the theorem is a statement about limits. Recall from @cor-closed-bounded-compact that a subset K of a finite-dimensional real space with a norm is compact if every sequence in K has a subsequence converging to a point of K. Compactness is what lets later sections take a maximum, or a nearest point, over a hull, and it is not obvious that a hull keeps it. A convex combination may use arbitrarily many points, so a sequence of combinations could use more and more of them, and there would be no single compact set of parameters from which to extract a convergent subsequence. Carathéodory’s bound removes that possibility: every point of the hull is described by exactly n + 1 points of K and n + 1 weights. [The Hull of a Compact Set Is Compact] Let V be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a norm, and let K \subseteq V be compact. 1. \conv K is compact. 2. If K is nonempty, then every linear functional \varphi on V attains a maximum on \conv K, and \max_{\elem{x} \in \conv K} \varphi(\elem{x}) = \max_{\elem{x} \in K} \varphi(\elem{x}) . For (a), write each term of a sequence in \conv K as a combination of exactly n + 1 points of K, using @thm-caratheodory and padding with zero weights. That turns one sequence into n + 2 sequences: one of weight vectors in \Delta_{n+1}, and n + 1 of points of K. Extract a convergent subsequence from each in turn, a subsequence of the previous one each time, and pass to the limit in the combination. For (b), a linear functional cannot do better on an average than on the best of the points averaged. Let n = \dim V. (a) If K = \emptyset, then \conv K = \emptyset, which is compact vacuously. Otherwise let (\elem{y}_k) be a sequence in \conv K. By @thm-caratheodory, each \elem{y}_k is a convex combination of at most n + 1 points of K; repeating one of those points with weight 0 if necessary, we may write \elem{y}_k = \sum_{i=0}^{n} t_{k,i}\,\elem{x}_{k,i} , \qquad \elem{x}_{k,i} \in K,\ \ \cvec{t}_k = (t_{k,0}, \dots, t_{k,n}) \in \Delta_{n+1} . Step 1: the weights. \Delta_{n+1} is closed in

Radon’s theorem and Helly’s theorem The dimension count behind Carathéodory’s theorem says something about intersections of convex sets as well. Its first form is a statement about n + 2 points. [Radon’s Theorem] Let V be a real vector space with \dim V = n, and let \elem{x}_1, \dots, \elem{x}_m \in V with m \ge n + 2. Then the index set \{1, \dots, m\} can be split into two disjoint nonempty sets I and J with \conv\{\elem{x}_i : i \in I\} \cap \conv\{\elem{x}_j : j \in J\} 
e \emptyset . Take an affine dependence and separate its positive coefficients from the rest. Moving the negative terms across the equation gives an equation between a positive combination of some points and a positive combination of the others, with the same total weight on each side, because the coefficients add up to zero. Divide by that total, and each side becomes a convex combination. By @lem-affine-dependence (b), the list (\elem{x}_1, \dots, \elem{x}_m) is affinely dependent: there are \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m, not all zero, with \sum_i\lambda_i\elem{x}_i = \elem{0} and \sum_i\lambda_i = 0. Let I = \{i : \lambda_i > 0\} and J = \{j : \lambda_j \le 0\}, which are disjoint with union \{1, \dots, m\}. Since the \lambda_i add up to 0 and are not all zero, some \lambda_i is positive and some is negative, so neither I nor J is empty. Put \sigma = \sum_{i \in I}\lambda_i > 0; then \sum_{j \in J}(-\lambda_j) = \sigma as well, since the total is 0. Moving the terms indexed by J across and dividing by \sigma, \elem{y} \coloneqq \sum_{i \in I}  rac{\lambda_i}{\sigma}\,\elem{x}_i = \sum_{j \in J}  rac{-\lambda_j}{\sigma}\,\elem{x}_j . On the left the coefficients are positive and add up to 1; on the right they are \ge 0 and add up to 1. So \elem{y} lies in both hulls, by @thm-convex-hull-combinations. This proves the theorem. A partition as in the theorem is a Radon partition. In the plane, four points in general position (no three on a line) either have one inside the triangle of the other three, or they form a quadrilateral whose two diagonals cross; @exr-caratheodory-b2 finds the partition in each case. The count n + 2 cannot be lowered: the n + 1 points \cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n have no Radon partition (@exr-caratheodory-c3). Helly’s theorem turns the counting around. Instead of asking how many points a hull needs, it asks how many sets of a family must be checked to know that all of them have a common point. Checking pairs is not enough, since three lines in the plane can meet pairwise in three different points; checking triples in the plane is. [Helly’s Theorem] Let V be a real vector space with \dim V = n, and let C_1, \dots, C_m be convex subsets of V, with m \ge n + 1. If every n + 1 of the sets have a point in common, then all m of them have a point in common. Induction on the number of sets. Given m \ge n + 2 sets, the inductive hypothesis provides, for each i, a point \elem{x}_i lying in every set except possibly C_i. That is m \ge n + 2 points, so Radon’s theorem splits them into two groups whose hulls meet at some \elem{y}. Any one set C_k misses at most one point, \elem{x}_k, and that point lies in only one of the two groups; the other group lies entirely in C_k, and so does its hull, which contains \elem{y}. We use induction on m. For m = n + 1, the hypothesis applied to all m sets is the conclusion. Let m \ge n + 2, and suppose the theorem holds for families of m - 1 convex sets. For each i = 1, \dots, m, the family \{C_k : k 
e i\} has m - 1 \ge n + 1 members, and every n + 1 of them have a common point by hypothesis. By the inductive hypothesis, there is a point \elem{x}_i with \elem{x}_i \in C_k \quad	ext{for every } k 
e i . Since m \ge n + 2, @thm-radon splits \{1, \dots, m\} into disjoint nonempty sets I, J and gives a point \elem{y} \in \conv\{\elem{x}_i : i \in I\} \cap \conv\{\elem{x}_j : j \in J\}. Fix k \in \{1, \dots, m\}. If k \in I, then k 
otin J, so every \elem{x}_j with j \in J lies in C_k. Since C_k is convex, @lem-convex-contains-combinations puts every convex combination of these points in C_k, so \conv\{\elem{x}_j : j \in J\} \subseteq C_k by @thm-convex-hull-combinations, and in particular \elem{y} \in C_k. If k \in J, the same argument with I in place of J gives \elem{y} \in C_k. Hence \elem{y} lies in every C_k. This completes the induction. [Helly’s proof run on four half-planes] In

Helly’s theorem is about finite families, and the finiteness cannot simply be dropped. The closed half-lines [k, \infty) \subseteq

Prove that \elem{x}_0, \dots, \elem{x}_n have no Radon partition, so that n + 2 in @thm-radon cannot be lowered. (a) If \sum_i t_i\elem{x}_i = \sum_i t_i'\elem{x}_i with \cvec{t}, \cvec{t}' \in \Delta_{n+1}, then \sum_i (t_i - t_i')\elem{x}_i = \elem{0} and \sum_i (t_i - t_i') = 1 - 1 = 0. By affine independence every t_i - t_i' = 0. (b) The point has the expression with all weights 	frac1{n+1}. A convex combination of n of the points is an expression of the form in (a) with the omitted point given weight 0. By the uniqueness in (a), it would have to coincide with the all-	frac1{n+1} expression, which has no zero weight. (c) Suppose I, J are disjoint, nonempty, and \sum_{i \in I} a_i\elem{x}_i = \sum_{j \in J} b_j\elem{x}_j with nonnegative weights, each family adding up to 1. Then \sum_{i \in I} a_i\elem{x}_i - \sum_{j \in J} b_j\elem{x}_j = \elem{0} is a relation among the \elem{x}_i whose coefficients add up to 1 - 1 = 0; an index lying in neither set gets coefficient 0, and no index lies in both, since I \cap J = \emptyset. By affine independence, all these coefficients are 0, so every a_i = 0, contradicting \sum_{i \in I} a_i = 1. Hence no Radon partition exists.

title: 18.3 Separating Hyperplanes
content:
Separating Hyperplanes Sections 01 and 02 looked at a convex set from the inside: which combinations of its points it contains, and how few points a combination needs. This section looks at it from the outside. A point that is not in a closed convex set can be cut off from it by a hyperplane, a set can be touched at its edge by a hyperplane that leaves the whole set on one side, and two disjoint convex sets can be pulled apart by one. All three facts come from a single construction, the point of the set nearest to a given point, and that construction is Chapter 11’s orthogonal projection with the subspace replaced by a convex set. Throughout, V is a finite-dimensional real inner product space, with inner product \inner{\cdot}{\cdot} (@def-inner-product), induced norm 
orm{\cdot} (@def-induced-norm), and n = \dim V. A sequence converges, \elem{x}_k 	o \elem{x}, when 
orm{\elem{x}_k - \elem{x}} 	o 0; closed means closed in the sense of @def-closed-set, so that a closed set contains the limit of every convergent sequence of its points. A set is compact if every sequence in it has a subsequence converging to a point of the set; this is the word of @cor-closed-bounded-compact, which says that every closed bounded subset of V is compact. The field is 
R because the whole section is about inequalities. The nearest point of a closed convex set Chapter 11 answered a question about subspaces: given \elem{v} and a finite-dimensional subspace U, which vector of U is closest to \elem{v}? @thm-best-approximation said there is exactly one, the orthogonal projection P_U\elem{v}, and that \elem{v} - P_U\elem{v} is perpendicular to U. Now replace U by a set with less structure, such as a disc, a box, or a half-plane, and ask the same question. Two small experiments in 
R^2 show which hypotheses the answer needs. - The open disc \{\cvec{y} : 
orm{\cvec{y}} < 1\} and the point \cvec{x} = (2, 0). The points (1 - 1/k, 0) of the disc come closer and closer to \cvec{x}, but the distance 1 is never reached, since the only candidate (1, 0) is missing. There is no nearest point. The set is convex but not closed. - The circle \{\cvec{y} : 
orm{\cvec{y}} = 1\} and the point \cvec{x} = \cvec{0}. Every point of the circle is at distance 1, so every point is a nearest point. The set is closed but not convex. So we ask for both properties, and then everything works. [Nearest Point Theorem] Let C be a nonempty, closed, convex subset of V, and let \elem{x} \in V. (a) There is exactly one point \elem{p} \in C with 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}} \le 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}} for every \elem{y} \in C. (b) A point \elem{p} \in C is this nearest point if and only if \inner{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}{\elem{y} - \elem{p}} \le 0 \qquad 	ext{for every } \elem{y} \in C . {#eq-variational-inequality} The nearest point is written P_C(\elem{x}), and the map P_C \colon V 	o C is the projection onto C. The number d(\elem{x}, C) = 
orm{\elem{x} - P_C(\elem{x})} is the distance from \elem{x} to C. Three jobs, three tools. ① Existence: a nearest point is a minimum of the continuous function \elem{y} \mapsto 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}}, and a minimum exists on a compact set; C itself may be unbounded, so cut it down to the part of C within a fixed distance of \elem{x}. ② The inequality @eq-variational-inequality is the first-order condition: slide from \elem{p} a little way towards another point \elem{y} of C, which convexity allows, and ask that the distance not decrease. ③ Read backwards, the inequality says that the angle at \elem{p} between \elem{x} - \elem{p} and \elem{y} - \elem{p} is at least a right angle, and expanding 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}}^2 then gives 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}}^2 \ge 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}^2 + 
orm{\elem{y} - \elem{p}}^2. That inequality proves both that \elem{p} is nearest and that nothing else is. Existence. Since C 
e \emptyset, pick \elem{y}_0 \in C and put R = 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}_0}. Let K = \{\elem{y} \in C : 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}} \le R\} . Then \elem{y}_0 \in K, and K is bounded, since 
orm{\elem{y}} \le 
orm{\elem{x}} + 
orm{\elem{y} - \elem{x}} \le 
orm{\elem{x}} + R for \elem{y} \in K by @cor-triangle-inequality. It is closed: if \elem{y}_k \in K and \elem{y}_k 	o \elem{y}, then \elem{y} \in C because C is closed, and 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}} \le 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}_k} + 
orm{\elem{y}_k - \elem{y}} \le R + 
orm{\elem{y}_k - \elem{y}} for every k; the right-hand side tends to R, and a nonstrict inequality survives a limit, so 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}} \le R. By @cor-closed-bounded-compact, the form in which Chapter 16 carried the compactness of closed bounded sets, fact (A3) of Chapter 16’s introduction, over to every finite-dimensional space, K is compact. The function f(\elem{y}) = 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}} is continuous, since \lvert f(\elem{y}) - f(\elem{y}')vert \le 
orm{\elem{y} - \elem{y}'} by @lem-reverse-triangle-norm. By the extreme value theorem, fact (A4) of Chapter 16’s introduction, f attains a minimum on K at some \elem{p} \in K. Every \elem{y} \in C \setminus K has f(\elem{y}) > R \ge f(\elem{p}). So 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}} \le 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}} for every \elem{y} \in C. (b), (\Rightarrow). Let \elem{p} be a nearest point and let \elem{y} \in C. For 0 < t \le 1, the point \elem{p} + t(\elem{y} - \elem{p}) = (1 - t)\elem{p} + t\elem{y} lies in C by @def-convex-set. Hence, expanding with @thm-norm-properties (c) over 
R, 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}^2 \le 
orm{(\elem{x} - \elem{p}) - t(\elem{y} - \elem{p})}^2 = 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}^2 - 2t\inner{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}{\elem{y} - \elem{p}} + t^2
orm{\elem{y} - \elem{p}}^2 . Cancel 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}^2 and divide by 2t > 0: \inner{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}{\elem{y} - \elem{p}} \le 	frac{t}{2}
orm{\elem{y} - \elem{p}}^2. This holds for every t = 1/k, and letting k 	o \infty gives @eq-variational-inequality. (b), (\Leftarrow), and uniqueness. Let \elem{p} \in C satisfy @eq-variational-inequality, and let \elem{y} \in C. The same expansion with t = 1 gives  egin{aligned} 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}}^2 &= 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}^2 - 2\inner{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}{\elem{y} - \elem{p}} + 
orm{\elem{y} - \elem{p}}^2 \ &\ge 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}^2 + 
orm{\elem{y} - \elem{p}}^2 . \end{aligned} 	ag{$\ast$} So 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}} \ge 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}, and \elem{p} is a nearest point. Finally, the nearest point \elem{p} found in the existence step satisfies @eq-variational-inequality by (\Rightarrow), so (\ast) applies to it; for \elem{y} \in C with \elem{y} 
e \elem{p} it gives 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{y}}^2 \ge 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}^2 + 
orm{\elem{y} - \elem{p}}^2 > 
orm{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}^2, and \elem{y} is not a nearest point. This proves the theorem. The inequality (\ast) is Pythagoras with the equality relaxed to an inequality. That is exactly the relation with Chapter 11, and it deserves to be said precisely. This theorem generalizes @thm-best-approximation. Let C = U be a subspace of V. It is convex, and closed by @prp-closed-open-basics (c). For \elem{p} \in U, the vector \elem{y} - \elem{p} runs over all of U as \elem{y} does, and with each \elem{u} \in U it also takes the value -\elem{u}. So @eq-variational-inequality says \inner{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}{\elem{u}} \le 0 and -\inner{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}{\elem{u}} \le 0, that is, \inner{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}{\elem{u}} = 0 \qquad 	ext{for every } \elem{u} \in U . For a subspace the variational inequality becomes an equality, the statement \elem{x} - \elem{p} \in U^{\perp}. Then \elem{x} = \elem{p} + (\elem{x} - \elem{p}) is the splitting of @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (a), so P_C(\elem{x}) = P_U\elem{x} by @def-orthogonal-projection, and (\ast) becomes the equation of @thm-pythagoras used in the proof of @thm-best-approximation. The projection onto a closed convex set is the orthogonal projection with “perpendicular” weakened to “at an obtuse angle”. [Three projections] Find P_C(\elem{x}) in each case, and check @eq-variational-inequality. 1. C is the closed unit ball \{\elem{y} : 
orm{\elem{y}} \le 1\} of V, and 
orm{\elem{x}} > 1. 2. C is the box [0,1]^3 = \{\cvec{y} \in 
R^3 : 0 \le y_i \le 1 	ext{ for each } i\} with the dot product, and \cvec{x} = (3, -1, 2). 3. C is the half-space \{\elem{y} : \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y}} \le c\}, where \elem{a} 
e \elem{0}, and \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x}} > c. (a) P_C(\elem{x}) = \elem{x}/
orm{\elem{x}}. With \elem{p} = \elem{x}/
orm{\elem{x}} we have 
orm{\elem{p}} = 1 and \elem{x} - \elem{p} = (
orm{\elem{x}} - 1)\elem{p}, so for \elem{y} \in C \inner{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}{\elem{y} - \elem{p}} = (
orm{\elem{x}} - 1) igl(\inner{\elem{p}}{\elem{y}} - 1 igr) \le 0 , because 
orm{\elem{x}} - 1 > 0 and \inner{\elem{p}}{\elem{y}} \le 
orm{\elem{p}}
orm{\elem{y}} \le 1 by @thm-cauchy-schwarz. By @thm-nearest-point (b), \elem{p} is the nearest point, and d(\elem{x}, C) = 
orm{\elem{x}} - 1. (b) Clamp each coordinate into [0, 1]: \cvec{p} = (1, 0, 1). Then \cvec{x} - \cvec{p} = (2, -1, 1) and, for \cvec{y} \in C, \inner{\cvec{x} - \cvec{p}}{\cvec{y} - \cvec{p}} = 2(y_1 - 1) - y_2 + (y_3 - 1) \le 0 , since y_1 \le 1, y_2 \ge 0, and y_3 \le 1. So P_C(\cvec{x}) = (1, 0, 1) and d(\cvec{x}, C) = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt6. The vector \cvec{a} = \cvec{x} - \cvec{p} = (2, -1, 1) also cuts \cvec{x} off: \inner{\cvec{a}}{\cvec{x}} = 9 and 
orm{\cvec{a}}^2 = 6, so c = \inner{\cvec{a}}{\cvec{x}} - 	frac12
orm{\cvec{a}}^2 = 6, and the plane 2y_1 - y_2 + y_3 = 6 strictly separates C from \cvec{x}, since its left side is at most 2 + 0 + 1 = 3 on C and equals 9 at \cvec{x}. @thm-separation-point below turns this recipe into a theorem. (c) Put \lambda = (\inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x}} - c)/
orm{\elem{a}}^2, which is positive, and \elem{p} = \elem{x} - \lambda\elem{a}. Then \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{p}} = \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x}} - \lambda
orm{\elem{a}}^2 = c, so \elem{p} \in C, and for \elem{y} \in C \inner{\elem{x} - \elem{p}}{\elem{y} - \elem{p}} = \lambda igl(\inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y}} - c igr) \le 0 . So P_C(\elem{x}) = \elem{x} - \lambda\elem{a}: drop the perpendicular to the boundary hyperplane, as Chapter 11 would have done. The distance is \lambda
orm{\elem{a}} = (\inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x}} - c)/
orm{\elem{a}}. Two degenerate cases fix the scale. If C = \{\elem{c}\} is a single point, then P_C(\elem{x}) = \elem{c} for every \elem{x}, and @eq-variational-inequality holds because \elem{y} - \elem{p} = \elem{0}. If C = V, then P_C is the identity. In every case P_C(\elem{x}) = \elem{x} exactly when \elem{x} \in C. Where did the proof of @thm-nearest-point use that C is closed, and where that it is convex? Match each use with one of the two failing experiments before the theorem. Closedness was used in the existence step, to make K closed and hence compact; the open disc fails there, since the minimizing candidates converge to a point outside it. Convexity was used in (\Rightarrow), to know that (1 - t)\elem{p} + t\elem{y} \in C, and uniqueness rests on that step. The circle fails there: with \cvec{x} = \cvec{0}, \cvec{p} = \cvec{e}_1, and \cvec{y} = -\cvec{e}_1, \inner{\cvec{x} - \cvec{p}}{\cvec{y} - \cvec{p}} = 2 > 0. The proof needs an inner product, and uniqueness can fail without one. In 
R^2 with 
orm{\cdot}_\infty, let C be the x_1-axis, which is closed and convex, and \cvec{x} = (0, 1). Then 
orm{\cvec{x} - (t, 0)}_\infty = \max(\lvert tvert, 1) = 1 for every t \in [-1, 1], so there is a whole segment of nearest points. Existence survives, since its proof used only (N3) and compactness. Uniqueness does not, because it came from the expansion of 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}}^2, which is available only for induced norms. Hyperplanes and half-spaces A hyperplane in the sense of Chapter 5 passes through \elem{0}: it is a subspace of codimension 1 (@def-hyperplane). To separate sets we need translates of hyperplanes, and Chapter 5 §06 called a coset \elem{p} + H of a hyperplane H (@def-coset) an affine hyperplane. In an inner product space these have a concrete form. By @thm-hyperplane-kernel-functional, H = \ker\varphi for a nonzero \varphi \in V^{*}; by @thm-riesz-representation, \varphi = \inner{\cdot}{\elem{a}} for a nonzero \elem{a} \in V. Hence \elem{p} + H = \{\elem{y} \in V : \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y}} = c\}, \qquad c = \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{p}} , and conversely every such set with \elem{a} 
e \elem{0} is an affine hyperplane, with \elem{a} as a normal vector. It cuts V into the two closed half-spaces \{\inner{\elem{a}}{\cdot} \le c\} and \{\inner{\elem{a}}{\cdot} \ge c\}. Both are convex, because \inner{\elem{a}}{\cdot} is linear, and closed by @prp-closed-open-basics (c). [Separation by a Hyperplane] Let A, B \subseteq V be nonempty. A nonzero vector \elem{a} \in V and a number c \in 
R separate A and B if \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x}} \le c \le \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y}} \qquad 	ext{for all } \elem{x} \in A 	ext{ and all } \elem{y} \in B . They strictly separate A and B if in addition there is a real \varepsilon > 0 with \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x}} \le c - \varepsilon and \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y}} \ge c + \varepsilon for all \elem{x} \in A, \elem{y} \in B. In words: A lies in one closed half-space of \{\inner{\elem{a}}{\cdot} = c\} and B in the other, and strict separation puts a slab of width 2\varepsilon/
orm{\elem{a}} between them. Replacing (\elem{a}, c) by (-\elem{a}, -c) swaps the roles of A and B. With \elem{a} = \elem{0} and c = 0 any two sets would be “separated”. Cutting off a point The first consequence of @thm-nearest-point is the one the chapter uses most. If \elem{x} is not in C, the vector from P_C(\elem{x}) to \elem{x} is a normal vector for a hyperplane that cuts \elem{x} off. [Separating a Point from a Closed Convex Set] Let C \subseteq V be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \elem{x} 
otin C. Put \elem{a} = \elem{x} - P_C(\elem{x}). Then \elem{a} 
e \elem{0} and \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y}} \le \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x}} - 
orm{\elem{a}}^2 \qquad 	ext{for every } \elem{y} \in C . In particular \elem{a} and c = \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x}} - 	frac12
orm{\elem{a}}^2 strictly separate C and \{\elem{x}\}. Write \elem{p} = P_C(\elem{x}). Since \elem{p} \in C and \elem{x} 
otin C, \elem{a} = \elem{x} - \elem{p} 
e \elem{0}. For \elem{y} \in C, @eq-variational-inequality gives \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y} - \elem{p}} \le 0, hence \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y}} \le \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{p}} = \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x}} - \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x} - \elem{p}} = \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x}} - 
orm{\elem{a}}^2 . With \varepsilon = 	frac12
orm{\elem{a}}^2 > 0 this reads \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y}} \le c - \varepsilon, while \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x}} = c + \varepsilon. This proves the theorem. In the picture after @thm-nearest-point, the hyperplane of the theorem is the line parallel to the dashed one, halfway between P_C(\elem{x}) and \elem{x}. The theorem turns into a description of a closed convex set from the outside. Sections 01 and 02 built convex sets up from points; this builds them down from half-spaces. [A Closed Convex Set Is an Intersection of Half-Spaces] Every nonempty closed convex subset C of V is the intersection of all the closed half-spaces \{\elem{y} : \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y}} \le c\}, with \elem{a} 
e \elem{0}, that contain C. Each of these half-spaces contains C, so C lies in their intersection. Conversely, let \elem{x} 
otin C. By @thm-separation-point, with \elem{a} = \elem{x} - P_C(\elem{x}) 
e \elem{0}, the half-space \{\elem{y} : \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y}} \le \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{x}} - 
orm{\elem{a}}^2\} contains C but not \elem{x}. So \elem{x} is not in the intersection. (If C = V, the family of half-spaces is empty and its intersection is V by convention.) The corollary has a converse that is immediate: an intersection of closed half-spaces is closed and convex, because each half-space is and both properties pass to intersections. So the closed convex sets are exactly the intersections of closed half-spaces. §04 turns this into a formula, the support function, and §09 studies the case of finitely many half-spaces. Supporting hyperplanes A point on the edge of C cannot be cut off, because it belongs to C. The best one can hope for is a hyperplane through the point with all of C on one side, touching C without cutting it. To say “on the edge” we need two more words. [Interior Point, Closure, Boundary Point] Let S \subseteq V. A point \elem{x} \in V is an interior point of S if there is a real r > 0 such that every \elem{y} with 
orm{\elem{y} - \elem{x}} < r lies in S; the set of interior points is written \interior{S}. The closure \closure{S} of S is the set of limits of all convergent sequences of points of S. A boundary point of S is a point of \closure{S} that is not an interior point of S. Constant sequences show S \subseteq \closure{S}, and by @def-closed-set, S is closed exactly when \closure{S} = S. By @thm-norm-equivalence neither notion depends on the norm used: a ball of radius r for one norm contains a ball of positive radius for any other. For the closed unit disc of 
R^2, the interior points are those with 
orm{\cvec{x}} < 1, and the boundary points form the unit circle. A segment in 
R^2 has no interior points at all, so every one of its points is a boundary point; that is the case the next lemma isolates. [A Convex Set Is Solid or Flat] Let V 
e \{\elem{0}\} and let C \subseteq V be nonempty and convex. Then either C has an interior point, or C lies in an affine hyperplane: there are \elem{a} 
e \elem{0} and c \in 
R with \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y}} = c for every \elem{y} \in C. Fix \elem{c}_0 \in C and look at the directions \elem{y} - \elem{c}_0 available inside C. If they span a proper subspace, a normal vector to that subspace is the \elem{a} we want. If they span V, then C contains n + 1 points in general position, hence the solid simplex they span, and the center of a solid simplex is an interior point: a point of the simplex is \sum_i t_i \elem{v}_i with t_i \ge 0 summing to 1, the t_i are determined by the point and depend continuously on it, and at the center they are all equal and positive, so every small enough move keeps them positive. Fix \elem{c}_0 \in C and let W = \Span\{\elem{y} - \elem{c}_0 : \elem{y} \in C\}. Case 1: W 
e V. Then \dim W < n, so \dim W^{\perp} = n - \dim W \ge 1 by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (c), and there is \elem{a} 
e \elem{0} in W^{\perp}. For \elem{y} \in C, \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y} - \elem{c}_0} = 0, that is, \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{y}} = \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{c}_0}. Take c = \inner{\elem{a}}{\elem{c}_0}. Case 2: W = V. Choose a linearly independent list (\elem{y}_1 - \elem{c}_0, \dots, \elem{y}_m - \elem{c}_0) with every \elem{y}_i \in C and m as large as possible; m \le n by @thm-size-bounds. Every vector \elem{y} - \elem{c}_0 with \elem{y} \in C lies in the span of this list, since otherwise @lem-append-independent would lengthen it. So the span contains every generator of W, hence equals V, and the list is a basis; thus m = n. Let \varphi_i(\elem{v}) be the i-th coordinate of \elem{v} in this basis, a linear functional by @thm-coordinates-linear, and write \varphi_i = \inner{\cdot}{\elem{w}_i} by @thm-riesz-representation. Put \mu_i(\elem{v}) = \varphi_i(\elem{v} - \elem{c}_0). Then for every \elem{v} \in V, \elem{v} = \Bigl(1 - \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_i(\elem{v})\Bigr)\elem{c}_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_i(\elem{v})\,\elem{y}_i , and when \mu_i(\elem{v}) \ge 0 for every i and \sum_i\mu_i(\elem{v}) \le 1, this is a convex combination of points of C, hence a point of C: by @thm-convex-hull-combinations it lies in \conv C, and \conv C = C by @def-convex-hull, since C is itself a convex set containing C. Let \elem{z} = \elem{c}_0 + 	frac{1}{n+1}\sum_i(\elem{y}_i - \elem{c}_0), so that \mu_i(\elem{z}) = 	frac{1}{n+1} for every i. Each \elem{w}_i 
e \elem{0}, because \varphi_i(\elem{y}_i - \elem{c}_0) = 1; put L = \max_i
orm{\elem{w}_i} > 0 and r = 1/ igl(n(n+1)L igr). If 
orm{\elem{v} - \elem{z}} < r, then by @thm-cauchy-schwarz \lvert\mu_i(\elem{v}) - \mu_i(\elem{z})vert = \lvert\inner{\elem{v} - \elem{z}}{\elem{w}_i}vert \le L
orm{\elem{v} - \elem{z}} <  rac{1}{n(n+1)} , so \mu_i(\elem{v}) > 	frac{1}{n+1} - 	frac{1}{n(n+1)} \ge 0 and \sum_i\mu_i(\elem{v}) < 	frac{n}{n+1} + 	frac{1}{n+1} = 1. Hence \elem{v} \in C, and \elem{z} is an interior point of C. The second ingredient says that from an interior point one can see the whole closure. [Closure and Interior of a Convex Set] Let C \subseteq V be convex. 1. \closure{C} is closed and convex. 2. If \elem{z} \in \interior{C}, \elem{w} \in \closure{C}, and 0 < t \le 1, then (1 - t)\elem{w} + t\elem{z} \in \interior{C}. Part (a) pushes limits through: a limit of limits is a limit, and a convex combination of limits is the limit of convex combinations. For (b), picture a small ball around \elem{z} inside C, and the cone from \elem{w} over it. The cone contains a smaller ball around (1 - t)\elem{w} + t\elem{z}; since \elem{w} is only a limit, replace it by a nearby point \elem{w}' of C, which shrinks the ball by half. (a) Let \elem{x}_k \in \closure{C} with \elem{x}_k 	o \elem{x}. Each \elem{x}_k is a limit of points of C, so there is \elem{c}_k \in C with 
orm{\elem{c}_k - \elem{x}_k} < 1/k. Then

title: 18.4 Gauges, Support Functions, and Dual Norms
content:
Gauges, Support Functions, and Dual Norms Chapter 16 §01 observed that the closed unit ball of every norm is convex and symmetric, and left the converse alone: does every convex, symmetric set arise as the unit ball of some norm? This section answers yes, by reading a norm off a convex set from the inside, the gauge. It then reads a function off a convex set from the outside, the support function, which turns §03’s description of a closed convex set by half-spaces into a formula. Applied to a unit ball, the support function is the dual norm, the measurement Chapter 16 never gave to a linear functional, and the last part of the section proves that taking the dual twice returns the norm we started with. Throughout, the field is 
R, and we work in 
R^n, n \ge 1, with the dot product \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y} and its norm 
orm{\cdot}_2. So everything proved in §03 is available, with V = 
R^n. A symbol 
orm{\cdot} without a subscript is an arbitrary norm on 
R^n in the sense of @def-norm, and B is its closed unit ball (@def-unit-ball). Interior points are meant in the sense of @def-interior-point, which does not depend on the norm. For a set K and a real t, we write tK = \{t\cvec{x} : \cvec{x} \in K\}. Gauges Every norm can be read off its unit ball. By (N2), for t > 0 we have 
orm{\cvec{x}} \le t exactly when 
orm{\cvec{x}/t} \le 1, that is, when \cvec{x} \in tB. Hence 
orm{\cvec{x}} = \inf\{t > 0 : \cvec{x} \in tB\} , the inflation factor by which B has to be blown up before it reaches \cvec{x}. The right-hand side makes sense for sets that are not unit balls, and this is the formula to study. The gauge of a convex set measures a vector by how far the set must be inflated to reach it. [Gauge] Let K \subseteq 
R^n be convex, with \cvec{0} an interior point of K. The gauge (or Minkowski functional) of K is the function p_K \colon 
R^n 	o 
R given by p_K(\cvec{x}) = \inf\{t > 0 : \cvec{x} \in tK\} . The infimum exists. Choose r > 0 with every \cvec{y} satisfying 
orm{\cvec{y}}_2 < r in K. If t > 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2/r, then 
orm{\cvec{x}/t}_2 < r, so \cvec{x}/t \in K and \cvec{x} \in tK. So the set of admissible t is nonempty, and it is bounded below by 0; by the completeness of 
R, fact (A1) of Chapter 16’s introduction, it has a greatest lower bound, and 0 \le p_K(\cvec{x}) \le 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2/r \qquad 	ext{for every } \cvec{x} \in 
R^n . The interior point is what makes p_K finite. For the segment [-\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1] \subseteq 
R^2, which has no interior points, the vector \cvec{e}_2 lies in no multiple tK, and the formula would give the infimum of the empty set. [Properties of the Gauge] Let K \subseteq 
R^n be convex with \cvec{0} an interior point, and let \cvec{x} \in 
R^n. 1. \cvec{x} \in tK for every t > p_K(\cvec{x}). 2. p_K is sublinear (@def-sublinear-functional). 3. \{\cvec{x} : p_K(\cvec{x}) < 1\} \subseteq K \subseteq \{\cvec{x} : p_K(\cvec{x}) \le 1\}. 4. If K is closed, then K = \{\cvec{x} : p_K(\cvec{x}) \le 1\}. Everything comes from one observation, (a): since \cvec{0} \in K and K is convex, shrinking a point of K towards \cvec{0} keeps it in K, so the admissible t form a whole half-line. Subadditivity is then convexity applied to \cvec{x}/s and \cvec{y}/t with weights proportional to s and t. (a) Let t > p_K(\cvec{x}). By the definition of an infimum there is s with p_K(\cvec{x}) \le s < t and \cvec{x} \in sK, so \cvec{x}/s \in K. Since \cvec{0} \in K and K is convex,  rac{\cvec{x}}{t} =  rac{s}{t}\cdot rac{\cvec{x}}{s} + \Bigl(1 -  rac{s}{t}\Bigr)\cvec{0} \in K , that is, \cvec{x} \in tK. (b) Let \lambda > 0. Since \lambda\cvec{x} \in tK exactly when \cvec{x} \in (t/\lambda)K, the admissible t for \lambda\cvec{x} are \lambda times those for \cvec{x}, and p_K(\lambda\cvec{x}) = \lambda p_K(\cvec{x}). For \lambda = 0, \cvec{0} \in tK for every t > 0, so p_K(\cvec{0}) = 0. For subadditivity, let \varepsilon > 0, s = p_K(\cvec{x}) + \varepsilon and t = p_K(\cvec{y}) + \varepsilon. By (a), \cvec{x}/s and \cvec{y}/t lie in K, so by convexity  rac{\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}}{s + t} =  rac{s}{s + t}\cdot rac{\cvec{x}}{s} +  rac{t}{s + t}\cdot rac{\cvec{y}}{t} \in K . Hence p_K(\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}) \le s + t = p_K(\cvec{x}) + p_K(\cvec{y}) + 2\varepsilon, for every \varepsilon > 0, and so p_K(\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}) \le p_K(\cvec{x}) + p_K(\cvec{y}). (c) If p_K(\cvec{x}) < 1, then \cvec{x} \in 1\cdot K by (a). If \cvec{x} \in K, then t = 1 is admissible, so p_K(\cvec{x}) \le 1. (d) Let p_K(\cvec{x}) \le 1. By (a), \cvec{x} \in (1 + 1/k)K for every k \ge 1, so the points \cvec{x}/(1 + 1/k) lie in K. They converge to \cvec{x}, and K is closed, so \cvec{x} \in K. With (c) this gives K = \{p_K \le 1\}. The gauge of a unit ball is its norm, by the computation that opened this section. A second example: for the rectangle K = [-2, 2] 	imes [-1, 1] \subseteq 
R^2, a vector lies in tK exactly when \lvert x_1vert \le 2t and \lvert x_2vert \le t, so p_K(\cvec{x}) = \max igl(	frac12\lvert x_1vert,\ \lvert x_2vert igr) , a weighted \infty-norm of the kind in @exm-induced-and-weighted-norms (b). At the degenerate extreme, K = 
R^n lies in every tK, and p_K is identically 0: sublinear, but no norm. The next theorem says exactly when a gauge is a norm. Its part (b) records the facts about unit balls that make the match perfect. [Convex Bodies and Norms] 1. Let K \subseteq 
R^n be closed, bounded, convex, and symmetric (-K = K), with \cvec{0} an interior point. Then p_K is a norm on 
R^n, and its closed unit ball is K. 2. Conversely, the closed unit ball B of any norm 
orm{\cdot} on 
R^n is closed, bounded, convex, and symmetric, with \cvec{0} an interior point, and p_B = 
orm{\cdot}. So the norms on 
R^n correspond one to one with the sets described in (a). Sublinearity is two thirds of a norm, and @prp-gauge-properties already has it. The missing third is absolute homogeneity for a scalar c < 0, which is what symmetry buys, and positive definiteness, which is what boundedness buys: a nonzero vector cannot fit inside every shrunken copy tK of a bounded set. Closedness makes the unit ball of p_K equal to K rather than squeezed between the two sets of @prp-gauge-properties (c). (a) By @prp-gauge-properties (b), p_K is sublinear, which gives (N3) and (N2) for c \ge 0. For c < 0, symmetry gives \cvec{x} \in tK if and only if -\cvec{x} \in t(-K) = tK, so p_K(-\cvec{x}) = p_K(\cvec{x}) and p_K(c\cvec{x}) = \lvert cvert p_K(-\cvec{x}) = \lvert cvert p_K(\cvec{x}). For (N1), p_K \ge 0 by definition. Let R be such that 
orm{\cvec{y}}_2 \le R for all \cvec{y} \in K. If p_K(\cvec{x}) = 0, then \cvec{x} \in tK for every t > 0 by @prp-gauge-properties (a), so 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le tR for every t > 0, and \cvec{x} = \cvec{0}. So p_K is a norm, and its closed unit ball \{p_K \le 1\} is K by @prp-gauge-properties (d). (b) Chapter 16 §01 showed, right after @def-unit-ball, that B is convex and symmetric. By @thm-norm-equivalence there are constants 0 < m \le M with m
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le 
orm{\cvec{x}} \le M
orm{\cvec{x}}_2. If 
orm{\cvec{x}} \le 1, then 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le 1/m, so B is bounded. If 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 < 1/M, then 
orm{\cvec{x}} < 1, so \cvec{0} is an interior point. If \cvec{x}_k \in B and \cvec{x}_k 	o \cvec{x}, then \lvert
orm{\cvec{x}_k} - 
orm{\cvec{x}}vert \le 
orm{\cvec{x}_k - \cvec{x}} \le M
orm{\cvec{x}_k - \cvec{x}}_2 	o 0 by @lem-reverse-triangle-norm, and 
orm{\cvec{x}} \le 1 because a nonstrict inequality survives the limit; so B is closed. Finally, \cvec{x} \in tB exactly when t \ge 
orm{\cvec{x}}, for t > 0, so p_B(\cvec{x}) = 
orm{\cvec{x}} (for \cvec{x} = \cvec{0}, the infimum of all t > 0 is 0). This proves the theorem. This is the converse of Chapter 16’s “every unit ball is convex”. There, a norm produced a convex symmetric set, the ball of @def-unit-ball, and convexity was what the triangle inequality bought. Here a convex symmetric set produces a norm, and the triangle inequality is what convexity buys: the subadditivity step in @prp-gauge-properties (b) is the convexity of K, used once. Norms and closed bounded symmetric convex sets with \cvec{0} inside are the same objects seen two ways, one analytic, one geometric. Each hypothesis in (a) carries one clause of @def-norm, and dropping one breaks exactly that clause. - Drop symmetry. The triangle T = \{\cvec{x} : x_1 \ge -1,\ x_2 \ge -1,\ x_1 + x_2 \le 1\}, with vertices (-1,-1), (2,-1), (-1,2), is closed, bounded, and convex, and contains the disc of radius 	frac12 about \cvec{0}. A vector lies in tT exactly when -x_1 \le t, -x_2 \le t, and x_1 + x_2 \le t, so p_T(\cvec{x}) = \max igl(-x_1,\ -x_2,\ x_1 + x_2 igr) , which is never negative, since the three numbers add up to 0. This is sublinear and satisfies (N1), but p_T igl((1,1) igr) = 2 while p_T igl((-1,-1) igr) = 1, so (N2) fails at c = -1. - Drop boundedness. The strip S = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^2 : \lvert x_2vert \le 1\} is closed, convex, and symmetric, and p_S(\cvec{x}) = \lvert x_2vert. Now (N2) and (N3) hold but (N1) fails: p_S(\cvec{e}_1) = 0. This is the seminorm of @exm-norm-non-example (b). Let K be the open unit disc \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^2 : 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 < 1\}, which is bounded, symmetric, and convex (if 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2, 
orm{\cvec{y}}_2 < 1 and 0 \le t \le 1, then 
orm{(1 - t)\cvec{x} + t\cvec{y}}_2 \le (1 - t)
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 + t
orm{\cvec{y}}_2 < 1) but not closed. What is p_K, and what is its closed unit ball? For t > 0, \cvec{x} \in tK exactly when 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 < t, so the admissible t form the interval (
orm{\cvec{x}}_2, \infty) and p_K(\cvec{x}) = 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2. So p_K is a norm after all, but its closed unit ball is the closed disc, not K. Closedness is used only for the last claim of @thm-gauge-is-norm (a), through @prp-gauge-properties (d). Support functions §03 described a closed convex set from the outside: by @cor-closed-convex-halfspaces it is the intersection of the closed half-spaces containing it. For a fixed normal vector \cvec{y}, the half-spaces \{\cvec{x} : \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} \le c\} containing K are those with c \ge \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} for every \cvec{x} \in K, and the tightest of them has c = \sup_{\cvec{x} \in K}\inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}}. That number, as a function of the direction \cvec{y}, deserves a name. The support function of a set records, for each direction, how far the set reaches in that direction. [Support Function] Let K \subseteq 
R^n be nonempty. The support function of K is h_K(\cvec{y}) = \sup_{\cvec{x} \in K}\inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} , \qquad \cvec{y} \in 
R^n , with the value +\infty when the numbers \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}}, \cvec{x} \in K, are unbounded above. When the numbers are bounded above, the supremum exists by (A1). If K is bounded, say 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le R on K, then \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} \le R
orm{\cvec{y}}_2 by @thm-cauchy-schwarz, so h_K is real-valued. If K is compact, the supremum is a maximum by the extreme value theorem, fact (A4) of Chapter 16’s introduction, since \cvec{x} \mapsto \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} is continuous: \lvert\inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} - \inner{\cvec{x}'}{\cvec{y}}vert \le 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{x}'}_2
orm{\cvec{y}}_2. For a unit vector \cvec{y}, the hyperplane \{\inner{\cdot}{\cvec{y}} = h_K(\cvec{y})\} is the one with normal \cvec{y} that touches K from outside, and h_K(\cvec{y}) is its signed distance from \cvec{0}. Some examples, each computed from the definition. - A point. h_{\{\cvec{x}_0\}}(\cvec{y}) = \inner{\cvec{x}_0}{\cvec{y}}, a linear function. - The Euclidean ball. h_{B_2}(\cvec{y}) = 
orm{\cvec{y}}_2: at most that by @thm-cauchy-schwarz, and attained at \cvec{x} = \cvec{y}/
orm{\cvec{y}}_2 when \cvec{y} 
e \cvec{0}. - The standard simplex \conv\{\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n\}. By @thm-convex-hull-combinations its points are \sum_i t_i\cvec{e}_i with t_i \ge 0 and \sum_i t_i = 1, and \sum_i t_iy_i \le \max_i y_i, with equality at a vertex \cvec{e}_k where y_k is largest. So h(\cvec{y}) = \max_i y_i. - A segment. h_{[-\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1]}(\cvec{y}) = \lvert y_1vert in 
R^2. - An unbounded set. For the half-line \{t\cvec{e}_1 : t \ge 0\}, h(\cvec{y}) = 0 if y_1 \le 0 and h(\cvec{y}) = +\infty if y_1 > 0. [Properties of the Support Function] Let K, L \subseteq 
R^n be nonempty and bounded. 1. h_K is sublinear. 2. If K \subseteq L, then h_K \le h_L. 3. h_{\conv K} = h_K. A supremum of linear functions of \cvec{y} inherits whatever inequalities each of them satisfies, which gives (a) and (b). For (c), a linear function takes on a convex combination a weighted average of its values, and an average never exceeds the largest value. (a) For \cvec{x} \in K, \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y} + \cvec{z}} = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} + \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{z}} \le h_K(\cvec{y}) + h_K(\cvec{z}), and taking the supremum over \cvec{x} gives h_K(\cvec{y} + \cvec{z}) \le h_K(\cvec{y}) + h_K(\cvec{z}). For t > 0, \inner{\cvec{x}}{t\cvec{y}} = t\inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}}, and a positive factor comes out of a supremum; for t = 0 both sides are 0, as K 
e \emptyset. (b) A supremum over a larger set is at least as large. (c) Since K \subseteq \conv K, (b) gives h_K \le h_{\conv K}, once we know \conv K is bounded: it lies in the ball \{
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le R\}, which is convex and contains K (@def-convex-hull). Conversely, by @thm-convex-hull-combinations a point of \conv K is \cvec{x} = \sum_i t_i\cvec{x}_i with \cvec{x}_i \in K, t_i \ge 0, \sum_i t_i = 1, and then \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \sum_i t_i\inner{\cvec{x}_i}{\cvec{y}} \le \sum_i t_i\,h_K(\cvec{y}) = h_K(\cvec{y}) . So h_{\conv K} \le h_K. A support function cannot see gaps. The two-point set \{\cvec{e}_1, -\cvec{e}_1\} and the segment [-\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1] in 
R^2 have the same support function \lvert y_1vert, by @prp-support-function-properties (c). So h_K does not determine K in general; it determines only the convex hull, and the next theorem shows that among closed convex sets it determines the set. Here is the promised formula. It is @cor-closed-convex-halfspaces with the family of half-spaces indexed by their normals. [The Support Function Determines a Closed Convex Set] Let K, L \subseteq 
R^n be nonempty, closed, and convex. Then 1. K = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^n : \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} \le h_K(\cvec{y}) 	ext{ for every } \cvec{y} \in 
R^n\}; 2. K \subseteq L if and only if h_K(\cvec{y}) \le h_L(\cvec{y}) for every \cvec{y}; in particular K = L if and only if h_K = h_L. R^n? What is the dual of that? 4. Which result of §03 does the proof of @thm-dual-dual-norm use, and at which point? 5. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: K^{\circ\circ} = K for every nonempty closed convex K \subseteq 
R^n. (a) For K convex with \cvec{0} an interior point, p_K(\cvec{x}) = \inf\{t > 0 : \cvec{x} \in tK\} (@def-gauge). For K nonempty, h_K(\cvec{y}) = \sup_{\cvec{x} \in K}\inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}}, possibly +\infty (@def-support-function). For a norm 
orm{\cdot} with ball B,

For the segment [-\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_1], h_K(\cvec{y}) = \lvert y_1vert vanishes at \cvec{e}_2. Support functions are sublinear (@prp-support-function-properties (a)) but need not be norms. (c)

orm{\cvec{x}} = 1, to produce a normal \cvec{a} at which the maximum defining 
orm{\cvec{a}}_{*} is attained at \cvec{x}. (e) Incorrect. For K = \{\cvec{e}_1\} in 
R^2, K^{\circ\circ} is the segment [\cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_1]. @thm-bipolar needs \cvec{0} \in K. B. Practice [B1: A weighted norm and its dual] On 
R^2 let N(\cvec{x}) = \max igl(\lvert x_1vert, 2\lvert x_2vert igr). 1. Prove that N_{*}(\cvec{y}) = \lvert y_1vert + 	frac12\lvert y_2vert. 2. Verify @thm-dual-dual-norm for N by computing N_{**} directly. (a) The ball of N is the rectangle \lvert x_1vert \le 1, \lvert x_2vert \le 	frac12. On it, \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} \le \lvert x_1vert\lvert y_1vert + \lvert x_2vert\lvert y_2vert \le \lvert y_1vert + 	frac12\lvert y_2vert. On it, \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} \le \lvert x_1vert\lvert y_1vert + 2\lvert x_2vert\cdot	frac12\lvert y_2vert \le N(\cvec{x}) igl(\lvert y_1vert + 	frac12\lvert y_2vert igr) \le N(\cvec{x}) . So N_{**} = N. [B2: A hexagonal norm] Let K = \{\cvec{x} \in

Justify your answer. (a) K is the intersection of six closed half-planes, such as \{x_1 \le 1\} and \{x_1 - x_2 \ge -1\}, each closed and convex (§03, before @def-separation); so K is closed and convex. It is bounded, since 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le \sqrt2 when \lvert x_1vert, \lvert x_2vert \le 1. It is symmetric, since each condition is unchanged by \cvec{x} \mapsto -\cvec{x}. And if

(b) For t > 0, \cvec{x} \in tK exactly when \cvec{x}/t \in K, that is, when \lvert x_1vert \le t, \lvert x_2vert \le t, and \lvert x_1 - x_2vert \le t. The infimum of such t is M = \max(\lvert x_1vert, \lvert x_2vert, \lvert x_1 - x_2vert) when \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}, and 0 = M when \cvec{x} = \cvec{0}. So p_K igl((2,-1) igr) = \max(2, 1, 3) = 3. (c) No. With \cvec{u} = \cvec{e}_1 and \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_2, p_K(\cvec{u} + \cvec{v}) = \max(1, 1, 0) = 1 and p_K(\cvec{u} - \cvec{v}) = \max(1, 1, 2) = 2, so the left side of the parallelogram law is 1 + 4 = 5, while the right side is 2\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 1 = 4. By @thm-parallelogram-characterization, no inner product induces p_K. [B3: The polar of a triangle] Let K = \conv\{(-1,-1), (2,-1), (-1,2)\} \subseteq 
R^2. 1. Compute h_K(\cvec{e}_1), h_K(-\cvec{e}_1), and h_K igl((1,1) igr). 2. Describe K^{\circ} by three linear inequalities. 3. Show that (-1, 0), (0, -1), and (1, 1) lie in K^{\circ}, and that (1, 0) does not. (a) By @prp-support-function-properties (c), h_K(\cvec{y}) is the largest of \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{y}} over the three vertices \cvec{v}, that is, of -y_1 - y_2, 2y_1 - y_2, -y_1 + 2y_2. So h_K(\cvec{e}_1) = \max(-1, 2, -1) = 2, h_K(-\cvec{e}_1) = \max(1, -2, 1) = 1, and h_K igl((1,1) igr) = \max(-2, 1, 1) = 1. (b) \cvec{y} \in K^{\circ} exactly when h_K(\cvec{y}) \le 1, that is, -y_1 - y_2 \le 1, \qquad 2y_1 - y_2 \le 1, \qquad -y_1 + 2y_2 \le 1 . (c) At (-1, 0) the three left sides are 1, -2, 1; at (0, -1) they are 1, 1, -2; at (1, 1) they are -2, 1, 1. All are \le 1. At (1, 0) the second is 2 > 1, so (1, 0) 
otin K^{\circ}, in agreement with h_K(\cvec{e}_1) = 2. C. Going deeper [C1: The norm from 1 to infinity] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R), and let

orm{\cdot}_1 on

R^n is the same number. 3. Explain why this does not contradict the warning of Chapter 16 §03 that the entrywise maximum is not a matrix norm. (a) By @prp-dual-of-one-two-infinity (b), the dual of 
orm{\cdot}_\infty is 
orm{\cdot}_1, so @prp-operator-norm-bilinear (a) gives
