orm{\cvec{y}}_1 \le 1\}. Write M = \max_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij}vert. For such \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}, \cvec{y}	p\A\cvec{x} = \sum_{i,j}y_ia_{ij}x_j \le M\sum_i\lvert y_ivert\sum_j\lvert x_jvert \le M . If \lvert a_{kl}vert = M, then \cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_l and \cvec{y} = \pm\cvec{e}_k, with the sign of a_{kl}, give \cvec{y}	p\A\cvec{x} = M. So 
orm{\A}_{1	o\infty} = M. (b) By @prp-operator-norm-bilinear (b) with \alpha = 1 and  eta = \infty, 
orm{\A	p}_{ eta*	o\alpha*} = 
orm{\A	p}_{1	o\infty} equals 
orm{\A}_{1	o\infty}, using  eta* = 1 and \alpha* = \infty from @prp-dual-of-one-two-infinity. This is consistent with (a), since \A and \A	p have the same entries. (c) 
orm{\cdot}_{1	o\infty} uses different norms on the source and the target, so the product \A\B of two square matrices is measured by a norm that does not compose: submultiplicativity in @thm-operator-norm-properties (d) needs the target norm of \B to be the source norm of \A. With one norm on M_n(
R) the entrywise maximum is not submultiplicative (@exm-entrywise-max-not-submultiplicative), and nothing here says otherwise. [C2: Equivalence constants dualize] Let N_1, N_2 be norms on 
R^n and 0 < m \le M constants with mN_1(\cvec{x}) \le N_2(\cvec{x}) \le MN_1(\cvec{x}) for every \cvec{x}. 1. Prove that 	frac1M N_{1*}(\cvec{y}) \le N_{2*}(\cvec{y}) \le 	frac1m N_{1*}(\cvec{y}) for every \cvec{y}. 2. Apply (a) to 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 \le \sqrt n\,
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 from @prp-p-norm-inequalities, and compare the result with that proposition. (a) If N_2(\cvec{x}) \le 1, then N_1(\cvec{x}) \le 1/m, so \cvec{x} = 	frac1m\cvec{x}' with N_1(\cvec{x}') \le 1, and \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = 	frac1m\inner{\cvec{x}'}{\cvec{y}} \le 	frac1m N_{1*}(\cvec{y}). Taking the maximum over the ball of N_2 gives N_{2*}(\cvec{y}) \le 	frac1m N_{1*}(\cvec{y}). If N_1(\cvec{x}) \le 1, then N_2(\cvec{x}) \le M, and @prp-dual-norm-properties (b) gives \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} \le N_2(\cvec{x})N_{2*}(\cvec{y}) \le MN_{2*}(\cvec{y}); so N_{1*}(\cvec{y}) \le MN_{2*}(\cvec{y}). (b) Take N_1 = 
orm{\cdot}_2, N_2 = 
orm{\cdot}_1, m = 1, M = \sqrt n. The duals are 
orm{\cdot}_2 and 
orm{\cdot}_\infty (@prp-dual-of-one-two-infinity), so (a) gives 	frac{1}{\sqrt n}
orm{\cvec{y}}_2 \le 
orm{\cvec{y}}_\infty \le 
orm{\cvec{y}}_2. These are exactly the other two inequalities 
orm{\cvec{y}}_\infty \le 
orm{\cvec{y}}_2 \le \sqrt n\,
orm{\cvec{y}}_\infty of @prp-p-norm-inequalities: that proposition is closed under duality, with the constants carried over unchanged. [C3: The gauge is the support function of the polar] Let K \subseteq 
R^n be closed and convex, with \cvec{0} an interior point. 1. Prove that p_K(\cvec{x}) = h_{K^{\circ}}(\cvec{x}) for every \cvec{x}. Hint: for t > 0, rewrite “\cvec{x} \in tK” using @thm-bipolar. 2. Deduce @thm-dual-dual-norm again from (a), @thm-gauge-is-norm (b) and @prp-dual-norm-properties (d). (a) The polar K^{\circ} contains \cvec{0}, so h_{K^{\circ}}(\cvec{x}) \ge \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{0}} = 0. Let t > 0. By @thm-bipolar, K = K^{\circ\circ}, so \cvec{x} \in tK \iff \cvec{x}/t \in K^{\circ\circ} \iff \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} \le t 	ext{ for every } \cvec{y} \in K^{\circ} \iff h_{K^{\circ}}(\cvec{x}) \le t . So the admissible t in @def-gauge are the t > 0 with t \ge h_{K^{\circ}}(\cvec{x}), and their infimum is h_{K^{\circ}}(\cvec{x}) (if h_{K^{\circ}}(\cvec{x}) = 0, the admissible t are all t > 0, with infimum 0). In particular h_{K^{\circ}}(\cvec{x}) is finite. (b) Let B be the ball of 
orm{\cdot}. By @thm-gauge-is-norm (b), B is closed and convex with \cvec{0} interior, and 
orm{\cdot} = p_B. By (a), p_B = h_{B^{\circ}}, and B^{\circ} is the ball of 
orm{\cdot}_{*} by @prp-dual-norm-properties (d). So 
orm{\cvec{x}} = \max\{\inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} : 
orm{\cvec{y}}_{*} \le 1\} = 
orm{\cvec{x}}_{**}, the maximum existing by @def-dual-norm applied to 
orm{\cdot}_{*}.

title: 18.5 Cones and Farkas's Lemma
content:
Cones and Farkas’s Lemma Chapter 3 answered one question about a linear system completely: \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} has a solution exactly when \cvec{b} lies in the column space of \A (@thm-consistent-iff-column-span). Its applications section then hit a wall. Traffic flows cannot be negative, and once the unknowns are required to satisfy \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}, the column space is the wrong set to look in. This section finds the right set, which is a cone, and answers the new question with the separation theorems of §03: either \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} has a nonnegative solution, or a single vector \cvec{y} certifies that it has none. That is Farkas’s lemma, and the next two sections run on it. One step is harder than it looks. Separation needs a closed set, and nothing proved so far says that the relevant cone is closed. Most of the work goes into that step, and the last part of the section shows, with an explicit cone, that it can really fail. Throughout, the field is 
R. Vectors in 
R^n are columns, \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \cvec{y}	p\cvec{x} is the standard inner product, and 
orm{\cdot} is the Euclidean norm it induces, the norm that @thm-nearest-point uses. Convergence \cvec{y}_k 	o \cvec{y} means 
orm{\cvec{y}_k - \cvec{y}} 	o 0, and “closed” is meant in the sequential sense of @def-closed-set: a set S is closed when every limit of a convergent sequence of points of S again lies in S. Convergence in this norm is entrywise convergence, by the elementary bound \lvert y_ivert \ \le\ 
orm{\cvec{y}} \ \le\ \lvert y_1vert + \dots + \lvert y_nvert \qquad 	ext{for } \cvec{y} \in 
R^n 	ext{ and } 1 \le i \le n . {#eq-euclidean-entry-bound} The left inequality holds because y_i^2 \le y_1^2 + \dots + y_n^2, and the right one is the triangle inequality for \cvec{y} = y_1\cvec{e}_1 + \dots + y_n\cvec{e}_n. Applied to \cvec{y}_k - \cvec{y}, with the algebra of limits of Chapter 16’s introduction on the right, it shows that 
orm{\cvec{y}_k - \cvec{y}} 	o 0 exactly when every entry of \cvec{y}_k - \cvec{y} tends to 0. Convex cones For a vector with real entries we write \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} when every entry of \cvec{x} is \ge 0, and \cvec{x} > \cvec{0} when every entry is > 0. The set 
R^m_{\ge 0} = \{ \cvec{x} \in 
R^m : \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} \} is the nonnegative orthant. The relation \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} is an entrywise statement about a vector, and it has nothing to do with the Loewner order \A \succeq \O of Chapter 13, which is a statement about a matrix. Here is the question. Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R) have columns \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_n. By @thm-matrix-times-vector-columns, \A\cvec{x} = x_1\cvec{a}_1 + \dots + x_n\cvec{a}_n, so \{ \cvec{b} \in 
R^m : \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} 	ext{ for some } \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} \} = \{ x_1\cvec{a}_1 + \dots + x_n\cvec{a}_n : 	ext{every } x_j \ge 0 \} . Without the sign condition this set would be the span of the columns, a subspace. With it, the set is closed under addition and under multiplication by nonnegative scalars, but not under multiplication by -1. Such sets turn up whenever quantities cannot be negative, so they get a name. A cone is a set you may stretch and add in, but never reflect. [Convex Cone] Let V be a vector space over 
R. A subset K \subseteq V is a convex cone if K is nonempty and a\elem{u} + b\elem{v} \in K \qquad 	ext{for all } \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in K 	ext{ and all real } a, b \ge 0 . In words: a convex cone contains every nonnegative combination of two of its members, and hence, by induction on the number of terms, every nonnegative combination of finitely many of its members. Three special cases unpack the single condition. Taking a = b = 0 shows \elem{0} \in K, so every convex cone contains the origin. Taking b = 0 shows that K is closed under multiplication by nonnegative scalars. Taking a = b = 1 shows that it is closed under addition, and conversely a nonempty set with these two closure properties is a convex cone. A convex cone is a convex set in the sense of @def-convex-set: take a = 1 - t and b = t with 0 \le t \le 1. The converse fails, and the next examples show how. Examples. Each is checked against the one condition of the definition. - The orthant. If \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \ge \cvec{0} and a, b \ge 0, then every entry of a\cvec{u} + b\cvec{v} is a sum of products of nonnegative numbers, so a\cvec{u} + b\cvec{v} \ge \cvec{0}. Hence 
R^m_{\ge 0} is a convex cone. - A half-space through the origin. Fix \cvec{a} \in 
R^n and let H = \{ \cvec{x} : \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{a}} \ge 0 \}. If \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \in H and a, b \ge 0, then \inner{a\cvec{u} + b\cvec{v}}{\cvec{a}} = a\inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{a}} + b\inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{a}} \ge 0. So H is a convex cone. When \cvec{a} 
e \cvec{0} it is one of the two closed half-spaces bounded by the hyperplane \cvec{a}^{\perp}. - The ice-cream cone. In 
R^{n+1}, write vectors as (\cvec{x}, t) with \cvec{x} \in 
R^n and t \in 
R, and let L = \{ (\cvec{x}, t) : 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le t \}. If (\cvec{x}, t), (\cvec{y}, s) \in L and a, b \ge 0, the triangle inequality and homogeneity of the norm (@def-norm) give 
orm{a\cvec{x} + b\cvec{y}}_2 \le a
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 + b
orm{\cvec{y}}_2 \le at + bs. So L is a convex cone. In 
R^3 it is the round solid cone that gives the family its name. - Positive semidefinite matrices. In the real vector space of real symmetric n 	imes n matrices, the set of \A \succeq \O is a convex cone. This is part (a) of @exr-positive-definite-matrices-c2. Chapter 13 used the phrase there, and this is the definition it was using. - Degenerate cases. \{\elem{0}\} and V are convex cones. More generally, every subspace is a convex cone, since it is closed under all linear combinations and in particular the nonnegative ones. A subspace is the extreme case of a cone that happens to be closed under reflection as well. Nonexamples by minimal change. In 
R^2, take the union of two opposite quadrants, Q = \{ \cvec{x} : x_1x_2 \ge 0 \}. It is closed under nonnegative scaling, since (ax_1)(ax_2) = a^2x_1x_2. The clause that fails is addition: (1, 0) and (0, -1) lie in Q, but their sum (1, -1) does not. Or keep convexity and lose the scaling: the closed unit disc is convex, but 2\cvec{e}_1 is not in it. Or translate the orthant to \1 + 
R^2_{\ge 0}: it is convex and closed under addition, but it does not contain \cvec{0}. Why this definition. The scalars must be nonnegative. With all real scalars allowed, the definition becomes the definition of a subspace, and the sign information that started this section would be lost. The requirement \elem{0} \in K is a convention that some authors drop: they call \{ \cvec{x} : \cvec{x} > \cvec{0} \} a cone as well. Including the origin costs nothing here and keeps the statements below free of exceptions. A convex cone need not be closed. In 
R^2 let C = \{ (x, y) : x > 0 \} \cup \{ (0, 0) \} . It is a convex cone. Let \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \in C and a, b \ge 0. The first entry of a\cvec{u} + b\cvec{v} is au_1 + bv_1 \ge 0. If it is positive, the vector lies in C. If it is zero, then au_1 = 0 and bv_1 = 0; since the only member of C with first entry 0 is \cvec{0}, this forces a\cvec{u} = \cvec{0} and b\cvec{v} = \cvec{0}, and the sum is \cvec{0} \in C. But (1/k, 1) \in C for every k \ge 1, while the limit (0, 1) is not in C. Separating a point from a cone needs the cone to be closed, so closedness must be proved. This particular cone comes back at the end of the section as the image of a closed cone. The cones in the question at the start of this section are the simplest kind. [Finitely Generated Cone] Let \elem{a}_1, \dots, \elem{a}_m be vectors in a real vector space V. The cone generated by them is \operatorname{cone}(\elem{a}_1, \dots, \elem{a}_m) = \Bigl\{ 	extstyle\sum_{i=1}^{m} x_i\elem{a}_i : x_1, \dots, x_m \ge 0 \Bigr\} . A cone of this form is finitely generated. For the empty list we set \operatorname{cone}() = \{\elem{0}\}, the value of the empty sum. When V = 
R^n and \A is the matrix with columns \cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_m, this is \{ \A\cvec{x} : \cvec{x} \in 
R^m_{\ge 0} \}, and we also write it \operatorname{cone}(\A). It is a convex cone: a nonnegative combination of two nonnegative combinations of the \elem{a}_i is again one, with coefficients ax_i + bx'_i \ge 0. It is also the smallest convex cone containing \elem{a}_1, \dots, \elem{a}_m, since any convex cone containing the \elem{a}_i contains all their nonnegative combinations, by the remark after @def-convex-cone. The orthant is \operatorname{cone}(\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_m). A subspace with basis \elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k is \operatorname{cone}(\elem{v}_1, -\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k, -\elem{v}_k), since c\elem{v}_i is c\elem{v}_i or \lvert cvert(-\elem{v}_i) according to the sign of c. The ice-cream cone is not finitely generated, a fact we shall neither need nor prove. Is \operatorname{cone} igl((1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1) igr) the same as \operatorname{cone} igl((1, 0), (0, 1) igr)? Is \operatorname{cone} igl((1, 0), (-1, 0) igr) a line or a half-line? Both cones are the quadrant 
R^2_{\ge 0}. The second list’s cone is the quadrant because x_1\cvec{e}_1 + x_2\cvec{e}_2 = (x_1, x_2). The first contains the second, and every generator of the first lies in the quadrant, which is a convex cone, so the first is contained in the quadrant too. A redundant generator changes nothing. The cone of (1, 0) and (-1, 0) is the whole x-axis \{ (t, 0) : t \in 
R \}, a line: for t \ge 0 use t(1, 0), and for t < 0 use \lvert tvert(-1, 0). The dual cone A certificate that \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} has no nonnegative solution will be a vector \cvec{y} that makes a nonnegative inner product with every column of \A but a negative one with \cvec{b}. Every nonnegative combination of the columns then also has a nonnegative inner product with \cvec{y}, so \cvec{b} cannot be such a combination. The set of vectors \cvec{y} that pass the first test deserves a name. The dual cone of K is the set of directions that make an angle of at most 90^\circ with everything in K. [Dual Cone] Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let S \subseteq V be any subset. The dual cone of S is S^{*} = \{ \elem{y} \in V : \inner{\elem{x}}{\elem{y}} \ge 0 	ext{ for every } \elem{x} \in S \} . We write S^{**} for (S^{*})^{*}. In words: \elem{y} \in S^{*} when the linear functional \inner{\cdot}{\elem{y}} is nonnegative on the whole of S, that is, when S lies in the closed half-space \{ \elem{x} : \inner{\elem{x}}{\elem{y}} \ge 0 \}. The inner product is what places S^{*} inside V rather than in the dual space of Chapter 5 (@thm-functionals-on-fn is the case V = 
R^n). S^{*} is not the dual space. The star here produces a subset of V itself, not a space of functionals, and it is defined for any subset, not only for a subspace. For a subspace U the dual cone is the orthogonal complement: if \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{y}} \ge 0 for every \elem{u} \in U, then applying this to -\elem{u} \in U gives \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{y}} \le 0 as well, so \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{y}} = 0, and the converse is immediate. So for a subspace we always write U^{\perp}, never U^{*}. The basic properties take one line each, and they explain why every dual cone is a good set to separate from. So it converges to q_{\cvec{k}}(s, t), and q_{\cvec{k}}(s, t) \ge 0 because a nonstrict inequality survives a limit. Hence K is closed. Membership. By @thm-psd-characterizations (a) \Leftrightarrow (e), (x, y, z) \in K exactly when the principal minors x, z, and xz - y^2 are all \ge 0. The image. (0, 0) = \P(\cvec{0}) \in \P(K). If x > 0 and y is arbitrary, put z = y^2/x. Then x \ge 0, z \ge 0, and xz - y^2 = 0, so (x, y, z) \in K and (x, y) \in \P(K). Conversely, if (x, y, z) \in K, then x \ge 0, and if x = 0 then 0 = xz \ge y^2 forces y = 0. So \P(K) is exactly the displayed set. It is not closed: (1/k, 1) \in \P(K) converges to (0, 1) 
otin \P(K). Neither alternative holds for \cvec{b} = (0, 1). Alternative (i) fails because \cvec{b} 
otin \P(K). For (ii), suppose \cvec{y} = (y_1, y_2) has \inner{\P\cvec{k}}{\cvec{y}} \ge 0 for every \cvec{k} \in K. Since (1, t) \in \P(K) for every real t, we get y_1 + ty_2 \ge 0 for all t. A nonconstant affine function of t takes negative values, so y_2 = 0. But then \inner{\cvec{b}}{\cvec{y}} = y_2 = 0, which is not < 0. So (ii) fails too. It is worth seeing exactly where the proof of @thm-farkas breaks. The vectors \cvec{k}_j = (1/j, 1, j) lie in K, their images (1/j, 1) converge to \cvec{b}, and the \cvec{k}_j themselves run off to infinity in the third coordinate. This is the escape that the left inverse in @lem-orthant-image-closed prevented. There is no nearest point of \P(K) to \cvec{b}: the distance is 0, but \cvec{b} is not in the set, so @lem-cone-separation has nothing to start from. What fails is closedness, which is why the finitely generated case needed its own theorem. The dual cone cannot see the difference either: \P(K)^{**} is the closed half-plane \{ x \ge 0 \}, strictly larger than \P(K), as @exr-cones-and-farkas-c3 shows. Exercises A. As a direct check, adding twice the first equation to the second gives 2x_1 + 3x_2 = -1, whose left side is \ge 0 for \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}. [B3: A dual cone and its dual] Let K = \operatorname{cone} igl((1, 0), (1, 1) igr) \subseteq

Given such a \cvec{y}, write \cvec{y} = (y_1 + y_2)(0, 1) + y_1(1, -1): indeed the right side is (y_1, y_1 + y_2 - y_1) = (y_1, y_2), and both coefficients are \ge 0. So \cvec{y} \in \operatorname{cone} igl((0,1),(1,-1) igr). Conversely, both generators satisfy the two inequalities, and the set defined by the inequalities is a convex cone, so it contains the cone they generate. (b) Applying @prp-dual-cone-basic (d) to the generators found in (a), K^{**} = \{ \cvec{x} : x_2 \ge 0,\ x_1 - x_2 \ge 0 \}. R with \A	p\cvec{y} + s\1 \ge \cvec{0} and \cvec{0}	p\cvec{y} + 1\cdot s < 0, that is, s < 0. Then \A	p\cvec{y} \ge -s\1 > \cvec{0}, so \cvec{y} solves the second system. (b) Here \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & 1 & -1\end{psmallmatrix}. The second system is impossible: \A	p\cvec{y} = (y_1, y_2, -y_1 - y_2), and its entries sum to 0, so they cannot all be positive. By (a) the first system is solvable. Indeed \cvec{x} = (1, 1, 1) gives \A\cvec{x} = (1 - 1, 1 - 1) = \cvec{0}. [C2: The ice-cream cone is its own dual] Let L = \{ (\cvec{x}, t) \in

Fix (\cvec{y}, s) \in L: we have shown that its inner product with every (\cvec{x}, t) \in L is \ge 0, so (\cvec{y}, s) \in L^{*}. Hence L \subseteq L^{*}. (b) Let (\cvec{y}, s) \in L^{*}. Explain why this does not contradict @thm-dual-cone-of-dual-cone, and show that C^{**} is the set of all limits of convergent sequences of points of C. (a) If (y_1, y_2) \in C^{*}, then testing against (1, t) \in C gives y_1 + ty_2 \ge 0 for every real t. This forces y_2 = 0, as in the example, and then t = 0 gives y_1 \ge 0. Conversely, if y_2 = 0 and y_1 \ge 0, then \inner{(x, y)}{(y_1, 0)} = xy_1 \ge 0 for every (x, y) \in C, since x \ge 0 on C. (b) By (a), C^{*} = \operatorname{cone} igl((1, 0) igr), so by @prp-dual-cone-basic (d), C^{**} = \{ (x, y) : \inner{(x, y)}{(1, 0)} \ge 0 \} = \{ (x, y) : x \ge 0 \} . title: 18.6 Linear Programming Duality
content:
Linear Programming Duality Chapter 3 ended its traffic example (@exm-traffic-network) by admitting what linear algebra alone cannot do: “Nonnegativity and street capacities turn the problem into one about inequalities, which is the subject of linear programming.” This section takes up that subject. A linear program asks for the largest value of a linear function on a region cut out by finitely many linear inequalities. The theory is almost entirely one idea. Every such maximum comes with a companion minimum, the dual program, and the two optimal values are equal. The proof of that equality is Farkas’s lemma of §05, applied to one combined system. The equality has a practical meaning that goes beyond the theorem. A feasible point proves a lower bound on the maximum, a dual feasible point proves an upper bound, and when the two bounds meet, the answer has been certified: anyone can check it by multiplying out, with no need to trust how it was found. Throughout, the field is 
R, vectors are columns, and \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}, \cvec{u} \le \cvec{v} are the entrywise relations of §05. Linear programs Here is a small instance of the kind of question we want to answer. A workshop makes two products. Each unit of the first uses 2 hours of machine time and 1 hour of labor, each unit of the second uses 1 hour of machine time and 3 hours of labor, and at most 3 units of the first can be sold. Machine time is limited to 7 hours, labor to 9, and the profits are 4 and 3 per unit. With x_1, x_2 units made, the question is:  egin{aligned} 	ext{maximize}\quad & 4x_1 + 3x_2 \ 	ext{subject to}\quad & 2x_1 + x_2 \le 7, \quad x_1 + 3x_2 \le 9, \quad x_1 \le 3, \ & x_1 \ge 0, \quad x_2 \ge 0 . \end{aligned} The objective and every constraint are linear, and there are finitely many constraints. In matrix form it reads “maximize \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} subject to \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}, \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}”. That shape deserves a name. A linear program is the search for the best value of a linear function over a region defined by finitely many linear inequalities. [Linear Program] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R), \cvec{b} \in 
R^m, and \cvec{c} \in 
R^n. The linear program with these data, in inequality form, is the problem 	ext{(P)}\qquad 	ext{maximize } \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \quad 	ext{subject to} \quad \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b},\ \ \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} . A vector \cvec{x} \in 
R^n with \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b} and \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} is a feasible point, and the set of all of them is the feasible region. The program is feasible if it has a feasible point and infeasible otherwise. It is unbounded if it is feasible and \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} takes arbitrarily large values on the feasible region. A feasible \cvec{x}^{\star} is an optimal solution if \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x}^{\star} \ge \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} for every feasible \cvec{x}, and then \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x}^{\star} is the optimal value. Clause by clause. The function \cvec{x} \mapsto \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} is the objective. The m rows of \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b} are the constraints, and \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} adds n more. An optimal solution is a feasible point at which the objective is as large as anywhere on the feasible region, and it need not be unique. The optimal value is unique when it exists. A program can fail to have an optimal solution in two ways: it can have no feasible point, or its objective can be unbounded above. Whether those are the only two ways is the question the section’s second theorem settles. Examples. The workshop problem is (P) with \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 3 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{b} =  egin{pmatrix} 7 \ 9 \ 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{c} =  egin{pmatrix} 4 \ 3 \end{pmatrix} . - One variable. With n = m = 1, “maximize x subject to x \le 2, x \ge 0” has the optimal solution x = 2. “Maximize x subject to -x \le -1, x \ge 0” asks for the largest x \ge 1, and it is unbounded. “Maximize x subject to x \le -1, x \ge 0” is infeasible. - Degenerate case. If \cvec{c} = \cvec{0}, every feasible point is optimal, with value 0. The program then asks only whether the system \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}, \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} has a solution. So the feasibility question of @cor-farkas-inequality is itself a linear program, the one with no objective. Nonexample by minimal change. Make one inequality strict: “maximize x subject to x < 2, x \ge 0”. Everything is still linear, but the supremum 2 is not attained, and no feasible point is optimal. The definition allows only nonstrict inequalities. They define closed regions, and closedness will again be what the proofs need. Why this form. Every problem with a linear objective and finitely many linear constraints can be brought to the shape (P). To minimize \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x}, maximize (-\cvec{c})	p\cvec{x}. A constraint \cvec{a}	p\cvec{x} \ge  eta is (-\cvec{a})	p\cvec{x} \le - eta. An equation \cvec{a}	p\cvec{x} =  eta is the pair \cvec{a}	p\cvec{x} \le  eta, -\cvec{a}	p\cvec{x} \le - eta. A variable x_j without a sign constraint can be written x_j = u_j - v_j with u_j, v_j \ge 0. @exr-linear-programming-duality-c2 carries out the last conversion. The form (P), with its sign constraints on \cvec{x}, is chosen because its dual, below, has the same shape, which makes the theory symmetric. [The workshop problem, drawn] Find the optimal solution of the workshop problem, and explain why it is optimal. The feasible region is the pentagon with corners (0, 0), (3, 0), (3, 1),  igl(	frac{12}{5}, 	frac{11}{5} igr), and (0, 3). For example, (3, 1) is where x_1 = 3 meets 2x_1 + x_2 = 7, and  igl(	frac{12}{5}, 	frac{11}{5} igr) solves 2x_1 + x_2 = 7, x_1 + 3x_2 = 9: subtracting twice the second equation from the first gives -5x_2 = -11. The level sets 4x_1 + 3x_2 = 	ext{const} are parallel lines, and the value grows in the direction \cvec{c} = (4, 3). Sliding the line in that direction, the last point of the region it meets appears to be \cvec{x}^{\star} =  igl(	frac{12}{5}, 	frac{11}{5} igr), with value 4\cdot	frac{12}{5} + 3\cdot	frac{11}{5} = 	frac{48 + 33}{5} = 	frac{81}{5} . Comparing the corners supports this: they give 0, 12, 15, 	frac{81}{5} = 16.2, and 9. A picture is not a proof, and neither is a list of five corners, since we have not proved that an optimum sits at a corner. Here is a proof. Multiply the first constraint by 	frac95 and the second by 	frac25, both nonnegative, and add: 	frac95(2x_1 + x_2) + 	frac25(x_1 + 3x_2) \le 	frac95\cdot 7 + 	frac25\cdot 9 = 	frac{81}{5} . The left side is  igl(	frac{18}{5} + 	frac25 igr)x_1 +  igl(	frac95 + 	frac65 igr)x_2 = 4x_1 + 3x_2. So every feasible point has 4x_1 + 3x_2 \le 	frac{81}{5}, and \cvec{x}^{\star}, which is feasible (	frac{12}{5} \le 3 as well), reaches this bound. It is optimal, and the optimal value is 	frac{81}{5}. The multipliers 	frac95 and 	frac25 are the heart of the matter. They were chosen so that the combined constraint had exactly the objective as its left side. The best upper bound obtainable this way is itself the answer to a linear program. The dual program Multiply the i-th constraint of (P) by a number y_i \ge 0 and add. For every feasible \cvec{x} this gives \cvec{y}	p\A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{y}	p\cvec{b}. If the combination dominates the objective coefficient by coefficient, \A	p\cvec{y} \ge \cvec{c}, then, since \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}, \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \le (\A	p\cvec{y})	p\cvec{x} = \cvec{y}	p\A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{y}	p\cvec{b} . Each such \cvec{y} proves an upper bound \cvec{b}	p\cvec{y} on the objective, and the natural question is how small that bound can be made. The dual program searches for the best upper bound that nonnegative combinations of the constraints can prove. [Dual Program] The dual of the linear program (P) of @def-linear-program is the problem 	ext{(D)}\qquad 	ext{minimize } \cvec{b}	p\cvec{y} \quad 	ext{subject to} \quad \A	p\cvec{y} \ge \cvec{c},\ \ \cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0} , with \cvec{y} \in 
R^m. The words feasible, infeasible, and optimal are used as for (P). (D) is unbounded if it is feasible and \cvec{b}	p\cvec{y} takes arbitrarily negative values on its feasible region. In this context (P) is called the primal program. The dual has one variable for each constraint of the primal and one constraint for each variable of the primal. The matrix is transposed, the roles of \cvec{b} and \cvec{c} are exchanged, and maximization becomes minimization. The dual of (D), written back in inequality form, is (P) again. @exr-linear-programming-duality-c1 checks this, and it explains why a statement about (P) always has a mirror statement about (D). For the workshop problem the dual is  egin{aligned} 	ext{minimize}\quad & 7y_1 + 9y_2 + 3y_3 \ 	ext{subject to}\quad & 2y_1 + y_2 + y_3 \ge 4, \quad y_1 + 3y_2 \ge 3, \ & y_1, y_2, y_3 \ge 0 , \end{aligned} and the multipliers of @exm-lp-workshop form the dual feasible point \cvec{y}^{\star} =  igl(	frac95, 	frac25, 0 igr), with \cvec{b}	p\cvec{y}^{\star} = 	frac{81}{5}. The dual has an economic reading too. y_i is a price for one unit of the i-th resource, and the constraints say that at these prices the resources used by one unit of each product are worth at least the profit it brings. Weak duality The computation that motivated (D) is the first theorem, and it is one line long. Weak Duality If \cvec{x} is feasible for (P) and \cvec{y} is feasible for (D), then \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}	p\cvec{y} . The feasible region is closed, but it may be unbounded, so the extreme value theorem (A4) of Chapter 16’s introduction does not apply to it. And a linear function that is bounded above on a closed convex set need not attain its supremum. The corollary is where finite generation pays off. Strong duality is a theorem about linear programs, not about optimization in general. For programs whose objective or constraints are convex but not linear, one can still write down a dual problem, and weak duality still holds, but the two optimal values may differ: a duality gap. Extra hypotheses are needed to close it, of which the best known is a strictly feasible point (Slater’s condition). That theory belongs to convex optimization and is not developed in this book. For linear programs no hypothesis beyond feasibility is needed, as @thm-strong-duality shows. Complementary slackness Strong duality says that at the optimum the two chains of inequalities in the proof of @thm-weak-duality are equalities. Reading that off term by term gives a test that locates the dual solution once the primal one is known. Complementary Slackness Let \cvec{x} be feasible for (P) and \cvec{y} feasible for (D). Optimality means the gap is zero, which means every product is zero. With f_4 = \alpha = 0 the conserving flows are \cvec{f} = (40 -  eta, 60 -  eta, 25, 0,  eta). The capacity of street 2 	o 3 gives 60 -  eta \le 30, so  eta \ge 30. The capacity of the diagonal gives  eta \le 30. So  eta = 30, and the only candidate is \cvec{f} = (10, 30, 25, 0, 30), which satisfies 0 \le f_i \le 30 for every street. It is the unique feasible flow. Lower bound: adding the balance equations at intersections 1 and 2 gives f_2 - f_4 + f_5 = 60, so f_5 = 60 - f_2 + f_4 = 60 - f_2 \ge 30 by the capacity f_2 \le 30, using f_4 = 0. Upper bound: f_5 \le 30 is itself a capacity constraint. Each certificate is a nonnegative combination of constraints, with free multipliers on the balance equations, as in the example. C. Going deeper [C1: The dual of the dual] 1. Rewrite (D) as a program in the inequality form of @def-linear-program, with data (-\A	p, -\cvec{c}, -\cvec{b}). Show that the dual of that program, rewritten as a maximization, is (P). 2. Deduce part (c) of @thm-strong-duality from part (b). (a) Minimizing \cvec{b}	p\cvec{y} is maximizing (-\cvec{b})	p\cvec{y}, and \A	p\cvec{y} \ge \cvec{c} is (-\A	p)\cvec{y} \le -\cvec{c}. So (D) is the inequality-form program (D'): maximize (-\cvec{b})	p\cvec{y} subject to (-\A	p)\cvec{y} \le -\cvec{c}, \cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0}, whose data are \A' = -\A	p, \cvec{b}' = -\cvec{c}, \cvec{c}' = -\cvec{b}. By @def-dual-program its dual is: minimize \cvec{b}'^{	op}\cvec{x} = (-\cvec{c})	p\cvec{x} subject to \A'^{	op}\cvec{x} = -\A\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{c}' = -\cvec{b}, \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}. That is: maximize \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} subject to \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}, \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}, which is (P). Its optimal value is the negative of the minimum above. (b) Suppose (D) is feasible and (P) is infeasible. Then (D') is feasible, with the same feasible points, and its dual, which by (a) has the same feasible points as (P), is infeasible. By @thm-strong-duality (b) applied to (D'), the objective (-\cvec{b})	p\cvec{y} takes arbitrarily large values on the feasible region. So \cvec{b}	p\cvec{y} takes arbitrarily negative values, and (D) is unbounded. [C2: Free variables] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R), \cvec{b} \in 
R^m, \cvec{c} \in 
R^n, and consider the program with no sign constraint on \cvec{x}: 	ext{(P}_{	ext{free}}	ext{)}\qquad 	ext{maximize } \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \ 	ext{ subject to } \ \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b} . 1. Prove weak duality between (P_{	ext{free}}) and (D_{	ext{eq}}): minimize \cvec{b}	p\cvec{y} subject to \A	p\cvec{y} = \cvec{c}, \cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0}. 2. Writing \cvec{x} = \cvec{u} - \cvec{v} with \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \ge \cvec{0}, show that (P_{	ext{free}}) has the same values as an inequality-form program whose dual is (D_{	ext{eq}}). Deduce that if both are feasible, both have optimal solutions with equal values. (a) If \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b} and \A	p\cvec{y} = \cvec{c} with \cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0}, then \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} = (\A	p\cvec{y})	p\cvec{x} = \cvec{y}	p\A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{y}	p\cvec{b}, the last step because \cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0} and \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}. No sign condition on \cvec{x} is needed, because the first step is an equality. (b) Every \cvec{x} \in 
R^n can be written as \cvec{u} - \cvec{v} with \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \ge \cvec{0}: take u_j = \max(x_j, 0) and v_j = \max(-x_j, 0). So (P_{	ext{free}}) has the same feasible objective values as the inequality-form program 	ext{maximize }  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{c} \ -\cvec{c} \end{pmatrix}	p egin{pmatrix} \cvec{u} \ \cvec{v} \end{pmatrix} \ 	ext{ subject to } \  egin{pmatrix} \A & -\A \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} \cvec{u} \ \cvec{v} \end{pmatrix} \le \cvec{b}, \quad  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{u} \ \cvec{v} \end{pmatrix} \ge \cvec{0} , with an optimal (\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) giving an optimal \cvec{x} = \cvec{u} - \cvec{v}, and conversely. By @def-dual-program its dual is: minimize \cvec{b}	p\cvec{y} subject to  egin{pmatrix} \A & -\A\end{pmatrix}	p\cvec{y} \ge (\cvec{c}, -\cvec{c}), \cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0}. The constraint reads \A	p\cvec{y} \ge \cvec{c} and -\A	p\cvec{y} \ge -\cvec{c}, that is, \A	p\cvec{y} = \cvec{c}. So the dual is (D_{	ext{eq}}). If both programs are feasible, @thm-strong-duality (a) gives optimal (\cvec{u}^{\star}, \cvec{v}^{\star}) and \cvec{y}^{\star} with equal values, and \cvec{x}^{\star} = \cvec{u}^{\star} - \cvec{v}^{\star} is optimal for (P_{	ext{free}}).

title: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content:
Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem Chapter 17 was built on a min–max formula: the Courant–Fischer theorem describes each eigenvalue of a Hermitian matrix as a minimum of maxima over subspaces. This section proves a second min–max theorem that looks similar and works for a completely different reason. It concerns a game in which two players choose simultaneously, and it says that if the players are allowed to randomize, it does not matter which of them has to reveal a plan first. The theorem is due to von Neumann, and with linear programming duality in hand (§06) it takes a page to prove. The two theorems are easy to confuse, and a reader who has just finished Chapter 17 will be tempted to. So the section also says precisely how they differ. Courant–Fischer is a statement about subspaces, and its equality comes from a dimension count. The minimax theorem is a statement about simplices, and its equality comes from convexity. Throughout, the field is 
R, \1 is the all-ones vector of whatever length the context requires, and \J = \1\1	p is the all-ones matrix. Inequalities between vectors are entrywise, as in §05. Matrix games Two players, Row and Column, play a game described by a real matrix \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R), the payoff matrix. Row secretly chooses a row i, Column secretly chooses a column j, both reveal their choices, and Column pays Row the amount a_{ij}. A negative entry means that Row pays Column. Whatever one player wins, the other loses, so the game is called zero-sum. Row wants a_{ij} large and Column wants it small. A choice of a row, or of a column, is a pure strategy. Suppose Row must announce a row in advance. Column will then answer with the smallest entry in that row, so the best Row can guarantee is \max_{i}\ \min_{j}\ a_{ij} . If instead Column must announce first, the best Column can guarantee is to pay at most \min_j \max_i a_{ij}. Announcing first is never an advantage, and that holds for any payoff function whatsoever. [Max–Min Never Exceeds Min–Max] Let X and Y be sets and f \colon X 	imes Y 	o 
R a function for which the extrema below exist. Then \max_{x \in X}\ \min_{y \in Y}\ f(x, y) \ \le\ \min_{y \in Y}\ \max_{x \in X}\ f(x, y) . Let x_0 \in X and y_0 \in Y. Then \min_{y \in Y} f(x_0, y) \ \le\ f(x_0, y_0) \ \le\ \max_{x \in X} f(x, y_0) . The left side does not depend on y_0 and the right side does not depend on x_0. Taking the maximum over x_0 on the left and then the minimum over y_0 on the right proves the lemma. The inequality can be strict. In the game with \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} , Row wins when the two choices match and loses when they differ. Every row contains a -1, so \max_i\min_j a_{ij} = -1. Every column contains a 1, so \min_j\max_i a_{ij} = 1. Whoever announces first loses a unit, and there is a gap of 2 between what the players can guarantee. Some games have no gap. In \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 4 \ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} the row minima are 1 and 0, whose maximum is 1, and the column maxima are 3, 1, 4, whose minimum is also 1. The entry a_{12} = 1 is the smallest in its row and the largest in its column. Such an entry is a saddle point. If Row plays row 1 and Column plays column 2, neither can gain by changing unilaterally, and the game is settled in pure strategies. The first game has no saddle point, and in that game the natural advice is: do not be predictable. Mixed strategies The way to be unpredictable is to randomize. Row chooses row i with probability x_i, and Column chooses column j with probability y_j, independently. The probabilities of the m rows form a vector with nonnegative entries summing to 1, that is, a point of the standard simplex of @def-standard-simplex, \Delta_m = \{ \cvec{x} \in 
R^m : \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} 	ext{ and } x_1 + \dots + x_m = 1 \} . A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over the pure strategies, and the simplex is the set of all of them. [Mixed Strategy] In the game with payoff matrix \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R), a mixed strategy for Row is a vector \cvec{x} \in \Delta_m, a mixed strategy for Column is a vector \cvec{y} \in \Delta_n, and the expected payoff is \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_i\,a_{ij}\,y_j . In words: a mixed strategy assigns to each pure strategy a weight that is nonnegative, and the weights sum to exactly 1. The payoff a_{ij} occurs with probability x_iy_j, since the two choices are independent, so \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} is the average payoff over many plays. The pure strategy “row i” is the mixed strategy \cvec{e}_i, a vertex of the simplex, and \cvec{e}_i	p\A\cvec{e}_j = a_{ij}. So mixed strategies extend pure ones, and the expected payoff extends the payoff. Examples. \Delta_2 is the segment from (1, 0) to (0, 1) in the plane, whose points (p, 1 - p) with 0 \le p \le 1 mean “row 1 with probability p”. \Delta_3 is the triangle with vertices \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3 in 
R^3, and its center 	frac13\1 is the uniform strategy. The degenerate case is \Delta_1 = \{1\}: a player with only one pure strategy has no choice, and the game is a single row or a single column. Nonexamples by minimal change.  igl(	frac12, 	frac12, 	frac12 igr) has nonnegative entries, but they sum to 	frac32, so it is not a probability distribution.  igl(	frac32, -	frac12 igr) sums to 1, but it has a negative entry. It lies on the line through \Delta_2, outside the segment. Why this definition. \Delta_n is exactly the set of convex combinations of \cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n, since \cvec{x} = \sum x_j\cvec{e}_j. So it is the convex hull of the pure strategies, by @thm-convex-hull-combinations, and in particular it is a convex set (@def-convex-set). That convexity is what makes the theorem below true. The convention of @def-standard-simplex, n weights for n pure strategies, is the one a game needs. The payoff \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} is linear in \cvec{y} for fixed \cvec{x}, and linear in \cvec{x} for fixed \cvec{y}, so a mixture of strategies earns the same mixture of payoffs. A mixed strategy is not a compromise move. Playing  igl(	frac12, 	frac12 igr) in the matching game does not mean playing “half of row 1 and half of row 2” in a single round. Each round Row plays one actual row, chosen at random, and \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} is an average over rounds. In the matching game with \cvec{x} = \cvec{y} =  igl(	frac12, 	frac12 igr), the expected payoff is 0, yet every single round pays +1 or -1, never 0. Against a fixed mixed strategy, the opponent never needs to randomize. That observation turns every “min over a simplex” into a min over finitely many numbers. [A Pure Best Response Exists] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R). For every \cvec{x} \in \Delta_m, \min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n} \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} = \min_{1 \le j \le n} (\A	p\cvec{x})_j , and the minimum on the left is attained at \cvec{y} = \cvec{e}_j for any j attaining the minimum on the right. Likewise, for every \cvec{y} \in \Delta_n, \max_{\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} = \max_{1 \le i \le m}(\A\cvec{y})_i, attained at a vertex \cvec{e}_i. For fixed \cvec{x}, the payoff \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} is an average of the entries of \A	p\cvec{x} with weights y_j, and an average is never below the smallest entry, which the vertex \cvec{e}_j attains. Write \cvec{w} = \A	p\cvec{x} \in 
R^n and \mu = \min_j w_j, a minimum of finitely many numbers. For \cvec{y} \in \Delta_n, \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} = \cvec{w}	p\cvec{y} = \sum_{j=1}^{n} y_jw_j \ \ge\ \sum_{j=1}^{n} y_j\mu = \mu , because every y_j \ge 0 and \sum_j y_j = 1. If w_{j_0} = \mu, then \cvec{e}_{j_0} \in \Delta_n gives \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{e}_{j_0} = w_{j_0} = \mu. So \mu is a value of \cvec{y} \mapsto \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} on \Delta_n and a lower bound for all its values, hence its minimum. The second statement is the same argument applied to \A\cvec{y} with the inequality reversed. So once Row fixes \cvec{x}, the amount Row can guarantee is g(\cvec{x}) = \min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} = \min_j (\A	p\cvec{x})_j , the smallest entry of \A	p\cvec{x}. Column, in the same way, guarantees by the second half of the lemma to pay at most h(\cvec{y}) = \max_{\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} = \max_i(\A\cvec{y})_i. In the matching game, \cvec{x} =  igl(	frac12, 	frac12 igr) gives \A	p\cvec{x} = (0, 0) and g(\cvec{x}) = 0, and the same holds for Column’s h. With mixing, both players can guarantee 0, and the gap of 2 has closed. The theorem says this always happens. The minimax theorem [Von Neumann’s Minimax Theorem] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R). There are \cvec{x}^{\star} \in \Delta_m, \cvec{y}^{\star} \in \Delta_n, and v \in 
R such that \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}^{\star} \ \le\ v \ \le\ \cvec{x}^{\star	op}\A\cvec{y} \qquad 	ext{for all } \cvec{x} \in \Delta_m,\ \cvec{y} \in \Delta_n . {#eq-minimax-saddle} Consequently \max_{\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m}\ \min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n}\ \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} \ =\ v\ =\ \min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n}\ \max_{\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m}\ \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} , where the outer maximum is attained at \cvec{x}^{\star} and the outer minimum at \cvec{y}^{\star}. Row wants the \cvec{x} \in \Delta_m that maximizes the smallest entry of \A	p\cvec{x}. If every entry of \A is positive, this can be rescaled into a linear program. Put \cvec{p} = \cvec{x}/v, where v is the guaranteed amount. Then “\A	p\cvec{x} \ge v\1 with \1	p\cvec{x} = 1, v as large as possible” becomes “\A	p\cvec{p} \ge \1, \cvec{p} \ge \cvec{0}, \1	p\cvec{p} as small as possible”. Column’s problem becomes the dual of that program, by the same substitution. Strong duality (§06) says the two optimal values agree, and that common value is 1/v. The plan: ① shift the entries by a constant to make them positive, which changes every payoff by the same constant; ② write down the two linear programs, check that both are feasible, and apply @thm-strong-duality; ③ rescale the optimal solutions into strategies and read off @eq-minimax-saddle. Step 1. We may assume every a_{ij} > 0. Choose c \in 
R with a_{ij} + c > 0 for all i, j, and put \B = \A + c\J. For \cvec{x} \in \Delta_m and \cvec{y} \in \Delta_n, \cvec{x}	p\J\cvec{y} = (\cvec{x}	p\1)(\1	p\cvec{y}) = 1 , \qquad	ext{so}\qquad \cvec{x}	p\B\cvec{y} = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} + c . Hence if \cvec{x}^{\star}, \cvec{y}^{\star}, w satisfy @eq-minimax-saddle for \B, then \cvec{x}^{\star}, \cvec{y}^{\star}, w - c satisfy it for \A. So it suffices to prove @eq-minimax-saddle when every entry of \A is positive, and we assume this from now on. Let \mu = \min_{i,j}a_{ij} > 0. Step 2. Two linear programs. Consider  egin{aligned} 	ext{(P)}\quad & 	ext{maximize } \1	p\cvec{q} \ 	ext{ subject to } \ \A\cvec{q} \le \1,\ \cvec{q} \ge \cvec{0} \quad (\cvec{q} \in 
R^n), \ 	ext{(D)}\quad & 	ext{minimize } \1	p\cvec{p} \ 	ext{ subject to } \ \A	p\cvec{p} \ge \1,\ \cvec{p} \ge \cvec{0} \quad (\cvec{p} \in 
R^m) . \end{aligned} (P) is a linear program in the inequality form of @def-linear-program, with data (\A, \1, \1), and (D) is its dual (@def-dual-program). (P) is feasible, with \cvec{q} = \cvec{0}. (D) is feasible, with \cvec{p} = \mu^{-1}\1: the j-th entry of \A	p\cvec{p} is \mu^{-1}\sum_i a_{ij} \ge \mu^{-1}a_{1j} \ge 1. By @thm-strong-duality (a), there are optimal \cvec{q}^{\star} and \cvec{p}^{\star} with equal values; call the common value \omega, so that \1	p\cvec{q}^{\star} = \1	p\cvec{p}^{\star} = \omega . Moreover \omega > 0. Since \A	p\cvec{p}^{\star} \ge \1, we have \cvec{p}^{\star} 
e \cvec{0}, and a nonzero vector with nonnegative entries has a positive entry sum. Step 3. Strategies from the programs. Put \cvec{x}^{\star} = \omega^{-1}\cvec{p}^{\star}, \qquad \cvec{y}^{\star} = \omega^{-1}\cvec{q}^{\star}, \qquad v = \omega^{-1} . Then \cvec{x}^{\star} \ge \cvec{0} with \1	p\cvec{x}^{\star} = \omega^{-1}\omega = 1, so \cvec{x}^{\star} \in \Delta_m, and likewise \cvec{y}^{\star} \in \Delta_n. The constraints of the two programs give \A	p\cvec{x}^{\star} = \omega^{-1}\A	p\cvec{p}^{\star} \ge v\1 , \qquad \A\cvec{y}^{\star} = \omega^{-1}\A\cvec{q}^{\star} \le v\1 . For every \cvec{y} \in \Delta_n, therefore, \cvec{x}^{\star	op}\A\cvec{y} = \sum_j y_j(\A	p\cvec{x}^{\star})_j \ge v\sum_j y_j = v. For every \cvec{x} \in \Delta_m, \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}^{\star} = \sum_i x_i(\A\cvec{y}^{\star})_i \le v. This is @eq-minimax-saddle. Step 4. The two extrema. For \cvec{x} \in \Delta_m let g(\cvec{x}) = \min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}, which exists by @lem-pure-best-response. By @eq-minimax-saddle, g(\cvec{x}^{\star}) \ge v, since every value of \cvec{y} \mapsto \cvec{x}^{\star	op}\A\cvec{y} is at least v. And g(\cvec{x}) \le \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}^{\star} \le v for every \cvec{x}. So v is a value of g and an upper bound for all its values: \max_{\cvec{x}}g(\cvec{x}) exists, equals v, and is attained at \cvec{x}^{\star}. In the same way h(\cvec{y}) = \max_{\cvec{x}}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} satisfies h(\cvec{y}^{\star}) \le v \le \cvec{x}^{\star	op}\A\cvec{y} \le h(\cvec{y}) for every \cvec{y}, so \min_{\cvec{y}}h(\cvec{y}) = v, attained at \cvec{y}^{\star}. This proves the theorem. [Value and Optimal Strategies] The number v of @thm-von-neumann-minimax is the value of the game with payoff matrix \A, written v(\A). A strategy \cvec{x} \in \Delta_m is optimal for Row if it guarantees the value, \min_{\cvec{y}}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} = v(\A), and \cvec{y} \in \Delta_n is optimal for Column if \max_{\cvec{x}}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} = v(\A). The value is well defined: it equals the max–min, and that depends only on \A. A strategy \cvec{x} is optimal for Row exactly when every entry of \A	p\cvec{x} is at least v(\A), and \cvec{y} is optimal for Column exactly when every entry of \A\cvec{y} is at most v(\A); both statements are @lem-pure-best-response. These are linear conditions, so each player’s set of optimal strategies is a convex subset of the simplex. Inequality @eq-minimax-saddle says that (\cvec{x}^{\star}, \cvec{y}^{\star}) is a saddle point in mixed strategies. If Row plays \cvec{x}^{\star}, Column cannot push the expected payment below v. If Column plays \cvec{y}^{\star}, Row cannot push it above v. Neither player gains by deviating alone, and announcing an optimal strategy in advance costs nothing. Alternatively, the theorem can be proved with no linear programming, by separation. The key fact is an alternative in the style of Farkas: either some \cvec{y} \in \Delta_n has \A\cvec{y} \le \cvec{0}, or some \cvec{x} \in \Delta_m has \A	p\cvec{x} > \cvec{0}. To prove it, separate the origin from the closed convex set \{ \A\cvec{y} + \cvec{z} : \cvec{y} \in \Delta_n,\ \cvec{z} \ge \cvec{0} \} using §03, and apply the result to \A - t\J for every real t. That route shows most directly that the theorem is about convexity. It also needs the compactness of \Delta_n, (A3) of Chapter 16’s introduction, to know that the set being separated is closed. The route taken above hides all of the analysis inside Farkas’s lemma. Two min–max theorems @thm-von-neumann-minimax and the Courant–Fischer theorem of Chapter 17 (@thm-courant-fischer) both have “min” and “max” in them, and both are called min–max theorems. They are different theorems, with different proofs. Put side by side, for a Hermitian \A \in M_n(F) (F = 
R or 
C) and a real \B \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R):  egin{aligned} \lambda_k(\A) &= \min_{\dim W = n-k+1}\ \max_{\cvec{0} 
e \cvec{x} \in W} R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) \ &= \max_{\dim W = k}\ \min_{\cvec{0} 
e \cvec{x} \in W} R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) , \[4pt] v(\B) &= \min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n}\ \max_{\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m} \cvec{x}	p\B\cvec{y} \ &= \max_{\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m}\ \min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n} \cvec{x}	p\B\cvec{y} . \end{aligned} What is being chosen. In Courant–Fischer the outer variable is a subspace W, and the inner variable is a vector inside that subspace. The inner set depends on the outer choice, so the formula is a nested optimization, not a game between two independent players. In von Neumann’s theorem the two variables range over fixed sets, \Delta_m and \Delta_n, neither of which depends on the other. What the theorem asserts. Von Neumann’s theorem is an exchange of order: the same function, with the max and the min taken in both orders, gives the same number. Courant–Fischer exchanges nothing. Its two forms use different dimensions, n - k + 1 and k, and swapping the order while keeping the dimension gives \lambda_{n+1-k}(\A), which differs from \lambda_k(\A) unless n = 2k - 1 or the two eigenvalues happen to be equal (the warning after @thm-courant-fischer). The sharpest contrast is in the inequality between the two forms. In von Neumann’s theorem, “max–min \le min–max” is @lem-max-min-le-min-max, and it is free for every function. In Courant–Fischer the corresponding inequality \max_{\dim W = k}\ \min_{\cvec{0} 
e \cvec{x} \in W} R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) \ \le\ \min_{\dim W' = n-k+1}\ \max_{\cvec{0} 
e \cvec{x} \in W'} R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) is not free: it is exactly the dimension count. Since k + (n - k + 1) > n, any W of dimension k meets any W' of dimension n - k + 1 in a nonzero vector \cvec{x} (@lem-subspace-intersection), and then \min_{W} R_{\A} \le R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) \le \max_{W'} R_{\A}. Where the equality comes from. In Courant–Fischer it is a dimension count. Any subspace of dimension n - k + 1 must meet the span of the top k eigenvectors, by @lem-subspace-intersection, and on the shared vector the Rayleigh quotient is pinned. Convexity plays no role: the subspaces of dimension n - k + 1 do not form a convex set in any sense used here, and R_{\A} is not linear. In von Neumann’s theorem it is convexity. The strategy sets are simplices, the payoff is linear in each variable separately, and the equality is linear programming duality, which is Farkas’s lemma, which is a separating hyperplane. No dimension is counted anywhere. What they need. Courant–Fischer needs a Hermitian matrix, since the spectral theorem supplies the eigenvectors that are its witnesses. Von Neumann’s theorem holds for every real matrix, square or not. How each fails when its key ingredient is removed. Replace the simplices by the finite sets of pure strategies, which are not convex, and von Neumann’s equality fails, as in the matching game above. Replace the dimension n - k + 1 by n - k, which is possible when k < n, so that the dimension count no longer forces an intersection, and Courant–Fischer’s formula returns \lambda_{k+1}(\A) instead of \lambda_k(\A). Solving a game [A game with an unused column] Find the value and optimal strategies for the game with payoff matrix \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 & 2 \ -2 & 4 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . No saddle point. The row minima are -1 and -2, so \max_i\min_j a_{ij} = -1. The column maxima are 3, 4, 2, so \min_j\max_i a_{ij} = 2. The two differ, so both players must mix. Row’s side. Write \cvec{x} = (p, 1 - p) with 0 \le p \le 1. Then \A	p\cvec{x} =  igl(5p - 2,\ 4 - 5p,\ 2p igr) , and by @lem-pure-best-response Row guarantees g(p) = \min\{5p - 2,\ 4 - 5p,\ 2p\}. The graph of g is the lower envelope of three lines. For p \le 	frac35 the first line is the lowest: 5p - 2 \le 4 - 5p exactly when p \le 	frac35, and 5p - 2 \le 2p exactly when p \le 	frac23. For p \ge 	frac35 the second line is the lowest: 4 - 5p \le 2p exactly when p \ge 	frac47, which holds since 	frac35 > 	frac47. So g(p) = 5p - 2 on [0, 	frac35] and g(p) = 4 - 5p on [	frac35, 1]. With slopes 5 and -5, g strictly increases on the first interval and strictly decreases on the second, so its maximum g igl(	frac35 igr) = 1 is attained at p = 	frac35 and nowhere else. The only optimal strategy for Row is \cvec{x}^{\star} =  igl(	frac35, 	frac25 igr), and \A	p\cvec{x}^{\star} =  igl(1, 1, 	frac65 igr). Column’s side. Against \cvec{x}^{\star}, column 3 costs Column 	frac65, which is more than the value, so we expect Column never to use it. Try \cvec{y} = (q, 1 - q, 0): then \A\cvec{y} = (4q - 1,\ 4 - 6q), and the two entries are equal when q = 	frac12. So \cvec{y}^{\star} =  igl(	frac12, 	frac12, 0 igr), with \A\cvec{y}^{\star} = (1, 1). Verification. \A	p\cvec{x}^{\star} =  igl(1, 1, 	frac65 igr) \ge 1\cdot\1 and \A\cvec{y}^{\star} = (1, 1) \le 1\cdot\1. As in Step 3 of the proof, these two inequalities give @eq-minimax-saddle with v = 1. So the value is v(\A) = 1, Row’s optimal strategy is  igl(	frac35, 	frac25 igr), and  igl(	frac12, 	frac12, 0 igr) is optimal for Column. Column’s optimal strategy is unique too. If \cvec{y} is optimal for Column, then \A\cvec{y} \le \1, so \cvec{x}^{\star	op}\A\cvec{y} \le 1. But \cvec{x}^{\star	op}\A\cvec{y} = y_1 + y_2 + 	frac65y_3 = 1 + 	frac15y_3, so y_3 = 0. With \cvec{y} = (q, 1-q, 0), the conditions 4q - 1 \le 1 and 4 - 6q \le 1 give q \le 	frac12 and q \ge 	frac12. This is complementary slackness (@thm-complementary-slackness) in the language of games: a column whose payoff against an optimal \cvec{x} exceeds the value is never used. In the game of @exm-game-two-by-three, is \cvec{x} =  igl(	frac12, 	frac12 igr) an optimal strategy for Row? What does Column do against it? No. \A	p\cvec{x} =  igl(	frac12, 	frac32, 1 igr), so g(\cvec{x}) = 	frac12 < 1 = v(\A). Column answers with column 1 and pays only 	frac12 on average. The symmetric-looking strategy is not the safe one. “Make the opponent indifferent between all columns” is not a method. In @exm-game-two-by-three, no \cvec{x} \in \Delta_2 makes all three entries of \A	p\cvec{x} equal: the first two are equal only at p = 	frac35, where the third is 	frac65, not 1. The optimal \cvec{x} equalizes only the columns that Column actually uses. Deciding which columns those are is the real content of solving the game, and it is what the linear program decides. Equalizing the wrong set of columns produces a strategy that is not optimal, or a “solution” with negative probabilities. Finally, optimal strategies need not be unique, although in the example both were. @exr-minimax-b3 gives a game in which Row has a whole segment of optimal strategies, which is what the convexity of the optimal set allows. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the standard simplex \Delta_n, a mixed strategy, and the value of a matrix game. 2. State von Neumann’s minimax theorem. 3. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: every matrix game has a saddle point in pure strategies. 4. Explain in two sentences why \max_{x}\min_{y} f(x, y) \le \min_{y}\max_{x} f(x, y) for every function f for which the extrema exist. 5. Name the mechanism that produces the equality in @thm-courant-fischer and the one that produces it in @thm-von-neumann-minimax. (a) \Delta_n = \{ \cvec{x} \in 
R^n : \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0},\ \sum_i x_i = 1 \}. In a game with payoff matrix \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R), a mixed strategy for Row is an \cvec{x} \in \Delta_m and one for Column is a \cvec{y} \in \Delta_n. The value is v(\A) = \max_{\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m}\min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}. (b) For every \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R), \max_{\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m}\min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} = \min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n}\max_{\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}, both extrema being attained. Equivalently, there are \cvec{x}^{\star}, \cvec{y}^{\star} and v with \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}^{\star} \le v \le \cvec{x}^{\star	op}\A\cvec{y} for all \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}. (c) Incorrect. In the matching game with \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}, \max_i\min_j a_{ij} = -1 < 1 = \min_j\max_i a_{ij}. An entry that is smallest in its row and largest in its column would make these equal. (d) For any x_0, y_0, \min_{y} f(x_0, y) \le f(x_0, y_0) \le \max_{x} f(x, y_0). The left side does not involve y_0 and the right side does not involve x_0, so we may maximize the left over x_0 and minimize the right over y_0. (e) For Courant–Fischer, a dimension count: @lem-subspace-intersection forces every competing subspace to meet a span of eigenvectors. For von Neumann, convexity: the strategy sets are simplices and the payoff is linear in each variable, and the equality is linear programming duality, which rests on separation. B. Practice [B1: A two-by-two game] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -3 \ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. 1. Show that the game has no saddle point in pure strategies. 2. Find the value and optimal strategies for both players, and verify the saddle inequality @eq-minimax-saddle. (a) The row minima are -3 and -1, so \max_i\min_j a_{ij} = -1. The column maxima are 2 and 1, so \min_j\max_i a_{ij} = 1. These differ, so no entry is both smallest in its row and largest in its column. (b) For \cvec{x} = (p, 1 - p), \A	p\cvec{x} = (3p - 1,\ 1 - 4p). The first entry increases and the second decreases in p, so their minimum is largest where they are equal: 3p - 1 = 1 - 4p, that is, p = 	frac27, with common value -	frac17. For \cvec{y} = (q, 1 - q), \A\cvec{y} = (5q - 3,\ 1 - 2q), and the entries are equal when q = 	frac47, with common value -	frac17. So take \cvec{x}^{\star} =  igl(	frac27, 	frac57 igr), \cvec{y}^{\star} =  igl(	frac47, 	frac37 igr), and v = -	frac17. Then \A	p\cvec{x}^{\star} = -	frac17\1 and \A\cvec{y}^{\star} = -	frac17\1. For every \cvec{y} \in \Delta_2, \cvec{x}^{\star	op}\A\cvec{y} = -	frac17(y_1 + y_2) = -	frac17, and, since \A\cvec{y}^{\star} = -	frac17\1, for every \cvec{x} \in \Delta_2 we have \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}^{\star} = -	frac17(x_1 + x_2) = -	frac17. So @eq-minimax-saddle holds with equality throughout, and v(\A) = -	frac17. The game slightly favors Column. [B2: A saddle point] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 4 \ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, the second game of this section. Show that \cvec{x}^{\star} = \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{y}^{\star} = \cvec{e}_2 satisfy @eq-minimax-saddle with v = 1, and deduce the value of the game. For \cvec{x} \in \Delta_2, \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{e}_2 = x_1\cdot 1 + x_2\cdot 0 = x_1 \le 1, since x_1 \le x_1 + x_2 = 1. For \cvec{y} \in \Delta_3, \cvec{e}_1	p\A\cvec{y} = 3y_1 + y_2 + 4y_3 \ge y_1 + y_2 + y_3 = 1. So \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{e}_2 \le 1 \le \cvec{e}_1	p\A\cvec{y} for all \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}, which is @eq-minimax-saddle with v = 1. By Step 4 of the proof of @thm-von-neumann-minimax (whose argument uses only @eq-minimax-saddle), the max–min and the min–max both equal 1, so v(\A) = 1. A pure saddle point is a special case of a mixed one. [B3: Many optimal strategies] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 & 1 \ -1 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. 1. Show that v(\A) = 1. 2. Find all optimal strategies for Row. 3. Show that Column has exactly one optimal strategy. (a) Column can play \cvec{e}_3, which gives \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{e}_3 = x_1 + x_2 = 1 for every \cvec{x}. Hence \min_{\cvec{y}}\max_{\cvec{x}}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} \le \max_{\cvec{x}}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{e}_3 = 1 . Row can play \cvec{x} =  igl(	frac12, 	frac12 igr), with \A	p\cvec{x} =  igl(	frac32, 	frac32, 1 igr) \ge \1, so \max_{\cvec{x}}\min_{\cvec{y}}\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} \ge 1 by @lem-pure-best-response. By @thm-von-neumann-minimax both equal v(\A), which is therefore 1. (b) By the remark after @def-value-of-game, \cvec{x} = (p, 1 - p) is optimal exactly when \A	p\cvec{x} = (5p - 1,\ 3 - 3p,\ 1) \ge \1, that is, p \ge 	frac25 and p \le 	frac23. So the optimal strategies for Row are the whole segment  igl\{ (p, 1 - p) : 	frac25 \le p \le 	frac23  igr\}. (c) \cvec{y} = (a, b, c) \in \Delta_3 is optimal exactly when \A\cvec{y} \le \1: 4a + c \le 1 and -a + 3b + c \le 1. Substituting c = 1 - a - b, these become 3a \le b and 2b \le 2a. Hence 3a \le b \le a, so a \le 0, and with a \ge 0 we get a = 0 and then b = 0. So \cvec{y} = \cvec{e}_3 is the unique optimal strategy for Column. C. Going deeper [C1: Symmetric games] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be skew-symmetric, \A	p = -\A. Such a game is symmetric: the two players have the same options, and swapping their roles swaps the payoff’s sign. 1. Prove that \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = 0 for every \cvec{x} \in 
R^n, and deduce that v(\A) = 0. 2. Prove that \cvec{x} is optimal for Row if and only if it is optimal for Column. 3. In rock–paper–scissors, with the pure strategies in that order and payoff 1 for a win, -1 for a loss, and 0 for a tie, \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & -1 \ -1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . Prove that the uniform strategy 	frac13\1 is the only optimal strategy. (a) \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} is a 1 	imes 1 matrix, so it equals its transpose: \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{x}	p\A	p\cvec{x} = -\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x}. Hence \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = 0. Let \cvec{x}^{\star}, \cvec{y}^{\star}, v be as in @thm-von-neumann-minimax. Taking \cvec{y} = \cvec{x}^{\star} in the right half of @eq-minimax-saddle gives v \le \cvec{x}^{\star	op}\A\cvec{x}^{\star} = 0. Taking \cvec{x} = \cvec{y}^{\star} in the left half gives 0 = \cvec{y}^{\star	op}\A\cvec{y}^{\star} \le v. So v(\A) = 0. (b) By the remark after @def-value-of-game and (a), \cvec{x} is optimal for Row exactly when \A	p\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}, and optimal for Column exactly when \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{0}. Since \A	p\cvec{x} = -\A\cvec{x}, the two conditions are the same. (c) With \cvec{x} = (x_1, x_2, x_3) \in \Delta_3, the condition \A	p\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} reads x_2 - x_3 \ge 0, \qquad x_3 - x_1 \ge 0, \qquad x_1 - x_2 \ge 0 . So x_2 \ge x_3 \ge x_1 \ge x_2, all three are equal, and since they sum to 1, each is 	frac13. By (a) and (b), 	frac13\1 is the unique optimal strategy for either player, and the value is 0. [C2: The value depends continuously on the payoffs] For \A, \B \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R), put \varepsilon = \max_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij} - b_{ij}vert. 1. Prove that \lvert v(\A) - v(\B)vert \le \varepsilon. 2. Prove also that if a_{ij} \ge b_{ij} for all i, j, then v(\A) \ge v(\B), and that v(\A + c\J) = v(\A) + c for every real c. (a) For \cvec{x} \in \Delta_m and \cvec{y} \in \Delta_n, \lvert \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} - \cvec{x}	p\B\cvec{y} vert \le \sum_{i,j} x_iy_j\lvert a_{ij} - b_{ij}vert \le \varepsilon\sum_{i,j}x_iy_j = \varepsilon , since \sum_{i,j}x_iy_j = (\sum_i x_i)(\sum_j y_j) = 1. So \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} \le \cvec{x}	p\B\cvec{y} + \varepsilon for all \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}. Taking the minimum over \cvec{y} preserves this inequality between two functions of \cvec{y}, and so does taking the maximum over \cvec{x}. By @thm-von-neumann-minimax the resulting max–mins are the values, so v(\A) \le v(\B) + \varepsilon. Exchanging \A and \B gives v(\B) \le v(\A) + \varepsilon. (b) If a_{ij} \ge b_{ij}, then \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} \ge \cvec{x}	p\B\cvec{y} for all strategies, since every x_iy_j \ge 0, and the same two steps give v(\A) \ge v(\B). For the shift, \cvec{x}	p(\A + c\J)\cvec{y} = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y} + c for all strategies, as in Step 1 of the proof of @thm-von-neumann-minimax, and adding a constant to a function adds it to every minimum and maximum. So v(\A + c\J) = v(\A) + c.

title: 18.8 Extreme Points
content:
Extreme Points Everything so far has gone from points to convex sets: a set of points has a convex hull, and Carathéodory’s theorem says how few points each element of the hull needs. This section asks the reverse question: given a convex set, which of its points cannot be manufactured from the others? A triangle is the hull of its three corners, and no smaller set will do. The corners are the extreme points, and the main theorem, due to Minkowski, says that a compact convex set is always the hull of its extreme points. We then find the extreme points of three unit balls and of the density matrices, show that the permutation matrices are extreme among the doubly stochastic matrices, and end with a compact convex set whose extreme points do not form a closed set. Throughout, the field is 
R, and V is a finite-dimensional real inner product space: 
R^n with the dot product, or M_n(
R) with the Frobenius inner product \inner{\A}{\B} = 	r(\B	p\A) of Chapter 11 §01. Compact is meant as in §03, and closed bounded sets are compact by @cor-closed-bounded-compact. Conversely a compact set is closed, as a subsequence has the limit of the whole sequence, and bounded, as a sequence with 
orm{\elem{x}_k} > k has no convergent subsequence, convergent sequences being bounded; both facts belong to the elementary algebra of limits that Chapter 16’s introduction imports. Points that are not in between A convex set contains the segment between any two of its points (@def-convex-set). In a filled triangle, a point in the middle of an edge sits between the two ends of that edge, and an interior point sits between many pairs. A corner sits between no pair: any segment of the triangle through a corner has the corner as an end. So the corners are the points you cannot do without: delete one from the list of points whose hull you take, and the hull shrinks. An extreme point of a convex set is a point that is not strictly between two other points of the set. [Extreme Point] Let C \subseteq V be a convex set. A point \elem{x} \in C is an extreme point of C if, whenever \elem{x} = t\elem{y} + (1 - t)\elem{z} with \elem{y}, \elem{z} \in C and 0 < t < 1 strictly, then \elem{y} = \elem{z} = \elem{x}. The set of extreme points of C is written \operatorname{ext} C. In words: the only way to put \elem{x} strictly inside a segment of C is the useless way, with both ends equal to \elem{x}. The word strictly matters. With t = 1 allowed, every point would be 1 \cdot \elem{x} + 0 \cdot \elem{z} for any \elem{z} \in C, and no point of a set with two elements or more would be extreme. To test the definition, midpoints are enough. [The Midpoint Test] Let C \subseteq V be convex and \elem{x} \in C. Then \elem{x} is an extreme point of C if and only if, whenever \elem{x} =  rac12(\elem{y} + \elem{z}) with \elem{y}, \elem{z} \in C, we have \elem{y} = \elem{z}. If \elem{x} sits at parameter t \le  rac12 on a segment [\elem{z}, \elem{y}], shorten the segment to [\elem{z}, \elem{y}'] with \elem{y}' at parameter 2t; then \elem{x} is its midpoint. (\Rightarrow) Take t =  rac12 in @def-extreme-point. (\Leftarrow) Let \elem{x} = t\elem{y} + (1 - t)\elem{z} with \elem{y}, \elem{z} \in C and 0 < t < 1. Swapping the names of \elem{y} and \elem{z} if necessary, we may assume t \le  rac12. Put \elem{y}' = 2t\elem{y} + (1 - 2t)\elem{z}. Since 0 < 2t \le 1, \elem{y}' lies on the segment from \elem{z} to \elem{y}, so \elem{y}' \in C by convexity. Moreover 	frac12(\elem{y}' + \elem{z}) = t\elem{y} + (1 - t)\elem{z} = \elem{x} , so the hypothesis gives \elem{y}' = \elem{z}, that is, 2t(\elem{y} - \elem{z}) = \elem{0}. As t 
e 0, \elem{y} = \elem{z}, and then \elem{x} = t\elem{y} + (1 - t)\elem{y} = \elem{y}. So \elem{y} = \elem{z} = \elem{x}, as claimed. Now some examples, simplest first. 1. A single point. C = \{\elem{x}\} is convex, and \elem{x} is extreme: any \elem{y}, \elem{z} \in C equal \elem{x}. 2. A closed segment C = \{t\elem{a} + (1 - t)\elem{b} : 0 \le t \le 1\} with \elem{a} 
e \elem{b} has exactly two extreme points, \elem{a} and \elem{b}. A point \elem{x} with parameter 0 < s < 1 is not extreme, since \elem{x} = s\elem{a} + (1 - s)\elem{b} with \elem{a} 
e \elem{b}. The end \elem{a} is extreme: if \elem{a} =  rac12(\elem{y} + \elem{z}) with \elem{y}, \elem{z} at parameters r, r' \in [0, 1], then comparing coefficients along the line gives  rac12(r + r') = 1, which forces r = r' = 1 and \elem{y} = \elem{z} = \elem{a}. (The coefficient comparison is legitimate because t \mapsto t\elem{a} + (1-t)\elem{b} = \elem{b} + t(\elem{a} - \elem{b}) is injective, as \elem{a} - \elem{b} 
e \elem{0}.) 3. The closed half-plane H = \{(x_1, x_2) \in 
R^2 : x_2 \ge 0\} has no extreme points. Every \cvec{x} \in H is the midpoint of \cvec{x} + \cvec{e}_1 and \cvec{x} - \cvec{e}_1, both in H, and they differ. 4. The empty set is convex and compact with no extreme points. It satisfies the main theorem below only because \conv\emptyset = \emptyset, which is why the theorem’s last sentence says “nonempty”. The closed disk B_2 \subseteq 
R^2 is a richer example: its extreme points are the whole unit circle. The section on unit balls below proves this for every n. A nonexample by minimal change. Take the closed triangle T = \conv\{(0,0), (2,0), (0,2)\} and slide from the corner (2, 0) along the edge to its midpoint (1, 1). The point (1,1) is still in T, still on its boundary, and still on a line with all of T on one side (x_1 + x_2 \le 2 on T). What fails is the one clause of @def-extreme-point: (1,1) =  rac12 igl((2,0) + (0,2) igr) with (2,0) 
e (0,2). Extreme is not the same as “on the boundary”. The point (1, 1) just used lies on the boundary of the triangle T, and every open disk around it contains points outside T; yet it is not extreme. The other direction does hold, for every convex set: an extreme point is never an interior point, since an interior point \cvec{x} is the midpoint of \cvec{x} \pm \varepsilon\cvec{e}_1 for small \varepsilon > 0. Let S = \{(0,0), (2,0), (0,2), (1,1), (1,0)\}. Which points of S are extreme points of \conv S? Only (0,0), (2,0), and (0,2). The hull is the triangle T = \{x_1 \ge 0,\ x_2 \ge 0,\ x_1 + x_2 \le 2\} above, because (1,1) and (1,0) =  rac12 igl((0,0) + (2,0) igr) already lie in T. Each of those two points is the midpoint of two distinct points of T, so neither is extreme. The corners are extreme. For (2, 0): if (2,0) =  rac12(\cvec{y} + \cvec{z}) with \cvec{y}, \cvec{z} \in T, then y_1, z_1 \le 2 and  rac12(y_1 + z_1) = 2 force y_1 = z_1 = 2, and the only point of T with first coordinate 2 is (2,0), because x_2 \ge 0 and x_1 + x_2 \le 2. The other two corners are handled the same way, with x_2 and with -x_1 - x_2 in place of x_1. Why this definition. It does not ask \elem{x} to be far from the rest of C, or on a corner; on the disk, extreme points have extreme neighbors arbitrarily close. It asks only that \elem{x} not be an average of other points of C, which is what “cannot be manufactured from the others” means for a convex hull. Exercise C1 shows that \elem{x} is extreme exactly when C \setminus \{\elem{x}\} is still convex. The first result makes the indispensability precise: if a convex set is the hull of S, then S contains every extreme point. [Extreme Points of a Hull Come From the Generators] Let S \subseteq V be any set. Then \operatorname{ext}(\conv S) \subseteq S. Split off one generator from a convex combination: what remains is again a point of the hull, and \elem{x} lies strictly between the two. Let \elem{x} be an extreme point of \conv S. By @thm-convex-hull-combinations, \elem{x} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i\elem{s}_i with \elem{s}_i \in S, every t_i > 0 (drop the zero terms) and \sum_i t_i = 1. If k = 1 then \elem{x} = \elem{s}_1 \in S. If k \ge 2, then 0 < t_1 < 1, and \elem{x} = t_1\elem{s}_1 + (1 - t_1)\elem{r} , \qquad \elem{r} = \sum_{i=2}^{k}  rac{t_i}{1 - t_1}\,\elem{s}_i . Faces A single extreme point is too small an object for an induction on dimension. The right object is a piece of the set that behaves like an extreme point as a whole. [Face] Let C \subseteq V be convex. A face of C is a convex subset F \subseteq C such that, whenever t\elem{y} + (1 - t)\elem{z} \in F with \elem{y}, \elem{z} \in C and 0 < t < 1, both \elem{y} and \elem{z} lie in F. So a face swallows every segment of C that passes through it at an inner point. The empty set and C itself are faces, and a one-point set \{\elem{x}\} is a face exactly when \elem{x} is an extreme point: that is @def-extreme-point word for word. The edges of a triangle are faces. The segment joining the midpoints of two edges is convex but is not a face: if the triangle has corners \elem{a}, \elem{b}, \elem{c} and the segment joins  rac12(\elem{a} + \elem{b}) to  rac12(\elem{a} + \elem{c}), its midpoint is  rac12\elem{a} +  rac12\cdot rac12(\elem{b} + \elem{c}), an inner point of a segment of the triangle whose ends \elem{a} and  rac12(\elem{b} + \elem{c}) do not lie on it. What makes faces useful for an induction is that they pass extremeness upwards. [Extreme Points of a Face] Let C \subseteq V be convex and F a face of C. Then \operatorname{ext} F = F \cap \operatorname{ext} C. In particular an extreme point of a face is an extreme point of C. Let \elem{x} \in \operatorname{ext} F, and let \elem{x} = t\elem{y} + (1 - t)\elem{z} with \elem{y}, \elem{z} \in C and 0 < t < 1. Since F is a face, \elem{y}, \elem{z} \in F, and since \elem{x} is extreme in F, \elem{y} = \elem{z} = \elem{x}. So \elem{x} \in \operatorname{ext} C. Conversely a point of F that is extreme in C is extreme in the smaller set F, because the definition then quantifies over fewer pairs \elem{y}, \elem{z}. The faces we can actually produce are the ones cut off by a hyperplane that has the whole set on one side. This is the situation of @thm-supporting-hyperplane. R) : \X	p = \X,\ \O \preceq \X \preceq \I\}, where \X \preceq \I means \I - \X \succeq \O (@def-loewner-order). 1. Prove that every symmetric \P with \P^2 = \P, that is, every orthogonal projection, is an extreme point of \cE. 2. Prove that no other point of \cE is extreme. 3. Deduce that every \X \in \cE is a convex combination of orthogonal projections, and give such a combination for \X = \diag( rac12,  rac14). Hint for (a): use @lem-psd-form-zero twice, once on \ker\P and once on \im\P. (a) First, \P \in \cE: its eigenvalues satisfy \lambda^2 = \lambda, so each is 0 or 1, and \P and \I - \P have eigenvalues in \{0, 1\}, hence are positive semidefinite (@thm-psd-characterizations). Let \P =  rac12(\A + \B) with \A, \B \in \cE. If \P\cvec{x} = \cvec{x}, then 0 = \cvec{x}	p(\I - \P)\cvec{x} =  rac12\cvec{x}	p(\I - \A)\cvec{x} +  rac12\cvec{x}	p(\I - \B)\cvec{x}, so \cvec{x}	p(\I - \A)\cvec{x} = 0 and, since \I - \A \succeq \O, (\I - \A)\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}, that is, \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{x}.
