The left and right eigenvectors for ho(\A) are unrelated in general; here \cvec{w}	p\cvec{v} = 10 + 11 + 14 = 35 for \cvec{v} = (1, 1, 2). @def-perron-vector below scales them so that this pairing is 1. The swap \S =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is nonnegative. Which conclusions of @thm-perron hold for \S, and which fail? \S has eigenvalues 1 and -1, with eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, -1). So ho(\S) = 1 is an eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector, it is simple, and the only nonnegative eigenvectors are the positive multiples of (1,1): (a), (b), (d) and (e) hold. Part (c) fails, since -1 
e 1 and \lvert -1vert = 1 = ho(\S). The hypothesis that fails is \S > \O: two entries are 0. This is the matrix whose powers do not converge in the warning of Chapter 9 §11, and (c) is exactly what was missing there. The positive eigenvector is so useful that it gets a name. [Perron Root, Perron Vector] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be positive. The number ho(\A) is the Perron root of \A. The Perron vector of \A is the unique \cvec{v} > \cvec{0} with \A\cvec{v} = ho(\A)\cvec{v} and v_1 + \dots + v_n = 1. The left Perron vector of \A is the unique \cvec{w} > \cvec{0} with \cvec{w}	p\A = ho(\A)\cvec{w}	p and \cvec{w}	p\cvec{v} = 1, where \cvec{v} is the Perron vector. Existence and uniqueness are @thm-perron (a) and (b): the eigenspace for ho(\A) is a line through a positive vector, and it meets the hyperplane \{\1	p\cvec{x} = 1\} in exactly one point, the vector \cvec{v}/(\1	p\cvec{v}). By (d), the Perron vector is also the only eigenvector of \A in \Delta_n. Likewise, by (e) and (b) applied to \A	p, the positive left eigenvectors for ho(\A) are the positive multiples of one \cvec{w}_0 > \cvec{0}, and since \cvec{w}_0	p\cvec{v} > 0, exactly one of them, \cvec{w}_0/(\cvec{w}_0	p\cvec{v}), pairs with the Perron vector to 1. The two normalizations differ on purpose: \cvec{v} is a probability vector, and \cvec{w}	p\cvec{v} = 1 makes \cvec{v}\cvec{w}	p a projection, the limit of (\A/ho(\A))^{k} that §05 finds. For @exm-perron-two-by-two the Perron vector is  rac15(2, 3) and the left Perron vector is (1, 1), since \1	p\cvec{v} = 1. For @exm-perron-three-by-three the Perron vector is  rac14(1, 1, 2), and the left Perron vector is  rac{4}{35}(10, 11, 7), since (10, 11, 7) pairs with  rac14(1, 1, 2) to  rac{35}{4}. Perron’s theorem says nothing about the other eigenvalues except their size. They may be negative, as -1 is in @exm-perron-two-by-two, or nonreal: the positive matrix  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \ 3 & 1 & 2 \ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix} has row sums 6, hence the eigenvector \1 for 6, and its other two eigenvalues are the roots of x^2 + 3x + 3, namely  rac{-3 \pm i\sqrt3}{2}, of modulus \sqrt3 < 6. They may also be repeated, as the eigenvalue 1 of  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} is. Simplicity is claimed for ho(\A) alone. What positivity buys, and what it costs Each hypothesis of @thm-perron has a job, and it is instructive to see where it went. Positivity of \A was used in the push-up claim, to turn a nonnegative, nonzero slack into a strictly positive one; in Step 4, to divide by a_{1j}; and in Step 1, to make r > 0. For a matrix that is only nonnegative, each of these uses fails, and so can each conclusion: Exercise C2 gives a nonnegative 2 	imes 2 matrix for each of (a)–(d), and the swap of the Quick check is the one for (c). §03 shows that one conclusion survives in general, that ho(\A) is an eigenvalue with a nonnegative eigenvector, and that most of the rest returns under a hypothesis much weaker than positivity. That hypothesis, irreducibility, is a condition on where the zero entries are, and §02 introduces it. Here is the payoff for Chapter 9. A stochastic matrix has \1	p\A = \1	p, so \1 is a positive left eigenvector for 1. If \A is stochastic and positive, @thm-perron (d) applied to \A	p says that \1 is a left eigenvector for ho(\A) and for no other eigenvalue, so ho(\A) = 1. Then (b) and (c) say that 1 is simple and every other eigenvalue has modulus less than 1: two of the three hypotheses of @thm-markov-limit-diagonalizable hold automatically. The third, diagonalizability, is the one §06 removes. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define what it means for a real matrix to be nonnegative and to be positive, and define \lvert\Mvert for a complex matrix \M. 2. State @thm-perron. 3. True or false: a positive symmetric matrix is positive definite. Justify your answer. 4. True or false: a positive matrix has no negative eigenvalue. Justify your answer. 5. True or false: if \O \le \A \le \B and \A 
e \B, then ho(\A) < ho(\B). Justify your answer. 6. In the proof of @thm-perron, which step uses compactness, and why is the quotient \min_i(\A\cvec{x})_i/x_i not maximized directly? (a) \A is nonnegative if every entry is \ge 0, and positive if every entry is > 0 (@def-entrywise-order). \lvert\Mvert is the real matrix whose (i,j) entry is \lvert m_{ij}vert. (b) If \A \in M_n(
R) and \A > \O, then r = ho(\A) > 0 is an eigenvalue of \A with a positive eigenvector \cvec{v}; it is algebraically simple; every other eigenvalue has modulus less than r; every nonnegative eigenvector is a positive multiple of \cvec{v}; and the same holds for \A	p, which gives a positive left eigenvector. (c) False.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} is positive and symmetric with the eigenvalue -1; the warning after @def-entrywise-order computes \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = -2 for \cvec{x} = (1, -1). (d) False.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix} has the eigenvalue -1 (@exm-perron-two-by-two). Perron’s theorem controls only the modulus of the other eigenvalues. (e) False. \diag(1, 0) \le \I_2, the two differ, and both have spectral radius 1. (f) Step 1: the set S is closed and bounded, so by (A3) and (A4) the coordinate t attains a maximum on it. The quotient is undefined where some x_i = 0. For a nonnegative matrix its natural repair can be discontinuous on the boundary of \Delta_n (for \diag(2, 1) it jumps at \cvec{e}_1), so the extreme value theorem does not apply to it directly. For positive \A the repair is in fact continuous, but proving that costs more than maximizing t over S. B. Practice [B1: A Perron vector by hand] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \ 3 & 4 & 3 \ 3 & 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}. Find the eigenvalues of \A, its Perron root, Perron vector, and left Perron vector. Check that no eigenvector for the other eigenvalues is nonnegative. Expanding \det(x\I - \A) along the first row,  egin{aligned} p_{\A}(x) &= (x - 2) igl((x - 4)^2 - 3 igr) +  igl(-3(x - 4) - 9 igr) -  igl(3 + 3(x - 4) igr) \ &= x^3 - 10x^2 + 23x - 14 = (x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 7) . \end{aligned} (Check: 	r\A = 10 and \det\A = 14.) So the eigenvalues are 7, 2, 1, and ho(\A) = 7. Solving (\A - 7\I)\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}, whose first two rows are -5x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0 and 3x_1 - 3x_2 + 3x_3 = 0, gives \cvec{x} = t(1, 3, 2); indeed \A(1, 3, 2) = (7, 21, 14). The entries of (1, 3, 2) add up to 6, so the Perron vector is  rac16(1, 3, 2). For the left eigenvector, (\A	p - 7\I)\cvec{w} = \cvec{0} gives the multiples of (3, 2, 3), and (3, 2, 3)\A = (21, 14, 21) = 7\,(3, 2, 3). Against the Perron vector, (3, 2, 3) \cdot  rac16(1, 3, 2) =  rac{15}{6} =  rac52, so by @def-perron-vector the left Perron vector is  rac25(3, 2, 3) =  igl( rac65,  rac45,  rac65 igr). For 2: (\A - 2\I)\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} gives \cvec{x} = t(1, 3, -3), since \A(1, 3, -3) = (2, 6, -6). For 1: \cvec{x} = t(1, 0, -1), since \A(1, 0, -1) = (1, 0, -1). For t 
e 0 each has entries of both signs, so neither is nonnegative, as @thm-perron (d) predicts. [B2: Which order?] For each matrix, decide whether it is nonnegative, whether it is positive, and whether it is positive definite. Justify your answers, and say whether @thm-perron applies. 1.  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} 2.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} 3.  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} 4.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} 5.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} For a real symmetric 2 	imes 2 matrix, positive definite means both eigenvalues are positive (@def-positive-semidefinite, with the spectral theorem). (a) Positive, hence nonnegative. Eigenvalues 3, 1, both positive, so positive definite. Perron applies: ho = 3 with eigenvector (1, 1). (b) Positive, hence nonnegative. Eigenvalues 4, -2, so not positive definite. Perron applies: ho = 4 with eigenvector (1,1), and \lvert -2vert < 4. (c) Not nonnegative, since the off-diagonal entries are -1; so not positive, and Perron does not apply. It is positive definite, with eigenvalues 1, 3. (d) Nonnegative, not positive (the (1,2) entry is 0), and not symmetric, so not positive definite by clause (P1). Perron does not apply, although here ho = 3 is an eigenvalue with the eigenvector \cvec{e}_2 \ge \cvec{0}, which is not positive. (e) Positive. Eigenvalues 2 and 0, so positive semidefinite but not positive definite, as \cvec{x} = (1, -1) gives \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = 0. Perron applies: ho = 2, eigenvector (1,1), and the eigenvalue 0 has modulus less than 2. [B3: Bounds from the smallest and largest entry] 1. Show that ho(c\J) = nc for every real c \ge 0, where \J is the n 	imes n all-ones matrix. 2. Let \A \in M_n(
R) with a \le a_{ij} \le b for all i, j, where 0 \le a \le b. Prove that na \le ho(\A) \le nb. 3. Hence bound ho(\A) for \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \ 2 & 3 & 1 \ 3 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, and compare with its exact value. (a) \J\1 = n\1, so n is an eigenvalue of \J. Also \J^2 = n\J, since every entry of \J^2 is a sum of n ones. If \J\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} with \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}, then \lambda^2\cvec{x} = \J^2\cvec{x} = n\J\cvec{x} = n\lambda\cvec{x}, so \lambda^2 = n\lambda and \lambda \in \{0, n\}. Hence ho(\J) = n, and ho(c\J) = c\,ho(\J) = nc because the eigenvalues of c\J are c times those of \J. (b) The hypothesis says \O \le a\J \le \A \le b\J. By @prp-spectral-radius-monotone (a), applied twice, ho(a\J) \le ho(\A) \le ho(b\J), and by (a) this reads na \le ho(\A) \le nb. (c) The entries lie between 1 and 3 and n = 3, so 3 \le ho(\A) \le 9. In fact every row sums to 6, so \A\1 = 6\,\1, and @thm-perron (d) says the positive eigenvector \1 belongs to ho(\A). Hence ho(\A) = 6. C. Going deeper [C1: Symmetry passes to the Perron vector] Let \A > \O be n 	imes n with Perron vector \cvec{v}, and let \P be a permutation matrix with \P	p\A\P = \A. 1. Prove that \P\cvec{v} = \cvec{v}. 2. Deduce that the Perron vector of \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 3 \ 1 & 1 & 3 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has equal first and second entries, and find it. 3. Deduce that if \A > \O commutes with the cyclic permutation matrix of 1 	o 2 	o \dots 	o n 	o 1, then its Perron vector is  rac1n\1. Hint: for (a), \P\cvec{v} is a positive vector in \Delta_n. (a) By @lem-permutation-matrices (b), \P\P	p = \I, so \A\P = \P\P	p\A\P = \P\A. Hence \A(\P\cvec{v}) = \P\A\cvec{v} = ho(\A)\,\P\cvec{v}. The entries of \P\cvec{v} are those of \cvec{v} in another order (\P = \P_\sigma sends \cvec{e}_j to \cvec{e}_{\sigma(j)}), so \P\cvec{v} > \cvec{0} and its entries add up to 1. By @def-perron-vector and the uniqueness proved after it, \P\cvec{v} = \cvec{v}. (b) Let \P be the permutation matrix that swaps \cvec{e}_1 and \cvec{e}_2. Then \P	p\A\P is \A with rows 1, 2 swapped and columns 1, 2 swapped, which is \A again, because rows 1 and 2 of \A are equal and so are columns 1 and 2. By (a), \P\cvec{v} = \cvec{v}, that is, v_1 = v_2. Now try \cvec{v} = (1, 1, c): \A\cvec{v} = (2 + 3c, 2 + 3c, 2 + c), and \A\cvec{v} = \lambda\cvec{v} requires \lambda = 2 + 3c and 2 + c = (2 + 3c)c, that is, 3c^2 + c - 2 = 0, so c =  rac23 or c = -1. The positive choice c =  rac23 gives the eigenvector (3, 3, 2) with eigenvalue 4, and by @thm-perron (d) this is the Perron eigenvector, so ho(\A) = 4 and the Perron vector is  rac18(3, 3, 2). (c) Let \C be the cyclic permutation matrix, \C\cvec{e}_j = \cvec{e}_{j+1} for j < n and \C\cvec{e}_n = \cvec{e}_1. If \A\C = \C\A, then \C	p\A\C = \C	p\C\A = \A by @lem-permutation-matrices (b). By (a), \C\cvec{v} = \cvec{v}, which says v_n = v_1 and v_j = v_{j+1} for j < n, so all entries are equal. As they add up to 1, \cvec{v} =  rac1n\1. [C2: Every conclusion fails for some nonnegative matrix] For each part of @thm-perron, (a) to (d), give a nonnegative 2 	imes 2 matrix for which that part fails, and name the step of the proof that breaks. Then give a nonnegative matrix for which (a), (b) and (c) fail at the same time. (a) \J_2(0) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has ho = 0, and its eigenvectors are the nonzero multiples of \cvec{e}_1, none positive. In the proof, r > 0 came from the smallest row sum, which here is 0; and the push-up claim fails, since \cvec{u} = \cvec{e}_1 satisfies \A\cvec{u} = 0\cdot\cvec{u} without being positive. (b) \I_2: ho = 1 is a double eigenvalue and E_1 = 
R^2. Step 5 fails: \cvec{u} - 	heta\cvec{v} can be nonzero and nonnegative with a zero entry, since \A\cvec{y} > \cvec{0} is no longer forced. (c)  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}: the eigenvalue -1 has modulus ho = 1. Step 4 fails: equality in the triangle inequality (@lem-triangle-equality-complex) is automatic when each row has a single nonzero term, so it aligns nothing. (d) \diag(2, 1): the eigenvector \cvec{e}_2 \ge \cvec{0} belongs to 1 
e 2 = ho. Step 7 fails, because the left eigenvector for 2 is \cvec{e}_1, which is not positive, and \cvec{e}_1	p\cvec{e}_2 = 0 is no contradiction. For all three at once, take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . It is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and (1), so p_{\A}(x) = (x^2 - 1)(x - 1) = (x - 1)^2(x + 1) by @thm-det-block-triangular, applied to x\I - \A over F[x], as the paragraph after it notes. Hence ho(\A) = 1 and a_{\A}(1) = 2, so (b) fails, and \lvert -1vert = ho(\A), so (c) fails. The system (\A - \I)\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} reads -x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0 and x_1 - x_2 = 0, which forces x_3 = 0; so every eigenvector for 1 is a multiple of (1, 1, 0), none of them positive, and (a) fails. [C3: The Perron root is strictly monotone] Let \A, \B \in M_n(
R) with \O < \A \le \B and \A 
e \B. 1. Prove that ho(\A) < ho(\B). 2. Show by an example that the conclusion fails if \A > \O is weakened to \A \ge \O. Hint: pair \B\cvec{v} with a positive left eigenvector of \B, where \cvec{v} is the Perron vector of \A. (a) \B \ge \A > \O, so \B is positive too. Let \cvec{v} > \cvec{0} be the Perron vector of \A, and by @thm-perron (e) let \cvec{w} > \cvec{0} satisfy \cvec{w}	p\B = ho(\B)\cvec{w}	p. Then ho(\B)\,\cvec{w}	p\cvec{v} = \cvec{w}	p\B\cvec{v} = \cvec{w}	p\A\cvec{v} + \cvec{w}	p(\B - \A)\cvec{v} = ho(\A)\,\cvec{w}	p\cvec{v} + \cvec{w}	p(\B - \A)\cvec{v} . The matrix \B - \A is nonnegative and nonzero, say b_{kl} - a_{kl} > 0, so \cvec{w}	p(\B - \A)\cvec{v} \ge w_k(b_{kl} - a_{kl})v_l > 0, every other term being \ge 0. Since \cvec{w}	p\cvec{v} > 0, dividing gives ho(\B) > ho(\A). (b) \A = \diag(1, 0) and \B = \I_2 satisfy \O \le \A \le \B and \A 
e \B, with ho(\A) = ho(\B) = 1. In the argument of (a), the Perron vector of \A is replaced by \cvec{e}_1, and (\B - \A)\cvec{e}_1 = \cvec{0}: the extra mass sits where the eigenvector does not look.

title: 19.2 Irreducibility and Graphs
content:
Irreducibility and Graphs Perron’s theorem (@thm-perron) asks for every entry to be positive, and most matrices that arise in practice do not oblige. The bicycle chain of Chapter 9 §11 has a zero entry, since a bicycle at station 3 never reaches station 1 in one night; the Leslie matrix of the same section is mostly zeros; the swap has only two nonzero entries. Some zeros are harmless and some are fatal: the swap keeps ho = 1 as a simple eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector, while for \I_2 the eigenvalue 1 is double and its positive eigenvectors are no longer all multiples of one. This section finds the dividing line. It depends only on where the zero entries are, and the right way to read that pattern is as a map of one-step moves between the indices: a directed graph. The matrices on the good side of the line are the irreducible ones, and §03 proves that they enjoy nearly all of Perron’s conclusions. Throughout, F is 
R or 
C. The definitions of this section use only whether an entry is zero, so they make sense for any matrix. The statements about powers and positivity need \A \ge \O, and say so. The graph of a matrix The question that recurs is this: which entries of \A^{k} are nonzero? For a nonnegative matrix, (\A^2)_{ij} = \sum_l a_{il}a_{lj} is positive exactly when some a_{il} and a_{lj} are both positive, that is, when one can go from j to some l and from l to i along nonzero entries. In a Markov chain (@def-markov-chain), a_{lj} is the probability of moving from state j to state l in one step, and the sentence says that state i can be reached from j in two steps. So we draw an arrow from j to i for each nonzero entry a_{ij} and count routes. The graph of a matrix has a vertex for each index and an arrow from j to i whenever the entry a_{ij} is not zero. [Directed Graph of a Matrix; Walks and Paths] Let n \ge 1 and \A = (a_{ij}) \in M_n(F). 1. The directed graph G(\A) of \A has vertices 1, 2, \dots, n, and an edge from j to i, written j 	o i, for each pair (i, j) with a_{ij} 
e 0. An edge j 	o j, from a nonzero diagonal entry, is a loop. 2. A walk of length k \ge 0 from j to i is a list of vertices j = i_0, i_1, \dots, i_k = i such that i_{t-1} 	o i_t is an edge for every t = 1, \dots, k. 3. A path is a walk whose vertices i_0, \dots, i_k are distinct. In words: (a) turns each nonzero entry into an arrow, and the arrow for a_{ij} points from the column index to the row index. That is the direction in which \A moves things: in \cvec{x} \mapsto \A\cvec{x}, entry j of \cvec{x} contributes a_{ij}x_j to entry i of the image, and in a column-stochastic chain a_{ij} is the probability of the move from j to i. Clause (b) allows k = 0: the one-vertex list (j) is a walk of length 0 from j to itself, whatever the matrix. A walk may revisit vertices and use an edge several times; a path may not. Many books draw the arrow for a_{ij} 
e 0 from i to j. The two graphs differ by reversing every edge, and nothing below depends on the choice except the wording “from j to i”. We take the direction that matches \cvec{x}_{k+1} = \A\cvec{x}_k and the column-stochastic convention of Chapter 9 §11. Examples, simplest first. - n = 1. G((a)) has one vertex, with a loop if a 
e 0 and no edge if a = 0. In either case there is the walk of length 0 from 1 to 1. - The zero matrix \O \in M_n(F) has n vertices and no edges at all. A positive matrix has every possible edge, loops included. - A cycle. The permutation matrix \C =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} has c_{21} = c_{32} = c_{13} = 1, so its edges are 1 	o 2, 2 	o 3 and 3 	o 1. - A path.  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} has the edges 1 	o 2 and 2 	o 3 only. There is a walk from 1 to 3, and none from 3 to anywhere but 3 itself. - \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 2 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \ 3 & 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix} has the edges 2 	o 1, 3 	o 2, 1 	o 3 and the loop 3 	o 3, drawn below. The values of the entries play no part in the graph. Nonexample by minimal change. The graph records whether an entry is zero, not how large it is. Change the entry 3 of the last matrix to 10^{-9}: the graph is unchanged. Change it to 0: the edge 1 	o 3 disappears, and with it every walk out of vertex 1 other than the one of length 0. The graph was built to count routes, and it does, for nonnegative matrices. The same lemma handles \I + \A, whose graph is that of \A with a loop added at every vertex; a loop lets a walk wait, so walks of length at most k become walks of length exactly k. [Powers Count Walks] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be nonnegative, and let k \ge 0 and i, j \in \{1, \dots, n\}. 1. (\A^{k})_{ij} > 0 if and only if G(\A) has a walk of length k from j to i. 2.  igl((\I + \A)^{k} igr)_{ij} > 0 if and only if G(\A) has a walk of length at most k from j to i. Induction on k, peeling off the first step of a walk. Expanding (\A^{k+1})_{ij} = \sum_l (\A^{k})_{il}a_{lj} gives a sum of nonnegative terms, so it is positive exactly when one term is: a first step j 	o l followed by a walk of length k from l to i. For \I + \A the diagonal 1 adds the option of waiting at j instead of stepping. (a) Induction on k. For k = 0, (\I)_{ij} > 0 exactly when i = j, which is exactly when there is a walk of length 0 from j to i. Suppose (a) holds for k. By @lem-entrywise-order-rules (c), \A^{k} \ge \O, so (\A^{k+1})_{ij} = \sum_{l=1}^{n}(\A^{k})_{il}\,a_{lj} is a sum of nonnegative terms. It is positive if and only if some term is, that is, if and only if there is an l with a_{lj} > 0 and (\A^{k})_{il} > 0. By the definition of G(\A) and the induction hypothesis, this says: there is an edge j 	o l and a walk of length k from l to i. Putting j in front of that walk gives a walk of length k + 1 from j to i, and every such walk arises this way, with l its second vertex. (b) Induction on k, with the same base case, since (\I + \A)^0 = \I. Suppose (b) holds for k. As (\I + \A)^{k} \ge \O and \I + \A \ge \O,  igl((\I + \A)^{k+1} igr)_{ij} = \sum_{l=1}^{n} igl((\I + \A)^{k} igr)_{il}\,(\delta_{lj} + a_{lj}) is positive if and only if there is an l with ((\I + \A)^{k})_{il} > 0 and either l = j or a_{lj} > 0. By the induction hypothesis this says: there is a walk of length at most k from l to i, where either l = j or j 	o l is an edge. In the first case we have a walk of length at most k from j to i; in the second, putting j in front gives one of length at most k + 1. Conversely, let a walk of length m \le k + 1 from j to i be given. If m \le k, take l = j. With \sigma = (3, 4, 1, 2), \P_\sigma	p\A\P_\sigma =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}. The edge 2 	o 3 goes into S, which is allowed; only edges out of S are forbidden. [B2: One power decides] For each matrix, compute (\I + \A)^2 and decide whether \A is irreducible. For the reducible one, read off from (\I + \A)^2 a set of vertices with no exit. 1. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} 2. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} (a) \I + \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}, and multiplying out, (\I + \A)^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 & 2 \ 2 & 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} > \O . Hence \A is irreducible by @thm-irreducible-power-positive. (b) \I + \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}, and (\I + \A)^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \ 3 & 2 & 2 \ 1 & 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} , which has zero entries, so \A is reducible. By @lem-powers-and-walks (b), column j of (\I + \A)^{2} is positive exactly in the rows i reachable from j. Column 2 is positive in rows 2, 3 only, so the vertices reachable from 2 form S = \{2, 3\}, and by the proof of @thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected no edge leaves it. Indeed a_{12} = a_{13} = 0. [B3: Eigenvalues from the normal form] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \ 1 & 3 & 0 \ 4 & 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}. Put \A in reducible normal form, and hence find its eigenvalues and ho(\A). The edges are 1 	o 1, 1 	o 2, 1 	o 3 (column 1), the loop 2 	o 2 (column 2), and 3 	o 1, 3 	o 3 (column 3). Vertex 2 has no exit, and 1, 3 reach each other. List 2 first: \sigma(1) = 2, \sigma(2) = 1, \sigma(3) = 3. By @lem-permutation-similarity-entries, \P_\sigma	p\A\P_\sigma =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 2 \ 0 & 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix} . The blocks (3) and  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 4 & 5 \end{psmallmatrix} are irreducible, the second because both its off-diagonal entries are nonzero. By @thm-reducible-normal-form (b), p_{\A}(x) = (x - 3)(x^2 - 6x - 3), so the eigenvalues are 3 and 3 \pm 2\sqrt3, and by (c), ho(\A) = 3 + 2\sqrt3 \approx 6.46, coming from the second block. C. Going deeper [C1: A necessary condition that is not sufficient] 1. Prove that if n \ge 2 and \A \in M_n(F) is irreducible, then every row and every column of \A contains a nonzero entry off the diagonal. 2. Show that the converse fails for every even n \ge 4. (a) Suppose column j has no nonzero entry off the diagonal: a_{ij} = 0 for all i 
e j. Then S = \{j\} has no exit, and S is neither empty nor everything because n \ge 2, so \A is reducible by @lem-reducible-closed-set. Suppose instead row i has a_{ij} = 0 for all j 
e i. Then S = \{1, \dots, n\} \setminus \{i\} has no exit, since the only entries a_{i'j} with j \in S and i' 
otin S are the a_{ij} with j 
e i; again \A is reducible. (b) Let n = 2m with m \ge 2, and let \M be the direct sum of m copies of the swap  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}. Every row and column has a 1 off the diagonal. But S = \{1, 2\} has no exit, since column 1 and column 2 are zero outside rows 1, 2, so \M is reducible. The Quick check is the case m = 2. [C2: The exponent n - 1 is sharp] Let n \ge 2 and let \C_n be the cyclic permutation matrix with \C_n\cvec{e}_j = \cvec{e}_{j+1} for j < n and \C_n\cvec{e}_n = \cvec{e}_1. 1. Prove that \C_n is irreducible, but that (\I + \C_n)^{n-2} is not positive. 2. Prove that if \A \ge \O is irreducible, then (\I + \A)^{k} > \O for every k \ge n - 1. (a) The nonzero entries of \C_n are (\C_n)_{j+1,j} = 1 for j < n and (\C_n)_{1n} = 1, so the edges of G(\C_n) are j 	o j + 1 and n 	o 1, and there are no others. Following them from any vertex visits every vertex, so G(\C_n) is strongly connected and \C_n is irreducible (@thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected). Each vertex has exactly one outgoing edge, so the only walk from 1 of length m \le n - 1 is 1 	o 2 	o \dots 	o m + 1. In particular the shortest walk from 1 to n has length n - 1, and there is no walk of length at most n - 2 from 1 to n. By @lem-powers-and-walks (b),  igl((\I + \C_n)^{n-2} igr)_{n1} = 0. (b) By @lem-powers-and-walks (b), ((\I + \A)^{k})_{ij} > 0 exactly when there is a walk of length at most k from j to i. For k \ge n - 1, a walk of length at most n - 1 is one of length at most k, and such walks exist for every pair by the proof of @thm-irreducible-power-positive. Hence (\I + \A)^{k} > \O. [C3: Irreducibility as growth of supports] Let n \ge 2 and \A \in M_n(
R) with \A \ge \O. For \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}, call \{i : x_i > 0\} the support of \cvec{x}. 1. Prove that the support of (\I + \A)\cvec{x} is the support S of \cvec{x} together with every vertex i for which there is an edge j 	o i with j \in S. 2. Prove that \A is irreducible if and only if, for every \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} with at least one zero entry and at least one positive entry, (\I + \A)\cvec{x} has more positive entries than \cvec{x}. 3. Deduce, without using walks, that (\I + \A)^{n-1}\cvec{x} > \cvec{0} for every nonzero \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} when \A is irreducible, and hence that (\I + \A)^{n-1} > \O. Hint for (b): use @lem-reducible-closed-set. (a) ((\I + \A)\cvec{x})_i = x_i + \sum_j a_{ij}x_j is a sum of nonnegative terms, so it is positive if and only if x_i > 0 or some a_{ij}x_j > 0, that is, i \in S or there is j \in S with a_{ij} > 0, which is an edge j 	o i. (b) Let \cvec{x} be as stated, with support S, which is neither empty nor everything. By (a), (\I + \A)\cvec{x} has support containing S, and strictly larger exactly when some edge goes from S to a vertex outside S. (\Rightarrow) If \A is irreducible, @lem-reducible-closed-set says every such S has an exit, so the support grows. (\Leftarrow) If \A were reducible, take S with no exit from @lem-reducible-closed-set, and let \cvec{x} have entry 1 on S and 0 elsewhere. Then (\I + \A)\cvec{x} has support exactly S, with the same number of positive entries, contradicting the hypothesis. (c) Let \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}, \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}, and put \cvec{x}_k = (\I + \A)^{k}\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}. By (a) the supports never shrink, and by (b) the support grows by at least one element at each step until it is everything. It starts with at least one element, so after at most n - 1 steps it has n, and then stays so: \cvec{x}_{n-1} > \cvec{0}. Applying this to \cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_j shows that column j of (\I + \A)^{n-1} is positive, for every j.

title: 19.3 The Perron–Frobenius Theorem
19.4 The Collatz–Wielandt Formula
19.5 Primitive Matrices
content:
Primitive Matrices The Perron–Frobenius theorem tells us what an irreducible nonnegative matrix looks like at its spectral radius: ho(\A) is an algebraically simple eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector. It says nothing about what the powers \A^{m} do, and Chapter 9 §11 already met the obstacle. The swap  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is irreducible, has a positive eigenvector for ho = 1, and its powers alternate forever. This section finds the extra hypothesis that makes the powers settle down, proves that under it (\A/ho)^{m} converges to an explicit rank-one matrix, and explains what goes wrong without it: the eigenvalues of modulus ho are then spread evenly around a circle, and their number is read off the zero pattern of \A. Throughout, matrices are real and \A \ge \O is meant entrywise, as are \A > \O, \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} and \cvec{x} > \cvec{0}. The spectrum is taken over 
C, and ho(\A) is the spectral radius (@def-spectral-radius). Walks in a nonnegative matrix Whether a power \A^{m} has a positive entry at position (i, j) depends only on which entries of \A are zero. The bookkeeping device is the directed graph G(\A) of §02 (@def-directed-graph-of-matrix): it has an edge j 	o i for each nonzero entry a_{ij}, and a walk of length m from j to i is a list j = i_0, i_1, \dots, i_m = i of vertices in which each i_{t-1} 	o i_t is an edge. The edge for a_{ij} points from the column index to the row index, the direction in which a column-stochastic chain moves. A walk is closed if i_0 = i_m and m \ge 1. By §02’s count of walks (@lem-powers-and-walks (a)), for \A \ge \O and m \ge 0, (\A^{m})_{ij} > 0 if and only if G(\A) has a walk of length m from j to i. Everything in this section about zero patterns rests on that fact. Primitive matrices Here is the property the swap lacks. Its powers are \I and the swap itself, and each of them has zero entries; no power ever mixes every state with every other. A primitive matrix is one that, after enough steps, connects every index to every index at once. [Primitive Matrix] A matrix \A \in M_n(
R), n \ge 1, with \A \ge \O is primitive if \A^{k} > \O for some integer k \ge 1, that is, if every entry of some power of \A is strictly positive. In words: we are allowed to wait, but only for a finite number k of steps, and after those k steps all n^{2} entries must be positive together. By @lem-powers-and-walks (a), \A is primitive exactly when there is one length k such that every vertex of G(\A) has a walk of length k to every vertex, including to itself. Examples. - Positive matrices. If \A > \O, take k = 1. Perron’s theorem (@thm-perron) is about these. - A matrix with zeros. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has a zero entry, but \A^{2} =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} > \O. So \A is primitive with k = 2. In the graph: the edges are 1 	o 1, 1 	o 2 and 2 	o 1, and 1 	o 1 	o 1, 1 	o 1 	o 2, 2 	o 1 	o 1, 2 	o 1 	o 2 are walks of length 2 between every ordered pair. - A slower one. \W =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Its edges are 2 	o 1, 3 	o 2, 1 	o 3, and 2 	o 3, so its closed walks include 1 	o 3 	o 2 	o 1 of length 3 and 2 	o 3 	o 2 of length 2. Multiplying out, \W^{4} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} still has a zero, and \W^{5} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} > \O. So \W is primitive, and the smallest k is 5. - Degenerate case. A 1 	imes 1 matrix (a) is primitive if and only if a > 0. The zero 1 	imes 1 matrix is not, which is why the statements below exclude it. Nonexample by minimal change. Change the (1,1)-entry of  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} to 0. The result \A' =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is still nonnegative, and it is still irreducible, since (\I + \A')^{1} > \O (@thm-irreducible-power-positive). But \A'^{2} = 2\I, so the even powers of \A' are multiples of \I and the odd powers multiples of \A', and every power has two zero entries: \A' is not primitive. The clause that fails is “some power is positive”; what was lost is the loop 1 	o 1; without it every edge joins 1 and 2, so every closed walk has even length. More generally, the powers of a permutation matrix are permutation matrices (@lem-permutation-matrices), and for n \ge 2 a permutation matrix has zeros; so no permutation matrix of size n \ge 2 is primitive. Why this definition. Asking for \A > \O itself would be too strong: it excludes the matrices above, whose powers behave exactly like those of a positive matrix. Asking only that each position (i, j) be positive in some power, possibly a different power for each position, is too weak: that is irreducibility, and the swap satisfies it. Primitivity sits between the two. It asks for a single power that is positive everywhere. Irreducible does not mean primitive. Irreducibility asks that each j be reachable from each i by a walk of some length; primitivity asks for walks of one common length. For the swap, every walk from 1 to 2 has odd length and every walk from 1 to 1 has even length, so no single power is positive at both (1,1) and (1,2). Is \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} primitive? Is \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}? \A^{2} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} > \O, so \A is primitive. For \B, every power is upper triangular, \B^{m} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & m \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, so the (2,1)-entry is always 0 and \B is not primitive: G(\B) has no walk from 1 to 2 at all. The first consequences of the definition come straight from the graph and from Perron’s theorem applied to the positive power. [First Properties of Primitive Matrices] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be primitive, with \A^{k} > \O. Then: 1. \A^{m} > \O for every m \ge k; 2. \A is irreducible; 3. ho(\A) > 0, and ho(\A) is the only eigenvalue of \A of modulus ho(\A). (a) Multiplying a positive matrix by a nonnegative matrix with no zero column keeps it positive. (b) A positive power gives walks between all vertices, which is strong connectivity. (c) The eigenvalues of \A^{k} are the k-th powers of those of \A. A second eigenvalue of \A on the circle of radius ho would land, after raising to the k-th power, on the circle where Perron’s theorem allows only the simple eigenvalue ho(\A^{k}). (a) Column j of \A^{k} is \A^{k-1} times column j of \A (@thm-three-views-of-product; for k = 1 read \A^{0} = \I). Since \A^{k} > \O, no column of \A is zero. Now suppose \A^{m} > \O for some m \ge k. Then (\A^{m+1})_{ij} = \sum_l (\A^{m})_{il}a_{lj} is a sum of nonnegative terms, and the term for an l with a_{lj} > 0 is positive. So \A^{m+1} > \O, and (a) follows by induction on m. (b) For every ordered pair (j, i), (\A^{k})_{ij} > 0, so @lem-powers-and-walks (a) gives a walk from j to i in G(\A). So G(\A) is strongly connected (@def-strongly-connected), and \A is irreducible by @thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected. (c) Over 
C, write p_{\A} = (x - \lambda_1)\cdots(x - \lambda_n), with each eigenvalue repeated according to its algebraic multiplicity. By the Spectral Mapping Theorem (@thm-spectral-mapping) with q = x^{k}, p_{\A^{k}} = (x - \lambda_1^{k})\cdots(x - \lambda_n^{k}) . So ho(\A^{k}) = \max_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^{k} = ho(\A)^{k}. By @thm-perron applied to \A^{k} > \O, ho(\A^{k}) > 0 is an algebraically simple eigenvalue of \A^{k}, and every other eigenvalue of \A^{k} has modulus less than ho(\A^{k}). In particular ho(\A)^{k} > 0, so ho(\A) > 0. By (b) and @thm-perron-frobenius, ho \coloneqq ho(\A) is an eigenvalue of \A; say \lambda_1 = ho. Suppose some \lambda_s with s \ge 2 had \lvert\lambda_svert = ho but \lambda_s 
e ho. Then \lambda_s^{k} is an eigenvalue of \A^{k} of modulus ho^{k} = ho(\A^{k}), so by Perron’s theorem it is not an “other” eigenvalue: \lambda_s^{k} = ho^{k}. Then ho^{k} occurs at least twice in the list \lambda_1^{k}, \dots, \lambda_n^{k}, at positions 1 and s, so a_{\A^{k}}(ho^{k}) \ge 2, contradicting simplicity. Hence ho is the only eigenvalue of modulus ho. Part (c) is the whole spectral content of primitivity, and the rest of the section shows that it is also enough. Part (a) says that once the powers become positive they stay positive, so the least such k, the exponent of \A, is well defined and marks a permanent change. The limit theorem For the swap, ho = 1 and the powers do not converge. We now show that primitivity is exactly what makes (\A/ho)^{m} converge, and we identify the limit. The answer involves eigenvectors on both sides. If \A \ge \O is irreducible, then @thm-perron-frobenius (a) and @cor-left-perron-vector (a)–(c) provide \cvec{v} > \cvec{0} and \cvec{w} > \cvec{0} with \A\cvec{v} = ho(\A)\cvec{v}, \cvec{w}	p\A = ho(\A)\cvec{w}	p, and \cvec{w}	p\cvec{v} > 0, and the right and left Perron vectors of @def-perron-root-and-vectors are the pair scaled so that \1	p\cvec{v} = 1 and \cvec{w}	p\cvec{v} = 1. Each of \cvec{v}, \cvec{w} is determined up to a positive factor, because ho(\A) is algebraically simple (@thm-perron-frobenius (b)), so its eigenspaces for \A and \A	p are lines (@thm-geometric-le-algebraic, @prp-left-eigenvectors-transpose (b)). [Limit Theorem for Primitive Matrices] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be primitive, ho = ho(\A), and let \cvec{v} > \cvec{0} and \cvec{w} > \cvec{0} satisfy \A\cvec{v} = ho\cvec{v} and \cvec{w}	p\A = ho\cvec{w}	p, for instance the right and left Perron vectors of \A. Then, entrywise, \Big( rac{1}{ho}\A\Big)^{m} \longrightarrow  rac{\cvec{v}\cvec{w}	p}{\cvec{w}	p\cvec{v}} \qquad (m 	o \infty). The limit is a positive matrix of rank one, and it does not depend on how \cvec{v} and \cvec{w} are scaled. The same conclusion holds for every irreducible \A \ge \O with ho(\A) > 0 whose only eigenvalue of modulus ho(\A) is ho(\A) itself. Divide by ho, so that the Perron eigenvalue becomes 1 and every other eigenvalue lies strictly inside the unit circle. Chapter 10 §10 then says the powers converge, with no diagonalizability needed, because it works with the Jordan form. It remains to name the limit \L. Three identities pin it down: \B\L = \L puts every column of \L on the line through \cvec{v}; \L\B = \L puts every row on the line through \cvec{w}	p; and \L\cvec{v} = \cvec{v} fixes the scale. It suffices to prove the last sentence, since a primitive matrix is irreducible with ho(\A) > 0 and has ho(\A) as its only eigenvalue of modulus ho(\A), by @prp-primitive-basic (b) and (c). So let \A \ge \O be irreducible with ho > 0 the only eigenvalue of modulus ho, and put \B = ho^{-1}\A. By @thm-spectral-mapping with q = x/ho, the eigenvalues of \B are the numbers \lambda/ho, \lambda \in \spec(\A), with the same algebraic multiplicities. So 1 is an eigenvalue of \B with a_{\B}(1) = a_{\A}(ho) = 1 by @thm-perron-frobenius, and every other eigenvalue of \B has modulus less than 1. Since the 1-blocks in a Jordan form of \B have total size a_{\B}(1) = 1 (@cor-jordan-invariants (a)), there is a single 1-block, of size 1. By @thm-matrix-powers-converge, \B^{m} converges to some \L \in M_n(
C). Three identities. By the algebra of limits, (B3) of Chapter 10 §10, applied entry by entry, \B^{m+1} = \B\,\B^{m} 	o \B\L and \B^{m+1} = \B^{m}\B 	o \L\B; but (\B^{m+1}) is a tail of (\B^{m}), so it also tends to \L. Hence \B\L = \L = \L\B. Also \B\cvec{v} = \cvec{v}, so \B^{m}\cvec{v} = \cvec{v} for every m, and letting m 	o \infty gives \L\cvec{v} = \cvec{v}. The columns. \B\L = \L says that every column of \L lies in E_1(\B) = E_{ho}(\A), which is the line \Span(\cvec{v}), as noted before the theorem. So column j of \L is u_j\cvec{v} for some u_j \in 
C, that is, \L = \cvec{v}\cvec{u}	p with \cvec{u} = (u_1, \dots, u_n). The rows. \L\B = \L reads \cvec{v}(\cvec{u}	p\B) = \cvec{v}\cvec{u}	p. Choose r with v_r 
e 0 and compare row r: \cvec{u}	p\B = \cvec{u}	p, so \B	p\cvec{u} = \cvec{u}, and \cvec{u} lies in the eigenspace of \A	p for ho. That eigenspace is the line through \cvec{w}, so \cvec{u} = c\cvec{w} for some c \in 
C. The scale. Now \cvec{v} = \L\cvec{v} = c\,\cvec{v}(\cvec{w}	p\cvec{v}), and comparing entry r gives c\,\cvec{w}	p\cvec{v} = 1. Since \cvec{w}	p\cvec{v} > 0, c = 1/(\cvec{w}	p\cvec{v}), and \L = \cvec{v}\cvec{w}	p/(\cvec{w}	p\cvec{v}). Finally, \cvec{v}\cvec{w}	p has (i,j)-entry v_iw_j > 0 and every column a multiple of \cvec{v}, so the limit is positive of rank one; replacing \cvec{v}, \cvec{w} by s\cvec{v}, t\cvec{w} with s, t > 0 multiplies numerator and denominator by st. This proves the theorem. Note what the proof did not use: no eigenvector basis, no computation of the other eigenvalues. Chapter 10’s Jordan-form criterion did the analysis once and for all; Perron–Frobenius supplied the simple eigenvalue and the two positive eigenvectors. With the normalization \cvec{w}	p\cvec{v} = 1 of §03, the limit is simply the idempotent \cvec{v}\cvec{w}	p. §06 turns the theorem into the long-run theorem for Markov chains. [A Limit Computed Two Ways] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, which is primitive since \A^{2} > \O. Find \lim_m (\A/ho)^{m} from @thm-primitive-limit, and confirm it with an exact formula for \A^{m}. The theorem. p_{\A} = x^{2} - x - 2 = (x - 2)(x + 1), so ho = 2. A positive right eigenvector solves (\A - 2\I)\cvec{v} = \cvec{0}, that is, -v_1 + v_2 = 0: take \cvec{v} = (1, 1). A positive left eigenvector solves (\A	p - 2\I)\cvec{w} = \cvec{0}, with \A	p - 2\I =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 \ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}: take \cvec{w} = (2, 1). Then \cvec{w}	p\cvec{v} = 3, and \Big( rac{1}{2}\A\Big)^{m} \longrightarrow \L =  rac13 egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 1 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} =  rac13 egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . The formula. \L^{2} = \L, because \cvec{w}	p\cvec{v}/3 = 1, and \L(\I - \L) = \O. A direct check gives 3\L - \I =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \A, so \A = 2\L - (\I - \L). Since \L and \I - \L are complementary projections, induction on m gives  egin{aligned} \A^{m} &= 2^{m}\L + (-1)^{m}(\I - \L), \ \Big( rac12\A\Big)^{m} &= \L + \Big(- rac12\Big)^{m} rac13 egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} . \end{aligned} For m = 2 this is  rac13 egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} +  rac1{12} egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} =  rac14 egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, which is \A^{2}/4. The error term is (- rac12)^{m} times a fixed matrix: it decays at the rate \lvert\lambda_2vert/ho =  rac12 and changes sign at every step. The limit uses the left eigenvector, not the transpose of the right one. For the matrix above, \cvec{v}\cvec{v}	p/(\cvec{v}	p\cvec{v}) =  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, which is not the limit. The two agree when \A is symmetric, since then \cvec{w} = \cvec{v}; in general \cvec{w} carries the information about how much each starting index contributes in the long run. The limit theorem also gives the converse of @prp-primitive-basic (c). [Primitivity from the Spectrum] Let \A \in M_n(
R), \A \ge \O, be irreducible with ho(\A) > 0. Then \A is primitive if and only if ho(\A) is the only eigenvalue of \A of modulus ho(\A). One direction is already proved. For the other, the limit theorem gives a positive limit, and a sequence that converges to a positive number is eventually positive. There are only n^{2} entries to wait for, so some single power is positive everywhere. (\Rightarrow) This is @prp-primitive-basic (c). (\Leftarrow) By the last sentence of @thm-primitive-limit, (\A/ho)^{m} 	o \L with \L > \O. Each of the n^{2} entries of (\A/ho)^{m} converges to a positive number c_{ij}, so it is positive for all m beyond some m_{ij}: this is the definition of the limit with \varepsilon = c_{ij}/2. For m larger than the largest of these finitely many m_{ij}, (\A/ho)^{m} > \O, and hence \A^{m} = ho^{m}(\A/ho)^{m} > \O. So \A is primitive. The nonzero entries of \P are p_{j+1,\,j} for j < n and p_{1n}, so the edges of G(\P) are j 	o j + 1 for j < n and n 	o 1: the graph is the cycle 1 	o 2 	o \dots 	o n 	o 1. Every walk runs round it, and a closed walk goes round a whole number of times, so its length is a multiple of n; the walk 1 	o 2 	o \dots 	o n 	o 1 has length n. So the period is n. Following the cycle, every vertex reaches every vertex, so G(\P) is strongly connected and \P is irreducible (@thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected). Eigenvalues. A sequence that returns to each of two different matrices infinitely often has no limit, so \P^{m} does not converge. R) is primitive, then \A^{(n-1)^{2}+1} > \O. The matrix \W_3 is the matrix \W of the examples, where we saw that \W^{4} has a zero at position (1, 1) and \W^{5} > \O; here (n-1)^{2} + 1 = 5.
