Directly, (\S + \I)/2 =  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, whose powers are all equal to itself, in agreement. [C2: Traces detect the period] Let \A \ge \O be irreducible, not the 1 	imes 1 zero matrix, with period h. 1. Prove that 	r(\A^{m}) = 0 for every m \ge 1 that is not a multiple of h, in two ways: from @thm-peripheral-spectrum (b), and from @lem-powers-and-walks (a). 2. Deduce that if 	r(\A^{2}) > 0 and 	r(\A^{3}) > 0, then \A is primitive. 3. Check (b) on the matrix \W of the examples. (a) Spectrum. Let \omega = e^{2\pi i/h} and p_{\A} = \prod_i(x - \lambda_i). By @thm-peripheral-spectrum (c), the period h is also the number of peripheral eigenvalues, so part (b) of that theorem applies with this \omega. By @cor-trace-det-of-polynomial, applied over 
C, 	r(\A^{m}) = \sum_i\lambda_i^{m}. By @thm-peripheral-spectrum (b), the list \omega\lambda_1, \dots, \omega\lambda_n is a rearrangement of \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, so \sum_i\lambda_i^{m} = \sum_i(\omega\lambda_i)^{m} = \omega^{m}\sum_i\lambda_i^{m}. If h 
mid m, then \omega^{m} 
e 1 (@exm-roots-of-unity), so 	r(\A^{m}) = 0. Walks. 	r(\A^{m}) = \sum_i(\A^{m})_{ii} is a sum of nonnegative terms, positive exactly when some (\A^{m})_{ii} > 0, that is, by @lem-powers-and-walks (a), when there is a closed walk of length m. Every closed walk has length a multiple of the period, so for h 
mid m the trace is 0. (b) By (a), h \mid 2 and h \mid 3, so h = 1, and \A is primitive by @cor-primitive-iff-aperiodic. (c) \W^{2} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has trace 2, and \W^{3} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has trace 3; so \W is primitive, as found directly. [C3: A finite test for primitivity] Let \A \in M_n(
R), \A \ge \O, and let \Z_m be the zero pattern of \A^{m}: the 0/1 matrix with a 1 exactly where \A^{m} is positive. 1. Prove that \Z_{m+1} is determined by \Z_m and \Z_1. 2. Deduce that if \Z_a = \Z_b with a < b, then \Z_{a+j} = \Z_{b+j} for every j \ge 0. 3. Prove that if \A is primitive, then \A^{k} > \O for some k \le 2^{n^{2}}. Compare with @thm-wielandt-bound. Hint: there are only 2^{n^{2}} zero patterns; use @prp-primitive-basic (a). (a) (\A^{m+1})_{ij} = \sum_l(\A^{m})_{il}a_{lj} is a sum of nonnegative terms, positive exactly when some l has (\A^{m})_{il} > 0 and a_{lj} > 0. So (\Z_{m+1})_{ij} = 1 if and only if (\Z_m)_{il} = (\Z_1)_{lj} = 1 for some l, which depends only on \Z_m and \Z_1. (b) By induction on j: the case j = 0 is the hypothesis, and if \Z_{a+j} = \Z_{b+j}, then (a) applied to both gives \Z_{a+j+1} = \Z_{b+j+1}. (c) Among \Z_1, \dots, \Z_{N+1}, N = 2^{n^{2}}, two agree, say \Z_a = \Z_b with a < b \le N + 1, so a \le N. By (b), \Z_{a + q(b-a)} = \Z_a for every q \ge 0, by induction on q. If \A^{k} > \O, then by @prp-primitive-basic (a) \A^{m} > \O for all m \ge k; choosing q with a + q(b - a) \ge k shows that \Z_a is the all-ones pattern, so \A^{a} > \O with a \le 2^{n^{2}}. Wielandt’s bound (n-1)^{2} + 1 is enormously smaller: for n = 3 it is 5 against 512.

title: 19.6 Markov Chains
content:
Markov Chains Chapter 9 §11 proved that a Markov chain settles down to a unique steady state, but only under three hypotheses on the eigenvalues of its transition matrix, one of them diagonalizability. It closed with a promise: the Perron–Frobenius theorem would give the same conclusions “for every stochastic matrix with some power having all entries positive, without assuming diagonalizability and without computing eigenvalues”. This section keeps that promise, using the limit theorem of §05. It then asks what happens when no power is positive. Irreducible chains still have a unique steady state, and they approach it on average even when they oscillate. Reducible chains can have many steady states, and among them the absorbing chains, which end in a trap, have an exact theory built on the Neumann series. Conventions. Stochastic means column-stochastic, as in @def-stochastic-matrix: \A \ge \O and every column sums to 1, that is, \1	p\A = \1	p. The entry a_{ij} is the probability of moving to state i from state j, and a Markov chain is \cvec{x}_{k+1} = \A\cvec{x}_k (@def-markov-chain). Many books use rows and the transposed matrix; we never do. The order \ge is entrywise. Steady states and the Perron root We first place stochastic matrices inside the theory of this chapter. Since \cvec{x}_m = \A^{m}\cvec{x}_0, the entry (\A^{m})_{ij} is the probability of being in state i after m steps when starting from state j. By @lem-powers-and-walks (a) it is positive exactly when the graph G(\A) has a walk of length m from j to i: the edges of the graph are the moves the chain can make in one step, and the walks are the routes it can take. [The Perron Root of a Stochastic Matrix] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be stochastic. Then: 1. ho(\A) = 1, and \1 is a positive left eigenvector for it; 2. the steady states of \A are exactly the nonnegative eigenvectors for ho(\A) whose entries sum to 1; 3. if \A is irreducible, then \A has exactly one steady state \cvec{v}, and \cvec{v} > \cvec{0}. @exm-irreducible-stochastic-perron already found these facts for one matrix, and the argument there is general. The column sums make \1	p a left eigenvector for 1, and no eigenvalue is larger in modulus; so a steady state is a nonnegative eigenvector for the Perron root; when \A is irreducible, Perron–Frobenius with the normalization \1	p\cvec{v} = 1 leaves room for only one. (a) By @prp-stochastic-properties (c), 1 \in \spec(\A) and \1	p\A = \1	p. By @cor-markov-powers-converge (a), every eigenvalue has modulus at most 1. So ho(\A) = 1. (b) This is @def-markov-chain read with (a): a steady state is a probability vector \cvec{v} with \A\cvec{v} = \cvec{v} = ho(\A)\cvec{v}. (c) By @thm-perron-frobenius (a), there is \cvec{u} > \cvec{0} with \A\cvec{u} = \cvec{u}; then \cvec{v} = \cvec{u}/(\1	p\cvec{u}) is a steady state with \cvec{v} > \cvec{0}. If \cvec{v}' is any steady state, it is a nonnegative eigenvector, so \cvec{v}' = c\cvec{v} with c > 0 by @thm-perron-frobenius (c), and 1 = \1	p\cvec{v}' = c\,\1	p\cvec{v} = c. Hence \cvec{v}' = \cvec{v}. In the notation of §03, the Perron root of a stochastic matrix is 1, the all-ones vector is a positive left eigenvector, and for an irreducible stochastic matrix the steady state is the right Perron vector. A unique positive steady state does not make the chain converge. The swap \S =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is stochastic and irreducible, so by (c) it has exactly one steady state, ( rac12,  rac12), and it is positive. Yet the chain started at \cvec{e}_1 alternates \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1, \dots and never approaches it. Existence and uniqueness of the steady state come from irreducibility; convergence needs more. The long-run theorem The “more” is primitivity. Here are the three conclusions of @thm-markov-limit-diagonalizable, in the same words, under the hypothesis that Chapter 9 §11 promised. [Long-Run Behavior of a Markov Chain] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be stochastic, and suppose that \A^{k} > \O for some k \ge 1. Then: 1. \A has exactly one steady state \cvec{v}, and \cvec{v} > \cvec{0}; 2. \A^{m} 	o \cvec{v}\1	p entrywise as m 	o \infty; 3. for every probability vector \cvec{x}_0, the Markov chain \cvec{x}_m = \A^{m}\cvec{x}_0 converges entrywise to \cvec{v}. For a stochastic matrix, @thm-primitive-limit has ho = 1, and the left eigenvector can be taken to be \1, so the limit \cvec{v}\cvec{w}	p/(\cvec{w}	p\cvec{v}) becomes \cvec{v}\1	p once the steady state is normalized by \1	p\cvec{v} = 1. The chain inherits the limit column by column. By hypothesis \A is primitive (@def-primitive), hence irreducible (@prp-primitive-basic (b)). So (a) is @prp-stochastic-perron (c). (b) By @prp-stochastic-perron (a), ho(\A) = 1 and \cvec{w} = \1 is positive with \cvec{w}	p\A = \cvec{w}	p; and \cvec{v} > \cvec{0} satisfies \A\cvec{v} = \cvec{v}. By @thm-primitive-limit, \A^{m} = \Big( rac{1}{ho(\A)}\A\Big)^{m} \longrightarrow  rac{\cvec{v}\1	p}{\1	p\cvec{v}} = \cvec{v}\1	p , since \1	p\cvec{v} = 1. (c) Entry r of \A^{m}\cvec{x}_0 is \sum_s(\A^{m})_{rs}(\cvec{x}_0)_s, which by (b) converges to \sum_s v_r(\cvec{x}_0)_s = v_r\,(\1	p\cvec{x}_0) = v_r. Compare the hypotheses with those of @thm-markov-limit-diagonalizable. That theorem asked for three facts about the eigenvalues: \A diagonalizable over 
C, a_{\A}(1) = 1, and \lvert\lambdavert < 1 for every other eigenvalue. Chapter 10 §10 (@cor-markov-powers-converge) removed the first, but still asked to locate every eigenvalue on the unit circle. The new hypothesis is a statement about the zero pattern of one power of \A, checked by multiplying matrices; no eigenvalue is computed, and none needs to be. The last two eigenvalue conditions become conclusions, by @prp-primitive-basic (c) and @thm-perron-frobenius (b), and diagonalizability is simply irrelevant. By @cor-primitive-iff-aperiodic the hypothesis can often be checked without multiplying at all: an irreducible stochastic matrix with one positive diagonal entry, a state that can stay put, qualifies. In the vocabulary of probability, a stochastic matrix with a positive power is called regular. [A Chain that Cannot Be Diagonalized] A token moves among three positions. From position 1 it always moves to 3; from 2 it moves to 1 or 3 with probability  rac12 each; from 3 it moves to 1 or 2 with probability  rac12 each. So \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1/2 & 1/2 \ 0 & 0 & 1/2 \ 1 & 1/2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . Show that @thm-markov-limit-diagonalizable does not apply but @thm-markov-limit-primitive does, and find the long-run distribution. Diagonalization fails. Expanding \det(x\I - \A) along the first column,  egin{aligned} p_{\A} &= x\Big(x^{2} -  rac14\Big) - \Big( rac14 +  rac{x}{2}\Big) \ &= x^{3} -  rac34x -  rac14 = (x - 1)\Big(x +  rac12\Big)^{2} . \end{aligned} For the double eigenvalue, \A +  rac12\I =  egin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 1/2 & 1/2 \ 0 & 1/2 & 1/2 \ 1 & 1/2 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix} has rank 2: its first two rows are independent, and the third is twice the first minus the second. So g_{\A}(- rac12) = 1 < 2 = a_{\A}(- rac12), and \A is not diagonalizable (@thm-diagonalization). @thm-markov-limit-diagonalizable does not apply. A positive power. Squaring, \A^{2} =  egin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 1/4 & 1/4 \ 1/2 & 1/4 & 0 \ 0 & 1/2 & 3/4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A^{4} = (\A^{2})^{2} =  egin{pmatrix} 3/8 & 5/16 & 5/16 \ 3/8 & 3/16 & 1/8 \ 1/4 & 1/2 & 9/16 \end{pmatrix} > \O . So @thm-markov-limit-primitive applies with k = 4. (\A^{3} still has a zero at position (2, 1): three steps cannot take the token from 1 to 2.) The steady state. (\A - \I)\cvec{v} = \cvec{0} reads -v_1 +  rac12v_2 +  rac12v_3 = 0 and -v_2 +  rac12v_3 = 0. So v_3 = 2v_2, then v_1 =  rac12v_2 + v_2 =  rac32v_2, and \cvec{v} is a multiple of (3, 2, 4). Scaling to sum 1, \cvec{v} = \Big( rac13,  rac29,  rac49\Big), \qquad \A^{m} \longrightarrow \cvec{v}\1	p . Check: \A\cvec{v} = ( rac19 +  rac29,\  rac29,\  rac13 +  rac19) = ( rac13,  rac29,  rac49). In the long run the token is at position 3 four times out of nine, wherever it starts. What the Jordan block does. Solving the recurrence exactly (for instance from the Jordan form, as in Chapter 10 §10) gives  egin{aligned} (\A^{m})_{11} &=  rac13\Big(1 + 2\Big(- rac12\Big)^{m}\Big), \ (\A^{m})_{21} &=  rac29\Big(1 + (3m - 1)\Big(- rac12\Big)^{m}\Big), \end{aligned} which one can confirm for m = 0, 1, 2 against \I, \A, \A^{2}. The factor m in the second formula comes from the 2 	imes 2 Jordan block for - rac12, whose powers carry the entry m\lambda^{m-1} (Chapter 10 §10): the error decays like m\,2^{-m} rather than 2^{-m}. It still decays, and the theorem never needed to know. Does @thm-markov-limit-primitive apply to \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 1 \ 1/2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}? If so, what is \lim_m \A^{m}? Yes: \A is stochastic and \A^{2} =  egin{pmatrix} 3/4 & 1/2 \ 1/4 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix} > \O. The steady state solves - rac12v_1 + v_2 = 0, so \cvec{v} = ( rac23,  rac13), and \A^{m} 	o \cvec{v}\1	p =  egin{pmatrix} 2/3 & 2/3 \ 1/3 & 1/3 \end{pmatrix}. The hypothesis of @thm-markov-limit-primitive is also necessary for the theorem as stated: if \A^{m} 	o \cvec{v}\1	p with \cvec{v} > \cvec{0}, then \A is primitive (exercise C2). Without the positivity of \cvec{v} it is not needed for convergence:  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1/2 \ 0 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix} has no positive power, yet its powers converge to \cvec{e}_1\1	p, whose steady state has a zero entry. Irreducible chains: convergence on average Now drop primitivity but keep irreducibility. By @prp-stochastic-perron (c) the steady state \cvec{v} is still unique and positive, but by @thm-primitive-iff-single-peripheral and @thm-peripheral-spectrum the chain has h \ge 2 eigenvalues on the unit circle, and its powers do not converge (@cor-markov-powers-converge (b)). What survives is convergence of averages. The average  rac1m(\cvec{x}_0 + \cvec{x}_1 + \dots + \cvec{x}_{m-1}) is, entry by entry, the average over the first m steps of the probability of being in each state; read through linearity of expectation (see the end of this section), it is the expected fraction of those steps spent there. It is this that settles down. [Averages of an Irreducible Chain] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be stochastic and irreducible, with steady state \cvec{v}. Then: 1.  rac1m ig(\I + \A + \A^{2} + \dots + \A^{m-1} ig) 	o \cvec{v}\1	p as m 	o \infty; 2. for every probability vector \cvec{x}_0, the averages  rac1m(\cvec{x}_0 + \cvec{x}_1 + \dots + \cvec{x}_{m-1}) of the chain converge to \cvec{v}; 3. \A^{m} converges if and only if \A is primitive. Split every vector into its component along \cvec{v} and a remainder whose entries sum to 0. The remainder lies in the image of \I - \A, by a dimension count, and on that image the sum \sum_{k<m}\A^{k} telescopes: \sum_{k<m}\A^{k}(\I - \A)\cvec{y} = \cvec{y} - \A^{m}\cvec{y}, which stays bounded, so dividing by m kills it. The component along \cvec{v} is fixed by every power. (a) Let U = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^{n} : \1	p\cvec{x} = 0\}, the kernel of the nonzero linear functional \cvec{x} \mapsto \1	p\cvec{x}, so \dim U = n - 1 by Rank–Nullity (@thm-rank-nullity). Since \1	p(\I - \A) = \1	p - \1	p = \cvec{0}	p, the image of \I - \A lies in U. The kernel of \I - \A on 
R^{n} is the real eigenspace of \A for 1; it contains \cvec{v} 
e \cvec{0}, and it has dimension at most g_{\A}(1) \le a_{\A}(1) = 1 by @thm-geometric-le-algebraic and @thm-perron-frobenius (b). (The real and the complex kernel of the real matrix \I - \A have the same dimension, n minus its rank, since row reduction uses only real arithmetic.) So ank(\I - \A) = n - 1 by Rank–Nullity, and an inclusion of subspaces of equal dimension is an equality: \im(\I - \A) = U. Now fix \cvec{x} \in 
R^{n}. Since \1	p\cvec{v} = 1, the vector \cvec{x} - (\1	p\cvec{x})\cvec{v} lies in U, so \cvec{x} = (\1	p\cvec{x})\cvec{v} + (\I - \A)\cvec{y} for some \cvec{y} \in 
R^{n}. As \A^{k}\cvec{v} = \cvec{v} for every k,  egin{aligned} \sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\A^{k}\cvec{x} &= m\,(\1	p\cvec{x})\cvec{v} + \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} ig(\A^{k}\cvec{y} - \A^{k+1}\cvec{y} ig) \ &= m\,(\1	p\cvec{x})\cvec{v} + \cvec{y} - \A^{m}\cvec{y} . \end{aligned} Every \A^{m} is stochastic (@prp-stochastic-properties (b)), so its entries lie in [0, 1] and \lvert(\A^{m}\cvec{y})_ivert \le \sum_j\lvert y_jvert. Hence each entry of  rac1m(\cvec{y} - \A^{m}\cvec{y}) has modulus at most  rac2m\sum_j\lvert y_jvert, which tends to 0 because  rac1m 	o 0, by the Archimedean property, a consequence of completeness (fact (A1) in the introduction to Chapter 16). Dividing the display by m,  rac1m\sum_{k<m}\A^{k}\cvec{x} 	o (\1	p\cvec{x})\cvec{v} = \cvec{v}\1	p\cvec{x}. Taking \cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_j gives the convergence of column j, for each j. (b)  rac1m\sum_{k<m}\cvec{x}_k =  igl( rac1m\sum_{k<m}\A^{k} igr)\cvec{x}_0 	o \cvec{v}\1	p\cvec{x}_0 = \cvec{v} by (a), entry by entry as in the proof of @thm-markov-limit-primitive (c). (c) (\Leftarrow) is @thm-markov-limit-primitive (b). (\Rightarrow) Suppose \A^{m} 	o \L. Then \A^{m+1} = \A\A^{m} tends both to \L and to \A\L, so \A\L = \L, and every column of \L lies in the real eigenspace for 1, which is \Span(\cvec{v}) by the proof of (a). Each column of \A^{m} has entries \ge 0 summing to 1, and both properties survive the limit, by the elementary algebra of limits recalled in the introduction to Chapter 16 (limits respect sums, and a nonstrict inequality survives a limit), so each column of \L is a probability vector on the line \Span(\cvec{v}), namely \cvec{v} itself. Thus \L = \cvec{v}\1	p > \O. As in the proof of @thm-primitive-iff-single-peripheral, the n^{2} entries of \A^{m} are then positive for all large m, so \A is primitive. The proof of (a) used irreducibility only to know that the eigenspace for 1 is a line through a probability vector \cvec{v}; nothing about the period or the other eigenvalues entered. [A Walk that Oscillates] A walker on three sites 1, 2, 3 in a row steps to a neighboring site at every step, choosing each neighbor with probability  rac12 when there are two. So \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1/2 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1/2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . Show that \A^{m} does not converge, and compute the averages of @thm-markov-cesaro exactly. The edges of G(\A) are 1 	o 2, 2 	o 1, 2 	o 3 and 3 	o 2. Every site reaches every other through site 2, so \A is irreducible (@thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected); and every edge joins site 2 to \{1, 3\}, so closed walks have even length and the period is 2. The steady state solves v_1 =  rac12v_2, v_3 =  rac12v_2, so \cvec{v} = ( rac14,  rac12,  rac14). Multiplying out, \A^{2} =  egin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 0 & 1/2 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \ 1/2 & 0 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A^{3} = \A\A^{2} = \A . So \A^{m} = \A for odd m and \A^{m} = \A^{2} for even m \ge 2, and since \A 
e \A^{2} the powers do not converge. A walker who starts at site 2 is at site 2 at every even step and never at an odd one. For the averages, note that  rac12(\A + \A^{2}) =  egin{pmatrix} 1/4 & 1/4 & 1/4 \ 1/2 & 1/2 & 1/2 \ 1/4 & 1/4 & 1/4 \end{pmatrix} = \cvec{v}\1	p. For m = 2p, the sum \sum_{k<2p}\A^{k} contains \I once, \A p times, and \A^{2} p - 1 times, so  egin{aligned}  rac1{2p}\sum_{k=0}^{2p-1}\A^{k} &=  rac{\I - \A^{2} + p(\A + \A^{2})}{2p} \ &= \cvec{v}\1	p +  rac1{2p} ig(\I - \A^{2} ig) \longrightarrow \cvec{v}\1	p . \end{aligned} For m = 2p + 1 there is one more term, \A^{2p} = \A^{2}, which changes the average by at most  rac1m in each entry. So the walker spends, in the long run, half its time at the middle site and a quarter at each end, although at no single time is its distribution close to \cvec{v} if it starts at a site. The oscillation can also be removed rather than averaged. The lazy chain  rac12(\I + \A), which at each step stays put with probability  rac12 and otherwise moves by \A, is stochastic, irreducible, and has positive diagonal, so it is primitive by @cor-primitive-iff-aperiodic, and it has the same steady state; exercise C1 works this out. Reducible chains: many steady states Without irreducibility, uniqueness fails too. The chain can split into parts that never communicate, and each can carry its own equilibrium. [Two Traps] States 1 and 2 exchange with each other and are never left; state 3 is never left either; state 4 stays with probability  rac14 and otherwise moves to 1, 2 or 3 with probability  rac14 each: \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 1/4 & 0 & 1/4 \ 1/2 & 3/4 & 0 & 1/4 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1/4 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1/4 \end{pmatrix} . Find all steady states, and the limit of the chain from each starting state. Steady states. Let \A\cvec{u} = \cvec{u} with \cvec{u} a probability vector. The last row gives  rac14u_4 = u_4, so u_4 = 0. The first row then gives  rac12u_1 +  rac14u_2 = u_1, so u_2 = 2u_1; the second and third rows then hold automatically. So \cvec{u} = (s, 2s, t, 0) with s, t \ge 0 and 3s + t = 1. Writing \cvec{v}_1 = ( rac13,  rac23, 0, 0) and \cvec{v}_2 = \cvec{e}_3, the steady states are exactly \cvec{u} = c\,\cvec{v}_1 + (1 - c)\,\cvec{v}_2, \qquad 0 \le c \le 1 , the whole segment [\cvec{v}_2, \cvec{v}_1] of Chapter 18. There are infinitely many, and E_1(\A) = \Span(\cvec{v}_1, \cvec{v}_2) is a plane: a_{\A}(1) = 2, since p_{\A} = (x - 1)^{2}(x -  rac14)^{2}, the first factor from the block of states 1, 2 and from state 3, the second from the block’s other eigenvalue  rac14 and from state 4. In particular \A is not irreducible, by @prp-stochastic-perron (c). Limits. The only eigenvalue of modulus 1 is 1, so \A^{m} converges by @cor-markov-powers-converge (b). Its limit \vPi satisfies \A\vPi = \vPi, as in the proof of @thm-markov-cesaro (c), and its columns are limits of probability vectors, hence probability vectors; so each column of \vPi is a steady state. Columns 1 and 2 of every \A^{m} have zeros in rows 3 and 4, by induction on m: \A maps a vector with zeros in those rows to a combination of its own first two columns, which again has zeros there. So columns 1 and 2 of \vPi are steady states with u_3 = 0, that is, \cvec{v}_1. Column 3 of \A is \cvec{e}_3, so column 3 of every power, and of \vPi, is \cvec{e}_3 = \cvec{v}_2. For column 4, write it as c\cvec{v}_1 + (1 - c)\cvec{v}_2 and find c from a conserved quantity: the row vector \cvec{y}	p = (1, 1, 0,  rac23) satisfies \cvec{y}	p\A = \cvec{y}	p, as a column-by-column check shows (column 4:  rac14 +  rac14 +  rac23\cdot rac14 =  rac23). Then \cvec{y}	p\A^{m} = \cvec{y}	p for all m, hence \cvec{y}	p\vPi = \cvec{y}	p, and entry 4 gives \cvec{y}	p(c\cvec{v}_1 + (1 - c)\cvec{v}_2) = c =  rac23. Thus \vPi =  egin{pmatrix} 1/3 & 1/3 & 0 & 2/9 \ 2/3 & 2/3 & 0 & 4/9 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1/3 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , with last column  rac23\cvec{v}_1 +  rac13\cvec{v}_2. The long run depends on where the chain starts: from state 4, the chain ends up in the pair \{1, 2\} with probability  rac23 and in state 3 with probability  rac13, the ratio  rac12 :  rac14 of the one-step probabilities of leaving 4 for each. In general the steady states of a stochastic matrix form a convex set, since a convex combination of probability vectors fixed by \A is again one; the example shows it can be a segment rather than a point. One steady state for each part of the chain that, once entered, is never left, and all convex combinations of these: that is the general picture, which we do not prove here. Absorbing chains The simplest traps are single states. A state j is absorbing if a_{jj} = 1, so that column j of \A is \cvec{e}_j: once there, the chain stays. Absorbing states model the end of a process: a game won or lost, a customer who has left, a molecule that has reacted. [Absorbing Chain] A stochastic matrix \A \in M_n(
R) is absorbing if it has at least one absorbing state, and from every state some absorbing state can be reached: for every j there are an absorbing state i and an m \ge 0 with (\A^{m})_{ij} > 0. The states that are not absorbing are called transient. Number the states so that the t \ge 1 transient states come first and the r \ge 1 absorbing states last. Column j for a transient j splits into the probabilities of moving to transient states and to absorbing states, and the column of an absorbing state is a standard basis vector. So \A has the block form \A =  egin{pmatrix} \Q & \O \ \R & \I_r \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Q \in M_t(
R), \quad \R \in M_{r 	imes t}(
R), with \Q, \R \ge \O and \1	p\Q + \1	p\R = \1	p. Multiplying blocks and inducting on m, \A^{m} =  egin{pmatrix} \Q^{m} & \O \ \R_m & \I_r \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \R_m = \R ig(\I + \Q + \dots + \Q^{m-1} ig) , since \A^{m+1} = \A\A^{m} has lower-left block \R\Q^{m} + \R_m = \R_{m+1}. The entry (\Q^{m})_{ij} is the probability of being at transient state i after m steps from transient state j; the column sums of \Q^{m} are the probabilities of not yet having been absorbed. [Transient Mass Dies Out] If \A is absorbing, with \Q as above, then every eigenvalue of \Q has modulus less than 1, and \Q^{m} 	o \O. Every column of \Q sums to at most 1, which only gives ho(\Q) \le 1. But after enough steps every transient state has leaked some mass into an absorbing state, so every column of a suitable power \Q^{M} sums to strictly less than 1, and the column-sum bound of Chapter 16 gives ho(\Q^{M}) < 1. For absorbing i and any j, (\A^{m+1})_{ij} = \sum_l a_{il}(\A^{m})_{lj} \ge a_{ii}(\A^{m})_{ij} = (\A^{m})_{ij}, since all terms are nonnegative; so the probability of being at i never decreases. Fix a transient j. By @def-absorbing-chain there are an absorbing i and m_j with (\A^{m_j})_{ij} > 0, and then (\A^{m})_{ij} > 0 for every m \ge m_j. Let M be the largest of the m_j over the transient j. Column j of \A^{M} sums to 1 (@prp-stochastic-properties (b)) and has a positive entry (\A^{M})_{ij} in the absorbing rows, so column j of \Q^{M} sums to less than 1. Since \Q^{M} \ge \O, its largest absolute column sum is some c < 1, and by @cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound, ho(\Q^{M}) \le c < 1. By @thm-spectral-mapping with q = x^{M}, the eigenvalues of \Q^{M} are the M-th powers of those of \Q, so ho(\Q)^{M} = ho(\Q^{M}) < 1 and ho(\Q) < 1. Finally \Q^{m} 	o \O by @thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero. The Neumann series now does all the work. Absorbing Chains Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} \Q & \O \ \R & \I_r \end{pmatrix} be absorbing, in the block form above. Then: 1. \I - \Q is invertible, and the fundamental matrix \N \coloneqq (\I - \Q)^{-1} = \sum_{k \ge 0}\Q^{k} satisfies \N \ge \O; 2. \A^{m} 	o  egin{pmatrix} \O & \O \ \R\N & \I_r \end{pmatrix} entrywise; 3. every column of the r 	imes t matrix \B \coloneqq \R\N is a probability vector. The lemma gives ho(\Q) < 1, which is exactly what the Neumann series needs. In the block formula for \A^{m}, the lower-left block is \R times a partial sum of that series, so it converges to \R\N; and column sums equal to 1 pass to the limit. (a) By @lem-absorbing-transient-decay and @thm-neumann-series-spectral, \sum_k\Q^{k} converges and equals (\I - \Q)^{-1}. Each partial sum is \ge \O, and a limit of nonnegative numbers is nonnegative, since a nonstrict inequality survives a limit (the elementary algebra of limits, recalled in the introduction to Chapter 16); so \N \ge \O. (b) By the block formula, the upper-left block of \A^{m} is \Q^{m} 	o \O (@lem-absorbing-transient-decay), and the lower-left block is \R_m = \R\sum_{k<m}\Q^{k}. Each entry of \R_m is a fixed linear combination of entries of the partial sum, so \R_m 	o \R\N by the algebra of limits, (B3) of Chapter 10 §10. The other two blocks do not depend on m. (c) Every column of \A^{m} sums to 1, and so does every column of the limit in (b). For a transient j, column j of the limit is (\cvec{0}, \B\cvec{e}_j), so the entries of \B\cvec{e}_j sum to 1; they are nonnegative because \R, \N \ge \O. Reading the answer. The theorem is pure algebra; its meaning comes from reading entries as probabilities. The (i, j)-entry of the limit in (b), for absorbing i and transient j, is the limit of the nondecreasing probabilities of being at i after m steps from j: the probability of being absorbed at i. So \B = \R\N is the matrix of absorption probabilities. Two further readings use a fact from probability that this book does not develop, linearity of expectation: the expected number of steps at which an event occurs is the sum over the steps of the probabilities of that event. With it, since (\Q^{k})_{ij} is the probability of being at transient i at step k from j,  egin{aligned} N_{ij} &= \sum_{k \ge 0}(\Q^{k})_{ij} \ &= 	ext{expected number of visits to } i 	ext{ starting from } j , \end{aligned} counting the visit at step 0 when i = j; and summing over i, the column sums 	au_j = (\1	p\N)_j are the expected numbers of steps before absorption. Nothing in the proofs depends on these readings. [Gambler’s Ruin] A gambler holds 1, 2, or 3 coins and bets one coin at a time on a fair toss, winning or losing a coin with probability  rac12 each. Play stops when the gambler holds 0 coins (ruin) or 4 coins (target). Find the fundamental matrix, the expected length of play, and the probability of reaching the target, from each starting fortune. The transient states are the fortunes 1, 2, 3, in that order, and the absorbing ones are 0 and 4, in that order. From fortune j the gambler moves to j - 1 or j + 1 with probability  rac12 each, so \Q =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1/2 & 0 \ 1/2 & 0 & 1/2 \ 0 & 1/2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \R =  egin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix} , the first row of \R recording ruin from fortune 1 and the second reaching the target from fortune 3. Each column of  egin{pmatrix} \Q \ \R \end{pmatrix} sums to 1, and every fortune reaches 0 by losing, so the chain is absorbing. The fundamental matrix. Solve (\I - \Q)\N = \I with \I - \Q =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1/2 & 0 \ -1/2 & 1 & -1/2 \ 0 & -1/2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. The result is \N =  egin{pmatrix} 3/2 & 1 & 1/2 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \ 1/2 & 1 & 3/2 \end{pmatrix} ; check the first column: (\I - \Q)( rac32, 1,  rac12) = ( rac32 -  rac12,\ - rac34 + 1 -  rac14,\ - rac12 +  rac12) = (1, 0, 0), and the other columns likewise. A gambler starting with 2 coins holds exactly 2 coins at 2 steps on average, counting the start, and holds 1 or 3 coins at one step each on average. Length of play. \1	p\N = (3, 4, 3): from fortunes 1, 2, 3 the game lasts 3, 4, 3 tosses on average. Absorption. \B = \R\N =  egin{pmatrix} 3/4 & 1/2 & 1/4 \ 1/4 & 1/2 & 3/4 \end{pmatrix} . From fortune j the gambler reaches the target with probability j/4 and is ruined with probability 1 - j/4. Each column sums to 1, as @thm-absorbing-chain (c) requires: the game ends with probability 1. Both answers match the classical formulas for a fair game with target T = 4: success probability j/T and expected length j(T - j), which gives 3, 4, 3. The matrix \Q of this example has eigenvalues 0 and \pm rac{1}{\sqrt2}, of modulus less than 1 as @lem-absorbing-transient-decay requires; but the lemma was proved without finding them, which is the pattern of this whole section. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the long-run theorem @thm-markov-limit-primitive, and name the three hypotheses of @thm-markov-limit-diagonalizable that it no longer needs. 2. True or false: every irreducible stochastic matrix has exactly one steady state. Justify your answer. 3. True or false: for every irreducible stochastic matrix, \A^{m} converges. Justify your answer. 4. True or false: if a stochastic matrix has two different steady states, it has infinitely many. Justify your answer. 5. In an absorbing chain, what do the column sums of the fundamental matrix measure, and why do the columns of \R\N sum to 1? (a) If \A is stochastic and \A^{k} > \O for some k, then \A has exactly one steady state \cvec{v}, it is positive, \A^{m} 	o \cvec{v}\1	p, and every chain \A^{m}\cvec{x}_0 converges to \cvec{v}. It no longer assumes that \A is diagonalizable, that a_{\A}(1) = 1, or that every other eigenvalue has modulus less than 1. (b) True, by @prp-stochastic-perron (c); moreover the steady state is positive. (c) False. The swap  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is irreducible and stochastic, and its powers alternate between \I and itself. By @thm-markov-cesaro (c), the powers converge exactly when the matrix is primitive. (d) True. If \cvec{u} 
e \cvec{u}' are steady states, then c\cvec{u} + (1 - c)\cvec{u}' for 0 \le c \le 1 is nonnegative, has entries summing to 1, and is fixed by \A; different c give different vectors, since \cvec{u} - \cvec{u}' 
e \cvec{0}. (e) The column sum (\1	p\N)_j is the expected number of steps before absorption from transient state j. The columns of \R\N sum to 1 because the columns of \A^{m} do and \Q^{m} 	o \O (@thm-absorbing-chain (c)): absorption is certain. B. Practice [B1: When does the long-run theorem apply?] For each stochastic matrix, determine whether @thm-markov-limit-primitive applies. Justify your answer, and when it applies, find the limit of \A^{m}. 1.  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1/2 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix}. 2.  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. 3.  egin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 0 \ 1/2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. (a) It applies. The edges of G(\A) are 1 	o 2, 2 	o 3, 3 	o 1 and the loop 3 	o 3. The cycle 1 	o 2 	o 3 	o 1 reaches every state from every state, so \A is irreducible (@thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected). It has the positive diagonal entry a_{33}, so it is primitive by @cor-primitive-iff-aperiodic. The steady state solves v_1 =  rac12v_3, v_2 = v_1, so \cvec{v} = (1, 1, 2)/4, and \A^{m} 	o \cvec{v}\1	p, every column equal to ( rac14,  rac14,  rac12). Check: \A\cvec{v} = ( rac14,  rac14,  rac14 +  rac14) = \cvec{v}. (b) It does not apply. This is a permutation matrix, so every power is a permutation matrix (@lem-permutation-matrices) and has zero entries. Its powers cycle with period 3 (@exm-cyclic-permutation) and do not converge. (c) It does not apply. Every power is lower triangular with (1,2)-entry 0, as one checks by induction: \A^{m} =  egin{pmatrix} 2^{-m} & 0 \ 1 - 2^{-m} & 1 \end{pmatrix}. The powers converge nonetheless, to  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \cvec{e}_2\1	p: state 2 is absorbing, and \cvec{e}_2 is the unique steady state, with a zero entry. [B2: A three-state chain] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 1/4 & 0 \ 1/2 & 1/2 & 1/2 \ 0 & 1/4 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix}. 1. Show that \A is stochastic and that \A^{2} > \O. 2. Find the steady state, and hence \lim_m \A^{m} and the long-run distribution of every chain with this transition matrix. (a) The entries are nonnegative and the columns sum to 1. Multiplying out, \A^{2} =  egin{pmatrix} 3/8 & 1/4 & 1/8 \ 1/2 & 1/2 & 1/2 \ 1/8 & 1/4 & 3/8 \end{pmatrix} > \O . (b) (\A - \I)\cvec{v} = \cvec{0}: the first row gives - rac12v_1 +  rac14v_2 = 0, so v_2 = 2v_1, and the third gives  rac14v_2 -  rac12v_3 = 0, so v_3 =  rac12v_2 = v_1. So \cvec{v} is a multiple of (1, 2, 1), and scaling to sum 1 gives \cvec{v} = ( rac14,  rac12,  rac14). By @thm-markov-limit-primitive, \A^{m} 	o \cvec{v}\1	p, every column equal to \cvec{v}, and every chain converges to \cvec{v} whatever its initial distribution. [B3: An unfair game] A gambler holds 1 or 2 coins and wins each toss with probability  rac13, losing with probability  rac23. Play stops at 0 or 3 coins. Find the fundamental matrix, the expected length of play, and the probability of reaching 3 coins from each starting fortune. Order the states as 1, 2 (transient) and 0, 3 (absorbing). From 1: to 2 with probability  rac13, to 0 with  rac23. From 2: to 3 with  rac13, to 1 with  rac23. So \Q =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2/3 \ 1/3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \R =  egin{pmatrix} 2/3 & 0 \ 0 & 1/3 \end{pmatrix} . The chain is absorbing, since from either fortune repeated losses reach 0. Then \I - \Q =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -2/3 \ -1/3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has determinant 1 -  rac29 =  rac79, so by @thm-two-by-two-inverse \N =  rac97 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2/3 \ 1/3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 9/7 & 6/7 \ 3/7 & 9/7 \end{pmatrix} . The expected lengths of play are \1	p\N = ( rac{12}{7},  rac{15}{7}), and \R\N =  egin{pmatrix} 6/7 & 4/7 \ 1/7 & 3/7 \end{pmatrix} . So the probability of reaching 3 coins is  rac17 from 1 coin and  rac37 from 2 coins, far below the fair values  rac13 and  rac23. The columns of \R\N sum to 1, as they must. C. Going deeper [C1: The lazy chain] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be stochastic and irreducible, with steady state \cvec{v}, and let \M =  rac12(\I + \A). 1. Prove that \M is stochastic and primitive, and that \cvec{v} is its unique steady state. Deduce that \M^{m} 	o \cvec{v}\1	p. 2. Let \A be the walk of @exm-reflecting-walk. Show that \M is the matrix of exercise B2, and that \M^{m} = \cvec{v}\1	p + 2^{-m}\F for every m \ge 1, where \F =  rac12 egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}. Hint: write \M in terms of \cvec{v}\1	p and \F. (a) \M \ge \O, and \1	p\M =  rac12(\1	p + \1	p\A) = \1	p, so \M is stochastic. By @exr-primitive-matrices-c1 (a) with t = 1, \A + \I is primitive, say (\A + \I)^{k} > \O; then \M^{k} = 2^{-k}(\A + \I)^{k} > \O, so \M is primitive. Also \M\cvec{v} =  rac12(\cvec{v} + \cvec{v}) = \cvec{v}. By @thm-markov-limit-primitive (a), \M has exactly one steady state, so it is \cvec{v}, and by part (b) of that theorem \M^{m} 	o \cvec{v}\1	p. (b) With \A as in @exm-reflecting-walk, \M =  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1/2 & 0 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1/2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 1/4 & 0 \ 1/2 & 1/2 & 1/2 \ 0 & 1/4 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix} , the matrix of @exr-markov-chains-b2, and \cvec{v} = ( rac14,  rac12,  rac14). Put \L = \cvec{v}\1	p, every column equal to \cvec{v}. Then \L^{2} = \cvec{v}(\1	p\cvec{v})\1	p = \L; \1	p\F = \cvec{0}	p, since each column of \F sums to 0, so \L\F = \cvec{v}(\1	p\F) = \O; and \F\cvec{v} =  rac12( rac14 -  rac14,\ 0,\ - rac14 +  rac14) = \cvec{0}, so \F\L = (\F\cvec{v})\1	p = \O. Also \F^{2} =  rac14 egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & -2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ -2 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \F. Subtracting, \M - \L =  rac14 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} =  rac12\F, so \M = \L +  rac12\F. If \M^{m} = \L + 2^{-m}\F, then  egin{aligned} \M^{m+1} &= \Big(\L +  rac12\F\Big) ig(\L + 2^{-m}\F ig) \ &= \L^{2} + 2^{-m}\L\F +  rac12\F\L + 2^{-m-1}\F^{2} = \L + 2^{-(m+1)}\F , \end{aligned} so the formula holds for every m \ge 1 by induction, starting from \M = \L +  rac12\F. The lazy walk converges although the walk itself oscillates, and its distance to the limit halves at every step. [C2: The converse of the long-run theorem] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be stochastic. 1. Prove that if \A^{m} 	o \cvec{v}\1	p for some \cvec{v} > \cvec{0}, then \A is primitive. 2. Give a stochastic \A with \A^{m} 	o \cvec{v}\1	p for a probability vector \cvec{v}, but no power of \A positive. Which entry of \cvec{v} is responsible? (a) The limit \cvec{v}\1	p has (i, j)-entry v_i > 0. Each of the n^{2} entries of \A^{m} converges to a positive number, so it is positive for all m beyond some m_{ij}; for m larger than all the m_{ij}, \A^{m} > \O. So \A is primitive. (b) \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1/2 \ 0 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix}. By induction \A^{m} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 - 2^{-m} \ 0 & 2^{-m} \end{pmatrix}: indeed \A\A^{m} has first row (1,\ 1 - 2^{-m} + 2^{-m-1}) = (1,\ 1 - 2^{-(m+1)}) and second row (0,\ 2^{-(m+1)}). So \A^{m} 	o  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \cvec{e}_1\1	p, while every power has (2,1)-entry 0. The responsible entry is v_2 = 0: (a) fails exactly because \cvec{v} is not positive. [C3: First-step analysis] Let \A be absorbing, with fundamental matrix \N and \vtau	p = \1	p\N. 1. Prove that \N = \I + \N\Q, and deduce that 	au_j = 1 + \sum_i q_{ij}	au_i for every transient j. Interpret this equation. 2. Prove, by multiplying by \R, that \B = \R\N satisfies \B = \R + \B\Q, and interpret it. 3. Use (a) to recompute the expected lengths of play (3, 4, 3) of @exm-gamblers-ruin without inverting a matrix. (a) \N(\I - \Q) = \I because \N is the inverse of \I - \Q, so \N = \I + \N\Q. Multiplying on the left by \1	p, \vtau	p = \1	p + \vtau	p\Q, whose j-th entry is 	au_j = 1 + \sum_i	au_iq_{ij}. In words: from j, one step is taken, the chain lands at transient i with probability q_{ij}, and from there the expected remaining time is 	au_i; landing at an absorbing state contributes nothing more. (b) Multiply \N = \I + \N\Q on the left by \R: \B = \R + \B\Q, that is, b_{ij} = r_{ij} + \sum_l b_{il}q_{lj}. The probability of absorption at i from j is the probability of stepping into i at once, plus the probability of stepping to a transient l and being absorbed at i from there. (c) With \Q as in @exm-gamblers-ruin, (a) reads 	au_1 = 1 +  rac12	au_2, 	au_2 = 1 +  rac12	au_1 +  rac12	au_3, 	au_3 = 1 +  rac12	au_2. The first and third equations give 	au_1 = 	au_3 = 1 +  rac12	au_2, so 	au_2 = 1 + 	au_1 = 1 + 1 +  rac12	au_2, giving 	au_2 = 4 and 	au_1 = 	au_3 = 3. (The system has only one solution, since its matrix is (\I - \Q)	p, which is invertible by @thm-absorbing-chain (a).)

title: 19.7 Birkhoff's Theorem
content:
Birkhoff’s Theorem Chapter 18 §08 met the doubly stochastic matrices, the nonnegative matrices whose rows and columns all add up to 1. It showed that every permutation matrix is an extreme point of the set \Omega_n they form, stated Birkhoff’s theorem that there are no other extreme points, proved that this is equivalent to “every doubly stochastic matrix is an average of permutation matrices”, and left the proof to this chapter. This section supplies it. The proof is a count: a corner of \Omega_n has so many zero entries that some row holds a single 1, and deleting that row and its column leaves a corner of \Omega_{n-1}. We then bound how many permutation matrices an average needs, turn the theorem into a procedure for finding them, and use it to give the second proof of Schur’s majorization theorem that Chapter 18 §08 sketched. Throughout, the field is 
R, and inequalities between matrices or vectors are entrywise, as in §01. Recall @def-doubly-stochastic: \M \in M_n(
R) is doubly stochastic if m_{ij} \ge 0 for all i, j, and every row and every column adds up to 1; in terms of the all-ones vector, \M\1 = \1 and \1	p\M = \1	p. So \M is stochastic in the book’s column sense (@def-stochastic-matrix), and so is \M	p. What is left to prove Here is where Chapter 18 §08 stopped. The set \Omega_n is convex and compact. The n! permutation matrices \P_\sigma, \sigma \in S_n (@def-permutation-matrix), lie in it, and each is an extreme point (@prp-permutation-matrices-extreme). The two forms of Birkhoff’s theorem, “the extreme points are the permutation matrices” and “\Omega_n is the convex hull of the permutation matrices”, were shown to be equivalent there, using Minkowski’s theorem (@thm-minkowski-extreme) in one direction and @prp-extreme-points-of-hull in the other. For n = 2, the Quick check after the statement found \Omega_2 by hand: it is the segment from \I to the swap matrix. So one implication is missing: every extreme point of \Omega_n is a permutation matrix. For n \ge 3 nothing as simple as the 2 	imes 2 computation is available, since \Omega_3 already has four free parameters. What does the work instead is a result of Chapter 18 §09 that recognizes a corner of a polyhedron from its tight constraints. The doubly stochastic matrices form a polyhedron Recall @def-polyhedron and @thm-vertices-basic-feasible. A polyhedron is a set \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^N : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\}; its extreme points are called vertices; and a point \cvec{x} of it is a vertex exactly when the rows \cvec{a}_i	p of the constraints that hold with equality at \cvec{x}, the active rows, include N linearly independent ones. An equation is allowed, as a pair of inequalities \cvec{a}	p\cvec{x} \le  eta and -\cvec{a}	p\cvec{x} \le - eta; both are active at every point of the polyhedron. To put \Omega_n in this form, list the n^2 entries of a matrix \X as one column, the vectorization \vecop\X \in 
R^{n^2} of Chapter 8. A linear expression \sum_{i,j} b_{ij}x_{ij} in the entries is then the dot product of \vecop\X with \vecop\B, and we may treat the coefficient matrix \B \in M_n(
R) itself as the row of the constraint. Three families of coefficient matrices appear. With \E_{ij} the matrix unit (a 1 in position (i,j), zeros elsewhere), let \R_i = \cvec{e}_i\1	p , \qquad \C_j = \1\cvec{e}_j	p \qquad (1 \le i, j \le n) , the matrices whose i-th row, respectively j-th column, consists of ones and whose other entries are zero. The letter \C_j is local to this section; elsewhere \C(p) is a companion matrix and \C_k(\lambda) a real Jordan block. Then \sum_{k,l}(\R_i)_{kl}x_{kl} is the i-th row sum of \X, and \C_j gives the j-th column sum. So \Omega_n \subseteq M_n(
R) \cong 
R^{n^2} is the polyhedron cut out by 1. the n^2 inequalities -x_{ij} \le 0, with rows -\E_{ij}; 2. the n row equations “row sum i equals 1”, with rows \pm\R_i; 3. the n column equations “column sum j equals 1”, with rows \pm\C_j. At a point \M \in \Omega_n, every row \pm\R_i and \pm\C_j is active, and -\E_{ij} is active exactly when m_{ij} = 0. The whole argument turns on how much the 2n equations are worth. They are not independent: adding all row sums and adding all column sums both give the sum of all entries, that is, \R_1 + \dots + \R_n = \J = \C_1 + \dots + \C_n , with \J the all-ones matrix. The next lemma says that this is the only relation. [The Row and Column Sum Conditions] Let n \ge 1, and let W_n = \{\X \in M_n(
R) : \X\1 = \cvec{0},\ \1	p\X = \cvec{0}	p\} be the space of real matrices whose rows and columns all add up to 0. Then: 1. \dim W_n = (n-1)^2; 2. the 2n matrices \R_1, \dots, \R_n, \C_1, \dots, \C_n span a subspace of M_n(
R) of dimension 2n - 1. A matrix in W_n is determined by its top-left (n-1) 	imes (n-1) block, which can be anything: the last column and the last row are then forced by the zero sums, and the corner comes out consistent. That gives (a). For (b), W_n is exactly the set of matrices killed by the 2n sum conditions, so rank–nullity converts one count into the other. (a) If n = 1, W_1 = \{\O\} and (n-1)^2 = 0.
