Check that \M \in \Omega_3, and write \M as a convex combination of permutation matrices by peeling. Hence confirm the bound of @cor-birkhoff-convex-combination for this \M. The entries are nonnegative; the rows of 6\M add up to 3 + 3 + 0, 1 + 2 + 3, 2 + 1 + 3, and the columns to 3 + 1 + 2, 3 + 2 + 1, 0 + 3 + 3, all 6. So \M \in \Omega_3. Peel \N = 6\M. Round 1. The diagonal 3, 2, 3 is positive; subtract 2\I:  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 3 \ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad (	ext{sums } 4) . Round 2. The positions (3,1), (1,2), (2,3) carry 2, 3, 3; subtract 2\P_1, where \P_1 has its 1’s there:  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad (	ext{sums } 2) . Round 3. The positions (1,1), (3,2), (2,3) carry 1, 1, 1; subtract \P_2, with 1’s there. What remains has 1’s at (2,1), (1,2), (3,3): a permutation matrix \P_3, with weight 1. So 6\M = 2\I + 2\P_1 + \P_2 + \P_3 and \M = 	frac13\,\I + 	frac13\,\P_1 + 	frac16\,\P_2 + 	frac16\,\P_3 , with weights nonnegative and adding up to 1. Hence \M uses four permutation matrices, within the bound (3-1)^2 + 1 = 5. [B3: Schur’s theorem by averaging] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. 1. Find \vlambda(\A) and an orthogonal \U with \A = \U\diag(\vlambda(\A))\U	p. 2. Compute \S = (u_{ij}^2) and check that \cvec{d}(\A) = \S\vlambda(\A). 3. Write \S as a convex combination of permutation matrices, and hence \cvec{d}(\A) as an average of rearrangements of \vlambda(\A). Confirm \cvec{d}(\A) \prec \vlambda(\A) from @def-majorization. (a) \A(2, 1) = (10, 5) = 5(2, 1) and \A(1, -2) = (0, 0), so \vlambda(\A) = (5, 0). With the unit eigenvectors 	frac{1}{\sqrt5}(2, 1) and 	frac{1}{\sqrt5}(1, -2) as columns, \U =  rac{1}{\sqrt5} egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix} , which is orthogonal, and \A = \U\diag(5, 0)\U	p by @cor-spectral-real-matrix. (b) \S = 	frac15 egin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, and \S(5, 0) = (4, 1) = \cvec{d}(\A). (c) \S = 	frac45\I + 	frac15 egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, so \cvec{d}(\A) = 	frac45(5, 0) + 	frac15(0, 5) = (4, 1). Directly: both vectors are decreasing, the totals are 5 = 5, and at k = 1, 4 \le 5. So \cvec{d}(\A) \prec \vlambda(\A). C. Going deeper [C1: Five permutation matrices can be needed] Let \P be the permutation matrix of the 3-cycle 1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 1, and let \T_{12}, \T_{13}, \T_{23} be those of the transpositions (1\ 2), (1\ 3), (2\ 3). The six permutation matrices of size 3 are \I, \P, \P^2 (the even ones) and \T_{12}, \T_{13}, \T_{23} (the odd ones). 1. Show that each of the nine positions (i, j) holds a 1 in exactly one even and exactly one odd permutation matrix, and that each even and each odd permutation matrix share exactly one position of a 1. 2. Deduce that if \sum_\sigma c_\sigma\P_\sigma = \O for real numbers c_\sigma, then c_\sigma = c for the even \sigma and c_\sigma = -c for the odd \sigma, for some c \in 
R. 3. Let \M = 	frac{1}{15} igl(\I + 2\P + 3\P^2 + 4\T_{12} + 5\T_{13} igr). Show that every way of writing \M as a convex combination of permutation matrices uses at least five of them with positive weight. Hint: in (a), a permutation of \{1, 2, 3\} is determined by where it sends any two points. (a) A permutation matrix \P_\sigma has a 1 in position (i, j) exactly when \sigma(j) = i. The permutations of \{1, 2, 3\} with \sigma(j) = i are determined by where they send the other two points, which must go to the other two values in one of two ways, so there are exactly two. If \sigma is one of them, the other is 	au\sigma, with 	au the transposition exchanging the two remaining values, so their signs are opposite (@def-sign-permutation, @thm-sign-multiplicative): one is even and one is odd. For the second claim, let \sigma be even and 	au odd. They cannot agree at all three points, since they differ; they cannot agree at exactly two, since two agreements force the third; and if they agreed nowhere, 	au^{-1}\sigma would fix no point and so be a 3-cycle, which is even, while 	au^{-1}\sigma is odd. So they agree at exactly one point j, that is, they share exactly one position (\sigma(j), j). (b) Look at position (i, j): by (a) exactly one even \sigma and one odd 	au have a 1 there, so the equation gives c_\sigma + c_	au = 0. By (a) again, every pair of an even \sigma and an odd 	au arises in this way at their shared position, so c_\sigma = -c_	au for every such pair. Fixing one odd 	au, all even c_\sigma equal c = -c_	au, and then every odd c_{	au'} = -c. (c) The given weights are 	frac{1}{15}(1, 2, 3) on \I, \P, \P^2 and 	frac{1}{15}(4, 5, 0) on \T_{12}, \T_{13}, \T_{23}; they are nonnegative with sum 1. If \M = \sum_\sigma t_\sigma\P_\sigma is any other convex combination, the difference of the two weight lists satisfies (b), so the even weights are 	frac{1}{15}(1, 2, 3) + s and the odd ones 	frac{1}{15}(4, 5, 0) - s for some real s. Nonnegativity needs s \ge -	frac1{15} (from \I) and s \le 0 (from \T_{23}). For -	frac1{15} < s < 0, all six weights are positive. At s = 0 exactly one vanishes, that of \T_{23}; at s = -	frac1{15} exactly one vanishes, that of \I, the others being 	frac{1}{15}(1, 2) and 	frac{1}{15}(5, 6, 1). So every representation has at least five positive weights, and the bound (3 - 1)^2 + 1 = 5 of @cor-birkhoff-convex-combination is attained. [C2: Integer matrices with equal line sums] Let k \ge 1, and let \N \in M_n(
R) have nonnegative integer entries, with every row and every column adding up to k. 1. Prove that \N is a sum of k permutation matrices, not necessarily distinct. 2. Carry this out for \N =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 2 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Hint: apply @cor-doubly-stochastic-positive-diagonal to 	frac1k\N. (a) By induction on k. The matrix 	frac1k\N is doubly stochastic, so by @cor-doubly-stochastic-positive-diagonal there is \sigma with n_{\sigma(j)j} > 0 for every j. These are positive integers, so each is at least 1, and \N - \P_\sigma has nonnegative integer entries with every row and column adding up to k - 1. If k = 1, then \N - \P_\sigma has line sums 0 and nonnegative entries, so it is \O and \N = \P_\sigma. If k \ge 2, the induction hypothesis writes \N - \P_\sigma as a sum of k - 1 permutation matrices, and adding \P_\sigma gives k. (b) Every row and column adds up to 3. The diagonal 2, 1, 1 is positive; subtracting \I leaves  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 2 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . The positions (1,1), (3,2), (2,3) are positive; subtracting that permutation matrix leaves the permutation matrix with 1’s at (3,1), (1,2), (2,3). So \N is \I plus these two permutation matrices. [C3: The dimension, and a matrix that is not unistochastic] Let n \ge 2. 1. Prove that if \X \in W_n has every \lvert x_{ij}vert \le 	frac1n, then 	frac1n\J + \X \in \Omega_n. Deduce that \operatorname{aff}\Omega_n = 	frac1n\J + W_n and \dim\Omega_n = (n-1)^2. 2. Show that \M = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} is doubly stochastic but is not of the form (\lvert u_{ij}vert^2) for any unitary \U \in M_3(
C). Hint for (b): two columns of \U must be orthogonal; look at which rows both can be nonzero in. (a) The entries of 	frac1n\J + \X are 	frac1n + x_{ij} \ge 	frac1n - 	frac1n = 0, and its rows and columns add up to 1 + 0 = 1, since \X \in W_n. So it lies in \Omega_n. The proof of @cor-birkhoff-convex-combination showed \Omega_n \subseteq 	frac1n\J + W_n, a coset, which is an affine set containing \Omega_n, so \operatorname{aff}\Omega_n \subseteq 	frac1n\J + W_n. Conversely, let \X \in W_n, \X 
e \O, and put c = n\max_{i,j}\lvert x_{ij}vert > 0. Then 	frac1n\J and 	frac1n\J + 	frac1c\X lie in \Omega_n, and the affine combination 	frac1n\J + \X = (1 - c)\,	frac1n\J + c\, igl(	frac1n\J + 	frac1c\X igr) lies in \operatorname{aff}\Omega_n. So \operatorname{aff}\Omega_n = 	frac1n\J + W_n, and \dim\Omega_n = \dim W_n = (n-1)^2 by @lem-doubly-stochastic-sum-conditions (a). (b) The entries are nonnegative and every row and column adds up to 1. Suppose \M = (\lvert u_{ij}vert^2) with \U unitary. The zero entries m_{13} = m_{21} = m_{32} = 0 force u_{13} = u_{21} = u_{32} = 0. Columns 1 and 2 of \U are (u_{11}, 0, u_{31}) and (u_{12}, u_{22}, 0), and they are orthogonal because \U is unitary: 0 = u_{11}\conj{u_{12}} + 0 \cdot \conj{u_{22}} + u_{31} \cdot 0 = u_{11}\conj{u_{12}} . But \lvert u_{11}vert^2 = \lvert u_{12}vert^2 = 	frac12, so u_{11}\conj{u_{12}} 
e 0, a contradiction. Hence \M is not unistochastic.

title: 19.8 PageRank
content:
PageRank A search engine that finds thousands of pages containing a word must decide which to list first. One answer, which made a search engine famous, is to let the pages vote. Each page spreads its vote over the pages it links to, a vote counts for more when it comes from a page that is itself important, and “important” is whatever this circular description settles on. Written out, the circle is an eigenvector equation for a stochastic matrix. This section sets up that matrix, shows why the raw web does not give a well-defined ranking, repairs it with a single parameter, and uses Perron’s theorem (@thm-perron) to prove that the repaired matrix has exactly one ranking, with every entry positive. We then prove how fast the ranking can be computed, and work a small web exactly. Throughout, the field is 
R, inequalities between vectors and matrices are entrywise as in §01, and stochastic means column-stochastic (@def-stochastic-matrix): nonnegative entries, every column adding up to 1. Many accounts of PageRank use rows instead; their matrices are the transposes of ours. We write \1 for the all-ones vector and \J = \1\1	p for the all-ones matrix. The web as a Markov chain Number the pages 1, \dots, n. Page j links to page i if it contains a link to it; we ignore links from a page to itself, and several links from j to i count as one. Let d_j be the number of pages that page j links to, its out-degree. A page with d_j = 0 is called dangling: a document with no links out, such as an image or a file. Imagine a surfer who, on page j, clicks one of its d_j links, each with probability 1/d_j. If \cvec{x}_k is the probability vector of the surfer’s position after k clicks, then, exactly as in Chapter 9 §11, \cvec{x}_{k+1} = \H\cvec{x}_k, where h_{ij} = 1/d_j if j links to i and h_{ij} = 0 otherwise. This hyperlink matrix \H is local to this section; elsewhere in the book \H is a Hessian. The long-run share of time the surfer spends on page i is the candidate for page i’s importance. It captures the circular description: page i receives, from each page j linking to it, the share 1/d_j of j’s own weight. At a dangling page the surfer has nowhere to go, and column j of \H is zero. The standard patch sends the surfer to a page chosen uniformly at random. [Link Matrix] Let a web have pages 1, \dots, n, with n \ge 1, and out-degrees d_1, \dots, d_n. Its link matrix is the n 	imes n matrix \P whose column j is: 1. if d_j \ge 1: the vector with entry 1/d_j in each position i such that page j links to page i, and 0 elsewhere; 2. if d_j = 0 (page j is dangling): the vector 	frac1n\1. Each column is a probability vector: in case (a) it has d_j entries equal to 1/d_j, and in case (b) n entries equal to 1/n. So \P is stochastic. For instance, the web on three pages in which page 1 links to pages 2 and 3, page 2 links to page 3, and page 3 links nowhere, has \P =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 	frac13 \ 	frac12 & 0 & 	frac13 \ 	frac12 & 1 & 	frac13 \end{pmatrix} . A ranking should then be a steady state of \P (@def-markov-chain): a probability vector \cvec{x} with \P\cvec{x} = \cvec{x}. When \P is irreducible (@def-irreducible), there is exactly one, with every entry positive, by @prp-stochastic-perron (c); part (a) of the same proposition gives ho(\P) = 1 for every stochastic \P. The real web is very far from irreducible, and the three failures below are the typical ones. [Three ways a web can fail to rank] For each web, describe what goes wrong with the surfer’s chain. 1. Two pages; page 1 links to page 2, and page 2 is dangling, but we use \H, without the patch. 2. Four pages; pages 1 and 2 link to each other, and so do pages 3 and 4. 3. Two pages that link to each other. (a) \H =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has a zero column, so it is not stochastic, and \H^2 = \O. From any start the surfer is gone after two clicks: \H^2\cvec{x}_0 = \cvec{0} is not a probability vector, and \H has no steady state at all, since \H\cvec{x} = \cvec{x} forces x_1 = 0 and then x_2 = x_1 = 0. The patched \P has second column (	frac12, 	frac12) and the steady state (	frac13, 	frac23), since \P(1, 2) = (0 \cdot 1 + 	frac12 \cdot 2,\ 1 \cdot 1 + 	frac12 \cdot 2) = (1, 2). (b) \P is block diagonal with two copies of the swap  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Both (	frac12, 	frac12, 0, 0) and (0, 0, 	frac12, 	frac12) are steady states, and so is every average of the two. The chain cannot say whether page 1 matters more than page 3: the ranking is not unique. (c) \P is the swap. Its steady state (	frac12, 	frac12) is unique, but from \cvec{x}_0 = \cvec{e}_1 the chain alternates \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_1, \dots and never settles. The eigenvalue -1 of the swap has the same modulus as 1. In (b) the matrix is reducible, and in (c) it is irreducible but not primitive (@def-primitive): the powers of the swap are \I and the swap, and neither is positive. Real webs have all three features, on a vast scale. The Google matrix The dangling patch of @def-link-matrix already repairs failure (a). One modification repairs the remaining two at once. Let the surfer, at every step, toss a biased coin: with probability \alpha follow a link as before, and with probability 1 - \alpha get bored and jump to a page chosen uniformly at random from all n. The jump is called teleportation, and \alpha the damping factor; a value around 0.85 is customary. The Google matrix mixes following links with jumping to a random page; its fixed probability vector is the ranking. [Google Matrix, PageRank Vector] Let \P \in M_n(
R) be the link matrix of a web with n \ge 1 pages, and let 0 < \alpha < 1. The matrix \G = \alpha\P +  rac{1 - \alpha}{n}\,\J is called the Google matrix in the literature, with damping factor \alpha. A PageRank vector of the web is a probability vector \vpi \in 
R^n with \G\vpi = \vpi. Page i is ranked above page k when \pi_i > \pi_k. In words: column j of \G is \alpha times column j of \P, the link step, plus 1 - \alpha times the uniform vector 	frac1n\1, the jump. A PageRank vector is a steady state of the surfer’s new chain. The letter \G is local to this section; elsewhere in the book \G is a Gram matrix. The theorem below shows that there is exactly one, which justifies calling it the PageRank vector. Two properties of \G do all the work. - \G is stochastic. Its entries are nonnegative, and column j adds up to \alpha \cdot 1 + (1 - \alpha)\cdot	frac1n \cdot n = 1. - \G is positive. Every entry is at least 	frac{1 - \alpha}{n} > 0, because \alpha\P \ge \O and \alpha < 1 strictly. Two degenerate values of \alpha are excluded, and each shows why. With \alpha = 1, \G = \P, and the failures (b) and (c) of @exm-link-matrix-failures come back. With \alpha = 0, \G = 	frac1n\J for every web, the PageRank vector is 	frac1n\1, and the links are ignored: every page ties. The damping factor trades faithfulness to the links against the good behavior of the chain, and we will see that the speed of the computation is governed by \alpha alone. For the three-page web above, with \alpha = 	frac12, \G =  rac12\P +  rac16\J =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac16 & 	frac16 & 	frac13 \ 	frac5{12} & 	frac16 & 	frac13 \ 	frac5{12} & 	frac23 & 	frac13 \end{pmatrix} , with columns adding up to 1 and every entry positive. A nonexample by minimal change. Replace the uniform jump by a jump to page 1 only: \G' = \alpha\P + (1 - \alpha)\cvec{e}_1\1	p. It is still stochastic, since each column of \cvec{e}_1\1	p is \cvec{e}_1. What fails is positivity: in the web of @exm-link-matrix-failures (b), \G' has zeros in rows 3 and 4 of columns 1 and 2, so Perron’s theorem no longer applies. (Here the ranking is still unique, but it gives pages 3 and 4 weight zero, since no surfer ever returns to them from pages 1 and 2.) Exercise B3 shows that any jump distribution with all entries positive works as well as the uniform one. PageRank is not a count of incoming links. A link is worth the rank of the page it comes from, divided by that page’s out-degree. In the four-page example at the end of this section, page 3 has more incoming links than any other page, yet page 1, with a single incoming link, ranks above it, because that link comes from page 3 and is page 3’s only link. A unique positive ranking Perron’s theorem, applied to the positive matrix \G, settles existence, uniqueness, and positivity at once. It also turns the eigenvector problem into a linear system. [The PageRank Vector] Let \P \in M_n(
R) be stochastic, 0 < \alpha < 1, and \G = \alpha\P +  rac{1-\alpha}{n}\J. Then: 1. ho(\G) = 1, and 1 is an eigenvalue of \G of algebraic multiplicity one; 2. there is exactly one probability vector \vpi with \G\vpi = \vpi, and every entry of \vpi is positive; 3. \I - \alpha\P is invertible, and \vpi is the unique solution of (\I - \alpha\P)\,\vpi =  rac{1 - \alpha}{n}\,\1 . Perron’s theorem hands us a simple eigenvalue ho(\G) with a positive eigenvector, so the only question is the value of ho(\G); the column sums pin it at 1. For (c), on probability vectors the rank-one part  rac{1-\alpha}{n}\J\cvec{x} is the constant vector  rac{1-\alpha}{n}\1, so the eigenvector equation becomes linear with a right-hand side. (a) By @thm-operator-norm-formulas (a), 
orm{\G}_1 is the largest column sum of \lvert\Gvert, which is 1 since \G is stochastic; so ho(\G) \le 1 by @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm (a). By @prp-stochastic-properties (c), 1 is an eigenvalue of \G. Hence ho(\G) = 1. Since every entry of \G is at least  rac{1-\alpha}{n} > 0, Perron’s theorem (@thm-perron) applies: by its parts (a) and (b), ho(\G) = 1 is an eigenvalue of algebraic multiplicity one, with an eigenvector \cvec{v} > \cvec{0} spanning E_1(\G). (b) Put \vpi = \cvec{v}/(\1	p\cvec{v}), which is defined because \1	p\cvec{v} > 0. It is a probability vector with positive entries and \G\vpi = \vpi. If \vpi' is another probability vector with \G\vpi' = \vpi', then \vpi' lies in E_1(\G) = \Span(\cvec{v}), so \vpi' = c\vpi for some c, and comparing entry sums gives 1 = c. Hence \vpi' = \vpi. In the language of §01, \vpi is the Perron vector of \G (@def-perron-vector). (c) If (\I - \alpha\P)\cvec{z} = \cvec{0} with \cvec{z} 
e \cvec{0}, then \P\cvec{z} = \alpha^{-1}\cvec{z}, so \alpha^{-1} > 1 is an eigenvalue of \P; but ho(\P) \le 
orm{\P}_1 = 1 as in (a). So 0 is not an eigenvalue of \I - \alpha\P, and \I - \alpha\P is invertible by @thm-invertible-tfae-eigen. For a probability vector \cvec{x}, \J\cvec{x} = \1(\1	p\cvec{x}) = \1, so \G\cvec{x} = \alpha\P\cvec{x} +  rac{1 - \alpha}{n}\,\1 , and \G\vpi = \vpi is the equation (\I - \alpha\P)\vpi =  rac{1-\alpha}{n}\1. So \vpi solves the system, and by invertibility it is the only solution. So the ranking exists, is unique, and gives every page a positive score: no page is ignored, however obscure. Part (c) is how one computes it for a small web: solve an n 	imes n linear system, with no eigenvalue in sight. A useful bonus is that the solution of (c) is automatically a probability vector. Multiplying the system on the left by \1	p, and using \1	p\P = \1	p, (1 - \alpha)\,\1	p\vpi =  rac{1 - \alpha}{n}\,\1	p\1 = 1 - \alpha , so \1	p\vpi = 1 without being imposed. Two pages link to each other, and \alpha = 	frac12. Write down \G, find \vpi, and find the eigenvalues of \G. \P is the swap, so \G =  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} +  rac14 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac14 & 	frac34 \ 	frac34 & 	frac14 \end{pmatrix} . Then \G(1, 1) = (1, 1) and \G(1, -1) = (-	frac12, 	frac12) = -	frac12(1, -1). So \vpi = (	frac12, 	frac12), and the eigenvalues are 1 and -	frac12. The swap has eigenvalues 1 and -1: the second one has been multiplied by \alpha. The next theorem says that this always happens. The second eigenvalue The PageRank vector of a real web is computed by iterating \cvec{x}_{k+1} = \G\cvec{x}_k, since the web has billions of pages and no one solves a system of that size exactly. How fast the iterates settle depends on the eigenvalues of \G other than 1. For a general positive matrix, Perron’s theorem says only that they are strictly smaller than ho in modulus, with no bound on how much smaller. For the Google matrix there is an exact description. [The Eigenvalues of the Google Matrix] Let n \ge 2, let \P \in M_n(
R) be stochastic, let 0 \le \alpha \le 1, and let \G = \alpha\P +  rac{1-\alpha}{n}\J. Since 1 is an eigenvalue of \P (@prp-stochastic-properties) and p_{\P} splits over 
C (@thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra), it factors as p_{\P}(x) = (x - 1)(x - \mu_2)\cdots(x - \mu_n) with \mu_2, \dots, \mu_n \in 
C. Then p_{\G}(x) = (x - 1)(x - \alpha\mu_2)\cdots(x - \alpha\mu_n) . In particular, if \alpha < 1, every eigenvalue \lambda 
e 1 of \G satisfies \lvert\lambdavert \le \alpha. Both \P and \G have \1	p as a left eigenvector for 1. Change basis so that \1	p becomes the first coordinate functional \cvec{e}_1	p; then both matrices become block lower triangular with a 1 in the corner. The teleportation term  rac1n\J =  rac1n\1\1	p only touches the first column in the new basis, so the lower-right blocks are \P_1 and \alpha\P_1 for the same \P_1. The eigenvalues of \P other than the 1 in the corner are those of \P_1; those of \G are \alpha times them. Let \N = \cvec{e}_1(\1 - \cvec{e}_1)	p, the matrix whose first row is (0, 1, \dots, 1) and whose other rows are zero, and let \S = \I + \N. Its first row is \1	p and its other rows are those of \I, so \cvec{e}_1	p\S = \1	p. Since (\1 - \cvec{e}_1)	p\cvec{e}_1 = 0, \N^2 = \cvec{e}_1 igl((\1 - \cvec{e}_1)	p\cvec{e}_1 igr)(\1 - \cvec{e}_1)	p = \O, and therefore (\I + \N)(\I - \N) = \I - \N^2 = \I. So \S is invertible with \S^{-1} = \I - \N (@thm-one-sided-inverse). Claim. If \M \in M_n(
R) satisfies \1	p\M = \1	p, then the first row of \S\M\S^{-1} is \cvec{e}_1	p. The first row is \cvec{e}_1	p\S\M\S^{-1} = \1	p\M\S^{-1} = \1	p\S^{-1} = \cvec{e}_1	p\S\S^{-1} = \cvec{e}_1	p. Since \P is stochastic, \1	p\P = \1	p, and the claim gives \S\P\S^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & \cvec{0}	p \ \cvec{b} & \P_1 \end{pmatrix} for some \cvec{b} \in 
R^{n-1} and \P_1 \in M_{n-1}(
R). For the teleportation term, \S igl(	frac1n\1\1	p igr)\S^{-1} = 	frac1n(\S\1)(\1	p\S^{-1}) = 	frac1n(\S\1)\,\cvec{e}_1	p , using \1	p\S^{-1} = \cvec{e}_1	p from the proof of the claim. Its only nonzero column is the first, 	frac1n\S\1, whose first entry is 	frac1n\1	p\1 = 1. So it equals  egin{pmatrix} 1 & \cvec{0}	p \ \cvec{c} & \O \end{pmatrix} for some \cvec{c} \in 
R^{n-1}, and  egin{aligned} \S\G\S^{-1} &= \alpha\,\S\P\S^{-1} + (1 - \alpha)\,\S igl(	frac1n\J igr)\S^{-1} \ &=  egin{pmatrix} 1 & \cvec{0}	p \ \alpha\cvec{b} + (1-\alpha)\cvec{c} & \alpha\P_1 \end{pmatrix} . \end{aligned} Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant), and x\I minus a block lower triangular matrix is block lower triangular, so by @thm-det-block-triangular p_{\P}(x) = (x - 1)\,p_{\P_1}(x) , \qquad p_{\G}(x) = (x - 1)\,p_{\alpha\P_1}(x) . Comparing the first with p_{\P}(x) = (x - 1)(x - \mu_2)\cdots(x - \mu_n) and canceling the nonzero factor x - 1 (in 
C[x], a product of nonzero polynomials is nonzero) gives p_{\P_1}(x) = (x - \mu_2)\cdots(x - \mu_n). If \alpha > 0, then  egin{aligned} p_{\alpha\P_1}(x) &= \det(x\I - \alpha\P_1) = \alpha^{n-1}\det igl(	frac{x}{\alpha}\I - \P_1 igr) \ &= \alpha^{n-1}\prod_{j=2}^{n}\Bigl( rac{x}{\alpha} - \mu_j\Bigr) = \prod_{j=2}^{n}(x - \alpha\mu_j) , \end{aligned} where the second step takes the factor \alpha out of each of the n - 1 rows. If \alpha = 0, then p_{\alpha\P_1}(x) = \det(x\I) = x^{n-1} = \prod_j(x - 0\cdot\mu_j). Either way the formula for p_{\G} follows. For the last sentence, each \mu_j is an eigenvalue of \P, so \lvert\mu_jvert \le ho(\P) \le 
orm{\P}_1 = 1 by @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm (a) and @thm-operator-norm-formulas (a). The eigenvalues of \G are the roots of p_{\G}: the number 1 and the \alpha\mu_j, each of modulus at most \alpha. If \alpha < 1, none of the \alpha\mu_j equals 1, so every eigenvalue \lambda 
e 1 is some \alpha\mu_j, and \lvert\lambdavert \le \alpha. This proves the theorem. The theorem gives more than a bound. It shows again that 1 is a simple eigenvalue of \G when \alpha < 1, without Perron’s theorem, and it says that the rest of the spectrum of \G is the rest of the spectrum of \P, shrunk by the factor \alpha. The bound is attained whenever \P itself has 1 as a repeated eigenvalue, as for the two separate webs of @exm-link-matrix-failures (b) (Exercise C2), and whenever \P has -1 as an eigenvalue, as in the Quick check. So for a web with two or more pieces that no link leaves, as large webs typically have, the second eigenvalue of \G has modulus exactly \alpha, and no better bound is possible. How fast the iteration converges The eigenvalue bound predicts that iterates approach \vpi at a rate like \alpha^k. For this particular matrix the prediction can be proved directly, with an explicit constant, by measuring errors in the 1-norm of Chapter 16. [Convergence at the Damping Rate] Let \P, \alpha, \G and \vpi be as in @thm-pagerank-vector, let \cvec{x}_0 be any probability vector, and let \cvec{x}_k = \G^k\cvec{x}_0. Then for every k \ge 0, 
orm{\cvec{x}_k - \vpi}_1 \le \alpha^k
orm{\cvec{x}_0 - \vpi}_1 \le 2\alpha^k . In particular, \cvec{x}_k 	o \vpi entrywise. The error \vepsilon_k = \cvec{x}_k - \vpi is a difference of probability vectors, so its entries add up to 0, and the teleportation term kills it. What remains is \alpha\P, and a stochastic matrix never increases the 1-norm. Each \cvec{x}_k is a probability vector by @prp-stochastic-properties (a), since \G is stochastic. Put \vepsilon_k = \cvec{x}_k - \vpi, so \1	p\vepsilon_k = 1 - 1 = 0. Since \G\vpi = \vpi, \vepsilon_{k+1} = \G\cvec{x}_k - \G\vpi = \G\vepsilon_k = \alpha\P\vepsilon_k +  rac{1 - \alpha}{n}\,\1(\1	p\vepsilon_k) = \alpha\P\vepsilon_k . By @thm-operator-norm-formulas (a), 
orm{\P}_1 = 1, the largest column sum of the nonnegative matrix \P, so 
orm{\P\vepsilon_k}_1 \le 
orm{\vepsilon_k}_1 (@def-operator-norm). Hence 
orm{\vepsilon_{k+1}}_1 \le \alpha
orm{\vepsilon_k}_1, and by induction on k, 
orm{\vepsilon_k}_1 \le \alpha^k
orm{\vepsilon_0}_1. Finally 
orm{\vepsilon_0}_1 \le 
orm{\cvec{x}_0}_1 + 
orm{\vpi}_1 = 2, as both are probability vectors. Each entry of \vepsilon_k has modulus at most 
orm{\vepsilon_k}_1 \le 2\alpha^k, and \alpha^k 	o 0 because 0 < \alpha < 1, one of the calculus facts recorded in Chapter 9 §11. A sequence whose terms are at most 2\alpha^k in absolute value, with 2\alpha^k 	o 0, tends to 0 straight from the definition of a limit: once 2\alpha^k < \varepsilon, so is every such term. So \cvec{x}_k 	o \vpi entrywise. The bound does not depend on the web at all: not on the number of pages, not on how they link. With \alpha = 0.85, fifty steps guarantee 
orm{\cvec{x}_{50} - \vpi}_1 \le 2(0.85)^{50} < 6 \cdot 10^{-4}, and ninety guarantee an error below 10^{-6}, for a web of any size. Each step is cheap, because \G is never formed: by the proof of @thm-pagerank-vector (c), \G\cvec{x} = \alpha\P\cvec{x} +  rac{1-\alpha}{n}\1 for a probability vector \cvec{x}, and \P\cvec{x} needs one operation per link, plus one shared correction for the dangling pages. In the language of §05, \G is primitive (@def-primitive), since \G^1 is already positive, and @thm-primitive-limit gives \G^k 	o \vpi\1	p, with right Perron vector \vpi and left Perron vector \1, normalized by \1	p\vpi = 1. The proposition adds the rate, and the rate is what makes the method practical. The iteration \cvec{x}_{k+1} = \G\cvec{x}_k is the power method; Chapter 24 studies it for general matrices, where the rate is governed by the ratio of the two largest eigenvalue moduli, here at most \alpha. A small web, exactly [Four pages, one dangling] A web has four pages. Page 1 links to pages 2 and 3; page 2 links to pages 3 and 4; page 3 links to page 1; page 4 is dangling. With \alpha = 	frac45, find the Google matrix, the PageRank vector, and the ranking, and compare \lvert\lambda_2vert with \alpha. The link matrix. Pages 1 and 2 have out-degree 2, page 3 has out-degree 1, and page 4 is dangling, so by @def-link-matrix \P =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 & 	frac14 \ 	frac12 & 0 & 0 & 	frac14 \ 	frac12 & 	frac12 & 0 & 	frac14 \ 0 & 	frac12 & 0 & 	frac14 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad 20\,\G = 16\,\P + \J =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 17 & 5 \ 9 & 1 & 1 & 5 \ 9 & 9 & 1 & 5 \ 1 & 9 & 1 & 5 \end{pmatrix} , since 20\alpha = 16 and 20 \cdot  rac{1-\alpha}{4} = 1. Every column of 20\G adds up to 20, and every entry is positive. The linear system. By @thm-pagerank-vector (c), (\I - 	frac45\P)\vpi = 	frac1{20}\1. Multiplying by 5 gives (5\I - 4\P)\vpi = 	frac14\1, that is,  egin{aligned} 5\pi_1 - 4\pi_3 - \pi_4 &= 	frac14 , &\qquad -2\pi_1 + 5\pi_2 - \pi_4 &= 	frac14 , \ -2\pi_1 - 2\pi_2 + 5\pi_3 - \pi_4 &= 	frac14 , &\qquad -2\pi_2 + 4\pi_4 &= 	frac14 . \end{aligned} Express everything through \pi_4. The fourth equation gives \pi_2 = 2\pi_4 - 	frac18. The second then gives 2\pi_1 = 5\pi_2 - \pi_4 - 	frac14 = 9\pi_4 - 	frac78, so \pi_1 = 	frac92\pi_4 - 	frac7{16}. The first gives 4\pi_3 = 5\pi_1 - \pi_4 - 	frac14 = 	frac{43}{2}\pi_4 - 	frac{39}{16}, so \pi_3 = 	frac{43}{8}\pi_4 - 	frac{39}{64}. Substituting into the third, \Bigl(-9 - 4 + 	frac{215}{8} - 1\Bigr)\pi_4 + \Bigl(	frac78 + 	frac14 - 	frac{195}{64}\Bigr) = 	frac{103}{8}\pi_4 - 	frac{123}{64} = 	frac14 , so 	frac{103}{8}\pi_4 = 	frac{139}{64} and \pi_4 = 	frac{139}{824}. Back-substituting, \vpi =  rac{1}{824}\,(265,\ 175,\ 245,\ 139) . Check. The entries add up to 824/824 = 1, as they must. With \cvec{y} = (265, 175, 245, 139), the first row of 20\G gives 265 + 175 + 17 \cdot 245 + 5 \cdot 139 = 5300 = 20 \cdot 265, and the other rows give 3500 = 20 \cdot 175, 4900 = 20 \cdot 245 and 2780 = 20 \cdot 139. So \G\vpi = \vpi. The ranking. Page 1 first (\approx 0.322), then page 3 (\approx 0.297), page 2 (\approx 0.212) and page 4 (\approx 0.169). Page 3 is linked from pages 1 and 2, while the dangling page 4 feeds every page equally; page 1 is linked only from page 3. Yet page 1 wins, because page 3 passes its whole weight to it, while pages 1, 2 and 4 split theirs. The second eigenvalue. Expanding the determinant gives  egin{aligned} p_{\P}(x) &= (x - 1)\Bigl(x^3 + 	frac34x^2 + 	frac18x - 	frac1{16}\Bigr) , \ p_{\G}(x) &= (x - 1)\Bigl(x^3 + 	frac35x^2 + 	frac{2}{25}x - 	frac{4}{125}\Bigr) , \end{aligned} and the second cubic is \alpha^3 times the first evaluated at x/\alpha, as @thm-google-matrix-eigenvalues predicts: 	frac34 \cdot 	frac45 = 	frac35, 	frac18 \cdot 	frac{16}{25} = 	frac{2}{25}, 	frac1{16} \cdot 	frac{64}{125} = 	frac{4}{125}. The cubic for \P has one real root near 0.199 and two complex ones of modulus about 0.560. So \lvert\lambda_2(\G)vert \approx 0.8 	imes 0.560 \approx 0.448, comfortably below \alpha = 0.8: for this web the iteration converges faster than @prp-pagerank-contraction guarantees. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the Google matrix of a web and its PageRank vector. 2. Why is every entry of \G positive, and which three conclusions does @thm-perron then give? 3. True or false: with \alpha = 1, every web has exactly one PageRank vector. Justify your answer. 4. True or false: the page with the most incoming links always has the highest PageRank. Justify your answer. 5. For \alpha = 0.85, what does @thm-google-matrix-eigenvalues say about the eigenvalues of \G other than 1? Can the bound be improved for every web? 6. True or false: after 10 steps of \cvec{x}_{k+1} = \G\cvec{x}_k from any probability vector, 
orm{\cvec{x}_{10} - \vpi}_1 \le 2\alpha^{10}. Justify your answer. (a) For a web with link matrix \P (@def-link-matrix) and 0 < \alpha < 1, \G = \alpha\P +  rac{1-\alpha}{n}\J. A PageRank vector is a probability vector \vpi with \G\vpi = \vpi. (b) \alpha\P has nonnegative entries and  rac{1-\alpha}{n}\J has every entry equal to  rac{1-\alpha}{n} > 0, since \alpha < 1. Perron’s theorem then gives: ho(\G) is an eigenvalue of algebraic multiplicity one; it has an eigenvector with all entries positive; every other eigenvalue has modulus strictly less than ho(\G). Here ho(\G) = 1. (c) False. With \alpha = 1, \G = \P, and for two pairs of pages linking only to each other, @exm-link-matrix-failures (b) gives two different steady states. (d) False. In @exm-pagerank-four-pages, page 3 has the most incoming links, but page 1 ranks first. (e) Every eigenvalue \lambda 
e 1 has \lvert\lambdavert \le 0.85. The bound cannot be improved for every web: when the link matrix has -1 or a repeated 1 among its eigenvalues, \G has an eigenvalue of modulus exactly 0.85 (the Quick check, and Exercise C2). (f) True, by @prp-pagerank-contraction with k = 10. B. Practice [B1: A three-page web] For the three-page web after @def-link-matrix (page 1 links to pages 2 and 3, page 2 to page 3, page 3 is dangling), with \alpha = 	frac12, find the PageRank vector by solving the system of @thm-pagerank-vector (c). Hence rank the pages. With \P as in the text, (\I - 	frac12\P)\vpi = 	frac16\1. Multiplying by 12 gives (12\I - 6\P)\vpi = 2\,\1:  egin{aligned} 12\pi_1 - 2\pi_3 &= 2 , \ -3\pi_1 + 12\pi_2 - 2\pi_3 &= 2 , \ -3\pi_1 - 6\pi_2 + 10\pi_3 &= 2 . \end{aligned} The first gives \pi_3 = 6\pi_1 - 1. The second becomes -3\pi_1 + 12\pi_2 - 12\pi_1 + 2 = 2, so \pi_2 = 	frac54\pi_1. The third becomes -3\pi_1 - 	frac{15}{2}\pi_1 + 60\pi_1 - 10 = 2, so 	frac{99}{2}\pi_1 = 12 and \pi_1 = 	frac{8}{33}. Then \pi_2 = 	frac{10}{33} and \pi_3 = 	frac{48}{33} - 1 = 	frac{15}{33}. So \vpi =  rac{1}{33}(8,\ 10,\ 15) , whose entries add up to 1. Check against the original system: 12 \cdot 8 - 2 \cdot 15 = 66 = 2 \cdot 33, -24 + 120 - 30 = 66, -24 - 60 + 150 = 66. Hence page 3 ranks first, then page 2, then page 1. [B2: A cycle of three pages] Three pages link in a cycle: 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 1. Let 0 < \alpha < 1. 1. Write down \P and show that p_{\P}(x) = x^3 - 1. 2. Use @thm-google-matrix-eigenvalues to find the eigenvalues of \G, and check your answer against 	r\G. 3. Find \vpi, and explain why the bound of @thm-google-matrix-eigenvalues is attained. (a) Column j of \P is \cvec{e}_{j+1}, with \cvec{e}_4 read as \cvec{e}_1:  egin{aligned} \P &=  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \det(x\I - \P) = \det egin{pmatrix} x & 0 & -1 \ -1 & x & 0 \ 0 & -1 & x \end{pmatrix} \ &= x \cdot x^2 + (-1)\cdot igl((-1)(-1) - x \cdot 0 igr) = x^3 - 1 , \end{aligned} expanding along the first row. (b) x^3 - 1 = (x - 1)(x - \omega)(x - \conj\omega) with \omega = -	frac12 + 	frac{\sqrt3}{2}i, so \mu_2 = \omega, \mu_3 = \conj\omega, and the eigenvalues of \G are 1, \alpha\omega, \alpha\conj\omega. Their sum is 1 + \alpha(\omega + \conj\omega) = 1 - \alpha. Directly, 	r\G = \alpha	r\P +  rac{1-\alpha}{3}	r\J = 0 + (1 - \alpha), which agrees (@thm-trace-det-eigenvalues). (c) \P\1 = \1 and \J\1 = 3\,\1, so \G\1 = \alpha\1 + (1 - \alpha)\1 = \1, and \vpi = 	frac13\1 by the uniqueness in @thm-pagerank-vector. The eigenvalues \alpha\omega and \alpha\conj\omega have modulus \alpha\lvert\omegavert = \alpha, so the bound \lvert\lambdavert \le \alpha holds with equality. [B3: Personalized jumps] Let \P \in M_n(
R) be stochastic, 0 < \alpha < 1, and let \cvec{v} be a probability vector with every v_i > 0. Put \G_{\cvec{v}} = \alpha\P + (1 - \alpha)\cvec{v}\1	p: the surfer now jumps to page i with probability v_i. 1. Prove that \G_{\cvec{v}} is stochastic and positive, and deduce that it has exactly one probability vector \vpi with \G_{\cvec{v}}\vpi = \vpi, and that \vpi > \cvec{0}. 2. Prove that \vpi is the unique solution of (\I - \alpha\P)\vpi = (1 - \alpha)\cvec{v}. 3. For two pages linking to each other, \alpha = 	frac12 and \cvec{v} = (	frac34, 	frac14), find \vpi. (a) The entries of \G_{\cvec{v}} are \alpha p_{ij} + (1 - \alpha)v_i \ge (1 - \alpha)v_i > 0. Column j adds up to \alpha + (1 - \alpha)\1	p\cvec{v} = \alpha + 1 - \alpha = 1. So \G_{\cvec{v}} is stochastic and positive. The proof of @thm-pagerank-vector (a) and (b) used only these two facts, so it applies word for word: ho(\G_{\cvec{v}}) = 1 is an eigenvalue of algebraic multiplicity one with a positive eigenvector, and its normalization \vpi is the only probability vector fixed by \G_{\cvec{v}}. (b) For a probability vector \cvec{x}, \G_{\cvec{v}}\cvec{x} = \alpha\P\cvec{x} + (1 - \alpha)\cvec{v}(\1	p\cvec{x}) = \alpha\P\cvec{x} + (1 - \alpha)\cvec{v}, so \G_{\cvec{v}}\vpi = \vpi says (\I - \alpha\P)\vpi = (1 - \alpha)\cvec{v}. The matrix \I - \alpha\P is invertible, as in the proof of @thm-pagerank-vector (c), so the solution is unique. (c) \P is the swap, and the system is \pi_1 - 	frac12\pi_2 = 	frac38, -	frac12\pi_1 + \pi_2 = 	frac18. The first gives \pi_1 = 	frac38 + 	frac12\pi_2, and the second becomes -	frac3{16} + 	frac34\pi_2 = 	frac18, so \pi_2 = 	frac{5}{12} and \pi_1 = 	frac38 + 	frac5{24} = 	frac{7}{12}. So \vpi = (	frac7{12}, 	frac5{12}): the preferred page 1 gains, but less than its jump weight 	frac34, because half the time the surfer follows the link to page 2. C. Going deeper [C1: PageRank as a sum over paths] Let \P, \alpha, \G and \vpi be as in @thm-pagerank-vector. 1. Prove that \displaystyle \vpi =  rac{1 - \alpha}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha^k\P^k\1. 2. Deduce that \pi_i \ge  rac{1-\alpha}{n} for every i. 3. Suppose no page is dangling and no page links to page i. Prove that \pi_i =  rac{1-\alpha}{n} exactly. Hint for (a): @thm-neumann-series with the 1-norm. (a) By @thm-operator-norm-formulas (a), 
orm{\alpha\P}_1 = \alpha
orm{\P}_1 = \alpha < 1, the largest column sum of \alpha\P. By @thm-neumann-series (a), \I - \alpha\P is invertible and (\I - \alpha\P)^{-1} = \sum_{k \ge 0}\alpha^k\P^k. By @thm-pagerank-vector (c), \vpi =  rac{1-\alpha}{n}(\I - \alpha\P)^{-1}\1, which is the stated series. (b) Every term \alpha^k\P^k\1 has nonnegative entries, and the term k = 0 is \1. So each entry of the sum is at least 1, since a limit of partial sums that are all at least 1 is at least 1, and \pi_i \ge  rac{1-\alpha}{n}. (c) From \G\vpi = \vpi and the proof of @thm-pagerank-vector (c), \vpi = \alpha\P\vpi +  rac{1-\alpha}{n}\1. Row i of \P is zero: p_{ij} 
e 0 only if page j links to page i or page j is dangling, and neither happens. So (\P\vpi)_i = 0 and \pi_i =  rac{1-\alpha}{n}, the smallest possible value by (b). [C2: When the bound is attained] Let \P \in M_n(
R) be stochastic, 0 < \alpha < 1, and \G = \alpha\P +  rac{1-\alpha}{n}\J. 1. Suppose \P has two different steady states \cvec{u} 
e \cvec{w}. Prove that \G(\cvec{u} - \cvec{w}) = \alpha(\cvec{u} - \cvec{w}), so that \alpha is an eigenvalue of \G. 2. For the web of @exm-link-matrix-failures (b), find all eigenvalues of \G, with multiplicity, and check your answer against (a). (a) Put \cvec{z} = \cvec{u} - \cvec{w} 
e \cvec{0}. Both are probability vectors, so \1	p\cvec{z} = 0 and \J\cvec{z} = \1(\1	p\cvec{z}) = \cvec{0}. Hence \G\cvec{z} = \alpha\P\cvec{u} - \alpha\P\cvec{w} + \cvec{0} = \alpha(\cvec{u} - \cvec{w}) = \alpha\cvec{z}, and \alpha is an eigenvalue of \G with eigenvector \cvec{z}. (b) \P is block diagonal with two blocks  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, each with characteristic polynomial x^2 - 1, so p_{\P}(x) = (x^2 - 1)^2 = (x - 1)(x - 1)(x + 1)(x + 1) by @thm-det-block-triangular. By @thm-google-matrix-eigenvalues, with \mu_2 = 1 and \mu_3 = \mu_4 = -1, the eigenvalues of \G are 1, \alpha, -\alpha, -\alpha. The eigenvalue \alpha is the one found in (a), with \cvec{u} = (	frac12, 	frac12, 0, 0), \cvec{w} = (0, 0, 	frac12, 	frac12) and eigenvector \cvec{z} = 	frac12(1, 1, -1, -1); indeed \P\cvec{z} = \cvec{z} and \J\cvec{z} = \cvec{0}, so \G\cvec{z} = \alpha\cvec{z}.

title: 19.9 M-Matrices
content:
M-Matrices Every section of this chapter so far has studied a nonnegative matrix \B through its spectral radius. This last section looks at the matrices s\I - \B built from one, which turn up wherever a quantity is balanced against what flows into it from its neighbors: a discretized differential equation, an economy that consumes part of its own output, the fundamental matrix of an absorbing Markov chain. The question is always the same. When is s\I - \B invertible with a nonnegative inverse, so that a nonnegative right-hand side is guaranteed a nonnegative solution? The answer is a single inequality, s > ho(\B), and the section’s main theorem shows that six other conditions, several of which can be checked by hand, say the same thing. The chapter’s summary closes the section. Throughout, matrices have real entries, the spectrum \spec(\A) of \A \in M_n(
R) is taken in 
C, as in the definition of the spectral radius (@def-spectral-radius), and \ge, > between matrices or vectors are entrywise. Z-matrices and M-matrices A matrix of the form s\I - \B with \B \ge \O has an unmistakable sign pattern: the diagonal entries s - b_{ii} can be anything, and every entry off the diagonal is -b_{ij} \le 0. The pattern comes first, because it is what one sees on the page. [Z-Matrix] A matrix \A = (a_{ij}) \in M_n(
R), n \ge 1, is a Z-matrix if a_{ij} \le 0 for every pair i 
e j. The diagonal is unrestricted. The identity is a Z-matrix, and so is -\I; every 1 	imes 1 matrix is one, since there is no off-diagonal entry to check. The matrix  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & -1 \ -1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} is one;  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ -1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} is not, because of the single entry a_{12} = 1 > 0. [Z-Matrices Are Shifts of Nonnegative Matrices] A matrix \A \in M_n(
R) is a Z-matrix if and only if \A = s\I - \B for some real s and some \B \in M_n(
R) with \B \ge \O. For a Z-matrix, every s \ge \max_i a_{ii} gives such a representation, with \B = s\I - \A. If \A = s\I - \B with \B \ge \O, then a_{ij} = -b_{ij} \le 0 for i 
e j. Conversely, let \A be a Z-matrix, let s \ge \max_i a_{ii} and put \B = s\I - \A. Its diagonal entries are s - a_{ii} \ge 0 by the choice of s, and its off-diagonal entries are -a_{ij} \ge 0 because \A is a Z-matrix. So \B \ge \O and \A = s\I - \B. The representation is far from unique: raising s by t raises every diagonal entry of \B by t. A definition built on it must therefore not depend on which representation is used, and that is the first thing to check below. Now the goal. For a Z-matrix \A = s\I - \B with s > 0, write \A = s(\I - s^{-1}\B). If ho(\B) < s, the Neumann series of Chapter 10 (@thm-neumann-series-spectral) inverts the second factor as \sum_k (s^{-1}\B)^k, a sum of nonnegative matrices. So a comparison between s and ho(\B) is exactly what decides whether the inverse is nonnegative, and it deserves a name. An M-matrix is a nonnegative matrix subtracted from a multiple of the identity large enough to dominate its spectral radius. [M-Matrix] A matrix \A \in M_n(
R), n \ge 1, is an M-matrix if it can be written as \A = s\I - \B \qquad 	ext{with } s \in 
R,\ \B \in M_n(
R),\ \B \ge \O 	ext{ and } s \ge ho(\B) . An M-matrix that is invertible is a nonsingular M-matrix. In words: the first clause asks that \A be a Z-matrix (by @lem-z-matrix-as-shift, that is what “s\I - \B with \B \ge \O” means), and the second asks that the shift s be at least the spectral radius of what is subtracted. The definition says “can be written”, so a single good representation suffices. The next lemma shows that one representation is as good as any other, and also identifies the singular case. [The Smallest Real Eigenvalue of a Z-Matrix] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be a Z-matrix, and let \A = s\I - \B with \B \ge \O be any representation as in @lem-z-matrix-as-shift. 1. s - ho(\B) is an eigenvalue of \A, and every \lambda \in \spec(\A) satisfies \operatorname{Re}\lambda \ge s - ho(\B). In particular s - ho(\B) is the smallest real eigenvalue of \A, and so it is the same number for every representation. 2. \A is an M-matrix if and only if s \ge ho(\B), and a nonsingular M-matrix if and only if s > ho(\B).
