A production plan \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} uses up \C\cvec{x} as inputs and leaves the net output \cvec{x} - \C\cvec{x} for outside use. Given a final demand \cvec{d} \ge \cvec{0}, the planner needs (\I - \C)\cvec{x} = \cvec{d}, \qquad \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} . The economy is productive if this has a solution for every \cvec{d} \ge \cvec{0}. The matrix \I - \C is a Z-matrix, and the theorem answers the question completely. [Productive Economies] Let \C \in M_n(
R) with \C \ge \O. The following are equivalent. 1. For every \cvec{d} \ge \cvec{0} there is \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} with (\I - \C)\cvec{x} = \cvec{d}. 2. There is \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} with \cvec{x} - \C\cvec{x} > \cvec{0}: some plan leaves a surplus of every good. 3. ho(\C) < 1. 4. \I - \C is invertible and (\I - \C)^{-1} \ge \O. 5. Every leading principal minor of \I - \C is positive. When they hold, the solution in (i) is unique, and (\I - \C)^{-1} = \I + \C + \C^2 + \cdots. They hold in particular when every column sum of \C is less than 1. The matrix \I - \C is a Z-matrix, so this is the main theorem read in economic terms: (iii) is (a) with s = 1; (ii), (iv) and (v) are (c), (b) and (g), where in (ii) a plan \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} with a surplus is automatically positive, since \cvec{x} > \C\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}; and (i) sits between (iv) and (ii). \I - \C is a Z-matrix with the representation s = 1, \B = \C, so (iii) says, by @lem-smallest-real-eigenvalue-z-matrix (b), that \I - \C is a nonsingular M-matrix. By @thm-m-matrix-characterizations, (iii) is therefore equivalent to (iv) (condition (b) there) and to (v) (condition (g)). It is also equivalent to (ii): if \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} and \cvec{x} - \C\cvec{x} > \cvec{0}, then \cvec{x} > \C\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}, so \cvec{x} > \cvec{0} and condition (c) of the theorem holds; conversely (c) supplies such an \cvec{x}. (iv) \Rightarrow (i): given \cvec{d} \ge \cvec{0}, the vector \cvec{x} = (\I - \C)^{-1}\cvec{d} is a product of nonnegative factors, hence \ge \cvec{0}, and it solves the system. (i) \Rightarrow (ii): take \cvec{d} = \1. When they hold, \I - \C is invertible, so the solution is unique, and ho(\C) < 1 gives the series by @thm-neumann-series-spectral. Finally, if every column sum of \C is less than 1, then ho(\C) \le 
orm{\C}_1 < 1 by @cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound, which is (iii). Condition (v) is known to economists as the Hawkins–Simon condition, and the series has a direct reading. To deliver \cvec{d}, the economy must first produce \cvec{d}; that production consumes \C\cvec{d}, which must also be produced; that consumes \C^2\cvec{d}; and so on. The Leontief inverse (\I - \C)^{-1} adds up all the rounds, and its (i, j)-entry is the total amount of good i that the economy must produce, directly and indirectly, to deliver one unit of good j. [Three Sectors] An economy has three sectors, agriculture, manufacturing, and services, with consumption matrix \C =  rac15 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 2 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . Show that it is productive, find ho(\C) exactly, compute the Leontief inverse, and find the production plan meeting the demand \cvec{d} = (12, 6, 6). Productive. Every column of 5\C sums to 3, so every column sum of \C is 	frac35 < 1, and @cor-leontief-productive applies. The spectral radius. Expanding \det(x\I - \C) along the first row gives p_{\C}(x) = x^3 - 	frac25x^2 - 	frac{3}{25}x = x igl(x - 	frac35 igr) igl(x + 	frac15 igr), so \spec(\C) = \{0, 	frac35, -	frac15\} and ho(\C) = 	frac35, equal to the column-sum bound 
orm{\C}_1 of @cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound. The bound is attained because all column sums are equal: \C	p\1 = 	frac35\1. The Leontief inverse. Here \I - \C = 	frac15 egin{psmallmatrix} 4 & -1 & -1 \ -2 & 5 & -1 \ 0 & -2 & 4 \end{psmallmatrix}, and (\I - \C)^{-1} =  rac16 egin{pmatrix} 9 & 3 & 3 \ 4 & 8 & 3 \ 2 & 4 & 9 \end{pmatrix} . To check, multiply  egin{psmallmatrix} 4 & -1 & -1 \ -2 & 5 & -1 \ 0 & -2 & 4 \end{psmallmatrix} by  egin{psmallmatrix} 9 & 3 & 3 \ 4 & 8 & 3 \ 2 & 4 & 9 \end{psmallmatrix}: the first row gives 36 - 4 - 2 = 30, 12 - 8 - 4 = 0, 12 - 3 - 9 = 0; the second -18 + 20 - 2 = 0, -6 + 40 - 4 = 30, -6 + 15 - 9 = 0; the third -8 + 8 = 0, -16 + 16 = 0, -6 + 36 = 30. The product is 30\I, and 	frac15\cdot	frac16\cdot 30 = 1. Every entry of the inverse is positive: extra demand for any one good raises the output of every sector. For instance, one extra unit of services requires 	frac12 unit of agricultural output in total, although services consume only 	frac15 unit of it directly. The plan. \cvec{x} = (\I - \C)^{-1}\cvec{d} =  rac16 egin{pmatrix} 108 + 18 + 18 \ 48 + 48 + 18 \ 24 + 24 + 54 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 24 \ 19 \ 17 \end{pmatrix} . Check: \C\cvec{x} = 	frac15(24 + 19 + 17,\ 48 + 17,\ 38 + 17) = (12, 13, 11), and \cvec{x} - \C\cvec{x} = (12, 6, 6) = \cvec{d}. Delivering this demand takes 24 units of agricultural output, twice the 12 that leave the economy. A two-sector economy has \C =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1/2 & 1 \ 1/2 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}. Is it productive? No. The leading principal minors of \I - \C =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1/2 & -1 \ -1/2 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix} are 	frac12 and 	frac12 - 	frac12 = 0, so (v) of @cor-leontief-productive fails. Indeed \C egin{psmallmatrix} 2 \ 1 \end{psmallmatrix} =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 \ 1 \end{psmallmatrix}: running the sectors in the ratio 2 : 1 exactly reproduces its own inputs and leaves nothing over, and ho(\C) = 1. Summary and transfer The chapter set out to explain what the sign of the entries alone forces on the spectrum. For a positive matrix the answer is Perron’s theorem (§01, Positive matrices and Perron’s theorem): the spectral radius is a simple eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector, and it strictly dominates every other eigenvalue in modulus. Irreducibility, a property of the zero pattern read off a directed graph (§02, Irreducibility and graphs), is what keeps most of that conclusion alive when zeros are allowed (§03, The Perron–Frobenius theorem), and without it one still has ho(\B) as an eigenvalue with a nonnegative eigenvector. From there the chapter drew the long-run behavior of powers (§05, Primitive matrices), Markov chains (§06, Markov chains), the extreme points of the doubly stochastic matrices (§07, Birkhoff’s theorem), a ranking of web pages (§08, PageRank), and in this section the matrices s\I - \B. Six moves did the work. - Compare entrywise, then take the spectral radius. Nonnegativity makes the spectral radius monotone and lets \lvert\A\cvec{x}vert \le \lvert\Avert\lvert\cvec{x}vert replace cancellation by an inequality (§01, Positive matrices and Perron’s theorem). Transfer: to bound the spectral radius of a matrix you do not understand, dominate it entrywise by one you do. - A positive test vector bounds ho from both sides. The ratios (\A\cvec{x})_i/x_i for a single \cvec{x} > \cvec{0} trap ho(\A) between their minimum and maximum (§04, The Collatz–Wielandt formula), and in this section one \cvec{x} > \cvec{0} with \A\cvec{x} > \cvec{0} certified a nonsingular M-matrix. The mechanism used here is the rescaling \D^{-1}\B\D with \D = \diag(\cvec{x}), which turns \B\cvec{x} into row sums. Transfer: guess a positive vector from the structure of the problem, the parabola for \K_n, and verify it by one multiplication. - Read the zero pattern as a graph. Which entries of \A^k are positive depends only on which entries of \A are, and that is a question about paths (§02, Irreducibility and graphs; §05, Primitive matrices). Transfer: when only signs matter, draw the graph and count paths. - Prove it for positive matrices, then reach the boundary. Perron’s theorem is proved where every entry is positive, and the nonnegative and irreducible cases are reached from it through positive matrices built from \A (§03, The Perron–Frobenius theorem). Transfer: when a hypothesis is an inequality that may hold with equality, prove the strict case and ask what survives the passage to the boundary; s > ho(\B) versus s \ge ho(\B) in this section is the same division. - Divide by the Perron root, then use Chapter 10. Once ho(\A) is known to be a simple eigenvalue dominating the others, \A/ho(\A) meets the hypotheses of the convergence theorems of Chapter 10 §10, and no diagonalizability is ever needed (§05, Primitive matrices; §06, Markov chains). Transfer: normalize the dominant eigenvalue to 1 before asking about limits. - Invert with a series of nonnegative terms. If \B \ge \O and ho(\B) < 1, then (\I - \B)^{-1} = \sum_k \B^k \ge \O. This is the fundamental matrix of an absorbing chain (§06, Markov chains), the Leontief inverse, and the nonnegativity of the inverse of every nonsingular M-matrix. Transfer: to prove that an inverse is nonnegative, or to interpret its entries, expand it as the sum of the rounds of a process. The chapter also paid promises made in earlier chapters. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The promise Made in Paid by ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- “Chapter 19 proves the Perron–Frobenius theorem, which gives the conclusions of @thm-markov-limit-diagonalizable for every stochastic matrix with some power having all entries positive, without assuming diagonalizability and without computing eigenvalues” Chapter 9 §11 §06 (Stochastic matrices and Markov chains), resting on §03 (The Perron–Frobenius theorem) and §05 (Primitive matrices and the limit theorem) “We do not prove Birkhoff’s theorem here; Chapter 19 does” Chapter 18 §08, and again in its summary, §11 §07 (Doubly stochastic matrices and Birkhoff’s theorem) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Some things the chapter did not do. The characterization of possibly singular M-matrices by nonnegative principal minors was stated here and proved in one direction only. The theorem of Hardy, Littlewood, and Pólya, that \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} exactly when \cvec{x} = \D\cvec{y} for a doubly stochastic \D, belongs to Chapter 21. And the power method, the algorithm that computes a Perron vector at the size of the web, belongs to Chapter 24. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define a Z-matrix and a nonsingular M-matrix. 2. True or false: every Z-matrix with positive diagonal entries is a nonsingular M-matrix. Justify your answer. 3. True or false: every principal submatrix of a nonsingular M-matrix is a nonsingular M-matrix. Justify your answer. 4. True or false: if \A is invertible and \A^{-1} \ge \O, then \A is an M-matrix. Justify your answer. 5. True or false: the inverse of a nonsingular M-matrix has every entry positive. Justify your answer. 6. Name a vector \cvec{x} > \cvec{0} with \K_n\cvec{x} > \cvec{0}, and explain why \cvec{x} = \1 does not work when n \ge 3. (a) \A \in M_n(
R) is a Z-matrix if a_{ij} \le 0 for all i 
e j (@def-z-matrix). It is a nonsingular M-matrix if \A = s\I - \B with \B \ge \O and s \ge ho(\B), and \A is invertible; equivalently, s > ho(\B) (@def-m-matrix, @lem-smallest-real-eigenvalue-z-matrix (b)). (b) False.  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -2 \ -2 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix} is a Z-matrix with positive diagonal, but its determinant is 1 - 4 = -3, so condition (g) of @thm-m-matrix-characterizations fails. (c) True. Let \A be a nonsingular M-matrix. By @thm-m-matrix-characterizations there is \cvec{x} > \cvec{0} with \A\cvec{x} > \cvec{0}. By @lem-test-vector-principal-submatrix, \A_{S,S} is a Z-matrix with \A_{S,S}\cvec{x}_S > \cvec{0} and \cvec{x}_S > \cvec{0}, so it is a nonsingular M-matrix by (c) \Rightarrow (a) of the theorem. (d) False. The swap \P =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} satisfies \P^{-1} = \P \ge \O, but p_{12} = 1 > 0, so \P is not a Z-matrix, and every M-matrix is one. (e) False. \I_2 is a nonsingular M-matrix, and \I_2^{-1} = \I_2 has zero off-diagonal entries. (f) x_i = i(n + 1 - i), for which \K_n\cvec{x} = 2\1 (@prp-second-difference-inverse). For \cvec{x} = \1, row i of \K_n\1 is 2 - 1 - 1 = 0 for every 2 \le i \le n - 1, and such rows exist when n \ge 3. B. Practice [B1: Which are nonsingular M-matrices?] Determine which of the following are nonsingular M-matrices. Justify your answer. 1.  egin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 & -1 \ -1 & 3 & -1 \ -1 & -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} 2.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \ -1 & 2 & -1 \ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} 3.  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -3 \ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} 4.  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} 5.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & -2 \ -2 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} (a) Yes. It is a Z-matrix, and every row sums to 1, so \cvec{x} = \1 > \cvec{0} gives \A\cvec{x} = \1 > \cvec{0}. By @thm-m-matrix-characterizations, (c) \Rightarrow (a), it is a nonsingular M-matrix. (Its inverse is 	frac14 egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} \ge \O, as (b) predicts.) (b) No. Every row sums to 0, so \A\1 = \cvec{0} and \A is singular. (It is a singular M-matrix: with s = 2, \B = 2\I - \A has every row sum equal to 2, so ho(\B) \le 2 by @cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound, while \B\1 = 2\1 gives ho(\B) \ge 2.) (c) Yes. It is a Z-matrix with leading principal minors 2 > 0 and 4 - 3 = 1 > 0, so (g) \Rightarrow (a) applies. Check: \A^{-1} =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 3 \ 1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} \ge \O. (d) No. The off-diagonal entries are 1 > 0, so it is not a Z-matrix. (It is positive definite, and its inverse 	frac13 egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & -1 \ -1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} has negative entries.) (e) No. It is a Z-matrix, but expanding along the first row, \det\A = 1\cdot(1 - 0) - (-2)\cdot(0 - 4) + 0 = 1 - 8 = -7 < 0 , so condition (f) of @thm-m-matrix-characterizations fails. [B2: A string with a free end] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \ -1 & 2 & -1 \ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . 1. Show that \A\1 is not positive, and find \cvec{x} > \cvec{0} with \A\cvec{x} > \cvec{0}. 2. Compute the leading principal minors of \A, and check that they agree with (a). 3. Compute \A^{-1} and check that \A^{-1} \ge \O. Hence solve \A\cvec{u} = \cvec{e}_3, and say why the answer had to be nonnegative. Hint: try an increasing \cvec{x} whose increments decrease. (a) \A\1 = (1, 0, 0), which is not positive. Take \cvec{x} = (3, 5, 6): then \A\cvec{x} = (6 - 5,\ -3 + 10 - 6,\ -5 + 6) = (1, 1, 1) > \cvec{0}. Since \A is a Z-matrix, it is a nonsingular M-matrix by @thm-m-matrix-characterizations, (c) \Rightarrow (a). (b) \det\A_1 = 2, \det\A_2 = 4 - 1 = 3, and, expanding along the first row, \det\A = 2(2 - 1) - (-1)(-1 - 0) = 2 - 1 = 1. All three are positive, which is condition (g), as (a) and the theorem require. (c) \A^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 2 \ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, the matrix with entries \min(i, j). Check: row 1 of \A against the columns gives 2 - 1 = 1, 2 - 2 = 0, 2 - 2 = 0; row 2 gives -1 + 2 - 1 = 0, -1 + 4 - 2 = 1, -1 + 4 - 3 = 0; row 3 gives -1 + 1 = 0, -2 + 2 = 0, -2 + 3 = 1. So \A\A^{-1} = \I, and \A^{-1} \ge \O. Hence \cvec{u} = \A^{-1}\cvec{e}_3 = (1, 2, 3). It had to be \ge \cvec{0} because \cvec{e}_3 \ge \cvec{0} and \A^{-1} \ge \O. Note that \A^{-1}\1 = (3, 5, 6) is the certificate of (a). [B3: A two-sector economy] Let \C =  egin{pmatrix} 1/5 & 2/5 \ 3/10 & 1/10 \end{pmatrix} . 1. Show that the economy with consumption matrix \C is productive. 2. Compute the Leontief inverse (\I - \C)^{-1}. 3. Find the production plan meeting the demand \cvec{d} = (30, 60), and check it. 4. Find ho(\C) exactly. (a) The column sums are 	frac15 + 	frac{3}{10} = 	frac12 and 	frac25 + 	frac{1}{10} = 	frac12, both less than 1, so the economy is productive by @cor-leontief-productive. (b) \I - \C =  egin{psmallmatrix} 4/5 & -2/5 \ -3/10 & 9/10 \end{psmallmatrix}, with determinant 	frac{36}{50} - 	frac{6}{50} = 	frac35. By @thm-two-by-two-inverse, (\I - \C)^{-1} =  rac53 egin{pmatrix} 9/10 & 2/5 \ 3/10 & 4/5 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 3/2 & 2/3 \ 1/2 & 4/3 \end{pmatrix} \ge \O . (c) \cvec{x} = (	frac32\cdot30 + 	frac23\cdot60,\ 	frac12\cdot30 + 	frac43\cdot60) = (85, 95). Check: \C\cvec{x} = (17 + 38,\ 	frac{51}{2} + 	frac{19}{2}) = (55, 35), and \cvec{x} - \C\cvec{x} = (30, 60). (d) p_{\C}(x) = x^2 - 	frac{3}{10}x +  igl(	frac{1}{50} - 	frac{12}{100} igr) = x^2 - 	frac{3}{10}x - 	frac{1}{10} = (x - 	frac12)(x + 	frac15). So \spec(\C) = \{	frac12, -	frac15\} and ho(\C) = 	frac12. Here the column-sum bound 
orm{\C}_1 = 	frac12 is attained, as it must be when all column sums are equal. C. Going deeper [C1: Raising the diagonal] 1. Let \A be a nonsingular M-matrix and \M a Z-matrix of the same size with \M \ge \A entrywise. Prove that \M is a nonsingular M-matrix and that \O \le \M^{-1} \le \A^{-1}. 2. Deduce that for every diagonal \D \ge \O, \K_n + \D is a nonsingular M-matrix with (\K_n + \D)^{-1} \le \K_n^{-1}. Check this for n = 2 and \D = \diag(1, 0). Hint: for the inequality, factor \A^{-1} - \M^{-1}. (a) By @thm-m-matrix-characterizations there is \cvec{x} > \cvec{0} with \A\cvec{x} > \cvec{0}. Since \M - \A \ge \O and \cvec{x} > \cvec{0}, (\M - \A)\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}, so \M\cvec{x} = \A\cvec{x} + (\M - \A)\cvec{x} > \cvec{0}. As \M is a Z-matrix, (c) \Rightarrow (a) of the theorem makes it a nonsingular M-matrix, and (a) \Rightarrow (b) gives \M^{-1} \ge \O. Next, \A^{-1} - \M^{-1} = \A^{-1}\M\M^{-1} - \A^{-1}\A\M^{-1} = \A^{-1}(\M - \A)\M^{-1} , a product of three nonnegative matrices, hence \ge \O. This proves \O \le \M^{-1} \le \A^{-1}. (b) \K_n is a nonsingular M-matrix by @prp-second-difference-inverse, and \K_n + \D is a Z-matrix with \K_n + \D \ge \K_n, since \D only changes the diagonal and does so upwards. Part (a) gives the claim. For n = 2: \K_2^{-1} = 	frac13 egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix}, and \K_2 + \D =  egin{psmallmatrix} 3 & -1 \ -1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} has determinant 5 and inverse 	frac15 egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 3 \end{psmallmatrix}. The difference is  rac13 egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} -  rac15 egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} =  rac{1}{15} egin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \ge \O . [C2: The singular case] 1. Show that the Z-matrix \Z =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 0 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix} has nonnegative leading principal minors but is not an M-matrix. 2. Let \A be an M-matrix. Prove that \A + \varepsilon\I is a nonsingular M-matrix for every real \varepsilon > 0. 3. Deduce that every principal minor of an M-matrix is nonnegative. 4. Check (c) for  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}, and explain why (a) does not contradict the stated converse in the remark after @thm-m-matrix-characterizations. (a) \det\Z_1 = 0 and \det\Z = 0\cdot(-1) - (-1)\cdot 0 = 0, both nonnegative. \Z is upper triangular, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries 0 and -1 (@thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form). Its smallest real eigenvalue is -1 < 0, so by @lem-smallest-real-eigenvalue-z-matrix it is not an M-matrix: for any representation \Z = s\I - \B, s - ho(\B) = -1. (b) Write \A = s\I - \B with \B \ge \O and s \ge ho(\B). Then \A + \varepsilon\I = (s + \varepsilon)\I - \B with s + \varepsilon > ho(\B), so it is a nonsingular M-matrix by @lem-smallest-real-eigenvalue-z-matrix (b). (c) Fix a nonempty S \subseteq [n] with k elements. Then (\A + \varepsilon\I)_{S,S} = \A_{S,S} + \varepsilon\I_k. By (b) and condition (f) of @thm-m-matrix-characterizations, q(\varepsilon) = \det(\A_{S,S} + \varepsilon\I_k) > 0 for every \varepsilon > 0. By the Leibniz formula, q is a polynomial in \varepsilon, hence continuous by the algebra of limits quoted in Chapter 16’s introduction, so q(1/m) 	o q(0) as m 	o \infty. A nonstrict inequality survives a limit, so \det\A_{S,S} = q(0) \ge 0. (d) It is an M-matrix (see the Quick check after @lem-smallest-real-eigenvalue-z-matrix). Its principal minors are 1, 1 and 1 - 1 = 0, all nonnegative. The converse in the remark asks for all principal minors to be nonnegative, and \Z of (a) has the principal minor \det\Z_{\{2\},\{2\}} = -1 < 0. Only its leading ones are nonnegative, and for the nonstrict inequality leading minors are not enough. [C3: Nonnegative dynamics] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be a Z-matrix, written as \A = s\I - \B with \B \ge \O. 1. Prove that e^{-t\A} \ge \O for every real t \ge 0. 2. Suppose \A is a nonsingular M-matrix, and let \cvec{x} be the solution of \cvec{x}' = -\A\cvec{x} with \cvec{x}(0) = \cvec{x}_0 \ge \cvec{0}. Prove that \cvec{x}(t) \ge \cvec{0} for every t \ge 0 and that \cvec{x}(t) 	o \cvec{0} as t 	o \infty. Hint: split -t\A into two commuting matrices. (a) -t\A = t\B + (-ts)\I, and the two terms commute because every matrix commutes with a multiple of \I. By @thm-exponential-properties (d), e^{-t\A} = e^{t\B}e^{-ts\I}. Every partial sum of the series for e^{-ts\I} is  igl(\sum_{m=0}^{M}(-ts)^m/m! igr)\I, so e^{-ts\I} = e^{-ts}\I. The series for e^{t\B} converges by @thm-exponential-series-converges, and its partial sums \sum_{m=0}^{M}t^m\B^m/m! are \ge \O because t \ge 0 and \B \ge \O; a nonstrict inequality survives a limit, so e^{t\B} \ge \O. Hence e^{-t\A} = e^{-ts}e^{t\B} \ge \O. (b) By @thm-linear-ode-solution, \cvec{x}(t) = e^{-t\A}\cvec{x}_0, which is \ge \cvec{0} for t \ge 0 by (a). By @thm-m-matrix-characterizations (d), every eigenvalue of \A has positive real part, so every eigenvalue of -\A has negative real part: -\A is stable. By @thm-exponential-decay, \cvec{x}(t) 	o \cvec{0}. Both conclusions matter in models of concentrations or populations, which must stay nonnegative and, when -\A is stable, die out.

title: Perturbation Theory
content:
Perturbation Theory Every matrix that comes from a measurement or a computation is slightly wrong, so the eigenvalues one actually knows are those of a nearby matrix \A + \E. Two earlier chapters began to say what that costs. Chapter 16 showed that the eigenvalues move continuously with the matrix (@cor-eigenvalues-continuous), and that “continuously” can be very bad: a perturbation of size \varepsilon moves the eigenvalue of a k 	imes k Jordan block by \varepsilon^{1/k} (@exm-jordan-block-perturbation). Chapter 17 showed that Hermitian matrices are as good as one could hope: each eigenvalue moves by at most 
orm{\E}_2 (@cor-weyl-perturbation). Most matrices are neither Jordan blocks nor Hermitian, and this chapter handles them. It asks four questions. - Where are the eigenvalues, before any of them is computed? Discs and ovals read off the entries, and the numerical range, locate them. - How far do they move when \A is not Hermitian? For every matrix there is a bound with an n-th root, and the Jordan block shows that the root cannot be removed. For a diagonalizable matrix, the Bauer–Fike theorem gives a bound proportional to 
orm{\E}, with a factor that measures how far the eigenvectors are from orthonormal. - Which eigenvalue goes where? A bound saying that each new eigenvalue is near some old one does not say that they can be paired off. For normal matrices they can, and the pairing comes from Birkhoff’s theorem of Chapter 19. - What happens to the rest? Eigenvectors and invariant subspaces, singular values, and the factors of the polar decomposition all move, and the chapter bounds each of them. It ends with the first-order sensitivity of a single simple eigenvalue. One result settles an old account. Chapter 16 quoted the theorem that the roots of a polynomial depend continuously on its coefficients (@thm-roots-depend-continuously) and left the proof to this chapter. §03 gives it from compactness and unique factorization alone, so @cor-eigenvalues-continuous, and everything Chapter 16 built on it, now rests on a proved theorem. The field is 
C throughout, unless a statement says 
R. A real matrix is read in M_n(
C) when its eigenvalues are wanted. Three conventions hold in every section. - The perturbation is \E, and the perturbed matrix is \A + \E, as in Chapters 16 and 17. A different letter, \widetilde\A, is used only where the perturbed matrix is not naturally written as a sum. - Every bound names its norm. 
orm{\cdot}_2 is the spectral norm and 
orm{\cdot}_F the Frobenius norm. A norm without a subscript means an arbitrary operator norm, and it is written that way only where the statement holds for all of them. There is one other use, announced where it starts: in §§09–10 a norm without a subscript stands for either the spectral or the Frobenius norm, the same one throughout the statement, and there it ranges over just those two. - Near some eigenvalue is not the same as matched. “Every eigenvalue of \A + \E lies within r of some eigenvalue of \A” is a one-sided statement. “The eigenvalues can be numbered so that each pair is within r” is a matching, and it is stronger. §§03–05 are largely about the difference, and the chapter never blurs it. The analysis this chapter imports The list is Chapter 16’s, facts (A1)–(A6) of that chapter’s introduction, together with the algebra of limits, and each fact is named again where it is used. Two carry most of the weight. (A3), compactness of closed bounded sets, is the engine of §03’s proof of the continuity of roots, and it is also what makes the numerical range of §02 compact. (A5), the intermediate value theorem, gives the convexity of the numerical range in §02. (A4), the extreme value theorem, is used once, also in §02, to know that the numerical radius — the largest modulus on the numerical range — is attained. §03’s counting theorem needs one more fact, that an integer-valued function on an interval that is locally constant is constant, and it derives this from (A5) as well. Nothing else analytic is used. In particular, the first-order formula of §11 for the derivative of a simple eigenvalue is proved without the implicit function theorem. What you need - Chapter 0 §06 and §09 — the triangle inequality for complex numbers, which is the first move of nearly every estimate in the chapter (§§01, 02, 03, 09, and 11), and the trace, which §08 computes with: @thm-complex-triangle-inequality, @thm-trace-properties. - Chapter 1 §06 — basis extension, once, in §11, to turn an eigenvector into the first column of an invertible matrix: @thm-basis-extension. - Chapter 3 §05 and §07 — Rank–Nullity for matrices and the factor theorem, both in §11: @thm-rank-nullity-matrix, @lem-factor-theorem-linear. - Chapter 4 §05 — that a projection’s image is the subspace it projects onto, which is what lets §08 compare two subspaces by comparing their projections: @thm-projection-direct-sum. - Chapter 6 — polynomials over 
C: @cor-complex-polynomial-splits, @thm-unique-factorization-polynomials, @thm-repeated-root-derivative. - Chapter 7 — determinants, the adjugate, and minors: @def-adjugate, @thm-adjugate-identity, @thm-rank-via-minors, @thm-charpoly-coefficients, @thm-charpoly-root-iff-singular, @thm-det-block-triangular. - Chapter 8 — block matrices and the Kronecker and vec identities: @thm-block-multiplication, @thm-vec-identity. - Chapter 9 — eigenvalues, multiplicities, diagonalization, and left eigenvectors: @thm-eigenvalue-characterizations, @def-algebraic-multiplicity, @thm-geometric-le-algebraic, @def-diagonalizable, @thm-diagonalization, @def-left-eigenvector, @prp-left-eigenvectors-transpose, @prp-left-right-eigen-expansion. - Chapter 10 — the Jordan form, and its warning that the form is unstable: @thm-jordan-canonical-form, @def-jordan-block. Here the Jordan form is the thing being measured rather than a tool: §§04 and 11 discuss it in the text and pay off Chapter 10’s promise, and no proof in the chapter cites it. - Chapter 11 — inner products, orthogonal projections, unitary maps, and the unitary invariance of the Frobenius norm: @thm-cauchy-schwarz, @def-orthogonal-projection, @thm-orthogonal-decomposition, @cor-extend-orthonormal-basis, @thm-isometry-characterizations, @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant. - Chapter 12 — Schur’s theorem, the spectral theorem, the Sylvester equation, and the departure from normality: @thm-schur-triangularization, @cor-spectral-complex-matrix, @thm-normal-eigenvector-shared, @def-sylvester-operator, @thm-sylvester-equation, @cor-block-diagonalization, @def-departure-from-normality, @exm-eigenvalue-sensitivity. - Chapter 13 — the singular value and polar decompositions, and Hadamard’s inequality: @thm-svd, @def-singular-values, @thm-polar-decomposition, @thm-hadamard-inequality. - Chapter 16 — operator norms, the Neumann series, continuity of eigenvalues, and condition numbers: @def-operator-norm, @thm-operator-norm-properties, @thm-operator-norm-formulas, @thm-neumann-series, @lem-entrywise-polynomial-continuous, @thm-roots-depend-continuously, @cor-eigenvalues-continuous, @exm-jordan-block-perturbation, @def-condition-number. - Chapter 17 — the Rayleigh quotient, Weyl’s inequalities, Lidskii’s inequality, majorization, the Hermitian dilation, and §10’s law of inertia for Hermitian matrices: @def-rayleigh-quotient, @thm-courant-fischer, @thm-weyl-inequalities, @cor-weyl-perturbation, @thm-lidskii-inequality, @def-majorization, @prp-hermitian-dilation, @cor-singular-value-perturbation, @def-inertia-triple, @thm-inertia-second-proof. - Chapter 18 — extreme points, and linear functions on compact convex sets: @def-extreme-point, @cor-linear-max-at-extreme. - Chapter 19 — irreducible matrices, and Birkhoff’s theorem: @def-irreducible, @thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected, @thm-birkhoff. Roadmap - Gershgorin discs. Every eigenvalue lies in a union of discs read off the rows, a diagonal rescaling moves the discs, and an irreducible matrix can have an eigenvalue on the boundary only if it lies on every circle. - Other inclusion regions. Brauer’s ovals, which are never worse than the discs, and the numerical range: it contains the spectrum, it is convex by the Toeplitz–Hausdorff theorem, and it equals the convex hull of the eigenvalues for a normal matrix. - Continuity of roots. Chapter 16’s quoted theorem, proved by compactness. Elsner’s bound, with its exponent 1/n shown to be sharp by a Jordan block, and its matching version. The counting theorem: a group of Gershgorin discs separated from the others contains exactly as many eigenvalues as discs. - The Bauer–Fike theorem. For a diagonalizable matrix, each perturbed eigenvalue lies within \kappa_2(\X)
orm{\E}_2 of an old one, with factor 1 for a normal matrix. It comes with a residual bound for computed eigenpairs and a version with an m-th root for defective matrices. - The Hoffman–Wielandt theorem. The eigenvalues of two normal matrices can be matched within their Frobenius distance, by Birkhoff’s theorem. The inequality fails for nonnormal matrices. - Hermitian perturbations. Residual bounds, the Kato–Temple bound, which is quadratic in the residual, and Ostrowski’s theorem, which says that a congruence changes each eigenvalue by a bounded relative factor. - The Sylvester equation, quantitatively. The separation of two matrices, which measures how badly conditioned \A\X - \X\B = \Y is. For normal matrices it is the distance between the spectra, and in general it can be much smaller. Bounds for separated Hermitian spectra follow. - Principal angles. The angles between two subspaces, their sines, and the distance 
orm{P_U - P_W}_2 between the orthogonal projections. - The Davis–Kahan theorem. An invariant subspace of a Hermitian matrix moves by at most the perturbation divided by the spectral gap. Single eigenvectors inside a cluster may not be stable, but the subspace of the whole cluster is. - Singular values and polar factors. Mirsky’s Frobenius bound for singular values, and bounds for the positive and the unitary factors of the polar decomposition of an invertible matrix. - Condition numbers of eigenvalues. The derivative of a simple eigenvalue, from a right and a left eigenvector, and its worst size, which is the condition number. The chapter’s summary closes this section. Named moves - Dominant coordinate plus the triangle inequality. Read the eigen-equation at the coordinate where the eigenvector is largest. - A determinant bounded two ways. A product of distances to the eigenvalues is a determinant, and Hadamard’s inequality bounds it by column lengths. - Compactness plus uniqueness. Bound the roots, extract a convergent subsequence, and let unique factorization identify the limit. - An integer-valued continuous function is constant. Count eigenvalues along a path on which none of them can escape the region. - Factor out the resolvent. Write \A + \E - \mu\I = (\A - \mu\I) igl(\I + (\A - \mu\I)^{-1}\E igr) and invert the second factor by the Neumann series. - Birkhoff turns a doubly stochastic weight into a permutation. Minimize a linear function over the doubly stochastic matrices, and the minimum sits at a permutation. - The perturbation of a subspace is a Sylvester equation. The block coupling an invariant subspace to the new complement solves one, so the spectral gap is the conditioning. - The singular-pair trick. Test a matrix equation against the top singular pair of the unknown. - The adjugate as a polynomial eigenvector. A column of \adj(\mu\I - \B) is an eigenvector whose entries are polynomials, so it moves continuously with the data.

title: 20.1 Gershgorin Discs
content:
Gershgorin Discs Chapter 16 bounded the whole spectrum with one number: every eigenvalue lies in the disc \lvert zvert \le 
orm{\A}_{\infty} (@cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound). That disc is centered at 0, and it knows nothing about where in it the eigenvalues sit. For a matrix that is nearly diagonal the answer ought to be visible at a glance: the eigenvalues should sit near the diagonal entries, and the off-diagonal entries should say how near. This section makes that precise. It puts one disc around each diagonal entry, with radius measured from the rest of its row, and proves that the discs together hold every eigenvalue. It then sharpens the picture twice: by rescaling the coordinates, and, for irreducible matrices, by looking at the boundary. Throughout, matrices are complex. A real matrix is read inside M_n(
C), as in Chapter 16 §04, because its eigenvalues may be nonreal, and they are what we want to locate. Discs around the diagonal Here is the situation to keep in mind. Take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 6 & 2 & 5 \ 1 & -1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} . The row-sum bound gives \lvert\lambdavert \le 
orm{\A}_{\infty} = 13 for every eigenvalue \lambda, a disc of radius 13 about 0. But if the off-diagonal entries were 0, the eigenvalues would be exactly 6, -1, -1. The off-diagonal entries are a perturbation of the diagonal matrix, and the natural guess is that each eigenvalue stays within reach of some diagonal entry, where the reach of row i is measured by the size of the entries of row i off the diagonal. We give that reach a name. Around each diagonal entry, draw the disc whose radius is the total size of the other entries in its row. Gershgorin Discs Let n \ge 1 and \A = (a_{ij}) \in M_n(
C). For i = 1, \dots, n, the i-th Gershgorin radius of \A is the real number r_i(\A) \coloneqq \sum_{j 
e i} \lvert a_{ij}vert \ \ge 0 , the sum over all j \in \{1, \dots, n\} other than i, and the i-th Gershgorin disc is the closed disc D_i(\A) \coloneqq \{\, z \in 
C : \lvert z - a_{ii}vert \le r_i(\A) \,\} . The discs D_i(\A	p), whose radii r_i(\A	p) = \sum_{j 
e i}\lvert a_{ji}vert are taken from the columns of \A, are the column discs. In words: the center of D_i(\A) is the diagonal entry a_{ii}, and the radius adds up the moduli of the entries of row i that are not on the diagonal. The disc includes its boundary circle. A radius may be 0, and then the disc is the single point a_{ii}. Since \A	p has the same diagonal as \A, the column discs have the same centers as the row discs and, in general, different radii. The letter r is lowercase on purpose, since R_{\A} is the Rayleigh quotient, and the plain D_i is a set of complex numbers, not the bold diagonal matrix \D. Some examples, simplest first. - Diagonal matrices and n = 1. For \A = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) every radius is 0, because every off-diagonal entry is 0, and D_i(\A) = \{d_i\}. The discs are the eigenvalues. A 1 	imes 1 matrix (a) is the case n = 1: the sum defining r_1 is empty, so D_1 = \{a\}. These degenerate cases are the ones any theorem about the discs must get exactly right. - A 2 	imes 2 matrix. For \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 4 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, r_1(\B) = 1 and r_2(\B) = 4, so the row discs are \lvert zvert \le 1 and \lvert zvert \le 4. The column discs swap the radii: \lvert zvert \le 4 and \lvert zvert \le 1. - The matrix above. r_1(\A) = 2 + 5 = 7, r_2(\A) = 1 + 1 = 2, and r_3(\A) = 1 + 1 = 2, so D_1(\A) = \{\lvert z - 6vert \le 7\} and D_2(\A) = D_3(\A) = \{\lvert z + 1vert \le 2\}. The column radii are 1 + 1 = 2, 2 + 1 = 3, and 5 + 1 = 6. Nonexample by minimal change. Keep the radius and move the center to 0: replace D_i(\A) by \{\lvert zvert \le r_i(\A)\}. For \diag(1, 2) both radii are 0 and the modified “discs” are both \{0\}, which misses both eigenvalues. The clause that changed is the center, and the diagonal example shows it is the part that carries the information: the radius only measures how far the off-diagonal part can pull an eigenvalue away from it. The theorem It turns out that the guess is right, with no loss at all in the constant: [Gershgorin’s Theorem] Let n \ge 1, \A \in M_n(
C), and let \lambda be an eigenvalue of \A with eigenvector \cvec{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n). If k is an index with \lvert x_kvert = \max_j \lvert x_jvert, then \lambda \in D_k(\A). Consequently: 1. every eigenvalue of \A lies in the union D_1(\A) \cup \dots \cup D_n(\A) of the row discs; 2. every eigenvalue of \A lies in the union D_1(\A	p) \cup \dots \cup D_n(\A	p) of the column discs; 3. hence every eigenvalue lies in the intersection of the two unions. We want \lvert\lambda - a_{kk}vert to be small for one well-chosen k, so look at row k of \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} and move the diagonal term across: (\lambda - a_{kk})x_k = \sum_{j 
e k} a_{kj}x_j. The triangle inequality bounds the right side by \sum_{j 
e k}\lvert a_{kj}vert\lvert x_jvert, and this becomes r_k(\A)\lvert x_kvert exactly when every \lvert x_jvert \le \lvert x_kvert. So choose k where the eigenvector is largest in modulus. Then divide by \lvert x_kvert, which is positive because \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}. Let \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} with \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}, and let k be as in the statement; such a k exists because a finite set of real numbers has a largest element. Since \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}, some x_j 
e 0, so \lvert x_kvert > 0. Row k of \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} reads \sum_{j} a_{kj}x_j = \lambda x_k, that is, (\lambda - a_{kk})\,x_k = \sum_{j 
e k} a_{kj}x_j . Taking moduli and using the triangle inequality (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality), then \lvert x_jvert \le \lvert x_kvert for every j, \lvert\lambda - a_{kk}vert\,\lvert x_kvert \le \sum_{j 
e k}\lvert a_{kj}vert\,\lvert x_jvert \le \Bigl(\sum_{j 
e k}\lvert a_{kj}vert\Bigr)\lvert x_kvert = r_k(\A)\,\lvert x_kvert . Dividing by \lvert x_kvert > 0 gives \lvert\lambda - a_{kk}vert \le r_k(\A), that is, \lambda \in D_k(\A). (a) Every eigenvalue has an eigenvector, and the disc just found is one of the D_i(\A). (b) By @prp-left-eigenvectors-transpose (b), \A	p has the same eigenvalues as \A. Applying (a) to \A	p puts each of them in D_1(\A	p) \cup \dots \cup D_n(\A	p). (c) A point lying in each of two sets lies in their intersection. This proves the theorem. The move in this proof is worth naming, since the chapter uses it again: choose the dominant coordinate of an eigenvector, then apply the triangle inequality to its row. The choice of the largest coordinate is exactly what lets every \lvert x_jvert be replaced by \lvert x_kvert without looking at the others. The theorem recovers Chapter 16’s bound and improves on it. If \lambda \in D_k(\A), then  egin{aligned} \lvert\lambdavert &\le \lvert a_{kk}vert + \lvert\lambda - a_{kk}vert \le \lvert a_{kk}vert + r_k(\A) \ &= \sum_{j}\lvert a_{kj}vert \le 
orm{\A}_{\infty} , \end{aligned} so (a) implies ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A}_{\infty}, and (b) likewise implies ho(\A) \le 
orm{\A}_1. The union of the discs is never larger than the row-sum disc, and it is usually much smaller, because it keeps the centers. [Discs, eigenvectors, and where each eigenvalue sits] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 6 & 2 & 5 \ 1 & -1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. Describe the regions given by @thm-gershgorin (a) and (b). Then check that (7, 1, 1), (-1, 1, 1), and (1, 1, -2) are eigenvectors, and locate each eigenvalue in the disc the theorem assigns to it. From the radii computed after @def-gershgorin-discs, the row discs give \{\lvert z - 6vert \le 7\} \cup \{\lvert z + 1vert \le 2\} , the second disc counted twice, and the column discs give \{\lvert z - 6vert \le 2\} \cup \{\lvert z + 1vert \le 3\} \cup \{\lvert z + 1vert \le 6\}, where the middle disc lies inside the last. So every eigenvalue lies in \{\lvert z - 6vert \le 2\} \cup \{\lvert z + 1vert \le 6\}, and also in \{\lvert z - 6vert \le 7\} \cup \{\lvert z + 1vert \le 2\}. The column discs have separated the two groups of centers; the row discs have not. Multiplying out, \A egin{pmatrix} 7 \ 1 \ 1 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 49 \ 7 \ 7 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \A egin{pmatrix} -1 \ 1 \ 1 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ -1 \ -1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \A egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 1 \ -2 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} -2 \ -2 \ 4 \end{pmatrix}, so the eigenvalues include 7, -1, and -2. These are three distinct eigenvalues of a 3 	imes 3 matrix, hence three distinct roots of the degree-3 polynomial p_{\A} (@thm-eigenvalue-characterizations), so by @cor-root-bound-general there are no others. - The eigenvector (7, 1, 1) peaks at k = 1, and indeed \lvert 7 - 6vert = 1 \le 7: 7 \in D_1(\A). - The eigenvector (1, 1, -2) peaks at k = 3, and \lvert -2 + 1vert = 1 \le 2: -2 \in D_3(\A). - The eigenvector (-1, 1, 1) has all three coordinates of modulus 1, so every k is a peak and -1 must lie in every row disc. It does: \lvert -1 - 6vert = 7 = r_1(\A), so it sits on the boundary circle of D_1(\A), and it is the center of the other two. Both unions pass the test, and the eigenvector tells us which disc to look in. The row-sum disc \lvert zvert \le 13 says only that \lvert\lambdavert \le 13. The union is the claim, not each disc. A single Gershgorin disc need not contain any eigenvalue. For \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 4 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, p_{\B}(x) = x^2 - 4, so the eigenvalues are \pm 2, while the first row disc is \lvert zvert \le 1: it contains neither. Both eigenvalues lie in the second disc \lvert zvert \le 4. Nor may the row disc and the column disc of the same index be intersected: D_1(\B) \cap D_1(\B	p) and D_2(\B) \cap D_2(\B	p) are both \lvert zvert \le 1, and \pm 2 lies in neither. Part (c) of the theorem intersects the two unions. Without computing any eigenvalue, show that every eigenvalue of \M =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 & -1 \ 1 & 6 & 2 \ -1 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} has real part at least 2. The row discs are \lvert z - 5vert \le 3, \lvert z - 6vert \le 3, and \lvert z - 3vert \le 1. A point z of the first has \operatorname{Re} z \ge 5 - \lvert z - 5vert \ge 2, of the second \operatorname{Re} z \ge 3, of the third \operatorname{Re} z \ge 2. By @thm-gershgorin (a) every eigenvalue lies in one of them, so its real part is at least 2. In particular 0 is not an eigenvalue, and \M is invertible. Diagonal dominance The last sentence of the Quick check is a pattern. If 0 lies outside every disc, then 0 is not an eigenvalue, and the matrix is invertible. The point 0 lies outside D_i(\A) exactly when \lvert 0 - a_{ii}vert > r_i(\A), which is a condition on row i alone. [Strict Diagonal Dominance Implies Invertibility] Let n \ge 1 and \A \in M_n(
C). Call \A strictly diagonally dominant (by rows) if \lvert a_{ii}vert > r_i(\A) = \sum_{j 
e i}\lvert a_{ij}vert \qquad	ext{for **every** } i = 1, \dots, n . A strictly diagonally dominant matrix is invertible. The same holds if \A is strictly diagonally dominant by columns, that is, if \A	p is strictly diagonally dominant. Suppose \A is strictly diagonally dominant. For every i, \lvert 0 - a_{ii}vert > r_i(\A), so 0 
otin D_i(\A). Hence 0 lies in no row disc, and by @thm-gershgorin (a) it is not an eigenvalue. By @thm-eigenvalue-characterizations, 0\I - \A = -\A is invertible, and so is \A. If instead \A	p is strictly diagonally dominant, then 0 lies in no column disc, and @thm-gershgorin (b) finishes in the same way. This is the Lévy–Desplanques theorem. The word strictly carries the weight, and the definition asks it of every row. Examples:  egin{psmallmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 & 1 \ 1 & -1 & 4 \end{psmallmatrix} is strictly dominant, since 3 > 2, 2 > 1, 4 > 2; every diagonal matrix with nonzero diagonal is, since every radius is 0; and a 1 	imes 1 matrix (a) is strictly dominant exactly when a 
e 0. A minimal change breaks it.  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix} has \lvert a_{ii}vert = 1 = r_i in both rows: it is dominant only weakly, and it is singular. The converse of the corollary is false:  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} is invertible and has zero diagonal. Diagonal dominance is a certificate of invertibility, cheap to check and often available, not a characterization. Hermitian matrices, and intervals For a Hermitian \A the eigenvalues are real (@thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues), and so are the diagonal entries, since a_{ii} = \conj{a_{ii}}. So only the part of each disc on the real line matters, which is the interval [a_{ii} - r_i(\A),\, a_{ii} + r_i(\A)]. @thm-gershgorin (a) then says \min_i igl(a_{ii} - r_i(\A) igr) \le \lambda_n(\A) \le \lambda_1(\A) \le \max_i igl(a_{ii} + r_i(\A) igr) . For \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 4 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 6 & 2 \ 0 & 2 & 9 \end{psmallmatrix} the intervals are [3, 5], [3, 9], and [7, 11], so every eigenvalue lies in [3, 11], and \A is positive definite by @thm-pd-characterizations, since its eigenvalues are positive; Exercise C1 turns this into a general criterion. For a Hermitian matrix the row and column discs coincide, since \lvert a_{ji}vert = \lvert\conj{a_{ij}}vert, so (b) adds nothing. Scaling the discs The discs depend on the matrix, and the eigenvalues depend only on its similarity class. So any similarity that is easy to compute gives new discs for the same eigenvalues. The cheapest one rescales the coordinates. [Rescaling the Gershgorin Discs] Let \A \in M_n(
C), let d_1, \dots, d_n be positive real numbers, and \D = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n). Then: 1. \D^{-1}\A\D has entries a_{ij}d_j/d_i. It has the same diagonal as \A, and the same eigenvalues with the same algebraic multiplicities. 2. r_i(\D^{-1}\A\D) = \dfrac{1}{d_i}\sum_{j 
e i}\lvert a_{ij}vert\,d_j for each i. 3. Every eigenvalue of \A lies in  igcup_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl\{\, z : \lvert z - a_{ii}vert \le  rac{1}{d_i}\sum_{j 
e i}\lvert a_{ij}vert\,d_j \,\Bigr\} . (a) \D is invertible with \D^{-1} = \diag(1/d_1, \dots, 1/d_n), because every d_i 
e 0. Multiplying by a diagonal matrix on the left scales rows and on the right scales columns, so (\D^{-1}\A\D)_{ij} = d_i^{-1}a_{ij}d_j, and for i = j this is a_{ii}. The matrices \A and \D^{-1}\A\D are similar, so they have the same characteristic polynomial (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant), hence the same eigenvalues with the same multiplicities. (b) By (a) and d_i, d_j > 0, \lvert a_{ij}d_j/d_ivert = \lvert a_{ij}vert d_j/d_i; sum over j 
e i. (c) Apply @thm-gershgorin (a) to \D^{-1}\A\D and use (a) and (b). Taking d_1 > 1 and the other d_j = 1 divides the first radius by d_1 and multiplies the entry \lvert a_{i1}vert inside every other radius by d_1. So scaling shrinks some discs at the expense of others, and the art is to shrink the disc we care about while the others can afford to grow. The same move appeared in Chapter 19 §09, where \D = \diag(\cvec{x}) turned the entries of \B\cvec{x} into row sums. [Separating a disc by scaling] For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 6 & 2 & 5 \ 1 & -1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} of @exm-gershgorin-three, the row disc D_1(\A) = \{\lvert z - 6vert \le 7\} overlaps \{\lvert z + 1vert \le 2\}. Find a scaling \D = \diag(d, 1, 1) whose row discs split into two disjoint groups, and find the range of d that does it. By @prp-gershgorin-scaling (b) with d_1 = d and d_2 = d_3 = 1, the scaled radii are r_1 =  rac{2 + 5}{d} =  rac{7}{d}, \qquad r_2 = 1\cdot d + 1 = d + 1, \qquad r_3 = d + 1 , with centers 6, -1, -1. The first disc is disjoint from the other two exactly when the distance 7 between the centers exceeds the sum of the radii:  rac{7}{d} + d + 1 < 7 \iff d^2 - 6d + 7 < 0 \iff 3 - \sqrt2 < d < 3 + \sqrt2 , where we multiplied by d > 0. For instance d = 2 gives \D^{-1}\A\D =  egin{psmallmatrix} 6 & 1 & 5/2 \ 2 & -1 & 1 \ 2 & 1 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix} and the discs \{\lvert z - 6vert \le 	frac72\} \quad	ext{and}\quad \{\lvert z + 1vert \le 3\} , the second counted twice, which are disjoint since 	frac72 + 3 < 7. The eigenvalues 7, -1, -2 are distributed one in the first disc and two in the second, as the figure shows. Scaling has bought a picture in which the eigenvalues fall into two groups, one near 6 and two near -1. What it has not yet bought is the statement that the first disc contains exactly one eigenvalue. @thm-gershgorin says only that the union holds all three, and nothing so far forbids all three from lying in the second disc. The counting statement is true, but it needs the eigenvalues to move continuously as the off-diagonal part is switched on, and §03 proves it. For a real matrix like this one, §03 will also show that an isolated disc centered on the real axis holds a real eigenvalue. Eigenvalues on the boundary Diagonal dominance fails for a matrix that matters. The second-difference matrix \K_n of Chapter 19 §09 has 2 on the diagonal and -1 beside it, so for n \ge 3 its interior rows have \lvert a_{ii}vert = 2 = r_i(\K_n). The discs \lvert z - 2vert \le 2 pass through 0, and @cor-diagonally-dominant-invertible says nothing, although \K_n is invertible. Only the first and last rows are strict. What rescues it is that the rows are linked: the dominant coordinate of an eigenvector cannot stay in the equality rows without spreading to the strict ones. The link is irreducibility, in the sense of @def-irreducible, and by @thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected it means that the graph G(\A), with an edge j 	o i whenever a_{ij} 
e 0, is strongly connected. [Taussky’s Theorem] Let n \ge 1, let \A \in M_n(
C) be irreducible, and let \lambda be an eigenvalue of \A with \lvert\lambda - a_{ii}vert \ge r_i(\A) \qquad	ext{for **every** } i , that is, \lambda lies in no open disc \{\lvert z - a_{ii}vert < r_i(\A)\}. Then \lvert\lambda - a_{ii}vert = r_i(\A) for every i: the eigenvalue lies on the boundary circle of every Gershgorin disc. Moreover, every eigenvector for \lambda has all its coordinates of the same modulus. The hypothesis holds in particular when \lambda is a boundary point (@def-interior-point) of D_1(\A) \cup \dots \cup D_n(\A). Run the proof of @thm-gershgorin at a peak index k. The hypothesis \lvert\lambda - a_{kk}vert \ge r_k makes the two ends of its chain of inequalities equal, so every inequality in the chain is an equality. The second one, \sum_{j 
e k}\lvert a_{kj}vert\lvert x_jvert \le r_k\lvert x_kvert, is an equality only if \lvert x_jvert = \lvert x_kvert whenever a_{kj} 
e 0. So the set of peak indices is closed under following edges of G(\A) backwards. Strong connectivity then drags every index into it. Let \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} with \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}, put m = \max_j\lvert x_jvert > 0 and S = \{k : \lvert x_kvert = m\}, which is nonempty. If k \in S, then \lvert\lambda - a_{kk}vert = r_k(\A), and every j 
e k with a_{kj} 
e 0 lies in S. By the hypothesis and the chain of inequalities in the proof of @thm-gershgorin, with \lvert x_kvert = m, r_k(\A)\,m \le \lvert\lambda - a_{kk}vert\,m \le \sum_{j 
e k}\lvert a_{kj}vert\,\lvert x_jvert \le r_k(\A)\,m . The two ends agree, so every inequality is an equality. The first gives \lvert\lambda - a_{kk}vert = r_k(\A), after dividing by m > 0. The last says \sum_{j 
e k}\lvert a_{kj}vert\,(m - \lvert x_jvert) = 0. Each term is nonnegative, so each is 0, and a_{kj} 
e 0 forces \lvert x_jvert = m, that is, j \in S. Now let i be any index and fix k \in S. By @thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected, G(\A) has a walk i = i_0, i_1, \dots, i_t = k. We show i_s \in S for s = t, t-1, \dots, 0. For s = t this is k \in S. If i_s \in S with s \ge 1, then i_{s-1} 	o i_s is an edge, so a_{i_s i_{s-1}} 
e 0; either i_{s-1} = i_s \in S, or the Claim applied to i_s puts i_{s-1} in S. Hence i \in S. So S = \{1, \dots, n\}: every coordinate of \cvec{x} has modulus m, and the Claim gives \lvert\lambda - a_{ii}vert = r_i(\A) for every i. For the last sentence, suppose \lvert\lambda - a_{ii}vert < r_i(\A) for some i, and put \delta = r_i(\A) - \lvert\lambda - a_{ii}vert > 0. Every z with \lvert z - \lambdavert < \delta satisfies \lvert z - a_{ii}vert \le \lvert z - \lambdavert + \lvert\lambda - a_{ii}vert < r_i(\A), so it lies in D_i(\A) and in the union. Then \lambda is an interior point of the union, not a boundary point. This proves the theorem. For n = 1 the theorem is empty but true: r_1 = 0 and the only eigenvalue is a_{11}. For the all-ones matrix \J \in M_n(
C), n \ge 2, which is irreducible because every entry is nonzero, every disc is \lvert z - 1vert \le n - 1, and the eigenvalue n, with eigenvector \1, satisfies \lvert n - 1vert = n - 1: it lies on all of the boundary circles at once, and its eigenvector has equal coordinates, exactly as the theorem predicts. The corollary is the one \K_n needed: equality in most rows is allowed, provided one row is strict and the rows are linked. [Irreducible Diagonal Dominance Implies Invertibility] Let n \ge 1 and let \A \in M_n(
C) be irreducible, with \lvert a_{ii}vert \ge r_i(\A) \quad	ext{for every } i, \qquad \lvert a_{ii}vert > r_i(\A) \quad	ext{for **at least one** } i . Then \A is invertible. Suppose \A is not invertible. By @thm-eigenvalue-characterizations, 0 is an eigenvalue. The first hypothesis says \lvert 0 - a_{ii}vert \ge r_i(\A) for every i, so @thm-taussky applies to \lambda = 0 and gives \lvert a_{ii}vert = r_i(\A) for every i. This contradicts the second hypothesis. Hence \A is invertible. Both hypotheses are needed.  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix} is irreducible and weakly dominant, with no strict row, and it is singular: its eigenvalue 0 lies on both circles \lvert z - 1vert = 1. Exercise C2 shows that irreducibility cannot be dropped either. [The second-difference matrix] Show that \K_n is invertible for every n \ge 1, and that its eigenvalues lie in the open interval (0, 4). For n = 1, \K_1 = (2), with eigenvalue 2. Let n \ge 2. (Chapter 19 §09 proved invertibility by exhibiting the inverse, @prp-second-difference-inverse; here the entries alone suffice.) The only nonzero entries off the diagonal are a_{i,i+1} = a_{i+1,i} = -1, so G(\K_n) has the edges i 	o i + 1 and i + 1 	o i, and walking along them reaches every vertex from every vertex. So \K_n is irreducible by @thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected. Its rows have r_1 = r_n = 1 < 2 and, when n \ge 3, r_i = 2 for 1 < i < n. So \lvert a_{ii}vert \ge r_i everywhere, strictly in row 1, and \K_n is invertible by @cor-irreducibly-dominant-invertible. \K_n is real symmetric, so its eigenvalues are real, and by @thm-gershgorin (a) they lie in  igcup_i[2 - r_i, 2 + r_i] \subseteq [0, 4]. The value 0 is excluded by invertibility. The value 4 satisfies \lvert 4 - 2vert = 2 \ge r_i for every i, so if it were an eigenvalue, @thm-taussky would give 2 = r_1 = 1, which is false. Hence every eigenvalue lies in (0, 4). In particular \K_n \succ \O, which Chapter 19 §09 obtained from its M-matrix structure. The all-ones matrix \J \in M_3(
C) is irreducible, and 0 is an eigenvalue of it, since \J has rank 1. But 0 does not lie on the circle \lvert z - 1vert = 2. Does this contradict @thm-taussky? No. The theorem applies only to an eigenvalue with \lvert\lambda - a_{ii}vert \ge r_i(\J) for every i, and \lvert 0 - 1vert = 1 < 2 = r_i(\J): the eigenvalue 0 lies inside every open disc, so the hypothesis fails and the theorem says nothing about it. The other eigenvalue, 3, satisfies \lvert 3 - 1vert = 2, and it does lie on every circle. The picture to take away is this. The union of the discs holds the spectrum. An eigenvalue sits in the disc of the row where its eigenvector peaks. Scaling moves radius from one disc to another. And for an irreducible matrix, an eigenvalue can reach the outer edge of the union only by reaching the edge of every disc at once. §02 replaces the discs by other regions built from the same entries, and §03 counts the eigenvalues inside a group of discs. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the Gershgorin radius r_i(\A) and the disc D_i(\A), and state @thm-gershgorin, including the statement about the peak coordinate of an eigenvector. 2. True or false: every Gershgorin disc of \A contains an eigenvalue of \A. Justify your answer. 3. True or false: every eigenvalue of \A lies in  igcup_i igl(D_i(\A) \cap D_i(\A	p) igr). Justify your answer. 4. True or false: an invertible matrix is strictly diagonally dominant by rows or by columns. Justify your answer. 5. True or false: an irreducible matrix with \lvert a_{ii}vert \ge r_i(\A) for every i is invertible. Justify your answer. 6. Name the method of proof of @thm-gershgorin in one line. (a) r_i(\A) = \sum_{j 
e i}\lvert a_{ij}vert and D_i(\A) = \{z \in 
C : \lvert z - a_{ii}vert \le r_i(\A)\}. If \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} with \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0} and \lvert x_kvert = \max_j\lvert x_jvert, then \lambda \in D_k(\A); hence every eigenvalue lies in  igcup_i D_i(\A), in  igcup_i D_i(\A	p), and in the intersection of these two unions. (b) False. For  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 4 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} the eigenvalues are \pm 2 and the first disc is \lvert zvert \le 1. (c) False. For the same matrix both intersections are \lvert zvert \le 1, which misses \pm 2. (d) False.  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} is invertible, and \lvert a_{11}vert = 0 < 1 both for rows and for columns. (e) False.  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix} is irreducible, with \lvert a_{ii}vert = 1 = r_i, and singular. @cor-irreducibly-dominant-invertible needs one strict row. (f) Choose the coordinate of the eigenvector of largest modulus, and apply the triangle inequality (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality) to that row of \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x}. B. Practice [B1: Deciding invertibility] Determine which of the following matrices are invertible. Justify your answers, using the results of this section where they apply and a direct computation where they do not. 1.  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 & -2 \ 1 & -4 & 2 \ 0 & 3 & 4i \end{pmatrix} 2.  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 2 \ 1 & 3 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} 3.  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} 4.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} (a) The radii are 4, 3, 3 and the diagonal moduli 5, 4, \lvert 4ivert = 4, so every row is strictly dominant. The matrix is invertible by @cor-diagonally-dominant-invertible. (b) Row 1 has 3 = 1 + 2, and rows 2 and 3 have 3 > 2. Every off-diagonal entry is nonzero, so every edge j 	o i with i 
e j is present in the graph, which is strongly connected, and the matrix is irreducible (@thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected). It is invertible by @cor-irreducibly-dominant-invertible. (Indeed its determinant is 18.) (c) Every row has 2 = 1 + 1: no row is strict, so neither corollary applies. Directly, the matrix is \I + \J, and \J\1 = 3\cdot\1, while \J\cvec{v} = \cvec{0} for \cvec{v} = (1, -1, 0) and \cvec{v} = (1, 0, -1). So the eigenvalues of \I + \J are 4, 1, 1, none zero, and the matrix is invertible, with determinant 4. The corollaries give sufficient conditions only. (d) Rows 1 and 2 have equality and row 3 is strict, but the matrix is singular: its first two rows are equal. The corollary does not apply because the matrix is reducible: column 3 is zero outside row 3, so no edge leaves vertex 3, and there is no walk from 3 to 1. [B2: An interval for a symmetric matrix] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 1 & -1 \ 1 & 3 & 1 \ -1 & 1 & 6 \end{pmatrix}. 1. Use @thm-gershgorin to find an interval containing every eigenvalue of \A, and compare it with the interval [-
orm{\A}_{\infty}, 
orm{\A}_{\infty}] given by @cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound. 2. Hence show that \A is positive definite, and that \det\A lies between 1 and 8^3. (a) \A is real symmetric, so its eigenvalues are real. The radii are 2, 2, 2, so the discs meet 
R in [3, 7], [1, 5], [4, 8], whose union is [1, 8]. By @thm-gershgorin (a), every eigenvalue lies in [1, 8]. The largest absolute row sum is 
orm{\A}_{\infty} = 8, so Chapter 16’s bound gives only [-8, 8]; the upper ends agree, but only the discs see that the eigenvalues are positive. (b) Every eigenvalue is at least 1 > 0, so \A \succ \O by @thm-pd-characterizations. The determinant is the product of the three eigenvalues, each in [1, 8], so 1 \le \det\A \le 8^3 = 512. (In fact \det\A = 74.) [B3: Choosing the scaling] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 7 & 4 & 4 \ 1 & 0 & -1 \ -1 & -2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. 1. Show that the row disc D_1(\A) meets the other two row discs. 2. For \D = \diag(d, 1, 1) with d > 0, find the scaled radii, and find all d for which the first scaled disc is disjoint from the other two. 3. Check that (-6, -1, 1) is an eigenvector of \A, and that its eigenvalue lies in the first scaled disc for d = 3. (a) The discs are \lvert z - 7vert \le 8, \lvert zvert \le 2, and \lvert z + 1vert \le 3. The point 0 lies in the first two, and -1 in the first and third. (b) By @prp-gershgorin-scaling (b), the radii of \D^{-1}\A\D are r_1 = 8/d, r_2 = 1\cdot d + 1 = d + 1, and r_3 = 1\cdot d + 2 = d + 2, with centers 7, 0, -1. The first disc misses the second when 8/d + d + 1 < 7, and misses the third when 8/d + d + 2 < 8: both say d + 8/d < 6. Multiplying by d > 0, this is d^2 - 6d + 8 < 0, that is, (d - 2)(d - 4) < 0, so 2 < d < 4. At d = 2 the discs touch. (c) Here  egin{aligned} \A(-6, -1, 1) &= (-42 - 4 + 4,\ -6 + 0 - 1,\ 6 + 2 - 1) \ &= (-42, -7, 7) = 7\,(-6, -1, 1) , \end{aligned} so 7 is an eigenvalue. For d = 3 the first scaled disc is \lvert z - 7vert \le 	frac83, which contains 7. The eigenvector peaks at the first coordinate, so @thm-gershgorin already placed 7 in D_1; the scaled theorem places it in the smaller disc. C. Going deeper [C1: Dominance and definiteness] 1. Prove that a Hermitian matrix \A with a_{ii} > r_i(\A) for every i is positive definite. 2. Prove that a Hermitian irreducible matrix with a_{ii} \ge r_i(\A) for every i, strictly for at least one i, is positive definite. 3. Deduce that for every n \ge 1 and every real t \ge 0, the matrix \K_n + t\,\cvec{e}_1\cvec{e}_1	p is positive definite. Hint for (b): apply (a)’s argument to find where the eigenvalues can be, and then use @thm-taussky. (a) The diagonal entries of a Hermitian matrix are real, and so are its eigenvalues (@thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues). By @thm-gershgorin (a), each eigenvalue \lambda lies in some D_k(\A), so \lambda \ge a_{kk} - \lvert\lambda - a_{kk}vert \ge a_{kk} - r_k(\A) > 0. A Hermitian matrix with only positive eigenvalues is positive definite (@thm-pd-characterizations). (b) As in (a), every eigenvalue satisfies \lambda \ge a_{kk} - r_k(\A) \ge 0 for some k, so it is enough to show that 0 is not an eigenvalue. The hypothesis gives \lvert 0 - a_{ii}vert = a_{ii} \ge r_i(\A) for every i, since a_{ii} \ge r_i(\A) \ge 0. If 0 were an eigenvalue, @thm-taussky would give a_{ii} = r_i(\A) for every i, contradicting the strict row. Hence all eigenvalues are positive and \A \succ \O. (This is also @cor-irreducibly-dominant-invertible, together with the sign information from (a).) (c) The matrix is real symmetric, and it differs from \K_n only in the (1,1) entry, which is 2 + t. The graph is unchanged, so for n \ge 2 it is irreducible, as shown in @exm-second-difference-taussky. Its rows satisfy a_{ii} \ge r_i, with 2 + t > 1 in row 1. By (b), it is positive definite. For n = 1 the matrix is (2 + t) with 2 + t > 0. [C2: Irreducibility cannot be dropped] 1. Give a 3 	imes 3 reducible matrix with \lvert a_{ii}vert \ge r_i(\A) for every i, strictly in at least one row, that is singular. Which step of the proof of @thm-taussky fails for it? 2. Let \A be irreducible and let \lambda be an eigenvalue with \lvert\lambda - a_{ii}vert \ge r_i(\A) for every i. Prove that the eigenspace E_\lambda(\A) has dimension 1. Hint for (b): given two independent eigenvectors, form a combination with a zero coordinate. (a) Take \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} from @exr-gershgorin-b1 (d): rows 1 and 2 have equality, row 3 is strict, and the first two rows are equal, so \A is singular. The eigenvector \cvec{x} = (1, -1, 	frac12) for 0 has \A\cvec{x} = (0, 0, -1 + 1) = \cvec{0}. Its peak set is S = \{1, 2\}, and the Claim of the proof holds: the rows in S have equality and their off-diagonal nonzero entries point into S. What fails is the spreading step. There is no walk from 3 to 1 in G(\A), so nothing forces 3 \in S, and the strict row 3 is never reached. (b) Suppose \cvec{x} and \cvec{y} are linearly independent eigenvectors for \lambda. Since \cvec{y} 
e \cvec{0}, choose i with y_i 
e 0, and put \cvec{z} = \cvec{x} - (x_i/y_i)\cvec{y}. Then \cvec{z} 
e \cvec{0}, by independence, and \A\cvec{z} = \lambda\cvec{z}, so \cvec{z} is an eigenvector for \lambda with z_i = 0. But by @thm-taussky every eigenvector for \lambda has all coordinates of the same modulus, which is positive because the vector is nonzero. This contradiction shows \dim E_\lambda(\A) \le 1, and \dim E_\lambda(\A) \ge 1 because \lambda is an eigenvalue.

title: 20.2 Other Inclusion Regions
content:
Other Inclusion Regions The Gershgorin discs of §01 come from one row of \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x}, read at the largest coordinate of \cvec{x}. That leaves two kinds of information unused. The first is the second largest coordinate, which the triangle inequality simply replaced by the largest; using it gives a region of ovals that is never worse than the discs. The second is the geometry of the inner product, which the discs ignore entirely: the number \cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x} over unit vectors \cvec{x} fills a region of the plane, the numerical range, that contains every eigenvalue. This section builds both regions. Its main theorem is that the numerical range is always convex. It ends with a rectangle for the spectrum whose sides are eigenvalues of Hermitian matrices, and with a warning about what these regions cannot do. Throughout, matrices are complex and n \ge 1, and 
orm{\cdot} on 
C^n is the Euclidean norm. As in §01, r_i(\A) = \sum_{j 
e i}\lvert a_{ij}vert is the i-th Gershgorin radius and D_i(\A) the i-th disc (@def-gershgorin-discs). The plane 
C is treated as a real vector space when convexity is discussed, as Chapter 18 §01 does. Using two coordinates: Brauer’s ovals In the proof of @thm-gershgorin every \lvert x_jvert with j 
e k was bounded by the largest one, \lvert x_kvert. That is wasteful when the second largest coordinate is much smaller. So keep two indices: p, where \lvert x_pvert is largest, and q 
e p, where it is largest among the rest. Row p bounds \lvert\lambda - a_{pp}vert\lvert x_pvert by r_p\lvert x_qvert, since every other coordinate is at most \lvert x_qvert. Row q bounds \lvert\lambda - a_{qq}vert\lvert x_qvert by r_q\lvert x_pvert. Multiplying the two bounds cancels the unknown coordinates. The result is a region defined by a product of distances. [Brauer’s Ovals of Cassini] Let n \ge 2 and \A \in M_n(
C). For i 
e j put O_{ij}(\A) \coloneqq  igl\{\, z \in 
C : \lvert z - a_{ii}vert\,\lvert z - a_{jj}vert \le r_i(\A)\,r_j(\A) \, igr\} . 1. Every eigenvalue of \A lies in  igcup_{i 
e j} O_{ij}(\A). 2. O_{ij}(\A) \subseteq D_i(\A) \cup D_j(\A) for every i 
e j. Hence  igcup_{i 
e j}O_{ij}(\A) \subseteq  igcup_i D_i(\A). For (a), take the two largest coordinates of an eigenvector as above and multiply the two row estimates. One case needs separate care: if the second largest coordinate is 0, there is nothing to divide by, but then \cvec{x} is a multiple of \cvec{e}_p and \lambda = a_{pp}, which lies in every oval through a_{pp}. For (b), a point outside both discs is farther than r_i from a_{ii} and farther than r_j from a_{jj}, so the product of its distances exceeds r_ir_j. (a) Let \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} with \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}. Choose p with \lvert x_pvert = \max_j\lvert x_jvert, which is positive, and then q 
e p with \lvert x_qvert = \max_{j 
e p}\lvert x_jvert; this is possible because n \ge 2. Case 1: x_q = 0. Then x_j = 0 for every j 
e p, and row p of \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} reads a_{pp}x_p = \lambda x_p. As x_p 
e 0, \lambda = a_{pp}. The left side of the inequality defining O_{pq}(\A) is then 0, and the right side is \ge 0, so \lambda \in O_{pq}(\A). Case 2: x_q 
e 0. Row p gives (\lambda - a_{pp})x_p = \sum_{j 
e p}a_{pj}x_j. Every j 
e p has \lvert x_jvert \le \lvert x_qvert, so by the triangle inequality (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality) \lvert\lambda - a_{pp}vert\,\lvert x_pvert \le r_p(\A)\,\lvert x_qvert . Row q gives (\lambda - a_{qq})x_q = \sum_{j 
e q}a_{qj}x_j. Every j has \lvert x_jvert \le \lvert x_pvert, so \lvert\lambda - a_{qq}vert\,\lvert x_qvert \le r_q(\A)\,\lvert x_pvert . Both sides of both inequalities are nonnegative, so they may be multiplied: \lvert\lambda - a_{pp}vert\,\lvert\lambda - a_{qq}vert\,\lvert x_pvert\,\lvert x_qvert \le r_p(\A)\,r_q(\A)\,\lvert x_pvert\,\lvert x_qvert . Dividing by \lvert x_pvert\lvert x_qvert > 0 gives \lambda \in O_{pq}(\A). (b) Let z 
otin D_i(\A) \cup D_j(\A), so a \coloneqq \lvert z - a_{ii}vert > r_i(\A) \ge 0 and c \coloneqq \lvert z - a_{jj}vert > r_j(\A) \ge 0. Since c > 0 and r_i(\A) \ge 0, ac > r_i(\A)\,c \ge r_i(\A)\,r_j(\A) , so z 
otin O_{ij}(\A). Taking complements, O_{ij}(\A) \subseteq D_i(\A) \cup D_j(\A), and taking the union over all pairs gives the last claim. This proves the theorem. The sets O_{ij}(\A) are the ovals of Cassini: the points whose distances to two fixed foci have product at most a constant. Since O_{ij}(\A) = O_{ji}(\A), there are n(n-1)/2 of them to draw, against n discs. The hypothesis n \ge 2 is there because an oval needs two distinct indices; for n = 1 there are none, and the eigenvalue a_{11} must be found some other way. For n = 2 the single oval is as good as a region can be. The eigenvalues satisfy (\lambda - a_{11})(\lambda - a_{22}) = a_{12}a_{21}, so taking moduli, \lvert\lambda - a_{11}vert\lvert\lambda - a_{22}vert = r_1r_2: both eigenvalues lie on the boundary curve of O_{12}. [Ovals where discs fail] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 4 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Show that the Gershgorin discs cannot prove \A invertible, and that the ovals can. The radii are r_1 = 1, r_2 = 1, r_3 = 2, and D_3(\A) = \{\lvert z - 1vert \le 2\} contains 0. So @thm-gershgorin (a) allows the eigenvalue 0. The column radii are 1, 2, 1, and the second column disc \lvert z - 4vert \le 2 misses 0, but the third, \lvert z - 1vert \le 1, contains it. So the discs cannot decide. Now test z = 0 against the three ovals:  egin{aligned} O_{12}&: \ \lvert 0 - 4vert\,\lvert 0 - 4vert = 16 > 1 = r_1r_2 ,\ O_{13}&: \ \lvert 0 - 4vert\,\lvert 0 - 1vert = 4 > 2 = r_1r_3 ,\ O_{23}&: \ \lvert 0 - 4vert\,\lvert 0 - 1vert = 4 > 2 = r_2r_3 . \end{aligned} So 0 lies in no oval, it is not an eigenvalue by @thm-brauer-ovals (a), and \A is invertible by @thm-eigenvalue-characterizations.
