None of them is a perturbation bound in the sense of the rest of this chapter, which asks how far the eigenvalues move when \A changes by a small \E. The numerical range does give a statement of that kind. For a unit \cvec{x}, \cvec{x}^{*}(\A + \E)\cvec{x} = \cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x} + \cvec{x}^{*}\E\cvec{x}, and \lvert\cvec{x}^{*}\E\cvec{x}vert \le 
orm{\E}_2 by @prp-numerical-range-basic (e). Hence W(\A + \E) \subseteq W(\A) + W(\E) \subseteq \{\, w + e : w \in W(\A),\ \lvert evert \le 
orm{\E}_2 \,\} , and so every eigenvalue of \A + \E lies within 
orm{\E}_2 of W(\A). This is only as good as W(\A) is small. W(\A) can be far larger than \spec(\A), so “within 
orm{\E}_2 of W(\A)” is not “within 
orm{\E}_2 of an eigenvalue”. For \A = M\J_2(0) with M > 0, @prp-numerical-range-basic (b) and @exm-numerical-range-jordan give W(\A) = \{\lvert zvert \le M/2\}, while \spec(\A) = \{0\}. So the bound above allows the eigenvalues of \A + \E to lie anywhere in \lvert zvert \le M/2 + 
orm{\E}_2, and this does not shrink as \E 	o \O. The eigenvalues do move a long way: \A + \varepsilon\cvec{e}_2\cvec{e}_1	p has characteristic polynomial x^2 - M\varepsilon, so for \varepsilon > 0 its eigenvalues \pm\sqrt{M\varepsilon} have moved by \sqrt{M\varepsilon}, far more than \varepsilon. For a normal \A, W(\A) = \conv\spec(\A) is small, but it still contains points far from every eigenvalue, such as the midpoint of two distant ones. The genuine perturbation bounds need a different mechanism: §03 proves that eigenvalues move continuously and at what rate in general, and §04 gives Bauer–Fike’s bound, in which the distance to the nearest eigenvalue is controlled. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the Brauer oval O_{ij}(\A) and the numerical range W(\A), and state the Toeplitz–Hausdorff theorem. 2. True or false: W(\A) = \conv\spec(\A) for every \A \in M_n(
C). Justify your answer. 3. True or false: W(\A) is contained in the union of the Gershgorin discs of \A. Justify your answer. 4. True or false: if \A + \A^{*} \succ \O, then \A is invertible. Justify your answer. 5. Why does @thm-brauer-ovals require n \ge 2? (a) For i 
e j, O_{ij}(\A) = \{z : \lvert z - a_{ii}vert\lvert z - a_{jj}vert \le r_i(\A)r_j(\A)\}, and W(\A) = \{\cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x} : 
orm{\cvec{x}} = 1\}. @thm-toeplitz-hausdorff: for every square complex \A, W(\A) is convex. (b) False. W(\J_2(0)) is the disc \lvert zvert \le 	frac12 (@exm-numerical-range-jordan), while \conv\spec(\J_2(0)) = \{0\}. Equality holds for normal matrices (@prp-numerical-range-normal). (c) False. For \A = \diag(1, -1) the discs are the two points \{1\} and \{-1\}, while W(\A) = [-1, 1] contains 0. The discs contain the spectrum, not the numerical range. (d) True. By @thm-bendixson every eigenvalue has \operatorname{Re}\lambda \ge \lambda_n(\H) > 0, with \H = (\A + \A^{*})/2 \succ \O. So 0 is not an eigenvalue, and \A is invertible (@thm-eigenvalue-characterizations). (e) An oval is built from two distinct indices i 
e j, and the proof needs a second index q 
e p. For n = 1 there are no ovals, and the union in (a) would be empty, although the matrix has an eigenvalue. B. Practice [B1: Invertibility from ovals] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 5 & 1 \ 2 & 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. 1. Show that neither the row discs nor the column discs of \A exclude 0. 2. Use @thm-brauer-ovals to show that \A is invertible. 3. Check that (1, -1, 0) is an eigenvector, and verify that its eigenvalue lies in O_{12}(\A). (a) The row radii are 2, 2, 4, and D_3(\A) = \{\lvert z - 2vert \le 4\} contains 0. The column radii are 3, 3, 2, and the third column disc \lvert z - 2vert \le 2 contains 0. (b) At z = 0: for O_{12}, 5 \cdot 5 = 25 > 4 = r_1r_2; for O_{13} and O_{23}, 5 \cdot 2 = 10 > 8 = r_1r_3 = r_2r_3. So 0 lies in no oval, is not an eigenvalue by @thm-brauer-ovals (a), and \A is invertible. (Its determinant is 32.) (c) \A(1, -1, 0) = (5 - 1, 1 - 5, 2 - 2) = (4, -4, 0), so the eigenvalue is 4. For O_{12}: \lvert 4 - 5vert\lvert 4 - 5vert = 1 \le 4. [B2: A Bendixson rectangle] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Find the rectangle of @thm-bendixson, and hence show that every eigenvalue of \A satisfies 0 \le \operatorname{Re}\lambda \le 2 and \lvert\operatorname{Im}\lambdavert \le 2. Compare with the eigenvalues. \H = 	frac12(\A + \A	p) =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}, with p_{\H}(x) = x^2 - 2x, so its eigenvalues are 0 and 2. \K = 	frac{1}{2i}(\A - \A	p) = 	frac{1}{2i} egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 4 \ -4 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & -2i \ 2i & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, with trace 0 and determinant -4, so its eigenvalues are \pm 2. By @thm-bendixson every eigenvalue has 0 \le \operatorname{Re}\lambda \le 2 and -2 \le \operatorname{Im}\lambda \le 2. Directly, p_{\A}(x) = x^2 - 2x + 4, so \lambda = 1 \pm i\sqrt3: the real part 1 lies in [0, 2], and \sqrt3 \approx 1.73 \le 2. [B3: Computing numerical ranges] Determine W(\A) for each matrix. Justify your answers. 1. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} 2. \A = \diag(1, i, -1, -i) 3. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} (a) \A = 2\J_2(0) + \I, so by @prp-numerical-range-basic (b) and @exm-numerical-range-jordan, W(\A) = 2W(\J_2(0)) + 1 = \{z : \lvert z - 1vert \le 1\}, the closed disc of radius 1 about 1. (b) A diagonal matrix is normal, so by @prp-numerical-range-normal W(\A) = \conv\{1, i, -1, -i\}, the filled square with these four vertices. (c) \A is real symmetric, with eigenvalues 3 and 1 (eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, -1)). By @prp-rayleigh-basic, or @prp-numerical-range-normal, W(\A) = [1, 3]. C. Going deeper [C1: Direct sums] 1. Let \B \in M_k(
C) and \C \in M_m(
C). Prove that W(\B \oplus \C) = \conv igl(W(\B) \cup W(\C) igr). 2. Deduce that \A = \diag(2, -2, 2i, -2i) \oplus \J_2(0) is not normal, but satisfies W(\A) = \conv\spec(\A). Hint for (a): one inclusion needs @thm-toeplitz-hausdorff. (a) (\subseteq) Write a unit vector of 
C^{k+m} as \cvec{x} = (\cvec{y}, \cvec{z}), with 
orm{\cvec{y}}^2 + 
orm{\cvec{z}}^2 = 1. Then \cvec{x}^{*}(\B \oplus \C)\cvec{x} = \cvec{y}^{*}\B\cvec{y} + \cvec{z}^{*}\C\cvec{z}. If \cvec{z} = \cvec{0} this is a point of W(\B), and if \cvec{y} = \cvec{0} a point of W(\C). Otherwise, with s = 
orm{\cvec{y}}^2 \in (0, 1), \cvec{x}^{*}(\B \oplus \C)\cvec{x} = s\, rac{\cvec{y}^{*}\B\cvec{y}}{
orm{\cvec{y}}^2} + (1 - s)\, rac{\cvec{z}^{*}\C\cvec{z}}{
orm{\cvec{z}}^2} , a convex combination of a point of W(\B), at the unit vector \cvec{y}/
orm{\cvec{y}}, and a point of W(\C). In every case the value lies in \conv(W(\B) \cup W(\C)), by @thm-convex-hull-combinations. (\supseteq) Taking \cvec{x} = (\cvec{y}, \cvec{0}) with \cvec{y} a unit vector shows W(\B) \subseteq W(\B \oplus \C), and likewise W(\C) \subseteq W(\B \oplus \C). By @thm-toeplitz-hausdorff, W(\B \oplus \C) is convex, so it contains the smallest convex set containing W(\B) \cup W(\C) (@def-convex-hull). (b) \A is not normal: its lower-right block is \J_2(0), and \A^{*}\A and \A\A^{*} differ in that block, since \J_2(0)^{*}\J_2(0) = \diag(0, 1) and \J_2(0)\J_2(0)^{*} = \diag(1, 0). By (a), @prp-numerical-range-normal, and @exm-numerical-range-jordan, W(\A) is the convex hull of the square Q = \conv\{\pm 2, \pm 2i\} and the disc \{\lvert zvert \le 	frac12\}. The square contains the disc: Q = \{ z : \lvert\operatorname{Re}zvert + \lvert\operatorname{Im}zvert \le 2 \}, and \lvert\operatorname{Re}zvert + \lvert\operatorname{Im}zvert \le 2\lvert zvert \le 1 on the disc. So W(\A) = Q. The spectrum is \{\pm 2, \pm 2i, 0\}, whose hull is also Q, since 0 \in Q. Hence W(\A) = \conv\spec(\A), although \A is not normal: the converse of @prp-numerical-range-normal fails. [C2: When the numerical range is real, or a point] Let \A \in M_n(
C). 1. Prove that W(\A) \subseteq 
R if and only if \A is Hermitian. 2. Deduce that W(\A) = \{c\} for a single c \in 
C if and only if \A = c\I. (a) (\Leftarrow) If \A is Hermitian, \cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x} = \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} is real by @prp-self-adjoint-immediate (a). (\Rightarrow) Write \A = \H + i\K as in @lem-hermitian-parts. If W(\A) \subseteq 
R, then \cvec{x}^{*}\K\cvec{x} = \operatorname{Im}(\cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x}) = 0 for every unit \cvec{x}. By @prp-rayleigh-basic, \lambda_1(\K) and \lambda_n(\K) are values of \cvec{x}^{*}\K\cvec{x} on unit vectors, so both are 0, and every eigenvalue of \K is 0. By @cor-spectral-complex-matrix, \K = \U\,\O\,\U^{*} = \O. Hence \A = \H is Hermitian. (b) (\Leftarrow) is the example W(c\I) = \{c\}. (\Rightarrow) By @prp-numerical-range-basic (b), W(\A - c\I) = W(\A) - c = \{0\} \subseteq 
R, so \A - c\I is Hermitian by (a). By @prp-rayleigh-basic its extreme eigenvalues are values of the form on unit vectors, hence both 0, and as in (a) the Hermitian matrix \A - c\I with all eigenvalues 0 is \O. [C3: The numerical radius] For \A \in M_n(
C), the numerical radius is w(\A) = \max\{\lvert zvert : z \in W(\A)\}. 1. Explain why the maximum exists, and prove that ho(\A) \le w(\A) \le 
orm{\A}_2. 2. Prove that 
orm{\A}_2 \le 2\,w(\A). 3. Show that both constants are attained: w(\A) = 
orm{\A}_2 for every normal \A, and 
orm{\A}_2 = 2\,w(\A) for \A = \J_2(0). Hint for (b): bound 
orm{\H}_2 and 
orm{\K}_2 separately. (a) W(\A) is nonempty and compact (@prp-numerical-range-basic (d)), and z \mapsto \lvert zvert is continuous, so the maximum is attained by the extreme value theorem, fact (A4) of Chapter 16’s introduction. Every eigenvalue lies in W(\A), by @prp-numerical-range-basic (a), so ho(\A) \le w(\A); and w(\A) \le 
orm{\A}_2 by @prp-numerical-range-basic (e). (b) Let \A = \H + i\K as in @lem-hermitian-parts. By @lem-hermitian-spectral-norm, 
orm{\H}_2 is the larger of \lambda_1(\H) and -\lambda_n(\H). By @prp-rayleigh-basic there is a unit \cvec{x} with \lambda_1(\H) = \cvec{x}^{*}\H\cvec{x} = \operatorname{Re}(\cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x}) \le \lvert\cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x}vert \le w(\A) , and a unit \cvec{y} with -\lambda_n(\H) = -\operatorname{Re}(\cvec{y}^{*}\A\cvec{y}) \le w(\A). So 
orm{\H}_2 \le w(\A), and the same argument with imaginary parts gives 
orm{\K}_2 \le w(\A). As the operator norm is a norm (@thm-operator-norm-properties (b)), 
orm{\A}_2 \le 
orm{\H}_2 + 
orm{i\K}_2 \le 2\,w(\A). (c) For normal \A, ho(\A) = 
orm{\A}_2, as Chapter 16 §04 showed after @def-spectral-radius, so the chain in (a) collapses to equalities. For \J_2(0), @exm-numerical-range-jordan gives w(\J_2(0)) = 	frac12, and 
orm{\J_2(0)}_2 = 1, since 
orm{\J_2(0)\cvec{x}} = \lvert x_2vert \le 
orm{\cvec{x}} with equality at \cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_2. So 
orm{\J_2(0)}_2 = 2\,w(\J_2(0)).

title: 20.3 Continuity of Roots
content:
Continuity of Roots Chapter 16 §07 proved that the eigenvalues of a matrix move continuously with the matrix, but only after quoting a theorem it did not prove: the roots of a monic polynomial move continuously with its coefficients (@thm-roots-depend-continuously). This section proves that theorem, with nothing more than the compactness of closed bounded sets. It then asks two quantitative questions the qualitative theorem cannot answer. How far can an eigenvalue move when the matrix moves by a given amount, with no hypothesis on the matrix at all? And how many eigenvalues does a region of the plane hold? The second question finishes the story of Gershgorin’s discs begun in Section 1: an isolated disc holds exactly one eigenvalue. Throughout, matrices are complex and eigenvalues are listed with algebraic multiplicity, so that \A \in M_n(
C) has exactly n of them (@cor-complex-polynomial-splits). Two imported facts of analysis are used, and each is named where it acts: compactness, fact (A3) of Chapter 16’s introduction, and the intermediate value theorem, fact (A5). A bound for the roots The proof of continuity will take a sequence of polynomials and follow their roots. For that to work, the roots must not escape to infinity, and the first step is a bound on the roots in terms of the coefficients. [Cauchy’s Bound for the Roots] Let n \ge 1 and let p(x) = x^n + c_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + c_1x + c_0 \in 
C[x] be monic. Put M = \max_{0 \le j \le n-1}\lvert c_jvert. Then every root z \in 
C of p satisfies \lvert zvert \le 1 + M . A root satisfies z^n = -(c_{n-1}z^{n-1} + \dots + c_0). If \lvert zvert is large, the left side is much bigger than every single term on the right, and there are only n terms; summing the geometric series on the right makes this precise. If \lvert zvert \le 1 there is nothing to prove, so suppose \lvert zvert > 1. Since p(z) = 0, we have z^n = -\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_jz^j, and the triangle inequality (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality) gives \lvert zvert^n \le M\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\lvert zvert^j = M\, rac{\lvert zvert^n - 1}{\lvert zvert - 1} \le M\, rac{\lvert zvert^n}{\lvert zvert - 1} , where the equality sums a geometric series with ratio \lvert zvert 
e 1. Dividing by \lvert zvert^n > 0 and multiplying by \lvert zvert - 1 > 0 gives \lvert zvert - 1 \le M, as claimed. The bound depends only on the size of the coefficients, and that is what the next proof needs. Polynomials whose coefficients stay bounded have roots that stay bounded. Show that the 1 in the bound cannot be dropped: find a monic polynomial with a root of modulus larger than M = \max_j\lvert c_jvert. Take p(x) = x^2 - x - 1, with M = 1. Its roots are (1 \pm \sqrt5)/2, and (1 + \sqrt5)/2 \approx 1.618 > 1. The bound 1 + M = 2 does hold. The roots move continuously Here is the theorem of Chapter 16 (@thm-roots-depend-continuously), restated in full under its own label, since from now on it is a proved result. [Continuous Dependence of the Roots on the Coefficients] Let n \ge 1 and let p(x) = x^n + c_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + c_1x + c_0 \in 
C[x] be monic, with roots \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n \in 
C listed with multiplicity. Let \varepsilon > 0. Then there is \delta > 0 with the following property. If q(x) = x^n + b_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + b_1x + b_0 is monic of the same degree n and \lvert b_j - c_jvert < \delta for every j, then the roots 
u_1, \dots, 
u_n of q, listed with multiplicity, can be numbered so that \lvert 
u_i - \mu_ivert < \varepsilon for i = 1, \dots, n. The hard direction, from coefficients to roots, has no formula. The easy direction does: expanding (x - 
u_1)\cdots(x - 
u_n) writes each coefficient as a polynomial in the roots. So argue by contradiction and let compactness supply the missing formula. ① A bad sequence q_k 	o p has root vectors that stay bounded, by Cauchy’s bound. ② By compactness, a subsequence of root vectors converges to some \vnu \in 
C^n. ③ Coefficients are polynomials in roots, so (x - 
u_1)\cdots(x - 
u_n) has the limiting coefficients, which are those of p. ④ Unique factorization says \vnu is a rearrangement of (\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n). ⑤ That rearrangement is a good numbering for the late q_k, which were supposed to have none. Suppose the conclusion fails for some \varepsilon > 0. Then no \delta works; in particular \delta = 1/k fails for every integer k \ge 1. So there is a monic q_k(x) = x^n + \sum_{j<n}b_j^{(k)}x^j with \lvert b_j^{(k)} - c_jvert < 1/k for every j, whose roots admit no numbering within \varepsilon of \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n. By @cor-complex-polynomial-splits (a), q_k = (x - 
u_1^{(k)})\cdots(x - 
u_n^{(k)}) for some \vnu^{(k)} = (
u_1^{(k)}, \dots, 
u_n^{(k)}) \in 
C^n, which lists the roots of q_k with multiplicity. The root vectors are bounded. Put M = \max_j\lvert c_jvert. Then \lvert b_j^{(k)}vert < M + 1, so by @lem-cauchy-root-bound every \lvert 
u_i^{(k)}vert \le M + 2, and 
orm{\vnu^{(k)}}_2 \le \sqrt n\,(M + 2). By compactness, fact (A3), the sequence (\vnu^{(k)}) has a subsequence (\vnu^{(k_l)})_{l \ge 1} converging in 
C^n to some \vnu = (
u_1, \dots, 
u_n). Since \lvert 
u_i^{(k_l)} - 
u_ivert \le 
orm{\vnu^{(k_l)} - \vnu}_2, each coordinate converges: 
u_i^{(k_l)} 	o 
u_i. The limit is a root vector of p. Expanding the product (x - z_1)\cdots(x - z_n) gives x^n + \sum_{j<n}s_j(z_1, \dots, z_n)x^j, where each s_j is a fixed polynomial with integer coefficients in z_1, \dots, z_n (it is \pm the sum of all products of n - j of the z_i with distinct indices). Hence b_j^{(k)} = s_j(\vnu^{(k)}). Along the subsequence, the algebra of limits gives s_j(\vnu^{(k_l)}) 	o s_j(\vnu), while b_j^{(k_l)} 	o c_j by the choice of q_k. Limits are unique, so s_j(\vnu) = c_j for every j, that is, (x - 
u_1)(x - 
u_2)\cdots(x - 
u_n) = p(x) = (x - \mu_1)(x - \mu_2)\cdots(x - \mu_n) . Each factor x - a is monic of degree 1, hence irreducible, so both sides are factorizations of p into monic irreducibles. By the uniqueness in @thm-unique-factorization-polynomials (b), there is a permutation \pi of \{1, \dots, n\} with 
u_{\pi(i)} = \mu_i for every i. The contradiction. For each i, 
u_{\pi(i)}^{(k_l)} 	o 
u_{\pi(i)} = \mu_i, so there is L_i with \lvert 
u_{\pi(i)}^{(k_l)} - \mu_ivert < \varepsilon for all l \ge L_i. Take l \ge \max_i L_i. Then the list 
u_{\pi(1)}^{(k_l)}, \dots, 
u_{\pi(n)}^{(k_l)} is a numbering of the roots of q_{k_l}, with multiplicity, within \varepsilon of \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n. This contradicts the choice of q_{k_l}, and proves the theorem. Chapter 16 quoted this statement as @thm-roots-depend-continuously and left its proof to this section. The proof needed nothing beyond compactness and unique factorization, and @cor-eigenvalues-continuous, with everything Chapter 16 built on it, now rests on a proved theorem. Each hypothesis of the theorem did a job in the proof. Monic of the same degree gave both the bound on the roots and the factorization of q_k with exactly n linear factors. Numbered so that is where the permutation \pi went. It was produced by unique factorization and depends on the subsequence, which is exactly the freedom that @prp-no-continuous-root-selection says cannot be removed. The proof is an instance of a move worth naming: compactness plus uniqueness. To show that x depends continuously on y when only the inverse relation y = F(x) is explicit, take a sequence, extract a convergent subsequence by compactness, and use the uniqueness of the solution of y = F(x) to identify its limit. Here F sends a root vector to the coefficients, and “unique” means unique up to order. How far: Elsner’s bound The theorem says that a small enough perturbation moves the roots a little, and it gives no rate. Chapter 16’s example @exm-jordan-block-perturbation showed that no bound of the form L
orm{\E} can hold. What does hold, for every matrix, is a bound by the n-th root of 
orm{\E}. The proof bounds one determinant in two ways: from below by the eigenvalues, and from above by Hadamard’s inequality. [Elsner’s Spectral Variation Bound] Let \A, \B \in M_n(
C), and let \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n be the eigenvalues of \A. Then every eigenvalue \mu of \B satisfies \min_{1 \le i \le n}\lvert \lambda_i - \muvert \le  igl(
orm{\A}_2 + 
orm{\B}_2 igr)^{1 - 1/n}\,
orm{\A - \B}_2^{1/n} . (For n = 1 the first factor is 1.) The quantity \prod_i\lvert \lambda_i - \muvert is \lvert \det(\A - \mu\I)vert, and it is at least the n-th power of the smallest factor. Bound the determinant above by Hadamard’s inequality, after rotating to an orthonormal basis whose first vector is an eigenvector \cvec{x} of \B. The first column is then (\A - \mu\I)\cvec{x} = (\A - \B)\cvec{x}, which is small. The other n - 1 columns are merely bounded. So one small factor meets n - 1 bounded ones, and taking n-th roots produces the exponent 1/n. Let \cvec{x} be an eigenvector of \B for \mu with 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 = 1. By @cor-extend-orthonormal-basis, extend (\cvec{x}) to an orthonormal basis (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_n) of 
C^n with \cvec{u}_1 = \cvec{x}, and let \U be the unitary matrix with these columns. Then \U^{*}\U = \I, so \lvert\det\Uvert^2 = \det\U^{*}\det\U = 1 by @thm-det-multiplicative and @thm-det-transpose. By @cor-det-product-eigenvalues-again applied to \A - \mu\I, whose eigenvalues are the \lambda_i - \mu, listed with the same multiplicities (@thm-spectral-mapping, with q(x) = x - \mu), and by @thm-det-multiplicative, \prod_{i=1}^{n}\lvert \lambda_i - \muvert = \lvert\det(\A - \mu\I)vert = \lvert\det igl((\A - \mu\I)\U igr)vert . The j-th column of (\A - \mu\I)\U is (\A - \mu\I)\cvec{u}_j. Hadamard’s inequality @thm-hadamard-inequality (b) bounds the determinant by the product of the column lengths. For j = 1, (\A - \mu\I)\cvec{x} = \A\cvec{x} - \B\cvec{x} = (\A - \B)\cvec{x}, so 
orm{(\A - \mu\I)\cvec{u}_1}_2 \le 
orm{\A - \B}_2 by @thm-operator-norm-properties (a). For j \ge 2, the triangle inequality (@cor-triangle-inequality) gives 
orm{(\A - \mu\I)\cvec{u}_j}_2 \le 
orm{\A}_2 + \lvert\muvert, and \lvert\muvert \le ho(\B) \le 
orm{\B}_2 by @thm-spectral-radius-le-norm. Writing \delta = \min_i\lvert \lambda_i - \muvert, each factor on the left is at least \delta, so \delta^{n} \le \prod_{i=1}^{n}\lvert \lambda_i - \muvert \le 
orm{\A - \B}_2\, igl(
orm{\A}_2 + 
orm{\B}_2 igr)^{n-1} . Taking nonnegative n-th roots, which preserves inequalities between nonnegative reals, gives the claim. The bound needs no hypothesis on \A: no diagonalizability, no normality. It is a Hölder modulus of continuity with exponent 1/n. The next example shows that the exponent cannot be improved, and that is the quantitative form of the instability that Chapter 10 §03 warned about. [The Jordan block meets Elsner’s bound] Let n \ge 2 and 0 < \varepsilon \le 1, and put \A = \J_n(0) and \B = \J_n(0) + \varepsilon\,\cvec{e}_n\cvec{e}_1	p. Compare the movement of the eigenvalues with Elsner’s bound, and show that no bound of the form C(
orm{\A}_2 + 
orm{\B}_2)^{1-\alpha}
orm{\A - \B}_2^{\alpha} with \alpha > 1/n can hold for all \A, \B \in M_n(
C). The eigenvalues. The matrix \B is the one of @exm-jordan-block-perturbation with k = n, where p_{\B}(x) = x^n - \varepsilon was computed. So the eigenvalues of \B are the n complex n-th roots of \varepsilon, each of modulus \varepsilon^{1/n}, while \A has the single eigenvalue 0. Every eigenvalue has moved exactly \varepsilon^{1/n}. The norms. \A - \B = -\varepsilon\,\cvec{e}_n\cvec{e}_1	p has the single nonzero entry -\varepsilon, so 
orm{\A - \B}_2 = \varepsilon (@thm-operator-norm-formulas (c)). Next, \B\cvec{e}_1 = \varepsilon\cvec{e}_n and \B\cvec{e}_j = \cvec{e}_{j-1} for j \ge 2, so for \cvec{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n) 
orm{\B\cvec{x}}_2^2 = \varepsilon^2\lvert x_1vert^2 + \sum_{j=2}^{n}\lvert x_jvert^2 \le 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2^2 , with equality at \cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_2. Hence 
orm{\B}_2 = 1, and the same computation with \varepsilon = 0 gives 
orm{\A}_2 = 1. The comparison. Elsner’s bound is 2^{1 - 1/n}\varepsilon^{1/n}, and the actual movement is \varepsilon^{1/n}. The bound is attained up to a factor 2^{1 - 1/n} < 2. The exponent is optimal. If a bound C\,2^{1-\alpha}\varepsilon^{\alpha} held for these pairs with \alpha > 1/n, then \varepsilon^{1/n} \le C\,2^{1-\alpha}\varepsilon^{\alpha}, that is, \varepsilon^{1/n - \alpha} \le 2^{1-\alpha}C, for every \varepsilon \in (0, 1]. But 1/n - \alpha < 0, so the left side tends to \infty as \varepsilon 	o 0^{+}. No such C exists. Put numbers on it. For n = 16 and \varepsilon = 10^{-16}, a change in the sixteenth decimal place of one entry, the eigenvalues of \J_{16}(0) move to the circle of radius (10^{-16})^{1/16} = 10^{-1}. This pays the debt of Chapter 10 §03, whose warning said that the Jordan form is not stable under small changes of the matrix and that Chapter 20 returns to this point. Elsner’s theorem says how unstable the eigenvalues can be: never worse than 
orm{\E}^{1/n}. The Jordan block says that this worst case happens. Arithmetic that keeps about sixteen significant digits commits errors of about this relative size at every step. So what such a computation returns are, at best, the eigenvalues of some matrix within about 10^{-16} of \J_{16}(0), and these may be spread around a circle of radius 0.1. The computation cannot tell a nilpotent Jordan block from a diagonalizable matrix with sixteen distinct eigenvalues. This is the numerical reason the Jordan form is not computed in floating-point arithmetic. Counting eigenvalues in a region Section 1 showed that every eigenvalue lies in the union of the Gershgorin discs (@thm-gershgorin), and left open how many lie in each part of that union. The tool for counting is a principle in the spirit of one the proof of @prp-no-continuous-root-selection already used: an integer-valued function that varies continuously cannot change. We apply it to the number of eigenvalues in a region, while the matrix moves along a segment. [Eigenvalue Counts Are Constant Along a Path] Let \A_0, \A_1 \in M_n(
C), and put \A(t) = (1 - t)\A_0 + t\A_1 for t \in [0, 1]. Let K, L \subseteq 
C be sets at positive distance: there is d > 0 with \lvert z - wvert \ge d for all z \in K and w \in L. Suppose that for every t \in [0, 1], every eigenvalue of \A(t) lies in K \cup L. Then the number N(t) of eigenvalues of \A(t) in K, counted with algebraic multiplicity, does not depend on t. In particular N(0) = N(1). The eigenvalues cannot jump across the gap between K and L, because they move continuously and are never allowed inside the gap. So near each t_0 the count is unchanged, and a function that is locally constant on an interval is constant. The last step is the intermediate value theorem: a continuous function with integer values cannot pass from one integer to another without taking the values in between. Fix t_0 \in [0, 1]. By @cor-eigenvalues-continuous, applied to \A(t_0) with the tolerance d and the norm 
orm{\cdot}_2, there is \delta > 0 such that every \B with 
orm{\B - \A(t_0)}_2 < \delta has its eigenvalues \mu_i numbered so that \lvert \mu_i - \lambda_ivert < d, where \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n are the eigenvalues of \A(t_0). Now \A(t) - \A(t_0) = (t - t_0)(\A_1 - \A_0), so 
orm{\A(t) - \A(t_0)}_2 < \delta whenever \lvert t - t_0vert\,
orm{\A_1 - \A_0}_2 < \delta, which holds for all t close enough to t_0. For such t, number the eigenvalues \mu_i of \A(t) in this way. Both \lambda_i and \mu_i lie in K \cup L, and a point of K is at distance at least d from every point of L. Since \lvert \mu_i - \lambda_ivert < d, the two lie in the same one of the two sets: \mu_i \in K if and only if \lambda_i \in K. Counting indices, N(t) = N(t_0). So N is constant on a neighborhood of each point of [0, 1]. In particular N is continuous: if t_k 	o t_0, then N(t_k) = N(t_0) for all large k. Suppose N(s) 
e N(0) for some s \in (0, 1], say N(s) > N(0); the other case is symmetric. By the intermediate value theorem, fact (A5), applied to N on [0, s], there is t with N(t) = N(0) + 	frac12, which is not an integer. This contradiction shows N(s) = N(0) for every s \in [0, 1], and proves the lemma. Now the counting theorem. The trick is to shrink the off-diagonal part of \A to zero. At the start of the path the matrix is diagonal and its eigenvalues are the disc centers, which we can count by looking. [Gershgorin’s Counting Theorem] Let \A \in M_n(
C), let S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\} have k elements with 1 \le k \le n - 1, and put U =  igcup_{i \in S} D_i(\A), \qquad V =  igcup_{i 
otin S} D_i(\A) . If U \cap V = \emptyset, then U contains exactly k eigenvalues of \A and V contains exactly n - k, counted with algebraic multiplicity. Let \D = \diag(a_{11}, \dots, a_{nn}) and slide from \D to \A along \A(t) = (1 - t)\D + t\A. The discs of \A(t) have the same centers and radii t\,r_i(\A), so they grow from points into the discs of \A and never leave U \cup V. By @thm-gershgorin the eigenvalues never leave either, and @lem-eigenvalue-count-constant carries the count from t = 0, where it is k, to t = 1. The two unions are at positive distance. Let i \in S and j 
otin S. The discs D_i(\A) and D_j(\A) are disjoint, so \lvert a_{ii} - a_{jj}vert > r_i(\A) + r_j(\A); otherwise the point on the segment from a_{ii} to a_{jj} at distance \min\{r_i(\A), \lvert a_{ii} - a_{jj}vert\} from a_{ii} would lie in both. For z \in D_i(\A) and w \in D_j(\A), the triangle inequality (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality) gives \lvert z - wvert \ge \lvert a_{ii} - a_{jj}vert - r_i(\A) - r_j(\A) > 0 . Call the middle quantity d_{ij}. The minimum d of the finitely many d_{ij} is positive, and every point of U is at distance at least d from every point of V. The path. Let \D = \diag(a_{11}, \dots, a_{nn}) and \A(t) = (1 - t)\D + t\A for t \in [0, 1]. The diagonal entries of \A(t) are the a_{ii}, and its off-diagonal entries are t\,a_{ij}, so r_i(\A(t)) = t\,r_i(\A) \le r_i(\A) and D_i(\A(t)) \subseteq D_i(\A). By @thm-gershgorin applied to \A(t), every eigenvalue of \A(t) lies in  igcup_i D_i(\A(t)) \subseteq U \cup V. By @lem-eigenvalue-count-constant with K = U and L = V, the number of eigenvalues of \A(t) in U is the same at t = 0 and at t = 1. The count at t = 0. \A(0) = \D is diagonal, so p_{\D}(x) = \prod_i(x - a_{ii}) by @thm-det-triangular, and its eigenvalue list is a_{11}, \dots, a_{nn}. For i \in S, a_{ii} is the center of D_i(\A), so a_{ii} \in U. For i 
otin S, a_{ii} \in V, hence a_{ii} 
otin U. So exactly k entries of the list lie in U. Therefore \A(1) = \A has exactly k eigenvalues in U. All n eigenvalues lie in U \cup V, and U \cap V = \emptyset, so the other n - k lie in V. This proves the theorem. The case k = 1 is the one used most, and for a real matrix it says something about reality as well. [An Isolated Disc Holds One Eigenvalue] Let \A \in M_n(
C) with n \ge 2, and suppose D_i(\A) is disjoint from D_j(\A) for every j 
e i. 1. D_i(\A) contains exactly one eigenvalue of \A, and it is algebraically simple. 2. If \A is real, that eigenvalue is real, and it lies in the interval [a_{ii} - r_i(\A), a_{ii} + r_i(\A)]. (a) Take S = \{i\}. Then U = D_i(\A) is disjoint from the union V of the other discs, because it is disjoint from each of them. By @thm-gershgorin-counting, D_i(\A) contains exactly one eigenvalue counted with algebraic multiplicity, so that eigenvalue \lambda has algebraic multiplicity 1. (b) Suppose \lambda 
otin 
R. By @thm-real-matrix-complex-eigenvalues, \conj{\lambda} 
e \lambda is also an eigenvalue of \A. The center a_{ii} is real, so \lvert \conj{\lambda} - a_{ii}vert = \lvert \conj{\lambda - a_{ii}}vert = \lvert \lambda - a_{ii}vert \le r_i(\A), and \conj{\lambda} \in D_i(\A) too. Then D_i(\A) contains two distinct eigenvalues, contradicting (a). So \lambda is real, and a real number within r_i(\A) of a_{ii} lies in the stated interval. Scaling (@prp-gershgorin-scaling) and counting work together. Scaling moves the radii around without changing the eigenvalues, and a disc that scaling manages to isolate then holds exactly one eigenvalue. [Isolating a real eigenvalue by scaling] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 7 & 3 & -1 \ 0 & -1 & -3 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . Show that \A has exactly one eigenvalue \lambda with \lvert \lambda - 7vert \le 2, and that it is real. The unscaled discs do not decide it. The row radii are r_1 = 4, r_2 = 3, r_3 = 2, so the discs are \lvert z - 7vert \le 4, \lvert z + 1vert \le 3, and \lvert z - 1vert \le 2. The first and the third meet at z = 3, since 7 - 1 = 4 + 2. So no disc is isolated, and @thm-gershgorin-counting does not apply. Scale. Take \D = \diag(2, 1, 1). By @prp-gershgorin-scaling, \D^{-1}\A\D has the same eigenvalues as \A, and its (i, j) entry is a_{ij}d_j/d_i: \D^{-1}\A\D =  egin{pmatrix} 7 & 3/2 & -1/2 \ 0 & -1 & -3 \ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . Its discs are \lvert z - 7vert \le 2, \lvert z + 1vert \le 3, and \lvert z - 1vert \le 3. The first is disjoint from the other two, because 7 - (-1) = 8 > 2 + 3 and 7 - 1 = 6 > 2 + 3. Count. By @cor-isolated-gershgorin-disc, applied to the real matrix \D^{-1}\A\D, the disc \lvert z - 7vert \le 2 contains exactly one eigenvalue, it is simple and real, and it lies in [5, 9]. The other two eigenvalues lie in \lvert z + 1vert \le 3 or \lvert z - 1vert \le 3, outside [5, 9]. A check by hand. Expanding along the first column, p_{\A}(x) = x^3 - 7x^2 + 3x - 4. Then p_{\A}(5) = -39 < 0 and p_{\A}(9) = 185 > 0, consistent with a real root in (5, 9). (It is about 6.64. The other two roots are the nonreal pair 0.18 \pm 0.75i, approximately, so here Gershgorin has isolated the only real eigenvalue.) A real 3 	imes 3 matrix has three pairwise disjoint Gershgorin discs. What can you say about its eigenvalues, and is it diagonalizable? By @cor-isolated-gershgorin-disc, each disc contains exactly one eigenvalue, which is real. The discs are disjoint, so the three eigenvalues are distinct and real, and the matrix is diagonalizable over 
R by @cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable. The count is for the union, not for each disc in it. Take \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 4 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 10 \end{psmallmatrix}. Its discs are \lvert zvert \le 1, \lvert zvert \le 4, and the single point \{10\}. The union of the first two is disjoint from the third, and it does contain two eigenvalues, \pm 2. But both lie in the second disc, and the first disc contains none. Inside a cluster of overlapping discs, the counting theorem says nothing about the individual discs. From one-sided to matched Elsner’s bound is one-sided. It says that every eigenvalue of \B is near some eigenvalue of \A, and it does not forbid two eigenvalues of \B from crowding near the same eigenvalue of \A while another eigenvalue of \A is left alone. The counting lemma turns it into a statement about a numbering. The price is a factor that grows with n. [Elsner’s Matching Bound] Let \A, \B \in M_n(
C) have eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n and \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n, and put R =  igl(
orm{\A}_2 + 
orm{\B}_2 igr)^{1 - 1/n}\,
orm{\A - \B}_2^{1/n} . Then the \mu_i can be numbered so that \lvert \lambda_i - \mu_ivert \le (2n - 1)R for every i. Slide from \A to \B along a segment. By @thm-elsner-spectral-variation, every matrix on the way has its eigenvalues in the discs of radius R about the \lambda_i. Group those discs into clusters that do not touch one another. By @lem-eigenvalue-count-constant a cluster built from m of the \lambda_i holds exactly m eigenvalues of \B, so we can pair within clusters. A cluster of m discs has diameter at most 2mR, which gives the factor 2n - 1. The conclusion is symmetric in \A and \B, and so is R, so we may assume 
orm{\A}_2 \le 
orm{\B}_2. For t \in [0, 1] put \A(t) = (1 - t)\A + t\B. Then 
orm{\A(t)}_2 \le (1 - t)
orm{\A}_2 + t
orm{\B}_2 \le 
orm{\B}_2 and 
orm{\A - \A(t)}_2 = t
orm{\A - \B}_2 \le 
orm{\A - \B}_2. By @thm-elsner-spectral-variation applied to \A and \A(t), and since the exponents 1 - 1/n and 1/n are nonnegative, every eigenvalue of \A(t) lies within R of some \lambda_i. Clusters. Call indices i and j linked if \lvert \lambda_i - \lambda_jvert \le 2R, and put two indices in the same cluster if a chain of links joins them. The clusters partition \{1, \dots, n\}. For a cluster C let K_C be the set of z with \lvert z - \lambda_ivert \le R for some i \in C, and let L_C be the union of the K_{C'} for the other clusters C'. If i \in C and j 
otin C, then i and j are not linked, so for z within R of \lambda_i and w within R of \lambda_j, \lvert z - wvert \ge \lvert \lambda_i - \lambda_jvert - 2R > 0 . Taking the minimum over the finitely many such pairs, K_C and L_C are at positive distance; and if C is the only cluster, L_C is empty, there is no pair to check, and the requirement holds with any d > 0. Every eigenvalue of every \A(t) lies in K_C \cup L_C. Counting. At t = 0 the eigenvalues are the \lambda_j. Those with j \in C lie in K_C, and the others lie in L_C, hence not in K_C; so \A(0) has exactly \lvert Cvert eigenvalues in K_C. By @lem-eigenvalue-count-constant, so does \A(1) = \B. Each \mu lies in exactly one K_C, since the K_C are pairwise disjoint and cover every eigenvalue. So we may number the \mu’s so that, for each cluster C, those in K_C receive the indices in C. Distances. Let i \in C, with m = \lvert Cvert. Since \mu_i \in K_C, there is j \in C with \lvert \mu_i - \lambda_jvert \le R. A chain of links from j to i inside C can be chosen without repeating an index, so it has at most m - 1 links, each of length at most 2R, and \lvert \lambda_j - \lambda_ivert \le 2(m - 1)R. Hence \lvert \mu_i - \lambda_ivert \le R + 2(m - 1)R = (2m - 1)R \le (2n - 1)R . This proves the theorem. The factor 2n - 1 is not the best possible, and bounds with a factor independent of n are known; we will not need them. What matters is the shape: a matching distance of order 
orm{\A - \B}^{1/n}, with no hypothesis on either matrix. Sections 4 and 5 replace the exponent 1/n by 1, and the price is a hypothesis on \A: diagonalizable in Section 4, and normal in Section 5. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State @thm-roots-continuous, including both hypotheses on q. 2. Which imported fact of analysis does the proof of @thm-roots-continuous use, and at which step? Which one does @lem-eigenvalue-count-constant use? 3. True or false: if 
orm{\B - \A}_2 \le 10^{-8}, then every eigenvalue of \B lies within 10^{-8} of an eigenvalue of \A. Justify your answer. 4. True or false: if \A \in M_3(
C) and D_1(\A) \cup D_2(\A) is disjoint from D_3(\A), then D_1(\A) contains exactly one eigenvalue. Justify your answer. 5. What is the difference between the conclusions of @thm-elsner-spectral-variation and @thm-elsner-matching? (a) See @thm-roots-continuous. The polynomial q must be monic and of the same degree n as p. (b) Compactness, fact (A3), supplies a convergent subsequence of the bounded root vectors \vnu^{(k)}. The lemma uses the intermediate value theorem, fact (A5), to show that a locally constant integer-valued function on [0, 1] is constant. (c) False. Take \A = \J_2(0) and \B = \J_2(0) + 10^{-8}\cvec{e}_2\cvec{e}_1	p, so 
orm{\B - \A}_2 = 10^{-8}. By @exm-jordan-root-perturbation with n = 2, the eigenvalues of \B are \pm 10^{-4}, at distance 10^{-4} from the only eigenvalue 0 of \A. (d) False. In the warning after @cor-isolated-gershgorin-disc, D_1 \cup D_2 is disjoint from D_3 = \{10\}, yet D_1 = \{\lvert zvert \le 1\} contains neither eigenvalue \pm 2. The counting theorem counts in the union. (e) The first is one-sided: every eigenvalue of \B is within R of some eigenvalue of \A, and several may be near the same one. The second gives a numbering pairing each \mu_i with its own \lambda_i, within (2n - 1)R. B. Practice [B1: Cauchy’s bound] Let p(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 12. 1. Use @lem-cauchy-root-bound to bound the moduli of the roots of p. 2. Find the roots exactly, and compare. (a) Here M = \max\{3, 4, 12\} = 12, so every root has \lvert zvert \le 13. (b) p(x) = x^2(x - 3) + 4(x - 3) = (x - 3)(x^2 + 4), so the roots are 3 and \pm 2i, of moduli 3 and 2. The bound 13 is true but crude, because the constant term 12 dominates M. [B2: Counting with discs] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 10 & 1 & -1 \ 1 & 2 & 2 \ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . 1. Show that \A has exactly one eigenvalue \lambda_1 with \lvert \lambda_1 - 10vert \le 2, and that it is real. 2. Explain why the Gershgorin discs cannot decide whether the other two eigenvalues are real. 3. Use the trace to locate the sum of the other two eigenvalues in an interval. (a) The row radii are r_1 = 2, r_2 = 3, r_3 = 2, so the discs are \lvert z - 10vert \le 2, \lvert z - 2vert \le 3, and \lvert z - 1vert \le 2. The first is disjoint from the other two, since 10 - 2 = 8 > 2 + 3 and 10 - 1 = 9 > 2 + 2. By @cor-isolated-gershgorin-disc, it contains exactly one eigenvalue, which is simple, real, and in [8, 12]. (b) The other two eigenvalues lie in \{\lvert z - 2vert \le 3\} \cup \{\lvert z - 1vert \le 2\}, a union of two overlapping discs that contains both real and nonreal points. The counting theorem only says that this union holds two eigenvalues. A conjugate pair and two real numbers are both consistent with that. (In fact they are the nonreal pair 1.43 \pm 1.99i, approximately.) (c) By @cor-trace-sum-eigenvalues-again, \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 = 	r\A = 13. Since 8 \le \lambda_1 \le 12, the sum \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 = 13 - \lambda_1 is real and lies in [1, 5]. C. Going deeper [C1: Stability is an open condition] 1. Let p be monic of degree n with every root in the open disc \{\lvert zvert < 1\}. Prove that there is \delta > 0 such that every monic q of degree n whose coefficients are within \delta of those of p also has every root in \{\lvert zvert < 1\}. 2. Deduce that the set of \A \in M_n(
C) with ho(\A) < 1 is open: for each such \A there is \eta > 0 with ho(\B) < 1 whenever 
orm{\B - \A}_2 < \eta. (a) Let \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n be the roots of p and put \varepsilon = 1 - \max_i\lvert \mu_ivert, which is positive since there are finitely many roots, each of modulus less than 1. Let \delta be given by @thm-roots-continuous for this \varepsilon. If q is within \delta, number its roots so that \lvert 
u_i - \mu_ivert < \varepsilon. Then \lvert 
u_ivert < \lvert \mu_ivert + \varepsilon \le 1 for every i. (b) Let ho(\A) < 1, so every root of p_{\A} lies in \{\lvert zvert < 1\} (@def-spectral-radius). Take \delta from (a) for p = p_{\A}. The coefficients of p_{\B} are polynomials in the entries of \B, as noted after @lem-entrywise-polynomial-continuous, so that lemma gives \eta > 0 such that 
orm{\B - \A}_2 < \eta makes every coefficient of p_{\B} within \delta of the corresponding coefficient of p_{\A}. For such \B, (a) puts every eigenvalue of \B in the open unit disc, and ho(\B) < 1 because there are finitely many of them. [C2: Why one-sided bounds do not give a matching] For lists (\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n) and (\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n) of complex numbers and r \ge 0, say that the list of \mu’s is r-close to the list of \lambda’s if every \mu_j is within r of some \lambda_i. 1. Let n = 2. Prove that if each list is r-close to the other, then the \mu_j can be numbered so that \lvert \lambda_i - \mu_ivert \le r for i = 1, 2. 2. Show that (a) fails for n = 3: give two lists of length 3, each 0-close to the other, such that every numbering has \max_i\lvert \lambda_i - \mu_ivert = 2. 3. Explain why the proof of @thm-elsner-matching needs @lem-eigenvalue-count-constant, and cannot simply apply @thm-elsner-spectral-variation twice, once in each direction. (a) By hypothesis, \lambda_2 is within r of some \mu_j; number the \mu’s so that this one is \mu_2, so \lvert \lambda_2 - \mu_2vert \le r. The other one, \mu_1, is within r of \lambda_1 or of \lambda_2. If of \lambda_1, we are done. If not, then \lvert \mu_1 - \lambda_2vert \le r and \lvert \mu_1 - \lambda_1vert > r. Now \lambda_1 is within r of some \mu_j, and not of \mu_1, so \lvert \lambda_1 - \mu_2vert \le r. Renumber by swapping \mu_1 and \mu_2. Then \lvert \lambda_1 - \mu_1vert \le r and \lvert \lambda_2 - \mu_2vert \le r. (b) Take (\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3) = (0, 2, 2) and (\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3) = (0, 0, 2). Every entry of each list occurs in the other, so each is 0-close to the other. But the \mu’s contain 0 twice and the \lambda’s only once, so every numbering pairs some \mu_i = 0 with some \lambda_i = 2, and \max_i\lvert \lambda_i - \mu_ivert = 2. (c) Applying @thm-elsner-spectral-variation to (\A, \B) and to (\B, \A) gives exactly the two-sided closeness of (a) with r = R, since R is symmetric in \A and \B. By (b), two-sided closeness does not produce a numbering once n \ge 3, because it ignores multiplicities. The counting lemma supplies the missing information: each cluster of discs holds as many eigenvalues of \B, counted with multiplicity, as it holds eigenvalues of \A. [C3: Sharpening Cauchy’s bound by rescaling] Let n \ge 1, let p(x) = x^n + c_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + c_1x + c_0 \in 
C[x] be monic, and let s > 0. 1. Prove that q(y) \coloneqq p(sy)/s^{n} is monic of degree n, with coefficients c_j/s^{\,n-j}, and that z is a root of p if and only if z/s is a root of q. Hence deduce that every root z of p satisfies \lvert zvert \le s\Bigl(1 + \max_{0 \le j \le n-1} rac{\lvert c_jvert}{s^{\,n-j}}\Bigr) . 2. Apply (a) with s = 3 to p(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 12, and compare the bound with the one @lem-cauchy-root-bound gives directly and with the roots found in @exr-continuity-of-roots-b1. (a) Substituting x = sy and dividing by s^{n} > 0, q(y) =  rac{p(sy)}{s^{n}} =  rac{s^{n}y^{n} + \sum_{j<n}c_js^{j}y^{j}}{s^{n}} = y^{n} + \sum_{j<n} rac{c_j}{s^{\,n-j}}\,y^{j} , which is monic of degree n with the stated coefficients. Since s^{n} 
e 0, the identity q(z/s) = p(z)/s^{n} shows that q(z/s) = 0 if and only if p(z) = 0. Now let z be a root of p. Then z/s is a root of q, so by @lem-cauchy-root-bound applied to q, whose coefficient maximum is M_s = \max_j\lvert c_jvert/s^{\,n-j}, we get \lvert zvert/s = \lvert z/svert \le 1 + M_s. Multiplying by s > 0 gives the bound. (b) For s = 3 the coefficients of q are -3/3 = -1, 4/9, and -12/27 = -4/9, so M_3 = 1 and every root of p has \lvert zvert \le 3(1 + 1) = 6. Applied to p itself, @lem-cauchy-root-bound gives only \lvert zvert \le 13, as in @exr-continuity-of-roots-b1 (a). The true moduli are 3 and 2, so the rescaled bound is closer, and the trade-off is visible in the formula: enlarging s shrinks every \lvert c_jvert/s^{\,n-j} but multiplies the whole bound by s.

title: 20.4 The Bauer–Fike Theorem
content:
The Bauer–Fike Theorem Section 3 bounded the movement of the eigenvalues of an arbitrary matrix by a constant times 
orm{\E}_2^{1/n}, and the Jordan block showed that nothing better holds in general. The culprit was the Jordan block itself. This section removes it by assuming that \A is diagonalizable, and the exponent 1/n becomes 1: every eigenvalue of \A + \E lies within \kappa_2(\X)

orm{\C_l\cvec{x}_l}_2^2 \le (\max_l
orm{\C_l}_2)^2
orm{\cvec{x}}_2^2. So 
orm{(\J - \mu\I)^{-1}}_2 \le \sum_{j=1}^{m}\delta^{-j}, and 1 \le  rac{	heta}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\delta^{-j} . Two cases. If \delta \ge 1, each \delta^{-j} \le \delta^{-1}, so 1 \le 	heta/\delta and \delta \le 	heta. If \delta < 1, each \delta^{-j} \le \delta^{-m}, so 1 \le 	heta\delta^{-m}, that is \delta^m \le 	heta and \delta \le 	heta^{1/m}. In both cases \delta \le \max(	heta, 	heta^{1/m}). orm{\E}_2, and the theorem is @thm-bauer-fike with p = 2. For m \ge 2 and small \E, the term 	heta^{1/m} dominates, and the eigenvalues move like the m-th root of the perturbation. That exponent is the Jordan block’s signature, and it is the answer to Chapter 10 §03’s warning that the Jordan form is not stable. Section 3’s @exm-jordan-root-perturbation shows it cannot be improved. There \A = \J_n(0), \X = \I, m = n, and

The two differ by the factor n^{1/n}, which never exceeds 3^{1/3} < 1.45. Only the size of the largest block enters, and a diagonalizable part of \A is charged the same m-th root as the defective part. Section 11 separates the eigenvalues. There a simple eigenvalue gets its own first-order condition number, and that number becomes infinite exactly when two eigenvalues merge into a Jordan block. Exercises A. By @exm-jordan-root-perturbation with n = 2, \A = \J_2(0) and \E = \varepsilon\cvec{e}_2\cvec{e}_1	p with 0 < \varepsilon < 1 give eigenvalues \pm\sqrt\varepsilon of \A + \E, at distance \sqrt\varepsilon > \varepsilon =

Then \X^{*}\X =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & q \ q & 1 \end{psmallmatrix} with q = 1/\sqrt2, with eigenvalues 1 \pm q, so \kappa_2(\X)^2 =  rac{1 + q}{1 - q} =  rac{\sqrt2 + 1}{\sqrt2 - 1} = (\sqrt2 + 1)^2 , and \kappa_2(\X) = 1 + \sqrt2 \approx 2.414. (b) By @thm-bauer-fike with p = 2, r = (1 + \sqrt2)(0.01) \approx 0.0241 works. (c) p(x) = (x - 1)(x - 3) - 0.02 = x^2 - 4x + 2.98, with roots 2 \pm \sqrt{1.02}. Each eigenvalue has moved by \sqrt{1.02} - 1 \approx 0.00995, well within r \approx 0.0241. [B2: A residual certificate] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \widehat{\cvec{x}} = (10, 9), and \mu = 3. 1. Compute the residual \cvec{r} = \A\widehat{\cvec{x}} - \mu\widehat{\cvec{x}} and \eta = 
orm{\cvec{r}}_2/

orm{\widehat{\cvec{x}}}_2 = \sqrt{181}, and \eta = \sqrt{2/181} \approx 0.105. (b) \A is real symmetric, hence normal. By @thm-residual-bound, some eigenvalue \lambda satisfies \lvert \lambda - 3vert \le \eta. The eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are real (@thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues), so \lambda \in [3 - \eta, 3 + \eta]. (In fact \lambda = 3, with eigenvector (1, 1).) [B3: A defective bound] Let \A = \J_2(3). 1. Explain why @thm-bauer-fike does not apply to \A. 2. Use @thm-bauer-fike-defective to find r such that every eigenvalue of \A + \E lies within r of 3 whenever 
orm{\E}_2 \le 10^{-4}. 3. Compute the eigenvalues of \A + 10^{-4}\cvec{e}_2\cvec{e}_1	p, and compare. (a) \A has the single eigenvalue 3 with algebraic multiplicity 2, and \A - 3\I = \J_2(0) has rank 1, so the eigenspace has dimension 1. Hence \A is not diagonalizable (@thm-diagonalization), and there is no \X to put in @thm-bauer-fike. (b) \A is its own Jordan form, so take \X = \I, with \kappa_2(\I) = 1, and m = 2. Then 	heta = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 10^{-4} = 2 	imes 10^{-4}, and \max(	heta, 	heta^{1/2}) = \sqrt2 	imes 10^{-2} \approx 0.0141. So r = \sqrt2 	imes 10^{-2} works. (c) p(x) = (x - 3)^2 - 10^{-4}, with roots 3 \pm 10^{-2}. The movement 0.01 is below r \approx 0.0141, and it is a hundred times the size 10^{-4} of the perturbation: the square root at work. C. Going deeper [C1: One eigenvalue in each disc] Let \A = \X\vLambda\X^{-1} have n distinct eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, put g = \min_{i 
e j}\lvert \lambda_i - \lambda_jvert, and let \E satisfy r = \kappa_2(\X)

Deduce that if \A and \E are real and every \lambda_i is real, then every eigenvalue of \A + \E is real. Hint: apply @lem-eigenvalue-count-constant to the path \A + t\E. e j, z \in Q_i, and w \in Q_j, the triangle inequality (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality) gives \lvert z - wvert \ge \lvert \lambda_i - \lambda_jvert - 2r \ge g - 2r > 0. So Q_i and the union L_i of the other Q_j are at distance at least g - 2r > 0. For t \in [0, 1], @thm-bauer-fike applied to \A and t\E puts every eigenvalue of \A + t\E within \kappa_2(\X)

The path \A + t\E = (1 - t)\A + t(\A + \E) is of the form in @lem-eigenvalue-count-constant, so the number of eigenvalues in Q_i is the same at t = 0 and t = 1. At t = 0 it is 1: \lambda_i \in Q_i, and \lambda_j \in Q_j \subseteq L_i is not in Q_i for j 
e i. So \A + \E has exactly one eigenvalue in each Q_i. The Q_i are pairwise disjoint, so these n eigenvalues are distinct, and \A + \E is diagonalizable by @cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable. (b) Let \mu be the eigenvalue of \A + \E in Q_i. Since \lambda_i is real, \lvert \conj{\mu} - \lambda_ivert = \lvert \mu - \lambda_ivert \le r, so \conj{\mu} \in Q_i. Since \A + \E is real, \conj{\mu} is also an eigenvalue (@thm-real-matrix-complex-eigenvalues). By (a), Q_i holds only one eigenvalue, so \conj{\mu} = \mu, and \mu is real.
