title: 20.5 The Hoffman–Wielandt Theorem
content:
The Hoffman–Wielandt Theorem Section 04 showed that for a normal \A, every eigenvalue of \A + \E lies within 
orm{\E}_2 of some eigenvalue of \A. That answers “how far”, one perturbed eigenvalue at a time. It does not answer “which goes where”: it never says that the eigenvalues of the two matrices can be paired off, each with a partner of its own. This section proves that for two normal matrices they can, with the total squared distance of the pairs bounded by 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2. The proof is short once the right tool is in hand, and the tool is Birkhoff’s theorem from Chapter 19 §07. We then sharpen the result for Hermitian matrices, where the pairing is simply the decreasing order, and show that without normality the inequality fails for every pairing. Throughout, the field is 
C, and eigenvalues are listed with algebraic multiplicity. For a Hermitian matrix, \lambda_1(\A) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(\A) is the decreasing list, as in Chapter 17. One-sided bounds do not pair eigenvalues Recall @cor-bauer-fike-normal (a): if \A \in M_n(
C) is normal and \E \in M_n(
C) is arbitrary, then every eigenvalue \mu of \A + \E satisfies \min_i\lvert\lambda_i - \muvert \le 
orm{\E}_2, where \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n are the eigenvalues of \A. The statement starts from a perturbed eigenvalue and finds a partner for it. Nothing in it stops two perturbed eigenvalues from choosing the same partner. Here is the smallest case. Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \A + \E =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac15 & 0 \ 0 & 	frac25 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \E =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac15 & 0 \ 0 & -	frac35 \end{pmatrix} . Then 
orm{\E}_2 = 	frac35, and both perturbed eigenvalues are within 	frac35 of an eigenvalue of \A, as the corollary promises. But if each one goes to its nearest eigenvalue of \A, both go to 0: the distances are 	frac15 and 	frac25 to 0, against 	frac45 and 	frac35 to 1. The nearest-eigenvalue map is not a bijection, and the eigenvalue 1 is left without a partner. A pairing does exist here, 0 \leftrightarrow 	frac15 and 1 \leftrightarrow 	frac25, with distances 	frac15 and 	frac35, but finding it was not the corollary’s doing. Why ask for a pairing at all? Because it is what “the eigenvalues move a little” should mean. Chapter 16’s @cor-eigenvalues-continuous is a pairing statement: the eigenvalues of a nearby matrix can be numbered so that each is close to its counterpart. It gives no rate. For Hermitian matrices, Weyl’s @cor-weyl-perturbation gives a pairing with a rate, and the pairing is the decreasing order. For normal matrices with complex eigenvalues there is no decreasing order, and the pairing has to be found. To say this precisely, let \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n and \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n be two lists of complex numbers. A pairing of them is a permutation \sigma \in S_n, which matches \lambda_i with \mu_{\sigma(i)}. Its cost, in the sense of this section, is the sum of squared distances \sum_{i=1}^{n}\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_{\sigma(i)}vert^2 . A one-sided statement, “every \mu_j is within r of some \lambda_i”, is a statement about sets. A pairing is a statement about lists with multiplicity, and it is strictly stronger. Let \A = \diag(0, 0, 1) and \B = \diag(0, 1, 1). Show that every eigenvalue of \B is an eigenvalue of \A and conversely, so each one-sided distance is 0. What is the smallest possible largest distance \max_i\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_{\sigma(i)}vert over all pairings \sigma? Both matrices have the eigenvalue set \{0, 1\}, so every eigenvalue of either one is at distance 0 from an eigenvalue of the other. As lists, \A has (0, 0, 1) and \B has (0, 1, 1). Any pairing must send one of the two 0’s of \A to a 1 of \B, since \B has only one 0. So every pairing has largest distance at least 1, and the identity pairing attains 1. Sets that agree can still be far apart as lists. Birkhoff turns weights into a permutation The proof below will produce a sum of the form \sum_{i,j}s_{ij}c_{ij}, in which c_{ij} = \lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert^2 is the cost of pairing \lambda_i with \mu_j, and the weights s_{ij} form a doubly stochastic matrix. Such a sum is a fractional pairing: every \lambda_i spreads a total weight 1 over the \mu_j, and every \mu_j receives a total weight 1. A genuine pairing is the special case where each weight is 0 or 1, that is, where (s_{ij}) is a permutation matrix. The lemma says that fractional pairings never beat the best genuine one. Recall @def-doubly-stochastic: \S \in M_n(
R) is doubly stochastic if its entries are nonnegative and every row and every column adds up to 1; the set of such matrices is \Omega_n. Recall also @def-permutation-matrix: \P_\sigma is the matrix whose j-th column is \cvec{e}_{\sigma(j)}, so its entry in position (\sigma(j), j) is 1 for each j, and all its other entries are 0. [A Fractional Pairing Is Never Cheaper] Let \C = (c_{ij}) \in M_n(
R) and \S = (s_{ij}) \in \Omega_n. Then there is a permutation \sigma \in S_n with \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_{\sigma(j)j} \ \le\ \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} s_{ij}c_{ij} . Write f(\X) = \sum_{i,j}x_{ij}c_{ij}, a linear function of \X. Birkhoff’s theorem writes \S as an average of permutation matrices, so f(\S) is the same average of the numbers f(\P_\sigma), and an average is at least its smallest term. Let f(\X) = \sum_{i,j}x_{ij}c_{ij} for \X \in M_n(
R); it is linear in \X. By @thm-birkhoff, \S = \sum_{k=1}^{m}t_k\P_{\sigma_k} for some permutations \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_m and weights t_k \ge 0 with \sum_k t_k = 1. By linearity, f(\S) = \sum_{k=1}^{m}t_k\,f(\P_{\sigma_k}) \ \ge\ \Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^{m}t_k\Bigr)\min_{k}f(\P_{\sigma_k}) = \min_{k}f(\P_{\sigma_k}) , where the inequality uses t_k \ge 0. Let \sigma be a \sigma_k attaining the minimum. The only nonzero entries of \P_\sigma are the 1’s in positions (\sigma(j), j), so f(\P_\sigma) = \sum_j c_{\sigma(j)j}. Hence \sum_j c_{\sigma(j)j} \le f(\S), as claimed. In the language of Chapter 18, this is @cor-linear-max-at-extreme applied to \Omega_n. With the Frobenius inner product \inner{\X}{\C} = 	r(\C	p\X) = \sum_{i,j}x_{ij}c_{ij}, the function f is \X \mapsto \inner{\X}{\C}. The set \Omega_n is nonempty, compact, and convex (Chapter 18 §08), so the minimum of f over it is attained at an extreme point, and by @thm-birkhoff the extreme points are the permutation matrices. The proof above uses the second form of Birkhoff’s theorem instead, so no compactness argument appears in it. The theorem We can now prove that two normal matrices have a pairing of their eigenvalues whose cost is at most the squared Frobenius distance between the matrices. [Hoffman–Wielandt Theorem] Let \A, \B \in M_n(
C) be normal, with eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n and \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n respectively, each listed with algebraic multiplicity in any order. Then there is a permutation \sigma \in S_n with \sum_{i=1}^{n} igl\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_{\sigma(i)} igrvert^2 \ \le\ 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 . Step roadmap. ① Diagonalize both. The spectral theorem gives \A = \U\vLambda\U^{*} and \B = \V\M\V^{*} with \U, \V unitary and \vLambda, \M diagonal. The two orthonormal bases of eigenvectors are different, and the unitary \W = \U^{*}\V records how they sit relative to each other. ② Compute the distance. The Frobenius norm does not see unitary factors, so 
orm{\A - \B}_F = 
orm{\vLambda\W - \W\M}_F. The (i,j) entry of \vLambda\W - \W\M is (\lambda_i - \mu_j)w_{ij}, so 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = \sum_{i,j}\lvert w_{ij}vert^2\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert^2. This is a fractional pairing with weights \lvert w_{ij}vert^2. ③ Round it. The weights form a doubly stochastic matrix, because the rows and the columns of a unitary matrix are unit vectors. The lemma replaces the fractional pairing by a genuine one that costs no more. By @cor-spectral-complex-matrix, since \A and \B are normal, there are unitary \U, \V \in \Unit(n) with \A = \U\vLambda\U^{*} , \qquad \B = \V\M\V^{*} , where \vLambda = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n) and \M = \diag(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n) in the given orders. Put \W = \U^{*}\V, which is unitary as a product of unitary matrices. Since \U^{*}\U = \I and \V^{*}\V = \I, \U^{*}(\A - \B)\V = \vLambda\U^{*}\V - \U^{*}\V\M = \vLambda\W - \W\M . By @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant, applied with the unitary factors \U^{*} on the left and \V on the right, 
orm{\A - \B}_F = 
orm{\vLambda\W - \W\M}_F. The (i,j) entry of \vLambda\W is \lambda_iw_{ij} and that of \W\M is w_{ij}\mu_j, since multiplying by a diagonal matrix on the left scales rows and on the right scales columns. Hence 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = \sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\lvert w_{ij}vert^2\,\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert^2 . {#eq-hoffman-wielandt-weights} Let \S = (s_{ij}) with s_{ij} = \lvert w_{ij}vert^2. Its entries are nonnegative. Row i adds up to \sum_j\lvert w_{ij}vert^2 = (\W\W^{*})_{ii} = 1, and column j adds up to \sum_i\lvert w_{ij}vert^2 = (\W^{*}\W)_{jj} = 1, since \W is unitary. So \S \in \Omega_n. Apply @lem-doubly-stochastic-linear-min to \S and the real matrix \C with c_{ij} = \lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert^2. It gives 	au \in S_n with \sum_{j=1}^{n}\lvert\lambda_{	au(j)} - \mu_jvert^2 \ \le\ \sum_{i,j}s_{ij}c_{ij} = 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 , the equality being @eq-hoffman-wielandt-weights. Put \sigma = 	au^{-1}. As j runs over 1, \dots, n, so does i = 	au(j), and j = \sigma(i); so the left-hand side is \sum_i\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_{\sigma(i)}vert^2. This proves the theorem. Both hypotheses were used in the first line and nowhere else: normality is what makes the diagonalizing matrices unitary. The rest of the proof is bookkeeping and Birkhoff’s theorem, which is where Chapter 19 §07’s theorem earns its keep. In words: the eigenvalues of a normal matrix, as a list with multiplicity, are a 1-Lipschitz function of the matrix, when matrices are measured in the Frobenius norm and lists by their best pairing. In particular every pair in the best pairing is within 
orm{\A - \B}_F, so each eigenvalue of \B has its own partner among those of \A within that distance. This is a matching bound, with a constant, valid for all normal matrices at once. Compare @cor-eigenvalues-continuous, which gives a matching with no constant for all matrices, and @cor-bauer-fike-normal, which gives a constant with no matching. The theorem asserts that some pairing is cheap. The proof does not say which, beyond what the lemma gives, but the cheapest of the n! pairings certainly works, since it costs no more than any other. The next example shows that a pairing chosen by any other rule can fail. [A Hermitian and a diagonal matrix] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix} i & 0 \ 0 & 2 + i \end{pmatrix} . Both are normal. Compute 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2, the cost of both pairings of the eigenvalues, and the matrix \S of the proof. Which pairings satisfy the conclusion of @thm-hoffman-wielandt? \A is real symmetric, hence Hermitian and normal, and \B is diagonal, hence normal. The eigenvalues of \A are \lambda_1 = 3 and \lambda_2 = 1, with unit eigenvectors 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1) and 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1): indeed \A(1,1) = (3,3) and \A(1,-1) = (1,-1). Those of \B are \mu_1 = i and \mu_2 = 2 + i, with eigenvectors \cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2. The distance. \A - \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 - i & 1 \ 1 & -i \end{psmallmatrix}, so 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = \lvert 2 - ivert^2 + 1 + 1 + \lvert -ivert^2 = 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 8 . The costs. The four squared distances c_{ij} = \lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert^2 are  egin{aligned} c_{11} &= \lvert 3 - ivert^2 = 10 , \qquad c_{12} = \lvert 1 - ivert^2 = 2 , \ c_{21} &= \lvert 1 - ivert^2 = 2 , \qquad c_{22} = \lvert -1 - ivert^2 = 2 . \end{aligned} The identity pairing 3 \leftrightarrow i, 1 \leftrightarrow 2 + i costs c_{11} + c_{22} = 12. The swap 3 \leftrightarrow 2 + i, 1 \leftrightarrow i costs c_{12} + c_{21} = 4. The weights. With \U = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix} and \V = \I, \W = \U^{*}, and every entry of \W has modulus 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}. So \S = 	frac12\J, and @eq-hoffman-wielandt-weights reads 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = 	frac12(10 + 2 + 2 + 2) = 8 , the average of the two costs, 	frac12(12 + 4). An average lies between its terms, so the cheaper pairing, the swap with cost 4, satisfies 4 \le 8. The identity pairing, with cost 12 > 8, does not. The theorem does not say that the given numbering works. In the example, the lists (3, 1) and (i, 2 + i), paired in the order written, cost 12 > 8 = 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2. Complex numbers have no natural order to sort by, so, unlike the Hermitian case below, there is no rule fixed in advance that always picks a good pairing. The safe reading is: the cheapest pairing satisfies the inequality. Normality cannot be dropped The proof used normality once, in its first line, to make the diagonalizing matrices unitary. For diagonalizable matrices \A = \X\vLambda\X^{-1} and \B = \Y\M\Y^{-1} with \X, \Y not unitary, @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant no longer applies, and 
orm{\A - \B}_F is no longer the norm of \vLambda\W - \W\M with \W = \X^{-1}\Y. The failure is real, not an artifact of the proof. [Every pairing fails] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} . Show that \A and \B are diagonalizable but not normal, and that the inequality of @thm-hoffman-wielandt fails for every pairing of their eigenvalues. \A is triangular with eigenvalues 1 and -1. The matrix \B has trace 0 and determinant -1 - 3 = -4, so its characteristic polynomial is x^2 - 4 and its eigenvalues are 2 and -2. Each has two distinct eigenvalues, so each is diagonalizable (@thm-diagonalization). Neither is normal:  egin{aligned} \A^{*}\A &=  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 3 & 10 \end{pmatrix} 
e  egin{pmatrix} 10 & -3 \ -3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \A\A^{*} , \ \B^{*}\B &=  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 & 10 \end{pmatrix} 
e  egin{pmatrix} 10 & -2 \ -2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \B\B^{*} . \end{aligned} The difference \A - \B has a single nonzero entry, -1 in position (2,1), so 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = 1. There are two pairings. The one that matches signs, 1 \leftrightarrow 2 and -1 \leftrightarrow -2, costs 1^2 + 1^2 = 2. The other, 1 \leftrightarrow -2 and -1 \leftrightarrow 2, costs 3^2 + 3^2 = 18. Both exceed 1, so no pairing satisfies the inequality. The entry 3 is what makes this work, and the failure is not confined to a perturbation as large as 1. Put \delta > 0 in the corner instead: \B_\delta =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 3 \ \delta & -1 \end{psmallmatrix} has determinant -1 - 3\delta and eigenvalues \pm\sqrt{1 + 3\delta}, each of which moves by \sqrt{1 + 3\delta} - 1, about 	frac32\delta for small \delta. So the cheaper pairing costs about 2 igl(	frac32\delta igr)^2 = 	frac92\delta^2, well above 
orm{\A - \B_\delta}_F^2 = \delta^2. With an entry m in place of 3 the cost is about 	frac12m^2\delta^2, so the inequality fails for small \delta as soon as m > \sqrt2. A large entry above the diagonal is exactly what Chapter 12 §11 measured as departure from normality, and it is what makes the eigenvalues sensitive. A Jordan block shows that no constant can repair the inequality. Let \A = \J_2(0) and, for \varepsilon > 0, \B_\varepsilon =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ \varepsilon & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}. Then \A has the eigenvalue 0 twice, \B_\varepsilon has characteristic polynomial x^2 - \varepsilon and eigenvalues \pm\sqrt\varepsilon, and 
orm{\A - \B_\varepsilon}_F^2 = \varepsilon^2. Both pairings cost the same, (\sqrt\varepsilon)^2 + (\sqrt\varepsilon)^2 = 2\varepsilon, and  rac{2\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^2} =  rac{2}{\varepsilon} \longrightarrow \infty \qquad (\varepsilon 	o 0^{+}) . So there is no constant K with \min_\sigma\sum_i\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_{\sigma(i)}vert^2 \le K
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 for all pairs of matrices. This is @exm-jordan-block-perturbation of Chapter 16 read in the language of pairings: the eigenvalues move like \sqrt\varepsilon while the matrix moves by \varepsilon. Diagonalizable is not enough, and one normal matrix is not enough. In @exm-hoffman-wielandt-fails both matrices are diagonalizable, and every pairing fails. Nor does it help to make just one of the two matrices normal: for \A = \J_2(0) and the Hermitian \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, with eigenvalues \pm 1, both pairings cost 1 + 1 = 2, while 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = 1. The theorem needs both matrices normal. Hermitian matrices: the pairing is the order When both matrices are Hermitian, the eigenvalues are real, and there is a natural guess for the best pairing: largest with largest, second with second, and so on. The guess is right, and the reason is a fact about real numbers alone. [The Sorted Pairing Is Cheapest] Let a_1 \ge a_2 \ge \dots \ge a_n and b_1 \ge b_2 \ge \dots \ge b_n be real numbers. Then for every \sigma \in S_n, \sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_i - b_i)^2 \ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_i - b_{\sigma(i)})^2 . Expanding the squares, \sum_i a_i^2 and \sum_i b_{\sigma(i)}^2 = \sum_j b_j^2 do not depend on \sigma, so the claim is that the cross term \sum_i a_ib_{\sigma(i)} is largest at the identity. If \sigma puts a smaller b before a larger one in two neighboring positions, swapping those two values can only increase the cross term, and it removes one inversion. Repeating the swap sorts \sigma into the identity. For every \sigma, since \sigma is a bijection, \sum_i b_{\sigma(i)}^2 = \sum_j b_j^2, and so  egin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_i - b_{\sigma(i)})^2 &= \sum_i a_i^2 + \sum_j b_j^2 - 2g(\sigma) , \ g(\sigma) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}a_ib_{\sigma(i)} . \end{aligned} It therefore suffices to show g(\sigma) \le g(\id) for every \sigma. The set S_n is finite, so g attains a maximum on it; among the permutations where it does, choose one, \sigma, with the fewest inversions (@def-inversion). Suppose \sigma 
e \id. Then \sigma(i) > \sigma(i+1) for some i, since a permutation with \sigma(1) < \sigma(2) < \dots < \sigma(n) is the identity. Let \sigma' agree with \sigma except that \sigma'(i) = \sigma(i+1) and \sigma'(i+1) = \sigma(i). Then g(\sigma') - g(\sigma) = (a_i - a_{i+1}) igl(b_{\sigma(i+1)} - b_{\sigma(i)} igr) \ \ge\ 0 , because a_i \ge a_{i+1}, and \sigma(i+1) < \sigma(i) gives b_{\sigma(i+1)} \ge b_{\sigma(i)}. So \sigma' also maximizes g. Now count inversions. The pair of positions (i, i+1) is an inversion of \sigma and not of \sigma'. A pair involving neither i nor i+1 sees the same values under both. For a position p 
otin \{i, i+1\}, the two pairs joining p to i and to i+1 compare \sigma(p) with the same two values \sigma(i), \sigma(i+1) under \sigma and under \sigma', from the same side, so together they contain the same number of inversions. Hence \sigma' has one inversion fewer than \sigma, contradicting the choice of \sigma. So \sigma = \id maximizes g, and g(\sigma) \le g(\id) for every \sigma. This proves the lemma. The move is an exchange argument: to show that an arrangement is optimal, show that repairing one local defect never makes things worse. The inequality \sum_i a_ib_{\sigma(i)} \le \sum_i a_ib_i is known as the rearrangement inequality. [Three numbers, six pairings] Let \cvec{a} = (4, 2, 1) and \cvec{b} = (3, 0, -1), both decreasing. Compute \sum_i(a_i - b_{\sigma(i)})^2 for all six \sigma \in S_3, and find the cheapest and the dearest. The nine squared distances (a_i - b_j)^2, with i the row and j the column, are  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 16 & 25 \ 1 & 4 & 9 \ 4 & 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix} . A pairing picks one entry from each row and each column. Writing \sigma by its values (\sigma(1), \sigma(2), \sigma(3)),  egin{aligned} (1,2,3) &: 1 + 4 + 4 = 9 , & (1,3,2) &: 1 + 9 + 1 = 11 , \ (2,1,3) &: 16 + 1 + 4 = 21 , & (2,3,1) &: 16 + 9 + 4 = 29 , \ (3,1,2) &: 25 + 1 + 1 = 27 , & (3,2,1) &: 25 + 4 + 4 = 33 . \end{aligned} The identity, which pairs the two sorted lists in order, costs 9, the least of the six, as @lem-sorted-pairing says. The dearest is the reversed pairing (3,2,1), at 33. One exchange step of the proof is visible here. The permutation (1,3,2) has the single inversion \sigma(2) > \sigma(3); undoing it gives the identity and lowers the cost by 2, which is 2(a_2 - a_3)(b_2 - b_3) = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 1. [Hoffman–Wielandt for Hermitian Matrices] Let \A, \B \in M_n(
C) be Hermitian. Then \sum_{i=1}^{n} igl(\lambda_i(\A) - \lambda_i(\B) igr)^2 \ \le\ 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 . Hermitian matrices are normal (@prp-self-adjoint-immediate (c)) and have real eigenvalues. By @thm-hoffman-wielandt applied to the lists \lambda_1(\A), \dots, \lambda_n(\A) and \lambda_1(\B), \dots, \lambda_n(\B), there is \sigma \in S_n with \sum_i igl(\lambda_i(\A) - \lambda_{\sigma(i)}(\B) igr)^2 \le 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2, where \lvert tvert^2 = t^2 for real t. Both lists are decreasing, so by @lem-sorted-pairing the sorted pairing costs no more than \sigma. This proves the corollary. This is the Frobenius-norm companion of Weyl’s bound. Put \E = \A - \B, Hermitian. By the spectral theorem \E = \U\D\U^{*} with \U unitary and \D = \diag(\lambda_1(\E), \dots, \lambda_n(\E)), so @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant gives 
orm{\E}_F^2 = 
orm{\D}_F^2 = \sum_i\lambda_i(\E)^2, while 
orm{\E}_2 = \max_i\lvert\lambda_i(\E)vert by @lem-hermitian-spectral-norm. So Weyl’s @cor-weyl-perturbation says \max_i\, igl\lvert\lambda_i(\A) - \lambda_i(\B) igrvert \ \le\ \max_i\,\lvert\lambda_i(\E)vert , and @cor-hoffman-wielandt-hermitian says \sum_i igl(\lambda_i(\A) - \lambda_i(\B) igr)^2 \ \le\ \sum_i\lambda_i(\E)^2 . In both, a norm of the vector of shifts \vlambda(\A) - \vlambda(\B) is bounded by the same norm of \vlambda(\E): the \infty-norm for Weyl, the 2-norm for Hoffman–Wielandt. Neither implies the other. For \E = t\I with t > 0, every eigenvalue shifts by t; Weyl’s bound t is exact for each shift, while Hoffman–Wielandt alone allows a single shift as large as 
orm{\E}_F = \sqrt n\,t. For a rank-one \E = t\,\cvec{x}\cvec{x}^{*} with 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 = 1, 
orm{\E}_F = 
orm{\E}_2 = t; Weyl lets every eigenvalue move by up to t, while Hoffman–Wielandt says that the squared shifts together use up at most t^2, so if one eigenvalue moves by t, none of the others moves at all. Lidskii’s inequality contains both. Chapter 17 §07 proved \vlambda(\A) - \vlambda(\B) \prec \vlambda(\A - \B) (the remark after @thm-lidskii-inequality), and Weyl’s bound follows from it there, as @cor-lidskii-special-cases (a). Chapter 21 shows that a majorization \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} gives \sum_i\phi(x_i) \le \sum_i\phi(y_i) for every convex \phi; with \phi(t) = t^2 this is @cor-hoffman-wielandt-hermitian again, and Chapter 21 turns the same majorization into one bound for every unitarily invariant norm. Nothing here depends on that route; the proof above goes through Birkhoff’s theorem, @thm-birkhoff. Let \A = \diag(3, 1) and \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix}. Compute 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 and both sides of @cor-hoffman-wielandt-hermitian. What does the reversed pairing \lambda_1(\A) \leftrightarrow \lambda_2(\B), \lambda_2(\A) \leftrightarrow \lambda_1(\B) cost? \A - \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix}, so 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = 4. The eigenvalues of \B are 3 and 1 (as in @exm-hoffman-wielandt-two-by-two), the same as those of \A. So the left side of the corollary is 0 \le 4: two matrices at Frobenius distance 2 can have identical spectra, and the inequality is only an upper bound. The reversed pairing costs (3 - 1)^2 + (1 - 3)^2 = 8 > 4. Even for Hermitian matrices, the pairing matters. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the Hoffman–Wielandt theorem, with its hypotheses. 2. True or false: if \A and \B are normal, the eigenvalues of \B listed in any order satisfy \sum_i\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_ivert^2 \le 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2. Justify your answer. 3. True or false: the Hoffman–Wielandt inequality holds for every pair of diagonalizable matrices. Justify your answer. 4. For normal \A and \B, what bound does the theorem give on the distance between an eigenvalue of \B and its partner? 5. Where exactly does Birkhoff’s theorem (@thm-birkhoff) enter the proof, and what would be missing without it? 6. For Hermitian \A, \B with \E = \A - \B of rank one, explain why at most one eigenvalue can move by the full amount 
orm{\E}_2. (a) If \A, \B \in M_n(
C) are normal, with eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n and \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n listed with multiplicity, then there is a permutation \sigma with \sum_i\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_{\sigma(i)}vert^2 \le 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2. (b) False. In @exm-hoffman-wielandt-two-by-two, the order (3, 1) and (i, 2 + i) costs 12 > 8. Only a suitable pairing, for instance the cheapest one, is guaranteed. (c) False. In @exm-hoffman-wielandt-fails both matrices have two distinct eigenvalues, hence are diagonalizable, and both pairings cost more than 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = 1. (d) Each summand is at most the whole sum, so \lvert\lambda_i - \mu_{\sigma(i)}vert \le 
orm{\A - \B}_F for every i, for the pairing \sigma of the theorem. (e) The proof writes 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 as \sum_{i,j}s_{ij}\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert^2 with (s_{ij}) doubly stochastic, a fractional pairing. Birkhoff’s theorem, through @lem-doubly-stochastic-linear-min, replaces it by a genuine pairing that costs no more. Without it, we would know only that a weighted average of the costs \lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert^2 is small, which does not produce a permutation. (f) For Hermitian \E of rank one, \E has at most one nonzero eigenvalue, so 
orm{\E}_F^2 = \sum_i\lambda_i(\E)^2 = 
orm{\E}_2^2. By @cor-hoffman-wielandt-hermitian the squared shifts add up to at most 
orm{\E}_2^2. If one shift equals 
orm{\E}_2 in absolute value, the others are 0. B. Practice [B1: A pair of normal matrices] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 + 2i \end{pmatrix} . Check that both are normal, compute 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 and the costs of both pairings of the eigenvalues, and compute the matrix \S of the proof of @thm-hoffman-wielandt. Hence decide which pairings satisfy the Hoffman–Wielandt inequality. \A is real symmetric, hence normal, and \B is diagonal, hence normal. \A(1,1) = (2,2) and \A(1,-1) = (-2,2), so \A has eigenvalues \lambda_1 = 2, \lambda_2 = -2 with unit eigenvectors 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, \pm1). \B has eigenvalues \mu_1 = 1, \mu_2 = -1 + 2i. \A - \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} -1 & 2 \ 2 & 1 - 2i \end{psmallmatrix}, so 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = 1 + 4 + 4 + 5 = 14. The squared distances are c_{11} = \lvert 2 - 1vert^2 = 1, c_{12} = \lvert 3 - 2ivert^2 = 13, c_{21} = \lvert -3vert^2 = 9, c_{22} = \lvert -1 - 2ivert^2 = 5. The identity pairing costs 1 + 5 = 6, and the swap costs 13 + 9 = 22. With \U = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix} and \V = \I, \W = \U^{*} has all entries of modulus 	frac1{\sqrt2}, so \S = 	frac12\J, and indeed 	frac12(1 + 13 + 9 + 5) = 14. Hence the identity pairing satisfies the inequality, 6 \le 14, and the swap does not, 22 > 14. [B2: Hermitian, compared with Weyl] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 2 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} . Compute \vlambda(\A), \vlambda(\B), 
orm{\A - \B}_F, and 
orm{\A - \B}_2. Verify @cor-hoffman-wielandt-hermitian and @cor-weyl-perturbation for this pair. Hence say which of the two bounds is closer to the truth here. \vlambda(\A) = (2, 1, 0). The top-left block of \B has eigenvalues 3 and 1 (with eigenvectors (1,1) and (1,-1)), and the last entry is -1, so \vlambda(\B) = (3, 1, -1). The shifts are \lambda_i(\B) - \lambda_i(\A) = 1, 0, -1. \E = \B - \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix}, so 
orm{\E}_F^2 = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 and 
orm{\E}_F = 2. Its top-left block has characteristic polynomial x^2 - x - 1, with roots 	frac{1 \pm \sqrt5}{2}, and its last eigenvalue is -1. By @lem-hermitian-spectral-norm, 
orm{\E}_2 = 	frac{1 + \sqrt5}{2} \approx 1.618. Hoffman–Wielandt: 1^2 + 0^2 + (-1)^2 = 2 \le 4. Weyl: each \lvert	ext{shift}vert \le 1 \le 1.618. Hence both hold. Weyl overestimates the largest shift by a factor of about 1.6; Hoffman–Wielandt overestimates the sum of squares by a factor of 2. Neither is sharp here, and neither dominates. [B3: Sorting] Let \cvec{a} = (5, 2, -1) and \cvec{b} = (4, 3, 0). Compute \sum_i(a_i - b_{\sigma(i)})^2 for all six \sigma \in S_3. Hence confirm @lem-sorted-pairing, and say which pairing is the most expensive. Write \sigma by its values (\sigma(1), \sigma(2), \sigma(3)). Then  egin{aligned} (1,2,3) &: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 , & (1,3,2) &: 1 + 4 + 16 = 21 , \ (2,1,3) &: 4 + 4 + 1 = 9 , & (2,3,1) &: 4 + 4 + 25 = 33 , \ (3,1,2) &: 25 + 4 + 16 = 45 , & (3,2,1) &: 25 + 1 + 25 = 51 . \end{aligned} The identity, which pairs the sorted lists in order, costs 3, the least of the six, as the lemma says. The most expensive is (3,2,1), which pairs the largest a with the smallest b and so on: the reversed order. Exercise C1 (b) shows this is no accident. C. Going deeper [C1: The most expensive pairing] 1. Let \A, \B \in M_n(
C) be normal, with eigenvalues \lambda_i and \mu_i. Prove that there is also a permutation \sigma with \sum_i\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_{\sigma(i)}vert^2 \ge 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2. 2. Deduce that for Hermitian \A, \B, \sum_{i=1}^{n} igl(\lambda_i(\A) - \lambda_{n+1-i}(\B) igr)^2 \ \ge\ 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 . Hint for (b): apply @lem-sorted-pairing to the list -\lambda_{n+1-i}(\B). (a) Apply @lem-doubly-stochastic-linear-min to the same \S \in \Omega_n as in the proof of @thm-hoffman-wielandt and to the matrix -\C, where c_{ij} = \lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert^2. It gives 	au with -\sum_j c_{	au(j)j} \le -\sum_{i,j}s_{ij}c_{ij} = -
orm{\A - \B}_F^2, by @eq-hoffman-wielandt-weights. Multiplying by -1 and putting \sigma = 	au^{-1}, as in that proof, gives \sum_i\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_{\sigma(i)}vert^2 \ge 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2. (b) Write a_i = \lambda_i(\A) and c_i = \lambda_i(\B), and let b_i = -c_{n+1-i}. Both (a_i) and (b_i) are decreasing, the second because c_{n+1-i} increases with i. Let \pi \in S_n, and let \sigma(i) = n + 1 - \pi(i), which is again a permutation, with b_{\sigma(i)} = -c_{\pi(i)}. By @lem-sorted-pairing, \sum_i(a_i - b_i)^2 \le \sum_i(a_i - b_{\sigma(i)})^2, that is, \sum_i(a_i + c_{n+1-i})^2 \ \le\ \sum_i(a_i + c_{\pi(i)})^2 . Expanding both sides, the squares \sum_i a_i^2 and \sum_j c_j^2 cancel, and what remains is \sum_i a_ic_{n+1-i} \le \sum_i a_ic_{\pi(i)}. Hence \sum_i(a_i - c_{\pi(i)})^2 = \sum_i a_i^2 + \sum_j c_j^2 - 2\sum_i a_ic_{\pi(i)} \ \le\ \sum_i(a_i - c_{n+1-i})^2 . So the reversed pairing i \mapsto n + 1 - i is the most expensive of all. By (a) some pairing costs at least 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2, so the most expensive one does too, which is the claim. [C2: Each eigenvalue keeps its own disc] Let \A \in M_n(
C) be normal with distinct eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, and let \delta = \min_{i 
e j}\lvert\lambda_i - \lambda_jvert. Let \B be normal with 
orm{\A - \B}_F < \delta/2. Prove that each open disc \{z : \lvert z - \lambda_ivert < \delta/2\} contains exactly one eigenvalue of \B, counted with multiplicity. Explain why @cor-bauer-fike-normal alone does not give this. The discs are pairwise disjoint: if \lvert z - \lambda_ivert < \delta/2 and \lvert z - \lambda_jvert < \delta/2 with i 
e j, the triangle inequality (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality) gives \lvert\lambda_i - \lambda_jvert < \delta, contradicting the definition of \delta. By @thm-hoffman-wielandt there is \sigma with \sum_i\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_{\sigma(i)}vert^2 \le 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 < \delta^2/4, so \lvert\lambda_i - \mu_{\sigma(i)}vert < \delta/2 for every i. Thus the entry \mu_{\sigma(i)} of the list lies in the i-th disc, and, the discs being disjoint, in no other. Since \sigma is a bijection, every entry of the list \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n is \mu_{\sigma(i)} for exactly one i. So the i-th disc contains exactly one entry of the list, namely \mu_{\sigma(i)}, which is the claim. @cor-bauer-fike-normal (a), with 
orm{\A - \B}_2 \le 
orm{\A - \B}_F < \delta/2 (@prp-spectral-vs-frobenius, or both norms being 0 if \A = \B, the case the proposition excludes), puts every eigenvalue of \B in the union of the discs, but, as in the first example of this section, it allows two of them to fall in the same disc and leave another disc empty. [C3: A Jordan block of any size] Let n \ge 2, \varepsilon > 0, \A = \J_n(0), and \B = \J_n(0) + \varepsilon\E_{n1}, where \E_{n1} is the matrix unit. 1. Show that the characteristic polynomial of \B is x^n - \varepsilon, and hence that every pairing of the eigenvalues of \A and \B costs n\varepsilon^{2/n}. 2. Deduce that the Hoffman–Wielandt inequality fails for every pairing whenever 0 < \varepsilon < n^{n/(2n-2)}, and that the ratio of the cost to 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 tends to \infty as \varepsilon 	o 0^{+}. Hint for (a): expand \det(x\I - \B) along the first column. (a) x\I - \B has x on the diagonal, -1 on the superdiagonal, -\varepsilon in position (n, 1), and zeros elsewhere. Expanding along the first column, the (1,1) entry x multiplies the determinant of an upper triangular matrix with diagonal x, which is x^{n-1}. The (n,1) entry -\varepsilon carries the sign (-1)^{n+1} and multiplies the determinant of the matrix left after deleting row n and column 1, which is lower triangular with diagonal entries -1, hence has determinant (-1)^{n-1}. So \det(x\I - \B) = x^n + (-1)^{n+1}(-\varepsilon)(-1)^{n-1} = x^n - \varepsilon . Its roots are the n complex numbers z with z^n = \varepsilon, each of modulus \varepsilon^{1/n} (these are Chapter 16’s computation in @exm-jordan-block-perturbation). Every eigenvalue of \A is 0, so every pairing costs \sum_i\lvert 0 - \mu_{\sigma(i)}vert^2 = n\,\varepsilon^{2/n}. (b) \A - \B = -\varepsilon\E_{n1}, so 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = \varepsilon^2. The inequality fails for every pairing exactly when n\varepsilon^{2/n} > \varepsilon^2, that is, \varepsilon^{2 - 2/n} < n, that is, \varepsilon < n^{1/(2 - 2/n)} = n^{n/(2n-2)}; for n = 2 this is \varepsilon < 2, as in the text. The ratio is n\varepsilon^{2/n}/\varepsilon^2 = n\varepsilon^{-(2n-2)/n}, and the exponent -(2n-2)/n is negative, so the ratio tends to \infty as \varepsilon 	o 0^{+}.

title: 20.6 Hermitian Perturbations
content:
Hermitian Perturbations For Hermitian matrices, Chapter 17 already gave the basic perturbation bound: each eigenvalue moves by at most 
orm{\E}_2, and no smaller constant is possible. This section asks what that bound does not tell us, and answers two such questions. The first is practical. A computation rarely hands us \E; it hands us an approximate eigenvector, and the question is how good the eigenvalue estimate it yields is. The answer is a residual bound, and when the eigenvalue is separated from the others it improves from linear to quadratic in the residual; that is the Kato–Temple theorem. The second concerns small eigenvalues. An absolute bound of size 
orm{\E}_2 says nothing about an eigenvalue much smaller than

By @thm-ostrowski-relative, \lambda_k(\S\A\S^{*}) = 	heta_k\lambda_k(\A) with 	heta_k > 0; a positive multiple has the same sign, and 0 goes to 0. (d) The residual bound needs nothing more. Kato–Temple needs a number \alpha or  eta beyond the neighboring eigenvalue, that is, a lower bound on the gap; in @exm-kato-temple-tridiagonal it came from interlacing. Ostrowski’s theorem is not about an approximate eigenvector, but it needs \S, or at least the extreme eigenvalues of \S\S^{*}. (e) \E = t\I moves every eigenvalue by exactly t = 
orm{\E}_2. Ostrowski’s theorem is about the perturbations \S\A\S^{*} - \A, which form a special class; \A + t\I is not of the form \S\A\S^{*} in general (for \A = \O it never is, when t 
e 0). A better bound for a smaller class contradicts nothing. B. Practice [B1: Three bounds for one estimate] Let \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 5 & 2 \ 2 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} and \cvec{x} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(3, 1). 1. Compute \mu = \cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x} and \varepsilon = 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \mu\cvec{x}}, and the interval given by @thm-hermitian-residual-bound. 2. Using @thm-cauchy-interlacing to bound \lambda_2(\A), apply @thm-kato-temple to bracket \lambda_1(\A). 3. Find the eigenvalues of \A exactly. Hence compare the actual error of \mu with \varepsilon and with the Kato–Temple bound. (a) \A(3, 1) = (17, 8), so \mu = 	frac{1}{10}(3 \cdot 17 + 1 \cdot 8) = 	frac{59}{10} = 5.9. The residual is 	frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} igl((17, 8) - 5.9(3, 1) igr) = 	frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(-0.7, 2.1), so \varepsilon^2 = 	frac{1}{10}(0.49 + 4.41) = 0.49 and \varepsilon = 0.7. Some eigenvalue lies in [5.2, 6.6]. (b) Deleting the first row and column leaves (2), so @thm-cauchy-interlacing gives \lambda_2(\A) \le 2. Also \lambda_1(\A) \ge \mu = 5.9 by @prp-rayleigh-basic. So with \alpha = 2 < \mu, no eigenvalue lies in (2, \lambda_1), and part (b) of @thm-kato-temple gives \lambda_1(\A) \ \le\ 5.9 +  rac{0.49}{5.9 - 2} = 5.9 +  rac{0.49}{3.9} \approx 6.026 . Hence 5.9 \le \lambda_1(\A) \le 6.026. (c) \A has trace 7 and determinant 6, so its eigenvalues are 6 and 1; indeed \A(2, 1) = (12, 6). The actual error of \mu is 6 - 5.9 = 0.1. The residual bound allows 0.7, seven times too much; Kato–Temple allows 0.126, within about 26\% of the truth. [B2: Ostrowski’s factors] Let \A = \diag(2, -1) and \S =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}. Compute \S\A\S^{*} and its eigenvalues, the eigenvalues of \S\S^{*}, and the factors 	heta_1, 	heta_2 of @thm-ostrowski-relative. Hence verify the theorem for this pair. \A\S^{*} = \diag(2, -1) egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 1 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix} =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 0 \ -1 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix}, and \S\A\S^{*} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} , with trace 0 and determinant -2, so eigenvalues \pm\sqrt2. Next \S\S^{*} =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}, with trace 3 and determinant 1, so eigenvalues 	frac{3 \pm \sqrt5}{2} \approx 2.618 and 0.382. Then 	heta_1 = \lambda_1(\S\A\S^{*})/\lambda_1(\A) = \sqrt2/2 \approx 0.707 and 	heta_2 = (-\sqrt2)/(-1) = \sqrt2 \approx 1.414. Both lie in [0.382, 2.618], as the theorem says, and both are positive, so the signs +, - are preserved. [B3: The Rayleigh quotient minimizes the residual] Let \A be Hermitian and \cvec{x} a unit vector, with ho = \cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x}. Prove that for every real 
u, 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - 
u\cvec{x}}^2 = 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - ho\cvec{x}}^2 + (
u - ho)^2 . Hence deduce that among all real 
u, the residual bound of @thm-hermitian-residual-bound is sharpest at 
u = ho. Write \A\cvec{x} - 
u\cvec{x} = (\A\cvec{x} - ho\cvec{x}) + (ho - 
u)\cvec{x}. The first vector is orthogonal to \cvec{x}, since \inner{\A\cvec{x} - ho\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x} - ho = 0. By @thm-pythagoras, 
orm{\A\cvec{x} -

orm{\A\cvec{x} - ho\cvec{x}}^2 + (ho - 
u)^2
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 = 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - ho\cvec{x}}^2 + (
u - ho)^2 . Hence

u\cvec{x}} \ge 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - ho\cvec{x}}, with equality only for 
u = ho. The interval [

orm{\A\cvec{x} -

orm{\A\cvec{x} - 
u\cvec{x}}] of @thm-hermitian-residual-bound therefore has its smallest radius at 
u = ho. C. Going deeper [C1: A residual that guarantees an eigenvalue] Let \A be Hermitian, \cvec{x} a unit vector, \mu = \cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x}, and \varepsilon = 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - \mu\cvec{x}}. 1. Let \alpha < \mu <  eta. Prove that if \varepsilon^2 < (\mu - \alpha)( eta - \mu), then \A has an eigenvalue in (\alpha,  eta). 2. Deduce that \A has an eigenvalue in [\mu - \varepsilon, \mu + \varepsilon], which is @thm-hermitian-residual-bound again, for this choice of \mu. Hint for (a): if there is none, consider \cvec{x}^{*}(\A - \alpha\I)(\A -  eta\I)\cvec{x}. (a) Suppose no eigenvalue lies in (\alpha,  eta). Then every eigenvalue t satisfies t \le \alpha or t \ge  eta, so (t - \alpha)(t -  eta) \ge 0. As in the proof of @thm-kato-temple, with \alpha in place of \lambda, 0 \ \le\ \cvec{x}^{*}(\A - \alpha\I)(\A -  eta\I)\cvec{x} = \varepsilon^2 + (\mu - \alpha)(\mu -  eta) , so \varepsilon^2 \ge (\mu - \alpha)( eta - \mu), contradicting the hypothesis. Hence some eigenvalue lies in (\alpha,  eta). (b) Let d be the smallest distance from \mu to an eigenvalue of \A, and suppose d > \varepsilon. Choose s with \varepsilon < s < d, and apply (a) with \alpha = \mu - s and  eta = \mu + s: the hypothesis holds, since (\mu - \alpha)( eta - \mu) = s^2 > \varepsilon^2. So some eigenvalue lies in (\mu - s, \mu + s), at distance less than s < d from \mu, contradicting the choice of d. Hence d \le \varepsilon, which is the claim. [C2: Relative bounds need structured perturbations] 1. Let \A be Hermitian and \S = \I + \F with \F \in M_n(
C). Prove that  igl\lvert\lambda_k(\S\A\S^{*}) - \lambda_k(\A) igrvert \ \le\  igl(2
orm{\F}_2 + 
orm{\F}_2^2 igr)\,\lvert\lambda_k(\A)vert for every k, whenever \S is invertible. 2. Show that there is no constant c such that \lvert\lambda_k(\A + \E) - \lambda_k(\A)vert \le c
orm{\E}_2\lvert\lambda_k(\A)vert for all Hermitian \A, \E and all k. Hint for (a): expand \S\S^{*} - \I, and show first that 
orm{\F^{*}}_2 = 
orm{\F}_2. (a) First, 
orm{\F^{*}}_2 \le 
orm{\F}_2: for every \cvec{x}, by @thm-cauchy-schwarz and @thm-operator-norm-properties (a), 
orm{\F^{*}\cvec{x}}^2 = \inner{\F\F^{*}\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} \le 
orm{\F\F^{*}\cvec{x}}\,
orm{\cvec{x}} \le 
orm{\F}_2
orm{\F^{*}\cvec{x}}\,
orm{\cvec{x}} , so 
orm{\F^{*}\cvec{x}} \le 
orm{\F}_2
orm{\cvec{x}} (trivially if \F^{*}\cvec{x} = \cvec{0}), and the reverse inequality follows by applying this to \F^{*}, since (\F^{*})^{*} = \F. Now \S\S^{*} - \I = \F + \F^{*} + \F\F^{*}, so by the triangle inequality for 
orm{\cdot}_2, which is a norm by @thm-operator-norm-properties (b), and by part (d) of the same theorem, 
orm{\S\S^{*} - \I}_2 \le 
orm{\F}_2 + 
orm{\F^{*}}_2 + 
orm{\F}_2
orm{\F^{*}}_2 = 2
orm{\F}_2 + 
orm{\F}_2^2 . The last inequality of @thm-ostrowski-relative then gives the claim. (b) Take \A = \diag(1, 0) and \E = \diag(0, t) with t > 0. Then \lambda_2(\A) = 0 and \lambda_2(\A + \E) = \min(1, t) > 0, so the left side is positive while the right side is c\,t \cdot 0 = 0. No constant c works. By (a), such an \E is not of the form \S\A\S^{*} - \A: congruence can never move the eigenvalue 0. [C3: Kato–Temple is sharp] Let \lambda_1 > \lambda_2 be real, \A = \diag(\lambda_1, \lambda_2), and \cvec{x} = (\cos\phi, \sin\phi) with 0 < \phi < \pi/2. 1. Compute \mu = \cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x} and show that \varepsilon^2 = (\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)^2\cos^2\phi\,\sin^2\phi. 2. Show that @thm-kato-temple (b), with \lambda = \lambda_1 and \alpha = \lambda_2, holds with equality. Hence the constant in the Kato–Temple bound cannot be improved. Write c = \cos\phi, s = \sin\phi, and d = \lambda_1 - \lambda_2 > 0. (a) \A\cvec{x} = (\lambda_1c, \lambda_2s), so \mu = \lambda_1c^2 + \lambda_2s^2. Using c^2 + s^2 = 1, \lambda_1 - \mu = ds^2 and \lambda_2 - \mu = -dc^2. The residual is \A\cvec{x} - \mu\cvec{x} =  igl((\lambda_1 - \mu)c, (\lambda_2 - \mu)s igr) = (ds^2c, -dc^2s), so \varepsilon^2 = d^2s^4c^2 + d^2c^4s^2 = d^2c^2s^2(s^2 + c^2) = d^2c^2s^2 . (b) Here \alpha = \lambda_2 < \mu, since \mu - \lambda_2 = dc^2 > 0, and no eigenvalue lies in (\lambda_2, \lambda_1). The bound reads \mu +  rac{\varepsilon^2}{\mu - \lambda_2} = \mu +  rac{d^2c^2s^2}{dc^2} = \mu + ds^2 = \lambda_1 . So equality holds for every \phi \in (0, \pi/2), and no smaller multiple of \varepsilon^2/(\mu - \alpha) would give a valid bound.

title: 20.7 The Sylvester Equation Revisited
content:
The Sylvester Equation Revisited Chapter 12 settled when the equation \A\X - \X\B = \C can be solved: over 
C it has exactly one solution for every \C if and only if \A and \B have no common eigenvalue (@thm-sylvester-equation). It then set a question aside. “The quantitative version — how badly conditioned the equation is when the spectra are close but disjoint — is a separate matter, and belongs with perturbation theory in Chapter 20.” Chapter 8, which first wrote the equation as a linear system, said the same thing more briefly: “its quantitative form appears in Chapter 20.” This section pays both debts. It attaches to each pair (\A, \B) a number that says how large a solution can be, computes it exactly for normal pairs, shows how badly it can behave otherwise, and proves a bound in the spectral norm for Hermitian pairs whose spectra sit on opposite sides of a gap. The reason to want these bounds now is that Sections 9 and 10 need them. In Section 9 the error in a computed invariant subspace turns out to satisfy a Sylvester equation, and in Section 10 so does the error in a square root or a polar factor. Each of those three errors is measured by one of the bounds proved here, applied once. Throughout, the field is 
C, \A \in M_m(
C) and \B \in M_n(
C), and \X, \C \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C). We write \cS = \cS_{\A,\B} for the Sylvester operator \X \mapsto \A\X - \X\B of @def-sylvester-operator, and \K = \I_n \otimes \A - \B	p \otimes \I_m for its matrix, so that \vecop(\cS(\X)) = \K\vecop\X by @eq-sylvester-kronecker. The eigenvalues of \A are \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m and those of \B are \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n, with multiplicity. Every bound names its norm: 
orm{\cdot}_F is the Frobenius norm and 
orm{\cdot}_2 the spectral norm. How large can the solution be? Start with the smallest case, m = n = 1. The equation is (a - b)x = c, and when a 
e b its solution is x = c/(a - b). So the size of the answer is governed by one number, the distance \lvert a - bvert between the two “spectra”: the closer they are, the larger x can be for a given c. The natural guess for larger matrices is that the distance between the two spectra, \min_{i,j}\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert, plays the same role, so that 
orm{\X}_F \le 
orm{\C}_F / \min_{i,j}\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert. We will see that this guess is right for normal pairs and can be wrong by any factor otherwise. The number that really controls the solution is the smallest amount by which \cS can stretch a matrix, and it deserves a name. The separation of \A and \B is the least that the Sylvester operator can shrink a matrix of unit size. [Separation] Let \A \in M_m(
C) and \B \in M_n(
C). The separation of \A and \B is  egin{aligned} \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) \coloneqq \min igl\{ &
orm{\A\X - \X\B}_F : \ &\X \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C),\ 
orm{\X}_F = 1  igr\} . \end{aligned} In words: we run over every matrix \X of the right shape whose Frobenius norm is exactly 1, apply the Sylvester operator, measure the result in the Frobenius norm, and take the smallest value. By homogeneity, 
orm{\A\X - \X\B}_F \ge \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B)
orm{\X}_F for every \X, and \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) is the largest constant with this property. The order matters: \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) belongs to \X \mapsto \A\X - \X\B, and \operatorname{sep}_F(\B, \A) to a different operator on a different space. The subscript F records the norm, as in 
orm{\cdot}_F. Well-definedness. A minimum over an infinite set needs to exist, and the first part of @prp-sep-properties below shows that it does, without any appeal to compactness: it is the smallest singular value of \K. Examples. 1. m = n = 1. Then \X = (x) with \lvert xvert = 1, and \lvert ax - xbvert = \lvert a - bvert. So \operatorname{sep}_F(a, b) = \lvert a - bvert, the one-dimensional picture above. 2. Equal matrices. For square \A, \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \A) = 0: the matrix \X = \I_m/\sqrt{m} has 
orm{\X}_F = 1 and \A\X - \X\A = \O. This degenerate case matters because it is the extreme of a shared eigenvalue, and the first property below says that any shared eigenvalue forces the separation to 0. 3. Diagonal matrices. If \A = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m) and \B = \diag(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n), then (\A\X - \X\B)_{ij} = (\lambda_i - \mu_j)x_{ij}, so \cS multiplies each entry by its own factor. The smallest stretch is the smallest factor in modulus, and \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) = \min_{i,j}\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert. The proof of @thm-sep-normal below writes this out. Nonexample by minimal change. Drop the normalization and take \min\{
orm{\A\X - \X\B}_F : \X 
e \O\} instead. The set of values is still nonempty and bounded below, but its infimum is 0 for every pair, and when the spectra are disjoint it is never attained: replacing \X by t\X multiplies the value by t, and t can be as small as we like, while the value 0 is taken at some \X 
e \O exactly when the two spectra meet (@thm-sylvester-equation), as they do in the second example above, where \A = \B and \X = \I_m. It is exactly the clause 
orm{\X}_F = 1 that fails, and it is what turns a meaningless infimum into a measurement of the operator. Why the Frobenius norm. Vectorization lists the entries of \X in one column, so 
orm{\vecop\X}_2 = 
orm{\X}_F: \vecop is an isometry from (M_{m 	imes n}(
C), 
orm{\cdot}_F) to (
C^{mn}, 
orm{\cdot}_2). That turns \operatorname{sep}_F into a question about the ordinary matrix \K, which the singular value decomposition answers. With 
orm{\cdot}_2 on both sides the minimum is also a sensible quantity, but it has no such formula, and we will not need it: the spectral-norm results below go through a different argument. The separation is not the distance between the spectra. It is at most that distance, by part (c) of the proposition below, but it can be far smaller. For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & t \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and the 1 	imes 1 matrix \B = \O_1, the spectra \{1\} and \{0\} are at distance 1 for every t, yet \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) < 1/t for t > 0 (@exm-sep-far-below-gap). Whenever \A or \B is not normal, compute the separation; do not read it off the eigenvalues. Everything we need about the separation is collected in one proposition. [Properties of the Separation] Let \A \in M_m(
C), \B \in M_n(
C), and \K = \I_n \otimes \A - \B	p \otimes \I_m. 1. The minimum defining \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) exists, and \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) = \sigma_{mn}(\K), the smallest singular value of \K. 2. \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) > 0 if and only if \spec(\A) \cap \spec(\B) = \varnothing. 3. \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) \le \min_{i,j}\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert. 4. If \spec(\A) \cap \spec(\B) = \varnothing, then for every \C the unique solution of \A\X - \X\B = \C satisfies 
orm{\X}_F \le  rac{
orm{\C}_F}{\operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B)} , and equality holds for some \C 
e \O. 5. For unitary \U \in \Unit(m) and \V \in \Unit(n), \operatorname{sep}_F(\U^{*}\A\U, \V^{*}\B\V) = \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B). 6. If n = 1 and \B = (\mu), then \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) = \sigma_m(\A - \mu\I_m), the smallest singular value of \A - \mu\I_m. Part (a) is the isometry \vecop plus the fact that the smallest stretch of a square matrix is its smallest singular value. Part (b) is Sylvester’s theorem, read through (a). Part (c) needs one good test matrix: an eigenvector of \A times a left eigenvector of \B is multiplied by \lambda - \mu under \cS, exactly as in the 1 	imes 1 case. Part (d) is the definition read backwards. Part (e) holds because unitary factors change neither the set of unit matrices nor the Frobenius norm. Part (f) is the case n = 1 of (a), where \K is nothing but \A - \mu\I_m. (a) Let \X \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C) and \cvec{x} = \vecop\X. The entries of \cvec{x} are those of \X, so 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 = 
orm{\X}_F, and likewise 
orm{\A\X - \X\B}_F = 
orm{\K\cvec{x}}_2 by @eq-sylvester-kronecker. Since \vecop is a bijection from M_{m 	imes n}(
C) onto 
C^{mn} (@def-vec-operator), the set whose minimum defines \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) equals \{
orm{\K\cvec{x}}_2 : 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 = 1\}. By @lem-stretch-in-singular-coordinates (b) with k equal to the size mn of \K, the head subspace is all of 
C^{mn}, and the minimum of 
orm{\K\cvec{x}}/
orm{\cvec{x}} over \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0} exists and equals \sigma_{mn}(\K). Restricting to unit vectors changes nothing, since the quotient is unchanged when \cvec{x} is scaled. (b) By @thm-svd, the number of nonzero singular values of \K is ank\K. Since \sigma_{mn}(\K) is the smallest, it is nonzero exactly when all mn of them are, that is, when ank\K = mn, which says that \K is invertible (@thm-invertible-tfae-det (d)). By @eq-sylvester-kronecker, \K is invertible exactly when \cS is, and by @thm-sylvester-equation ((a) \Leftrightarrow (b)) that happens exactly when \spec(\A) \cap \spec(\B) = \varnothing. Combining with (a) proves (b). (c) Fix i, j. Choose an eigenvector \cvec{x} of \A for \lambda_i, and, by @prp-left-eigenvectors-transpose (b), a left eigenvector \cvec{y} of \B for \mu_j, so that \cvec{y}	p\B = \mu_j\cvec{y}	p (@def-left-eigenvector). Scale both to length 1, and put \X = \cvec{x}\cvec{y}	p. Its (p, q) entry is x_py_q, so 
orm{\X}_F^2 = \sum_{p,q}\lvert x_pvert^2\lvert y_qvert^2 = 
orm{\cvec{x}}^2
orm{\cvec{y}}^2 = 1 . By associativity, \A\X - \X\B = (\A\cvec{x})\cvec{y}	p - \cvec{x}(\cvec{y}	p\B) = (\lambda_i - \mu_j)\X. Hence \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) \le 
orm{(\lambda_i - \mu_j)\X}_F = \lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert. This holds for every pair (i, j), so it holds for the minimum. (d) By @thm-sylvester-equation the solution \X exists and is unique. If \X = \O there is nothing to prove. Otherwise \X/
orm{\X}_F has Frobenius norm 1, so by @def-sep \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) \le  rac{
orm{\A\X - \X\B}_F}{
orm{\X}_F} =  rac{
orm{\C}_F}{
orm{\X}_F} , and \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) > 0 by (b), so we may rearrange. For equality, take \X_0 with 
orm{\X_0}_F = 1 attaining the minimum, which exists by (a), and put \C = \A\X_0 - \X_0\B. Then \C 
e \O, because 
orm{\C}_F = \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) > 0, and the unique solution is \X_0, for which the two sides are both 1. (e) Put \A' = \U^{*}\A\U and \B' = \V^{*}\B\V. For every \X, \A'(\U^{*}\X\V) - (\U^{*}\X\V)\B' = \U^{*}(\A\X - \X\B)\V , because \U\U^{*} = \I_m and \V\V^{*} = \I_n. By @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant, 
orm{\U^{*}\X\V}_F = 
orm{\X}_F and the right side has Frobenius norm 
orm{\A\X - \X\B}_F. The map \X \mapsto \U^{*}\X\V is a bijection of M_{m 	imes n}(
C), with inverse \Y \mapsto \U\Y\V^{*}, so it carries the matrices of Frobenius norm 1 onto themselves. Hence the two minima are taken over the same set of values, and they are equal. (f) With n = 1 and \B = (\mu), the Kronecker matrix is \K = \I_1 \otimes \A - (\mu) \otimes \I_m = \A - \mu\I_m, of size mn = m. So (a) gives \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) = \sigma_m(\A - \mu\I_m). Part (d) is the quantitative form that Chapter 8 and Chapter 12 promised, and it says more than an inequality. The number 1/\operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) is exactly the largest factor by which solving the equation can magnify the data, measured in the Frobenius norm. Since \cS is linear, it is also the factor for errors: if \C is replaced by \C + \Delta\C, the solution moves by \cS^{-1}(\Delta\C), whose norm is at most 
orm{\Delta\C}_F/\operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B), and some \Delta\C achieves this. A small separation is the precise meaning of “badly conditioned”. Part (c) says that close spectra always make the separation small. The rest of the section asks whether the converse holds, that is, whether well-separated spectra make it large. Part (f) of @prp-sep-properties was read off the Kronecker matrix. Prove it instead straight from @def-sep, without vectorizing: for \B = (\mu), unwind what the matrices \X of Frobenius norm 1 are. Here n = 1, so \X = \cvec{x} is a column in 
C^m with 
orm{\cvec{x}}_F = 
orm{\cvec{x}}, and \A\cvec{x} - \cvec{x}\mu = (\A - \mu\I_m)\cvec{x}. So \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) = \min_{
orm{\cvec{x}} = 1}
orm{(\A - \mu\I_m)\cvec{x}}, which is \sigma_m(\A - \mu\I_m) by @lem-stretch-in-singular-coordinates (b) with k = m. Normal pairs: the separation is the gap For normal matrices the naive guess is right, and the proof is the diagonal example written out. [Separation of Normal Matrices] Let \A \in M_m(
C) and \B \in M_n(
C) be normal, with eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m and \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n. Then \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) = \min_{i,j}\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert . Consequently, if \delta = \min_{i,j}\lvert\lambda_i - \mu_jvert > 0, the unique solution of \A\X - \X\B = \C satisfies

orm{\F}_2 . \end{aligned} Taking the minimum over \X gives \operatorname{sep}_F(\A + \E, \B + \F) \ge \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) - 
orm{\E}_2 - 
orm{\F}_2. Applying this to the pair (\A + \E, \B + \F) with the perturbations -\E, -\F gives the reverse inequality, and together they are the claim. (c) By @prp-sep-properties (f), s \coloneqq \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) = \sigma_m(\A - \mu\I_m). Let \A - \mu\I_m = \U\vSigma\V^{*} be a singular value decomposition (@thm-svd), with last columns \cvec{u}_m of \U and \cvec{v}_m of \V. Then (\A - \mu\I_m)\cvec{v}_m = s\cvec{u}_m, comparing column m of (\A - \mu\I_m)\V = \U\vSigma. Put \E = -s\,\cvec{u}_m\cvec{v}_m^{*}. Then (\A + \E - \mu\I_m)\cvec{v}_m = s\cvec{u}_m - s\cvec{u}_m(\cvec{v}_m^{*}\cvec{v}_m) = \cvec{0} with \cvec{v}_m 
e \cvec{0}, so \mu is an eigenvalue of \A + \E. Also 
orm{\E\cvec{x}} = s\lvert\cvec{v}_m^{*}\cvec{x}vert \le s
orm{\cvec{x}} by Cauchy–Schwarz, with equality at \cvec{x} = \cvec{v}_m, so 
orm{\E}_2 = s. (d) With \mu = 0 and \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \O_1) = 1/10, part (c) gives a perturbation of spectral norm 1/10 after which 0 is an eigenvalue of \A + \E, so \A + \E and \B share an eigenvalue. The eigenvalues 1 and 0 are at distance 1, but a perturbation ten times smaller than that distance destroys the solvability of the equation. By (b) with \F = \O, no perturbation of spectral norm less than 1/10 can do it, since it leaves the separation positive. So the separation, not the eigenvalue gap, is the distance to a shared eigenvalue here. [C2: Interlaced spectra break the spectral-norm bound] Let \A = \diag(0, 2), \B = \diag(1, 3), and \C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. 1. Show that every eigenvalue of \A is at distance at least 1 from every eigenvalue of \B, and explain why @thm-sylvester-one-sided does not apply with \alpha -  eta = 1. 2. Solve \A\X - \X\B = \C. 3. Show that 
orm{\X}_2 > 
orm{\C}_2. 4. Verify directly that 
orm{\X}_F \le 
orm{\C}_F, as @thm-sep-normal requires. Hint for (c): compute \C	p\C, and test \X on the vector (1, 1). (a) The eigenvalues are 0, 2 and 1, 3, and the four differences \lambda_i - \mu_j are -1, -3, 1, -1, all of modulus at least 1. The theorem needs \A \succeq \alpha\I and \B \preceq  eta\I with \alpha >  eta, that is, every eigenvalue of \A above every eigenvalue of \B, or, applying it to (-\A, -\B), every one below. Neither holds, since 0 < 1 < 2 < 3 interlace. Applied honestly, the best one-sided constants are \alpha = 0 and  eta = 3, and \alpha >  eta fails. (b) As in the diagonal example after @def-sep, (\A\X - \X\B)_{ij} = (a_{ii} - b_{jj})x_{ij}, so x_{ij} = c_{ij}/(a_{ii} - b_{jj}): \X =  egin{pmatrix} 1/(0 - 1) & 1/(0 - 3) \ 1/(2 - 1) & -1/(2 - 3) \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & -1/3 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . (c) \C	p\C = 2\I_2, so both singular values of \C are \sqrt2 and 
orm{\C}_2 = \sqrt2 (@thm-operator-norm-formulas (c)). For \cvec{x} = (1, 1)/\sqrt2, a unit vector, \X\cvec{x} = (-4/3, 2)/\sqrt2, so 
orm{\X\cvec{x}}^2 =  rac{1}{2}\Bigl( rac{16}{9} + 4\Bigr) =  rac{26}{9} > 2 . Hence 
orm{\X}_2 \ge \sqrt{26}/3 > \sqrt2 = 
orm{\C}_2. (d) 
orm{\X}_F^2 = 1 + 	frac19 + 1 + 1 = 	frac{28}{9} and 
orm{\C}_F^2 = 4, so 
orm{\X}_F \le 
orm{\C}_F, in agreement with @thm-sep-normal, which gives \operatorname{sep}_F(\A, \B) = 1. So the Frobenius bound with constant 1/\delta survives interlacing, while the spectral-norm bound with the same constant does not.

title: 20.8 Principal Angles
content:
Principal Angles The sections so far measured how far eigenvalues move. The next section asks how far eigenvectors move, and more generally invariant subspaces, and before it can answer it needs a way to say how far apart two subspaces are. For two lines there is an obvious answer, the angle between them. This section shows that for subspaces of dimension k \ge 2 one angle is not enough, and that the right replacement is a list of k angles read off from a singular value decomposition. It then proves the two facts Section 9 will use: the sines of these angles are the singular values of a matrix built from the orthogonal complement, and the largest sine is the distance between the two orthogonal projections. Throughout, F is 
R or 
C, and F^n carries its standard inner product \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x}, with \cvec{x}^{*} = \cvec{x}	p when F = 
R. For a subspace U of F^n, P_U is the orthogonal projection onto U (@def-orthogonal-projection), identified with its matrix in the standard basis. Singular values of a matrix with k columns follow the convention of Chapter 17 §09: \sigma_i \coloneqq 0 for \min(	ext{rows}, k) < i \le k, so that \sigma_i^2 is the i-th largest eigenvalue of \A^{*}\A for every i \le k (@eq-sv-eigen). One angle is not enough For two lines \Span(\cvec{u}) and \Span(\cvec{w}) there is one number to compute, the angle between them. For planes the first idea is to copy it: call the angle between U and W the smallest angle between a line in U and a line in W. That idea fails at once in 
R^3. Two distinct planes U, W \subseteq 
R^3 always meet in a line, since \dim(U \cap W) = 2 + 2 - \dim(U + W) \ge 4 - 3 = 1 by @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim. So the smallest angle is 0 for every pair of planes: it cannot tell a plane tilted by one degree from a plane at right angles. Taking the largest such angle instead does no better in 
R^4. Let U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) and compare W_1 = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_3), \qquad W_2 = \Span(\cvec{e}_3, \cvec{e}_4) . Each contains a vector perpendicular to all of U (namely \cvec{e}_3), so each has a line at angle \pi/2 from U. But W_1 shares the whole line \Span(\cvec{e}_1) with U, while W_2 is perpendicular to U in every direction. One number cannot record both facts. A list can: (0, \pi/2) for W_1 and (\pi/2, \pi/2) for W_2. The rest of this section explains where such a list comes from in general, when the subspaces are not lined up with the coordinate axes. Two subspaces can be given orthonormal bases that face each other in pairs; the principal angles are the angles between the partners. Principal angles Everything will be computed from orthonormal bases written as the columns of a matrix, so we first record how such matrices behave. Let U \subseteq F^n be a subspace with \dim U = k \ge 1. An orthonormal basis matrix of U is a matrix \Q \in M_{n 	imes k}(F) whose columns form an orthonormal basis of U. One exists: apply Gram–Schmidt (@thm-gram-schmidt) to any basis of U. [Orthonormal Basis Matrices] Let U \subseteq F^n have dimension k \ge 1 and let \Q \in M_{n 	imes k}(F) be an orthonormal basis matrix of U. 1. \Q^{*}\Q = \I_k and P_U = \Q\Q^{*}. 2. 
orm{\Q\cvec{y}} = 
orm{\cvec{y}} for every \cvec{y} \in F^k. For every matrix \Y with k rows and every matrix \Z with k columns,  egin{aligned} 
orm{\Q\Y}_2 &= 
orm{\Y}_2, & 
orm{\Q\Y}_F &= 
orm{\Y}_F, \ 
orm{\Z\Q^{*}}_2 &= 
orm{\Z}_2, & 
orm{\Z\Q^{*}}_F &= 
orm{\Z}_F . \end{aligned} 3. Every orthonormal basis matrix of U is \Q\R for some \R \in \Unit(k) (orthogonal when F = 
R). 4. \I_n - P_U = P_{U^{\perp}}. If moreover k < n and \Q_{\perp} \in M_{n 	imes (n-k)}(F) is an orthonormal basis matrix of U^{\perp}, then the square matrix (\Q \mid \Q_{\perp}) is unitary, and \Q\Q^{*} + \Q_{\perp}\Q_{\perp}^{*} = \I_n . (a) The (i, j) entry of \Q^{*}\Q is \cvec{q}_i^{*}\cvec{q}_j = \inner{\cvec{q}_j}{\cvec{q}_i} = \delta_{ij}, because the columns \cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_k are orthonormal. By @thm-projection-formula (a), for every \cvec{v} \in F^n, P_U\cvec{v} = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{q}_i}\cvec{q}_i = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\cvec{q}_i(\cvec{q}_i^{*}\cvec{v}) = \Q\Q^{*}\cvec{v} , the last step being column-times-row expansion of \Q\Q^{*}. (b) By (a), 
orm{\Q\cvec{y}}^2 = \cvec{y}^{*}\Q^{*}\Q\cvec{y} = \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{y} = 
orm{\cvec{y}}^2. Hence 
orm{\Q\Y\cvec{x}} = 
orm{\Y\cvec{x}} for every \cvec{x}, and taking the maximum over unit \cvec{x} (@def-operator-norm) gives 
orm{\Q\Y}_2 = 
orm{\Y}_2. For the Frobenius norm, 
orm{\Q\Y}_F^2 = 	r(\Y^{*}\Q^{*}\Q\Y) = 	r(\Y^{*}\Y) = 
orm{\Y}_F^2. Next, 
orm{\Z\Q^{*}}_F^2 = 	r(\Q\Z^{*}\Z\Q^{*}) = 	r(\Z^{*}\Z\Q^{*}\Q) = 
orm{\Z}_F^2, by @thm-trace-properties (3). For the spectral norm, let \cvec{x} \in F^n. By the first sentence and (a), 
orm{\Q^{*}\cvec{x}} = 
orm{\Q\Q^{*}\cvec{x}} = 
orm{P_U\cvec{x}} \le 
orm{\cvec{x}} (@thm-projection-formula (c)). So 
orm{\Z\Q^{*}\cvec{x}} \le 
orm{\Z}_2
orm{\Q^{*}\cvec{x}} \le 
orm{\Z}_2
orm{\cvec{x}} by @thm-operator-norm-properties (a), and 
orm{\Z\Q^{*}}_2 \le 
orm{\Z}_2. Conversely, choose a unit \cvec{y} \in F^k with 
orm{\Z\cvec{y}} = 
orm{\Z}_2 (@lem-operator-norm-attained). Then \cvec{x} = \Q\cvec{y} is a unit vector with \Z\Q^{*}\cvec{x} = \Z\cvec{y}, so 
orm{\Z\Q^{*}}_2 \ge 
orm{\Z}_2. (c) Let \Q' be another orthonormal basis matrix of U, and put \R = \Q^{*}\Q' \in M_k(F). Each column of \Q' lies in U, where P_U is the identity, so \Q' = P_U\Q' = \Q\Q^{*}\Q' = \Q\R by (a). Then \R^{*}\R = \Q'^{*}\Q\Q^{*}\Q' = \Q'^{*}P_U\Q' = \Q'^{*}\Q' = \I_k, so the square matrix \R is unitary (@def-unitary-orthogonal). (d) For the first identity, let \cvec{v} \in F^n and write \cvec{v} = \cvec{u} + \cvec{w} with \cvec{u} \in U and \cvec{w} \in U^{\perp}, which is possible in exactly one way by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (a). Then P_U\cvec{v} = \cvec{u} by @def-orthogonal-projection. Since (U^{\perp})^{\perp} = U by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (b), the splitting \cvec{v} = \cvec{w} + \cvec{u} is also the one that defines P_{U^{\perp}}, so P_{U^{\perp}}\cvec{v} = \cvec{w} = \cvec{v} - P_U\cvec{v}. As \cvec{v} was arbitrary, \I_n - P_U = P_{U^{\perp}}. Nothing here restricts k: when k = n, U^{\perp} = \{\cvec{0}\} and both sides are \O. Now let k < n. The columns of \Q and of \Q_{\perp} are orthonormal, and each column of \Q is orthogonal to each column of \Q_{\perp} because U \perp U^{\perp}. Their number is k + (n - k) = n, by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (c). So the square matrix \W = (\Q \mid \Q_{\perp}) \in M_n(F) satisfies \W^{*}\W = \I_n, hence is unitary, and then \W\W^{*} = \I_n as well, since \W^{*} = \W^{-1}. By block multiplication (@thm-block-multiplication), \W\W^{*} = \Q\Q^{*} + \Q_{\perp}\Q_{\perp}^{*}. This also re-proves the first identity here, since \Q_{\perp}\Q_{\perp}^{*} = P_{U^{\perp}} by (a) applied to U^{\perp}. Now the definition. The question is how much of U survives when it is projected into W. By parts (a) and (b) of the lemma, for a unit vector \cvec{u} = \Q_U\cvec{y} of U the surviving length is 
orm{P_W\cvec{u}} = 
orm{\Q_W\Q_W^{*}\cvec{u}} = 
orm{\Q_W^{*}\cvec{u}} = 
orm{(\Q_W^{*}\Q_U)\cvec{y}}. So the matrix \Q_W^{*}\Q_U records the answer for every direction of U at once, and its singular values are the stretch factors along the best directions. Principal Angles Let U, W \subseteq F^n be subspaces with 1 \le k = \dim U \le l = \dim W , and let \Q_U \in M_{n 	imes k}(F) and \Q_W \in M_{n 	imes l}(F) be orthonormal basis matrices of U and W. The principal angles between U and W are the k numbers 0 \le 	heta_1 \le 	heta_2 \le \dots \le 	heta_k \le  rac{\pi}{2} determined by \cos	heta_i = \sigma_i(\Q_W^{*}\Q_U) \qquad (i = 1, \dots, k) . We write \Theta(U, W) = \diag(	heta_1, \dots, 	heta_k) and \sin\Theta(U, W) = \diag(\sin	heta_1, \dots, \sin	heta_k). In words: fix orthonormal bases of the two subspaces, form the l 	imes k matrix whose (i, j) entry is the inner product of the j-th basis vector of U with the i-th basis vector of W, and take its k singular values. These lie in [0, 1], as we check next, so each is the cosine of exactly one angle in [0, \pi/2]. The largest cosine gives the smallest angle, so the decreasing singular values produce increasing angles. The number of angles is the smaller dimension, k, and the definition asks for k \le l; for a pair with \dim U > \dim W, swap the names. The two notations at the end are for use in norms: 
orm{\sin\Theta(U, W)}_2 = \sin	heta_k, the largest entry of a nonnegative diagonal matrix (@lem-hermitian-spectral-norm), and 
orm{\sin\Theta(U, W)}_F =  igl(\sum_i\sin^2	heta_i igr)^{1/2}. Well-definedness. Three things need checking. The answer must not depend on the orthonormal bases chosen. The singular values must be at most 1, or there is no angle. And when k = l the definition treats U and W asymmetrically, so we should check that swapping them changes nothing. [Principal Angles Are Well Defined] In the setting of @def-principal-angles, put \M = \Q_W^{*}\Q_U \in M_{l 	imes k}(F). 1. The singular values of \M do not depend on the choice of the orthonormal basis matrices \Q_U and \Q_W. 2. 1 \ge \sigma_1(\M) \ge \dots \ge \sigma_k(\M) \ge 0, so 	heta_1, \dots, 	heta_k exist, are unique, and are nondecreasing. 3. \sigma_i(\Q_U^{*}\Q_W) = \sigma_i(\M) for i = 1, \dots, k. In particular, if k = l, the principal angles between W and U are those between U and W. 4. If k = 1 and U = \Span(\cvec{u}) with 
orm{\cvec{u}} = 1, then \cos	heta_1 = 
orm{P_W\cvec{u}}. If also l = 1 and W = \Span(\cvec{w}) with 
orm{\cvec{w}} = 1, then \cos	heta_1 = \lvert\inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}}vert. (a) By @lem-orthonormal-basis-matrix (c), any other choices are \Q_U\R and \Q_W\R' with \R \in \Unit(k) and \R' \in \Unit(l). The new matrix is \M' = \R'^{*}\M\R, and \M'^{*}\M' = \R^{*}\M^{*}\R'\R'^{*}\M\R = \R^{*}(\M^{*}\M)\R , using \R'\R'^{*} = \I_l. Since \R^{*} = \R^{-1}, this is similar to \M^{*}\M, so the two have the same characteristic polynomial (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant) and the same eigenvalues with multiplicity. By @def-singular-values, \M' and \M have the same singular values. (b) By @thm-operator-norm-properties (d) and @lem-orthonormal-basis-matrix (b), 
orm{\M}_2 \le 
orm{\Q_W^{*}}_2
orm{\Q_U}_2, and 
orm{\Q_U}_2 = 
orm{\Q_U\I_k}_2 = 
orm{\I_k}_2 = 1 by @thm-operator-norm-properties (c). Also 
orm{\Q_W^{*}\cvec{x}} = 
orm{P_W\cvec{x}} \le 
orm{\cvec{x}}, as in the proof of that lemma, so 
orm{\Q_W^{*}}_2 \le 1. Hence \sigma_1(\M) = 
orm{\M}_2 \le 1 by @thm-operator-norm-formulas (c), and all singular values lie in [0, 1]. The cosine is a strictly decreasing bijection from [0, \pi/2] onto [0, 1], so each \sigma_i(\M) is \cos	heta_i for exactly one 	heta_i \in [0, \pi/2], and \sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_k gives 	heta_1 \le \dots \le 	heta_k. (c) Let \M = \Y\vSigma\Z^{*} be a singular value decomposition (@thm-svd). Then \M^{*} = \Z\vSigma	p\Y^{*}, where \Z, \Y are unitary and \vSigma	p \in M_{k 	imes l}(
R) carries the same diagonal entries \sigma_1(\M) \ge \dots \ge \sigma_k(\M) and zeros elsewhere. So this is a factorization of \M^{*} of the shape in @thm-svd, and @thm-singular-values-unique gives \sigma_i(\M^{*}) = \sigma_i(\M). Since \M^{*} = \Q_U^{*}\Q_W, this is the first claim. When k = l, the principal angles between W and U are defined by \sigma_i(\Q_U^{*}\Q_W), so they coincide with those between U and W. (d) With \Q_U = \cvec{u}, the matrix \M = \Q_W^{*}\cvec{u} is a single column, and its one singular value is (\M^{*}\M)^{1/2} = 
orm{\Q_W^{*}\cvec{u}}. By @lem-orthonormal-basis-matrix (b) and (a), 
orm{\Q_W^{*}\cvec{u}} = 
orm{\Q_W\Q_W^{*}\cvec{u}} = 
orm{P_W\cvec{u}}. If l = 1 and \Q_W = \cvec{w}, then \M = \cvec{w}^{*}\cvec{u} = \inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}}, whose singular value is \lvert\inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}}vert. Examples. 1. Two lines in 
R^2. For \cvec{u} = \cvec{e}_1 and \cvec{w} = (1, 1)/\sqrt2, part (d) gives \cos	heta_1 = 1/\sqrt2, so 	heta_1 = \pi/4. Replacing \cvec{w} by -\cvec{w} changes neither the line nor the answer. 2. Nested subspaces. If U \subseteq W, then every column of \Q_U is fixed by P_W, so \M^{*}\M = \Q_U^{*}\Q_W\Q_W^{*}\Q_U = \Q_U^{*}P_W\Q_U = \Q_U^{*}\Q_U = \I_k. All singular values are 1 and all principal angles are 0. The degenerate case U = W is included, and it is the reason the angles start at 0. 3. Perpendicular subspaces. If U \subseteq W^{\perp}, every entry of \M is the inner product of a vector of U with a vector of W, hence 0, so all principal angles are \pi/2. 4. The planes of the opening. For U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) and W_1 = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_3), take the standard vectors as orthonormal bases. Then \M = \Q_{W_1}	p\Q_U =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, with singular values 1, 0, so the principal angles are (0, \pi/2). For W_2 = \Span(\cvec{e}_3, \cvec{e}_4) we are in Example 3, with angles (\pi/2, \pi/2). These are the two lists that the single-number attempts could not tell apart. Nonexample by minimal change. In Example 4, replace the orthonormal basis (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_3) of W_1 by the basis (\cvec{e}_1, (\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_3)/\sqrt2), whose vectors still have length 1 but are no longer orthogonal. The matrix of inner products becomes  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 1/\sqrt2 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, with largest singular value \sqrt{3/2} > 1, and no angle has that cosine. What fails is the orthogonality of the columns of \Q_W: without it, \Q_W\Q_W^{*} is not the projection P_W, and the matrix no longer measures how much of U survives in W. Why this definition: the principal vectors. The singular value decomposition of \M does more than produce numbers. It produces bases of U and W in which the whole configuration is visible, and this is the precise meaning of the slogan. [Principal Vectors] In the setting of @def-principal-angles, let \Q_W^{*}\Q_U = \Y\vSigma\Z^{*} be a singular value decomposition (@thm-svd), with \Y \in M_l(F) and \Z \in M_k(F) unitary, columns \cvec{y}_1, \dots, \cvec{y}_l and \cvec{z}_1, \dots, \cvec{z}_k. Put \cvec{u}_i = \Q_U\cvec{z}_i \ (1 \le i \le k), \qquad \cvec{w}_j = \Q_W\cvec{y}_j \ (1 \le j \le l) . Then (\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_k) is an orthonormal basis of U, (\cvec{w}_1, \dots, \cvec{w}_l) is an orthonormal basis of W, and \inner{\cvec{u}_i}{\cvec{w}_j} =  egin{cases} \cos	heta_i & 	ext{if } i = j, \ 0 & 	ext{if } i 
e j . \end{cases} The matrix \Q_U\Z has columns \cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_k, all in U, and (\Q_U\Z)^{*}(\Q_U\Z) = \Z^{*}\Z = \I_k by @lem-orthonormal-basis-matrix (a). So the \cvec{u}_i are k orthonormal vectors of U. They are linearly independent (@thm-orthogonal-independent), and \dim U = k, so they form a basis. The same argument applies to the \cvec{w}_j in W. Finally, \inner{\cvec{u}_i}{\cvec{w}_j} = \cvec{w}_j^{*}\cvec{u}_i = \cvec{y}_j^{*}(\Q_W^{*}\Q_U)\cvec{z}_i = \cvec{y}_j^{*}\Y\vSigma\Z^{*}\cvec{z}_i = \cvec{e}_j^{*}\vSigma\cvec{e}_i , which is the (j, i) entry of \vSigma: it equals \sigma_i = \cos	heta_i when j = i, and 0 otherwise. So U and W have orthonormal bases that face each other in pairs. Each \cvec{u}_i makes the angle 	heta_i with its partner \cvec{w}_i, in the sense of part (d) of the proposition, and is perpendicular to every other \cvec{w}_j. The last l - k vectors of W have no partner, and they are perpendicular to all of U. The vectors \cvec{u}_i, \cvec{w}_i are called principal vectors. Two subspaces, however they sit in F^n, look like a list of k independent pairs of lines, and the principal angles are the angles within the pairs. The principal vectors are usually not the basis vectors one started with. For U = W = 
R^2 with bases (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) and ((\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2)/\sqrt2, (\cvec{e}_1 - \cvec{e}_2)/\sqrt2), each given basis vector of U is at angle \pi/4 from each given basis vector of W. The principal angles are nevertheless 0, 0, by Example 2, since the subspaces are equal. Pairing the given columns one by one measures the bases, not the subspaces. Lines have no orientation, so principal angles use \lvert\inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}}vert and lie in [0, \pi/2]. The angle of @def-angle is between vectors in a real space, and it can reach \pi. For \cvec{u} = \cvec{e}_1 and \cvec{w} = -\cvec{e}_1 in 
R^2 that angle is \pi, yet \Span(\cvec{u}) = \Span(\cvec{w}) and the principal angle is 0. Over 
C the vector angle is not even defined: \cvec{u} = \cvec{e}_1 and \cvec{w} = i\cvec{e}_1 span the same complex line, \inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}} = \conj{i} = -i is not real, and the principal angle is again 0 because \lvert -ivert = 1. Find the principal angle between the line U = \Span igl((1, 2, 2) igr) and the plane W = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^3 : x_3 = 0\}. Here k = 1 \le 2 = l. The unit vector \cvec{u} = 	frac13(1, 2, 2) spans U, and P_W\cvec{u} = 	frac13(1, 2, 0), since (\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) is an orthonormal basis of W (@thm-projection-formula (a)). By @prp-principal-angles-well-defined (d), \cos	heta_1 = 
orm{P_W\cvec{u}} = \sqrt5/3. So 	heta_1 = \arccos(\sqrt5/3) \approx 41.8^\circ, and \sin	heta_1 = 2/3, which is the distance from \cvec{u} to the plane. Sines and the orthogonal complement The cosines measure how much of U survives projection into W. What Section 9 can actually bound is the part that does not survive: the component of U in W^{\perp}. Pythagoras says the two parts are complementary, and the theorem makes this exact. R^3 meet in a line (@thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim, as in the opening of the section), and a common unit vector forces \cos	heta_1 = 1 (Exercise A1 (d)). Here the common line is \Span(\cvec{e}_1). [B2: Which projections are at distance one?] Determine, for each pair, whether 
orm{P_U - P_W}_2 = 1. Justify your answer. 1. U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) and W = \Span(\cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3) in 
R^3. 2. U = \Span igl((1, 1, 0) igr) and W = \Span igl((1, -1, 1) igr) in 
R^3. 3. U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2) and W = \Span igl((1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1) igr) in 
R^3. 4. U = \Span igl((1, 2, 3) igr) and W = \Span igl((1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) igr) in 
R^3. (a) Yes. W^{\perp} = \Span(\cvec{e}_1) \subseteq U, so U \cap W^{\perp} 
e \{\cvec{0}\}, and @thm-projection-difference-norm (c) applies since both dimensions are 2. (b) Yes. \inner{(1, 1, 0)}{(1, -1, 1)} = 0, so U \subseteq W^{\perp}, and (c) of the theorem applies with k = 1. (c) No. Both are planes, and W^{\perp} = \Span igl((1, 1, -1) igr), since (1, 1, -1) is orthogonal to both spanning vectors of W and \dim W^{\perp} = 1. This vector has nonzero third entry, so it is not in U, and U \cap W^{\perp} = \{\cvec{0}\}. By the theorem, 
orm{P_U - P_W}_2 < 1. (In fact the principal angles are 0 and \arccos(1/\sqrt3), so the distance is \sqrt{2/3}.) (d) Yes, for a different reason: the dimensions are 1 and 2, and the remark after @exm-two-planes-in-r4 shows that

Its principal angle 	heta_1 = \arccos(\sqrt5/\sqrt{14}) is far from \pi/2, which illustrates why the projection distance is only used for equal dimensions. [B3: Two lines] Let \cvec{u}, \cvec{w} \in F^n be unit vectors and c = \lvert\inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}}vert. Prove that
