By @lem-orthonormal-basis-matrix (a) with \Q_U = \cvec{u} and \Q_W = \cvec{w}, P_U = \cvec{u}\cvec{u}^{*} and P_W = \cvec{w}\cvec{w}^{*}. By @prp-principal-angles-well-defined (d), the single principal angle satisfies \cos	heta_1 = c, so \sin	heta_1 = \sqrt{1 - c^2}, since \sin	heta_1 \ge 0 on [0, \pi/2]. Now @thm-projection-difference-norm (a) and (b) with k = 1 give 
orm{P_U - P_W}_2 = \sin	heta_1 and 
orm{P_U - P_W}_F = \sqrt2\sin	heta_1, which are the two claims. C. Going deeper [C1: Counting zero and right angles] Let U, W \subseteq F^n with 1 \le k = \dim U \le l = \dim W, orthonormal basis matrices \Q_U, \Q_W, and \M = \Q_W^{*}\Q_U. 1. Prove that \cvec{y}^{*}(\I_k - \M^{*}\M)\cvec{y} = 
orm{(\I - P_W)\Q_U\cvec{y}}^2 for every \cvec{y} \in F^k. 2. Deduce that the number of principal angles equal to 0 is \dim(U \cap W). 3. Prove that the number of principal angles equal to \pi/2 is \dim(U \cap W^{\perp}). Hint for (b): a positive semidefinite matrix \B with \cvec{y}^{*}\B\cvec{y} = 0 has \B\cvec{y} = \cvec{0}. (a) Let \cvec{u} = \Q_U\cvec{y}. By @lem-orthonormal-basis-matrix (a) and (b), \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{y} = 
orm{\cvec{u}}^2 and \cvec{y}^{*}\M^{*}\M\cvec{y} = 
orm{\Q_W^{*}\cvec{u}}^2 = 
orm{P_W\cvec{u}}^2. Since \cvec{u} = P_W\cvec{u} + (\I - P_W)\cvec{u} with the two parts orthogonal (@thm-orthogonal-decomposition), @thm-pythagoras gives 
orm{\cvec{u}}^2 - 
orm{P_W\cvec{u}}^2 = 
orm{(\I - P_W)\cvec{u}}^2. (b) Put \B = \I_k - \M^{*}\M. It is Hermitian, and by (a) it is positive semidefinite (@def-positive-semidefinite). Its eigenvalues are 1 - \cos^2	heta_i = \sin^2	heta_i, with an orthonormal eigenbasis \cvec{z}_1, \dots, \cvec{z}_k (as in the proof of @thm-sines-of-principal-angles). So the number of i with 	heta_i = 0 is the number of zero eigenvalues, which is \dim\ker\B. We claim \ker\B = \{\cvec{y} : \Q_U\cvec{y} \in W\}. If \B\cvec{y} = \cvec{0}, then \cvec{y}^{*}\B\cvec{y} = 0, so (\I - P_W)\Q_U\cvec{y} = \cvec{0} by (a), and \Q_U\cvec{y} = P_W\Q_U\cvec{y} \in W. Conversely, if \Q_U\cvec{y} \in W, then \cvec{y}^{*}\B\cvec{y} = 0 by (a). Writing \cvec{y} = \sum_ic_i\cvec{z}_i, this says \sum_i\sin^2	heta_i\lvert c_ivert^2 = 0. So c_i = 0 whenever \sin	heta_i 
e 0, and then \B\cvec{y} = \sum_ic_i\sin^2	heta_i\cvec{z}_i = \cvec{0}. This proves the claim; the second half of it is the fact in the hint, proved here for this \B. The map \cvec{y} \mapsto \Q_U\cvec{y} is linear and injective (@lem-orthonormal-basis-matrix (b)). It carries \ker\B onto \{\cvec{u} \in U : \cvec{u} \in W\} = U \cap W, because every vector of U is \Q_U\cvec{y} for some \cvec{y}. So \dim\ker\B = \dim(U \cap W). (c) 	heta_i = \pi/2 exactly when \sigma_i(\M) = 0. The number of nonzero singular values of \M is ank\M (@thm-svd), so the number of zero ones among the k is k - ank\M = \dim\ker\M, by the Rank–Nullity Theorem (@thm-rank-nullity) for \cvec{y} \mapsto \M\cvec{y} on F^k. Next, \M\cvec{y} = \Q_W^{*}\Q_U\cvec{y} = \cvec{0} if and only if P_W\Q_U\cvec{y} = \Q_W(\Q_W^{*}\Q_U\cvec{y}) = \cvec{0}, because \Q_W is injective. That holds if and only if \Q_U\cvec{y} \in W^{\perp}. As in (b), \cvec{y} \mapsto \Q_U\cvec{y} carries \ker\M injectively onto U \cap W^{\perp}, so the count is \dim(U \cap W^{\perp}). [C2: The smallest angle as a maximum] Let U, W \subseteq F^n with 1 \le k = \dim U \le l = \dim W and principal angles 	heta_1 \le \dots \le 	heta_k. 1. Prove that \cos	heta_1 = \max igl\{\lvert\inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}}vert : \cvec{u} \in U,\ \cvec{w} \in W,\ 
orm{\cvec{u}} = 
orm{\cvec{w}} = 1 igr\} , and that the maximum is attained at the principal vectors \cvec{u}_1, \cvec{w}_1. 2. Deduce that 	heta_1 is the smallest principal angle between a line of U and a line of W, which is the notion tried and rejected at the start of the section. 3. Hence explain, in one sentence, why 	heta_1 alone cannot distinguish the pairs (U, W_1) and (U, U) of the opening, but the full list 	heta_1, 	heta_2 can. (a) Let \cvec{u} \in U and \cvec{w} \in W be unit vectors. By @lem-orthonormal-basis-matrix (a) and (b), \cvec{u} = \Q_U\cvec{y} and \cvec{w} = \Q_W\cvec{z} with \cvec{y} = \Q_U^{*}\cvec{u} and \cvec{z} = \Q_W^{*}\cvec{w} unit vectors. Then \inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}} = \cvec{z}^{*}\Q_W^{*}\Q_U\cvec{y} = \cvec{z}^{*}\M\cvec{y}, and by Cauchy–Schwarz and @thm-operator-norm-properties (a), \lvert\inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}}vert \le 
orm{\cvec{z}}\,
orm{\M\cvec{y}} \le 
orm{\M}_2 = \sigma_1(\M) = \cos	heta_1 , using @thm-operator-norm-formulas (c). By @prp-principal-vectors, the unit vectors \cvec{u}_1 \in U and \cvec{w}_1 \in W satisfy \inner{\cvec{u}_1}{\cvec{w}_1} = \cos	heta_1, so the maximum exists and equals \cos	heta_1. (b) By @prp-principal-angles-well-defined (d), the principal angle between the lines \Span(\cvec{u}) and \Span(\cvec{w}) is \arccos\lvert\inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}}vert. Since \arccos is decreasing, the smallest such angle corresponds to the largest \lvert\inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{w}}vert, which by (a) is \cos	heta_1. (c) Both pairs share a line, so both have 	heta_1 = 0, and the first number cannot separate them. The second angle is \pi/2 for (U, W_1) and 0 for (U, U), by Examples 4 and 2 after @prp-principal-angles-well-defined.

title: 20.9 The Davis–Kahan Theorem
content:
The Davis–Kahan Theorem Weyl’s inequality settled the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix: under a Hermitian perturbation \E, each of them moves by at most 
orm{\E}_2, whatever the matrix and however its eigenvalues are spaced. Eigenvectors are a different matter, and this section is about them. Section 8 supplied the yardstick, the principal angles between two subspaces, and Section 7 supplied the tool, bounds for the equation \A\X - \X\B = \Y. The theorem of this section is what happens when the two meet: the perturbation of an invariant subspace satisfies a Sylvester equation, and the bounds of Section 7 then measure it. Throughout, \A and \widetilde{\A} = \A + \E are Hermitian matrices in M_n(
C), so \E = \widetilde{\A} - \A is Hermitian too, and 1 \le k \le n - 1. As everywhere in this chapter, 
orm{\cdot}_2 is the spectral norm and 
orm{\cdot}_F the Frobenius norm, and every bound names the norm it holds in. For a subspace we write \col(\Q) for the column space of a matrix \Q whose columns span it. Eigenvectors can move a long way Before any theorem, here is what goes wrong. The example is as small as it can be, and every number in it is exact. [A tiny perturbation that turns the eigenvectors through 45°] Let 0 < \eta < 1 and \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 + \eta & 0 \ 0 & 1 - \eta \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \E = \eta egin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . Compare the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of \A and of \widetilde{\A} = \A + \E, and compute 
orm{\E}_2. Adding, \widetilde{\A} =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & \eta \ \eta & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}. Since \widetilde{\A} egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 1 \end{pmatrix} = (1 + \eta) egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \widetilde{\A} egin{pmatrix} 1 \ -1 \end{pmatrix} = (1 - \eta) egin{pmatrix} 1 \ -1 \end{pmatrix}, the eigenvalues of \widetilde{\A} are 1 + \eta and 1 - \eta: exactly those of \A. The eigenvectors are another story. For the eigenvalue 1 + \eta, the matrix \A has the unit eigenvector \cvec{e}_1 and \widetilde{\A} has 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1); the two lines they span meet at the angle \pi/4, because \lvert\inner{\cvec{e}_1}{	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)}vert = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} = \cos	frac{\pi}{4}. The same happens for 1 - \eta, with \cvec{e}_2 and 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1). The matrix \E/\eta is Hermitian and squares to 2\I_2, so its eigenvalues are \pm\sqrt2 (it has trace 0), and by @lem-hermitian-spectral-norm 
orm{\E}_2 = \sqrt2\,\eta . So as \eta 	o 0^{+} the perturbation vanishes, the eigenvalues do not move at all, and yet the eigenvectors of \widetilde{\A} stay a full 45^\circ away from those of \A. The rotation does not shrink with \eta. What does shrink with \eta is the distance 2\eta between the two eigenvalues of \A, and that is the whole story: the two eigenvalues are so close that a perturbation of their own size can mix their eigenvectors freely. An eigenvector bound must therefore divide by a gap, and the natural guess is “angle \lesssim perturbation / gap”. Here that ratio is \sqrt2\eta/2\eta = 1/\sqrt2 = \sin(\pi/4), which is exactly the sine of the angle. The theorem below turns the guess into an inequality, and this example will turn out to attain it. Well-conditioned eigenvalues do not make well-conditioned eigenvectors. @cor-weyl-perturbation guarantees that every eigenvalue of a Hermitian matrix moves by at most 
orm{\E}_2, with no mention of gaps, and it is tempting to expect the same of eigenvectors. @exm-davis-kahan-small-gap refutes this: a perturbation of size \sqrt2\,\eta leaves every eigenvalue fixed and turns every eigenvector through \pi/4, however small \eta is. No inequality of the form \sin	heta \le C
orm{\E}_2, with C depending only on n, can hold. Two norms, three facts The proofs of this section and the next shuffle unitary factors and matrices with orthonormal columns in and out of norms, sometimes the spectral one and sometimes the Frobenius one. The facts needed are elementary, but they are needed so often that they are worth collecting once. Part (c) is mostly quoted: its norm identities for a matrix with orthonormal columns are @lem-orthonormal-basis-matrix (b) of Section 8, read with U = \col(\X), and for the Frobenius norm the unitary invariance is @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant. The rest — (a), (b), and the inequality 
orm{\X^{*}\N} \le 
orm{\N} — is proved below, and what the lemma is really for is to have all of it, in both norms, in one place. [Moving Factors in and out of the Two Norms] Let 
orm{\cdot} stand for either 
orm{\cdot}_2 or 
orm{\cdot}_F, the same one throughout each statement. 1. 
orm{\M^{*}} = 
orm{\M} for every \M \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C). 2. 
orm{\X\M\Y} \le 
orm{\X}_2\,
orm{\M}\,
orm{\Y}_2 whenever the product is defined. 3. If \X \in M_{m 	imes k}(
C) has orthonormal columns, that is \X^{*}\X = \I_k, then 
orm{\X}_2 = 1, 
orm{\X\M} = 
orm{\M}, and 
orm{\X^{*}\N} \le 
orm{\N} for all \M \in M_{k 	imes n}(
C) and \N \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C). In particular 
orm{\U\M\V} = 
orm{\M} for unitary \U and \V. (a) For 
orm{\cdot}_F this holds because \M^{*} has the same entries as \M up to position and conjugation. For 
orm{\cdot}_2, let \cvec{x} \in 
C^n. By @thm-cauchy-schwarz and @thm-operator-norm-properties (a), applied twice, 
orm{\M\cvec{x}}^2 = \inner{\M^{*}\M\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} \le 
orm{\M^{*}\M\cvec{x}}\,
orm{\cvec{x}} \le 
orm{\M^{*}}_2
orm{\M}_2
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 . Taking the maximum over unit \cvec{x} gives 
orm{\M}_2^2 \le 
orm{\M^{*}}_2
orm{\M}_2, hence 
orm{\M}_2 \le 
orm{\M^{*}}_2 when \M 
e \O (and trivially when \M = \O). Applying this to \M^{*}, whose conjugate transpose is \M, gives the reverse inequality. (b) For 
orm{\cdot}_2 this is @thm-operator-norm-properties (d) used twice. For 
orm{\cdot}_F, let \cvec{m}_1, \dots, \cvec{m}_n be the columns of \M. The columns of \X\M are the \X\cvec{m}_j, and the squared Frobenius norm is the sum of the squared lengths of the columns, so 
orm{\X\M}_F^2 = \sum_j 
orm{\X\cvec{m}_j}^2 \le 
orm{\X}_2^2\sum_j
orm{\cvec{m}_j}^2 = 
orm{\X}_2^2
orm{\M}_F^2 . For a factor on the right, (a) and the left-hand case give 
orm{\M\Y}_F = 
orm{\Y^{*}\M^{*}}_F \le 
orm{\Y^{*}}_2
orm{\M^{*}}_F = 
orm{\Y}_2
orm{\M}_F. Combining the two cases gives (b). (c) For every \cvec{v} \in 
C^k, 
orm{\X\cvec{v}}^2 = \cvec{v}^{*}\X^{*}\X\cvec{v} = 
orm{\cvec{v}}^2. Hence 
orm{\X}_2 = 1, and multiplying by \X changes the length of no column, so 
orm{\X\M}_F = 
orm{\M}_F and 
orm{\X\M\cvec{v}} = 
orm{\M\cvec{v}} for every \cvec{v}, which gives 
orm{\X\M}_2 = 
orm{\M}_2. Next, 
orm{\X^{*}}_2 = 
orm{\X}_2 = 1 by (a), so 
orm{\X^{*}\N} \le 
orm{\N} by (b). Finally, for unitary \U and \V both \U and \V^{*} have orthonormal columns, so 
orm{\U\M\V} = 
orm{\M\V} = 
orm{\V^{*}\M^{*}} = 
orm{\M^{*}} = 
orm{\M}, using (a) twice. Part (c) is the one used most. Its inequality 
orm{\X^{*}\N} \le 
orm{\N} says that reading \N in only some of the coordinates of an orthonormal basis can only lose mass, never gain it. The perturbation of a subspace is a Sylvester equation Fix the data. A Hermitian matrix is normal, so by @cor-spectral-complex-matrix there is a unitary \Q \in M_n(
C) with \Q^{*}\A\Q diagonal, the eigenvalues appearing in any order we like, and they are real by @thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues. Choose k of them, list them first, and split the columns accordingly: \Q =  egin{pmatrix} \Q_1 & \Q_2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Q^{*}\A\Q =  egin{pmatrix} \vLambda_1 & \O \ \O & \vLambda_2 \end{pmatrix}, with \Q_1 \in M_{n 	imes k}(
C) and \vLambda_1 \in M_k(
R), \vLambda_2 \in M_{n-k}(
R) diagonal. Do the same for \widetilde{\A}, producing \widetilde{\Q} =  egin{pmatrix} \widetilde{\Q}_1 & \widetilde{\Q}_2 \end{pmatrix}, \widetilde{\vLambda}_1, and \widetilde{\vLambda}_2. Reading \A\Q = \Q(\vLambda_1 \oplus \vLambda_2) column by column, \A\Q_1 = \Q_1\vLambda_1, \qquad \widetilde{\A}\widetilde{\Q}_2 = \widetilde{\Q}_2\widetilde{\vLambda}_2 , so the columns of \Q_1 are orthonormal eigenvectors of \A, and U = \col(\Q_1) is a k-dimensional subspace invariant under \A. Likewise W = \col(\widetilde{\Q}_1) is a k-dimensional subspace invariant under \widetilde{\A}. The question is how far apart U and W are, and Section 8 answers “measure the principal angles 	heta_1 \le \dots \le 	heta_k of @def-principal-angles”. Put \X \coloneqq \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\Q_1 \in M_{(n-k) 	imes k}(
C) . It measures the angles, and it satisfies an equation. The unperturbed subspace, read in the perturbed complement, solves a Sylvester equation whose coefficients are the two spectra and whose right-hand side is the perturbation. [The Subspace Perturbation Equation] In the notation above, \widetilde{\vLambda}_2\X - \X\vLambda_1 = \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\E\Q_1 , {#eq-davis-kahan-identity} and the nonzero singular values of \X are the nonzero sines \sin	heta_i of the principal angles between U = \col(\Q_1) and W = \col(\widetilde{\Q}_1), with multiplicity. In particular 
orm{\X}_F = 
orm{\sin\Theta(U, W)}_F , \qquad 
orm{\X}_2 = \sin	heta_k = 
orm{\sin\Theta(U, W)}_2 , where \sin\Theta(U, W) = \diag(\sin	heta_1, \dots, \sin	heta_k). Compute \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\widetilde{\A}\Q_1 twice. Letting \widetilde{\A} act to the left, on the perturbed eigenvectors, produces \widetilde{\vLambda}_2. Writing \widetilde{\A} = \A + \E and letting \A act to the right, on the unperturbed ones, produces \vLambda_1, plus an error term that carries \E. The difference of the two computations is the identity. Taking conjugate transposes in \widetilde{\A}\widetilde{\Q}_2 = \widetilde{\Q}_2\widetilde{\vLambda}_2, and using \widetilde{\A}^{*} = \widetilde{\A} and \widetilde{\vLambda}_2^{*} = \widetilde{\vLambda}_2 (a real diagonal matrix), gives \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\widetilde{\A} = \widetilde{\vLambda}_2\widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}. Hence \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\widetilde{\A}\Q_1 = \widetilde{\vLambda}_2\widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\Q_1 = \widetilde{\vLambda}_2\X . On the other hand \widetilde{\A} = \A + \E and \A\Q_1 = \Q_1\vLambda_1, so  egin{aligned} \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\widetilde{\A}\Q_1 &= \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\Q_1\vLambda_1 + \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\E\Q_1 \ &= \X\vLambda_1 + \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\E\Q_1 . \end{aligned} Subtracting the two expressions gives @eq-davis-kahan-identity. For the angles: the columns of the unitary \widetilde{\Q} form an orthonormal basis of 
C^n (@thm-isometry-characterizations), so the n - k columns of \widetilde{\Q}_2 are orthonormal and orthogonal to every column of \widetilde{\Q}_1. They therefore span a subspace of W^{\perp} of dimension n - k, which is all of W^{\perp} because \dim W^{\perp} = n - k by @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (c). So \widetilde{\Q}_2 is a matrix whose columns are an orthonormal basis of W^{\perp}, and @thm-sines-of-principal-angles (a) says that the singular values of \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\Q_1 = \X are the \sin	heta_i, as a multiset completed by zeros; zeros change neither a sum of squares nor a maximum of nonnegative numbers. For the two norms, \I - P_W = P_{W^{\perp}} = \widetilde{\Q}_2\widetilde{\Q}_2^{*} by @lem-orthonormal-basis-matrix (d) and (a), so (\I - P_W)\Q_1 = \widetilde{\Q}_2\X, and @lem-spectral-frobenius-toolkit (c) removes the factor \widetilde{\Q}_2: 
orm{\X}_F = 
orm{(\I - P_W)\Q_1}_F, \qquad 
orm{\X}_2 = 
orm{(\I - P_W)\Q_1}_2 . By @thm-sines-of-principal-angles (b), applied with U and W, these are 
orm{\sin\Theta(U, W)}_F and \sin	heta_k = 
orm{\sin\Theta(U, W)}_2. This proves the lemma. Take \A = \widetilde{\A} = \I_2, so \E = \O, with k = 1, \Q_1 = \cvec{e}_1, and \widetilde{\Q}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1); both are legitimate choices of unit eigenvector. The subspaces U and W are 45^\circ apart, although the matrices are equal. What does @eq-davis-kahan-identity say here, and why is there no contradiction? Here \vLambda_1 = (1) and \widetilde{\vLambda}_2 = (1), so the equation reads 1\cdot\X - \X\cdot 1 = \O, which every 1 	imes 1 matrix satisfies. The equation holds, as it must, but it does not determine \X, and \X = \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\Q_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1)\cdot\cvec{e}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} = \sin	frac{\pi}{4} is one of its many solutions. The trouble is that the spectra of \widetilde{\vLambda}_2 and \vLambda_1 overlap. The theorems below assume that they are separated, and then the equation has exactly one solution (@thm-sylvester-equation), which is small when the right-hand side is. The \sin\Theta theorem in the Frobenius norm With the identity in hand, the theorem is a matter of dividing by the gap. The gap that matters compares perturbed eigenvalues outside the subspace with unperturbed eigenvalues inside it, because those are the two coefficient matrices of the equation. [The Davis–Kahan \sin\Theta Theorem] Let \A, \widetilde{\A} = \A + \E \in M_n(
C) be Hermitian, let 1 \le k \le n-1, and let \Q =  egin{pmatrix} \Q_1 & \Q_2 \end{pmatrix} and \widetilde{\Q} =  egin{pmatrix} \widetilde{\Q}_1 & \widetilde{\Q}_2 \end{pmatrix} be unitary, with \Q_1, \widetilde{\Q}_1 \in M_{n 	imes k}(
C), such that \Q^{*}\A\Q = \vLambda_1 \oplus \vLambda_2, \qquad \widetilde{\Q}^{*}\widetilde{\A}\widetilde{\Q} = \widetilde{\vLambda}_1 \oplus \widetilde{\vLambda}_2 are real diagonal. Suppose there is a \delta > 0 such that \lvert\mu - \lambdavert \ge \delta for every diagonal entry \mu of \widetilde{\vLambda}_2 and every diagonal entry \lambda of \vLambda_1. Then the principal angles \Theta = \Theta(\col(\Q_1), \col(\widetilde{\Q}_1)) satisfy 
orm{\sin\Theta}_F \ \le\  rac{
orm{\E\Q_1}_F}{\delta} \ \le\  rac{\sqrt{k}\,
orm{\E}_2}{\delta} . @eq-davis-kahan-identity is a Sylvester equation whose two coefficient matrices are diagonal, hence normal, and for a normal pair the separation of Section 7 is exactly the distance between the two spectra. The hypothesis says that this distance is at least \delta, so Section 7’s bound divides the right-hand side by \delta. What is left is @lem-davis-kahan-identity, which reads the size of \X as the size of \sin\Theta. Write \mu_1, \dots, \mu_{n-k} for the diagonal entries of \widetilde{\vLambda}_2, \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k for those of \vLambda_1, and \Y = \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\E\Q_1, so that \widetilde{\vLambda}_2\X - \X\vLambda_1 = \Y by @lem-davis-kahan-identity. A diagonal matrix is normal, and its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, so @thm-sep-normal gives \operatorname{sep}_F(\widetilde{\vLambda}_2, \vLambda_1) = \min_{i,j}\lvert\mu_i - \lambda_jvert \ \ge\ \delta > 0 . As in the proof of @lem-davis-kahan-identity, \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\widetilde{\A} = \widetilde{\vLambda}_2\widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}, so with \X' = \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\Z', \widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\R\V = \widetilde{\vLambda}_2\X' - \X'\D . Both coefficient matrices are real diagonal, hence normal, and their diagonal entries differ by at least \delta, so, as in the proof of @thm-davis-kahan-frobenius, @thm-sep-normal and @prp-sep-properties (d) give 
orm{\X'}_F \le 
orm{\widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\R\V}_F/\delta. By @lem-spectral-frobenius-toolkit (c), 
orm{\widetilde{\Q}_2^{*}\R\V}_F \le 
orm{\R\V}_F = 
orm{\R}_F. Finally, by @thm-sines-of-principal-angles applied as in @lem-davis-kahan-identity, with \col(\Z') = \col(\Z) in place of \col(\Q_1), 
orm{\X'}_F = 
orm{\sin\Theta}_F. This proves (a). (b) Take k = 1 and \Z = \cvec{z}. Then \M = (\mu), \R = \cvec{r}, and the only eigenvalue of \M is \mu. Since \lambda_i(\widetilde{\A}) is simple, its eigenspace is the line \Span(\widetilde{\cvec{x}}), so we may choose \widetilde{\Q} with first column \widetilde{\cvec{x}} and \widetilde{\vLambda}_2 holding the other eigenvalues of \widetilde{\A}, as in the proof of @cor-eigenvector-perturbation. Part (a) gives \sin	heta(\cvec{z}, \widetilde{\cvec{x}}) \le 
orm{\cvec{r}}/\delta. This is the eigenvector companion of a residual bound: everything on the right is computable from \cvec{z} and \widetilde{\A} and a gap estimate, with no unperturbed matrix in sight. [C2: The constant in the eigenvector bound is sharp] Let g > 0 and e > 0, and let \A = \diag(g, 0), \E = e egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}. 1. Show that a unit eigenvector \widetilde{\cvec{x}} of \A + \E for its larger eigenvalue makes an angle 	heta \in [0, \pi/4) with \cvec{e}_1 satisfying 	an 2	heta = 2e/g. 2. Deduce that \sin	heta \cdot g/e 	o 1 as e 	o 0^{+}. 3. Hence show that for no constant c < 1 is it true that \sin	heta(\cvec{x}, \widetilde{\cvec{x}}) \le c\,
orm{\E}_2/\gamma for all sufficiently small Hermitian \E, in the setting of @cor-eigenvector-perturbation. (a) The larger eigenvalue of \widetilde{\A} =  egin{psmallmatrix} g & e \ e & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} is \lambda_+ = h + s, where h = g/2 and s = \sqrt{h^2 + e^2}. The first row of \widetilde{\A} - \lambda_+\I is (g - \lambda_+, e) = (h - s, e), so (e, s - h) spans the eigenline, and s - h > 0. The angle with \cvec{e}_1 therefore satisfies 	an	heta = t \coloneqq (s - h)/e > 0. Using s^2 = h^2 + e^2, 1 - t^2 =  rac{e^2 - (s - h)^2}{e^2} =  rac{2h(s - h)}{e^2} > 0 , so t < 1, that is 	heta < \pi/4, and  egin{aligned} 	an 2	heta =  rac{2t}{1 - t^2} &=  rac{2(s - h)}{e}\cdot rac{e^2}{2h(s - h)} \ &=  rac{e}{h} =  rac{2e}{g} . \end{aligned} (b) From (a), \cos 2	heta = 1/\sqrt{1 + 	an^2 2	heta} = g/\sqrt{g^2 + 4e^2}, since 2	heta \in [0, \pi/2). Hence  egin{aligned} \sin^2	heta =  rac{1 - \cos 2	heta}{2} &=  rac{\sqrt{g^2 + 4e^2} - g}{2\sqrt{g^2 + 4e^2}} \ &=  rac{2e^2}{\sqrt{g^2 + 4e^2}\, igl(\sqrt{g^2 + 4e^2} + g igr)} , \end{aligned} multiplying above and below by \sqrt{g^2 + 4e^2} + g. So \Bigl( rac{g\sin	heta}{e}\Bigr)^2 =  rac{2g^2}{\sqrt{g^2 + 4e^2}\, igl(\sqrt{g^2 + 4e^2} + g igr)} , which tends to 2g^2/(g \cdot 2g) = 1 as e 	o 0^{+}, by continuity of the square root. (c) Here \cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_1, \gamma = g, and 
orm{\E}_2 = e, since \E/e is Hermitian with eigenvalues \pm1. If \sin	heta \le c\,e/g held for all small e > 0 with some c < 1, then \sin	heta \cdot g/e \le c for those e, contradicting (b). So to first order in 
orm{\E}_2, the bound 
orm{\E}_2/(\gamma - 
orm{\E}_2) of @cor-eigenvector-perturbation cannot be improved by any constant factor.

title: 20.10 Singular Values and Polar Factors
content:
Singular Values and Polar Factors Chapter 17 §09 proved that singular values are perfectly conditioned: \lvert\sigma_i(\A + \E) - \sigma_i(\A)vert \le 
orm{\E}_2, for any matrices at all. This section finishes that story and then starts a new one. First the Frobenius-norm version, Mirsky’s theorem, which follows from Section 5’s Hoffman–Wielandt inequality once the Hermitian dilation of Chapter 17 turns singular values into eigenvalues. Then the polar decomposition \A = \U\P: how far do the unitary factor and the positive factor move when \A does? Both answers come from one tool used twice, the bound of Section 7 for a Sylvester equation with positive coefficients. Throughout, the field is 
C, 
orm{\cdot}_2 is the spectral norm and 
orm{\cdot}_F the Frobenius norm, and @lem-spectral-frobenius-toolkit of Section 9 is used freely to move unitary factors and conjugate transposes in and out of either norm. For \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C) we put p = \min(m, n), and \sigma_1(\A) \ge \dots \ge \sigma_p(\A) \ge 0 are its singular values (@def-singular-values). Singular values in the Frobenius norm Here is where Chapter 17 left the question. Its @cor-singular-value-perturbation says that for any \A, \E \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C), \lvert\sigma_i(\A + \E) - \sigma_i(\A)vert \le 
orm{\E}_2 \qquad (1 \le i \le p) , with no symmetry, squareness, or smallness assumed. In the language of Section 5 this is a bound on the largest entry of the vector of differences, and the matching is simply by index. What it does not give is a good bound on all the differences together. Squaring and adding p copies of it gives \sum_{i=1}^{p} igl(\sigma_i(\A + \E) - \sigma_i(\A) igr)^2 \le p\,
orm{\E}_2^2 , and the factor p grows with the size of the matrices. For Hermitian eigenvalues, Section 5 removed that factor: @cor-hoffman-wielandt-hermitian bounds the sum of squares by 
orm{\E}_F^2, with no dependence on n. Chapter 17 recorded, in @prp-hermitian-dilation, a device for carrying any theorem about Hermitian eigenvalues over to singular values, and promised that this chapter would lean on it. Here it is. [Mirsky’s Theorem] Let \A, \B \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C) and p = \min(m, n). Then \sum_{i=1}^{p} igl(\sigma_i(\A) - \sigma_i(\B) igr)^2 \ \le\ 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 . Replace each matrix by its Hermitian dilation \cH(\cdot), whose eigenvalues are \pm\sigma_i and zeros. Listed decreasingly, the eigenvalues of \cH(\A) are \sigma_1(\A), \dots, \sigma_p(\A), then the zeros, then -\sigma_p(\A), \dots, -\sigma_1(\A), and the positions depend only on m and n, so \cH(\B) has the same pattern. Apply the Hermitian Hoffman–Wielandt inequality to the two dilations. On the left each difference \sigma_i(\A) - \sigma_i(\B) appears twice, once from the top and once from the bottom, while the zeros cancel against zeros. On the right each entry of \A - \B appears twice, once in each off-diagonal block. The two factors of 2 cancel. For \M \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C), \cH(\M) =  egin{psmallmatrix} \O & \M \ \M^{*} & \O \end{psmallmatrix} is Hermitian (@prp-hermitian-dilation). Since conjugate transposition is additive, \cH(\A) - \cH(\B) =  egin{pmatrix} \O & \A - \B \ (\A - \B)^{*} & \O \end{pmatrix} = \cH(\A - \B) , and since the entries of \cH(\M) are those of \M, those of \M^{*}, and zeros, 
orm{\cH(\M)}_F^2 = 
orm{\M}_F^2 + 
orm{\M^{*}}_F^2 = 2
orm{\M}_F^2 . {#eq-dilation-frobenius} By @prp-hermitian-dilation, \cH(\A) \in M_{m+n}(
C) has eigenvalues \pm\sigma_1(\A), \dots, \pm\sigma_p(\A) and m + n - 2p zeros, with multiplicity. Since every \sigma_i(\A) \ge 0, the list  egin{aligned} &\sigma_1(\A) \ge \dots \ge \sigma_p(\A) \ \ge\ \underbrace{0 \ge \dots \ge 0}_{m+n-2p} \ &\qquad \ge\ -\sigma_p(\A) \ge \dots \ge -\sigma_1(\A) \end{aligned} is decreasing, and a multiset of real numbers has only one decreasing listing. So, with N = m + n, \lambda_i(\cH(\A)) =  egin{cases} \sigma_i(\A) & 1 \le i \le p, \ 0 & p < i \le N - p, \ -\sigma_{N+1-i}(\A) & N - p < i \le N . \end{cases} The same formula holds for \B, with the same three ranges of i, because m, n, and p are the same. Hence, summing over the three ranges, and writing j = N + 1 - i in the third,  egin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^{N} igl(\lambda_i(\cH(\A)) - \lambda_i(\cH(\B)) igr)^2 &= \sum_{i=1}^{p} igl(\sigma_i(\A) - \sigma_i(\B) igr)^2 + 0 \ &\qquad + \sum_{j=1}^{p} igl(-\sigma_j(\A) + \sigma_j(\B) igr)^2 \ &= 2\sum_{i=1}^{p} igl(\sigma_i(\A) - \sigma_i(\B) igr)^2 . \end{aligned} By @cor-hoffman-wielandt-hermitian, applied to the Hermitian matrices \cH(\A) and \cH(\B), the left-hand side is at most 
orm{\cH(\A) - \cH(\B)}_F^2 = 
orm{\cH(\A - \B)}_F^2 = 2
orm{\A - \B}_F^2, by @eq-dilation-frobenius. Dividing by 2 proves the theorem. This is the payment Chapter 17 §09 promised when it said that Chapter 20 leans on the dilation for perturbation bounds. Together with @cor-singular-value-perturbation, it bounds the vector of singular-value differences in the two norms one reaches for first: its largest entry by 
orm{\A - \B}_2, its Euclidean length by 
orm{\A - \B}_F. Chapter 21 puts both inside one statement covering every unitarily invariant norm. Note what was not assumed. @thm-hoffman-wielandt needs normal matrices, and Section 5 showed by a Jordan-block pair that it fails without normality. Mirsky’s theorem holds for every pair of matrices, square or not, because the dilation manufactures the Hermitian hypothesis instead of assuming it. [Two matrices that differ in one entry] Let \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} and \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix}. Compute the singular values of both, and compare the two sides of @thm-mirsky-frobenius with what @cor-singular-value-perturbation alone would give. \A is symmetric with \A(1,1) = 3(1,1) and \A(1,-1) = (1,-1), so \A	p\A = \A^2 has eigenvalues 9 and 1, and \sigma(\A) = (3, 1). For \B, \B	p\B =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, with trace 9 and determinant 16, so its eigenvalues are 	frac{9 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}. These are perfect squares:  igl(	frac{\sqrt{17} \pm 1}{2} igr)^2 = 	frac{18 \pm 2\sqrt{17}}{4} = 	frac{9 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}. Hence \sigma_1(\B) = 	frac{\sqrt{17} + 1}{2} \approx 2.562, \qquad \sigma_2(\B) = 	frac{\sqrt{17} - 1}{2} \approx 1.562 . The difference \A - \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} has 
orm{\A - \B}_F = 
orm{\A - \B}_2 = 1. The left side of Mirsky’s inequality is \Bigl(	frac{5 - \sqrt{17}}{2}\Bigr)^2 + \Bigl(	frac{3 - \sqrt{17}}{2}\Bigr)^2 = 	frac{(42 - 10\sqrt{17}) + (26 - 6\sqrt{17})}{4} = 17 - 4\sqrt{17} \approx 0.508 , comfortably below 1. The index-by-index bound gives \lvert\sigma_i(\A) - \sigma_i(\B)vert \le 1 for each i; the actual values are about 0.438 and 0.562. On its own it bounds the sum of squares only by 2, and Mirsky halves that. Let \A = \diag(3, 1) and \B = \diag(1, 3). Compute both sides of @thm-mirsky-frobenius. Why is the left side not (3 - 1)^2 + (1 - 3)^2? Both matrices have singular values (3, 1) in decreasing order, so the left side is 0, while 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = 
orm{\diag(2, -2)}_F^2 = 8. The theorem compares the sorted lists, the i-th largest with the i-th largest. Pairing the diagonal entries by position would give 8, which is also allowed, but it is not what the theorem measures. Stable singular values do not mean stable singular vectors. Take 0 < \eta < 1, \A = \diag(1 + \eta, 1 - \eta) and \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & \eta \ \eta & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}, the pair of @exm-davis-kahan-small-gap. Both are positive definite with eigenvalues 1 \pm \eta, so both have singular values 1 \pm \eta, and the left side of Mirsky’s inequality is 0. But the right singular vector for \sigma_1 is \cvec{e}_1 for \A and 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1) for \B, a 45^\circ turn, while 
orm{\A - \B}_F = 2\eta is as small as we like. As with eigenvectors, singular vectors are controlled by gaps. Applying Section 9 to the dilations \cH(\A) and \cH(\B), whose eigenvectors are built from the singular vectors, is one way to bound them. The square root is Lipschitz away from zero The second half of the section is about the polar decomposition, and its positive factor is a square root, \lvert\Avert = (\A^{*}\A)^{1/2}. So we start with square roots. For positive numbers there is an exact formula for how far a square root moves: \sqrt{p} - \sqrt{q} =  rac{p - q}{\sqrt{p} + \sqrt{q}} , the usual trick of multiplying by the conjugate. It shows that the square root is Lipschitz on [c, \infty) with constant 1/(2\sqrt{c}), and that no constant works near 0. For matrices the trick fails as written: with \S = \P^{1/2} and \T = \Q^{1/2}, the product (\S - \T)(\S + \T) = \S^2 + \S\T - \T\S - \T^2 is \P - \Q only when \S and \T commute. But a different grouping of the same terms works with no commuting at all: \S(\S - \T) + (\S - \T)\T = \S^2 - \S\T + \S\T - \T^2 = \P - \Q . {#eq-sqrt-sylvester} This says that \X = \S - \T solves the Sylvester equation \S\X + \X\T = \P - \Q, whose coefficients are positive definite. That is exactly the situation of @cor-positive-sylvester. [Perturbation of the Square Root] Let \P, \Q \in M_n(
C) be positive definite. Then 
orm{\P^{1/2} - \Q^{1/2}} \ \le\  rac{
orm{\P - \Q}}{\lambda_n(\P)^{1/2} + \lambda_n(\Q)^{1/2}} , where 
orm{\cdot} is either 
orm{\cdot}_2 or 
orm{\cdot}_F. Put \S = \P^{1/2} and \T = \Q^{1/2}, the positive square roots of @thm-psd-square-root. By that theorem the eigenvalues of \S are the nonnegative square roots of those of \P, and t \mapsto \sqrt{t} is increasing, so the smallest eigenvalue of \S is \alpha \coloneqq \lambda_n(\P)^{1/2}, which is positive because \P \succ \O. Every eigenvalue of the Hermitian matrix \S - \alpha\I is therefore nonnegative, so \S \succeq \alpha\I by @thm-psd-characterizations (b). In the same way \T \succeq  eta\I with  eta \coloneqq \lambda_n(\Q)^{1/2} > 0. By @eq-sqrt-sylvester, \X = \S - \T satisfies \S\X + \X\T = \P - \Q. Since \alpha +  eta > 0, @cor-positive-sylvester applies to this equation, whose solution is therefore unique and equal to \X, and gives 
orm{\S - \T} \le  rac{
orm{\P - \Q}}{\alpha +  eta} in both the spectral and the Frobenius norm. This proves the theorem. For n = 1 this is the scalar identity, as an inequality that happens to be an equality. It is sharp for every n: with \P = \diag(4, 100) and \Q = \diag(1, 100), \P^{1/2} - \Q^{1/2} = \diag(1, 0) has both norms equal to 1, and the bound is 3/(2 + 1) = 1; padding both matrices with a further block 100\,\I_{n-2} changes neither side of the inequality, so the equality holds for every n \ge 2. The difference sits exactly in the direction where both matrices are smallest, which is the worst place for it. The proof used only \alpha +  eta > 0, so the conclusion holds as soon as one of \P and \Q is positive definite and the other positive semidefinite. The square root is not Lipschitz on all positive semidefinite matrices. Take \P = \varepsilon\I_n with 0 < \varepsilon < 1 and \Q = \O. Then 
orm{\P - \Q}_2 = \varepsilon, while \P^{1/2} - \Q^{1/2} = \sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\I_n has spectral norm \sqrt{\varepsilon}, which is larger by the factor 1/\sqrt{\varepsilon}. That factor is unbounded as \varepsilon 	o 0^{+}, so no inequality 
orm{\P^{1/2} - \Q^{1/2}}_2 \le C
orm{\P - \Q}_2 can hold for all \P, \Q \succeq \O. The denominator of the theorem is what records this. By the remark the theorem still applies, with denominator \sqrt{\varepsilon} + 0, and the bound \varepsilon/\sqrt{\varepsilon} = \sqrt{\varepsilon} is attained. @exr-singular-values-and-polar-c1 shows that the square root is nevertheless continuous everywhere, with a square-root modulus. The positive polar factor Recall @thm-polar-decomposition: every \A \in M_n(
C) is a unitary matrix times the positive semidefinite \lvert\Avert = (\A^{*}\A)^{1/2}, and when \A is invertible both factors are unique. In this section we write the decomposition as \A = \U\P, \qquad \U 	ext{ unitary}, \qquad \P = \lvert\Avert , keeping the letter \W for another use below. For invertible \A the matrix \A^{*}\A is positive definite, since \cvec{x}^{*}\A^{*}\A\cvec{x} = 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}^2 > 0 for \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}. Its eigenvalues are the \sigma_i(\A)^2 (@def-singular-values), so \lambda_n(\A^{*}\A) = \sigma_n(\A)^2 > 0, \qquad \P = \lvert\Avert \succeq \sigma_n(\A)\,\I , the second because the eigenvalues of \lvert\Avert are the square roots \sigma_i(\A) (@thm-psd-square-root) and @thm-psd-characterizations (b) applies to \lvert\Avert - \sigma_n(\A)\I as before. [Perturbation of the Positive Polar Factor] Let \A, \B \in M_n(
C) be invertible. Then 
orm{\,\lvert\Avert - \lvert\Bvert\,} \ \le\  rac{ igl(
orm{\A}_2 + 
orm{\B}_2 igr)\,
orm{\A - \B}}{\sigma_n(\A) + \sigma_n(\B)} , where 
orm{\cdot} is either 
orm{\cdot}_2 or 
orm{\cdot}_F. Both \A^{*}\A and \B^{*}\B are positive definite, with \lambda_n(\A^{*}\A)^{1/2} = \sigma_n(\A) and \lambda_n(\B^{*}\B)^{1/2} = \sigma_n(\B), as just shown. So @thm-sqrt-perturbation gives 
orm{\,\lvert\Avert - \lvert\Bvert\,} \le  rac{
orm{\A^{*}\A - \B^{*}\B}}{\sigma_n(\A) + \sigma_n(\B)} . Now \A^{*}\A - \B^{*}\B = \A^{*}(\A - \B) + (\A - \B)^{*}\B, as expanding the right side shows. By @lem-spectral-frobenius-toolkit (b) and (a), 
orm{\A^{*}(\A - \B)} \le 
orm{\A^{*}}_2
orm{\A - \B} = 
orm{\A}_2
orm{\A - \B}, and likewise 
orm{(\A - \B)^{*}\B} \le 
orm{(\A - \B)^{*}}\,
orm{\B}_2 = 
orm{\A - \B}\,
orm{\B}_2. The triangle inequality for the norm (@thm-operator-norm-properties (b) for 
orm{\cdot}_2, @cor-triangle-inequality for the Frobenius norm, which is induced by an inner product) gives 
orm{\A^{*}\A - \B^{*}\B} \le (
orm{\A}_2 + 
orm{\B}_2)
orm{\A - \B}, and substituting proves the theorem. When \B is close to \A, the constant is about 2
orm{\A}_2/(2\sigma_n(\A)) = \kappa_2(\A), the condition number of Chapter 16. So by this estimate \lvert\Avert is as sensitive as \A is ill-conditioned. It is a crude estimate, as the example below shows. Sharper ones are known, but this is the one the Sylvester bound gives with no extra work. The unitary polar factor For a nonzero complex number, the unitary polar factor is the phase z/\lvert zvert. If two numbers z and w have the same modulus r, their phases differ by exactly \lvert z - wvert/r. So the phase moves at the rate of the perturbation divided by the modulus, and it is undefined at z = 0. The theorem below is the matrix form of this, with \sigma_n as the modulus. [Perturbation of the Unitary Polar Factor] Let \A, \B \in M_n(
C) be invertible, with polar decompositions (@thm-polar-decomposition) \A = \U\P and \B = \V\Q, where \U, \V are unitary, \P = \lvert\Avert, and \Q = \lvert\Bvert. Then 
orm{\U - \V} \ \le\  rac{2\,
orm{\A - \B}}{\sigma_n(\A) + \sigma_n(\B)} , where 
orm{\cdot} is either 
orm{\cdot}_2 or 
orm{\cdot}_F. Measure \U against \V by the single unitary matrix \W = \V^{*}\U, which equals \I exactly when \U = \V; then 
orm{\U - \V} = 
orm{\W - \I}. Now write \A - \B in the two polar frames. Seen through \V^{*} on the left it is \W\P - \Q. Its conjugate transpose, seen through \U on the right, is \P - \Q\W. The difference of these two expressions is (\W - \I)\P + \Q(\W - \I), a Sylvester equation for \W - \I with positive definite coefficients \Q and \P, and its right-hand side has norm at most 2
orm{\A - \B}. Put \W = \V^{*}\U, which is unitary. Since \U^{*}\U = \V^{*}\V = \I, \P^{*} = \P, and \Q^{*} = \Q,  egin{aligned} \V^{*}(\A - \B) &= \V^{*}\U\P - \V^{*}\V\Q = \W\P - \Q, \ (\A - \B)^{*}\U &= \P\U^{*}\U - \Q\V^{*}\U = \P - \Q\W . \end{aligned} Subtracting the second identity from the first,  egin{aligned} \V^{*}(\A - \B) - (\A - \B)^{*}\U &= \W\P - \P + \Q\W - \Q \ &= \Q(\W - \I) + (\W - \I)\P . \end{aligned} {#eq-polar-factor-identity} So \X = \W - \I solves \Q\X + \X\P = \Y, with \Y the left side of @eq-polar-factor-identity. As shown before @thm-polar-positive-perturbation, \Q \succeq \sigma_n(\B)\I and \P \succeq \sigma_n(\A)\I, and \sigma_n(\A) + \sigma_n(\B) > 0. So @cor-positive-sylvester, applied with \Q and \P as its two coefficients, gives 
orm{\W - \I} \le  rac{
orm{\Y}}{\sigma_n(\A) + \sigma_n(\B)} in both norms. By @lem-spectral-frobenius-toolkit (c) and (a), 
orm{\V^{*}(\A - \B)} = 
orm{\A - \B} and 
orm{(\A - \B)^{*}\U} = 
orm{(\A - \B)^{*}} = 
orm{\A - \B}, so 
orm{\Y} \le 2
orm{\A - \B} by the triangle inequality in either norm (@thm-operator-norm-properties (b), @cor-triangle-inequality). Finally \U - \V = \V(\V^{*}\U - \I) = \V(\W - \I), so 
orm{\U - \V} = 
orm{\W - \I} by @lem-spectral-frobenius-toolkit (c). Combining the three displays proves the theorem. Notice the difference from @thm-polar-positive-perturbation. There the constant was a condition number, but here only \sigma_n appears. The unitary factor feels how close \A is to the singular matrices, which is \sigma_n(\A) by @cor-distance-to-singular, and nothing else. For n = 1, what does the theorem say about two nonzero complex numbers z and w? Test it on z = 1, w = -1. A nonzero z \in 
C = M_1(
C) has polar decomposition z = 	frac{z}{\lvert zvert}\cdot\lvert zvert, with \sigma_1(z) = \lvert zvert, and both norms are the modulus. So the theorem says \Bigl\lvert rac{z}{\lvert zvert} -  rac{w}{\lvert wvert}\Bigrvert \le  rac{2\lvert z - wvert}{\lvert zvert + \lvert wvert} . For z = 1, w = -1 both sides equal 2. So the constant 2 in the theorem cannot be lowered, even for n = 1. [The polar factors of two nearby matrices] Let \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 4 & 5 \end{psmallmatrix}, whose polar decomposition @exm-polar-2x2 found to be \U = 	frac{1}{\sqrt5} egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & -1 \ 1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix}, \lvert\Avert = \sqrt5 egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix}, with \sigma(\A) = (3\sqrt5, \sqrt5). Let \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 6 & 5 \end{psmallmatrix}. Find the polar decomposition of \B, compute 
orm{\U - \V}, and compare it with @thm-polar-unitary-perturbation. Finding \V. For a real 2 	imes 2 matrix of positive determinant, look for \V among the rotations \R_{\varphi} =  egin{psmallmatrix} c & -s \ s & c \end{psmallmatrix}, with c = \cos\varphi, s = \sin\varphi. For \B = (b_{ij}), the off-diagonal entries of \R_{\varphi}	p\B are cb_{12} + sb_{22} and -sb_{11} + cb_{21}, and they agree exactly when (b_{11} + b_{22})s = (b_{21} - b_{12})c. For our \B this reads 8s = 6c, so (c, s) = (	frac45, 	frac35), and  egin{aligned} \V &= 	frac15 egin{pmatrix} 4 & -3 \ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, \ \V	p\B &= 	frac15 egin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \ -3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 6 & 5 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 6 & 3 \ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} . \end{aligned} This symmetric matrix has trace 10 and determinant 15, so both its eigenvalues, 5 \pm \sqrt{10}, are positive, and it is positive definite. Thus \B = \V(\V	p\B) is a unitary matrix times a positive definite one. Squaring gives (\V	p\B)^2 = \B	p\V\V	p\B = \B	p\B, so \V	p\B = \lvert\Bvert by uniqueness of the positive square root (@thm-psd-square-root). Since \B is invertible, @thm-polar-decomposition now gives \V as its unitary polar factor. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of \lvert\Bvert, \sigma(\B) = (5 + \sqrt{10}, 5 - \sqrt{10}) \approx (8.162, 1.838). The same recipe applied to \A gives 8s = 4c, which recovers \U. The distance. \U and \V are the rotations through angles \varphi_{\A} and \varphi_{\B} with \cos(\varphi_{\B} - \varphi_{\A}) = 	frac{2}{\sqrt5}\cdot	frac45 + 	frac{1}{\sqrt5}\cdot	frac35 = 	frac{11}{5\sqrt5} . For two rotations, (\U - \V)	p(\U - \V) = 2\I - (\U	p\V + \V	p\U) =  igl(2 - 2\cos(\varphi_{\B} - \varphi_{\A}) igr)\I, so both singular values of \U - \V equal \sqrt{2 - 22/(5\sqrt5)} and 
orm{\U - \V}_2 \approx 0.180, \qquad 
orm{\U - \V}_F \approx 0.254 . The bound. \A - \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 \ -2 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, so 
orm{\A - \B}_2 = 
orm{\A - \B}_F = 2, and  rac{2 \cdot 2}{\sigma_2(\A) + \sigma_2(\B)} =  rac{4}{\sqrt5 + 5 - \sqrt{10}} \approx 0.982 in both norms. The theorem holds, with a factor of about 5 to spare in the spectral norm and 4 in the Frobenius norm. For the positive factors, @thm-polar-positive-perturbation gives 
orm{\,\lvert\Avert - \lvert\Bvert\,} \le  rac{(3\sqrt5 + 5 + \sqrt{10}) \cdot 2}{\sqrt5 + 5 - \sqrt{10}} \approx 7.30 , while \lvert\Avert - \lvert\Bvert =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2\sqrt5 - 6 & \sqrt5 - 3 \ \sqrt5 - 3 & 2\sqrt5 - 4 \end{psmallmatrix} has spectral norm about 1.79 and Frobenius norm about 1.93. That bound is correct but crude, as promised. At a singular matrix the unitary factor jumps, and no bound of this kind survives. For 0 < \varepsilon \le 1 let  egin{aligned} \A_{\varepsilon} &= \diag(1, \varepsilon) = \I\,\diag(1, \varepsilon), \ \B_{\varepsilon} &= \diag(1, -\varepsilon) = \diag(1, -1)\,\diag(1, \varepsilon) . \end{aligned} These are polar decompositions: the unitary factors are \U = \I and \V = \diag(1, -1), and both positive factors are \diag(1, \varepsilon). As \varepsilon 	o 0^{+}, both matrices tend to the singular \diag(1, 0), and 
orm{\A_{\varepsilon} - \B_{\varepsilon}} = 2\varepsilon 	o 0 in both norms. Yet \U - \V = \diag(0, 2) has spectral and Frobenius norm 2 for every \varepsilon. So the unitary factor has no limit at \diag(1, 0), and it cannot be chosen continuously there. This matches the nonuniqueness in @thm-polar-decomposition: both \I and \diag(1, -1) are unitary polar factors of \diag(1, 0). The theorem, with \sigma_2(\A_{\varepsilon}) = \sigma_2(\B_{\varepsilon}) = \varepsilon, gives the bound (2 \cdot 2\varepsilon)/(2\varepsilon) = 2, which is attained. Padding both matrices with an identity block, \A_{\varepsilon} \oplus \I_{n-2} and \B_{\varepsilon} \oplus \I_{n-2}, gives the same equality for every n \ge 2: the constant 2 cannot be improved, and the denominator cannot be dropped. @cor-unitary-nearest identified the unitary polar factor as the unitary matrix nearest to \A in the Frobenius norm. @thm-polar-unitary-perturbation adds that for invertible \A this nearest unitary matrix moves continuously with \A, at a rate no worse than 2/(\sigma_n(\A) + \sigma_n(\B)). A matrix that has drifted from unitarity can therefore be put back reliably, as long as it stays well away from the singular matrices. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State Mirsky’s theorem. In its proof by the Hermitian dilation of @prp-hermitian-dilation, where does each of the two factors of 2 come from? 2. True or false: \lvert\sigma_i(\A) - \sigma_i(\B)vert \le 
orm{\A - \B}_F for every i. Justify. 3. True or false: the unitary polar factor is a continuous function of \A on the invertible matrices, and it extends continuously to all of M_n(
C). Justify. 4. Which identity turns the perturbation of a square root into a Sylvester equation, and which result then bounds it? 5. Why does @thm-polar-unitary-perturbation hold in both the spectral and the Frobenius norm? (a) @thm-mirsky-frobenius: \sum_{i=1}^{p}(\sigma_i(\A) - \sigma_i(\B))^2 \le 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2. On the eigenvalue side, each difference \sigma_i(\A) - \sigma_i(\B) occurs twice in the sorted spectra of the dilations, once as \sigma_i near the top and once as -\sigma_i near the bottom. On the norm side, each entry of \A - \B occurs twice in \cH(\A - \B), once in \A - \B and once, conjugated, in (\A - \B)^{*} (@eq-dilation-frobenius). (b) True. Every term of the sum in Mirsky’s theorem is nonnegative, so each one is at most the sum, which is at most 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2. (It also follows from @cor-singular-value-perturbation and 
orm{\cdot}_2 \le 
orm{\cdot}_F, @prp-spectral-vs-frobenius.) (c) False as a whole. The first half is true: by @thm-polar-unitary-perturbation, 
orm{\U - \V}_2 \le 2
orm{\A - \B}_2/(\sigma_n(\A) + \sigma_n(\B)), which tends to 0 as \B 	o \A for fixed invertible \A, because \sigma_n(\B) \ge 0. The second half is false: in the last warning of the section, \A_{\varepsilon} and \B_{\varepsilon} both tend to \diag(1, 0) while their unitary factors stay at distance 2, so no value at \diag(1, 0) makes the factor continuous there. (d) \S(\S - \T) + (\S - \T)\T = \S^2 - \T^2 (@eq-sqrt-sylvester), which exhibits \S - \T as the solution of \S\X + \X\T = \P - \Q. Section 7’s @cor-positive-sylvester bounds that solution. (e) Each step holds in both norms: @cor-positive-sylvester is stated for both, and so are the facts of @lem-spectral-frobenius-toolkit used to remove the unitary factors and conjugate transposes. B. Practice [B1: Mirsky by hand] Let \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 4 & 5 \end{psmallmatrix}, with \sigma(\A) = (3\sqrt5, \sqrt5) from @exm-polar-2x2, and \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 4 & 3 \end{psmallmatrix}. 1. Show that \sigma(\B) = (\sqrt{13} + 2, \sqrt{13} - 2). 2. Verify @thm-mirsky-frobenius for this pair. 3. What bound on \sum_i(\sigma_i(\A) - \sigma_i(\B))^2 does @cor-singular-value-perturbation give? Hence say what Mirsky’s theorem gains here. (a) \B	p\B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 25 & 12 \ 12 & 9 \end{psmallmatrix} has trace 34 and determinant 225 - 144 = 81, so its eigenvalues are 17 \pm \sqrt{289 - 81} = 17 \pm 4\sqrt{13}. Since (\sqrt{13} \pm 2)^2 = 17 \pm 4\sqrt{13} and \sqrt{13} - 2 > 0, the singular values are \sqrt{13} \pm 2 \approx 5.606, 1.606. (b) \A - \B = \diag(0, 2), so 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = 4. The left side is  egin{aligned} &(3\sqrt5 - \sqrt{13} - 2)^2 + (\sqrt5 - \sqrt{13} + 2)^2 \ &\qquad = 84 - 8\sqrt{65} - 8\sqrt5 \approx 1.613 , \end{aligned} expanding each square (the \sqrt{13} terms cancel). Indeed 1.613 \le 4. (c) 
orm{\A - \B}_2 = 2, so each \lvert\sigma_i(\A) - \sigma_i(\B)vert \le 2, and the sum of the two squares is at most 8. Mirsky’s theorem gives 4, half as much. The true value is about 1.613: the differences are about 1.103 and 0.631. [B2: A square root that does not commute] Let \S =  egin{psmallmatrix} 3 & 2 \ 2 & 3 \end{psmallmatrix}, \T =  egin{psmallmatrix} 3 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{psmallmatrix}, \P = \S^2, and \Q = \T^2. 1. Compute \P and \Q, and explain why \S = \P^{1/2} and \T = \Q^{1/2}. 2. Find \lambda_2(\P) and \lambda_2(\Q)^{1/2}. 3. Compute 
orm{\P - \Q}_2 and 
orm{\P - \Q}_F, and hence the two bounds of @thm-sqrt-perturbation. Compare them with 
orm{\S - \T}. (a) Squaring, \P =  egin{psmallmatrix} 13 & 12 \ 12 & 13 \end{psmallmatrix} and \Q =  egin{psmallmatrix} 13 & 14 \ 14 & 20 \end{psmallmatrix}. \S is symmetric with eigenvalues 5 and 1 (eigenvectors (1, \pm1)), and \T is symmetric with trace 7 and determinant 8, so both eigenvalues of each are positive, and \S, \T \succ \O. By the uniqueness in @thm-psd-square-root, \S = \P^{1/2} and \T = \Q^{1/2}. (b) The eigenvalues of \P are 25 and 1, so \lambda_2(\P) = 1. The eigenvalues of \T are 	frac{7 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}, and by @thm-psd-square-root those of \Q are their squares, so \lambda_2(\Q)^{1/2} = \lambda_2(\T) = 	frac{7 - \sqrt{17}}{2} \approx 1.438. (c) \P - \Q =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & -2 \ -2 & -7 \end{psmallmatrix} is symmetric with characteristic polynomial t^2 + 7t - 4, so its eigenvalues are 	frac{-7 \pm \sqrt{65}}{2}, and by @lem-hermitian-spectral-norm 
orm{\P - \Q}_2 = 	frac{7 + \sqrt{65}}{2} \approx 7.531. Also 
orm{\P - \Q}_F = \sqrt{4 + 4 + 49} = \sqrt{57} \approx 7.550. The denominator is 1 + 1.438 = 2.438, so the bounds are about 3.089 (spectral) and 3.096 (Frobenius). Since \S - \T = \diag(0, -1), both of its norms equal 1. Hence the theorem holds here with a factor of about 3 to spare. It is not an equality because \S - \T does not sit along the eigenvector of \P and \Q where both are smallest. [B3: A nearly sharp instance] Let \A = 2\I_2 and \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & -1 \ 1 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix}. 1. Find the polar decompositions of \A and \B. 2. Compute 
orm{\U - \V}_2 and 
orm{\U - \V}_F, and compare them with the bounds of @thm-polar-unitary-perturbation. 3. Compute 
orm{\,\lvert\Avert - \lvert\Bvert\,}_2 and the bound of @thm-polar-positive-perturbation. (a) \A = \I \cdot 2\I, with \U = \I and \lvert\Avert = 2\I \succ \O. The columns of \B are orthogonal, each of length \sqrt5, so \V = 	frac{1}{\sqrt5}\B is orthogonal and \B = \V \cdot \sqrt5\,\I, with \sqrt5\,\I \succ \O. Both matrices are invertible, so these are their polar decompositions (@thm-polar-decomposition), and \sigma_2(\A) = 2, \sigma_2(\B) = \sqrt5. (b) \V is the rotation with \cos\varphi = 	frac{2}{\sqrt5}, so, as in @exm-polar-factors-nearby, (\U - \V)	p(\U - \V) = (2 - 2\cos\varphi)\I = (2 - 	frac{4}{\sqrt5})\I. Hence 
orm{\U - \V}_2 = \sqrt{2 - 4/\sqrt5} \approx 0.4595 and 
orm{\U - \V}_F = \sqrt2\,
orm{\U - \V}_2 \approx 0.6498. Next, \A - \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} is orthogonal, so 
orm{\A - \B}_2 = 1 and 
orm{\A - \B}_F = \sqrt2. The bounds are  rac{2 \cdot 1}{2 + \sqrt5} \approx 0.4721, \qquad  rac{2\sqrt2}{2 + \sqrt5} \approx 0.6677 . Both hold, and each is within 3\% of the true value. (c) \lvert\Avert - \lvert\Bvert = (2 - \sqrt5)\I, of spectral norm \sqrt5 - 2 \approx 0.236. The bound is (
orm{\A}_2 + 
orm{\B}_2)
orm{\A - \B}_2/(2 + \sqrt5) = (2 + \sqrt5) \cdot 1/(2 + \sqrt5) = 1, a factor of about 4 larger. C. Going deeper [C1: The square root is continuous everywhere] Let \S, \T \in M_n(
C) be positive semidefinite. 1. Let \lambda be an eigenvalue of the Hermitian matrix \S - \T, with unit eigenvector \cvec{x}. Prove that \S^2 - \T^2 = (\S - \T)^2 + (\S - \T)\T + \T(\S - \T), and that \cvec{x}^{*}(\S^2 - \T^2)\cvec{x} = \lambda^2 + 2\lambda\,\cvec{x}^{*}\T\cvec{x}. 2. Deduce that if \lambda \ge 0 then \lambda^2 \le 
orm{\S^2 - \T^2}_2. 3. Prove that 
orm{\P^{1/2} - \Q^{1/2}}_2 \le 
orm{\P - \Q}_2^{1/2} for all positive semidefinite \P, \Q \in M_n(
C), and show that the exponent 	frac12 cannot be replaced by anything larger. Hint: for (c), apply (b) to the pair (\S, \T) or to the pair (\T, \S), according to the sign of the eigenvalue of \S - \T of largest modulus. (a) Expanding,  egin{aligned} &(\S - \T)^2 + (\S - \T)\T + \T(\S - \T) \ &\qquad = \S^2 - \S\T - \T\S + \T^2 + \S\T - \T^2 + \T\S - \T^2 = \S^2 - \T^2 . \end{aligned} Since (\S - \T)\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} with \lambda real (@thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues) and \S - \T Hermitian, also \cvec{x}^{*}(\S - \T) = \lambda\cvec{x}^{*}. Hence \cvec{x}^{*}(\S - \T)^2\cvec{x} = \lambda^2\cvec{x}^{*}\cvec{x} = \lambda^2, \cvec{x}^{*}(\S - \T)\T\cvec{x} = \lambda\,\cvec{x}^{*}\T\cvec{x}, and \cvec{x}^{*}\T(\S - \T)\cvec{x} = \lambda\,\cvec{x}^{*}\T\cvec{x}. Adding gives the claim. (b) \cvec{x}^{*}\T\cvec{x} \ge 0 because \T \succeq \O, so if \lambda \ge 0, (a) gives \lambda^2 \le \cvec{x}^{*}(\S^2 - \T^2)\cvec{x}. By @thm-cauchy-schwarz and @thm-operator-norm-properties (a), \cvec{x}^{*}\M\cvec{x} \le 
orm{\M\cvec{x}}
orm{\cvec{x}} \le 
orm{\M}_2 for any \M and unit \cvec{x}. So \lambda^2 \le 
orm{\S^2 - \T^2}_2. (c) Put \S = \P^{1/2} and \T = \Q^{1/2}, so \S^2 - \T^2 = \P - \Q. By @lem-hermitian-spectral-norm, 
orm{\S - \T}_2 = \lvert\lambdavert for some eigenvalue \lambda of \S - \T. If \lambda \ge 0, (b) gives \lambda^2 \le 
orm{\P - \Q}_2. If \lambda < 0, then -\lambda > 0 is an eigenvalue of \T - \S, and (b) applied to the pair (\T, \S) gives \lambda^2 \le 
orm{\T^2 - \S^2}_2 = 
orm{\P - \Q}_2. In both cases 
orm{\P^{1/2} - \Q^{1/2}}_2 = \lvert\lambdavert \le 
orm{\P - \Q}_2^{1/2}. For the exponent, take \P = \varepsilon\I and \Q = \O with 0 < \varepsilon < 1, as in the warning after @thm-sqrt-perturbation. Then 
orm{\P^{1/2} - \Q^{1/2}}_2 = \varepsilon^{1/2} and 
orm{\P - \Q}_2 = \varepsilon. If \varepsilon^{1/2} \le C\varepsilon^{r} held for all small \varepsilon with some r > 	frac12, then C \ge \varepsilon^{1/2 - r} 	o \infty as \varepsilon 	o 0^{+}, which is impossible. So the square root, which is not Lipschitz near singular matrices, is still continuous on all positive semidefinite matrices, with modulus t \mapsto t^{1/2}. [C2: Both Eckart–Young lower bounds from perturbation theory] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C), let 0 \le k < p = \min(m, n), and let \B \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C) have rank at most k. 1. Explain why \sigma_i(\B) = 0 for i > k. 2. Prove, using @thm-mirsky-frobenius, that 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 \ge \sum_{i=k+1}^{p}\sigma_i(\A)^2. 3. Prove, using @cor-singular-value-perturbation, that 
orm{\A - \B}_2 \ge \sigma_{k+1}(\A). 4. Compare with @thm-eckart-young and @thm-eckart-young-spectral. (a) By @thm-compact-svd the number of nonzero singular values of \B is ank\B \le k, and they come first in the decreasing list, so \sigma_i(\B) = 0 for i > k. (b) By @thm-mirsky-frobenius, and dropping the nonnegative terms with i \le k,  egin{aligned} 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 &\ge \sum_{i=1}^{p} igl(\sigma_i(\A) - \sigma_i(\B) igr)^2 \ &\ge \sum_{i=k+1}^{p} igl(\sigma_i(\A) - 0 igr)^2 , \end{aligned} using (a) in the last step. (c) By @cor-singular-value-perturbation with i = k + 1 \le p and \E = \B - \A, \sigma_{k+1}(\A) =  igl\lvert\sigma_{k+1}(\A) - \sigma_{k+1}(\B) igrvert \le 
orm{\B - \A}_2 = 
orm{\A - \B}_2 , using (a) and \sigma_{k+1}(\A) \ge 0. (d) These are exactly the lower-bound halves of the Frobenius and the spectral Eckart–Young theorems. Both theorems also show that the bounds are attained, by the truncation \A_k, which has singular values \sigma_1(\A), \dots, \sigma_k(\A), 0, \dots, 0, so that it makes every term with i \le k vanish. So “the best rank-k approximation” is a perturbation theorem read backwards: no matrix of rank k can be closer to \A than the singular values of \A allow, because singular values cannot move further than the perturbation. [C3: The nearest unitary to an almost-unitary matrix] Let \E \in M_n(
C) with 
orm{\E}_2 < 1, let \A = \I + \E, and let \U be the unitary polar factor of \A. 1. Prove that \sigma_n(\A) \ge 1 - 
orm{\E}_2 > 0, so that \A is invertible. 2. Prove that 
orm{\U - \I} \le 2
orm{\E}/(2 - 
orm{\E}_2) in both the spectral and the Frobenius norm. 3. Deduce that if 
orm{\E}_2 \le 	frac12 then 
orm{\U - \I}_F \le 	frac43
orm{\E}_F. Compare with the bound 
orm{\U - \I}_F \le 2
orm{\E}_F that @cor-unitary-nearest and the triangle inequality give with no computation. (a) The identity has all singular values equal to 1. By @cor-singular-value-perturbation with i = n, \lvert\sigma_n(\I + \E) - 1vert \le 
orm{\E}_2, so \sigma_n(\A) \ge 1 - 
orm{\E}_2 > 0. An n 	imes n matrix with n nonzero singular values has rank n (@thm-compact-svd), so \A is invertible. (b) Apply @thm-polar-unitary-perturbation to \A and \B = \I, whose polar decomposition is \I = \I \cdot \I, with \V = \I and \sigma_n(\I) = 1. Since \A - \I = \E, 
orm{\U - \I} \le  rac{2
orm{\E}}{\sigma_n(\A) + 1} \le  rac{2
orm{\E}}{2 - 
orm{\E}_2} , using (a) to bound the denominator from below. This holds in both norms because the theorem does. (c) If 
orm{\E}_2 \le 	frac12 then 2 - 
orm{\E}_2 \ge 	frac32, and (b) in the Frobenius norm gives 
orm{\U - \I}_F \le 	frac43
orm{\E}_F. For comparison, @cor-unitary-nearest says that \U is at least as close to \A as any unitary matrix is, and \I is one, so 
orm{\A - \U}_F \le 
orm{\A - \I}_F = 
orm{\E}_F. The triangle inequality (@cor-triangle-inequality) then gives 
orm{\U - \I}_F \le 
orm{\U - \A}_F + 
orm{\A - \I}_F \le 2
orm{\E}_F . So the soft argument already locates \U within 2
orm{\E}_F of \I. Part (b) improves the constant to 	frac43 when 
orm{\E}_2 \le 	frac12, and to 2/(2 - 
orm{\E}_2), which tends to 1, as \E 	o \O. It also gives the spectral-norm statement, about which @cor-unitary-nearest says nothing.

title: 20.11 Condition Numbers of Eigenvalues
content:
Condition Numbers of Eigenvalues The Bauer–Fike theorem of §04 bounds the movement of every eigenvalue of a diagonalizable matrix at once, by \kappa_2(\X)
orm{\E}_2 (@thm-bauer-fike). That is one number for the whole spectrum, and it depends on a choice of eigenvector matrix \X. §04 warned that a well-behaved eigenvalue can sit inside a badly conditioned \X, so the bound can be far too pessimistic for some eigenvalues. This section asks about one eigenvalue at a time. If \lambda is a simple eigenvalue of \A, how fast does it move when \A is pushed in a direction \E? The answer is an exact derivative, \cvec{y}^{*}\E\cvec{x}/(\cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x}), built from a right and a left eigenvector. Its worst size over all \E with 
orm{\E}_2 = 1 is the condition number of that eigenvalue. The field is 
C. Throughout, \A, \E \in M_n(
C), and 
orm{\cdot} on vectors is the Euclidean norm. Left and right eigenvectors Chapter 9 defined a left eigenvector as a nonzero \cvec{y} with \cvec{y}	p\A = \lambda\cvec{y}	p (@def-left-eigenvector). Over 
C it is more convenient to put a conjugate on it. In this section, a left eigenvector of \A for \lambda is a nonzero \cvec{y} \in 
C^n with \cvec{y}^{*}\A = \lambda\,\cvec{y}^{*} , which is the same as \A^{*}\cvec{y} = \conj{\lambda}\,\cvec{y}. Since \cvec{y}^{*} = \conj{\cvec{y}}	p, the equation \cvec{y}^{*}\A = \lambda\cvec{y}^{*} says exactly that \conj{\cvec{y}} is a left eigenvector in the sense of @def-left-eigenvector. So the two conventions differ only by conjugating the vector. The conjugate is worth it for one reason: the number \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x} is then the standard inner product \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} of Chapter 11, and Cauchy–Schwarz applies to it. For a simple eigenvalue, that is, one of algebraic multiplicity 1 (@def-algebraic-multiplicity), the right and left eigenvectors are as rigid as they can be, and they are never orthogonal. That last fact is what the whole section divides by. [Left and Right Eigenvectors of a Simple Eigenvalue] Let \A \in M_n(
C) and let \lambda be a simple eigenvalue of \A, with a right eigenvector \cvec{x} and a left eigenvector \cvec{y}. 1. The right eigenvectors of \A for \lambda are exactly the nonzero multiples of \cvec{x}, and the left eigenvectors are exactly the nonzero multiples of \cvec{y}. 2. \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x} 
eq 0. Split \lambda off from the rest of the spectrum. In a basis that begins with \cvec{x}, the matrix becomes block triangular with the 1 	imes 1 block (\lambda) in the corner and a block \B with \lambda 
otin \spec(\B). Chapter 12 §10 clears the off-diagonal corner whenever the two diagonal blocks have disjoint spectra, so \A is similar to (\lambda) \oplus \B. In that picture everything is visible: \cvec{e}_1 is the right eigenvector, \cvec{e}_1^{*} the left one, and \cvec{e}_1^{*}\cvec{e}_1 = 1. If n = 1, both claims hold because every nonzero vector of 
C^1 is a multiple of every other, and \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x} = \conj{y_1}x_1 is a product of two nonzero numbers. Let n \ge 2. By @thm-basis-extension, extend the independent list (\cvec{x}) to a basis of 
C^n, and let \P_0 be the invertible matrix with these columns, so that \P_0\cvec{e}_1 = \cvec{x}. Then \P_0^{-1}\A\P_0\cvec{e}_1 = \P_0^{-1}\lambda\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{e}_1, so \P_0^{-1}\A\P_0 =  egin{pmatrix} \lambda & \cvec{c} \ \cvec{0} & \B \end{pmatrix} for some \cvec{c} \in M_{1 	imes (n-1)}(
C) and \B \in M_{n-1}(
C). By @thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant and @thm-det-block-triangular, p_{\A}(x) = (x - \lambda)\,p_{\B}(x). If p_{\B}(\lambda) = 0, then x - \lambda would divide p_{\B} by the Factor Theorem (@lem-factor-theorem-linear), so (x - \lambda)^2 would divide p_{\A}, against a_{\A}(\lambda) = 1. Hence \lambda 
otin \spec(\B) (@thm-eigenvalue-characterizations). The spectra \{\lambda\} and \spec(\B) are disjoint, so by @cor-block-diagonalization (c) and (a) there is \Q =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & \cvec{z} \ \O & \I_{n-1} \end{psmallmatrix} with \Q^{-1}\P_0^{-1}\A\P_0\Q = (\lambda) \oplus \B. Summary and transfer The chapter set out to answer four questions about a perturbed matrix \A + \E: where its eigenvalues are, how far they move, which one goes where, and what happens to eigenvectors, invariant subspaces, singular values, and polar factors. - Where. Gershgorin’s discs (§01) and the other inclusion regions (§02) locate the eigenvalues without computing any of them. - How far. The continuity of roots (§03) is now a theorem of the book, proved by compactness. It comes with Elsner’s Hölder bound, whose exponent 1/n cannot be improved, and with a matching version of that bound. Bauer–Fike (§04) replaces the exponent by 1 for diagonalizable matrices, at the price of the factor \kappa_2(\X). - Which goes where. Hoffman–Wielandt (§05) matches the eigenvalues of two normal matrices in the Frobenius norm. - Hermitian matrices (§06) got sharper tools: residual bounds, a quadratic bound for the Rayleigh quotient, and relative bounds under congruence. - Eigenvectors and subspaces. The Sylvester equation (§07) and principal angles (§08) together give Davis–Kahan (§09): an invariant subspace moves by at most the perturbation divided by the gap. - Singular values and polar factors (§10) follow by the dilation and by the Sylvester bounds. - To first order. This section gave each simple eigenvalue its own derivative and condition number. Nine moves did the work. - Dominant coordinate plus the triangle inequality. Look at the row of the eigen-equation where the eigenvector is largest (§01), or at the two largest coordinates (§02). Transfer: to locate an eigenvalue without computing it, read the eigen-equation at the coordinate where the eigenvector peaks. There the eigenvalue cannot hide behind the other terms. - A determinant bounded two ways. The product of the distances from \mu to the eigenvalues of \A is \lvert\det(\A - \mu\I)vert, and Hadamard’s inequality bounds that determinant by column lengths (§03, Elsner). Transfer: when a product of unknown quantities is a determinant, bound the determinant from above and the product from below, and read off the smallest factor. - Compactness plus uniqueness. Roots are bounded, so a subsequence of root vectors converges. Its limit is a root vector of the limit polynomial, and unique factorization says which one (§03). Transfer: to prove that a solution depends continuously on the data, bound the solutions, extract a convergent subsequence, and let uniqueness of the limiting solution do the rest. - An integer-valued continuous function is constant. Deform \A to its diagonal, and count the eigenvalues in a region whose boundary no eigenvalue crosses (§03, the counting theorem). Transfer: to count objects that move continuously, move to a case where the count is obvious, along a path that never lets one of them escape. - Factor out the resolvent. Write \A + \E - \mu\I = (\A - \mu\I) igl(\I + (\A - \mu\I)^{-1}\E igr), so that the Neumann series makes the second factor invertible whenever 
orm{(\A - \mu\I)^{-1}\E} < 1 (§04). Transfer: to show a perturbed matrix is invertible, factor out the unperturbed one and ask whether what remains is close to \I. - Birkhoff turns a doubly stochastic weight into a permutation. The weights \lvert w_{ij}vert^2 of a unitary matrix form a doubly stochastic matrix, and a linear function on those attains its minimum at a permutation matrix (§05). Transfer: to optimize over matchings, relax to doubly stochastic matrices. A linear objective has its optimum at a vertex, and the vertices are the matchings. - The perturbation of a subspace is a Sylvester equation. The block that couples the old invariant subspace to the new complement satisfies \widetilde\vLambda_2\X - \X\vLambda_1 = (a piece of \E), so the separation of the two spectra is the conditioning (§07, §09). Transfer: to measure how far an invariant subspace moves, write down the coupling block and recognize the equation it solves. - The singular-pair trick. Test a matrix equation against the top singular pair of the unknown \X. This turns 
orm{\X}_2 into a scalar that the hypotheses bound directly (§07, used twice in §10). Transfer: to bound the spectral norm of the solution of a linear matrix equation, evaluate the equation at the vectors where that norm is attained. - The adjugate as a polynomial eigenvector. A column of \adj(\mu\I - \B) is an eigenvector of \B whenever \mu is an eigenvalue, and its entries are polynomials in \mu and the entries of \B. So it moves continuously when they do (this section). Transfer: when an object must be chosen continuously and there is no canonical choice, look for a formula that is polynomial in the data. The implicit function theorem then becomes unnecessary. orm{\cvec{x}}/\lvert\cvec{x}^{*}\cvec{y}vert = \kappa_{\A}(\lambda), since \lvert\cvec{x}^{*}\cvec{y}vert = \lvert\conj{\cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x}}vert = \lvert\cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x}vert. (b) \U^{*}\A\U has the same characteristic polynomial as \A (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant), so \lambda is simple for it. From \A\cvec{x} = \lambda\cvec{x} and \cvec{y}^{*}\A = \lambda\cvec{y}^{*} we get (\U^{*}\A\U)(\U^{*}\cvec{x}) = \lambda\,\U^{*}\cvec{x} and (\U^{*}\cvec{y})^{*}(\U^{*}\A\U) = \cvec{y}^{*}\A\U = \lambda\,(\U^{*}\cvec{y})^{*}. Since \U^{*} is unitary, 
orm{\U^{*}\cvec{x}} = 
orm{\cvec{x}} and 
orm{\U^{*}\cvec{y}} = 
orm{\cvec{y}} (@thm-isometry-characterizations), and (\U^{*}\cvec{y})^{*}(\U^{*}\cvec{x}) = \cvec{y}^{*}\U\U^{*}\cvec{x} = \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x}. So all three ingredients of @def-eigenvalue-condition-number are unchanged. (c) For \S =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}, \S^{-1}\A\S =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix} egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 0 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix}. By @exm-triangular-eigenvalue-condition (a) with b = -1 and \lvert a - dvert = 1, its eigenvalue 1 has condition number \sqrt2, whereas \kappa_{\A}(1) = 1 because \A is normal. A nonunitary similarity changes lengths and angles, so it changes the angle between \cvec{x} and \cvec{y} in @prp-eigenvalue-condition-properties (e). C. Going deeper [C1: Perfect conditioning characterizes normality] 1. Let \A \in M_n(
C) have n distinct eigenvalues. Prove that \A is normal if and only if \kappa_{\A}(\lambda) = 1 for every eigenvalue \lambda. 2. Show that the hypothesis of distinct eigenvalues cannot be replaced by “\kappa_{\A}(\lambda) = 1 for every simple eigenvalue \lambda”: give a nonnormal \A \in M_3(
C) with a simple eigenvalue, all of whose simple eigenvalues have condition number 1. Hint: in (a), what does \kappa = 1 say about \cvec{y}, and what does the computation in @thm-left-right-biorthogonal say about \cvec{y}_j^{*}\cvec{x}_i? (a) (\Rightarrow) This is @prp-eigenvalue-condition-properties (c). (\Leftarrow) Let \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n be the distinct eigenvalues, with right eigenvectors \cvec{x}_1, \dots, \cvec{x}_n. Since \kappa_{\A}(\lambda_j) = 1, @prp-eigenvalue-condition-properties (a) says that a left eigenvector for \lambda_j is a multiple of \cvec{x}_j, so \cvec{x}_j itself is one: \cvec{x}_j^{*}\A = \lambda_j\cvec{x}_j^{*}. Let i

Computing \cvec{x}_j^{*}\A\cvec{x}_i in two ways, \lambda_j\,\cvec{x}_j^{*}\cvec{x}_i = (\cvec{x}_j^{*}\A)\cvec{x}_i = \cvec{x}_j^{*}(\A\cvec{x}_i) = \lambda_i\,\cvec{x}_j^{*}\cvec{x}_i , so (\lambda_j - \lambda_i)\cvec{x}_j^{*}\cvec{x}_i = 0, and \cvec{x}_j^{*}\cvec{x}_i = 0 because \lambda_i 
e \lambda_j. So the vectors \cvec{x}_i/
orm{\cvec{x}_i} form an orthonormal list of n vectors in 
C^n, hence an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. With \U the unitary matrix having these columns, \A = \U\diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)\U^{*}, so \A is normal by @cor-spectral-complex-matrix. (b) Let \A = \J_2(0) \oplus (1) =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}. Its eigenvalues are 0, 0, 1, so 1 is the only simple eigenvalue. Its right and left eigenvectors are both \cvec{e}_3, since \A\cvec{e}_3 = \cvec{e}_3 and \cvec{e}_3^{*}\A = \cvec{e}_3^{*}, so \kappa_{\A}(1) = 1. But \A is not normal: \A^{*}\A = \diag(0, 1, 1) while \A\A^{*} = \diag(1, 0, 1). [C2: The derivatives add up to the trace] Let \A \in M_n(
C) have n distinct eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, and let \E \in M_n(
C). Write \lambda_i(t) for the eigenvalue of \A + t\E near \lambda_i, from @thm-simple-eigenvalue-derivative. 1. Prove that \lambda_1'(0) + \dots + \lambda_n'(0) = 	r\E. 2. Deduce this again from 	r(\A + t\E) = \lambda_1(t) + \dots + \lambda_n(t), valid for all small t, and explain why the two arguments agree. Hint: in (a), use a diagonalizing \X and the rows of \X^{-1} as left eigenvectors. (a) \A is diagonalizable by @cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable, say \A = \X\vLambda\X^{-1}. As in the proof of @prp-eigenvalue-condition-properties (d), \cvec{x}_i = \X\cvec{e}_i and \cvec{y}_i^{*} = \cvec{e}_i^{*}\X^{-1} are right and left eigenvectors for \lambda_i, with \cvec{y}_i^{*}\cvec{x}_i = 1. So by @thm-simple-eigenvalue-derivative, \sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i'(0) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\cvec{e}_i^{*}\X^{-1}\E\X\cvec{e}_i = 	r(\X^{-1}\E\X) = 	r\E , where the middle equality sums the diagonal entries of \X^{-1}\E\X and the last uses 	r(\B\C) = 	r(\C\B) (@thm-trace-properties (3)). (b) Let g be the smallest distance between two of the \lambda_i. By @thm-simple-eigenvalue-derivative (b), \lvert\lambda_i(t) - \lambda_ivert < g/2 for every i once \lvert tvert is small enough, so \lambda_1(t), \dots, \lambda_n(t) are n distinct eigenvalues of \A + t\E. They are therefore all of its eigenvalues, each simple, and @thm-trace-det-eigenvalues gives 	r(\A + t\E) = \sum_i\lambda_i(t). The left side is 	r\A + t	r\E and 	r\A = \sum_i\lambda_i, so \sum_i(\lambda_i(t) - \lambda_i)/t = 	r\E for small t

The two arguments agree because both express the same fact: the sum of the eigenvalues is a linear function of the matrix, so its derivative in the direction \E is 	r\E, whatever the individual derivatives are. [C3: The adjugate at a simple eigenvalue] Let n \ge 2, let \lambda be a simple eigenvalue of \A \in M_n(
C) with right eigenvector \cvec{x} and left eigenvector \cvec{y}, and put \N = \lambda\I - \A. 1. Prove that \adj\N = c\,\cvec{x}\cvec{y}^{*} for some scalar c

Hint: for (a), use both products in @thm-adjugate-identity; for (b), apply @thm-derivative-of-det to t \mapsto (\lambda + t)\I - \A. (a) Since \lambda is an eigenvalue, \det\N = 0, so @thm-adjugate-identity gives \N\adj\N = \O and \adj\N\,\N = \O. The first says every column of \adj\N lies in \ker(\lambda\I - \A), so by @lem-simple-eigenvalue-left-right (a) every column is a multiple of \cvec{x}: \adj\N = \cvec{x}\cvec{w}^{*} for some \cvec{w} \in 
C^n, whose conjugated entries are those multiples. Step 3 of the proof of @thm-simple-eigenvalue-derivative showed that \adj\N 
e \O, so \cvec{w} 
e \cvec{0}. The second identity gives \cvec{x}(\cvec{w}^{*}\N) = \O, and since \cvec{x}
