By @thm-derivative-of-det, t \mapsto \det\B(t) is differentiable at 0 with derivative 	r(\adj\N\,\I) = 	r(\adj\N). On the other hand \det\B(t) = p_{\A}(\lambda + t). Expanding each power (\lambda + t)^k by the binomial theorem gives p_{\A}(\lambda + t) = p_{\A}(\lambda) + p_{\A}'(\lambda)\,t + t^2h(t) for a polynomial h, because the coefficient of t in \sum_k c_k(\lambda + t)^k is \sum_k kc_k\lambda^{k-1} = p_{\A}'(\lambda). So the difference quotient at 0 is p_{\A}'(\lambda) + t\,h(t) 	o p_{\A}'(\lambda). The two derivatives agree: 	r(\adj\N) = p_{\A}'(\lambda). (c) By (a) and (b), p_{\A}'(\lambda) = 	r(c\,\cvec{x}\cvec{y}^{*}) = c\,\cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x}, since the trace of \cvec{x}\cvec{y}^{*} is \sum_i x_i\conj{y_i} = \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x}. Because \lambda is a simple root of p_{\A}, @thm-repeated-root-derivative (a) gives p_{\A}'(\lambda) 
e 0. Hence \cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x} 
e 0, which reproves @lem-simple-eigenvalue-left-right (b) from (a) of that lemma. Moreover c = p_{\A}'(\lambda)/(\cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x}), which is the displayed formula. For example, for \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & M \ 0 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix} and \lambda = 1, we have \adj(\I - \A) =  egin{psmallmatrix} -1 & M \ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} and p_{\A}'(1) = -1, while \cvec{x}\cvec{y}^{*}/(\cvec{y}^{*}\cvec{x}) =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -M \ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, in agreement.

title: Matrix Inequalities
content:
Matrix Inequalities Five chapters have left inequalities unpaid, and they turn out to be one inequality seen from five sides. Chapter 13 §10 and §11 said that the truncated singular value decomposition and the unitary polar factor are nearest in “every unitarily invariant norm”, a phrase it could not define. Chapter 16 §08 admitted that it had never said which norms those are. Chapter 17 §06 found a family of functionals that fail to be norms on Hermitian matrices and guessed the repair; §07 proved a majorization and left its consequences open; §11 stated Loewner’s theorem once, promised this chapter’s proof four times, and proved none of it. Chapter 18 §10 and §11 deferred the convexity of \A \mapsto 	r f(\A). Chapter 19 §07 and §09 deferred the theorem of Hardy, Littlewood, and Pólya. Chapter 20 §05, §10, and §11 wanted Weyl’s, Mirsky’s, and Hoffman–Wielandt’s bounds inside one statement. The organizing fact behind all of them is majorization, the order \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} that Chapter 17 §08 defined. This chapter closes the circle in four movements. - Majorization is a doubly stochastic map. \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} exactly when \cvec{x} = \D\cvec{y} for a doubly stochastic \D, and with Birkhoff’s theorem, exactly when \cvec{x} lies in the convex hull of the permutations of \cvec{y}. Convexity then acts one row at a time, and every convex function respects the order. - A majorization becomes a norm inequality. The norms that cannot tell coordinates apart are the symmetric gauge functions; composing one with the singular values gives a unitarily invariant norm, and every unitarily invariant norm arises this way exactly once. Ky Fan dominance then says that “\uinorm{\A} \le \uinorm{\B} for every unitarily invariant norm” and “\sigma(\A) \prec_w \sigma(\B)” are the same statement. - The deferred theorems fall out. Eckart–Young, the nearest unitary matrix, Lidskii, and Mirsky, each in every unitarily invariant norm at once. - The order-theoretic side. Which functions preserve the Loewner order \A \succeq \B? Very few: Loewner’s theorem says they are exactly the functions with a particular integral representation, and the powers t^{p} qualify only for 0 \le p \le 1. The chapter ends with the exponential, where Golden and Thompson’s trace inequality replaces the identity e^{a+b} = e^{a}e^{b} that matrices cannot have. Matrices are complex unless a statement says otherwise, and f applied to a Hermitian matrix always means the spectral functional calculus of Chapter 12 §08 (@def-function-of-normal-operator). Four notational conventions hold throughout. - \vlambda(\A) is the decreasing eigenvalue list of a Hermitian \A, \sigma(\A) the decreasing singular value list, and \cvec{x}^{\downarrow} the decreasing rearrangement of a real vector, as in Chapter 17. - Majorization is Chapter 17 §08’s (@def-majorization), with \prec_w the top-sums version. - A unitarily invariant norm is written \uinorm{\A}, with triple bars, to keep it apart from any particular norm. Symmetric gauge functions are \Phi; Chapter 18 §04’s gauge p_K of a convex set is a different object with the same word, and §03 says so once. - The order on matrices is always the Loewner order \A \succeq \B of Chapter 13 §05 (@def-loewner-order). No matrix is ever compared entrywise: the order of Chapters 18 and 19 is used here only on vectors, as \cvec{x} \le \cvec{y} in §03, which says so at its head. The analysis this chapter imports The list is Chapter 16’s, facts (A1)–(A6) of that chapter’s introduction — completeness, monotone convergence, compactness of closed bounded sets, the extreme value theorem, the intermediate value theorem, and the mean value theorem — together with the algebra of limits. Each is named again where it is used, except the intermediate value theorem (A5), which this chapter never needs. The weight falls on three: (A1) and (A3) build §10’s integral, completeness for the convergence of the Riemann sums and compactness for the uniform continuity of the integrand, and (A6) is how §09 turns a nonnegative derivative into monotonicity along a segment. Section 9 also uses (A3) and (A4) for the same two jobs, uniform continuity and boundedness on a compact interval, and (A2) bounds the improper integral of §10 that represents t^{p}. One fact is quoted beyond that list, and it is this chapter’s own. Loewner’s theorem cannot be proved from (A1)–(A6): its analytic half is a theorem about functions of a complex variable. The book’s practice, as with Taylor’s theorem in Chapter 14 §06 and the theorem of Abel and Ruffini in Chapter 11, is to quote one named result at its point of use and prove everything else. So: (A7) (Pick and Nevanlinna.) Let I \subseteq 
R be an open interval and f \colon I 	o 
R. Suppose the Loewner matrix  igl[f[t_i, t_j] igr]_{i,j=1}^{n} of divided differences is positive semidefinite for every n and all t_1, \dots, t_n \in I. Then f is the restriction to I of a function that is analytic on 
C \setminus (
R \setminus I) and maps the upper half plane into its closure; and every such function has the integral representation of Chapter 17 §11’s @thm-loewner-statement (ii). In particular such an f is automatically infinitely differentiable on I. (A7) is stated once, in §10, and used three times there. Its clause (c) supplies the smoothness that §09’s criterion asks for, its clause (a) the implication (i) \Rightarrow (iii) of Loewner’s theorem, and its clause (b) the implication (iii) \Rightarrow (ii). Together they give the one thing the chapter cannot prove: that a function which is operator monotone of every order has the integral representation. No other section uses it, and everything else in the chapter is proved. What this means in practice is worth spelling out, because the reader should know which results are conditional. - Resting on (A7): only the implication just named, and therefore only the “hard” direction of @thm-loewner-statement — that (i) implies (ii). Section 10 marks each step where it enters. - Not resting on (A7): everything in §§01–08, §11, and §12; the whole of §09, including the criterion that, for a continuously differentiable f, monotonicity of order n is exactly positivity of every n 	imes n Loewner matrix, which is the elementary heart of Loewner’s theorem and is proved in full; the easy direction of Loewner’s theorem, that the integral representation forces operator monotonicity, which §10 proves outright; the operator monotonicity of t^{p} for 0 \le p \le 1 and of \log t, both obtained from that easy direction together with an explicit representation; and the three negative results — that t^{p} fails for every p > 1, that t^{2} fails already at order 2, and that e^{t} is not operator monotone — which come from §09’s criterion and from explicit two-by-two witnesses. Section 10 also integrates a continuous matrix-valued function over a compact interval. That is not imported: the section builds the integral entrywise as a limit of Riemann sums, using only (A1)–(A4), and proves the one property it needs, that an integral of positive semidefinite matrices is positive semidefinite. Beyond the list, the only analytic fact quoted is the fundamental theorem of calculus, which §10 uses twice and flags both times: in a remark, to check the logarithm’s integral representation, and in an exercise, to evaluate the constant K_{1/2}. Neither use is a step in a proof. In particular §09’s derivative of a matrix function is obtained without the implicit function theorem, exactly as Chapter 20 §11’s derivative of a simple eigenvalue was. What you need - Chapter 0 §09 — matrix multiplication, and the trace with its cyclic invariance: @def-matrix-multiplication, @thm-trace-properties. - Chapter 3 — the invertibility criteria and permutation matrices: @thm-invertible-tfae, @def-permutation-matrix, @lem-permutation-matrices. - Chapter 6 §06 — Lagrange interpolation: @thm-lagrange-interpolation. - Chapter 7 §05 — multiplicativity of the determinant and the determinant test for invertibility, in the exercises of §§06 and 11 only; no proof in the chapter needs a determinant: @thm-det-multiplicative, @thm-invertible-tfae-det. - Chapter 8 §01 — block multiplication: @thm-block-multiplication. - Chapter 9 — the trace and determinant read off the eigenvalues, and the spectra of \A\B and \B\A: @thm-trace-det-eigenvalues, @thm-ab-ba-eigenvalues. - Chapter 10 §09 — the matrix exponential: @def-matrix-exponential, @thm-exponential-properties. - Chapter 11 §01 and §07 — the Frobenius inner product, Pythagoras and Cauchy–Schwarz, and the unitary invariance of the Frobenius norm: @thm-pythagoras, @thm-cauchy-schwarz, @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant. - Chapter 12 — the spectral theorem, the spectral resolution, and the functional calculus: @cor-trace-sum-eigenvalues-again, @thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues, @cor-spectral-complex-matrix, @cor-spectral-real-matrix, @def-spectral-resolution, @thm-spectral-resolution, @thm-spectral-resolution-unique, @def-function-of-normal-operator, @thm-functional-calculus-properties, @thm-unitary-exponential. - Chapter 13 — positive semidefiniteness, square roots, the Loewner order, the Schur product theorem, and the singular value and polar decompositions: @def-positive-semidefinite, @prp-congruence-positivity, @thm-psd-characterizations, @thm-pd-characterizations, @thm-psd-square-root, @def-loewner-order, @prp-loewner-partial-order, @lem-extreme-eigenvalues-quadratic-form, @thm-loewner-basic, @exm-loewner-not-monotone, @prp-square-root-monotone, @thm-block-psd-schur, @def-hadamard-product, @thm-schur-product, @def-singular-values, @thm-svd, @thm-singular-values-unique, @thm-polar-decomposition, @cor-unitary-nearest, @def-truncated-svd, @thm-eckart-young. - Chapter 15 §04 — the pairing Chapter 15 calls a contraction, a word §08 gives a different meaning: @def-contraction (named so that the clash is visible, not used). - Chapter 16 — norms, the operator norm, entrywise convergence, bounds for the exponential, and the derivative of a matrix-valued function: @def-norm, @exm-p-norms, @cor-entrywise-convergence-is-the-convergence, @def-operator-norm, @thm-operator-norm-properties, @thm-operator-norm-formulas, @thm-exponential-norm-bound, @def-matrix-valued-derivative. - Chapter 17 — the variational descriptions, Weyl’s and Lidskii’s inequalities, majorization, the Hermitian dilation, and the operator monotone functions: @cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone, @lem-hermitian-spectral-norm, @cor-weyl-perturbation, @thm-ky-fan, @cor-ky-fan-subadditive, @exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-c2, @thm-lidskii-inequality, @def-majorization, @exm-majorization-first-examples, @prp-majorization-basic, @lem-horn-two-by-two, @lem-am-gm, @lem-stretch-in-singular-coordinates, @thm-singular-value-minmax, @prp-hermitian-dilation, @thm-weyl-singular-values, @cor-singular-value-perturbation, @thm-eckart-young-spectral, @def-operator-monotone, @prp-operator-monotone-increasing, @prp-affine-operator-monotone, @prp-inverse-operator-monotone, @prp-operator-monotone-cone, @cor-shifted-inverse-operator-monotone, @prp-square-operator-convex, @thm-loewner-statement. - Chapter 18 — convex sets and hulls, convex functions, Jensen’s inequality, gauges and duality, and the classical inequalities: @exm-majorization-set-convex, @prp-convexity-operations, @lem-convex-contains-combinations, @def-convex-hull, @thm-convex-hull-combinations, @def-gauge, @def-dual-norm, @prp-dual-norm-properties, @prp-dual-of-one-two-infinity, @thm-dual-dual-norm, @def-density-matrix, @def-doubly-stochastic, @def-convex-function, @exm-first-convex-functions, @thm-jensen, @prp-sup-of-affine-convex, @lem-convex-one-variable, @thm-convex-second-derivative, @lem-exp-log, @cor-minkowski-inequality, @thm-dual-p-norm. - Chapter 19 §07 — Birkhoff’s theorem and the half of Hardy–Littlewood–Pólya already proved: @thm-birkhoff, @prp-doubly-stochastic-image-majorized. - Chapter 20 — the derivative of a simple eigenvalue, the norm toolkit behind Davis–Kahan, and the perturbation bounds this chapter upgrades: @cor-hoffman-wielandt-hermitian, @lem-spectral-frobenius-toolkit, @thm-mirsky-frobenius, @thm-simple-eigenvalue-derivative. Roadmap - Doubly stochastic maps. T-transforms average two coordinates, and finitely many of them turn \cvec{y} into any \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}. That is the theorem of Hardy, Littlewood, and Pólya, and with Birkhoff’s theorem it says that the majorization order is containment of permutation polytopes. - Convex functions of a majorization. Karamata’s inequality, its converse, Schur-convex and Schur-concave functions, and the convexity of \A \mapsto 	r f(\A) for every convex f. - Symmetric gauge functions. Norms on 
R^{n} blind to the order and the signs of the coordinates. They are monotone under weak majorization, and they have a duality theory of their own. - Unitarily invariant norms. The norms unchanged by unitary factors on either side: the Frobenius and spectral norms, the Ky Fan k-norms, and the Schatten p-norms. Von Neumann’s correspondence matches them exactly with the symmetric gauges, through \uinorm{\A} = \Phi(\sigma(\A)). - The trace inequality. \lvert	r(\A^{*}\B)vert \le \sum_i\sigma_i(\A)\sigma_i(\B), and the duality it gives between a unitarily invariant norm and the norm of the dual gauge. - Ky Fan dominance. Weak majorization of singular values is equivalent to domination in every unitarily invariant norm. Eckart–Young and the nearest unitary matrix follow, in every such norm. - Lidskii in majorization form. Chapter 17’s majorization, run through the previous three sections, yields one bound for every convex function and one for every unitarily invariant norm, with Hoffman–Wielandt and Mirsky as special cases. - Operator convex functions. The Hansen–Pedersen–Jensen inequality f(\V^{*}\A\V) \preceq \V^{*}f(\A)\V for a contraction \V, proved by dilating \V to a unitary matrix, and the contrast with the far weaker trace convexity of §02. - Loewner matrices. The derivative of f at a diagonal matrix is a Hadamard product with the matrix of divided differences. With the Schur product theorem this makes monotonicity of order n equivalent to positivity of every n 	imes n Loewner matrix. - Loewner’s theorem. The three conditions of Chapter 17 §11 are equivalent. One implication quotes (A7); the rest is proved, including the integral machinery. The powers t^{p} are operator monotone exactly for 0 \le p \le 1, \log t is, and e^{t} is not. - Means and matrix Cauchy–Schwarz. Cauchy–Schwarz and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for matrices, each holding in every unitarily invariant norm at once; then the matrix geometric mean \A \# \B, its surprising symmetry, and the chain from the harmonic through the geometric to the arithmetic mean in the Loewner order. - Golden–Thompson. Lie’s product formula, a trace inequality for powers of a product of two positive matrices, and 	r e^{\A+\B} \le 	r(e^{\A}e^{\B}). Three matrices break it. Then Klein’s inequality and the relative entropy, Lieb’s concavity theorem stated and not proved, and a summary that closes the chapter and Part V. Named moves - A majorization is a doubly stochastic map. Turn the family of partial-sum inequalities into a single linear map, and let convexity act one row at a time. - A symmetric gauge turns a weak majorization into a norm inequality. To prove one inequality for a whole family of norms, find the combinatorial statement about the underlying numbers that every member of the family respects. - A Hermitian dilation turns singular values into eigenvalues. Every theorem about the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix has a singular-value twin, obtained by applying it to \cH(\A). - The Schur product theorem turns a Loewner matrix into monotonicity. Differentiate a matrix function, recognize the derivative as an entrywise product with a positive semidefinite matrix, and integrate along a segment. - A limit of Riemann sums carries the Loewner order through an integral. An order defined by a closed convex cone survives every limit, so it survives integration. - Lie’s product formula turns a sum in the exponent into a product. Split one operation into k small steps, make the error of a single step O(1/k^{2}), and let telescoping absorb the factor k.

title: 21.1 Doubly Stochastic Maps
content:
Doubly Stochastic Maps Chapter 17 §08 defined majorization and Chapter 19 §07 proved one half of the fact that makes it useful: a doubly stochastic matrix can only even a vector out, \S\cvec{y} \prec \cvec{y}. The other half was promised twice. Chapter 19 §07 ended by saying that “this converse of the proposition is part of the theorem of Hardy, Littlewood, and Pólya, which Chapter 21 takes up”, and Chapter 19 §09 listed among its unfinished business “the theorem of Hardy, Littlewood, and Pólya, that \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} exactly when \cvec{x} = \D\cvec{y} for a doubly stochastic \D”. This section pays both. The proof builds \D out of one very simple move, repeated: average two coordinates and leave the rest alone. Throughout, vectors are real, \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n, and \prec and \prec_w are Chapter 17 §08’s @def-majorization. By @thm-birkhoff, \D \in \conv\{\P_\sigma : \sigma \in S_n\}, so by @thm-convex-hull-combinations, \D = \sum_{i=1}^{m}t_i\P_{\sigma_i} with t_i \ge 0 and \sum_i t_i = 1. Hence \cvec{x} = \sum_i t_i\P_{\sigma_i}\cvec{y}, a convex combination of the vectors \P_\sigma\cvec{y}, which lies in their convex hull by @thm-convex-hull-combinations. (\Leftarrow) By @thm-convex-hull-combinations, \cvec{x} = \sum_i t_i\P_{\sigma_i}\cvec{y} with (t_1, \dots, t_m) a list of nonnegative weights adding up to 1. Put \D = \sum_i t_i\P_{\sigma_i}. Its entries are nonnegative, and \D\1 = \sum_i t_i\1 = \1, \1	p\D = \1	p, so \D \in \Omega_n and \cvec{x} = \D\cvec{y}. By @prp-doubly-stochastic-image-majorized, \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}. The set \conv\{\P_\sigma\cvec{y}\} is the permutation polytope of \cvec{y}: the convex hull of the n! rearrangements of \cvec{y}. It lies in the affine subspace where the coordinate sum equals \sum_i y_i, so its dimension is at most n - 1. For n = 3 and distinct entries it is a hexagon. The solid hexagon is the permutation polytope of \cvec{y} = (3, 2, 1), drawn inside the plane x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 6; the dashed one, at half the size, is the polytope of (	frac52, 2, 	frac32). By @cor-majorization-convex-hull, \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} says that \cvec{x} lies in the solid hexagon, and \cvec{x} \prec (	frac52, 2, 	frac32) \prec \cvec{y} says that the dashed hexagon sits inside the solid one. The majorization order is containment of permutation polytopes. The center (2,2,2), the flat vector, lies in every one of them, which is @exm-majorization-first-examples (b) again. Use @cor-majorization-convex-hull to give a second proof that \{\cvec{x} : \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}\} is convex, a fact Chapter 18 proved by hand in @exm-majorization-set-convex. By the corollary, \{\cvec{x} : \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}\} = \conv\{\P_\sigma\cvec{y} : \sigma \in S_n\}. A convex hull is convex (@thm-convex-hull-combinations, or @def-convex-hull directly). So the set is convex. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define a T-transform, and say which coordinates of a vector it can change. 2. State the Hardy–Littlewood–Pólya theorem in full. 3. True or false: if \cvec{x} = \S\cvec{y} with \S row-stochastic (nonnegative entries, every row adding up to 1), then \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}. Justify your answer. 4. True or false: if \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}, the doubly stochastic \D with \cvec{x} = \D\cvec{y} is unique. Justify your answer. 5. In @lem-t-transform-step, why is j chosen as the largest index with y_j > x_j rather than the smallest? 6. Why can the number of coordinates in which two decreasing vectors \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} agree never be exactly n - 1? (a) For 1 \le j < k \le n and 0 \le t \le 1, it is \T = (1-t)\I + t\Q with \Q the permutation matrix of the transposition of j and k (@def-t-transform). It changes only the coordinates j and k, replacing each by an average of the two old values. (b) For \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n, \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} if and only if \cvec{x} = \D\cvec{y} for some doubly stochastic \D; and when \cvec{x} and \cvec{y} are both decreasing, \D may be taken to be a product of at most n-1 T-transforms (@thm-hardy-littlewood-polya). (c) False. With \cvec{y} = (1,0) and \S =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, \S\cvec{y} = (1,1) has total 2 while \cvec{y} has total 1, so (M2) fails. Row sums alone control nothing but the individual entries; the column sums are what preserve the total. (d) False. For \cvec{y} = (2,1,0) and \cvec{x} = (1,1,1), both 	frac13\J and the matrix \D_2 of the warning after @exm-hlp-four-vector send \cvec{y} to \cvec{x}. (e) Because it makes the entries strictly between j and k agree with \cvec{x}’s, which is what Step 4 needs in order to keep \cvec{y}' decreasing. The majorization would survive the other choice: with j smallest, the slack Y_m - X_m is nondecreasing on j \le m \le k - 1 rather than constant, hence still at least \delta throughout, and Step 5 goes through. The sorted order is what fails, and with it the possibility of applying the lemma again. For \cvec{x} = (5,5,0) and \cvec{y} = (6,6,-2), taking j smallest gives j = 1, k = 3, \delta = 1, and \cvec{y}' = (5, 6, -1), which is not decreasing, while the rule of the lemma gives j = 2 and \cvec{y}' = (6, 5, -1), which is. (f) Suppose they agree in all indices but i_0. Subtracting the n - 1 equalities x_i = y_i from the equal totals of (M2) leaves x_{i_0} = y_{i_0}, so in fact they agree everywhere. B. Practice [B1: Run the construction] Let \cvec{y} = (9, 5, 4) and \cvec{x} = (6, 6, 6). Verify \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}, produce T-transforms \T_1, \T_2 with \cvec{x} = \T_2\T_1\cvec{y} by the recipe of @lem-t-transform-step, and write out \D = \T_2\T_1. Hence check that \D is doubly stochastic. Both vectors are decreasing with total 18, and the running totals are 6, 12 against 9, 14. So (M1) and (M2) hold and \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}. First step. \cvec{y} - \cvec{x} = (3, -1, -2), so j = 1 and k = 2. Then \delta = \min\{3, 1\} = 1 and t = 1/(9-5) = 	frac14, and \T_1 acts on \{1,2\}: \cvec{y}' =  igl(	frac34\cdot 9 + 	frac14\cdot 5,\ 	frac14\cdot 9 + 	frac34\cdot 5,\ 4 igr) = (8, 6, 4) . Second step. \cvec{y}' - \cvec{x} = (2, 0, -2), so j = 1, k = 3, \delta = \min\{2,2\} = 2, and t = 2/(8-4) = 	frac12. Then \T_2\cvec{y}' =  igl(	frac12\cdot 8 + 	frac12\cdot 4,\ 6,\ 	frac12\cdot 8 + 	frac12\cdot 4 igr) = (6, 6, 6) = \cvec{x} . The matrix. \T_1 has rows (	frac34, 	frac14, 0), (	frac14, 	frac34, 0), (0,0,1), and \T_2 has rows (	frac12, 0, 	frac12), (0,1,0), (	frac12, 0, 	frac12). Multiplying, \D = \T_2\T_1 =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac38 & 	frac18 & 	frac12 \[2pt] 	frac14 & 	frac34 & 0 \[2pt] 	frac38 & 	frac18 & 	frac12 \end{pmatrix} . Each row adds up to 1, and the columns add up to 	frac38 + 	frac14 + 	frac38 = 1, 	frac18 + 	frac34 + 	frac18 = 1, and 	frac12 + 0 + 	frac12 = 1. So \D \in \Omega_3, and \D\cvec{y} = (	frac{27}{8} + 	frac58 + 2,\ 	frac94 + 	frac{15}4,\ 	frac{27}8 + 	frac58 + 2) = (6,6,6). [B2: Determine which are majorizations] For each pair, determine whether \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}. Where it holds, exhibit a doubly stochastic \D with \cvec{x} = \D\cvec{y}; where it fails, name the clause of @def-majorization and the value of k at which it fails. Justify your answer. 1. \cvec{x} = (2, 2, 2), \cvec{y} = (4, 1, 1). 2. \cvec{x} = (3, 1, 0), \cvec{y} = (2, 2, 0). 3. \cvec{x} = (1, 3, 0), \cvec{y} = (2, 0, 2). 4. \cvec{x} = (1, 1), \cvec{y} = (2, 1). (a) Both decreasing, totals 6 = 6; running totals 2, 4 against 4, 5. So \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}. Here \cvec{x} is the flat vector, and \D = 	frac13\J works: every entry of 	frac13\J\cvec{y} is 	frac13(4+1+1) = 2. (b) Totals 4 = 4, but at k = 1 the sorted first entries are 3 > 2, so (M1) fails at k = 1 and \cvec{x} 
ot\prec \cvec{y}. (c) Sorted, \cvec{x}^{\downarrow} = (3,1,0) and \cvec{y}^{\downarrow} = (2,2,0); this is (b) again, so \cvec{x} 
ot\prec \cvec{y}, with (M1) failing at k = 1. (d) Totals 2 
e 3, so (M2) fails and \cvec{x} 
ot\prec \cvec{y}. (Both running totals do satisfy (M1), so \cvec{x} \prec_w \cvec{y}.) [B3: Into the polytope] Let \cvec{y} = (4, 2, 0) and \cvec{x} = (2, 2, 2). Using @cor-majorization-convex-hull, write \cvec{x} explicitly as a convex combination of rearrangements of \cvec{y}, in two different ways. The six rearrangements of \cvec{y} are the vectors with entries 4, 2, 0 in some order. Averaging the three cyclic shifts, 	frac13 igl[(4,2,0) + (0,4,2) + (2,0,4) igr] = 	frac13(6,6,6) = (2,2,2) = \cvec{x} . Alternatively, average a vector with its reversal: 	frac12 igl[(4,2,0) + (0,2,4) igr] = 	frac12(4,4,4) = (2,2,2) = \cvec{x} . Both are convex combinations, with weights (	frac13,	frac13,	frac13) and (	frac12,	frac12). This is the nonuniqueness of the warning after @exm-hlp-four-vector, seen on the polytope: \cvec{x} is the center of the hexagon, lying strictly inside it rather than on an edge, and such a point has many representations. (The hexagon itself has empty interior in 
R^3, since it lies in the plane x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 6; “inside” here means inside the hexagon, within that plane.) C. Going deeper [C1: Row-stochastic is not enough, twice over] Let \S \in M_n(
R) be row-stochastic: every entry is nonnegative and every row adds up to 1. 1. Give such an \S and a \cvec{y} \in 
R^2 with \S\cvec{y} 
ot\prec \cvec{y}. 2. Prove that if \S\cvec{y} \prec \cvec{y} for every \cvec{y} \in 
R^n, then \S is doubly stochastic. Hint for (b): test the hypothesis on the standard basis vectors. (a) Take \S =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} and \cvec{y} = (1, 0). Then \S\cvec{y} = (1,1), whose total is 2, while \cvec{y} has total 1. So (M2) fails. (b) Apply the hypothesis with \cvec{y} = \cvec{e}_j. The vector \S\cvec{e}_j is the j-th column of \S, by @def-matrix-multiplication. From \S\cvec{e}_j \prec \cvec{e}_j, clause (M2) gives \sum_{i=1}^{n}s_{ij} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(\cvec{e}_j)_i = 1 . So every column of \S adds up to 1. The entries are nonnegative and the rows add up to 1 by hypothesis, so \S is doubly stochastic by @def-doubly-stochastic. [C2: Transitivity, a second time] 1. Prove that if \A, \B \in \Omega_n then \A\B \in \Omega_n. 2. Hence deduce that \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} and \cvec{y} \prec \cvec{z} imply \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{z}, and compare this route with the proof of @prp-majorization-basic (b). (a) The entries of \A\B are \sum_k a_{ik}b_{kj}, sums of products of nonnegative numbers, hence nonnegative. Since \A\1 = \1 and \B\1 = \1, we get (\A\B)\1 = \A(\B\1) = \A\1 = \1, so every row of \A\B adds up to 1. Since \1	p\A = \1	p and \1	p\B = \1	p, we get \1	p(\A\B) = (\1	p\A)\B = \1	p\B = \1	p, so every column does too. By @def-doubly-stochastic, \A\B \in \Omega_n. (b) By @thm-hardy-littlewood-polya there are \D, \E \in \Omega_n with \cvec{x} = \D\cvec{y} and \cvec{y} = \E\cvec{z}. Then \cvec{x} = \D\E\cvec{z}, and \D\E \in \Omega_n by (a). By @thm-hardy-littlewood-polya again, \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{z}. @prp-majorization-basic (b) proved the same thing in one line, by chaining the inequalities X_k \le Y_k \le Z_k between running totals. That proof is shorter and uses nothing. The route here is longer, but it explains transitivity rather than verifying it: a majorization is an averaging, and averaging twice is averaging. [C3: The count n - 1 cannot be improved] Let n \ge 2, \cvec{y} = (n, 0, \dots, 0), and \cvec{x} = (1, 1, \dots, 1) in 
R^n. For \cvec{z} \in 
R^n, write \operatorname{supp}(\cvec{z}) = \{i : z_i 
e 0\}. 1. Show that \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}. 2. Let \T be a T-transform. Prove that \lvert\operatorname{supp}(\T\cvec{z})vert \le \lvert\operatorname{supp}(\cvec{z})vert + 1 for every \cvec{z} \in 
R^n. 3. Deduce that no product of fewer than n - 1 T-transforms sends \cvec{y} to \cvec{x}. (a) Both vectors are decreasing with total n. Every running total of \cvec{y} is n, and the k-th running total of \cvec{x} is k \le n. So (M1) and (M2) hold. (b) Let \T act on \{j, k\} with parameter t. By @eq-t-transform-action, (\T\cvec{z})_i = z_i for i 
otin \{j, k\}, so \operatorname{supp}(\T\cvec{z}) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}(\cvec{z}) \cup \{j, k\} . If both j, k \in \operatorname{supp}(\cvec{z}), the right side is \operatorname{supp}(\cvec{z}) and there is nothing to prove. If neither is, then z_j = z_k = 0, so (\T\cvec{z})_j = (\T\cvec{z})_k = 0 and again \operatorname{supp}(\T\cvec{z}) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}(\cvec{z}). In the remaining case exactly one of them, say j, lies in \operatorname{supp}(\cvec{z}), and then \operatorname{supp}(\T\cvec{z}) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}(\cvec{z}) \cup \{k\}, a set with one more element. In all cases the bound holds. (c) Suppose \cvec{x} = \T_r\cdots\T_1\cvec{y}. Put \cvec{z}^{(0)} = \cvec{y} and \cvec{z}^{(i)} = \T_i\cvec{z}^{(i-1)}. Then \lvert\operatorname{supp}(\cvec{z}^{(0)})vert = 1 and \lvert\operatorname{supp}(\cvec{z}^{(r)})vert = \lvert\operatorname{supp}(\cvec{x})vert = n. By (b), the size of the support grows by at most 1 at each step, so n \le 1 + r , \qquad	ext{that is,}\qquad r \ge n - 1 . Together with @thm-hardy-littlewood-polya, which gives such a product with r \le n-1, exactly n - 1 transforms are needed for this pair.

title: 21.2 Convex Functions of a Majorization
content:
Convex Functions of a Majorization Section 1 turned the n inequalities of a majorization into a single identity, \cvec{x} = \D\cvec{y} with \D doubly stochastic. This section spends it. Chapter 17 §07 left to this chapter “the general consequences of a majorization \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}, namely \sum_i\phi(x_i) \le \sum_i\phi(y_i) for every convex \phi \colon 
R 	o 
R, …”; that is the first theorem below, and its converse says that the convex functions see nothing but the majorization. Two more promises are paid from it: Chapter 17 §08’s claim that for nonnegative vectors “\cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} implies x_1\cdots x_n \ge y_1\cdots y_n”, and Chapters 18 §10 and §11’s claim that “\A \mapsto 	r f(\A) = \sum_i f(\lambda_i(\A)) is convex on the Hermitian matrices with spectrum in that interval” for every convex f. Conventions. Vectors are real and \prec, \prec_w are @def-majorization. A convex function is one in the sense of @def-convex-function, and an interval of 
R is a convex subset of 
R, since it contains every number lying between two of its points. In the last subsection F = 
R or 
C, matrices in M_n(F) written \A, \B, \C are Hermitian, and f(\A) is the spectral functional calculus of Chapter 12 §08, @def-function-of-normal-operator. There \P_j, with an integer subscript, is an orthogonal projection of a spectral resolution; \P_\sigma always means a permutation matrix. No analysis is imported here: the only facts used from outside linear algebra reach us through Chapter 18’s already proved results. Karamata’s inequality A majorization is a statement about sums of the largest entries. A convex function is one whose graph lies below its chords. The link between them is that an averaging matrix turns one into the other, and §01 says that a majorization is an averaging matrix. Karamata’s Inequality Let I \subseteq 
R be an interval, let \phi \colon I 	o 
R be convex, and let \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n satisfy \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}, with every entry of \cvec{y} lying in I. Then every entry of \cvec{x} lies in I, and \sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi(x_i) \ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi(y_i) . Write \cvec{x} = \D\cvec{y} with \D doubly stochastic. Each x_i is then a weighted average of the y_j, with the weights in row i of \D; Jensen’s inequality bounds \phi(x_i) by the same average of the \phi(y_j). Add these n inequalities. The coefficient of \phi(y_j) on the right is the sum of column j of \D, which is 1. The rows and the columns do two different jobs, and this is where “doubly” earns its keep. By @thm-hardy-littlewood-polya there is a doubly stochastic \D = (d_{ij}) with \cvec{x} = \D\cvec{y}, that is, x_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}y_j \qquad (i = 1, \dots, n) . Fix i. The numbers d_{i1}, \dots, d_{in} are nonnegative and add up to 1, since row i of \D is a row of a doubly stochastic matrix (@def-doubly-stochastic). So x_i is a convex combination of y_1, \dots, y_n, all of which lie in the convex set I; by @lem-convex-contains-combinations, x_i \in I. Now @thm-jensen, applied to the convex \phi on I with the points y_1, \dots, y_n and the weights d_{i1}, \dots, d_{in}, gives \phi(x_i) = \phi\Bigl(\sum_j d_{ij}y_j\Bigr) \ \le\ \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}\,\phi(y_j) . Summing over i and exchanging the order of the two finite sums, \sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi(x_i) \ \le\ \sum_{j=1}^{n}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{ij}\Bigr)\phi(y_j) = \sum_{j=1}^{n}\phi(y_j) , because every column of \D adds up to 1. This proves the theorem. The proof is three lines and uses @thm-hardy-littlewood-polya once. That is what §01 was for: without it we would be comparing sorted partial sums with the values of an arbitrary convex function, and there is no route from one to the other. [One majorization, four inequalities] Let \cvec{y} = (5, 3, 1, 1) and \cvec{x} = (3, 3, 2, 2). Check that \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}, and write down what @thm-karamata gives for \phi(t) = t^2, for \phi(t) = \lvert t - 2vert, and for \phi(t) = \max\{t - 2, 0\}. Both vectors are decreasing with total 10, and the running totals are 3, 6, 8 for \cvec{x} against 5, 8, 9 for \cvec{y}. So (M1) and (M2) hold, and \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}. All three functions are convex on I = 
R: t^2 by @lem-convex-one-variable, since its derivative 2t is increasing, and the other two as pointwise maxima of affine functions, by @prp-sup-of-affine-convex (\lvert t - 2vert = \max\{t-2,\ 2-t\}). So:  egin{aligned} 	extstyle\sum_i x_i^2 &= 9 + 9 + 4 + 4 = 26 \ \le\ 25 + 9 + 1 + 1 = 36 = 	extstyle\sum_i y_i^2 , \ 	extstyle\sum_i\lvert x_i - 2vert &= 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 2 \ \le\ 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 , \ 	extstyle\sum_i\max\{x_i - 2, 0\} &= 1 + 1 = 2 \ \le\ 3 + 1 = 4 . \end{aligned} Each is an instance of the one theorem. The last one measures how much of each vector sits above the level 2, and it is the test function the converse below is built from. Does @thm-karamata apply to \phi(t) = t^3 on I = 
R? Test it on \cvec{x} = (0,0,0) \prec \cvec{y} = (1, 1, -2). No. On 
R the function t^3 is not convex: at a = -2, b = 0, and t = 	frac12 the midpoint value is \phi(-1) = -1, while the chord gives 	frac12\phi(-2) + 	frac12\phi(0) = -4, and -1 > -4. The conclusion of the theorem does fail here. Both vectors have total 0, and the running totals 0, 0 of \cvec{x} are at most 1, 2, so \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}. But \sum_i x_i^3 = 0 while \sum_i y_i^3 = 1 + 1 - 8 = -6, and 0 > -6. On I = (0, \infty), where t^3 is convex, since its derivative 3t^2 is increasing there (@lem-convex-one-variable), the theorem does apply, and no such failure is possible for vectors with strictly positive entries. The converse, and the weak version Karamata’s inequality is not merely a consequence of majorization; it is equivalent to it. Two families of test functions do the work: the affine ones pin down the totals, and the “hockey sticks” t \mapsto \max\{t - c, 0\} pin down the partial sums. [Convex Functions Detect Majorization] Let \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n. If \sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi(x_i) \ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi(y_i) for every convex \phi \colon 
R 	o 
R, then \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}. Use \phi(t) = t and \phi(t) = -t to get the equal totals. For the k-th partial sum, use the function that is 0 below a level c and rises with slope 1 above it. Summed over a vector it always exceeds “top k sum minus kc”, and it equals that when c is the k-th largest entry. Setting c = y^{\downarrow}_k makes the right-hand side exact and the left-hand side an over-estimate, which is the direction we need. Both \phi(t) = t and \phi(t) = -t are affine, hence convex by @exm-first-convex-functions (a). They give \sum_i x_i \le \sum_i y_i and -\sum_i x_i \le -\sum_i y_i, so the totals are equal. This is (M2). Fix k with 1 \le k \le n - 1, put c = y^{\downarrow}_k, and let \phi_c(t) = \max\{t - c,\ 0\} , the pointwise maximum of the two affine functions t \mapsto t - c and t \mapsto 0, hence convex by @prp-sup-of-affine-convex. For any \cvec{z} \in 
R^n the sum \sum_i\phi_c(z_i) does not depend on the order of the entries, so it equals \sum_i\phi_c(z^{\downarrow}_i). Every term is \ge 0, and each of the first k terms satisfies \phi_c(z^{\downarrow}_i) \ge z^{\downarrow}_i - c. Hence \sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi_c(z_i) \ \ge\ \sum_{i=1}^{k}z^{\downarrow}_i - kc . 	ag{$\ast$} For \cvec{z} = \cvec{y} and this particular c, (\ast) is an equality: for i \le k we have y^{\downarrow}_i \ge y^{\downarrow}_k = c, so \phi_c(y^{\downarrow}_i) = y^{\downarrow}_i - c; and for i > k we have y^{\downarrow}_i \le c, so \phi_c(y^{\downarrow}_i) = 0. Therefore \sum_{i=1}^{k}x^{\downarrow}_i - kc \ \overset{(\ast)}{\le}\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi_c(x_i) \ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi_c(y_i) = \sum_{i=1}^{k}y^{\downarrow}_i - kc , the middle step being the hypothesis applied to \phi_c. Canceling kc gives (M1) at k. As k was arbitrary, \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}. Together with @thm-karamata this is an equivalence: \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} if and only if \sum_i\phi(x_i) \le \sum_i\phi(y_i) for every convex \phi \colon 
R 	o 
R. So majorization is exactly the order that all convex functions agree on. The proof also shows how few test functions are needed: the two affine ones and the n - 1 hockey sticks at the levels y^{\downarrow}_1, \dots, y^{\downarrow}_{n-1}. Weak majorization has a matching statement, with the class of test functions cut down. [Karamata for Weak Majorization] Let \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n with \cvec{x} \prec_w \cvec{y}, and let \phi \colon 
R 	o 
R be convex and increasing. Then \sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi(x_i) \ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi(y_i) . The only thing wrong with \cvec{y} is that its total may be too big. Take the excess away from the smallest entry of \cvec{y}. That keeps the vector sorted, leaves all the partial sums before the last one untouched, and produces a genuine majorization, to which @thm-karamata applies. Lowering an entry can only lower \phi, which is where “increasing” is used. Let s = \sum_i y_i - \sum_i x_i. Taking k = n in (M1) for \cvec{x} \prec_w \cvec{y} gives s \ge 0. Define \cvec{w} \in 
R^n by w_i = y^{\downarrow}_i \ \ (i \le n-1) , \qquad w_n = y^{\downarrow}_n - s . R^n, and every entry of \cvec{y} lies in I, then every entry of \cvec{x} lies in I and \sum_i\phi(x_i) \le \sum_i\phi(y_i) (@thm-karamata). (b) The affine functions \phi(t) = t and \phi(t) = -t give the equal totals, (M2). The hockey stick \phi_c(t) = \max\{t - c, 0\} with c = y^{\downarrow}_k gives (M1) at k. (c) For a symmetric convex A \subseteq 
R^n, G \colon A 	o 
R is Schur-convex if \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} implies G(\cvec{x}) \le G(\cvec{y}) (@def-schur-convex), and Schur-concave if \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} implies G(\cvec{x}) \ge G(\cvec{y}) (@def-schur-concave). (d) False. G(\cvec{x}) = -x_1x_2 on the nonnegative quadrant is Schur-convex by @cor-product-schur-concave, but the warning after that corollary shows that G(	frac32,	frac32) = -2.25 exceeds the average -2.5 of G(1,1) and G(2,2). (e) False. A Schur-convex function must be symmetric, as shown after @def-schur-concave, and G(\cvec{x}) = x_1 is linear, hence convex, but not symmetric: G(1,0) = 1 
e 0 = G(0,1), while (1,0) and (0,1) majorize each other. Symmetry is exactly the missing hypothesis of @thm-symmetric-convex-is-schur-convex. (f) For I = 
R and f(t) = t^2, it says that \A \mapsto 	r(\A^2) is convex on the Hermitian matrices. Since \A is Hermitian, 	r(\A^2) = 	r(\A^{*}\A) = 
orm{\A}_F^2, the squared Frobenius norm. B. Practice [B1: Four consequences of one majorization] Let \cvec{y} = (6, 2, 1, 1) and \cvec{x} = (4, 3, 2, 1). 1. Verify that \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}. 2. Compute \sum_i x_i^2 and \sum_i y_i^2, and \sum_i\max\{x_i - 3, 0\} and \sum_i\max\{y_i - 3, 0\}. Name the theorem each comparison illustrates. 3. Compute \prod_i x_i and \prod_i y_i. Hence check @cor-product-schur-concave. 4. Give a convex \phi \colon 
R 	o 
R for which the two sides are equal. (a) Both vectors are decreasing with total 10; the running totals are 4, 7, 9 for \cvec{x} against 6, 8, 9 for \cvec{y}. So (M1) and (M2) hold. (b) \sum_i x_i^2 = 16 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 30 and \sum_i y_i^2 = 36 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 42, so 30 \le 42. Also \sum_i\max\{x_i - 3, 0\} = 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1 and \sum_i\max\{y_i-3,0\} = 3, so 1 \le 3. Both illustrate @thm-karamata, the first with \phi(t) = t^2 and the second with the hockey stick at level 3. (c) \prod_i x_i = 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 24 and \prod_i y_i = 6 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 12. Indeed 24 \ge 12, as @cor-product-schur-concave requires for nonnegative vectors. (d) Any affine \phi, for instance \phi(t) = t: both sides are the common total 10, by (M2). Affine functions are the ones on which majorization gives no information. [B2: Which are Schur-convex?] Determine which of the following functions are Schur-convex on the stated symmetric convex set. Justify your answer, naming the theorem used or giving a counterexample. 1. G(\cvec{x}) = \max_i x_i - \min_i x_i on 
R^n. 2. G(\cvec{x}) = \sum_i \lvert x_i vert on 
R^n. 3. G(\cvec{x}) = x_1 + 2x_2 on 
R^2. 4. G(\cvec{x}) = \sum_i\sqrt{x_i} on A = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^n : x_i > 0 	ext{ for every } i\}. (a) Schur-convex. G(\cvec{x}) = x^{\downarrow}_1 - x^{\downarrow}_n, and \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} gives x^{\downarrow}_1 \le y^{\downarrow}_1 by (M1) at k = 1 and x^{\downarrow}_n \ge y^{\downarrow}_n by subtracting (M1) at k = n-1 from (M2). Subtracting the second from the first gives G(\cvec{x}) \le G(\cvec{y}). (b) Schur-convex, by @thm-karamata with \phi(t) = \lvert tvert, convex as a maximum of two affine functions (@prp-sup-of-affine-convex). (c) Not Schur-convex. It is not symmetric, and a Schur-convex function must be. Concretely (1,0) and (0,1) are rearrangements of each other, so (1,0) \prec (0,1) and (0,1) \prec (1,0). Schur-convexity would give G(1,0) \le G(0,1) from the first and G(0,1) \le G(1,0) from the second, hence G(1,0) = G(0,1). But G(1,0) = 1 and G(0,1) = 2. (d) Not Schur-convex; it is Schur-concave. First, t \mapsto \sqrt t is concave on (0, \infty): for a, b > 0 and 0 \le 	heta \le 1, @lem-am-gm gives 2\sqrt{ab} \le a + b, so  egin{aligned}  igl(	heta\sqrt a + (1-	heta)\sqrt b igr)^2 &= 	heta^2a + (1-	heta)^2b + 2	heta(1-	heta)\sqrt{ab} \ &\le 	heta^2a + (1-	heta)^2b + 	heta(1-	heta)(a + b) \ &= 	heta a + (1-	heta)b , \end{aligned} using 	heta^2 + 	heta(1-	heta) = 	heta and (1-	heta)^2 + 	heta(1-	heta) = 1-	heta; taking square roots of two nonnegative numbers preserves the inequality. So \phi(t) = -\sqrt t is convex on (0,\infty), and @thm-karamata turns \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} into \sum_i(-\sqrt{x_i}) \le \sum_i(-\sqrt{y_i}), that is, G(\cvec{x}) \ge G(\cvec{y}). For a concrete instance, (2,2) \prec (3,1) and G(2,2) = 2\sqrt2 \approx 2.83, while G(3,1) = \sqrt3 + 1 \approx 2.73, so G went down as the vector spread out. [B3: Trace convexity on two-by-two matrices] 1. Let f(t) = t^2, \A = \diag(2, 0), \B =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}, and 	heta = 	frac12. Compute 	r f(\A), 	r f(\B), and 	r f(\C) for \C = 	frac12(\A + \B), and verify @thm-trace-convex. 2. Let f(t) = -\log t, \A = \I_2, \B = \diag(4, 	frac14), and 	heta = 	frac12. Do the same, and state the inequality in terms of determinants. (a) Both matrices are real symmetric, hence Hermitian. \A^2 = \diag(4,0), so 	r f(\A) = 4; and \B^2 =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}, so 	r f(\B) = 4. Next \C = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac32 & 	frac12 \[2pt] 	frac12 & 	frac12\end{pmatrix} , \qquad \C^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 	frac52 & 1 \[2pt] 1 & 	frac12\end{pmatrix} , so 	r f(\C) = 	frac52 + 	frac12 = 3. The theorem asserts 3 \le 	frac12\cdot 4 + 	frac12\cdot 4 = 4, which holds. (b) Both are positive definite, so their spectra lie in (0, \infty). By @exm-logdet-convex, 	r f(\M) = -\log\det\M. Here \det\A = 1 and \det\B = 4 \cdot 	frac14 = 1, so both traces are -\log 1 = 0. The midpoint is \C = \diag(	frac52, 	frac58), with \det\C = 	frac{25}{16}, so 	r f(\C) = -\log	frac{25}{16}. The theorem asserts -\log	frac{25}{16} \ \le\ 	frac12\cdot 0 + 	frac12\cdot 0 = 0 , which holds because 	frac{25}{16} > 1 and \log is increasing with \log 1 = 0 (@lem-exp-log (c)). In determinant form: \det\C = 	frac{25}{16} \ge 1 = \sqrt{\det\A\,\det\B}. C. Going deeper [C1: Entropy] For \cvec{x} in A = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^n : x_i > 0 	ext{ for every } i\}, let H(\cvec{x}) = -\sum_i x_i\log x_i. 1. Prove that g(t) = t\log t is convex on (0, \infty). Hint: apply @thm-jensen to the concave \log, with the points 1/a, 1/b and cleverly chosen weights. 2. Deduce that H is Schur-concave on A. 3. Deduce that H(\cvec{x}) \le \log n for every \cvec{x} \in A with \sum_i x_i = 1, with equality when \cvec{x} = (	frac1n, \dots, 	frac1n). (a) Let a, b > 0 and 0 \le 	heta \le 1, and put c = 	heta a + (1-	heta)b > 0. Set w_1 =  rac{	heta a}{c} , \qquad w_2 =  rac{(1-	heta)b}{c} , which are nonnegative and satisfy w_1 + w_2 = (	heta a + (1-	heta)b)/c = 1. The function -\log is convex on (0,\infty) by @lem-exp-log (c), so @thm-jensen with the points 1/a and 1/b gives -\log\Bigl(w_1 rac1a + w_2 rac1b\Bigr) \ \le\ -w_1\log rac1a - w_2\log rac1b . Now w_1/a + w_2/b = 	heta/c + (1-	heta)/c = 1/c, and \log(1/a) = -\log a since \log a + \log(1/a) = \log 1 = 0 (@lem-exp-log (c)). So the display reads \log c \ \le\ w_1\log a + w_2\log b =  rac{	heta a\log a + (1-	heta)b\log b}{c} . Multiplying by c > 0 gives c\log c \le 	heta a\log a + (1-	heta)b\log b, which is @def-convex-function for g. (b) By (a) and @thm-karamata with I = (0,\infty), \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} in A implies \sum_i x_i\log x_i \le \sum_i y_i\log y_i, that is, H(\cvec{x}) \ge H(\cvec{y}). By @def-schur-concave, H is Schur-concave. (The set A is symmetric and convex, so @def-schur-concave applies.) (c) Let \cvec{x} \in A with \sum_i x_i = 1. Its mean is 	frac1n, so the flat vector \cvec{f} = (	frac1n, \dots, 	frac1n) satisfies \cvec{f} \prec \cvec{x} by @exm-majorization-first-examples (b), and \cvec{f} \in A. By (b), H(\cvec{f}) \ge H(\cvec{x}). Finally H(\cvec{f}) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n}	frac1n\log	frac1n = -\log	frac1n = \log n , using \log	frac1n = -\log n. So H(\cvec{x}) \le \log n, with equality at \cvec{x} = \cvec{f}. [C2: Three norms under majorization] Let \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} in 
R^n. Prove that 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 \le 
orm{\cvec{y}}_1 , \qquad 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le 
orm{\cvec{y}}_2 , \qquad 
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty \le 
orm{\cvec{y}}_\infty . Which of the three needs @thm-karamata, and which follows from @def-majorization alone? For 
orm{\cdot}_1, apply @thm-karamata with \phi(t) = \lvert tvert, convex on 
R by @prp-sup-of-affine-convex: \sum_i\lvert x_ivert \le \sum_i\lvert y_ivert. For 
orm{\cdot}_2, apply @thm-karamata with \phi(t) = t^2, convex on 
R by @lem-convex-one-variable, since its derivative 2t is increasing: \sum_i x_i^2 \le \sum_i y_i^2. Both sides are nonnegative and t \mapsto \sqrt t is increasing on [0,\infty), so 
orm{\cvec{x}}_2 \le 
orm{\cvec{y}}_2. For 
orm{\cdot}_\infty, no convexity is needed. Since 
orm{\cvec{z}}_\infty = \max_i\lvert z_ivert = \max\{z^{\downarrow}_1,\ -z^{\downarrow}_n\}, and (M1) at k = 1 gives x^{\downarrow}_1 \le y^{\downarrow}_1 while subtracting (M1) at k = n-1 from (M2) gives x^{\downarrow}_n \ge y^{\downarrow}_n, hence -x^{\downarrow}_n \le -y^{\downarrow}_n. The maximum of the two smaller numbers is at most the maximum of the two larger ones. So the \infty-norm follows from @def-majorization directly, and the other two from @thm-karamata. A later section of this chapter proves the same for every norm that is invariant under permuting and changing the signs of the coordinates. [C3: One convex function is not enough] Let \cvec{x} = (2, -1, -1) and \cvec{y} = (1, 1, -2). 1. Show that \sum_i x_i = \sum_i y_i and \sum_i x_i^2 = \sum_i y_i^2, yet neither \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} nor \cvec{y} \prec \cvec{x}. 2. Exhibit a convex \phi with \sum_i\phi(x_i) > \sum_i\phi(y_i), and another with the inequality reversed. Explain how this is consistent with @prp-majorization-from-convex. (a) Both totals are 0, and \sum_i x_i^2 = 4 + 1 + 1 = 6 = 1 + 1 + 4 = \sum_i y_i^2. Both vectors are already decreasing, with running totals 2, 1 for \cvec{x} and 1, 2 for \cvec{y}. (M1) at k = 1 fails for \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y}, since 2 > 1, and (M1) at k = 2 fails for \cvec{y} \prec \cvec{x}, since 2 > 1. (b) Take \phi(t) = \max\{t - 1, 0\}, convex by @prp-sup-of-affine-convex. Then \sum_i\phi(x_i) = 1 + 0 + 0 = 1 and \sum_i\phi(y_i) = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0, so 1 > 0. This is the test function of @prp-majorization-from-convex at c = y^{\downarrow}_1 = 1, and it certifies \cvec{x} 
ot\prec \cvec{y}. Take \psi(t) = \max\{t + 1, 0\}. Then \sum_i\psi(x_i) = 3 + 0 + 0 = 3 and \sum_i\psi(y_i) = 2 + 2 + 0 = 4, so 3 < 4, certifying \cvec{y} 
ot\prec \cvec{x} by the same proposition applied with the roles exchanged, at c = x^{\downarrow}_2 = -1. There is no contradiction: @prp-majorization-from-convex asks the inequality to hold for every convex \phi. Agreeing on the affine functions and on t^2 is far from agreeing on all of them, and here two hockey sticks pull in opposite directions.

title: 21.3 Symmetric Gauge Functions
content:
Symmetric Gauge Functions The last two sections turned a majorization into an inequality between sums of a convex function. This section turns it into an inequality between norms. The norms that work are the ones blind to exactly the information a majorization discards — the order of the entries and their signs — and Section 4 will show that these are precisely the norms a matrix inherits from its singular values. Throughout, the field is 
R and the space is 
R^n with the dot product \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y}, n \ge 1. Majorization \prec and weak majorization \prec_w are Chapter 17 §08’s (@def-majorization), and \cvec{x}^{\downarrow} is the decreasing rearrangement. A permutation matrix \P_\sigma is @def-permutation-matrix; \P_\sigma\cvec{x} rearranges the entries of \cvec{x}. We write \lvert\cvec{x}vert = (\lvert x_1vert, \dots, \lvert x_nvert), and \cvec{x} \le \cvec{y} means x_i \le y_i for every i — the entrywise order of Chapter 18 §05, never the Loewner order. From §01 we use @cor-majorization-convex-hull, which rests on @thm-hardy-littlewood-polya; the exercises also use §02’s @thm-karamata. What a norm must forget Chapter 17 §06 measured a Hermitian matrix by its Ky Fan partial sum s_k(\A) = \lambda_1(\A) + \dots + \lambda_k(\A), and @exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-c2 asked whether s_k is a norm. On the positive semidefinite matrices it behaves like one; on all Hermitian matrices it fails, because s_1(\diag(0,-1)) = 0 with \diag(0,-1) 
e \O. The exercise ended by naming the repair: apply s_k to the singular values instead of the eigenvalues. Singular values are nonnegative, so nothing can cancel, and the failure disappears. That repair suggests the shape of the whole chapter’s answer. A measurement of a matrix built from its singular values is a function of a list of n nonnegative numbers. Two things about that list are accidents of bookkeeping. Its order is one: the singular values of a matrix form a multiset, and Chapter 13 chose to write them decreasingly. Its signs are the other: a formula that is to extend from nonnegative lists to all of 
R^n, and be a norm there, cannot notice which entries are negative, since \cvec{x} and the vector obtained by flipping one sign have the same absolute values and must be measured alike. A symmetric gauge function is a norm that cannot tell the entries of a vector apart by where they sit or which way they point. [Symmetric Gauge Function] A symmetric gauge function on 
R^n is a norm \Phi \colon 
R^n 	o 
R (@def-norm) such that 1. \Phi(\P_\sigma\cvec{x}) = \Phi(\cvec{x}) for every permutation matrix \P_\sigma and every \cvec{x} \in 
R^n (permutation invariance); 2. \Phi(\varepsilon_1x_1, \dots, \varepsilon_nx_n) = \Phi(\cvec{x}) for all signs \varepsilon_i \in \{+1, -1\} and every \cvec{x} \in 
R^n (sign invariance). In words: (G1) says that shuffling the entries does not change the measurement, and (G2) says that flipping any of their signs does not either. The word every does the work in both, and the two clauses are genuinely separate: below are a norm with (G1) and not (G2), and one with (G2) and not (G1). Together they say that \Phi(\cvec{x}) depends only on the multiset \{\lvert x_1vert, \dots, \lvert x_nvert\}, that is, \Phi(\cvec{x}) = \Phi igl(\lvert\cvec{x}vert^{\downarrow} igr) \qquad (\cvec{x} \in 
R^n) , {#eq-gauge-depends-on-sorted-moduli} since \lvert\cvec{x}vert is obtained from \cvec{x} by (G2) and \lvert\cvec{x}vert^{\downarrow} from \lvert\cvec{x}vert by (G1). Note also that (N2) of @def-norm already gives \Phi(-\cvec{x}) = \Phi(\cvec{x}); (G2) is much stronger, because it flips the signs one entry at a time. The word “gauge” is used here in a different sense from Chapter 18 §04. There, @def-gauge attached to a convex set K the function p_K(\cvec{x}) = \inf\{t > 0 : \cvec{x} \in tK\}, which measures a vector by inflating K. That object is not this one. The name “symmetric gauge function” is standard and traditional for @def-symmetric-gauge, and the two never appear in the same argument in this book; where confusion is possible, this chapter writes \Phi and never p_K. The first examples are the norms already at hand. [The p-norms, the Ky Fan gauges, and size one] Check each against @def-symmetric-gauge. 1. 
orm{\cdot}_p for 1 \le p \le \infty. 2. For 1 \le k \le n, the function \Phi_k(\cvec{x}) = \sum_{i \le k}\lvert xvert^{\downarrow}_i, the sum of the k largest absolute values. 3. On 
R^1, the function \Phi(x) = c\lvert xvert for a constant c > 0. (a) These are norms: @exm-p-norms for p = 1, 2, \infty, and @cor-minkowski-inequality supplies the triangle inequality for the rest. The formulas  igl(\sum_i\lvert x_ivert^p igr)^{1/p} and \max_i\lvert x_ivert are built from the absolute values alone and are unchanged by reordering the sum or the maximum, so (G1) and (G2) hold. (b) Rewrite the definition as a maximum: \Phi_k(\cvec{x}) = \max\Bigl\{\sum_{i \in S}\lvert x_ivert \ :\ S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\},\ \lvert Svert = k\Bigr\} , since the largest such sum is the one over the indices of the k largest absolute values. Each function \cvec{x} \mapsto \sum_{i \in S}\lvert x_ivert is nonnegative, absolutely homogeneous, and subadditive, so the maximum of finitely many of them is too, which gives (N2) and (N3). For (N1), every singleton is contained in some S, so \Phi_k(\cvec{x}) \ge \max_i\lvert x_ivert, and \Phi_k(\cvec{x}) = 0 forces \cvec{x} = \cvec{0}. Both (G1) and (G2) are visible in the displayed formula. At the two ends, \Phi_1 = 
orm{\cdot}_\infty and \Phi_n = 
orm{\cdot}_1. (c) A norm on 
R^1 by inspection. There is only one permutation and \Phi(-x) = \Phi(x), so (G1) and (G2) are automatic: on 
R^1 every norm is a symmetric gauge function. The degenerate case is worth keeping in mind, because it shows that the two clauses carry no information until n \ge 2. The functions in (b) will be used constantly, so they get a name of their own. [Ky Fan Gauge] For 1 \le k \le n, the k-th Ky Fan gauge on 
R^n is \Phi_k(\cvec{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\lvert xvert^{\downarrow}_i , the sum of the k largest absolute values of the entries of \cvec{x}. Nonexamples by minimal change. Each drops exactly one clause. - A norm with (G1) and not (G2). On 
R^2 let \Phi(\cvec{x}) = \max igl(\lvert x_1 + x_2vert,\ \lvert x_1vert,\ \lvert x_2vert igr) . Each of the three expressions is nonnegative, absolutely homogeneous, and subadditive, so their maximum is too; and \Phi(\cvec{x}) = 0 forces x_1 = x_2 = 0, so \Phi is a norm. Swapping x_1 and x_2 permutes the three expressions, so (G1) holds. But \Phi(1,1) = 2 while \Phi(1,-1) = 1: (G2) fails. - A norm with (G2) and not (G1). On 
R^2 let \Phi(\cvec{x}) = \lvert x_1vert + 2\lvert x_2vert. This is a norm, and it is built from absolute values, so (G2) holds. But \Phi(1, 0) = 1 and \Phi(0,1) = 2: (G1) fails. Why this definition. The two clauses are exactly what a norm needs in order to be computable from an unordered list of nonnegative numbers, and nothing more is demanded — in particular, no relation to any other norm, and no smoothness. Dropping (G1) allows a norm to prefer one coordinate to another, which no measurement of singular values can do, since relabeling the singular values of a matrix is not an operation on the matrix at all. Dropping (G2) allows a norm to see cancellation between coordinates, which is fatal: Section 7 needs \Phi evaluated at differences of eigenvalue lists and of singular value lists, whose entries have both signs (@thm-lidskii-ui and @thm-mirsky-ui). Is \Phi(\cvec{x}) = \max_i x_i (no absolute values) a symmetric gauge function on 
R^n for n \ge 2? Which clause fails first? It is not, and it fails before (G1) or (G2) are reached: it is not a norm. Absolute homogeneity (N2) fails at c = -1, since \max_i(-x_i) = -\min_i x_i, which for \cvec{x} = (1, 0) is 0 while \max_i x_i = 1. Positive definiteness (N1) fails too: \Phi(-1,-1) = -1 < 0. Restricted to vectors with nonnegative entries the formula is perfectly reasonable, and it equals 
orm{\cvec{x}}_\infty there; the definition insists on a norm on all of 
R^n precisely so that this kind of one-sided formula is excluded. A symmetric gauge is monotone The first payoff is that a symmetric gauge respects the crudest comparison there is: if every entry of \cvec{x} is smaller in absolute value than the matching entry of \cvec{y}, then \Phi(\cvec{x}) \le \Phi(\cvec{y}). This is not automatic for a norm. The function N(\cvec{x}) = \lvert x_1 - x_2vert + \lvert x_1vert is a norm on 
R^2, and N(1, 0) = 2 is larger than N(1,1) = 1 although (1,0) is dominated entrywise by (1,1). Sign invariance is what rules this out. [Symmetric Gauges Are Monotone] Let \Phi be a symmetric gauge function on 
R^n, and let \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n satisfy \lvert x_ivert \le \lvert y_ivert for every i. Then \Phi(\cvec{x}) \le \Phi(\cvec{y}). Change one coordinate at a time. Shrinking a single entry towards 0 is taking an average of two vectors: the vector itself and the one with that entry’s sign flipped. Sign invariance says those two have the same \Phi, and the triangle inequality says the average has no larger one. Step 1: one coordinate. Suppose \cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \in 
R^n agree in every coordinate except the j-th, where \lvert u_jvert \le \lvert v_jvert. If v_j = 0 then u_j = 0 and \cvec{u} = \cvec{v}. Otherwise put 	heta =  rac12\Bigl(1 +  rac{u_j}{v_j}\Bigr) , which lies in [0, 1] because \lvert u_j/v_jvert \le 1. Let \cvec{v}' be \cvec{v} with its j-th coordinate negated. Then 	heta v_j + (1-	heta)(-v_j) = u_j, while in every other coordinate \cvec{v} and \cvec{v}' agree with \cvec{u}, so \cvec{u} = 	heta\cvec{v} + (1 - 	heta)\cvec{v}' . By (N3) and (N2) of @def-norm, \Phi(\cvec{u}) \le 	heta\Phi(\cvec{v}) + (1-	heta)\Phi(\cvec{v}'), and \Phi(\cvec{v}') = \Phi(\cvec{v}) by (G2). Hence \Phi(\cvec{u}) \le \Phi(\cvec{v}). Step 2: all coordinates. Put \cvec{z}^{(0)} = \cvec{y} and, for 1 \le j \le n, \cvec{z}^{(j)} = (x_1, \dots, x_j, y_{j+1}, \dots, y_n) , so that \cvec{z}^{(n)} = \cvec{x}. Consecutive vectors \cvec{z}^{(j-1)} and \cvec{z}^{(j)} agree except in coordinate j, where \lvert x_jvert \le \lvert y_jvert. By Step 1, \Phi(\cvec{z}^{(j)}) \le \Phi(\cvec{z}^{(j-1)}) for each j. Going deeper [C1: Symmetric gauges detect weak majorization] Let \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n have nonnegative entries. 1. Prove that \cvec{x} \prec_w \cvec{y} if and only if \Phi(\cvec{x}) \le \Phi(\cvec{y}) for every symmetric gauge function \Phi on 
R^n. 2. Prove that \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} if and only if \cvec{x} \prec_w \cvec{y} and \sum_ix_i = \sum_iy_i. 3. Deduce that \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} if and only if \Phi(\cvec{x}) \le \Phi(\cvec{y}) for every symmetric gauge and \sum_ix_i = \sum_iy_i. Hint for (a): only finitely many gauges are needed. (a) (\Rightarrow) is @thm-gauge-monotone-under-majorization (b). (\Leftarrow) Apply the hypothesis to the Ky Fan gauges \Phi_k of @def-ky-fan-gauge, k = 1, \dots, n. Since \cvec{x} and \cvec{y} have nonnegative entries, \lvert\cvec{x}vert^{\downarrow} = \cvec{x}^{\downarrow} and likewise for \cvec{y}, so \Phi_k(\cvec{x}) = \sum_{i\le k}x^{\downarrow}_i and \Phi_k(\cvec{y}) = \sum_{i\le k}y^{\downarrow}_i. The inequalities \Phi_k(\cvec{x}) \le \Phi_k(\cvec{y}) for k = 1, \dots, n are exactly (M1) extended to k = n, which is @def-majorization’s \cvec{x} \prec_w \cvec{y}. (b) This is a restatement of @def-majorization: \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} means (M1) for k \le n-1 together with equality of totals, and \cvec{x} \prec_w \cvec{y} means (M1) for k \le n. Given equality of totals, the case k = n of (M1) is automatic, so the two lists of conditions agree. (c) Combine (a) and (b): \cvec{x} \prec \cvec{y} holds exactly when \cvec{x} \prec_w \cvec{y} and the totals are equal, and by (a) the first of these is equivalent to \Phi(\cvec{x}) \le \Phi(\cvec{y}) for every symmetric gauge. [C2: The dual of a Ky Fan gauge] Fix 1 \le k \le n and let \Phi_k be the Ky Fan gauge of @def-ky-fan-gauge. 1. Prove that \Phi_k^{*}(\cvec{y}) \ge \max igl(
orm{\cvec{y}}_\infty,\ 	frac1k
orm{\cvec{y}}_1 igr) by exhibiting two competitors. 2. Let \Phi_k(\cvec{x}) \le 1 and let \cvec{y} have nonnegative, decreasing entries. Put t = \lvert xvert^{\downarrow}_k and split each \lvert x_ivert as (\lvert x_ivert - t)_{+} + \min(\lvert x_ivert, t). Prove that \sum_i(\lvert x_ivert - t)_{+} \le 1 - kt and that 0 \le t \le 1/k. 3. Deduce \Phi_k^{*}(\cvec{y}) = \max igl(
orm{\cvec{y}}_\infty, 	frac1k

orm{\cvec{y}}_\infty. The vector \cvec{x} with x_i = \pm1/k, the sign of y_i, has \Phi_k(\cvec{x}) = k\cdot	frac1k = 1 and \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = 	frac1k
orm{\cvec{y}}_1. So \Phi_k^{*}(\cvec{y}) is at least both numbers. (b) Since \lvert xvert^{\downarrow} is decreasing, (\lvert xvert^{\downarrow}_i - t)_{+} = 0 for i > k, so \sum_i(\lvert x_ivert - t)_{+} = \sum_{i\le k} igl(\lvert xvert^{\downarrow}_i - t igr) = \Phi_k(\cvec{x}) - kt \le 1 - kt . Also kt \le \sum_{i\le k}\lvert xvert^{\downarrow}_i = \Phi_k(\cvec{x}) \le 1, so 0 \le t \le 1/k. (c) By @thm-dual-gauge, \Phi_k^{*} is a symmetric gauge, so its value at \cvec{y} depends only on \lvert\cvec{y}vert^{\downarrow}; and replacing \cvec{x} by \lvert\cvec{x}vert leaves \Phi_k(\cvec{x}) unchanged and does not decrease \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} when \cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0}. So we may assume \cvec{y} has nonnegative decreasing entries and \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}. With t as in (b), and using y_i \le y_1 = 
orm{\cvec{y}}_\infty in the first sum and \min(x_i, t) \le t in the second, \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} \le 
orm{\cvec{y}}_\infty(1 - kt) + t

orm{\cvec{y}}_1 - k

orm{\cvec{y}}_\infty. If

orm{\cvec{y}}_\infty, 	frac1k
