title: Affine and Projective Geometry
content:
Affine and Projective Geometry Twenty chapters have studied the vector space, and a vector space has an origin. Geometry does not. Nothing a geometer says — these three points are collinear, these two lines are parallel, this point is the midpoint of that segment — mentions a zero vector, and the sets that geometry actually hands us are usually not subspaces at all. Chapter 3’s solution set of \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} with \cvec{b} 
e \cvec{0} is the first example in the book: it misses \cvec{0}, the sum of two of its points is not one of its points, and yet it is a perfectly good flat piece of space. Something is being described there that the word “subspace” does not reach. There are two classical repairs, and this chapter is both of them. Affine geometry deletes the origin and keeps what survives: points, differences of points, flats, parallelism, ratios along a line, and the maps that send lines to lines. Projective geometry goes the other way and adds points — one for every direction — so that two lines in a plane always meet, the dimension formula for a join loses its second case, every quadric in a plane is one of a very short list, and interchanging “point” with “hyperplane” turns every theorem into another theorem. Everything here is proved with linear algebra, and mostly with the linear algebra of Chapters 1 to 5. An affine space is a vector space acting freely and transitively on a set; a projective space is the set of lines through the origin of a vector space; a projectivity is an invertible linear map read on those lines; a conic is a quadratic form; a line in space is a wedge of two vectors. The geometry is the payoff, not the method. Conventions - Points are not bold. P, Q, R are points of an affine space \cA, and \overrightarrow{PQ} \in V is the vector from P to Q; vectors follow the book’s rule by type, bold in coordinates, \cvec{x} \in F^n, and plain in an abstract space, \elem{v} \in V. We write 
A^n for affine n-space, the set F^n with its origin deliberately forgotten. - A flat is an affine subspace, and \vec{A} is its direction space, a subspace of V. The join A \vee B is the smallest flat containing both, the affine counterpart of U + W. - 
P(V) is the projective space of V, of dimension \dim V - 1, with 
P^n(F) = 
P(F^{n+1}); [\cvec{x}] = [x_0 : x_1 : \dots : x_n] is the point determined by \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}. The empty projective space has dimension -1, and that convention is used, not merely tolerated. The projective linear group is \operatorname{PGL}(V). - The cross-ratio (A, B; C, D) is a point of 
P^1(F), not a scalar. Over a field where the affine chart applies it is the familiar number, and Section 7 gives the formula; keeping it projective is what lets it take the value [1:0] without apology. - V^{*} is Chapter 5’s dual space and 
P(V^{*}) the dual projective space, whose points are the hyperplanes of 
P(V). Section 8 writes S^{0} for the subspace of 
P(V^{*}) dual to S, built from the annihilator. - Z(q) is the zero set of a quadratic form, and “conic” means Z(q) in a projective plane. Section 5’s affine quadric is instead the zero set of a degree-two polynomial \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} + 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} + c, and carries the (n+1) 	imes (n+1) matrix \widetilde{\A} alongside the small matrix \A. Which field, and where the characteristic bites Sections 1, 2, 6, 7, 8 and 9 work over an arbitrary field F, with no hypothesis on the characteristic at all. That includes the chapter’s finite-field computations: the four-point affine plane over 
F_2 in Section 1, and the count of 
P^n(
F_q) with the Fano plane in Section 6. Characteristic 2 is barred exactly where quadratic forms appear, which is Section 5 throughout and Section 10 up to the Plücker material. The reason is Chapter 14’s: over 
F_2 a quadratic form is not determined by a symmetric matrix, and Section 5 opens by showing that there is then nothing left to classify — every \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} with \A symmetric collapses to the square of a linear form. Section 5 names the hypothesis at each of the three places it does work, and Section 10 states it at the head and lifts it explicitly for the Plücker subsection, which needs no assumption on F. Two smaller restrictions are local and flagged where they occur: Section 2’s centroid needs 3 
e 0 as well as 2 
e 0, and over 
F_3 the three medians really are parallel; Section 7’s negative result about n+1 points needs F to have at least three elements, and Section 7 proves that over 
F_2 the negative result is false. Three sections are metric, and they are over 
R with the standard inner product: Section 4 entirely, the second half of Section 5, and Section 3, which inherits Chapter 18’s setting of 
R^n with the dot product. Everywhere else a distance would be meaningless: a projectivity does not preserve one. What the chapter quotes, and what it does not prove The chapter imports no analysis. It develops none of its own — no limits, no continuity, no compactness argument — and it adds nothing to the list of analytic facts (A1)–(A6) that Chapter 16 introduced. It uses that list exactly once, at one remove: Section 3’s proof that a bounded polyhedron is the hull of its vertices cites Chapter 16’s @cor-closed-bounded-compact to supply the compactness hypothesis of Chapter 18’s @thm-minkowski-extreme. That is the whole of it. Section 3 says so at its head, and uses the words “closed”, “bounded”, and “compact” only inside the results it cites. Topology is likewise absent. 
P^2(
R) is a famous topological object, and a reader who has met it will expect the words “compact” and “nonorientable”; Section 6 says plainly that this chapter does not use them, because every argument here is a statement about subspaces of a vector space, valid over any field, including finite ones where topology has nothing to say. Six things are quoted and not proved. Each is flagged again where it appears, and nothing in the chapter rests on any of them. - Section 9 — the coordinatization theory of axiomatic projective planes: that Desargues’s theorem holds in a plane exactly when the plane comes from a division ring, that Pappus’s theorem holds exactly when that ring is commutative, that Pappus therefore implies Desargues, and that non-Desarguesian planes exist. This book has built neither division rings nor synthetic planes, and “projective plane” has meant 
P(V) throughout. Section 9 states these with credit in one remark and proves Desargues and Pappus itself, over an arbitrary field, by linear algebra. - Section 8 — the duality principle is claimed as a working method, not a meta-theorem. What Section 8 proves is a list of five equivalences about the correspondence S \mapsto S^{0}; to turn “every incidence statement has a dual” into a theorem one has to define a formal language and induct on it, which this book has not set up. So every dual statement the chapter uses is proved individually, and Section 8 says this in as many words. - Section 4 — the classification of motions is proved in full for 
R^2 and 
R^3, both the direct and the opposite cases. The general shape in 
R^n — a translation along a flat together with mutually orthogonal rotation planes — is described in a warning and is not proved; the warning says so, and gives \R_{\pi/2} \oplus \R_{\pi/3} in 
R^4 as the witness that the three-dimensional list does not extend. - Section 3 — that a dual variable is the exact rate at which the optimal value gains when a constraint is loosened. Section 3 proves the inequality, that y_i bounds the gain, and then exhibits a two-row program where the exact reading fails. It also declines to develop the finite description of an unbounded polyhedron as a polytope plus a cone, pointing at Chapter 18’s exercise instead. - Section 10 — which quadric the Klein quadric is. The main text records that it is smooth, with inertia (3,3,0) over 
R; the Gram matrix that shows this is computed in @exr-conics-and-plucker-c2, and nothing in the section rests on the answer. - Section 10 — which proportionality factors turn the parametrization of the circle into primitive Pythagorean triples. That is arithmetic about parities and common factors, not linear algebra, and Section 10 says so where it stops. Two exercises from earlier chapters are cited, both for credit only: Chapter 15 §10’s @exr-grassmann-and-clifford-c1, which reaches the Plücker relation by the \omega \wedge \omega route, and Chapter 18 §09’s @exr-polytopes-c1. Section 10 proves the Plücker relation in both directions from results in the text, and its proof needs no hypothesis on the characteristic, which the exercise’s route does. No theorem here rests on an exercise. One debt is paid. Chapter 15 §08 hinted at Plücker coordinates without naming the chapter that would build them; Section 10 does. What you need The chapter leans hard on Chapters 0 to 5 and on Chapters 12, 14, and 18, and lightly on everything else. Chapters 9, 10, 13, 19, 20, and 21 are not used at all. Eigenvalues appear only through Chapter 12’s spectral theorem and Chapter 14’s inertia; no canonical form of an operator, no positive semidefinite matrix, no singular value, and no matrix inequality is needed anywhere. - Chapter 0 — sets, maps, and the algebra the constructions rest on: functions and their inverses for Section 4, equivalence relations and quotient sets for Section 6’s construction of 
P(V), the characteristic of a field for Section 5, and the group axioms, which the affine, Euclidean, and projective groups each verify: @thm-bijective-iff-invertible, @thm-composition-associative, @def-equivalence-relation, @def-quotient-set, @thm-partition, @def-characteristic, @thm-matrix-times-vector-columns, @thm-three-views-of-product, @def-group, @def-subgroup, @def-group-homomorphism, @exm-groups, @thm-group-basic-properties, @thm-homomorphism-basic-properties. - Chapter 1 — the chapter’s constant companion, and above all the dimension formula for a sum of subspaces, which is what both the affine join formula and the projective dimension formula reduce to: @thm-subspace-test, @thm-intersection-subspaces, @thm-span-subspace, @def-linear-independence, @lem-append-independent, @thm-unique-representation, @thm-basis-extension, @thm-dim-impl-eq, @thm-right-size-basis, @thm-size-bounds, @thm-subspace-sum, @thm-direct-sum-criteria, @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim, @thm-basis-extension-general. - Chapter 3 — the object that opens Section 1, the solution set of a system with \cvec{b} 
e \cvec{0}; the rank facts Sections 2, 3 and 10 count with; and the observation that a homogeneous system with more unknowns than equations has a nontrivial solution, which is the whole existence half of “five points determine a conic”: @thm-consistent-iff-column-span, @thm-general-solution-structure, @cor-more-unknowns-than-equations, @thm-invertible-tfae, @thm-rank-nullity-matrix, @thm-rouche-capelli, @thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank, @lem-root-bound. - Chapter 2 — linear maps, which are the linear parts of affine maps and the representatives of projectivities: @exm-translation, @thm-linear-map-from-any-basis, @thm-linear-transform-basis, @thm-prop-kernel, @thm-prop-image, @thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel, @thm-injective-preserves-independence, @thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images, @thm-rank-nullity, @cor-rank-nullity-consequences, @thm-composition-linear, @thm-inverse-is-linear, @thm-invertible-operator-tfae, @thm-isomorphic-equivalence-relation, @thm-isomorphic-iff-same-dimension, @cor-coordinate-isomorphism. - Chapter 4 — the rank of a map read off its matrix, and the cosets that flats turn out to be: @thm-rank-map-equals-rank-matrix, @def-coset, @lem-coset-equality, @thm-dimension-quotient, @thm-projection-direct-sum. - Chapter 5 — the whole of Section 8 and half of Sections 2 and 6. The annihilator is what makes projective duality a bijection, and the hyperplane-as-kernel-of-a-functional is what makes a flat a solution set: @def-dual-space, @thm-dual-basis, @thm-functionals-on-fn, @prp-nonzero-functional-surjective, @cor-dimension-dual-space, @def-annihilator, @thm-annihilator-properties, @thm-dimension-annihilator, @cor-annihilator-of-annihilator, @cor-subspaces-determined-by-annihilator, @thm-double-dual-isomorphism, @def-dual-map, @thm-dual-map-properties, @def-hyperplane, @thm-hyperplane-kernel-functional, @thm-subspace-is-solution-set, @lem-subspace-cut-out-by-annihilator, @cor-same-null-space-iff-same-row-space, @prp-affine-subspace-intersection, @exm-implicit-equations. - Chapter 6 §01 — one fact: a nonzero polynomial of degree at most d over a field has at most d roots, which is how an exercise of Section 5 knows that a line meeting a quadric in three points lies inside it. Section 10 uses Chapter 3 §07’s version of the same bound for the same purpose, and that one is in the text: @cor-root-bound-general. - Chapter 7 — determinants, for the direct-or-opposite dichotomy of Section 4 and for the coordinate computations; the Vandermonde determinant is how Section 7 certifies a list of points in general position: @cor-parity-well-defined, @thm-det-transpose, @thm-det-multiplicative, @thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible, @thm-vandermonde-determinant, @cor-vandermonde-nonzero, @thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant. - Chapter 8 §01 — block multiplication, which is what the (n+1) 	imes (n+1) matrix of an affine map is for: @thm-block-multiplication. - Chapter 11 — the Euclidean sections’ toolkit: the inner product and Cauchy–Schwarz, orthogonal decomposition, the characterizations of an isometry, and the polarization identity that turns distance-preservation into linearity: @thm-cauchy-schwarz, @thm-norm-properties, @thm-orthonormal-coordinates, @cor-extend-orthonormal-basis, @thm-orthogonal-decomposition, @thm-four-subspaces-orthogonal, @lem-polarization-identities, @thm-isometry-characterizations, @prp-orthogonal-group-properties, @thm-orthogonal-2x2, @def-householder-reflection, @prp-householder-properties. - Chapter 12 — the real spectral theorem, which rotates a quadric onto its principal axes, and the canonical form of an orthogonal matrix, which is the entire engine of Section 4’s two classification theorems: @cor-spectral-real-matrix, @thm-principal-axes, @exm-principal-axes-ellipse, @thm-orthogonal-canonical-form, @cor-so3-is-rotation, @thm-rodrigues, @thm-rotation-angle-trace, @thm-cartan-dieudonne-small. - Chapter 14 — the classification of quadratic forms, which Sections 5 and 10 turn into the classification of quadrics. Congruence is what an affine change of coordinates does to the big matrix, and Sylvester’s law is what separates an ellipse from an empty set: @def-form-matrix, @prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible, @def-congruent, @prp-congruence-equivalence, @prp-congruence-preserves-symmetry, @thm-congruence-preserves-rank, @def-quadratic-form, @thm-polarization-forms, @thm-alternating-vs-skew, @prp-alternating-form-matrix, @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable, @prp-diagonal-entries-square-classes, @cor-complex-symmetric-classification, @thm-sylvester-inertia, @cor-real-symmetric-classification, @def-signature, @thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues, @def-isotropic-vector, @cor-alternating-even-rank, @exm-pfaffian-small. - Chapter 15 §§08–10 — exterior powers, for Plücker coordinates alone: the basis of \Lambda^2 F^4, that a wedge is nonzero exactly when the factors are independent, and that its coordinates are the minors: @lem-alternating-map-properties, @thm-exterior-power-basis, @thm-wedge-nonzero-iff-independent, @cor-top-exterior-power-is-a-line, @thm-wedge-coordinates-are-minors, @exr-grassmann-and-clifford-c1 (credited, not used). - Chapter 16 — two facts, both in the metric sections: the reverse triangle inequality for Section 4’s nonexample, and the compactness of closed bounded sets, which is the chapter’s only contact with analysis: @lem-reverse-triangle-norm, @cor-closed-bounded-compact. - Chapter 17 — the Rayleigh quotient, which reads Section 5’s semi-axes off the eigenvalues, and the inertia triple: @prp-rayleigh-basic, @def-inertia-triple. - Chapter 18 — all of Section 3, and the affine vocabulary of Sections 1, 2 and 5. Convex hulls and affine hulls, separation, extreme points and faces, polytopes and Minkowski–Weyl, and linear programming duality: @def-affine-hull, @prp-affine-hull-coset, @thm-convex-hull-combinations, @prp-convexity-operations, @def-standard-simplex, @def-affine-independence, @lem-affine-dependence, @thm-supporting-hyperplane, @def-dual-program, @thm-weak-duality, @thm-strong-duality, @cor-duality-certificate, @thm-complementary-slackness, @def-extreme-point, @def-face, @prp-exposed-face, @lem-extreme-points-of-face, @thm-minkowski-extreme, @cor-linear-max-at-extreme, @def-polyhedron, @prp-polyhedron-closed-convex, @thm-minkowski-weyl, @thm-vertices-basic-feasible, @cor-finitely-many-vertices, @exm-cube-cross-polytope, @exr-polytopes-c1 (pointed at, not used). Roadmap - Affine Spaces and Affine Maps. A set on which a vector space acts freely and transitively: differences of points are vectors, sums of points are meaningless, and Chasles’s relation is the one law. Choosing an origin identifies the space with V, and the identification is canonical only after the choice. Affine combinations are exactly the combinations whose coefficients sum to 1, and no other coefficient sum survives a change of origin. An affine map is a linear map plus a translation, for a unique linear part, and the whole affine group fits in one (n+1) 	imes (n+1) block matrix — the device the rest of the chapter computes with. - Flats, Independence, and Coordinates. Flats are the cosets, parallelism is an equivalence relation on flats of equal dimension, and two flats either meet or lie in two distinct parallel hyperplanes. The dimension of a join has two cases: the subspace formula when they meet, and a corrected formula with a +1 when they miss, in which the intersection of directions takes over. No convention for \dim\emptyset merges the two. Then affine frames, barycentric coordinates, and an affine map pinned down by its values on an affine frame of n+1 points; on any set lying inside a proper flat — in particular on any n points — two distinct affine maps agree. The medians of a triangle meet at the centroid, in one line of barycentric coordinates — and over 
F_3 they do not meet at all. - Convex Polyhedra, Geometrically. A reading of Chapter 18, not a reproof: it says so in its first paragraph. A face is what a supporting hyperplane cuts out; faces are polyhedra and there are finitely many; vertex, extreme point, and basic feasible solution are three names for one thing. The face lattices of a cube and of a simplex are computed in full. A linear program is a family of parallel hyperplanes sweeping across a solid, the optimal set is a whole face, and the dual variables are the nonnegative weights expressing the objective as a combination of the active outer normals. Negative cases: an unbounded slab with no vertex at all, whose optimum is nonetheless attained on a face that contains none, and a quadrant that has a vertex and no optimum. No algorithm appears here or anywhere in this book; Chapter 24 is where algorithms live. - Euclidean Motions. Distance alone forces everything: a map of 
R^n preserving distances is affine with orthogonal linear part, and surjectivity is not assumed — it is proved. Polarization is the move, and the Euclidean norm is doing real work, as a distance-preserving nonaffine map for the maximum norm shows. Motions form a group with the translations normal in it and the orthogonal group as the quotient’s content, recorded without quotient groups, which this book has not built. Then both classifications in full: in the plane, translation, rotation, reflection, glide reflection; in space, translation, rotation, screw, reflection, glide, rotatory reflection, told apart by the fixed set. From 
R^4 on the list breaks, and the section says so. - Affine and Euclidean Quadrics. A quadric is a quadratic form that has forgotten where the origin is. An affine substitution acts on the (n+1) 	imes (n+1) matrix by congruence, a center exists exactly when the linear vector lies in the column space of the small matrix, and the parabola is precisely the centerless case. Over 
R every quadric is affinely equivalent to exactly one of three families, separated by the pair of inertias; for n = 2 that is nine normal forms, two of which have empty zero sets and are still inequivalent, and for n = 3 it is seventeen. Allowing only motions instead keeps the eigenvalues, and they are the reciprocal squared semi-axes — the Rayleigh quotient read on an ellipsoid. - Projective Space. Stop working with the points of a vector space and start working with its lines through the origin. The affine chart splits 
P^n(F) into a copy of 
A^n and a hyperplane at infinity of directions, and the two parallel lines of the opening now meet, at a point whose coordinates are computed. The dimension formula \dim(S \vee T) + \dim(S \cap T) = \dim S + \dim T has no exceptional case, which is the whole reason for the construction; two distinct lines of a projective plane meet in exactly one point. Finite fields give \lvert 
P^n(
F_q)vert = (q^{n+1}-1)/(q-1), and the Fano plane is drawn and checked. - Projective Transformations. An invertible linear map descends to 
P(V), and two of them give the same projectivity exactly when they differ by a nonzero scalar — so \operatorname{PGL}(V) is \GL(V) modulo scalars, said without quotient groups. The fundamental theorem: n+2 points in general position can be carried to any other such list by exactly one projectivity. n+1 points are not enough, and the explicit failure is a diagonal matrix; over 
F_2, and only there, n+1 points do suffice, which is proved. Then the cross-ratio, invariant under projectivities and a complete invariant of four points on a line, computed exactly; perspectivities; and the sentence that ties the chapter together — affine maps are exactly the projectivities fixing the hyperplane at infinity as a set. - Duality. A point of 
P(V^{*}) is a hyperplane of 
P(V). The annihilator gives an inclusion-reversing bijection S \mapsto S^{0} between the projective subspaces of the two spaces, with \dim S^{0} = n - 1 - \dim S, exchanging joins with meets and the two extreme subspaces with each other. Dualizing twice returns the original. The duality principle is then stated as five equivalences and used as a recipe, each application being its own proof; “two distinct points lie on a unique line” dualizes to “two distinct lines meet in a unique point”, and the projective dimension formula turns out to be self-dual. The trap is spelled out: the dual of “point” is “hyperplane”, and in 
P^3 two lines need not meet. - Desargues and Pappus. Two triangles are perspective from a point if and only if they are perspective from a line, proved inside 
P^2 by choosing representatives so that the hypothesis reads \elem{a}' = \elem{a} + \elem{o}, with every scaling step verified — that is where such proofs go wrong. The converse costs no second theorem: the same lemma, applied to a pair of auxiliary triangles built out of the same picture. Pappus follows in coordinates, with the frame chosen by the previous section’s fundamental theorem to make the computation short, and the degenerate configurations excluded by hypothesis. Both hold over every field, and the remark that closes the section records, with credit and without proof, that Desargues means “division ring” and Pappus means “commutative”. - Conics and Lines in Space. Over an algebraically closed field a projective quadric is classified by rank alone; over 
R by rank and inertia up to sign, giving five conics in 
P^2(
R): empty, a point, a line, two lines, a smooth conic. Five points in general position lie on exactly one conic, and the independence of the five conditions is proved, not assumed. A smooth conic with one point is in bijection with 
P^1 by projection from that point, which turns one Pythagorean triple into all of them. Pole, polar, and the dual conic use Section 8’s duality. Finally Plücker coordinates, over any field: a line of 
P^3 is a point of 
P^5, the six coordinates satisfy p_{01}p_{23} - p_{02}p_{13} + p_{03}p_{12} = 0, and every point of that Klein quadric is a line — both directions proved. A summary closes the chapter. Named moves - Choose an origin, then say that you chose it. An affine space becomes a vector space the moment a point is picked, and every affine statement is then a linear statement about the difference vectors. The discipline is to record which conclusions survive a different choice: those are the affine ones, and the coefficient sum 1 is exactly the test. - Add a coordinate to linearize. An affine map of F^n is not linear, but \cvec{x} \mapsto (1, \cvec{x}) — Section 1 writes the extra coordinate last instead — makes it the restriction of a linear map of F^{n+1}, with matrix  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & \cvec{0}	p \ \cvec{b} & \M \end{psmallmatrix}. The same extra coordinate is what turns a quadric polynomial into a quadratic form and an affine space into a chart of a projective space. Three of this chapter’s theorems are that one observation in three costumes. - Pass from points to lines through the origin. Scaling is the enemy of a well-defined point and the friend of a well-defined condition: q(\lambda\elem{x}) = \lambda^2 q(\elem{x}) vanishes when q(\elem{x}) does. Anything homogeneous descends to 
P(V), which is why every object in the second half of the chapter is the solution set of homogeneous polynomial equations. - Choose the representatives so the hypothesis becomes an equation. A projective point is a whole line of vectors, and the content of most projective proofs is the scaling chosen at the start: \elem{a}' = \elem{a} + \elem{o} in Desargues, a normalized frame in the fundamental theorem, the second intersection point in the conic parametrization. State out loud which scalings remain free afterwards. - Split the translation and ask what \I - \Q can absorb. To classify a map \cvec{x} \mapsto \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b}, decompose \cvec{b} along the kernel of \I - \Q and its complement. The part in the image is absorbed by moving the fixed set; the part in the kernel survives and is the glide. That single question produces both of Section 4’s classification theorems. - Read an old theorem geometrically instead of proving a new one. Section 3 adds no convexity theorem to Chapter 18. It renames the objects — face, vertex, edge, facet — and the theorems become statements about a solid with flat sides. Knowing when a chapter is a translation rather than a construction is worth as much as the construction. - Count the conditions, then prove they are independent. Five points impose five linear conditions on a 6-dimensional space of forms, so a conic exists by counting alone. Uniqueness is the real theorem, and it is where general position earns its keep: a second independent solution would let us push a conic through a sixth point on one of the lines, a conic meeting a line three times contains it, so it splits into two lines, and the second line then carries three of the original five. The count is cheap; the independence is the content. - Dualize by the dimension formula, never by the words. The dual of a d-dimensional subspace has dimension n - 1 - d. Compute that number before translating any statement: in a plane it sends points to lines, but in 
P^3 it sends points to planes and lines to lines, and translating “point” to “line” there produces a false theorem.

title: 22.1 Affine Spaces and Affine Maps
content:
Affine Spaces and Affine Maps Every space in this book so far has had a distinguished point: the zero vector. Geometry does not. A plane drawn on paper has no privileged spot, and none of the statements a geometer cares about — three points are collinear, two lines are parallel, this point is the midpoint of that segment — mentions one. This section builds the object that has all the structure of a vector space except the origin, and the maps between such objects. Everything in the rest of the chapter is written in this language. A set with no zero in it Chapter 3 already produced such an object without naming it. Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \cvec{b} \in F^m, and suppose \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} is consistent. By @thm-general-solution-structure the solution set is \cvec{p} + N, where N = 
ul(\A) and \cvec{p} is any one solution. When \cvec{b} 
e \cvec{0} this set is not a subspace: it misses \cvec{0}, and the sum of two solutions is not a solution. Yet it is not shapeless either. The difference of two solutions is a vector of N, and adding a vector of N to a solution gives a solution. So the solution set carries an action of N, and N records exactly how any two solutions differ. That is the whole structure, and it deserves a name. The only operation is: subtract two points and get a vector; add a vector to a point and get a point. Adding two points is meaningless, and so is multiplying a point by a scalar. An affine space is a set of points in which differences of points are vectors, and every vector moves every point to exactly one other. [Affine Space] Let V be a vector space over a field F. An affine space with direction space V is a nonempty set \cA, whose elements are called points, together with a map \cA 	imes \cA 	o V, \qquad (P, Q) \mapsto \overrightarrow{PQ}, such that: 1. (Chasles’s relation) \overrightarrow{PQ} + \overrightarrow{QR} = \overrightarrow{PR} for all P, Q, R \in \cA; 2. for every P \in \cA, the map \cA 	o V, Q \mapsto \overrightarrow{PQ}, is a bijection. The dimension of \cA is \dim \cA \coloneqq \dim V. For P \in \cA and \elem{v} \in V we write P + \elem{v} for the unique point Q with \overrightarrow{PQ} = \elem{v}, which exists and is unique by (AS2). Read the two clauses. (AS1) says that traveling from P to Q and then from Q to R is traveling from P to R; it is the one law that makes the arrows behave like displacements. (AS2) says that from any fixed point P, every vector of V is the displacement to exactly one point: existence makes \cA big enough (the action is transitive), uniqueness makes it no bigger (the action is free). The set \cA is not a vector space and has no zero; V is a vector space and has one. Two consequences are immediate and will be used constantly. [First consequences of Chasles] Let \cA be an affine space with direction space V. For all P, Q \in \cA and \elem{u}, \elem{w} \in V: 1. \overrightarrow{PP} = \elem{0}, and \overrightarrow{QP} = -\overrightarrow{PQ}; 2. P + \elem{0} = P and (P + \elem{u}) + \elem{w} = P + (\elem{u} + \elem{w}); 3. \overrightarrow{PQ} = \elem{0} if and only if P = Q. (a) Taking P = Q = R in (AS1) gives \overrightarrow{PP} + \overrightarrow{PP} = \overrightarrow{PP}, so \overrightarrow{PP} = \elem{0} by cancellation in the group (V, +) (@thm-group-basic-properties). Taking R = P in (AS1) gives \overrightarrow{PQ} + \overrightarrow{QP} = \overrightarrow{PP} = \elem{0}. (b) P + \elem{0} = P restates \overrightarrow{PP} = \elem{0}. For the second identity, put Q = P + \elem{u} and R = Q + \elem{w}, so that \overrightarrow{PQ} = \elem{u} and \overrightarrow{QR} = \elem{w}. By (AS1), \overrightarrow{PR} = \elem{u} + \elem{w}, which says R = P + (\elem{u} + \elem{w}). (c) (\Leftarrow) is (a). (\Rightarrow) If \overrightarrow{PQ} = \elem{0} = \overrightarrow{PP}, then Q = P by the injectivity in (AS2). The clauses in part (b) are the axioms of an action of the additive group of V on \cA, and the definition is often given that way instead. The two presentations carry the same information. [The two forms of the definition agree] Let V be a vector space over F and \cA a nonempty set. Giving a map \cA 	imes \cA 	o V satisfying (AS1) and (AS2) is the same as giving a map \cA 	imes V 	o \cA, written (P, \elem{v}) \mapsto P + \elem{v}, such that 1. P + \elem{0} = P for every P \in \cA; 2. (P + \elem{u}) + \elem{w} = P + (\elem{u} + \elem{w}) for all P \in \cA and \elem{u}, \elem{w} \in V; 3. for all P, Q \in \cA there is exactly one \elem{v} \in V with P + \elem{v} = Q. The two constructions are inverse to each other. There is nothing to find: in one direction the addition was already defined after @def-affine-space, in the other the vector \overrightarrow{PQ} is the one whose uniqueness (AC3) asserts. The work is checking the axioms, and each check is one line. Suppose first that (P, Q) \mapsto \overrightarrow{PQ} satisfies (AS1) and (AS2), and define P + \elem{v} as after @def-affine-space. Then (AC1) and (AC2) are @lem-chasles-consequences (b), and (AC3) is (AS2), since P + \elem{v} = Q says \overrightarrow{PQ} = \elem{v}. Conversely, suppose (P, \elem{v}) \mapsto P + \elem{v} satisfies (AC1)–(AC3), and let \overrightarrow{PQ} be the unique \elem{v} with P + \elem{v} = Q. For (AS1), put \elem{u} = \overrightarrow{PQ} and \elem{w} = \overrightarrow{QR}; then by (AC2), P + (\elem{u} + \elem{w}) = (P + \elem{u}) + \elem{w} = Q + \elem{w} = R , so \overrightarrow{PR} = \elem{u} + \elem{w} by the uniqueness in (AC3). For (AS2), fix P. The map Q \mapsto \overrightarrow{PQ} is surjective because \elem{v} is the image of P + \elem{v}, and injective because \overrightarrow{PQ} = \overrightarrow{PQ'} = \elem{v} gives Q = P + \elem{v} = Q'. The two passages are inverse: starting from \overrightarrow{\ \cdot\ }, the constructed addition has P + \elem{v} = Q exactly when \overrightarrow{PQ} = \elem{v}, so the difference map it returns is the original one; and starting from an addition, the same equivalence returns it unchanged. This proves the proposition. The converse half used only (AC2) and (AC3), and it could not have used more: (AC1) follows from the other two. Indeed (AC3) with Q = P gives exactly one \elem{v} with P + \elem{v} = P, and that \elem{v} has P + (\elem{v} + \elem{v}) = (P + \elem{v}) + \elem{v} = P + \elem{v} = P by (AC2), so \elem{v} + \elem{v} = \elem{v} by the same uniqueness and \elem{v} = \elem{0}. We list (AC1) anyway, because that is how the axioms of a group action are usually written. Now the examples. The first is the one every other example is modeled on. [Four affine spaces] Check each of the following against @def-affine-space, and say what its direction space and dimension are. 1. A vector space V over F, with \overrightarrow{\elem{x}\elem{y}} \coloneqq \elem{y} - \elem{x}. 2. A coset \elem{p} + U of a subspace U of V (@def-coset), with the same difference map. 3. The solution set of a consistent system \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}, \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). 4. The set 
F_2^2 of four points, with \overrightarrow{\cvec{x}\cvec{y}} = \cvec{y} - \cvec{x}. (a) Chasles reads (\elem{y} - \elem{x}) + (\elem{z} - \elem{y}) = \elem{z} - \elem{x}, which is true in any vector space. For fixed \elem{x}, the map \elem{y} \mapsto \elem{y} - \elem{x} is a bijection V 	o V with inverse \elem{v} \mapsto \elem{x} + \elem{v}. Direction space V; dimension \dim V. Here the point \elem{x} and the vector \elem{x} are the same object, and only the language distinguishes them. (b) The set \elem{p} + U is nonempty (it contains \elem{p}) and the difference of two of its elements is (\elem{p} + \elem{u}) - (\elem{p} + \elem{w}) = \elem{u} - \elem{w} \in U, so the map does land in U. Chasles is again the identity in (a). For fixed \elem{x} \in \elem{p} + U, the map \elem{y} \mapsto \elem{y} - \elem{x} is a bijection \elem{p} + U 	o U: it is injective, and \elem{u} \in U is the image of \elem{x} + \elem{u}, which lies in \elem{p} + U because U is closed under addition. Direction space U; dimension \dim U. Over 
R these are exactly Chapter 18’s affine subspaces of V (@def-affine-hull (b)), with the same dimension. (c) By @thm-general-solution-structure the solution set is \cvec{p} + 
ul(\A) for any one solution \cvec{p}, so this is a special case of (b). Direction space 
ul(\A); dimension 
ullity(\A) = n - ank\A by @thm-rank-nullity-matrix. Consistency is what makes the set nonempty, and @thm-rouche-capelli says when it holds. (d) A special case of (a) with V = 
F_2^2: four points, direction space 
F_2^2, dimension 2. It is worth seeing because it is so small. Every pair of distinct points P 
e Q has \overrightarrow{PQ} = \overrightarrow{QP}, since -1 = 1 in 
F_2; the next section will call a coset of a one-dimensional subspace a line, and here each such coset has exactly two points. So every one of the  inom{4}{2} = 6 pairs of distinct points is itself a line, and the six lines fall into three pairs with no point in common. A nonexample, by minimal change. Delete one point from the plane: let \cA = 
R^2 \setminus \{\cvec{0}\}, with \overrightarrow{\cvec{x}\cvec{y}} = \cvec{y} - \cvec{x}. Chasles still holds, because it is an identity about subtraction. But (AS2) fails: for P = (1, 0), no point Q of \cA has \overrightarrow{PQ} = (-1, 0), since the only candidate is \cvec{0}, which we removed. The map Q \mapsto \overrightarrow{PQ} is injective but not surjective. It is exactly the transitivity of the action that fails: the set has a hole. A point is not a vector. In an affine space there is no zero point; and over a field in which 2 
e 0 and 3 
e 0 there is no sum P + Q of two points and no multiple 3P. The only legal expressions are \overrightarrow{PQ} \in V, P + \elem{v} \in \cA, and the affine combinations defined below. If you find yourself writing P + Q, you have silently chosen an origin; the next subsection says what that costs. Choosing an origin An affine space looks like its direction space as soon as one point is nominated as the zero. This is the chapter’s first named move, and it is used in almost every proof that follows: to compute, pick an origin; to state a result, do not. [Choice of Origin] Let \cA be an affine space with direction space V, and let O \in \cA. Then 	heta_O \colon \cA 	o V, \qquad 	heta_O(P) = \overrightarrow{OP} , is a bijection with 	heta_O(O) = \elem{0}, and it carries the affine structure of \cA to that of V in @exm-affine-space-basic (a): \overrightarrow{PQ} = 	heta_O(Q) - 	heta_O(P) \qquad (P, Q \in \cA). If O' \in \cA is another point, then 	heta_{O'}(P) = 	heta_O(P) - 	heta_O(O') for every P: the two identifications differ by a translation of V. 	heta_O is a bijection by (AS2), and 	heta_O(O) = \overrightarrow{OO} = \elem{0} by @lem-chasles-consequences (a). By Chasles and the same lemma, 	heta_O(Q) - 	heta_O(P) = \overrightarrow{OQ} - \overrightarrow{OP} = \overrightarrow{OQ} + \overrightarrow{PO} = \overrightarrow{PQ} . For the last statement, apply this with P and O' in place of Q and P: 	heta_{O'}(P) = \overrightarrow{O'P} = 	heta_O(P) - 	heta_O(O'). So an n-dimensional affine space over F is a copy of F^n with the labels rubbed off. Choosing O writes the labels back on, and any two choices differ by a translation. We write 
A^n(F) for F^n regarded as an affine space over itself, and 
A^n when F = 
R; its points are written P = (p_1, \dots, p_n), in plain type, even though the same list of numbers written \cvec{p} would be a vector. The identification is never canonical. @prp-choice-of-origin does not say that \cA “is” V; it says that each point of \cA gives one isomorphism, and there are as many as there are points. A statement proved after choosing O is a statement about \cA only if it does not depend on which O was chosen. Checking that independence is a real obligation, and the next subsection is nothing but that check, done once for all. Affine combinations Sums of points are forbidden, and yet the centroid 	frac13(P_1 + P_2 + P_3) of a triangle is a genuine point of the plane, independent of any coordinate system. Something with weights adding up to 1 survives the loss of the origin. Here is the computation that says which expressions survive. Fix O \in \cA, points P_1, \dots, P_k \in \cA and scalars t_1, \dots, t_k \in F with s \coloneqq t_1 + \dots + t_k. Let O' \in \cA and \elem{w} = \overrightarrow{OO'}. Since \overrightarrow{O'P_i} = \overrightarrow{O'O} + \overrightarrow{OP_i} = \overrightarrow{OP_i} - \elem{w}, \sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i \overrightarrow{O'P_i} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i \overrightarrow{OP_i} - s\elem{w} , {#eq-affine-combination-shift} and therefore, adding this vector to the point O' = O + \elem{w} and using @lem-chasles-consequences (b), we get the companion identity for points. O' + \sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i \overrightarrow{O'P_i} = \Bigl( O + \sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i \overrightarrow{OP_i} \Bigr) + (1 - s)\elem{w} . {#eq-affine-combination-point-shift} The vector on the left of @eq-affine-combination-shift does not depend on the origin exactly when s = 0; the point on the left of @eq-affine-combination-point-shift does not depend on it exactly when s = 1. Both cases are worth a name. Weights adding to one make a point; weights adding to zero make a vector; nothing else means anything. [Affine Combination] Let \cA be an affine space with direction space V, let P_1, \dots, P_k \in \cA with k \ge 1, and let t_1, \dots, t_k \in F. 1. If t_1 + \dots + t_k = 1, the affine combination \sum_{i} t_iP_i is the point O + \sum_{i} t_i\overrightarrow{OP_i}, for any O \in \cA. 2. If t_1 + \dots + t_k = 0, the expression \sum_{i} t_iP_i denotes the vector \sum_{i} t_i\overrightarrow{OP_i} \in V, for any O \in \cA. For no other value of t_1 + \dots + t_k is \sum_i t_iP_i defined. In words: the same symbol means a point when the weights add up to 1 and a vector when they add up to 0, and the type of the answer is read off from the weights. The simplest instance of (b) is k = 2 with weights (-1, 1): the vector Q - P is \overrightarrow{PQ}. The simplest instance of (a) is k = 1 with t_1 = 1, which is P_1. [Affine combinations are exactly the origin-free ones] With the notation of @def-affine-combination, put s = t_1 + \dots + t_k. 1. If s = 1, the point O + \sum_i t_i\overrightarrow{OP_i} is the same for every O \in \cA. 2. If s = 0, the vector \sum_i t_i\overrightarrow{OP_i} is the same for every O \in \cA. 3. Suppose \dim \cA \ge 1. If s 
e 1, there are points P_1, \dots, P_k and origins O, O' for which O + \sum_i t_i\overrightarrow{OP_i} and O' + \sum_i t_i\overrightarrow{O'P_i} differ; and if s 
e 0, the same is true of the vectors \sum_i t_i\overrightarrow{OP_i}. (a) and (b) are @eq-affine-combination-point-shift and @eq-affine-combination-shift with 1 - s = 0 and s = 0 respectively, since O' was an arbitrary point of \cA. (b) Since \dim \cA \ge 1, the direction space V contains some \elem{w} 
e \elem{0}. Take any O \in \cA, put O' = O + \elem{w}, and take P_1 = \dots = P_k = O, so that \overrightarrow{OP_i} = \elem{0} for every i. Then @eq-affine-combination-point-shift reads O' + \sum_i t_i\overrightarrow{O'P_i} = O + (1-s)\elem{w} , which differs from O + \sum_i t_i \overrightarrow{OP_i} = O when (1-s)\elem{w} 
e \elem{0}, that is, when s 
e 1, by @lem-chasles-consequences (c). Likewise @eq-affine-combination-shift reads \sum_i t_i\overrightarrow{O'P_i} = -s\elem{w}, which differs from \sum_i t_i\overrightarrow{OP_i} = \elem{0} when s 
e 0. Taking \cA = V over 
R and O = \elem{0}, part (a) becomes the ordinary vector expression \sum_i t_i\elem{x}_i with \sum_i t_i = 1, which is Chapter 18’s affine combination (@def-affine-hull (a)). So @def-affine-combination extends that notion from a real vector space to an affine space over any field, and adds the companion vector-valued case. Chapter 18’s affine hull \operatorname{aff} S and its description as a coset (@prp-affine-hull-coset) are the real case of the flats of the next section. Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R be f(x) = 2x + 3, which is not linear. Compute f(3 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 2) and 3f(1) - 2f(2); then compute f(1 + 2) and f(1) + f(2). What do the two pairs show? First pair: 3 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 2 = -1 and f(-1) = 1, while 3f(1) - 2f(2) = 3 \cdot 5 - 2 \cdot 7 = 1. They agree, and the weights 3 and -2 add up to 1. Second pair: f(3) = 9, while f(1) + f(2) = 5 + 7 = 12. They differ, and the weights 1 and 1 add up to 2. So f respects combinations whose weights add up to 1 and destroys the others: it is affine but not linear. That is the content of the next subsection. Affine maps Linear maps are the functions that respect the structure of a vector space. Affine maps should be the functions that respect the structure of an affine space, and by @def-affine-combination that structure is: which affine combinations equal which points. So there is only one reasonable definition. An affine map is one that can be applied inside an affine combination. Then \I - \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix} and \col(\I - \A) = \Span(\cvec{e}_2), which does not contain \cvec{b} = \cvec{e}_1; so there is no fixed point, by (a). And \A 
e \I. [C2: Affine maps on two points, over two fields] Let f \colon \cA 	o \cB be a map of affine spaces over F that preserves affine combinations of two points, that is, f((1-t)P + tQ) = (1-t)f(P) + tf(Q) for all P, Q \in \cA and t \in F. 1. Prove that if \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, then f is affine. Hint: run the proof of @thm-affine-map-is-linear-plus-translation, replacing the three-point combination by two two-point ones. 2. Show that over 
F_2 the hypothesis is empty, and give a nonaffine map 
F_2^2 	o 
F_2 satisfying it. (a) Fix O \in \cA and define T(\elem{v}) = \overrightarrow{f(O)f(O + \elem{v})} as in @thm-affine-map-is-linear-plus-translation. Homogeneity is the hypothesis with P = O + \elem{v}, Q = O: O + \lambda\elem{v} = \lambda(O + \elem{v}) + (1-\lambda)O, so f(O + \lambda\elem{v}) = \lambda f(O+\elem{v}) + (1-\lambda)f(O) = f(O) + \lambda T(\elem{v}), giving T(\lambda\elem{v}) = \lambda T(\elem{v}). For additivity, let \elem{u}, \elem{w} \in V and let M = 	frac12(O + \elem{u}) + 	frac12(O + \elem{w}), which is legal since 2 
e 0 in F. With origin O, M = O + 	frac12(\elem{u} + \elem{w}). By the hypothesis, f(M) = 	frac12 f(O + \elem{u}) + 	frac12 f(O + \elem{w}), which with origin f(O) reads f(M) = f(O) + 	frac12(T(\elem{u}) + T(\elem{w})). So T igl(	frac12(\elem{u} + \elem{w}) igr) = 	frac12 igl(T(\elem{u}) + T(\elem{w}) igr). Applying homogeneity with \lambda = 2 to the left-hand side gives T(\elem{u} + \elem{w}) = T(\elem{u}) + T(\elem{w}). Hence T is linear, and f(P) = f(O) + T(\overrightarrow{OP}) by construction, so f is affine by @thm-affine-map-is-linear-plus-translation (c). (b) Over 
F_2 the only scalars are t = 0 and t = 1, for which (1-t)P + tQ is P or Q; the required identity then reads f(P) = f(P) or f(Q) = f(Q). So every map satisfies the hypothesis. Take f \colon 
F_2^2 	o 
F_2 with f(0,0) = f(1,0) = f(0,1) = 0 and f(1,1) = 1. It is not affine: by @exr-affine-spaces-b3 (b), (1,1) is the affine combination O + P + Q of the other three points with weights (1,1,1), so an affine f would have f(1,1) = f(O) + f(P) + f(Q) = 0. [C3: Conjugating a translation] Let \cA be an affine space with direction space V, let f \in \operatorname{Aff}(\cA) and let \elem{v} \in V. 1. Prove that f \circ 	au_{\elem{v}} \circ f^{-1} = 	au_{\vec{f}(\elem{v})}. 2. Hence prove that the translations form a subgroup of \operatorname{Aff}(\cA) that is carried to itself by every conjugation, and that \elem{v} \mapsto 	au_{\elem{v}} is an isomorphism from (V, +) onto it. 3. Deduce that if \dim \cA \ge 2, then \operatorname{Aff}(\cA) is not abelian. (a) Both sides are affine maps \cA 	o \cA. By @thm-affine-group (a) the linear part of the left-hand side is \vec f \circ \id_V \circ (\vec f)^{-1} = \id_V, so by the kernel description in @thm-affine-group (c) it is a translation 	au_{\elem{u}} for some \elem{u}. To identify \elem{u}, fix O \in \cA and put P = f^{-1}(O). Then \elem{u} = \overrightarrow{O\,(f \circ 	au_{\elem{v}} \circ f^{-1})(O)} = \overrightarrow{f(P)\, f(P + \elem{v})} = \vec{f}(\elem{v}) , using @thm-affine-map-is-linear-plus-translation (b) and \overrightarrow{P(P+\elem{v})} = \elem{v}. (b) The translations are the kernel of f \mapsto \vec f (@thm-affine-group (c)), hence a subgroup by @thm-homomorphism-basic-properties, and (a) says every conjugate of a translation is a translation. The map \elem{v} \mapsto 	au_{\elem{v}} satisfies 	au_{\elem{u}} \circ 	au_{\elem{w}} = 	au_{\elem{u} + \elem{w}} by @lem-chasles-consequences (b), so it is a homomorphism (V, +) 	o \operatorname{Aff}(\cA); it is surjective onto the translations by definition, and injective because 	au_{\elem{v}} = \id forces P + \elem{v} = P, hence \elem{v} = \elem{0}. (c) Since \dim V \ge 2, pick independent \elem{v}, \elem{w} \in V and T \in \GL(V) with T(\elem{v}) = \elem{w} (extend \{\elem{v}, \elem{w}\} to a basis of V by @thm-basis-extension-general, and map that basis to itself with \elem{v} and \elem{w} swapped, using @thm-linear-map-from-any-basis; this T is invertible because T \circ T fixes every basis vector and so is \id_V, by the uniqueness in that theorem). By @thm-affine-group (c) there is f \in \operatorname{Aff}(\cA) with \vec f = T. If \operatorname{Aff}(\cA) were abelian then f \circ 	au_{\elem{v}} \circ f^{-1} = 	au_{\elem{v}}, while (a) gives 	au_{T(\elem{v})} = 	au_{\elem{w}}; by the injectivity in (b) that forces \elem{v} = \elem{w}, contradicting independence.

title: 22.2 Flats, Independence, and Coordinates
content:
Flats, Independence, and Coordinates An affine space has no origin, so it has no subspaces in the sense of Chapter 1: a subspace must contain \elem{0}, and there is no \elem{0}. What it has instead are its flats — the lines, planes, and hyperplanes that sit inside it. This section defines them, settles when two of them meet and how big the smallest flat containing both is, puts coordinates on an affine space using n + 1 points rather than n vectors, and shows that in 
A^n(F) the flats are exactly the solution sets of linear systems. The join formula has two cases, and the second one is where affine geometry parts company with linear algebra. Throughout, \cA is an affine space over a field F with direction space V (@def-affine-space), and from the dimension formula onward \dim \cA = \dim V = n is finite, except where a statement says otherwise. Flats A subset of \cA deserves to be called flat when it is an affine space in its own right, using the same difference map. By @def-affine-combination there is only one thing to require. A flat is a nonempty set of points closed under taking affine combinations. [Flat] A subset A \subseteq \cA is a flat, or an affine subspace of \cA, if it is nonempty and contains every affine combination of its own points: whenever k \ge 1, P_1, \dots, P_k \in A and t_1, \dots, t_k \in F satisfy t_1 + \dots + t_k = 1, the point \sum_{i=1}^{k}t_iP_i lies in A. The requirement that A be nonempty is a convention, and it is the useful one: a flat is going to have a direction space and a dimension, and the empty set has neither. Intersections of flats may of course be empty, and we will say so each time. [Flats Are the Cosets] Let A \subseteq \cA be nonempty. Then A is a flat if and only if there are P \in \cA and a subspace U of V with A = P + U \coloneqq \{ P + \elem{u} : \elem{u} \in U \}. In that case: 1. U = \{ \overrightarrow{XY} : X, Y \in A \} is determined by A alone; it is written \vec{A} and called the direction space of A. 2. A = Q + \vec{A} for every Q \in A, and A, with the difference map of \cA restricted to it, is an affine space with direction space \vec{A}. The dimension of A is \dim A \coloneqq \dim \vec{A}. A flat of dimension 0 is a single point, one of dimension 1 is a line, one of dimension 2 is a plane, and, when \dim\cA = n is finite, one of dimension n - 1 is a hyperplane of \cA. One direction is a computation with origin P. For the other, fix P \in A and let U be the set of displacements from P to points of A; the three subspace axioms come from three affine combinations, with weight lists (1), (\lambda, 1 - \lambda) and (1, 1, -1). (\Leftarrow) Let A = P + U with U a subspace, and let P + \elem{u}_1, \dots, P + \elem{u}_k \in A with \sum_i t_i = 1. Computing the affine combination with origin P (@def-affine-combination), \sum_{i} t_i(P + \elem{u}_i) = P + \sum_i t_i\elem{u}_i \in P + U , since U is closed under linear combinations. And A 
i P is nonempty. (\Rightarrow) Let A be a flat, fix P \in A and put U = \{ \overrightarrow{PX} : X \in A \}. Then \elem{0} = \overrightarrow{PP} \in U. If \elem{u} = \overrightarrow{PX} \in U and \lambda \in F, the point \lambda X + (1 - \lambda)P lies in A and equals P + \lambda\elem{u} when computed with origin P, so \lambda\elem{u} \in U. If also \elem{w} = \overrightarrow{PY} \in U, the point X + Y - P lies in A (weights 1 + 1 - 1 = 1) and equals P + (\elem{u} + \elem{w}), so \elem{u} + \elem{w} \in U. By @thm-subspace-test, U is a subspace, and A = P + U by construction. (a) Let X, Y \in A. Then \overrightarrow{XY} = \overrightarrow{XP} + \overrightarrow{PY} \in U by Chasles, since U is closed under negation and addition; so \{\overrightarrow{XY} : X, Y \in A\} \subseteq U. Conversely each \elem{u} \in U is \overrightarrow{PX} for some X \in A, and P \in A. Hence the two sets are equal, and the right-hand side mentions only A. (b) Let Q \in A. For X \in A we have \overrightarrow{QX} \in \vec{A} by (a), so A \subseteq Q + \vec{A}; and for \elem{u} \in \vec{A}, writing \elem{u} = \overrightarrow{XY} with X, Y \in A, the point Q + \elem{u} is the affine combination Q + Y - X of points of A, hence lies in A. So A = Q + \vec{A}. Finally the restricted difference map takes values in \vec{A} by (a), Chasles is inherited, and for fixed P \in A the map X \mapsto \overrightarrow{PX} is a bijection A 	o \vec A, being the restriction of the bijection of (AS2) to A = P + \vec A. So (AS1) and (AS2) hold and A is an affine space with direction space \vec A. Over 
R, with \cA = V, a flat is exactly Chapter 18’s affine subspace of V (@def-affine-hull (b)), and the two dimensions agree: Chapter 18 also reads the subspace off the coset as the set of differences. Chapter 5’s affine hyperplane \cvec{p} + H (the paragraph before @prp-affine-subspace-intersection) is the case \dim A = n - 1 in 
A^n(F). A one-point set \{P\} = P + \{\elem{0}\} is a flat, and \cA = P + V is a flat: the two degenerate cases. A nonexample, by minimal change. A line is a flat; the union of two lines is not. Let X = \{ (x, y) \in 
A^2 : xy = 0 \}, the union of the two coordinate axes. It is nonempty, and it contains every affine combination of points taken from one axis, each axis being a flat. But @def-flat asks for all of them: the points P = (1, 0) and Q = (0, 1) lie in X, the weights of 	frac12P + 	frac12Q add up to 1, and 	frac12P + 	frac12Q =  igl(	frac12, 	frac12 igr) has xy = 	frac14 
e 0. So the closure clause fails for one pair of points, and X is not a coset of a subspace, although it is a union of two of them. [Intersections of Flats] Let (A_i)_{i \in I} be a nonempty family of flats of \cA and put A =  igcap_{i \in I}A_i. If A 
e \emptyset, then A is a flat and \vec{A} =  igcap_{i \in I}\vec{A_i}. Suppose A 
e \emptyset and fix P \in A. If P_1, \dots, P_k \in A and \sum_j t_j = 1, then the point \sum_j t_jP_j lies in each A_i, because each A_i is a flat containing all the P_j; so it lies in A. Hence A is a flat. By @prp-flat-is-coset (b), A_i = P + \vec{A_i} for each i and A = P + \vec{A}, so \vec{A} = \{ \overrightarrow{PX} : X \in A \} =  igcap_{i \in I} \{ \overrightarrow{PX} : X \in A_i \} =  igcap_{i \in I}\vec{A_i} , where the middle equality holds because X \mapsto \overrightarrow{PX} is injective (AS2). Since \cA itself is a flat containing every subset, the following is well defined. [Join of Flats] Let A, B be flats of \cA. Their join A \vee B is the intersection of all flats of \cA containing A \cup B. The intersection contains A, so it is nonempty, and it is a flat by @prp-flat-intersection: A \vee B is the smallest flat containing both. A single point P is a flat, and we write P \vee Q, A \vee P for joins in which a one-point flat \{P\} appears. This is the affine analogue of U + W, and Chapter 18’s affine hull is the same construction over 
R (@prp-affine-hull-coset). Parallelism is what an affine space has and a vector space does not notice. [Parallel Flats] Two flats A, B of \cA are parallel, written A \parallel B, if \vec{A} = \vec{B}. [Parallelism] Parallelism is an equivalence relation on the set of flats of \cA. Two parallel flats are either equal or disjoint, and each equivalence class consists of the flats P + U, P \in \cA, for one fixed subspace U. Equality of direction spaces is an equivalence relation, so \parallel is one. Let A \parallel B with common direction U, and suppose X \in A \cap B. Then A = X + U = B by @prp-flat-is-coset (b). So A and B are equal or disjoint. Finally, the flats with direction space U are exactly the sets P + U with P \in \cA, again by @prp-flat-is-coset. Parallel flats have the same dimension. Some authors also call a line parallel to a plane containing its direction; we do not, and we say “\vec{A} \subseteq \vec{B}” when we mean that. When two flats meet, and how big their join is Here is the central computation of the section. Two subspaces of a vector space always meet, in \elem{0} at least. Two flats need not, and the dimension formula splits accordingly. [Intersection and Join of Two Flats] Let A, B be flats of \cA, and choose P \in A and Q \in B. Parts (a) and (b) need no hypothesis on \dim\cA. 1. A \vee B = P +  igl( \vec{A} + \vec{B} + \Span(\overrightarrow{PQ})  igr). 2. A \cap B 
e \emptyset if and only if \overrightarrow{PQ} \in \vec{A} + \vec{B}; and then A \cap B is a flat whose direction space is \vec{A} \cap \vec{B}. 3. Let \dim\cA = n be finite. If A \cap B 
e \emptyset, then \dim(A \vee B) = \dim A + \dim B - \dim(A \cap B) . If A \cap B = \emptyset, then \dim(A \vee B) = \dim A + \dim B - \dim(\vec{A} \cap \vec{B}) + 1 . 4. Let \dim\cA = n be finite. If A \cap B = \emptyset, there is a hyperplane H of V with A \subseteq P + H and B \subseteq Q + H, and the two flats P + H, Q + H are parallel, distinct, and disjoint. Everything is read off from one subspace, W = \vec{A} + \vec{B} + \Span(\overrightarrow{PQ}). The three summands are forced: the join must contain the directions of A and of B, and it must contain a way of getting from A to B. Whether the third summand is already inside the first two is exactly whether A and B meet — and that one extra dimension, present precisely when they miss each other, is the whole difference between (c)’s two cases. Put W = \vec{A} + \vec{B} + \Span(\overrightarrow{PQ}), a subspace of V, and C = P + W, a flat by @prp-flat-is-coset. (a) First, A \cup B \subseteq C. Indeed A = P + \vec{A} \subseteq P + W. And each point of B is Q + \elem{b} with \elem{b} \in \vec{B}, which equals P + (\overrightarrow{PQ} + \elem{b}) by @lem-chasles-consequences (b), and \overrightarrow{PQ} + \elem{b} \in W. So C is one of the flats being intersected in @def-affine-join, whence A \vee B \subseteq C. Conversely, A \vee B is a flat containing P, so A \vee B = P + U by @prp-flat-is-coset (b), where U is the direction space of A \vee B. Since A \subseteq A \vee B and P \in A, part (a) of that proposition gives \vec{A} \subseteq U. Since Q \in A \vee B, also \overrightarrow{PQ} \in U. And for \elem{b} \in \vec{B} the point Q + \elem{b} lies in B \subseteq A \vee B, so \overrightarrow{PQ} + \elem{b} = \overrightarrow{P\,(Q + \elem{b})} \in U, and therefore \elem{b} \in U. Hence W \subseteq U, that is, C \subseteq A \vee B. The two inclusions give (a). (b) (\Leftarrow) Suppose \overrightarrow{PQ} = \elem{a} + \elem{b} with \elem{a} \in \vec{A}, \elem{b} \in \vec{B}. Put X = P + \elem{a}, a point of A. Then \overrightarrow{QX} = \overrightarrow{QP} + \overrightarrow{PX} = -(\elem{a} + \elem{b}) + \elem{a} = -\elem{b} \in \vec{B} , so X \in Q + \vec{B} = B. Hence X \in A \cap B. (\Rightarrow) If X \in A \cap B, then \overrightarrow{PX} \in \vec{A} and \overrightarrow{XQ} \in \vec{B} by @prp-flat-is-coset (a), so \overrightarrow{PQ} = \overrightarrow{PX} + \overrightarrow{XQ} \in \vec{A} + \vec{B}. The last clause is @prp-flat-intersection applied to the two flats A and B. (c) Case 1: A \cap B 
e \emptyset. By (b), \overrightarrow{PQ} \in \vec{A} + \vec{B}, so W = \vec{A} + \vec{B}. By (a) and @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim,  egin{aligned} \dim(A \vee B) &= \dim(\vec{A} + \vec{B}) \ &= \dim\vec{A} + \dim\vec{B} - \dim(\vec{A} \cap \vec{B}) , \end{aligned} and \dim(\vec A \cap \vec B) = \dim(A \cap B) by (b), which is the first formula. Case 2: A \cap B = \emptyset. By (b), \overrightarrow{PQ} 
otin \vec{A} + \vec{B}; in particular \overrightarrow{PQ} 
e \elem{0}. Then \Span(\overrightarrow{PQ}) \cap (\vec{A} + \vec{B}) = \{\elem{0}\} , since a nonzero \lambda\overrightarrow{PQ} lying in \vec{A} + \vec{B} would give \overrightarrow{PQ} = \lambda^{-1}(\lambda\overrightarrow{PQ}) \in \vec{A} + \vec{B}, \lambda being nonzero and hence invertible. So @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim applied to the two subspaces \vec A + \vec B and \Span(\overrightarrow{PQ}) gives \dim W = \dim(\vec{A} + \vec{B}) + 1, and one more application, as in Case 1, gives the second formula. (d) Put U = \vec{A} + \vec{B} and r = \dim U. By (b), \overrightarrow{PQ} 
otin U, so appending \overrightarrow{PQ} to a basis (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_r) of U leaves an independent list (@lem-append-independent). Extend it to a basis (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_r,\ \overrightarrow{PQ},\ \elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_{n - r - 1}) of V by @thm-basis-extension, and let H = \Span(\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_r, \elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_{n-r-1}). Then \dim H = n - 1, so \dim(V/H) = 1 by @thm-dimension-quotient and H is a hyperplane (@def-hyperplane). Now \vec{A} \subseteq U \subseteq H gives A = P + \vec{A} \subseteq P + H, and likewise B \subseteq Q + H. The flats P + H and Q + H are parallel by @def-parallel-flats. They are distinct: if they were equal, then Q \in P + H would give \overrightarrow{PQ} \in H, contradicting the independence of the displayed basis. Being parallel and distinct, they are disjoint by @prp-parallel-equivalence. This proves the theorem. The two formulas in (c) are best read side by side. When the flats meet, the count is the subspace count of @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim, with A \cap B in the role of \vec A \cap \vec B. When they miss, the correction term is taken among the directions, where the flats always do meet, and a +1 is paid for the displacement that carries one flat to the other. Part (b) is what the two pictures below show. On the left the displacement \overrightarrow{PQ} splits as a step inside \vec{A} followed by a step inside \vec{B}, and the flats meet; on the right it does not split, so it contributes a direction of its own to the join. [Two lines in space, twice] In 
A^3 let  egin{aligned} A &= (1, 0, 0) + \Span igl((1, 1, 0) igr) , \ B &= (0, 0, 1) + \Span igl((1, -1, 0) igr) , \ B' &= (0, 0, 1) + \Span igl((1, 1, 0) igr) . \end{aligned} Decide in each case whether the lines meet, and compute \dim(A \vee B) and \dim(A \vee B'). Here P = (1,0,0), Q = (0,0,1) and \overrightarrow{PQ} = (-1, 0, 1). A and B. The directions (1,1,0) and (1,-1,0) are independent, and \vec{A} + \vec{B} is the plane of vectors with third coordinate 0. Since \overrightarrow{PQ} = (-1,0,1) has third coordinate 1, it is not in \vec A + \vec B, so A \cap B = \emptyset by @thm-flat-intersection-and-join (b): the lines are skew, that is, disjoint and not parallel. (Directly: (1 + s, s, 0) = (t, -t, 1) forces 0 = 1.) Also \vec A \cap \vec B = \{\cvec{0}\}, the two directions being independent. The second formula of (c) gives \dim(A \vee B) = 1 + 1 - 0 + 1 = 3 , so A \vee B = 
A^3: two skew lines span the whole space. A and B'. Now \vec{A} = \vec{B'}, so the lines are parallel, and they are distinct because \overrightarrow{PQ} = (-1,0,1) 
otin \vec{A}; hence they are disjoint (@prp-parallel-equivalence). Here \vec A \cap \vec{B'} = \vec A has dimension 1, so \dim(A \vee B') = 1 + 1 - 1 + 1 = 2 , and A \vee B' is the plane (1,0,0) + \Span igl((1,1,0), (-1,0,1) igr), by part (a). There is no convention for \dim\emptyset that makes one formula do both cases. It is tempting to set \dim\emptyset = -1 and keep writing \dim(A \vee B) = \dim A + \dim B - \dim(A \cap B). For the skew lines of @exm-skew-lines-join that gives 1 + 1 - (-1) = 3, which is right; for the parallel lines A and B' it gives 3 as well, and the correct answer is 2. The two disjoint cases differ in \dim(\vec A \cap \vec B), which the empty intersection cannot record. Use the second formula of @thm-flat-intersection-and-join (c), and always check first whether the flats meet. In 
A^4, let A and B be planes (flats of dimension 2) with \vec{A} \cap \vec{B} = \{\cvec{0}\}. Must they meet? Yes. By @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim, \dim(\vec A + \vec B) = 2 + 2 - 0 = 4 = \dim V, so \vec A + \vec B = V by @thm-dim-impl-eq. Hence \overrightarrow{PQ} \in \vec A + \vec B for any P \in A, Q \in B, and @thm-flat-intersection-and-join (b) gives A \cap B 
e \emptyset. (The dimension formula agrees: the disjoint case would predict 2 + 2 - 0 + 1 = 5 > 4, which is impossible.) Their intersection is then a single point, since its direction space is \vec A \cap \vec B = \{\cvec{0}\}. Affine frames and barycentric coordinates To put coordinates on an n-dimensional vector space we choose n vectors. To put coordinates on an n-dimensional affine space we must also say where the origin is, so we choose n + 1 points — and if we refuse to single out one of them, the coordinates come out symmetric in all n + 1. That symmetry is what makes the centroid computation below one line. Chapter 18 §02 defined a list (\elem{x}_0, \dots, \elem{x}_m) in a real vector space to be affinely independent when the only scalars with \sum_i\lambda_i = 0 and \sum_i \lambda_i\elem{x}_i = \elem{0} are all zero (@def-affine-independence). By @def-affine-combination (b) the expression \sum_i\lambda_iP_i is a well-defined vector for points of an affine space whenever \sum_i\lambda_i = 0, so the same words apply here verbatim. The next lemma is @lem-affine-dependence (a) in that setting; its proof uses nothing about 
R, so we give it again over an arbitrary field. [Affine Independence by Differences] Let P_0, P_1, \dots, P_m \in \cA. The following are equivalent. 1. The only \lambda_0, \dots, \lambda_m \in F with \sum_{i=0}^m\lambda_i = 0 and \sum_{i=0}^m \lambda_iP_i = \elem{0} are \lambda_0 = \dots = \lambda_m = 0. 2. The list (\overrightarrow{P_0P_1}, \dots, \overrightarrow{P_0P_m}) is linearly independent in V. A list satisfying these is called affinely independent. Condition (a) does not mention P_0 specially, so (b) holds with any P_j in place of P_0 as soon as it holds for one. By @def-affine-combination (b) computed with origin P_0, and since \overrightarrow{P_0P_0} = \elem{0}, \sum_{i=0}^{m}\lambda_iP_i = \sum_{i=0}^{m}\lambda_i\overrightarrow{P_0P_i} = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i\overrightarrow{P_0P_i} . Given \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m, the condition \sum_{i=0}^m\lambda_i = 0 holds for exactly one \lambda_0, namely \lambda_0 = -\sum_{i \ge 1}\lambda_i; and (\lambda_0, \dots, \lambda_m) is the zero list exactly when (\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m) is. So the relations forbidden by (a) correspond, one for one, to the nontrivial linear relations among \overrightarrow{P_0P_1}, \dots, \overrightarrow{P_0P_m}, and (a) holds if and only if there are none, which is (b). A^3. C. Going deeper [C1: Affine maps and flats] Let f \colon \cA 	o \cB be affine and let A \subseteq \cA be a flat. 1. Prove that f(A) is a flat of \cB whose direction space is \vec{f}(\vec{A}), and deduce \dim f(A) \le \dim A. 2. Prove that if B \subseteq \cB is a flat with f^{-1}(B) 
e \emptyset, then f^{-1}(B) is a flat with direction space (\vec f)^{-1}(\vec B). 3. Hence prove that an injective affine map sends flats to flats of the same dimension, and lines to lines. Hence f(A) = f(P) + \vec f(\vec A), and \vec{f}(\vec{A}) is a subspace of W, being the image of the linear map \vec f restricted to the subspace \vec{A} (@thm-prop-image applied to that restriction). So f(A) is a flat by @prp-flat-is-coset, with the stated direction space, and \dim f(A) = \dim\vec f(\vec A) \le \dim\vec A = \dim A, because the images of a basis of \vec A span \vec f(\vec A) (@thm-image-spanned-by-basis-images) and a spanning list is at least as long as the dimension (@thm-size-bounds (b)). (b) Let P \in f^{-1}(B), so f(P) \in B. For \elem{u} \in V, f(P + \elem{u}) = f(P) + \vec f(\elem{u}) lies in B = f(P) + \vec B exactly when \vec f(\elem{u}) \in \vec B. So f^{-1}(B) = P + (\vec f)^{-1}(\vec B), and (\vec f)^{-1}(\vec B) is a subspace: it contains \elem{0} and is closed under linear combinations by linearity of \vec f and the subspace test (@thm-subspace-test). By @prp-flat-is-coset, f^{-1}(B) is a flat with that direction space. (c) If f is injective, then \vec f is injective: \vec f(\elem{u}) = \elem{0} gives f(P + \elem{u}) = f(P), hence P + \elem{u} = P and \elem{u} = \elem{0}. An injective linear map carries a basis of \vec A to a linearly independent list (@thm-injective-preserves-independence) that spans \vec f(\vec A), hence to a basis of it; so \dim f(A) = \dim\vec f(\vec A) = \dim\vec A = \dim A by (a). A line has dimension 1, so its image is a flat of dimension 1, a line. [C2: The midpoint quadrilateral] Let F be a field with 2 
e 0, let \cA be an affine space over F, and let P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4 \in \cA be any four points. Put M_{12} = 	frac12P_1 + 	frac12P_2, and define M_{23}, M_{34}, M_{41} likewise. 1. Prove that \overrightarrow{M_{12}M_{23}} = \overrightarrow{M_{41}M_{34}} = 	frac12\overrightarrow{P_1P_3}. 2. Deduce that if M_{12}, M_{23}, M_{34}, M_{41} are distinct, then M_{12} \vee M_{23} and M_{41} \vee M_{34} are parallel lines, and likewise for the other pair of opposite sides: the four midpoints form a parallelogram. 3. What does the statement say when P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4 are not coplanar, for instance in 
A^3? (a) Fix any origin O and write \elem{p}_i = \overrightarrow{OP_i}. By @def-affine-combination, \overrightarrow{O M_{12}} = 	frac12(\elem{p}_1 + \elem{p}_2) and similarly for the others. Hence, by @prp-choice-of-origin, \overrightarrow{M_{12}M_{23}} = 	frac12(\elem{p}_2 + \elem{p}_3) - 	frac12(\elem{p}_1 + \elem{p}_2) = 	frac12(\elem{p}_3 - \elem{p}_1) = 	frac12\overrightarrow{P_1P_3} , and \overrightarrow{M_{41}M_{34}} = 	frac12(\elem{p}_3 + \elem{p}_4) - 	frac12(\elem{p}_4 + \elem{p}_1) = 	frac12(\elem{p}_3 - \elem{p}_1) . The answer does not depend on O, as it must not. (b) If M_{12}

By (a) the two lines M_{12} \vee M_{23} and M_{41} \vee M_{34} have the same direction space \Span igl(	frac12\overrightarrow{P_1P_3} igr), so they are parallel (@def-parallel-flats). Running (a) with the indices shifted by one gives \overrightarrow{M_{23}M_{34}} = \overrightarrow{M_{12}M_{41}} = 	frac12\overrightarrow{P_2P_4}, so the other two sides are parallel too. (c) Nothing in (a) used coplanarity, so the conclusion holds for a skew quadrilateral in

Four noncoplanar points are affinely independent: otherwise (\overrightarrow{P_1P_2}, \overrightarrow{P_1P_3}, \overrightarrow{P_1P_4}) would be dependent (@lem-affine-independence-differences) and span a subspace of dimension at most 2, putting all four points in a flat of dimension at most 2. The two parallel lines M_{12} \vee M_{23} and M_{41} \vee M_{34} are also distinct: were they equal, their common direction space would contain \overrightarrow{M_{12}M_{41}}, which is 	frac12\overrightarrow{P_2P_4} by (b), so 	frac12\overrightarrow{P_2P_4} = \mu \cdot 	frac12\overrightarrow{P_1P_3} for some \mu \in F (@prp-flat-is-coset (a)) — a relation \sum_i\lambda_iP_i = \elem{0} with weights summing to 0 and -	frac12 
e 0 at P_2, again against affine independence. Their join is therefore a plane, of dimension 1 + 1 - 1 + 1 = 2 by @thm-flat-intersection-and-join (c), and it contains all four midpoints. [C3: Medians over the field with three elements] Work in 
A^2(
F_3) with the affinely independent list P_1 = (0,0), P_2 = (1,0), P_3 = (0,1). (Nothing is lost by this choice: by @thm-affine-map-determined-by-frame any other affinely independent triple is carried to this one by an affine bijection, which preserves midpoints, being an affine combination, and carries lines to lines by @exr-affine-subspaces-c1.) 1. Compute the three midpoints M_i and the three medians m_i = P_i \vee M_i. 2. Prove that the three medians are pairwise parallel and pairwise disjoint, so that @prp-medians-meet-at-centroid fails over 
F_3. 3. Explain which step of the proof of @prp-medians-meet-at-centroid breaks, and why the hypothesis 3

F_3 we have 2^{-1} = 2, since 2 \cdot 2 = 4 = 1. So  egin{aligned} M_1 &= 2P_2 + 2P_3 = 2(1,0) + 2(0,1) = (2,2) , \ M_2 &= 2P_1 + 2P_3 = (0,2) , \ M_3 &= 2P_1 + 2P_2 = (2,0) . \end{aligned} Then \overrightarrow{P_1M_1} = (2,2), \overrightarrow{P_2M_2} = (0,2) - (1,0) = (2,2) and \overrightarrow{P_3M_3} = (2,0) - (0,1) = (2,2). So  egin{aligned} m_1 &= (0,0) + \Span igl((2,2) igr), \ m_2 &= (1,0) + \Span igl((2,2) igr), \ m_3 &= (0,1) + \Span igl((2,2) igr) . \end{aligned} (b) All three have the same direction space \Span((2,2)) = \Span((1,1)), so they are parallel (@def-parallel-flats). They are distinct: \overrightarrow{P_1P_2} = (1,0)

Hence the three medians have no common point, and the conclusion of @prp-medians-meet-at-centroid is false here. (c) The proof solved 	frac32 s = 1 for s, which needs 3 to be invertible. Over
