title: 22.3 Convex Polyhedra, Geometrically
content:
Convex Polyhedra, Geometrically Chapter 18 built the theory of convex sets and proved its main theorems: that a compact convex set is the hull of its extreme points, that a bounded polyhedron and a polytope are the same thing, and that a feasible, bounded linear program and its dual have the same optimal value. This section proves none of that again. It reads those theorems as statements about the geometry of a solid with flat sides: what its faces are, how they fit together, and what a linear program looks like when the objective is a family of parallel hyperplanes sliding across it. Everything here is a corollary of Chapter 18 or a short argument on top of it, and every citation points back there. Throughout, the field is 
R and the space is 
R^n with the dot product, as in Chapter 18. A polyhedron is a set P = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\} (@def-polyhedron), with \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R) whose rows we write \cvec{a}_1	p, \dots, \cvec{a}_m	p, so that \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b} is the list of inequalities \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} \le b_i. A vertex of P is an extreme point of it (@def-extreme-point), and \operatorname{ext} P is the set of them. We use Chapters 16 and 18’s topological words — closed, bounded, compact — only inside the results we cite; nothing here develops them further. Faces, cut by a supporting hyperplane A cube has six square sides, twelve edges, and eight corners, and each of them is the part of the cube touched by a plane that has the whole cube on one side. That is the picture to formalize. The tool is Chapter 18’s supporting hyperplane (@thm-supporting-hyperplane): a hyperplane through a point of a convex set with the set in one of its closed half-spaces. A face of a polyhedron is the part of it touched by a hyperplane that does not cut into it. [Face of a Polyhedron] Let P \subseteq 
R^n be a polyhedron. A face of P is a set of the form F = \{\cvec{x} \in P : \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} =  eta\} for some \cvec{c} \in 
R^n and  eta \in 
R such that \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \le  eta for every \cvec{x} \in P. A face other than P itself is called proper. Clause by clause. The pair (\cvec{c},  eta) must be a valid inequality for P: the whole polyhedron lies in the closed half-space \{\cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \le  eta\}. The face is then what the boundary hyperplane \{\cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} =  eta\} actually touches. Note that \cvec{c} is allowed to be \cvec{0}. Two faces come free. Taking \cvec{c} = \cvec{0} and  eta = 0 makes the inequality 0 \le 0, valid everywhere, and F = P: the whole polyhedron is a face of itself. Taking \cvec{c} = \cvec{0} and  eta = 1 makes the inequality 0 \le 1, again valid, and F = \emptyset: the empty set is a face. These two are the degenerate cases, and they are kept because the theorems below are cleaner with them than without. Chapter 18 §08 already has a notion of face for an arbitrary convex set, @def-face: a convex subset F \subseteq C that swallows every segment of C passing through it at an inner point. The two agree here in one direction at once. Every face in the sense of @def-polyhedron-face is a face in the sense of @def-face. That is exactly @prp-exposed-face (a), applied with \cvec{w} = \cvec{c} and \alpha =  eta, since on 
R^n the inner product \inner{\cvec{c}}{\cvec{x}} is \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x}. So everything Chapter 18 proves about faces applies to ours; in particular @lem-extreme-points-of-face gives \operatorname{ext} F = F \cap \operatorname{ext} P. The converse — that every face of a polyhedron in Chapter 18’s sense is cut out by a supporting hyperplane — is also true, and @exr-polyhedra-and-linear-programming-c2 proves it. It uses flatness: the same exercise ends with a round convex set having a one-point face in the sense of @def-face that no supporting hyperplane isolates, so the converse fails for general convex sets. Examples, in 
R^2, with P the triangle \{x_1 \ge 0,\ x_2 \ge 0,\ x_1 + x_2 \le 3\} of Chapter 18 §09. 1. \cvec{c} = (1,1),  eta = 3. The inequality is valid by the third row, and the face is the slanted edge from (3,0) to (0,3). 2. \cvec{c} = (1,0),  eta = 3. Valid, since x_1 \le x_1 + x_2 \le 3 on P. The face is the single point (3, 0): the hyperplane x_1 = 3 touches the triangle at one corner. 3. \cvec{c} = (-1, 0),  eta = 0. Valid by the first row, and the face is the vertical edge \{0\} 	imes [0,3]. 4. \cvec{c} = (1, 1),  eta = 4. Valid, but never attained: the face is \emptyset. A nonexample by minimal change. In example 1 replace  eta = 3 by  eta = 2. The set \{\cvec{x} \in P : x_1 + x_2 = 2\} is still a segment inside P, still convex, and still a slice by a hyperplane. What fails is the one clause the definition insists on: x_1 + x_2 \le 2 is not valid for P, since (3,0) \in P violates it. The hyperplane cuts through the triangle instead of resting against it, and the slice is not a face. It also fails @def-face: the segment from (0,0) to (3,0) passes through (2,0) at an inner point but is not contained in the slice. The reason faces are useful is that there are only finitely many of them, and each is again a polyhedron described by the same rows, some of them turned into equations. [Faces Are Polyhedra, and There Are Finitely Many] Let P = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\} with m rows. For J \subseteq \{1, \dots, m\} put P_J = \{\cvec{x} \in P : \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} = b_i 	ext{ for every } i \in J\} . Then: 1. every P_J is a face of P, and it is a polyhedron; 2. every nonempty face of P equals P_J for some J; 3. consequently P has at most 2^m nonempty faces, and every face of P is a polyhedron. For (a), add up the rows indexed by J: the sum \sum_{i \in J}\cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} is at most \sum_{i \in J}b_i on P, and a sum of numbers each at most its bound hits the total bound only if every one of them does. So one valid inequality encodes all of J at once. For (b), let F be a nonempty face and let J collect the rows that are tight at every point of F. Certainly F \subseteq P_J. For the other inclusion we need a point \cvec{x}^{*} of F at which every row outside J is slack; averaging finitely many points of F, one per slack row, produces it. Then, given \cvec{y} \in P_J with \cvec{c}	p\cvec{y} <  eta, step from \cvec{x}^{*} away from \cvec{y}. The rows in J are equations satisfied by both points, so they survive the step exactly; the rows outside J have room at \cvec{x}^{*}, so they survive a short step. But the step raises \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} above  eta, which no point of P may do. (a) Put \cvec{c} = \sum_{i \in J}\cvec{a}_i and  eta = \sum_{i \in J}b_i, with the empty sums \cvec{0} and 0. For \cvec{x} \in P, \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} = \sum_{i \in J}\cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} \le \sum_{i \in J}b_i =  eta , so the inequality is valid. If \cvec{x} \in P and \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} =  eta, then \sum_{i \in J}(b_i - \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}) = 0 is a sum of nonnegative numbers, so each is zero and \cvec{x} \in P_J; conversely every \cvec{x} \in P_J has \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} =  eta. Hence P_J = \{\cvec{x} \in P : \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} =  eta\} is a face. It is a polyhedron because each equation \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} = b_i is the pair of inequalities \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} \le b_i and -\cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} \le -b_i, so P_J is cut out by m + \lvert Jvert inequalities. (b) Let F = \{\cvec{x} \in P : \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} =  eta\} be nonempty, with \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \le  eta on P. Put J = \{i : \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} = b_i 	ext{ for every } \cvec{x} \in F\} . Then F \subseteq P_J by the definition of J, and it remains to prove P_J \subseteq F. First note that F is convex: it is the intersection of the convex set P (@prp-polyhedron-closed-convex) with the solution set of a linear equation, which is convex as the preimage of a point under \cvec{x} \mapsto \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} (@prp-convexity-operations (b)); an intersection of convex sets is convex by @prp-convexity-operations (a). Step 1: a point of F with every row outside J slack. For each i 
otin J choose, by the definition of J, a point \cvec{x}_i \in F with \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}_i < b_i. If J = \{1, \dots, m\} let \cvec{x}^{*} be any point of F. Otherwise let k \ge 1 be the number of indices outside J and let \cvec{x}^{*} =  rac1k\sum_{i 
otin J}\cvec{x}_i, which lies in F by convexity. For each i 
otin J, every term of \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}^{*} =  rac1k\sum_{j 
otin J}\cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}_j is at most b_i and the term j = i is strictly less, so \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}^{*} < b_i. Step 2: the step away from \cvec{y}. Let \cvec{y} \in P_J and suppose, for a contradiction, that \cvec{c}	p\cvec{y} <  eta. For t > 0 put \cvec{z}_t = \cvec{x}^{*} + t(\cvec{x}^{*} - \cvec{y}). For i \in J we have \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}^{*} = b_i, because \cvec{x}^{*} \in F \subseteq P_J, and \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{y} = b_i, because \cvec{y} \in P_J; hence \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{z}_t = b_i + t(b_i - b_i) = b_i \le b_i . For i 
otin J put \delta = \min_{i 
otin J}(b_i - \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}^{*}) > 0 and M = \max_{i 
otin J}\lvert\cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}^{*} - \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{y}vert; both are minima and maxima of finitely many numbers. Choose t > 0 with tM < \delta, which is possible (any t will do if M = 0). Then for i 
otin J, \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{z}_t = \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}^{*} + t igl(\cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}^{*} - \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{y} igr) \le \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}^{*} + tM < \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}^{*} + \delta \le b_i . So \cvec{z}_t \in P. But \cvec{c}	p\cvec{z}_t = \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x}^{*} + t(\cvec{c}	p\cvec{x}^{*} - \cvec{c}	p\cvec{y}) =  eta + t( eta - \cvec{c}	p\cvec{y}) >  eta , since t > 0 and  eta - \cvec{c}	p\cvec{y} > 0. This contradicts the validity of \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \le  eta on P. Hence \cvec{c}	p\cvec{y} =  eta and \cvec{y} \in F, so P_J \subseteq F and F = P_J. (c) There are 2^m subsets J, so by (b) at most that many nonempty faces. Each of them is a polyhedron by (a), and the empty face is the polyhedron \{\cvec{x} : 0 \le -1\}. This proves the proposition. The map J \mapsto P_J is surjective onto the nonempty faces but is very far from injective: adding to J a row that is already tight everywhere on P_J changes nothing, and adding two incompatible rows gives \emptyset. A row of the system need not be a side of the solid. In P = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^2 : x_1 \le 1,\ x_2 \le 1,\ x_1 + x_2 \le 3\} the third row is implied by the first two, since x_1 + x_2 \le 2 on P. It defines no face except the empty one: P_{\{3\}} = \{\cvec{x} \in P : x_1 + x_2 = 3\} = \emptyset. So a polyhedron with m rows can have far fewer than m sides, and counting rows is not counting geometry. Conversely, @def-polyhedron-face never mentions the rows at all, which is why @prp-face-is-polyhedron has to prove that the faces can be read off them. Vertices, edges, facets A nonempty face F is a nonempty convex set, so it has a dimension: \dim F = \dim \operatorname{aff} F, as in Chapter 18 §01, and \operatorname{aff} F is the flat \cvec{p} + U of @prp-affine-hull-coset — a flat in the sense of @def-flat. The graded vocabulary follows. [Edge, Facet] Let P \subseteq 
R^n be a nonempty polyhedron. A face of P of dimension 1 is an edge; a face of dimension \dim P - 1 is a facet. A face of dimension 0 is a single point, and the next proposition shows that these are exactly the vertices. [Three Descriptions of a Corner] Let P = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\} and \cvec{v} \in P. The following are equivalent. 1. \cvec{v} is a vertex of P, that is, an extreme point. 2. \{\cvec{v}\} is a face of P. 3. Among the rows active at \cvec{v} there are n linearly independent ones, that is, \cvec{v} is a basic feasible point. (a) and (c) are @thm-vertices-basic-feasible, already proved. A one-point face is an extreme point by @prp-exposed-face (b). For the remaining implication, take J to be the active set: if the active rows have rank n, the system \A_J\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}_J has \cvec{v} as its only solution, so P_J = \{\cvec{v}\}, and @prp-face-is-polyhedron makes that a face. (a) \Leftrightarrow (c) is @thm-vertices-basic-feasible. (b) \Rightarrow (a). Write \{\cvec{v}\} = \{\cvec{x} \in P : \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} =  eta\} with \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \le  eta on P. By @prp-exposed-face (b), applied with \cvec{w} = \cvec{c} and \alpha =  eta, \cvec{v} \in \operatorname{ext} P. (c) \Rightarrow (b). Let I = I(\cvec{v}) be the active set and \A_I the matrix of active rows, of rank n by hypothesis. Its null space is \{\cvec{0}\} by @thm-rank-nullity-matrix, so \A_I\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}_I has at most one solution; since \cvec{v} is one, it is the only one. Hence P_I = \{\cvec{x} \in P : \A_I\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}_I\} = \{\cvec{v}\} , and P_I is a face by @prp-face-is-polyhedron (a). This proves the equivalence. So a corner of a polyhedron can be recognized three ways: by convexity (it is not an average), by geometry (a hyperplane touches P there and nowhere else), or by algebra (enough constraints are tight). The three are used interchangeably from here on. Bounded polyhedra are the ones with enough corners to rebuild them. This is the bounded half of the Minkowski–Weyl theorem, and it is the sentence this whole section is arranged around. [A Bounded Polyhedron Is the Hull of Its Vertices] Let P \subseteq 
R^n be a bounded polyhedron. Then \operatorname{ext} P is finite and P = \conv(\operatorname{ext} P) . Conversely, every polytope is a bounded polyhedron. If P = \emptyset, both sides are \emptyset and \operatorname{ext}P = \emptyset. Otherwise P is closed and convex by @prp-polyhedron-closed-convex, and bounded by hypothesis, so it is compact by @cor-closed-bounded-compact. By @thm-minkowski-extreme, P = \conv(\operatorname{ext} P), and \operatorname{ext} P is finite by @cor-finitely-many-vertices. The converse is @thm-minkowski-weyl (a). The same theorem applied to a face is what makes an edge a segment between two corners — the statement that lets one speak of walking along the edges of a solid. [An Edge Joins Two Vertices] Let P \subseteq 
R^n be a bounded polyhedron and F an edge of P. Then F = [\cvec{v}, \cvec{w}] for two distinct vertices \cvec{v}, \cvec{w} of P. An edge is itself a bounded polyhedron, so it is the hull of its own vertices; those are vertices of P because a face passes extremeness upwards. Being 1-dimensional, it sits on a line, and the hull of finitely many points of a line is the segment between the outermost two. By @prp-face-is-polyhedron, F is a polyhedron, and it is bounded because F \subseteq P. By @thm-polytope-is-hull-of-vertices, F = \conv(\operatorname{ext} F) with \operatorname{ext} F finite, and F 
e \emptyset since it has a dimension. By the remark after @def-polyhedron-face, F is a face of P in the sense of @def-face, so @lem-extreme-points-of-face gives \operatorname{ext} F = F \cap \operatorname{ext} P: every vertex of F is a vertex of P. A polyhedron can have corners and still have no optimum. “Vertex” and “corner of the picture” can both be empty words for an unbounded polyhedron. The slab above is a perfectly ordinary convex solid, closed, with a genuine boundary, and it has no vertices, no edges, and no bounded face. Nothing in this section rebuilds it from finitely many points, and nothing should: by @thm-minkowski-weyl (a) a polyhedron is a polytope exactly when it is bounded. Row (4) is inactive at \cvec{x}^{\star}, so its weight is y_2 = 0; and x^{\star}_2 = 4 > 0, so the slack on the second sign constraint is s_2 = 0. So \A has rows (1,2) and (2,1), with \cvec{b} = (8, 10) and \cvec{c} = (1,3). The dual solution read off is \cvec{y} = (	frac32, 0), which satisfies \cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0} and \A	p\cvec{y} = 	frac32(1,2) =  igl(	frac32, 3 igr) \ge (1,3) = \cvec{c} , so it is dual feasible, with value \cvec{b}	p\cvec{y} = 8\cdot	frac32 = 12. Since the primal value at (0,4) is also 12, @cor-duality-certificate (a) confirms that both are optimal. [B3: Faces of the cross-polytope] Let B_1 = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^n : \cvec{s}	p\cvec{x} \le 1 	ext{ for every sign vector } \cvec{s} \in \{-1,1\}^n\}, the cross-polytope of @exm-cube-cross-polytope. Determine the face P_J for J a single sign vector \cvec{s}, and its dimension. How many facets does B_1 have? For a single sign vector \cvec{s}, P_{\{\cvec{s}\}} = \{\cvec{x} \in B_1 : \cvec{s}	p\cvec{x} = 1\}. Now \cvec{s}	p\cvec{x} = \sum_i s_ix_i \le \sum_i\lvert x_ivert = 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1, term by term, so equality holds exactly when s_ix_i = \lvert x_ivert for every i; and 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 = \max_{\cvec{s}}\cvec{s}	p\cvec{x} \le 1 on B_1, as @exm-cube-cross-polytope records. So \cvec{s}	p\cvec{x} = 1 forces 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 = 1 and s_ix_i = \lvert x_ivert \ge 0 for every i; conversely those conditions give \cvec{s}	p\cvec{x} = 
orm{\cvec{x}}_1 = 1. Writing \cvec{x} = \sum_i x_i\cvec{e}_i with x_i = s_i\lvert x_ivert, we get P_{\{\cvec{s}\}} = \Bigl\{\sum_i t_i(s_i\cvec{e}_i) : t_i \ge 0,\ \sum_i t_i = 1\Bigr\} = \conv\{s_1\cvec{e}_1, \dots, s_n\cvec{e}_n\} , using @thm-convex-hull-combinations. This is a copy of \Delta_n, of dimension n - 1 by the computation after @prp-affine-hull-coset. Since \dim B_1 = n — it contains \cvec{0} and every \pm\cvec{e}_i, and the differences \cvec{e}_i - \cvec{0} span 
R^n, so @prp-affine-hull-coset gives \operatorname{aff}B_1 = 
R^n — each P_{\{\cvec{s}\}} is a facet. Distinct \cvec{s} give distinct facets, since \cvec{s} is recovered from P_{\{\cvec{s}\}} by the signs of the vertices s_i\cvec{e}_i. There are no others. Every nonempty face is P_J for a set J of sign vectors, by @prp-face-is-polyhedron (b), and if \cvec{s} 
e \cvec{s}' both lie in J then P_J \subseteq P_{\{\cvec{s}\}} \cap P_{\{\cvec{s}'\}}. A point of that intersection has x_i = s_i\lvert x_ivert = s'_i\lvert x_ivert, so x_i = 0 whenever s_i 
e s'_i; hence the intersection is \conv\{s_i\cvec{e}_i : s_i = s'_i\}, of dimension at most n - 2, since at least one index is missing. So B_1 has exactly 2^n facets: in 
R^n it has 2n vertices and 2^n facets, exactly the reverse of the cube. C. Going deeper [C1: A face of a face] Let P be a polyhedron and F a face of P. 1. Prove that every face of F is a face of P. 2. Deduce that the faces of P contained in a fixed face F are exactly the faces of F. Hint: for (a), use @prp-face-is-polyhedron to write both F and the face of F in the form P_J. (a) We may assume the face G of F is nonempty, since \emptyset is a face of P. Fix a system \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b} with P = \{\cvec{x} : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\} and rows \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} \le b_i, i = 1, \dots, m. By @prp-face-is-polyhedron (b), F = P_J for some J. By part (a) of the same proposition, F is cut out by the m original rows together with the rows -\cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} \le -b_i for i \in J. By (b) applied to F with this system, G = F_K for some set K of those rows; since the rows -\cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} \le -b_i with i \in J are tight everywhere on F, including them in K changes nothing, so we may take K \subseteq \{1, \dots, m\}. Then G = \{\cvec{x} \in F : \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} = b_i 	ext{ for } i \in K\} = \{\cvec{x} \in P : \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} = b_i 	ext{ for } i \in J \cup K\} = P_{J \cup K} , which is a face of P by @prp-face-is-polyhedron (a). (b) By (a), every face of F is a face of P, and it is contained in F. Conversely let G be a face of P with G \subseteq F, say G = \{\cvec{x} \in P : \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} =  eta\} with \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \le  eta on P. Then \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \le  eta holds in particular on F \subseteq P, and \{\cvec{x} \in F : \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} =  eta\} = \{\cvec{x} \in P : \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} =  eta\} \cap F = G \cap F = G , so G is a face of F. [C2: The two notions of face agree for a polyhedron] Let P = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\} and let F \subseteq P be a nonempty face in the sense of @def-face: F is convex, and whenever t\cvec{y} + (1-t)\cvec{z} \in F with \cvec{y}, \cvec{z} \in P and 0 < t < 1, both \cvec{y} and \cvec{z} lie in F. 1. Let J = \{i : \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} = b_i 	ext{ for every } \cvec{x} \in F\}. Prove that F = P_J. 2. Deduce that F is a face in the sense of @def-polyhedron-face, so the two notions agree for polyhedra. Hint: for (a), Step 1 of the proof of @prp-face-is-polyhedron produces a point of F at which every row outside J is slack; use it as the midpoint of a short segment. (a) F \subseteq P_J by the definition of J. For the reverse inclusion, note first that F is convex, so Step 1 of the proof of @prp-face-is-polyhedron applies verbatim and yields \cvec{x}^{*} \in F with \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x}^{*} < b_i for every i 
otin J. Let \cvec{y} \in P_J. If \cvec{y} = \cvec{x}^{*} we are done, so assume \cvec{y} 
e \cvec{x}^{*} and put \cvec{z}_t = \cvec{x}^{*} + t(\cvec{x}^{*} - \cvec{y}) for t > 0. Exactly as in Step 2 of that proof, \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{z}_t = b_i for i \in J and, for small enough t > 0, \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{z}_t < b_i for i 
otin J; so \cvec{z}_t \in P. Fix such a t. Then \cvec{x}^{*} =  rac{t}{1+t}\,\cvec{y} +  rac{1}{1+t}\,\cvec{z}_t , a combination with positive coefficients adding to 1: the right side is  rac{t\cvec{y} + \cvec{x}^{*} + t\cvec{x}^{*} - t\cvec{y}}{1+t} = \cvec{x}^{*}. Both \cvec{y} and \cvec{z}_t lie in P and \cvec{x}^{*} \in F, so the face property of @def-face forces \cvec{y} \in F. Hence P_J \subseteq F and F = P_J. (b) By @prp-face-is-polyhedron (a), P_J is a face in the sense of @def-polyhedron-face. Together with the remark after @def-polyhedron-face, which gives the other direction for every face, the two notions coincide on polyhedra. They do not coincide for general convex sets, and one round set shows it. Let D = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^2 : 
orm{\cvec{x}} \le 1\}, let \cvec{q} = (2,0), let C = \conv(D \cup \{\cvec{q}\}), and put \cvec{p} =  igl(	frac12, 	frac{\sqrt3}{2} igr), so that 
orm{\cvec{p}} = 1 and \inner{\cvec{p}}{\cvec{q}} = 1. Since D is convex, @thm-convex-hull-combinations writes every point of C as (1-s)\cvec{d} + s\cvec{q} with \cvec{d} \in D and s \in [0,1], whence \inner{\cvec{p}}{(1-s)\cvec{d} + s\cvec{q}} = (1-s)\inner{\cvec{p}}{\cvec{d}} + s \le (1-s)
orm{\cvec{d}} + s \le 1 , the first inequality by @thm-cauchy-schwarz. Equality with s < 1 forces \inner{\cvec{p}}{\cvec{d}} = 
orm{\cvec{d}} = 1, hence (\cvec{p}, \cvec{d}) dependent and \cvec{d} = \cvec{p}; so \{\cvec{x} \in C : \inner{\cvec{p}}{\cvec{x}} = 1\} = [\cvec{p}, \cvec{q}]. Now \{\cvec{p}\} is a face of C in the sense of @def-face: if \cvec{p} = t\cvec{y} + (1-t)\cvec{z} with \cvec{y}, \cvec{z} \in C and 0 < t < 1, then 1 = t\inner{\cvec{p}}{\cvec{y}} + (1-t)\inner{\cvec{p}}{\cvec{z}}, and both inner products are at most 1, so both equal 1 and \cvec{y} = \cvec{p} + a(\cvec{q} - \cvec{p}), \cvec{z} = \cvec{p} + b(\cvec{q} - \cvec{p}) with a, b \in [0,1]; then ta + (1-t)b = 0 forces a = b = 0. But no supporting hyperplane isolates \cvec{p}. If \inner{\cvec{c}}{\cvec{x}} \le  eta on C with \inner{\cvec{c}}{\cvec{p}} =  eta, then \cvec{c} 
e \cvec{0}, since \cvec{c} = \cvec{0} gives the face C or \emptyset; testing the inequality at the point \cvec{c}/
orm{\cvec{c}} of D gives 
orm{\cvec{c}} \le  eta = \inner{\cvec{c}}{\cvec{p}} \le 
orm{\cvec{c}}, so equality holds in @thm-cauchy-schwarz and \cvec{c} = 
orm{\cvec{c}}\cvec{p},  eta = 
orm{\cvec{c}}. Then \inner{\cvec{c}}{\cvec{q}} = 
orm{\cvec{c}}\inner{\cvec{p}}{\cvec{q}} =  eta, so \cvec{q} lies in the face too, and the face is not \{\cvec{p}\}. [C3: The optimal face has no better vertex outside it] Let P \subseteq 
R^n be a nonempty bounded polyhedron, \cvec{c} \in 
R^n, and let F^{\star} be the optimal face of @prp-optimal-set-is-a-face. 1. Prove that F^{\star} = \conv(F^{\star} \cap \operatorname{ext} P). 2. Deduce that the optimal value of the program equals \max\{\cvec{c}	p\cvec{v} : \cvec{v} \in \operatorname{ext}P\}, a maximum over a finite set, and that this finite maximum is attained exactly at the vertices lying in F^{\star}. (a) F^{\star} is a nonempty bounded polyhedron by @prp-face-is-polyhedron, so @thm-polytope-is-hull-of-vertices gives F^{\star} = \conv(\operatorname{ext}F^{\star}). By the remark after @def-polyhedron-face, F^{\star} is a face of P in the sense of @def-face, so @lem-extreme-points-of-face gives \operatorname{ext}F^{\star} = F^{\star} \cap \operatorname{ext}P. Substituting proves (a). (b) By @cor-finitely-many-vertices, \operatorname{ext}P is finite, and it is nonempty by @thm-polytope-is-hull-of-vertices since P 
e \emptyset. Write \gamma^{\star} for the optimal value. Every vertex lies in P, so \cvec{c}	p\cvec{v} \le \gamma^{\star} for \cvec{v} \in \operatorname{ext}P; and by (a) F^{\star} contains a vertex, at which \cvec{c}	p\cvec{v} = \gamma^{\star}. So the finite maximum equals \gamma^{\star}. A vertex \cvec{v} attains it exactly when \cvec{c}	p\cvec{v} = \gamma^{\star}, which is exactly the condition \cvec{v} \in F^{\star} defining the optimal face.

title: 22.4 Euclidean Motions
content:
Euclidean Motions Affine geometry knows about lines, parallels, and ratios along a line, but not about length. Put the standard inner product back on 
R^n and a new question appears: which maps of space leave every distance unchanged? One might expect a large and unruly collection, since the condition says nothing about linearity, nothing about continuity, and nothing about where the origin goes. The first theorem of this section says otherwise. A map that preserves distances is forced to be affine, with an orthogonal linear part — and it is forced without assuming that it is surjective, which most treatments quietly do. The rest of the section turns that structure theorem into a complete list of the motions of the plane and of space. Throughout, the field is 
R, the space is 
R^n with the standard inner product, and the distance between \cvec{x} and \cvec{y} is 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}}. Matrices are bold, points of 
R^n are bold vectors as usual, and we write \R_{	heta} and the reflections of @thm-orthogonal-2x2 for the elements of \Orth(2). Distance alone Chapter 11 studied the linear maps preserving distance: the isometries, which in 
R^n are the orthogonal matrices (@thm-isometry-characterizations). But a translation \cvec{x} \mapsto \cvec{x} + \cvec{b} with \cvec{b} 
e \cvec{0} also preserves every distance and is not linear, since it moves the origin. So the linear theory misses exactly what affine geometry was invented to supply, and the right notion drops linearity from the hypotheses altogether. A Euclidean motion is a map of space that changes no distance. [Euclidean Motion] A Euclidean motion of 
R^n, or simply a motion, is a map f \colon 
R^n 	o 
R^n such that 
orm{f(\cvec{x}) - f(\cvec{y})} = 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}} \qquad 	ext{for all } \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n . No linearity, continuity, or surjectivity is assumed. In words: the only requirement is that the distance between any two points equals the distance between their images. The quantifier is for all pairs, not for pairs at some special distance, and that turns out to be exactly the right amount of information. Examples. 1. Translations. t_{\cvec{b}}(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x} + \cvec{b} satisfies t_{\cvec{b}}(\cvec{x}) - t_{\cvec{b}}(\cvec{y}) = \cvec{x} - \cvec{y}, so it is a motion for every \cvec{b}. It is linear only when \cvec{b} = \cvec{0}. 2. Orthogonal maps. For \Q \in \Orth(n), the map \cvec{x} \mapsto \Q\cvec{x} is a motion: 
orm{\Q\cvec{x} - \Q\cvec{y}} = 
orm{\Q(\cvec{x} - \cvec{y})} = 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}}, the last equality by @thm-isometry-characterizations (a) applied to T_{\Q}, which is an isometry by part (f) of that theorem. 3. Compositions. If f and g are motions then so is g \circ f, since 
orm{g(f(\cvec{x})) - g(f(\cvec{y}))} = 
orm{f(\cvec{x}) - f(\cvec{y})} = 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}}. In particular \cvec{x} \mapsto \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b} is a motion for every \Q \in \Orth(n) and \cvec{b} \in 
R^n. 4. The degenerate case n = 0 is the one-point space and its only motion is the identity; for n = 1 the motions are x \mapsto \pm x + b, as the theorem below will confirm. A nonexample by minimal change. Take f(\cvec{x}) = 2\cvec{x}. It is linear, continuous, and bijective, and it multiplies every distance by the same factor 2. The one clause of @def-euclidean-motion it fails is the only one there is: 
orm{f(\cvec{x}) - f(\cvec{y})} = 2
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}} 
e 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}} as soon as \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{y}. A map that rescales all distances equally is a similarity, not a motion, and this book does not pursue them. Why this definition, and why it is enough. Nothing in it mentions the vector space structure of 
R^n; it is a statement about 
R^n as a set with a distance. The content of the next theorem is that the vector space structure is recoverable anyway. That is worth pausing on: distances alone remember which points are midpoints, hence which maps are affine, hence all of the linear algebra. [Every Motion Is Affine] Let f \colon 
R^n 	o 
R^n be a Euclidean motion. Then there are a unique \Q \in \Orth(n) and a unique \cvec{b} \in 
R^n with f(\cvec{x}) = \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b} \qquad 	ext{for every } \cvec{x} \in 
R^n . In particular f is an affine map (@def-affine-map) whose linear part \vec f (@thm-affine-map-is-linear-plus-translation) is the isometry T_{\Q}. Three steps. ① Move the origin out of the way: g(\cvec{x}) = f(\cvec{x}) - f(\cvec{0}) is a motion fixing \cvec{0}, so it preserves norms as well as distances. ② A map preserving both norms and distances preserves inner products, because the inner product is built from those two by polarization: 2\inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = 
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 + 
orm{\cvec{y}}^2 - 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}}^2. ③ A map preserving inner products is linear, and the way to see it is the reflex for showing a vector is zero: pair the vector g(\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}) - g(\cvec{x}) - g(\cvec{y}) with itself. Expanding the square turns it into a combination of inner products, each of which g has just been shown to preserve, and the combination is the square of (\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}) - \cvec{x} - \cvec{y} = \cvec{0}. Step 1: reduce to a motion fixing the origin. Put \cvec{b} = f(\cvec{0}) and g(\cvec{x}) = f(\cvec{x}) - \cvec{b}. For all \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}, 
orm{g(\cvec{x}) - g(\cvec{y})} = 
orm{f(\cvec{x}) - f(\cvec{y})} = 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}} , so g is a motion, and g(\cvec{0}) = \cvec{0}. Taking \cvec{y} = \cvec{0} gives 
orm{g(\cvec{x})} = 
orm{g(\cvec{x}) - g(\cvec{0})} = 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{0}} = 
orm{\cvec{x}} for every \cvec{x}: g preserves norms. Step 2: g preserves inner products. By @thm-norm-properties (c), for real vectors \cvec{u}, \cvec{v},  egin{aligned} 
orm{\cvec{u} - \cvec{v}}^2 &= 
orm{\cvec{u}}^2 - 2\inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{v}} + 
orm{\cvec{v}}^2 , \ 	ext{so}\qquad 2\inner{\cvec{u}}{\cvec{v}} &= 
orm{\cvec{u}}^2 + 
orm{\cvec{v}}^2 - 
orm{\cvec{u} - \cvec{v}}^2 . \end{aligned} This is the polarization identity of @lem-polarization-identities in the form that uses the distance: the inner product is determined by norms and distances alone. Applying it to g(\cvec{x}), g(\cvec{y}) and then to \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}, and using Step 1 three times,  egin{aligned} 2\inner{g(\cvec{x})}{g(\cvec{y})} &= 
orm{g(\cvec{x})}^2 + 
orm{g(\cvec{y})}^2 - 
orm{g(\cvec{x}) - g(\cvec{y})}^2 \ &= 
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 + 
orm{\cvec{y}}^2 - 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}}^2 = 2\inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} . \end{aligned} So \inner{g(\cvec{x})}{g(\cvec{y})} = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} for all \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}. Step 3: g is linear. Fix \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n and expand the squared norm of \cvec{d} = g(\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}) - g(\cvec{x}) - g(\cvec{y}). For any three vectors \cvec{r}, \cvec{s}, \cvec{z}, repeated use of @thm-norm-properties (c) gives  egin{aligned} 
orm{\cvec{r} - \cvec{s} - \cvec{z}}^2 = \ &
orm{\cvec{r}}^2 + 
orm{\cvec{s}}^2 + 
orm{\cvec{z}}^2 \ &- 2\inner{\cvec{r}}{\cvec{s}} - 2\inner{\cvec{r}}{\cvec{z}} + 2\inner{\cvec{s}}{\cvec{z}} . \end{aligned} Apply this with \cvec{r} = g(\cvec{x}+\cvec{y}), \cvec{s} = g(\cvec{x}), \cvec{z} = g(\cvec{y}). Every term on the right is a norm or an inner product of values of g, and Steps 1 and 2 replace each by the corresponding quantity for \cvec{x} + \cvec{y}, \cvec{x}, \cvec{y}. The result is the same expression with \cvec{r} = \cvec{x} + \cvec{y}, \cvec{s} = \cvec{x}, \cvec{z} = \cvec{y}, that is, 
orm{(\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}) - \cvec{x} - \cvec{y}}^2 = 0. Hence 
orm{\cvec{d}}^2 = 0 and \cvec{d} = \cvec{0} by @thm-norm-properties (a), so g(\cvec{x} + \cvec{y}) = g(\cvec{x}) + g(\cvec{y}) . For scalars, let \lambda \in 
R and expand in the same way:  egin{aligned} 
orm{g(\lambda\cvec{x}) - \lambda g(\cvec{x})}^2 &= 
orm{g(\lambda\cvec{x})}^2 - 2\lambda\inner{g(\lambda\cvec{x})}{g(\cvec{x})} + \lambda^2
orm{g(\cvec{x})}^2 \ &= 
orm{\lambda\cvec{x}}^2 - 2\lambda\inner{\lambda\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} + \lambda^2
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 \ &= \lambda^2
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 - 2\lambda^2
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 + \lambda^2
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 = 0 , \end{aligned} so g(\lambda\cvec{x}) = \lambda g(\cvec{x}). Therefore g is linear. Step 4: the matrix. Let \Q be the matrix of g in the standard basis, so g(\cvec{x}) = \Q\cvec{x}. By Step 2, g preserves inner products, so \Q \in \Orth(n) by @thm-isometry-characterizations (b) and (f), the standard basis being orthonormal. Then f(\cvec{x}) = g(\cvec{x}) + \cvec{b} = \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b}. Uniqueness. If \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b} = \Q'\cvec{x} + \cvec{b}' for every \cvec{x}, then \cvec{x} = \cvec{0} gives \cvec{b} = \cvec{b}', and then (\Q - \Q')\cvec{x} = \cvec{0} for every \cvec{x} gives \Q = \Q'. This proves the theorem. Surjectivity was never used. The definition of a motion asks only that distances be preserved, and the proof never produces a preimage of anything. Most treatments define a motion to be a distance-preserving bijection, and then the bijectivity is an unused hypothesis — as the next corollary shows, it comes for free. [Motions Are Bijections] Every Euclidean motion f of 
R^n is a bijection, and f^{-1} is again a motion. The linear part of f^{-1} is \Q	p, where \Q is the linear part of f. Write f(\cvec{x}) = \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b} by @thm-motion-is-affine. Since \Q \in \Orth(n), \Q is invertible with \Q^{-1} = \Q	p (@thm-isometry-characterizations (g1)), so the map h(\cvec{y}) = \Q	p(\cvec{y} - \cvec{b}) = \Q	p\cvec{y} - \Q	p\cvec{b} satisfies h(f(\cvec{x})) = \cvec{x} and f(h(\cvec{y})) = \cvec{y}. Hence f is a bijection with inverse h, which is a motion by examples 2 and 3 after @def-euclidean-motion, with linear part \Q	p. The Euclidean norm is doing real work. Step 2 is the only place where the special shape of 
orm{\cdot} is used, and for other norms the phenomenon fails. Here is a distance-preserving map that is not affine, for a norm of Chapter 16 and between spaces of different dimensions. Give 
R^2 the norm 
orm{(y_1,y_2)}_{\infty} = \max(\lvert y_1vert, \lvert y_2vert) of Chapter 16 and consider \varphi \colon 
R 	o 
R^2, \varphi(t) = (t, \lvert tvert). For s, t \in 
R, @lem-reverse-triangle-norm applied to the absolute value as a norm on 
R gives  igl\lvert\lvert svert - \lvert tvert igrvert \le \lvert s - tvert, so 
orm{\varphi(s) - \varphi(t)}_{\infty} = \max igl(\lvert s - tvert,\  igl\lvert\lvert svert - \lvert tvert igrvert igr) = \lvert s - tvert . So \varphi preserves distances exactly, and it is visibly not affine: \varphi(-1) = (-1,1), \varphi(0) = (0,0), and \varphi(1) = (1,1), yet \varphi(0) is not the midpoint of \varphi(-1) and \varphi(1), which is (0,1). Replacing \lvert tvert by any function 
R 	o 
R that never changes by more than its input does gives another one. What makes @thm-motion-is-affine true is polarization, an identity special to the norms that come from an inner product, and not any property shared by all norms. The determinant of the linear part now splits the motions into two halves, exactly as it splits \Orth(n). [Direct and Opposite Motions] Let f(\cvec{x}) = \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b} be a motion of 
R^n. It is direct, or orientation-preserving, if \det\Q = 1, and opposite, or orientation-reversing, if \det\Q = -1. (b) If f and g are motions with f(\cvec{p}_i) = g(\cvec{p}_i) = \cvec{q}_i for all i, then h = g^{-1}\circ f is a motion (@cor-motion-bijective) fixing every \cvec{p}_i. Write h(\cvec{x}) = \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b} by @thm-motion-is-affine. Subtracting h(\cvec{p}_0) = \cvec{p}_0 from h(\cvec{p}_i) = \cvec{p}_i gives \Q(\cvec{p}_i - \cvec{p}_0) = \cvec{p}_i - \cvec{p}_0 for i \ge 1, so \Q fixes a basis and \Q = \I; then \cvec{b} = \cvec{p}_0 - \cvec{p}_0 = \cvec{0} and h = \id, so f = g. With fewer points the spanning hypothesis fails and uniqueness goes with it. In 
R^2, take the single pair \cvec{p}_0 = \cvec{q}_0 = (0,0) and \cvec{p}_1 = \cvec{q}_1 = (1,0). Both the identity and the reflection in the first coordinate axis are motions carrying \cvec{p}_i to \cvec{q}_i, and they differ at (0,1). Here \cvec{p}_1 - \cvec{p}_0 = \cvec{e}_1 spans only a line. [C3: Motions of a finite set] Let S \subseteq 
R^n be a finite nonempty set and let G = \{f \in \operatorname{E}(n) : f(S) = S\} be its symmetry group. 1. Prove that G is a subgroup of \operatorname{E}(n), and that every f \in G fixes the centroid \cvec{c} = 	frac{1}{\lvert Svert}\sum_{\cvec{p} \in S}\cvec{p}. 2. Deduce that G is isomorphic to a subgroup of \Orth(n), and that G contains no translation other than the identity. (a) The identity lies in G. If f, g \in G then (g\circ f)(S) = g(S) = S, and f(S) = S with f a bijection (@cor-motion-bijective) gives f^{-1}(S) = S; so G is a subgroup by @def-subgroup, using @prp-motion-group (a). Let f \in G, with f(\cvec{x}) = \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b}. Since f restricts to a bijection of the finite set S, \sum_{\cvec{p} \in S} f(\cvec{p}) = \sum_{\cvec{q} \in S}\cvec{q} = \lvert Svert\,\cvec{c} , while on the other hand \sum_{\cvec{p}\in S}f(\cvec{p}) = \Q igl(\sum_{\cvec{p}\in S}\cvec{p} igr) + \lvert Svert\cvec{b} = \lvert Svert(\Q\cvec{c} + \cvec{b}) = \lvert Svert f(\cvec{c}). Dividing by \lvert Svert 
e 0 gives f(\cvec{c}) = \cvec{c}. (b) Conjugating by the translation t_{-\cvec{c}} gives an injective homomorphism G 	o \operatorname{E}(n), f \mapsto t_{-\cvec{c}}\circ f\circ t_{\cvec{c}}, whose image consists of motions fixing \cvec{0}, hence of linear ones by @thm-motion-is-affine; those are the orthogonal maps. So G is isomorphic to a subgroup of \Orth(n), namely \{\lambda(f) : f \in G\} in the notation of @prp-motion-group. If t_{\cvec{b}} \in G then t_{\cvec{b}}(\cvec{c}) = \cvec{c} by (a), so \cvec{b} = \cvec{0}. Geometrically: a finite figure cannot be carried onto itself by a nontrivial translation, because a translation would move its centroid.

title: 22.5 Affine and Euclidean Quadrics
content:
Affine and Euclidean Quadrics Chapter 14 classified quadratic forms up to congruence, and the answer over 
R was the inertia. A curve like 5x^2 + 4xy + 5y^2 - 14x - 14y - 7 = 0 is not a quadratic form, though: it has linear terms and a constant, and its zero set does not pass through the origin. This section asks what the inertia classification becomes once the origin is given up, which is exactly the question affine geometry was built for. Two answers come out, one for affine changes of coordinates and one for the rigid motions of @def-euclidean-motion, and the difference between them is the difference between “it is an ellipse” and “its semi-axes are \sqrt7 and \sqrt3”. Where characteristic two bites Everything in this section needs a field in which 2 
e 0, and it is worth seeing why before any definition is written down. A degree-two polynomial in x_1, \dots, x_n has a homogeneous quadratic part, and we want to write that part as \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} with \A symmetric, so that Chapter 14 applies to it. For a symmetric \A the coefficient of x_ix_j with i 
e j is a_{ij} + a_{ji} = 2a_{ij}. Recovering a_{ij} from the polynomial means halving, which is the division by 1 + 1 that @thm-polarization-forms performs, and on which the uniqueness of the symmetric matrix attached to a quadratic form (@def-quadratic-form) depends. Over 
F_2 the halving is not merely inconvenient; the target is not there. Every symmetric \A \in M_n(
F_2) gives \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = \sum_i a_{ii}x_i^2 + 2\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}x_ix_j = \sum_i a_{ii}x_i^2 , and since a^2 = a for a \in 
F_2 and squaring is additive there, this is  igl(\sum_i a_{ii}x_i igr)^2, the square of a linear form. So over 
F_2 no expression \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} with \A symmetric ever has an xy term, the polynomial xy is not of that shape at all, and the ones that are have already collapsed to squares of linear forms. There is nothing left to classify. So: throughout this section F is a field with \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 (@def-characteristic), and from the affine classification onward F = 
R. The hypothesis will be invoked by name at each of the three places where it does work: writing the linear part as 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x}, reading off a symmetric \A, and solving for a center. The equation of a quadric Fix an origin O and a basis of the direction space, which by @prp-choice-of-origin identifies the affine space \cA of dimension n with F^n. Every polynomial of degree 2 in the resulting coordinates can then be written in one standard shape. A quadric is what you get when a quadratic form is allowed to forget where the origin is. [Quadric] Let \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 and let \cA be an affine space of dimension n over F, identified with F^n by a choice of origin and basis (@prp-choice-of-origin). A quadric polynomial on \cA is a function Q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} + 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} + c with \A \in M_n(F) symmetric and nonzero, \cvec{b} \in F^n and c \in F. Its quadratic part is the quadratic form q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x}. The quadric defined by Q is its zero set \{\, \cvec{x} \in F^n : Q(\cvec{x}) = 0 \,\} . For n = 2 a quadric is called a conic. Read the clauses. “Symmetric” is a normalization, not a restriction: \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{x}	p\A	p\cvec{x} because a 1 	imes 1 matrix equals its transpose, so \A may always be replaced by 	frac12(\A + \A	p), and once symmetric it is determined by q (@thm-polarization-forms). “Nonzero” excludes \A = \O, where Q would be affine and its zero set a flat (@def-flat) already handled in Section 2; it is the clause that makes the object genuinely quadratic. The factor 2 in 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} is a convention we may adopt because 2 is invertible: a linear part  eta_1x_1 + \dots +  eta_nx_n is 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} with b_i =  eta_i/2. It pays for itself in every formula below. The data are recoverable from the function. @def-quadric calls Q a function, so before speaking of “its” quadratic part or “its” constant we must check that \A, \cvec{b} and c are determined by Q. They are, over any field of characteristic 
e 2. First Q(\cvec{0}) = c. Next Q(\cvec{x}) - Q(-\cvec{x}) = 4\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} \qquad 	ext{for every } \cvec{x} \in F^n , and 4 = 2\cdot 2 
e 0, so taking \cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_i recovers b_i for each i. Finally \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} = Q(\cvec{x}) - 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} - c is then determined as a function of \cvec{x}, and a symmetric \A is determined by that quadratic form (@thm-polarization-forms). So the triple (\A, \cvec{b}, c) is unique. Examples. Over 
R with n = 2: - x^2 + y^2 - 1, with \A = \I_2, \cvec{b} = \cvec{0}, c = -1: the unit circle. - x^2 - y, with \A = \diag(1, 0), \cvec{b} = (0, -	frac12), c = 0: a parabola. Here the halving convention is visible, and \A is singular. - x^2 + y^2: the zero set is the single point \cvec{0}, although the polynomial has degree 2. - x^2: the zero set is the line x = 0, traced “twice” in the sense that \A = \diag(1,0) has rank 1 and the polynomial is a square. This is the degenerate case, and it matters because the classification must find room for it. - x^2 + y^2 + 1: the zero set is empty. Over 
R a quadric may have no points at all, and the classification below has two different normal forms whose zero sets are both empty. Nonexample by minimal change. Replace x^2 + y^2 - 1 by x^4 + y^2 - 1: the quadratic part is no longer a quadratic form, and there is no \A. Replace it instead by 2x + 3y - 1: now \A = \O, the clause “nonzero” fails, and the zero set is a line, not a quadric. A quadric is classified through its polynomial, not through its point set. Over 
R the polynomials x^2 + y^2 + 1 and x^2 + 1 both have empty zero set, and no coordinate change can be expected to tell empty from empty; yet the two polynomials will land in different classes below, and rightly so, because their behavior over 
C and their intersections with lines differ. Everything in the affine classification below is a statement about the polynomial Q up to an invertible affine substitution and a nonzero scalar factor. When the zero set determines Q up to a scalar it will be said explicitly. The matrix of a quadric The whole point of writing the linear part as 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} is that Q then becomes a single quadratic form in one extra variable. Write 	ilde{\cvec{x}} =  egin{pmatrix} \cvec{x} \ 1 \end{pmatrix} \in F^{n+1}, \qquad \widetilde{\A} =  egin{pmatrix} \A & \cvec{b} \ \cvec{b}	p & c \end{pmatrix} \in M_{n+1}(F) , so that \widetilde\A is symmetric and 	ilde{\cvec{x}}	p\widetilde\A\,	ilde{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} + \cvec{x}	p\cvec{b} + \cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} + c = Q(\cvec{x}) , the two middle terms being equal because each is a 1 	imes 1 matrix and one is the transpose of the other. We call \widetilde\A the big matrix of Q and \A its small matrix. The extra coordinate is the same trick that turned an affine map into an (n+1) 	imes (n+1) block matrix in @prp-affine-map-block-matrix, and the two devices fit together exactly. [Affine Substitution Is Congruence of the Big Matrix] Let Q have big matrix \widetilde\A, let \M \in M_n(F) be invertible, let \cvec{t} \in F^n, and let g(\cvec{y}) = \M\cvec{y} + \cvec{t} be the corresponding invertible affine map (@def-affine-map), with block matrix (@prp-affine-map-block-matrix) \widehat{g} =  egin{pmatrix} \M & \cvec{t} \ \cvec{0}	p & 1 \end{pmatrix} . Then Q \circ g is again a quadric polynomial, its big matrix is \widehat{g}	p\widetilde\A\widehat{g}, and its small matrix, linear vector, and constant are \A' = \M	p\A\M, \qquad \cvec{b}' = \M	p(\A\cvec{t} + \cvec{b}), \qquad c' = Q(\cvec{t}) . By @prp-affine-map-block-matrix, \widehat{g}\,	ilde{\cvec{y}} =  igl(\M\cvec{y} + \cvec{t},\, 1 igr) = \widetilde{g(\cvec{y})}. Hence Q(g(\cvec{y})) = \widetilde{g(\cvec{y})}	p\widetilde\A\,\widetilde{g(\cvec{y})} = 	ilde{\cvec{y}}	p igl(\widehat{g}	p\widetilde\A\widehat{g} igr)	ilde{\cvec{y}} , and \widehat{g}	p\widetilde\A\widehat{g} is symmetric, being a congruence of a symmetric matrix (@prp-congruence-preserves-symmetry). Multiplying the blocks out,  egin{aligned}  egin{pmatrix} \M	p & \cvec{0} \ \cvec{t}	p & 1\end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} \A & \cvec{b} \ \cvec{b}	p & c\end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} \M & \cvec{t} \ \cvec{0}	p & 1\end{pmatrix} &=  egin{pmatrix} \M	p\A & \M	p\cvec{b} \ \cvec{t}	p\A + \cvec{b}	p & \cvec{t}	p\cvec{b} + c\end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} \M & \cvec{t} \ \cvec{0}	p & 1\end{pmatrix} \ &=  egin{pmatrix} \M	p\A\M & \M	p(\A\cvec{t} + \cvec{b}) \ (\A\cvec{t} + \cvec{b})	p\M & \cvec{t}	p\A\cvec{t} + 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{t} + c\end{pmatrix}, \end{aligned} where the bottom-left block was transposed using \A	p = \A. Reading off the blocks gives \A', \cvec{b}' and c' = \cvec{t}	p\A\cvec{t} + 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{t} + c = Q(\cvec{t}). Finally \A' = \M	p\A\M is nonzero, since \M is invertible and congruence preserves rank (@thm-congruence-preserves-rank), so Q \circ g is a quadric polynomial. This proves the proposition. Three consequences are worth naming at once. The new constant is Q evaluated at the new origin — obvious in hindsight, since \cvec{y} = \cvec{0} means \cvec{x} = \cvec{t}. The new small matrix is a congruence of the old one, so the rank of \A is an affine invariant of Q by @thm-congruence-preserves-rank, and over 
R so is its inertia by @cor-real-symmetric-classification (b) — the latter only up to the simultaneous exchange of n_+ with n_- that a negative scalar factor forces, as Step 4 of the classification theorem below records. And \widetilde\A itself only undergoes congruences by matrices whose last row is (\cvec{0}	p, 1), which is a strictly smaller set than all congruences: that restriction is exactly why the affine classification is finer than Chapter 14’s. Replacing Q by \lambda Q with \lambda 
e 0 does not change the zero set and replaces \widetilde\A by \lambda\widetilde\A, so a scalar factor costs nothing geometrically and is worth allowing alongside the substitution. [Affine Equivalence of Quadric Polynomials] Two quadric polynomials Q_1, Q_2 on F^n are affinely equivalent when Q_2 = \lambda\,(Q_1 \circ g) for some invertible affine map g (@def-affine-map) and some \lambda \in F with \lambda 
e 0. This is an equivalence relation, because the invertible affine maps form a group and the nonzero scalars do too. Centers A circle has a center and a parabola does not, and the difference is visible in the equation before any picture is drawn. A center is a point about which the equation is symmetric. [Center of a Quadric] Let Q be a quadric polynomial on F^n. A point \cvec{p} \in F^n is a center of Q if Q(\cvec{p} + \cvec{v}) = Q(\cvec{p} - \cvec{v}) \qquad 	ext{for every } \cvec{v} \in F^n . Q is central if it has at least one center, and centerless otherwise. In words: reflecting in \cvec{p}, the map \cvec{p} + \cvec{v} \mapsto \cvec{p} - \cvec{v}, carries the quadric to itself, and more than that, leaves the whole polynomial unchanged. The next proposition turns this into a linear system. [When a Center Exists] Let \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 and let Q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} + 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} + c be a quadric polynomial on F^n. Then: 1. \cvec{p} is a center of Q if and only if \A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b} = \cvec{0}; 2. Q is central if and only if \cvec{b} \in \col(\A); in particular Q is central whenever \A is invertible, and the center is then the unique point -\A^{-1}\cvec{b}; 3. if \cvec{p} is a center then Q(\cvec{p} + \cvec{v}) = Q(\cvec{p}) + \cvec{v}	p\A\cvec{v} for every \cvec{v}, and the value Q(\cvec{p}) is the same at every center. Expand Q(\cvec{p} \pm \cvec{v}) and subtract. Everything even in \cvec{v} cancels and what is left is 4\cvec{v}	p(\A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b}), a linear functional of \cvec{v}. A linear functional vanishes identically exactly when its vector vanishes, so the condition on \cvec{p} is one linear equation per coordinate. The 4 is where \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 is spent. (a) Expanding and using \A	p = \A, so that \cvec{p}	p\A\cvec{v} = \cvec{v}	p\A\cvec{p}, Q(\cvec{p} \pm \cvec{v}) = \cvec{p}	p\A\cvec{p} \pm 2\cvec{v}	p\A\cvec{p} + \cvec{v}	p\A\cvec{v} + 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{p} \pm 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{v} + c . Subtracting the two, Q(\cvec{p}+\cvec{v}) - Q(\cvec{p}-\cvec{v}) = 4\cvec{v}	p\A\cvec{p} + 4\cvec{b}	p\cvec{v} = 4\,\cvec{v}	p(\A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b}) . {#eq-center-difference} Since \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, the element 4 = 2 \cdot 2 is nonzero. So \cvec{p} is a center exactly when \cvec{v}	p(\A\cvec{p}+\cvec{b}) = 0 for every \cvec{v}. Taking \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_i shows that this forces every entry of \A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b} to vanish; conversely \A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b} = \cvec{0} makes @eq-center-difference zero for every \cvec{v}. Hence (a). (b) By (a), a center is a solution of \A\cvec{p} = -\cvec{b}, and such a solution exists exactly when -\cvec{b}, equivalently \cvec{b}, lies in \col(\A) (@thm-matrix-times-vector-columns). If \A is invertible then \col(\A) = F^n and \cvec{p} = -\A^{-1}\cvec{b} is the only solution. (c) With \A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b} = \cvec{0}, the expansion above with the sign + reads Q(\cvec{p} + \cvec{v}) =  igl(\cvec{p}	p\A\cvec{p} + 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{p} + c igr) + 2\cvec{v}	p(\A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b}) + \cvec{v}	p\A\cvec{v} = Q(\cvec{p}) + \cvec{v}	p\A\cvec{v} . If \cvec{p}' is a second center then \A(\cvec{p}' - \cvec{p}) = (-\cvec{b}) - (-\cvec{b}) = \cvec{0}, so putting \cvec{v} = \cvec{p}' - \cvec{p} in the last identity gives Q(\cvec{p}') = Q(\cvec{p}) + \cvec{v}	p\A\cvec{v} = Q(\cvec{p}) + \cvec{v}	p\cvec{0} = Q(\cvec{p}). This proves the proposition. Part (c) is the useful half. Translating the origin to a center — that is, applying @prp-quadric-congruence with \M = \I and \cvec{t} = \cvec{p} — gives \cvec{b}' = \A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b} = \cvec{0}, so the equation becomes \cvec{v}	p\A\cvec{v} + Q(\cvec{p}) = 0 with no linear term at all, and Chapter 14 applies verbatim. That single move is the engine of the classification. [The parabola is centerless] Show that Q(x,y) = x^2 - y over 
R has no center, and find all centers of Q_1(x,y) = x^2 - 1. For Q, \A = \diag(1,0) and \cvec{b} = (0, -	frac12). Then \col(\A) = \Span(\cvec{e}_1) and \cvec{b} 
otin \col(\A) because its second entry is nonzero, so by @prp-centre-exists-iff (b) there is no center. Concretely, Q(\cvec{p} + \cvec{v}) - Q(\cvec{p} - \cvec{v}) = 4\cvec{v}	p(\A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b}) = 4(v_1p_1 - 	frac12 v_2), which is -2 
e 0 at \cvec{v} = \cvec{e}_2 whatever \cvec{p} is. For Q_1, \A = \diag(1,0) and \cvec{b} = \cvec{0} \in \col(\A), so the centers are the solutions of \A\cvec{p} = \cvec{0}, namely the whole y-axis. That is right: Q_1 defines the pair of lines x = \pm1, and reflecting in any point of the y-axis swaps them. And Q_1(\cvec{p}) = -1 at every one of those centers, as @prp-centre-exists-iff (c) promises. A quadric polynomial on F^n with ank\A = n has exactly one center, and one with ank\A = n - 1 has either none or a whole line of them. Which is it for x^2 + y^2 - 2x on 
R^2, and which for x^2 + 2y? For x^2 + y^2 - 2x we have \A = \I_2 of rank 2 and \cvec{b} = (-1, 0), so the unique center is -\A^{-1}\cvec{b} = (1,0); indeed the curve is the circle (x-1)^2 + y^2 = 1. For x^2 + 2y we have \A = \diag(1,0) of rank 1 and \cvec{b} = (0,1) 
otin \col(\A) = \Span(\cvec{e}_1), so there is no center at all: it is a parabola. The line of centers occurs instead for x^2 - 1, where \cvec{b} = \cvec{0} does lie in \col(\A). The affine classification over the reals Now the theorem. Over 
R we may diagonalize the small matrix by Sylvester (@cor-real-symmetric-classification), translate to kill as much of the linear part as a center allows, and then scale. What survives is a short list. [Affine Classification of Real Quadrics] Let Q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} + 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} + c be a quadric polynomial on 
R^n and let r = ank\A, which is \ge 1 because \A 
e \O (@def-quadric). Then Q is affinely equivalent to exactly one polynomial from the following list, for one value of p in the range shown, where \sigma_{r,p}(\cvec{y}) = y_1^2 + \dots + y_p^2 - y_{p+1}^2 - \dots - y_r^2: 1. \sigma_{r,p}(\cvec{y}) - 1, with 0 \le p \le r; 2. \sigma_{r,p}(\cvec{y}), with r \le 2p \le 2r; 3. \sigma_{r,p}(\cvec{y}) - y_{r+1}, with r < n and r \le 2p \le 2r. Case (III) occurs exactly when Q is centerless. The parameter p that occurs is n_+(\A) or n_-(\A), the two being interchanged by a negative scalar factor (@def-signature). Three moves, in this order, and each is a result already proved. ① Diagonalize the quadratic part. Sylvester’s law (@cor-real-symmetric-classification) produces coordinates in which the quadratic part is \sigma_{r,p}; by @prp-quadric-congruence this changes \cvec{b} and c but nothing else. ② Complete the square in the first r variables. A translation kills the linear coefficients b_1, \dots, b_r, because those are exactly the coordinates in which \A is invertible. This is @prp-centre-exists-iff read one coordinate at a time. ③ Deal with what is left, a polynomial \sigma_{r,p} + 2\sum_{i>r}b_iy_i + c in which the y_i with i > r appear only linearly. If they do not appear at all, scaling clears the constant to 0 or -1, giving (II) or (I). If one of them does appear, it can be used as a new coordinate that swallows the constant too, giving (III). That the list has no repetitions is a separate, purely computational matter: the pair (inertia of \A, inertia of \widetilde\A) is an affine invariant by @prp-quadric-congruence, and reading it off the three families separates them. Step 1: diagonalize. Write (p, r-p, n-r) for the inertia of \A (@def-signature); this p is the one carried through Steps 1 to 3. By @cor-real-symmetric-classification (a) there is an invertible \M_1 with \M_1	p\A\M_1 = \D, where \D = \diag(\epsilon_1, \dots, \epsilon_n) has \epsilon_i = 1 for i \le p, \epsilon_i = -1 for p < i \le r, and \epsilon_i = 0 for i > r. Substituting \cvec{x} = \M_1\cvec{y} and applying @prp-quadric-congruence with \cvec{t} = \cvec{0}, the polynomial becomes Q_1(\cvec{y}) = \sigma_{r,p}(\cvec{y}) + 2\cvec{b}_1	p\cvec{y} + c, \qquad \cvec{b}_1 = \M_1	p\cvec{b} . Step 2: complete the square. Let \cvec{t} have entries t_i = -\epsilon_i b_{1,i} for i \le r and t_i = 0 for i > r, and substitute \cvec{y} = \cvec{z} + \cvec{t}. By @prp-quadric-congruence with \M = \I, the new linear vector is \cvec{b}_2 = \D\cvec{t} + \cvec{b}_1, whose i-th entry for i \le r is \epsilon_it_i + b_{1,i} = -\epsilon_i^2b_{1,i} + b_{1,i} = 0, since \epsilon_i^2 = 1 there; for i > r it is b_{1,i}, unchanged. The new constant is c_2 = Q_1(\cvec{t}). So Q_2(\cvec{z}) = \sigma_{r,p}(\cvec{z}) + 2\sum_{i>r}b_{1,i}z_i + c_2 . Step 3, Case A: b_{1,i} = 0 for every i > r. Then Q_2 = \sigma_{r,p} + c_2. If c_2 = 0, this is \sigma_{r,p}. If r \le 2p we are in case (II). Otherwise multiply by \lambda = -1 and reverse the order of the first r coordinates, which turns \sigma_{r,p} into \sigma_{r,\,r-p} with r \le 2(r-p); again case (II). If c_2 
e 0, substitute z_i = \lvert c_2vert^{1/2}w_i for i \le r and z_i = w_i otherwise, an invertible linear change, and then multiply by \lambda = 1/\lvert c_2vert. The result is \sigma_{r,p}(\cvec{w}) + \sgn(c_2). If \sgn(c_2) = -1 this is case (I) with parameter p. The eigenvalues of \A are 4 and -2, from x^2 - 2x - 8 = (x-4)(x+2), so \operatorname{In}\A = (1,1,0) by @thm-inertia-from-eigenvalues, and \det\A = -8 
e 0. The unique center solves \A\cvec{p} = (2,2), giving \cvec{p} = (	frac12, 	frac12), and c_0 = Q(\cvec{p}) = 	frac14 + 	frac32 + 	frac14 - 2 - 2 + 3 = 1. Translating, the equation becomes X^2 + 6XY + Y^2 + 1 = 0 with X = x - 	frac12, Y = y - 	frac12. Completing the square, X^2 + 6XY + Y^2 = (X + 3Y)^2 - 8Y^2, so with s = X + 3Y, t = Y the equation is s^2 - 8t^2 = -1. Multiplying by -1 and setting w_1 = 2\sqrt2\,t, w_2 = s gives w_1^2 - w_2^2 = 1. So \widetilde\A is congruent to \diag(1,-8,1) up to the translation, giving \operatorname{In}\widetilde\A = (2,1,0); up to the simultaneous exchange this is the invariant  igl((1,1,0),(1,2,0) igr) of row 2. The conic is a hyperbola. [B3: Principal axes] Find the center, principal axes, and semi-axes of 2x^2 - 4xy + 5y^2 - 4x + 2y - 7 = 0 over 
R. \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 2 & -2 \ -2 & 5\end{psmallmatrix}, \cvec{b} = (-2, 1), c = -7. Since \det\A = 6 
e 0 the center solves \A\cvec{p} = (2,-1): from 2p_1 - 2p_2 = 2 and -2p_1 + 5p_2 = -1 we get p_2 = 	frac13, p_1 = 	frac43. Then c_0 = Q(\cvec{p}) = \cvec{b}	p\cvec{p} + c = (-2)	frac43 + 1\cdot	frac13 - 7 = -	frac{28}{3} , using Q(\cvec{p}) = \cvec{p}	p(\A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b}) + \cvec{b}	p\cvec{p} + c = \cvec{b}	p\cvec{p} + c, valid because \A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b} = \cvec{0}. The characteristic polynomial is x^2 - 7x + 6 = (x-1)(x-6), so \lambda = 1, 6 with unit eigenvectors \cvec{q}_1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt5}(2,1) and \cvec{q}_2 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt5}(1,-2); indeed \A(2,1) = (2,1) and \A(1,-2) = (6,-12). By @thm-euclidean-classification the normal form is y_1^2 + 6y_2^2 - 	frac{28}{3} = 0, that is  rac{y_1^2}{28/3} +  rac{y_2^2}{14/9} = 1 . So the curve is an ellipse centered at (	frac43, 	frac13), with semi-axis 2\sqrt{21}/3 = \sqrt{28/3} along \cvec{q}_1 and semi-axis \sqrt{14}/3 along \cvec{q}_2. C. Going deeper [C1: Which quadrics are determined by their points] Work over 
R with n = 2. 1. Give two quadric polynomials with the same zero set that are not proportional. 2. Prove that if Q is a quadric polynomial whose zero set contains three points of some line L, then Q vanishes on all of L. 3. Deduce that the zero set of a quadric polynomial is never exactly a set of three noncollinear points. Hint for (b): restrict Q to a parametrization of L. (a) Take Q_1 = x^2 + y^2 and Q_2 = x^2 + 2y^2. Both vanish exactly at \cvec{0}, since a sum of squares of reals is zero only when each is, but Q_2 
e \lambda Q_1 for any \lambda: comparing the coefficients of x^2 forces \lambda = 1, and then the coefficients of y^2 disagree. (b) Write L = \{\cvec{p} + t\cvec{v} : t \in 
R\} with \cvec{v} 
e \cvec{0}, a flat of dimension 1 (@def-flat). Then f(t) = Q(\cvec{p} + t\cvec{v}) = (\cvec{v}	p\A\cvec{v})t^2 + 2 igl(\cvec{v}	p(\A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b}) igr)t + Q(\cvec{p}) by the expansion in the proof of @prp-centre-exists-iff, so f is a polynomial of degree at most 2 in t. If Q vanishes at three distinct points of L, then f has three distinct roots. A nonzero polynomial of degree at most 2 over a field has at most 2 roots (@cor-root-bound-general), so f is the zero polynomial and Q vanishes on all of L. (c) Suppose, for a contradiction, that the zero set of a quadric polynomial Q is exactly \{P_1, P_2, P_3\} with the three points not collinear, that is affinely independent (@def-affine-independence). Then (P_1, P_2, P_3) is an affine frame of 
R^2 (@def-affine-frame), so by @thm-affine-map-determined-by-frame there is an affine map f carrying it to the frame  igl((0,0), (1,0), (0,1) igr). That f is invertible: by @thm-affine-map-is-linear-plus-translation (b) its linear part sends \overrightarrow{P_1P_2} to \cvec{e}_1 and \overrightarrow{P_1P_3} to \cvec{e}_2, so it carries a basis to a basis and is invertible, whence f is bijective by @prp-affine-map-block-matrix. Substituting by f^{-1}, we may therefore assume the three points are (0,0), (1,0), (0,1), since an invertible affine substitution carries the zero set bijectively to the zero set (@prp-quadric-congruence). Write Q = ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 + 2dx + 2ey + c. Then Q(0,0) = c = 0, Q(1,0) = a + 2d = 0 and Q(0,1) = b + 2e = 0, so Q = a\,x(x-1) + b\,y(y-1) + 2hxy . Restricting to the line y = 0 gives a\,x(x-1). If a = 0 this vanishes identically and the whole line lies in the zero set, which is impossible for a three-point set; so a 
e 0, and by the same argument on x = 0, b 
e 0. Now fix m \in 
R with m 
e 0 and restrict to the line y = mx: Q(t, mt) = t igl[(a + 2hm + bm^2)\,t - (a + bm) igr] . The only point of \{P_1,P_2,P_3\} on that line is (0,0), because (1,0) needs m = 0 and (0,1) is not of the form (t, mt). So t = 0 must be the only root. If a + 2hm + bm^2 
e 0, the bracket vanishes at t = (a+bm)/(a+2hm+bm^2), and that must be 0, forcing a + bm = 0. Hence for every m 
e 0, a + 2hm + bm^2 = 0 \qquad 	ext{or} \qquad a + bm = 0 . The first equation is a quadratic in m with leading coefficient b 
e 0, so it has at most 2 roots, and the second has exactly one since b 
e 0 (@cor-root-bound-general). That is at most three permitted values of m, while 
R \setminus \{0\} is infinite. Contradiction. Hence no quadric polynomial over 
R has exactly three noncollinear points as its zero set. [C2: Over another field] 1. Over 
C, prove that every quadric polynomial in n variables is equivalent, under an invertible affine substitution and a nonzero scalar, to one of \sigma_r(\cvec{y}) - 1, \sigma_r(\cvec{y}), or \sigma_r(\cvec{y}) - y_{r+1} with r < n, where \sigma_r(\cvec{y}) = y_1^2 + \dots + y_r^2. How many normal forms are there for n = 2? 2. Over 
F_3, how many points does the conic x^2 + y^2 - 1 = 0 have in 
F_3^2? And x^2 + y^2 = 0? (a) Repeat the proof of @thm-affine-classification-of-quadrics, replacing @cor-real-symmetric-classification by @cor-complex-symmetric-classification, which says that over 
C a symmetric matrix of rank r is congruent to \I_r \oplus \O_{n-r}: rank alone is the congruence invariant. Step 1 gives \sigma_r + 2\cvec{b}_1	p\cvec{y} + c; Step 2 is unchanged; and in Step 3 Case A with c_2 
e 0 we substitute z_i = \gamma w_i for i \le r with \gamma^2 = -c_2, possible because every complex number has a square root, and obtain \sigma_r - 1 after dividing by -c_2. No sign remains to normalize, and no p survives, so the invariants reduce to (ank\A, ank\widetilde\A) = (r, r+1), (r,r), (r, r+2), which are pairwise distinct. For n = 2: r = 1 gives three forms and r = 2 gives two (family (III) needs r < n), so five in all, against nine over 
R. The four forms that disappear are accounted for by inertia: over 
C the ellipse, the hyperbola, and the empty conic x^2+y^2+1 all become \sigma_2 - 1; the point and the crossing lines both become \sigma_2; and x^2 = 1 and x^2 = -1 both become \sigma_1 - 1, the last two because i^2 = -1. (b) The squares in 
F_3 are 0^2 = 0, 1^2 = 1, 2^2 = 1, so x^2 \in \{0,1\} and x^2 = 1 has two solutions while x^2 = 0 has one. For x^2 + y^2 = 1: either x^2 = 1 and y^2 = 0, giving 2 \cdot 1 = 2 points, or x^2 = 0 and y^2 = 1, giving 1 \cdot 2 = 2 points; and 1 + 1 = 2 
e 1 rules out the remaining combination. Total 4 points, namely (\pm1, 0) and (0,\pm1). For x^2 + y^2 = 0: the options are 0 + 0 only, since 1 + 1 = 2 
e 0 and 1 + 0 = 1 
e 0. Total 1 point, the origin. So over 
F_3 this “circle” behaves like a real circle in the first case and like the real point-conic in the second, because -1 is not a square in 
F_3. [C3: The center as a projection] Let Q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} + 2\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} + c be a central quadric polynomial on 
R^n with r = ank\A. 1. Prove that the set of centers is a flat of dimension n - r (@def-flat). 2. Prove that the set of centers is contained in the zero set of Q if and only if Q(\cvec{p}) = 0 for one, hence every, center \cvec{p}. 3. Give an example on 
R^3 with a line of centers, none of which lies on the quadric. (a) By @prp-centre-exists-iff (a) the centers are the solutions of \A\cvec{p} = -\cvec{b}, a consistent linear system. By @thm-general-solution-structure its solution set is \cvec{p}_0 + 
ul(\A) for any particular solution \cvec{p}_0, a coset of 
ul(\A), hence a flat with direction space 
ul(\A). Its dimension is \dim
ul(\A) = n - ank\A = n - r by the Rank-Nullity Theorem (@thm-rank-nullity). (b) By @prp-centre-exists-iff (c) the value Q(\cvec{p}) is the same at every center, so “for one” and “for every” agree; and the set of centers lies in the zero set exactly when that common value is 0. (c) Take Q(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 - 1 on 
R^3. Here \A = \diag(1,1,0) has rank 2, \cvec{b} = \cvec{0} \in \col(\A), and the centers are the solutions of \A\cvec{p} = \cvec{0}, namely the z-axis, a line as (a) predicts with n - r = 1. The common value is Q(0,0,z) = -1 
e 0, so no center lies on the quadric, which is the cylinder of radius 1 about the z-axis.

title: 22.6 Projective Space
content:
Projective Space The affine geometry of the first two sections has one flaw, and it is visible in the statement of @thm-flat-intersection-and-join: the formula for the dimension of a join has two cases, because two flats may fail to meet. This section builds a geometry in which that never happens. The construction is entirely linear — a projective space is the set of lines through the origin of a vector space — and the payoff is a dimension formula with no exceptional case at all. Everything here works over an arbitrary field F, and neither analysis nor topology enters. Two lines that do not meet In the affine plane 
A^2(
R), take L_1 = \{(y_1,y_2) : y_2 - y_1 = 0\}, \qquad L_2 = \{(y_1,y_2) : y_2 - y_1 = 1\} . A point in both would satisfy 0 = 1, so L_1 \cap L_2 = \emptyset. Both are flats of dimension 1 with the same direction space \Span((1,1)), and their join is the whole plane. So @thm-flat-intersection-and-join (c) is in its second case: \dim(L_1 \vee L_2) = 1 + 1 - 1 + 1 = 2, with the extra +1 paid for by the failure to meet, and there is nothing to substitute for \dim(L_1 \cap L_2), because the empty set has no dimension. The two lines do have something in common: a direction. They are going the same way, and the natural thing to say is that they meet “at infinity”. The whole of this section is the work of turning that phrase into mathematics without losing linearity. The repair, in one sentence: stop working with points of a vector space and start working with its lines through the origin. The projective space of a vector space Let V be a vector space over F. On V \setminus \{\elem{0}\} define \elem{x} \sim \elem{y} \quad 	ext{if and only if} \quad \elem{y} = \lambda\elem{x} 	ext{ for some } \lambda \in F, \ \lambda 
e 0 . This is an equivalence relation (@def-equivalence-relation): it is reflexive with \lambda = 1; symmetric, because \elem{y} = \lambda\elem{x} with \lambda 
e 0 gives \elem{x} = \lambda^{-1}\elem{y}; and transitive, because \elem{y} = \lambda\elem{x} and \elem{z} = \mu\elem{y} give \elem{z} = (\mu\lambda)\elem{x} with \mu\lambda 
e 0, a field having no zero divisors. Note that \elem{0} had to be removed: it is equivalent only to itself, and keeping it would put a single extra point into every picture with no geometric job. A point of projective space is a line through the origin, with the origin itself thrown away. Projective Space Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field F with \dim V = n + 1. The projective space of V is the quotient set (@def-quotient-set) 
P(V) = (V \setminus \{\elem{0}\})/{\sim} , whose elements are called points. The point determined by \elem{x} 
e \elem{0} is written [\elem{x}]. The dimension of 
P(V) is \dim
P(V) = \dim V - 1 = n , so that 
P(\{\elem{0}\}) = \emptyset has dimension -1. We write 
P^n(F) = 
P(F^{n+1}) for projective n-space over F. A projective space of dimension 1 is a projective line, and one of dimension 2 a projective plane. Two clauses need comment. The shift by one in the dimension is not a decoration: it is what makes a projective line behave like a line and a projective plane like a plane, as @thm-affine-chart is about to confirm. And the convention \dim\emptyset = -1 looks like a dodge, but it is forced by the same shift — the empty set is 
P(\{\elem{0}\}) and \dim\{\elem{0}\} = 0 — and it will do real work in @thm-projective-dimension-formula. [Points Are Lines Through the Origin] Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F. The map [\elem{x}] \mapsto \Span(\elem{x}) is a bijection from 
P(V) onto the set of 1-dimensional subspaces of V. Well defined. If [\elem{x}] = [\elem{y}] then \elem{y} = \lambda\elem{x} with \lambda 
e 0, so \Span(\elem{y}) = \Span(\elem{x}) because each of \elem{x}, \elem{y} is a scalar multiple of the other. Also \elem{x} 
e \elem{0}, so \Span(\elem{x}) has dimension 1. Injective. If \Span(\elem{x}) = \Span(\elem{y}) with \elem{x}, \elem{y} 
e \elem{0}, then \elem{y} = \lambda\elem{x} for some \lambda \in F, and \lambda 
e 0 since \elem{y} 
e \elem{0}. Hence [\elem{x}] = [\elem{y}]. Surjective. A 1-dimensional subspace has a basis (\elem{x}) with \elem{x} 
e \elem{0}, and then it is \Span(\elem{x}), the image of [\elem{x}]. This proves the proposition. So a point of 
P^2(F) is a line through the origin of F^3, and a “line” of the projective plane will turn out to be a plane through the origin of F^3. Every statement below can be read twice: once about 
P(V) and once about subspaces of V. [Homogeneous Coordinates] Let \cvec{x} = (x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n) \in F^{n+1} be nonzero. The homogeneous coordinates of the point [\cvec{x}] \in 
P^n(F) are written [\cvec{x}] = [x_0 : x_1 : \dots : x_n] , the colons recording that only the ratios are determined: for every \lambda 
e 0, [x_0 : x_1 : \dots : x_n] = [\lambda x_0 : \lambda x_1 : \dots : \lambda x_n] , and not all of x_0, \dots, x_n are zero. Coordinates run from 0. In F^{n+1} we index the entries and the standard basis from 0, writing \cvec{x} = (x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n) and \cvec{e}_0, \dots, \cvec{e}_n, and every projective section of this chapter does the same. Subscripts start at 1 everywhere else in the book; the exception pays for itself here, because it keeps the n of 
P^n(F) equal to the dimension while the coordinates number n+1. Examples. - 
P^0(F) = 
P(F^1) has exactly one point, [1], since every nonzero scalar is a nonzero multiple of 1. Its dimension is 0, as a single point should have. - 
P^1(F) consists of the points [1 : a] for a \in F, all distinct, together with the single point [0 : 1]. Indeed if x_0 
e 0 then [x_0 : x_1] = [1 : x_1/x_0], and if x_0 = 0 then x_1 
e 0 and [0 : x_1] = [0:1]. - 
P^1(
F_2) = \{[1:0], [1:1], [0:1]\} has three points. The three lines through the origin of 
F_2^2 are \Span((1,0)), \Span((1,1)), \Span((0,1)), matching @prp-projective-points-are-lines. - The degenerate case 
P(\{\elem{0}\}) = \emptyset. It is worth keeping, because intersections produce it. Nonexample by minimal change. Over 
R, replace the relation by \elem{x} \approx \elem{y} when \elem{y} = \lambda\elem{x} with \lambda > 0. This is still an equivalence relation, but the quotient is not 
P(V): every projective point [\elem{x}] splits into the two classes of \elem{x} and -\elem{x}. The clause that fails is the one allowing every nonzero \lambda, and what is lost is precisely the identification of a line with itself traversed backwards. A single homogeneous coordinate means nothing. The expression “x_1 = 3” is not a statement about a point of 
P^n(F), since [1:3:0] = [2:6:0] and the second coordinate changed. Only two kinds of statement survive scaling: a ratio such as x_1/x_0 where x_0 
e 0, and the vanishing or nonvanishing of a homogeneous expression, such as x_1 = 0 or x_0x_2 - x_1^2 = 0. Whenever a formula below names a coordinate, check that it survives replacing \cvec{x} by \lambda\cvec{x}. The affine chart, and where the missing points live Here is the theorem that makes the construction worth doing: projective space is an affine space plus a smaller projective space. [The Standard Affine Chart] Let n \ge 1 and let  egin{aligned} U_0 &= \{[x_0 : \dots : x_n] \in 
P^n(F) : x_0 
e 0\}, \ H_{\infty} &= \{[x_0 : \dots : x_n] \in 
P^n(F) : x_0 = 0\} . \end{aligned} Then: 1. both conditions are independent of the representative, and 
P^n(F) = U_0 \sqcup H_{\infty}, a disjoint union; 2. the map \iota \colon F^n 	o U_0, \iota(a_1, \dots, a_n) = [1 : a_1 : \dots : a_n], is a bijection, with inverse [x_0 : \dots : x_n] \mapsto (x_1/x_0, \dots, x_n/x_0); 3. H_{\infty} = 
P(W) with W = \{\cvec{x} \in F^{n+1} : x_0 = 0\}, so H_{\infty} has dimension n-1, and [0 : x_1 : \dots : x_n] \mapsto [x_1 : \dots : x_n] is a bijection H_{\infty} 	o 
P^{n-1}(F). U_0 is the standard affine chart and H_{\infty} the hyperplane at infinity. Scaling multiplies x_0 by a nonzero number, so it cannot create or destroy a zero there: that single observation makes both halves well defined. On the half where x_0 
e 0 we may normalize x_0 to 1, and once x_0 = 1 the remaining coordinates are no longer ambiguous, which is why the affine points come back one for one. On the other half x_0 carries no information at all, so it may be deleted, and what is left is one dimension smaller. (a) If \cvec{y} = \lambda\cvec{x} with \lambda 
e 0 then y_0 = \lambda x_0, and a product of two elements of a field is zero only if one of them is, so y_0 = 0 exactly when x_0 = 0. Hence both defining conditions depend only on the point. Every point satisfies exactly one of them, so the union is disjoint and exhausts 
P^n(F). (b) Well defined: (1, a_1, \dots, a_n) 
e \cvec{0}, and its zeroth entry is 1 
e 0, so \iota(\cvec{a}) \in U_0. Injective: if [1 : \cvec{a}] = [1 : \cvec{a}'] then (1, \cvec{a}') = \lambda(1, \cvec{a}) for some \lambda 
e 0; comparing zeroth entries gives \lambda = 1, hence \cvec{a}' = \cvec{a}. Surjective: let [\cvec{x}] \in U_0, so x_0 
e 0 and x_0^{-1} exists. Then x_0^{-1}\cvec{x} = (1, x_1/x_0, \dots, x_n/x_0), so [\cvec{x}] = \iota(x_1/x_0, \dots, x_n/x_0). The displayed formula for the inverse is exactly this computation, and it is independent of the representative because replacing \cvec{x} by \lambda\cvec{x} multiplies numerator and denominator of each ratio by \lambda. (c) W is a subspace of F^{n+1}, being the kernel of the linear functional \cvec{x} \mapsto x_0, and \dim W = n by the Rank-Nullity Theorem (@thm-rank-nullity), the functional being nonzero and hence surjective onto F (@prp-nonzero-functional-surjective). A nonzero \cvec{x} has x_0 = 0 exactly when \cvec{x} \in W \setminus \{\cvec{0}\}, so H_{\infty} = 
P(W) and \dim H_{\infty} = n - 1 by @def-projective-space. The stated map is well defined, because deleting the zeroth coordinate turns \lambda\cvec{x} into \lambda times the deletion and cannot produce \cvec{0} from a nonzero \cvec{x} with x_0 = 0; it is injective and surjective because inserting a zeroth coordinate 0 inverts it. This proves the theorem. For n = 2 the statement reads: the projective plane is the affine plane together with a projective line. Writing it out, every point of 
P^2(F) is exactly one of [1 : a : b] \ \ (a, b \in F), \qquad [0 : 1 : m] \ \ (m \in F), \qquad [0 : 0 : 1] , the first family being the affine plane through \iota, and the last two being the line at infinity H_\infty \cong 
P^1(F), which has \lvert F vert + 1 points when F is finite. The label m is chosen deliberately: the next proposition shows [0:1:m] is the point where all affine lines of slope m meet. [Completing an Affine Line] Let a_1, a_2 \in F be not both zero, let b \in F, and let L = \{(y_1, y_2) \in F^2 : a_1y_1 + a_2y_2 = b\} , a flat of dimension 1 in 
A^2 by @thm-flat-is-solution-set, the single row (a_1, a_2) being nonzero, with direction space \Span((-a_2, a_1)). Let \varphi(x_0,x_1,x_2) = a_1x_1 + a_2x_2 - bx_0 and  ar L = 
P(\ker\varphi) \subseteq 
P^2(F). Then: 1.  ar L is a projective line; 2. \iota(L) =  ar L \cap U_0, so  ar L contains a faithful copy of L; 3.  ar L \setminus U_0 is the single point [0 : -a_2 : a_1]; 4. two such lines L, L' have the same direction space if and only if  ar L and  ar{L'} meet H_{\infty} in the same point. (a) \varphi is linear and nonzero, since \varphi(0,1,0) = a_1 and \varphi(0,0,1) = a_2 are not both zero. So \varphi is surjective onto F (@prp-nonzero-functional-surjective) and \dim\ker\varphi = 3 - 1 = 2 by @thm-rank-nullity. Hence  ar L = 
P(\ker\varphi) has dimension 1. (b) A point of U_0 is \iota(y_1,y_2) = [1 : y_1 : y_2] by @thm-affine-chart (b), and \varphi(1, y_1, y_2) = a_1y_1 + a_2y_2 - b. This vanishes exactly when (y_1,y_2) \in L. Since \varphi is homogeneous of degree 1, the vanishing does not depend on the representative. (c) A point of  ar L \setminus U_0 has x_0 = 0 and a_1x_1 + a_2x_2 = 0 with (x_1,x_2) 
e (0,0). The solution set of that single nontrivial equation in F^2 is \Span((-a_2,a_1)), of dimension 1, so there is exactly one such projective point, namely [0 : -a_2 : a_1]. (d) By (c) the point in question is [0 : -a_2 : a_1], which by @prp-projective-points-are-lines determines and is determined by \Span((-a_2,a_1)), the direction space of L. This proves the proposition. Now return to the hook. The lines L_1 : y_2 - y_1 = 0 and L_2 : y_2 - y_1 = 1 have (a_1, a_2) = (-1, 1) and b = 0 respectively b = 1, so  ar L_1 : x_2 - x_1 = 0, \qquad  ar L_2 : x_2 - x_1 - x_0 = 0 . Subtracting the two equations gives x_0 = 0, and then x_2 = x_1 with (x_1,x_2) 
e (0,0). So  ar L_1 \cap  ar L_2 = \{[0 : 1 : 1]\} , exactly one point, and it lies on the line at infinity. By @prp-completing-an-affine-line (c) that point is [0 : -a_2 : a_1] = [0 : -1 : -1] = [0:1:1] for both lines, which is their common direction \Span((1,1)) read as a point. Two parallel lines meet at their shared direction, and nowhere else. In 
P^2(
R), which point of the line at infinity do all the vertical affine lines y_1 = c pass through, and which point do all lines of slope m pass through?
