R and identify it. (a) \Q^2 = -\I_2, so A is closed under multiplication and is a subalgebra containing \I_2, of dimension 2. Every nonzero element x\I_2 + y\Q has determinant x^2 + y^2 > 0, hence is invertible in M_2(
R), and its inverse (x^2+y^2)^{-1}(x\I_2 - y\Q) lies in A. So every nonzero left ideal contains an invertible element and hence equals A; the only left ideals are \{\O\} and A, and each has a complementary left ideal (the other one). So A is semisimple. (b) A product with \sum n_i^2 = 2 must be 
R 	imes 
R, which contains the nonzero element (1, 0) with (1,0)(0,1) = (0,0); but in A the product of two nonzero elements is nonzero, since both are invertible. So no such isomorphism exists. The hypothesis that fails is algebraic closure: 
R is not algebraically closed. (c) By (a) every nonzero element of A is invertible, and its inverse again lies in A, so A is a division algebra over 
R; it is a copy of 
C, the map x\I_2 + y\Q \mapsto x + yi being a bijective algebra homomorphism. This is the D_1 that would appear in the quoted Wedderburn–Artin form of A.

title: 23.7 Group Representations
content:
Group Representations Sections 01–06 studied an algebra of operators in the abstract. A group is not an algebra — its elements cannot be added — but a group can be made to act by operators, and then the operators it produces span an algebra. This section sets up that translation: a representation of a group G over F is the same thing as a representation of the group algebra F[G], so everything proved about algebras applies at once. The section’s main theorem, Maschke’s, says when the resulting algebra is semisimple, and its hypothesis on the field is not decoration: we exhibit a group and a field where the conclusion fails outright. Throughout, G is a finite group, written multiplicatively, with its identity element written 1, and F is a field. All vector spaces are finite-dimensional over F. Where a statement needs F to be 
C, or needs a condition on \operatorname{char} F, the statement says so. Letting a group act by operators The book’s groups so far have been groups of matrices or of permutations: \GL_n(F) (@exm-groups), the symmetric group S_n, the classical groups of Chapter 14. Such a group arrives with its linear algebra attached. An abstract group does not. If all we know about G is its multiplication table, the only way to bring linear algebra to bear is to manufacture operators out of it. The manufacture has one requirement. Group multiplication must become composition of operators, since composition is the only product on \cL(V), and every group element must become an invertible operator, since every group element can be undone. That is exactly the definition of a homomorphism into the group \GL(V) of invertible operators on V, a group under composition by the same argument that makes \GL_n(F) one (@exm-groups). A representation is a way of realizing the elements of a group as invertible operators, so that multiplying in the group means composing the operators. [Representation of a group] Let G be a group, F a field, and V a finite-dimensional vector space over F. A representation of G on V over F is a group homomorphism ho \colon G 	o \GL(V), that is, a map assigning to each g \in G an invertible operator ho(g) on V such that ho(gh) = ho(g)ho(h) for all g, h \in G. The space V is the representation space, and \dim V is the degree of ho. The representation is faithful if ho is injective. When V = F^n we speak of a matrix representation and write ho(g) \in \GL_n(F). In words: to give a representation is to attach to each g \in G an invertible operator ho(g) on one fixed space V, in such a way that the operator attached to a product is the composition of the operators attached to the factors. Two conditions that look like extra demands are already implied by @thm-homomorphism-basic-properties: ho(1) = \id_V, and ho(g^{-1}) = ho(g)^{-1} for every g. So we never have to check them. Note what is not required. Nothing says ho is injective, and nothing says the operators ho(g) are distinct. The constant map g \mapsto \id_V is a perfectly good representation; it simply carries no information about G. Examples. Fix a finite group G and a field F. - The trivial representation. V = F and ho(g) = \id_F for every g. It is a representation because \id_F \cdot \id_F = \id_F, matching ho(gh) = ho(g)ho(h). Its degree is 1. This is the degenerate case, and it is not a curiosity: it is one of the basic building blocks, and in Section 08 it is the piece that detects averages. - The sign representation of S_n. V = F and ho(\sigma) = \sgn(\sigma)\,\id_F, where \sgn is the sign of a permutation (@def-sign-permutation). It is a homomorphism because \sgn(\sigma	au) = \sgn(\sigma)\sgn(	au) (@thm-sign-multiplicative). Over a field of characteristic 2 we have -1 = 1, so the sign representation coincides with the trivial one; over 
C it does not. It is faithful on S_2, whose two elements have signs 1 and -1, but not on S_n for n \ge 3, where \sgn((1\ 2\ 3)) = 1 = \sgn(\id) while (1\ 2\ 3) 
e \id. - The permutation representation of S_n. V = F^n and ho(\sigma)\cvec{e}_i = \cvec{e}_{\sigma(i)}, extended linearly (@thm-linear-map-from-any-basis). Then ho(\sigma)ho(	au)\cvec{e}_i = ho(\sigma)\cvec{e}_{	au(i)} = \cvec{e}_{\sigma(	au(i))} = ho(\sigma	au)\cvec{e}_i, where the last step uses that \sigma	au means “first 	au, then \sigma”. So ho is a homomorphism, and each ho(\sigma) is invertible with inverse ho(\sigma^{-1}). The matrix of ho(\sigma) in the standard basis is the permutation matrix \P_\sigma of @def-permutation-matrix. The same recipe works for any subgroup of S_n. - The rotation representation of 
Z/n
Z over 
R. V = 
R^2 and ho([k]) is rotation by 2\pi k/n, with matrix  egin{pmatrix} \cos(2\pi k/n) & -\sin(2\pi k/n) \ \sin(2\pi k/n) & \cos(2\pi k/n)\end{pmatrix}. Composing rotations adds angles, so ho([k])ho([l]) = ho([k+l]); and rotating by 2\pi n/n = 2\pi is the identity, so the recipe does not depend on the representative k. For n \ge 3 this representation has no invariant line. A line invariant under ho([1]) would give that matrix a real eigenvalue (@prp-one-dimensional-invariant), but with c = \cos(2\pi/n) and s = \sin(2\pi/n) its characteristic polynomial is x^2 - 2cx + 1, of discriminant 4c^2 - 4 = -4s^2, which is negative because 0 < 2\pi/n < \pi forces s 
e 0 when n \ge 3. (The quarter-turn case is @exm-rotation-invariant-subspaces.) Section 04 turned this into the standard warning about Schur’s lemma over 
R. - The regular representation. V = F[G], the group algebra of @def-group-algebra: the free vector space on the set G (@def-free-vector-space), with basis \{\delta_g : g \in G\} and multiplication determined by \delta_g\delta_h = \delta_{gh}. Its dimension is \lvert Gvert. Put ho_{\mathrm{reg}}(g)\delta_h = \delta_{gh}, extended linearly. Then ho_{\mathrm{reg}}(g)ho_{\mathrm{reg}}(g')\delta_h = \delta_{gg'h} = ho_{\mathrm{reg}}(gg')\delta_h, so ho_{\mathrm{reg}} is a homomorphism, and ho_{\mathrm{reg}}(g) is invertible with inverse ho_{\mathrm{reg}}(g^{-1}). It is faithful: if ho_{\mathrm{reg}}(g) = \id then \delta_g = ho_{\mathrm{reg}}(g)\delta_1 = \delta_1, so g = 1 because the \delta_h are distinct basis vectors. Its degree is \lvert Gvert. Nonexample by minimal change. Keep V = F^2 and G = 
Z/4
Z, and try ho([k]) =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & k \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} over 
Q. Each matrix is invertible, and ho([k])ho([l]) =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & k+l \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}, so multiplicativity holds on representatives. But the recipe is not well defined on 
Z/4
Z: the class [0] is also [4], and  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} 
e \I_2. The clause that fails is that ho must be a function on G. Over 
F_2 the same recipe on 
Z/2
Z is well defined, because  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \I_2 there; we return to that example when Maschke’s theorem breaks. A representation need not remember the group. The trivial representation of any group is a representation, and it forgets everything. Conversely, a noninjective ho can still be useful: the sign representation of S_n has a huge kernel yet separates even from odd permutations. When a statement needs ho to see all of G, it must say faithful; none of the theorems below does. Is ho \colon 
Z/3
Z 	o \GL_1(
R) = 
R \setminus \{0\}, ho([k]) = (-1)^k, a representation? No: it is not well defined. We have [0] = [3] in 
Z/3
Z, but (-1)^0 = 1 while (-1)^3 = -1. Equivalently, a representation of degree 1 is a homomorphism 
Z/3
Z 	o 
R\setminus\{0\}, and ho([1])^3 = ho([0]) = 1 forces ho([1]) = 1, since 1 is the only real cube root of 1. So the only degree-1 real representation of 
Z/3
Z is the trivial one. Subrepresentations, equivalence, and irreducibility Having made operators, we ask the question this book always asks of a family of operators: can the space be broken into smaller pieces that the family preserves? Chapter 9 called such a piece an invariant subspace (@def-invariant-subspace). Here the family is \{ho(g) : g \in G\}. [Subrepresentation] Let ho be a representation of G on V. A subspace U \subseteq V is G-invariant if ho(g)\elem{u} \in U for every g \in G and every \elem{u} \in U. In that case the restrictions ho(g)|_U define a representation ho|_U of G on U, the subrepresentation of ho on U. Two checks make this legitimate. First, ho(g)|_U really is an operator on U, by invariance. Second, it is invertible on U: applying invariance to g^{-1} gives ho(g)^{-1}U = ho(g^{-1})U \subseteq U, so ho(g)|_U has a two-sided inverse on U, namely ho(g^{-1})|_U. Multiplicativity is inherited. The subspaces \{\elem{0}\} and V are always G-invariant; we call them the trivial invariant subspaces. [Equivalence of representations] Let ho and ho' be representations of G on V and V', over the same field. A linear map S \colon V 	o V' intertwines ho and ho' if S\,ho(g) = ho'(g)\,S \qquad 	ext{for every } g \in G . The representations are equivalent, written ho \cong ho', if some intertwining S is an isomorphism; equivalently, if ho'(g) = Sho(g)S^{-1} for all g. Equivalence is what “the same representation written in another basis” means. Indeed, if V = V' = F^n and S is an invertible matrix, then ho'(g) = Sho(g)S^{-1} is simultaneous similarity of the whole family \{ho(g)\} by one matrix. It is an equivalence relation: \id_V intertwines ho with itself; if S intertwines ho with ho' and is invertible then S^{-1} intertwines ho' with ho, since Sho(g) = ho'(g)S gives ho(g)S^{-1} = S^{-1}ho'(g); and a composition of intertwining isomorphisms intertwines. [Irreducible representation] A representation ho of G on V is irreducible if V 
e \{\elem{0}\} and the only G-invariant subspaces of V are \{\elem{0}\} and V. A representation with V 
e \{\elem{0}\} that is not irreducible is reducible. Read the two clauses separately. The zero space is excluded by decree, exactly as 1 is excluded from the primes: keeping it would break every statement of the form “every representation is built from irreducible ones”. The second clause is the real content. Examples and a nonexample. - Every representation of degree 1 is irreducible: a one-dimensional space has no subspaces but \{\elem{0}\} and itself. - The permutation representation of S_3 on F^3 is reducible for every F. The line L = \Span(\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2 + \cvec{e}_3) is S_3-invariant, since ho(\sigma)(\cvec{e}_1+\cvec{e}_2+\cvec{e}_3) = \cvec{e}_{\sigma(1)}+\cvec{e}_{\sigma(2)}+\cvec{e}_{\sigma(3)} = \cvec{e}_1+\cvec{e}_2+\cvec{e}_3, the same three basis vectors in another order. And L 
e \{\cvec{0}\}, L 
e F^3. - So is the sum-zero subspace W = \{\cvec{x} \in F^3 : x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0\}, of dimension 2: permuting the coordinates of \cvec{x} does not change their sum. We will see below that over 
C the subrepresentation on W is irreducible; this is the standard representation of S_3. - Nonexample by minimal change. Replace S_3 by the subgroup H = \{\id, (1\ 2)\} \subseteq S_3 and keep V = F^3. Then \Span(\cvec{e}_3) is H-invariant, though it is not S_3-invariant. Invariance depends on the whole group, not on one element of it. Finally, the operation that puts representations together. If ho_1, ho_2 are representations of G on V_1, V_2, their direct sum is the representation ho_1 \oplus ho_2 on V_1 \oplus V_2 given by (ho_1\oplusho_2)(g)(\elem{v}_1, \elem{v}_2) = (ho_1(g)\elem{v}_1, ho_2(g)\elem{v}_2). In a basis adapted to the decomposition its matrix is block diagonal, ho_1(g) \oplus ho_2(g). Conversely, if V = U \oplus W with both summands G-invariant, then the map U \oplus W 	o V, (\elem{u}, \elem{w}) \mapsto \elem{u} + \elem{w}, is an isomorphism intertwining ho|_U \oplus ho|_W with ho, so ho \cong ho|_U \oplus ho|_W. So “decomposing a representation” and “finding an invariant complement” are the same task. Representations of G and representations of F[G] Here is the bridge that puts Sections 01–06 to work. The group algebra F[G] was built in @def-group-algebra precisely so that the next theorem is true. [Representations of G are representations of F[G]] Let G be a finite group, F a field, and V a finite-dimensional vector space over F. The assignment ho \ \longmapsto \ \widetildeho, \qquad \widetildeho\Bigl(\sum_{g \in G} a_g \delta_g\Bigr) \coloneqq \sum_{g \in G} a_g\,ho(g), is a bijection from the set of representations ho \colon G 	o \GL(V) onto the set of algebra homomorphisms F[G] 	o \End(V) (@def-algebra-homomorphism) — that is, onto the ways of making V an F[G]-space in the sense of @def-representation-of-an-algebra. Moreover a subspace U \subseteq V is G-invariant for ho if and only if \widetildeho(a)U \subseteq U for every a \in F[G]. An element of F[G] is a formal linear combination of group elements, so a linear map out of F[G] is determined by, and may be prescribed freely on, the basis \{\delta_g\}. The only thing to check is that “multiplicative on the basis” upgrades to “multiplicative everywhere”, and that is bilinearity of both products. The inverse map recovers ho by restricting to the basis; the one point needing care is why \widetildeho(\delta_g) is automatically invertible, which is where \delta_g\delta_{g^{-1}} = \delta_1 earns its keep. Let ho \colon G 	o \GL(V) be a representation. The formula defines a linear map \widetildeho \colon F[G] 	o \End(V), because \{\delta_g\} is a basis of F[G] and a linear map may be prescribed on a basis (@thm-linear-map-from-any-basis). It sends \delta_1 to ho(1) = \id_V (@thm-homomorphism-basic-properties). For multiplicativity, take a = \sum_g a_g\delta_g and b = \sum_h b_h\delta_h. Multiplication in F[G] and composition in \End(V) are both bilinear, so  egin{aligned} \widetildeho(ab) &= \widetildeho\Bigl(\sum_{g, h} a_g b_h\, \delta_{gh}\Bigr) = \sum_{g, h} a_g b_h\, ho(gh) \ &= \sum_{g, h} a_g b_h\, ho(g)ho(h) = \Bigl(\sum_g a_g ho(g)\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_h b_h ho(h)\Bigr) = \widetildeho(a)\widetildeho(b), \end{aligned} where the third equality is the homomorphism property of ho. Hence \widetildeho is an algebra homomorphism. Conversely, let \varphi \colon F[G] 	o \End(V) be an algebra homomorphism, and set ho(g) \coloneqq \varphi(\delta_g). Since \delta_1 is the identity of F[G] (@def-group-algebra) and \id_V is the identity of \End(V), the unital clause of @def-algebra-homomorphism gives \varphi(\delta_1) = \id_V. Then ho(g)ho(h) = \varphi(\delta_g\delta_h) = \varphi(\delta_{gh}) = ho(gh). In particular ho(g)ho(g^{-1}) = \varphi(\delta_1) = \id_V and likewise in the other order, so each ho(g) is invertible and ho maps into \GL(V). Thus ho is a representation, and \widetildeho = \varphi because the two agree on the basis \{\delta_g\} and both are linear. Since also \widetildeho(\delta_g) = ho(g), the two constructions are mutually inverse, and the assignment is a bijection. For the last sentence, suppose U is G-invariant. For a = \sum_g a_g\delta_g and \elem{u} \in U, each ho(g)\elem{u} lies in U, and U is a subspace, so \widetildeho(a)\elem{u} = \sum_g a_g ho(g)\elem{u} \in U. Conversely, if \widetildeho(a)U \subseteq U for all a, take a = \delta_g. This proves the theorem. So the two languages are interchangeable, and we use whichever is shorter. A G-invariant subspace is an F[G]-invariant subspace; an irreducible representation of G on V is exactly a simple F[G]-space in the sense of @def-simple-module; and a map intertwining two representations of G is exactly an F[G]-map in the sense of @def-intertwining-map, since the condition Sho(g) = ho'(g)S for all g extends by linearity to all of F[G]. In particular Schur’s lemma (@thm-schurs-lemma) applies verbatim to irreducible representations of groups, and we use it that way in Section 08. Working with F[G] rather than with G buys one thing that matters: the ability to add group elements. Every averaging argument below lives in F[G], not in G. Chapter 10 §07 made the same move for a single operator, replacing T by the algebra F[T] and the space by an F[x]-module. Maschke’s theorem We now know that a reducible representation has a proper nonzero invariant subspace U. To break V into pieces we need more: an invariant complement, a G-invariant W with V = U \oplus W. An ordinary complement always exists (@thm-complement-exists), but it has no reason to be invariant. The idea for repairing it is the one move this chapter uses over and over. Start with an object that is not invariant, and average its G-translates. The average is invariant because translating it permutes the terms of the sum. Averaging divides by \lvert Gvert, and that is the whole hypothesis. [When the group order is invertible] Let F be a field and m a positive integer. Then m \cdot 1_F 
e 0 in F if and only if \operatorname{char} F does not divide m. If \operatorname{char} F = 0, then m \cdot 1_F 
e 0 for every positive integer m (@def-characteristic), and 0 divides no positive integer, so both sides of the equivalence hold. Assume from now on that p \coloneqq \operatorname{char} F > 0, so p is the smallest positive integer with p\cdot 1_F = 0. (\Rightarrow) We prove the contrapositive: if p \mid m, then m\cdot 1_F = 0. Write m = qp with q \ge 1. By @lem-integer-multiples, m\cdot 1_F = (qp)\cdot 1_F = (q\cdot 1_F)(p\cdot 1_F) = (q\cdot 1_F)\cdot 0 = 0. (\Leftarrow) Suppose, for a contradiction, that some positive integer m has m\cdot 1_F = 0 and p 
mid m. Choose such an m as small as possible. Now m 
e p, since p \mid p, and m > p, since p is the smallest positive integer killing 1_F. So m - p is a positive integer, and by @lem-integer-multiples (m - p)\cdot 1_F + p \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F = 0 , whence (m-p)\cdot 1_F = 0. Also p 
mid m - p, for otherwise p would divide (m-p) + p = m. This contradicts the minimality of m. This proves the lemma. Maschke’s Theorem Let G be a finite group and F a field whose characteristic does not divide \lvert Gvert. Let ho be a representation of G on a finite-dimensional space V over F, and let U \subseteq V be a G-invariant subspace. Then there is a G-invariant subspace W \subseteq V with V = U \oplus W . Pick any projection P of V onto U; its kernel is a complement, but the wrong one, because P need not commute with the ho(g). Repair it by averaging the conjugates ho(g)Pho(g)^{-1} over g \in G. ① Each conjugate is again a projection onto U, because U is invariant. ② Their average P_0 is therefore again a projection onto U — here we divide by \lvert Gvert. ③ Conjugating P_0 by ho(h) only permutes the terms of the sum, so P_0 commutes with every ho(h), and then its kernel is invariant. Write n = \lvert Gvert. By hypothesis and @lem-group-order-invertible, n \cdot 1_F 
e 0, so the scalar 	frac{1}{n} \coloneqq (n\cdot 1_F)^{-1} exists in F. By @thm-complement-exists there is a subspace W_0 with V = U \oplus W_0; let P \in \cL(V) be the projection onto U along W_0 (@thm-projection-direct-sum (b)), so \im P = U and P\elem{u} = \elem{u} for all \elem{u} \in U. Define P_0 \coloneqq  rac{1}{n}\sum_{g \in G} ho(g)\, P\, ho(g)^{-1} \ \in \cL(V). Step 1: \im P_0 \subseteq U. Let \elem{v} \in V and g \in G. Then Pho(g)^{-1}\elem{v} \in \im P = U, and U is G-invariant, so ho(g)Pho(g)^{-1}\elem{v} \in U. A subspace is closed under sums and scalar multiples, so P_0\elem{v} \in U. Step 2: P_0\elem{u} = \elem{u} for \elem{u} \in U. Let \elem{u} \in U and g \in G. Since U is G-invariant and ho(g)^{-1} = ho(g^{-1}), we have ho(g)^{-1}\elem{u} \in U, so Pho(g)^{-1}\elem{u} = ho(g)^{-1}\elem{u} and hence ho(g)Pho(g)^{-1}\elem{u} = \elem{u}. Summing over the n elements of G gives \sum_g ho(g)Pho(g)^{-1}\elem{u} = (n\cdot 1_F)\elem{u}, and multiplying by 	frac1n gives P_0\elem{u} = \elem{u}. By Steps 1 and 2, P_0\elem{v} \in U for every \elem{v}, and P_0 fixes U pointwise; therefore P_0^2\elem{v} = P_0(P_0\elem{v}) = P_0\elem{v}, so P_0 is a projection (@def-projection-operator) with \im P_0 = U. Step 3: P_0 commutes with every ho(h). Fix h \in G. Then ho(h)P_0ho(h)^{-1} =  rac1n \sum_{g \in G} ho(hg)\,P\,ho(hg)^{-1}, using ho(h)ho(g) = ho(hg) and ho(g)^{-1}ho(h)^{-1} = (ho(h)ho(g))^{-1} = ho(hg)^{-1}. The map g \mapsto hg is a bijection G 	o G, with inverse g \mapsto h^{-1}g by @thm-group-basic-properties, so as g runs over G so does hg, and the sum is unchanged: ho(h)P_0ho(h)^{-1} = P_0. Multiplying on the right by ho(h) gives ho(h)P_0 = P_0ho(h). Step 4: conclusion. Put W \coloneqq \ker P_0. By @thm-projection-direct-sum (a), V = \im P_0 \oplus \ker P_0 = U \oplus W. And W is G-invariant: if P_0\elem{w} = \elem{0} and h \in G, then by Step 3, P_0ho(h)\elem{w} = ho(h)P_0\elem{w} = \elem{0}, so ho(h)\elem{w} \in W. This proves the theorem. Two hypotheses did real work, and it is worth naming where. Finiteness of G is what makes the sum \sum_{g} a finite sum, hence an operator at all. The condition on the characteristic is what makes 	frac1n exist, and Step 2 is where it is spent: without the division, the computation in Step 2 gives \sum_g ho(g)Pho(g)^{-1}\elem{u} = (n\cdot 1_F)\elem{u}, which is \elem{0} for every \elem{u} \in U when \operatorname{char} F divides n. The unnormalized sum then annihilates U instead of fixing it, and there is nothing to rescue. Both failures are real, not artifacts of the proof. [Maschke fails when the characteristic divides the order] Let p be a prime, F = 
F_p, G = 
Z/p
Z, and V = 
F_p^2. Define ho([k]) \coloneqq  egin{pmatrix} 1 & k \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in \GL_2(
F_p). Show that ho is a well-defined representation, that U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1) is G-invariant, and that U has no G-invariant complement. Well defined. The entry k is read in 
F_p, so the matrix depends only on k modulo p; and  egin{psmallmatrix}1&k\0&1\end{psmallmatrix} egin{psmallmatrix}1&l\0&1\end{psmallmatrix} =  egin{psmallmatrix}1&k+l\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}, so ho([k])ho([l]) = ho([k]+[l]). Each matrix is invertible, with inverse ho([-k]). So ho is a representation of the additive group 
Z/p
Z. Here \lvert Gvert = p = \operatorname{char}
F_p, so the characteristic does divide the order and the hypothesis of @thm-maschke fails. The invariant line. ho([k])\cvec{e}_1 = \cvec{e}_1 for every k, so U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1) is G-invariant, and U 
e \{\cvec{0}\}, V. No invariant complement. If V = U \oplus W, then \dim W = 2 - 1 = 1 by @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim, so W = \Span(\cvec{v}) for some \cvec{v} = (a, b) 
e \cvec{0}; and b 
e 0, since b = 0 would force a 
e 0 and W = \Span(\cvec{e}_1) = U, which is not a complement of itself. Suppose W is G-invariant. Then ho([1])\cvec{v} = (a + b,\, b) must be a scalar multiple \lambda\cvec{v} = (\lambda a, \lambda b). Comparing second coordinates and dividing by b 
e 0 gives \lambda = 1; comparing first coordinates then gives a + b = a, so b = 0, a contradiction. Hence U has no G-invariant complement. In fact U is the only nontrivial invariant subspace, so V is neither irreducible nor a direct sum of irreducibles. Do not drop finiteness either. Let G = 
Z (infinite) act on 
Q^2 by ho(k) =  egin{psmallmatrix}1&k\0&1\end{psmallmatrix} — now well defined, since 
Z has no relations to respect. The computation just made, with b 
e 0 in 
Q, again shows \Span(\cvec{e}_1) is invariant with no invariant complement, and here the characteristic is 0. Averaging over 
Z is not an option: the sum has infinitely many terms. Once one invariant complement can always be found, the full decomposition follows by induction. [Complete Reducibility of Group Representations] Let G be a finite group and F a field with \operatorname{char} F 
mid \lvert Gvert — for instance F = 
C. Then every representation ho of G on a nonzero finite-dimensional space V over F decomposes as V = V_1 \oplus V_2 \oplus \dots \oplus V_r with each V_i a G-invariant subspace on which the subrepresentation is irreducible. We argue by strong induction on \dim V \ge 1 (@thm-strong-induction). If ho is irreducible, take r = 1 and V_1 = V. Otherwise V has a G-invariant subspace U with U 
e \{\elem{0}\} and U 
e V. By @thm-maschke there is a G-invariant W with V = U \oplus W, and W 
e \{\elem{0}\} since U 
e V. Both \dim U and \dim W are at least 1, and since U \cap W = \{\elem{0}\} (@thm-direct-sum-criteria) the dimension formula @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim gives \dim U + \dim W = \dim V; hence both are smaller than \dim V. The induction hypothesis decomposes U and W into irreducible invariant subspaces, and concatenating the two lists decomposes V, because a subspace of U invariant under ho|_U is invariant under ho. This proves the corollary. In the language of Section 03, the corollary says that F[G] acts semisimply on every representation (@def-semisimple-algebra, @thm-semisimple-iff-sum-of-simples); applied to the regular representation, it says F[G] is a semisimple algebra. Section 06’s structure theorem then applies to 
C[G], and Section 08 cashes that in. Where exactly does the proof of @cor-complete-reducibility use that V 
e \{\elem{0}\}? In the base of the induction and in the meaning of the conclusion. If V = \{\elem{0}\} it is not irreducible (@def-irreducible-representation excludes the zero space) and it has no nonzero invariant subspace to split off, so neither branch of the argument applies. The usual convention is that \{\elem{0}\} is the empty direct sum, r = 0; the corollary is stated with V 
e \{\elem{0}\} so that r \ge 1. Two families worked out We close with the two examples Section 08 will compute characters for. Both are over 
C, where @cor-complete-reducibility applies to every finite group. [The irreducible complex representations of a cyclic group] Let G = 
Z/n
Z and F = 
C. Determine all irreducible representations of G up to equivalence. Every irreducible is one-dimensional. Let ho be a representation of G on V 
e \{\elem{0}\} over 
C, and set A = ho([1]). By @thm-complex-operator-has-eigenvalue, A has an eigenvector \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}, say A\elem{v} = \lambda\elem{v}. The line L = \Span(\elem{v}) is invariant under A, hence under every power A^k = ho([k]), so L is G-invariant. If ho is irreducible then L = V, so \dim V = 1. (For abelian G the algebra 
C[G] is commutative, since \delta_g\delta_h = \delta_{gh} = \delta_{hg} = \delta_h\delta_g and multiplication is bilinear; so this is also @cor-abelian-irreducibles-are-lines read through @thm-representations-are-modules-over-the-group-algebra.) Listing them. A one-dimensional representation is a homomorphism \chi \colon 
Z/n
Z 	o 
C\setminus\{0\}, determined by z = \chi([1]), which must satisfy z^n = \chi([n]) = \chi([0]) = 1. So z is an n-th root of unity, z = \omega^k with \omega = e^{2\pi i/n} and 0 \le k \le n-1 (@exm-roots-of-unity). Conversely each such z does define a homomorphism \chi_k([j]) = \omega^{jk}: the recipe respects representatives because \omega^{n} = 1, and \omega^{(j+l)k} = \omega^{jk}\omega^{lk}. They are pairwise inequivalent. Two one-dimensional representations are equivalent exactly when they are equal, since on a one-dimensional space every operator is \lambda\,\id for a scalar \lambda, and S(\lambda\,\id)S^{-1} = \lambda\,\id for every isomorphism S. And \chi_k 
e \chi_l for 0 \le k < l \le n-1, because \chi_k([1]) = \omega^k 
e \omega^l = \chi_l([1]), the n-th roots of unity being distinct. So 
Z/n
Z has exactly n irreducible complex representations, all of degree 1, namely \chi_0, \dots, \chi_{n-1}. Their degrees satisfy \sum_k 1^2 = n = \lvert Gvert, the count @cor-dimension-count gives for the semisimple algebra 
C[G]. [The irreducible complex representations of the symmetric group on three letters] Write down three pairwise inequivalent irreducible complex representations of S_3, with explicit matrices for the two-dimensional one. Trivial and sign. ho_{\mathrm{triv}}(\sigma) = 1 and ho_{\mathrm{sgn}}(\sigma) = \sgn(\sigma), both on 
C, both irreducible because their degree is 1. They are inequivalent: ho_{\mathrm{triv}}((1\ 2)) = 1 
e -1 = ho_{\mathrm{sgn}}((1\ 2)). The standard representation. Take the permutation representation on 
C^3 and restrict it to the invariant plane W = \{\cvec{x} : x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0\}. A basis of W is \sB = (\cvec{f}_1, \cvec{f}_2) with \cvec{f}_1 = \cvec{e}_1 - \cvec{e}_2 and \cvec{f}_2 = \cvec{e}_2 - \cvec{e}_3: they lie in W, they are independent, and \dim W = 2 because W is the kernel of the surjective functional \cvec{x} \mapsto x_1+x_2+x_3 on 
C^3 (@thm-rank-nullity). With ho(\sigma)\cvec{e}_i = \cvec{e}_{\sigma(i)}:  egin{aligned} ho((1\ 2))\cvec{f}_1 &= \cvec{e}_2 - \cvec{e}_1 = -\cvec{f}_1, \ ho((1\ 2))\cvec{f}_2 &= \cvec{e}_1 - \cvec{e}_3 = \cvec{f}_1 + \cvec{f}_2, \ ho((1\ 2\ 3))\cvec{f}_1 &= \cvec{e}_2 - \cvec{e}_3 = \cvec{f}_2, \ ho((1\ 2\ 3))\cvec{f}_2 &= \cvec{e}_3 - \cvec{e}_1 = -\cvec{f}_1 - \cvec{f}_2 . \end{aligned} Writing R_\sigma \coloneqq ho(\sigma)|_W, the two matrices in the basis \sB are \mtx{R_{(1\ 2)}}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mtx{R_{(1\ 2\ 3)}}{\sB}{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. The remaining four matrices follow by multiplying: \I_2 for \id,  egin{psmallmatrix}0&-1\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix} for (1\ 3),  egin{psmallmatrix}1&0\1&-1\end{psmallmatrix} for (2\ 3), and  egin{psmallmatrix}-1&1\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix} for (1\ 3\ 2). Irreducibility. A proper nonzero invariant subspace of the plane W would be a line \Span(\cvec{v}), and \cvec{v} would be an eigenvector of both displayed matrices. The first has eigenvalues -1 and 1, with eigenvectors spanned by (1, 0) and (1, 2) respectively. The second has characteristic polynomial x^2 + x + 1, whose roots are the two primitive cube roots of unity; neither (1,0) nor (1,2) is an eigenvector of it, since  egin{psmallmatrix}0&-1\1&-1\end{psmallmatrix}(1,0) = (0,1) and  egin{psmallmatrix}0&-1\1&-1\end{psmallmatrix}(1,2) = (-2,-1) are not multiples of (1,0), (1,2). So there is no common eigenvector, and the standard representation is irreducible. Inequivalent. It has degree 2, the others degree 1, and equivalent representations act on spaces of the same dimension. The degrees satisfy 1^2 + 1^2 + 2^2 = 6 = \lvert S_3vert, which is the count @cor-dimension-count gives for the semisimple algebra 
C[S_3]. That count runs over all isomorphism classes of irreducible 
C[S_3]-spaces (@thm-wedderburn), and a further class would add at least 1 to a total already equal to 6; so these three are all of the irreducible complex representations of S_3. Section 08 reaches the same conclusion by counting conjugacy classes, which does not require the list to be found first. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. C, ho([k]) =  egin{pmatrix} \omega^k & 0 \ 0 & \omega^{-k}\end{pmatrix} with \omega = e^{\pi i/3}. 2. G = S_3, F =

Scalars commute with matrices, so ho(\sigma)ho(	au) = \sgn(\sigma	au)\P_{\sigma	au} = ho(\sigma	au), and ho(\sigma) is invertible because \P_\sigma is and \sgn(\sigma) 
e 0. 3. No. Taking transposes reverses products: ho(\sigma)ho(	au) = \P_\sigma	p\P_	au	p = (\P_	au\P_\sigma)	p = \P_{	au\sigma}	p = ho(	au\sigma). Since S_3 is not abelian this differs from ho(\sigma	au): with \sigma = (1\ 2), 	au = (1\ 3) we get 	au\sigma = (1\ 2\ 3)

(IP3). For \elem{v} 
e \elem{0}, each ho(g)\elem{v}

Z/3

So the three summands realize \chi_0, \chi_1, \chi_2: every irreducible representation of

Prove that every representation of degree 1 satisfies ho(ghg^{-1}h^{-1}) = 1 for all g, h \in G. 2. Deduce that the only degree-1 complex representation of G = S_3 other than the trivial one is the sign representation. So ho(ghg^{-1}h^{-1}) = ho(g)ho(h)ho(g)^{-1}ho(h)^{-1} = ho(g)ho(g)^{-1}ho(h)ho(h)^{-1} = 1, using @thm-homomorphism-basic-properties for the inverses. (b) Let ho have degree 1 over

Applying this product to each point, rightmost factor first: 1 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 3, and 3 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 1. So the product is (1\ 2\ 3). By (a), ho((1\ 2\ 3)) = 1, and then ho((1\ 3\ 2)) = ho((1\ 2\ 3))^{2} = 1. Let c = ho((1\ 2)). Since (1\ 2)^2 = \id, c^2 = 1, so c = \pm 1. Finally (1\ 3) = (1\ 2\ 3)(1\ 2) and (2\ 3) = (1\ 2)(1\ 2\ 3), so ho((1\ 3)) = ho((2\ 3)) = c as well. Thus ho is determined by c: for c = 1 it is trivial, and for c = -1 it agrees with \sgn on every element. Both values do occur, so there are exactly two. [C2: Maschke over a field of the right characteristic] Let G = 
Z/2

Q, find two G-invariant lines whose direct sum is V. 2. For F = 
F_2, prove that V has exactly one nontrivial G-invariant subspace, and conclude that @thm-maschke fails here. Which hypothesis is violated? 3. For F = 
F_3, decompose V into irreducible subrepresentations. (a) ho([1]) swaps the coordinates, so \cvec{u} = (1,1) and \cvec{w} = (1,-1) satisfy ho([1])\cvec{u} = \cvec{u} and ho([1])\cvec{w} = -\cvec{w}. F_2 = 2 = \lvert Gvert. (c) Over 
F_3, -1 = 2

By @thm-dual-map-properties (b),  egin{aligned} 	au(g)	au(h) &= T'S' = (ST)' =  igl(ho(h)^{-1}ho(g)^{-1} igr)' \ &=  igl((ho(g)ho(h))^{-1} igr)' =  igl(ho(gh)^{-1} igr)' = 	au(gh), \end{aligned} where the fourth equality is @thm-group-basic-properties (3) applied in \GL(V). e \{\elem{0}\}, so V 
e \{\elem{0}\} by @cor-dimension-dual-space. Let U be a G-invariant subspace of V with U 
e \{\elem{0}\} and U 
e V. By (b), U^{0} is G-invariant, and by @thm-dimension-annihilator, \dim U^{0} = \dim V - \dim U. title: 23.8 Characters and Orthogonality
content:
Characters and Orthogonality Complete reducibility (@cor-complete-reducibility) promises that every complex representation of a finite group breaks into irreducible pieces, but the promise is not constructive: it says nothing about which pieces, or how many of each. This section produces a small table of numbers that answers both questions. To each representation we attach one function G 	o 
C, its character, and we prove that the characters of the irreducible representations are an orthonormal basis of a space of functions we can compute the dimension of by counting. Everything a complex representation is, up to equivalence, is then read off from one row of numbers. Throughout, G is a finite group and the field is 
C. The hypothesis matters twice over: \operatorname{char}
C = 0 never divides \lvert Gvert, so @thm-maschke applies; and 
C is algebraically closed, so Schur’s lemma (@thm-schurs-lemma) gives that the only operators commuting with an irreducible representation are the scalars. The theory over a field whose characteristic divides \lvert G vert — modular representation theory — is a different subject, and this book does not enter it. Conjugacy classes Before characters we need the sets they are constant on. The book has met them only in an exercise of Section 1 (@exr-associative-algebras-c1), so we build them here. [Conjugate elements, conjugacy class] Let G be a group. Elements g, h \in G are conjugate if h = xgx^{-1} for some x \in G. The conjugacy class of g is C(g) \coloneqq \{ xgx^{-1} : x \in G \} . Conjugacy is an equivalence relation (@def-equivalence-relation): g = 1g1^{-1} gives reflexivity; if h = xgx^{-1}, then g = x^{-1}h(x^{-1})^{-1}, which gives symmetry using @thm-group-basic-properties; and if h = xgx^{-1} and k = yhy^{-1}, then k = (yx)g(yx)^{-1}, which gives transitivity. Hence the conjugacy classes are the equivalence classes, and by @thm-partition they partition G: every element lies in exactly one class. We write k for the number of conjugacy classes of G, a finite number since G is finite. In an abelian group xgx^{-1} = g for every x, so every class is a single element and k = \lvert Gvert. At the other extreme, C(1) = \{1\} always. [The conjugacy classes of the symmetric group on three letters] Find the conjugacy classes of S_3. First a rule that does the work. For \sigma \in S_n and a cycle (i_1\ i_2\ \cdots\ i_r), \sigma\,(i_1\ i_2\ \cdots\ i_r)\,\sigma^{-1} = (\sigma(i_1)\ \sigma(i_2)\ \cdots\ \sigma(i_r)) . Both sides are permutations, so it is enough to check they agree at every point. At \sigma(i_j): the left side applies \sigma^{-1} to get i_j, then the cycle to get i_{j+1} (indices read cyclically), then \sigma to get \sigma(i_{j+1}); the right side does the same in one step. At a point \sigma(m) with m 
otin \{i_1, \dots, i_r\}: the left side gives \sigma(m) back, and so does the right side, since \sigma(m) is not among the \sigma(i_j) by injectivity. Every point of \{1, \dots, n\} is \sigma(m) for exactly one m, so the two agree. So conjugation relabels the entries of a cycle. Choose such a list ho_1, \dots, ho_s with s as large as possible; by maximality every irreducible complex representation of G is equivalent to some ho_i. Write \chi_i = \chi_{ho_i}, and let U = \Span(\chi_1, \dots, \chi_s) \subseteq \operatorname{Cl}(G), using @prp-character-basic (b). Let f \in U^{\perp}, the orthogonal complement of U in \operatorname{Cl}(G) (@def-orthogonal-complement), so f is a class function with \inner{f}{\chi_i} = 0, hence also \inner{\chi_i}{f} = \conj{\inner{f}{\chi_i}} = 0, for every i. For any representation ho of G on V, define T_f^{ho} \coloneqq \sum_{g \in G}\conj{f(g)}\,ho(g) \in \cL(V). Claim 1. T_f^ho commutes with ho(h) for every h \in G. Fix h. Then ho(h)\,T_f^ho\,ho(h)^{-1} = \sum_{g \in G}\conj{f(g)}\,ho(hgh^{-1}) . The map g \mapsto hgh^{-1} is a bijection G 	o G, with inverse g \mapsto h^{-1}gh. Substituting g' = hgh^{-1}, so that g = h^{-1}g'h, the sum becomes \sum_{g'}\conj{f(h^{-1}g'h)}ho(g'). Since f is a class function, f(h^{-1}g'h) = f(g'), so the sum is T_f^ho. Multiplying on the right by ho(h) gives the claim. Claim 2. If ho is irreducible, then T_f^ho = 0. By Claim 1 and @cor-commuting-with-irreducible, over the algebraically closed field 
C we get T_f^ho = \lambda\,\id_V for some \lambda \in 
C. Taking traces and using linearity of the trace (@thm-trace-operator-properties), \lambda\,\dim V = 	r T_f^ho = \sum_{g}\conj{f(g)}\,\chi_ho(g) = \lvert Gvert\,\inner{\chi_ho}{f} . Now ho is equivalent to some ho_i, so \chi_ho = \chi_i by @prp-character-basic (c), and \inner{\chi_i}{f} = 0. Since \dim V \ge 1, \lambda = 0. Claim 3. T_f^ho = 0 for every representation ho. We may assume V 
e \{\elem{0}\}. By @cor-complete-reducibility, V = V_1\oplus\dots\oplus V_r with each V_j invariant and ho|_{V_j} irreducible. Each ho(g) maps V_j into V_j, hence so does T_f^ho, and its restriction to V_j is \sum_g \conj{f(g)}\,ho|_{V_j}(g) = T_f^{ho|_{V_j}}, which is 0 by Claim 2. So T_f^ho vanishes on each V_j, hence on their sum V. Now apply Claim 3 to the regular representation ho_{\mathrm{reg}} on 
C[G], where ho_{\mathrm{reg}}(g)\delta_h = \delta_{gh}. Evaluating at the basis vector \delta_1, 0 = T_f^{ho_{\mathrm{reg}}}\delta_1 = \sum_{g \in G}\conj{f(g)}\,\delta_g . The \delta_g are a basis of 
C[G], so every coefficient vanishes: \conj{f(g)} = 0, that is f(g) = 0, for all g. Hence U^{\perp} = \{0\}. By @thm-orthogonal-decomposition, \operatorname{Cl}(G) = U \oplus U^{\perp} = U. So (\chi_1, \dots, \chi_s) is an orthonormal spanning list, hence a basis, and s = \dim\operatorname{Cl}(G) = k by @prp-dimension-class-functions. Finally, inequivalent irreducibles have different characters, since orthonormality gives \inner{\chi_i}{\chi_j} = 0 
e 1 = \inner{\chi_i}{\chi_i} for i 
e j; so the k characters correspond to the k equivalence classes of irreducible representations. This proves the theorem. [The sum of the squares of the degrees] Let G be a finite group and let ho_1, \dots, ho_k on V_1, \dots, V_k be a complete list of pairwise inequivalent irreducible complex representations of G, one for each of the k conjugacy classes (@thm-characters-span-class-functions). Then each ho_i occurs in the regular representation with multiplicity exactly \dim V_i, and \lvert Gvert = \sum_{i=1}^{k}(\dim V_i)^2 . The regular character is \chi_{\mathrm{reg}}(1) = \lvert Gvert and \chi_{\mathrm{reg}}(g) = 0 for g 
e 1, as computed after @def-character. Hence \inner{\chi_{\mathrm{reg}}}{\chi_i} =  rac{1}{\lvert Gvert}\sum_{g}\chi_{\mathrm{reg}}(g)\conj{\chi_i(g)} =  rac{1}{\lvert Gvert}\,\lvert Gvert\,\conj{\chi_i(1)} = \dim V_i, the value \chi_i(1) = \dim V_i being a real number (@prp-character-basic (a)). By @cor-irreducibility-criterion this inner product is the multiplicity of ho_i in ho_{\mathrm{reg}}, so \chi_{\mathrm{reg}} = \sum_i (\dim V_i)\chi_i. Evaluating at g = 1 gives \lvert Gvert = \sum_i (\dim V_i)\chi_i(1) = \sum_i(\dim V_i)^2. This is @cor-dimension-count, the count \dim A = \sum n_i^2 of the structure theorem, applied to A = 
C[G]: the two proofs are different and the answer is the same. [Orthogonality of the columns] Let G be a finite group with conjugacy classes C_1, \dots, C_k, representatives g_j \in C_j and sizes c_j = \lvert C_jvert, and irreducible characters \chi_1, \dots, \chi_k. Then for all j, l, \sum_{i=1}^{k}\chi_i(g_j)\,\conj{\chi_i(g_l)} =  egin{cases} \lvert Gvert / c_j, & j = l, \ 0, & j 
e l . \end{cases} @thm-characters-span-class-functions makes the table of character values a square array. Rescale it so that orthonormality of the rows says the matrix is unitary; then its columns are orthonormal too, because a one-sided inverse of a square matrix is two-sided. Let \U \in M_k(
C) have entries u_{ij} = \sqrt{c_j/\lvert Gvert}\ \chi_i(g_j); the square root is a positive real. By @eq-class-inner-product and @thm-character-orthogonality, (\U\U^{*})_{i i'} = \sum_{j=1}^{k} u_{ij}\conj{u_{i'j}} =  rac{1}{\lvert Gvert}\sum_{j=1}^{k} c_j\,\chi_i(g_j)\conj{\chi_{i'}(g_j)} = \inner{\chi_i}{\chi_{i'}}, which is 1 for i = i' and 0 otherwise. Hence \U\U^{*} = \I_k. By @thm-one-sided-inverse, \U^{*}\U = \I_k as well, so for all j, l \sum_{i=1}^{k}\conj{u_{ij}}u_{il} =  rac{\sqrt{c_jc_l}}{\lvert Gvert}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\conj{\chi_i(g_j)}\chi_i(g_l) equals 1 when j = l and 0 otherwise. For j = l this gives \sum_i \lvert\chi_i(g_j)vert^2 = \lvert Gvert/c_j, and for j 
e l it gives \sum_i \conj{\chi_i(g_j)}\chi_i(g_l) = 0. Conjugating the second identity, which is a sum of complex numbers, gives the stated form. This proves the corollary. Two character tables The character table of G is the k 	imes k array whose (i, j)-entry is \chi_i(g_j): one row per irreducible character, one column per conjugacy class. By @thm-characters-span-class-functions it is square, by @thm-character-orthogonality its rows are orthonormal, and by @cor-column-orthogonality its columns are orthogonal. [The character table of the symmetric group on three letters] Write down the character table of S_3 and verify every orthogonality relation. By @exm-conjugacy-classes-s3 there are k = 3 classes, with representatives \id, (1\ 2), (1\ 2\ 3) and sizes 1, 3, 2. So there are three irreducible complex representations (@thm-characters-span-class-functions), and @exm-s3-irreducibles produced three: the trivial, the sign, and the standard one. Their characters, from the definitions and the traces computed in @exm-s3-standard-is-irreducible, are: \id (1\ 2) (1\ 2\ 3) ---------------------- ----- -------- ----------- class size 1 3 2 \chi_{\mathrm{triv}} 1 1 1 \chi_{\mathrm{sgn}} 1 -1 1 \chi_{\mathrm{std}} 2 0 -1 Degrees. 1^2 + 1^2 + 2^2 = 6 = \lvert S_3vert, as @cor-sum-of-squares requires. Row orthogonality, from @eq-class-inner-product with weights 1, 3, 2 and divisor 6. All values are real, so conjugation does nothing:  egin{aligned} \inner{\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}}{\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}} &= 	frac16(1 + 3 + 2) = 1, \ \inner{\chi_{\mathrm{sgn}}}{\chi_{\mathrm{sgn}}} &= 	frac16(1 + 3 + 2) = 1, \ \inner{\chi_{\mathrm{std}}}{\chi_{\mathrm{std}}} &= 	frac16(4 + 0 + 2) = 1, \ \inner{\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}}{\chi_{\mathrm{sgn}}} &= 	frac16(1 - 3 + 2) = 0, \ \inner{\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}}{\chi_{\mathrm{std}}} &= 	frac16(2 + 0 - 2) = 0, \ \inner{\chi_{\mathrm{sgn}}}{\chi_{\mathrm{std}}} &= 	frac16(2 + 0 - 2) = 0 . \end{aligned} Column orthogonality, from @cor-column-orthogonality, with no weights this time:  egin{aligned} 	ext{column } \id: &\quad 1 + 1 + 4 = 6 = 6/1, \ 	ext{column } (1\ 2): &\quad 1 + 1 + 0 = 2 = 6/3, \ 	ext{column } (1\ 2\ 3): &\quad 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 = 6/2, \ \id 	ext{ against } (1\ 2): &\quad 1\cdot1 + 1\cdot(-1) + 2\cdot 0 = 0, \ \id 	ext{ against } (1\ 2\ 3): &\quad 1 + 1 - 2 = 0, \ (1\ 2) 	ext{ against } (1\ 2\ 3): &\quad 1 - 1 + 0 = 0 . \end{aligned} Every relation holds. [The character table of a cyclic group of order four] Write down the character table of 
Z/4
Z and verify the orthogonality relations. The group is abelian, so every conjugacy class is a single element and k = 4. By @thm-characters-span-class-functions there are four irreducible complex representations, and @exm-cyclic-irreducibles produced four, all of degree 1: \chi_m([j]) = i^{jm}, using \omega = e^{2\pi i/4} = i. Their degrees satisfy 1^2+1^2+1^2+1^2 = 4 = \lvert Gvert. [0] [1] [2] [3] -------- ----- ----- ----- ----- \chi_0 1 1 1 1 \chi_1 1 i -1 -i \chi_2 1 -1 1 -1 \chi_3 1 -i -1 i Row orthogonality. For characters of degree 1, \conj{\chi_l([j])} = i^{-jl}, so \inner{\chi_m}{\chi_l} =  rac14\sum_{j=0}^{3} i^{j(m-l)} . If m = l every term is 1 and the sum is 4/4 = 1. If m 
e l, put d = m - l, so i^{d} 
e 1 and (i^d)^4 = 1; then (i^d - 1)\sum_{j=0}^{3}(i^d)^j = (i^d)^4 - 1 = 0, and dividing by i^d - 1 
e 0 gives \sum_j i^{jd} = 0. For instance \inner{\chi_1}{\chi_0} = 	frac14(1 + i - 1 - i) = 0 and \inner{\chi_3}{\chi_1} = 	frac14(1 - 1 + 1 - 1) = 0. Column orthogonality. Every class has size 1, so @cor-column-orthogonality predicts 4 down the diagonal and 0 off it. The same geometric sum settles every one of them: column [j] against column [l] gives \sum_{m=0}^{3}\chi_m([j])\conj{\chi_m([l])} = \sum_{m=0}^{3} i^{m(j-l)}, which is 4 when j = l, and is 0 otherwise by the computation just made, read with d = j - l. Three of them written out. Column [1] against itself: 1 + \lvert ivert^2 + 1 + \lvert -ivert^2 = 4. Column [0] against [2]: the entries of column [0] are 1, 1, 1, 1 and those of column [2] are 1, -1, 1, -1, so the sum is 1\cdot 1 + 1\cdot(-1) + 1\cdot 1 + 1\cdot(-1) = 0. Column [1] against [3]: 1 + i\cdot\conj{(-i)} + (-1)\conj{(-1)} + (-i)\conj{i} = 1 + i\cdot i + 1 + (-i)(-i) = 1 - 1 + 1 - 1 = 0. Read as a matrix, the table is (i^{jm})_{m, j}, which up to the factor 1/2 is the 4 	imes 4 Fourier matrix of @exm-fourier-matrix-4. That is not a coincidence, and Section 09 explains it. The character table does not determine the group. Two nonisomorphic groups can have identical character tables. The standard witness is a pair of groups of order 8: the eight symmetries of a square (four rotations and four reflections), and the group \{\pm\I_2, \pm\elem{i}, \pm\elem{j}, \pm\elem{k}\} sitting inside the quaternions 
H of @def-quaternions under multiplication. Both have five conjugacy classes and degrees 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, and their tables agree entry for entry, yet the groups are not isomorphic. This is stated on credit and not proved here; nothing below depends on it. What the character table does determine is every complex representation of the group, up to equivalence (@cor-irreducibility-criterion). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the character of a representation, and state why it does not depend on a choice of basis. 2. State the orthogonality relation for irreducible complex characters. 3. Determine whether the following is true: “if \chi is a character of G then \chi(gh) = \chi(g)\chi(h).” Justify your answer. 4. A group of order 12 has exactly four conjugacy classes. Determine the degrees of its irreducible complex representations. 5. Explain why the number of irreducible complex representations of an abelian group G is \lvert Gvert. 1. \chi_ho(g) = 	rho(g) (@def-character). The trace of an operator is computed from its matrix in any basis and the answer is the same for all of them (@def-trace-operator), so \chi_ho depends only on ho. 2. For irreducible complex representations ho, \sigma of a finite group, \inner{\chi_\sigma}{\chi_ho} is 1 if ho \cong \sigma and 0 otherwise (@thm-character-orthogonality). 3. False. See the warning after @prp-character-basic: for the standard representation of S_3, \chi((1\ 2))\chi((1\ 3)) = 0 but \chi((1\ 3\ 2)) = -1. It is true precisely for characters of degree 1. 4. Four classes means four irreducible representations (@thm-characters-span-class-functions), with degrees d_1, \dots, d_4 \ge 1 satisfying d_1^2 + d_2^2 + d_3^2 + d_4^2 = 12 (@cor-sum-of-squares). Every group has the trivial representation, so we may take d_1 = 1 and need d_2^2+d_3^2+d_4^2 = 11 with each d_i \ge 1. The squares available are 1, 4, 9, since 4^2 = 16 > 11. A triple containing a 9 has its other two terms summing to 2, so it is 9 + 1 + 1 = 11, which works; and a triple with no 9 is one of 4+4+4 = 12, 4+4+1 = 9, 4+1+1 = 6, and 1+1+1 = 3, none of them 11. So the degrees are 1, 1, 1, 3. 5. In an abelian group xgx^{-1} = g, so every conjugacy class is a singleton and k = \lvert Gvert; now apply @thm-characters-span-class-functions. B. Practice [B1: A character computed and decomposed] Let \P_	au be the permutation matrix of 	au \in S_3, so that \P_	au\cvec{e}_i = \cvec{e}_{	au(i)} (@def-permutation-matrix), and let \pi be the representation of S_3 on \cL(
C^3) given by \pi(	au)(f) = \P_	au\, f\, \P_	au^{-1}. 1. Compute the character of \pi on the three conjugacy classes. 2. Decompose \pi into irreducibles. (a) This is the construction of @prp-hom-representation with both representations equal to the permutation representation ho_{\mathrm{perm}} on 
C^3. So its character is \chi_\pi(	au) = \chi_{\mathrm{perm}}(	au)\conj{\chi_{\mathrm{perm}}(	au)} = \lvert\chi_{\mathrm{perm}}(	au)vert^2. From @exm-s3-standard-is-irreducible, \chi_{\mathrm{perm}} = (3, 1, 0) on the classes of \id, (1\ 2), (1\ 2\ 3), so \chi_\pi = (9, 1, 0). (b) With weights 1, 3, 2 and divisor 6:  egin{aligned} \inner{\chi_\pi}{\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}} &= 	frac16(9 + 3 + 0) = 2, \ \inner{\chi_\pi}{\chi_{\mathrm{sgn}}} &= 	frac16(9 - 3 + 0) = 1, \ \inner{\chi_\pi}{\chi_{\mathrm{std}}} &= 	frac16(9\cdot2 + 0 + 0) = 3 . \end{aligned} So \chi_\pi = 2\chi_{\mathrm{triv}} + \chi_{\mathrm{sgn}} + 3\chi_{\mathrm{std}}, and the degrees check: 2 + 1 + 6 = 9 = \dim\cL(
C^3). As a check on the arithmetic, \inner{\chi_\pi}{\chi_\pi} = 	frac16(81 + 3 + 0) = 14 = 2^2+1^2+3^2, as @cor-irreducibility-criterion requires. In particular \dim\cL_G(
C^3, 
C^3) = 2: the G-equivariant operators on 
C^3 form a plane, spanned by the identity and the all-ones matrix. [B2: Which of these are characters?] Let G = S_3, with classes ordered \id, (1\ 2), (1\ 2\ 3) of sizes 1, 3, 2. Determine which of the following class functions are characters of complex representations of S_3. Justify your answer. 1. (4, 0, 1); 2. (3, 1, 0); 3. (2, 2, -1); 4. (1, 1, -1). A class function is a character exactly when it is a nonnegative integer combination of \chi_{\mathrm{triv}} = (1,1,1), \chi_{\mathrm{sgn}} = (1,-1,1), and \chi_{\mathrm{std}} = (2,0,-1), by @cor-complete-reducibility and @prp-character-basic (d); the coefficients are the inner products \inner{\cdot}{\chi_i}. (a) \inner{(4,0,1)}{\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}} = 	frac16(4 + 0 + 2) = 1, \inner{\cdot}{\chi_{\mathrm{sgn}}} = 	frac16(4 - 0 + 2) = 1, \inner{\cdot}{\chi_{\mathrm{std}}} = 	frac16(8 + 0 - 2) = 1. All nonnegative integers, and 1\cdot1+1\cdot1+1\cdot2 = 4 matches the degree. Yes: it is the character of the direct sum of the trivial, the sign, and the standard representation, equivalently of the direct sum of the permutation representation and the sign representation, since (3,1,0) + (1,-1,1) = (4,0,1). (b) Inner products 1, 0, 1 as computed in @exm-s3-standard-is-irreducible. Yes: the permutation representation. (c) \inner{\cdot}{\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}} = 	frac16(2 + 6 - 2) = 1, \inner{\cdot}{\chi_{\mathrm{sgn}}} = 	frac16(2 - 6 - 2) = -1. A negative multiplicity is impossible, so no. (It is a difference of characters, called a virtual character, but not a character.) (d) \inner{(1,1,-1)}{\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}} = 	frac16(1 + 3 - 2) = 	frac13, which is not an integer. So no: it is not even a combination of the three irreducible characters with integer coefficients, let alone nonnegative ones. [B3: Degree-one characters of a cyclic group] Let G = 
Z/6
Z. 1. Write down the character table. 2. Verify \inner{\chi_1}{\chi_4} = 0 and \inner{\chi_2}{\chi_2} = 1 by direct computation. (a) The group is abelian of order 6, so there are six classes, six irreducible characters, all of degree 1, given by \chi_m([j]) = \omega^{jm} with \omega = e^{2\pi i/6} (@exm-cyclic-irreducibles). The table has (m, j)-entry \omega^{jm}, with \omega^6 = 1. (b) Here  egin{aligned} \inner{\chi_1}{\chi_4} &= 	frac16\sum_{j=0}^{5}\omega^{j}\conj{\omega^{4j}} = 	frac16\sum_j \omega^{-3j} \ &= 	frac16\sum_j(-1)^{j} = 	frac16(1-1+1-1+1-1) = 0 , \end{aligned} using \omega^{-3} = \omega^{3} = -1. And \inner{\chi_2}{\chi_2} = 	frac16\sum_j \omega^{2j}\conj{\omega^{2j}} = 	frac16\sum_j \lvert\omega^{2j}vert^2 = 	frac16\cdot 6 = 1. C. Going deeper [C1: Counting fixed points] Let G be a finite group acting on \{1, \dots, n\} through a homomorphism \varphi \colon G 	o S_n, and let ho(g) = \P_{\varphi(g)} be the corresponding permutation representation on 
C^n, where \P_\sigma is the permutation matrix of @def-permutation-matrix (so \P_\sigma\P_	au = \P_{\sigma	au} by @lem-permutation-matrices (a)). 1. Prove that \inner{\chi_ho}{\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}} equals the average number of fixed points of the permutations \varphi(g), and also equals \dim (
C^n)^{G}. 2. Deduce that for every n \ge 1, the average number of fixed points of a permutation in S_n is exactly 1. 3. For G = S_3 with \varphi = \id, verify (a) numerically. (a) By the computation after @def-character, \chi_ho(g) is the number of i with \varphi(g)(i) = i. Hence \inner{\chi_ho}{\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}} =  rac{1}{\lvert Gvert}\sum_{g}\chi_ho(g)\cdot\conj{1} is exactly the average of those counts. By @lem-average-projection applied to ho, the same quantity is \dim(
C^n)^G. (b) Take G = S_n and \varphi = \id. A vector \cvec{x} \in 
C^n fixed by every ho(	au) has x_i = x_j for all i 
e j, by taking 	au the transposition (i\ j); conversely every vector with equal coordinates is fixed. So (
C^n)^{S_n} = \Span(\cvec{e}_1 + \dots + \cvec{e}_n), of dimension 1 (for n = 1 this is 
C itself). By (a) the average number of fixed points equals that dimension, namely 1. (c) For S_3, \chi_ho = (3, 1, 0) on classes of sizes 1, 3, 2, so the average number of fixed points is 	frac16(1\cdot3 + 3\cdot1 + 2\cdot0) = 1. Directly: \id fixes three points, each of the three transpositions fixes one, and each of the two 3-cycles fixes none, giving (3 + 3 + 0)/6 = 1. And \dim(
C^3)^{S_3} = 1 by (b). The three agree. [C2: Degree-one characters form a group] Let G be a finite group and let X(G) be the set of characters of degree 1 of complex representations of G. (For abelian G this group is the subject of Section 09.) 1. Prove that the pointwise product of two degree-one characters is a degree-one character, and that X(G) is a group under this product. 2. Prove that \lvert X(G)vert \le k, the number of conjugacy classes, with equality if and only if G is abelian. Hint: use @cor-sum-of-squares in one direction and @cor-abelian-irreducibles-are-lines in the other. (a) A degree-one character is a homomorphism \chi \colon G 	o 
C\setminus\{0\} (the representation is the scalar it multiplies by). If \chi, \psi are two of them then (\chi\psi)(gh) = \chi(gh)\psi(gh) = \chi(g)\psi(g)\chi(h)\psi(h) = (\chi\psi)(g)(\chi\psi)(h), using commutativity of 
C; so \chi\psi is again a homomorphism into 
C\setminus\{0\}, hence a degree-one character. The product is associative because multiplication in 
C is; \chi_{\mathrm{triv}} is an identity; and g \mapsto \chi(g)^{-1} is a homomorphism and satisfies \chi \cdot \chi^{-1} = \chi_{\mathrm{triv}}. So X(G) is a group (@def-group). (b) Degree-one characters are irreducible (a one-dimensional representation has no nontrivial invariant subspace) and pairwise distinct elements of X(G) are inequivalent representations, since for degree one, equivalence means equality. So X(G) is a subset of the k irreducible characters (@thm-characters-span-class-functions) and \lvert X(G)vert \le k. Equality says every irreducible character has degree 1. If G is abelian then 
C[G] is a commutative algebra, so every irreducible 
C[G]-space is one-dimensional by @cor-abelian-irreducibles-are-lines; by @thm-representations-are-modules-over-the-group-algebra those are exactly the irreducible representations of G. Conversely, if every irreducible has degree 1 then \lvert Gvert = \sum_{i=1}^{k}1 = k by @cor-sum-of-squares, so every conjugacy class is a singleton; that is, xgx^{-1} = g for all x, g, which says G is abelian. [C3: The second orthogonality relation] Let G be a finite group with irreducible complex characters \chi_1, \dots, \chi_k. 1. Prove that \sum_{i=1}^{k}\lvert\chi_i(g)vert^2 = \lvert Gvert/\lvert C(g)vert for every g \in G. 2. Deduce that \sum_{i}\lvert\chi_i(g)vert^2 = 1 if and only if the class of g is all of G, and that this happens only for the trivial group. Hint: C(1) = \{1\} always. 3. For G = S_3 compute \sum_i \lvert\chi_i(g)vert^2 at each of the three classes and check (a). (a) This is the diagonal case j = l of @cor-column-orthogonality, with g = g_j a representative of its own class and c_j = \lvert C(g)vert. The value is independent of the representative chosen, as it must be, since characters are class functions. (b) By (a), the sum equals 1 exactly when \lvert C(g)vert = \lvert Gvert, that is, when the class of g is all of G. But C(1) = \{1\}, and the classes partition G, so a class equal to G forces G = \{1\}. Conversely for the trivial group the only class is \{1\} = G and the single character has \lvert\chi_1(1)vert^2 = 1. (c) From @exm-character-table-s3: at \id, 1 + 1 + 4 = 6 = 6/1; at (1\ 2), 1 + 1 + 0 = 2 = 6/3; at (1\ 2\ 3), 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 = 6/2. Each matches \lvert Gvert/\lvert C(g)vert with class sizes 1, 3, 2.

title: 23.9 Finite Abelian Groups and the Fourier Transform
content:
Finite Abelian Groups and the Fourier Transform Everything in this chapter has been building a machine, and for one family of groups the machine produces an object the book already owns. When G is abelian and the field is 
C, Section 4 forces every irreducible representation down to a single dimension, Section 8 makes the resulting characters orthonormal, and what is left is one unitary matrix. For the cyclic group that matrix is the Fourier matrix of Chapter 12 Section 9, entry for entry. This section proves that, and two companion statements: the convolution theorem is the group algebra splitting into a product of copies of 
C, and a circulant is an element of that group algebra multiplying. Throughout, G is a finite abelian group, with identity written e, and the field is
