By @thm-fourier-inversion-on-a-group (a), \U is unitary, hence invertible, hence so is \sqrt n\,\U	p. A linear bijection that is a homomorphism of algebras is an isomorphism of algebras. For G = 
Z/n
Z, write a = \sum_m c_m\delta_{[m]}. Then \Phi(a)(\chi_j) = \sum_m c_m\omega^{jm} = p_{\cvec{c}}(\omega^j), the j-th entry of the vector \widehat{\cvec{c}} = \sqrt n\,\F\cvec{c} of Chapter 12 Section 9, with p_{\cvec{c}} the symbol of @def-circulant. Multiplicativity of \Phi then reads p_{\cvec{c}\ast\cvec{d}}(\omega^j) = p_{\cvec{c}}(\omega^j)p_{\cvec{d}}(\omega^j), which is @thm-convolution-theorem (b). So the convolution theorem is a splitting theorem. Convolution is hard to look at because it is multiplication in 
C[G] written in the basis of point masses; in the basis of characters the same multiplication is diagonal, because there the algebra has fallen apart into n independent copies of 
C. Seen from Section 6 this is no surprise: 
C[G] is semisimple by @thm-maschke applied to the regular representation, and a commutative semisimple algebra over 
C is a product of matrix algebras by @thm-wedderburn, all of whose blocks must be 1	imes1 because M_k(
C) is commutative only for k = 1. Then \dim
C[G] = \lvert Gvert and @cor-dimension-count force the number of blocks to be \lvert Gvert. The content of @thm-group-algebra-splits over and above that is the explicit isomorphism. The third identification puts Chapter 12’s matrices back into the picture. [Circulants Are the Group Algebra of the Cyclic Group] Let n \ge 1 and let \cC_n\subseteq M_n(
C) be the algebra of circulants (@cor-circulants-algebra). Let \Psi\colon
C[
Z/n
Z]	o M_n(
C) be the linear map with \Psi(\delta_{[m]}) \coloneqq \S^{m} \qquad (m = 0, 1, \dots, n-1), where \S is the cyclic shift. Then: 1. \Psi is an isomorphism of algebras onto \cC_n, and \Psi igl(\sum_m c_m\delta_{[m]} igr) is the circulant \C with first row \cvec{c}; 2. \Psi(a) is the matrix of the map “multiply by a” on 
C[
Z/n
Z], in the ordered basis \sB =  igl(\delta_{[0]},\ \delta_{[-1]},\ \delta_{[-2]},\ \dots,\ \delta_{[-(n-1)]} igr) ; 3. \F^{*}\Psi(a)\F is the diagonal matrix whose j-th entry is \Phi(a)(\chi_j); that is, \Phi is \Psi followed by conjugating with \F and reading off the diagonal. Part (a) is almost a tautology once the right map is chosen: \Psi sends the basis element \delta_{[m]} to \S^m, and the only relation in the group, [m] + [k] = [m+k] read modulo n, matches the only relation among the powers, \S^n = \I. Part (b) is an index computation, and the reversal of the basis in it is forced by Chapter 12’s convention (\C)_{jk} = c_{k-j}. Part (c) is @thm-circulant-diagonalization restated. (a) By @thm-circulant-is-polynomial-in-shift (a), \sum_m c_m\S^m = p_{\cvec{c}}(\S) is the circulant with first row \cvec{c}, so \Psi has the stated values and its image is \cC_n, which by @cor-circulants-algebra (a) has \I,\S,\dots,\S^{n-1} as a basis. Hence \Psi carries a basis to a basis and is a linear bijection onto \cC_n. For multiplicativity it suffices, by bilinearity of both products, to check it on basis vectors: \Psi igl(\delta_{[m]}\delta_{[k]} igr) = \Psi igl(\delta_{[m+k]} igr) = \S^{(m+k) mod n} = \S^{m}\S^{k}, the last equality because \S^n = \I. Finally \Psi(\delta_{[0]}) = \I, so \Psi is an isomorphism of algebras onto \cC_n. (b) Write \sB = (u_0,\dots,u_{n-1}) with u_k = \delta_{[-k]}; this is a reordering of the basis of point masses, hence a basis. For a = \sum_m c_m\delta_{[m]}, a\,u_k = \sum_m c_m\,\delta_{[m-k]} = \sum_m c_m\,u_{k-m} = \sum_j c_{k-j}\,u_j , substituting j = k-m and reading all subscripts modulo n. So the (j,k)-entry of the matrix of multiplication by a in \sB is c_{k-j}, which is (\C)_{jk} by @def-circulant. Hence that matrix is \C = \Psi(a). (c) By (a) and @thm-circulant-diagonalization, \F^{*}\Psi(a)\F = \diag(p_{\cvec{c}}(1),\dots,p_{\cvec{c}}(\omega^{n-1})), and p_{\cvec{c}}(\omega^j) = \Phi(a)(\chi_j) was computed at the end of the proof of @thm-group-algebra-splits. Part (b) reverses the basis, and the reversal is not cosmetic. With Chapter 12’s convention (\C)_{jk} = c_{k-j}, applying a circulant to a vector is not convolution: (\C\cvec{x})_j = \sum_t c_t x_{j+t}, with a plus sign, whereas (\cvec{c}\ast\cvec{x})_j = \sum_t c_tx_{j-t}. What is true is that \C\cvec{x} = \cvec{c}^{-}\ast\cvec{x}, where \cvec{c}^{-} is the vector with (\cvec{c}^{-})_t = c_{-t}, and that the product of two circulants is the circulant of the convolution of their first rows (@thm-convolution-theorem (a)). The group algebra sees the product, which is why @thm-circulants-are-the-group-algebra (a) needs no reversal while (b) does. If you keep only one of these, keep the product statement. [The case n = 4, checked against Chapter 12] For G = 
Z/4
Z, write down the character table, the character matrix, and the image under \Phi of the element a = \delta_{[0]} + 2\delta_{[1]} + 3\delta_{[2]} + 4\delta_{[3]}. Compare with Chapter 12 Section 9. Here \omega = e^{2\pi i/4} = i and \chi_j([m]) = i^{jm}. The table of values, rows \chi_0,\chi_1,\chi_2,\chi_3 and columns [0],[1],[2],[3], is  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & i & -1 & -i \ 1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \ 1 & -i & -1 & i \end{pmatrix} . The array is symmetric, since i^{jm} = i^{mj}, so reading it with rows indexed by m and columns by j and dividing by \sqrt4 = 2 gives the character matrix \U =  rac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & i & -1 & -i \ 1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \ 1 & -i & -1 & i \end{pmatrix} . This is exactly the matrix \F of @exm-fourier-matrix-4. By @thm-circulants-are-the-group-algebra (a), \Psi(a) is the circulant with first row (1,2,3,4), the running example of Chapter 12 Section 9. By @thm-group-algebra-splits,  egin{aligned} \Phi(a)(\chi_0) &= 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, \ \Phi(a)(\chi_1) &= 1 + 2i - 3 - 4i = -2 - 2i, \ \Phi(a)(\chi_2) &= 1 - 2 + 3 - 4 = -2, \ \Phi(a)(\chi_3) &= 1 - 2i - 3 + 4i = -2 + 2i, \end{aligned} using i^2 = -1 and i^3 = -i. These are the four eigenvalues found in @exm-circulant-4x4-eigenvalues, in the same order, and @thm-circulants-are-the-group-algebra (c) says that \F^{*}\Psi(a)\F = \diag(10, -2-2i, -2, -2+2i), which is what that example computed. As a check on the first value, \chi_0 is the trivial character, so \Phi(a)(\chi_0) is the sum of the coefficients, which is the common row sum 10 of the circulant. What has been bought? Chapter 12 said that a circulant is a polynomial in the shift, and proved it with an induction on the entries of \S^m. That statement is now structural: 
C[
Z/n
Z] is generated as an algebra by one element \delta_{[1]}, whose image is \S, so every element of the algebra is a polynomial in \S. What the structural reading does not hand over free is that those polynomials are exactly the circulants; that is still Chapter 12’s entry computation (@thm-circulant-is-polynomial-in-shift (a)), quoted in the proof of @thm-circulants-are-the-group-algebra (a). The one matrix \F that diagonalizes every circulant simultaneously is the character matrix, which exists before any circulant is named because the characters of G exist before any element of 
C[G] is named. And the reason the eigenvalues came out as n evaluations of one polynomial is that they are the n coordinates of a in the product decomposition 
C[G]\cong
C^{\widehat G}. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the dual group \widehat G of a finite abelian group G, and say what its identity and inverses are. 2. State why \lvert\widehat Gvert = \lvert Gvert, naming the two results used. 3. Write down the character matrix of G and state what its unitarity says about the characters. 4. Determine whether the following are true, with a reason. (i) Every irreducible complex representation of a finite abelian group is one-dimensional. (ii) The book has proved \widehat G\cong G for every finite abelian G. (iii) The Fourier matrix of Chapter 12 Section 9 is the character matrix of 
Z/n
Z. (iv) For \A \in \cC_n and \cvec{x}\in
C^n, \A\cvec{x} is the convolution of the first row of \A with \cvec{x}. 5. Explain in one sentence why the values of a character of a finite abelian group are roots of unity. (a) \widehat G is the set of group homomorphisms G	o
C^{	imes} with the pointwise product (@def-dual-group). Its identity is the trivial character \chi_0 \equiv 1, and the inverse of \chi is \conj\chi (@prp-dual-group-is-a-group). (b) Because G is abelian, each conjugacy class is a single element, so there are \lvert Gvert classes; @thm-characters-span-class-functions makes the number of irreducible characters equal to that, and @thm-abelian-characters-are-homomorphisms identifies the irreducible characters with the elements of \widehat G (@prp-dual-group-order). (c) (\U)_{mj} = \chi_j(g_m)/\sqrt n for fixed orderings of G and \widehat G (@def-character-matrix). Unitarity says the columns are orthonormal, that is, 	frac1n\sum_g\chi_j(g)\conj{\chi_k(g)} = \delta_{jk}: the characters are an orthonormal basis of the functions on G (@thm-fourier-inversion-on-a-group). (d) (i) True over 
C, by @thm-abelian-characters-are-homomorphisms (a); it is false over 
R. (ii) False. It is proved here only for direct products of cyclic groups (@thm-dual-group-iso), and the book does not prove that every finite abelian group is such a product. (iii) True, entry for entry (@thm-character-matrix-is-fourier-matrix). (iv) False: (\A\cvec{x})_j = \sum_t c_tx_{j+t}, while convolution has x_{j-t}. The product of two circulants, however, is the circulant of the convolution. (e) Each g has finite order m (@lem-element-has-finite-order), and applying \chi to g^m = e gives \chi(g)^m = 1. B. Practice [B1: The character table of the group of order three] Let G = 
Z/3
Z and \omega = e^{2\pi i/3}. 1. Write down the three characters and the character matrix. 2. Verify one off-diagonal orthogonality relation by hand. 3. Let a = 2\delta_{[0]} - \delta_{[1]} - \delta_{[2]} \in
C[G]. Compute \Phi(a), write down the circulant \Psi(a), and state its eigenvalues. (a) By @exm-characters-of-a-cyclic-group, \chi_j([m]) = \omega^{jm} for j = 0, 1, 2, and \U =  rac{1}{\sqrt3} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & \omega & \omega^2 \ 1 & \omega^2 & \omega^4 \end{pmatrix} =  rac{1}{\sqrt3} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & \omega & \omega^2 \ 1 & \omega^2 & \omega \end{pmatrix}, using \omega^4 = \omega^3\omega = \omega. (b) Take j = 1, k = 0. Then 	frac13\sum_{m=0}^{2}\chi_1([m])\conj{\chi_0([m])} = 	frac13(1 + \omega + \omega^2) = 0, since \omega 
e 1 and (\omega-1)(1+\omega+\omega^2) = \omega^3-1 = 0. (c) Here \cvec{c} = (2,-1,-1), so \Phi(a)(\chi_j) = 2 - \omega^{j} - \omega^{2j}. For j = 0 this is 2 - 1 - 1 = 0. For j = 1 and j = 2 the two subtracted terms are \omega and \omega^2 in one order or the other, and \omega + \omega^2 = -1 by (b), so the value is 2 + 1 = 3 both times. By @thm-circulants-are-the-group-algebra (a), \Psi(a) =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & -1 \ -1 & 2 & -1 \ -1 & -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}, with eigenvalues 0, 3, 3. The eigenvalue 0 is visible directly: every row sums to 0, so the all-ones vector is in the kernel. [B2: A product of two cyclic groups] Let G = 
Z/2
Z	imes
Z/3
Z and \omega = e^{2\pi i/3}. 1. Use @thm-dual-group-iso (b) to list the six characters of G explicitly. 2. Show that G is cyclic by exhibiting a generator, and say which character of G corresponds to which character of 
Z/6
Z under your isomorphism. (a) By @thm-dual-group-iso (b) every character of G is (x,y)\mapsto\chi(x)\psi(y) with \chi\in\widehat{
Z/2
Z} and \psi\in\widehat{
Z/3
Z}. By @exm-characters-of-a-cyclic-group these are \chi_a(x) = (-1)^{ax} for a \in\{0,1\} and \psi_b(y) = \omega^{by} for b\in\{0,1,2\}. So the six characters are 	heta_{a,b}(x,y) = (-1)^{ax}\omega^{by} \qquad (a\in\{0,1\},\ b\in\{0,1,2\}), and there are 2\cdot3 = 6 = \lvert Gvert of them, as @prp-dual-group-order requires. (b) Let g = ([1],[1]). Its multiples are ([1],[1]), ([0],[2]), ([1],[0]), ([0],[1]), ([1],[2]), ([0],[0]) for k = 1,\dots,6, all six distinct, so g has order 6 and G = \langle gangle is cyclic. Send [k]\in
Z/6
Z to kg; this is the isomorphism. Under it the character \chi_j of 
Z/6
Z with \chi_j([k]) = \zeta^{jk}, \zeta = e^{2\pi i/6}, pulls back to 	heta_{a,b} with 	heta_{a,b}(g) = (-1)^{a}\omega^{b} = \zeta^{3a+2b}, so j \equiv 3a + 2b \pmod 6. As (a,b) runs over the six pairs, 3a+2b runs over 0, 2, 4, 3, 5, 1 modulo 6, hitting each residue once. [B3: A transform and its inversion] Let G = 
Z/4
Z and let f be the function with values f([0]), f([1]), f([2]), f([3]) = 1, 1, -1, -1. 1. Compute \widehat f(\chi_j) for j = 0, 1, 2, 3. 2. Recover f([1]) from @thm-fourier-inversion-on-a-group (b). 3. Check Plancherel’s identity for f. (a) With \chi_j([m]) = i^{jm} and @def-fourier-transform-on-a-group,  egin{aligned} \widehat f(\chi_0) &= 1 + 1 - 1 - 1 = 0, \ \widehat f(\chi_1) &= 1 + i - (-1) - (-i) = 2 + 2i, \ \widehat f(\chi_2) &= 1 - 1 - 1 + 1 = 0, \ \widehat f(\chi_3) &= 1 - i + 1 - i = 2 - 2i . \end{aligned} For j = 3 the powers are i^0, i^3, i^6, i^9 = 1, -i, -1, i, so the sum is 1 - i + 1 - i. (b) Only j = 1, 3 contribute, and \conj{\chi_1([1])} = \conj i = -i, \conj{\chi_3([1])} = \conj{-i} = i. So 	frac14 igl((2+2i)(-i) + (2-2i)(i) igr) = 	frac14 igl((2 - 2i) + (2 + 2i) igr) = 1 , using (2+2i)(-i) = -2i - 2i^2 = 2 - 2i and (2-2i)(i) = 2i - 2i^2 = 2 + 2i. This is f([1]), as it should be. (c) The left side is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4. The right side is 	frac14(0 + \lvert2+2ivert^2 + 0 + \lvert2-2ivert^2) = 	frac14(8 + 8) = 4. They agree. C. Going deeper [C1: The idempotents that do the splitting] Let G be a finite abelian group of order n. For \chi\in\widehat G put \varepsilon_\chi \coloneqq  rac1n\sum_{g\in G}\conj{\chi(g)}\,\delta_g \in 
C[G]. 1. Prove that \Phi(\varepsilon_\chi)(\psi) equals 1 when \psi = \chi and 0 otherwise. 2. Deduce that \varepsilon_\chi\varepsilon_\psi = 0 for \chi
e\psi, that \varepsilon_\chi^2 = \varepsilon_\chi, and that \sum_\chi\varepsilon_\chi = \delta_e. 3. For G = 
Z/4
Z write \varepsilon_{\chi_1} out, and identify the matrix \Psi(\varepsilon_{\chi_1}) in terms of the Fourier vector \cvec{f}_1 of Chapter 12 Section 9. Hint for (a): the sum is an inner product of two characters. (a) By @def-fourier-transform-on-a-group and the definition of \Phi, \Phi(\varepsilon_\chi)(\psi) =  rac1n\sum_{g}\conj{\chi(g)}\,\psi(g) =  rac1n\sum_g \psi(g)\conj{\chi(g)} , which is the inner product of the irreducible characters \psi and \chi (@def-character-inner-product). By @thm-character-orthogonality it is 1 if \psi = \chi and 0 otherwise. (b) \Phi is an isomorphism of algebras (@thm-group-algebra-splits), and in 
C^{\widehat G} the functions \Phi(\varepsilon_\chi) are the point masses at the various \chi. Point masses satisfy exactly the three relations claimed: the pointwise product of two distinct ones is 0, each is its own square, and their sum is the constant function 1, which is \Phi(\delta_e). Applying \Phi^{-1} transfers the relations to 
C[G]. (c) With \chi_1([m]) = i^m, \conj{\chi_1([m])} = (-i)^m, so \varepsilon_{\chi_1} = 	frac14 igl(\delta_{[0]} - i\,\delta_{[1]} - \delta_{[2]} + i\,\delta_{[3]} igr). By @thm-circulants-are-the-group-algebra (a), \Psi(\varepsilon_{\chi_1}) is the circulant with first row 	frac14(1,-i,-1,i), whose (j,k)-entry is 	frac14(-i)^{k-j} = 	frac14 i^{\,j-k}. With \cvec{f}_1 = 	frac12(1,i,-1,-i), the matrix \cvec{f}_1\cvec{f}_1^{*} has (j,k)-entry 	frac14 i^{j}\conj{i^{k}} = 	frac14 i^{\,j-k}. This \varepsilon_{\chi_1} is the idempotent called e_2 in @exm-wedderburn-of-c4, whose list runs from 1 and is written in the generator g = [1]. So \Psi(\varepsilon_{\chi_1}) = \cvec{f}_1\cvec{f}_1^{*}, the orthogonal projection onto the line spanned by \cvec{f}_1. The idempotents of the group algebra are the spectral projections of Chapter 12. [C2: The double dual needs no choices] Let G be a finite abelian group. For g\in G define \ev_g \colon \widehat G	o
C^{	imes} by \ev_g(\chi) \coloneqq \chi(g). 1. Prove that \ev_g \in \widehat{\widehat G} and that g\mapsto\ev_g is a group homomorphism G	o\widehat{\widehat G}. 2. Prove that it is injective. Hint: the rows of the character matrix are indexed by the elements of G. 3. Deduce that it is an isomorphism, and explain why this is not a second proof of @thm-dual-group-iso. (a) For \chi,\psi\in\widehat G, \ev_g(\chi\psi) = (\chi\psi)(g) = \chi(g)\psi(g) = \ev_g(\chi)\ev_g(\psi), so \ev_g is a homomorphism \widehat G	o
C^{	imes}, that is an element of \widehat{\widehat G}. And \ev_{gh}(\chi) = \chi(gh) = \chi(g)\chi(h) = (\ev_g\ev_h)(\chi), so g\mapsto\ev_g is a homomorphism. (b) Suppose \ev_g is the trivial character of \widehat G, that is \chi(g) = 1 = \chi(e) for every \chi\in\widehat G. Then the rows of the character matrix indexed by g and by e are equal, so \U has two equal rows and is singular, contradicting @thm-fourier-inversion-on-a-group (a) unless g = e. Hence the kernel is trivial and the map is injective (@thm-homomorphism-basic-properties gives that the kernel is a subgroup, and a homomorphism with trivial kernel is injective by cancellation). (c) By @prp-dual-group-order applied twice, \lvert\widehat{\widehat G}vert = \lvert\widehat Gvert = \lvert Gvert, so an injective homomorphism between them is a bijection, hence an isomorphism. It is not a proof that \widehat G\cong G: it compares G with the dual of its dual, and gives no map between G and \widehat G at all. The difference is exactly the one Chapter 5 drew between V\cong V^{*}, which needs a choice of basis, and V\cong V^{**}, which does not. [C3: The same theory over a finite field] Two properties of 
C were in use throughout this section: it contains n distinct n-th roots of unity, and n is invertible in it. They are not everything 
C contributed: algebraic closure was spent in @thm-abelian-characters-are-homomorphisms (a), and Section 8’s orthogonality relations were proved for complex representations only. But for one group and one field the conclusions can be checked directly with nothing more than those two properties. Take F = 
F_5, G = 
Z/4
Z, and \omega = 2 \in
F_5. 1. Verify that \omega has order 4 in 
F_5^{	imes}, and that 4 is invertible in 
F_5. 2. Write down the 4	imes4 matrix \M with (\M)_{mj} = \omega^{jm} over 
F_5 and check that 4^{-1}\sum_m\omega^{jm}\omega^{-km} = \delta_{jk} for j = 1 and k = 0, 1. 3. Let \C be the circulant over 
F_5 with first row (1,2,3,4). Compute \M^{-1}\C\M without inverting \M, by evaluating the symbol at the powers of \omega. Hint for (c): the proof of @thm-circulant-diagonalization used only \S^n = \I and the geometric-series identity, both of which hold over 
F_5. (a) 2^1 = 2, 2^2 = 4, 2^3 = 3, 2^4 = 1 in 
F_5, so \omega = 2 has order 4 and 1, 2, 4, 3 are four distinct fourth roots of 1. Also 4\cdot4 = 16 = 1, so 4 is invertible with 4^{-1} = 4. Note \operatorname{char}
F_5 = 5 does not divide \lvert Gvert = 4, which is Maschke’s hypothesis. (b) Reading rows m = 0,1,2,3 and columns j = 0,1,2,3, \M =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 4 & 3 \ 1 & 4 & 1 & 4 \ 1 & 3 & 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix} . For j = k = 1 every term is \omega^{m}\omega^{-m} = 1, so the sum is 4^{-1}\cdot4 = 1. For j = 1, k = 0 it is 4^{-1}(1 + 2 + 4 + 3) = 4\cdot 10 = 4\cdot 0 = 0 in 
F_5. (c) The symbol is p_{\cvec{c}}(x) = 1 + 2x + 3x^2 + 4x^3. Evaluating over 
F_5:  egin{aligned} p_{\cvec{c}}(1) &= 1+2+3+4 = 10 = 0, \ p_{\cvec{c}}(2) &= 1+4+12+32 = 49 = 4, \ p_{\cvec{c}}(4) &= 1+8+48+256 = 313 = 3, \ p_{\cvec{c}}(3) &= 1+6+27+108 = 142 = 2 . \end{aligned} The columns of \M are the eigenvectors, so \M^{-1}\C\M = \diag(0, 4, 3, 2). The matrix \C is singular over 
F_5, as it must be: its row sums are 10 = 0. Every conclusion checked here holds over 
F_5 for this G, except that “unitary” has no meaning and \M is merely invertible; the orthogonality relations survive with \conj{\,\cdot\,} replaced by inversion in 
F_5^{	imes}.

title: 23.10 What the Chapter Buys
content:
What the Chapter Buys Nine sections is a lot of new vocabulary, and vocabulary is not what you should carry away. This closing section introduces nothing. It names the four moves the chapter actually used, reads four earlier theorems of the book again from the height we have reached, sets out in one place which hypothesis on the field each result needed and what breaks without it, and says plainly what was quoted rather than proved and what was left outside the door on purpose. Four moves Average over the group to build an invariant object. This is the whole of @thm-maschke. Given a projection onto a subrepresentation that is not invariant, replace it by the average of its conjugates ho(g)Pho(g)^{-1} over g \in G; the average is invariant because translating the summation index permutes the summands, and it is still a projection onto the same subspace. The hypothesis \operatorname{char}F 
mid \lvert Gvert is not decoration: the average is divided by \lvert Gvert, and if that number is 0 in F there is nothing to divide by. The same move produced the intertwiner in @thm-character-orthogonality, where an arbitrary linear map is averaged into an equivariant one. Once you have seen it, you will recognize it elsewhere: whenever a construction depends on a choice and a finite group acts on the choices, averaging over the group removes the dependence. Use Schur’s lemma to force a scalar. @thm-schurs-lemma has two halves, and the useful one in practice is the second: over an algebraically closed field, an operator commuting with an irreducible family is a scalar (@cor-commuting-with-irreducible). The pattern of use is always the same. You have an operator built by some construction, you check it commutes with everything in sight, and you conclude it is \lambda\,\id; then you take a trace to find \lambda. That single step is what turns the averaged intertwiner of the previous paragraph into the orthogonality relations, and it is what collapses the representations of an abelian group to lines (@cor-abelian-irreducibles-are-lines). Count with \sum n_i^2. Wedderburn’s theorem gives \dim A = \sum_i n_i^2 (@cor-dimension-count), which for a group algebra reads \lvert Gvert = \sum_i (\dim V_i)^2 (@cor-sum-of-squares). This is a very strong constraint for a small group: once you know the number of conjugacy classes, the sum of squares often has only one solution, and you have the dimensions of all the irreducible representations before you have written down a single matrix. It plays the role Rank–Nullity plays in Chapter 2: an identity that pins down what you were otherwise going to have to compute. Read a commuting family as a commutative algebra. Chapters 9 and 12 studied families \cF \subseteq \cL(V) whose members commute. The algebra generated by \cF is then commutative, and the chapter’s theorems apply to it directly. This is not a reformulation for its own sake; it is what makes the next four paragraphs possible. Four old theorems, seen from here Commuting operators have a common eigenvector (@thm-commuting-common-eigenvector). Chapter 9 proved this by restricting to an eigenspace and inducting. From here: the algebra A generated by the family is commutative, and V contains an irreducible A-invariant subspace U, namely a nonzero invariant subspace of least dimension. By @cor-abelian-irreducibles-are-lines, over an algebraically closed field U is a line, and a line invariant under every member of the family is precisely a common eigenvector. Chapter 9’s hypothesis — that each characteristic polynomial splits — is what algebraic closure was standing in for. @thm-simultaneous-diagonalization then follows by decomposing V into such lines. No product of matrix algebras has a nonzero radical. Before applying Wedderburn, check semisimplicity — and for a group algebra that check is @thm-maschke, which is a statement about the characteristic and nothing else. Quoted, not proved The chapter stated six things with credit and proved none of them. Nothing in the chapter rests on any of them, and each is flagged where it appears. - Wedderburn–Artin over a division ring. A finite-dimensional semisimple algebra over any field is a product of matrix algebras over division rings. We proved only the algebraically closed case, where the division rings are the field itself. The book has not built division rings, and the general theorem needs them. - Wedderburn’s little theorem, that a finite division ring is a field. Same reason. - The character table does not determine the group. There are two nonisomorphic groups of order 8 with identical character tables. The book has neither the group theory to construct them nor the need. - The structure theorem for finite abelian groups, that every one is a direct product of cyclic groups. Section 9 proved \widehat G \cong G only for such products, and said so. Chapter 10’s Smith normal form is the linear-algebra shadow of the missing argument. - The converse of @prp-semisimple-has-zero-radical, that a finite-dimensional algebra with zero radical is semisimple. Section 3 states it and does not use it; wherever semisimplicity is needed later it is established directly. - When the commutant of a single matrix is the algebra of polynomials in it, namely when the minimal and characteristic polynomials agree. Section 1 states the criterion in a remark and computes examples on both sides of it, and proves nothing about it. Left outside on purpose The subject continues, and the chapter stopped where the book’s tools stopped rather than where the subject does. Four directions, in rough order of how soon you would meet them. Induced representations and Frobenius reciprocity. Given a subgroup H \le G and a representation of H, there is a way to build a representation of G, and the characters of the two are related by an adjunction. This is the standard next tool, and it is the standard way to produce the irreducible representations of a group rather than merely count them. It needs cosets of a subgroup, which Chapter 0 does not have. Modular representation theory. What happens when \operatorname{char}F divides \lvert Gvert and @thm-maschke fails. Representations no longer decompose into irreducibles, the group algebra is not semisimple, and a genuinely different theory takes over. Section 7’s unipotent example is the whole of what we said about it. Character tables as a computational subject. We computed a few small ones: the symmetric group on three letters, the cyclic group

Every theorem here used finiteness twice: to average, and to count. For compact groups an integral replaces the sum and most of the chapter survives; for other infinite groups almost none of it does. One more look back The book began with one linear map and asked for a basis making it simple. Chapter 9 found eigenvectors, Chapter 10 found the Jordan and rational forms, Chapters 11 to 13 found orthonormal bases when there was an inner product to respect. Then the question widened: Chapter 9 Section 9 and Chapter 12 Section 7 asked for a basis good for a whole commuting family at once. This chapter widened it once more, to a set of operators closed under composition, and found that over an algebraically closed field there is essentially one building block, a full matrix algebra, and that everything semisimple is a product of those. That is a satisfying place to stop, but notice what it cost. The answer is clean only over an algebraically closed field, only for semisimple algebras, and — on the group side — only when the characteristic is coprime to the order. Every one of those three conditions was a real restriction with a two-by-two counterexample behind it. A structure theorem that applies to everything is usually a structure theorem that says nothing; this one says a great deal, and the price is printed on the label. Exercises A.
