title: Computation and Applications
content: Computation and Applications Chapter 21 closed Part V by naming a debt: “every proof here is an existence or a comparison, and not one of them is an algorithm. That is the subject of Chapter 24.” It is the book’s largest single debt — twenty-six promises across eighteen files — and it has been accumulating since Chapter 3, where partial pivoting was recommended for a reason the book could not yet give. Twenty chapters have built objects and proved things about them. Not one has said how to produce those objects from data of finite accuracy, in finitely many arithmetic operations, and not one has been able to say what an answer computed that way even means. This chapter answers three questions in that order. What does a computed answer mean? It is the exact answer to a nearby question, and the whole of numerical linear algebra lies in making “nearby” precise: a model of arithmetic, backward error, and the rule that ties the two to Chapter 16’s condition number, with Chapter 20’s residual bounds supplying the error bars. How are the objects of this book actually computed? Elimination with pivoting, least squares by reflections, eigenvalues by iteration — because no finite eigenvalue algorithm can exist — Krylov subspaces, conjugate gradients, the fast Fourier transform, and fast multiplication. What is linear algebra for? Vibrations, principal components, and graphs, each an application in which a theorem already proved does the work. The chapter is about arithmetic, algorithms, and cost. No product, library, or language is named anywhere in it: an algorithm here is a rule for producing numbers from numbers, and its cost is a count of arithmetic operations. Conventions Seven conventions hold throughout, and each is stated once where it is introduced. - u is the unit roundoff and \fl(\cdot) the rounding map of §01’s model, with \cR the set of representable numbers and \gamma_k = ku/(1-ku) the accumulated-rounding constant, defined in §01 and used in every section that mentions arithmetic. - A flop is one arithmetic operation, and costs are leading-order counts, written \tfrac23 n^3 + O(n^2). The constant matters and the exponent matters more; §§02 and 13 are where that sentence is made quantitative. - Perturbations of data are \Delta\A and \Delta\cvec{b}, and a computed object carries a hat: \widehat{\cvec{x}}, \widehat{\L}. Chapters 16, 17, and 20 wrote a perturbation \E; \E is kept here for a perturbation whose size is given, and \Delta for one produced by an algorithm. - \kappa(\A) always means Chapter 16 §08’s condition number (@def-condition-number). Chapter 20 §11’s condition number of a simple eigenvalue does not appear in this chapter, so the two never have to be told apart. - Iteration indices are superscripts in parentheses, \cvec{x}^{(k)}, \A^{(k)}, leaving subscripts free for coordinates. - \lvert\A\rvert is the entrywise absolute value (\lvert a_{ij}\rvert), as in Chapter 19, and \A \le \B the entrywise order. This is a local override of Chapter 13’s \lvert\A\rvert = (\A^{*}\A)^{1/2}, which does not appear in this chapter. - New symbols, each defined at its first use: the growth factor g_n (§02), the Krylov space \cK_k(\A, \cvec{b}) and the Ritz values (§06), the energy norm \norm{\cdot}_{\A} and the Chebyshev polynomials T_k (§07, the same polynomials as Chapter 11 §10), the mass and stiffness matrices \M and \K (§09), the data matrix \X with its centered form \X_c and sample covariance \S (§10), the graph Laplacian and its reduced form (§11, following Chapter 3 §07), the unnormalized Fourier matrix \W_n = \sqrt n\,\F_n (§12), and the arithmetic cost M(n) with the exponent \omega (§13). Two letters are reused, each with a warning where it happens: \L is the flowed matrix of §08 and the Laplacian of §11, and \K is §09’s stiffness matrix, not Chapter 19 §09’s second-difference matrix \K_n. What the chapter assumes Every earlier chapter assumed only field axioms, and Part V added a short list of facts from analysis. This chapter adds assumptions of a different kind, and both are stated as definitions so that the reader can see exactly where mathematics stops. Floating-point arithmetic is not a theorem of linear algebra. It is a model of a machine. A machine stores finitely many numbers and rounds every result to one of them, and the statement that it does so with a small relative error is a description of a device, not a fact to be proved. So §01 states it as a definition, @def-floating-point-model, in the register this book uses for definitions: a finite set of representable numbers, a rounding map \fl, and the requirement \fl(x \odot y) = (x \odot y)(1 + \delta), \qquad \lvert\delta\rvert \le u, for \odot \in \{+, -, \times, \div\} and for the square root, with overflow and underflow excluded by assumption. Everything after §01 is a theorem about that model. The model is an idealization: the arithmetic in common use satisfies it for those five operations, with u about 10^{-16}, and every rounding claim in this chapter is a consequence of it and of nothing else. Section 9 does the same for a piece of physics. Newton’s second law and Hooke’s law are not theorems either, so @def-mass-spring-model names them as clauses (P1) and (P2), says that Hooke’s law holds only for small displacements and that no real system is free of friction, and every statement about vibrations is then a theorem about that idealization. Nothing outside §09 uses it. No new analysis is imported. The list remains Chapter 16’s facts (A1)–(A6) — completeness, monotone convergence, compactness of closed bounded sets, the extreme value theorem, the intermediate value theorem, and the mean value theorem — together with the algebra of limits. Each is named again where it is used. Chapter 21’s quoted fact (A7), the Nevanlinna–Pick characterization behind Loewner’s theorem, is not used anywhere in this chapter, and neither is any consequence of it that Chapter 21 marked as resting on it. What is quoted and not proved Several classical results in this subject have proofs longer than the sections that need them. The book’s practice is to prove everything or to name the result at its point of use and say plainly that it is not proved. Here is the complete list, section by section; each item is flagged again in the section that quotes it. - §02 — that Chapter 3’s ordering of elimination, which updates the whole trailing block at each step, satisfies the same backward error bound as the ordering §02 displays. The section also declines to quantify the seam between that bound, which is about the factors the model computes, and the growth bound, which is about exact elimination. Separately, and not a quoted theorem at all: partial pivoting is not shown to be backward stable, and §02 says so rather than tidying it. - §03 — Wilkinson’s accumulated backward error for a complete Householder factorization, of which §03 proves the one-reflection case; and the rates at which classical and modified Gram–Schmidt lose orthogonality, u\kappa_2(\A)^2 and u\kappa_2(\A). - §04 — that Rayleigh quotient iteration converges at a quadratic rate, not a cubic one, for a general diagonalizable matrix. The cubic Hermitian rate is proved. - §05 — the theorem of Abel and Ruffini, quoted from Chapter 11 §08, which is the reason every eigenvalue method in this chapter iterates; and the general convergence theorem of the QR algorithm, of which §05 proves the first column and hence the whole 2 \times 2 case. - §06 — the Kaniel–Paige–Saad estimate for the extreme Ritz values, of which §06 proves a clean special case; and the analysis of the loss of orthogonality in Lanczos, which §06 describes and names without proving. - §08 — the differentiability of t \mapsto \Q(t), which the continuous form of the Toda statement rests on. The discrete form, that the QR iterates sit on the flow at integer times, is proved. - §10 — not a quoted theorem but a missing subject. Chapter 13 §11 promised an argument that a sample says something about a population, and that is statistics, which this book does not develop. Section 10 proves everything deterministic, supplies the finite-population reading, and says plainly where it stops. - §13 — the recursive form of Strassen’s error bound; Winograd’s lower bound of seven multiplications for the 2 \times 2 product; the equality of the two definitions of \omega, through all arithmetic operations and through multiplications alone; every bound on \omega below \log_2 7; and Laderman’s twenty-three-product identity for 3 \times 3 matrices, which an exercise hands to the reader. Nothing in this book is proved from any of them. Every theorem in the chapter either proves its own case or carries what it needs as an explicit hypothesis, and since all of these enter the book here, no earlier chapter can rest on them either. The one place a quoted result is used at all is exercise C1 (b) of §13, where Laderman’s identity is given to the reader as a hypothesis and the deduction from it is the reader’s own. What you need This chapter draws on almost the whole book. Chapters 5, 14, 15, 22, and 23 are the exceptions: duality, bilinear forms, tensor products, affine and projective geometry, and algebras and representations are not used here. Chapter 21 supplies the sentence the chapter answers, but none of its theorems. - Chapter 0 §06 and §09 — the complex numbers §07 and §12 work in, and the definition of the matrix product with its three views and the trace, which between them supply every operation count in the chapter: @thm-conjugate-properties, @thm-complex-triangle-inequality, @exm-roots-of-unity, @def-matrix-multiplication, @exm-matrix-multiplication, @thm-three-views-of-product, @thm-trace-properties. - Chapter 1 §06 — basis extension, which §06 uses to finish an orthonormal list, and “a subspace of the full dimension is the whole space”, which §11 uses to identify a column space: @thm-basis-extension, @thm-dim-impl-eq. - Chapter 3 — the invertibility criteria, rank, elimination and the LU factorization, and the incidence matrix of a network that §11 turns into the Laplacian: @thm-invertible-tfae, @thm-rank-nullity-matrix, @thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank, @lem-elimination-matrices, @lem-unit-lower-triangular-closed, @lem-triangular-invertible, @thm-lu-exists-without-swaps, @thm-lu-unique, @exm-no-lu-factorization, @def-incidence-matrix, @prp-incidence-rank-connected, @cor-flow-solvable, @exr-applications-c3. - Chapter 4 §02 — similarity, the relation every eigenvalue iteration in §§04–08 preserves: @def-similar-matrices. - Chapter 6 §01 — that a polynomial over an infinite field is determined by the function it defines, which is how §08 turns an equality of values into an equality of characteristic polynomials: @thm-polynomial-function-determines-polynomial. - Chapter 7 — determinants, almost all of them for §11: the alternating properties, the definition with the triangular and transpose rules, multiplicativity and the invertibility criterion, Laplace expansion and the adjugate identity, minors and rank, and the Gram determinant that §11 turns into the matrix-tree theorem. Section 6 also uses the tridiagonal recurrence and the Vandermonde determinant, and §§05, 07, and 08 the characteristic polynomial: @thm-alternating-properties, @def-determinant, @thm-det-transpose, @thm-det-triangular, @thm-det-multiplicative, @thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible, @thm-laplace-expansion, @thm-adjugate-identity, @thm-rank-via-minors, @cor-gram-determinant-nonnegative, @exr-minors-and-rank-c1, @thm-tridiagonal-recurrence, @thm-vandermonde-determinant, @thm-charpoly-coefficients, @thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant. - Chapter 8 — block multiplication, which is what makes both fast algorithms recurse, and Schur complements, which are what elimination is: @thm-block-multiplication, @def-schur-complement, @thm-block-ldu, @thm-schur-determinant. - Chapter 9 — diagonalization for §04, the eigenvalues on the diagonal of a triangular form for §05, and Cayley–Hamilton for §08: @thm-diagonalization, @thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form, @thm-cayley-hamilton. - Chapter 10 — cyclic subspaces, which are Krylov subspaces under another name, and the matrix exponential, which §08 flows along and §09 solves with: @def-cyclic-subspace, @def-cyclic-vector, @def-t-annihilator, @def-companion-matrix, @prp-cyclic-subspace-smallest, @thm-cyclic-subspace-basis, @thm-cyclic-iff-min-equals-char, @def-matrix-exponential, @thm-exponential-properties, @cor-exponential-of-jordan-block, @thm-linear-ode-solution, @exm-second-order-scalar-ode. - Chapter 11 — the chapter’s largest single source: inner products and Pythagoras, orthonormal bases and Gram–Schmidt, projections and best approximation, least squares, self-adjointness and isometries, reflections and rotations with the QR factorization and Hessenberg form, Parseval’s identity, and the orthogonal polynomials behind the three-term recurrence: @thm-cauchy-schwarz, @cor-triangle-inequality, @thm-pythagoras, @thm-orthogonal-independent, @def-induced-norm, @thm-gram-schmidt, @thm-orthonormal-coordinates, @def-orthogonal-projection, @def-distance-to-subspace, @thm-orthogonal-decomposition, @thm-best-approximation, @thm-least-squares, @cor-least-squares-unique, @prp-self-adjoint-immediate, @def-unitary-orthogonal, @prp-orthogonal-group-properties, @thm-isometry-characterizations, @def-householder-reflection, @prp-householder-properties, @thm-householder-maps-vector, @thm-qr-factorization, @thm-qr-householder, @def-givens-rotation, @thm-hessenberg-form, @thm-parseval-identity, @def-orthogonal-polynomial-sequence, @prp-multiplication-by-x-symmetric, @thm-three-term-recurrence. - Chapter 12 — the spectral theorem in both forms, and the circulants and the discrete Fourier transform that §§11 and 12 rest on: @cor-spectral-complex-matrix, @cor-spectral-real-matrix, @def-circulant, @thm-circulant-diagonalization, @cor-circulants-algebra, @thm-fourier-matrix-unitary, @thm-convolution-theorem, @exm-fourier-matrix-4, @exr-circulants-and-the-dft-b1. - Chapter 13 — positive definiteness and Cholesky, simultaneous congruence, which is exactly §09’s basis of normal modes, the Loewner order, the singular value decomposition with low-rank approximation for §10, and the pseudoinverse: @def-positive-semidefinite, @thm-pd-characterizations, @thm-psd-characterizations, @prp-congruence-positivity, @thm-cholesky, @exm-cholesky-by-hand, @def-generalized-eigenvalue, @thm-generalized-eigenvalues-real, @thm-simultaneous-congruence, @exm-generalized-eigenproblem-2x2, @def-loewner-order, @def-singular-values, @thm-svd, @def-truncated-svd, @thm-eckart-young, @cor-best-fitting-subspace, @def-pseudoinverse. - Chapter 16 — norms and operator norms, the derivative of a matrix-valued function, and above all the condition number and the theorem that bounds a relative error by it: @lem-reverse-triangle-norm, @thm-operator-norm-formulas, @thm-operator-norm-properties, @def-matrix-valued-derivative, @lem-matrix-product-rule, @thm-derivative-of-inverse, @thm-derivative-of-det, @def-condition-number, @prp-condition-number-properties, @thm-relative-error-bound, @thm-normal-equations-squares-conditioning. - Chapter 17 — the Rayleigh quotient and its critical points, the min–max description of the eigenvalues, Weyl’s inequalities, interlacing, and the variational description of the singular values: @def-rayleigh-quotient, @prp-rayleigh-basic, @prp-rayleigh-critical-points, @prp-rayleigh-deflation, @thm-courant-fischer, @cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone, @cor-weyl-perturbation, @lem-hermitian-spectral-norm, @thm-cauchy-interlacing, @cor-interlacing-general-submatrix, @lem-tridiagonal-eigenvector-ends, @thm-weyl-singular-values, @cor-singular-value-perturbation. - Chapter 18 — two small facts, one from each end of the chapter: the coset description of an affine hull, which §10 minimizes over, and the logarithm of a positive definite matrix, which §08 needs to know which matrices its theorem covers: @prp-affine-hull-coset, @lem-exp-log. Both are cited in the text, in §10’s opening and §08’s warning, and neither is a step in a proof. - Chapter 19 — the cyclic permutation that defeats the power method, the Google matrix and the PageRank rate that §04 explains, and the second-difference matrix that §09’s uniform chain turns out to be: @exm-cyclic-permutation, @thm-google-matrix-eigenvalues, @prp-pagerank-contraction, @prp-second-difference-inverse. These are examples the chapter re-reads rather than results it argues from: they appear in §04’s and §09’s examples, and in no proof. - Chapter 20 — the perturbation bounds that turn a residual into an error bar, which is what makes every iteration in this chapter stoppable: @thm-residual-bound, @thm-hermitian-residual-bound, @thm-kato-temple. They are quoted where they are needed — the warnings of §§01 and 06 — and applied in the examples and exercises of §§04, 05, and 06, but no proof here is built on one. Roadmap - Floating point and backward error. The model, the constant \gamma_k, the backward error of an inner product, and the three words the chapter runs on: backward stable, forward error, mixed stability. Then the rule, made a theorem: forward error at most condition number times backward error. - Elimination, pivoting, and cost. One step of elimination is a Schur complement of a 1 \times 1 pivot. The cost is \tfrac23 n^3, and half that for Cholesky. A triangular solve is backward stable, and so is the factorization, up to a growth factor that partial pivoting bounds by 2^{n-1} — a bound that is attained, which is why the section stops short of calling partial pivoting stable. - Least squares in practice. The sensitivity of the least-squares solution involves the residual as well as \kappa_2(\A). Forming the normal equations loses twice the digits; the reflection route loses them once, because one reflection is backward stable, and classical Gram–Schmidt loses orthogonality at a rate this section states with credit. - The power method. Repeated multiplication finds the dominant eigenvector at rate \lvert\lambda_2/\lambda_1\rvert, the Rayleigh quotient squares that for Hermitian matrices, a shift and an inverse pick out any eigenvalue, and updating the shift from the Rayleigh quotient makes the convergence cubic. It all fails when two eigenvalues share a modulus. - The QR algorithm. Factor and reverse, repeatedly. The iterates are orthogonal iteration applied to the powers of the matrix, which is where the convergence comes from; Hessenberg form brings the cost of a step down to about 6n^2 flops; and a shift is what turns slow convergence into fast. - Krylov subspaces. The right home for an iteration that can afford only one matrix–vector product at a time. Gram–Schmidt inside that space is the Arnoldi process and gives a Hessenberg matrix, with a three-term recurrence — the Lanczos process — when the matrix is Hermitian; the eigenvalues of the small matrix interlace the large one’s, and Chapter 20’s bounds apply to them verbatim. In floating point the three-term economy costs orthogonality, and the section says so. - Steepest descent and conjugate gradients. Solving \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} by minimizing a quadratic. Steepest descent converges like (\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1); conjugate gradients minimizes over the whole Krylov space and converges like (\sqrt\kappa - 1)/(\sqrt\kappa + 1). The square root is the point, and Chebyshev polynomials, small on an interval and large just outside it, are where it comes from. - Lax pairs and the Toda flow. The chapter’s one piece of pure mathematics: a differential equation whose flow preserves the spectrum, and which the QR iterates sit on at integer times. That the flow’s time-one map is a step of the algorithm is derived, but only after granting a differentiability this book has not set up. An algorithm and a differential equation can be the same object seen at two resolutions. - Vibrations. Masses and springs give \M\ddot{\cvec{x}} = -\K\cvec{x}, the substitution \cvec{x} = e^{i\omega t}\cvec{v} gives a generalized eigenproblem, and Chapter 13 gives the \M-orthonormal basis of normal modes. Stiffening raises every frequency, adding mass lowers them, and pinning a mass interlaces them. - Principal components. The best-fitting k-dimensional affine subspace of a finite set of points is spanned by the leading singular vectors of the centered data matrix, and “variance explained” is a theorem rather than a convention. The covariance matrix is never formed, for §03’s reason, and the inference from a sample to a population is handed back to statistics. - Graph Laplacians. \L = \N\N\tp for the incidence matrix of Chapter 3 §07. The multiplicity of the eigenvalue 0 counts components, the second smallest eigenvalue measures connectivity and the signs of its eigenvector split the graph, and the determinant of a reduced Laplacian counts spanning trees, which completes Chapter 7 §07. - The fast Fourier transform. The Fourier matrix factors into a permutation, two half-size copies of itself, and a diagonal factor. Solving the resulting recurrence gives O(n\log n), and with it fast convolution, fast polynomial multiplication, and fast circulant solves. - Fast matrix multiplication. Two 2 \times 2 matrices multiply with seven products instead of eight, and the recursion gives O(n^{\log_2 7}). The exponent \omega is at least 2, which is proved; everything known about it below \log_2 7 is stated with credit and not proved. Strassen’s algorithm satisfies a norm error bound but no entrywise one, and a small entry really can come out with every digit wrong. The section closes the chapter. Named moves - State the machine as a definition, then prove theorems about it. When a subject rests on something that is not mathematics, isolate it in one definition, say what kind of statement it is, and derive the rest. Everything in this chapter that mentions rounding is a consequence of @def-floating-point-model alone, and §09 treats its two physical laws the same way. - Measure an answer by a change in the data that makes it exact. The forward error is what one wants and cannot see; the backward error is what one can bound. Prove the backward statement and let the condition number convert it. - Count the operations, and solve the recurrence exactly. An asymptotic order hides the constant that decides whether an algorithm is worth using. Every cost in this chapter is a closed form or an explicit leading term. - A residual is an error bar. Chapter 20’s perturbation bounds turn a quantity the algorithm already has into a certificate, which is what allows an iteration to know when to stop. - Iterate in a subspace, not along a direction. The Krylov space is generated by the one operation an iteration can afford, and it is large enough to contain the answer to a polynomial approximation problem whose solution is the algorithm. - A conserved spectrum comes from a commutator. If \dot{\L} = [\B, \L], then \L(t) is a similarity orbit and its eigenvalues do not move; differentiating a conjugation is the whole proof. - A fast algorithm is a factorization. Factor the linear map (the Fourier matrix) or the bilinear map (the matrix product) into cheap pieces and recursive calls, then count the calls against the size reduction.

title: 24.1 Floating Point and Backward Error
content:
Floating Point and Backward Error Chapter 16 ended with a number and a warning. The number was \kappa(\A), which bounds how much a relative error in the data can be magnified on the way to the answer. The warning was that \kappa says nothing about arithmetic: it “describes a problem”, and an error bound of its shape “only becomes a statement about a computation once one knows how large a perturbation the computation itself introduces”. That chapter closed the door with a sentence we now have to walk through: “Conditioning bounds what any method can promise; whether a given method keeps that promise is stability, and it is Chapter 24’s subject.” This section builds the two things that were missing. First a model of machine arithmetic — an assumption, stated plainly as one, because floating-point arithmetic is not a theorem of linear algebra. Then the vocabulary that turns the model into verdicts about algorithms: forward error, backward error, and stability. Two answers to one question Chapter 16 §08 left a small experiment on the reader’s desk. The system was  egin{aligned} 10^{-15}x_1 + x_2 &= 1, \ x_1 + x_2 &= 2 , \end{aligned} whose coefficient matrix has \kappa_{\infty} < 5: by every measure of Chapter 16 this problem is as well behaved as a problem can be, and its exact solution is (1, 1) to fourteen places. Eliminating x_1 with the first equation as the pivot row, and rounding to twelve significant decimal digits at every step, returns (0, 1). Exchanging the two equations first, and rounding in exactly the same way, returns (1, 1). Two algorithms, one problem, one arithmetic, and one of the two answers has no correct digit in it. Nothing in Chapter 16 can tell the two apart, because \kappa never mentions a method. Section 2 works that example in the model below and says exactly what the exchange achieved. This section builds the language it will be said in. A model of machine arithmetic A machine holds finitely many numbers. It cannot hold 1/3, it cannot hold \sqrt2, and between any two numbers it does hold there are infinitely many it does not. So the result of an arithmetic operation on two stored numbers is usually not a stored number, and the machine must replace it by a neighbor. We could try to describe which numbers a particular machine stores and exactly how it rounds. That would be a description of a machine, not mathematics, and it would be obsolete before the ink dried. What is wanted instead is the one property of rounding that every later argument uses, elevated into an assumption. Every operation is performed exactly and then moved to the nearest stored number, so each operation multiplies its exact answer by something within u of 1. [The floating-point model] A floating-point model consists of a finite set \cR \subseteq 
R of representable numbers with 0, 1 \in \cR and -\cR = \cR, a map  l \colon 
R 	o \cR sending each real number to a nearest element of \cR, and a real number u > 0 called the unit roundoff, subject to the following. 1. (Rounding.) For every t \in 
R in range,  l(t) = t(1 + \delta) for some \delta with \lvert\deltavert \le u. 2. (Arithmetic.) For x, y \in \cR and \odot \in \{+, -, 	imes, \div\} with y 
e 0 when \odot is \div, the computed value of x \odot y is  l(x \odot y); the computed value of \sqrt{x} for x \in \cR, x \ge 0, is  l(\sqrt{x}\,). Hence  l(x \odot y) = (x \odot y)(1 + \delta), \qquad \lvert\deltavert \le u , and likewise  l(\sqrt x) = \sqrt x\,(1 + \delta) with \lvert\deltavert \le u. 3. (No overflow or underflow.) Every quantity occurring in a computation we analyze is assumed to be in range, so that (FP1) applies to it. Clause by clause. “A nearest element” is a mild requirement, and the only use we make of it is the observation that \lvert tvert \le 1 forces \lvert l(t)vert \le 1, because 1 \in \cR. (FP1) is the whole content of the word roundoff: the error made in storing a real number is relative, of size at most u, and that is essentially the only thing we will ever know about  l. (FP2) says an operation is as accurate as storing its answer would be — the machine does not do anything stupid in between. The displayed identity is what every proof in this chapter actually uses, and it is worth reading aloud: the computed product is the exact product times 1 + \delta. (FP3) is an honest exclusion. Numbers too large or too small for \cR break (FP1) completely, and analyzing them is a separate subject; we assume the problem away and say so each time it matters. This is a definition, not a theorem. Nothing in Chapters 1 to 21 implies it, and nothing in this chapter proves it. It is an idealization of a machine, in the way that a frictionless plane is an idealization of a table. The arithmetic in common use satisfies it for the four operations and the square root, with u a little over 10^{-16}; a decimal machine carrying t significant digits satisfies it with u = 	frac12 \cdot 10^{1-t}. Every statement in this chapter that mentions rounding is a theorem about the model, and carries exactly as much authority as the model does. [The model we compute in] Throughout this chapter, a worked number comes from the six-digit decimal model: \cR is the set of numbers \pm d_1.d_2d_3d_4d_5d_6 	imes 10^{e} with digits d_i, d_1 
e 0 and e in some fixed finite range, together with 0; and  l rounds to the nearest such number. (The range of e is what (FP3) lets us stop thinking about.) What is u, and what is  l(99999996)? Two consecutive representable numbers of the same exponent e differ by 10^{e-5}, and a number t with that exponent has \lvert tvert \ge 10^{e}. Rounding to the nearest moves t by at most half the gap, so \lvert l(t) - tvert \le 	frac12 \cdot 10^{e-5} \le 	frac12 \cdot 10^{-5}\lvert tvert , which is (FP1) with u = 	frac12 \cdot 10^{-5} = 5 	imes 10^{-6}. For  l(99999996): the number is 9.9999996 	imes 10^{7}, and the two neighbors with six digits are 9.99999 	imes 10^{7} and 1.00000 	imes 10^{8}. The second is nearer, so  l(99999996) = 10^{8}. Note what happened: eight digits went in, six came out, and the two digits that were lost were the only two that distinguished 99999996 from 10^8. A model with an absolute error bound would be a different, and false, model. Suppose we had written  l(x + y) = (x + y) + \delta with \lvert\deltavert \le u. Then  l(10^{6} + 1) would have to be within u = 5	imes10^{-6} of 10^{6} + 1, whereas a six-digit machine returns 10^{6}, an absolute error of 1. The error a machine makes is proportional to the size of the number it is storing; a machine is accurate in ratio, never in amount. Confusing the two is the commonest mistake in the subject, and (FP1) exists to prevent it. In the six-digit model, is  l(x + y) = x + y possible when x and y are representable and both nonzero? Is  l(x - y) = x - y possible when x 
e y? Yes to both, and easily. 1 + 2 = 3 is representable, so the first addition is exact. For the second, 10^{8} - 99999.9 = 99900000.1, which is not representable, so that particular subtraction is inexact; but 1.00001 - 1.00000 = 10^{-5} is representable exactly, so that subtraction is exact. The model never claims an operation is inexact. It claims only a bound on how inexact it can be. That both extremes occur is what makes the subject interesting: the second subtraction is performed exactly, and it is nevertheless the shape of subtraction that destroys answers, as the last example of this section will show. Accumulated rounding: the constant \gamma_k A single operation costs a factor 1 + \delta. An algorithm performs many, and the factors pile up: an answer typically carries a product like (1 + \delta_1)(1 + \delta_2)\cdots(1 + \delta_k), sometimes with an inverted factor where a division occurred. Carrying such products around is unbearable, so we bound them once and for all. The constant that results is used in every remaining section of this chapter. [Accumulated rounding] Let k \ge 1 and let \delta_1, \dots, \delta_k satisfy \lvert\delta_ivert \le u, and let ho_1, \dots, ho_k \in \{+1, -1\}. If ku < 1, then \prod_{i=1}^{k}(1 + \delta_i)^{ho_i} = 1 + 	heta \qquad	ext{with}\qquad \lvert	hetavert \le \gamma_k \coloneqq  rac{ku}{1 - ku} . Induction on k, with the two signs treated as two cases. The only thing to watch is that the recursion for \gamma_k survives division, where the denominator 1 - u costs something; the definition \gamma_k = ku/(1-ku) is exactly the bound that absorbs that cost. Note first that ku < 1 forces ju < 1 for j \le k, so every \gamma_j with j \le k is defined and positive, and \gamma_1 \le \gamma_2 \le \dots \le \gamma_k. Base case k = 1. If ho_1 = +1, then 	heta = \delta_1 and \lvert	hetavert \le u \le u/(1-u) = \gamma_1. If ho_1 = -1, then 	heta =  rac{1}{1 + \delta_1} - 1 =  rac{-\delta_1}{1 + \delta_1}, \qquad \lvert	hetavert \le  rac{u}{1 - u} = \gamma_1 , where 1 + \delta_1 \ge 1 - u > 0 because u < 1. Inductive step. Suppose the product of the first k-1 factors is 1 + 	heta' with \lvert	heta'vert \le \gamma_{k-1}, and write \delta = \delta_k. If ho_k = +1, then 1 + 	heta = (1 + 	heta')(1 + \delta), so 	heta = 	heta' + \delta + 	heta'\delta and  egin{aligned} \lvert	hetavert &\le \gamma_{k-1} + u + \gamma_{k-1}u\ &=  rac{(k-1)u + u igl(1 - (k-1)u igr) + (k-1)u^2}{1 - (k-1)u} =  rac{ku}{1 - (k-1)u} , \end{aligned} and 1 - (k-1)u \ge 1 - ku > 0, so this is at most ku/(1-ku) = \gamma_k. If ho_k = -1, then 1 + 	heta = (1 + 	heta')/(1 + \delta), so 	heta = (	heta' - \delta)/(1 + \delta) and \lvert	hetavert \le (\gamma_{k-1} + u)/(1 - u). It remains to check that this is at most \gamma_k. Clearing the positive denominators 1 - (k-1)u, 1 - u, and 1 - ku, the inequality (\gamma_{k-1}+u)/(1-u) \le \gamma_k is equivalent to u igl(k - (k-1)u igr)(1 - ku) \le ku igl(1 - ku + (k-1)u^2 igr) , and expanding both sides gives k - k^2u - (k-1)u + k(k-1)u^2 on the left against k - k^2u + k(k-1)u^2 on the right, after dividing by u > 0. The left side is the right side minus (k-1)u, which is at least 0, so the left side is at most the right side and the inequality holds. This proves the lemma. Read \gamma_k as “about ku”. Indeed if ku \le 0.01 then \gamma_k \le ku/0.99 < 1.02\,ku. The denominator is there only so that the induction above closes; it is never the point of a bound. We will also use, without further comment, that \gamma_j \le \gamma_k for j \le k, and we set \gamma_0 = 0, which is what the formula gives and what the empty product deserves. The first backward error analysis Here is the simplest algorithm in the book: add up n products. What comes out is not \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y}. But it is exactly \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y} for a slightly different \cvec{x} — and that turns out to be the useful thing to say. [Backward Error of an Inner Product] Let \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^{n} have representable entries, let nu < 1, and let the inner product be computed in the model of @def-floating-point-model in the natural order, s_1 =  l(x_1y_1), \qquad s_k =  l igl(s_{k-1} +  l(x_ky_k) igr) \quad (k = 2, \dots, n). Then there is a vector \Delta\cvec{x} \in 
R^n with s_n = (\cvec{x} + \Delta\cvec{x})	p\cvec{y} \qquad	ext{and}\qquad \lvert\Delta x_ivert \le \gamma_n \lvert x_ivert \ 	ext{ for every } i . Unroll the recursion and see which rounding factors touch which term. The term x_ky_k picks up one factor from its own multiplication and one from each addition it takes part in afterwards, so no term collects more than n factors. @lem-gamma-bound converts “at most n factors” into “1 + 	heta with \lvert	hetavert \le \gamma_n”, and a factor attached to x_ky_k can be blamed on x_k alone. By (FP2) there are numbers \delta_k and \varepsilon_k, all of modulus at most u, with  egin{aligned}  l(x_ky_k) &= x_ky_k(1 + \delta_k) \quad (1 \le k \le n),\ s_k &=  igl(s_{k-1} +  l(x_ky_k) igr)(1 + \varepsilon_k) \quad (2 \le k \le n). \end{aligned} An induction on m gives s_m = \sum_{k=1}^{m} x_ky_k(1 + \delta_k)\prod_{j = \max(k,2)}^{m}(1 + \varepsilon_j) , the empty product being 1: for m = 1 this is s_1 = x_1y_1(1+\delta_1), and the step from m-1 to m multiplies every existing term by 1 + \varepsilon_m and adds the new term x_my_m(1+\delta_m)(1+\varepsilon_m), which is what the formula says. Take m = n and count factors in the k-th term. For k = 1 there are 1 + (n-1) = n of them; for k \ge 2 there are 1 + (n - k + 1) = n - k + 2 \le n. Every factor has the form 1 + \delta with \lvert\deltavert \le u, and nu < 1, so @lem-gamma-bound (with all ho_i = +1) gives numbers 	heta_k with s_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} x_ky_k(1 + 	heta_k), \qquad \lvert	heta_kvert \le \gamma_n . Put \Delta x_k = x_k	heta_k. Then \lvert\Delta x_kvert \le \gamma_n\lvert x_kvert and s_n = \sum_k (x_k + \Delta x_k)y_k = (\cvec{x} + \Delta\cvec{x})	p\cvec{y}. This proves the theorem. The conclusion is worth staring at. The computed number is not close to \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y} — if \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y} happens to be tiny compared with \sum_k \lvert x_ky_kvert, it can be wrong in every digit. What the theorem says is different and stronger in kind: the computed number is an inner product, exactly, of data within a relative \gamma_n of the given data. The algorithm has not solved a nearby problem approximately; it has solved a nearby problem exactly. The same proof, with the roles of \cvec{x} and \cvec{y} exchanged, gives s_n = \cvec{x}	p(\cvec{y} + \Delta\cvec{y}) with \lvert\Delta\cvec{y}vert \le \gamma_n\lvert\cvec{y}vert entrywise. What it does not give is a perturbation of both at once with half the constant, and it does not give a bound on \lvert s_n - \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y}vert relative to \lvert\cvec{x}	p\cvec{y}vert. @exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-c1 makes the last point precise. For complex \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} the operations +, 	imes are themselves built from several real operations, so the model must be applied to those; the resulting bound has the same shape with a modestly larger constant, and we do not prove it here or use it. Forward error, backward error, stability We can now name what @thm-inner-product-backward-error did, and the alternative it declined to do. Fix a problem: a map f \colon D 	o 
R^{m} from data to answers, where D is a set of admissible data in some 
R^{N}. The set D always consists of real data and is never cut down to the representable ones: for the problems of this chapter it is all of 
R^{N}, or all invertible matrices, and it has to be, because the perturbed datum \cvec{a} + \Delta\cvec{a} below must lie in it. An algorithm for f is a map \widehat f — defined at the representable data, and sending each of them to whatever the computation actually returns in the model, rounding and all. Two numbers measure how the second differs from the first. [Forward and backward error] Let f be a problem, \widehat f an algorithm for it, and \cvec{a} \in D a representable datum with f(\cvec{a}) 
e \cvec{0}. The forward error of \widehat f at \cvec{a} is the relative error in the answer,  rac{
orm{\widehat f(\cvec{a}) - f(\cvec{a})}}{
orm{f(\cvec{a})}} . The backward error of \widehat f at \cvec{a} is the smallest relative perturbation of the data that accounts for the computed answer exactly, \inf\Bigl\{ rac{
orm{\Delta\cvec{a}}}{
orm{\cvec{a}}} \;:\; \cvec{a} + \Delta\cvec{a} \in D 	ext{ and } f(\cvec{a} + \Delta\cvec{a}) = \widehat f(\cvec{a})\Bigr\} , with the convention that it is \infty when no such \Delta\cvec{a} exists. The forward error is what a user wants to know and can almost never compute, since it needs f(\cvec{a}). The backward error is what an analyst can bound, because bounding it only requires exhibiting one \Delta\cvec{a}, which a proof like the one above hands over for free. An algorithm whose backward error is always as small as the arithmetic allows is the best one can hope for. A backward stable algorithm returns the exact answer to a question you might as well have asked. [Backward stability] Let f \colon D 	o 
R^m be a problem. An algorithm \widehat f for f, running in a floating-point model with unit roundoff u, is backward stable if there is a constant c, depending only on the dimensions of the data and not on the data itself or on u, such that for every representable \cvec{a} \in D there exists \Delta\cvec{a} \in 
R^{N} with \cvec{a} + \Delta\cvec{a} \in D, \qquad \widehat f(\cvec{a}) = f(\cvec{a} + \Delta\cvec{a}), \qquad 
orm{\Delta\cvec{a}} \le c\,u\,
orm{\cvec{a}} . The small words carry the weight. For every \cvec{a}: one lucky datum proves nothing. c independent of the data: a “constant” allowed to grow with 
orm{\cvec{a}} or with \kappa would make the definition vacuous. c independent of u: the bound must improve when the arithmetic does. The constant is allowed to depend on n, and in practice always does — \gamma_n is about nu, not u — which is why “backward stable” is a statement about a family of algorithms indexed by size, and why nobody worries much about a factor of n. By @thm-inner-product-backward-error, the natural inner product algorithm is backward stable as an algorithm in \cvec{x} for the problem \cvec{x} \mapsto \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y} with \cvec{y} fixed, on the domain D = 
R^n. Take c = 1.02\,n, which depends on the dimension alone. Indeed the entrywise bound \lvert\Delta\cvec{x}vert \le \gamma_n\lvert\cvec{x}vert implies 
orm{\Delta\cvec{x}} \le \gamma_n
orm{\cvec{x}} in each of the norms 
orm{\cdot}_1, 
orm{\cdot}_2, 
orm{\cdot}_{\infty}, and \gamma_n \le 1.02\,nu in every model with nu \le 0.01, by the remark after @lem-gamma-bound. (Restricting to such models is how a bound stated with \gamma_n is turned into one with a constant independent of u, and we do it silently from here on.) Some algorithms are not backward stable and are not bad either: they perturb the data a little and the answer a little, and neither perturbation alone accounts for the result. The weaker notion that covers them is worth naming, so that we never have to claim more than we have proved. [Mixed forward-backward stability] An algorithm \widehat f for f \colon D 	o 
R^m is mixed forward-backward stable if there is a constant c, depending only on the dimensions, such that for every representable \cvec{a} \in D there are \Delta\cvec{a} and \Delta\cvec{y} with \cvec{a} + \Delta\cvec{a} \in D and \widehat f(\cvec{a}) = f(\cvec{a} + \Delta\cvec{a}) + \Delta\cvec{y}, \qquad 
orm{\Delta\cvec{a}} \le cu
orm{\cvec{a}}, \qquad 
orm{\Delta\cvec{y}} \le cu
orm{f(\cvec{a} + \Delta\cvec{a})} . Backward stability is the special case \Delta\cvec{y} = \cvec{0}, so it is the stronger statement of the two. A mixed stable algorithm does not satisfy the hypothesis of the next theorem: its \Delta\cvec{y} contributes a further term to the forward error, and we do not estimate that term anywhere in this chapter. Where a method in this chapter is only mixed stable, we say so, and we claim nothing more about it than the definition gives. Backward stable does not mean accurate, and inaccurate does not mean unstable. A backward stable algorithm commits to nothing about the forward error except what the problem allows, and for an ill-conditioned problem that is very little. Conversely, an algorithm can return an accurate answer on one datum by luck while being backward unstable. The two words describe different objects: conditioning belongs to f, stability belongs to \widehat f. Chapter 16 §08 promised exactly this: “Chapter 24 draws the distinction properly, defines backward stability, and proves which of the algorithms in this book have it.” @def-backward-stable is the definition; the proofs occupy Sections 2 and 3, and the next theorem is the only bridge between the two sides. Multiplying the two together The rule of thumb everyone quotes is forward error \lesssim condition number 	imes backward error. For linear systems it is not a rule of thumb at all. It is @thm-relative-error-bound with a different reading of the same symbols. [Forward Error from Backward Error] Let \A \in M_n(
C) be invertible, \cvec{b} 
e \cvec{0}, and \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}. Let \widehat{\cvec{x}} be any vector which is the exact solution of a perturbed system, (\A + \Delta\A)\widehat{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{b}, \qquad  rac{
orm{\Delta\A}}{
orm{\A}} \le \eta , and suppose r \coloneqq \kappa(\A)\,\eta < 1. Then \A + \Delta\A is invertible and  rac{
orm{\widehat{\cvec{x}} - \cvec{x}}}{
orm{\cvec{x}}} \;\le\;  rac{r}{1 - r} \;=\;  rac{\kappa(\A)\eta}{1 - \kappa(\A)\eta} . In particular, if \eta = cu is admissible — as it is when the algorithm producing \widehat{\cvec{x}} is backward stable with constant c for the problem \A \mapsto \A^{-1}\cvec{b} with \cvec{b} held fixed, so that only \A is perturbed — and if \kappa(\A)cu \le 	frac12, then the forward relative error is at most 2\kappa(\A)cu. There is nothing to do: backward stability says the computed answer solves a perturbed system exactly, and Chapter 16 already bounded the effect of perturbing \A. The content of the theorem is the translation, not the estimate. Since 
orm{\Delta\A}/
orm{\A} \le \eta, we have \kappa(\A)
orm{\Delta\A}/
orm{\A} \le r < 1, so @thm-relative-error-bound (b), applied with \E = \Delta\A, says that \A + \Delta\A is invertible and that  rac{
orm{\widehat{\cvec{x}} - \cvec{x}}}{
orm{\cvec{x}}} \le  rac{r'}{1 - r'}, \qquad r' \coloneqq \kappa(\A) rac{
orm{\Delta\A}}{
orm{\A}} \le r . The function s \mapsto s/(1-s) is increasing on [0, 1), since its derivative (1-s)^{-2} is positive there, so r'/(1-r') \le r/(1-r). For the last claim put \eta = cu; then r = \kappa(\A)cu \le 	frac12 gives 1 - r \ge 	frac12 and r/(1-r) \le 2r. This proves the theorem. When the right-hand side is perturbed too. A solver for \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} normally perturbs the pair (\A, \cvec{b}), returning \widehat{\cvec{x}} 
e \cvec{0} with (\A + \Delta\A)\widehat{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{b} + \Delta\cvec{b}, \qquad 
orm{\Delta\A}_2 \le cu
orm{\A}_2, \qquad 
orm{\Delta\cvec{b}}_2 \le cu
orm{\cvec{b}}_2 , which is not literally the hypothesis above. One absorption repairs that. Put \Delta\A' = \Delta\A - \Delta\cvec{b}\,\widehat{\cvec{x}}^{*}/
orm{\widehat{\cvec{x}}}_2^2; then (\A + \Delta\A')\widehat{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{b} + \Delta\cvec{b} - \Delta\cvec{b} = \cvec{b}, and the subtracted matrix is an outer product, of 2-norm 
orm{\Delta\cvec{b}}_2/
orm{\widehat{\cvec{x}}}_2. So @thm-forward-from-backward applies in the 2-norm with \eta = cu\Bigl(1 +  rac{
orm{\cvec{b}}_2}{
orm{\A}_2
orm{\widehat{\cvec{x}}}_2}\Bigr) \;\le\; cu\Bigl(1 +  rac{
orm{\cvec{x}}_2}{
orm{\widehat{\cvec{x}}}_2}\Bigr) , the last step because 
orm{\cvec{b}}_2 = 
orm{\A\cvec{x}}_2 \le 
orm{\A}_2
orm{\cvec{x}}_2. That is a small multiple of cu as soon as the computed \widehat{\cvec{x}} is not much shorter than \cvec{x}, and it is how every later appeal to the theorem for a linear solver is to be read. Reading the bound in digits. Suppose the arithmetic has u \approx 10^{-16} and the algorithm is backward stable with a modest c. The bound then reads: relative forward error at most about \kappa(\A) \cdot 10^{-16}. Taking logarithms, the computed answer may be wrong from about the  igl(16 - \log_{10}\kappa(\A) igr)-th significant digit onward. This is the origin of the sentence “a stable solve loses about \log_{10}\kappa decimal digits”. Two cautions, both real. It is an upper bound, so the loss may be smaller — Chapter 16 §08’s warning that “the condition number bounds the error; it does not produce it” applies verbatim. And it is a statement about \kappa(\A) for the problem as posed: an algorithm that quietly poses a different problem pays that problem’s condition number instead. That last point is the whole of Chapter 16 §08’s remaining ledger. Its third unpaid item read: “Hence the comparison of the two algorithms — that a stable implementation of the QR route loses about \log_{10}\kappa_2(\A) decimal digits while forming and solving the normal equations loses about 2\log_{10}\kappa_2(\A) — is still Chapter 24’s to prove.” The theorem above supplies the first half of the sentence for any backward stable method. Section 3 supplies the second half and the two algorithms, using Chapter 16’s own @thm-normal-equations-squares-conditioning for the square. An algorithm for \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} is backward stable, \kappa(\A) = 10^{8}, and u = 10^{-16}. A user reports that the computed \widehat{\cvec{x}} has only eight correct digits and concludes that the algorithm is broken. What is wrong with the conclusion? Nothing at all is wrong with the algorithm: @thm-forward-from-backward — applied after absorbing any perturbation of \cvec{b} into \Delta\A, as in the remark following it — predicts a relative forward error of about \kappa(\A)u = 10^{-8}, up to the modest constant c, which is exactly eight correct digits. The loss is charged to the problem, not to the method. Chapter 16 §08 put it as sharply as it can be put: with data of limited accuracy, an ill-conditioned answer is not determined to more digits than that, whatever anybody computes with. Cancellation, and where the damage really happens Backward stability is a property of a whole algorithm, and algorithms are usually wrecked in one place. That place is almost always a subtraction of two nearly equal numbers. The following example is the standard one, and it repays being done digit by digit. [Two ways to solve a quadratic] In the six-digit decimal model of @exm-six-digit-model, find the two roots of x^2 - 10^{4}x + 1 = 0 by the quadratic formula x_{\pm} = 	frac12 igl(10^4 \pm \sqrt{10^8 - 4} igr), and then again with the smaller root computed as x_- = 1/x_+. Compare with the exact roots. The exact roots. Their sum is 10^4 and their product is 1. Now 9999.9998^2 = 10^{8} - 4 + 4	imes10^{-8}, which is just above 10^8 - 4, so \sqrt{10^8 - 4} = 9999.99979999\ldots and x_+ = 9999.99989999\ldots, \qquad x_- =  rac{1}{x_+} = 1.0000000100\ldots 	imes 10^{-4} . The formula, step by step. Each line is one operation of the model. -  l(10^4 	imes 10^4) = 10^{8}, exactly representable, no error. -  l(10^{8} - 4) =  l(99999996) = 1.00000 	imes 10^{8}, by @exm-six-digit-model. Here the two informative digits are lost, and the relative error committed is about 4 	imes 10^{-8}, comfortably inside u = 5 	imes 10^{-6}. The model is behaving perfectly. -  l(\sqrt{10^{8}}) = 10^{4}, exactly. -  l(10^4 + 10^4) = 2 	imes 10^4 and  l(2	imes10^4 \div 2) = 10^4: the computed x_+ is 10^{4}, with relative error 10^{-8}. Excellent. -  l(10^4 - 10^4) = 0, exactly, and  l(0 \div 2) = 0: the computed x_- is \mathbf{0}. The repair. Compute x_+ = 10^4 as above, then  l(1 \div 10^4) = 10^{-4}, whose relative error against 1.00000001 	imes 10^{-4} is 10^{-8}. What to conclude. The second route loses nothing; the first returns a root with no correct digit, indeed with no digits at all. And notice where the damage was done. The fatal subtraction 10^4 - 10^4 was performed exactly: both operands were representable and so was their difference. The error was already present, manufactured four lines earlier when 99999996 was rounded to 10^8, and the subtraction merely deleted the digits the two operands had in common, which was all of them. Cancellation does not create error. It exposes error, by deleting the digits that were correct and promoting the ones that were not. A small residual is not a small error, and a small error is not a small residual. For a computed solution \widehat{\cvec{x}} of \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} with \widehat{\cvec{x}} 
e \cvec{0}, put \cvec{r} = \cvec{b} - \A\widehat{\cvec{x}} and \Delta\A =  rac{\cvec{r}\,\widehat{\cvec{x}}^{*}}{
orm{\widehat{\cvec{x}}}_2^2}, \qquad	ext{so that}\qquad (\A + \Delta\A)\widehat{\cvec{x}} = \A\widehat{\cvec{x}} + \cvec{r} = \cvec{b} , and 
orm{\Delta\A}_2 = 
orm{\cvec{r}}_2/
orm{\widehat{\cvec{x}}}_2: Cauchy–Schwarz gives \le, and \Delta\A\widehat{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{r} attains it — the computation is the one in the proof of @thm-residual-bound, with \cvec{b} in place of \mu\widehat{\cvec{x}}. So a small relative residual is a small backward error, and nothing more: by @thm-forward-from-backward the forward error may still be \kappa(\A) times as large. In the other direction, an accurate \widehat{\cvec{x}} for a badly scaled \A can have a residual far larger than one expects. Chapter 20 §04’s @thm-residual-bound is the eigenvalue version of exactly this move, and that section named the technique: “An error analysis of this kind, which measures an answer by a change in the data that makes it exact, is a backward error analysis. Chapter 24 builds on it.” Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the three clauses of @def-floating-point-model, and say which one is an exclusion rather than an assumption about accuracy. 2. Define the unit roundoff, and give its value for a decimal model carrying t significant digits. 3. Define the forward error and the backward error of an algorithm at a datum, and say which of the two a user can usually measure. 4. Decide whether each statement is correct, with a reason: (i) “a backward stable algorithm returns an answer with small forward error”; (ii) “if the computed \widehat{\cvec{x}} has a tiny residual, then \widehat{\cvec{x}} is close to \cvec{x}”. 5. Why is @def-floating-point-model called a model rather than a theorem? (a) (FP1) rounding is relative, with error at most u; (FP2) each operation returns the rounding of its exact result, so  l(x \odot y) = (x\odot y)(1+\delta) with \lvert\deltavert \le u; (FP3) no overflow or underflow. (FP3) is the exclusion: it does not say the arithmetic is good, it says we decline to analyze the case where it is not. (b) u is the bound in (FP1): \lvert  l(t) - tvert \le u\lvert tvert for every in-range t. For a decimal model with t significant digits, u = 	frac12 \cdot 10^{1-t} (@exm-six-digit-model does the case t = 6). (c) See @def-forward-error. The forward error is 
orm{\widehat f(\cvec{a}) - f(\cvec{a})}/
orm{f(\cvec{a})}, the backward error the smallest 
orm{\Delta\cvec{a}}/
orm{\cvec{a}} with f(\cvec{a} + \Delta\cvec{a}) = \widehat f(\cvec{a}). A user can usually measure neither directly, but the backward error is the one an analyst can bound, because a bound needs only one exhibited \Delta\cvec{a}; computing the forward error needs the exact answer, which is what the computation was for. (d) (i) Incorrect. It returns an answer with small backward error; the forward error is then at most about \kappa times that, by @thm-forward-from-backward (after absorbing any perturbation of \cvec{b}, as the remark after that theorem does), and for large \kappa that is no guarantee at all. (ii) Incorrect, for the same reason: a small residual is a small backward error (see the warning above), which bounds the forward error only after multiplication by \kappa(\A). (e) Because it is an assumption about a physical machine, not a consequence of anything proved earlier in the book. Nothing in Chapters 1 to 21 mentions rounding. Everything this chapter proves about arithmetic is a theorem about the model, true of any machine that satisfies it and silent about one that does not. B. Practice [B1: The \gamma calculus] Assume (j + k)u < 1. 1. Prove that 1 + \gamma_k = 1/(1 - ku). 2. Hence prove that \gamma_j + \gamma_k + \gamma_j\gamma_k \le \gamma_{j+k}. 3. Explain in one sentence why (b) is the statement one needs when two separately analyzed computations are performed one after the other. (a) 1 + \gamma_k = 1 + ku/(1-ku) =  igl((1-ku) + ku igr)/(1-ku) = 1/(1-ku). (b) Using (a) twice, 1 + \gamma_j + \gamma_k + \gamma_j\gamma_k = (1+\gamma_j)(1+\gamma_k) =  rac{1}{(1-ju)(1-ku)} . Now (1-ju)(1-ku) = 1 - (j+k)u + jku^2 \ge 1 - (j+k)u > 0, and inverting reverses the inequality between positive numbers, so the right-hand side is at most 1/ igl(1-(j+k)u igr) = 1 + \gamma_{j+k}. Subtracting 1 gives the claim. (c) If one stage multiplies the exact answer by 1 + 	heta_1 with \lvert	heta_1vert \le \gamma_j and the next by 1 + 	heta_2 with \lvert	heta_2vert \le \gamma_k, the combined factor is 1 + 	heta_1 + 	heta_2 + 	heta_1	heta_2, and (b) says the total is still of the form 1 + 	heta with \lvert	hetavert \le \gamma_{j+k} — the counts simply add. [B2: Summation] Let x_1, \dots, x_n be representable, let nu < 1, and let s_n be computed by s_1 = x_1, s_k =  l(s_{k-1} + x_k). 1. Prove that s_n = \sum_{k=1}^n x_k(1 + 	heta_k) with \lvert	heta_kvert \le \gamma_{n-1}. 2. Deduce \lvert s_n - \sum_k x_kvert \le \gamma_{n-1}\sum_k\lvert x_kvert, and explain why this is not a bound on the relative error of s_n. 3. Give three representable numbers in the six-digit model for which the computed sum has relative error larger than u. (a) By (FP2), s_k = (s_{k-1} + x_k)(1 + \varepsilon_k) for 2 \le k \le n, with \lvert\varepsilon_kvert \le u. Unrolling as in the proof of @thm-inner-product-backward-error, s_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k \prod_{j = \max(k,2)}^{n}(1 + \varepsilon_j) . The k = 1 and k = 2 terms carry n - 1 factors and the rest carry fewer, so @lem-gamma-bound gives \lvert	heta_kvert \le \gamma_{n-1}. (b) Subtract \sum_k x_k and use the triangle inequality: \lvert s_n - \sum_k x_kvert = \lvert\sum_k x_k	heta_kvert \le \gamma_{n-1}\sum_k\lvert x_kvert. It is not a relative error bound because the right-hand side involves \sum_k\lvert x_kvert, not \lvert\sum_k x_kvert, and the two differ by an arbitrarily large factor when the x_k have mixed signs and cancel. (c) Take x_1 = 1, x_2 = 10^{-7}, x_3 = -1, summed in that order. Then  l(1 + 10^{-7}) = 1, since 1 + 10^{-7} lies strictly between the representable neighbors 1 and 1.00001 and is nearer the first; and  l(1 - 1) = 0. The computed sum is 0, the true sum is 10^{-7}, and the relative error is 1. This is (b) at work: \sum\lvert x_kvert = 2 while \lvert\sum x_kvert = 10^{-7}. [B3: The model by hand] Work in the six-digit decimal model. 1. Compute  l(1/3) and verify (FP1) for it. 2. Compute the two sides of  l igl( l(a + b) + c igr) and  l igl(a +  l(b + c) igr) for a = 10^{5}, b = 1, c = 1, and say what this shows about the model. (a) 1/3 = 3.33333\overline{3} 	imes 10^{-1}, so  l(1/3) = 0.333333 and \lvert l(1/3) - 1/3vert = 	frac13 	imes 10^{-6}. Dividing by 1/3 gives a relative error of 10^{-6}, which is at most u = 5 	imes 10^{-6}. (b) Left:  l(10^5 + 1) = 100001 exactly (six digits), and  l(100001 + 1) = 100002. Right:  l(1 + 1) = 2, and  l(10^5 + 2) = 100002. Here the two agree. Change a to 10^{6}: left gives  l(10^6 + 1) = 10^6, then  l(10^6 + 1) = 10^{6}; right gives  l(1+1) = 2, then  l(10^6 + 2) = 10^{6} as well, since 1000002 rounds to 1.00000 	imes 10^6. Try a = 10^{6}, b = c = 3: left is 10^6 then 10^{6}; right is 6 then  l(1000006) = 1.00001 	imes 10^{6}. The two differ. Floating-point addition is commutative but not associative, so the order of a summation is part of the algorithm, not an irrelevance — which is why @thm-inner-product-backward-error names the order it analyzes. C. Going deeper [C1: When backward stability says nothing] Let \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n and let s_n be the computed inner product of @thm-inner-product-backward-error. 1. Prove that \lvert s_n - \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y}vert \le \gamma_n \lvert\cvec{x}vert	p\lvert\cvec{y}vert, where \lvert\cdotvert is entrywise. 2. Deduce that if all x_iy_i \ge 0 then the relative error of s_n is at most \gamma_n. 3. Give \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^3 with representable entries, in the six-digit model, for which the relative error of s_n is at least 1. Explain why this does not contradict @thm-inner-product-backward-error. (a) By the theorem’s proof, s_n = \sum_k x_ky_k(1+	heta_k) with \lvert	heta_kvert \le \gamma_n, so \lvert s_n - \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y}vert = \Bigl\lvert\sum_k x_ky_k	heta_k\Bigrvert \le \gamma_n\sum_k\lvert x_kvert\lvert y_kvert = \gamma_n\lvert\cvec{x}vert	p\lvert\cvec{y}vert . (b) If every x_ky_k \ge 0 then \lvert\cvec{x}vert	p\lvert\cvec{y}vert = \sum_k x_ky_k = \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y}, so (a) reads \lvert s_n - \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y}vert \le \gamma_n\,\cvec{x}	p\cvec{y}, which is the relative bound (and \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y} > 0 unless every term vanishes, in which case s_n = 0 too). (c) Take \cvec{x} = (1, 10^{-7}, -1) and \cvec{y} = (1, 1, 1), all representable. Each product x_ky_k is computed exactly, so \delta_1 = \delta_2 = \delta_3 = 0. Then s_1 = 1; next s_2 =  l(1 + 10^{-7}) = 1, which is (1 + 10^{-7})(1 + \varepsilon_2) with \varepsilon_2 =  rac{-10^{-7}}{1 + 10^{-7}}, \qquad \lvert\varepsilon_2vert < 10^{-7} < u ; finally s_3 =  l(1 - 1) = 0, exactly, so \varepsilon_3 = 0 serves. The true value is \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y} = 10^{-7}, so the forward relative error is 1. There is no contradiction. Following the proof, 	heta_1 = 	heta_2 = \varepsilon_2 and 	heta_3 = 0, all of modulus below u \le \gamma_3, and indeed (1 + \varepsilon_2) + 10^{-7}(1 + \varepsilon_2) - 1 = (1 + 10^{-7})(1 + \varepsilon_2) - 1 = 0 = s_3 . So the backward perturbation \Delta\cvec{x} = (\varepsilon_2, 10^{-7}\varepsilon_2, 0) is of relative size about 10^{-7} in every coordinate: the algorithm solved a neighboring problem exactly. What made the answer worthless is the problem, not the method: here \lvert\cvec{x}vert	p\lvert\cvec{y}vert = 2 + 10^{-7} while \cvec{x}	p\cvec{y} = 10^{-7}, so part (a)’s bound is twenty million times the quantity being computed. This is the same phenomenon as @exm-cancellation, seen through the backward error. [C2: An unstable way to compute a variance] Given x_1, \dots, x_N with mean \overline x = 	frac1N\sum_i x_i, the quantity S = \sum_i (x_i - \overline x)^2 can be computed in one pass as S = \sum_i x_i^2 - 	frac1N igl(\sum_i x_i igr)^2, or in two passes by forming \overline x first. 1. Verify the identity \sum_i (x_i - \overline x)^2 = \sum_i x_i^2 - 	frac1N(\sum_i x_i)^2. 2. In the six-digit model, run both routes on x = (10000, 10001, 10002), showing every operation, and compare with the exact value S = 2. 3. Say which route is to be preferred and why, in the vocabulary of this section. (a) Expand: \sum_i(x_i - \overline x)^2 = \sum_i x_i^2 - 2\overline x\sum_i x_i + N\overline x^2. Since \sum_i x_i = N\overline x, the last two terms are -2N\overline x^2 + N\overline x^2 = -N\overline x^2 = -	frac1N(\sum_i x_i)^2. (b) One pass. The squares are 10^{8}, 100020001, 100040004; rounding each to six digits gives 1.00000	imes10^{8}, 1.00020 	imes 10^{8}, and 1.00040 	imes 10^{8}, and accumulating gives  l(1.00000	imes10^8 + 1.00020	imes10^8) = 2.00020	imes10^{8} and then 3.00060 	imes 10^{8}. The sum \sum_i x_i = 30003 is exact, its square is 900180009, which rounds to 9.00180 	imes 10^{8}, and dividing by 3 gives 3.00060 	imes 10^{8}. Subtracting:  l(3.00060	imes10^8 - 3.00060	imes10^8) = \mathbf{0}. Two passes. \overline x =  l(30003/3) = 10001, exactly. The deviations -1, 0, 1 are computed exactly, their squares are 1, 0, 1, and the sum is \mathbf{2}, the exact answer. (c) The two-pass route. The one-pass route subtracts two nine-digit numbers that agree in their first six digits, so in a six-digit model it commits catastrophic cancellation and returns 0; worse, 0 is not the value of S for any small relative perturbation of the data. Indeed S(\cvec{x} + \Delta\cvec{x}) = 0 forces the three perturbed entries to be equal, say to v; and for \cvec{x} = (10000, 10001, 10002) the largest of \lvert x_i - vvert is at least 1, whatever v is, because x_3 - x_1 = 2. So every \Delta\cvec{x} that accounts for the computed answer has  rac{
orm{\Delta\cvec{x}}_{\infty}}{
orm{\cvec{x}}_{\infty}} \ge  rac{1}{10002} > 19\,u , whereas @def-backward-stable allows cu. One datum bounds the constant rather than disposing of it — what this shows exactly is that no c \le 19 will serve for the one-pass route — but the mechanism is general, and it is the one @exm-cancellation identified. The two-pass route performs the subtraction x_i - \overline x first, while the operands are still exactly representable, and nothing is ever lost. Same identity, same arithmetic, different algorithm — which is precisely the distinction between a problem and a method.

title: 24.2 Elimination, Pivoting, and Cost
