Elimination, Pivoting, and Cost Chapter 3 solved \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} by elimination and packaged the work as \A = \L\U or \P\A = \L\U. It said nothing about how much arithmetic that costs, and almost nothing about what rounding does to it — only a remark, about a two-by-two matrix with a tiny corner entry, ending: “Chapter 24 makes this precise.” Chapter 8 left a second note: “Chapter 24 reads Gaussian elimination itself as a sequence of Schur complements of 1 	imes 1 pivots.” Chapter 13 left a third, that Cholesky “does about half the arithmetic of a general LU factorization” and needs no pivoting. This section pays all three. Section 1 supplied the model and the word backward stable; here that word is applied to the oldest algorithm in the book. Throughout, matrices are real, since the representable numbers of @def-floating-point-model are real, and \lvert\Mvert denotes the entrywise absolute value (\lvert m_{ij}vert), with \lvert\Mvert \le \lvert\Nvert read entrywise. Elimination is a sequence of Schur complements Chapter 8 built a machine for one block elimination: if \M =  egin{psmallmatrix}\A & \B\ \C & \D\end{psmallmatrix} with \A invertible, then subtracting \C\A^{-1} times the first block row from the second leaves  egin{psmallmatrix}\A & \B\ \O & \M/\A\end{psmallmatrix}, where \M/\A = \D - \C\A^{-1}\B is the Schur complement (@def-schur-complement, @thm-block-ldu). Gaussian elimination is that machine run with a 1 	imes 1 block, n - 1 times. Saying so exactly is the cleanest description of the algorithm there is, and it is what makes block versions of it possible. [Elimination Produces Schur Complements] Let \A \in M_n(F) and 1 \le k \le n - 1, and suppose the first k steps of elimination without row swaps (Chapter 3 §06) are carried out with nonzero pivots, producing \A^{(k)}. Partition \A =  egin{pmatrix} \A_k & \B \ \C & \D\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A^{(k)} =  egin{pmatrix} \V & \B' \ \O & \S\end{pmatrix}, with \A_k, \V \in M_k(F), the zero block being what the first k steps created. Then \A_k is invertible and \S = \A/\A_k = \D - \C\,\A_k^{-1}\B . In particular, for k = 1 and a_{11} 
e 0, one step of elimination replaces the trailing (n-1) 	imes (n-1) block by the Schur complement of the 1 	imes 1 pivot block. The first k steps multiply \A on the left by a unit lower triangular matrix whose columns k+1, \dots, n are those of the identity — that is exactly what @lem-elimination-matrices (c) says, and it is the whole point. Such a matrix has block form  egin{psmallmatrix}\L_{11} & \O\ \L_{21} & \I\end{psmallmatrix}. Multiply that by the partitioned \A^{(k)}, match the four blocks against \A, and the \L_{11} cancels out of the bottom-right block, leaving the Schur complement. Write  oldsymbol{\ell}_j for the j-th multiplier vector, whose first j entries are zero, and recall from Chapter 3 §06 that step j multiplies on the left by \G_j(- oldsymbol{\ell}_j), with inverse \G_j( oldsymbol{\ell}_j) by @lem-elimination-matrices (b). Hence \A = \L_k\A^{(k)} where, by @lem-elimination-matrices (c), \L_k = \G_1( oldsymbol{\ell}_1)\cdots\G_k( oldsymbol{\ell}_k) = \I + \sum_{j=1}^{k} oldsymbol{\ell}_j\cvec{e}_j	p . Only columns 1, \dots, k of \L_k differ from those of \I, so partitioning \L_k as \A is partitioned gives \L_k =  egin{pmatrix} \L_{11} & \O \ \L_{21} & \I_{n-k}\end{pmatrix}, with \L_{11} \in M_k(F) unit lower triangular, hence invertible by @lem-unit-lower-triangular-closed (b). By @thm-block-multiplication,  egin{pmatrix} \A_k & \B \ \C & \D\end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \L_{11} & \O \ \L_{21} & \I\end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix} \V & \B' \ \O & \S\end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} \L_{11}\V & \L_{11}\B' \ \L_{21}\V & \L_{21}\B' + \S\end{pmatrix} . Comparing blocks: \A_k = \L_{11}\V, \B = \L_{11}\B', \C = \L_{21}\V, and \D = \L_{21}\B' + \S. Now \V is upper triangular with the first k pivots on its diagonal, and those are nonzero by hypothesis, so \V is invertible by @lem-triangular-invertible. Therefore \A_k = \L_{11}\V is invertible, and \A_k^{-1} = \V^{-1}\L_{11}^{-1}. Hence \C\,\A_k^{-1}\B = (\L_{21}\V)(\V^{-1}\L_{11}^{-1})(\L_{11}\B') = \L_{21}\B' , and so \S = \D - \L_{21}\B' = \D - \C\A_k^{-1}\B = \A/\A_k. This proves the theorem. [Two steps, two Schur complements] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3\ 2 & 7 & 5\ -1 & 4 & 8\end{pmatrix} . Carry out two steps of elimination without row swaps, then compute \A/\A_1 and \A/\A_2 directly from @def-schur-complement, and check @thm-elimination-is-schur-complements in both cases. The elimination. The first multipliers are \ell_{21} = 2/1 = 2 and \ell_{31} = -1/1 = -1; subtracting \ell_{i1} times row 1 from row i gives \A^{(1)}. The second multiplier is \ell_{32} = 6/3 = 2, and row 3 becomes (0, 0, 11 - 2(-1)) = (0,0,13): \A^{(1)} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3\ 0 & 3 & -1\ 0 & 6 & 11\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A^{(2)} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3\ 0 & 3 & -1\ 0 & 0 & 13\end{pmatrix} . The Schur complement of the 1 	imes 1 block. Here \A_1 = (1), \B =  egin{pmatrix}2 & 3\end{pmatrix}, \C =  egin{pmatrix}2 & -1\end{pmatrix}	p, and \D =  egin{psmallmatrix}7&5\4&8\end{psmallmatrix}, so  egin{aligned} \A/\A_1 &= \D - \C\A_1^{-1}\B =  egin{pmatrix}7&5\4&8\end{pmatrix} -  egin{pmatrix}2\-1\end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix}2&3\end{pmatrix}\ &=  egin{pmatrix}7&5\4&8\end{pmatrix} -  egin{pmatrix}4&6\-2&-3\end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix}3&-1\6&11\end{pmatrix} , \end{aligned} which is exactly the trailing block of \A^{(1)}. The Schur complement of the 2 	imes 2 block. Now \A_2 =  egin{psmallmatrix}1&2\2&7\end{psmallmatrix}, with \det\A_2 = 3 and \A_2^{-1} = 	frac13 egin{psmallmatrix}7&-2\-2&1\end{psmallmatrix}, while \C =  egin{pmatrix}-1 & 4\end{pmatrix} and \B =  egin{pmatrix}3 & 5\end{pmatrix}	p. Then  egin{aligned} \C\A_2^{-1} &= 	frac13 egin{pmatrix}-15 & 6\end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix}-5 & 2\end{pmatrix},\ \A/\A_2 &= 8 -  egin{pmatrix}-5 & 2\end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix}3\5\end{pmatrix} = 8 - (-5) = 13 , \end{aligned} the trailing 1 	imes 1 block of \A^{(2)}. Both readings agree with @thm-elimination-is-schur-complements, and as an arithmetic check the pivots 1, 3, 13 multiply to 39, which is \det\A — the corollary below says why that is no coincidence. Two consequences come out for free. The first identifies the pivots with ratios of minors, which is how Chapter 13 §01 wrote them in Sylvester’s criterion. [Pivots Are Ratios of Leading Minors] Let \A \in M_n(F), let 1 \le k \le n-1, and write \A_j for the leading principal j 	imes j submatrix of \A, with \det\A_0 \coloneqq 1. 1. If the first k pivots of elimination without row swaps are nonzero, then \A_1, \dots, \A_k are invertible and the j-th pivot equals \det\A_j/\det\A_{j-1} for j \le k. 2. Conversely, if \A_1, \dots, \A_{n-1} are invertible then elimination without row swaps succeeds on \A with nonzero pivots, and \A = \L\U by @thm-lu-exists-without-swaps. (a) Invertibility of \A_1, \dots, \A_k is @thm-elimination-is-schur-complements applied with 1, \dots, k in place of k. For j = 1 the pivot is a_{11} = \det\A_1/\det\A_0, as claimed. For 2 \le j \le k, the j-th pivot is the (j,j) entry of \A^{(j-1)}, which by the theorem (with j - 1 in place of k) is the (1,1) entry of \A/\A_{j-1}. That entry is a_{jj} minus row j of \C times \A_{j-1}^{-1} times column j of \B, so it involves only rows and columns 1, \dots, j of \A: it equals the 1 	imes 1 matrix \A_j/\A_{j-1}. By @thm-schur-determinant (a), \det\A_j = \det\A_{j-1}\cdot\det(\A_j/\A_{j-1}), which is the claim. (b) We show by induction on j that the j-th pivot is nonzero, for j = 1, \dots, n-1. For j = 1 the pivot is a_{11} = \det\A_1 
e 0. Let 2 \le j \le n-1 and suppose the first j-1 pivots are nonzero. Then @thm-elimination-is-schur-complements applies with j - 1 in place of k, and the calculation in (a) identifies the j-th pivot as \det\A_j/\det\A_{j-1}, which is nonzero because \A_j and \A_{j-1} are invertible (@thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible). So elimination never stops, and @thm-lu-exists-without-swaps gives \A = \L\U. The matrix  egin{psmallmatrix}0 & 1\ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix} has no LU factorization (@exm-no-lu-factorization). Which hypothesis of @cor-pivots-and-minors (b) fails, and what does @thm-elimination-is-schur-complements say about it? \A_1 = \O_1 is not invertible, so (b) does not apply. @thm-elimination-is-schur-complements does not apply either: it assumes the first pivot is nonzero, and here it is 0, so the Schur complement \A/\A_1 is not even defined — @def-schur-complement requires the pivot block to be invertible. This is the whole content of Chapter 3’s “elimination stops”: there is no Schur complement to form. What elimination costs A flop is one arithmetic operation: one addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division, or one square root. Counting flops is crude — it ignores which operations are slow and how data moves — but it captures how the work grows with n. We quote leading terms, writing 	frac23 n^3 + O(n^2) and meaning it. The constant matters and the exponent matters more: halving the constant is worth having, but a smaller exponent overtakes it at some size and stays ahead forever. [The Cost of Elimination] Counting each of the five operations as one flop, and counting only arithmetic on matrix and vector entries: 1. Elimination without row swaps on \A \in M_n(
R) costs  rac{n(n-1)(4n+1)}{6} = 	frac23 n^3 - 	frac12 n^2 - 	frac16 n flops, that is 	frac23 n^3 + O(n^2). 2. Forward substitution with a unit lower triangular \L costs n^2 - n flops and back substitution with an upper triangular \U costs n^2, so solving \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} from a factorization costs 2n^2 - n flops. 3. The Cholesky recursion of Chapter 13 §02 on a positive definite \A \in M_n(
R) costs  rac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} = 	frac13 n^3 + 	frac12 n^2 + 	frac16 n flops, that is 	frac13 n^3 + O(n^2), of which n are square roots. (a) At step k the algorithm computes n - k multipliers, one division each, and then replaces each of the (n-k)^2 entries of the trailing block by a_{ij} - \ell_{ik}a_{kj}, two flops each. The entries below the pivot are set to zero without arithmetic. So the cost is \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\Bigl[(n-k) + 2(n-k)^2\Bigr] = \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} igl(j + 2j^2 igr) =  rac{(n-1)n}{2} +  rac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{3} , using \sum_{j\le m} j = m(m+1)/2 and \sum_{j \le m}j^2 = m(m+1)(2m+1)/6 with m = n-1. Putting the two terms over 6 gives n(n-1) igl(3 + 2(2n-1) igr)/6 = n(n-1)(4n+1)/6. (b) Forward substitution computes x_i = b_i - \sum_{j<i}\ell_{ij}x_j with no division, since \ell_{ii} = 1: that is 2(i-1) flops, and \sum_{i\le n}2(i-1) = n(n-1). Back substitution computes x_i =  igl(b_i - \sum_{j>i}u_{ij}x_j igr)/u_{ii}, which is 2(n-i) + 1 flops, and \sum_{i \le n} igl(2(n-i)+1 igr) = n(n-1) + n = n^2. (c) Column j of the recursion computes \ell_{jj} =  igl(a_{jj} - \sum_{k<j}\ell_{jk}^2 igr)^{1/2}, costing 2(j-1) flops for the sum and one square root, and then \ell_{ij} =  igl(a_{ij} - \sum_{k<j}\ell_{ik}\ell_{jk} igr)/\ell_{jj} for each of the n - j rows below, costing 2(j-1) + 1 flops each. The total is  egin{aligned} \sum_{j=1}^{n}(n - j + 1) igl(2j - 1 igr) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} i\,(2n - 2i + 1)\ &= (2n+1) rac{n(n+1)}{2} - 2\cdot rac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} , \end{aligned} substituting i = n - j + 1; the two terms combine to n(n+1)(2n+1) igl(	frac12 - 	frac13 igr) = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. Comparing (a) and (c): 	frac13 n^3 against 	frac23 n^3. This is Chapter 13 §02’s “Cholesky does about half the arithmetic of a general LU factorization”, now a count rather than a claim, for the reason that section gave — the recursion produces one triangular factor instead of two. Part (b) says the factorization is the expensive part: solving m systems with the same \A costs 	frac23n^3 + 2mn^2, not m times 	frac23 n^3. One row at a time Every algorithm below computes its entries the same way: accumulate a sum of products into a running total, then possibly divide. Analyzing that pattern once saves doing it three times. [One Row of Substitution] Let m \ge 0, let t_1, \dots, t_m, y_1, \dots, y_m, c, and d 
e 0 be representable, and suppose s_0 = c, \qquad s_p =  l igl(s_{p-1} -  l(t_py_p) igr) \quad (p = 1, \dots, m), \qquad z =  l(s_m/d) are computed in the model of @def-floating-point-model, with (m+1)u < 1. Then there are 	heta_0, \dots, 	heta_m with c = d\,z\,(1 + 	heta_0) + \sum_{p=1}^{m} t_py_p(1 + 	heta_p), \qquad \lvert	heta_pvert \le \gamma_{m+1} \ 	ext{ for all } p . If the final division is omitted, so that z = s_m, the same identity holds with d = 1 and \lvert	heta_pvert \le \gamma_m. Unroll the recursion, then divide the whole identity by the product of the accumulation factors. Dividing is the trick: it moves those factors onto c’s neighbors as inverse factors, which is exactly what @lem-gamma-bound was stated to allow. By (FP2) there are \delta_p, \varepsilon_p, \eta, all of modulus at most u, with  l(t_py_p) = t_py_p(1+\delta_p), s_p =  igl(s_{p-1} - t_py_p(1+\delta_p) igr)(1+\varepsilon_p), and z = (s_m/d)(1+\eta). Induction on m gives s_m = c\prod_{p=1}^{m}(1+\varepsilon_p) - \sum_{p=1}^{m}t_py_p(1+\delta_p)\prod_{q=p}^{m}(1+\varepsilon_q) , the case m = 0 being s_0 = c, and the step from m-1 to m multiplying everything by 1 + \varepsilon_m and subtracting the new term. Each 1 + \varepsilon_p is nonzero, since \lvert\varepsilon_pvert \le u < 1, so we may divide the identity by \prod_{p \le m}(1+\varepsilon_p) and rearrange: c = s_m\prod_{p=1}^{m}(1+\varepsilon_p)^{-1} + \sum_{p=1}^{m}t_py_p(1+\delta_p)\prod_{q=1}^{p-1}(1+\varepsilon_q)^{-1} . From z = (s_m/d)(1+\eta) we get s_m = d\,z\,(1+\eta)^{-1}. So the first term is d\,z times a product of m + 1 factors of the form (1+\delta)^{\pm1} with \lvert\deltavert \le u, which by @lem-gamma-bound is 1 + 	heta_0 with \lvert	heta_0vert \le \gamma_{m+1}. The p-th term of the sum carries 1 + (p-1) = p \le m such factors, so it is t_py_p(1+	heta_p) with \lvert	heta_pvert \le \gamma_p \le \gamma_{m+1}. If the division is omitted, the first term carries only the m inverse factors, so \lvert	heta_0vert \le \gamma_m, and the rest of the argument is unchanged. This proves the lemma. Solving a triangular system Here is the cleanest backward error analysis in the subject, and the model for every other one in this chapter. Note in advance what it does not assume: nothing about the size of the diagonal entries of \T, nothing about its conditioning, and no pivoting of any kind. [Backward Error of a Triangular Solve] Let \T \in M_n(
R) be lower triangular with representable entries and nonzero diagonal, let \cvec{b} \in 
R^n be representable, and let nu < 1. Let \widehat{\cvec{x}} be computed by forward substitution in the model: for each i, the products t_{ij}\widehat x_j are subtracted from b_i one at a time in increasing order of j, and the result is divided by t_{ii} — that is, exactly the computation of @lem-substitution-row with m = i-1. Then there is a lower triangular \Delta\T with (\T + \Delta\T)\widehat{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{b} \qquad	ext{and}\qquad \lvert\Delta t_{ij}vert \le \gamma_i\,\lvert t_{ij}vert \le \gamma_n\,\lvert t_{ij}vert \quad (j \le i) . The same statement, with \gamma_{n+1-i} in place of \gamma_i, holds for back substitution with an upper triangular \T. Row i is the pattern of @lem-substitution-row, with c = b_i, the m = i-1 products t_{ij}\widehat x_j, and the final division by t_{ii}. The lemma hands back an identity in which every coefficient of \widehat x_j is t_{ij} times something within \gamma_i of 1; that “something minus one”, times t_{ij}, is \Delta t_{ij}. Fix i. The quantities \widehat x_1, \dots, \widehat x_{i-1} are already computed, hence representable, so @lem-substitution-row applies with m = i - 1, c = b_i, t_p = t_{ip}, y_p = \widehat x_p, d = t_{ii}, and z = \widehat x_i. Since m + 1 = i \le n and nu < 1, it gives 	heta_0, \dots, 	heta_{i-1} of modulus at most \gamma_i with b_i = t_{ii}\widehat x_i(1+	heta_0) + \sum_{j<i} t_{ij}\widehat x_j(1+	heta_j) . Define \Delta t_{ii} = t_{ii}	heta_0, \Delta t_{ij} = t_{ij}	heta_j for j < i, and \Delta t_{ij} = 0 for j > i. Then \Delta\T is lower triangular, \lvert\Delta t_{ij}vert \le \gamma_i\lvert t_{ij}vert \le \gamma_n\lvert t_{ij}vert since \gamma_i \le \gamma_n, and the display says precisely that row i of (\T + \Delta\T)\widehat{\cvec{x}} equals b_i. As i was arbitrary, (\T+\Delta\T)\widehat{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{b}. For back substitution, row i has n - i products instead of i - 1, so the lemma applies with m = n - i and the bound is \gamma_{n+1-i}. This proves the theorem. This is as strong as a backward error statement gets. The perturbation is bounded entrywise, and entrywise relative to the entries of \T itself: a zero entry of \T is not perturbed at all, and a tiny entry is perturbed only in its own last digits. So a triangular solve is backward stable in the sense of @def-backward-stable — with the constant c = 1.02\,n in any model with nu \le 0.01, since \gamma_n \le 1.02\,nu there — whatever \kappa(\T) may be. Backward stable is not accurate, and this theorem is where the point bites hardest. @thm-triangular-solve-backward-error holds for every nonsingular triangular \T. It does not say \widehat{\cvec{x}} is near \cvec{x}. By @thm-forward-from-backward the forward error can be about \kappa(\T)\gamma_n, and triangular matrices can be spectacularly ill-conditioned. Take the n 	imes n matrix \T with 1 on the diagonal and -1 everywhere above it. Its row sums of moduli are n, n-1, \dots, 1, so 
orm{\T}_{\infty} = n. Its inverse has 1 on the diagonal and 2^{j-i-1} in position (i,j) for j > i: back substitution on \T\cvec{x} = \cvec{e}_j gives x_j = 1 and x_i = \sum_{p > i} x_p for i < j, and each partial sum of 1, 1, 2, 4, \dots is the next term. Hence 
orm{\T^{-1}}_{\infty} = 1 + (1 + 2 + \dots + 2^{n-2}) = 2^{n-1} and \kappa_{\infty}(\T) = n2^{n-1}, so for n = 60 a backward stable solve can still return nonsense. Stability is a promise about the data, and a promise about the data is worth only what the conditioning of the problem makes it worth. The factorization itself For the factorization we analyze the ordering that computes each entry of \L and \U by one accumulation. In exact arithmetic it produces the same factors as Chapter 3’s row operations — for invertible \A this is @thm-lu-unique — but it groups the arithmetic differently, and rounding notices the difference. Elimination, one entry at a time. Input: \A \in M_n(
R). Set \ell_{ii} = 1. For i = 1, 2, \dots, n: - for j = i, \dots, n, put u_{ij} = a_{ij} - \sum_{k<i}\ell_{ik}u_{kj}; - if u_{ii} = 0, stop; otherwise for r = i+1, \dots, n, put \ell_{ri} =  igl(a_{ri} - \sum_{k<i}\ell_{rk}u_{ki} igr)/u_{ii}. [Backward Error of a Factorization] Let \A \in M_n(
R) have representable entries, let nu < 1, and suppose the algorithm above runs to completion in the model of @def-floating-point-model, producing \widehat\L and \widehat\U. Then \widehat\L\widehat\U = \A + \Delta\A \qquad	ext{with}\qquad \lvert\Delta\Avert \le \gamma_n\,\lvert\widehat\Lvert\,\lvert\widehat\Uvert entrywise. Each entry is one application of @lem-substitution-row: the entries of \U with no division, the entries of \L with one. In both cases the lemma returns a_{ij} as a sum of the products \widehat\ell_{ip}\widehat u_{pj}, each with its own factor 1 + 	heta_p. Collecting the terms is exactly forming the (i,j) entry of \widehat\L\widehat\U, and the 	heta_p are what is left over. Case i \le j. The computation of \widehat u_{ij} is @lem-substitution-row with m = i - 1, c = a_{ij}, t_p = \widehat\ell_{ip}, y_p = \widehat u_{pj}, no division, and z = \widehat u_{ij}. Writing 	heta_i for the 	heta_0 of the lemma, and using \widehat\ell_{ii} = 1, a_{ij} = \sum_{p=1}^{i}\widehat\ell_{ip}\widehat u_{pj}(1 + 	heta_p), \qquad \lvert	heta_pvert \le \gamma_{i-1} . (For i = 1 the sum has one term and 	heta_1 = 0.) Since \widehat\ell_{ip} = 0 for p > i, the sum without the 	heta_p is (\widehat\L\widehat\U)_{ij}. Hence  igl\lvert a_{ij} - (\widehat\L\widehat\U)_{ij} igrvert = \Bigl\lvert\sum_{p\le i}\widehat\ell_{ip}\widehat u_{pj}	heta_p\Bigrvert \le \gamma_{i-1}\sum_{p\le i}\lvert\widehat\ell_{ip}vert\lvert\widehat u_{pj}vert = \gamma_{i-1} igl(\lvert\widehat\Lvert\lvert\widehat\Uvert igr)_{ij} , the last equality again because \widehat\ell_{ip} = 0 for p > i. Case i > j. The computation of \widehat\ell_{ij} is @lem-substitution-row with m = j-1, c = a_{ij}, t_p = \widehat\ell_{ip}, y_p = \widehat u_{pj}, d = \widehat u_{jj}, and z = \widehat\ell_{ij}. Writing 	heta_j for 	heta_0, a_{ij} = \sum_{p=1}^{j}\widehat\ell_{ip}\widehat u_{pj}(1 + 	heta_p), \qquad \lvert	heta_pvert \le \gamma_{j} . Since \widehat u_{pj} = 0 for p > j, the sum without the 	heta_p is again (\widehat\L\widehat\U)_{ij}, and the same estimate gives \lvert a_{ij} - (\widehat\L\widehat\U)_{ij}vert \le \gamma_j(\lvert\widehat\Lvert\lvert\widehat\Uvert)_{ij}. In both cases the constant is at most \gamma_n. This proves the theorem. What is proved and what is not. The theorem is about the ordering displayed above. Chapter 3’s ordering, which updates the whole trailing block at each step, satisfies the same bound \lvert\Delta\Avert \le \gamma_n\lvert\widehat\Lvert\lvert\widehat\Uvert; the proof is a different induction of comparable length, and we do not give it here. Nothing later in this chapter uses it. Also, the theorem assumes the algorithm completes, which in the model means every computed \widehat u_{ii} is nonzero; it says nothing about what happens when one of them is zero, or about the case where a pivot is nonzero only by a rounding accident. One more seam will appear below: the growth bound for partial pivoting, proved in the next subsection, concerns the exact elimination in Chapter 3’s ordering, whereas the bound just proved concerns the factors this ordering computes in the model. In exact arithmetic, and for invertible \A, the two orderings produce the same \L and \U, by @thm-lu-unique; in the model they agree only to within rounding, and we do not quantify that here. Nothing below is allowed to cross that seam quietly. @eq-lu-growth-bound, proved next, measures growth in the computed factors, which is a quantity one can read off after the fact; the a priori bound 2^{n-1} of @thm-growth-partial-pivoting is a statement about exact elimination. The three places that put the two together — the warning after @exm-growth-attained and the solutions to A1 and B3 — say that they are doing so, and each of them uses the combination only to show that even its most favorable reading proves nothing. The bound is useless until we know how big \lvert\widehat\Lvert\lvert\widehat\Uvert is, and that is not controlled by \A. It is controlled by what the algorithm does to \A, which is why elimination needs a pivoting rule at all. The quantity to watch has a name. [Growth factor] Let elimination — with whatever pivoting rule is in force — be run on \A \in M_n(
R), producing an upper factor \U. The growth factor of that run is g_n \coloneqq  rac{\max_{i,j}\lvert u_{ij}vert}{\max_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij}vert} , the largest entry in modulus the algorithm produces, relative to the largest entry in modulus it was given. [B3: The Cholesky entry bound] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & -2 & 6 \ -2 & 5 & -1 \ 6 & -1 & 26\end{pmatrix}, whose Cholesky factor was computed in @exm-cholesky-by-hand to be \L with rows (2,0,0), (-1,2,0), (3,1,4). 1. Check @thm-cholesky-stability (a) entry by entry. 2. Compute \lvert\Lvert\lvert\L	pvert and check that every entry is at most \max_{p,q}\lvert a_{pq}vert. 3. What would the bound of @eq-lu-growth-bound require if \A were factored by general elimination with partial pivoting instead? (a) The bound is \lvert\ell_{ij}vert \le \sqrt{a_{ii}}. Row 1: 2 \le \sqrt4 = 2, with equality. Row 2: 1, 2 \le \sqrt5 \approx 2.236. Row 3: 3, 1, 4 \le \sqrt{26} \approx 5.099. All hold, and the row sums of squares are 4, 5, 26, which are a_{11}, a_{22}, a_{33} exactly. (b) \lvert\Lvert has rows (2,0,0), (1,2,0), (3,1,4), so \lvert\Lvert\lvert\L	pvert =  egin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 & 6\ 2 & 5 & 5\ 6 & 5 & 26\end{pmatrix} . The largest entry of \A in modulus is 26, and every entry above is at most 26 — indeed the (i,k) entry is at most \sqrt{a_{ii}a_{kk}}: for instance 5 \le \sqrt{5 \cdot 26} \approx 11.4. (c) It would require knowing g_3 for the computed factors, and the only bound available is @thm-growth-partial-pivoting’s exact-arithmetic 2^{2} = 4; granting the transfer between the two (the remark after @thm-lu-backward-error), @eq-lu-growth-bound permits \max\lvert\Delta a_{ij}vert \le 3\gamma_3\cdot4\cdot26 = 12\gamma_3\cdot 26. @thm-cholesky-stability (c) permits  igl(\gamma_4/(1-\gamma_4) igr)\cdot 26 instead: the factor 3g_3 = 12 disappears entirely, and the price is the step from \gamma_3 to \gamma_4/(1-\gamma_4), which is about 	frac43\gamma_3. No pivoting is needed to get it. C. Going deeper [C1: Column diagonal dominance needs no pivoting] Call \A \in M_n(
R) strictly column diagonally dominant if \lvert a_{jj}vert > \sum_{i 
e j}\lvert a_{ij}vert for every j. 1. Show that partial pivoting makes no exchange at the first step. 2. Show that \A/\A_1 is again strictly column diagonally dominant, and that each of its column sums \sum_{i\ge2}\lvert a'_{ij}vert is at most the corresponding column sum \sum_{i\ge1}\lvert a_{ij}vert of \A. 3. Deduce that elimination without any exchanges succeeds and that g_n < 2. Hint: for (c), bound every entry of every \A^{(k)} by a column sum of \A. (a) Column 1 satisfies \lvert a_{11}vert > \sum_{i \ge 2}\lvert a_{i1}vert \ge \lvert a_{i1}vert for each i \ge 2, so the entry of largest modulus in column 1 is already a_{11}, and it is nonzero. (b) Write a'_{ij} = a_{ij} - (a_{i1}/a_{11})a_{1j} for i, j \ge 2. For the column sums, the triangle inequality gives \sum_{i\ge2}\lvert a'_{ij}vert \le \sum_{i\ge2}\lvert a_{ij}vert +  rac{\lvert a_{1j}vert}{\lvert a_{11}vert}\sum_{i\ge2}\lvert a_{i1}vert \le \sum_{i\ge2}\lvert a_{ij}vert + \lvert a_{1j}vert = \sum_{i\ge1}\lvert a_{ij}vert , using \sum_{i\ge2}\lvert a_{i1}vert < \lvert a_{11}vert. For dominance, fix j \ge 2. Then \sum_{\substack{i\ge2\ i
e j}}\lvert a'_{ij}vert \le \sum_{\substack{i\ge2\ i
e j}}\lvert a_{ij}vert +  rac{\lvert a_{1j}vert}{\lvert a_{11}vert}\sum_{\substack{i\ge2\ i
e j}}\lvert a_{i1}vert <  igl(\lvert a_{jj}vert - \lvert a_{1j}vert igr) +  rac{\lvert a_{1j}vert}{\lvert a_{11}vert} igl(\lvert a_{11}vert - \lvert a_{j1}vert igr) , where the two strict bounds are column-j and column-1 dominance. The right side equals \lvert a_{jj}vert - \lvert a_{1j}vert\lvert a_{j1}vert/\lvert a_{11}vert, which is at most \lvert a_{jj} - a_{j1}a_{1j}/a_{11}vert = \lvert a'_{jj}vert by the reverse triangle inequality. So \sum_{i \ge 2, i
e j}\lvert a'_{ij}vert < \lvert a'_{jj}vert. (c) By (a) and (b) and induction, every Schur complement \A^{(k)} restricted to its active block is strictly column diagonally dominant, so no exchange is ever made and no pivot is zero. By (b) and induction, the column sums of the active blocks never increase, so every entry of every \A^{(k)} is bounded by \max_j\sum_i\lvert a_{ij}vert — and the rows that have been frozen into \U were bounded the same way when they were created. Finally, dominance gives \sum_i\lvert a_{ij}vert < 2\lvert a_{jj}vert \le 2\max_{p,q}\lvert a_{pq}vert, so g_n < 2. Hence such matrices need no pivoting at all. [C2: The growth bound is attained for every n] Let \Y_n be the matrix of @exm-growth-attained: y_{ii} = 1, y_{ij} = -1 for i > j, y_{in} = 1 for all i, and y_{ij} = 0 for j > i with j < n. 1. Prove that partial pivoting makes no exchange at any step, and that every multiplier equals -1. 2. Prove by induction on k that after k steps the active trailing block is again of the form \Y_{n-k}, except that its last column is 2^{k} times the all-ones vector. 3. Deduce g_n = 2^{n-1}, and explain why this does not contradict the practical success of partial pivoting. (a) and (b) together, by induction. At step k = 1, column 1 is (1, -1, \dots, -1), every entry of modulus 1, so the pivot y_{11} = 1 is already of largest modulus and no exchange is made; the multipliers are -1/1 = -1. Subtracting -1 times row 1 from row i adds row 1 to row i. Row 1 is (1, 0, \dots, 0, 1), so for i \ge 2 the entries in columns 2, \dots, n-1 are unchanged, the entry in column 1 becomes 0, and the entry in column n becomes 1 + 1 = 2. The trailing (n-1)	imes(n-1) block therefore has 1 on its diagonal, -1 below, 0 above except in the last column, and 2 throughout its last column: it is \Y_{n-1} with the last column doubled. Since doubling one column changes neither which entry of a column has largest modulus nor the ratios within the other columns, the same applies at every subsequent step, and after k steps the active block is \Y_{n-k} with last column 2^{k} times the all-ones vector. (b) Every entry of \Y_n has modulus 1, so M_0 = 1. By (b) the largest entry ever created is the (n,n) entry after step n-1, namely 2^{n-1}. So g_n = 2^{n-1}, meeting @thm-growth-partial-pivoting exactly. This does not contradict anything practical: \Y_n is a constructed matrix, and the theorem only says the worst case is 2^{n-1}. What the example does destroy is the hope of a theorem: no bound better than 2^{n-1} can be proved for partial pivoting, so any claim that partial pivoting is backward stable is a claim about the matrices one meets, not about all matrices. That is why @thm-cholesky-stability matters — it is a genuine theorem, for a class of matrices identified in advance.

content:
The QR Algorithm Chapter 11 §08 brought a square matrix to upper Hessenberg form with reflections and then stopped, with a warning attached: no finite procedure built from arithmetic and square roots can carry that reduction on to triangular form, because such a procedure would extract the roots of an arbitrary polynomial from its coefficients, and the theorem of Abel and Ruffini forbids it — a theorem this book quotes, there and here, and does not prove. Every eigenvalue method must therefore iterate, and nothing proved below rests on that quotation. The iteration this section develops is the one Chapter 11 named in a single sentence — factor \Z = \Q\R, then replace \Z by \R\Q — and we now ask why it works, why it is always started from a Hessenberg matrix, and why it is always run with a shift. Factor and multiply back Section 4 iterated a matrix against a vector: the power method drives \cvec{x}^{(k)} = \A\cvec{x}^{(k-1)} towards the dominant eigenvector, one eigenvalue at a time. The whole spectrum at once needs an iteration on matrices, and it must be an iteration by similarity, or the spectrum would not survive it. Chapter 11’s reflections already gave us a supply of similarities that cost little: \A \mapsto \Q^{*}\A\Q with \Q unitary. The question is which \Q to take. Here is the answer, and it looks like sleight of hand. Factor \A = \Q\R and then multiply the two factors back in the other order. Since \Q^{*}\Q = \I, the product \R\Q is \Q^{*}(\Q\R)\Q = \Q^{*}\A\Q, so nothing has been lost; and the reversal shifts weight from the upper triangle into the lower one in a way that, repeated, empties the lower triangle altogether. Factor the matrix, then put the factors back the wrong way round, and repeat. [The QR Iteration] Let \A \in M_n(F), where F = 
R or F = 
C. Set \A^{(1)} = \A, and for k \ge 1 define \A^{(k)} = \Q^{(k)}\R^{(k)}, \qquad \A^{(k+1)} = \R^{(k)}\Q^{(k)}, where \A^{(k)} = \Q^{(k)}\R^{(k)} is a factorization with \Q^{(k)} \in M_n(F) unitary and \R^{(k)} \in M_n(F) upper triangular. The sequence \A^{(1)}, \A^{(2)}, \dots is the unshifted QR iteration started at \A. In words: at every step we factor the current matrix, then form the product of its factors in the reversed order, and that product is the next matrix. The superscript in parentheses counts steps, never coordinates. Well-definedness. A factorization exists at every step, for every square matrix and with no hypothesis on its columns, by @thm-qr-householder. It need not be unique: if \D is diagonal with \lvert d_j vert = 1, then (\Q\D)(\D^{*}\R) is another one. When \A^{(k)} is invertible the ambiguity is exactly that, and demanding a positive real diagonal in \R^{(k)} removes it, by @thm-qr-factorization; and if \A is invertible then so is every \A^{(k)}, being similar to \A. We do not need the normalization for anything below, so the definition leaves the choice open. [Every Step Is a Unitary Similarity] In the notation of @def-qr-iteration, \A^{(k+1)} = (\Q^{(k)})^{*}\A^{(k)}\Q^{(k)} for every k. Consequently all the matrices \A^{(k)} are unitarily similar to \A, and they share its characteristic polynomial, its eigenvalues with multiplicities, its trace, and its determinant. Since \Q^{(k)} is unitary, (\Q^{(k)})^{*}\Q^{(k)} = \I_n (@def-unitary-orthogonal), so (\Q^{(k)})^{*}\A^{(k)}\Q^{(k)} = (\Q^{(k)})^{*}\Q^{(k)}\R^{(k)}\Q^{(k)} = \R^{(k)}\Q^{(k)} = \A^{(k+1)} . A unitary matrix is invertible with \Q^{-1} = \Q^{*}, so this exhibits \A^{(k+1)} as similar to \A^{(k)} (@def-similar-matrices); composing these similarities for 1, \dots, k-1 makes \A^{(k)} similar to \A^{(1)} = \A. Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant), hence the same eigenvalues with multiplicities, and the same trace and determinant. This proves the proposition. Two examples fix what the iteration does and does not do. [Two matrices the iteration cannot move] Determine the QR iterates of \A = \diag(3, 1) and of the rotation \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}. For \A: the factorization \A = \I_2\A has \I_2 unitary and \A upper triangular with positive diagonal, so by the uniqueness in @thm-qr-factorization it is the factorization. Then \A^{(2)} = \A\I_2 = \A, and the iteration stands still. It has nothing to do: \A is already triangular and its diagonal already lists the eigenvalues (@thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form). For \B: here \B is itself unitary, since its columns (0,1) and (-1,0) are orthonormal, so \B = \B\,\I_2 is a factorization with \I_2 upper triangular with positive diagonal — again the unique one. So \B^{(2)} = \I_2\B = \B, and the iteration stands still here too. This time it has everything to do: the eigenvalues of \B are \pm i, and \B is not triangular. The iteration is stuck. The second matrix is the section’s standing negative example, and the reason it is stuck is visible already: \lvert ivert = \lvert -ivert. We return to it after the convergence theorem, and repair it with a shift. Reversing the factors is not a similarity for just any factorization. The step works because \Q is unitary, so that \Q^{-1} = \Q^{*} and \R\Q = \Q^{*}\A\Q. Do the same with an \L\U factorization and you get \U\L = \L^{-1}\A\L, which is still a similarity — but with \L^{-1} in place of \L^{*}, and \L^{-1} can be enormous. That is the older \L\R iteration, and its instability under rounding is exactly the instability of elimination without pivoting met in Section 2. The iteration is the power method in disguise Nothing said so far suggests that the iterates go anywhere. The identity that explains them is the following, and it is the heart of the section: the accumulated factors of k steps are a QR factorization of the k-th power of \A. Powers of \A are what the power method of Section 4 runs on, so the identity says the two methods are the same method, one applied to a vector and the other to a whole basis at once. Write \U_k = \Q^{(1)}\Q^{(2)}\cdots\Q^{(k)}, \qquad \T_k = \R^{(k)}\cdots\R^{(2)}\R^{(1)} . The first is unitary, as a product of unitary matrices (@prp-orthogonal-group-properties), and the second is upper triangular, as a product of upper triangular matrices. [QR Iterates Factor the Powers] Let \A \in M_n(F) and let \A^{(k)}, \Q^{(k)}, \R^{(k)} be as in @def-qr-iteration. Then for every k \ge 1, \A^{(k+1)} = \U_k^{*}\,\A\,\U_k \qquad	ext{and}\qquad \A^{k} = \U_k\T_k . In particular \U_k\T_k is a QR factorization of \A^{k}. Induction on k, with the two statements proved together, because each feeds the other. The similarity statement is @prp-qr-iteration-similar telescoped. For the factorization, the move to find is the one that turns \A\U_k into something with a \Q at the front: the similarity statement, read backwards, says \A\U_k = \U_k\A^{(k+1)}, and \A^{(k+1)} is by definition \Q^{(k+1)}\R^{(k+1)}. One line of bookkeeping then converts \A\cdot\A^{k} into \U_{k+1}\T_{k+1}. Both statements by induction on k. For k = 1: \U_1 = \Q^{(1)} and \T_1 = \R^{(1)}, so \U_1\T_1 = \Q^{(1)}\R^{(1)} = \A^{(1)} = \A, and \U_1^{*}\A\U_1 = \A^{(2)} by @prp-qr-iteration-similar. Let k \ge 1 and suppose both statements hold for k. By @prp-qr-iteration-similar applied at step k+1 and the inductive hypothesis, \A^{(k+2)} = (\Q^{(k+1)})^{*}\A^{(k+1)}\Q^{(k+1)} = (\Q^{(k+1)})^{*}\U_k^{*}\A\,\U_k\Q^{(k+1)} = \U_{k+1}^{*}\A\,\U_{k+1}, where the last equality uses \U_{k+1} = \U_k\Q^{(k+1)} and (\X\Y)^{*} = \Y^{*}\X^{*}. That is the first statement for k+1. For the second, multiply the inductive similarity \A^{(k+1)} = \U_k^{*}\A\U_k on the left by \U_k, which is legitimate because \U_k\U_k^{*} = \I_n: \A\,\U_k = \U_k\A^{(k+1)} = \U_k\Q^{(k+1)}\R^{(k+1)} = \U_{k+1}\R^{(k+1)} . Hence, using the inductive factorization \A^{k} = \U_k\T_k, \A^{k+1} = \A\,(\U_k\T_k) = (\A\,\U_k)\T_k = \U_{k+1}\R^{(k+1)}\T_k = \U_{k+1}\T_{k+1}, since \T_{k+1} = \R^{(k+1)}\T_k by definition. As \U_{k+1} is unitary and \T_{k+1} upper triangular, this is a QR factorization of \A^{k+1}, and the induction is complete. The consequence to keep is about the first column. Comparing first columns in \A^{k} = \U_k\T_k and writing 	au_k = (\T_k)_{11}, we get \A^{k}\cvec{e}_1 = \U_k\T_k\cvec{e}_1 = 	au_k\,\U_k\cvec{e}_1 , {#eq-qr-first-column} because the first column of an upper triangular matrix is 	au_k\cvec{e}_1. So whenever 	au_k 
eq 0, which the Quick check just below records for invertible \A, the first column of \U_k is the normalized vector \A^{k}\cvec{e}_1/
orm{\A^{k}\cvec{e}_1}, up to a scalar of modulus one — which is precisely the k-th iterate of the power method (@thm-power-method) started at \cvec{e}_1. The QR algorithm runs the power method in its first column, and, as the next theorem shows, that alone forces the first column of \A^{(k+1)} to converge. Why is 	au_k 
eq 0 when \A is invertible? Each \A^{(j)} is similar to \A (@prp-qr-iteration-similar), hence invertible, and \R^{(j)} = (\Q^{(j)})^{*}\A^{(j)} is then invertible as a product of invertible matrices. So \T_k is invertible, being a product of invertible matrices; an upper triangular matrix is invertible exactly when its diagonal entries are all nonzero (@lem-triangular-invertible), so 	au_k = (\T_k)_{11}

C) be invertible and diagonalizable, say \A = \X\vLambda\X^{-1} with \vLambda = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n) and with \cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n the columns of \X. Assume a single dominant eigenvalue, \lvert\lambda_1vert > \lvert\lambda_2vert \ge \dots \ge \lvert\lambda_nvert > 0 , and write \cvec{e}_1 = c_1\cvec{v}_1 + \dots + c_n\cvec{v}_n, assuming c_1 
eq 0. Put t = \lvert\lambda_2/\lambda_1vert < 1. Then there is a constant C, depending on \A and \X but not on k, such that the unshifted QR iterates satisfy 
orm{\A^{(k+1)}\cvec{e}_1 - \lambda_1\cvec{e}_1}_2 \le C\,t^{k} \qquad (k \ge 1) . In particular a^{(k)}_{11} 	o \lambda_1 and a^{(k)}_{i1} 	o 0 for every i \ge 2, each at the rate t^{k}. For n = 2 this says that the iterates converge to upper triangular form, with a^{(k)}_{11} 	o \lambda_1 and a^{(k)}_{22} 	o \lambda_2. By @eq-qr-first-column the first column \cvec{u}_1 of \U_k is the power-method iterate, so it is close to the dominant eigenvector, and the vector \A\cvec{u}_1 - \lambda_1\cvec{u}_1 is small. Now read \A^{(k+1)} = \U_k^{*}\A\U_k column by column: its first column is \U_k^{*}\A\cvec{u}_1, and subtracting \lambda_1\cvec{e}_1 = \U_k^{*}(\lambda_1\cvec{u}_1) leaves \U_k^{*}(\A\cvec{u}_1 - \lambda_1\cvec{u}_1). A unitary matrix does not change lengths, so the whole error in the first column equals the length of that small vector. Nothing else is needed. Write \cvec{u}_1 = \U_k\cvec{e}_1 for the first column of \U_k, suppressing k from the notation. Step 1: the error in the first column is a residual. Since \U_k is unitary and \A^{(k+1)} = \U_k^{*}\A\U_k by @thm-qr-is-orthogonal-iteration, \A^{(k+1)}\cvec{e}_1 - \lambda_1\cvec{e}_1 = \U_k^{*}\A\cvec{u}_1 - \lambda_1\U_k^{*}\cvec{u}_1 = \U_k^{*} igl(\A\cvec{u}_1 - \lambda_1\cvec{u}_1 igr), using \cvec{u}_1 = \U_k\cvec{e}_1 twice. A unitary matrix preserves the Euclidean norm (@thm-isometry-characterizations), so 
orm{\A^{(k+1)}\cvec{e}_1 - \lambda_1\cvec{e}_1}_2 = 
orm{\A\cvec{u}_1 - \lambda_1\cvec{u}_1}_2 . 	ag{$\ast$} Step 2: \cvec{u}_1 is a power-method iterate. By @eq-qr-first-column, \A^{k}\cvec{e}_1 = 	au_k\cvec{u}_1 with 	au_k 
eq 0, as the Quick check above records. Since \A\cvec{v}_i = \lambda_i\cvec{v}_i, \A^{k}\cvec{e}_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i\lambda_i^{k}\cvec{v}_i = c_1\lambda_1^{k} igl(\cvec{v}_1 + \cvec{z}_k igr), \qquad \cvec{z}_k = \sum_{i \ge 2} rac{c_i}{c_1}\Bigl( rac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_1}\Bigr)^{k}\cvec{v}_i , which is legitimate because c_1

orm{\cvec{v}_1}_2 > 0, whence

orm{\A}_2 + \lvert\lambda_1vert igr)M}{

orm{\A}_2 + \lvert\lambda_1vert holds, since 
orm{\cvec{u}_1}_2 = 1. So the displayed estimate holds for all k \ge 1 with C = \max\Bigl\{\,C_1,\  igl(
orm{\A}_2 + \lvert\lambda_1vert igr)t^{-k_0}\,\Bigr\} , and combining with (\ast) proves the main estimate. The entrywise statements follow because each coordinate of a vector is at most its Euclidean norm. For n = 2, the estimate forces a^{(k)}_{21} 	o 0 and a^{(k)}_{11} 	o \lambda_1; and a^{(k)}_{22} = 	r\A^{(k)} - a^{(k)}_{11} = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 - a^{(k)}_{11} 	o \lambda_2, the trace being preserved by @prp-qr-iteration-similar. This proves the theorem. What is proved here, and what is not. The theorem above settles the first column, for every n, and with it the whole 2 	imes 2 case. The general statement is this: if \A is diagonalizable with \lvert\lambda_1vert > \lvert\lambda_2vert > \dots > \lvert\lambda_nvert > 0, and if \X^{-1} admits an \L\U factorization without row swaps (@thm-lu-exists-without-swaps), then the whole of \A^{(k)} below the diagonal tends to zero, with a^{(k)}_{i+1,i} = O igl(\lvert\lambda_{i+1}/\lambda_ivert^{k} igr) \quad	ext{and}\quad a^{(k)}_{ii} 	o \lambda_i \quad (1 \le i \le n). This is the classical convergence theorem of the algorithm, due to Rutishauser, Francis, and Kublanovskaya; it is not proved here. The proof runs through the factorization \A^{k} = \X\vLambda^{k}\L\U of @thm-qr-is-orthogonal-iteration’s identity, the observation that \vLambda^{k}\L\vLambda^{-k} 	o \I, and a continuity argument for the QR factorization that this book has not developed. Nothing in this section or later depends on it: the Hessenberg and shifting results below are proved outright, and the worked example at the end exhibits the rates rather than assuming them. The extra hypothesis on \X^{-1} is not cosmetic, and the strict ordering of the moduli is not either — the next example shows what happens without it. [The unshifted algorithm on a rotation] Let \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}. Explain why no unshifted QR iteration can bring \B closer to triangular form, and say which hypothesis of @thm-qr-convergence fails. By @exm-qr-fixed-points, \B^{(k)} = \B for every k: the iteration is stationary, and \B is as far from triangular as a 2 	imes 2 matrix can be, with b_{21} = 1. The eigenvalues are \pm i, so \lvert\lambda_1vert = \lvert\lambda_2vert = 1 and the hypothesis \lvert\lambda_1vert > \lvert\lambda_2vert fails. The failure is not an artifact of the proof. Over 
R the matrix is orthogonally similar to no real triangular matrix at all, since a real triangular matrix has real eigenvalues; and over 
C the power method has nothing to converge to, because \B^{k}\cvec{e}_1 simply rotates around the plane forever (@thm-power-method). Convergence is to triangular form, not to diagonal form. Even when the iterates do converge, the strictly upper triangular part generally does not: only the entries below the diagonal die out. What is more, in the convergence theorem quoted above — the one this section does not prove — the order in which the eigenvalues appear on the diagonal is decided by the moduli, largest first, so that a run it covers reveals \lambda_1 in the top-left corner and \lambda_n in the bottom-right. With shifts, which is how the algorithm is actually run, even that ordering goes away. Hessenberg first As written, one step costs a QR factorization of a full n 	imes n matrix and a matrix product: that is O(n^3) flops, in the counting convention of @prp-lu-cost, and the count really does grow like n^3, since the product alone touches n^2 entries with n terms each. The iteration needs many steps, and no amount of cleverness about the steps rescues a method that spends n^3 operations on each of them. The remedy is Chapter 11’s. Reduce \A once to upper Hessenberg form by @thm-hessenberg-form, at a cost of O(n^3) paid a single time, and then iterate. R) be upper Hessenberg, n \ge 2. Then \Z has a factorization \Z = \Q\R with \Q orthogonal and \R upper triangular in which \Q is a product of n-1 Givens rotations and is itself upper Hessenberg; and for this factorization \R\Q is again upper Hessenberg. Producing \R and then \R\Q costs about 6n^2 flops. A Hessenberg matrix has only n-1 entries in the way of triangularity, one per column, and @def-givens-rotation removes one entry per rotation. So the natural factorization to use is the rotation one, not the reflection one — this is the case Chapter 11 §08 flagged, where “the count reverses”. Then two bookkeeping facts finish it: the accumulated product of the rotations is Hessenberg, and upper triangular times upper Hessenberg is upper Hessenberg. For 1 \le i \le n-1 let \G_i = \G(i, i+1; c_i, s_i) be a Givens rotation in the coordinates i, i+1 (@def-givens-rotation). Working left to right, choose \G_i to annihilate the entry in position (i+1, i) of the matrix produced so far: if that matrix has entries a in position (i,i) and b in position (i+1, i) with (a, b)

Two shifts are standard. The Rayleigh shift takes \mu_k = a^{(k)}_{nn}, the trailing diagonal entry; when \A is Hermitian this is the Rayleigh quotient R_{\A^{(k)}}(\cvec{e}_n) of @def-rayleigh-quotient, hence a good eigenvalue estimate as soon as \cvec{e}_n is nearly an eigenvector. Prove that if \Z is upper Hessenberg with z_{m+1,m} = 0 for some 1 \le m \le n-1, then \spec(\Z) = \spec(\Z_{11}) \cup \spec(\Z_{22}), where \Z_{11} is the leading m 	imes m block and \Z_{22} the trailing (n-m) 	imes (n-m) block. 2. Deduce that a QR implementation may, at every step, replace the problem by two smaller ones as soon as one subdiagonal entry vanishes. 3. Give a 3 	imes 3 upper Hessenberg matrix with no zero subdiagonal entry for which the unshifted iteration never reduces any subdiagonal entry at all. (a) With z_{m+1,m} = 0 and \Z upper Hessenberg, every entry z_{ij} with i > m \ge j vanishes: for i > m+1 this is i > j+1, and for i = m+1 it is either j < m, again i > j+1, or j = m, the assumed entry. So \Z is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks \Z_{11} and \Z_{22}. By @thm-block-multiplication and the determinant of a block triangular matrix (@thm-det-block-triangular), p_{\Z}(x) = p_{\Z_{11}}(x)\,p_{\Z_{22}}(x), so the eigenvalues of \Z are those of the two blocks together. (b) The two blocks are again upper Hessenberg, and by (a) computing their spectra computes that of \Z. Each step on a block of size m costs about 6m^2 rather than 6n^2 (@prp-hessenberg-preserved), so splitting is a strict gain; and part (a) guarantees no eigenvalue is lost. This is deflation. (c) Take the cyclic permutation matrix \Z =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, which is upper Hessenberg with subdiagonal entries 1, 1, and is orthogonal. By @exr-the-qr-algorithm-b2 (b) it is a fixed point of the unshifted iteration, so no subdiagonal entry ever moves. Its eigenvalues are the three cube roots of 1, all of modulus 1 — the obstruction of @thm-qr-convergence in its purest form. [C2: Hermitian iterates and the Rayleigh quotient] Let \A \in M_n(
C) be Hermitian and let \A^{(k)} be its unshifted QR iterates. 1. Prove that every \A^{(k)} is Hermitian with the same eigenvalues as \A. 2. Prove that a^{(k)}_{nn} = R_{\A}(\cvec{u}_n^{(k)}), where \cvec{u}_n^{(k)} is the last column of \U_{k-1} and R_{\A} is the Rayleigh quotient of @def-rayleigh-quotient. 3. Hence explain, citing @thm-hermitian-residual-bound, why the Rayleigh shift \mu_k = a^{(k)}_{nn} is a certified eigenvalue estimate, and say what the certificate is. (a) By @thm-qr-is-orthogonal-iteration, \A^{(k)} = \U_{k-1}^{*}\A\U_{k-1}, with \U_0 = \I at k = 1, so (\A^{(k)})^{*} = \U_{k-1}^{*}\A^{*}\U_{k-1} = \A^{(k)}, and unitary similarity preserves eigenvalues. (b) Writing \cvec{u}_n = \U_{k-1}\cvec{e}_n, which is a unit vector since \U_{k-1} is unitary, a^{(k)}_{nn} = \cvec{e}_n^{*}\A^{(k)}\cvec{e}_n = \cvec{e}_n^{*}\U_{k-1}^{*}\A\U_{k-1}\cvec{e}_n = \cvec{u}_n^{*}\A\cvec{u}_n = R_{\A}(\cvec{u}_n), the last equality because R_{\A}(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}^{*}\A\cvec{x}/\cvec{x}^{*}\cvec{x} and \cvec{u}_n^{*}\cvec{u}_n = 1. (c) Put \mu = a^{(k)}_{nn} and \cvec{r} = \A\cvec{u}_n - \mu\cvec{u}_n. Then \mu is real, \A being Hermitian, and @thm-hermitian-residual-bound says that \A has an eigenvalue in [\mu - 
orm{\cvec{r}}_2, \mu + 
orm{\cvec{r}}_2]. The certificate is 
orm{\cvec{r}}_2, and it costs nothing extra: by the computation in (b), \U_{k-1}^{*}\cvec{r} = \A^{(k)}\cvec{e}_n - \mu\cvec{e}_n is the last column of \A^{(k)} with its diagonal entry removed, so 
orm{\cvec{r}}_2 is the Euclidean norm of the entries of that column other than the diagonal one. If \A was first reduced to Hessenberg form, so that every \A^{(k)} is Hermitian and upper Hessenberg, hence tridiagonal, that norm is the single entry \lvert a^{(k)}_{n-1,n}vert. The algorithm is already watching that number. [C3: Why the powers are the right object] Let \A \in M_n(
C) be invertible, with unshifted QR iterates as in @def-qr-iteration. 1. Prove that for 1 \le j \le n, the subspace spanned by the first j columns of \U_k equals \A^{k}(\Span(\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_j)). 2. Deduce that if the first j columns of \U_k converge to a basis of an \A-invariant subspace W, then the entries of \A^{(k+1)} in rows j+1, \dots, n of columns 1, \dots, j tend to 0. Hint for (b): write the entries as inner products of \A applied to one column against another. (a) By @thm-qr-is-orthogonal-iteration, \A^{k} = \U_k\T_k with \T_k upper triangular and invertible (Quick check above), so \A^{k}\cvec{e}_i = \U_k\T_k\cvec{e}_i lies in \Span(\U_k\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \U_k\cvec{e}_i) for each i, since \T_k\cvec{e}_i has zeros below row i. Hence \A^{k}(\Span(\cvec{e}_1,\dots,\cvec{e}_j)) \subseteq \Span(\U_k\cvec{e}_1,\dots,\U_k\cvec{e}_j). Both sides have dimension j: the left because \A^{k} is invertible, the right because the columns of a unitary matrix are independent. One inclusion plus equal dimension gives equality. (b) Write \cvec{u}_i = \U_k\cvec{e}_i. For p > j \ge q, a^{(k+1)}_{pq} = \cvec{e}_p^{*}\U_k^{*}\A\U_k\cvec{e}_q = \cvec{u}_p^{*}\A\cvec{u}_q = \inner{\A\cvec{u}_q}{\cvec{u}_p} . Suppose \cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_j converge to an orthonormal basis \cvec{w}_1, \dots, \cvec{w}_j of an \A-invariant subspace W, let P be the orthogonal projection onto W (@def-orthogonal-projection) and put \delta_k = \max_{q \le j}
orm{\cvec{u}_q - \cvec{w}_q}_2, so \delta_k 	o 0. Since \A\cvec{w}_q \in W, we have (\I - P)\A\cvec{w}_q = \cvec{0} and hence 
orm{(\I - P)\A\cvec{u}_q}_2 = 
orm{(\I-P)\A(\cvec{u}_q - \cvec{w}_q)}_2 \le 
orm{\A}_2\delta_k. Since \inner{\cvec{u}_p}{\cvec{u}_q} = 0 for q \le j < p, we have \lvert\inner{\cvec{u}_p}{\cvec{w}_q}vert = \lvert\inner{\cvec{u}_p}{\cvec{w}_q - \cvec{u}_q}vert \le \delta_k by Cauchy–Schwarz (@thm-cauchy-schwarz), so 
orm{P\cvec{u}_p}_2 \le j\,\delta_k. Splitting \cvec{u}_p and using that P is self-adjoint,  egin{aligned} \lvert\inner{\A\cvec{u}_q}{\cvec{u}_p}vert &=  igl\lvert\inner{(\I-P)\A\cvec{u}_q}{\cvec{u}_p} + \inner{\A\cvec{u}_q}{P\cvec{u}_p} igrvert \ &\le 
orm{(\I-P)\A\cvec{u}_q}_2 + 
orm{\A}_2
orm{P\cvec{u}_p}_2 \ \le\ (1 + j)
orm{\A}_2\,\delta_k , \end{aligned} by Cauchy–Schwarz again and 
orm{\cvec{u}_p}_2 = 
orm{\cvec{u}_q}_2 = 1. The right-hand side tends to 0, so a^{(k+1)}_{pq} 	o 0. This is @thm-qr-convergence for j = 1, read as a statement about invariant subspaces rather than about eigenvectors, and it is the form in which the general convergence theorem quoted above is proved.

title: 24.6 Krylov Subspaces
24.7 Steepest Descent and Conjugate Gradients
content:
Steepest Descent and Conjugate Gradients Section 2 solved \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} by elimination: about 	frac23 n^3 operations, an exact answer after finitely many of them, and a factorization that fills in most of the zeros the matrix had. For a large sparse matrix that is the wrong bargain. This section builds two iterations that touch \A only through the product \cvec{x} \mapsto \A\cvec{x}, for the case where \A is positive definite, and counts what each of them buys. The first costs about \kappa steps per decimal digit of accuracy, the second about \sqrt{\kappa}. Where that square root comes from is the point of the section. Throughout, \A \in M_n(
R) is symmetric and positive definite, \cvec{b} \in 
R^n, and \cvec{x}^{\star} = \A^{-1}\cvec{b} is the exact solution. Iteration indices are superscripts in parentheses. We work over 
R because the function this section minimizes is built from \cvec{b}	p\cvec{x}, which over 
C is not a real number; everything below survives over 
C with \cvec{b}^{*}\cvec{x} replaced by its real part, and nothing else changes. A linear system is a minimization problem Positive definiteness is a statement about the number \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} (@def-positive-semidefinite), so it invites us to look for a quantity that the solution makes small, rather than an equation the solution satisfies. There is one, and it is the simplest possible candidate: a quadratic minus a linear term. Solving \A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b} is the same as sitting at the bottom of a bowl. [The Energy Inner Product and the Energy Norm] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be symmetric positive definite. The energy inner product is \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}}_{\A} \coloneqq \cvec{y}	p\A\cvec{x} \qquad (\cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n), and the energy norm is 
orm{\cvec{x}}_{\A} \coloneqq \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}}_{\A}^{1/2} = (\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x})^{1/2}. Two vectors are \A-orthogonal, or conjugate, when \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}}_{\A} = 0. This is the inner product of Chapter 13 §04, written there as \cvec{y}^{*}\A\cvec{x}. It really is one: it is bilinear because matrix multiplication is; it is symmetric because the 1 	imes 1 matrix \cvec{y}	p\A\cvec{x} equals its own transpose \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}; and \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}}_{\A} > 0 for \cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0} is clause (P2) of @def-positive-semidefinite in its strict form. So 
orm{\cdot}_{\A} is the induced norm of @def-induced-norm, and every fact about norms and orthogonality from Chapter 11 applies verbatim. That is the reason for introducing it: it lets us reuse the Pythagorean theorem in a geometry bent by \A. The word energy comes from the springs of Section 9, where 	frac12\cvec{x}	p\K\cvec{x} is the potential energy stored in a displacement \cvec{x}. [The Solution Minimizes the Energy Functional] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be symmetric positive definite, \cvec{b} \in 
R^n, and define \phi(\cvec{x}) \coloneqq 	frac12\,\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} \qquad (\cvec{x} \in 
R^n). Then, with \cvec{x}^{\star} = \A^{-1}\cvec{b}, \phi(\cvec{x}) - \phi(\cvec{x}^{\star}) = 	frac12
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_{\A}^{2} \qquad 	ext{for every } \cvec{x} \in 
R^n . In particular \cvec{x}^{\star} is the unique minimizer of \phi. \A is invertible, since \A \succ \O has only positive eigenvalues (@thm-pd-characterizations, (a) \Rightarrow (b)), so \cvec{x}^{\star} is defined and \A\cvec{x}^{\star} = \cvec{b}. Expand, using \A	p = \A:  egin{aligned} 	frac12
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_{\A}^{2} &= 	frac12\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x}^{\star} + 	frac12(\cvec{x}^{\star})	p\A\cvec{x}^{\star}\ &= 	frac12\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} + 	frac12\,\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x}^{\star} , \end{aligned} where the second line uses \A\cvec{x}^{\star} = \cvec{b} twice and \cvec{x}	p\cvec{b} = \cvec{b}	p\cvec{x}. The first two terms are \phi(\cvec{x}). Putting \cvec{x} = \cvec{x}^{\star} gives 0 = \phi(\cvec{x}^{\star}) + 	frac12\cvec{b}	p\cvec{x}^{\star}, so the leftover constant is -\phi(\cvec{x}^{\star}), which is the identity. Since 
orm{\cdot}_{\A} is a norm, the right-hand side is \ge 0 with equality only at \cvec{x} = \cvec{x}^{\star}. This proves the proposition. So every iteration below may be read twice: as an attempt to solve a linear system, and as an attempt to walk downhill on a bowl whose shape is \A. The identity also tells us which error to measure. The natural yardstick is not 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_2 but 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_{\A}, because that is the one the algorithms actually make small. Two quantities recur. The error is  oldsymbol{\varepsilon} = \cvec{x} - \cvec{x}^{\star} and the residual is \cvec{r} = \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x}, and they are related by \cvec{r} = \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x} = \A\cvec{x}^{\star} - \A\cvec{x} = -\A oldsymbol{\varepsilon} . {#eq-residual-error} The residual is computable and the error is not; @eq-residual-error is the exchange rate between them. Steepest descent Fix \cvec{x} and a direction \cvec{d} 
e \cvec{0}, and ask what happens along the line \cvec{x} + t\cvec{d}. Expanding \phi and using \A	p = \A, \phi(\cvec{x} + t\cvec{d}) = \phi(\cvec{x}) - t\,\cvec{d}	p\cvec{r} + 	frac12 t^2\,\cvec{d}	p\A\cvec{d} , {#eq-line-search} where \cvec{r} = \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x}. Since \cvec{d}	p\A\cvec{d} > 0, the right-hand side is a parabola in t opening upwards, so it has one minimum, at t =  rac{\cvec{d}	p\cvec{r}}{\cvec{d}	p\A\cvec{d}}, \qquad	ext{with decrease}\quad  rac{(\cvec{d}	p\cvec{r})^2}{2\,\cvec{d}	p\A\cvec{d}} . {#eq-exact-line-search} Choosing t this way is an exact line search; it costs one product \A\cvec{d}. Which \cvec{d} should we take? Read @eq-line-search for small t: the decrease is t\,\cvec{d}	p\cvec{r} to first order, and among unit vectors \cvec{d} the quantity \cvec{d}	p\cvec{r} is largest exactly at \cvec{d} = \cvec{r}/
orm{\cvec{r}}_2, by Cauchy–Schwarz (@thm-cauchy-schwarz) with its equality case. So the residual is the direction in which \phi falls fastest at the starting point, measured in the ordinary Euclidean norm. “Steepest” is a statement about the first instant, not about the step. The direction that minimizes \phi over the whole line is not \cvec{r} but \A^{-1}\cvec{r}: with \cvec{d} = \A^{-1}\cvec{r}, @eq-exact-line-search gives t = 1 and \cvec{x} + \cvec{d} = \cvec{x} + \A^{-1}(\cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}^{\star}, the exact answer in one step. That direction is unavailable, because producing it means solving the very system we are trying to solve. Every method in this section is an attempt to approximate \A^{-1}\cvec{r} cheaply. Steepest Descent Let \A \succ \O and \cvec{b} \in 
R^n, and let \cvec{x}^{(0)} \in 
R^n. Steepest descent is the iteration: for k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, set \cvec{r}^{(k)} = \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x}^{(k)}; if \cvec{r}^{(k)} = \cvec{0}, stop, since \cvec{x}^{(k)} = \cvec{x}^{\star}; otherwise put t_k =  rac{(\cvec{r}^{(k)})	p\cvec{r}^{(k)}}{(\cvec{r}^{(k)})	p\A\cvec{r}^{(k)}}, \qquad \cvec{x}^{(k+1)} = \cvec{x}^{(k)} + t_k\,\cvec{r}^{(k)} . The denominator is positive because \cvec{r}^{(k)} 
e \cvec{0} and \A \succ \O, so t_k is defined, and t_k > 0. One step costs one matrix–vector product. To see how fast this is we need one inequality, and it is a statement about weighted averages, not about matrices at all. [Kantorovich’s Inequality] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be symmetric positive definite with eigenvalues \lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n > 0. Then for every \cvec{y} \in 
R^n, (\cvec{y}	p\A\cvec{y})(\cvec{y}	p\A^{-1}\cvec{y}) \le  rac{(\lambda_1 + \lambda_n)^2}{4\lambda_1\lambda_n}\,(\cvec{y}	p\cvec{y})^2 . In an orthonormal eigenbasis both factors become weighted averages of the eigenvalues, one of \lambda and one of 1/\lambda, with the same weights. The obstacle is that 1/\lambda is not linear, so the second average is not determined by the first. It is, however, bounded by it: on the interval [\lambda_n, \lambda_1] the curve 1/\lambda lies below the straight line joining its endpoints. Replacing the curve by that line makes the second average a linear function of the first, and the product becomes a scalar quadratic that we maximize by hand. Write a = \lambda_1 and c = \lambda_n. For every \lambda with c \le \lambda \le a,  rac{a + c - \lambda}{ac} -  rac{1}{\lambda} =  rac{\lambda(a + c - \lambda) - ac}{ac\lambda} =  rac{-(\lambda - a)(\lambda - c)}{ac\lambda} \ \ge\ 0 , 	ag{$\ast$} because \lambda - a \le 0, \lambda - c \ge 0, and ac\lambda > 0. We may assume \cvec{y} 
e \cvec{0}, the case \cvec{y} = \cvec{0} being an equality 0 = 0, and by homogeneity (both sides scale by s^4 under \cvec{y} \mapsto s\cvec{y}) we may assume \cvec{y}	p\cvec{y} = 1. By the spectral theorem (@cor-spectral-real-matrix) there is an orthonormal basis \cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_n of 
R^n with \A\cvec{q}_i = \lambda_i\cvec{q}_i. Let u_i = \cvec{q}_i	p\cvec{y} be the coordinates of \cvec{y} in that basis, and put w_i = u_i^2. Then \sum_i w_i = 
orm{\cvec{y}}_2^2 = 1 by Parseval’s identity (@thm-parseval-identity), every w_i \ge 0, and \cvec{y}	p\A\cvec{y} = \sum_i \lambda_i w_i \eqqcolon \mu , \qquad \cvec{y}	p\A^{-1}\cvec{y} = \sum_i  rac{w_i}{\lambda_i} , the second because \A^{-1}\cvec{q}_i = \lambda_i^{-1}\cvec{q}_i. Since the w_i are weights summing to 1 and every \lambda_i \in [c, a], the number \mu lies in [c, a]. Averaging (\ast) with the weights w_i, \cvec{y}	p\A^{-1}\cvec{y} \le \sum_i w_i\, rac{a + c - \lambda_i}{ac} =  rac{a + c - \mu}{ac} . Hence (\cvec{y}	p\A\cvec{y})(\cvec{y}	p\A^{-1}\cvec{y}) \le \mu(a + c - \mu)/(ac). Finally, for any real \mu, \mu(a + c - \mu) =  rac{(a+c)^2}{4} - \Bigl( rac{a+c}{2} - \mu\Bigr)^{2} \le  rac{(a+c)^2}{4} , and dividing by ac gives the bound. This proves the lemma. Equality is attainable: take \cvec{y} = (\cvec{q}_1 + \cvec{q}_n)/\sqrt2, so that w_1 = w_n = 	frac12 and every other weight is 0. Then (\ast) is an equality at each \lambda_i carrying weight, since those are a and c, and \mu = (a+c)/2 makes the last step an equality too. Only the weights w_i = u_i^2 enter, so (\cvec{q}_1 - \cvec{q}_n)/\sqrt2 serves just as well, and so does any nonzero multiple of either. @exm-steepest-descent-sharp does exactly this, up to sign and scale. We also record the condition number in the form we shall use it. For \A \succ \O, @lem-hermitian-spectral-norm gives 
orm{\A}_2 = \lambda_1, since all eigenvalues are positive; the eigenvalues of \A^{-1} are the \lambda_i^{-1}, so the same lemma gives 
orm{\A^{-1}}_2 = \lambda_n^{-1}. Hence, by @def-condition-number, \kappa \coloneqq \kappa_2(\A) =  rac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_n} \ \ge 1 . {#eq-kappa-of-a-positive-matrix} [Convergence of Steepest Descent] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be symmetric positive definite with \kappa = \kappa_2(\A), let \cvec{b} \in 
R^n, and let \cvec{x}^{(0)}, \cvec{x}^{(1)}, \dots be the steepest descent iterates. Then for every k for which \cvec{x}^{(k)} is defined, 
orm{\cvec{x}^{(k)} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_{\A} \le \Bigl( rac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}\Bigr)^{k}\,
orm{\cvec{x}^{(0)} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_{\A} . One step at a time. Write the new energy-norm error in terms of the old one; the exact line search makes the difference a single explicit fraction, whose numerator and denominator are exactly the three quantities Kantorovich’s inequality compares. What comes out is 1 - 4\lambda_1\lambda_n/(\lambda_1+\lambda_n)^2, and that number is the square of (\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1). It is enough to prove the estimate for one step and then iterate. Fix k and write \cvec{x} = \cvec{x}^{(k)}, \cvec{r} = \cvec{r}^{(k)}, t = t_k, and  oldsymbol{\varepsilon} =  oldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(k)} \coloneqq \cvec{x}^{(k)} - \cvec{x}^{\star}, and assume \cvec{r} 
e \cvec{0}. By @eq-residual-error, \cvec{r} = -\A oldsymbol{\varepsilon}, so 
orm{ oldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_{\A}^2 =  oldsymbol{\varepsilon}	p\A oldsymbol{\varepsilon} = (\A^{-1}\cvec{r})	p\A(\A^{-1}\cvec{r}) = \cvec{r}	p\A^{-1}\cvec{r} , using \A	p = \A and (\A^{-1})	p = \A^{-1}. The new error is  oldsymbol{\varepsilon} + t\cvec{r}, so  egin{aligned} 
orm{ oldsymbol{\varepsilon} + t\cvec{r}}_{\A}^2 &= 
orm{ oldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_{\A}^2 + 2t\,\cvec{r}	p\A oldsymbol{\varepsilon} + t^2\,\cvec{r}	p\A\cvec{r}\ &= 
orm{ oldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_{\A}^2 - 2t\,\cvec{r}	p\cvec{r} + t^2\,\cvec{r}	p\A\cvec{r} , \end{aligned} the second line because \A oldsymbol{\varepsilon} = -\cvec{r}. Substituting t = (\cvec{r}	p\cvec{r})/(\cvec{r}	p\A\cvec{r}) collapses the last two terms: 
orm{ oldsymbol{\varepsilon} + t\cvec{r}}_{\A}^2 = 
orm{ oldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_{\A}^2 -  rac{(\cvec{r}	p\cvec{r})^2}{\cvec{r}	p\A\cvec{r}} = 
orm{ oldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_{\A}^2\Bigl(1 -  rac{(\cvec{r}	p\cvec{r})^2}{(\cvec{r}	p\A\cvec{r})(\cvec{r}	p\A^{-1}\cvec{r})}\Bigr), where the last step divides and multiplies by 
orm{ oldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_{\A}^2 = \cvec{r}	p\A^{-1}\cvec{r}, which is nonzero because \cvec{r} 
e \cvec{0}. By @lem-kantorovich applied to \cvec{y} = \cvec{r},  rac{(\cvec{r}	p\cvec{r})^2}{(\cvec{r}	p\A\cvec{r})(\cvec{r}	p\A^{-1}\cvec{r})} \ \ge\  rac{4\lambda_1\lambda_n}{(\lambda_1+\lambda_n)^2}, so the bracket is at most 1 -  rac{4\lambda_1\lambda_n}{(\lambda_1 + \lambda_n)^2} =  rac{(\lambda_1 - \lambda_n)^2}{(\lambda_1 + \lambda_n)^2} = \Bigl( rac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}\Bigr)^{2}, the last equality on dividing numerator and denominator by \lambda_n^2 and using @eq-kappa-of-a-positive-matrix. Since  oldsymbol{\varepsilon} + t\cvec{r} = \cvec{x}^{(k+1)} - \cvec{x}^{\star} =  oldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(k+1)}, taking square roots gives 
orm{ oldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(k+1)}}_{\A} \le  rac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}
orm{ oldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(k)}}_{\A}, and an induction on k proves the theorem. [The bound is attained] Let \A = \diag(9, 1), \cvec{b} = (9, 1), and \cvec{x}^{(0)} = (2, -8). Run three steps of steepest descent and compare with @thm-steepest-descent. Here \cvec{x}^{\star} = (1, 1) and \kappa = 9, so the bound’s factor is 	frac45. The first residual is \cvec{r}^{(0)} = \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x}^{(0)} = (9,1) - (18, -8) = (-9, 9), so \cvec{r}	p\cvec{r} = 162 and \cvec{r}	p\A\cvec{r} = 9\cdot 81 + 81 = 810, giving t_0 = 	frac15. Then \cvec{x}^{(1)} = (2,-8) + 	frac15(-9,9) =  igl(	frac15, -	frac{31}{5} igr), \qquad \cvec{r}^{(1)} =  igl(	frac{36}{5}, 	frac{36}{5} igr). The two components of \cvec{r}^{(1)} are again equal in absolute value, so t_1 = 	frac15 as well, and \cvec{x}^{(2)} =  igl(	frac{41}{25}, -	frac{119}{25} igr), \cvec{x}^{(3)} =  igl(	frac{61}{125}, -	frac{451}{125} igr). The squared energy-norm errors are 90, \qquad 	frac{288}{5}, \qquad 	frac{4608}{125}, \qquad 	frac{73728}{3125}, and each is exactly 	frac{16}{25} times the one before.
