content: Determine whether each pair of matrices is similar. Justify your answer. \(\J_2(4) \oplus \J_1(4)\) and \(\J_1(4) \oplus \J_2(4)\) . \(\J_3(0) \oplus \J_1(0)\) and \(\J_2(0) \oplus \J_2(0)\) . \(\J_2(1) \oplus \J_2(1)\) and \(\J_2(1) \oplus \J_1(1) \oplus \J_1(1)\) . \(\diag(2, 2, 5)\) and the matrix \(\A_2\) of @exr-jordan-canonical-form-b2 (b).

title: Exercise (C1: A matrix is similar to its transpose)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) with \(p_{\A}\) split over \(F\) . Let \(\R \in M_k(F)\) be the reversal permutation matrix, with \(1\) in each position \((j, k + 1 - j)\) and \(0\) elsewhere. Prove that \(\R^{-1} = \R\) and \(\R^{-1}\J_k(\lambda)\R = \J_k(\lambda)^{\tp}\) . Deduce that every Jordan matrix \(\J\) satisfies \(\J \sim \J^{\tp}\) . Deduce that \(\A \sim \A^{\tp}\) . Hint: for (c), transpose a similarity \(\A = \P \J \P^{-1}\) . The conclusion holds over every field; Section 7 removes the hypothesis that \(p_{\A}\) splits.

title: Exercise (C2: How much do p and m decide?)
content: Work over \(\nC\) . Find all Jordan forms with \(p_T = (x - 1)^3(x - 2)^2\) and \(m_T = (x - 1)^2(x - 2)\) . Find all Jordan forms with \(p_T = (x - 1)^4(x - 2)^2\) and \(m_T = (x - 1)^2(x - 2)\) . In (b), what is the least amount of extra information that determines the Jordan form? Prove that \(p_T\) and \(m_T\) determine the Jordan form whenever \(a(\lambda) \le 3\) for every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) .

title: Theorem 10.3.1 (Jordan Canonical Form Theorem)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) with \(\dim V = n \ge 1\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . (Existence) \(T\) has a Jordan form if and only if \(p_T\) splits over \(F\) . (Uniqueness) Suppose \(\J\) is a Jordan form of \(T\) . Then for every \(\lambda \in F\) and every integer \(j \ge 1\) , the number of blocks \(\J_k(\lambda)\) in \(\J\) with \(k \ge j\) equals \[ \rank(T - \lambda\,\id_V)^{j-1} - \rank(T - \lambda\,\id_V)^{j} , \] a number depending only on \(T\) , \(\lambda\) , and \(j\) . Consequently any two Jordan forms of \(T\) have the same blocks, up to the order in which they are listed. Equivalently, for \(\A \in M_n(F)\) with \(p_{\A}\) split: \(\A\) is similar to a Jordan matrix, and that matrix is unique up to the order of its blocks. We call it the Jordan form of \(\A\) .

title: Definition 10.4.2 (Basic Weyr Matrix, Weyr Structure, Weyr Form)
page: 10.4 The Real Jordan Form and the Weyr Form
content: Let \(\lambda \in F\) and let \(w_1 \ge w_2 \ge \dots \ge w_s \ge 1\) be a partition of an integer \(m \ge 1\) ( @def-partition-of-n ). The basic Weyr matrix with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) and Weyr structure \((w_1, \dots, w_s)\) is the matrix \(\W \in M_m(F)\) , partitioned into blocks according to \(m = w_1 + \dots + w_s\) , whose blocks are \[ \W_{jj} = \lambda \I_{w_j}, \qquad \W_{j,j+1} = \begin{pmatrix} \I_{w_{j+1}} \\ \O \end{pmatrix} \in M_{w_j \times w_{j+1}}(F), \qquad \W_{jl} = \O \ \text{ otherwise} . \] A Weyr matrix is a direct sum of basic Weyr matrices. A Weyr form of \(T \in \cL(V)\) is a Weyr matrix \(\W\) with \(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} = \W\) for some basis \(\sB\) of \(V\) ; for \(\A \in M_n(F)\) , a Weyr form of \(\A\) is a Weyr matrix similar to \(\A\) .

title: Exercise (B1: Real forms of two by two matrices)

title: Theorem 10.4.5 (Weyr Form)
page: 10.4 The Real Jordan Form and the Weyr Form
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) with \(\dim V = n \ge 1\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . (Existence) \(T\) has a Weyr form if and only if \(p_T\) splits over \(F\) . One can be arranged with one basic Weyr block per eigenvalue. (Uniqueness) In any Weyr form of \(T\) with one basic block per eigenvalue, the block for \(\lambda\) has Weyr structure \[ w_j = \dim\ker(T - \lambda\,\id_V)^{j} - \dim\ker(T - \lambda\,\id_V)^{j-1} \qquad (j \ge 1), \] the nonzero terms of this sequence; equivalently \((w_1, w_2, \dots)\) is the dual partition of the partition formed by the sizes of the \(\lambda\) -blocks of the Jordan form of \(T\) . So the Weyr form is determined by \(T\) up to the order of its basic blocks.

title: Definition 10.5.3 (Companion Matrix)
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) and let \(p = x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + a_1x + a_0 \in F[x]\) be monic of degree \(n\) . The companion matrix of \(p\) is the matrix \(\C(p) \in M_n(F)\) with \(1\) in each position \((j+1, j)\) just below the diagonal, last column \((-a_0, -a_1, \dots, -a_{n-1})\) , and \(0\) elsewhere: \[ \C(p) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & -a_0 \\ 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & -a_1 \\ 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & -a_2 \\ \vdots & & \ddots & & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 & -a_{n-1} \end{pmatrix} . \] For \(n = 1\) and \(p = x + a_0\) this reads \(\C(p) = (-a_0)\) .

title: Definition 10.5.1 (Cyclic Subspace)
content: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\) , let \(T \in \cL(V)\) , and let \(\elem{v} \in V\) . The cyclic subspace generated by \(\elem{v}\) is \[ Z(\elem{v}; T) \coloneqq \Span\big(\elem{v},\ T\elem{v},\ T^2\elem{v},\ \dots\big) = \Span\big(\{\, T^j\elem{v} : j \ge 0 \,\}\big), \] where \(T^0 = \id_V\) . For \(\A \in M_n(F)\) we write \(Z(\elem{v}; \A) = Z(\elem{v}; T_{\A})\) .

title: Definition 10.5.4 (Cyclic Vector, Cyclic Operator)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) with \(\dim V = n \ge 1\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . A vector \(\elem{v} \in V\) is a cyclic vector for \(T\) if \[ Z(\elem{v}; T) = V . \] We call \(T\) cyclic if it has a cyclic vector, and \(\A \in M_n(F)\) cyclic if \(T_{\A}\) is.

title: Definition 10.5.2 (The T-Annihilator of a Vector)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) , let \(T \in \cL(V)\) , and let \(\elem{v} \in V\) . The set \[ I_{\elem{v}} \coloneqq \{\, p \in F[x] : p(T)\elem{v} = \elem{0} \,\} \] is a nonzero ideal of \(F[x]\) , and the \(T\) -annihilator of \(\elem{v}\) , written \(m_{T,\elem{v}}\) , is its unique monic generator: \[ I_{\elem{v}} = \langle m_{T,\elem{v}} \rangle . \] Equivalently, \(m_{T,\elem{v}}\) is the monic polynomial of least degree with \(m_{T,\elem{v}}(T)\elem{v} = \elem{0}\) . For \(\A \in M_n(F)\) we write \(m_{\A,\elem{v}}\) .

title: Example (A Cyclic Subspace and a Cyclic Vector)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(\nQ) . \] Find \(p_{\A}\) and \(m_{\A}\) . Find \(m_{\A,\cvec{e}_1}\) , the subspace \(Z(\cvec{e}_1; \A)\) , and the matrix of \(T_{\A}\) restricted to it. Find a cyclic vector for \(\A\) and an invertible \(\P\) with \(\P^{-1}\A \P\) a companion matrix.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define \(Z(\elem{v}; T)\) and the \(T\) -annihilator \(m_{T,\elem{v}}\) . State the formula for \(\dim Z(\elem{v}; T)\) and say which basis of \(Z(\elem{v}; T)\) the theorem provides. Write down \(\C(p)\) for \(p = x^3 - 2x + 5\) , and say what \(p_{\C(p)}\) and \(m_{\C(p)}\) are. True or false: every operator on a space of dimension \(n \ge 2\) has a cyclic vector. Justify your answer. What is \(m_{T,\elem{v}}\) when \(\elem{v}\) is an eigenvector of \(T\) for \(\lambda\) ? What is \(Z(\elem{v}; T)\) then? True or false: if \(m_{T,\elem{v}} = m_T\) for some \(\elem{v}\) , then \(\elem{v}\) is a cyclic vector. Justify your answer.

content: Let \(V = \nR[x]_{\le 3}\) and let \(D \in \cL(V)\) be differentiation. Find \(m_{D,q}\) for \(q = 1\) , \(q = x\) , \(q = x^2\) , and \(q = x^3\) . title: Exercise (C1: What commutes with a cyclic operator)
content: Let \(V\) be finite-dimensional with \(\dim V = n \ge 1\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \(m_T = p_T\) . Prove that every \(S \in \cL(V)\) with \(ST = TS\) is a polynomial in \(T\) , that is, \(S = q(T)\) for some \(q \in F[x]\) . Deduce that the set \(\{\, S \in \cL(V) : ST = TS \,\}\) is a subspace of \(\cL(V)\) of dimension exactly \(n\) . Show that (a) fails without the hypothesis \(m_T = p_T\) , by taking \(T = \id_V\) with \(n \ge 2\) . Hint for (a): apply \(S\) to a cyclic vector.

title: Exercise (C2: How many cyclic vectors?)
content:
Let \(V\) be finite-dimensional with \(\dim V = n \ge 1\) and \(T \in \cL(V)\) . Prove that \(\elem{v}\) is a cyclic vector for \(T\) if and only if \(\elem{v}\) lies in no \(T\) -invariant subspace \(U\) with \(U 
e V\) . Prove that if \(\elem{v}\) is cyclic, then so is \(c\elem{v}\) for every \(c \in F\) with \(c 
e 0\) . Deduce that over an infinite field a cyclic operator has infinitely many cyclic vectors. Let \(F = 
F_2\) and \(T = T_{\J}\) with \(\J =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . Find all cyclic vectors of \(T\) . Deduce from (c) that the set of cyclic vectors, together with \(\elem{0}\) , need not be a subspace.

title: Lemma 10.5.4 (Annihilator of a Sum with Coprime Annihilators)
content: Let \(V\) be finite-dimensional, \(T \in \cL(V)\) , and \(\elem{u}, \elem{w} \in V\) with \(f = m_{T,\elem{u}}\) and \(g = m_{T,\elem{w}}\) coprime . Then \[ m_{T, \elem{u} + \elem{w}} = fg . \] More generally, if \(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k \in V\) have pairwise coprime \(T\) -annihilators \(f_1, \dots, f_k\) , then \(m_{T, \elem{v}_1 + \dots + \elem{v}_k} = f_1 f_2 \cdots f_k\) .

title: Proposition 10.5.1 (The Cyclic Subspace Is the Smallest Invariant Subspace Containing the Vector)
content: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\) , \(T \in \cL(V)\) , and \(\elem{v} \in V\) . Then: \(Z(\elem{v}; T) = \{\, p(T)\elem{v} : p \in F[x] \,\}\) ; \(Z(\elem{v}; T)\) is \(T\) -invariant; if \(U\) is a \(T\) -invariant subspace of \(V\) with \(\elem{v} \in U\) , then \(Z(\elem{v}; T) \subseteq U\) .

title: Proposition 10.5.5 (Some Vector Has the Minimal Polynomial as Its Annihilator)
content: Let \(V \ne \{\elem{0}\}\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) and \(T \in \cL(V)\) . Then there is \(\elem{v} \in V\) with \[ m_{T,\elem{v}} = m_T . \]

title: Theorem 10.5.3 (The Companion Matrix Realizes Its Polynomial Twice)
content: Let \(p \in F[x]\) be monic of degree \(n \ge 1\) and \(\C = \C(p)\) . Then \[ p_{\C} = m_{\C} = p , \] and \(\cvec{e}_1\) satisfies \(Z(\cvec{e}_1; \C) = F^n\) with \(m_{\C,\cvec{e}_1} = p\) . Consequently every monic polynomial over \(F\) is both the characteristic and the minimal polynomial of some square matrix over \(F\) .

title: Theorem 10.5.6 (Cyclic Operators)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) with \(\dim V = n \ge 1\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . The following are equivalent: \(T\) is cyclic, that is, \(T\) has a cyclic vector; \(\deg m_T = n\) ; \(m_T = p_T\) . In that case \(\elem{v}\) is a cyclic vector if and only if \(m_{T,\elem{v}} = m_T\) , and in the basis \((\elem{v}, T\elem{v}, \dots, T^{n-1}\elem{v})\) the matrix of \(T\) is \(\C(m_T)\) . The same holds for \(\A \in M_n(F)\) .

title: Theorem 10.5.2 (Basis and Matrix of a Cyclic Subspace)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) , let \(T \in \cL(V)\) , and let \(\elem{v} \in V\) with \(\elem{v} \ne \elem{0}\) . Write \(Z = Z(\elem{v}; T)\) and \[ m_{T,\elem{v}} = x^{k} + a_{k-1}x^{k-1} + \dots + a_1x + a_0, \qquad k = \deg m_{T,\elem{v}} \ge 1 . \] Then: \(\big(\elem{v},\ T\elem{v},\ \dots,\ T^{k-1}\elem{v}\big)\) is a basis of \(Z\) ; in particular \(\dim Z = \deg m_{T,\elem{v}}\) ; \(T^{k}\elem{v} = -\big(a_0\elem{v} + a_1T\elem{v} + \dots + a_{k-1}T^{k-1}\elem{v}\big)\) , and the matrix of \(T|_{Z}\) in the basis of (a) is the companion matrix of \(m_{T,\elem{v}}\) ( @exr-characteristic-polynomial-c1 ; the definition is repeated in full as @def-companion-matrix below); \(m_{T|_{Z}} = p_{T|_{Z}} = m_{T,\elem{v}}\) ; \(m_{T,\elem{v}} \mid m_T\) , and \(\deg m_{T,\elem{v}} \le \deg m_T \le \dim V\) .

title: Corollary 10.6.8 (Companion Blocks of Linear Powers Are Jordan Blocks)
content: Let \(\lambda \in F\) and \(k \ge 1\) . Then \[ \C\big((x - \lambda)^k\big) \sim \J_k(\lambda) . \] Consequently, if \(p_T\) splits over \(F\) , then the elementary divisors of \(T\) are the polynomials \((x - \lambda)^k\) for the Jordan blocks \(\J_k(\lambda)\) of \(T\) , and the elementary divisor form of @thm-elementary-divisor-form and the Jordan form of \(T\) are obtained from one another by replacing each block \(\C\big((x-\lambda)^k\big)\) by \(\J_k(\lambda)\) and conversely.

title: Corollary 10.6.4 (Uniqueness of the Chain and of the Prime Powers)
content: Let \(V \ne \{\elem{0}\}\) be finite-dimensional over \(F\) and \(T \in \cL(V)\) . Any two decompositions as in @thm-cyclic-decomposition give the same ordered list \(d_1 \mid \dots \mid d_r\) . Any decomposition \(V = Z(\elem{u}_1;T) \oplus \dots \oplus Z(\elem{u}_N;T)\) whose annihilators \(m_{T,\elem{u}_i}\) are powers of monic irreducibles gives the same list of annihilators, up to order, namely the prime powers occurring in \(d_1, \dots, d_r\) . Explicitly, writing \[ c_p(k) = \frac{\dim\ker p(T)^{k} - \dim\ker p(T)^{k-1}}{\deg p} \qquad (p \text{ monic irreducible},\ k \ge 1), \] the list is recovered by \(r = \max_p c_p(1)\) and \[ v_p(d_j) = \#\{\, k \ge 1 : c_p(k) \ge r + 1 - j \,\} \qquad (1 \le j \le r) . \] In particular the invariant factors of \(T\) are determined by the numbers \(\dim\ker p(T)^{k}\) alone.

title: Corollary 10.6.6 (Similarity via the Invariant Factors)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(F)\) with \(n \ge 1\) . The following are equivalent: \(\A \sim \B\) ; \(\A\) and \(\B\) have the same invariant factors; \(\A\) and \(\B\) have the same elementary divisors, up to order; \(\dim\ker p(\A)^{k} = \dim\ker p(\B)^{k}\) for every monic irreducible \(p \in F[x]\) and every \(k \ge 1\) .

title: Corollary 10.6.10 (Similarity Is Independent of the Field)
content: Let \(K\) be a subfield of \(L\) and let \(\A, \B \in M_n(K)\) , \(n \ge 1\) . If \(\A\) and \(\B\) are similar over \(L\) , then they are similar over \(K\) : \[ \begin{aligned} &\A = \Q^{-1}\B \Q \ \text{ for some invertible } \Q \in M_n(L) \\ &\qquad \implies \A = \P^{-1}\B \P \ \text{ for some invertible } \P \in M_n(K) . \end{aligned} \]

title: Definition 10.6.1 (Invariant Factors, Elementary Divisors)
content: Let \(V \ne \{\elem{0}\}\) be finite-dimensional over \(F\) and \(T \in \cL(V)\) . The invariant factors of \(T\) are the monic nonconstant polynomials \[ d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \dots \mid d_r \] of @thm-cyclic-decomposition , which by @cor-invariant-factors-unique (a) do not depend on the decomposition. The elementary divisors of \(T\) are the prime powers occurring in the factorizations of \(d_1, \dots, d_r\) , listed with repetition; by @cor-invariant-factors-unique (b) they are the annihilators of the pieces in any decomposition of \(V\) into cyclic subspaces with prime-power annihilators. For \(\A \in M_n(F)\) the invariant factors and elementary divisors are those of \(T_{\A}\) .

title: Example (Invariant Factors from Polynomial Data)
content: Let \(T\) be an operator on a \(6\) -dimensional \(\nQ\) -vector space with \[ p_T = (x-1)^2(x^2+1)^2, \qquad m_T = (x-1)(x^2+1)^2 . \] Find the elementary divisors, the invariant factors, the rational canonical form ( @thm-rational-canonical-form ), and the elementary divisor form ( @thm-elementary-divisor-form ).

title: Example (The Rational Canonical Form of a Matrix over the Rationals)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in M_4(\nQ), \qquad p_{\A} = (x^2+1)^2 . \] Find the invariant factors of \(\A\) , its rational canonical form ( @thm-rational-canonical-form ), and an invertible \(\P \in M_4(\nQ)\) realizing it.

What is the rational canonical form of \(T\) , and over which fields does it exist? True or false: two matrices in \(M_n(
Q)\) that are similar over \(

Q\) . Justify your answer. An operator on a \(5\) -dimensional \(

title: Lemma 10.6.9 (Rank Does Not Change with the Field)
content: Let \(K\) be a subfield of a field \(L\) and let \(\M \in M_{m \times n}(K)\) . Then the rank of \(\M\) computed over \(K\) equals its rank computed over \(L\) .

title: Proposition 10.6.3 (Counting the Exponents)
content: Let \(V \ne \{\elem{0}\}\) be finite-dimensional over \(F\) , let \(T \in \cL(V)\) , and suppose \[ V = Z(\elem{u}_1; T) \oplus \dots \oplus Z(\elem{u}_N; T), \qquad m_{T,\elem{u}_i} = g_i , \] with every \(g_i\) monic and nonconstant. Then for every monic irreducible \(p \in F[x]\) : \(\displaystyle \dim\ker p(T)^{k} = \deg p \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{N} \min\big(k, v_p(g_i)\big)\) for every integer \(k \ge 0\) ; for every \(k \ge 1\) , \[ \#\{\, i : v_p(g_i) \ge k \,\} = \frac{\dim\ker p(T)^{k} - \dim\ker p(T)^{k-1}}{\deg p} , \] a number depending only on \(T\) , \(p\) , and \(k\) .

title: Theorem 10.6.2 (Cyclic Decomposition Theorem)
content: Let \(V \ne \{\elem{0}\}\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . Then there are an integer \(r \ge 1\) , vectors \(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_r \in V\) , and monic nonconstant polynomials \(d_1, \dots, d_r \in F[x]\) such that \[ V = Z(\elem{v}_1; T) \oplus \dots \oplus Z(\elem{v}_r; T), \qquad m_{T,\elem{v}_j} = d_j , \] and \(d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \dots \mid d_r\) ; \(d_r = m_T\) ; \(d_1d_2\cdots d_r = p_T\) ; in particular \(\sum_j \deg d_j = \dim V\) ; there is a finer decomposition \(V = \bigoplus_{i,j} Z(\elem{v}_{ij}; T)\) into cyclic subspaces whose annihilators \(m_{T,\elem{v}_{ij}}\) are powers of monic irreducibles, and the list of these prime powers, with repetitions, consists exactly of the prime powers occurring in the factorizations of \(d_1, \dots, d_r\) .

title: Theorem 10.6.7 (Elementary Divisor Form)
content: Let \(V \ne \{\elem{0}\}\) be finite-dimensional over \(F\) , let \(T \in \cL(V)\) , and let \(q_1, \dots, q_N\) be the elementary divisors of \(T\) . Then there is a basis \(\sB\) of \(V\) with \[ \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} = \C(q_1) \oplus \C(q_2) \oplus \dots \oplus \C(q_N) , \] and the blocks are determined by \(T\) up to their order.

title: Theorem 10.6.1 (Cyclic Decomposition for a Single Prime Power)
content: Let \(V \ne \{\elem{0}\}\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) , let \(T \in \cL(V)\) , and suppose \[ m_T = p^{e}, \qquad p \in F[x] \text{ monic irreducible of degree } d, \quad e \ge 1 . \] Then there are an integer \(m \ge 1\) , vectors \(\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_m \in V\) , and exponents \[ e = k_1 \ge k_2 \ge \dots \ge k_m \ge 1 \] such that \[ V = Z(\elem{u}_1; T) \oplus Z(\elem{u}_2; T) \oplus \dots \oplus Z(\elem{u}_m; T), \qquad m_{T,\elem{u}_i} = p^{k_i} \quad (1 \le i \le m) . \] In particular \(\dim V = d(k_1 + \dots + k_m)\) .

title: Theorem 10.6.5 (Rational Canonical Form)
content: Let \(V \ne \{\elem{0}\}\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over any field \(F\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) have invariant factors \(d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \dots \mid d_r\) . Then there is a basis \(\sB\) of \(V\) with \[ \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB} = \C(d_1) \oplus \C(d_2) \oplus \dots \oplus \C(d_r) , \] and this matrix is determined by \(T\) . It is called the rational canonical form of \(T\) . Equivalently, every \(\A \in M_n(F)\) with \(n \ge 1\) is similar to exactly one matrix of the form \(\C(d_1) \oplus \dots \oplus \C(d_r)\) with \(d_1 \mid \dots \mid d_r\) monic and nonconstant.

title: Corollary 10.7.7 (A Matrix Is Similar to Its Transpose)
page: 10.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form
content: Let \(F\) be any field and \(\A \in M_n(F)\) . Then \(\A \sim \A\tp\) .

title: Corollary 10.7.6 (The Smith Form of x\I - \A Carries the Invariant Factors)
page: 10.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) with invariant factors \(d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \dots \mid d_r\) as in @thm-rational-canonical-form . Then the Smith normal form of \(x\I - \A\) is \[ \diag\big(\underbrace{1, \dots, 1}_{n - r},\, d_1,\, d_2,\, \dots,\, d_r\big) . \] In particular the invariant factors of \(\A\) are exactly the nonconstant diagonal entries of the Smith normal form of \(x\I - \A\) , read from the top down, and two matrices in \(M_n(F)\) are similar if and only if \(x\I - \A\) and \(x\I - \B\) have the same Smith normal form.

title: Definition 10.7.1 (Elementary Operations over F\lbrack x\rbrack)
page: 10.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form
content: Let \(\M \in M_n(F[x])\) . An elementary row operation over \(F[x]\) on \(\M\) is one of: interchanging two rows; multiplying one row by a nonzero scalar \(c \in F\) ; adding \(h\) times one row to a different row, where \(h \in F[x]\) is any polynomial. Elementary column operations over \(F[x]\) are defined the same way with “column” in place of “row”.

title: Definition 10.7.2 (Equivalence over F\lbrack x\rbrack)
page: 10.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form
content: Let \(\M, \M' \in M_n(F[x])\) . We say \(\M\) and \(\M'\) are equivalent over \(F[x]\) , written \(\M \approx \M'\) , if there are \(\U, \V \in M_n(F[x])\) , each invertible in \(M_n(F[x])\) , with \[ \M' = \U \M \V . \]

title: Example (A Smith Normal Form Computed by Hand)
page: 10.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(\nQ). \] Find the Smith normal form of \(x\I - \A\) over \(\nQ[x]\) , naming every operation, and check the answer with determinantal divisors.

page: 10.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form

title: Exercise (C2: Uniqueness by hand in the smallest case)
page: 10.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form
content: Let \(\M \in M_2(F[x])\) be nonzero. Prove directly, without using determinantal divisors, that \(\Delta_1(\M)\) — the monic gcd of the four entries of \(\M\) — is unchanged by each of the six elementary operations of @def-polynomial-elementary-operations . Prove that \(\det(\U \M \V) = c\det \M\) for a nonzero constant \(c\) whenever \(\U, \V\) are invertible over \(F[x]\) . Deduce that if \(\diag(d_1, d_2) \approx \diag(e_1, e_2)\) with all four entries monic or zero, \(d_1 \mid d_2\) , and \(e_1 \mid e_2\) , then \(d_1 = e_1\) and \(d_2 = e_2\) .

title: Lemma 10.7.4 (Division of a Polynomial Matrix by x\I - \A)
page: 10.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) and \(\M \in M_n(F[x])\) . Then there are \(\Q \in M_n(F[x])\) and \(\R \in M_n(F)\) with \[ \M = (x\I - \A)\,\Q + \R . \]

title: Proposition 10.7.2 (Operations and Equivalence)
page: 10.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form
content: Let \(\M, \M' \in M_n(F[x])\) . \(\approx\) is an equivalence relation on \(M_n(F[x])\) . If \(\M'\) is obtained from \(\M\) by a finite sequence of elementary row and column operations over \(F[x]\) , then \(\M \approx \M'\) .

title: Proposition 10.7.1 (Invertible Polynomial Matrices)
page: 10.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form
content: Let \(\U \in M_n(F[x])\) . Then \(\U\) has an inverse in \(M_n(F[x])\) if and only if \(\det \U\) is a nonzero constant .

title: Theorem 10.7.5 (Similarity as Equivalence of x\I - \A and x\I - \B)
page: 10.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(n \ge 1\) , and \(\A, \B \in M_n(F)\) . Then \[ \A \sim \B \quad \text{over } F \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad x\I - \A \approx x\I - \B \quad \text{over } F[x]. \]

title: Theorem 10.7.3 (Smith Normal Form)
page: 10.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(n \ge 1\) , and \(\M \in M_n(F[x])\) . Then: (Existence) \(\M\) is equivalent over \(F[x]\) , by a finite sequence of elementary row and column operations, to a diagonal matrix \[ \D = \diag(d_1, d_2, \dots, d_n) \] in which every \(d_i\) is monic or zero and \(d_i \mid d_{i+1}\) for \(i = 1, \dots, n-1\) . (Uniqueness) The list \((d_1, \dots, d_n)\) is determined by \(\M\) : if \(\M \approx \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) \approx \diag(e_1, \dots, e_n)\) with both lists as in (a), then \(d_i = e_i\) for every \(i\) . The matrix \(\D\) is called the Smith normal form of \(\M\) , and \(d_1, \dots, d_n\) its invariant divisors .

title: Definition 10.8.1 (Semisimple Operator)
page: 10.8 Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) with \(\dim V \ge 1\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . We say \(T\) is semisimple if \[ m_T = p_1p_2\cdots p_k \] for distinct monic irreducible \(p_1, \dots, p_k \in F[x]\) ; equivalently, if no irreducible polynomial \(p \in F[x]\) satisfies \(p^2 \mid m_T\) . A matrix \(\A \in M_n(F)\) is semisimple over \(F\) if \(T_{\A}\) is.

title: Example (The Semisimple and Nilpotent Parts of a 3 \times 3 Matrix)
page: 10.8 Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(\nQ), \qquad p_{\A} = (x - 2)^2(x - 3). \] Find the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition \(\A = \S + \N\) , and exhibit \(\S\) and \(\N\) as polynomials in \(\A\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 10.8 Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
content: Define a semisimple operator, and say how the definition specializes to Chapter 9’s criterion for diagonalizability. State the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition Theorem, including all three conditions on \(S\) and \(N\) and the uniqueness clause. True or false: \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nR)\) is semisimple. Justify your answer. True or false: if \(\A = \D + \E\) with \(\D\) the diagonal part of \(\A\) and \(\E\) the off-diagonal part, then \(\D\) is the semisimple part of \(\A\) . Justify your answer. Which hypothesis of the uniqueness clause does the pair \((\D, \E)\) of part (d) typically violate? Why does every operator commuting with \(T\) commute with the semisimple part of \(T\) ?

title: Exercise (B1: Semisimple and nilpotent parts)
page: 10.8 Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
content: For each matrix over \(\nQ\) , find the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition \(\A = \S + \N\) and express \(\S\) as a polynomial in \(\A\) . \(\A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}\) . \(\A_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}\) . \(\A_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: When is the nilpotent part zero?)
page: 10.8 Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
content: Let \(V\) be finite-dimensional with \(\dim V \ge 1\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) with \(p_T\) split, with Jordan–Chevalley decomposition \(T = S + N\) . Prove that \(N = 0\) if and only if \(T\) is diagonalizable, and that \(S = 0\) if and only if \(T\) is nilpotent.

title: Exercise (B3: Block diagonal matrices)
page: 10.8 Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
content: Let \(\A_1 \in M_p(F)\) and \(\A_2 \in M_q(F)\) have split characteristic polynomials, with Jordan–Chevalley decompositions \(\A_i = \S_i + \N_i\) . Prove that the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition of \(\A_1 \oplus \A_2\) is \[ \A_1 \oplus \A_2 = (\S_1 \oplus \S_2) + (\N_1 \oplus \N_2). \]

title: Exercise (C1: The multiplicative version)
page: 10.8 Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
content: Call \(U \in \cL(V)\) unipotent if \(U - \id_V\) is nilpotent. Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be invertible with \(p_T\) split, and let \(T = S + N\) be its Jordan–Chevalley decomposition. Prove that \(S\) is invertible. Prove that \(S^{-1}\) commutes with \(N\) , and that \(S^{-1}N\) is nilpotent. Deduce that \(T = SU\) with \(S\) diagonalizable, \(U\) unipotent, and \(SU = US\) . Prove that this multiplicative decomposition is unique: if \(T = S'U'\) with \(S'\) diagonalizable, \(U'\) unipotent, and \(S'U' = U'S'\) , then \(S' = S\) and \(U' = U\) . Hint: for (d), turn the multiplicative statement into an additive one by writing \(T = S' + S'(U' - \id_V)\) .

title: Exercise (C2: The parts inherit every symmetry)
page: 10.8 Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
content: Let \(V\) be finite-dimensional with \(\dim V \ge 1\) , let \(T \in \cL(V)\) with \(p_T\) split, and let \(T = S + N\) be its Jordan–Chevalley decomposition. Prove that if \(X \in \cL(V)\) satisfies \(XT = TX\) , then \(XS = SX\) and \(XN = NX\) . Deduce that every \(T\) -invariant subspace is \(S\) -invariant and \(N\) -invariant, and that \(S\) and \(N\) map each \(G_\lambda(T)\) into itself. Give an example of a diagonalizable \(S\) and a nilpotent \(N\) with \(SN \ne NS\) for which \(S + N\) is not the operator whose semisimple part is \(S\) . (So the commuting hypothesis cannot be dropped from the uniqueness statement.)

title: Lemma 10.8.1 (The Minimal Polynomial Does Not Notice a Larger Field)
page: 10.8 Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
content: Let \(K \subseteq L\) be fields and \(\A \in M_n(K)\) , \(n \ge 1\) . Then the minimal polynomial of \(\A\) computed in \(K[x]\) equals the minimal polynomial of \(\A\) computed in \(L[x]\) .

title: Proposition 10.8.2 (Semisimple Means Diagonalizable After Enlarging the Field)
page: 10.8 Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
content: Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic \(0\) , let \(\A \in M_n(K)\) with \(n \ge 1\) , and let \(L \supseteq K\) be a field over which \(m_{\A}\) splits. Then \[ \A \text{ is semisimple over } K \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \A \text{ is diagonalizable over } L . \]

title: Theorem 10.8.3 (Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition)
page: 10.8 Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) with \(\dim V = n \ge 1\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) with \(p_T\) split over \(F\) . Then: (Existence) There are \(S, N \in \cL(V)\) with \[ T = S + N, \qquad S \text{ diagonalizable}, \qquad N \text{ nilpotent}, \qquad SN = NS ; \] moreover \(S = g(T)\) and \(N = h(T)\) for some \(g, h \in F[x]\) . (Uniqueness) If \(T = S' + N'\) with \(S'\) diagonalizable, \(N'\) nilpotent, and \(S'N' = N'S'\) , then \(S' = S\) and \(N' = N\) . We call \(S\) the semisimple part and \(N\) the nilpotent part of \(T\) .

title: Corollary 10.9.5 (Exponential of a Jordan Block, with a Parameter)
page: 10.9 Functions of Matrices, the Exponential, and Linear Differential Equations
content: Let \(k \ge 1\) , \(\lambda \in \nC\) , and \(t \in \nR\) . Then \(e^{t\J_k(\lambda)}\) is the upper triangular matrix with \[ \bigl(e^{t\J_k(\lambda)}\bigr)_{r,\,r+j} = \frac{t^{j}e^{\lambda t}}{j!} \qquad (0 \le j \le k-1) \] and zeros below the diagonal. Consequently, if \(\A = \P \J \P^{-1}\) with \(\J = \J_{k_1}(\lambda_1) \oplus \dots \oplus \J_{k_m}(\lambda_m)\) , then \[ e^{t\A} = \P\Bigl(e^{t\J_{k_1}(\lambda_1)} \oplus \dots \oplus e^{t\J_{k_m}(\lambda_m)}\Bigr)\P^{-1} . \] In particular, for a diagonal \(\D = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n)\) , \(e^{t\D} = \diag(e^{td_1}, \dots, e^{td_n})\) .

title: Definition 10.9.2 (Matrix Exponential)
page: 10.9 Functions of Matrices, the Exponential, and Linear Differential Equations
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) . The matrix exponential of \(\A\) is \[ e^{\A} \coloneqq \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{\A^{m}}{m!} = \lim_{\M \to \infty}\ \sum_{m=0}^{\M}\frac{\A^{m}}{m!}, \] the limit taken entrywise, provided it exists; \(\A^{0} = \I\) .

title: Definition 10.9.1 (Function of a Matrix)
page: 10.9 Functions of Matrices, the Exponential, and Linear Differential Equations
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) with Jordan form \(\J = \J_{k_1}(\lambda_1) \oplus \dots \oplus \J_{k_m}(\lambda_m)\) and \(\A = \P \J \P^{-1}\) . Let \(f\) be a complex-valued function that is defined and at least \(k_i - 1\) times differentiable at \(\lambda_i\) for every \(i\) — for instance, a function given by a convergent power series on a disc around each eigenvalue. Define \[ f\bigl(\J_k(\lambda)\bigr) \coloneqq \begin{pmatrix} f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \tfrac{f''(\lambda)}{2!} & \cdots & \tfrac{f^{(k-1)}(\lambda)}{(k-1)!} \\ & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \ddots & \vdots \\ & & \ddots & \ddots & \tfrac{f''(\lambda)}{2!} \\ & & & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\ & & & & f(\lambda) \end{pmatrix} \in M_k(\nC), \] the upper triangular matrix with \(f^{(j)}(\lambda)/j!\) in every position \((r, r+j)\) , and \[ f(\A) \coloneqq \P\,\Bigl( f\bigl(\J_{k_1}(\lambda_1)\bigr) \oplus \dots \oplus f\bigl(\J_{k_m}(\lambda_m)\bigr) \Bigr)\,\P^{-1} . \]

title: Lemma 10.9.1 (A Polynomial of a Jordan Block)
page: 10.9 Functions of Matrices, the Exponential, and Linear Differential Equations
content: Let \(F\) have characteristic \(0\) , let \(k \ge 1\) , \(\lambda \in F\) , and \(p \in F[x]\) . Then \(p(\J_k(\lambda))\) is the upper triangular matrix whose \((r, r+j)\) -entry is \[ \bigl(p(\J_k(\lambda))\bigr)_{r, r+j} = \frac{p^{(j)}(\lambda)}{j!} \qquad (0 \le j \le k - 1, \ 1 \le r \le k - j), \] with all entries below the diagonal equal to \(0\) . In particular the value \(p(\lambda)\) fills the diagonal, \(p'(\lambda)\) the superdiagonal, and only the first \(k\) derivatives of \(p\) at \(\lambda\) are involved.

title: Definition 10.10.1 (Entrywise Convergence and Boundedness)
content: Let \(\M_1, \M_2, \dots\) be matrices in \(M_{p \times q}(\nC)\) and \(\M \in M_{p \times q}(\nC)\) . The sequence \((\M_m)\) converges to \(\M\) , written \(\M_m \to \M\) , if for every position \((r, s)\) the sequence of complex numbers \((\M_m)_{rs}\) converges to \(\M_{rs}\) . We then write \(\M = \lim_m \M_m\) . The sequence \((\M_m)\) is bounded if there is a real \(c \ge 0\) with \(\lvert (\M_m)_{rs}\rvert \le c\) for all \(m\) and all positions \((r, s)\) . A series \(\sum_{k \ge 0} \M_k\) converges to \(\M\) if its sequence of partial sums \(\sum_{k=0}^{K}\M_k\) converges to \(\M\) .

title: Theorem 10.10.3 (Power-Bounded Matrices)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) , \(n \ge 1\) , with Jordan form \(\J\) . The sequence \((\A^{m})_{m \ge 0}\) is bounded if and only if every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(\A\) satisfies \(\lvert\lambda\rvert \le 1\) , and every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) with \(\lvert\lambda\rvert = 1\) has all of its blocks in \(\J\) of size \(1\) , equivalently \(a_{\A}(\lambda) = g_{\A}(\lambda)\) , equivalently \(x - \lambda\) occurs to the first power in \(m_{\A}\) .

title: Theorem 10.10.2 (Powers Tending to Zero)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) , \(n \ge 1\) . Then \(\A^{m} \to \O\) if and only if every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(\A\) satisfies \(\lvert\lambda\rvert < 1\) .

title: Theorem 10.10.6 (Neumann Series)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) , \(n \ge 1\) . Then the series \(\sum_{k \ge 0}\A^{k}\) converges if and only if every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(\A\) satisfies \(\lvert\lambda\rvert < 1\) . In that case \(\I - \A\) is invertible and \[ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\A^{k} = (\I - \A)^{-1} . \]

title: Corollary 11.1.6 (Triangle Inequality)
content:
Let \(V\) be an inner product space and \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) . Then \[

title: Definition 11.1.5 (Angle Between Vectors)
content: Let \(V\) be a real inner product space and let \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) be nonzero . The angle between \(\elem{u}\) and \(\elem{v}\) is the unique \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) with \[ \cos\theta = \frac{\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}}}{\norm{\elem{u}}\,\norm{\elem{v}}} . \]

title: Definition 11.1.2 (Conjugate Transpose)
content: For \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) , the conjugate transpose \(\A^{*} \in M_{n \times m}(F)\) is the matrix with entries \((\A^{*})_{ij} = \conj{a_{ji}}\) . A square matrix with \(\A^{*} = \A\) is Hermitian .

title: Definition 11.1.3 (Induced Norm)
content:
Let \(V\) be an inner product space. The norm of \(\elem{v} \in V\) is \[ 
orm{\elem{v}} \coloneqq \sqrt{\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}} , \] the nonnegative real square root. A vector with \(
orm{\elem{v}} = 1\) is a unit vector , and replacing a nonzero \(\elem{v}\) by \(\elem{v} / 
orm{\elem{v}}\) is called normalizing it.

title: Definition 11.1.1 (Inner Product)
content:
Let \(F\) be \(
R\) or \(
C\) , and let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\) . An inner product on \(V\) is a map \[ \inner{\cdot}{\cdot} \colon V 	imes V 	o F \] such that for all \(\elem{u}, \elem{v}, \elem{w} \in V\) and all \(a, b \in F\) : \(\inner{a\elem{u} + b\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} = a\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} + b\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}}\) ( linear in the first slot ); \(\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{u}} = \conj{\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}}}\) ( conjugate symmetry ); \(\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} > 0\) for every nonzero \(\elem{v} \in V\) ( positive definiteness ). A vector space equipped with an inner product is an inner product space . When \(F = 
R\) it is a real inner product space, when \(F = 
C\) a complex one.

title: Definition 11.1.4 (Orthogonal Vectors)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space. Vectors \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) are orthogonal , written \(\elem{u} \perp \elem{v}\) , if \(\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = 0\) . A list \((\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k)\) is orthogonal if \(\elem{v}_i \perp \elem{v}_j\) whenever \(i \ne j\) .

orm{\cvec{u} + \cvec{v}}^2 - 
orm{\cvec{u} - \cvec{v}}^2 ig)\) . Show that \( eta(\cvec{u}, \cvec{u}) = 
orm{\cvec{u}}^2\) , that \( eta(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) =  eta(\cvec{v}, \cvec{u})\) , and that \( eta(\cvec{u}, \cvec{0}) = 0\) . Prove that \( eta(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) +  eta(\cvec{u}, \cvec{w}) = 2 eta ig(\cvec{u}, 	frac12(\cvec{v} + \cvec{w}) ig)\) for all \(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}, \cvec{w}\) . Deduce that \( eta(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v}) +  eta(\cvec{u}, \cvec{w}) =  eta(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} + \cvec{w})\) . Granting that \( eta(\cvec{u}, t\cvec{v}) = t eta(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v})\) for all \(t \in 
R\) , conclude that \( eta\) is an inner product on \(
R^2\) whose induced norm is \(
orm{\cdot}\) . Hint: for (b), apply the parallelogram law to the pair \(\cvec{u} + 	frac12(\cvec{v} + \cvec{w})\) , \(	frac12(\cvec{v} - \cvec{w})\) , and then to the pair \(\cvec{u} - 	frac12(\cvec{v} + \cvec{w})\) , \(	frac12(\cvec{w} - \cvec{v})\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Recovering the inner product from the norm)
content:
Let \(V\) be an inner product space over \(F\) . For \(F = 
R\) , prove the polarization identity \(\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = 	frac14 ig(
orm{\elem{u} + \elem{v}}^2 - 
orm{\elem{u} - \elem{v}}^2 ig)\) . For \(F = 
C\) , prove that \[ \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} =  rac14\sum_{k=0}^{3} i^{k}\,
orm{\elem{u} + i^{k}\elem{v}}^2 . \] Deduce that two inner products on \(V\) with the same induced norm are equal.

title: Exercise (C3: The equality cases)
content:
Let \(V\) be an inner product space. Prove that \(
orm{\elem{u} + \elem{v}} = 
orm{\elem{u}} + 
orm{\elem{v}}\) if and only if one of \(\elem{u}, \elem{v}\) is a nonnegative real multiple of the other. Deduce the equality condition in the classical inequality of @exr-inner-products-b3 (b): for real \(a_i, b_i\) , equality holds if and only if one of the vectors \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) , \((b_1, \dots, b_n)\) is a multiple of the other. Give real numbers \(a_i, b_i\) , not all zero, with \(\sum a_ib_i < 0\) and equality in the classical inequality, and explain why this does not contradict (a).

title: Theorem 11.1.5 (Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space and \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) . Then \[ \lvert \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} \rvert \le \norm{\elem{u}}\,\norm{\elem{v}} , \] with equality if and only if the list \((\elem{u}, \elem{v})\) is linearly dependent.

title: Theorem 11.1.1 (First Properties of an Inner Product)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space over \(F\) . For all \(\elem{u}, \elem{v}, \elem{w} \in V\) and \(a, b \in F\) : \(\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}\) is a real number, and \(\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} \ge 0\) with equality if and only if \(\elem{v} = \elem{0}\) ; \(\inner{\elem{u}}{a\elem{v} + b\elem{w}} = \conj{a}\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} + \conj{b}\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{w}}\) ( conjugate-linear in the second slot ); \(\inner{\elem{0}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{0}} = 0\) ; if \(\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{w}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}}\) for every \(\elem{w} \in V\) , then \(\elem{u} = \elem{v}\) .

title: Theorem 11.1.2 (Properties of the Induced Norm)
content:
Let \(V\) be an inner product space over \(F\) , \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) and \(c \in F\) . Then: \(
orm{\elem{v}} \ge 0\) , with \(
orm{\elem{v}} = 0\) if and only if \(\elem{v} = \elem{0}\) ; \(
orm{c\elem{v}} = \lvert c vert 
orm{\elem{v}}\) ; \(
orm{\elem{u} + \elem{v}}^2 = 
orm{\elem{u}}^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} + 
orm{\elem{v}}^2\) .

title: Theorem 11.1.4 (Orthogonal Nonzero Vectors Are Independent)
content: Let \((\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k)\) be an orthogonal list of nonzero vectors in an inner product space. Then the list is linearly independent.

title: Theorem 11.1.3 (Pythagorean Theorem)
content:
Let \((\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k)\) be an orthogonal list in an inner product space. Then \[ 
orm{\elem{v}_1 + \dots + \elem{v}_k}^2 = 
orm{\elem{v}_1}^2 + \dots + 
orm{\elem{v}_k}^2 . \]

title: Corollary 11.2.3 (Extending an Orthonormal List)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space and let \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_r)\) be an orthonormal list in \(V\) . Then there are vectors \(\elem{e}_{r+1}, \dots, \elem{e}_n \in V\) such that \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n)\) is an orthonormal basis of \(V\) .

title: Corollary 11.2.4 (Classification of Finite-Dimensional Inner Product Spaces)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space over \(F\) with \(\dim V = n\) . Then there is an isomorphism \(T \colon V \to F^n\) with \[ \inner{T\elem{u}}{T\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} \qquad \text{for all } \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V , \] where the right-hand inner product is that of \(V\) and the left-hand one is the standard inner product of \(F^n\) . An isomorphism with this property is an isometric isomorphism , so every \(n\) -dimensional inner product space over \(F\) is isometrically isomorphic to \(F^n\) .

title: Definition 11.2.3 (Gram Matrix)
content: Let \((\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k)\) be a list in an inner product space \(V\) over \(F\) . Its Gram matrix is \(\G \in M_k(F)\) with entries \[ (\G)_{ij} = \inner{\elem{v}_j}{\elem{v}_i} \qquad (1 \le i, j \le k). \]

title: Definition 11.2.2 (Orthonormal Basis)
content: An orthonormal basis of an inner product space \(V\) is an orthonormal list that is a basis of \(V\) .

title: Definition 11.2.1 (Orthonormal List)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space. A list \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k)\) of vectors of \(V\) is orthonormal if \[ \inner{\elem{e}_i}{\elem{e}_j} = \delta_{ij} \qquad \text{for all } i, j \in \{1, \dots, k\}, \] that is, if \(\inner{\elem{e}_i}{\elem{e}_j} = 0\) whenever \(i \ne j\) ( orthogonal ) and \(\norm{\elem{e}_i} = 1\) for every \(i\) ( normalized ).

title: Example (Deciding Independence with a Gram Matrix)
content: Decide whether \(((1,1,0), (1,0,1), (0,1,-1))\) is independent in \(\nR^3\) , using its Gram matrix.

title: Example (Gram–Schmidt on 1, x, x^2)
content: Apply the Gram–Schmidt process of @thm-gram-schmidt to \((1, x, x^2)\) in \(\nR[x]_{\le 2}\) with \[ \inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1} p(t)q(t)\,\dd t . \]

title: Example (Gram–Schmidt in \nR^3)
content: Apply the Gram–Schmidt process of @thm-gram-schmidt to \(\cvec{v}_1 = (1, 1, 1)\) , \(\cvec{v}_2 = (0, 1, 1)\) , \(\cvec{v}_3 = (0, 0, 1)\) in \(\nR^3\) with the dot product.

title: Example (Reading Off Coordinates)
content: Let \(\cvec{e}_1 = \tfrac13(1, 2, 2)\) , \(\cvec{e}_2 = \tfrac13(2, 1, -2)\) , \(\cvec{e}_3 = \tfrac13(2, -2, 1)\) , the orthonormal basis of \(\nR^3\) found above. Write \(\cvec{v} = (3, 0, 3)\) in this basis, and check Parseval’s identity.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define an orthonormal list, using the Kronecker delta, and say what an orthonormal basis is. Why is every orthonormal list linearly independent? Name the result used. Write down the coordinates of \(\elem{v}\) in an orthonormal basis \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n)\) , and state Parseval’s identity. True or false: the Gram–Schmidt process ( @thm-gram-schmidt ) applied to a list and to the same list in reverse order produces the same orthonormal list. Justify your answer. State the criterion for linear independence in terms of the Gram matrix. True or false: every \(3\) -dimensional real inner product space is isometrically isomorphic to \(\nR^3\) with the dot product. Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: Gram–Schmidt with numbers)
content: Apply the Gram–Schmidt process of @thm-gram-schmidt to each list, with the dot product. \(((1,0,1), (1,1,0), (0,1,1))\) in \(\nR^3\) . \(((1,1,0,0), (1,0,1,0), (0,0,1,1))\) in \(\nR^4\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Gram–Schmidt on polynomials)
content: In \(\nR[x]_{\le 2}\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{0}^{1} p(t)q(t)\,\dd t\) , apply the Gram–Schmidt process of @thm-gram-schmidt to \((1, x, x^2)\) . Compare the monic outputs with those of @exm-gram-schmidt-legendre and explain the difference.

title: Exercise (B3: Coordinates without solving a system)
content: Let \(\cvec{e}_1 = \tfrac13(1,2,2)\) , \(\cvec{e}_2 = \tfrac13(2,1,-2)\) , \(\cvec{e}_3 = \tfrac13(2,-2,1)\) in \(\nR^3\) . Write \(\cvec{v} = (1, -1, 4)\) in this basis. Compute \(\norm{\cvec{v}}^2\) in two ways, and state which theorem says the answers agree. Compute \(\inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{u}}\) for \(\cvec{u} = (3, 0, 3)\) from the coordinates of \(\cvec{v}\) and \(\cvec{u}\) , using @exm-orthonormal-coordinates-r3 for \(\cvec{u}\) .

title: Exercise (B4: Gram matrices)
content:
For each list, write down the Gram matrix and use it to decide whether the list is independent. \(((1,1,0), (1,0,1), (0,1,1))\) in \(
R^3\) with the dot product. \(((1, i), (i, 1))\) in \(
C^2\) with the standard inner product. \((1, x, x^2 - 	frac13)\) in \(
R[x]_{\le 2}\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1} pq\) .

title: Exercise (C1: The Gram matrix determines the list)
content: Let \((\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k)\) be a list in an inner product space \(V\) and \((\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_k)\) a list in an inner product space \(W\) , both over \(F\) , with the same Gram matrix: \(\inner{\elem{v}_j}{\elem{v}_i} = \inner{\elem{w}_j}{\elem{w}_i}\) for all \(i, j\) . Prove that \(\sum_j x_j\elem{v}_j = \elem{0}\) if and only if \(\sum_j x_j\elem{w}_j = \elem{0}\) , for every \(\cvec{x} \in F^k\) . Deduce that there is an isomorphism \(T \colon \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k) \to \Span(\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_k)\) , well defined by \(T\elem{v}_j = \elem{w}_j\) for every \(j\) . Prove that \(T\) is an isometric isomorphism, that is, \(\inner{T\elem{u}}{T\elem{u}'} = \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{u}'}\) for all \(\elem{u}, \elem{u}'\) in the domain.

title: Exercise (C2: Gram–Schmidt on a dependent list)
content: Let \((\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_m)\) be a list in an inner product space, not assumed independent, and run the recursion of @thm-gram-schmidt . Let \(k\) be the smallest index with \(\elem{v}_k \in \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_{k-1})\) . Prove that the recursion is defined up to \(\elem{e}_{k-1}\) and that \(\elem{w}_k = \elem{0}\) , so the step \(\elem{e}_k = \elem{w}_k/\norm{\elem{w}_k}\) fails. Repair the process: show that if, whenever \(\elem{w}_k = \elem{0}\) , we discard \(\elem{v}_k\) and continue with \(\elem{v}_{k+1}\) , the output is an orthonormal basis of \(\Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_m)\) . Run the repaired process on \(((1,1,0), (2,2,0), (1,0,1))\) in \(\nR^3\) .

title: Theorem 11.2.5 (Properties of the Gram Matrix)
content: Let \((\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k)\) be a list in an inner product space \(V\) over \(F\) , with Gram matrix \(\G\) . Then: \(\G\) is Hermitian , \(\G^{*} = \G\) , and its diagonal entries are the real numbers \(\norm{\elem{v}_i}^2 \ge 0\) ; \(\cvec{x}^{*}\G\cvec{x} = \big\lVert \textstyle\sum_{j} x_j\elem{v}_j \big\rVert^2\) for every \(\cvec{x} \in F^k\) ; \(\G\) is invertible if and only if \((\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k)\) is linearly independent; \(\det \G\) is a real number with \(\det \G \ge 0\) , and \(\det \G > 0\) exactly when the list is linearly independent.

title: Theorem 11.2.2 (Gram–Schmidt Process)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space and let \((\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_m)\) be a linearly independent list in \(V\) . Define recursively \[ \elem{w}_k = \elem{v}_k - \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} \inner{\elem{v}_k}{\elem{e}_i}\,\elem{e}_i , \qquad \elem{e}_k = \frac{\elem{w}_k}{\norm{\elem{w}_k}} \qquad (k = 1, \dots, m). \] Then every \(\elem{w}_k\) is nonzero, so the recursion is defined, and: \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_m)\) is an orthonormal list; \(\Span(\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k) = \Span(\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_k)\) for every \(k = 1, \dots, m\) ; if \((\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_r)\) is already orthonormal for some \(r \le m\) , then \(\elem{e}_i = \elem{v}_i\) for \(i \le r\) . In particular, every finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis.

title: Theorem 11.2.1 (Coordinates, Inner Products, and Norms in an Orthonormal Basis)
content: Let \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n)\) be an orthonormal basis of an inner product space \(V\) , and let \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) . Then: \(\displaystyle \elem{v} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}\,\elem{e}_i\) ; \(\displaystyle \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{e}_i}\,\conj{\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}}\) ; \(\displaystyle \norm{\elem{v}}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i} \rvert^2\) ( Parseval’s identity for a finite orthonormal basis).

title: Corollary 11.3.4 (Projecting with an orthogonal basis)
content: Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space \(V\) , and let \((\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_k)\) be an orthogonal basis of \(U\) , so that \(\inner{\elem{u}_i}{\elem{u}_j} = 0\) for \(i \neq j\) and every \(\elem{u}_i \neq \elem{0}\) . Then \[ P_U\elem{v} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{u}_i}}{\inner{\elem{u}_i}{\elem{u}_i}}\,\elem{u}_i \qquad \text{for every } \elem{v} \in V . \]

title: Definition 11.3.3 (Distance to a subspace)
content: Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space \(V\) and let \(\elem{v} \in V\) . The distance from \(\elem{v}\) to \(U\) is \[ d(\elem{v}, U) = \min_{\elem{u} \in U} \norm{\elem{v} - \elem{u}} = \norm{\elem{v} - P_U\elem{v}} . \]

title: Definition 11.3.1 (Orthogonal complement)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space over \(F\) and let \(S \subseteq V\) be any subset. The orthogonal complement of \(S\) is \[ S^{\perp} = \{\, \elem{v} \in V : \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{s}} = 0 \text{ for every } \elem{s} \in S \,\}, \] read “ \(S\) perp”.

title: Definition 11.3.2 (Orthogonal projection)
content: Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space \(V\) . By @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (a), every \(\elem{v} \in V\) has a unique splitting \(\elem{v} = \elem{u} + \elem{w}\) with \(\elem{u} \in U\) and \(\elem{w} \in U^{\perp}\) . The orthogonal projection onto \(U\) is the operator \(P_U \in \cL(V)\) defined by \[ P_U\elem{v} = \elem{u} . \]

title: Example (The best quadratic approximation to a cubic)
content: On \(V = \nR[x]_{\le 3}\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1} p(t)q(t)\,\dd t\) , let \(U = \nR[x]_{\le 2}\) . Find the polynomial of \(U\) closest to \(x^3\) , and the distance.

title: Example (Distance from a point to a plane)
content: In \(\nR^3\) with the dot product, let \(U = \{ (x, y, z) : x + y + z = 0 \}\) and \(\cvec{v} = (1, 2, 3)\) . Find \(P_U\cvec{v}\) and \(d(\cvec{v}, U)\) , twice: once through \(U^{\perp}\) , and once through an orthonormal basis of \(U\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define the orthogonal complement \(S^{\perp}\) of a subset \(S\) of an inner product space. True or false: \(S^{\perp}\) is a subspace only when \(S\) is a subspace. Justify your answer. State the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem, including every hypothesis. Let \(U\) be a \(3\) -dimensional subspace of \(\nR^7\) . What is \(\dim U^{\perp}\) , and what is \(\dim(U^{\perp})^{\perp}\) ? What quantity does \(P_U\elem{v}\) minimize, and over what set? Name two differences between \(U^{\perp}\) and the annihilator \(U^{0}\) .

title: Exercise (B1: A complement and a projection in \nR^4)
content: In \(\nR^4\) with the dot product, let \(U = \Span\bigl((1, 1, 0, 0),\ (0, 0, 1, 1)\bigr)\) . Find a basis of \(U^{\perp}\) and verify the dimension count. Compute \(P_U\cvec{v}\) and \(d(\cvec{v}, U)\) for \(\cvec{v} = (1, 2, 3, 4)\) . Verify directly that \(\cvec{v} - P_U\cvec{v} \in U^{\perp}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Distance from a point to a plane)
content: In \(\nR^3\) with the dot product, let \(U = \{ (x, y, z) : 2x - y + 2z = 0 \}\) and \(\cvec{v} = (1, 2, 3)\) . Compute \(d(\cvec{v}, U)\) and \(P_U\cvec{v}\) , and check that \(P_U\cvec{v}\) lies in \(U\) . Hence write down the general formula for the distance from \(\cvec{v}\) to the plane \(\{ \cvec{x} : \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{n}} = 0 \}\) , \(\cvec{n} \neq \cvec{0}\) .

title: Exercise (B3: The best quadratic approximation to a quartic)
content: On \(\nR[x]_{\le 4}\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1}p(t)q(t)\,\dd t\) , let \(U = \nR[x]_{\le 2}\) . Find \(P_U(x^4)\) and \(d(x^4, U)\) . Hint: the orthogonal basis of @exm-best-quadratic-approximation still works.

title: Exercise (C1: Perp turns sums into intersections)
content: Let \(U\) and \(W\) be subspaces of an inner product space \(V\) . Prove that \((U + W)^{\perp} = U^{\perp} \cap W^{\perp}\) . (No finiteness is needed.) Assume now that \(V\) is finite-dimensional. Deduce that \((U \cap W)^{\perp} = U^{\perp} + W^{\perp}\) .

title: Exercise (C2: A subspace with no orthogonal complement)
content:
Let \(V = 
R[x]\) , with the coefficient inner product \[ \inner{p}{q} = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_kb_k \quad 	ext{for } p = \sum_k a_kx^k,\ q = \sum_k b_kx^k, \] a finite sum, since a polynomial has only finitely many nonzero coefficients. Let \(U = \{\, p \in V : p(1) = 0 \,\}\) . Verify that \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}\) is an inner product on \(V\) and that \(U\) is a subspace with \(U 
eq V\) . Prove that \(U^{\perp} = \{0\}\) . Conclude that \(U \oplus U^{\perp} 
eq V\) , so @thm-orthogonal-decomposition fails without the hypothesis that \(U\) is finite-dimensional. Explain what goes wrong geometrically by exhibiting, for each \(m \ge 1\) , an element \(p_m \in U\) with \(
orm{p_m - 1} = 1/\sqrt{m}\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Which projections are orthogonal)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space and let \(P \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \(P^2 = P\) . Prove that the following are equivalent: \(P = P_U\) for some subspace \(U\) ; \(\inner{P\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{P\elem{v}}\) for all \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) ; \(\ker P = (\im P)^{\perp}\) . Hint: for (b) \(\Rightarrow\) (c), pair a vector of \(\ker P\) with \(P\elem{v}\) .

title: Proposition 11.3.1 (Perp is always a subspace)
content: For every subset \(S\) of an inner product space \(V\) , the set \(S^{\perp}\) is a subspace of \(V\) . Moreover \(S^{\perp} = \Span(S)^{\perp}\) .

title: Theorem 11.3.5 (Best Approximation Theorem)
content: Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space \(V\) , and let \(\elem{v} \in V\) . Then \[ \norm{\elem{v} - P_U\elem{v}} \le \norm{\elem{v} - \elem{u}} \qquad \text{for every } \elem{u} \in U, \] and equality holds only for \(\elem{u} = P_U\elem{v}\) .

title: Theorem 11.3.2 (Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space over \(F\) and let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of \(V\) . Then: \(V = U \oplus U^{\perp}\) ; \((U^{\perp})^{\perp} = U\) ; if in addition \(V\) is finite-dimensional, then \(\dim U^{\perp} = \dim V - \dim U\) .

title: Theorem 11.3.3 (Projection formula)
content: Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space \(V\) , with orthonormal basis \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k)\) . Then for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) : \(\displaystyle P_U\elem{v} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}\elem{e}_i\) ; \(\inner{P_U\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{P_U\elem{v}}\) for all \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) ; \(\norm{P_U\elem{v}} \le \norm{\elem{v}}\) , with equality if and only if \(\elem{v} \in U\) .

title: Corollary 11.4.4 (Uniqueness of the least-squares solution)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) and \(\cvec{b} \in F^m\) . The following are equivalent: \(\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}\) has exactly one least-squares solution (for one, equivalently for every, \(\cvec{b}\) ); the columns of \(\A\) are linearly independent, that is \(\rank \A = n\) ; \(\A^{*}\A\) is invertible. In that case the least-squares solution is \(\cvec{x} = (\A^{*}\A)^{-1}\A^{*}\cvec{b}\) .

title: Example (The least-squares line through four points)
content: Find the line \(y = c + dt\) that minimizes the sum of the squared vertical errors at the four data points \[ (1, 3), \quad (2, 1), \quad (3, 5), \quad (4, 5). \] Compute the residual and the minimum value of the sum of squares.

title: Example (The least-squares parabola)
content: Find the quadratic \(y = a + bt + ct^2\) minimizing the sum of squared errors at \[ (-2, 7), \quad (-1, 6), \quad (0, 2), \quad (1, 0), \quad (2, 5). \]

title: Example (A minimum-norm solution)
content: Find the solution of smallest norm of \[ \begin{cases} x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 3, \\ x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 7. \end{cases} \]

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define a least-squares solution of \(\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}\) , and write down the normal equations. True or false: if \(\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}\) is consistent, then its solutions are exactly its least-squares solutions. Justify your answer. Explain in one sentence why the normal equations are always consistent. Give a condition on the columns of \(\A\) equivalent to uniqueness of the least-squares solution. Where does the minimum-norm solution of a consistent system live, and why is it unique there? True or false: \((\A^{*}\A)^{-1} = \A^{-1}(\A^{*})^{-1}\) . Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: A least-squares line)
content: Find the least-squares line \(y = c + dt\) for the data \((0, 3), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 6)\) . Compute the residual, verify that it is orthogonal to both columns of \(\A\) , and give the minimum sum of squares.

title: Exercise (B2: A least-squares parabola)
content: Find the least-squares quadratic \(y = a + bt + ct^2\) for the data \((-1, 2), (0, 8), (1, 6), (2, 16)\) , and the minimum sum of squares. Hint: write down \(\A\tp\A\) from the power sums \(\sum t_i^k\) , \(k = 0, \dots, 4\) .

content: Find the minimum-norm solution of \[ \begin{cases} x_1 + x_3 = 2, \\ x_2 + x_3 = 3, \end{cases} \] and verify that it is orthogonal to \(\nul(\A)\) .

Describe all least-squares solutions. Find the one of smallest norm, and the minimum sum of squares.

title: Lemma 11.4.1 (Moving a matrix across the inner product)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) . Then for all \(\cvec{x} \in F^n\) and \(\cvec{y} \in F^m\) , \[ \inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}} = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\A^{*}\cvec{y}}, \qquad \inner{\cvec{y}}{\A\cvec{x}} = \inner{\A^{*}\cvec{y}}{\cvec{x}} . \]

title: Lemma 11.4.3 (The null space of \A^{*}\A)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) . Then \(\nul(\A^{*}\A) = \nul(\A)\) .

title: Theorem 11.4.2 (Least Squares Theorem)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) and \(\cvec{b} \in F^m\) , and write \(U = \col(\A)\) . For \(\cvec{x} \in F^n\) , the following are equivalent: \(\norm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}} \le \norm{\A\cvec{z} - \cvec{b}}\) for every \(\cvec{z} \in F^n\) ; \(\A\cvec{x} = P_U\cvec{b}\) ; \(\A^{*}\A\cvec{x} = \A^{*}\cvec{b}\) . Moreover such an \(\cvec{x}\) always exists. A vector satisfying these conditions is called a least-squares solution of \(\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}\) , and the equations in (c) are the normal equations .

title: Theorem 11.4.5 (Minimum-Norm Solution)
content:

title: Corollary 11.5.2 (The Riesz map)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) . Define \[ \Phi \colon V \to V^{*}, \qquad \Phi(\elem{w}) = \inner{\cdot}{\elem{w}} . \] Then \(\Phi\) is a bijection, and for all \(\elem{w}, \elem{w}' \in V\) and \(c \in F\) , \[ \Phi(\elem{w} + \elem{w}') = \Phi(\elem{w}) + \Phi(\elem{w}'), \qquad \Phi(c\elem{w}) = \conj{c}\,\Phi(\elem{w}). \] In particular \(\Phi\) is an isomorphism of vector spaces when \(F = \nR\) , and is conjugate-linear when \(F = \nC\) .

title: Example (A functional with no Riesz vector)
content: Let \(V = \nR[x]\) with the coefficient inner product \(\inner{p}{q} = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_kb_k\) for \(p = \sum_k a_kx^k\) and \(q = \sum_k b_kx^k\) (a finite sum, and an inner product by @exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projections-c2 (a)). Show that \(\varphi(p) = p(1)\) has no Riesz vector.

title: Example (Two Riesz vectors)
content: On \(V = \nR[x]_{\le 1}\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{0}^{1} p(t)q(t)\,\dd t\) , find the Riesz vector of \(\varphi(p) = p(0)\) . On \(V = M_n(\nC)\) with the Frobenius inner product \(\inner{\A}{\B} = \tr(\B^{*}\A)\) , find the Riesz vector of \(\varphi(\A) = \tr\A\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the Riesz Representation Theorem, including every hypothesis. Write down the formula for the Riesz vector of \(\varphi\) in terms of an orthonormal basis, and say where the conjugate comes from. True or false: over \(\nC\) , the Riesz map \(\Phi \colon V \to V^{*}\) is a linear isomorphism. Justify your answer. In what sense does an inner product answer the question Chapter 5 left open about \(V \cong V^{*}\) ? Under \(\Phi\) , which subspace of \(V^{*}\) corresponds to \(U^{\perp}\) ? Give an example showing that the theorem fails in infinite dimension.

title: Exercise (B1: Riesz vectors for evaluation)
content: On \(V = \nR[x]_{\le 2}\) use the node inner product \(\inner{p}{q} = p(-1)q(-1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)\) . Find the Riesz vectors of \(\varphi(p) = p(0)\) and of \(\psi(p) = p(1)\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Riesz vectors on matrices)
content: On \(M_n(\nC)\) with the Frobenius inner product \(\inner{\A}{\B} = \tr(\B^{*}\A)\) , find the Riesz vector of: \(\varphi(\A) = a_{12}\) (assume \(n \ge 2\) ); \(\varphi_{\C}(\A) = \tr(\C\A)\) , for a fixed \(\C \in M_n(\nC)\) .

title: Exercise (B3: The correspondence in \nR^4)
content: In \(\nR^4\) with the dot product, let \(U = \Span\bigl((1, 0, 1, 0), (0, 1, 0, 1)\bigr)\) . Find a basis of \(U^{\perp}\) and a basis of \(U^{0}\) , and verify that \(\Phi\) carries the first to the second.

title: Exercise (C1: Riesz without an orthonormal basis)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space and let \(\varphi \in V^{*}\) be nonzero. Write \(K = \ker\varphi\) . Prove that \(\dim K^{\perp} = 1\) . Let \(\elem{u}\) span \(K^{\perp}\) with \(\norm{\elem{u}} = 1\) . Prove that \(\elem{w} = \conj{\varphi(\elem{u})}\,\elem{u}\) satisfies \(\varphi(\elem{v}) = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}}\) for all \(\elem{v} \in V\) . Deduce @thm-riesz-representation , including the case \(\varphi = 0\) . Hint for (b): split \(\elem{v}\) using \(V = K \oplus K^{\perp}\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Evaluation at 0 is not represented)
content: Let \(V = \nR[x]\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{0}^{1}p(t)q(t)\,\dd t\) , and let \(\varphi(p) = p(0)\) . Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(w = \sum_{j=0}^{d} c_jx^j\) satisfied \(\inner{p}{w} = p(0)\) for every \(p \in V\) . Show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{d} \frac{c_j}{k + j + 1} = 0\) for every integer \(k \ge 1\) , and that the same sum equals \(1\) for \(k = 0\) . Let \(N(s) = \sum_{j=0}^{d} c_j \prod_{i \neq j}(s + i + 1)\) , the product running over \(i \in \{0, \dots, d\}\setminus\{j\}\) . Show that \(N(k) = 0\) for every integer \(k \ge 1\) , and deduce that \(N\) is the zero polynomial. Deduce that every \(c_j = 0\) , and hence a contradiction.

title: Theorem 11.5.3 (Perp corresponds to the annihilator)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) , let \(U\) be a subspace, and let \(\Phi\) be the Riesz map. Then \[ \Phi(U^{\perp}) = U^{0} . \] Equivalently, a functional \(\varphi \in V^{*}\) annihilates \(U\) if and only if its Riesz vector lies in \(U^{\perp}\) .

title: Theorem 11.5.1 (Riesz Representation Theorem)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) and let \(\varphi \in V^{*}\) . Then there is a unique \(\elem{w} \in V\) such that \[ \varphi(\elem{v}) = \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} \qquad \text{for every } \elem{v} \in V . \] If \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_n)\) is any orthonormal basis of \(V\) , then \(\elem{w} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \conj{\varphi(\elem{e}_i)}\,\elem{e}_i\) .

title: Corollary 11.6.6 (Rank of the Adjoint)
content: Let \(V, W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) and \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . Then \(\rank T^{*} = \rank T\) ; \(\ker(T^{*}T) = \ker T\) , and consequently \(\rank(T^{*}T) = \rank T\) .

title: Definition 11.6.1 (Adjoint)
content: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) and let \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . The adjoint of \(T\) is the unique linear map \(T^{*} \in \cL(W, V)\) satisfying \[ \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}} = \inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}\elem{w}} \qquad \text{for all } \elem{v} \in V \text{ and all } \elem{w} \in W . \]

title: Definition 11.6.3 (Normal Operator)
content: An operator \(T \in \cL(V)\) on a finite-dimensional inner product space is normal if it commutes with its adjoint: \[ T^{*}T = TT^{*} . \]

title: Definition 11.6.2 (Self-adjoint Operator)
content: An operator \(T \in \cL(V)\) on a finite-dimensional inner product space is self-adjoint if \(T^{*} = T\) , that is, if \[ \inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{T\elem{v}} \qquad \text{for all } \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V . \] The matrix counterpart is the Hermitian matrix of @def-conjugate-transpose , \(\A^{*} = \A\) ; over \(\nR\) this says \(\A\tp = \A\) , and the matrix is symmetric .

title: Example (Differentiation on a Polynomial Space)
content: On \(V = \nR[x]_{\le 2}\) define \(\inner{p}{q} \coloneqq a_0b_0 + a_1b_1 + a_2b_2\) for \(p = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2\) and \(q = b_0 + b_1x + b_2x^2\) . (This is the standard inner product of \(\nR^3\) transported by the coordinate map, so it is an inner product, and \(\sE = (1, x, x^2)\) is an orthonormal basis.) Find the adjoint of \(D \colon V \to V\) , \(D(p) = p'\) .

title: Example (Four Adjoints)
content: Compute the adjoint in each case. In (a) and (b) the spaces carry the standard inner product; in (c) and (d), \(V\) and \(W\) are arbitrary finite-dimensional inner product spaces. \(T_{\A} \colon \nC^3 \to \nC^2\) for \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + i & 0 & 2 \\ i & 1 & -i \end{pmatrix}\) . The forward shift \(S \colon F^3 \to F^3\) , \(S(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (0, x_1, x_2)\) . \(\id_V\) and the zero map \(V \to W\) . The orthogonal projection \(P_U \colon V \to V\) onto a subspace \(U \subseteq V\) .

title: Example (The Transpose Rule Breaks)
content: Work in \(\nR^2\) with the standard inner product and let \(T(x_1, x_2) = (x_2, 0)\) . Let \(\sB = (\cvec{b}_1, \cvec{b}_2)\) with \(\cvec{b}_1 = (1, 0)\) and \(\cvec{b}_2 = (1, 1)\) . Compute \(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\) and \(\mtx{T^{*}}{\sB}{\sB}\) , and compare the second with the transpose of the first.

title: Example (All Four Subspaces of a 3 × 3 Matrix)
content: For \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(\nR\) , find bases of the four subspaces and verify the two orthogonality statements.

title: Example (A Map With No Adjoint)
content: On \(V = \nR[x]\) , all polynomials, define \(\inner{p}{q} \coloneqq \sum_{k \ge 0} a_kb_k\) , a finite sum since the coefficients vanish eventually. Show that \(T \colon V \to V\) , \(T(p) \coloneqq p(1) \cdot 1\) , has no adjoint.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the defining property of the adjoint \(T^{*}\) of \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) , including the domain and codomain of \(T^{*}\) and all quantifiers. Which hypothesis of @thm-adjoint-exists is used to produce \(T^{*}\) , and which theorem supplies it? True or false: \((cT)^{*} = cT^{*}\) for every scalar \(c\) . Justify your answer. title: Exercise (C3: The adjoint in an arbitrary basis)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space, let \(\sB = (\elem{b}_1, \dots, \elem{b}_n)\) be any ordered basis of \(V\) , let \(\G\) be its Gram matrix, \(g_{ij} = \inner{\elem{b}_j}{\elem{b}_i}\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . Prove that \(\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB}^{*}\,\G\,\coord{\elem{u}}{\sB}\) for all \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) . Deduce that \(\mtx{T^{*}}{\sB}{\sB} = \G^{-1}\left(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\right)^{*}\G\) . Check that (b) returns @thm-matrix-of-adjoint when \(\sB\) is orthonormal, and verify it on @exm-adjoint-nonorthonormal-basis . title: Proposition 11.6.7 (First Properties of Self-adjoint Operators)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint on a finite-dimensional inner product space \(V\) over \(F\) . \(\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} \in \nR\) for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) , even when \(F = \nC\) . If \(\sB\) is an orthonormal basis of \(V\) , the diagonal entries of \(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\) are real. \(T\) is normal.

title: Theorem 11.6.1 (Existence and Uniqueness of the Adjoint)
content: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . Then there is exactly one map \(T^{*} \colon W \to V\) such that \[ \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{w}}_W = \inner{\elem{v}}{T^{*}\elem{w}}_V \qquad \text{for all } \elem{v} \in V,\ \elem{w} \in W, \] and this \(T^{*}\) is linear.

title: Theorem 11.6.2 (Properties of the Adjoint)
content: Let \(U, V, W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) . For \(S, T \in \cL(V, W)\) , \((S + T)^{*} = S^{*} + T^{*}\) . For \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) and \(c \in F\) , \((cT)^{*} = \conj{c}\,T^{*}\) . For \(T \in \cL(U, V)\) and \(S \in \cL(V, W)\) , \((ST)^{*} = T^{*}S^{*}\) . \(T^{**} = T\) for every \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) , and \((\id_V)^{*} = \id_V\) . If \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) is invertible, then \(T^{*}\) is invertible and \((T^{*})^{-1} = (T^{-1})^{*}\) .

title: Theorem 11.6.4 (The Adjoint Is the Dual Map Read Through Riesz)
content: Let \(V, W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) and \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . Then \[ \Phi_V \circ T^{*} = T' \circ \Phi_W . \]

title: Theorem 11.6.5 (The Four Fundamental Subspaces)
content: Let \(V, W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) and let \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . Then \(\ker T^{*} = (\im T)^{\perp}\) ; \(\im T^{*} = (\ker T)^{\perp}\) ; \(V = \ker T \oplus \im T^{*}\) ; \(W = \im T \oplus \ker T^{*}\) .

title: Theorem 11.6.3 (The Matrix of the Adjoint Is the Conjugate Transpose)
content: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) , let \(\sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n)\) be an orthonormal basis of \(V\) and \(\sC = (\elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_m)\) an orthonormal basis of \(W\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . Then \[ \mtx{T^{*}}{\sC}{\sB} = \left(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sC}\right)^{*} . \]

title: Definition 11.7.1 (Isometry)
content: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be inner product spaces over \(F\) . A linear map \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) is an isometry if \[ \norm{T\elem{v}} = \norm{\elem{v}} \qquad \text{for every } \elem{v} \in V . \]

title: Definition 11.7.2 (Unitary and Orthogonal)
content:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) . An operator \(T \in \cL(V)\) is unitary if \[ T^{*}T = TT^{*} = \id_V , \] equivalently if \(T\) is an invertible isometry. When \(F = 
R\) , such a \(T\) is also called orthogonal . A matrix \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) with \(\A^{*}\A = \I_n\) is a unitary matrix ; a matrix \(\A \in M_n(
R)\) with \(\A	p\A = \I_n\) is an orthogonal matrix .

title: Definition 11.7.3 (The Unitary and Orthogonal Groups)
content: For \(n \ge 1\) set \[ \Unit(n) \coloneqq \{ \A \in M_n(\nC) : \A^{*}\A = \I_n \}, \qquad \Orth(n) \coloneqq \{ \A \in M_n(\nR) : \A\tp\A = \I_n \}, \] and \(\SO(n) \coloneqq \{ \A \in \Orth(n) : \det \A = 1 \}\) , the special orthogonal group .

title: Exercise (B3: Permutations are orthogonal)
content: Let \(\sigma \in S_n\) and let \(\P_{\sigma} \in M_n(\nR)\) be its permutation matrix ( @def-permutation-matrix ), whose \(j\) -th column is \(\cvec{e}_{\sigma(j)}\) . Prove that \(\P_{\sigma} \in \Orth(n)\) . Deduce that \(\det \P_{\sigma} = \pm1\) , and identify the sign. Show that \(\P_{\sigma}^{-1} = \P_{\sigma}\tp = \P_{\sigma^{-1}}\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Determinant as a homomorphism)
content: Prove that \(\det \colon \Orth(n) \to \{1, -1\}\) is a surjective group homomorphism with kernel \(\SO(n)\) , and deduce that exactly half of \(\Orth(n)\) has determinant \(-1\) , in the sense that \(\Orth(n)\) is the disjoint union of \(\SO(n)\) and one coset \(\A_0\SO(n)\) . Prove that \(\det \colon \Unit(n) \to \{ z \in \nC : \lvert z\rvert = 1 \}\) is a surjective group homomorphism. Describe \(\Orth(1)\) and \(\Unit(1)\) completely.

title: Exercise (C3: Two reflections make a rotation)
content: Let \(\alpha, \beta \in \nR\) and let \(\M_{\alpha}, \M_{\beta} \in \Orth(2)\) be the reflections of @thm-orthogonal-2x2 , in the lines \(L_{\alpha}\) and \(L_{\beta}\) at angles \(\alpha/2\) and \(\beta/2\) . Prove that \(\M_{\alpha}\M_{\beta} = \R_{\alpha - \beta}\) . Deduce that the composite of the reflections in two lines through the origin is the rotation by twice the angle from the second line to the first, and that every rotation of the plane is a product of two reflections. Deduce that \(\Orth(2)\) is not abelian, by computing \(\M_{\beta}\M_{\alpha}\) .

title: Proposition 11.7.1 (Eigenvalues of an Isometry Have Modulus 1)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be an isometry of an inner product space over \(F\) , and let \(\lambda \in F\) be an eigenvalue of \(T\) . Then \(\lvert\lambda\rvert = 1\) . In particular, if \(F = \nR\) then \(\lambda = 1\) or \(\lambda = -1\) .

title: Proposition 11.7.4 (The Groups and Their Determinants)
content: \(\Unit(n)\) and \(\Orth(n)\) are groups under matrix multiplication, and \(\Orth(n) = \Unit(n) \cap M_n(\nR)\) . If \(\A \in \Unit(n)\) then \(\lvert\det \A\rvert = 1\) . If \(\A \in \Orth(n)\) then \(\det \A = 1\) or \(\det \A = -1\) . \(\SO(n)\) is a subgroup of \(\Orth(n)\) .

title: Theorem 11.7.3 (Characterizations of Isometries)
content: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . The following are equivalent. \(T\) is an isometry: \(\norm{T\elem{v}} = \norm{\elem{v}}\) for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) . \(T\) preserves inner products: \(\inner{T\elem{u}}{T\elem{v}} = \inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}}\) for all \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) . \(T^{*}T = \id_V\) . \(T\) sends every orthonormal list in \(V\) to an orthonormal list in \(W\) . \(T\) sends some orthonormal basis of \(V\) to an orthonormal list in \(W\) . For one (equivalently every) pair of orthonormal bases \(\sB\) of \(V\) and \(\sC\) of \(W\) , the matrix \(\A = \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sC} \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) , where \(n = \dim V\) and \(m = \dim W\) , satisfies \(\A^{*}\A = \I_n\) ; that is, the \(n\) columns of \(\A\) are orthonormal vectors of \(F^m\) . If in addition \(\dim W = \dim V\) , then (a)–(f) are further equivalent to each of \(T\) is invertible with \(T^{-1} = T^{*}\) ; \(TT^{*} = \id_W\) .

title: Theorem 11.7.6 (Classification of the Plane Isometries)
content: Let \(\A \in \Orth(2)\) . If \(\det \A = 1\) , then \(\A = \R_{\theta}\) for a unique \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi)\) . If \(\det \A = -1\) , then \(\A = \M_{\theta}\) for a unique \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi)\) . In this case \(\A^2 = \I\) , the eigenvalues of \(\A\) are \(1\) and \(-1\) , and \(\A\) is the reflection in the line \(L = \Span\bigl((\cos\tfrac\theta2, \sin\tfrac\theta2)\bigr)\) : it fixes \(L\) pointwise and negates \(L^{\perp}\) . Consequently \(\Orth(2) = \{\R_{\theta}\} \cup \{\M_{\theta}\}\) , and \(\SO(2) = \{\R_{\theta} : \theta \in [0, 2\pi)\}\) .
