title: Theorem 11.7.7 (Every Element of SO(3) Is a Rotation)
content: Let \(\A \in \SO(3)\) . Then there is a unit vector \(\cvec{u} \in \nR^3\) with \(\A\cvec{u} = \cvec{u}\) , and an orthonormal basis \(\sB = (\cvec{u}, \cvec{w}_1, \cvec{w}_2)\) of \(\nR^3\) in which \[ \mtx{T_{\A}}{\sB}{\sB} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ 0 & \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix} \] for some \(\theta\) . That is, \(\A\) fixes the axis \(\Span(\cvec{u})\) and rotates the plane \(\Span(\cvec{u})^{\perp}\) by \(\theta\) . Moreover \(\tr \A = 1 + 2\cos\theta\) .

title: Definition 11.8.2 (Givens Rotation)
content: Let \(1 \le i < j \le m\) and let \(c, s \in \nR\) with \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\) . The Givens rotation \(\G(i, j; c, s) \in M_m(\nR)\) is the identity matrix with the four entries in rows and columns \(i, j\) replaced by \[ \begin{pmatrix} g_{ii} & g_{ij} \\ g_{ji} & g_{jj} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} c & s \\ -s & c \end{pmatrix} . \]

title: Definition 11.8.1 (Householder Reflection)
content: Let \(\cvec{w} \in F^m\) be nonzero . The Householder reflection determined by \(\cvec{w}\) is \[ \H_{\cvec{w}} = \I_m - \frac{2\,\cvec{w}\cvec{w}^{*}}{\norm{\cvec{w}}^2} \in M_m(F) . \]

title: Example (Hessenberg form of a 3 \times 3 matrix)
content: Reduce \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \] to upper Hessenberg form by a unitary similarity.

title: Example (A 3 \times 3 QR by reflections)
content: Triangularize \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \] by Householder reflections, and read off \(\Q\) and \(\R\) .

title: Example (A 3 \times 2 QR, and a least-squares problem)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} . \] Find the QR factorization of \(\A\) . Find the \(\cvec{x} \in \nR^2\) minimizing \(\norm{\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}}\) , using (a).

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State @thm-qr-factorization in full, including the two normalizations that make \(\Q\) and \(\R\) unique. Which hypothesis on \(\A\) does @thm-qr-factorization need, and which does @thm-qr-householder need? Explain the difference in one sentence. Write down the Householder reflection determined by \(\cvec{w}\) , and list three of its properties. In @thm-householder-maps-vector , which of the two possible targets \(\pm\norm{\cvec{x}}\cvec{e}_1\) is chosen, and why? True or false: applying reflections on both sides, as in @thm-hessenberg-form , can be pushed to make every complex matrix unitarily similar to an upper triangular one. Justify your answer. Why must the reflection used at step \(k\) of @thm-hessenberg-form fix \(\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_k\) ?

title: Exercise (B1: QR by Gram–Schmidt)
content: Find the QR factorization of \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \] in the sense of @thm-qr-factorization , and verify that \(\R = \Q\tp\A\) for the top-left \(2 \times 2\) entries.

title: Exercise (B2: The same matrix by reflections)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}\) , the matrix of @exm-qr-3x2 . Find \(\cvec{w}_1\) and the reflection \(\H_1\) of @thm-householder-maps-vector for the first column of \(\A\) , and compute \(\H_1\A\) . Find the second reflection and hence a factorization \(\A = \Q\R\) with \(\Q \in M_3(\nR)\) orthogonal and \(\R \in M_{3\times2}(\nR)\) upper triangular. Compare the \(\R\) of (b) with the \(\R\) of @exm-qr-3x2 , and say exactly how the two factorizations differ.

title: Exercise (B3: A least-squares fit through QR)
content: Fit a line \(y = c_0 + c_1t\) to the data \((t, y) = (0,1), (1,3), (2,2)\) in the least-squares sense, by finding the QR factorization of the design matrix and solving \(\R\cvec{x} = \Q\tp\cvec{b}\) . Compute the residual and check the answer against the normal equations.

title: Exercise (B4: Determine which are QR factorizations)
content: Determine which of the following are QR factorizations of the matrix on the left in the sense of @thm-qr-factorization . Justify your answer; for those that are not, name the clause that fails and repair it if possible. \(\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 7\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac15\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 4 & 3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 5 & \tfrac{31}{5} \\ 0 & \tfrac{17}{5}\end{pmatrix}\) . \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \tfrac12 \\ 0 & \tfrac12\end{pmatrix}\) . \(\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (C1: All the QR factorizations of a matrix)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m\times n}(F)\) have independent columns, with QR factorization \(\A = \Q\R\) as in @thm-qr-factorization . Prove that an upper triangular \(\S \in M_n(F)\) with \(\S^{*}\S = \I_n\) is diagonal, with diagonal entries of modulus \(1\) . Deduce that the pairs \((\Q_1, \R_1)\) with \(\Q_1^{*}\Q_1 = \I_n\) , \(\R_1\) upper triangular and invertible, and \(\A = \Q_1\R_1\) , are exactly the pairs \((\Q\D^{-1}, \D\R)\) for \(\D = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n)\) with \(\lvert d_k\rvert = 1\) . Hence give a second proof of the uniqueness statement of @thm-qr-factorization .

title: Exercise (C2: Reflections do not mind dependence)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, \] whose third column is the sum of the first two. Run the Gram–Schmidt process of @thm-gram-schmidt on the columns of \(\A\) and say precisely which step fails. Carry out the Householder reduction of @thm-qr-householder on \(\A\) and exhibit \(\R\) . Explain, using @thm-qr-factorization , why no factorization \(\A = \Q\R\) with \(\Q^{*}\Q = \I_3\) and \(\R\) upper triangular with positive diagonal can exist.

title: Exercise (C3: Triangularizing with rotations)
content: Let \((a, b) \in \nR^2\) be nonzero and \(r = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) . Verify that the Givens rotation \(\G\) of @def-givens-rotation with \(c = a/r\) and \(s = b/r\) satisfies \(\G(a,b) = (r, 0)\) , and that \(\G \in \SO(2)\) . Use (a) to write \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) as \(\Q\R\) with \(\Q \in \SO(2)\) and \(\R\) upper triangular with positive diagonal. How many Givens rotations does it take to triangularize a general \(3\times3\) real matrix, and which entries does each one kill? Compare with the number of Householder reflections.

title: Proposition 11.8.2 (Properties of a Householder Reflection)
content: Let \(\cvec{w} \in F^m\) be nonzero and \(\H = \H_{\cvec{w}}\) . Then \(\H^{*} = \H\) ( \(\H\) is Hermitian); \(\H^2 = \I_m\) , so \(\H^{-1} = \H\) ; \(\H\) is unitary; \(\H\cvec{w} = -\cvec{w}\) , and \(\H\cvec{v} = \cvec{v}\) for every \(\cvec{v} \perp \cvec{w}\) ; \(\det \H = -1\) .

title: Theorem 11.8.5 (Reduction to Hessenberg Form)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) , \(n \ge 1\) . Then there is a unitary \(\Q \in M_n(F)\) such that \(\Z = \Q^{*}\A\Q\) is upper Hessenberg , that is, \[ z_{ij} = 0 \qquad \text{whenever } i > j + 1 . \] The matrix \(\Q\) can be taken to be a product of \(n - 2\) factors, each a Householder reflection or an identity matrix (and \(\Q = \I_n\) when \(n \le 2\) ). For \(n = 4\) the pattern is \[ \Z = \begin{pmatrix} \ast & \ast & \ast & \ast \\ \ast & \ast & \ast & \ast \\ 0 & \ast & \ast & \ast \\ 0 & 0 & \ast & \ast \end{pmatrix}. \]

title: Theorem 11.8.1 (QR Factorization)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) have linearly independent columns. Then there are matrices \(\Q \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) and \(\R \in M_n(F)\) with the columns of \(\Q\) orthonormal, equivalently \(\Q^{*}\Q = \I_n\) ; \(\R\) upper triangular with positive real diagonal entries; \(\A = \Q\R\) . Moreover \(\Q\) and \(\R\) are unique : any pair satisfying (a), (b), (c) is this one. The pair \((\Q, \R)\) is the QR factorization of \(\A\) .

title: Theorem 11.8.4 (QR by Householder Reflections)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) . Then there are a unitary \(\Q \in M_m(F)\) and an \(\R \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) with \(r_{ij} = 0\) whenever \(i > j\) , such that \[ \A = \Q\R . \] Moreover \(\Q\) can be taken to be a product of at most \(\min(n, m-1)\) Householder reflections. No hypothesis on the columns of \(\A\) is needed.

title: Definition 11.9.1 (Fourier Coefficients With Respect to an Orthonormal List)
content: Let \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k)\) be an orthonormal list in an inner product space \(V\) and let \(\elem{v} \in V\) . The scalars \[ \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_1},\ \dots,\ \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_k} \in F \] are the Fourier coefficients of \(\elem{v}\) with respect to the list.

title: Example (The Fourier Coefficients of f(x) = x)
content: In \(C[-\pi, \pi]\) with \(\inner{f}{g} = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg\) , let \(f(x) = x\) . Find all \(a_k\) and \(b_k\) , write down \(S_nf\) , and say what @thm-fourier-best-approximation (c) gives.

title: Example (The Trigonometric System Is Orthonormal)
content: Fix \(n \ge 1\) . Show that the list of \(2n + 1\) functions \[ \frac{1}{\sqrt2},\ \cos x,\ \sin x,\ \cos 2x,\ \sin 2x,\ \dots,\ \cos nx,\ \sin nx \] is orthonormal in \(V = C[-\pi, \pi]\) with \(\inner{f}{g} = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State Bessel’s inequality, saying exactly what is assumed about the space and what is assumed about the list. State Parseval’s identity, including the condition under which equality holds for a given vector. True or false: Bessel’s inequality requires the ambient space to be finite-dimensional. Justify your answer. Write down the inner product used on \(C[-\pi, \pi]\) in this section, including its normalizing constant, and say what the constant is for. State what @thm-fourier-best-approximation gives about \(S_nf\) , and name one thing it does not give. True or false: if \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k)\) is an orthonormal list and \(\sum_i\lvert\inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i}\rvert^2 = \norm{\elem{v}}^2\) for one particular \(\elem{v} \ne \elem{0}\) , then the list is an orthonormal basis of \(V\) . Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: Fourier coefficients)
content: Work in \(C[-\pi, \pi]\) with \(\inner{f}{g} = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg\) . Find all Fourier coefficients \(a_k\) and \(b_k\) of each of the following, and in each case write down \(S_2f\) . \(f(x) = \lvert x \rvert\) . \(f(x) = x^2\) . \(f(x) = 3 - 2\sin x + \sin 3x\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Verifying Bessel for a truncation)
content: In \(\nR^4\) with the dot product let \(\cvec{e}_1 = \tfrac12(1, 1, 1, 1)\) , \(\cvec{e}_2 = \tfrac12(1, -1, 1, -1)\) and \(\cvec{v} = (2, 0, 0, 2)\) . Verify @thm-bessel-inequality for \(\cvec{v}\) and this list, compute the deficit, and check against \((\ast)\) by computing \(\norm{\cvec{v} - P_U\cvec{v}}\) directly, where \(U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1, \cvec{e}_2)\) . For \(f(x) = \lvert x \rvert\) and \(n = 1\) , write out both sides of @thm-fourier-best-approximation (c) using @exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-b1 (a), and show that the resulting inequality is equivalent to \(96 \le \pi^4\) .

title: Exercise (B3: The best approximation by \Span(1, \cos x))
content: In \(C[-\pi, \pi]\) with \(\inner{f}{g} = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg\) , let \(U = \Span(1, \cos x)\) and \(f(x) = x^2\) . Find \(P_Uf\) and \(d(f, U)^2\) . Hint: the list \((1, \cos x)\) is orthogonal but not orthonormal.

title: Exercise (C1: Parseval for the full trigonometric system)
content: This exercise uses an input from analysis that this book does not prove : the trigonometric system is complete in \(C[-\pi, \pi]\) , meaning that for every \(f \in C[-\pi, \pi]\) , \[ \frac{a_0^2}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\big(a_k^2 + b_k^2\big) = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(t)^2\,\dd t . \] Apply this to \(f(x) = x\) and deduce that \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 1/k^2 = \pi^2/6\) . Hence deduce that \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 1/(2k - 1)^2 = \pi^2/8\) . Say precisely which step used the analysis input, and explain why no result of this section can supply it.

title: Exercise (C2: Chebyshev orthogonality by substitution)
content: Let \(\inner{p}{q}_w = \int_{-1}^{1} p(t)q(t)(1 - t^2)^{-1/2}\,\dd t\) on \(\nR[x]\) , the Chebyshev inner product of the text. Prove that for every \(n \ge 0\) there is a polynomial \(T_n\) of degree \(n\) with \(T_n(\cos\theta) = \cos n\theta\) for all \(\theta\) , and find \(T_0, T_1, T_2, T_3\) . Prove that \(\inner{p}{q}_w = \int_0^{\pi} p(\cos\theta)\,q(\cos\theta)\,\dd\theta\) for all polynomials \(p, q\) . Deduce that \(\inner{T_m}{T_n}_w = 0\) for \(m \ne n\) , and compute \(\inner{T_n}{T_n}_w\) . Hint for (a): the identity \(\cos((n+1)\theta) + \cos((n-1)\theta) = 2\cos\theta\cos n\theta\) .

title: Theorem 11.9.1 (Bessel’s Inequality)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space over \(F\) , not assumed finite-dimensional , and let \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k)\) be an orthonormal list in \(V\) . Then for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) , \[ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lvert \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i} \rvert^2 \;\le\; \norm{\elem{v}}^2 . \]

title: Theorem 11.9.3 (Fourier Partial Sums Are Best Approximations)
content: Let \(f \in C[-\pi, \pi]\) , let \(n \ge 1\) , and let \(a_k, b_k\) be the Fourier coefficients of \(f\) . Put \[ S_nf = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{n}\big(a_k\cos kx + b_k\sin kx\big) . \] Then, with \(\inner{f}{g} = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg\) : \(S_nf = P_{W_n}f\) ; \(\norm{f - S_nf} \le \norm{f - g}\) for every \(g \in W_n\) , with equality only for \(g = S_nf\) ; \(\displaystyle \frac{a_0^2}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{n}\big(a_k^2 + b_k^2\big) \le \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(t)^2\,\dd t\) .

title: Theorem 11.9.2 (Parseval’s Identity)
content: Let \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k)\) be an orthonormal list in an inner product space \(V\) and let \(\elem{v} \in V\) . Then \[ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lvert \inner{\elem{v}}{\elem{e}_i} \rvert^2 = \norm{\elem{v}}^2 \quad\text{if and only if}\quad \elem{v} \in \Span(\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k) . \] In particular, if \((\elem{e}_1, \dots, \elem{e}_k)\) is an orthonormal basis of \(V\) , the identity holds for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) .

title: Definition 11.10.1 (Orthogonal Polynomial Sequence)
content:
Let \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}\) be an inner product on \(
R[x]\) , or on \(
R[x]_{\le n}\) . An orthogonal polynomial sequence for it is a sequence \(p_0, p_1, p_2, \dots\) of polynomials (a finite list \(p_0, \dots, p_n\) in the second case) such that \(\deg p_k = k\) for every index \(k\) ; \(\inner{p_j}{p_k} = 0\) whenever \(j 
e k\) . The sequence is monic if every \(p_k\) has leading coefficient \(1\) .

title: Example (The monic Legendre polynomials, continued)
content: For \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1} pq\) , @exm-gram-schmidt-legendre gave \(p_0 = 1\) , \(p_1 = x\) , \(p_2 = x^2 - \tfrac13\) , with \(\inner{p_0}{p_0} = 2\) , \(\inner{p_1}{p_1} = \tfrac23\) , and \(\inner{p_2}{p_2} = \tfrac{8}{45}\) . Use @thm-three-term-recurrence to obtain \(p_3\) , and check the recurrence reproduces \(p_2\) .

title: Example (Two-point Gauss–Legendre)
content: Take \(w = 1\) on \((-1, 1)\) and \(k = 2\) . Find the nodes and weights, and test the resulting rule on \(f = 1 + 2x + 3x^2 + 4x^3\) and on \(f = x^4\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define what it means for \(p_0, p_1, p_2, \dots\) to be a monic orthogonal polynomial sequence for an inner product on \(\nR[x]\) . State the three-term recurrence, including the formulas for \(a_k\) and \(b_k\) and the starting values. True or false: \(b_k > 0\) for every \(k \ge 1\) . Justify your answer. For \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1} pq\) , how many roots does \(p_7\) have, of what kind, and where? True or false: for every inner product on \(\nR[x]\) one has \(\inner{xp}{q} = \inner{p}{xq}\) . Justify your answer. How many nodes does a Gaussian rule need in order to integrate every polynomial of degree at most \(11\) exactly?

title: Exercise (B1: A weighted interval)
content: On \(\nR[x]\) put \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_0^1 p(t)q(t)\,t\,\dd t\) . Compute the monic \(p_0\) , \(p_1\) , and \(p_2\) , and verify directly that \(p_2 \perp \nR[x]_{\le 1}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Two rows of the table)
content: Verify the degree- \(1\) and degree- \(2\) entries of the table for two of the classical families. Chebyshev: \(w(t) = (1 - t^2)^{-1/2}\) on \((-1, 1)\) . You may use, without proof, that \(\int_{-1}^{1} (1 - t^2)^{-1/2}\dd t = \pi\) and \(\int_{-1}^{1} t^2(1 - t^2)^{-1/2}\dd t = \pi/2\) . Laguerre: \(w(t) = e^{-t}\) on \((0, \infty)\) . You may use, without proof, that \(\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-t}\,\dd t = k!\) .

title: Exercise (B3: One more Legendre polynomial)
content: Continue @exm-legendre-recurrence : compute \(\inner{p_3}{p_3}\) for \(p_3 = x^3 - \tfrac35 x\) , then use @thm-three-term-recurrence to find \(p_4\) . Verify that \(\inner{p_4}{1} = \inner{p_4}{x^2} = 0\) .

title: Exercise (B4: A two-point rule on the unit interval)
content: Work on \((0, 1)\) with \(w = 1\) . Exercise B2 of Section 2 ( @exr-orthonormal-bases-b2 ) found the monic orthogonal polynomials \(1\) , \(x - \tfrac12\) , \(x^2 - x + \tfrac16\) . Write down the two-point Gaussian rule for \(\int_0^1 f\) . Check it on \(f = x^3\) , and show that it fails on \(f = x^4\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Interlacing roots)
content: Let \(w\) be a weight on \((a, b)\) and let \((p_k)\) be its monic orthogonal polynomial sequence. The roots of \(p_k\) are said to interlace those of \(p_{k+1}\) when exactly one root of \(p_k\) lies strictly between each pair of consecutive roots of \(p_{k+1}\) . This is true for every \(k\) ; prove the first two cases by hand. Let \(r\) be the root of \(p_1\) and \(s_1 < s_2\) the roots of \(p_2\) . Prove that \(s_1 < r < s_2\) . Let \(u_1 < u_2 < u_3\) be the roots of \(p_3\) . Prove that \(u_1 < s_1 < u_2 < s_2 < u_3\) . Hint: evaluate the three-term recurrence at a root.

title: Exercise (C2: The ceiling is 2k − 1)
content:
Let \(w\) be a weight on \((a, b)\) and let \(k \ge 1\) . Let \(t_1, \dots, t_k\) be any \(k\) distinct real numbers and \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k\) any real numbers. Prove that there is an \(f \in 
R[x]_{\le 2k}\) with \(\int_a^b fw 
e \sum_i \alpha_i f(t_i)\) . Hence deduce that the Gaussian rule of @thm-gaussian-quadrature is exact on \(
R[x]_{\le 2k-1}\) and on no larger space \(
R[x]_{\le d}\) .

title: Lemma 11.10.4 (Even multiplicities mean no sign change)
content: Let \(I \subseteq \nR\) be an open interval and let \(f \in \nR[x]\) be nonzero. If \(\operatorname{mult}_r(f)\) is even for every \(r \in I\) , then \(f \ge 0\) throughout \(I\) , or \(f \le 0\) throughout \(I\) .

title: Proposition 11.10.2 (Existence and uniqueness of the monic sequence)
content:
Let \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}\) be an inner product on \(
R[x]\) . For each \(k \in 
N\) there is exactly one monic \(p_k\) of degree \(k\) with \(\inner{p_k}{q} = 0\) for every \(q \in 
R[x]_{\le k-1}\) . These \(p_k\) form the unique monic orthogonal polynomial sequence, and \((p_0, \dots, p_k)\) is an orthogonal basis of \(
R[x]_{\le k}\) for every \(k\) . The same holds on \(
R[x]_{\le n}\) for \(k \le n\) .

title: Proposition 11.10.1 (Multiplication by x is symmetric)
content: Let \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}\) be an inner product on \(\nR[x]\) coming from a weight, or the node inner product on \(\nR[x]_{\le n}\) . Then \[ \inner{xp}{q} = \inner{p}{xq} \] for all polynomials \(p, q\) in the space (in the node case, for all \(p, q\) of degree at most \(n - 1\) , so that \(xp\) and \(xq\) still lie in it).

title: Theorem 11.10.6 (Gaussian Quadrature)
content: Let \(w\) be a weight on \((a, b)\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_a^b pqw\) , let \(k \ge 1\) , and let \(t_1 < \dots < t_k\) be the roots of the monic orthogonal polynomial \(p_k\) , which lie in \((a, b)\) by @thm-orthogonal-polynomial-roots . Let \(\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k \in \nR[x]_{\le k-1}\) be the Lagrange polynomials for these nodes ( @def-lagrange-basis ) and set \[ \alpha_i = \int_a^b \ell_i(t)\,w(t)\,\dd t \qquad (i = 1, \dots, k). \] Then every \(\alpha_i\) is strictly positive , and \[ \int_a^b f(t)\,w(t)\,\dd t = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_i\,f(t_i) \] for every \(f \in \nR[x]_{\le 2k-1}\) .

title: Theorem 11.10.5 (Roots of an Orthogonal Polynomial)
content: Let \(w\) be a weight on \((a, b)\) , let \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_a^b pqw\) , and let \((p_k)\) be the monic orthogonal polynomial sequence. For every \(k \ge 1\) , the polynomial \(p_k\) has \(k\) distinct real roots, and every one of them lies in the open interval \((a, b)\) .

title: Theorem 11.10.3 (Three-Term Recurrence)
content: Let \((p_k)\) be the monic orthogonal polynomial sequence of @prp-monic-orthogonal-sequence , for an inner product satisfying @prp-multiplication-by-x-symmetric . For a weight on an interval this covers every \(k\) ; for the node inner product on \(n\) nodes, where @prp-multiplication-by-x-symmetric holds only up to degree \(n - 1\) , read the statement for \(k + 1 \le n\) . Put \(p_{-1} = 0\) and, for \(k \ge 0\) , \[ a_k = \frac{\inner{xp_k}{p_k}}{\inner{p_k}{p_k}}, \qquad b_k = \frac{\inner{p_k}{p_k}}{\inner{p_{k-1}}{p_{k-1}}} \ \ (k \ge 1). \] Then \(p_0 = 1\) , \(p_1 = x - a_0\) , and \[ p_{k+1} = (x - a_k)\,p_k - b_k\,p_{k-1} \qquad \text{for every } k \ge 1 . \] Moreover \(b_k > 0\) for every \(k \ge 1\) .

title: Corollary 12.1.5 (Determinant Is the Product of the Eigenvalues)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) have eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) , listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then \(\det\A = \lambda_1\cdots\lambda_n\) .

title: Corollary 12.1.3 (Schur Factorization)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) with \(n \ge 1\) , and let \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) be the eigenvalues of \(\A\) , each listed as often as its algebraic multiplicity, in any prescribed order. Then there are a unitary \(\U \in M_n(
C)\) and an upper triangular \(\T \in M_n(
C)\) with \[ \A = \U\T\U^{*}, \qquad t_{ii} = \lambda_i \quad (1 \le i \le n) . \]

title: Corollary 12.1.6 (Diagonalizable Matrices Are Everywhere)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) and let \(\varepsilon > 0\) . Then there is a diagonalizable \(\A' \in M_n(\nC)\) with \[ \lvert a_{ij} - a'_{ij} \rvert < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for all } i, j . \] In this sense every complex square matrix is a limit of diagonalizable ones.

title: Corollary 12.1.4 (Trace Is the Sum of the Eigenvalues)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) have eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) , listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then \(\tr\A = \lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_n\) .

title: Example (An Eigenline Whose Complement Is Not Invariant)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) act on \(\nC^2\) . Check that \(\cvec{e}_1\) is an eigenvector and decide whether \((\Span(\cvec{e}_1))^{\perp}\) is invariant.

title: Example (A Two-by-Two Schur Factorization)
content: Find a unitary \(\U\) and an upper triangular \(\T\) with \(\U^{*}\A\U = \T\) , as in @cor-schur-matrix , for \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix} . \]

title: Example (A Three-by-Three Schur Factorization)
content: Find a unitary \(\U\) and an upper triangular \(\T\) with \(\U^{*}\A\U = \T\) , as in @cor-schur-matrix , for \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 4 & -3 & -2 \end{pmatrix} . \]

title: Exercise (A1)
content:
State @thm-schur-triangularization , including the field and every hypothesis. In the proof, an eigenvector of \(T^{*}\) is taken rather than one of \(T\) . Say why, in one sentence, and name the property of \((\Span(\elem{v}))^{\perp}\) that is wanted. True or false: if \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) is upper triangular in some orthonormal basis, then its eigenvalues are the diagonal entries of that triangular matrix. Justify your answer. Which step of the proof of @thm-schur-triangularization fails over \(
R\) ? Give a matrix in \(M_2(
C)\) that is upper triangular in an orthonormal basis but is not diagonal in any.

title: Exercise (B1: A Schur form with complex entries)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) , regarded as a complex matrix. Find the eigenvalues of \(\A\) . Find a unitary \(\U \in M_2(\nC)\) with \(\U^{*}\A\U\) upper triangular, and compute that triangular matrix. Explain why no real orthogonal \(\Q\) makes \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) upper triangular.

title: Exercise (B2: A three-by-three Schur form)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) . Verify that \((1, -1, 0)\) is an eigenvector and find the corresponding eigenvalue. Extend it to an orthonormal basis of \(\nR^3\) and compute \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) for the resulting \(\Q\) . Hence write down the eigenvalues of \(\A\) with their algebraic multiplicities.

title: Exercise (B3: The field matters)
content:
Let \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} a & -b \ b & a \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
R)\) with \(b 
e 0\) . Find the eigenvalues of \(\A\) over \(
C\) and show that \(\A\) is unitarily similar to a diagonal matrix in \(M_2(
C)\) . Prove that there is no invertible \(\P \in M_2(
R)\) at all, orthogonal or otherwise, with \(\P^{-1}\A\P\) upper triangular. Say what @thm-real-schur produces for this \(\A\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Cayley–Hamilton from the triangular factors)
content: Let \(\T \in M_n(\nC)\) be upper triangular with diagonal entries \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) , and set \(\N_k = (\T - \lambda_1\I)(\T - \lambda_2\I)\cdots(\T - \lambda_k\I)\) for \(1 \le k \le n\) . Prove by induction on \(k\) that the first \(k\) columns of \(\N_k\) are zero. Deduce that \(p_{\T}(\T) = \O\) . Deduce the Cayley–Hamilton Theorem ( @thm-cayley-hamilton ) for every \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) , using @cor-schur-matrix . Hint for (a): the \(j\) -th column of \(\T - \lambda_j\I\) has its only possibly nonzero entries in rows \(1, \dots, j - 1\) .

title: Exercise (C2: The Frobenius norm is unitarily invariant)
content:
Chapter 11 §07 introduced the Frobenius norm \(
orm{\A}_F =  igl(\sum_{i, j} \lvert a_{ij} vert^2 igr)^{1/2}\) and proved (a) and (b) below as @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant . Prove them again here without looking, since the argument is two lines and (c) is what this section is for. Prove that \(
orm{\A}_F^2 = 	r(\A^{*}\A)\) . Prove that \(
orm{\U\A}_F = 
orm{\A}_F = 
orm{\A\V}_F\) whenever \(\U \in M_m(
C)\) and \(\V \in M_n(
C)\) are unitary. Deduce that if \(\A = \U\T\U^{*}\) is a Schur factorization ( @cor-schur-matrix ), then \(
orm{\A}_F = 
orm{\T}_F\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Distinct eigenvalues are dense, but not over the reals)
content: Sharpen @cor-schur-normal-matrix-nearby : prove that for every \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) and every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is \(\A'\) with \(n\) distinct eigenvalues and \(\lvert a_{ij} - a'_{ij} \rvert < \varepsilon\) for all \(i, j\) . Show that the analogous statement fails over \(\nR\) : for \(\R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) there is an \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that no real matrix within \(\varepsilon\) of \(\R\) , entry by entry, has a real eigenvalue at all. Hint for (b): a real \(2 \times 2\) matrix with entries \(a, b, c, d\) has real eigenvalues exactly when \((a - d)^2 + 4bc \ge 0\) .

title: Lemma 12.1.1 (Eigenvectors of the Adjoint Cut Out Invariant Subspaces)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) , let \(T \in \cL(V)\) , and let \(W \subseteq V\) be a \(T^{*}\) -invariant subspace. Then \(W^{\perp}\) is \(T\) -invariant.

title: Theorem 12.1.7 (Real Schur Form)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) with \(n \ge 1\) . Then there are an orthogonal \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) and a matrix \(\T \in M_n(\nR)\) with \[ \A = \Q\T\Q\tp, \] where \(\T\) is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks of size \(1 \times 1\) and \(2 \times 2\) , and every \(2 \times 2\) diagonal block has a conjugate pair of nonreal eigenvalues.

title: Theorem 12.1.2 (Schur’s Unitary Triangularization)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(\nC\) with \(\dim V = n \ge 1\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . There is an orthonormal basis \(\sB\) of \(V\) such that \(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\) is upper triangular. More precisely, let \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) be the eigenvalues of \(T\) , each listed as often as its algebraic multiplicity, in any order we please. Then \(\sB\) can be chosen so that the \(i\) -th diagonal entry of \(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\) is \(\lambda_i\) .

title: Example (A Hermitian Two-by-Two)
content: For \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 - i \\ 1 + i & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) on \(\nC^2\) , find the eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each, and verify that the two eigenvectors are orthogonal.

title: Example (Four Tests)
content:
Determine which of the following are self-adjoint. Justify your answer; for those that are not, name the failing pair of vectors. \(T_{\A}\) on \(
C^2\) with the standard inner product, \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 - i \ 1 + i & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(T_{\B}\) on \(
C^2\) with the standard inner product, \(\B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ i & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . Differentiation \(D\) on \(V = 
R[x]_{\le 2}\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_0^1 pq\) . The orthogonal projection \(P_U\) onto a subspace \(U\) of any \(V\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State what it means for \(T \in \cL(V)\) to be self-adjoint, in terms of \(T^{*}\) and in terms of inner products, and say what the matrix condition is and in which bases it may be used. True or false: a symmetric matrix in \(M_2(\nC)\) has real eigenvalues. Justify your answer. Which field does @thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue concern, and which earlier theorem supplies the eigenvalue it borrows? True or false: if \(T\) is self-adjoint and \(U\) is any subspace, then \(U^{\perp}\) is \(T\) -invariant. Justify your answer. State the difference between @thm-self-adjoint-zero-test and @thm-complex-zero-test , and give the standard example showing the second has no real analogue. Give a normal operator on \(\nR^2\) that is not self-adjoint.

title: Exercise (B1: Determine which are self-adjoint)
content:
Determine which of the following operators are self-adjoint. Justify your answer; for those that are not, exhibit a pair \(\elem{u}, \elem{v}\) with \(\inner{T\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} 
e \inner{\elem{u}}{T\elem{v}}\) , or compute \(T^{*}\) . \(T_{\A}\) on \(
C^2\) , \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 + i \ 2 - i & -5 \end{pmatrix}\) , standard inner product. \(T_{\B}\) on \(
C^2\) , \(\B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) , standard inner product. \(T_{\C}\) on \(
R^3\) , \(\C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \ 2 & 1 & 3 \ 0 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) , standard inner product. \(S^{*}S\) , for an arbitrary \(S \in \cL(V, W)\) between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. \(P_U - P_{U^{\perp}}\) , for a subspace \(U\) of a finite-dimensional \(V\) . \(T(x_1, x_2) = (x_2, x_1)\) on \(
R^2\) with the standard inner product, whose matrix in the basis \(\sC = ((1, 0), (1, 2))\) is \( egin{pmatrix} -	frac12 & 	frac32 \ 	frac12 & 	frac12 \end{pmatrix}\) , which is not symmetric.

title: Exercise (B2: Eigenvalues and orthogonality)
content:
For \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \ i & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
C)\) , check that \(\A\) is Hermitian, find its eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each, and verify that the eigenvectors are orthogonal. For \(\S =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 3 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(
R)\) , find the eigenvalues with their multiplicities and bases of the eigenspaces, and verify that the two eigenspaces are orthogonal. Hence write down an orthonormal basis of \(
R^3\) consisting of eigenvectors of \(\S\) .

title: Exercise (B3: A self-adjoint square root of zero)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint with \(T^2 = 0\) . Prove that \(T = 0\) . Deduce that a self-adjoint \(T\) with \(T^k = 0\) for some \(k \ge 1\) is zero.

title: Exercise (C1: The operator S^{*}S)
content: Let \(S \in \cL(V, W)\) between finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) , and set \(T = S^{*}S \in \cL(V)\) . Prove that \(T\) is self-adjoint and that \(\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} \ge 0\) for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) , with equality if and only if \(S\elem{v} = \elem{0}\) . Deduce that every eigenvalue of \(T\) is a nonnegative real number. Prove that \(T\) is invertible if and only if \(S\) is injective. Hint for (a): the quantity \(\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}\) is a norm squared in disguise.

title: Exercise (C2: Sums and products)
content: Let \(S, T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint. Prove that \(S + T\) and \(cT\) are self-adjoint for every real scalar \(c\) , and show by example that \(cT\) need not be self-adjoint for \(c \in \nC\) . Prove that \(ST\) is self-adjoint if and only if \(ST = TS\) . Give self-adjoint \(S, T \in \cL(\nC^2)\) with \(ST\) not self-adjoint.

title: Exercise (C3: What the real quadratic form does determine)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(\nR\) and \(T \in \cL(V)\) . Call \(T\) skew-adjoint if \(T^{*} = -T\) . Prove that \(\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0\) for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) if and only if \(T\) is skew-adjoint. Deduce that every \(T \in \cL(V)\) can be written uniquely as \(T = A + B\) with \(A\) self-adjoint and \(B\) skew-adjoint, and that \(\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = \inner{A\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}\) for every \(\elem{v}\) . Conclude that over \(\nR\) the function \(\elem{v} \mapsto \inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}\) determines \(A\) and nothing about \(B\) . Contrast this with the complex case.

title: Theorem 12.2.6 (The Zero Test over the Complex Numbers)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be any operator. If \(\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0\) for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) , then \(T = 0\) .

title: Theorem 12.2.2 (Real Self-adjoint Operators Have an Eigenvalue)
content:
Let \(V 
e \{\elem{0}\}\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(
R\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint. Then: every root of \(p_T\) in \(
C\) is real, so \(p_T\) splits over \(
R\) ; \(T\) has an eigenvalue.

title: Theorem 12.2.4 (Self-adjointness Passes to Orthogonal Complements)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint and let \(U \subseteq V\) be a \(T\) -invariant subspace. Then: \(U^{\perp}\) is \(T\) -invariant; \(T|_U \in \cL(U)\) and \(T|_{U^{\perp}} \in \cL(U^{\perp})\) are self-adjoint, for the inner products inherited from \(V\) .

title: Theorem 12.2.3 (Distinct Eigenvalues Give Orthogonal Eigenvectors)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint, and let \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) satisfy \(T\elem{u} = \lambda\elem{u}\) and \(T\elem{v} = \mu\elem{v}\) with \(\lambda \ne \mu\) . Then \(\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = 0\) . Consequently \(E_\lambda(T) \perp E_\mu(T)\) for distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda, \mu\) .

title: Theorem 12.2.1 (Self-adjoint Operators Have Real Eigenvalues)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F = \nR\) or \(F = \nC\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint. Then every eigenvalue of \(T\) is real.

title: Theorem 12.2.5 (The Zero Test for Self-adjoint Operators)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F = \nR\) or \(F = \nC\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint . If \(\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}} = 0\) for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) , then \(T = 0\) .

title: Corollary 12.3.2 (Kernel, Image, and an Orthogonal Splitting)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal on a finite-dimensional inner product space \(V\) . Then: \(\ker T = \ker T^{*}\) ; \(\im T = \im T^{*}\) ; \(V = \ker T \oplus \im T\) , and the two summands are orthogonal to each other.

title: Corollary 12.3.4 (Eigenvectors for Distinct Eigenvalues Are Orthogonal)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal, let \(\lambda \neq \mu\) be eigenvalues of \(T\) , and let \(T\elem{u} = \lambda\elem{u}\) and \(T\elem{v} = \mu\elem{v}\) . Then \(\inner{\elem{u}}{\elem{v}} = 0\) . Hence \(E_{\lambda}(T) \perp E_{\mu}(T)\) whenever \(\lambda \neq \mu\) .

title: Example (Which of these are normal?)
content:
Decide which of the following matrices are normal, with the standard inner product on \(
C^n\) or \(
R^n\) . For those that are, say which familiar family they belong to. \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 + i \ 1 - i & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
C\) . \(\B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ -2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
R\) . \(\U = 	frac1{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ i & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
C\) . \(\C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \ 3 & 1 & 2 \ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
C\) . \(\M =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
R\) . \(\N =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
R\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the definition of a normal operator, and state one equivalent condition phrased in terms of norms. True or false: every self-adjoint operator is normal, and every normal operator is self-adjoint. Justify both halves. Let \(T\) be normal with \(T\elem{v} = 3\elem{v}\) . What is \(T^{*}\elem{v}\) ? What if \(T\elem{v} = 3i\elem{v}\) ? Give a normal operator on \(\nR^2\) that is neither self-adjoint nor unitary. True or false: if \(S\) and \(T\) are normal then \(S + T\) is normal. Justify your answer. Explain in one sentence why a normal operator cannot be nilpotent unless it is zero.

title: Exercise (B1: Determine which are normal)
content:
Determine which of the following matrices are normal, with the standard inner product. Justify your answer; for those that are not, exhibit a vector \(\cvec{v}\) with \(
orm{\A\cvec{v}} 
eq 
orm{\A^{*}\cvec{v}}\) . \( egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
R\) . \( egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
R\) . \( egin{pmatrix} 0 & i \ i & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
C\) . \( egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
R\) . \( egin{pmatrix} i & 1 \ 0 & i \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
C\) .

title: Exercise (B2: The splitting of a singular normal operator)
content:
Let \(\C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & -1 \ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(
R)\) , and let \(T = T_{\C}\) be the operator it defines on \(
R^3\) . Verify that \(T\) is normal. Compute \(\ker T\) and \(\ker T^{*}\) and check that they agree. Compute \(\im T\) , and verify directly that \(
R^3 = \ker T \oplus \im T\) with the two summands orthogonal, as @cor-normal-kernel (c) predicts.

title: Exercise (B3: Triangular and normal, by hand)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & d \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nC)\) . Compute the \((1,1)\) entries of \(\A^{*}\A\) and of \(\A\A^{*}\) . Hence prove that \(\A\) is normal if and only if \(b = 0\) , that is, if and only if \(\A\) is diagonal. Which upper triangular matrices in \(M_2(\nC)\) are unitary? Hint: for (a), you only need one entry of each product.

title: Exercise (C1: A normal operator with no proper invariant subspace)
content:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space with \(V 
eq \{\elem{0}\}\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal. Suppose the only \(T\) -invariant subspaces of \(V\) are \(\{\elem{0}\}\) and \(V\) . Show that \(\dim V = 1\) . Show that the conclusion fails over \(
R\) , by exhibiting a normal operator on \(
R^2\) whose only invariant subspaces are \(\{\cvec{0}\}\) and \(
R^2\) . Where exactly does the argument of (a) use that the field is \(
C\) ? Hint: an eigenvector spans an invariant subspace.

title: Exercise (C2: Arithmetic of normal operators)
content: Let \(S, T \in \cL(V)\) be normal. Prove that \(T^{*}\) is normal and that \(cT\) is normal for every \(c \in F\) . Prove that \(p(T)\) is normal for every polynomial \(p \in F[x]\) . Give a concrete \(S\) and \(T\) , both normal, with \(ST\) not normal. (Part (b) shows that this cannot happen when \(S\) is a polynomial in \(T\) .)

title: Exercise (C3: Normality depends on the inner product)
content: Normality is a property of \(T\) together with an inner product, not of \(T\) alone. Work on \(V = \nR^2\) with the operator \(T\) whose standard matrix is \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) . Verify that \(T\) is normal for the standard inner product. Now use \(\inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}}_{\G} = \cvec{y}\tp\G\cvec{x}\) with \(\G = \diag(1, 2)\) , which is an inner product on \(\nR^2\) . Using the rule \(\mtx{T^{*}}{\sE}{\sE} = \G^{-1}\A\tp\G\) in the standard basis \(\sE\) ( @exr-adjoints-c3 ), compute the matrix of the adjoint of \(T\) for this inner product. Show that \(T\) is not normal for \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\G}\) , and reconcile this with (a).

title: Proposition 12.3.6 (An Invariant Subspace of a Normal Operator Is Reducing)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal on a finite-dimensional inner product space, and let \(U \subseteq V\) be \(T\) -invariant. Then \(U\) is \(T^{*}\) -invariant, \(U^{\perp}\) is \(T\) -invariant, and \(T|_U\) is a normal operator on \(U\) .

title: Theorem 12.3.1 (Characterizations of Normality)
content:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . The following are equivalent. \(T\) is normal. \(
orm{T\elem{v}} = 
orm{T^{*}\elem{v}}\) for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) . \(\inner{T\elem{u}}{T\elem{v}} = \inner{T^{*}\elem{u}}{T^{*}\elem{v}}\) for all \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) . Suppose in addition that \(F = 
C\) , and set \[ A = 	frac12(T + T^{*}), \qquad B = 	frac1{2i}(T - T^{*}), \] so that \(A\) and \(B\) are self-adjoint and \(T = A + iB\) . Then (a)–(c) are further equivalent to \(AB = BA\) .

title: Theorem 12.3.3 (An Eigenvector of a Normal Operator Is an Eigenvector of Its Adjoint)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal, let \(\lambda \in F\) , and let \(\elem{v} \in V\) . Then \[ T\elem{v} = \lambda\elem{v} \quad \text{if and only if} \quad T^{*}\elem{v} = \conj{\lambda}\,\elem{v} . \] In particular \(E_{\lambda}(T) = E_{\conj{\lambda}}(T^{*})\) , and \(\lambda \in \spec(T)\) if and only if \(\conj{\lambda} \in \spec(T^{*})\) .

title: Theorem 12.3.5 (A Normal Operator Has No Hidden Kernel)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal. Then \(\ker T^{k} = \ker T\) for every integer \(k \ge 1\) . In particular, if \(T^{k} = 0\) for some \(k \ge 1\) — that is, if \(T\) is nilpotent ( @def-nilpotent ) — then \(T = 0\) .

title: Corollary 12.4.5 (The Adjoint of a Normal Operator Is a Polynomial in It)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, with distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\) . Then there is a polynomial \(p \in \nC[x]\) of degree less than \(k\) with \(T^{*} = p(T)\) .

title: Corollary 12.4.4 (The Spectrum Decides)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space. \(T\) is self-adjoint if and only if every eigenvalue of \(T\) is real. \(T\) is unitary if and only if every eigenvalue of \(T\) has modulus \(1\) . \(\inner{T\elem{v}}{\elem{v}}\) is a nonnegative real number for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) if and only if every eigenvalue of \(T\) is a nonnegative real.

title: Corollary 12.4.3 (Unitary Diagonalization)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) . Then \(\A\) is normal if and only if there exist a unitary \(\U \in \Unit(n)\) and a diagonal \(\D \in M_n(\nC)\) with \[ \A = \U\D\U^{*} . \] A matrix admitting such a factorization is called unitarily diagonalizable . The diagonal of \(\D\) is the list of eigenvalues of \(\A\) with multiplicity, in an order that may be prescribed in advance, and the columns of \(\U\) are a corresponding orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

title: Example (Diagonalizable, and no orthonormal eigenbasis)
content: For \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nR)\) , find an invertible \(\P\) with \(\P^{-1}\A\P\) diagonal, and show that no orthogonal \(\Q\) makes \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) diagonal.

title: Example (Unitarily diagonalizing a Hermitian matrix)
content: Find a unitary \(\U\) and a diagonal \(\D\) with \(\U^{*}\A\U = \D\) , for \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 - i \\ 1 + i & 3 \end{pmatrix} . \]

title: Exercise (A1)
content:
State the complex spectral theorem, including every hypothesis, and state its matrix form. What goes wrong with the proof if the field is \(
R\) ? Name the exact step. True or false: a matrix in \(M_n(
C)\) with \(n\) distinct eigenvalues is unitarily diagonalizable. Justify your answer. Let \(\A \in M_3(
C)\) be normal with \(\spec(\A) = \{2, 2, -1\}\) as a list with multiplicity. Is the unitary \(\U\) in \(\A = \U\D\U^{*}\) determined by \(\A\) and the order of \(\D\) ? What is determined? A normal operator \(T\) satisfies \(T^{*} = T^{3}\) . What can you say about its eigenvalues? Explain why @lem-triangular-normal-diagonal cannot be weakened to “a normal matrix with some of its below-diagonal entries zero is diagonal”.

title: Exercise (B1: Unitarily diagonalize)
content: For each matrix, find a unitary \(\U\) and a diagonal \(\D\) with \(\U^{*}\A\U = \D\) . \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -i \\ i & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\A = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & i \\ i & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: A circulant, diagonalized)
content: Let \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}\) , so \(\omega^3 = 1\) and \(1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0\) , and let \[ \C = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(\nC) . \] Verify that \(\C\) is normal. Show that \(\cvec{f}_j = \tfrac1{\sqrt3}(1, \omega^{j}, \omega^{2j})\) is an eigenvector of \(\C\) for \(j = 0, 1, 2\) , and find the eigenvalue. Deduce a unitary \(\F\) with \(\F^{*}\C\F\) diagonal, and write down the diagonal explicitly.

title: Exercise (B3: Decide unitary diagonalizability)
content: Determine which of the following matrices are unitarily diagonalizable over \(\nC\) , and which are merely diagonalizable. Justify your answer. \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Operators of finite order)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, and suppose \(T^{k} = \id_V\) for some integer \(k \ge 1\) . Prove that every eigenvalue of \(T\) is a \(k\) -th root of unity. Deduce that \(T\) is unitary and unitarily diagonalizable. Show that the hypothesis “normal” cannot be dropped from (b) by exhibiting a \(T\) with \(T^{2} = \id_V\) that is not unitary.

title: Exercise (C2: Same spectrum, same multiplicities)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(\nC)\) be normal, and suppose they have the same eigenvalues with the same multiplicities, that is, the same characteristic polynomial. Prove that there is a unitary \(\W\) with \(\B = \W\A\W^{*}\) (one says \(\A\) and \(\B\) are unitarily similar ). Give two matrices in \(M_2(\nC)\) with the same characteristic polynomial that are not unitarily similar, and say which hypothesis of (a) they violate. Deduce that two normal matrices are unitarily similar if and only if they are similar.

title: Exercise (C3: Normality cannot be dropped)
content:
@cor-normal-spectral-corollaries reads the class of a normal operator off its spectrum. This exercise shows that each part fails without that hypothesis. Give \(\A \in M_2(
C)\) with both eigenvalues real that is not Hermitian. Give \(\A \in M_2(
C)\) with both eigenvalues of modulus \(1\) that is not unitary. Over \(
R\) , give \(\A \in M_2(
R)\) with \(\inner{\A\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}} \ge 0\) for every \(\cvec{x} \in 
R^2\) whose eigenvalues are not nonnegative reals. Why does no such example exist over \(
C\) ?

title: Lemma 12.4.1 (A Normal Triangular Matrix Is Diagonal)
content: Let \(\T = (t_{ij}) \in M_n(\nC)\) be upper triangular and normal. Then \(\T\) is diagonal.

title: Theorem 12.4.2 (Complex Spectral Theorem)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(\nC\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . The following are equivalent. \(T\) is normal. \(V\) has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of \(T\) .

title: Corollary 12.5.2 (Orthogonal Diagonalization)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) . Then \(\A\) is symmetric if and only if there are an orthogonal \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) and a real diagonal \(\D\) with \[ \A = \Q\D\Q\tp . \] The diagonal of \(\D\) is the eigenvalue list of \(\A\) with multiplicity, in any prescribed order, and the columns of \(\Q\) are a corresponding orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

title: Corollary 12.5.4 (Spectral Decomposition of a Symmetric Matrix)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
R)\) be symmetric, and let \((\cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_n)\) be an orthonormal basis of \(
R^n\) with \(\A\cvec{q}_i = \lambda_i\cvec{q}_i\) . Then \[ \A = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i\,\cvec{q}_i\cvec{q}_i	p , \] and each \(\cvec{q}_i\cvec{q}_i	p\) is the matrix of the orthogonal projection of \(
R^n\) onto the line \(\Span(\cvec{q}_i)\) .

title: Example (Finding the axes of a conic)
content: Identify the curve \(3x^2 - 2xy + 3y^2 = 1\) in \(\nR^2\) , and find its axes and their half-lengths.

title: Example (A normal real operator with no eigenvector)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(\nR^2)\) be the quarter turn, with matrix \[ \R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \] in the standard basis. Show that \(T\) is normal, and that \(T\) has no eigenvalue and no eigenvector in \(\nR^2\) .

title: Example (Orthogonally diagonalizing a 3 by 3 matrix)
content: Orthogonally diagonalize \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \] and write it as a sum of rank-one orthogonal projections.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the real spectral theorem and its matrix form, with every hypothesis. Which two results from Section 2 does the induction use, and what does each one supply? True or false: a normal operator on a real inner product space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Justify your answer. What are the possible diagonal blocks in the real normal form of a normal operator, and what does the condition \(b > 0\) rule out? Given a symmetric \(\A\) with orthonormal eigenvectors \(\cvec{q}_1, \cvec{q}_2\) and eigenvalues \(9\) and \(1\) , describe the curve \(\cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{x} = 1\) . True or false: a real matrix with real eigenvalues is symmetric. Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: Orthogonally diagonalize)
content: For each symmetric matrix, find an orthogonal \(\Q\) and a diagonal \(\D\) with \(\Q\tp\A\Q = \D\) . \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Identify the conic)
content: Identify the curve \(5x^2 + 4xy + 5y^2 = 1\) : say what kind of conic it is, find its axes, and find their half-lengths.

title: Exercise (B3: A sum of rank-one projections)
content: Using your answer to @exr-spectral-theorem-real-b1 (b), write \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \] as \(\sum_i \lambda_i\cvec{q}_i\cvec{q}_i\tp\) , with the three matrices \(\cvec{q}_i\cvec{q}_i\tp\) written out, and verify the identity by adding them.

title: Exercise (C1: One eigenvalue only)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric with every eigenvalue equal to \(\lambda\) . Prove that \(\A = \lambda\I\) . Show that (a) fails without symmetry, by exhibiting a matrix in \(M_2(\nR)\) whose only eigenvalue is \(0\) and which is not \(\O\) . Deduce that a symmetric \(\A\) with \(\A^2 = \A\) is the matrix of an orthogonal projection.

title: Exercise (C2: Diagonalizing two matrices at once)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric with \(\A\B = \B\A\) . Prove that each eigenspace \(E_{\lambda}(\A)\) is \(\B\) -invariant, and that the restriction of \(T_{\B}\) to it is self-adjoint. Prove that there is a single \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) with \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) and \(\Q\tp\B\Q\) both diagonal. Show that the conclusion fails without commutativity, using \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) . Hint for (b): apply @thm-spectral-real inside each eigenspace of \(\A\) .

title: Exercise (C3: A rotation-scaling in normal form)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ -4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nR)\) . Verify that \(\A\) is normal and not symmetric, and find its complex eigenvalues. Find an orthogonal \(\Q\) with \(\Q\tp\A\Q = \vLambda(\lambda)\) for the eigenvalue \(\lambda\) with positive imaginary part. Explain why no orthogonal \(\Q\) makes \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) diagonal, and why this does not contradict @thm-spectral-complex .

title: Theorem 12.5.5 (Principal Axis Theorem)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric, let \(q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{x}\) , and let \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) with \(\Q\tp\A\Q = \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)\) , the columns \(\cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_n\) of \(\Q\) being an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Substituting \(\cvec{x} = \Q\cvec{y}\) , that is, taking \(y_i = \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{q}_i}\) to be the coordinates of \(\cvec{x}\) in that basis, \[ q(\cvec{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i y_i^2 . \] In particular, for \(n = 2\) with \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2 > 0\) , the level set \(\{q = 1\}\) is an ellipse whose axes lie along \(\cvec{q}_1\) and \(\cvec{q}_2\) , with half-lengths \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_1}\) and \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_2}\) .

title: Theorem 12.5.3 (Real Normal Form of a Normal Operator)
content:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(
R\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal. Then \(V\) has an orthonormal basis in which the matrix of \(T\) is block diagonal, \[ (c_1) \oplus \dots \oplus (c_p) \oplus \vLambda(\lambda_1) \oplus \dots \oplus \vLambda(\lambda_q), \] with \(c_1, \dots, c_p \in 
R\) and, for each \(j\) , \(\lambda_j = a_j + b_ji\) with \(b_j > 0\) and \[ \vLambda(\lambda_j) =  egin{pmatrix} a_j & -b_j \ b_j & a_j \end{pmatrix} \] the rotation-scaling block of @def-real-jordan-block . In matrix form: \(\A \in M_n(
R)\) is normal if and only if \(\A = \Q\B\Q	p\) with \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) and \(\B\) of the displayed shape.

title: Theorem 12.5.1 (Real Spectral Theorem)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(\nR\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . The following are equivalent. \(T\) is self-adjoint. \(V\) has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of \(T\) .

title: Corollary 12.6.2 (Orthogonal Matrices in Dimension Three)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Let \(\Q \in \Orth(3)\) . Then there are an orthonormal basis \((\cvec{u}, \cvec{w}_1, \cvec{w}_2)\) of \(\nR^3\) and an angle \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) such that, in that basis, the matrix of \(T_{\Q}\) is \[ [1] \oplus \R_{\theta} \quad\text{if } \det\Q = 1, \qquad [-1] \oplus \R_{\theta} \quad\text{if } \det\Q = -1 . \] In particular every \(\Q \in \SO(3)\) fixes the line \(\Span(\cvec{u})\) pointwise and rotates the plane \(\Span(\cvec{u})^{\perp}\) by \(\theta\) .

title: Definition 12.6.1 (Cross-product Matrix)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content:
For \(\cvec{n} = (n_1, n_2, n_3) \in 
R^3\) , the cross-product matrix of \(\cvec{n}\) is \[ \K_{\cvec{n}} \coloneqq  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -n_3 & n_2 \ n_3 & 0 & -n_1 \ -n_2 & n_1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(
R), \] so that \(\K_{\cvec{n}}\cvec{v} = \cvec{n} 	imes \cvec{v}\) for every \(\cvec{v} \in 
R^3\) .

title: Example (Axis and Angle of a Space Rotation)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Let \[ \Q = \tfrac19\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -4 & 8 \\ 8 & 4 & 1 \\ -4 & 7 & 4 \end{pmatrix} . \] Verify that \(\Q \in \SO(3)\) , find its axis and angle, and confirm the answer with Rodrigues’ formula.

title: Example (Two Quarter Turns in Two Orders)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Let \(\A = \R_{\cvec{e}_1, \pi/2}\) and \(\B = \R_{\cvec{e}_3, \pi/2}\) , the quarter turns about the first and third coordinate axes. Compute \(\A\B\) and \(\B\A\) , and find the axis and angle of each.

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: State the canonical form of an element of \(\Orth(n)\) , saying what the blocks are and which angles are allowed. Which hypothesis on \(\Q\) turns the rotation-scaling blocks of the real normal form into rotation blocks, and why? Write down the cross-product matrix \(\K_{\cvec{n}}\) and state the identity \(\K_{\cvec{n}}^3 = ?\) for a unit \(\cvec{n}\) . Given \(\Q \in \SO(3)\) , how do you find its angle, and how do you find its axis? Name the two degenerate cases. True or false: if \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) and \(\det\Q = 1\) , then \(\Q\) fixes a nonzero vector. Justify your answer. How many Householder reflections can be needed to write an element of \(\Orth(n)\) , and what does the parity of that number say?

title: Exercise (B1: Axis and angle)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: For each of the following, decide whether it lies in \(\SO(3)\) , \(\Orth(3) \setminus \SO(3)\) , or neither. For those in \(\SO(3)\) , find the axis and the angle; for those in \(\Orth(3)\) with determinant \(-1\) , give the canonical form \([-1] \oplus \R_{\theta}\) and say what the map is geometrically. \(\tfrac19\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -8 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 & -8 \\ 7 & 4 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\tfrac19\begin{pmatrix} -7 & 4 & 4 \\ 4 & -1 & 8 \\ 4 & 8 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\tfrac19\begin{pmatrix} 7 & -4 & -4 \\ -4 & 1 & -8 \\ -4 & -8 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\tfrac19\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -8 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 & -8 \\ 7 & 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Mirrors)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Write the matrix \(\M = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) as a Householder reflection \(\H_{\cvec{w}}\) , and say which plane is its mirror. Following the proof of @thm-cartan-dieudonne-small , write \(\Q = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) as a product of Householder reflections, and check the count against \(\det\Q\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Rodrigues in an example)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Compute \(\R_{\cvec{e}_3, \theta}\) from Rodrigues’ formula and check that it is \(\R_{\theta} \oplus [1]\) . Compute \(\R_{\cvec{n}, 2\pi/3}\) for \(\cvec{n} = \tfrac1{\sqrt3}(1, 1, 1)\) , and identify the resulting matrix.

title: Exercise (C1: The plane, re-derived)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Use @thm-orthogonal-canonical-form to prove that every \(\Q \in \Orth(2)\) is either orthogonally similar to \(\R_{\theta}\) for a unique \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) , or orthogonally similar to \(\diag(1, -1)\) . Chapter 11 proved more: \(\Q\) equals \(\R_{\theta}\) or \(\M_{\theta}\) ( @thm-orthogonal-2x2 ). Explain exactly what information (a) loses, and why the canonical form must lose it. Deduce that any two reflections of \(\nR^2\) are orthogonally similar, and that \(\R_{\alpha}\) and \(\R_{\beta}\) are orthogonally similar if and only if \(\beta = \pm\alpha\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Products of rotations)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content:
Prove that the product of two rotations of \(
R^3\) is a rotation of \(
R^3\) , and explain which theorem supplies the axis. Let \(\A\) and \(\B\) be the half-turns about two perpendicular axes \(\Span(\cvec{a})\) and \(\Span(\cvec{b})\) , with \(\cvec{a} \perp \cvec{b}\) unit vectors. Prove that \(\A\B\) is the half-turn about the axis \(\Span(\cvec{a} 	imes \cvec{b})\) . Deduce that every rotation of \(
R^3\) is a product of two half-turns. Hint for (c): use @thm-cartan-dieudonne-small , or the description of a half-turn in the Quick check after @thm-rodrigues .

title: Exercise (C3: Moving one point of the sphere to another)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content:
Let \(S = \{ \cvec{x} \in 
R^3 : 
orm{\cvec{x}} = 1 \}\) . Prove that for all \(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \in S\) there is \(\Q \in \SO(3)\) with \(\Q\cvec{u} = \cvec{v}\) . (One says that \(\SO(3)\) acts transitively on \(S\) .) Prove that \(\{ \Q \in \SO(3) : \Q\cvec{u} = \cvec{u} \} = \{ \R_{\cvec{u},	heta} : 	heta \in 
R \}\) , and that this set is an abelian subgroup of \(\SO(3)\) . Is the analogue of (a) true for \(\SO(2)\) acting on the unit circle of \(
R^2\) ? And for \(\SO(4)\) acting on the unit sphere of \(
R^4\) ? Justify your answers.

title: Lemma 12.6.3 (Properties of the Cross-product Matrix)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content:
Let \(\cvec{n} \in 
R^3\) with \(
orm{\cvec{n}} = 1\) , and write \(\K = \K_{\cvec{n}}\) . title: Lemma 12.6.6 (A Mirror Between Two Vectors of Equal Length)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix

Let \(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in

title: Theorem 12.6.7 (Reflections Generate the Orthogonal Group)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) and \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) . Then \(\Q\) is a product of at most \(n\) Householder reflections. (The identity is the empty product, of zero reflections.)

title: Theorem 12.6.1 (Canonical Form of an Orthogonal Matrix)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Let \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) . Then there are integers \(p, q, m \ge 0\) with \(p + q + 2m = n\) , and angles \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_m\) with \(0 < \theta_j < \pi\) , and a matrix \(\P \in \Orth(n)\) , such that \[ \P\tp\Q\P = \I_p \oplus (-\I_q) \oplus \R_{\theta_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus \R_{\theta_m} . \] Moreover \(\det \Q = (-1)^q\) , and \(p\) , \(q\) , and the multiset \(\{\theta_1, \dots, \theta_m\}\) are determined by \(\Q\) .

title: Theorem 12.6.4 (Rodrigues’ Rotation Formula)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content:
Let \(\cvec{n} \in 
R^3\) be a unit vector, let \(	heta \in 
R\) , and write \(\K = \K_{\cvec{n}}\) . Define \[ \R_{\cvec{n},	heta} \coloneqq \I_3 + \sin	heta\,\K + (1 - \cos	heta)\,\K^2 . \] For every \(\cvec{v} \in 
R^3\) , \[ \R_{\cvec{n},	heta}\cvec{v} = \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{n}}\cvec{n} + \cos	heta\, igl(\cvec{v} - \inner{\cvec{v}}{\cvec{n}}\cvec{n} igr) + \sin	heta\,(\cvec{n} 	imes \cvec{v}) . \] \(\R_{\cvec{n},	heta}\cvec{n} = \cvec{n}\) , and for every unit \(\cvec{w} \perp \cvec{n}\) the list \(\sB = (\cvec{n}, \cvec{w}, \cvec{n} 	imes \cvec{w})\) is an orthonormal basis of \(
R^3\) with \(\mtx{T_{\R_{\cvec{n},	heta}}}{\sB}{\sB} = [1] \oplus \R_{	heta}\) . In particular \(\R_{\cvec{n},	heta} \in \SO(3)\) . Conversely, every \(\Q \in \SO(3)\) equals \(\R_{\cvec{n},	heta}\) for some unit vector \(\cvec{n}\) and some \(	heta \in [0, \pi]\) .

title: Theorem 12.6.5 (Axis and Angle from the Matrix)
page: 12.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Let \(\Q = \R_{\cvec{n},\theta} \in \SO(3)\) with \(\cvec{n}\) a unit vector and \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) . Then \(\tr\Q = 1 + 2\cos\theta\) , so \(\cos\theta = \tfrac12(\tr\Q - 1)\) and \(\theta\) is determined by \(\Q\) ; \(\Q - \Q\tp = 2\sin\theta\,\K_{\cvec{n}}\) ; if \(0 < \theta < \pi\) , then \(\sin\theta > 0\) and \[ \cvec{n} = \frac{1}{2\sin\theta}\,(q_{32} - q_{23},\ q_{13} - q_{31},\ q_{21} - q_{12}) ; \] if \(\theta = 0\) then \(\Q = \I_3\) and the axis is arbitrary; and if \(\theta = \pi\) then \(\Q + \I_3 = 2\cvec{n}\cvec{n}\tp\) , whose nonzero columns are the multiples \(2n_i\cvec{n}\) of \(\cvec{n}\) .

title: Corollary 12.7.3 (Commuting Symmetric Matrices)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let \(\cF \subseteq \cL(V)\) be a nonempty commuting family of self-adjoint operators. Then \(V\) has an orthonormal basis of common eigenvectors. Equivalently, if \(\A_1, \dots, \A_r \in M_n(\nR)\) are symmetric and pairwise commuting, there is \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) with every \(\Q\tp\A_i\Q\) diagonal.

title: Corollary 12.7.2 (Commuting Normal Matrices)
content: Let \(\A_1, \dots, \A_r \in M_n(\nC)\) be normal and pairwise commuting. Then there is a unitary \(\U \in \Unit(n)\) such that \(\U^{*}\A_i\U\) is diagonal for every \(i\) . The same holds for an arbitrary commuting family of normal matrices in \(M_n(\nC)\) .

title: Example (Two Commuting Symmetric Matrices, Diagonalized Together)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(\nR) . \] Check that \(\A\B = \B\A\) and find \(\Q \in \Orth(3)\) with \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) and \(\Q\tp\B\Q\) both diagonal.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State @thm-simultaneous-unitary-diagonalization , naming every hypothesis. Which result of Chapter 9 makes the eigenspaces of one member invariant under the others, and which hypothesis does it use? Why is the restriction of a normal operator to an invariant subspace again normal, and which earlier result says so? Why does the same fail for a subspace that is not invariant? True or false: two commuting diagonalizable matrices are simultaneously unitarily diagonalizable. Justify your answer. True or false: if \(S\) and \(T\) are normal then \(S + T\) is normal. Justify your answer. Which hypothesis of @thm-simultaneous-unitary-diagonalization is dropped in @thm-simultaneous-unitary-triangularization , and what is lost in the conclusion?

title: Exercise (B1: Diagonalize two at once)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(\nR) . \] Verify that \(\A\B = \B\A\) and that both are symmetric. Find \(\Q \in \Orth(3)\) with \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) and \(\Q\tp\B\Q\) both diagonal, and write down the two diagonal matrices. Explain why \(\A\) on its own does not determine \(\Q\) up to permuting and rescaling columns, but the pair does.

title: Exercise (B2: Check the two warnings)
content: For \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) , find an invertible \(\P\) with \(\P^{-1}\A\P\) and \(\P^{-1}\B\P\) diagonal, and show that no unitary \(\P\) does this. For \(\X = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\Z = \diag(1,-1)\) , write down an orthogonal \(\Q_1\) diagonalizing \(\X\) and an orthogonal \(\Q_2\) diagonalizing \(\Z\) , and prove that no single invertible matrix diagonalizes both.

title: Exercise (B3: Triangularize two at once)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) in \(M_2(\nC)\) . Verify that \(\A\B = \B\A\) . Determine whether \(\A\) and \(\B\) are simultaneously diagonalizable, and justify your answer. Exhibit a unitary \(\U\) with \(\U^{*}\A\U\) and \(\U^{*}\B\U\) both upper triangular, as @thm-simultaneous-unitary-triangularization promises.

title: Exercise (C1: A special case of a theorem of Fuglede)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let \(S, T \in \cL(V)\) be both normal , with \(ST = TS\) . Prove that \(ST^{*} = T^{*}S\) and \(S^{*}T = TS^{*}\) . Deduce that \(S + T^{*}\) and \(ST^{*}\) are normal. Give an example of two commuting operators, not both normal, for which the conclusion of (a) fails as stated for the pair — that is, exhibit commuting \(S, T\) with \(ST^{*} \neq T^{*}S\) . Note on the hypotheses: a theorem of Fuglede says that in (a) the operator \(S\) need not be assumed normal — it is enough that \(T\) be normal and that \(S\) commute with \(T\) . That stronger statement is true and is not proved in this book; (a) is only the case in which both are normal, and its proof uses the normality of \(S\) in an essential way.

title: Exercise (C2: A commuting family of orthogonal projections)
content:
Let \(V 
eq \{\elem{0}\}\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F = 
R\) or \(
C\) , and let \(P_1, \dots, P_r \in \cL(V)\) be the orthogonal projections onto subspaces \(U_1, \dots, U_r\) , pairwise commuting. Prove that there is an orthonormal basis \(\sB\) of \(V\) such that every vector of \(\sB\) lies in \(U_i\) or in \(U_i^{\perp}\) , for every \(i\) . Deduce that \(P_iP_j\) is the orthogonal projection onto \(U_i \cap U_j\) . Prove that \(P_i + P_j\) is an orthogonal projection if and only if \(U_i \perp U_j\) , and identify the subspace in that case. Hint for (a): the eigenvalues of an idempotent operator.

title: Theorem 12.7.4 (Sums and Products of Commuting Normal Operators)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let \(S, T \in \cL(V)\) be normal with \(ST = TS\) . Then \(S + T\) and \(ST\) are normal.

title: Theorem 12.7.1 (One Orthonormal Eigenbasis for a Commuting Family)
content: Let \(V \neq \{\elem{0}\}\) be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let \(\cF \subseteq \cL(V)\) be a nonempty commuting family of normal operators. Then \(V\) has an orthonormal basis \(\sB\) each of whose vectors is an eigenvector of every \(T \in \cF\) ; equivalently, \(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\) is diagonal for every \(T \in \cF\) . Conversely, if some orthonormal basis \(\sB\) makes every \(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\) diagonal, then \(\cF\) is commuting and every member of \(\cF\) is normal.

title: Theorem 12.7.5 (Simultaneous Unitary Triangularization)
content: Let \(V \neq \{\elem{0}\}\) be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let \(\cF \subseteq \cL(V)\) be a nonempty commuting family. Then there is an orthonormal basis \(\sB\) of \(V\) such that \(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\) is upper triangular for every \(T \in \cF\) . In particular, if \(\A_1, \dots, \A_r \in M_n(\nC)\) commute pairwise, there is \(\U \in \Unit(n)\) with every \(\U^{*}\A_i\U\) upper triangular.

title: Definition 12.8.2 (Function of an Operator)
page: 12.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \((\ast)\) , with distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\) and spectral resolution \(T = \sum_i\lambda_iP_i\) . For any function \(f \colon \spec(T) \to F\) , define \[ f(T) \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^{k}f(\lambda_i)\,P_i \ \in \cL(V) . \]

title: Definition 12.8.1 (Spectral Resolution)
page: 12.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \((\ast)\) , let \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\) be the distinct eigenvalues of \(T\) , and write \(E_i = E_{\lambda_i}(T)\) for the corresponding eigenspaces. Let \[ P_i \coloneqq P_{E_i} \in \cL(V) \] be the orthogonal projection onto \(E_i\) ( @def-orthogonal-projection ). The identity \[ T = \lambda_1P_1 + \lambda_2P_2 + \dots + \lambda_kP_k \] is the spectral resolution of \(T\) , and the family \((P_1, \dots, P_k)\) is the resolution of the identity attached to \(T\) .

title: Example (A Square Root, and Three Impostors)
page: 12.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nR)\) . Find its spectral resolution, compute \(\sqrt{\A}\) and \(\A^{m}\) , and find a symmetric square root of \(\A\) other than \(\sqrt{\A}\) .

title: Example (Two Projections That Are Not Orthogonal)
page: 12.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nR)\) , which is diagonalizable with eigenvalues \(1\) and \(2\) . Compute the projections \(\vpi_1, \vpi_2\) of @thm-primary-decomposition for \(\A\) , verify that \(\A = \vpi_1 + 2\vpi_2\) , and decide whether they are orthogonal projections.

title: Example (A Symmetric 3 \times 3 Matrix)
page: 12.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(\nR)\) . Find the spectral resolution of \(\A\) .

title: Example (Exponentiating a Hermitian Matrix, and Undoing It)
page: 12.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(\H = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) . Compute \(e^{\,i\theta\H}\) for \(\theta \in \nR\) . Then find a Hermitian \(\K\) with \(e^{i\K} = \Q\) , where \(\Q = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) .

page: 12.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator

page: 12.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content:
