Prove that \[ (\A\B)^{+} = \B^{+}\A^{+} . \] Hint: write both pseudoinverses with the formulas of @thm-pseudoinverse-properties (e) and verify the Penrose conditions for the product.

title: Exercise (C3: When the pseudoinverse is the adjoint)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) . Prove that \(\A^{+} = \A^{*}\) if and only if \(\A\A^{*}\A = \A\) . Deduce that \(\A^{+} = \A^{*}\) if and only if every nonzero singular value of \(\A\) equals \(1\) . Give an example of such an \(\A\) in \(M_2(\nR)\) which is neither unitary nor an orthogonal projection.

title: Proposition 13.12.5 (The Semidefinite Block Criterion)
content: Let \(\A \in M_k(F)\) and \(\C \in M_l(F)\) be self-adjoint and put \[ \M = \begin{pmatrix} \A & \B \\ \B^{*} & \C \end{pmatrix} \in M_{k+l}(F) . \] Then \(\M \succeq \O\) if and only if \(\A \succeq \O\) , every column of \(\B\) lies in \(\col(\A)\) , and \(\C - \B^{*}\A^{+}\B \succeq \O\) .

title: Proposition 13.12.1 (The pseudoinverse does not depend on the decomposition)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) and let \(\A = \U\vSigma\V^{*}\) be any singular value decomposition ( @thm-svd ). Then \(\X = \V\vSigma^{+}\U^{*}\) is the unique matrix in \(M_{n \times m}(F)\) such that for every \(\cvec{y} \in \col(\A)\) , \(\X\cvec{y}\) is the unique vector of \(\col(\A^{*})\) that \(\A\) sends to \(\cvec{y}\) ; \(\X\cvec{y} = \cvec{0}\) for every \(\cvec{y} \in \col(\A)^{\perp}\) . In particular \(\A^{+}\) depends on \(\A\) alone.

title: Theorem 13.12.2 (The Penrose Conditions)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) . Then \(\X = \A^{+}\) is the unique matrix in \(M_{n \times m}(F)\) satisfying all four of \(\A\X\A = \A\) ; \(\X\A\X = \X\) ; \((\A\X)^{*} = \A\X\) ; \((\X\A)^{*} = \X\A\) .

title: Theorem 13.12.4 (The pseudoinverse solves both problems at once)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F)\) and \(\cvec{b} \in F^m\) , and put \(\cvec{x}^{+} = \A^{+}\cvec{b}\) . Then: \(\cvec{x}^{+}\) is a least-squares solution of \(\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}\) , that is, \(
orm{\A\cvec{x}^{+} - \cvec{b}} \le 
orm{\A\cvec{z} - \cvec{b}}\) for every \(\cvec{z} \in F^n\) ; \(
orm{\cvec{x}^{+}} < 
orm{\cvec{x}}\) for every other least-squares solution \(\cvec{x}\) ; if \(\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}\) is consistent, \(\cvec{x}^{+}\) is its minimum-norm solution in the sense of @thm-minimum-norm-solution ; if \(\A\) is invertible, \(\cvec{x}^{+} = \A^{-1}\cvec{b}\) .

title: Theorem 13.12.3 (Properties of the pseudoinverse)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) . Then: \(\A\A^{+} = P_{\col(\A)}\) and \(\A^{+}\A = P_{\col(\A^{*})}\) , the orthogonal projections onto the column space of \(\A\) in \(F^m\) and onto the column space of \(\A^{*}\) in \(F^n\) ; \((\A^{+})^{+} = \A\) ; \((\A^{+})^{*} = (\A^{*})^{+}\) ; \(\rank\A^{+} = \rank\A\) ; \(\A^{+} = \A^{-1}\) if \(\A\) is invertible; \(\A^{+} = (\A^{*}\A)^{-1}\A^{*}\) if \(\rank\A = n\) ; and \(\A^{+} = \A^{*}(\A\A^{*})^{-1}\) if \(\rank\A = m\) .

title: Corollary 13.13.2 (One Orthogonal Projection per Subspace)
content: Let \(U\) be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space \(V\) . Among the projections of \(V\) with image \(U\) — one for each complement of \(U\) , by @thm-projection-direct-sum — exactly one is self-adjoint, namely \(P_U\) .

title: Example (Two Oblique Projections, Measured)
content: For each of \[ \P' = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Q = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \] on \(\nR^2\) , verify that it is a projection, put it in the form of @thm-idempotent-canonical-form , and find the angle between its image and its kernel and the largest length of an image of a unit vector.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define what it means for \(P \in \cL(V)\) to be a projection, and what it means for it to be the orthogonal projection onto a subspace \(U\) . Which of the two definitions needs an inner product? State three conditions on a projection \(P\) , each equivalent to “ \(P\) is an orthogonal projection”. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if \(\norm{P\elem{v}} \le \norm{\elem{v}}\) for some nonzero \(\elem{v}\) , then the projection \(P\) is orthogonal. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: every projection of rank \(r\) on an \(n\) -dimensional inner product space has matrix \(\I_r \oplus \O\) in some orthonormal basis.

title: Exercise (B1: Which are orthogonal projections?)
content:
Determine which of the following matrices are projections, and among those, which are orthogonal projections. Justify your answer. For the oblique ones over \(
R\) , find the angle between image and kernel. \(\A =  rac{1}{5} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) on \(
R^2\) . \(\B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ -2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) on \(
R^2\) . \(\C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) on \(
R^2\) . \(\D =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) on \(
C^2\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Putting a projection in canonical form)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) act on \(\nR^3\) with the dot product. Verify that \(\A\) is a projection and find \(\im\A\) and \(\ker\A\) . Find an orthonormal basis \(\sB\) of \(\nR^3\) as in @thm-idempotent-canonical-form and write down \(\mtx{T_{\A}}{\sB}{\sB}\) . Hence determine whether \(\A\) is an orthogonal projection, and find \(\rank\A\) without row reducing.

title: Exercise (B3: The complementary projection)
content: Let \(P \in \cL(V)\) be a projection on a finite-dimensional inner product space, with \(U = \im P\) . Prove that \(P\) is an orthogonal projection if and only if \(\id_V - P\) is. Prove that in that case \(\id_V - P = P_{U^{\perp}}\) . Hint: @exr-projections-and-trace-b2 identifies the image and the kernel of \(\id_V - P\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Products of orthogonal projections)
content: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be orthogonal projections on a finite-dimensional inner product space \(V\) , with images \(U\) and \(W\) . Prove that \(PQ\) is an orthogonal projection if and only if \(PQ = QP\) . Suppose \(PQ = QP\) . Prove that \(PQ = P_{U \cap W}\) . Give an explicit example of two orthogonal projections on \(\nR^2\) whose product is not a projection.

title: Exercise (C2: The Frobenius norm detects obliqueness)
content: Let \(\P \in M_n(F)\) be idempotent, of rank \(r\) . Prove that \(\norm{\P}_F^2 \ge r\) . Prove that equality holds if and only if \(\P\) is an orthogonal projection. Hint: the canonical form of @thm-idempotent-canonical-form , together with the invariance of the Frobenius norm under a unitary change of orthonormal basis.

title: Exercise (C3: How far an oblique projection can stretch)
content:
Let \(P\) be a projection of rank \(r\) on an \(n\) -dimensional inner product space \(V\) over \(F\) , with \(0 < r < n\) , and let \(\X\) be the block of @thm-idempotent-canonical-form , with largest singular value \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_1(\X)\) . Prove that \(
orm{\X\cvec{z}} \le \sigma_1
orm{\cvec{z}}\) for every \(\cvec{z} \in F^{\,n-r}\) , with equality for some \(\cvec{z} 
e \cvec{0}\) . Prove that the largest value of \(
orm{P\elem{v}}\) over unit vectors \(\elem{v} \in V\) is \(\sqrt{1 + \sigma_1^2}\) . Deduce the two-dimensional formula \(\sqrt{1 + \lvert xvert^2}\) of the text, and state what the answer becomes when \(P\) is an orthogonal projection.

title: Theorem 13.13.3 (Canonical Form of an Idempotent in an Orthonormal Basis)
content: Let \(V\) be an \(n\) -dimensional inner product space over \(F\) and let \(P \in \cL(V)\) be a projection of rank \(r\) . Let \((\elem{f}_1, \dots, \elem{f}_r)\) be any orthonormal basis of \(\im P\) and \((\elem{f}_{r+1}, \dots, \elem{f}_n)\) any orthonormal basis of \((\im P)^{\perp}\) . Then \(\sB = (\elem{f}_1, \dots, \elem{f}_n)\) is an orthonormal basis of \(V\) , and \[ \mtx{P}{\sB}{\sB} = \begin{pmatrix} \I_r & \X \\ \O & \O \end{pmatrix} \] for some \(\X \in M_{r \times (n - r)}(F)\) . Moreover \(P\) is an orthogonal projection if and only if \(\X = \O\) .

title: Theorem 13.13.1 (Orthogonal Projections Among the Idempotents)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) and let \(P \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \(P^2 = P\) . The following are equivalent. \(P\) is the orthogonal projection onto its image: \(P = P_U\) with \(U = \im P\) . \(\ker P = (\im P)^{\perp}\) . \(P^{*} = P\) . \(P\) is normal. \(\norm{P\elem{v}} \le \norm{\elem{v}}\) for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) .

title: Definition 14.1.1 (Bilinear Form)
content: Let \(V\) be a vector space over a field \(F\) . A bilinear form on \(V\) is a function \(\beta \colon V \times V \to F\) that is linear in each argument when the other is held fixed: for all \(\elem{u}, \elem{u}', \elem{v}, \elem{v}' \in V\) and all \(c \in F\) , \(\beta(\elem{u} + \elem{u}', \elem{v}) = \beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) + \beta(\elem{u}', \elem{v})\) and \(\beta(c\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = c\,\beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v})\) ; \(\beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v} + \elem{v}') = \beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) + \beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}')\) and \(\beta(\elem{u}, c\elem{v}) = c\,\beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v})\) . Equivalently, \(\beta\) is a \(2\) -linear form on \(V\) in the sense of @def-multilinear-form .

title: Definition 14.1.2 (Matrix of a Bilinear Form)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional \(V\) with ordered basis \(\sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n)\) . The matrix of \(\beta\) with respect to \(\sB\) , also called its Gram matrix , is the matrix \(\mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB} \in M_n(F)\) with entries \[ \bigl(\mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\bigr)_{ij} \coloneqq \beta(\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j) . \]

title: Definition 14.1.4 (Nondegenerate Form)
content: A bilinear form \(\beta\) on \(V\) is nondegenerate if \(\operatorname{rad}(\beta) = \{\elem{0}\}\) , that is, if for every nonzero \(\elem{v} \in V\) there exists \(\elem{u} \in V\) with \(\beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) \ne 0\) . Otherwise \(\beta\) is degenerate .

title: Definition 14.1.3 (Radical of a Form)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a bilinear form on \(V\) . The radical of \(\beta\) is \[ \operatorname{rad}(\beta) \coloneqq \{\, \elem{v} \in V : \beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = 0 \text{ for every } \elem{u} \in V \,\} = \ker R_\beta , \] a subspace of \(V\) . Its elements are the vectors that every vector is orthogonal to.

title: Example (Six two-slot functions)
content:
Decide which of the following are bilinear forms on the given space over the given field. The dot product on \(F^n\) : \( eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n\) . On \(F^n\) , for a fixed \(\A \in M_n(F)\) : \( eta_{\A}(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}\) . On \(F^2\) : \( eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_2 - x_2y_1\) . On \(
R[x]_{\le 2}\) : \( eta(f, g) = \int_0^1 f(t)g(t)\,\dd t\) . On any \(V\) : the zero function \( eta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = 0\) . On \(
R^n\) : \( eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = 
orm{\cvec{x}}\,
orm{\cvec{y}}\) , the product of the Euclidean lengths.

title: Example (Four Gram matrices)
content: Compute \(\mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) in each case. The dot product on \(F^n\) , with \(\sB = \sE\) the standard basis. \(\beta_{\A}(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y}\) on \(F^n\) , with \(\sB = \sE\) . The signed area \(\beta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_2 - x_2y_1\) on \(F^2\) , with \(\sB = \sE\) . \(\beta(f, g) = \int_0^1 fg\) on \(\nR[x]_{\le 2}\) , with \(\sB = (1, x, x^2)\) .

title: Example (Three radicals)
content: Find \(\operatorname{rad}(\beta)\) and decide degeneracy. \(\beta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1\) on \(F^2\) . \(\beta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 - x_2y_2\) on \(\nR^2\) . The zero form on any \(V \ne \{\elem{0}\}\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define what it means for \(\beta \colon V \times V \to F\) to be a bilinear form, stating both clauses in full. Define the matrix \(\mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) of a bilinear form with respect to an ordered basis \(\sB\) , and state how \(\beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v})\) is recovered from it. Determine whether the following is correct, with a reason: every bilinear form on \(F^n\) is \(\beta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y}\) for exactly one \(\A \in M_n(F)\) . Define the radical of \(\beta\) and state what it means for \(\beta\) to be nondegenerate. Determine whether the following is correct, with a reason: if \(\beta(\elem{v}, \elem{v}) = 0\) for some \(\elem{v} \ne \elem{0}\) , then \(\beta\) is degenerate.

title: Exercise (B1: Which are forms?)
content:
Determine which of the following are bilinear forms on the given space. Justify your answer; for those that fail, name the clause that fails and give a witness. On \(
R^2\) : \( eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + 2x_1y_2 - 3x_2y_1\) . On \(
R^2\) : \( eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + 1\) . On \(
R[x]_{\le 2}\) : \( eta(f, g) = f(1)g(2) - f(0)g(0)\) . On \(
R^2\) : \( eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1^2y_1\) . On \(M_2(
R)\) : \( eta(\X, \Y) = 	r(\X	p\Y)\) .

title: Exercise (B2: A Gram matrix from sample values)
content: On \(V = \nR[x]_{\le 2}\) , define \(\beta(f, g) = f(0)g(0) + f(1)g(1) + f(2)g(2)\) . Verify that \(\beta\) is a bilinear form and compute \(\mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) for \(\sB = (1, x, x^2)\) . Compute \(\beta(1 + x,\ x^2 - 1)\) directly from the definition, and again from the matrix. Check that the answers agree. Hence decide whether \(\beta\) is nondegenerate.

title: Exercise (B3: Two radicals)
content: On \(F^3\) , let \(\beta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y}\) with \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. \] Find \(\operatorname{rad}(\beta)\) and the left radical, give a basis of each, and decide whether they are equal.

title: Exercise (C1: Over \nF_2)
content: Let \(\beta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + x_2y_2\) on \(V = \nF_2^2\) . Write down \(\mtx{\beta}{\sE}{\sE}\) and prove that \(\beta\) is nondegenerate. Find every \(\cvec{v} \in V\) with \(\beta(\cvec{v}, \cvec{v}) = 0\) . Hence explain why the argument “ \(\beta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) = 0\) only for \(\cvec{v} = \cvec{0}\) ” cannot be used to prove nondegeneracy over a general field, even for the dot product.

title: Exercise (C2: Orthogonal complements for a form)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a bilinear form on a vector space \(V\) with \(\dim V = n\) , and for a subspace \(U \subseteq V\) put \[ U^{\perp_\beta} \coloneqq \{\, \elem{v} \in V : \beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = 0 \text{ for every } \elem{u} \in U \,\}. \] Prove that \(U^{\perp_\beta}\) is a subspace and that \(\dim U^{\perp_\beta} \ge n - \dim U\) . Prove that equality holds when \(\beta\) is nondegenerate. Give an example with \(\dim U = 1\) in which the inequality in (a) is strict. Hint: consider the map \(V \to U^{*}\) that sends \(\elem{v}\) to the restriction of \(\beta(\cdot, \elem{v})\) to \(U\) .

title: Exercise (C3: The evaluation pairing)
content: Let \(V\) be finite-dimensional and let \(W = V^{*} \times V\) . Define \(\beta\) on \(W\) by \[ \beta\bigl((\varphi, \elem{v}), (\psi, \elem{w})\bigr) \coloneqq \psi(\elem{v}) + \varphi(\elem{w}). \] Prove that \(\beta\) is a bilinear form on \(W\) . Prove that \(\beta\) is nondegenerate. Hint: the two summands of an element of the radical can be killed separately. Deduce that if \(\elem{v} \in V\) satisfies \(\varphi(\elem{v}) = 0\) for every \(\varphi \in V^{*}\) , then \(\elem{v} = \elem{0}\) , and name the result of Chapter 5 this recovers.

title: Proposition 14.1.2 (Nondegeneracy is invertibility of the Gram matrix)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a bilinear form on an \(n\) -dimensional \(V\) with ordered basis \(\sB\) , and put \(\A = \mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) . Then: \(\A\) is the matrix of \(R_\beta\) from the basis \(\sB\) to the dual basis \(\sB^{*}\) ; that is, \(\A = \mtx{R_\beta}{\sB}{\sB^{*}}\) . \(\dim\operatorname{rad}(\beta) = n - \rank\A\) . The following are equivalent: \(\beta\) is nondegenerate; \(\A\) is invertible; \(R_\beta\) is an isomorphism \(V \to V^{*}\) .

title: Theorem 14.1.1 (Forms and Matrices Correspond)
content: Let \(V\) be an \(n\) -dimensional vector space over \(F\) with ordered basis \(\sB\) , and let \(\beta\) be a bilinear form on \(V\) with \(\A = \mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) . For all \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) , \[ \beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = \coord{\elem{u}}{\sB}\tp\,\A\,\coord{\elem{v}}{\sB} . \] \(\A\) is the only matrix in \(M_n(F)\) with this property. The assignment \(\beta \mapsto \mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) is a bijection from the set of bilinear forms on \(V\) onto \(M_n(F)\) , and it respects sums and scalar multiples: \(\mtx{\beta + \gamma}{\sB}{\sB} = \mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB} + \mtx{\gamma}{\sB}{\sB}\) and \(\mtx{c\beta}{\sB}{\sB} = c\,\mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) .

title: Definition 14.2.1 (Congruent Matrices)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(F)\) . We say \(\A\) is congruent to \(\B\) , written \(\A \simeq \B\) , if there exists an invertible \(\P \in M_n(F)\) such that \[ \B = \P\tp\A\P . \]

title: Definition 14.2.2 (Discriminant)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate bilinear form on an \(n\) -dimensional \(V\) . The discriminant of \(\beta\) is the square class of \(\det\mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) in \(F^{\times}\) , for any ordered basis \(\sB\) of \(V\) .

title: Example (Congruences and a noncongruence)
content: \(\I_2 \simeq \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}\) over any field. \(\I_2 \simeq \diag(4, 1)\) over \(\nQ\) . \(\A \simeq \A\) for every \(\A\) . \(\I_2 \not\simeq \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}\) over any field.

title: Example (Congruent, with no eigenvalue in common)
content: \(\I_2 \simeq \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}\) by @exm-congruence-first (a). Compare their eigenvalues. \(\begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} \simeq \diag(1, -3)\) by @exm-form-in-a-new-basis . Compare their eigenvalues.

title: Example (Killing the cross term)
content: On \(\nR^2\) , let \(\beta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + 2x_1y_2 + 2x_2y_1 + x_2y_2\) , so that \[ \A = \mtx{\beta}{\sE}{\sE} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \] Compute \(\mtx{\beta}{\sB'}{\sB'}\) for \(\sB' = \bigl((1, 0),\ (-2, 1)\bigr)\) , both by @thm-change-of-basis-form and directly from @def-form-matrix .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the change-of-basis rule for the matrix of a bilinear form, saying which matrix \(\P\) appears. Define what it means for \(\A, \B \in M_n(F)\) to be congruent. For each of rank, symmetry, determinant, eigenvalues, and the square class of a nonzero determinant, say whether it is a congruence invariant. Determine whether the following is correct, with a reason: congruent matrices are similar. State the one circumstance in which a change of basis is simultaneously a similarity and a congruence.

title: Exercise (B1: A congruence in \nQ)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}\) and \(\P = \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix}\) , both over \(\nQ\) . Compute \(\P\tp\A\P\) , and hence write down a matrix congruent to \(\A\) that is diagonal. Find the eigenvalues of both matrices and compare them. Compute the discriminant of the form \(\cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y}\) and check that it agrees for the two matrices.

title: Exercise (B2: A noncongruence over \nQ)
content: Prove that \(\diag(1,1)\) and \(\diag(1,2)\) are not congruent over \(\nQ\) . Prove that they are congruent over \(\nR\) , by exhibiting \(\P\) . Explain in one sentence why (a) and (b) are consistent.

title: Exercise (B3: Completing the square, again)
content: On \(\nR^2\) , let \(\beta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 - x_1y_2 - x_2y_1 + 2x_2y_2\) . Write down \(\A = \mtx{\beta}{\sE}{\sE}\) and expand \(q(\cvec{x}) = \beta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{x})\) as a polynomial in \(x_1, x_2\) . Complete the square to find a basis \(\sB'\) with \(\mtx{\beta}{\sB'}{\sB'} = \I_2\) . Verify by computing \(\P\tp\A\P\) . Hence find the eigenvalues of \(\A\) and compare them with those of \(\I_2\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Congruence versus equivalence)
content: Prove that if \(\A \simeq \B\) then \(\A\) and \(\B\) are equivalent in the sense of @def-equivalent-matrices . Give two matrices in \(M_2(\nQ)\) that are equivalent but not congruent, and justify your example. Hence explain what “the congruence classes refine the equivalence classes” means, and say what extra information a congruence class carries that a rank does not.

title: Exercise (C2: Orthogonal congruence)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) , listed with multiplicity. Prove that \(\A \simeq \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)\) . Deduce that if every \(\lambda_i\) is nonzero, then \(\A\) is congruent to a diagonal matrix all of whose entries are \(\pm1\) . Give two real symmetric \(2 \times 2\) matrices that are congruent and have no eigenvalue in common. Hint for (b): recall from @exm-congruence-first (b) what scaling a basis vector does to a diagonal entry.

title: Exercise (C3: How much the discriminant sees)
content:
Show that \(
C^{	imes}\) has exactly one square class, and that \(
R^{	imes}\) has exactly two. List the squares in \(
F_5^{	imes}\) and show that \(
F_5^{	imes}\) has exactly two square classes. Hence determine, for each of \(
C\) , \(
R\) , and \(
F_5\) , the largest number of pairwise noncongruent invertible matrices in \(M_n\) that the discriminant alone can distinguish.

title: Proposition 14.2.2 (Congruence is an equivalence relation)
content: Congruence is an equivalence relation on \(M_n(F)\) ( @def-equivalence-relation ).

title: Proposition 14.2.4 (Congruence preserves the symmetry type)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(F)\) with \(\B = \P\tp\A\P\) for an invertible \(\P\) . If \(\A\tp = \A\) , then \(\B\tp = \B\) . If \(\A\tp = -\A\) , then \(\B\tp = -\B\) . If \(\A\tp = -\A\) and every diagonal entry of \(\A\) is \(0\) , the same holds for \(\B\) . Each implication is an equivalence, since congruence is symmetric ( @prp-congruence-equivalence ).

title: Proposition 14.2.6 (An orthogonal change of basis is both)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) and \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) . Then \(\Q\tp\A\Q = \Q^{-1}\A\Q\) , so this matrix is at once congruent and similar to \(\A\) . Consequently, if \(\A\) is symmetric, then \(\A\) is congruent to the diagonal matrix \(\D\) of its eigenvalues, listed with multiplicity in any prescribed order.

title: Theorem 14.2.1 (Change of Basis for a Form)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional \(V\) , let \(\sB\) and \(\sB'\) be ordered bases of \(V\) , and let \(\P = \mtx{\id}{\sB'}{\sB}\) be the change-of-coordinates matrix from \(\sB'\) to \(\sB\) . Then \[ \mtx{\beta}{\sB'}{\sB'} = \P\tp\,\mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\,\P . \]

title: Theorem 14.2.5 (Congruence changes the determinant by a square)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(F)\) with \(\B = \P\tp\A\P\) for an invertible \(\P\) . Then \[ \det\B = (\det\P)^2\,\det\A , \] with \(\det\P \ne 0\) . In particular \(\det\A = 0\) if and only if \(\det\B = 0\) , and when they are nonzero, \(\det\B = c^2\det\A\) for some \(c \in F \setminus\{0\}\) .

title: Theorem 14.2.3 (Congruence preserves rank)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(F)\) with \(\A \simeq \B\) . Then \(\rank\A = \rank\B\) . Consequently, whether the associated form is nondegenerate is a property of the congruence class, and it is legitimate to speak of the rank of a bilinear form , meaning the rank of its matrix in any basis.

title: Definition 14.3.3 (Hermitian Form)
content: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(\nC\) . A function \(\beta \colon V \times V \to \nC\) is a Hermitian form if it is linear in the first argument , and \[ \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{u}) = \conj{\beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v})} \qquad \text{for all } \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V . \]

title: Definition 14.3.2 (Quadratic Form)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a bilinear form on \(V\) . The quadratic form associated with \(\beta\) is the function \[ q \colon V \to F, \qquad q(\elem{v}) = \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{v}) . \] A function \(q \colon V \to F\) is called a quadratic form on \(V\) if \(q(\elem{v}) = \beta(\elem{v},\elem{v})\) for some symmetric bilinear form \(\beta\) on \(V\) .

title: Definition 14.3.1 (Symmetric Bilinear Form)
content: A bilinear form \(\beta \colon V \times V \to F\) is symmetric if \[ \beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = \beta(\elem{v}, \elem{u}) \] for all \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) .

title: Example (The dot product over the field with two elements)
content: Let \(F = \nF_2\) and \(V = \nF_2^2\) , and let \(\beta\) be the dot product, \(\beta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 + x_2y_2\) . Decide whether \(\beta\) is symmetric, skew-symmetric, and alternating, and compute the function \(\cvec{v} \mapsto \beta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v})\) on all four vectors of \(V\) .

title: Example (From a polynomial to its matrix and back)
content: Over \(\nQ\) , let \(q(x_1, x_2, x_3) = 2x_1^2 - x_2^2 + 6x_1x_2 - 4x_2x_3\) . Find the symmetric matrix \(\A\) with \(q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{x}\) , and evaluate \(q(1, 1, 1)\) both from the polynomial and from \(\A\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define what it means for a bilinear form \(\beta\) on \(V\) to be symmetric , alternating , and skew-symmetric . State the relationship between alternating and skew-symmetric forms, including the exact role of the characteristic. Write down the matrix condition, in a fixed basis, for each of the three notions in (a). Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: over \(\nQ\) , a bilinear form is determined by the function \(\elem{v} \mapsto \beta(\elem{v},\elem{v})\) . Why is a Hermitian form not an example of @def-bilinear-form ?

title: Exercise (B1: Determine which of the following)
content: Over \(\nQ\) , with \(V = \nQ^2\) and \(\cvec{x} = (x_1,x_2)\) , \(\cvec{y} = (y_1,y_2)\) , determine for each of the following bilinear forms whether it is symmetric, whether it is alternating, and whether it is skew-symmetric. Justify each answer. \(\beta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = x_1y_1 - x_2y_2\) . \(\beta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = 3x_1y_2 - 3x_2y_1\) . \(\beta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = x_1y_2 + 2x_2y_1\) . \(\beta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = 0\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Polarizing a quadratic form)
content: Over \(\nR\) , let \(q(x_1,x_2,x_3) = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 - 2x_2x_3 + 5x_3^2\) . Find the symmetric matrix \(\A\) with \(q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{x}\) . Compute \(\beta(\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2, \cvec{e}_3)\) directly from \(\A\) , and again from the polarization formula \(\tfrac12(q(\cvec{u}+\cvec{v}) - q(\cvec{u}) - q(\cvec{v}))\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Splitting a form)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ -1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(\nQ\) , and let \(\beta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y}\) . Write \(\beta = \beta_s + \beta_a\) as in @thm-symmetric-alternating-decomposition , giving the matrix of each part, and verify that \(\beta\) and \(\beta_s\) have the same quadratic form.

title: Exercise (C1: Is this still true over \nF_2?)
content: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(\nF_2\) with \(\dim V = n \ge 1\) . Prove that every alternating bilinear form on \(V\) is symmetric. Prove that the alternating forms on \(V\) form a subspace of the space of all bilinear forms, and compute its dimension. Deduce that for \(n = 2\) there is exactly one nonzero alternating form on \(V\) , and write down its matrix. Hint: for (b), use @prp-alternating-form-matrix .

title: Exercise (C2: How much of a form does q see?)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) and let \(\beta\) be any bilinear form on \(V\) , with \(q(\elem{v}) = \beta(\elem{v},\elem{v})\) . Prove that two bilinear forms have the same quadratic form if and only if their difference is alternating. Deduce that the set of bilinear forms with a given quadratic form \(q\) contains exactly one symmetric form. For \(\dim V = n\) , how many bilinear forms share a given quadratic form when \(F = \nF_3\) ?

title: Exercise (C3: A Hermitian form is a real symmetric form in disguise)
content:
Let \( eta\) be a Hermitian form on \(
C^n\) with matrix \(\A = \A^{*}\) as in @prp-hermitian-form-matrix , and regard \(
C^n\) as a real vector space of dimension \(2n\) by forgetting multiplication by \(i\) . Prove that \(	au(\cvec{u},\cvec{v}) = \operatorname{Re} eta(\cvec{u},\cvec{v})\) is a symmetric \(
R\) -bilinear form on that real space, with \(	au(\cvec{v},\cvec{v}) =  eta(\cvec{v},\cvec{v})\) . Prove that \(\omega(\cvec{u},\cvec{v}) = \operatorname{Im} eta(\cvec{u},\cvec{v})\) is an alternating \(
R\) -bilinear form. For \(n = 1\) and \(\A = (1)\) , write both \(	au\) and \(\omega\) as explicit forms on \(
R^2\) .

title: Proposition 14.3.2 (Alternation and Skewness in the Matrix)
content: Let \(\sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n)\) be a basis of \(V\) and \(\A = \mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) . Then: \(\beta\) is skew-symmetric if and only if \(\A\tp = -\A\) ; \(\beta\) is alternating if and only if \(\A\tp = -\A\) and \(a_{ii} = 0\) for every \(i\) .

title: Proposition 14.3.1 (Symmetry Is Visible in the Matrix)
content: Let \(\sB\) be a basis of \(V\) and \(\A = \mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) . Then \(\beta\) is symmetric if and only if \(\A\tp = \A\) .

title: Proposition 14.3.6 (Hermitian Forms and Hermitian Matrices)
content: Let \(\beta\) be linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, let \(\sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n)\) be a basis of \(V\) , and let \(\A\) be the matrix with entries \(a_{ij} = \beta(\elem{v}_j, \elem{v}_i)\) . Then \(\beta\) is Hermitian if and only if \(\A^{*} = \A\) , and in that case \(\beta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) = \coord{\elem{v}}{\sB}^{*}\A\coord{\elem{u}}{\sB}\) .

title: Theorem 14.3.3 (Alternating Versus Skew-Symmetric)
content:
Let \(F\) be a field and let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\) . Every alternating bilinear form on \(V\) is skew-symmetric. No hypothesis on \(F\) or on \(V\) is needed. If \(\operatorname{char} F 
e 2\) , every skew-symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) is alternating. Again \(V\) is arbitrary. If \(\operatorname{char} F = 2\) and \(V 
e \{\elem{0}\}\) , there is a skew-symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) that is not alternating. So the converse of (a) holds if and only if \(\operatorname{char} F 
e 2\) .

title: Theorem 14.3.5 (Polarization)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) . The map \(\beta \mapsto q\) , \(q(\elem{v}) = \beta(\elem{v},\elem{v})\) , is a bijection from the set of symmetric bilinear forms on \(V\) onto the set of quadratic forms on \(V\) . Its inverse is given by either of \[ \begin{aligned} \beta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) &= \tfrac12\bigl(q(\elem{u}+\elem{v}) - q(\elem{u}) - q(\elem{v})\bigr) \\ &= \tfrac14\bigl(q(\elem{u}+\elem{v}) - q(\elem{u}-\elem{v})\bigr). \end{aligned} \] In particular a symmetric form is determined by its quadratic form: if \(\beta(\elem{v},\elem{v}) = \beta'(\elem{v},\elem{v})\) for all \(\elem{v}\) , then \(\beta = \beta'\) .

title: Theorem 14.3.4 (Symmetric Plus Alternating)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) and let \(\beta\) be a bilinear form on \(V\) . Then there are a unique symmetric form \(\beta_{s}\) and a unique alternating form \(\beta_{a}\) on \(V\) with \(\beta = \beta_{s} + \beta_{a}\) , namely \[ \begin{aligned} \beta_{s}(\elem{u},\elem{v}) &= \tfrac12\bigl(\beta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) + \beta(\elem{v},\elem{u})\bigr), \\ \beta_{a}(\elem{u},\elem{v}) &= \tfrac12\bigl(\beta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) - \beta(\elem{v},\elem{u})\bigr). \end{aligned} \] In matrices: \(\A = \tfrac12(\A + \A\tp) + \tfrac12(\A - \A\tp)\) .

title: Corollary 14.4.4 (Classification of Complex Symmetric Matrices by Rank)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) be symmetric of rank \(r\) . Then \(\A\) is congruent to \[ \I_r \oplus \O_{n-r} = \diag(\underbrace{1, \dots, 1}_{r}, 0, \dots, 0). \] Consequently two symmetric matrices in \(M_n(\nC)\) are congruent if and only if they have the same rank, and there are exactly \(n + 1\) congruence classes.

title: Definition 14.4.1 (Orthogonal Basis for a Form)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a bilinear form on \(V\) . Vectors \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) are orthogonal with respect to \(\beta\) if \(\beta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) = 0\) . An ordered basis \(\sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n)\) of \(V\) is an orthogonal basis for \(\beta\) if \[ \beta(\elem{v}_i, \elem{v}_j) = 0 \qquad \text{whenever } i \ne j . \]

title: Example (Diagonalizing a symmetric matrix with zero diagonal)
content: Over \(\nQ\) , diagonalize \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \] by congruence, producing an invertible \(\P\) with \(\P\tp\A\P\) diagonal.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define what it means for an ordered basis to be an orthogonal basis for a bilinear form \(\beta\) , and say what that means about \(\mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) . State @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable with all of its hypotheses. Which step of the proof uses \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) , and what exactly is divided by? Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if \(\P\tp\A\P = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n)\) , then the \(d_i\) are the eigenvalues of \(\A\) . Describe the pair of operations that a congruence by an elementary matrix performs.

title: Exercise (B1: Symmetric elimination)
content: Over \(\nQ\) , let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \] Diagonalize \(\A\) by paired row and column operations, exhibiting \(\P\) and \(\P\tp\A\P\) .

title: Exercise (B2: No pivot on the diagonal)
content: Over \(\nQ\) , let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(q(\cvec{x}) = 2x_1x_2\) . Find a vector \(\cvec{v}\) with \(q(\cvec{v}) \ne 0\) , as in @lem-anisotropic-vector-exists . Diagonalize \(\A\) by paired operations and exhibit \(\P\) . Write \(q\) as a difference of two squares in the new coordinates.

title: Exercise (B3: Reading off the rank)
content: Let \(\A \in M_4(\nC)\) be symmetric with \(\rank\A = 3\) . Write down the normal form of \(\A\) under congruence, and say how many congruence classes of symmetric matrices there are in \(M_4(\nC)\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Square classes over a finite field)
content:
Work over \(
F_5\) , whose nonzero squares are \(1\) and \(4\) . Prove that the \(1 	imes 1\) matrices \((1)\) and \((2)\) are not congruent over \(
F_5\) . Prove that \(\I_2\) and \(2\I_2\) are congruent over \(
F_5\) , by exhibiting a \(\P\) . Explain why (a) and (b) are consistent with @prp-diagonal-entries-square-classes . Hint: for (b), look for two vectors \(\cvec{p}_1, \cvec{p}_2\) with \(\cvec{p}_i \cdot \cvec{p}_i = 2\) and \(\cvec{p}_1 \cdot \cvec{p}_2 = 0\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Is this still true over \nF_2?)
content:
Let \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
F_2\) , and let \( eta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{y}\) on \(
F_2^2\) . Prove that \( eta\) is alternating. Prove that if \(\P \in M_2(
F_2)\) is invertible, then every diagonal entry of \(\P	p\A\P\) is \(0\) . Deduce that \(\A\) is congruent to no diagonal matrix except the zero matrix, and hence that @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable fails over \(
F_2\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Diagonalizing the restriction)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) , let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) , and let \(U \subseteq V\) be a subspace. Prove that \(U\) has an orthogonal basis for the restriction of \(\beta\) to \(U\) . Give an example, with \(\dim V = 2\) , in which \(\beta\) is nondegenerate but its restriction to some \(1\) -dimensional \(U\) is the zero form. Deduce that an orthogonal basis of \(U\) cannot always be extended to an orthogonal basis of \(V\) by adding vectors of \(U\) alone, and say in one sentence what @thm-symmetric-form-diagonalizable does guarantee instead.

title: Lemma 14.4.1 (A Non-Zero Form Is Non-Zero Somewhere on the Diagonal)
content:
Let \(\operatorname{char} F 
e 2\) and let \( eta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) with \( eta 
e 0\) . Then there exists \(\elem{v} \in V\) with \(q(\elem{v}) 
e 0\) .

title: Proposition 14.4.3 (Diagonal Entries Are Defined Only up to Squares)
content: Let \(\sB = (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_n)\) be an orthogonal basis for \(\beta\) with \(d_i = q(\elem{v}_i)\) , and let \(t_1, \dots, t_n \in F\) be nonzero. Then \((t_1\elem{v}_1, \dots, t_n\elem{v}_n)\) is again an orthogonal basis for \(\beta\) , with diagonal entries \(t_i^2d_i\) .

title: Theorem 14.4.2 (Diagonalization of a Symmetric Form)
content: Let \(F\) be a field with \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) , let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) , and let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) . Then \(V\) has an orthogonal basis for \(\beta\) . Equivalently: every symmetric \(\A \in M_n(F)\) is congruent to a diagonal matrix, that is, there is an invertible \(\P \in M_n(F)\) with \(\P\tp\A\P\) diagonal.

title: Corollary 14.5.2 (Classification of Real Symmetric Matrices by Signature)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric. Then: \(\A\) is congruent to \(\I_{n_+} \oplus (-\I_{n_-}) \oplus \O_{n_0}\) , where \((n_+, n_-, n_0)\) is the inertia of \(\A\) , and to no other matrix of this shape; \(\A \simeq \B\) if and only if \(\A\) and \(\B\) have the same inertia; the number of congruence classes of symmetric matrices in \(M_n(\nR)\) is \(\tfrac12(n+1)(n+2)\) .

title: Definition 14.5.1 (Inertia and Signature)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space \(V\) of dimension \(n\) , diagonalized in some orthogonal basis. The triple \[ (n_+, n_-, n_0) \] of numbers of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries is the inertia of \(\beta\) , and it is well defined by @thm-sylvester-inertia . The pair \((n_+, n_-)\) is the signature of \(\beta\) , and \(n_+ + n_- = \rank\beta\) while \(n_0 = n - \rank\beta\) . The same words are used for a real symmetric matrix \(\A\) , through the form \(\beta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y}\) , and we write \(n_+(\A)\) , \(n_-(\A)\) , \(n_0(\A)\) .

title: Example (A signature by symmetric elimination)
content: Find the inertia of \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \] and say whether the form \(q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{x}\) is positive definite.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define the inertia and the signature of a real symmetric matrix. State @thm-sylvester-inertia , with all hypotheses. Which part of the inertia is already an invariant before the law of inertia is proved, and by which earlier result? Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: congruent real symmetric matrices have the same trace. Explain in one sentence why an orthogonal change of basis lets the spectral theorem compute an inertia.

title: Exercise (B1: Signatures by elimination)
content: Find the inertia of each of the following real symmetric matrices by paired row and column operations. Do not compute any eigenvalues. \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\C = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Which of these are congruent?)
content: Sort the following real symmetric matrices into congruence classes, justifying each answer. \[ \A_1 = \diag(1, 1, -1), \quad \A_2 = \diag(5, 2, -7), \quad \A_3 = \diag(1, -1, -1), \] \[ \A_4 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A_5 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 \end{pmatrix}. \]

title: Exercise (B3: Inertia from a characteristic polynomial)
content: Let \(\A \in M_3(\nR)\) be symmetric with \(\det(x\I - \A) = x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6\) . Find the inertia of \(\A\) . Is \(\A\) congruent to \(\diag(1, 1, -1)\) ? Is it similar to it?

title: Exercise (C1: An intrinsic description of n_+)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space \(V\) of dimension \(n\) , with quadratic form \(q\) . Call a subspace \(U \subseteq V\) positive if \(q(\elem{v}) > 0\) for every \(\elem{v} \in U\) with \(\elem{v} \ne \elem{0}\) . Prove that \(n_+\) is the largest dimension of a positive subspace of \(V\) . Deduce @thm-sylvester-inertia again from (a), in two lines. State and prove the corresponding description of \(n_-\) . Hint: for (a), use an orthogonal basis to produce one positive subspace of dimension \(n_+\) , and the dimension formula to rule out a larger one.

title: Exercise (C2: Congruence cannot be read off the eigenvalues, and inertia can)
content: Give two real symmetric \(2\times2\) matrices that are congruent but have no eigenvalue in common. Prove that if \(\A\) and \(\B\) are real symmetric and similar , then they are congruent. Give two real symmetric \(2\times2\) matrices that are congruent but not similar, so that the converse of (b) fails.

title: Exercise (C3: Inertia of a block matrix)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_m(
R)\) and \(\B \in M_k(
R)\) be symmetric. Let also \(\D \in M_n(
R)\) be symmetric and invertible, let \(\cvec{b} \in 
R^n\) , let \(c \in 
R\) , and put \[ \M =  egin{pmatrix} \D & \cvec{b} \ \cvec{b}	p & c \end{pmatrix} \in M_{n+1}(
R). \] Prove that the inertia of \(\A \oplus \B\) is the entrywise sum of the inertias of \(\A\) and \(\B\) . Prove that \(\M\) is congruent to \(\D \oplus (c - \cvec{b}	p\D^{-1}\cvec{b})\) . Hence find the inertia of \(\M\) when \(\D = \diag(1,-1)\) , \(\cvec{b} = (1,1)\) , and \(c = 0\) . Hint: for (b), the congruence is the block elimination of Chapter 8, and the leftover scalar is a Schur complement.

title: Theorem 14.5.3 (Inertia Is the Sign Pattern of the Spectrum)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric. Then \(n_+(\A)\) is the number of positive eigenvalues of \(\A\) , counted with multiplicity, \(n_-(\A)\) the number of negative ones, and \(n_0(\A)\) the multiplicity of \(0\) .

title: Theorem 14.5.1 (Sylvester’s Law of Inertia)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space \(V\) with \(\dim V = n\) , and let \(\sB\) and \(\sB'\) be two orthogonal bases for \(\beta\) . Let \((n_+, n_-, n_0)\) be the numbers of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries of \(\mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) , and \((n_+', n_-', n_0')\) the corresponding numbers for \(\mtx{\beta}{\sB'}{\sB'}\) . Then \[ n_+ = n_+', \qquad n_- = n_-', \qquad n_0 = n_0' . \]

title: Definition 14.6.1 (Definiteness of a Real Symmetric Form)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space \(V\) , with quadratic form \(q\) . Then \(\beta\) is: positive definite if \(q(\elem{v}) > 0\) for every nonzero \(\elem{v} \in V\) ; positive semidefinite if \(q(\elem{v}) \ge 0\) for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) ; negative definite if \(q(\elem{v}) < 0\) for every nonzero \(\elem{v} \in V\) ; negative semidefinite if \(q(\elem{v}) \le 0\) for every \(\elem{v} \in V\) ; indefinite if there exist \(\elem{u}, \elem{w} \in V\) with \(q(\elem{u}) > 0\) and \(q(\elem{w}) < 0\) . The same five words apply to a real symmetric matrix \(\A\) , through the form \(\beta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y}\) on \(\nR^n\) .

title: Definition 14.6.2 (Hessian)
content:
Let \(f\) be a real-valued function on an open set \(U \subseteq 
R^n\) , twice continuously differentiable on \(U\) , and let \(\cvec{a} \in U\) . The Hessian of \(f\) at \(\cvec{a}\) is the matrix \[ \H_f(\cvec{a}) \in M_n(
R), \qquad  igl(\H_f(\cvec{a}) igr)_{ij} =  rac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i\,\partial x_j}(\cvec{a}) . \] A point \(\cvec{a} \in U\) with \(
abla f(\cvec{a}) = \cvec{0}\) is a critical point of \(f\) .

title: Example (Two critical points of a cubic surface)
content: Find the critical points of \(f(x,y) = x^3 - 3xy + y^3\) on \(\nR^2\) and classify each one.

title: Example (One Hessian, three answers)
content: The three functions \[ g_1 = x^2 + y^4, \qquad g_2 = x^2 - y^4, \qquad g_3 = x^2 \] all have \(\nabla g_i(0,0) = \cvec{0}\) and the same Hessian at the origin. What is that Hessian, and what happens at the origin in each case?

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define what it means for a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space to be indefinite . State the signature condition equivalent to negative semidefiniteness, and the one equivalent to positive definiteness. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: a symmetric form that is not positive semidefinite is indefinite. Name the two results of analysis that @thm-second-derivative-test assumes, and say which part of its proof uses each. A critical point has \(n_0 = 2\) and \(n_- = 0\) . What does @thm-second-derivative-test conclude?

title: Exercise (B1: Classify by the signature)
content: Determine the definiteness of each of the following real symmetric matrices, and give the inertia of each. Justify your answers. \[ \A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix},\quad \A_2 = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -5\end{pmatrix},\quad \A_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}. \]

title: Exercise (B2: Critical points of a quartic)
content: Find all critical points of \(f(x,y) = x^4 + y^4 - 4xy\) and classify each with @thm-second-derivative-test .

title: Exercise (C1: The signature measures positive subspaces)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space \(V\) of dimension \(n\) , with inertia \((n_+, n_-, n_0)\) . Call a subspace \(U \subseteq V\) positive if \(q(\elem{v}) > 0\) for every nonzero \(\elem{v} \in U\) . Prove that \(V\) has a positive subspace of dimension \(n_+\) . Prove that every positive subspace has dimension at most \(n_+\) . Hint: consider a subspace on which \(q \le 0\) of the largest available dimension. Hence deduce that \(n_+\) equals the largest dimension of a positive subspace, and that this gives a second proof that \(n_+\) does not depend on the orthogonal basis.

title: Exercise (C2: A saddle the determinant hides)
content:
Let \(f(x,y,z) = x^2 - y^2 - z^2 + xyz\) . Verify that the origin is a critical point and compute \(\H_f(\cvec{0})\) and its determinant. Classify the origin, and explain why the sign of \(\det \H_f(\cvec{0})\) alone would have been useless. Prove that no twice continuously differentiable \(g \colon 
R^3 	o 
R\) has a strict local maximum at a critical point \(\cvec{0}\) with \(\det\H_g(\cvec{0}) > 0\) , and give a \(g \colon 
R^2 	o 
R\) that does. Which feature of the dimension is responsible?

title: Lemma 14.6.3 (A Positive Definite Form Is Bounded Below by a Multiple of the Norm Squared)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
R)\) be symmetric and positive definite, and let \(\lambda\) be its smallest eigenvalue. Then \(\lambda > 0\) and \[ \cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} \ \ge\ \lambda
orm{\cvec{x}}^2 \qquad 	ext{for every } \cvec{x} \in 
R^n . \]

title: Proposition 14.6.2 (Chapter 13’s Tests, in the Language of Forms)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on an \(n\) -dimensional real vector space, \(\A = \mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB}\) its matrix in any basis, and \(\A_k\) the top-left \(k \times k\) corner of \(\A\) . Then: \(\beta\) is positive definite \(\iff\) every eigenvalue of \(\A\) is positive \(\iff\) \(\det \A_k > 0\) for \(k = 1, \dots, n\) ; \(\beta\) is negative definite \(\iff\) every eigenvalue of \(\A\) is negative \(\iff\) \((-1)^k\det \A_k > 0\) for \(k = 1, \dots, n\) .

title: Theorem 14.6.1 (Definiteness Is the Signature)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space \(V\) of dimension \(n\) , with inertia \((n_+, n_-, n_0)\) ( @def-signature ). Then: \(\beta\) is positive definite \(\iff\) \((n_+, n_-, n_0) = (n, 0, 0)\) ; \(\beta\) is positive semidefinite \(\iff\) \(n_- = 0\) ; \(\beta\) is negative definite \(\iff\) \((n_+, n_-, n_0) = (0, n, 0)\) ; \(\beta\) is negative semidefinite \(\iff\) \(n_+ = 0\) ; \(\beta\) is indefinite \(\iff\) \(n_+ > 0\) and \(n_- > 0\) .

title: Theorem 14.6.4 (The Second-Derivative Test)
content: Let \(f\) be a real-valued function, twice continuously differentiable on an open set \(U \subseteq \nR^n\) , let \(\cvec{a} \in U\) be a critical point of \(f\) , and let \((n_+, n_-, n_0)\) be the inertia of \(\H_f(\cvec{a})\) . Then: if \(\H_f(\cvec{a})\) is positive definite, that is \((n_+, n_-, n_0) = (n, 0, 0)\) , then \(\cvec{a}\) is a strict local minimum of \(f\) ; if \(\H_f(\cvec{a})\) is negative definite, that is \((n_+, n_-, n_0) = (0, n, 0)\) , then \(\cvec{a}\) is a strict local maximum of \(f\) ; if \(\H_f(\cvec{a})\) is indefinite, that is \(n_+ > 0\) and \(n_- > 0\) , then \(\cvec{a}\) is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum: every neighborhood of \(\cvec{a}\) contains points where \(f > f(\cvec{a})\) and points where \(f < f(\cvec{a})\) . Such an \(\cvec{a}\) is a saddle point . If \(n_0 > 0\) and \(\cvec{a}\) is not covered by (a)–(c), the test gives no information.

title: Definition 14.7.3 (Hyperbolic Pair, Hyperbolic Plane)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) . A hyperbolic pair is an ordered pair \((\elem{e}, \elem{f})\) of vectors of \(V\) with \[ q(\elem{e}) = 0, \qquad q(\elem{f}) = 0, \qquad \beta(\elem{e},\elem{f}) = 1 . \] The subspace \(H = \Span(\elem{e},\elem{f})\) is then called a hyperbolic plane , and \((\elem{e},\elem{f})\) is a hyperbolic basis of it.

title: Definition 14.7.1 (Isotropic and Anisotropic)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) with quadratic form \(q\) . A vector \(\elem{v} \in V\) is isotropic if \(\elem{v} \ne \elem{0}\) and \(q(\elem{v}) = 0\) , and anisotropic if \(q(\elem{v}) \ne 0\) . The form \(\beta\) is anisotropic if it has no isotropic vectors: that is, if \(q(\elem{v}) = 0\) implies \(\elem{v} = \elem{0}\) . Otherwise \(\beta\) is isotropic .

title: Definition 14.7.2 (Totally Isotropic Subspace)
content: A subspace \(W \subseteq V\) is totally isotropic for \(\beta\) if \(\beta(\elem{u},\elem{w}) = 0\) for all \(\elem{u}, \elem{w} \in W\) ; equivalently, if \(W \subseteq W^{\perp_\beta}\) . The zero subspace is totally isotropic, trivially.

title: Definition 14.7.4 (Witt Index)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional \(V\) . The Witt index of \(\beta\) is \[ \operatorname{ind}(\beta) \coloneqq \max\{\, \dim W : W \subseteq V \text{ totally isotropic} \,\} , \] the largest dimension of a totally isotropic subspace. By @prp-totally-isotropic-bound it satisfies \(\operatorname{ind}(\beta) \le n/2\) , and it is \(0\) exactly when \(\beta\) is anisotropic.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define isotropic vector , totally isotropic subspace , and hyperbolic pair . Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: a nondegenerate form has no isotropic vectors. What is the Witt index of a positive definite form on a space of dimension \(n\) ? Of a form of signature \((4,4)\) ? State the Gram matrix of a hyperbolic plane in a hyperbolic basis, and say why it shows the restricted form is nondegenerate. Which hypothesis of @lem-isotropic-extends-to-hyperbolic fails for the form \(q(\cvec{x}) = x_1^2\) on \(\nR^2\) at the isotropic vector \(\cvec{e}_2\) ?

title: Exercise (B1: Find the isotropic vectors)
content:
For each of the following real quadratic forms, find all isotropic vectors, give the signature, and state the Witt index. \(q(x_1,x_2) = x_1^2 + 2x_1x_2\) on \(
R^2\) . \(q(x_1,x_2,x_3) = x_1x_2\) on \(
R^3\) . (Is this form nondegenerate?) \(q(x_1,x_2,x_3) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2\) on \(
R^3\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Build a hyperbolic basis)
content: For \(q(x_1,x_2) = x_1^2 + x_2^2\) on \(\nC^2\) , find a hyperbolic pair. For \(q(x_1,x_2,x_3) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 - x_3^2\) on \(\nR^3\) , find a hyperbolic pair \((\cvec{e},\cvec{f})\) with \(\cvec{e} = \cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_3\) , and identify the anisotropic part \(\Span(\cvec{e},\cvec{f})^{\perp_\beta}\) .

title: Exercise (B3: A totally isotropic subspace of the largest size)
content: Let \(q(\cvec{x}) = x_1x_4 + x_2x_3\) on \(\nR^4\) . Write down the Gram matrix and verify that \(\beta\) is nondegenerate. Exhibit a totally isotropic subspace of dimension \(2\) , and explain why none of dimension \(3\) exists. Determine the signature of \(q\) and confirm the Witt index by @prp-witt-index-real-complex (a).

title: Exercise (C1: Isotropy makes the form surjective)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate symmetric form on \(V\) over a field \(F\) with \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) . Prove that if \(\beta\) has an isotropic vector, then \(q \colon V \to F\) is surjective. Deduce that if some \(c \in F\) is not of the form \(q(\elem{v})\) , then \(\beta\) is anisotropic. Use (b) to show that the form \(q(x_1,x_2) = x_1^2 + x_2^2\) on \(\nF_3^2\) is anisotropic, and give its Witt index.

title: Exercise (C2: A maximal totally isotropic subspace and its complement)
content: Let \(\beta\) be nondegenerate symmetric on \(V\) with \(\dim V = n\) , and let \(W \subseteq V\) be totally isotropic with \(\dim W = \operatorname{ind}(\beta) = m\) . Prove that \(\dim W^{\perp_\beta} = n - m\) and \(W \subseteq W^{\perp_\beta}\) . Prove that the form induced by \(\beta\) on the quotient \(W^{\perp_\beta}/W\) is well defined and anisotropic. Hint: a coset with an isotropic representative would enlarge \(W\) . Deduce that \(n - 2m = \dim(W^{\perp_\beta}/W)\) agrees with the dimension of the anisotropic part in @thm-witt-decomposition .

title: Exercise (C3: Where characteristic 2 breaks)
content:
Work over \(
F_2\) and let \( eta\) be the dot product on \(
F_2^2\) , with Gram matrix \(\I_2\) . Verify that \( eta\) is symmetric and nondegenerate, and find all \(\cvec{v}\) with \(q(\cvec{v}) = 0\) . Show that \( eta\) has a vector with \(q(\cvec{v}) = 0\) and \(\cvec{v} 
e \cvec{0}\) that lies in no hyperbolic plane, and identify which line of the proof of @lem-isotropic-extends-to-hyperbolic fails. Explain in one sentence why the third description of “totally isotropic” given after @def-totally-isotropic-subspace is unavailable here.

title: Lemma 14.7.4 (Every Isotropic Vector Lies in a Hyperbolic Plane)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) , let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) , and let \(\elem{e} \in V\) be isotropic. Then there is \(\elem{f} \in V\) such that \((\elem{e}, \elem{f})\) is a hyperbolic pair. In particular \(\elem{e}\) lies in a hyperbolic plane \(H = \Span(\elem{e},\elem{f})\) , and \(\beta|_H\) is nondegenerate.

title: Lemma 14.7.1 (Dimension of an Orthogonal Complement)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate bilinear form on \(V\) with \(\dim V = n\) , and let \(U \subseteq V\) be a subspace. Then \(U^{\perp_\beta}\) is a subspace of \(V\) , and \[ \dim U^{\perp_\beta} = n - \dim U . \]

title: Proposition 14.7.3 (A Nondegenerate Subspace Splits Off)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate symmetric form on \(V\) with \(\dim V = n\) , and let \(U \subseteq V\) be a subspace such that \(\beta|_{U \times U}\) is nondegenerate. Then \[ V = U \perp U^{\perp_\beta} , \] and \(\beta\) restricted to \(U^{\perp_\beta}\) is nondegenerate.

title: Proposition 14.7.2 (Half the Dimension, at Most)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate symmetric form on \(V\) with \(\dim V = n\) , and let \(W \subseteq V\) be totally isotropic. Then \(\dim W \le n/2\) .

title: Proposition 14.7.6 (The Number of Hyperbolic Planes Is the Witt Index)
content: In any decomposition \(V = H_1 \perp \dots \perp H_m \perp V_0\) as in @thm-witt-decomposition , \(m = \operatorname{ind}(\beta)\) . In particular \(m\) is the same for every such decomposition, and so is \(\dim V_0 = n - 2m\) .

title: Proposition 14.7.7 (The Witt Index over the Reals and the Complexes)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate symmetric form on a real \(V\) with signature \((n_+, n_-)\) ( @def-signature ), so \(n_+ + n_- = n\) . Then \(\operatorname{ind}(\beta) = \min(n_+, n_-)\) , and the anisotropic part has dimension \(\lvert n_+ - n_-\rvert\) and is definite. Let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate symmetric form on a complex \(V\) with \(\dim V = n\) . Then \(\operatorname{ind}(\beta) = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\) . In particular every such form with \(n \ge 2\) has an isotropic vector, and the anisotropic part has dimension \(0\) or \(1\) .

title: Theorem 14.7.5 (Witt Decomposition)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) and let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional \(V\) . Then there are an integer \(m \ge 0\) , hyperbolic planes \(H_1, \dots, H_m \subseteq V\) , and a subspace \(V_0 \subseteq V\) such that \[ V = H_1 \perp H_2 \perp \dots \perp H_m \perp V_0 \] and \(\beta\) restricted to \(V_0\) is anisotropic . In particular \(\dim V = 2m + \dim V_0\) .

title: Corollary 14.8.4 (Witt’s Cancellation Theorem)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) . Let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate symmetric form on \(V\) , and let \(U, U' \subseteq V\) be isometric subspaces. Then \(U^{\perp_\beta} \cong U'^{\perp_\beta}\) . Let \((V,\beta)\) and \((V',\beta')\) be finite-dimensional spaces with nondegenerate symmetric forms, and suppose \[ V = U \perp W, \qquad V' = U' \perp W' . \] If \(V \cong V'\) and \(U \cong U'\) , then \(W \cong W'\) .

title: Corollary 14.8.5 (The Anisotropic Part Is Determined)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) , let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate symmetric form on a finite-dimensional \(V\) , and let \[ V = H_1 \perp \dots \perp H_m \perp V_0 = H_1' \perp \dots \perp H_{m'}' \perp V_0' \] be two decompositions as in @thm-witt-decomposition . Then \(m = m' = \operatorname{ind}(\beta)\) and \(V_0 \cong V_0'\) .

title: Definition 14.8.1 (Isometry of Bilinear Spaces)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a bilinear form on \(V\) and \(\beta'\) one on \(V'\) . An isometry from \((V,\beta)\) to \((V',\beta')\) is a linear bijection \(\sigma \colon V \to V'\) with \[ \beta'\bigl(\sigma(\elem{u}), \sigma(\elem{v})\bigr) = \beta(\elem{u},\elem{v}) \qquad \text{for all } \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V . \] The two spaces are isometric , written \((V,\beta) \cong (V',\beta')\) or just \(V \cong V'\) , if such a \(\sigma\) exists. An isometry of \((V,\beta)\) with itself is an isometry of \(V\) . When \(U \subseteq V\) and \(U' \subseteq V'\) are subspaces, “an isometry \(U \to U'\) ” always means an isometry for the restricted forms \(\beta|_{U\times U}\) and \(\beta'|_{U'\times U'}\) .

title: Definition 14.8.2 (Reflection in an Anisotropic Vector)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) and let \(\elem{w} \in V\) be anisotropic, that is \(q(\elem{w}) \ne 0\) . The reflection in \(\elem{w}\) is the map \[ \tau_{\elem{w}} \colon V \to V, \qquad \tau_{\elem{w}}(\elem{v}) = \elem{v} - \frac{2\beta(\elem{v},\elem{w})}{q(\elem{w})}\,\elem{w} . \]

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State Witt’s extension theorem, with all its hypotheses. Define the reflection \(\tau_{\elem{w}}\) and say which vectors it fixes. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if \(U \subseteq V\) and \(U' \subseteq V'\) are isometric subspaces of nondegenerate spaces, then \(U^{\perp}\) and \(U'^{\perp}\) are isometric. Where is \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) used in the proof of @thm-witt-extension ? Two real nondegenerate forms of dimension \(6\) both have Witt index \(2\) . Must they be isometric?

title: Exercise (B1: Extend an isometry by hand)
content: Let \(V = \nR^3\) with \(q(\cvec{x}) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 - x_3^2\) , let \(U = \Span(\cvec{e}_1)\) , \(U' = \Span(\cvec{e}_2)\) , and let \(\sigma(\cvec{e}_1) = \cvec{e}_2\) . Verify that \(\sigma\) is an isometry of \(U\) onto \(U'\) . Extend \(\sigma\) to an isometry of \(V\) , and write down its matrix in the standard basis. Determine \(U^{\perp_\beta}\) and \(U'^{\perp_\beta}\) and exhibit the isometry between them produced by your extension.

title: Exercise (B2: Cancel a hyperbolic plane)
content: Let \(H\) denote a hyperbolic plane over \(\nR\) , and let \(A\) and \(B\) be nondegenerate real spaces with forms, with \(\dim A = \dim B = 3\) . Suppose \(H \perp A \cong H \perp B\) . Prove that \(A \cong B\) . If \(A\) has signature \((2,1)\) , what is the signature of \(B\) ? Does \(A \perp B \cong A \perp B\) with \(A \cong A\) allow us to conclude \(B \cong B\) ? Say which part of @cor-witt-cancellation is being used and why the statement is not vacuous.

title: Exercise (B3: Reflections in an indefinite space)
content: In \(\nR^2\) with \(q(\cvec{x}) = x_1^2 - x_2^2\) : Compute the matrix of \(\tau_{\cvec{e}_1}\) and of \(\tau_{\cvec{e}_2}\) in the standard basis, and check each satisfies \(\P\tp\A\P = \A\) with \(\A = \diag(1,-1)\) . Explain why \(\tau_{\cvec{v}}\) is undefined for \(\cvec{v} = (1,1)\) , and say what fails. Find an isometry carrying \((1,0)\) to \((-1,0)\) and one carrying \((2,\sqrt3)\) to \((-2,\sqrt3)\) . (Check the values of \(q\) first.)

title: Exercise (C1: Inertia from cancellation)
content:
Work over \(
R\) and let \(V\) be an \(n\) -dimensional space with a nondegenerate symmetric form. Prove that if \(
R^{p,q}\) denotes \(
R^{p+q}\) with the form \(x_1^2 + \dots + x_p^2 - x_{p+1}^2 - \dots - x_{p+q}^2\) , then \(
R^{p,q} \cong 
R^{p',q'}\) forces \(p = p'\) and \(q = q'\) , using only @cor-witt-cancellation and @prp-witt-index-real-complex . Explain in one sentence how this compares with the proof of @thm-sylvester-inertia in Section 5.

e 0\) then some \(\varphi \in G\) has \(\varphi(\elem{u}) = \elem{u}'\) . Prove that if \(\elem{u}\) and \(\elem{u}'\) are both isotropic and nonzero, then some \(\varphi \in G\) has \(\varphi(\elem{u}) = \elem{u}'\) . e 0\) , and on the set of nonzero isotropic vectors.

title: Exercise (C3: What extension does not say)
content: Give an example of a nondegenerate \((V,\beta)\) and subspaces \(U, U'\) of the same dimension that are not isometric, and say why @thm-witt-extension does not apply. Let \(\beta\) be nondegenerate on \(V\) and let \(U \subseteq V\) be totally isotropic with \(\dim U = \operatorname{ind}(\beta)\) . Prove that any two such \(U\) are carried onto one another by an isometry of \(V\) . Deduce that all maximal totally isotropic subspaces of a nondegenerate space have the same dimension, and compare with @prp-totally-isotropic-bound .

title: Lemma 14.8.2 (Moving One Anisotropic Vector to Another)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) , let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) , and let \(\elem{u}, \elem{u}' \in V\) satisfy \[ q(\elem{u}) = q(\elem{u}') \ne 0 . \] Then there is an isometry \(\rho\) of \(V\) with \(\rho(\elem{u}) = \elem{u}'\) , and \(\rho\) may be taken to be a reflection or a product of two reflections.

title: Proposition 14.8.1 (Reflections Are Involutive Isometries)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) and \(\elem{w} \in V\) anisotropic. Then \(\tau_{\elem{w}}\) is linear, and: \(\tau_{\elem{w}}(\elem{w}) = -\elem{w}\) , and \(\tau_{\elem{w}}(\elem{v}) = \elem{v}\) for every \(\elem{v}\) with \(\beta(\elem{v},\elem{w}) = 0\) ; \(\tau_{\elem{w}} \circ \tau_{\elem{w}} = \id_V\) ; in particular \(\tau_{\elem{w}}\) is bijective; \(\beta(\tau_{\elem{w}}\elem{u}, \tau_{\elem{w}}\elem{v}) = \beta(\elem{u},\elem{v})\) for all \(\elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V\) . Hence \(\tau_{\elem{w}}\) is an isometry of \(V\) .

title: Theorem 14.8.3 (Witt’s Extension Theorem)
content: Let \(F\) be a field with \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) , let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) , and let \(\beta\) be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) . Let \(U, U' \subseteq V\) be subspaces and let \[ \sigma \colon U \to U' \] be an isometry for the restricted forms. Then there is an isometry \(\varphi\) of \(V\) with \(\varphi|_U = \sigma\) .

title: Corollary 14.9.4 (The Determinant of an Alternating Matrix Is a Square)
content: Let \(F\) be any field and let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) be alternating. Then \(\det\A\) is a square in \(F\) : there is \(c \in F\) with \(\det\A = c^2\) .

title: Corollary 14.9.3 (Alternating Matrices Are Classified by Rank)
content: Let \(F\) be any field and let \(\A, \B \in M_n(F)\) be alternating. \(\rank\A\) is even . \(\A \simeq \B\) if and only if \(\rank\A = \rank\B\) . There are exactly \(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1\) congruence classes of alternating matrices in \(M_n(F)\) , one for each even rank \(0, 2, 4, \dots\) up to \(n\) . If \(n\) is odd, every alternating \(\A \in M_n(F)\) is singular.

title: Definition 14.9.2 (Symplectic Basis)
content: A basis of \(V\) as in @thm-symplectic-standard-form is a symplectic basis , or a Darboux basis , for the alternating form \(\beta\) . A nondegenerate alternating form on a finite-dimensional space is called a symplectic form , and the pair \((V, \beta)\) a symplectic vector space .

title: Definition 14.9.1 (Hyperbolic Pair)
content: Let \(\beta\) be an alternating form on \(V\) . A hyperbolic pair for \(\beta\) is an ordered pair \((\elem{u}, \elem{w})\) of vectors of \(V\) with \[ \beta(\elem{u}, \elem{w}) = 1 . \] Its span \(H = \Span(\elem{u}, \elem{w})\) is called a hyperbolic plane for \(\beta\) .

title: Example (Alternating Forms on a Plane)
content: Describe all alternating bilinear forms on \(F^2\) , and decide which are nondegenerate.

title: Example (A Symplectic Basis for a 4 × 4 Form)
content: Let \(\beta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y}\) on \(\nQ^4\) , where \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . \] Find a symplectic basis, and the matrix \(\P\) with \(\P\tp\A\P = \vOmega_4\) .

title: Example (The Pfaffian in Sizes 2 and 4)
content: For \(n = 2\) , \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & a \\ -a & 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det\A = a^2, \qquad \operatorname{Pf}(\A) = a . \] For \(n = 4\) , write the six independent entries as \(a = a_{12}\) , \(b = a_{13}\) , \(c = a_{14}\) , \(d = a_{23}\) , \(e = a_{24}\) , \(f = a_{34}\) . Expanding the \(4 \times 4\) determinant gives \[ \det\A = (af - be + cd)^2, \qquad \operatorname{Pf}(\A) = af - be + cd . \] The three terms pair up \(\{1,2\}\{3,4\}\) , \(\{1,3\}\{2,4\}\) , and \(\{1,4\}\{2,3\}\) : the Pfaffian sums over the ways of splitting \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) into two pairs, with a sign. For the matrix \(\A\) of @exm-darboux-basis-4x4 this reads \(\operatorname{Pf}(\A) = 1\cdot 0 - 2\cdot 1 + 3\cdot 1 = 1\) , and indeed \(\det\A = 1\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define a hyperbolic pair for an alternating form, and say why its two vectors are automatically linearly independent. State @thm-symplectic-standard-form , and say which hypothesis on \(F\) it needs. Determine whether the following is correct: every skew-symmetric matrix over every field has even rank. Justify your answer. Why can an alternating form never have a diagonal Gram matrix, unless the form is zero? How many congruence classes of alternating matrices are there in \(M_5(\nR)\) ? In \(M_5(\nF_7)\) ?

title: Exercise (B1: A symplectic basis)
content: Let \(\beta(\cvec{x},\cvec{y}) = \cvec{x}\tp\B\cvec{y}\) on \(\nQ^4\) , with \[ \B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . \] Find a symplectic basis for \(\beta\) and an invertible \(\P \in M_4(\nQ)\) with \(\P\tp\B\P = \vOmega_4\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Pfaffians and determinants)
content: For each matrix below, compute the Pfaffian using the formula of @exm-pfaffian-small , and verify that its square is the determinant. \[ \A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 3 \\ -1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . \] Hence write down, for each, an invertible matrix congruence class in the sense of @cor-alternating-even-rank .

title: Exercise (B3: Determine which of the following)
content:

title: Exercise (C1: Lagrangian subspaces)
content: Let \(\beta\) be a symplectic form on \(V\) with \(\dim V = 2m\) ( @def-darboux-basis ), and call a subspace \(U \subseteq V\) totally isotropic if \(\beta(\elem{u}, \elem{u}') = 0\) for all \(\elem{u}, \elem{u}' \in U\) . Prove that \(\Span(\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_m)\) is totally isotropic, for any symplectic basis. Prove that every totally isotropic subspace satisfies \(\dim U \le m\) . Deduce that a symplectic form on a space of dimension \(2m\) has a totally isotropic subspace of dimension exactly \(m\) , and no larger one. (These are the Lagrangian subspaces.) Hint for (b): compare \(U\) with \(U^{\perp_\beta}\) of @exr-bilinear-forms-c2 .

title: Exercise (C2: The inverse of an alternating matrix)
content: Let \(F\) be any field. Prove that every alternating matrix of odd size over \(F\) is singular, without using determinants. Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) be alternating and invertible. Prove that \(\A^{-1}\) is alternating. Hint for (b): the adjugate. The \((i,i)\) entry of \(\adj\A\) is a minor of \(\A\) of size \(n - 1\) .

content:

F_q^{2m}\) ? How many symmetric ones? How many of the alternating forms on \(
F_q^{2}\) are nondegenerate, and how many congruence classes do they fall into? How many of the symmetric forms on \(
F_q^{1}\) are nondegenerate, and how many congruence classes do they fall into? Hint: the squaring map \(
F_q^{	imes} 	o 
F_q^{	imes}\) has kernel \(\{1, -1\}\) . Explain in one or two sentences why the answers to (b) and (c) differ, in terms of what a change of basis can do to the single free parameter in each case.

title: Lemma 14.9.1 (Peeling Off a Hyperbolic Plane)
content: Let \(\beta\) be an alternating form on a finite-dimensional \(V\) , and suppose \(\beta \ne 0\) . There is a hyperbolic pair \((\elem{u}, \elem{w})\) for \(\beta\) . For any such pair, with \(H = \Span(\elem{u}, \elem{w})\) and \[ H^{\perp_\beta} = \{\, \elem{v} \in V : \beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) = \beta(\elem{w}, \elem{v}) = 0 \,\} , \] we have \(V = H \oplus H^{\perp_\beta}\) and \(\dim H^{\perp_\beta} = \dim V - 2\) . \(\operatorname{rad}(\beta) = \operatorname{rad}\bigl(\beta|_{H^{\perp_\beta}}\bigr)\) . In particular, if \(\beta\) is nondegenerate then so is its restriction to \(H^{\perp_\beta}\) .

title: Theorem 14.9.2 (Standard Form of an Alternating Form)
content: Let \(F\) be any field, let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\) with \(\dim V = n\) , and let \(\beta\) be an alternating bilinear form on \(V\) . Then there are an integer \(m \ge 0\) with \(2m \le n\) and a basis \[ \sB = (\elem{u}_1, \dots, \elem{u}_m, \elem{w}_1, \dots, \elem{w}_m, \elem{z}_1, \dots, \elem{z}_{n-2m}) \] of \(V\) such that, for all \(i, j\) , \[ \beta(\elem{u}_i, \elem{w}_j) = \delta_{ij}, \qquad \beta(\elem{u}_i, \elem{u}_j) = \beta(\elem{w}_i, \elem{w}_j) = 0 , \] and \(\beta(\elem{z}_k, \elem{v}) = 0\) for every \(k\) and every \(\elem{v} \in V\) . Equivalently, in this basis \[ \mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB} = \vOmega_{2m} \oplus \O_{n-2m}, \qquad \vOmega_{2m} \coloneqq \begin{pmatrix} \O & \I_m \\ -\I_m & \O \end{pmatrix} . \] {#eq-standard-alternating-matrix} In particular: every alternating \(\A \in M_n(F)\) is congruent to \(\vOmega_{2m} \oplus \O_{n-2m}\) for exactly one \(m\) ; if \(\beta\) is nondegenerate then \(n = 2m\) is even and \(\mtx{\beta}{\sB}{\sB} = \vOmega_{n}\) .

title: Definition 14.10.2 (The Indefinite Orthogonal and Symplectic Groups)
content: For \(p, q \ge 0\) with \(p + q = n\) , set \(\I_{p,q} \coloneqq \I_p \oplus (-\I_q) \in M_n(\nR)\) and \[ \Orth(p, q) \coloneqq \operatorname{Isom}(\I_{p,q}) = \{\, \P \in M_n(\nR) : \P\tp\I_{p,q}\P = \I_{p,q} \,\} , \] the indefinite orthogonal group of signature \((p, q)\) . For \(m \ge 1\) and any field \(F\) , set \[ \Sp(2m, F) \coloneqq \operatorname{Isom}(\vOmega_{2m}) = \{\, \P \in M_{2m}(F) : \P\tp\vOmega_{2m}\P = \vOmega_{2m} \,\} , \] the symplectic group , where \(\vOmega_{2m}\) is the standard alternating matrix of @eq-standard-alternating-matrix .

title: Definition 14.10.1 (Isometry Group of a Form)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) and \(\beta\) a nondegenerate bilinear form on \(V\) ( @def-nondegenerate ). An operator \(T \in \cL(V)\) is an isometry of \(\beta\) if \[ \beta(T\elem{u}, T\elem{v}) = \beta(\elem{u}, \elem{v}) \qquad \text{for all } \elem{u}, \elem{v} \in V , \] and the set of all of them is written \(\operatorname{Isom}(\beta)\) . For a nonsingular \(\A \in M_n(F)\) , the corresponding matrix group is \[ \operatorname{Isom}(\A) \coloneqq \{\, \P \in M_n(F) : \P\tp\A\P = \A \,\} . \] When \(F = \nC\) and \(\A^{*} = \A\) is nonsingular Hermitian, \(\operatorname{Isom}(\A)\) means instead \(\{\, \P : \P^{*}\A\P = \A \,\}\) .

title: Example (Members of Each Family)
content: Verify the following memberships, with \(\vOmega_{2m}\) as above. \(\begin{psmallmatrix} \cosh t & \sinh t \\ \sinh t & \cosh t\end{psmallmatrix} \in \Orth(1,1)\) for every \(t \in \nR\) . \(\begin{psmallmatrix} \M & \O \\ \O & (\M\tp)^{-1}\end{psmallmatrix} \in \Sp(2m, F)\) for every invertible \(\M \in M_m(F)\) . \(\begin{psmallmatrix} \I_m & \S \\ \O & \I_m\end{psmallmatrix} \in \Sp(2m, F)\) if and only if \(\S\tp = \S\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define \(\operatorname{Isom}(\A)\) for a nonsingular \(\A \in M_n(F)\) , and explain why its elements are automatically invertible. Which form does \(\Orth(p,q)\) preserve, and which does \(\Sp(2m,F)\) preserve? Determine whether the following is correct: if \(\A \simeq \B\) , then \(\operatorname{Isom}(\A) = \operatorname{Isom}(\B)\) . Justify your answer. State what is known here about \(\det\P\) for \(\P \in \Sp(2m,F)\) , distinguishing what is proved from what is only recorded. In the parameter count, what exactly does the word “dimension” mean, and what is not being claimed?

title: Exercise (B1: Determine which of the following)
content: For each matrix, determine whether it lies in \(\Orth(2)\) , in \(\Orth(1,1)\) , in \(\Sp(2,\nR)\) — where the relevant forms are \(\I_2\) , \(\I_{1,1} = \diag(1,-1)\) , and \(\vOmega_2\) — listing all that apply. Justify each answer. \(\begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{psmallmatrix}\) . \(\begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}\) . \(\begin{psmallmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/3\end{psmallmatrix}\) . \(\begin{psmallmatrix} 5/3 & 4/3 \\ 4/3 & 5/3\end{psmallmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: A symplectic matrix of size four)
content: Let \(\M = \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}\) and \(\S = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}\) , and put \[ \P_1 = \begin{pmatrix} \M & \O \\ \O & (\M\tp)^{-1}\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \P_2 = \begin{pmatrix} \I_2 & \S \\ \O & \I_2\end{pmatrix} . \] Write out \(\P_1\) explicitly and verify \(\P_1 \in \Sp(4, \nQ)\) directly from the definition. Explain why \(\P_1\P_2 \in \Sp(4,\nQ)\) without computing the product. Compute \(\det\P_1\) and \(\det\P_2\) , and check them against @thm-classical-group-determinants .

title: Exercise (B3: Counting parameters)
content: Compute the expected dimensions of \(\Orth(4)\) , \(\Orth(2,2)\) , \(\Unit(3)\) , and \(\Sp(4,\nR)\) . For which \(n\) and \(m\) do \(\Orth(n)\) and \(\Sp(2m,\nR)\) have the same expected dimension? Solve the resulting equation. The group \(\SO(n)\) is cut out of \(\Orth(n)\) by the single equation \(\det\P = 1\) . Why does this not reduce the expected dimension by one?

title: Exercise (C1: Isometries of a degenerate form)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} \in M_2(\nR)\) and let \(G = \{\, \P \in M_2(\nR) : \P\tp\A\P = \A \,\}\) , the set produced by dropping the nondegeneracy hypothesis from @def-isometry-group-of-form . Determine \(G\) explicitly. Exhibit an element of \(G\) that is not invertible, and explain which step of the proof of @thm-classical-groups-are-groups it defeats. Prove that the invertible elements of \(G\) do form a group.

title: Exercise (C3: Bounded and unbounded)
content: Prove that every entry of a matrix \(\P \in \Orth(n)\) satisfies \(\lvert p_{ij}\rvert \le 1\) . Prove that for every \(n \ge 2\) and every real \(M\) , the group \(\Orth(n-1, 1)\) contains a matrix with an entry larger than \(M\) . Explain in two sentences why (a) and (b) together make it plausible that \(\Orth(n)\) is compact and \(\Orth(n-1,1)\) is not, and say precisely what has and has not been proved.

title: Proposition 14.10.2 (Congruence Conjugates the Isometry Group)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(F)\) be nonsingular with \(\B = \Q\tp\A\Q\) for an invertible \(\Q\) ( @def-congruent ). Then \[ \operatorname{Isom}(\B) = \Q^{-1}\operatorname{Isom}(\A)\,\Q , \] so the two groups are conjugate subgroups of \(\GL_n(F)\) ; in particular they are isomorphic as groups, by \(\P \mapsto \Q\P\Q^{-1}\) .

title: Theorem 14.10.3 (Determinants in the Classical Groups)
content: Let \(F\) be any field and \(\A \in M_n(F)\) nonsingular. Then \(\det\P = \pm 1\) for every \(\P \in \operatorname{Isom}(\A)\) . In particular \(\det\P = \pm 1\) for \(\P \in \Orth(p,q)\) , and both signs occur when \(n \ge 1\) . If \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) is Hermitian and nonsingular, then \(\lvert\det\P\rvert = 1\) for every \(\P \in \operatorname{Isom}(\A)\) ; in particular for \(\P \in \Unit(n)\) . \(\Sp(2, F) = \SL_2(F)\) . In particular every \(\P \in \Sp(2,F)\) has \(\det\P = 1\) exactly, and \(-1\) does not occur.

title: Theorem 14.10.1 (Isometry Groups Are Groups)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) be nonsingular. Then every \(\P \in \operatorname{Isom}(\A)\) is invertible, and \(\operatorname{Isom}(\A)\) is a subgroup of \(\GL_n(F)\) . The same holds for \(\operatorname{Isom}(\beta)\) inside the group of invertible operators on \(V\) , and for the Hermitian version.

title: Definition 14.11.2 (Timelike, Spacelike, Null)
content:
Let \(\cvec{x} \in 
R^{1,3}\) with \(\cvec{x} 
e \cvec{0}\) . Then \(\cvec{x}\) is timelike if \(q(\cvec{x}) > 0\) ; null , or lightlike , if \(q(\cvec{x}) = 0\) ; spacelike if \(q(\cvec{x}) < 0\) . The set \(\{\cvec{x} \in 
R^{1,3} : q(\cvec{x}) = 0\}\) is the light cone . A timelike \(\cvec{x}\) is future-pointing if \(x_1 > 0\) and past-pointing if \(x_1 < 0\) .

title: Definition 14.11.3 (Boost)
content: For \(t \in \nR\) , the boost of rapidity \(t\) is \[ \B_t \coloneqq \begin{pmatrix} \cosh t & \sinh t \\ \sinh t & \cosh t \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nR) . \]

title: Definition 14.11.1 (Minkowski Space)
content:
Minkowski space \(
R^{1,3}\) is the real vector space \(
R^4\) equipped with the symmetric bilinear form \[ \eta(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}) \coloneqq x_1y_1 - x_2y_2 - x_3y_3 - x_4y_4 , \] whose quadratic form is \(q(\cvec{x}) = x_1^2 - x_2^2 - x_3^2 - x_4^2\) . The first coordinate is the time coordinate and the remaining three are the space coordinates. More generally, for \(p, m \ge 0\) , \(
R^{p,m}\) is \(
R^{p+m}\) with the form whose matrix in the standard basis is \(\I_p \oplus (-\I_m)\) .

title: Example (Reading off the three types)
content: Classify \(\cvec{e}_1\) , \(\cvec{e}_2\) , \(\cvec{e}_1 + \cvec{e}_2\) , and \((2, 1, 1, 1)\) in \(\nR^{1,3}\) , and decide which of them are isotropic.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the sign convention used in this section, give the matrix of \(\eta\) in the standard basis, and say what its signature and inertia are. Define timelike, null, and spacelike, and say which earlier notion the word “null” renames. True or false: the sum of two spacelike vectors is spacelike. Justify your answer. Justify your answer. \[ \A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 5/3 & 4/3 \\ 4/3 & 5/3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \A_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \A_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 5/3 & -4/3 \\ 4/3 & -5/3 \end{pmatrix}. \]

content: Classify \(\cvec{x} = (3, 1, 2, 2)\) , \(\cvec{y} = (1, 0, 1, 0)\) , and \(\cvec{z} = (0, 1, 1, 1)\) in \(\nR^{1,3}\) as timelike, null, or spacelike. The vector \(\cvec{y}\) is null.
