title: Proposition 18.5.1 (Basic Properties of the Dual Cone)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let \(S, T \subseteq V\) . \(S^{*}\) is a closed convex cone. If \(S \subseteq T\) , then \(T^{*} \subseteq S^{*}\) . \(S \subseteq S^{**}\) . \(\operatorname{cone}(\elem{a}_1, \dots, \elem{a}_m)^{*} = \{ \elem{y} : \inner{\elem{a}_i}{\elem{y}} \ge 0 \text{ for } i = 1, \dots, m \}\) . In \(\nR^n\) , with \(\A\) the matrix of columns \(\cvec{a}_i\) , this is \(\{ \cvec{y} : \A\tp\cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0} \}\) .

title: Theorem 18.5.2 (Carathéodory’s Theorem for Cones)
content: Let \(V\) be a real vector space and let \(\elem{a}_1, \dots, \elem{a}_m \in V\) . Every \(\elem{b} \in \operatorname{cone}(\elem{a}_1, \dots, \elem{a}_m)\) lies in \(\operatorname{cone}(\elem{a}_i : i \in S)\) for some set of indices \(S \subseteq \{1, \dots, m\}\) such that the list \((\elem{a}_i)_{i \in S}\) is linearly independent . In particular, if \(\dim V = n\) , then \(\elem{b}\) is a nonnegative combination of at most \(n\) of the \(\elem{a}_i\) .

title: Theorem 18.5.8 (The Bidual of a Closed Cone)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let \(K \subseteq V\) be a closed convex cone. Then \(K^{**} = K\) .

title: Theorem 18.5.6 (Farkas’s Lemma)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R)\) and \(\cvec{b} \in 
R^m\) . Exactly one of the following has a solution: \(\A\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}\) with \(\cvec{x} \in 
R^n\) , \(\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}\) ; \(\A	p\cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0}\) and \(\cvec{b}	p\cvec{y} < 0\) , with \(\cvec{y} \in 
R^m\) .

title: Theorem 18.5.4 (Finitely Generated Cones Are Closed)
content: Let \(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_m \in \nR^n\) . Then \(\operatorname{cone}(\cvec{a}_1, \dots, \cvec{a}_m)\) is a closed convex cone.

title: Corollary 18.6.2 (Certificates from Weak Duality)
content: If \(\cvec{x}\) is feasible for (P), \(\cvec{y}\) is feasible for (D), and \(\cvec{c}\tp\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}\tp\cvec{y}\) , then \(\cvec{x}\) is optimal for (P) and \(\cvec{y}\) is optimal for (D). If (P) is unbounded, then (D) is infeasible. If (D) is unbounded, then (P) is infeasible.

title: Corollary 18.6.4 (Bounded Linear Programs Attain Their Optimum)
content: If (P) is feasible and its objective is bounded above on the feasible region, that is, \(\cvec{c}\tp\cvec{x} \le N\) for some \(N\) and every feasible \(\cvec{x}\) , then (P) has an optimal solution. The same holds for (D) with “bounded below”.

title: Definition 18.6.2 (Dual Program)
content: The dual of the linear program (P) of @def-linear-program is the problem \[ \text{(D)}\qquad \text{minimize } \cvec{b}\tp\cvec{y} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \A\tp\cvec{y} \ge \cvec{c},\ \ \cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0} , \] with \(\cvec{y} \in \nR^m\) . The words feasible , infeasible , and optimal are used as for (P). (D) is unbounded if it is feasible and \(\cvec{b}\tp\cvec{y}\) takes arbitrarily negative values on its feasible region. In this context (P) is called the primal program.

title: Definition 18.6.1 (Linear Program)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R)\) , \(\cvec{b} \in 
R^m\) , and \(\cvec{c} \in 
R^n\) . The linear program with these data, in inequality form , is the problem \[ 	ext{(P)}\qquad 	ext{maximize } \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \quad 	ext{subject to} \quad \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b},\ \ \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} . \] A vector \(\cvec{x} \in 
R^n\) with \(\A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\) and \(\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}\) is a feasible point , and the set of all of them is the feasible region . The program is feasible if it has a feasible point and infeasible otherwise. It is unbounded if it is feasible and \(\cvec{c}	p\cvec{x}\) takes arbitrarily large values on the feasible region. A feasible \(\cvec{x}^{\star}\) is an optimal solution if \(\cvec{c}	p\cvec{x}^{\star} \ge \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x}\) for every feasible \(\cvec{x}\) , and then \(\cvec{c}	p\cvec{x}^{\star}\) is the optimal value .

title: Example (The workshop problem, drawn)
content: Find the optimal solution of the workshop problem, and explain why it is optimal.

title: Example (Capacities on every street)
content: Suppose street \(4 \to 1\) is open again, but every street can carry at most \(35\) cars per minute. What is the smallest flow the diagonal street \(1 \to 3\) can carry, and how would you convince someone that it cannot be smaller?

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Write down the dual of: maximize \(2x_1 + x_2\) subject to \(x_1 + x_2 \le 3\) , \(x_1 - x_2 \le 1\) , \(\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}\) . State weak duality and strong duality. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if (P) is infeasible, then (D) is unbounded. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if (P) is feasible and \(\cvec{c}\tp\cvec{x} \le 100\) for every feasible \(\cvec{x}\) , then (P) has an optimal solution. At an optimal pair \(\cvec{x}, \cvec{y}\) , suppose \(x_2 > 0\) . What does complementary slackness say about the second constraint of (D)?

title: Exercise (B1: Solve and certify)
content: Consider: maximize \(x_1 + 2x_2\) subject to \[ x_1 + x_2 \le 5, \qquad -x_1 + x_2 \le 1, \qquad 2x_1 - x_2 \le 4, \qquad \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0} . \] Sketch the feasible region and guess an optimal solution. Write down the dual, and use complementary slackness to find a candidate dual solution. Prove that both candidates are optimal, and state the optimal value.

title: Exercise (B2: Which case?)
content: For each program, write down its dual, and determine which of the four cases of @thm-strong-duality occurs. Justify your answer, giving the optimal values where they exist. Maximize \(x_1 + x_2\) subject to \(x_1 - x_2 \le 1\) , \(\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}\) . Maximize \(-x_1\) subject to \(x_1 \le 2\) , \(-x_1 \le -1\) , \(x_1 \ge 0\) . Maximize \(x_1\) subject to \(x_1 + x_2 \le -1\) , \(\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}\) .

title: Exercise (B3: A network with one flow)
content: In the traffic network of this section, close street \(4 \to 1\) and give every other street a capacity of \(30\) cars per minute. Show that there is exactly one feasible flow. For its diagonal flow \(f_5 = 30\) , give a certificate, in the style of @exm-traffic-lp , that \(f_5 \ge 30\) for every feasible flow, and one that \(f_5 \le 30\) .

title: Exercise (C1: The dual of the dual)
content: Rewrite (D) as a program in the inequality form of @def-linear-program , with data \((-\A\tp, -\cvec{c}, -\cvec{b})\) . Show that the dual of that program, rewritten as a maximization, is (P). Deduce part (c) of @thm-strong-duality from part (b).

title: Exercise (C2: Free variables)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R)\) , \(\cvec{b} \in 
R^m\) , \(\cvec{c} \in 
R^n\) , and consider the program with no sign constraint on \(\cvec{x}\) : \[ 	ext{(P}_{	ext{free}}	ext{)}\qquad 	ext{maximize } \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \ 	ext{ subject to } \ \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b} . \] Prove weak duality between (P \(_{	ext{free}}\) ) and (D \(_{	ext{eq}}\) ): minimize \(\cvec{b}	p\cvec{y}\) subject to \(\A	p\cvec{y} = \cvec{c}\) , \(\cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0}\) . Writing \(\cvec{x} = \cvec{u} - \cvec{v}\) with \(\cvec{u}, \cvec{v} \ge \cvec{0}\) , show that (P \(_{	ext{free}}\) ) has the same values as an inequality-form program whose dual is (D \(_{	ext{eq}}\) ). Deduce that if both are feasible, both have optimal solutions with equal values.

title: Theorem 18.6.5 (Complementary Slackness)
content: Let \(\cvec{x}\) be feasible for (P) and \(\cvec{y}\) feasible for (D). Then \(\cvec{x}\) and \(\cvec{y}\) are both optimal if and only if for every \(i\) , \(y_i > 0\) implies \((\A\cvec{x})_i = b_i\) ; and for every \(j\) , \(x_j > 0\) implies \((\A\tp\cvec{y})_j = c_j\) .

title: Theorem 18.6.3 (Strong Duality for Linear Programs)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R)\) , \(\cvec{b} \in 
R^m\) , and \(\cvec{c} \in 
R^n\) , and let (P) and (D) be as in @def-linear-program and @def-dual-program . If (P) and (D) are both feasible, then both have optimal solutions, and their optimal values are equal : there are feasible \(\cvec{x}^{\star}\) and \(\cvec{y}^{\star}\) with \(\cvec{c}	p\cvec{x}^{\star} = \cvec{b}	p\cvec{y}^{\star}\) . If (P) is feasible and (D) is infeasible, then (P) is unbounded. If (D) is feasible and (P) is infeasible, then (D) is unbounded.

title: Theorem 18.6.1 (Weak Duality)
content: If \(\cvec{x}\) is feasible for (P) and \(\cvec{y}\) is feasible for (D), then \[ \cvec{c}\tp\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\tp\cvec{y} . \]

title: Definition 18.7.1 (Mixed Strategy)
page: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content: In the game with payoff matrix \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(\nR)\) , a mixed strategy for Row is a vector \(\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m\) , a mixed strategy for Column is a vector \(\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n\) , and the expected payoff is \[ \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_i\,a_{ij}\,y_j . \]

title: Definition 18.7.2 (Value and Optimal Strategies)
page: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content: The number \(v\) of @thm-von-neumann-minimax is the value of the game with payoff matrix \(\A\) , written \(v(\A)\) . A strategy \(\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m\) is optimal for Row if it guarantees the value, \(\min_{\cvec{y}}\cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y} = v(\A)\) , and \(\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n\) is optimal for Column if \(\max_{\cvec{x}}\cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y} = v(\A)\) .

title: Example (A game with an unused column)
page: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content: Find the value and optimal strategies for the game with payoff matrix \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 4 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . \]

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content: Define the standard simplex \(\Delta_n\) , a mixed strategy, and the value of a matrix game. State von Neumann’s minimax theorem. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: every matrix game has a saddle point in pure strategies. Explain in two sentences why \(\max_{x}\min_{y} f(x, y) \le \min_{y}\max_{x} f(x, y)\) for every function \(f\) for which the extrema exist. Name the mechanism that produces the equality in @thm-courant-fischer and the one that produces it in @thm-von-neumann-minimax .

title: Exercise (B1: A two-by-two game)
page: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . Show that the game has no saddle point in pure strategies. Find the value and optimal strategies for both players, and verify the saddle inequality @eq-minimax-saddle .

title: Exercise (B2: A saddle point)
page: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) , the second game of this section. Show that \(\cvec{x}^{\star} = \cvec{e}_1\) , \(\cvec{y}^{\star} = \cvec{e}_2\) satisfy @eq-minimax-saddle with \(v = 1\) , and deduce the value of the game.

title: Exercise (B3: Many optimal strategies)
page: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . Show that \(v(\A) = 1\) . Find all optimal strategies for Row. Show that Column has exactly one optimal strategy.

title: Exercise (C1: Symmetric games)
page: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) be skew-symmetric, \(\A\tp = -\A\) . Such a game is symmetric : the two players have the same options, and swapping their roles swaps the payoff’s sign. Prove that \(\cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{x} = 0\) for every \(\cvec{x} \in \nR^n\) , and deduce that \(v(\A) = 0\) . Prove that \(\cvec{x}\) is optimal for Row if and only if it is optimal for Column. In rock–paper–scissors, with the pure strategies in that order and payoff \(1\) for a win, \(-1\) for a loss, and \(0\) for a tie, \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . \] Prove that the uniform strategy \(\tfrac13\1\) is the only optimal strategy.

title: Exercise (C2: The value depends continuously on the payoffs)
page: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content: For \(\A, \B \in M_{m \times n}(\nR)\) , put \(\varepsilon = \max_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij} - b_{ij}\rvert\) . Prove that \(\lvert v(\A) - v(\B)\rvert \le \varepsilon\) . Prove also that if \(a_{ij} \ge b_{ij}\) for all \(i, j\) , then \(v(\A) \ge v(\B)\) , and that \(v(\A + c\J) = v(\A) + c\) for every real \(c\) .

title: Lemma 18.7.1 (Max–Min Never Exceeds Min–Max)
page: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets and \(f \colon X \times Y \to \nR\) a function for which the extrema below exist. Then \[ \max_{x \in X}\ \min_{y \in Y}\ f(x, y) \ \le\ \min_{y \in Y}\ \max_{x \in X}\ f(x, y) . \]

title: Lemma 18.7.2 (A Pure Best Response Exists)
page: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(\nR)\) . For every \(\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m\) , \[ \min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n} \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y} = \min_{1 \le j \le n} (\A\tp\cvec{x})_j , \] and the minimum on the left is attained at \(\cvec{y} = \cvec{e}_j\) for any \(j\) attaining the minimum on the right. Likewise, for every \(\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n\) , \(\max_{\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m}\cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y} = \max_{1 \le i \le m}(\A\cvec{y})_i\) , attained at a vertex \(\cvec{e}_i\) .

title: Theorem 18.7.3 (Von Neumann’s Minimax Theorem)
page: 18.7 Matrix Games and the Minimax Theorem
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(\nR)\) . There are \(\cvec{x}^{\star} \in \Delta_m\) , \(\cvec{y}^{\star} \in \Delta_n\) , and \(v \in \nR\) such that \[ \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y}^{\star} \ \le\ v \ \le\ \cvec{x}^{\star\top}\A\cvec{y} \qquad \text{for all } \cvec{x} \in \Delta_m,\ \cvec{y} \in \Delta_n . \] {#eq-minimax-saddle} Consequently \[ \max_{\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m}\ \min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n}\ \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y} \ =\ v\ =\ \min_{\cvec{y} \in \Delta_n}\ \max_{\cvec{x} \in \Delta_m}\ \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{y} , \] where the outer maximum is attained at \(\cvec{x}^{\star}\) and the outer minimum at \(\cvec{y}^{\star}\) .

title: Corollary 18.8.6 (Linear Functions Peak at Extreme Points)
content: Let \(K \subseteq V\) be a nonempty compact convex set and \(\elem{a} \in V\) . Then the maximum of \(\elem{x} \mapsto \inner{\elem{x}}{\elem{a}}\) over \(K\) exists and is attained at an extreme point of \(K\) . The same holds for the minimum.

title: Definition 18.8.3 (Density Matrix)
content: A density matrix of size \(n\) is a real symmetric matrix \(\X \in M_n(\nR)\) with \(\X \succeq \O\) and \(\tr\X = 1\) . We write \(\cD_n\) for the set of them.

title: Definition 18.8.4 (Doubly Stochastic Matrix)
content: A matrix \(\M \in M_n(\nR)\) is doubly stochastic if all its entries are nonnegative and every row and every column adds up to \(1\) . We write \(\Omega_n\) for the set of doubly stochastic \(n \times n\) matrices.

title: Definition 18.8.1 (Extreme Point)
content: Let \(C \subseteq V\) be a convex set. A point \(\elem{x} \in C\) is an extreme point of \(C\) if, whenever \(\elem{x} = t\elem{y} + (1 - t)\elem{z}\) with \(\elem{y}, \elem{z} \in C\) and \(0 < t < 1\) strictly , then \(\elem{y} = \elem{z} = \elem{x}\) . The set of extreme points of \(C\) is written \(\operatorname{ext} C\) .

title: Definition 18.8.2 (Face)
content: Let \(C \subseteq V\) be convex. A face of \(C\) is a convex subset \(F \subseteq C\) such that, whenever \(t\elem{y} + (1 - t)\elem{z} \in F\) with \(\elem{y}, \elem{z} \in C\) and \(0 < t < 1\) , both \(\elem{y}\) and \(\elem{z}\) lie in \(F\) .

title: Example (A double cone over a circle)
content:
In \(
R^3\) , let \(\Gamma = \{(1, 0, 0) + (\cvec{u}, 0) : \cvec{u} \in 
R^2,\ 
orm{\cvec{u}} = 1\}\) be the circle of radius \(1\) centered at \((1, 0, 0)\) in the plane \(x_3 = 0\) , where \((\cvec{u}, 0) = (u_1, u_2, 0)\) ; it passes through the origin, at \(\cvec{u} = (-1, 0)\) . Let \(\cvec{p} = (0, 0, 1)\) , \(\cvec{q} = (0, 0, -1)\) , \(S = \Gamma \cup \{\cvec{p}, \cvec{q}\}\) , and \(K = \conv S\) . Show that \(K\) is compact and convex, that \[ \operatorname{ext} K = (\Gamma \setminus \{\cvec{0}\}) \cup \{\cvec{p}, \cvec{q}\} , \] and that this set is not closed.

title: Example (The diamond, the cube, and the sphere)
content: In \(\nR^n\) with \(n \ge 1\) , show that: \(\operatorname{ext} B_1 = \{\pm\cvec{e}_1, \dots, \pm\cvec{e}_n\}\) , \(2n\) points; \(\operatorname{ext} B_\infty = \{\cvec{s} : \text{every } s_i = \pm 1\}\) , the \(2^n\) sign vectors; \(\operatorname{ext} B_2 = \{\cvec{x} : \norm{\cvec{x}}_2 = 1\}\) , the whole unit sphere.

title: Example (The largest eigenvalue as a linear maximum)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric. Show that \(\lambda_1(\A) = \max\{\tr(\A\X) : \X \in \cD_n\}\) , and find the maximum for \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the definition of an extreme point of a convex set \(C \subseteq V\) . True or false: every boundary point of a compact convex set in \(\nR^2\) is an extreme point. Justify your answer. True or false: there is a nonempty closed convex subset of \(\nR^2\) with no extreme points. Justify your answer. State @thm-minkowski-extreme , and name the two facts from Chapter 16’s introduction that its proof uses. True or false: if \(K = \conv S\) with \(S\) finite, then every point of \(S\) is an extreme point of \(K\) . Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: Finding extreme points)
content: Determine the extreme points of each of the following convex subsets of \(\nR^2\) . Justify your answer. \(\conv\{(0,0), (4,0), (0,2), (2,1), (1,1)\}\) . \(P = \{(x, y) : x^2 \le y \le 1\}\) . The strip \(\{(x, y) : 0 \le y \le 1\}\) . Hint: for (b), use @prp-exposed-face (b) with a tangent line.

title: Exercise (B2: A density matrix split into pure pieces)
content: Let \[ \X = \begin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 1/4 \\ 1/4 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Y = \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Z = \begin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix} . \] For each of the three matrices, decide whether it lies in \(\cD_2\) , and if so whether it is an extreme point. Write \(\X\) as a convex combination of two extreme points of \(\cD_2\) .

title: Exercise (B3: A doubly stochastic matrix from permutations)
content: Let \[ \M = \frac16\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} . \] Check that \(\M \in \Omega_3\) . Write \(\M\) as a convex combination of three permutation matrices. Hence explain why \(\M\) is not an extreme point of \(\Omega_3\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Deleting an extreme point)
content: Let \(C \subseteq V\) be convex and \(\elem{x} \in C\) . Prove that \(\elem{x}\) is an extreme point of \(C\) if and only if \(C \setminus \{\elem{x}\}\) is convex. Deduce that \(\elem{x}\) is an extreme point of \(C\) if and only if \(\elem{x} \notin \conv(C \setminus \{\elem{x}\})\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Every contraction is an average of orthogonal matrices)
content:
Let \(\cB = \{\A \in M_n(
R) : 
orm{\A}_2 \le 1\}\) , the unit ball of the operator \(2\) -norm ( @def-operator-norm ), so that \(\A \in \cB\) exactly when \(
orm{\A\cvec{x}} \le 
orm{\cvec{x}}\) for every \(\cvec{x} \in 
R^n\) . Prove that every orthogonal matrix is an extreme point of \(\cB\) . Prove that every \(\A \in \cB\) that is not orthogonal is not an extreme point of \(\cB\) . Deduce that every \(\A \in \cB\) is a convex combination of orthogonal matrices. Hint for (b): use the singular value decomposition ( @thm-svd ) and change only the smallest singular value.

title: Exercise (C3: The corners of the Loewner interval)
content: Let \(\cE = \{\X \in M_n(\nR) : \X\tp = \X,\ \O \preceq \X \preceq \I\}\) , where \(\X \preceq \I\) means \(\I - \X \succeq \O\) ( @def-loewner-order ). Prove that every symmetric \(\P\) with \(\P^2 = \P\) , that is, every orthogonal projection, is an extreme point of \(\cE\) . Prove that no other point of \(\cE\) is extreme. Deduce that every \(\X \in \cE\) is a convex combination of orthogonal projections, and give such a combination for \(\X = \diag(\frac12, \frac14)\) . Hint for (a): use @lem-psd-form-zero twice, once on \(\ker\P\) and once on \(\im\P\) .

title: Lemma 18.8.1 (The Midpoint Test)
content: Let \(C \subseteq V\) be convex and \(\elem{x} \in C\) . Then \(\elem{x}\) is an extreme point of \(C\) if and only if, whenever \(\elem{x} = \frac12(\elem{y} + \elem{z})\) with \(\elem{y}, \elem{z} \in C\) , we have \(\elem{y} = \elem{z}\) .

title: Lemma 18.8.3 (Extreme Points of a Face)
content: Let \(C \subseteq V\) be convex and \(F\) a face of \(C\) . Then \(\operatorname{ext} F = F \cap \operatorname{ext} C\) . In particular an extreme point of a face is an extreme point of \(C\) .

title: Lemma 18.8.7 (A Zero of the Form Is a Null Vector)
content: Let \(\B \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric with \(\B \succeq \O\) , and let \(\cvec{y} \in \nR^n\) satisfy \(\cvec{y}\tp\B\cvec{y} = 0\) . Then \(\B\cvec{y} = \cvec{0}\) .

title: Proposition 18.8.4 (Supporting Slices Are Faces)
content: Let \(C \subseteq V\) be convex, let \(\elem{w} \in V\) and \(\alpha \in \nR\) , and suppose \(\inner{\elem{w}}{\elem{x}} \le \alpha\) for every \(\elem{x} \in C\) . Then: \(F = \{\elem{x} \in C : \inner{\elem{w}}{\elem{x}} = \alpha\}\) is a face of \(C\) ; if \(F\) is a single point \(\{\elem{c}\}\) , then \(\elem{c}\) is an extreme point of \(C\) .

title: Proposition 18.8.2 (Extreme Points of a Hull Come From the Generators)
content: Let \(S \subseteq V\) be any set. Then \(\operatorname{ext}(\conv S) \subseteq S\) .

title: Proposition 18.8.9 (Permutation Matrices Are Extreme)
content: Every permutation matrix is an extreme point of \(\Omega_n\) .

title: Theorem 18.8.8 (Extreme Points of the Density Matrices)
content: For \(n \ge 1\) , \[ \operatorname{ext}\cD_n = \{\cvec{x}\cvec{x}\tp : \cvec{x} \in \nR^n,\ \norm{\cvec{x}} = 1\} , \] the orthogonal projections of rank one. Every \(\X \in \cD_n\) is a convex combination of at most \(n\) of them.

title: Theorem 18.8.5 (Minkowski’s Theorem)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let \(K \subseteq V\) be a compact convex set. Then \[ K = \conv(\operatorname{ext} K) . \] In particular, a nonempty compact convex set has at least one extreme point.

title: Corollary 18.9.3 (A Polyhedron Has Finitely Many Vertices)
content: Let \(P = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\}\) with \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(\nR)\) . Every vertex of \(P\) is the unique solution of \(\A_J\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}_J\) for some set \(J\) of \(n\) row indices with \(\A_J\) invertible. In particular \(P\) has at most \(\binom{m}{n}\) vertices.

title: Definition 18.9.3 (Active Set, Basic Feasible Point)
content: Let \(P = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\}\) and \(\cvec{x} \in P\) . The active set of \(\cvec{x}\) is \(I(\cvec{x}) = \{i : \cvec{a}_i\tp\cvec{x} = b_i\}\) , the indices of the inequalities that hold with equality at \(\cvec{x}\) . The point \(\cvec{x}\) is a basic feasible point of the system if among the active rows \(\{\cvec{a}_i : i \in I(\cvec{x})\}\) there are \(n\) linearly independent ones.

title: Definition 18.9.4 (Polyhedral Cone)
content:
A polyhedral cone in \(
R^n\) is a set of the form \(C = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{0}\}\) for some \(m \ge 0\) and \(\A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R)\) .

title: Definition 18.9.2 (Polyhedron)
content:
A polyhedron in \(
R^n\) is a set of the form \[ P = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\} \] for some \(m \ge 0\) , \(\A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
R)\) , and \(\cvec{b} \in 
R^m\) ; that is, the intersection of finitely many sets \(\{\cvec{x} : \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} \le b_i\}\) . An extreme point of a polyhedron or of a polytope ( @def-extreme-point ) is called a vertex .

title: Definition 18.9.1 (Polytope)
content: A polytope in \(\nR^n\) is a set of the form \(\conv\{\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_k\}\) for finitely many points \(\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_k \in \nR^n\) , \(k \ge 0\) .

title: Example (The cube and the cross-polytope)
content: For \(n \ge 1\) , describe \(B_\infty\) and \(B_1\) both as polytopes and as polyhedra, and find their vertices from the inequalities by @thm-vertices-basic-feasible .

title: Example (A triangle, both ways)
content: Let \(Q = \conv\{(0,0), (3,0), (0,3), (1,1)\} \subseteq \nR^2\) . Find a system of inequalities describing \(Q\) , and then recover the vertices of \(Q\) from it.

title: Example (The vertices of a quadrilateral)
content: Find the vertices of \[ P = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^2 : x_1 \ge 0,\ x_2 \ge 0,\ x_1 + 2x_2 \le 4,\ 3x_1 + x_2 \le 6\} , \] and the maximum of \(\varphi(\cvec{x}) = x_1 + x_2\) over \(P\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the definitions of a polytope and of a polyhedron in \(\nR^n\) . True or false: every polyhedron is a polytope. Justify your answer. True or false: the intersection of two polytopes in \(\nR^n\) is a polytope. Justify your answer. State the criterion of @thm-vertices-basic-feasible for a point of \(\{\cvec{x} : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\}\) to be a vertex. True or false: every inequality produced by Fourier–Motzkin elimination ( @lem-fourier-motzkin ) is needed to describe the projection. Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: Vertices of a pentagon)
content: Find all vertices of \[ P = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^2 : x_1 \ge 0,\ x_2 \ge 0,\ x_1 + x_2 \le 4,\ x_1 - x_2 \le 2,\ -x_1 + 2x_2 \le 5\} , \] and the maximum of \(2x_1 + 3x_2\) over \(P\) . Hence write \(P\) as a polytope.

title: Exercise (B2: Inequalities for a quadrilateral)
content: Use Fourier–Motzkin elimination to find a system of inequalities describing the quadrilateral \[ Q = \conv\{(0,0), (2,0), (2,1), (0,2)\} . \] Hence find the vertices of \(Q\) . Hint: substitute away \(t_1, t_2, t_4\) and keep \(s = t_3\) , the weight of \((2,1)\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Which of these are vertices?)
content: Let \(P = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^3 : \cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0},\ x_1 + x_2 + x_3 \le 3,\ x_1 + x_2 \le 2\}\) . Determine which of the following points are vertices of \(P\) . Justify your answer. \((0, 2, 1)\) \((1, 1, 1)\) \((0, 0, 3)\) \((3, 0, 0)\) \((1, 0, 0)\)

title: Exercise (C1: Unbounded polyhedra)
content:
Let \(P = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\}\) be a nonempty polyhedron, and let \(C = \{(\cvec{x}, t) \in 
R^n 	imes 
R : \A\cvec{x} - t\cvec{b} \le \cvec{0},\ -t \le 0\}\) . Prove that \(\cvec{x} \in P\) if and only if \((\cvec{x}, 1) \in C\) . By @thm-minkowski-weyl (b), \(C\) is generated by finitely many vectors \((\cvec{w}_j, t_j)\) , \(j = 1, \dots, k\) . Prove that every \(t_j \ge 0\) , and that \[ P = \conv\{\cvec{w}_j/t_j : t_j > 0\} + \Bigl\{\sum_{t_j = 0} c_j\cvec{w}_j : c_j \ge 0\Bigr\} , \] the set of sums of a point of the polytope and a point of the cone. So every nonempty polyhedron is a polytope plus a finitely generated cone. Check the statement for \(P = \{\cvec{x} \in 
R^2 : x_1 \ge 0,\ 0 \le x_2 \le 1\}\) , with the polytope \(\conv\{(0,0), (0,1)\}\) and the cone generated by \(\cvec{e}_1\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Linear images of polyhedra)
content:
Let \(\M \in M_{p 	imes n}(
R)\) . Prove that if \(P \subseteq 
R^n\) is a polyhedron, then \(\M(P) = \{\M\cvec{x} : \cvec{x} \in P\}\) is a polyhedron in \(
R^p\) , and that if \(P\) is a polyhedral cone, so is \(\M(P)\) . Prove that if \(Q\) is a polytope, then \(\M(Q)\) is a polytope, directly from @def-polytope . Deduce that a linear image of a polyhedral cone is closed. Why does this not contradict the existence of a closed convex cone with a nonclosed linear image?

content:
Let \(\A \in M_{m 	imes n}(

Deduce that a vertex of \(P\) has at most \(ank \A\) positive entries. Find the vertices of \(P = \{\cvec{x} \in

title: Lemma 18.9.4 (Fourier–Motzkin Elimination)
content:
Let \(P = \{(\cvec{x}, s) \in 
R^{n} 	imes 
R : \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} + c_is \le b_i 	ext{ for } i = 1, \dots, m\}\) . Split the indices by the sign of the coefficient of \(s\) : \(I_+ = \{i : c_i > 0\}\) , \(I_- = \{i : c_i < 0\}\) , \(I_0 = \{i : c_i = 0\}\) . Then \(\pi(P)\) is the set of \(\cvec{x} \in 
R^n\) satisfying \[  egin{aligned} \cvec{a}_i	p\cvec{x} &\le b_i && 	ext{for } i \in I_0 , \ (c_i\cvec{a}_j - c_j\cvec{a}_i)	p\cvec{x} &\le c_ib_j - c_jb_i && 	ext{for } i \in I_+,\ j \in I_- . \end{aligned} \] In particular \(\pi(P)\) is a polyhedron, and if every \(b_i = 0\) , every right-hand side above is \(0\) .

title: Proposition 18.9.1 (Polyhedra Are Closed and Convex)
content: Every polyhedron \(P = \{\cvec{x} : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\}\) is convex and closed.

title: Theorem 18.9.5 (Minkowski–Weyl Theorem)
content: A subset of \(\nR^n\) is a polytope if and only if it is a bounded polyhedron. A subset of \(\nR^n\) is a finitely generated cone if and only if it is a polyhedral cone.

title: Theorem 18.9.2 (Vertices Are Basic Feasible Points)
content: Let \(P = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\}\) and \(\cvec{x} \in P\) . Then \(\cvec{x}\) is a vertex of \(P\) if and only if \(\cvec{x}\) is a basic feasible point.

title: Corollary 18.10.4 (The Top Eigenvalue Sums Are Convex)
content: Let \(1 \le k \le n\) . On the real vector space of Hermitian \(n \times n\) matrices over \(F\) , the function \[ s_k(\A) = \lambda_1(\A) + \dots + \lambda_k(\A) \] is convex. In particular \(\A \mapsto \lambda_1(\A)\) is convex, and \(\A \mapsto \lambda_n(\A)\) is concave.

title: Definition 18.10.1 (Convex Function)
content:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space \(V\) , and let \(f \colon C 	o 
R\) . Then \(f\) is convex if \[ f igl(t\elem{x} + (1-t)\elem{y} igr) \ \le\ tf(\elem{x}) + (1-t)f(\elem{y}) \] for all \(\elem{x}, \elem{y} \in C\) and all real \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\) . It is strictly convex if the inequality is strict whenever \(\elem{x} 
e \elem{y}\) and \(0 < t < 1\) . It is concave , or strictly concave , if \(-f\) is convex, or strictly convex. The epigraph of \(f\) is the subset of the real vector space \(V 	imes 
R\) , with componentwise operations, \[ \operatorname{epi} f = \{ (\elem{x}, s) \in V 	imes 
R : \elem{x} \in C,\ s \ge f(\elem{x}) \} . \]

title: Exercise (C1: Subadditive and homogeneous)
content: Let \(g \colon V \to \nR\) be positively homogeneous : \(g(t\elem{x}) = tg(\elem{x})\) for every \(\elem{x} \in V\) and every real \(t \ge 0\) . Prove that \(g\) is convex if and only if \(g(\elem{x} + \elem{y}) \le g(\elem{x}) + g(\elem{y})\) for all \(\elem{x}, \elem{y} \in V\) . Deduce that every norm on \(\nR^n\) is convex, and that @cor-ky-fan-subadditive and @cor-eigenvalue-sums-convex are equivalent statements about \(s_k\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Tangent lines)
content: Let \(I \subseteq \nR\) be an open interval and let \(g \colon I \to \nR\) be differentiable and convex. Prove that \(g(y) \ge g(x) + g'(x)(y - x)\) for all \(x, y \in I\) . Deduce that \(g(y) = \max_{x \in I}\bigl(g(x) + g'(x)(y - x)\bigr)\) for every \(y \in I\) : a differentiable convex function is the maximum of its tangent lines. Hint: in (a), apply the definition to the points \(x\) and \(y\) with weight \(s\) on \(y\) , and let \(s \to 0\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Where a convex function is largest)
content: Let \(f \colon \nR^n \to \nR\) be convex, and let \(P\) be the convex hull \(\conv\{\cvec{x}_1, \dots, \cvec{x}_m\}\) . Prove that \(\max_{\cvec{x} \in P}f(\cvec{x}) = \max_i f(\cvec{x}_i)\) . Let \(f(x, y) = x^2 - xy + y^2\) and let \(P\) be the triangle \(\conv\{(2, 0), (0, 2), (-2, -2)\}\) . Find the maximum and the minimum of \(f\) on \(P\) , and say where each is attained.

title: Lemma 18.10.5 (Increasing Derivative Gives Convexity)
content: Let \(I \subseteq \nR\) be an open interval and let \(g \colon I \to \nR\) be differentiable. If \(g'\) is increasing on \(I\) , then \(g\) is convex; if \(g'\) is strictly increasing, then \(g\) is strictly convex. In particular, if \(g\) is twice differentiable with \(g'' \ge 0\) on \(I\) , then \(g\) is convex, and if \(g'' > 0\) on \(I\) , then \(g\) is strictly convex.

title: Proposition 18.10.1 (Convex Function, Convex Epigraph)
content: Let \(C \subseteq V\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f \colon C \to \nR\) . Then \(f\) is convex if and only if \(\operatorname{epi} f\) is a convex subset of \(V \times \nR\) .

title: Proposition 18.10.3 (A Supremum of Affine Functions Is Convex)
content: Let \(C \subseteq V\) be nonempty and convex, and let \((a_i)_{i \in I}\) be a nonempty family of affine functions on \(V\) . Suppose that for every \(\elem{x} \in C\) the set \(\{a_i(\elem{x}) : i \in I\}\) is bounded above, and put \[ g(\elem{x}) = \sup_{i \in I} a_i(\elem{x}) \qquad (\elem{x} \in C) . \] Then \(g \colon C \to \nR\) is convex.

title: Theorem 18.10.7 (Convex Functions Are Continuous)
content:
Let \(U \subseteq 
R^n\) be a nonempty open convex set and let \(f \colon U 	o 
R\) be convex. Then \(f\) is continuous on \(U\) . More precisely, for every \(\cvec{a} \in U\) there are \(\delta > 0\) and \(L \ge 0\) with \[ \lvert f(\cvec{a} + \cvec{h}) - f(\cvec{a})vert \le L
orm{\cvec{h}} \qquad 	ext{whenever } 
orm{\cvec{h}} \le \delta . \]

title: Theorem 18.10.6 (Convexity from the Hessian)
content: Let \(U \subseteq \nR^n\) be a nonempty open convex set, and let \(f \colon U \to \nR\) be twice continuously differentiable. \(f\) is convex on \(U\) if and only if \(\H_f(\cvec{a}) \succeq \O\) for every \(\cvec{a} \in U\) . If \(\H_f(\cvec{a}) \succ \O\) for every \(\cvec{a} \in U\) , then \(f\) is strictly convex on \(U\) .

title: Theorem 18.10.2 (Jensen’s Inequality)
content: Let \(C \subseteq V\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f \colon C \to \nR\) be convex. Let \(\elem{x}_1, \dots, \elem{x}_m \in C\) , and let \(w_1, \dots, w_m \ge 0\) with \(w_1 + \dots + w_m = 1\) . Then \(\sum_i w_i\elem{x}_i \in C\) and \[ f\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{m} w_i\elem{x}_i\Bigr) \ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^{m} w_if(\elem{x}_i) . \] If \(f\) is strictly convex and every \(w_i > 0\) , equality holds only when \(\elem{x}_1 = \elem{x}_2 = \dots = \elem{x}_m\) .

content: Let \(x_1, \dots, x_n > 0\) . Prove that \[ \frac{n}{\frac{1}{x_1} + \dots + \frac{1}{x_n}} \ \le\ \frac{x_1 + \dots + x_n}{n} , \] with equality if and only if \(x_1 = \dots = x_n\) .

title: Lemma 18.11.1 (Exponential and Logarithm)
content: \(e^{s} > 0\) for every real \(s\) , and \(s \mapsto e^s\) is strictly increasing and strictly convex on \(\nR\) . For every real \(y > 0\) there is exactly one real \(s\) with \(e^s = y\) ; write \(s = \log y\) . \(\log \colon (0, \infty) \to \nR\) is strictly increasing and strictly concave , with \(\log(xy) = \log x + \log y\) and \(\log 1 = 0\) .

title: Lemma 18.11.3 (Young’s Inequality)
content: Let \(p, q > 1\) with \(\frac1p + \frac1q = 1\) . Then for all real \(a, b \ge 0\) , \[ ab \ \le\ \frac{a^p}{p} + \frac{b^q}{q} , \] with equality if and only if \(a^p = b^q\) .

title: Theorem 18.11.2 (Weighted Arithmetic–Geometric Mean Inequality)
content: Let \(t_1, \dots, t_m \ge 0\) , and let \(w_1, \dots, w_m > 0\) with \(w_1 + \dots + w_m = 1\) . Then \[ t_1^{w_1}t_2^{w_2}\cdots t_m^{w_m} \ \le\ w_1t_1 + w_2t_2 + \dots + w_mt_m , \] with equality if and only if \(t_1 = t_2 = \dots = t_m\) .

title: Definition 19.1.1 (Entrywise Order; Nonnegative and Positive Matrices)
content: Let \(\A = (a_{ij})\) and \(\B = (b_{ij})\) be real \(m \times n\) matrices. \(\A \ge \B\) means \(a_{ij} \ge b_{ij}\) for every \(i, j\) , and \(\A > \B\) means \(a_{ij} > b_{ij}\) for every \(i, j\) . We write \(\B \le \A\) and \(\B < \A\) for the same statements. \(\A\) is nonnegative if \(\A \ge \O\) , and positive if \(\A > \O\) , where \(\O\) is the zero matrix of the same shape. For a complex \(m \times n\) matrix \(\M = (m_{ij})\) , the entrywise absolute value is the real matrix \(\lvert\M\rvert \coloneqq (\lvert m_{ij}\rvert)\) . Vectors are the case \(n = 1\) , so \(\cvec{x} \ge \cvec{0}\) , \(\cvec{x} > \cvec{0}\) and \(\lvert\cvec{x}\rvert = (\lvert x_1\rvert, \dots, \lvert x_n\rvert)\) have the same meaning as in Chapter 18 §05.

title: Definition 19.1.2 (Perron Root, Perron Vector)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) be positive. The number \(\rho(\A)\) is the Perron root of \(\A\) . The Perron vector of \(\A\) is the unique \(\cvec{v} > \cvec{0}\) with \(\A\cvec{v} = \rho(\A)\cvec{v}\) and \(v_1 + \dots + v_n = 1\) . The left Perron vector of \(\A\) is the unique \(\cvec{w} > \cvec{0}\) with \(\cvec{w}\tp\A = \rho(\A)\cvec{w}\tp\) and \(\cvec{w}\tp\cvec{v} = 1\) , where \(\cvec{v}\) is the Perron vector.

title: Example (A positive 3 \times 3 matrix)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) . Find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and its positive left eigenvector.

title: Example (Perron’s theorem for Chapter 9’s first example)
content: Check each part of @thm-perron for \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Example (Enlarging one entry)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . Compute both spectral radii and compare with @prp-spectral-radius-monotone .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define what it means for a real matrix to be nonnegative and to be positive , and define \(\lvert\M\rvert\) for a complex matrix \(\M\) . State @thm-perron . True or false: a positive symmetric matrix is positive definite. Justify your answer. True or false: a positive matrix has no negative eigenvalue. Justify your answer. True or false: if \(\O \le \A \le \B\) and \(\A \ne \B\) , then \(\rho(\A) < \rho(\B)\) . Justify your answer. In the proof of @thm-perron , which step uses compactness, and why is the quotient \(\min_i(\A\cvec{x})_i/x_i\) not maximized directly?

title: Exercise (B1: A Perron vector by hand)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) . Find the eigenvalues of \(\A\) , its Perron root, Perron vector, and left Perron vector. Check that no eigenvector for the other eigenvalues is nonnegative.

title: Exercise (B2: Which order?)
content: For each matrix, decide whether it is nonnegative, whether it is positive, and whether it is positive definite. Justify your answers, and say whether @thm-perron applies. \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\)

title: Exercise (B3: Bounds from the smallest and largest entry)
content: Show that \(\rho(c\J) = nc\) for every real \(c \ge 0\) , where \(\J\) is the \(n \times n\) all-ones matrix. Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) with \(a \le a_{ij} \le b\) for all \(i, j\) , where \(0 \le a \le b\) . Prove that \(na \le \rho(\A) \le nb\) . Hence bound \(\rho(\A)\) for \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) , and compare with its exact value.

title: Exercise (C1: Symmetry passes to the Perron vector)
content: Let \(\A > \O\) be \(n \times n\) with Perron vector \(\cvec{v}\) , and let \(\P\) be a permutation matrix with \(\P\tp\A\P = \A\) . Prove that \(\P\cvec{v} = \cvec{v}\) . Deduce that the Perron vector of \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) has equal first and second entries, and find it. Deduce that if \(\A > \O\) commutes with the cyclic permutation matrix of \(1 \to 2 \to \dots \to n \to 1\) , then its Perron vector is \(\frac1n\1\) . Hint: for (a), \(\P\cvec{v}\) is a positive vector in \(\Delta_n\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Every conclusion fails for some nonnegative matrix)
content: For each part of @thm-perron , (a) to (d), give a nonnegative \(2 \times 2\) matrix for which that part fails, and name the step of the proof that breaks. Then give a nonnegative matrix for which (a), (b) and (c) fail at the same time.

title: Exercise (C3: The Perron root is strictly monotone)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(\nR)\) with \(\O < \A \le \B\) and \(\A \ne \B\) . Prove that \(\rho(\A) < \rho(\B)\) . Show by an example that the conclusion fails if \(\A > \O\) is weakened to \(\A \ge \O\) . Hint: pair \(\B\cvec{v}\) with a positive left eigenvector of \(\B\) , where \(\cvec{v}\) is the Perron vector of \(\A\) .

content:

content:

title: Lemma 19.1.3 (Equality in the Triangle Inequality)
content: Let \(z_1, \dots, z_m \in \nC\) , put \(s = z_1 + \dots + z_m\) , and suppose \(\lvert s\rvert = \lvert z_1\rvert + \dots + \lvert z_m\rvert\) and \(s \ne 0\) . Then \(z_j = \lvert z_j\rvert\,c\) for every \(j\) , where \(c = s/\lvert s\rvert\) has \(\lvert c\rvert = 1\) .

content:
Let \(n \ge 1\) and let \(\A \in M_n(
