A^p(F)\) one has \(\widehat{g \circ f} = \widehat{g}\,\widehat{f}\) . For \(m = n\) , \(f\) is bijective if and only if \(\A\) is invertible, and then \[ \widehat{f^{-1}} = (\widehat{f})^{-1} =  egin{pmatrix} \A^{-1} & -\A^{-1}\cvec{b} \ \cvec{0}	p & 1 \end{pmatrix} . \]

title: Proposition 22.1.2 (The two forms of the definition agree)
content: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\) and \(\cA\) a nonempty set. Giving a map \(\cA \times \cA \to V\) satisfying (AS1) and (AS2) is the same as giving a map \(\cA \times V \to \cA\) , written \((P, \elem{v}) \mapsto P + \elem{v}\) , such that \(P + \elem{0} = P\) for every \(P \in \cA\) ; \((P + \elem{u}) + \elem{w} = P + (\elem{u} + \elem{w})\) for all \(P \in \cA\) and \(\elem{u}, \elem{w} \in V\) ; for all \(P, Q \in \cA\) there is exactly one \(\elem{v} \in V\) with \(P + \elem{v} = Q\) . The two constructions are inverse to each other.

title: Proposition 22.1.3 (Choice of Origin)
content: Let \(\cA\) be an affine space with direction space \(V\) , and let \(O \in \cA\) . Then \[ \theta_O \colon \cA \to V, \qquad \theta_O(P) = \overrightarrow{OP} , \] is a bijection with \(\theta_O(O) = \elem{0}\) , and it carries the affine structure of \(\cA\) to that of \(V\) in @exm-affine-space-basic (a): \[ \overrightarrow{PQ} = \theta_O(Q) - \theta_O(P) \qquad (P, Q \in \cA). \] If \(O' \in \cA\) is another point, then \(\theta_{O'}(P) = \theta_O(P) - \theta_O(O')\) for every \(P\) : the two identifications differ by a translation of \(V\) .

title: Theorem 22.1.6 (Composition, Inverses, and the Affine Group)
content: Let \(\cA, \cB, \cC\) be affine spaces over \(F\) , and write \(V\) and \(W\) for the direction spaces of \(\cA\) and \(\cB\) . If \(f \colon \cA \to \cB\) and \(g \colon \cB \to \cC\) are affine, then \(g \circ f\) is affine and \(\overrightarrow{g \circ f} = \vec{g} \circ \vec{f}\) . An affine \(f \colon \cA \to \cB\) is bijective if and only if \(\vec{f}\) is bijective, and then \(f^{-1}\) is affine with \(\overrightarrow{f^{-1}} = (\vec{f})^{-1}\) . The bijective affine maps \(\cA \to \cA\) form a group \(\operatorname{Aff}(\cA)\) under composition, and \(f \mapsto \vec{f}\) is a surjective group homomorphism \(\operatorname{Aff}(\cA) \to \GL(V)\) whose kernel is the set of translations \(\tau_{\elem{v}} \colon P \mapsto P + \elem{v}\) , \(\elem{v} \in V\) .

title: Theorem 22.1.5 (An Affine Map Is Linear Plus a Translation)
content: Let \(\cA, \cB\) be affine spaces over \(F\) with direction spaces \(V, W\) , and let \(f \colon \cA \to \cB\) . The following are equivalent. \(f\) is affine. There is a linear map \(T \colon V \to W\) with \(\overrightarrow{f(P)f(Q)} = T(\overrightarrow{PQ})\) for all \(P, Q \in \cA\) . For some \(O \in \cA\) there is a linear map \(T \colon V \to W\) with \(f(P) = f(O) + T(\overrightarrow{OP})\) for all \(P \in \cA\) . The map \(T\) in (b) and (c) is unique, is the same in both, and does not depend on \(O\) . It is called the linear part of \(f\) and written \(\vec{f}\) .

title: Definition 22.2.4 (Affine Frame)
content: Let \(\dim \cA = n\) . An affine frame of \(\cA\) is a list \((P_0, P_1, \dots, P_n)\) of \(n + 1\) affinely independent points of \(\cA\) .

title: Definition 22.2.2 (Join of Flats)
content: Let \(A, B\) be flats of \(\cA\) . Their join \(A \vee B\) is the intersection of all flats of \(\cA\) containing \(A \cup B\) .

title: Definition 22.2.1 (Flat)
content: A subset \(A \subseteq \cA\) is a flat , or an affine subspace of \(\cA\) , if it is nonempty and contains every affine combination of its own points: whenever \(k \ge 1\) , \(P_1, \dots, P_k \in A\) and \(t_1, \dots, t_k \in F\) satisfy \(t_1 + \dots + t_k = 1\) , the point \(\sum_{i=1}^{k}t_iP_i\) lies in \(A\) .

title: Definition 22.2.3 (Parallel Flats)
content: Two flats \(A, B\) of \(\cA\) are parallel , written \(A \parallel B\) , if \(\vec{A} = \vec{B}\) .

title: Example (Reading a triangle)
content: In \(\nA^2\) take the frame \(P_0 = (0,0)\) , \(P_1 = (4, 0)\) , \(P_2 = (0, 3)\) . Check that it is a frame, and find the barycentric coordinates ( @thm-barycentric-coordinates ) of \(X = (1, 1)\) . Find the point with barycentric coordinates \((\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac14)\) . Describe the line \(P_1 \vee P_2\) in barycentric coordinates.

title: Example (Equations for a plane in four-space)
content: In @exm-implicit-equations the subspace \(U = \Span\bigl((1,1,0,1), (0,1,1,1)\bigr)\) of \(\nR^4\) was found to be \(\{ \cvec{x} : x_1 - x_2 + x_3 = 0,\ x_4 - x_2 = 0 \}\) . Find equations for the flat \(A = \cvec{p} + U\) with \(\cvec{p} = (1, 0, 0, 0)\) , and give two of its points.

title: Example (Two lines in space, twice)
content: In \(\nA^3\) let \[ \begin{aligned} A &= (1, 0, 0) + \Span\bigl((1, 1, 0)\bigr) , \\ B &= (0, 0, 1) + \Span\bigl((1, -1, 0)\bigr) , \\ B' &= (0, 0, 1) + \Span\bigl((1, 1, 0)\bigr) . \end{aligned} \] Decide in each case whether the lines meet, and compute \(\dim(A \vee B)\) and \(\dim(A \vee B')\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define a flat and its direction space, and say why the direction space does not depend on the point used to compute it. State both cases of the dimension formula for \(\dim(A \vee B)\) , and say which one applies to two distinct parallel planes in \(\nA^3\) . True or false, with a reason: the intersection of two flats is a flat. What are the barycentric coordinates of \(P_2\) with respect to the frame \((P_0, P_1, P_2, P_3)\) of a three-dimensional affine space?

title: Exercise (B1: Two flats in four-space)
content: In \(\nA^4\) let \(A = (1,0,0,0) + \Span\bigl((1,1,0,0), (0,0,1,1)\bigr)\) , and let \[ B = (0,1,0,0) + \Span\bigl((1,0,1,0)\bigr), \qquad B' = (2,1,0,0) + \Span\bigl((1,0,1,0)\bigr) . \] For each of \(B\) and \(B'\) , decide whether it meets \(A\) , and compute \(\dim(A \vee \cdot)\) . Justify your answers with @thm-flat-intersection-and-join .

title: Exercise (B2: Barycentric arithmetic)
content: In \(\nA^2\) take the frame \(P_0 = (1, 1)\) , \(P_1 = (3, 1)\) , \(P_2 = (1, 4)\) . Verify that it is a frame. Find the barycentric coordinates ( @thm-barycentric-coordinates ) of \(X = (2, 2)\) . Find the centroid of \((P_0, P_1, P_2)\) in ordinary coordinates, and check its barycentric coordinates.

title: Exercise (B3: From parameters to equations and back)
content: Find a system of equations whose solution set is the line \(A = (1, 2, 3) + \Span\bigl((1, 1, 1)\bigr)\) in \(\nA^3\) , using as few equations as possible. The set \(B = \{ \cvec{x} \in \nR^3 : x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 6 \}\) is a flat. Find its dimension, a point of it, and its direction space. Decide whether \(A \subseteq B\) , and compute \(\dim(A \vee B)\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Affine maps and flats)
content: Let \(f \colon \cA \to \cB\) be affine and let \(A \subseteq \cA\) be a flat. Prove that \(f(A)\) is a flat of \(\cB\) whose direction space is \(\vec{f}(\vec{A})\) , and deduce \(\dim f(A) \le \dim A\) . Prove that if \(B \subseteq \cB\) is a flat with \(f^{-1}(B) \ne \emptyset\) , then \(f^{-1}(B)\) is a flat with direction space \((\vec f)^{-1}(\vec B)\) . Hence prove that an injective affine map sends flats to flats of the same dimension, and lines to lines.

title: Exercise (C2: The midpoint quadrilateral)
content: Let \(F\) be a field with \(2 \ne 0\) , let \(\cA\) be an affine space over \(F\) , and let \(P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4 \in \cA\) be any four points. Put \(M_{12} = \tfrac12P_1 + \tfrac12P_2\) , and define \(M_{23}, M_{34}, M_{41}\) likewise. Prove that \(\overrightarrow{M_{12}M_{23}} = \overrightarrow{M_{41}M_{34}} = \tfrac12\overrightarrow{P_1P_3}\) . Deduce that if \(M_{12}, M_{23}, M_{34}, M_{41}\) are distinct, then \(M_{12} \vee M_{23}\) and \(M_{41} \vee M_{34}\) are parallel lines, and likewise for the other pair of opposite sides: the four midpoints form a parallelogram. What does the statement say when \(P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4\) are not coplanar, for instance in \(\nA^3\) ?

title: Exercise (C3: Medians over the field with three elements)
content:
Work in \(
A^2(
F_3)\) with the affinely independent list \(P_1 = (0,0)\) , \(P_2 = (1,0)\) , \(P_3 = (0,1)\) . (Nothing is lost by this choice: by @thm-affine-map-determined-by-frame any other affinely independent triple is carried to this one by an affine bijection, which preserves midpoints, being an affine combination, and carries lines to lines by @exr-affine-subspaces-c1 .) Compute the three midpoints \(M_i\) and the three medians \(m_i = P_i \vee M_i\) . Prove that the three medians are pairwise parallel and pairwise disjoint, so that @prp-medians-meet-at-centroid fails over \(
F_3\) . Explain which step of the proof of @prp-medians-meet-at-centroid breaks, and why the hypothesis \(3 
e 0\) cannot be dropped.

title: Lemma 22.2.5 (Affine Independence by Differences)
content: Let \(P_0, P_1, \dots, P_m \in \cA\) . The following are equivalent. The only \(\lambda_0, \dots, \lambda_m \in F\) with \(\sum_{i=0}^m\lambda_i = 0\) and \(\sum_{i=0}^m \lambda_iP_i = \elem{0}\) are \(\lambda_0 = \dots = \lambda_m = 0\) . The list \((\overrightarrow{P_0P_1}, \dots, \overrightarrow{P_0P_m})\) is linearly independent in \(V\) . A list satisfying these is called affinely independent . Condition (a) does not mention \(P_0\) specially, so (b) holds with any \(P_j\) in place of \(P_0\) as soon as it holds for one.

title: Proposition 22.2.9 (Points inside a proper flat do not determine an affine map)
content: Let \(\dim \cA = n \ge 1\) and let \(S \subseteq \cA\) be contained in a flat \(A\) with \(\dim A < n\) — for instance, any set of at most \(n\) points. Then there are two distinct affine maps \(\cA \to \cA\) that agree at every point of \(S\) .

title: Proposition 22.2.2 (Intersections of Flats)
content: Let \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) be a nonempty family of flats of \(\cA\) and put \(A = \bigcap_{i \in I}A_i\) . If \(A \ne \emptyset\) , then \(A\) is a flat and \(\vec{A} = \bigcap_{i \in I}\vec{A_i}\) .

title: Proposition 22.2.1 (Flats Are the Cosets)
content: Let \(A \subseteq \cA\) be nonempty. Then \(A\) is a flat if and only if there are \(P \in \cA\) and a subspace \(U\) of \(V\) with \(A = P + U \coloneqq \{ P + \elem{u} : \elem{u} \in U \}\) . In that case: \(U = \{ \overrightarrow{XY} : X, Y \in A \}\) is determined by \(A\) alone; it is written \(\vec{A}\) and called the direction space of \(A\) . \(A = Q + \vec{A}\) for every \(Q \in A\) , and \(A\) , with the difference map of \(\cA\) restricted to it, is an affine space with direction space \(\vec{A}\) . The dimension of \(A\) is \(\dim A \coloneqq \dim \vec{A}\) . A flat of dimension \(0\) is a single point , one of dimension \(1\) is a line , one of dimension \(2\) is a plane , and, when \(\dim\cA = n\) is finite, one of dimension \(n - 1\) is a hyperplane of \(\cA\) .

title: Proposition 22.2.7 (The Medians Meet at the Centroid)
content: Let \(F\) be a field in which \(2 \ne 0\) and \(3 \ne 0\) , let \(\cA\) be an affine space over \(F\) , and let \((P_1, P_2, P_3)\) be an affinely independent list in \(\cA\) . Put \[ M_1 = \tfrac12 P_2 + \tfrac12 P_3, \qquad M_2 = \tfrac12 P_1 + \tfrac12 P_3, \qquad M_3 = \tfrac12 P_1 + \tfrac12 P_2 , \] the midpoints of the sides, and let \(m_i = P_i \vee M_i\) be the medians . Then \(m_1, m_2, m_3\) are lines meeting in exactly one point, the centroid \[ G = \tfrac13 P_1 + \tfrac13 P_2 + \tfrac13 P_3 , \] and \(\overrightarrow{P_iG} = 2\,\overrightarrow{GM_i}\) for each \(i\) .

title: Proposition 22.2.3 (Parallelism)
content: Parallelism is an equivalence relation on the set of flats of \(\cA\) . Two parallel flats are either equal or disjoint, and each equivalence class consists of the flats \(P + U\) , \(P \in \cA\) , for one fixed subspace \(U\) .

title: Theorem 22.2.8 (An Affine Map Is Determined by a Frame)
content: Let \(\cA\) have dimension \(n\) with affine frame \((P_0, \dots, P_n)\) , let \(\cB\) be an affine space over the same field with direction space \(W\) , and let \(Q_0, \dots, Q_n \in \cB\) be any points. Then there is exactly one affine map \(f \colon \cA \to \cB\) with \(f(P_i) = Q_i\) for \(i = 0, \dots, n\) . Moreover \(f\) carries the barycentric coordinates of @thm-barycentric-coordinates across: \[ f\Bigl( \sum_{i=0}^{n}t_iP_i \Bigr) = \sum_{i=0}^{n}t_iQ_i \qquad \Bigl( \sum_i t_i = 1 \Bigr) . \]

title: Theorem 22.2.6 (Barycentric Coordinates)
content: Let \(\dim \cA = n\) and let \((P_0, \dots, P_n)\) be an affine frame of \(\cA\) . For every \(X \in \cA\) there are unique scalars \(t_0, \dots, t_n \in F\) with \[ t_0 + t_1 + \dots + t_n = 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad X = \sum_{i=0}^{n} t_iP_i . \] They are called the barycentric coordinates of \(X\) with respect to the frame.

title: Theorem 22.2.4 (Intersection and Join of Two Flats)
content: Let \(A, B\) be flats of \(\cA\) , and choose \(P \in A\) and \(Q \in B\) . Parts (a) and (b) need no hypothesis on \(\dim\cA\) . \(A \vee B = P + \bigl( \vec{A} + \vec{B} + \Span(\overrightarrow{PQ}) \bigr)\) . \(A \cap B \ne \emptyset\) if and only if \(\overrightarrow{PQ} \in \vec{A} + \vec{B}\) ; and then \(A \cap B\) is a flat whose direction space is \(\vec{A} \cap \vec{B}\) . Let \(\dim\cA = n\) be finite. If \(A \cap B \ne \emptyset\) , then \[ \dim(A \vee B) = \dim A + \dim B - \dim(A \cap B) . \] If \(A \cap B = \emptyset\) , then \[ \dim(A \vee B) = \dim A + \dim B - \dim(\vec{A} \cap \vec{B}) + 1 . \] Let \(\dim\cA = n\) be finite. If \(A \cap B = \emptyset\) , there is a hyperplane \(H\) of \(V\) with \(A \subseteq P + H\) and \(B \subseteq Q + H\) , and the two flats \(P + H\) , \(Q + H\) are parallel, distinct, and disjoint.

title: Theorem 22.2.10 (Flats Are Exactly the Solution Sets)
content: Let \(A \subseteq \nA^n(F)\) be nonempty and \(0 \le k \le n\) . The following are equivalent. \(A\) is a flat of dimension \(k\) . \(A = \{ \cvec{x} \in F^n : \M\cvec{x} = \cvec{c} \}\) for some \(\M \in M_{(n-k) \times n}(F)\) with linearly independent rows and some \(\cvec{c} \in F^{n-k}\) . In that case no system with fewer than \(n - k\) equations has solution set \(A\) , and for \(k < n\) the flat \(A\) is an intersection of exactly \(n - k\) affine hyperplanes.

title: Definition 22.3.2 (Edge, Facet)
content: Let \(P \subseteq \nR^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. A face of \(P\) of dimension \(1\) is an edge ; a face of dimension \(\dim P - 1\) is a facet . A face of dimension \(0\) is a single point, and the next proposition shows that these are exactly the vertices.

title: Definition 22.3.1 (Face of a Polyhedron)
content:
Let \(P \subseteq 
R^n\) be a polyhedron. A face of \(P\) is a set of the form \[ F = \{\cvec{x} \in P : \cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} =  eta\} \] for some \(\cvec{c} \in 
R^n\) and \( eta \in 
R\) such that \(\cvec{c}	p\cvec{x} \le  eta\) for every \(\cvec{x} \in P\) . A face other than \(P\) itself is called proper .

title: Example (The faces of a cube)
content: Let \(B_\infty = [-1, 1]^n\) , described by the \(2n\) rows \(\cvec{e}_i\tp\cvec{x} \le 1\) and \(-\cvec{e}_i\tp\cvec{x} \le 1\) . Find all faces of \(B_\infty\) and their dimensions.

title: Example (A linear program and its picture)
content: Maximize \(3x_1 + 2x_2\) over \[ P = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^2 : x_1 \ge 0,\ x_2 \ge 0,\ x_1 + x_2 \le 5,\ 2x_1 + x_2 \le 8\} . \] Find the vertices, the optimum, the optimal face, and the dual optimal solution.

title: Example (The faces of a simplex)
content: Let \(\Delta_n = \{\cvec{t} \in \nR^n : t_i \ge 0,\ \sum_i t_i = 1\}\) be the standard simplex ( @def-standard-simplex ), described by the \(n\) rows \(-t_i \le 0\) together with \(\1\tp\cvec{t} \le 1\) and \(-\1\tp\cvec{t} \le -1\) . Find all faces of \(\Delta_n\) .

title: Example (A slab, and a quadrant)
content: Find the faces of the slab \(S = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^3 : 0 \le x_3 \le 1\}\) , and its vertices. Show that \(\max\{x_1 + x_2 : \cvec{x} \in Q\}\) does not exist for the quadrant \(Q = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^2 : x_1 \ge 0,\ x_2 \ge 0\}\) , although \(Q\) has a vertex.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State @def-polyhedron-face , and say which pair \((\cvec{c}, \beta)\) exhibits \(P\) itself as a face and which exhibits \(\emptyset\) . True or false: a polyhedron given by \(m\) inequalities in \(\nR^n\) has exactly \(2^m\) nonempty faces. Justify your answer. Give the three equivalent descriptions of a vertex from @prp-vertex-iff-point-face . True or false: if a linear program over a bounded nonempty polyhedron has two distinct optimal solutions, it has infinitely many. Justify your answer. How many faces of dimension \(2\) does the cube \([-1,1]^4\) have?

title: Exercise (B1: Vertices and faces of a region)
content: Let \[ P = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^2 : x_1 \ge 0,\ x_2 \ge 0,\ x_1 + 2x_2 \le 8,\ 2x_1 + x_2 \le 10\} . \] Find all vertices of \(P\) , list all of its faces, and maximize \(x_1 + 3x_2\) over \(P\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Reading the dual off the normals)
content: For the program of @exr-polyhedra-and-linear-programming-b1 with objective \(x_1 + 3x_2\) , use @prp-dual-normal-cone to write \(\cvec{c} = (1,3)\) as a nonnegative combination of the outer normals of the constraints active at the optimum, and check the resulting dual solution against @cor-duality-certificate .

title: Exercise (B3: Faces of the cross-polytope)
content: Let \(B_1 = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^n : \cvec{s}\tp\cvec{x} \le 1 \text{ for every sign vector } \cvec{s} \in \{-1,1\}^n\}\) , the cross-polytope of @exm-cube-cross-polytope . Determine the face \(P_J\) for \(J\) a single sign vector \(\cvec{s}\) , and its dimension. How many facets does \(B_1\) have?

title: Exercise (C1: A face of a face)
content: Let \(P\) be a polyhedron and \(F\) a face of \(P\) . Prove that every face of \(F\) is a face of \(P\) . Deduce that the faces of \(P\) contained in a fixed face \(F\) are exactly the faces of \(F\) . Hint: for (a), use @prp-face-is-polyhedron to write both \(F\) and the face of \(F\) in the form \(P_J\) .

title: Exercise (C2: The two notions of face agree for a polyhedron)
content: Let \(P = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\}\) and let \(F \subseteq P\) be a nonempty face in the sense of @def-face : \(F\) is convex, and whenever \(t\cvec{y} + (1-t)\cvec{z} \in F\) with \(\cvec{y}, \cvec{z} \in P\) and \(0 < t < 1\) , both \(\cvec{y}\) and \(\cvec{z}\) lie in \(F\) . Let \(J = \{i : \cvec{a}_i\tp\cvec{x} = b_i \text{ for every } \cvec{x} \in F\}\) . Prove that \(F = P_J\) . Deduce that \(F\) is a face in the sense of @def-polyhedron-face , so the two notions agree for polyhedra. Hint: for (a), Step 1 of the proof of @prp-face-is-polyhedron produces a point of \(F\) at which every row outside \(J\) is slack; use it as the midpoint of a short segment.

title: Exercise (C3: The optimal face has no better vertex outside it)
content: Let \(P \subseteq \nR^n\) be a nonempty bounded polyhedron, \(\cvec{c} \in \nR^n\) , and let \(F^{\star}\) be the optimal face of @prp-optimal-set-is-a-face . Prove that \(F^{\star} = \conv(F^{\star} \cap \operatorname{ext} P)\) . Deduce that the optimal value of the program equals \(\max\{\cvec{c}\tp\cvec{v} : \cvec{v} \in \operatorname{ext}P\}\) , a maximum over a finite set, and that this finite maximum is attained exactly at the vertices lying in \(F^{\star}\) .

title: Proposition 22.3.6 (Dual Variables Are the Weights of the Active Normals)
content: Let \(\cvec{x}^{\star}\) be an optimal solution of (P). Then there are \(\cvec{y} \in \nR^m\) and \(\cvec{s} \in \nR^n\) with \(\cvec{y} \ge \cvec{0}\) and \(\cvec{s} \ge \cvec{0}\) such that \[ \cvec{c} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} y_i\cvec{a}_i + \sum_{j=1}^{n} s_j(-\cvec{e}_j) , \] where \(y_i = 0\) whenever \(\cvec{a}_i\tp\cvec{x}^{\star} < b_i\) , and \(s_j = 0\) whenever \(x^{\star}_j > 0\) . That is, \(\cvec{c}\) is a nonnegative combination of the outer normals of the constraints active at \(\cvec{x}^{\star}\) , and the weights are an optimal solution of (D).

title: Proposition 22.3.4 (An Edge Joins Two Vertices)
content: Let \(P \subseteq \nR^n\) be a bounded polyhedron and \(F\) an edge of \(P\) . Then \(F = [\cvec{v}, \cvec{w}]\) for two distinct vertices \(\cvec{v}, \cvec{w}\) of \(P\) .

title: Proposition 22.3.1 (Faces Are Polyhedra, and There Are Finitely Many)
content: Let \(P = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\}\) with \(m\) rows. For \(J \subseteq \{1, \dots, m\}\) put \[ P_J = \{\cvec{x} \in P : \cvec{a}_i\tp\cvec{x} = b_i \text{ for every } i \in J\} . \] Then: every \(P_J\) is a face of \(P\) , and it is a polyhedron; every nonempty face of \(P\) equals \(P_J\) for some \(J\) ; consequently \(P\) has at most \(2^m\) nonempty faces, and every face of \(P\) is a polyhedron.

title: Proposition 22.3.5 (The Optimal Set Is a Face)
content: Let \(P \subseteq \nR^n\) be a polyhedron, \(\cvec{c} \in \nR^n\) , and suppose \(\cvec{c}\tp\cvec{x}\) attains a maximum \(\gamma^{\star}\) on \(P\) . Then the set \(F^{\star}\) of maximizers is a nonempty face of \(P\) . If \(P\) is bounded, \(F^{\star}\) contains a vertex of \(P\) .

title: Proposition 22.3.2 (Three Descriptions of a Corner)
content: Let \(P = \{\cvec{x} \in \nR^n : \A\cvec{x} \le \cvec{b}\}\) and \(\cvec{v} \in P\) . The following are equivalent. \(\cvec{v}\) is a vertex of \(P\) , that is, an extreme point. \(\{\cvec{v}\}\) is a face of \(P\) . Among the rows active at \(\cvec{v}\) there are \(n\) linearly independent ones, that is, \(\cvec{v}\) is a basic feasible point.

title: Theorem 22.3.3 (A Bounded Polyhedron Is the Hull of Its Vertices)
content: Let \(P \subseteq \nR^n\) be a bounded polyhedron. Then \(\operatorname{ext} P\) is finite and \[ P = \conv(\operatorname{ext} P) . \] Conversely, every polytope is a bounded polyhedron.

title: Corollary 22.4.2 (Motions Are Bijections)
content: Every Euclidean motion \(f\) of \(\nR^n\) is a bijection, and \(f^{-1}\) is again a motion. The linear part of \(f^{-1}\) is \(\Q\tp\) , where \(\Q\) is the linear part of \(f\) .

title: Definition 22.4.2 (Direct and Opposite Motions)
content: Let \(f(\cvec{x}) = \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b}\) be a motion of \(\nR^n\) . It is direct , or orientation-preserving, if \(\det\Q = 1\) , and opposite , or orientation-reversing, if \(\det\Q = -1\) . These are the only possibilities: \(\Q\tp\Q = \I_n\) , and \(\det\Q\tp = \det\Q\) ( @thm-det-transpose ), so \((\det\Q)^2 = \det(\Q\tp\Q) = 1\) by @thm-det-multiplicative .

title: Definition 22.4.1 (Euclidean Motion)
content:
A Euclidean motion of \(
R^n\) , or simply a motion , is a map \(f \colon 
R^n 	o 
R^n\) such that \[ 
orm{f(\cvec{x}) - f(\cvec{y})} = 
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{y}} \qquad 	ext{for all } \cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n . \] No linearity, continuity, or surjectivity is assumed.

title: Definition 22.4.3 (Translation, Rotation, Reflection, Glide Reflection)
Definition 22.4.4 (Screw Motion, Rotatory Reflection)
content:
Let \(L = \cvec{p} + \Span(\cvec{u})\) be a line in \(
R^3\) with \(
orm{\cvec{u}} = 1\) , and let \(\Pi = \cvec{p} + W\) be a plane. A rotation about the axis \(L\) is a motion \(\cvec{x} \mapsto \Q(\cvec{x} - \cvec{p}) + \cvec{p}\) with \(\Q \in \SO(3)\) , \(\Q 
e \I\) and \(\Q\cvec{u} = \cvec{u}\) . It fixes \(L\) pointwise, and by @cor-so3-is-rotation it turns the plane \(\Span(\cvec{u})^{\perp}\) by a single angle \(	heta \in (0, \pi]\) , the angle of the rotation. The requirement \(\Q 
e \I\) keeps the identity out: it is a translation, and a translation should not also count as a rotation about every line at once. A screw motion is \(t_{\cvec{v}} \circ r\) , where \(r\) is a rotation about \(L\) — so its angle is again nonzero — and \(\cvec{v} 
e \cvec{0}\) is parallel to \(L\) . The reflection in the plane \(\Pi\) is \(\cvec{x} \mapsto \Q_{\Pi}(\cvec{x} - \cvec{p}) + \cvec{p}\) , with \(\Q_{\Pi}\) the linear map fixing \(W\) pointwise and negating \(W^{\perp}\) ; a glide reflection is \(t_{\cvec{v}} \circ s_{\Pi}\) with \(\cvec{v} 
e \cvec{0}\) lying in \(W\) . A rotatory reflection about the point \(\cvec{p}\) is the composite of a rotation about an axis \(L = \cvec{p} + \Span(\cvec{u})\) by an angle \(	heta \in (0, \pi]\) with the reflection in the plane \(\cvec{p} + \Span(\cvec{u})^{\perp}\) perpendicular to that axis. The two commute, and the composite is \(\cvec{x} \mapsto \Q(\cvec{x} - \cvec{p}) + \cvec{p}\) where \(\Q\) is \([-1] \oplus \R_{	heta}\) in an orthonormal basis beginning with \(\cvec{u}\) ; in particular \(\det\Q = -1\) . The case \(	heta = \pi\) gives \(\Q = -\I_3\) and the point reflection \(\cvec{x} \mapsto 2\cvec{p} - \cvec{x}\) .

title: Example (Naming a plane motion)
content: Classify the motion \(f(\cvec{x}) = \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b}\) of \(\nR^2\) with \[ \Q = \tfrac15\begin{pmatrix} -3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \cvec{b} = (5, 0) . \]

title: Example (Naming a space motion)
content: Classify the motion \(f(\cvec{x}) = \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b}\) of \(\nR^3\) with \[ \Q = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \cvec{b} = (4, 1, -2) . \]

title: Example (Two mirrors)
content: Reflect in the line \(L_1 = \Span((1,0))\) and then in \(L_2 = \Span((1,1))\) . Identify the composite. Reflect in \(M_1 = \{x_2 = 0\}\) and then in \(M_2 = \{x_2 = 1\}\) . Identify the composite. Prove the general statements: two reflections in lines through a common point \(\cvec{p}\) meeting at angle \(\alpha\) compose to the rotation about \(\cvec{p}\) by \(2\alpha\) ; two reflections in parallel lines compose to a translation by twice the perpendicular vector between them.

title: Exercise (A1)
content:
State @def-euclidean-motion , and say which of linearity, continuity, and surjectivity it assumes. True or false: every motion of \(
R^n\) with a fixed point is linear. Justify your answer. Name the four kinds of motion of \(
R^2\) and give the fixed-point set of each. True or false: the composite of two opposite motions of \(
R^3\) is opposite. Justify your answer. A motion of \(
R^3\) has exactly one fixed point. What kind is it?

title: Exercise (B1: Classify three plane motions)
content: Classify each motion \(f(\cvec{x}) = \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b}\) of \(\nR^2\) , giving the center and angle, the axis, or the axis and glide vector, as appropriate. \(\Q = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}\) , \(\cvec{b} = (2, 4)\) . \(\Q = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}\) , \(\cvec{b} = (3, 3)\) . \(\Q = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}\) , \(\cvec{b} = (1, -1)\) .

title: Exercise (B2: A space motion)
content: Classify the motion \(f(\cvec{x}) = \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b}\) of \(\nR^3\) with \[ \Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \cvec{b} = (0, 2, 0) , \] giving the axis and the glide vector if there is one.

title: Exercise (B3: A motion is determined by few points)
content: Let \(f\) and \(g\) be motions of \(\nR^n\) that agree on \(\cvec{0}, \cvec{e}_1, \dots, \cvec{e}_n\) . Prove that \(f = g\) . Hint: consider \(h = g^{-1} \circ f\) and use @thm-motion-is-affine .

title: Exercise (C1: Reflections generate the motions)
content:
Prove that every motion of \(
R^n\) is a composite of at most \(n + 1\) reflections in affine hyperplanes, where the reflection in the hyperplane \(\cvec{p} + \Span(\cvec{w})^{\perp}\) is \(\cvec{x} \mapsto \H_{\cvec{w}}(\cvec{x} - \cvec{p}) + \cvec{p}\) with \(\H_{\cvec{w}}\) the Householder reflection of @def-householder-reflection . Deduce that a translation of \(
R^n\) by \(\cvec{b} 
e \cvec{0}\) is a composite of exactly two such reflections, and identify them. Hint: for (a), first make the motion fix a point, then quote @thm-cartan-dieudonne-small .

title: Exercise (C2: Matching two congruent frames)
content:
Let \(\cvec{p}_0, \dots, \cvec{p}_n\) and \(\cvec{q}_0, \dots, \cvec{q}_n\) be points of \(
R^n\) with \(
orm{\cvec{p}_i - \cvec{p}_j} = 
orm{\cvec{q}_i - \cvec{q}_j}\) for all \(i, j\) , and suppose \(\cvec{p}_1 - \cvec{p}_0, \dots, \cvec{p}_n - \cvec{p}_0\) is a basis of \(
R^n\) . Prove that there is a motion \(f\) of \(
R^n\) with \(f(\cvec{p}_i) = \cvec{q}_i\) for every \(i\) . Prove that \(f\) is unique, and give an example with fewer points where it is not. Hint: for (a), translate both lists so that \(\cvec{p}_0 = \cvec{q}_0 = \cvec{0}\) , then compare the inner products of the two lists.

title: Exercise (C3: Motions of a finite set)
content: Let \(S \subseteq \nR^n\) be a finite nonempty set and let \(G = \{f \in \operatorname{E}(n) : f(S) = S\}\) be its symmetry group. Prove that \(G\) is a subgroup of \(\operatorname{E}(n)\) , and that every \(f \in G\) fixes the centroid \(\cvec{c} = \tfrac{1}{\lvert S\rvert}\sum_{\cvec{p} \in S}\cvec{p}\) . Deduce that \(G\) is isomorphic to a subgroup of \(\Orth(n)\) , and that \(G\) contains no translation other than the identity.

title: Proposition 22.4.3 (The Euclidean Group)
content: \(\operatorname{E}(n)\) is a group under composition. The map \(\lambda \colon \operatorname{E}(n) \to \Orth(n)\) sending a motion to its linear part is a surjective group homomorphism. \(\ker\lambda = \operatorname{Trans}(n)\) , and \(\cvec{b} \mapsto t_{\cvec{b}}\) is a group isomorphism \((\nR^n, +) \to \operatorname{Trans}(n)\) . For every motion \(f\) with linear part \(\Q\) and every \(\cvec{b} \in \nR^n\) , \[ f \circ t_{\cvec{b}} \circ f^{-1} = t_{\Q\cvec{b}} . \] In particular a conjugate of a translation is a translation.

title: Theorem 22.4.1 (Every Motion Is Affine)
content:
Let \(f \colon 
R^n 	o 
R^n\) be a Euclidean motion. Then there are a unique \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) and a unique \(\cvec{b} \in 
R^n\) with \[ f(\cvec{x}) = \Q\cvec{x} + \cvec{b} \qquad 	ext{for every } \cvec{x} \in 
R^n . \] In particular \(f\) is an affine map ( @def-affine-map ) whose linear part \(\vec f\) ( @thm-affine-map-is-linear-plus-translation ) is the isometry \(T_{\Q}\) .

title: Definition 22.5.2 (Affine Equivalence of Quadric Polynomials)
content: Two quadric polynomials \(Q_1, Q_2\) on \(F^n\) are affinely equivalent when \[ Q_2 = \lambda\,(Q_1 \circ g) \] for some invertible affine map \(g\) ( @def-affine-map ) and some \(\lambda \in F\) with \(\lambda \ne 0\) .

title: Definition 22.5.3 (Center of a Quadric)
content: Let \(Q\) be a quadric polynomial on \(F^n\) . A point \(\cvec{p} \in F^n\) is a center of \(Q\) if \[ Q(\cvec{p} + \cvec{v}) = Q(\cvec{p} - \cvec{v}) \qquad \text{for every } \cvec{v} \in F^n . \] \(Q\) is central if it has at least one center, and centerless otherwise.

title: Definition 22.5.1 (Quadric)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) and let \(\cA\) be an affine space of dimension \(n\) over \(F\) , identified with \(F^n\) by a choice of origin and basis ( @prp-choice-of-origin ). A quadric polynomial on \(\cA\) is a function \[ Q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{x} + 2\cvec{b}\tp\cvec{x} + c \] with \(\A \in M_n(F)\) symmetric and nonzero , \(\cvec{b} \in F^n\) and \(c \in F\) . Its quadratic part is the quadratic form \(q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{x}\) . The quadric defined by \(Q\) is its zero set \[ \{\, \cvec{x} \in F^n : Q(\cvec{x}) = 0 \,\} . \] For \(n = 2\) a quadric is called a conic .

title: Example (One conic, two classifications)
content: Over \(\nR\) , consider \[ Q(x,y) = 5x^2 + 4xy + 5y^2 - 14x - 14y - 7 . \] Classify its zero set affinely, and then find its center, principal axes, and semi-axes.

title: Example (The parabola is centerless)
content: Show that \(Q(x,y) = x^2 - y\) over \(\nR\) has no center, and find all centers of \(Q_1(x,y) = x^2 - 1\) .

R\) . Name the three places in this section where \(\operatorname{char} F

title: Exercise (C3: The center as a projection)
content: Let \(Q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{x} + 2\cvec{b}\tp\cvec{x} + c\) be a central quadric polynomial on \(\nR^n\) with \(r = \rank\A\) . Prove that the set of centers is a flat of dimension \(n - r\) ( @def-flat ). Prove that the set of centers is contained in the zero set of \(Q\) if and only if \(Q(\cvec{p}) = 0\) for one, hence every, center \(\cvec{p}\) . Give an example on \(\nR^3\) with a line of centers, none of which lies on the quadric.

title: Proposition 22.5.2 (When a Center Exists)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) and let \(Q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{x} + 2\cvec{b}\tp\cvec{x} + c\) be a quadric polynomial on \(F^n\) . Then: \(\cvec{p}\) is a center of \(Q\) if and only if \(\A\cvec{p} + \cvec{b} = \cvec{0}\) ; \(Q\) is central if and only if \(\cvec{b} \in \col(\A)\) ; in particular \(Q\) is central whenever \(\A\) is invertible, and the center is then the unique point \(-\A^{-1}\cvec{b}\) ; if \(\cvec{p}\) is a center then \(Q(\cvec{p} + \cvec{v}) = Q(\cvec{p}) + \cvec{v}\tp\A\cvec{v}\) for every \(\cvec{v}\) , and the value \(Q(\cvec{p})\) is the same at every center.

title: Proposition 22.5.1 (Affine Substitution Is Congruence of the Big Matrix)
content: Let \(Q\) have big matrix \(\widetilde\A\) , let \(\M \in M_n(F)\) be invertible, let \(\cvec{t} \in F^n\) , and let \(g(\cvec{y}) = \M\cvec{y} + \cvec{t}\) be the corresponding invertible affine map ( @def-affine-map ), with block matrix ( @prp-affine-map-block-matrix ) \[ \widehat{g} = \begin{pmatrix} \M & \cvec{t} \\ \cvec{0}\tp & 1 \end{pmatrix} . \] Then \(Q \circ g\) is again a quadric polynomial, its big matrix is \(\widehat{g}\tp\widetilde\A\widehat{g}\) , and its small matrix, linear vector, and constant are \[ \A' = \M\tp\A\M, \qquad \cvec{b}' = \M\tp(\A\cvec{t} + \cvec{b}), \qquad c' = Q(\cvec{t}) . \]

title: Theorem 22.5.3 (Affine Classification of Real Quadrics)
content: Let \(Q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{x} + 2\cvec{b}\tp\cvec{x} + c\) be a quadric polynomial on \(\nR^n\) and let \(r = \rank\A\) , which is \(\ge 1\) because \(\A \ne \O\) ( @def-quadric ). Then \(Q\) is affinely equivalent to exactly one polynomial from the following list, for one value of \(p\) in the range shown, where \(\sigma_{r,p}(\cvec{y}) = y_1^2 + \dots + y_p^2 - y_{p+1}^2 - \dots - y_r^2\) : \(\sigma_{r,p}(\cvec{y}) - 1\) , with \(0 \le p \le r\) ; \(\sigma_{r,p}(\cvec{y})\) , with \(r \le 2p \le 2r\) ; \(\sigma_{r,p}(\cvec{y}) - y_{r+1}\) , with \(r < n\) and \(r \le 2p \le 2r\) . Case (III) occurs exactly when \(Q\) is centerless. The parameter \(p\) that occurs is \(n_+(\A)\) or \(n_-(\A)\) , the two being interchanged by a negative scalar factor ( @def-signature ).

title: Theorem 22.5.4 (Euclidean Classification of Real Quadrics)
content: Let \(Q(\cvec{x}) = \cvec{x}\tp\A\cvec{x} + 2\cvec{b}\tp\cvec{x} + c\) be a quadric polynomial on \(\nR^n\) , let \(r = \rank\A\) , and let \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_r\) be the nonzero eigenvalues of \(\A\) , listed with multiplicity. Then there is a Euclidean motion \(\cvec{x} = \U\cvec{y} + \cvec{t}\) , with \(\U \in \Orth(n)\) , after which \(Q\) becomes exactly one of \(\lambda_1y_1^2 + \dots + \lambda_ry_r^2 + c_0\) , when \(Q\) is central, where \(c_0 = Q(\cvec{p})\) at any center \(\cvec{p}\) ; \(\lambda_1y_1^2 + \dots + \lambda_ry_r^2 + 2\mu\,y_{r+1}\) , when \(Q\) is centerless, where \(\mu = \norm{\cvec{b} - P_{\col(\A)}\cvec{b}} > 0\) . The columns of \(\U\) are an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of \(\A\) , the first \(r\) of them for \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_r\) ; these are the principal axes of \(Q\) . The multiset \(\{\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_r\}\) and the number \(c_0\) , respectively \(\mu\) , are unchanged by every Euclidean motion, so the normal form is unique up to the order of its terms.

title: Corollary 22.6.7 (Two Lines in a Projective Plane Meet)
content: Let \(P\) be a projective plane, that is \(P = \nP(V)\) with \(\dim V = 3\) . Then any two distinct lines of \(P\) meet in exactly one point.

title: Definition 22.6.2 (Homogeneous Coordinates)
content: Let \(\cvec{x} = (x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n) \in F^{n+1}\) be nonzero. The homogeneous coordinates of the point \([\cvec{x}] \in \nP^n(F)\) are written \[ [\cvec{x}] = [x_0 : x_1 : \dots : x_n] , \] the colons recording that only the ratios are determined: for every \(\lambda \ne 0\) , \[ [x_0 : x_1 : \dots : x_n] = [\lambda x_0 : \lambda x_1 : \dots : \lambda x_n] , \] and not all of \(x_0, \dots, x_n\) are zero.

title: Definition 22.6.1 (Projective Space)
content:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field \(F\) with \(\dim V = n + 1\) . The projective space of \(V\) is the quotient set ( @def-quotient-set ) \[ 
P(V) = (V \setminus \{\elem{0}\})/{\sim} , \] whose elements are called points . The point determined by \(\elem{x} 
e \elem{0}\) is written \([\elem{x}]\) . The dimension of \(
P(V)\) is \[ \dim
P(V) = \dim V - 1 = n , \] so that \(
P(\{\elem{0}\}) = \emptyset\) has dimension \(-1\) . We write \(
P^n(F) = 
P(F^{n+1})\) for projective \(n\) -space over \(F\) . A projective space of dimension \(1\) is a projective line , and one of dimension \(2\) a projective plane .

title: Definition 22.6.3 (Projective Subspace)
content:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) . A projective subspace of \(
P(V)\) is a subset of the form \[ 
P(U) = \{[\elem{x}] : \elem{x} \in U \setminus \{\elem{0}\}\} \] for a subspace \(U\) of \(V\) . Its dimension is \(\dim U - 1\) . A projective subspace of dimension \(0\) is a point , of dimension \(1\) a line , of dimension \(2\) a plane , and of dimension \(\dim
P(V) - 1\) a hyperplane .

title: Lemma 22.6.4 (A Projective Subspace Remembers Its Subspace)
content:
Let \(U\) and \(W\) be subspaces of \(V\) . Then \(
P(U) \subseteq 
P(W)\) if and only if \(U \subseteq W\) ; in particular \(
P(U) = 
P(W)\) forces \(U = W\) .

title: Proposition 22.6.3 (Completing an Affine Line)
content:
Let \(a_1, a_2 \in F\) be not both zero, let \(b \in F\) , and let \[ L = \{(y_1, y_2) \in F^2 : a_1y_1 + a_2y_2 = b\} , \] a flat of dimension \(1\) in \(
A^2\) by @thm-flat-is-solution-set , the single row \((a_1, a_2)\) being nonzero, with direction space \(\Span((-a_2, a_1))\) . Let \(\varphi(x_0,x_1,x_2) = a_1x_1 + a_2x_2 - bx_0\) and \( ar L = 
P(\ker\varphi) \subseteq 
P^2(F)\) . Then: \( ar L\) is a projective line; \(\iota(L) =  ar L \cap U_0\) , so \( ar L\) contains a faithful copy of \(L\) ; \( ar L \setminus U_0\) is the single point \([0 : -a_2 : a_1]\) ; two such lines \(L, L'\) have the same direction space if and only if \( ar L\) and \( ar{L'}\) meet \(H_{\infty}\) in the same point.

title: Proposition 22.6.5 (Meet and Join)
content:
Let \(S = 
P(U)\) and \(T = 
P(W)\) be projective subspaces of \(
P(V)\) . Then: \(S \cap T = 
P(U \cap W)\) , so an intersection of projective subspaces is a projective subspace; among all projective subspaces containing \(S \cup T\) there is a smallest one, namely \(
P(U + W)\) . We write \(S \vee T = 
P(U + W)\) and call it the join of \(S\) and \(T\) .

title: Proposition 22.6.9 (The Number of Points of a Finite Projective Space)
content: Let \(F\) be a finite field with \(q\) elements and let \(n \ge 0\) . Then \[ \lvert \nP^n(F)\rvert = 1 + q + q^2 + \dots + q^n = \frac{q^{n+1} - 1}{q - 1} . \] More generally a projective subspace of dimension \(d\) has \((q^{d+1}-1)/(q-1)\) points.

title: Proposition 22.6.1 (Points Are Lines Through the Origin)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) . The map \([\elem{x}] \mapsto \Span(\elem{x})\) is a bijection from \(\nP(V)\) onto the set of \(1\) -dimensional subspaces of \(V\) .

title: Proposition 22.6.8 (Two Points Determine a Line)
content: Let \(\nP(V)\) be a projective space of dimension at least \(1\) . Any two distinct points of \(\nP(V)\) lie on exactly one line.

title: Theorem 22.6.2 (The Standard Affine Chart)
content:
Let \(n \ge 1\) and let \[  egin{aligned} U_0 &= \{[x_0 : \dots : x_n] \in 
P^n(F) : x_0 
e 0\}, \ H_{\infty} &= \{[x_0 : \dots : x_n] \in 
P^n(F) : x_0 = 0\} . \end{aligned} \] Then: both conditions are independent of the representative, and \(
P^n(F) = U_0 \sqcup H_{\infty}\) , a disjoint union; the map \(\iota \colon F^n 	o U_0\) , \(\iota(a_1, \dots, a_n) = [1 : a_1 : \dots : a_n]\) , is a bijection, with inverse \([x_0 : \dots : x_n] \mapsto (x_1/x_0, \dots, x_n/x_0)\) ; \(H_{\infty} = 
P(W)\) with \(W = \{\cvec{x} \in F^{n+1} : x_0 = 0\}\) , so \(H_{\infty}\) has dimension \(n-1\) , and \([0 : x_1 : \dots : x_n] \mapsto [x_1 : \dots : x_n]\) is a bijection \(H_{\infty} 	o 
P^{n-1}(F)\) . \(U_0\) is the standard affine chart and \(H_{\infty}\) the hyperplane at infinity .

title: Theorem 22.6.6 (Projective Dimension Formula)
content: Let \(S\) and \(T\) be projective subspaces of a finite-dimensional projective space. Then \[ \dim(S \vee T) + \dim(S \cap T) = \dim S + \dim T . \] {#eq-projective-dimension} There is no exceptional case : the identity holds for all \(S\) and \(T\) , including when \(S \cap T = \emptyset\) , where \(\dim(S \cap T) = -1\) .

title: Definition 22.7.3 (Cross-Ratio)
content: Let \(L\) be a projective line, that is, a projective space of dimension \(1\) over \(F\) , let \(A, B, C \in L\) be pairwise distinct , and let \(D \in L\) be arbitrary. Let \(f \colon L \to \nP^1(F)\) be the unique projectivity with \[ f(A) = [1:0], \qquad f(B) = [0:1], \qquad f(C) = [1:1] . \] The cross-ratio of the ordered quadruple is the point \[ (A, B; C, D) \coloneqq f(D) \in \nP^1(F) . \]

title: Definition 22.7.2 (General Position)
content: Let \(\dim V = n + 1\) . A list \(P_1, \dots, P_m\) of points of \(\nP(V)\) is in general position if for every subset \(I \subseteq \{1, \dots, m\}\) with \(\lvert I \rvert \le n + 1\) , and any choice of representatives \(\elem{v}_i\) with \(P_i = [\elem{v}_i]\) , the list \((\elem{v}_i)_{i \in I}\) is linearly independent.

title: Definition 22.7.1 (Projective Transformation)
content:
Let \(T \colon V 	o W\) be an isomorphism of vector spaces over \(F\) . The projective transformation , or projectivity , induced by \(T\) is the map \[ [T] \colon 
P(V) 	o 
P(W), \qquad [T] igl([\elem{x}] igr) \coloneqq [T\elem{x}] . \] A map \(
P(V) 	o 
P(W)\) is a projectivity if it equals \([T]\) for some isomorphism \(T\) .

title: Example (A cross-ratio, before and after)
content: On \(\nP^1(\nQ)\) , use the chart \([t : 1] \mapsto t\) and take the points with parameters \(a = 0\) , \(b = 1\) , \(c = 3\) , \(d = 7\) . Compute \((A, B; C, D)\) . Then apply the projectivity \([\A]\) with \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) and compute the cross-ratio of the images.

title: Example (Moving the standard frame)
content: Work in \(\nP^2(\nQ)\) . Find the projectivity carrying \[ [1:0:0],\quad [0:1:0],\quad [0:0:1],\quad [1:1:1] \] to \[ Q_0 = [1:1:0],\quad Q_1 = [0:1:1],\quad Q_2 = [1:0:1],\quad Q_3 = [4:3:5], \] after checking that the second list is in general position.

title: Exercise (C2: Rearranging the four points)
content: Let \(A, B, C\) be pairwise distinct points of a projective line and \(D\) a fourth point. Prove that \((B, A; C, D)\) is obtained from \((A, B; C, D) = [\lambda : \mu]\) by exchanging the two entries. Suppose all four points lie in a chart, with parameters \(a, b, c, d\) , and that \((A,B;C,D)\) is the scalar \(\chi\) . Prove that \((A, C; B, D) = 1 - \chi\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Cross-ratio characterizes projectivities of a line)
content: Let \(L\) and \(L'\) be projective lines over \(F\) and let \(g \colon L \to L'\) be an injection such that \[ \bigl(g(A), g(B); g(C), g(D)\bigr) = (A, B; C, D) \] for all \(A, B, C, D \in L\) with \(A, B, C\) pairwise distinct. Prove that \(g\) is a projectivity. Hint: pin \(g\) down on three points first.

title: Lemma 22.7.4 (Normalizing a Frame)
content: Let \(\dim V = n + 1 \ge 1\) and let \(P_1, \dots, P_{n+2}\) be points of \(\nP(V)\) in general position. Then there are representatives \(\elem{v}_i\) with \(P_i = [\elem{v}_i]\) such that \[ (\elem{v}_1, \dots, \elem{v}_{n+1}) \text{ is a basis of } V \qquad\text{and}\qquad \elem{v}_{n+2} = \elem{v}_1 + \dots + \elem{v}_{n+1} . \] Moreover such a list is unique up to one common scalar: if \((\elem{v}'_1, \dots, \elem{v}'_{n+2})\) is another, then \(\elem{v}'_i = a\elem{v}_i\) for all \(i\) , with a single \(a \in F^{\times}\) .

title: Proposition 22.7.8 (Computing the Cross-Ratio)
content:
In the situation of @def-cross-ratio , write \(L = 
P(U)\) with \(\dim U = 2\) , choose representatives \(A = [\elem{a}]\) , \(B = [\elem{b}]\) , and expand \[ \elem{c} = c_1\elem{a} + c_2\elem{b}, \qquad \elem{d} = d_1\elem{a} + d_2\elem{b} \] for representatives \(\elem{c}\) of \(C\) and \(\elem{d}\) of \(D\) . Then \(c_1 
e 0\) , \(c_2 
e 0\) , and \[ (A, B; C, D) = [\, d_1c_2 : d_2c_1 \,] . \] If moreover \(L = 
P^1(F)\) and the four points lie in the chart \(\mu 
e 0\) , with scalars \(a, b, c, d\) given by \([t : 1] \mapsto t\) , then \[ (A, B; C, D) = \Bigl[\, (c - a)(d - b) \,:\, (c - b)(d - a) \,\Bigr] . \]

title: Proposition 22.7.10 (Projection From a Point Is a Projectivity)
content:
Let \(\dim V = 3\) , let \(L = 
P(U)\) and \(L' = 
P(U')\) be lines in the projective plane \(
P(V)\) , and let \(O = [\elem{o}]\) be a point lying on neither. For \(P \in L\) , let \(\pi(P)\) be the unique point in which the line \(O \vee P\) meets \(L'\) . Then \(\pi \colon L 	o L'\) is well defined, and it is the projectivity induced by the restriction to \(U\) of the projection of \(V\) onto \(U'\) along \(\Span(\elem{o})\) . In particular \(\pi\) preserves cross-ratio.

title: Proposition 22.7.1 (Projectivities Compose and Invert)
content: Let \(T \colon V \to W\) and \(S \colon W \to X\) be isomorphisms of finite-dimensional vector spaces over \(F\) . Then \([S] \circ [T] = [ST]\) , the map \([T]\) is a bijection with inverse \([T^{-1}]\) , and \([\id_V] = \id_{\nP(V)}\) .

title: Proposition 22.7.2 (Projectivities Preserve Subspaces, Joins, and Meets)
content:
Let \(T \colon V 	o W\) be an isomorphism and let \(U\) be a subspace of \(V\) . Then \[ [T] igl(
P(U) igr) = 
P(T(U)) , \] a projective subspace of \(
P(W)\) of the same dimension as \(
P(U)\) , and the restriction of \([T]\) to \(
P(U)\) is the projectivity induced by the isomorphism \(T|_U \colon U 	o T(U)\) . Consequently \([T]\) preserves inclusion, intersections, and joins of projective subspaces.

title: Proposition 22.7.6 (What Fixes the Coordinate Points)
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) . A projectivity of \(\nP^n(F)\) fixes each of the \(n+1\) points \([\cvec{e}_0], \dots, [\cvec{e}_n]\) if and only if it is \([\D]\) for an invertible diagonal matrix \(\D\) . The group of such projectivities is trivial if and only if \(F = \nF_2\) .

title: Proposition 22.7.7 (Over the Two-Element Field, n+1 Points Suffice)
content:
Let \(n \ge 1\) and \(F = 
F_2\) . Given two lists \(P_0, \dots, P_n\) and \(Q_0, \dots, Q_n\) of \(n+1\) points of \(
P^n(
F_2)\) , each in general position, there is exactly one projectivity of \(
P^n(
F_2)\) carrying \(P_i\) to \(Q_i\) for every \(i\) .

title: Theorem 22.7.9 (Invariance and Completeness of the Cross-Ratio)
content: Let \(L\) and \(L'\) be projective lines over \(F\) . (Invariance) If \(g \colon L \to L'\) is a projectivity and \(A, B, C \in L\) are pairwise distinct, then for every \(D \in L\) , \(\bigl(g(A), g(B); g(C), g(D)\bigr) = (A, B; C, D)\) . (Completeness) Let \(A, B, C \in L\) be pairwise distinct and \(A', B', C' \in L'\) pairwise distinct, and let \(D \in L\) , \(D' \in L'\) . Then there is a projectivity \(L \to L'\) carrying \(A, B, C, D\) to \(A', B', C', D'\) if and only if \((A,B;C,D) = (A',B';C',D')\) .

title: Theorem 22.7.5 (Fundamental Theorem of Projective Geometry)
content:
Let \(\dim V = \dim W = n + 1 \ge 1\) . Let \(P_1, \dots, P_{n+2}\) be points of \(
P(V)\) in general position and \(Q_1, \dots, Q_{n+2}\) points of \(
P(W)\) in general position. Then there is exactly one projectivity \(f \colon 
P(V) 	o 
P(W)\) with \[ f(P_i) = Q_i \qquad 	ext{for } i = 1, \dots, n+2 . \]

title: Theorem 22.7.3 (Projectivities and Scalars)
content: Let \(\dim V = \dim W \ge 1\) and let \(S, T \colon V \to W\) be isomorphisms. \([S] = [T]\) if and only if \(S = \lambda T\) for some \(\lambda \in F^{\times}\) . The set \(\operatorname{PGL}(V) \coloneqq \{[T] : T \in \GL(V)\}\) of projectivities of \(\nP(V)\) is a group under composition, the projective linear group of \(V\) . The map \(\Pi \colon \GL(V) \to \operatorname{PGL}(V)\) , \(T \mapsto [T]\) , is a surjective group homomorphism, and \(\ker \Pi = \{\lambda\,\id_V : \lambda \in F^{\times}\}\) .

title: Theorem 22.7.11 (Affine Maps Are the Projectivities Fixing Infinity)
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) and let \(g\) be a projectivity of \(\nP^n(F)\) . Then \(g(H_{\infty}) = H_{\infty}\) if and only if \(g = [\A]\) for a matrix of the block form \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \cvec{0}\tp \\ \cvec{b} & \M \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{b} \in F^n, \quad \M \in \GL_n(F) . \] In that case \(g\) maps the chart \(\{x_0 \ne 0\}\) onto itself, and in the affine coordinates above it acts as \[ \cvec{x} \longmapsto \M\cvec{x} + \cvec{b} , \] an invertible affine map with linear part \(\cvec{x} \mapsto \M\cvec{x}\) ( @def-affine-map , @thm-affine-map-is-linear-plus-translation ). Conversely every invertible affine map of \(F^n\) arises from exactly one such \(\A\) .

title: Corollary 22.8.7 (Two Points, Two Lines)
content:
Let \(\dim V = 3\) , so that \(
P(V)\) is a projective plane. Two distinct points of \(
P(V)\) lie on exactly one line. Two distinct lines of \(
P(V)\) meet in exactly one point.

title: Definition 22.8.1 (Dual Projective Space)
content:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) with \(\dim V = n + 1 \ge 1\) . The dual projective space of \(
P(V)\) is the projective space \[ 
P(V^{*}) \] of the dual space \(V^{*}\) ( @def-dual-space ). A point of \(
P(V^{*})\) is a class \([\varphi]\) with \(\varphi \in V^{*}\) nonzero , and \([\varphi] = [\psi]\) exactly when \(\psi = \lambda\varphi\) for some \(\lambda \in F \setminus \{0\}\) .

title: Example (A line and its point)
content: In \(\nP^2(\nQ)\) , find the point of the dual plane naming the line through \([1:1:0]\) and \([0:1:1]\) . Then find the point where the lines \(x_0 - x_1 + x_2 = 0\) and \(x_0 + x_2 = 0\) meet.

title: Exercise (A1)
content:
Define the dual projective space of \(
P(V)\) , and say what its dimension is. Let \(S\) be a plane in \(
P^4(F)\) . Compute \(\dim S^{0}\) . True or false, with a reason: the duality correspondence of @thm-duality-correspondence is a bijection from the points of \(
P(V)\) to the points of \(
P(V)\) . In \(
P^2\) , what is the dual of the statement “three distinct points are collinear”? What are \(\emptyset^{0}\) and \(
P(V)^{0}\) ?

title: Exercise (B1: Lines and dual points)
content: Work in \(\nP^2(\nQ)\) . Find the dual point of the line through \([1:2:1]\) and \([0:1:3]\) . Find the point where the lines \(x_0 + x_1 - x_2 = 0\) and \(2x_0 - x_1 = 0\) meet.

title: Exercise (B2: Dimension bookkeeping)
content: Let \(n = 5\) , so \(\nP(V) = \nP^5(F)\) . For each of the following \(S\) , give \(\dim S^{0}\) , and say which of the two is larger. \(S\) a point. \(S\) a line. \(S\) of dimension \(2\) . \(S\) a hyperplane. \(S = \emptyset\) . Then determine whether there is any \(S\) with \(\dim S^{0} = \dim S\) . Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B3: Dualize a statement)
content: For each statement about \(\nP^3(F)\) , write the dual statement, using @thm-duality-principle with \(n = 3\) , and say whether both are true. A point and a line not through it lie in exactly one plane. Three planes with no common line meet in at most one point.

title: Exercise (C1: Counting in a finite projective plane)
content:
Let \(q\) be a prime power and \(F = 
F_q\) . Show that a projective space of dimension \(d\) over \(
F_q\) has \((q^{d+1} - 1)/(q - 1)\) points. Deduce that \(
P^2(
F_q)\) has as many lines as points, and that every point lies on exactly \(q + 1\) lines.

title: Exercise (C2: A form makes a self-duality)
content:
Let \( eta\) be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on \(V\) , with \(\dim V = n+1\) . Show that \(R_{ eta} \colon V 	o V^{*}\) , \(\elem{v} \mapsto  eta(\cdot, \elem{v})\) , is an isomorphism, and deduce that it induces a projectivity \([R_{ eta}] \colon 
P(V) 	o 
P(V^{*})\) . Hence define, for a projective subspace \(S\) of \(
P(V)\) , a projective subspace \(S^{\perp}\) of \(
P(V)\) with \(\dim S^{\perp} = n - 1 - \dim S\) , and show that the assignment \(S \mapsto S^{\perp}\) is an inclusion-reversing bijection of the set of projective subspaces of \(
P(V)\) with itself. Give an example over \(
R\) with \(n = 2\) in which \(S \subseteq S^{\perp}\) for some point \(S\) , and explain why this cannot happen if \( eta\) is positive definite.

title: Exercise (C3: What the correspondence does to a chain)
content:
Let \(\dim V = n + 1\) and let \[ \emptyset = S_{-1} \subsetneq S_0 \subsetneq S_1 \subsetneq \dots \subsetneq S_n = 
P(V) \] be projective subspaces with \(\dim S_d = d\) for each \(d\) . Prove that \(S_n^{0} \subsetneq S_{n-1}^{0} \subsetneq \dots \subsetneq S_{-1}^{0}\) is again such a chain, and identify \(\dim S_d^{0}\) . Deduce that \(S \mapsto S^{0}\) carries the chains of this shape in \(
P(V)\) bijectively to those in \(
P(V^{*})\) , and that it reverses their order.

title: Lemma 22.8.1 (Passing Between U and \nP(U))
content:
Let \(U, U_1, U_2\) be subspaces of \(V\) . \(
P(U_1) \subseteq 
P(U_2)\) if and only if \(U_1 \subseteq U_2\) . In particular \(U \mapsto 
P(U)\) is injective, so a projective subspace determines its subspace. \(
P(U_1 \cap U_2) = 
P(U_1) \cap 
P(U_2)\) . \(
P(U_1) \vee 
P(U_2) = 
P(U_1 + U_2)\) , where \(\vee\) is the join, the smallest projective subspace containing both ( @prp-join-and-meet ).

title: Proposition 22.8.5 (Duality and Projectivities)
content: Let \(T \colon V \to W\) be an isomorphism of \((n+1)\) -dimensional spaces, with dual map \(T' \colon W^{*} \to V^{*}\) ( @def-dual-map ), which is an isomorphism by @thm-dual-map-properties (d). Then for every projective subspace \(S\) of \(\nP(V)\) , \[ \bigl([T](S)\bigr)^{0} = \bigl[(T')^{-1}\bigr]\bigl(S^{0}\bigr) . \]

title: Proposition 22.8.2 (Points of the Dual Are Hyperplanes)
content:
Let \(\dim V = n + 1 \ge 1\) . The map \[ [\varphi] \longmapsto 
P(\ker\varphi) \] is a well-defined bijection from \(
P(V^{*})\) onto the set of hyperplanes of \(
P(V)\) .

title: Theorem 22.8.4 (Dualizing Twice Returns the Original)
content:
Let \(\dim V = n + 1 \ge 1\) . The evaluation map \(\ev_V \colon V 	o V^{**}\) is an isomorphism ( @thm-double-dual-isomorphism ), so it induces a projectivity \([\ev_V] \colon 
P(V) 	o 
P(V^{**})\) ( @def-projective-transformation ). For every projective subspace \(S\) of \(
P(V)\) , \[ S^{00} = [\ev_V](S), \] so that under the identification \(
P(V) = 
P(V^{**})\) given by \([\ev_V]\) we have \(S^{00} = S\) . Moreover the inverse of the bijection of @thm-duality-correspondence (d) is \(R \mapsto [\ev_V]^{-1} igl(R^{0} igr)\) .

title: Theorem 22.8.3 (The Duality Correspondence)
content:
Let \(\dim V = n + 1 \ge 1\) , and let \(S, T\) be projective subspaces of \(
P(V)\) , the empty set and \(
P(V)\) included. Then: \(\dim S^{0} = n - 1 - \dim S\) ; \(S \subseteq T\) if and only if \(T^{0} \subseteq S^{0}\) ; \((S \vee T)^{0} = S^{0} \cap T^{0}\) and \((S \cap T)^{0} = S^{0} \vee T^{0}\) ; \(S \mapsto S^{0}\) is a bijection from the set of projective subspaces of \(
P(V)\) onto the set of projective subspaces of \(
P(V^{*})\) .

title: Theorem 22.8.6 (The Duality Principle)
content:
Let \(\dim V = n + 1 \ge 1\) , and let \(S \mapsto S^{0}\) be the correspondence of @thm-duality-correspondence , from the projective subspaces of the \(n\) -dimensional space \(
P(V)\) onto those of the \(n\) -dimensional space \(
P(V^{*})\) . Let \(R, S, T\) be projective subspaces of \(
P(V)\) and let \(d\) be an integer. Then: \(S \subseteq T\) if and only if \(T^{0} \subseteq S^{0}\) ; and \(S = T\) if and only if \(S^{0} = T^{0}\) ; \(\dim S = d\) if and only if \(\dim S^{0} = n - 1 - d\) ; \(R = S \vee T\) if and only if \(R^{0} = S^{0} \cap T^{0}\) ; \(R = S \cap T\) if and only if \(R^{0} = S^{0} \vee T^{0}\) ; as \(S\) runs over all projective subspaces of \(
P(V)\) , the subspace \(S^{0}\) runs exactly once over all projective subspaces of \(
P(V^{*})\) .

title: Definition 22.9.1 (Triangles, and the Two Perspectives)
content:
Let \(\dim V = 3\) , so that \(
P(V)\) is a projective plane ( @def-projective-subspace ). A triangle in \(
P(V)\) is an ordered triple \((A, B, C)\) of noncollinear points, called its vertices ; its sides are the three lines \(AB\) , \(BC\) , \(CA\) . Let \((A,B,C)\) and \((A',B',C')\) be triangles with \(A 
e A'\) , \(B 
e B'\) and \(C 
e C'\) . They are: perspective from a point if some point \(O\) lies on all three of the lines \(AA'\) , \(BB'\) , \(CC'\) ; such an \(O\) is a center ; perspective from a line if the three pairs of corresponding sides \(\{AB, A'B'\}\) , \(\{BC, B'C'\}\) , \(\{CA, C'A'\}\) consist of distinct lines and the three intersection points \[ AB \cap A'B', \qquad BC \cap B'C', \qquad CA \cap C'A' \] are collinear; a line through all three is an axis .

title: Example (Desargues with exact coordinates)
content: In \(\nP^2(\nQ)\) take \(O = [1:1:1]\) and the triangle \(A = [1:0:0]\) , \(B = [0:1:0]\) , \(C = [0:0:1]\) , and on the three lines through \(O\) take \[ A' = [3:1:1], \qquad B' = [1:4:1], \qquad C' = [1:1:2] . \] Verify the hypotheses, scale the representatives as in the proof, and find the axis.

title: Exercise (A1)
content:
Define “perspective from a point” and “perspective from a line” for two triangles in a projective plane. In @lem-collinear-representatives , which hypothesis makes \(\mu 
e 0\) and which makes \(
u 
e 0\) ? State @thm-desargues , with both of its hypotheses on the configuration. True or false, with a reason: in @thm-pappus the six points are required to be pairwise distinct. Name the one place in the proof of @thm-pappus where the hypothesis \(\ell 
e m\) is used.

title: Exercise (B1: A Desargues configuration)
content: In \(\nP^2(\nQ)\) let \(O = [1:1:1]\) , \(A = [1:0:0]\) , \(B = [0:1:0]\) , \(C = [0:0:1]\) , and \[ A' = [0:1:1], \qquad B' = [1:0:1], \qquad C' = [1:1:0] . \] Check that each primed point lies on the corresponding line through \(O\) , scale the representatives as in @lem-desargues-from-a-point , and compute the axis.

title: Exercise (B2: A Pappus configuration)
content: In \(\nP^2(\nQ)\) let \(\ell = \{x_1 = 0\}\) and \(m = \{x_0 = 0\}\) , and take \[ \begin{aligned} A &= [1:0:1], & B &= [1:0:2], & C &= [1:0:4], \\ A' &= [0:1:1], & B' &= [0:1:3], & C' &= [0:1:4] . \end{aligned} \] Compute \(R\) , \(Q\) , \(P\) and the line through them, and verify \(\cvec{p} + \cvec{r} - \cvec{q} = \cvec{0}\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Concurrency from collinearity)
content: In \(\nP^2(\nQ)\) let \(A = [1:0:0]\) , \(B = [0:1:0]\) , \(C = [0:0:1]\) and \[ A' = [1:2:2], \qquad B' = [2:1:2], \qquad C' = [2:2:1] . \] Verify the hypotheses of @thm-desargues , then decide whether \(AA'\) , \(BB'\) , \(CC'\) are concurrent by computing the three points \(AB\cap A'B'\) , \(BC \cap B'C'\) , \(CA \cap C'A'\) and testing them for collinearity. Do not compute the three lines \(AA'\) , \(BB'\) , \(CC'\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Desargues in space)
content:
Let \(\dim V = 4\) , so \(
P(V) = 
P^3\) . Let \((A,B,C)\) and \((A',B',C')\) be triangles spanning distinct planes \(\Pi\) and \(\Pi'\) of \(
P^3\) , with the six vertices distinct, and suppose a point \(O 
otin \Pi \cup \Pi'\) lies on each of \(AA'\) , \(BB'\) , \(CC'\) . Prove that \(A\) , \(B\) , \(A'\) , \(B'\) lie in one plane of \(
P^3\) , and deduce that the lines \(AB\) and \(A'B'\) meet. Prove that \(\Pi \cap \Pi'\) is a line. Deduce that the three points \(AB \cap A'B'\) , \(BC \cap B'C'\) , \(CA \cap C'A'\) lie on that line, and so are collinear. Hint: for (a), all four points lie on lines through \(O\) ; for (b), use the dimension formula for subspaces.

title: Exercise (C2: Pappus over the two smallest fields)
content:
Prove that the hypotheses of @thm-pappus cannot be satisfied when \(F = 
F_2\) . Over \(F = 
F_3\) , take \(\ell\) , \(m\) , \(\cvec{o}\) , \(\cvec{u}\) , \(\cvec{w}\) as in the proof of @thm-pappus and the parameters \(a = a' = 0\) , \(b = b' = 1\) , \(c = c' = 2\) . Compute \(\cvec{r}, \cvec{q}, \cvec{p}\) and exhibit a line containing all three points. Explain why the choice of parameters in (b) is the only one available over \(
F_3\) , up to renaming the points.

title: Exercise (C3: Why the side hypothesis is there)
content: In \(\nP^2(\nQ)\) let \[ \begin{aligned} A &= [1:0:0], & B &= [0:1:0], & C &= [0:0:1], \\ A' &= [1:1:0], & B' &= [1:2:0], & C' &= [1:3:1], \end{aligned} \] and let \(O = [1:3:0]\) . Prove that \((A,B,C)\) and \((A',B',C')\) are triangles with six distinct vertices, and that \(O\) lies on each of \(AA'\) , \(BB'\) , \(CC'\) . Prove that the two triangles are not perspective from a line, in the strict sense of @def-perspective-triangles . Say which clause of hypothesis (ii) of @thm-desargues fails here.

title: Lemma 22.9.1 (Scaling Three Collinear Points)
content: Let \(W \subseteq V\) be a \(2\) -dimensional subspace and let \(O, A, A'\) be three distinct points of the line \(\nP(W)\) . Let \(\elem{o}\) be any nonzero vector representing \(O\) . Then there are vectors \(\elem{a}\) representing \(A\) and \(\elem{a}'\) representing \(A'\) with \[ \elem{a}' = \elem{a} + \elem{o} . \]

title: Lemma 22.9.2 (Perspective from a Point Gives an Axis)
content:
Let \(\dim V = 3\) . Let \((A,B,C)\) and \((A',B',C')\) be triangles in \(
P(V)\) with \(A 
e A'\) , \(B 
e B'\) , \(C 
e C'\) , and suppose: some point \(O\) , distinct from all six vertices , lies on each of \(AA'\) , \(BB'\) , \(CC'\) ; \(AB 
e A'B'\) , \(BC 
e B'C'\) and \(CA 
e C'A'\) . Then the three points \(AB \cap A'B'\) , \(BC \cap B'C'\) , \(CA \cap C'A'\) are collinear.

title: Theorem 22.9.3 (Desargues’s Theorem)
content: Let \(\dim V = 3\) and let \((A,B,C)\) and \((A',B',C')\) be triangles in \(\nP(V)\) such that the six vertices are distinct, and no vertex of either triangle lies on a side of the other. Then the two triangles are perspective from a point if and only if they are perspective from a line.

title: Theorem 22.9.4 (Pappus’s Theorem)
content: Let \(\dim V = 3\) , let \(\ell\) and \(m\) be distinct lines of \(\nP(V)\) and let \(O\) be their common point. Let \(A, B, C\) be three distinct points of \(\ell\) , none equal to \(O\) , and let \(A', B', C'\) be three distinct points of \(m\) , none equal to \(O\) . Then the three points \[ \begin{aligned} R &= AB' \cap A'B, \\ Q &= AC' \cap A'C, \\ P &= BC' \cap B'C \end{aligned} \] exist and are collinear.

title: Corollary 22.10.2 (The Conics of a Projective Plane)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) and let \(q\) be a nonzero quadratic form on a \(3\) -dimensional space. Over an algebraically closed \(F\) there are three classes, with zero sets: a line (rank \(1\) ), two distinct lines (rank \(2\) ), a smooth conic (rank \(3\) ). Over \(\nR\) there are five classes, listed by \((n_+, n_-)\) with \(n_+ \ge n_-\) , with zero sets: \[ \begin{aligned} (1,0) &: \ \text{a line}, &\quad (2,0) &: \ \text{a single point}, \\ (1,1) &: \ \text{two distinct lines}, &\quad (3,0) &: \ \text{empty}, \\ (2,1) &: \ \text{a smooth conic, nonempty.} & & \end{aligned} \]

title: Corollary 22.10.7 (The Dual Conic)
content:
Let \(C\) be a smooth conic in \(
P(V)\) with matrix \(\A\) in some basis, and identify each line of \(
P(V)\) with the point \([\varphi]\) of \(
P(V^{*})\) for which the line is \(
P(\ker\varphi)\) , as @prp-points-of-dual-are-hyperplanes allows. Then the set of tangent lines of \(C\) is the smooth conic of \(
P(V^{*})\) with matrix \(\A^{-1}\) .

title: Definition 22.10.3 (Plücker Coordinates of a Line)
content:
Let \(L = 
P(W)\) be a line of \(
P^3\) and let \((\cvec{u}, \cvec{w})\) be a basis of \(W\) . The Plücker coordinates of \(L\) relative to that basis are the six scalars \[ p_{ij} \coloneqq u_iw_j - u_jw_i , \qquad 0 \le i < j \le 3 , \] that is, the \(2 	imes 2\) minors of the \(4	imes 2\) matrix with columns \(\cvec{u}\) and \(\cvec{w}\) . By @thm-wedge-coordinates-are-minors they are the coordinates of the wedge: \[ \cvec{u}\wedge\cvec{w} = \sum_{i<j} p_{ij}\,\elem{e}_{ij} . \] The point \([\cvec{u}\wedge\cvec{w}] \in 
P(\Lambda^2F^4) = 
P^5\) is the Plücker point of \(L\) , written \([L]\) .

title: Definition 22.10.2 (Polar Line, Tangent Line)
content: Let \(C = Z(q)\) be a smooth conic in \(\nP(V)\) , \(\dim V = 3\) , with symmetric bilinear form \(\beta\) , and let \(P = [\elem{x}]\) . The polar of \(P\) with respect to \(C\) is \[ P^{\beta} \coloneqq \{\, [\elem{y}] \in \nP(V) : \beta(\elem{x},\elem{y}) = 0 \,\} , \] and \(P\) is the pole of that line. For \(P \in C\) , the polar \(P^{\beta}\) is called the tangent line to \(C\) at \(P\) .

title: Definition 22.10.1 (Projective Quadric, Conic, Smooth Quadric)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) , let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(F\) and let \(q\) be a nonzero quadratic form on \(V\) ( @def-quadratic-form ), with associated symmetric bilinear form \(\beta\) ( @thm-polarization-forms ). The projective quadric defined by \(q\) is \[ Z(q) \coloneqq \{\, [\elem{x}] \in \nP(V) : q(\elem{x}) = 0 \,\} . \] The rank of the quadric is \(\rank\beta\) , and the quadric is smooth (or nondegenerate ) when \(\beta\) is nondegenerate, that is, when the rank is \(\dim V\) . A quadric in a projective plane is called a conic , the same word Section 5 used for the affine case ( @def-quadric ).

title: Example (Classifying a conic by hand)
content:

title: Lemma 22.10.3 (A Conic Containing a Line Is Degenerate)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) , let \(\dim V = 3\) and let \(q \ne 0\) be a quadratic form on \(V\) vanishing on every vector of a \(2\) -dimensional subspace \(W\) . Then \(q = \varphi\chi\) for two nonzero linear functionals \(\varphi, \chi\) on \(V\) with \(\ker\varphi = W\) , and the rank of \(q\) is at most \(2\) . In particular a smooth conic contains no line.

title: Proposition 22.10.8 (The Plücker Point Determines the Line)
content:
Let \(L = 
P(W)\) be a line of \(
P^3\) and let \((\cvec{u},\cvec{w})\) be a basis of \(W\) . \(\cvec{u}\wedge\cvec{w} 
e \elem{0}\) , and \([\cvec{u}\wedge\cvec{w}]\) does not depend on the choice of basis \((\cvec{u},\cvec{w})\) of \(W\) , so \([L]\) is well defined. \(W = \{\, \cvec{v} \in F^4 : \cvec{v}\wedge\cvec{u}\wedge\cvec{w} = \elem{0} \,\}\) . Consequently \(L \mapsto [L]\) is injective on lines.

title: Proposition 22.10.6 (Reciprocity and Tangency)
content: With the notation of @def-pole-and-polar , let \(P = [\elem{x}]\) and \(Q = [\elem{y}]\) . \(Q \in P^{\beta}\) if and only if \(P \in Q^{\beta}\) . \(P \in C\) if and only if \(P \in P^{\beta}\) . Let \(P \in C\) and let \(L\) be a line through \(P\) . Then \(L \cap C = \{P\}\) if and only if \(L = P^{\beta}\) ; every other line through \(P\) meets \(C\) in exactly two points.

title: Theorem 22.10.5 (Projection from a Point of a Conic)
content:
Let \(\operatorname{char} F 
e 2\) , let \(C = Z(q)\) be a smooth conic in \(
P(V)\) , \(\dim V = 3\) , and suppose \(C\) contains a point \(P_0 = [\elem{p}]\) . Let \(\ell\) be any line of \(
P(V)\) with \(P_0 
otin \ell\) . Then the map \[ \psi \colon \ell 	o C, \qquad \psi([\elem{x}]) =  igl[\, -q(\elem{x})\,\elem{p} + 2 eta(\elem{p},\elem{x})\,\elem{x} \, igr] \] is a well-defined bijection. In particular \(C\) is in bijection with \(
P^1\) .

title: Theorem 22.10.4 (Five Points Determine a Conic)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) and let \(P_1, \dots, P_5\) be five points of \(\nP^2\) in general position ( @def-general-position ), that is, pairwise distinct with no three collinear. Then there is a nonzero quadratic form \(q\) on \(F^3\) vanishing at all five, and it is unique up to a nonzero scalar. Consequently exactly one conic passes through the five points.

title: Theorem 22.10.9 (The Plücker Relation and the Klein Quadric)
content:
Let \(F\) be any field and let \(\elem{0} 
e \omega = \sum_{i<j} p_{ij}\elem{e}_{ij} \in \Lambda^2F^4\) . Then \(\omega = \cvec{u}\wedge\cvec{w}\) for some \(\cvec{u},\cvec{w} \in F^4\) if and only if \[ p_{01}p_{23} - p_{02}p_{13} + p_{03}p_{12} = 0 . \] {#eq-plucker-relation} Consequently \(L \mapsto [L]\) is a bijection from the set of lines of \(
P^3\) onto the set \[ \cK \coloneqq  igl\{\, [\omega] \in 
P^5 : p_{01}p_{23} - p_{02}p_{13} + p_{03}p_{12} = 0 \, igr\} , \] the Klein quadric .

title: Theorem 22.10.1 (Classification of Projective Quadrics)
content: Let \(\operatorname{char} F \ne 2\) and \(\dim V = n+1\) , and let \(q, q'\) be nonzero quadratic forms on \(V\) with matrices \(\A, \A'\) in some basis. If \(F\) is algebraically closed, then \(q\) and \(q'\) are projectively equivalent if and only if \(\rank\A = \rank\A'\) . There are exactly \(n+1\) classes, one for each rank \(r = 1, \dots, n+1\) , with normal form \(x_0^2 + \dots + x_{r-1}^2\) . If \(F = \nR\) , then \(q\) and \(q'\) are projectively equivalent if and only if their inertias \((n_+, n_-, n_0)\) and \((n_+', n_-', n_0')\) agree up to interchanging \(n_+\) with \(n_-\) . A normal form is \(x_0^2 + \dots + x_{n_+-1}^2 - x_{n_+}^2 - \dots - x_{r-1}^2\) with \(n_+ \ge n_-\) , \(r = n_+ + n_-\) .

title: Definition 23.1.2 (Algebra Homomorphism, Kernel, and Image)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be algebras over \(F\) . An algebra homomorphism \(\varphi \colon A \to B\) is an \(F\) -linear map with \[ \varphi(xy) = \varphi(x)\varphi(y) \quad \text{for all } x, y \in A, \qquad \varphi(1_A) = 1_B , \] as in @def-algebra-over-field . Its kernel is \(\ker\varphi = \{x \in A : \varphi(x) = 0\}\) and its image is \(\im\varphi = \{\varphi(x) : x \in A\}\) , the kernel and image of \(\varphi\) as a linear map.

title: Definition 23.1.3 (Isomorphic Algebras)
content: An algebra isomorphism is a bijective algebra homomorphism. Algebras \(A\) and \(B\) are isomorphic , written \(A \cong B\) , if there is an algebra isomorphism \(A \to B\) .

title: Definition 23.1.6 (Commutant and Center)
content: Let \(A\) be an algebra over \(F\) and let \(S \subseteq A\) be any subset . The commutant of \(S\) in \(A\) is \[ S' \coloneqq \{ a \in A : as = sa \text{ for every } s \in S \} . \] The center of \(A\) is \(Z(A) \coloneqq A'\) , the set of elements commuting with every element of \(A\) . We write \(S''\) for \((S')'\) .

title: Definition 23.1.4 (The Subalgebra Generated by a Set)
content: Let \(A\) be an algebra over \(F\) and \(S \subseteq A\) . The subalgebra generated by \(S\) , written \(F\langle S\rangle\) , is the intersection of all subalgebras of \(A\) containing \(S\) .

title: Definition 23.1.5 (Group Algebra)
content: Let \(G\) be a finite group with identity \(e\) , and let \(F\) be a field. The group algebra \(F[G]\) is the free vector space \(F^{(G)}\) on the set \(G\) ( @def-free-vector-space ), with basis \(\{\delta_g : g \in G\}\) , equipped with the unique bilinear multiplication satisfying \[ \delta_g\,\delta_h = \delta_{gh} \qquad \text{for all } g, h \in G . \] We write \(g\) for \(\delta_g\) and \(1\) for \(\delta_e\) , so that a general element is a formal sum \(\sum_{g \in G} a_g\,g\) with all \(a_g \in F\) , two such sums are equal exactly when all their coefficients agree, and \[ \Bigl(\sum_{g} a_g\,g\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{h} b_h\,h\Bigr) = \sum_{k \in G}\Bigl(\sum_{g \in G} a_g\,b_{g^{-1}k}\Bigr)k . \]

title: Definition 23.1.1 (Subalgebra)
content: Let \(A\) be an algebra over \(F\) . A subset \(B \subseteq A\) is a subalgebra of \(A\) if \(B\) is a subspace of \(A\) ; \(xy \in B\) for all \(x, y \in B\) ; \(1_A \in B\) .

title: Proposition 23.1.5 (The Center of the Matrix Algebra Is the Scalars)
content: Let \(F\) be any field and \(n \ge 1\) . Then \(Z(M_n(F)) = F\I_n\) . Equivalently, for a finite-dimensional \(V \ne \{\elem{0}\}\) , the operators commuting with every operator on \(V\) are exactly the scalar multiples of \(\id_V\) .

title: Proposition 23.1.4 (Properties of the Commutant)
content: Let \(A\) be an algebra over \(F\) and \(S, T \subseteq A\) . \(S'\) is a subalgebra of \(A\) ; in particular \(Z(A)\) is a commutative subalgebra. If \(S \subseteq T\) , then \(T' \subseteq S'\) . \(S \subseteq S''\) . \(S' = S'''\) .

title: Proposition 23.1.1 (What the Generated Subalgebra Contains)
content: Let \(A\) be an algebra over \(F\) and \(S \subseteq A\) . Then \(F\langle S\rangle\) is the span of \(1_A\) together with all finite products \(s_1s_2\cdots s_k\) with \(k \ge 1\) and \(s_1, \dots, s_k \in S\) .

title: Proposition 23.1.2 (The Algebra Generated by One Operator)
content: Let \(V \ne \{\elem{0}\}\) be finite-dimensional over \(F\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) have minimal polynomial \(m_T\) , of degree \(d\) . Then \[ F[T] \coloneqq \{p(T) : p \in F[x]\} \] is a commutative subalgebra of \(\cL(V)\) , it equals \(F\langle\{T\}\rangle\) , and \((\id_V, T, T^2, \dots, T^{d-1})\) is a basis of it. In particular \(\dim F[T] = \deg m_T\) .

title: Theorem 23.1.3 (Left Multiplication Embeds an Algebra in Its Own Operators)
content: Let \(A\) be an algebra over \(F\) . For \(a \in A\) define \(L_a \colon A \to A\) by \(L_a(x) = ax\) . Then \[ L \colon A \to \cL(A), \qquad a \mapsto L_a , \] is an injective algebra homomorphism. If \(\dim_F A = n < \infty\) , then \(A\) is isomorphic to a subalgebra of \(M_n(F)\) .

title: Corollary 23.2.3 (Homomorphisms out of a Matrix Algebra Are Injective)
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(n \ge 1\) , and let \(\varphi \colon M_n(F) \to B\) be an algebra homomorphism into any \(F\) -algebra \(B \ne \{0\}\) . Then \(\varphi\) is injective.

title: Definition 23.2.1 (Left and Right Ideals)
content: Let \(A\) be an algebra over \(F\) and let \(I \subseteq A\) be a subspace . Then \(I\) is a left ideal of \(A\) if \(ax \in I\) for every \(a \in A\) and every \(x \in I\) ; a right ideal of \(A\) if \(xa \in I\) for every \(a \in A\) and every \(x \in I\) . A two-sided ideal is a subspace that is both, which is @def-two-sided-ideal . When \(A\) is commutative the three notions coincide, and we say ideal .

title: Definition 23.2.2 (Quotient Algebra)
content: Let \(A\) be an algebra over \(F\) and \(\cI\) a two-sided ideal of \(A\) . The quotient algebra \(A/\cI\) is the quotient vector space \(A/\cI\) with the multiplication \((x + \cI)(y + \cI) = xy + \cI\) of @lem-quotient-algebra , and \(\pi \colon A \to A/\cI\) , \(\pi(x) = x + \cI\) , is the quotient homomorphism .

title: Example (The group algebra of a cyclic group)
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(n \ge 1\) , and \(G = \nZ/n\nZ\) written multiplicatively as \(\{1, g, \dots, g^{n-1}\}\) with \(g^n = 1\) . Show that \[ F[G] \cong F[x]/\langle x^n - 1\rangle . \]

title: Example (Ideals in five algebras)
content: In any algebra \(A\) : \(\{0\}\) and \(A\) . In \(F[x]\) : the sets \(\langle p\rangle\) of @def-ideal-polynomials . In \(M_n(F)\) : the column ideal \(C_j\) of matrices whose columns other than the \(j\) -th are zero. In \(M_n(F)\) : the set \(R_U = \{\X : \col(\X) \subseteq U\}\) for a subspace \(U \subseteq F^n\) . In any algebra \(A\) : the kernel of an algebra homomorphism \(\varphi \colon A \to B\) . Say in each case which of the three kinds of ideal is meant.
