content: In the notation of @def-qr-iteration , \(\A^{(k+1)} = (\Q^{(k)})^{*}\A^{(k)}\Q^{(k)}\) for every \(k\) . Consequently all the matrices \(\A^{(k)}\) are unitarily similar to \(\A\) , and they share its characteristic polynomial, its eigenvalues with multiplicities, its trace, and its determinant.

title: Theorem 24.5.3 (Convergence of the First Column)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) be invertible and diagonalizable, say \(\A = \X\vLambda\X^{-1}\) with \(\vLambda = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)\) and with \(\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n\) the columns of \(\X\) . Assume a single dominant eigenvalue , \[ \lvert\lambda_1vert > \lvert\lambda_2vert \ge \dots \ge \lvert\lambda_nvert > 0 , \] and write \(\cvec{e}_1 = c_1\cvec{v}_1 + \dots + c_n\cvec{v}_n\) , assuming \(c_1 
eq 0\) . Put \(t = \lvert\lambda_2/\lambda_1vert < 1\) . Then there is a constant \(C\) , depending on \(\A\) and \(\X\) but not on \(k\) , such that the unshifted QR iterates satisfy \[ 
orm{\A^{(k+1)}\cvec{e}_1 - \lambda_1\cvec{e}_1}_2 \le C\,t^{k} \qquad (k \ge 1) . \] In particular \(a^{(k)}_{11} 	o \lambda_1\) and \(a^{(k)}_{i1} 	o 0\) for every \(i \ge 2\) , each at the rate \(t^{k}\) . For \(n = 2\) this says that the iterates converge to upper triangular form, with \(a^{(k)}_{11} 	o \lambda_1\) and \(a^{(k)}_{22} 	o \lambda_2\) .

title: Theorem 24.5.2 (QR Iterates Factor the Powers)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) and let \(\A^{(k)}\) , \(\Q^{(k)}\) , \(\R^{(k)}\) be as in @def-qr-iteration . Then for every \(k \ge 1\) , \[ \A^{(k+1)} = \U_k^{*}\,\A\,\U_k \qquad\text{and}\qquad \A^{k} = \U_k\T_k . \] In particular \(\U_k\T_k\) is a QR factorization of \(\A^{k}\) .

title: Definition 24.6.1 (Krylov Subspace)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) , let \(\cvec{b} \in F^n\) , and let \(k \ge 1\) be an integer. The \(k\) -th Krylov subspace of the pair \((\A, \cvec{b})\) is \[ \cK_k(\A, \cvec{b}) \coloneqq \Span\bigl(\cvec{b},\ \A\cvec{b},\ \A^2\cvec{b},\ \dots,\ \A^{k-1}\cvec{b}\bigr) \subseteq F^n . \]

title: Definition 24.6.2 (Ritz Values and Ritz Vectors)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) , let \(\Q_k \in M_{n\times k}(F)\) have orthonormal columns, and put \(\H_k = \Q_k^{*}\A\Q_k\) . The eigenvalues \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_k\) of \(\H_k\) are the Ritz values of \(\A\) from the subspace \(\Span(\cvec{q}_1,\dots,\cvec{q}_k)\) , and for an eigenvector \(\cvec{y}\) of \(\H_k\) with \(\H_k\cvec{y} = \theta\cvec{y}\) and \(\norm{\cvec{y}} = 1\) , the vector \(\cvec{x} = \Q_k\cvec{y}\) is the corresponding Ritz vector ; the pair \((\theta, \cvec{x})\) is a Ritz pair .

title: Example (A breakdown at step two)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\cvec{b} = \cvec{e}_1\) . Run the Lanczos recurrence of @thm-lanczos , and identify what it finds.

title: Example (Ritz values closing in on the extremes)
content: Let \(\A = \diag(4,3,2,1)\) and \(\cvec{b} = (1,1,1,1)\) . Compute the Lanczos coefficients, the Ritz values for \(k = 1, 2, 3\) , and the residual of the largest Ritz pair at \(k = 3\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define \(\cK_k(\A,\cvec{b})\) and state its dimension in terms of \(m_{\A,\cvec{b}}\) . State the Arnoldi identity of @thm-arnoldi (b), naming the shape of every matrix in it. True or false: for Hermitian \(\A\) , the Arnoldi process needs all of \(\cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_j\) to produce \(\cvec{q}_{j+1}\) . Justify your answer. What does a breakdown \(h_{k+1,k} = 0\) mean, and why is it good news? Give the formula for the residual of a Ritz pair, and say why it costs nothing to evaluate.

title: Exercise (B1: Dimensions)
content: For each pair \((\A, \cvec{b})\) , determine \(\dim\cK_k(\A,\cvec{b})\) for every \(k \ge 1\) . Justify your answer. \(\A = \diag(2,2,5)\) , \(\cvec{b} = (1,1,1)\) . \(\A = \diag(2,2,5)\) , \(\cvec{b} = (1,-1,0)\) . \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) , \(\cvec{b} = \cvec{e}_2\) . \(\A\) the \(4 \times 4\) matrix with \(\A\cvec{e}_j = \cvec{e}_{j+1}\) for \(j \le 3\) and \(\A\cvec{e}_4 = \cvec{0}\) , \(\cvec{b} = \cvec{e}_1\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Two Arnoldi steps)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \cvec{b} = \cvec{e}_3 . \] Carry out two Arnoldi steps. Write down \(\Q_2\) , \(\widetilde{\H}_2\) , and \(\H_2\) , verify @eq-arnoldi , and compute the two Ritz values with their residuals. Hence say which, if either, is a converged eigenvalue estimate.

title: Exercise (B3: Lanczos on a tridiagonal matrix)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric tridiagonal with every subdiagonal entry nonzero, and let \(\cvec{b} = \cvec{e}_1\) . Prove that the Lanczos process produces \(\cvec{q}_j = \pm\cvec{e}_j\) for every \(j\) , and hence that \(\T_n = \A\) up to signs. What does this say about the cost of Lanczos on a matrix that is already tridiagonal?

title: Exercise (C1: Ritz values from the other end)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) be Hermitian and let \(\theta_1^{(k)} \ge \dots \ge \theta_k^{(k)}\) be the Ritz values from \(\cK_k(\A,\cvec{b})\) , \(1 \le k \le d\) . Prove that \(\theta_k^{(k)}\) is nonincreasing in \(k\) and that \(\theta_k^{(k)} \ge \lambda_n(\A)\) . Deduce a bound for \(\theta_k^{(k)} - \lambda_n(\A)\) from @thm-ritz-extreme-convergence , with no new argument. Show that at \(k = d\) the Ritz values are \(d\) of the eigenvalues of \(\A\) , and say which.

title: Exercise (C2: Shift invariance, and what it costs)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) , \(\cvec{b} \neq \cvec{0}\) , and let \(\sigma, c \in F\) with \(c \neq 0\) . Prove that \(\cK_k(c\A + \sigma\I, \cvec{b}) = \cK_k(\A, \cvec{b})\) for every \(k\) . Deduce that the Arnoldi vectors \(\cvec{q}_j\) are the same for \(\A\) and for \(c\A + \sigma\I\) , up to a scalar of modulus one, and that the Ritz values transform by \(\theta \mapsto c\theta + \sigma\) . Contrast this with Section 5: explain in two sentences why shifting accelerates the QR algorithm but does not accelerate a Krylov method, and what one must do instead to get the effect.

title: Exercise (C3: When the Krylov space is everything)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) . Prove that there exists \(\cvec{b}\) with \(\cK_n(\A,\cvec{b}) = F^n\) if and only if \(m_{\A} = p_{\A}\) . Prove that in that case the Arnoldi process run to \(k = n\) produces a unitary \(\Q_n\) with \(\Q_n^{*}\A\Q_n\) upper Hessenberg, all of whose subdiagonal entries are nonzero. Hence give a second proof of @thm-hessenberg-form over \(\nC\) for such \(\A\) , and explain why it does not replace Chapter 11’s. Hint for (a): Chapter 10 §05 calls such a \(\cvec{b}\) a cyclic vector.

title: Proposition 24.6.1 (Krylov Spaces: Nesting, Dimension, Invariance)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) and \(\cvec{b} \in F^n\) with \(\cvec{b} \neq \cvec{0}\) , and let \(d = \deg m_{\A,\cvec{b}} \ge 1\) be the degree of the \(\A\) -annihilator of \(\cvec{b}\) ( @def-t-annihilator ). Then, for every \(k \ge 1\) : \(\cK_k(\A,\cvec{b}) = \{\, p(\A)\cvec{b} : p \in F[x],\ \deg p \le k-1 \,\}\) , and \(\cK_k \subseteq \cK_{k+1}\) and \(\A\,\cK_k \subseteq \cK_{k+1}\) ; \(\dim\cK_k(\A,\cvec{b}) = \min(k, d)\) ; \(\cK_{k+1} = \cK_k\) if and only if \(k \ge d\) , and in that case \(\cK_k = Z(\cvec{b};\A)\) is \(\A\) -invariant.

title: Theorem 24.6.2 (The Arnoldi Process)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) , let \(\cvec{b} \in F^n\) be nonzero, let \(d = \deg m_{\A,\cvec{b}}\) , and run the Arnoldi process. Then the Arnoldi relation \[ \A\Q_k = \Q_k\H_k + h_{k+1,k}\,\cvec{q}_{k+1}\cvec{e}_k\tp \qquad (1 \le k \le d) \] {#eq-arnoldi} holds, the last term being \(\O\) when \(k = d\) . Moreover: For every \(j \le d\) , the list \((\cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_j)\) is an orthonormal basis of \(\cK_j(\A,\cvec{b})\) ; moreover \(h_{j+1,j} > 0\) for \(j < d\) , and \(h_{d+1,d} = 0\) , so the process breaks down at step \(d\) and at no earlier step. For \(1 \le k \le d\) we have \(\Q_k^{*}\Q_k = \I_k\) , and \(\H_k = \Q_k^{*}\A\Q_k\) is upper Hessenberg . For \(k < d\) , @eq-arnoldi can also be written \(\A\Q_k = \Q_{k+1}\widetilde{\H}_k\) . A breakdown means an invariant subspace: if \(h_{k+1,k} = 0\) , then \(\A\cK_k \subseteq \cK_k\) , and every eigenvalue of \(\H_k\) is an eigenvalue of \(\A\) .

title: Theorem 24.6.3 (The Lanczos Recurrence)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) be Hermitian , let \(\cvec{b} 
eq \cvec{0}\) , and run the Arnoldi process. Then \(\H_k\) is Hermitian for every \(k \le d\) , hence tridiagonal , with real diagonal entries; writing \(\alpha_j = h_{jj} \in 
R\) and \( eta_j = h_{j+1,j}\) , which is \(> 0\) for \(j < d\) and \(0\) for \(j = d\) , we have \(h_{j,j+1} =  eta_j\) and \[ \A\cvec{q}_j =  eta_{j-1}\cvec{q}_{j-1} + \alpha_j\cvec{q}_j +  eta_j\cvec{q}_{j+1} \qquad (1 \le j \le d), \] {#eq-lanczos} with \( eta_0\cvec{q}_0\) read as \(\cvec{0}\) and \( eta_d\cvec{q}_{d+1}\) as \(\cvec{0}\) . Consequently \(\H_k = \T_k\) is the real symmetric tridiagonal matrix with diagonal \((\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k)\) and off-diagonal \(( eta_1, \dots,  eta_{k-1})\) , and each step of the process needs only \(\cvec{q}_{j-1}\) and \(\cvec{q}_j\) .

title: Theorem 24.6.5 (A Rate for the Largest Ritz Value)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) be Hermitian with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 > \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n\) and an orthonormal eigenbasis \(\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n\) . Let \(\cvec{b}\) be a unit vector with \(\cvec{b} = \sum_i c_i\cvec{v}_i\) and \(c_1 \neq 0\) , and put \[ \tau^2 = \frac{\sum_{i \ge 2}\lvert c_i\rvert^2}{\lvert c_1\rvert^2}, \qquad \rho = \frac{\lambda_2 - \lambda_n}{2\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 - \lambda_n} \in [0, 1) . \] Then the largest Ritz value \(\theta_1^{(k)}\) from \(\cK_k(\A,\cvec{b})\) satisfies, for \(1 \le k \le d\) , \[ 0 \ \le\ \lambda_1 - \theta_1^{(k)} \ \le\ (\lambda_1 - \lambda_n)\,\tau^2\,\rho^{2(k-1)} , \] and \(\theta_1^{(k)}\) is nondecreasing in \(k\) .

title: Theorem 24.6.4 (Ritz Values Interlace, and Their Residual Is One Number)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) be Hermitian with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1(\A) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(\A)\) , let \(1 \le k \le d\) , and let \(	heta_1 \ge \dots \ge 	heta_k\) be the Ritz values from \(\cK_k(\A,\cvec{b})\) , that is, the eigenvalues of \(\T_k\) . \(\lambda_i(\A) \ \ge\ 	heta_i \ \ge\ \lambda_{i + n - k}(\A)\) for \(1 \le i \le k\) . If \(\T_k\cvec{y} = 	heta\cvec{y}\) with \(
orm{\cvec{y}} = 1\) and \(\cvec{x} = \Q_k\cvec{y}\) , then \[ \A\cvec{x} - 	heta\cvec{x} =  eta_k\,y_k\,\cvec{q}_{k+1}, \qquad	ext{so}\qquad 
orm{\A\cvec{x} - 	heta\cvec{x}} =  eta_k\,\lvert y_kvert , \] where \(y_k\) is the last coordinate of \(\cvec{y}\) and \( eta_k = h_{k+1,k}\) , with \( eta_d\cvec{q}_{d+1}\) read as \(\cvec{0}\) .

title: Corollary 24.7.5 (Finite Termination)
content: In exact arithmetic the conjugate gradient iteration reaches \(\cvec{r}^{(m)} = \cvec{0}\) , and hence \(\cvec{x}^{(m)} = \cvec{x}^{\star}\) , for some \(m \le n\) . If \(\A\) has only \(d\) distinct eigenvalues, then \(m \le d\) .

title: Definition 24.7.4 (Chebyshev Polynomials)
content: The Chebyshev polynomials \(T_0, T_1, T_2, \dots \in \nR[x]\) are defined by \[ T_0 = 1, \qquad T_1 = x, \qquad T_{k+1} = 2x\,T_k - T_{k-1} \ \ (k \ge 1). \]

title: Definition 24.7.3 (The Conjugate Gradient Iteration)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
R)\) be symmetric positive definite, \(\cvec{b} \in 
R^n\) , and \(\cvec{x}^{(0)} \in 
R^n\) . Set \[ \cvec{r}^{(0)} = \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x}^{(0)}, \qquad \cvec{p}^{(0)} = \cvec{r}^{(0)} . \] For \(k = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) : if \(\cvec{r}^{(k)} = \cvec{0}\) , stop. Otherwise put \[  egin{aligned} \alpha_k &=  rac{(\cvec{r}^{(k)})	p\cvec{r}^{(k)}}{(\cvec{p}^{(k)})	p\A\cvec{p}^{(k)}}, & \cvec{x}^{(k+1)} &= \cvec{x}^{(k)} + \alpha_k\cvec{p}^{(k)},\ \cvec{r}^{(k+1)} &= \cvec{r}^{(k)} - \alpha_k\A\cvec{p}^{(k)}, &  eta_k &=  rac{(\cvec{r}^{(k+1)})	p\cvec{r}^{(k+1)}}{(\cvec{r}^{(k)})	p\cvec{r}^{(k)}}, \end{aligned} \] and \(\cvec{p}^{(k+1)} = \cvec{r}^{(k+1)} +  eta_k\cvec{p}^{(k)}\) . This is the conjugate gradient iteration, or CG .

title: Definition 24.7.1 (The Energy Inner Product and the Energy Norm)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
R)\) be symmetric positive definite. The energy inner product is \[ \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}}_{\A} \coloneqq \cvec{y}	p\A\cvec{x} \qquad (\cvec{x}, \cvec{y} \in 
R^n), \] and the energy norm is \(
orm{\cvec{x}}_{\A} \coloneqq \inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}}_{\A}^{1/2} = (\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x})^{1/2}\) . Two vectors are \(\A\) -orthogonal , or conjugate , when \(\inner{\cvec{x}}{\cvec{y}}_{\A} = 0\) .

title: Definition 24.7.2 (Steepest Descent)
content: Let \(\A \succ \O\) and \(\cvec{b} \in \nR^n\) , and let \(\cvec{x}^{(0)} \in \nR^n\) . Steepest descent is the iteration: for \(k = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) , set \(\cvec{r}^{(k)} = \cvec{b} - \A\cvec{x}^{(k)}\) ; if \(\cvec{r}^{(k)} = \cvec{0}\) , stop, since \(\cvec{x}^{(k)} = \cvec{x}^{\star}\) ; otherwise put \[ t_k = \frac{(\cvec{r}^{(k)})\tp\cvec{r}^{(k)}}{(\cvec{r}^{(k)})\tp\A\cvec{r}^{(k)}}, \qquad \cvec{x}^{(k+1)} = \cvec{x}^{(k)} + t_k\,\cvec{r}^{(k)} . \]

title: Example (Two distinct eigenvalues, two steps)
content: Let \(\A = \I_3 + \J\) , where \(\J\) is the all-ones matrix, let \(\cvec{b} = \cvec{e}_1\) and \(\cvec{x}^{(0)} = \cvec{0}\) . Run CG.

title: Example (The bound is attained)
content: Let \(\A = \diag(9, 1)\) , \(\cvec{b} = (9, 1)\) , and \(\cvec{x}^{(0)} = (2, -8)\) . Run three steps of steepest descent and compare with @thm-steepest-descent .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define the energy inner product of a symmetric positive definite \(\A\) , and say which clause of @def-positive-semidefinite makes it an inner product. State @prp-quadratic-minimizer , and explain in one sentence why it makes \(\norm{\cdot}_{\A}\) the natural yardstick for the error. State the optimality property of the \(k\) -th conjugate gradient iterate, naming the set over which it is optimal. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: in exact arithmetic, conjugate gradients applied to a \(1000 \times 1000\) positive definite matrix with \(5\) distinct eigenvalues terminates after at most \(5\) steps. Write down the two Chebyshev facts of @lem-chebyshev-extremal , and say which of the two supplies the \(\sqrt\kappa\) in @thm-cg-convergence .

title: Exercise (B1: Steepest descent by hand)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) , \(\cvec{b} = (2, 1)\) , and \(\cvec{x}^{(0)} = (0, 0)\) . Compute \(\cvec{x}^{(1)}\) and \(\cvec{x}^{(2)}\) by steepest descent. Compute \(\norm{\cvec{x}^{(k)} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_{\A}^2\) for \(k = 0, 1, 2\) and compare the ratios with the bound of @thm-steepest-descent .

title: Exercise (B2: Conjugate gradients by hand)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\) , \(\cvec{b} = (1, 2)\) , and \(\cvec{x}^{(0)} = (0,0)\) . Run conjugate gradients to termination, and verify at each stage that the residuals are orthogonal and the directions \(\A\) -orthogonal.

title: Exercise (B3: Chebyshev by recurrence)
content: Compute \(T_5\) from @def-chebyshev-polynomials . Evaluate \(T_5(1)\) , \(T_5(-1)\) , and \(T_5(0)\) , and check them against @lem-chebyshev-extremal (a). Evaluate \(T_5(2)\) from the polynomial, and check it against the closed formula of @lem-chebyshev-extremal (b).

title: Exercise (C1: Sharpness of Kantorovich)
content: Let \(a \ge c > 0\) and let \(\A = \diag(a, c)\) . Prove that for \(\cvec{y} = (1, 1)\) the inequality of @lem-kantorovich is an equality. Hence deduce that the constant \((\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1)\) in @thm-steepest-descent cannot be replaced by any smaller one.

title: Exercise (C2: Finite termination, from polynomials)
content: Give a second proof of the second statement of @cor-cg-finite-termination — that \(d\) distinct eigenvalues force termination in at most \(d\) steps — using @eq-cg-polynomial-min instead of a dimension count. Hint: consider \(q(x) = \prod_{i=1}^{d}(1 - x/\mu_i)\) .

title: Exercise (C3: What preconditioning does to the spectrum)
content: Let \(\A, \M \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric positive definite and write \(\M = \C\C\tp\) with \(\C\) invertible, which is possible by @thm-cholesky . Prove that \(\C^{-1}\A\C^{-\top}\) is symmetric positive definite. Prove that \(\C^{-1}\A\C^{-\top}\) and \(\M^{-1}\A\) are similar, and deduce that their eigenvalues coincide. Hence show that those eigenvalues are exactly the generalized eigenvalues of the pencil \(\A - \lambda\M\) in the sense of @def-generalized-eigenvalue , and say what @thm-cg-convergence then predicts for preconditioned conjugate gradients.

title: Lemma 24.7.6 (Chebyshev Polynomials: Size Inside and Growth Outside)
content: For every \(k \ge 0\) and every \(w \in \nC \setminus\{0\}\) , \[ T_k\Bigl(\frac{w + w^{-1}}{2}\Bigr) = \frac{w^{k} + w^{-k}}{2} . \] {#eq-chebyshev-substitution} Consequently: \(\lvert T_k(x)\rvert \le 1\) for every real \(x \in [-1, 1]\) , and \(T_k(1) = 1\) ; for every real \(z > 1\) , \[ T_k(z) = \tfrac12\Bigl(\bigl(z + \sqrt{z^2-1}\bigr)^{k} + \bigl(z + \sqrt{z^2-1}\bigr)^{-k}\Bigr) \ \ge\ \tfrac12\bigl(z + \sqrt{z^2-1}\bigr)^{k} , \] and, separately, \(T_k(z) \ge 1\) .

title: Lemma 24.7.2 (Kantorovich’s Inequality)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric positive definite with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n > 0\) . Then for every \(\cvec{y} \in \nR^n\) , \[ (\cvec{y}\tp\A\cvec{y})(\cvec{y}\tp\A^{-1}\cvec{y}) \le \frac{(\lambda_1 + \lambda_n)^2}{4\lambda_1\lambda_n}\,(\cvec{y}\tp\cvec{y})^2 . \]

title: Proposition 24.7.1 (The Solution Minimizes the Energy Functional)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
R)\) be symmetric positive definite, \(\cvec{b} \in 
R^n\) , and define \[ \phi(\cvec{x}) \coloneqq 	frac12\,\cvec{x}	p\A\cvec{x} - \cvec{b}	p\cvec{x} \qquad (\cvec{x} \in 
R^n). \] Then, with \(\cvec{x}^{\star} = \A^{-1}\cvec{b}\) , \[ \phi(\cvec{x}) - \phi(\cvec{x}^{\star}) = 	frac12
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_{\A}^{2} \qquad 	ext{for every } \cvec{x} \in 
R^n . \] In particular \(\cvec{x}^{\star}\) is the unique minimizer of \(\phi\) .

title: Theorem 24.7.7 (Convergence of Conjugate Gradients)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
R)\) be symmetric positive definite with \(\kappa = \kappa_2(\A)\) , let \(\cvec{b} \in 
R^n\) , and let \(\cvec{x}^{(k)}\) be the conjugate gradient iterates from \(\cvec{x}^{(0)}\) , with \(\cvec{x}^{(k)} \coloneqq \cvec{x}^{\star}\) once the iteration has terminated. Then for every \(k \ge 0\) , \[ 
orm{\cvec{x}^{(k)} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_{\A} \ \le\ 2\Bigl( rac{\sqrt{\kappa} - 1}{\sqrt{\kappa} + 1}\Bigr)^{k}\,
orm{\cvec{x}^{(0)} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_{\A} . \]

title: Theorem 24.7.4 (Conjugate Gradients: Orthogonality and Optimality)
content:
Let \(\A \succ \O\) , \(\cvec{b} \in 
R^n\) , \(\cvec{x}^{(0)} \in 
R^n\) , and write \(\cK_k = \cK_k(\A, \cvec{r}^{(0)})\) for the Krylov subspaces of @def-krylov-subspace , with \(\cK_0 = \{\cvec{0}\}\) . Suppose the iteration of @def-conjugate-gradient has produced nonzero \(\cvec{r}^{(0)}, \dots, \cvec{r}^{(k)}\) . Then: \(\cvec{p}^{(0)}, \dots, \cvec{p}^{(k)}\) are nonzero and pairwise \(\A\) -orthogonal, and every \(\alpha_j\) and \( eta_j\) with \(j \le k\) is defined, with \(\alpha_j > 0\) ; \(\cvec{r}^{(0)}, \dots, \cvec{r}^{(k)}\) are pairwise orthogonal, and \((\cvec{r}^{(k+1)})	p\cvec{p}^{(j)} = 0\) for every \(j \le k\) ; \(\Span(\cvec{r}^{(0)}, \dots, \cvec{r}^{(k)}) = \Span(\cvec{p}^{(0)}, \dots, \cvec{p}^{(k)}) = \cK_{k+1}\) , a space of dimension \(k+1\) ; \(\cvec{x}^{(k+1)}\) is the unique minimizer of \(
orm{\cvec{x} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_{\A}\) over the affine set \(\cvec{x}^{(0)} + \cK_{k+1}\) .

title: Theorem 24.7.3 (Convergence of Steepest Descent)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
R)\) be symmetric positive definite with \(\kappa = \kappa_2(\A)\) , let \(\cvec{b} \in 
R^n\) , and let \(\cvec{x}^{(0)}, \cvec{x}^{(1)}, \dots\) be the steepest descent iterates. Then for every \(k\) for which \(\cvec{x}^{(k)}\) is defined, \[ 
orm{\cvec{x}^{(k)} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_{\A} \le \Bigl( rac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}\Bigr)^{k}\,
orm{\cvec{x}^{(0)} - \cvec{x}^{\star}}_{\A} . \]

title: Corollary 24.8.2 (Constant \B: the flow is conjugation by the exponential)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content:
Let \(\B \in M_n(
C)\) be a fixed matrix and let \(\L \colon 
R 	o M_n(
C)\) be differentiable with \(\L' = [\B, \L]\) . Then \[ \L(t) = e^{t\B}\,\L(0)\,e^{-t\B} \qquad (t \in 
R), \] so \(\L(t)\) is similar to \(\L(0)\) for every \(t\) .

title: Definition 24.8.1 (Lax Pair)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Let \(I \subseteq \nR\) be an open interval. A Lax pair on \(I\) is a pair of functions \(\L, \B \colon I \to M_n(\nC)\) , with \(\L\) differentiable, such that \[ \L'(t) = [\B(t), \L(t)] \coloneqq \B(t)\L(t) - \L(t)\B(t) \qquad \text{for every } t \in I . \] The equation itself is called a Lax equation , and \(\L\) is said to flow under it.

title: Definition 24.8.2 (The Toda Flow)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: For \(\M \in M_n(\nR)\) write \(\M_{+}\) for its strictly upper triangular part and \(\M_{-}\) for its strictly lower triangular part , so that \(\M\) is the sum of \(\M_{-}\) , its diagonal part, and \(\M_{+}\) , and set \[ \B(\M) \coloneqq \M_{+} - \M_{-} . \] The Toda flow is the Lax equation \[ \L'(t) = \bigl[\B(\L(t)),\ \L(t)\bigr] \] for a differentiable \(\L \colon I \to M_n(\nR)\) taking symmetric tridiagonal values.

title: Example (A curve of matrices with a frozen spectrum)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Take \(\B = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}\) and \(\L_0 = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}\) . Since \(\B^2 = \O\) , @def-matrix-exponential gives \(e^{t\B} = \I + t\B\) , and the recipe of the previous example produces \[ \L(t) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & t \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -t \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} t & -t^2 \\ 1 & -t\end{pmatrix} . \] Three of the four entries move — only the corner \(\ell_{21} = 1\) stands still — and yet \(\tr\L(t) = 0\) and \(\det\L(t) = -t^2 + t^2 = 0\) , so \(p_{\L(t)}(x) = x^2\) for every \(t\) . The curve stays inside one similarity class the whole time.

title: Example (The 2 \times 2 flow, twice)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Let \(n = 2\) , so \(\L = \begin{psmallmatrix} d_1 & e_1 \\ e_1 & d_2\end{psmallmatrix}\) and @eq-toda-coordinates reads \[ d_1' = 2e_1^2, \qquad d_2' = -2e_1^2, \qquad e_1' = e_1(d_2 - d_1) . \] Verify by hand that \(\tr\L\) and \(\det\L\) are constant along the flow. Solve the flow explicitly for \(\L(0) = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Define a Lax pair, and say which of the two functions is required to be differentiable. State @thm-lax-isospectral , and name the two results from earlier chapters its proof uses. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if \(\L' = [\B, \L]\) then \(\L(t) = \L(0)\) for all \(t\) . Explain in one sentence why the proof of @thm-lax-isospectral does not construct the conjugating matrix \(\S(t)\) . Write down the Toda equations @eq-toda-coordinates for \(n = 3\) , and check that the sum of the three diagonal equations is \(0\) .

title: Exercise (B1: A Lax pair verified)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Let \(\B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\L(t) = \begin{pmatrix} t & -t^2 \\ 1 & -t \end{pmatrix}\) . Verify directly that \(\L'(t) = [\B, \L(t)]\) . Compute \(p_{\L(t)}\) and confirm @thm-lax-isospectral in this case. Determine whether \(\L(t)\) and \(\L(0)\) are similar for every \(t\) , and exhibit the similarity.

title: Exercise (B2: The bracket by hand)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Let \[ \L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}. \] Compute \(\B(\L)\) and \([\B(\L), \L]\) directly, and check the answer against @prp-toda-equations .

title: Exercise (B3: One QR step on an exponential)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Let \(\L_0 = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}\) and \(\A^{(1)} = e^{\L_0}\) . Show that \(e^{t\L_0} = \begin{psmallmatrix} c(t) & s(t) \\ s(t) & c(t)\end{psmallmatrix}\) with \(c(t) = \tfrac12(e^{t} + e^{-t})\) and \(s(t) = \tfrac12(e^{t} - e^{-t})\) . Find the QR factorization of \(e^{t\L_0}\) with positive diagonal, and hence \(\L(t) = \Q(t)\tp\L_0\Q(t)\) . Compare your \(\L(1)\) with @exm-toda-two-by-two (b).

title: Exercise (C1: The power sums are constants of the motion)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Let \((\L, \B)\) be a Lax pair on \(I\) . Prove that \(t \mapsto \tr\bigl(\L(t)^{m}\bigr)\) is constant for every integer \(m \ge 1\) . Hint: the product rule, then @thm-trace-properties (3). Deduce, for \(n = 2\) , that the characteristic polynomial of \(\L(t)\) is constant, without using @thm-lax-isospectral .

title: Exercise (C2: How far \B is from being determined)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Let \((\L, \B)\) be a Lax pair on \(I\) and let \(\C \colon I \to M_n(\nC)\) satisfy \([\C(t), \L(t)] = \O\) for every \(t\) . Prove that \((\L, \B + \C)\) is also a Lax pair. Give an example with \(\C \ne \O\) , and conclude that a Lax equation does not determine \(\B\) . Prove, using @lem-skew-upper-splitting , that there is nevertheless exactly one skew-symmetric \(\B\) for which \(\B +\) (upper triangular) equals a given symmetric \(\L\) — that is, the \(\B(\L)\) of @def-toda-flow is the only natural candidate once “skew-symmetric” and “upper triangular” are the two slots.

title: Exercise (C3: Symmetry constrains \B)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Let \((\L, \B)\) be a Lax pair of real matrices on \(I\) with \(\L(t)\) symmetric for every \(t\) . Prove that \([\B(t) + \B(t)\tp,\ \L(t)] = \O\) for every \(t\) . Deduce that \(\bigl(\L, \tfrac12(\B - \B\tp)\bigr)\) is also a Lax pair, so that \(\B\) may always be taken skew-symmetric. Determine whether the Toda \(\B(\L)\) of @def-toda-flow satisfies the hypothesis of (a). Justify your answer.

title: Lemma 24.8.4 (Skew plus upper triangular, uniquely)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Every \(\M \in M_n(\nR)\) is \(\M = \K + \U\) for exactly one skew-symmetric \(\K\) and one upper triangular \(\U\) . If \(\M\) is symmetric then \(\K = \M_{-} - \M_{+} = -\B(\M)\) .

title: Proposition 24.8.3 (The Toda Flow in Coordinates)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Let \(\L \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric and tridiagonal, with diagonal entries \(d_1, \dots, d_n\) and off-diagonal entries \(e_1, \dots, e_{n-1}\) , so \(\ell_{i,i+1} = \ell_{i+1,i} = e_i\) . Put \(e_0 = e_n = 0\) . Then \([\B(\L), \L]\) is again symmetric and tridiagonal, with \[ \bigl[\B(\L), \L\bigr]_{ii} = 2\bigl(e_i^2 - e_{i-1}^2\bigr), \qquad \bigl[\B(\L), \L\bigr]_{i,i+1} = e_i\,(d_{i+1} - d_i) . \] Consequently the Toda flow is the system \[ d_i' = 2\bigl(e_i^2 - e_{i-1}^2\bigr) \ \ (1 \le i \le n), \qquad e_i' = e_i\,(d_{i+1} - d_i) \ \ (1 \le i \le n-1) . \] {#eq-toda-coordinates}

title: Theorem 24.8.1 (Lax Pairs Are Isospectral)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Let \((\L, \B)\) be a Lax pair on an open interval \(I\) . Then the characteristic polynomial of \(\L(t)\) does not depend on \(t\) : \[ p_{\L(t)} = p_{\L(s)} \qquad \text{for all } s, t \in I . \] In particular \(\L(t)\) has the same eigenvalues as \(\L(s)\) , with the same algebraic multiplicities, and \(\tr\L(t)\) and \(\det\L(t)\) are constant.

title: Theorem 24.8.5 (One QR Step Is One Unit of Toda Time)
page: 24.8 Lax Pairs and the Toda Flow
content: Let \(\L_0 \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric and let \(\A^{(1)}, \A^{(2)}, \A^{(3)}, \dots\) be the unshifted QR iterates of @def-qr-iteration started at \(\A^{(1)} = e^{\L_0}\) , with the factorizations \[ \A^{(k)} = \Q^{(k)}\R^{(k)}, \qquad \A^{(k+1)} = \R^{(k)}\Q^{(k)} \qquad (k \ge 1) \] normalized so that each \(\R^{(k)}\) has positive diagonal entries, and write \(\W_k = \Q^{(1)}\Q^{(2)}\cdots\Q^{(k)}\) , with \(\W_0 = \I\) . Then for every \(k \ge 0\) : the factorizations exist and are unique, and \(\A^{(k+1)} = \W_k\tp\,\A^{(1)}\,\W_k\) ; \(\W_k\) is the orthogonal factor in the QR factorization of \(e^{k\L_0}\) ; \(\A^{(k+1)} = e^{\L_k}\) , where \(\L_k = \W_k\tp\,\L_0\,\W_k\) is symmetric and has the same eigenvalues as \(\L_0\) .

title: Corollary 24.9.3 (Frequencies from the Rayleigh Quotient)
Definition 24.9.3 (Generalized Rayleigh quotient)
content: Let \((\M, \K)\) be a mass–spring system. Its generalized Rayleigh quotient is \[ \rho(\cvec{v}) \coloneqq \frac{\cvec{v}\tp\K\cvec{v}}{\cvec{v}\tp\M\cvec{v}} , \] defined for every \(\cvec{v} \in \nR^n\) with \(\cvec{v} \ne \cvec{0}\) , and at no other vector.

title: Definition 24.9.1 (The mass–spring model)
content: (Newton’s second law.) A mass \(m_i > 0\) whose displacement is \(x_i(t)\) obeys \(m_i x_i''(t) = f_i(t)\) , where \(f_i\) is the total force on it. (Hooke’s law.) A spring of stiffness \(k \ge 0\) whose two ends have moved by \(a\) and \(b\) pulls its ends together with force \(k(b - a)\) acting on the end at \(a\) , and \(-k(b-a)\) on the end at \(b\) . A wall is an end whose displacement is \(0\) . A spring of stiffness \(0\) exerts no force whatever, so it is the same thing as no spring at all.

title: Definition 24.9.2 (Mass–spring system)
content:
A mass–spring system with \(n\) degrees of freedom is a pair of real symmetric matrices \(\M, \K \in M_n(
R)\) with \(\M \succ \O\) and \(\K \succeq \O\) , called the mass matrix and the stiffness matrix . A motion of the system is a twice-differentiable function \(\cvec{x} \colon 
R 	o 
R^n\) with \[ \M\cvec{x}''(t) = -\K\cvec{x}(t) \qquad 	ext{for every } t \in 
R . \] {#eq-mass-spring} The same equation is read for a function \(\cvec{x} \colon 
R 	o 
C^n\) whenever a complex trial solution is convenient; a motion without qualification is real.

title: Example (Three systems)
content: \(n = 1\) : one mass \(m\) between two walls with springs \(k_1, k_2\) . Then \(\M = (m)\) and \(\K = (k_1 + k_2)\) , both \(1 \times 1\) . \(n = 3\) with all masses equal to \(m\) and all four stiffnesses equal to \(k\) . Then \(\M = m\I_3\) and \(\K = k\K_3\) , where \(\K_3\) is the second-difference matrix met in @prp-second-difference-inverse . The free chain: the same three masses joined to each other by \(k_2, k_3\) but with no walls , so \(k_1 = k_4 = 0\) . Then \(\K\) is still symmetric and still \(\B\tp\D_k\B\) , hence \(\succeq \O\) , but now \(\K\1 = \cvec{0}\) : sliding the whole chain sideways stretches nothing.

title: Example (Pinning the middle mass)
content: In @exm-three-mass-chain with \(k = m = 1\) , hold mass \(2\) fixed. Deleting row and column \(2\) from \(\K_3\) and from \(\I_3\) gives \(\K' = \diag(2, 2)\) and \(\M' = \I_2\) , so the pinned frequencies are \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \sqrt2\) . The unpinned ones are \(\sqrt{2-\sqrt2} \approx 0.765\) , \(\sqrt2 \approx 1.414\) , and \(\sqrt{2+\sqrt2} \approx 1.848\) , and indeed \[ 0.765 \le 1.414 \le 1.414 \le 1.414 \le 1.848 , \] which is @prp-pinning-interlaces , here with two of the four inequalities equalities. The answer is also visible: with the middle mass pinned, the two outer masses no longer interact, and each is a single mass between two unit springs, of frequency \(\sqrt2\) .

title: Example (Guessing the lowest mode of the chain)
content: For the chain of @exm-three-mass-chain with \(k = m = 1\) , estimate \(\omega_1^2\) by guessing a shape, without computing any eigenvalue.

title: Example (Three equal masses, four equal springs)
content: Take \(n = 3\) with every mass \(m\) and every stiffness \(k\) , so that \(\M = m\I_3\) and \(\K = k\K_3\) as in @exm-mass-spring-examples (b). Find the natural frequencies and the normal modes of @thm-normal-modes .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the two hypotheses on \(\M\) and \(\K\) in @def-mass-spring-system , and say which one guarantees that \(\rho(\cvec{v})\) is defined for every \(\cvec{v} \ne \cvec{0}\) . State @thm-normal-modes (b), including the normalization of the eigenvectors. A system has \(\K\) invertible. What does @thm-normal-modes say about \(\omega_1\) ? What if \(\K\) is singular? True or false: if every stiffness \(k_e\) of a chain is doubled and every mass is left alone, every natural frequency is multiplied by \(\sqrt2\) . Justify your answer. True or false: for \(\M = \diag(1,4)\) the squared natural frequencies are the eigenvalues of \(\K\) divided by \(1\) and by \(4\) in some order. Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: Two masses, two springs)
content: A cart of mass \(2\) is joined to a wall by a spring of stiffness \(2\) , and a cart of mass \(1\) is joined to the first cart by a spring of stiffness \(1\) ; the second cart is free on the right. Write down \(\M\) and \(\K\) . Find the natural frequencies and an \(\M\) -orthonormal basis of normal modes. Verify directly that the two modes are \(\M\) -orthogonal but not orthogonal for the standard inner product.

title: Exercise (B2: Bounding the slowest mode)
content: For the system of Exercise B1, estimate \(\omega_1^2\) from above using the guesses \(\cvec{g} = (1,1)\) and \(\cvec{g} = (2,3)\) , and compare with the exact value.

title: Exercise (B3: Stiffening a chain)
content: In the system of Exercise B1, the stiffness of the second spring is increased from \(1\) to \(2\) , so that \(\K\) becomes \(\K' = \begin{psmallmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}\) . Verify that \(\K' \succeq \K\) . Compute the new squared frequencies and check @prp-frequency-monotonicity (a).

title: Exercise (C1: The free chain drifts)
content: Let \((\M, \K)\) be a mass–spring system. Prove that \(\omega_1 = 0\) if and only if \(\K\) is singular, and that in that case the generalized eigenvectors for \(\omega = 0\) are exactly the nonzero vectors of \(\ker\K\) . Hence describe all motions of the free chain of @exm-mass-spring-examples (c) with three equal masses \(m\) and equal inner stiffnesses \(k\) , given that \(\ker\K\) is spanned by \(\1\) . Deduce that the total momentum \(\sum_i m_ix_i'(t)\) of the free chain is constant in time.

title: Exercise (C2: Adding a mass cannot raise a frequency, and can lower it a lot)
content: Let \((\M, \K)\) be a mass–spring system and let \(t > 0\) . Prove that the system \((\M + t\cvec{e}_p\cvec{e}_p\tp, \K)\) , obtained by adding mass \(t\) to the \(p\) -th degree of freedom, has \(\omega_j'(t) \le \omega_j\) for every \(j\) , and that \(t \mapsto \omega_j'(t)\) is nonincreasing. For the single mass of @exm-mass-spring-examples (a) with \(m = k_1 = k_2 = 1\) , compute \(\omega_1'(t)\) exactly and find \(\lim_{t\to\infty}\omega_1'(t)\) . Give an example of a mass–spring system and a \(p\) for which adding mass at \(p\) leaves the largest frequency unchanged. Hint: look for a mode that does not move the \(p\) -th mass.

title: Lemma 24.9.1 (The scalar oscillator)
content: Let \(\omega \ge 0\) and let \(y \colon \nR \to \nC\) be twice differentiable with \(y'' = -\omega^2 y\) . If \(\omega > 0\) , then \[ y(t) = y(0)\cos\omega t + \frac{y'(0)}{\omega}\sin\omega t \] for every \(t\) ; if \(\omega = 0\) , then \(y(t) = y(0) + y'(0)t\) . Conversely every function of these two shapes satisfies \(y'' = -\omega^2y\) .

title: Proposition 24.9.4 (Stiffening Raises, Loading Lowers)
content: Let \((\M, \K)\) and \((\M', \K')\) be mass–spring systems with \(n\) degrees of freedom, with natural frequencies \(\omega_j\) and \(\omega_j'\) . If \(\M' = \M\) and \(\K' \succeq \K\) , then \(\omega_j' \ge \omega_j\) for every \(j\) . If \(\K' = \K\) and \(\M' \succeq \M\) , then \(\omega_j' \le \omega_j\) for every \(j\) .

title: Proposition 24.9.5 (Pinning Interlaces the Frequencies)
content: Let \((\M, \K)\) be a mass–spring system with \(n \ge 2\) degrees of freedom and natural frequencies \(\omega_1 \le \dots \le \omega_n\) . Fix \(p\) , let \(I = \{1, \dots, n\}\setminus\{p\}\) , and let \(\M' = \M_{I,I}\) and \(\K' = \K_{I,I}\) be the principal submatrices on \(I\) . Then \((\M', \K')\) is a mass–spring system with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom, and its natural frequencies \(\mu_1 \le \dots \le \mu_{n-1}\) satisfy \[ \omega_j \ \le\ \mu_j \ \le\ \omega_{j+1} \qquad (1 \le j \le n-1) . \]

title: Theorem 24.9.2 (Normal Modes)
content:
Let \((\M, \K)\) be a mass–spring system with \(n\) degrees of freedom ( @def-mass-spring-system ). For \(\omega \in 
R\) and \(\cvec{v} \in 
R^n\) with \(\cvec{v} 
e \cvec{0}\) , the complex-valued function \(\cvec{x}(t) = e^{i\omega t}\cvec{v}\) satisfies @eq-mass-spring if and only if \[ \K\cvec{v} = \omega^2\M\cvec{v} . \] There are real numbers \(0 \le \omega_1 \le \dots \le \omega_n\) and vectors \(\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n \in 
R^n\) with \[ \K\cvec{v}_j = \omega_j^2\M\cvec{v}_j \quad	ext{and}\quad \cvec{v}_i	p\M\cvec{v}_j = \delta_{ij} , \] and \((\cvec{v}_1, \dots, \cvec{v}_n)\) is a basis of \(
R^n\) . Every motion of the system is \[ \cvec{x}(t) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j(t)\,\cvec{v}_j , \] where \[ c_j(t) =  egin{cases} a_j\cos\omega_jt + b_j\sin\omega_jt, & \omega_j > 0, \ a_j + b_jt, & \omega_j = 0, \end{cases} \] for uniquely determined real \(a_j, b_j\) ; conversely every such function is a motion. The coefficients are \(a_j = \cvec{v}_j	p\M\cvec{x}(0)\) , and \(b_j = \cvec{v}_j	p\M\cvec{x}'(0)/\omega_j\) when \(\omega_j > 0\) , \(b_j = \cvec{v}_j	p\M\cvec{x}'(0)\) when \(\omega_j = 0\) . The numbers \(\omega_j\) do not depend on the construction in (b): by @thm-generalized-eigenvalues-real (b) the \(\omega_j^2\) are exactly the roots of \(\det(\K - \lambda\M)\) , with multiplicity. They are the natural frequencies , and the pairs \((\omega_j, \cvec{v}_j)\) are the normal modes of the system.

title: Definition 24.10.1 (Data matrix, mean, and centered data matrix)
content:
Let \(\cvec{x}_1, \dots, \cvec{x}_N \in 
R^n\) . The data matrix is the matrix \(\X \in M_{n 	imes N}(
R)\) whose \(j\) -th column is \(\cvec{x}_j\) . The mean of the data is \[  ar{\cvec{x}} \coloneqq  rac1N\sum_{j=1}^{N}\cvec{x}_j \in 
R^n , \] and the centered data matrix is \[ \X_c \coloneqq \X -  ar{\cvec{x}}\,\1	p \in M_{n 	imes N}(
R) , \] whose \(j\) -th column is \(\cvec{c}_j \coloneqq \cvec{x}_j -  ar{\cvec{x}}\) .

title: Definition 24.10.3 (Principal directions and components)
content: In the situation of @prp-covariance-and-svd , the unit vectors \(\cvec{u}_1, \cvec{u}_2, \dots\) are the principal directions of the data, and the numbers \(\cvec{u}_i\tp\cvec{c}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_i\tp\cvec{c}_N\) are the \(i\) -th principal components : the coordinates of the centered data along \(\cvec{u}_i\) .

title: Definition 24.10.2 (Sample covariance matrix)
content:
Let \(\cvec{x}_1, \dots, \cvec{x}_N \in 
R^n\) with centered data matrix \(\X_c\) ( @def-centered-data-matrix ). The sample covariance matrix of the data is \[ \S \coloneqq  rac1N\,\X_c\X_c	p \in M_n(
R) , \] with entries \[ s_{ab} =  rac1N\sum_{j=1}^{N}(x_{aj} -  ar x_a)(x_{bj} -  ar x_b) \qquad (1 \le a, b \le n) . \] For \(\cvec{w} \in 
R^n\) with \(\cvec{w} 
e \cvec{0}\) , the variance of the data in the direction \(\cvec{w}\) is the number \(\cvec{w}	p\S\cvec{w}/
orm{\cvec{w}}^2\) , which for a unit \(\cvec{w}\) is \(\cvec{w}	p\S\cvec{w}\) ; and the total variance of the data is \(	r\S\) .

title: Example (Centering three data sets)
content: \(N = 4\) points in \(\nR^2\) : \((5,4), (4,1), (2,3), (1,0)\) . Their sum is \((12, 8)\) , so \(\bar{\cvec{x}} = (3,2)\) and \[ \X_c = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & -2\end{pmatrix} . \] Both rows sum to \(0\) . \(N = 1\) . Then \(\bar{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{x}_1\) and \(\X_c = \O\) : a single point carries no shape at all. This degenerate case matters, because every ratio below has \(0/0\) here and the statements must exclude it or say what they mean. Data already centered: if \(\X\1 = \cvec{0}\) then \(\bar{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{0}\) and \(\X_c = \X\) . Centering is idempotent, since \(\X_c\1 = \cvec{0}\) always.

title: Example (Three covariance matrices)
content: The four points of @exm-centering-examples (a). Then \[ \X_c\X_c\tp = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \S = \begin{pmatrix} 5/2 & 3/2 \\ 3/2 & 5/2\end{pmatrix} . \] Both coordinates have variance \(5/2\) , and the positive off-diagonal entry says they rise and fall together. Two points \(\pm\cvec{v}\) in \(\nR^n\) with \(\cvec{v} \ne \cvec{0}\) , so \(N = 2\) and \(\bar{\cvec{x}} = \cvec{0}\) . Then \(\X_c\X_c\tp = 2\cvec{v}\cvec{v}\tp\) and \(\S = \cvec{v}\cvec{v}\tp\) , of rank one: all the spread is in one direction, and \(\cvec{w}\tp\S\cvec{w} = (\cvec{w}\tp\cvec{v})^2\) vanishes for every \(\cvec{w} \perp \cvec{v}\) . \(N = 1\) . Then \(\X_c = \O\) and \(\S = \O\) : no direction has any spread.

title: Example (Four points, done exactly)
content: Take the four points \((5,4), (4,1), (2,3), (1,0)\) of @exm-centering-examples (a). Find the mean, the sample covariance matrix, the principal directions, the best-fitting line, the total squared distance to it, and the fraction of variance it explains.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define the centered data matrix and the sample covariance matrix, and say what \(\cvec{w}\tp\S\cvec{w}\) means for a unit vector \(\cvec{w}\) . State @thm-best-fitting-affine-subspace , including the value of the minimum and the claim about the mean. True or false: the principal directions of a data set are the eigenvectors of \(\X\X\tp\) . Justify your answer. True or false: if \(N = 3\) points in \(\nR^{10}\) are given, then \(\S\) has rank at most \(2\) . Justify your answer. Why should a computation of the principal directions avoid forming \(\X_c\X_c\tp\) ?

title: Exercise (B1: A four-point cloud)
content: The points \((1,1), (3,5), (5,3), (7,7)\) are given in \(\nR^2\) . Compute \(\bar{\cvec{x}}\) , \(\X_c\) , \(\X_c\X_c\tp\) , and \(\S\) . Find the singular values of \(\X_c\) and the principal directions. Find the best-fitting line, the total squared distance to it, and the fraction of variance it explains. Verify the total squared distance directly.

title: Exercise (B2: Variance direction by direction)
content: For the data of Exercise B1, compute the variance in the directions \(\cvec{e}_1\) , \(\cvec{e}_2\) , \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,1)\) , and \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1)\) , and say which of them is largest and why that was predictable.

title: Exercise (B3: Changing the units)
content: The centered data matrix of a two-coordinate data set is \(\X_c = \begin{psmallmatrix} 3 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & -4\end{psmallmatrix}\) . The second coordinate is then re-expressed in units \(c\) times smaller, which multiplies row \(2\) by \(c > 0\) . Find the principal directions before the change. Find the value of \(c\) at which the first principal direction switches from one coordinate axis to the other, and say what happens exactly at that value.

title: Exercise (C1: The mean is forced, and the projection is not a shortcut)
content:
Let \(\cvec{x}_1, \dots, \cvec{x}_N \in 
R^n\) with mean \( ar{\cvec{x}}\) . Prove that the point \(\cvec{p} \in 
R^n\) minimizing \(\sum_j
orm{\cvec{x}_j - \cvec{p}}^2\) is unique and equals \( ar{\cvec{x}}\) . (This is the case \(k = 0\) , which @thm-best-fitting-affine-subspace excludes, so it has to be proved rather than quoted.) Hence deduce that for every subspace \(U\) , the affine subspace \(\cvec{p} + U\) minimizing \(D\) over translates of \(U\) is \( ar{\cvec{x}} + U\) . Give an example of data and a subspace \(U\) for which \( ar{\cvec{x}} + U\) is not the best-fitting affine subspace of its dimension, so that the choice of \(U\) still matters.

title: Exercise (C2: Total variance is a trace, and what that buys)
content:
Let \(\cvec{x}_1, \dots, \cvec{x}_N \in 
R^n\) with sample covariance \(\S\) , and let \(\Q \in M_n(
R)\) be orthogonal. Prove that the data \(\Q\cvec{x}_1, \dots, \Q\cvec{x}_N\) have sample covariance \(\Q\S\Q	p\) , and deduce that the total variance \(	r\S\) is unchanged. Prove that for any orthonormal basis \((\cvec{q}_1, \dots, \cvec{q}_n)\) of \(
R^n\) , the sum of the variances of the data in the \(n\) directions \(\cvec{q}_i\) equals \(	r\S\) . Deduce that no orthonormal frame can make every coordinate variance small: some \(\cvec{q}_i\) always has variance at least \(	r\S/n\) . For the data of @exm-pca-four-points , which frames attain that bound?

title: Lemma 24.10.1 (Distance to a flat, and where its translate wants to be)
content:
Let \(U \subseteq 
R^n\) be a subspace, let \(Q = \I_n - P_U\) be the orthogonal projection onto \(U^{\perp}\) , and let \(\cvec{p} \in 
R^n\) . For every \(\cvec{x} \in 
R^n\) , \(\ d(\cvec{x}, \cvec{p} + U) = 
orm{Q(\cvec{x} - \cvec{p})}\) , and the nearest point of \(\cvec{p} + U\) exists. For points \(\cvec{x}_1, \dots, \cvec{x}_N\) with mean \( ar{\cvec{x}}\) , \[ \sum_{j=1}^{N}
orm{Q(\cvec{x}_j - \cvec{p})}^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{N}
orm{Q(\cvec{x}_j -  ar{\cvec{x}})}^2 + N
orm{Q( ar{\cvec{x}} - \cvec{p})}^2 . \] In particular the left side is smallest exactly when \( ar{\cvec{x}} \in \cvec{p} + U\) .

title: Proposition 24.10.3 (The Covariance Matrix and the Singular Value Decomposition)
Theorem 24.10.2 (The Best-Fitting Affine Subspace)
content: Let \(\cvec{x}_1, \dots, \cvec{x}_N \in \nR^n\) have mean \(\bar{\cvec{x}}\) and centered data matrix \(\X_c\) ( @def-centered-data-matrix ), let \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge 0\) be the singular values of \(\X_c\) ( @def-singular-values ), and let \(\cvec{u}_1, \cvec{u}_2, \dots\) be the left singular vectors of a fixed singular value decomposition of \(\X_c\) ( @thm-svd ). Let \(1 \le k \le \min(n, N)\) . Among all affine subspaces \(A \subseteq \nR^n\) of dimension at most \(k\) , the total squared distance \[ D(A) \coloneqq \sum_{j=1}^{N} d(\cvec{x}_j, A)^2 \] is smallest for \[ A_0 = \bar{\cvec{x}} + \Span(\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_k) , \] and its smallest value is \(\sum_{i > k}\sigma_i^2\) . Moreover every minimizing \(A\) contains \(\bar{\cvec{x}}\) .

title: Theorem 24.10.4 (Variance Captured by the Principal Directions)
content: In the situation of @prp-covariance-and-svd , let \(1 \le k \le \min(n, N)\) , let \(U_0 = \Span(\cvec{u}_1, \dots, \cvec{u}_k)\) , and let \(P\) be the orthogonal projection onto a subspace \(U\) with \(\dim U \le k\) . Write \[ \operatorname{var}(U) \coloneqq \frac1N\sum_{j=1}^{N}\norm{P(\cvec{x}_j - \bar{\cvec{x}})}^2 . \] Then: \(\operatorname{var}(U)\) is the total variance of the projected points \(P\cvec{x}_1, \dots, P\cvec{x}_N\) , whose mean is \(P\bar{\cvec{x}}\) ; \(\operatorname{var}(U) + \dfrac1N D(\bar{\cvec{x}} + U) = \tr\S\) , where \(D\) is as in @thm-best-fitting-affine-subspace ; \(\operatorname{var}(U) \le \operatorname{var}(U_0) = \dfrac1N\sum_{i \le k}\sigma_i^2\) ; if \(\X_c \ne \O\) , the fraction of the total variance captured by \(U_0\) is \[ \frac{\operatorname{var}(U_0)}{\tr\S} = \frac{\sigma_1^2 + \dots + \sigma_k^2}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \dots} . \]

title: Definition 24.11.2 (Fiedler value)
content: Let \(G\) be a graph on \(m \ge 2\) vertices with at least one edge. The Fiedler value , or algebraic connectivity , of \(G\) is the second smallest eigenvalue \(\mu_2(\L)\) of its Laplacian, counted with multiplicity.

title: Definition 24.11.1 (Graph Laplacian)
content: Let \(G\) be a graph with vertices \(1, \dots, m\) and \(k \ge 1\) edges, and fix any orientation of \(G\) , with incidence matrix \(\N \in M_{m \times k}(\nR)\) . The Laplacian of \(G\) is \[ \L \coloneqq \N\N\tp \in M_m(\nR) . \]

title: Example (Two triangles and a bridge)
content: Let \(G\) have vertices \(1, \dots, 6\) and edges \(\{1,2\}\) , \(\{1,3\}\) , \(\{2,3\}\) , \(\{3,4\}\) , \(\{4,5\}\) , \(\{4,6\}\) , \(\{5,6\}\) : two triangles joined by a single edge. Find the Fiedler value and a Fiedler vector, and read off the partition.

title: Example (A Laplacian computed twice)
content: Let \(G\) be the four-vertex graph of @exr-minors-and-rank-c1 : vertices \(1, 2, 3, 4\) and edges \(e_1 = \{1,2\}\) , \(e_2 = \{2,3\}\) , \(e_3 = \{3,4\}\) , \(e_4 = \{4,1\}\) , \(e_5 = \{1,3\}\) . Compute \(\L\) from \(\D - \A\) and from \(\N\N\tp\) , and check them against each other.

title: Example (The four-vertex graph, counted both ways)
content: For the graph of @exm-laplacian-two-ways , compute \(\det\L_0\) with \(r = 4\) , and list the spanning trees.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define the Laplacian of a graph, and say why it does not depend on the orientation used to define it. Write down the formula for \(\cvec{x}\tp\L\cvec{x}\) as a sum over edges, and deduce that \(\L \succeq \O\) . State the matrix-tree theorem, including all its hypotheses. True or false: a graph on \(m\) vertices is connected if and only if \(\rank\L = m - 1\) . Justify your answer. True or false: if \(\L\) has eigenvalue \(0\) with multiplicity \(1\) , then \(\det\L_0 > 0\) . Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: The four-cycle)
content: Let \(C_4\) be the graph on vertices \(1, 2, 3, 4\) with edges \(\{1,2\}, \{2,3\}, \{3,4\}, \{4,1\}\) . Write down \(\L\) and explain why it is a circulant in the sense of @def-circulant . Find all eigenvalues of \(\L\) , the Fiedler value, and a Fiedler vector. Compute \(\det\L_0\) and list the spanning trees.

title: Exercise (B2: Counting trees in a bowtie)
content: Let \(G\) have vertices \(1, \dots, 5\) and edges \(\{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{2,3\}, \{3,4\}, \{3,5\}, \{4,5\}\) : two triangles sharing the vertex \(3\) . Write down \(\L\) and compute \(\det\L_0\) with \(r = 1\) . Count the spanning trees directly, and check that the two answers agree. Verify that \(\cvec{x} = (1,1,0,-1,-1)\) is an eigenvector of \(\L\) , and say what its eigenvalue tells you.

title: Exercise (B3: Which minors are \pm 1?)
content: Let \(G\) be the graph on vertices \(1, 2, 3\) with edges \(e_1 = \{1,2\}\) , \(e_2 = \{2,3\}\) , \(e_3 = \{1,3\}\) , \(e_4 = \{1,2\}\) (so \(e_1\) and \(e_4\) are parallel). Orient every edge from the smaller vertex to the larger, let \(r = 3\) and \(I = \{1,2\}\) . Write down \(\N\) and \(\N_0 = \N_{I,[4]}\) . Compute \(\det\N_{I,S}\) for all six sets \(S\) of two edges, and say in each case whether \(S\) is a spanning tree. Hence find the number of spanning trees, and check it against \(\det\L_0\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Cayley’s formula)
content: Let \(K_m\) be the complete graph on \(m \ge 2\) vertices, in which every pair of distinct vertices is joined by exactly one edge, and let \(\J_t \in M_t(\nR)\) be the all-ones matrix. Show that the Laplacian of \(K_m\) is \(m\I_m - \J_m\) , and that \(\L_0 = m\I_{m-1} - \J_{m-1}\) for every choice of deleted vertex. Prove that \(\det(m\I_{m-1} - \J_{m-1}) = m^{m-2}\) . Deduce Cayley’s formula : \(K_m\) has exactly \(m^{m-2}\) spanning trees. Check it for \(m = 2, 3, 4\) against a direct count. Hint for (b): the eigenvalues of \(\J_t\) are visible from its rank and its row sums.

title: Exercise (C2: Weighted graphs)
content: Give each edge \(e\) of a graph \(G\) on \(m \ge 2\) vertices a weight \(w_e > 0\) , let \(\W = \diag(w_1, \dots, w_k)\) , and define the weighted Laplacian \(\L^{\cvec{w}} \coloneqq \N\W\N\tp\) , with \(\N\) the incidence matrix of any orientation. Prove that \(\cvec{x}\tp\L^{\cvec{w}}\cvec{x} = \sum_{e} w_e (x_{u_e} - x_{v_e})^2\) , and deduce that \(\L^{\cvec{w}} \succeq \O\) with the same kernel as \(\L\) . Prove the weighted matrix-tree theorem: for any vertex \(r\) , \[ \det\L^{\cvec{w}}_0 = \sum_{T} \ \prod_{e \in T} w_e , \] the sum running over all spanning trees \(T\) of \(G\) . Check (b) on the graph of @exm-laplacian-two-ways by comparing the coefficient of \(w_1w_2w_3\) on both sides, and confirm that setting every \(w_e = 1\) recovers @thm-matrix-tree . Hint for (b): \(\N\W\N\tp = (\N\W^{1/2})(\N\W^{1/2})\tp\) .

title: Lemma 24.11.6 (Unimodularity of Incidence Minors)
content: Let \(\N \in M_{m \times k}(\nR)\) be the incidence matrix of an oriented graph \(G\) with \(m\) vertices and \(k \ge 1\) edges. Write \(\cvec{n}_e \in \nR^m\) for the column of \(\N\) belonging to the edge \(e\) . Every square submatrix of \(\N\) has determinant \(0\) , \(1\) , or \(-1\) . For a set \(S\) of edges, the list \((\cvec{n}_e)_{e \in S}\) is linearly independent if and only if \(S\) contains no cycle. Fix a vertex \(r\) and put \(I = [m] \setminus \{r\}\) . For a set \(S\) of exactly \(m - 1\) edges, \(S\) is a spanning tree of \(G\) if and only if it contains no cycle, and \[ \det \N_{I,S} = \begin{cases} \pm 1 & \text{if } S \text{ is a spanning tree of } G, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]

title: Proposition 24.11.5 (Adding an Edge Raises No Eigenvalue)
content: Let \(G\) be a graph on \(m\) vertices with at least one edge, and let \(G'\) be \(G\) with one extra edge joining \(u \ne v\) . Then \(\L' = \L + \cvec{w}\cvec{w}\tp\) with \(\cvec{w} = \cvec{e}_u - \cvec{e}_v\) , and \[ \mu_j(\L') \ \ge\ \mu_j(\L) \qquad (j = 1, \dots, m). \] In particular the Fiedler value does not decrease when an edge is added.

title: Proposition 24.11.4 (The Fiedler Value as a Minimum)
content: Let \(G\) be a graph on \(m \ge 2\) vertices with at least one edge. Then \[ \mu_2(\L) = \min\Bigl\{ \tfrac{\cvec{x}\tp\L\cvec{x}}{\cvec{x}\tp\cvec{x}} \ : \ \cvec{x} \in \nR^m,\ \cvec{x} \ne \cvec{0},\ \cvec{x}\tp\1 = 0 \Bigr\} , \] and the minimum is attained at an eigenvector for \(\mu_2(\L)\) .

title: Proposition 24.11.3 (Positive Fiedler Value Means Connected)
content: Let \(G\) be a graph on \(m \ge 2\) vertices with at least one edge. Then \(\mu_2(\L) > 0\) if and only if \(G\) is connected.

title: Proposition 24.11.1 (First Properties of the Laplacian)
content: Let \(G\) be a graph on \(m\) vertices with \(k \ge 1\) edges and Laplacian \(\L\) . Then: \(\L = \D - \A\) ; in particular \(\L\) is symmetric and does not depend on the orientation chosen in @def-graph-laplacian . For every \(\cvec{x} \in \nR^m\) , \[ \cvec{x}\tp\L\cvec{x} = \sum_{e = 1}^{k} \bigl(x_{u_e} - x_{v_e}\bigr)^2 , \] where \(u_e\) and \(v_e\) are the two ends of the edge \(e\) . Consequently \(\L \succeq \O\) . \(\L\1 = \cvec{0}\) , where \(\1 = (1, \dots, 1) \in \nR^m\) .

title: Proposition 24.11.7 (A Spanning Tree Has m - 1 Edges)
content: Let \(G\) be a graph on \(m \ge 2\) vertices. Every spanning tree of \(G\) has exactly \(m - 1\) edges. Conversely, if a set \(S\) of exactly \(m - 1\) edges is such that the graph on all \(m\) vertices with edge set \(S\) is connected, then \(S\) is a spanning tree.

title: Theorem 24.11.2 (The Kernel of the Laplacian)
content:
Let \(G\) be a graph on \(m\) vertices with \(k \ge 1\) edges, with components \(C_1, \dots, C_c\) , and let \(\1_{C_r} \in 
R^m\) be the vector with entry \(1\) at the vertices of \(C_r\) and \(0\) elsewhere. Then \[ 
ul(\L) = \Span igl(\1_{C_1}, \dots, \1_{C_c} igr), \] this list is a basis, and the eigenvalue \(0\) of \(\L\) has multiplicity exactly \(c\) . In particular \(\L\) is singular, and \(
ul(\L) = \Span(\1)\) exactly when \(G\) is connected.

title: Theorem 24.11.8 (Matrix-Tree Theorem)
content: Let \(G\) be a graph on \(m \ge 2\) vertices with \(k \ge 1\) edges and Laplacian \(\L\) . Fix a vertex \(r\) , and let \(\L_0 = \L_{I,I} \in M_{m-1}(\nR)\) be \(\L\) with the row and the column of \(r\) deleted, where \(I = [m] \setminus \{r\}\) . Then \[ \det\L_0 = \#\{\text{spanning trees of } G\} . \] In particular the answer does not depend on which vertex \(r\) is deleted, and \(\det\L_0 = 0\) exactly when \(G\) is disconnected.

title: Corollary 24.12.4 (Solving a Circulant System in O(n\log n))
content: Let \(n = 2^p\) , let \(\C \in M_n(\nC)\) be an invertible circulant with first row \(\cvec{c}\) , and let \(\cvec{b} \in \nC^n\) . Then the solution of \(\C\cvec{x} = \cvec{b}\) can be computed in \(3C(n) + 2n\) operations.

title: Corollary 24.12.3 (Convolution in O(n\log n))
content: Let \(n = 2^p\) . The cyclic convolution \(\cvec{c} \ast \cvec{d}\) of two vectors in \(\nC^n\) can be computed in \[ 3C(n) + 2n = \tfrac92\,n\log_2 n - n + 3 \] operations, where \(C\) is as in @thm-fft-cost . Consequently, the product of two polynomials in \(\nC[x]\) of degree at most \(d\) can be computed in \(O(d\log d)\) operations.

title: Definition 24.12.2 (The even-odd permutation, the twiddle matrix, and the butterfly)
content:
Let \(n = 2m\) with \(m \ge 1\) . The even-odd permutation matrix \(\P_n \in M_n(
C)\) is the permutation matrix determined by \[ (\P_n\cvec{x})_t = x_{2t}, \qquad (\P_n\cvec{x})_{m+t} = x_{2t+1} \qquad (0 \le t \le m-1); \] it lists the even-numbered entries of \(\cvec{x}\) first, then the odd-numbered ones, each in their original order. The twiddle matrix is \(\D_m \coloneqq \diag igl(1, \omega_n, \omega_n^2, \dots, \omega_n^{m-1} igr) \in M_m(
C)\) . Its entries are powers of \(\omega_n\) , not of \(\omega_m\) . The butterfly matrix is \[ \B_n \coloneqq  egin{pmatrix} \I_m & \D_m \ \I_m & -\D_m \end{pmatrix} \in M_n(
C) . \]

title: Definition 24.12.1 (The transform matrix)
content: For \(n \ge 1\) let \[ \W_n \coloneqq \sqrt n\,\F_n \in M_n(\nC), \qquad (\W_n)_{jk} = \omega_n^{jk} \quad (0 \le j,k \le n-1), \] so that \(\widehat{\cvec{c}} = \W_n\cvec{c}\) for every \(\cvec{c} \in \nC^n\) .

title: Example (A transform of length eight)
content: Compute \(\W_8\cvec{c}\) for \(\cvec{c} = (1,2,3,4,1,2,3,4)\) by the procedure, showing every level, and check the result against the direct definition at one entry.

title: Example (The factorization for n = 4)
content: Write out @thm-fft-factorization for \(n = 4\) , and check it against the matrix \(\F\) of @exm-fourier-matrix-4 .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Write down the matrix \(\W_n\) , and say how it is related to the Fourier matrix \(\F_n\) of Chapter 12. State @thm-fft-factorization , and say what each of the three factors on the right costs to apply. How many operations does \(\W_n\cvec{x}\) cost as a plain matrix–vector product, and how many by the fast algorithm when \(n = 2^p\) ? True or false: the fast Fourier transform computes a different transform from the one in Chapter 12, which is why it is faster. Justify your answer. Why does the algorithm require \(n\) to be a power of two, and what is done when it is not?

title: Exercise (B1: A transform of length four)
content: Let \(\cvec{c} = (1, 1, -1, -1) \in \nC^4\) . Compute \(\W_4\cvec{c}\) by the procedure of this section, showing the two halves and the twiddles. Check the answer by evaluating the symbol \(p_{\cvec{c}}\) at the fourth roots of unity. Count the operations your computation in (a) used, and compare with \(C(4)\) .

title: Exercise (B2: A transform of length eight)
content: Let \(\cvec{c} = (2, 1, 0, 3, 2, 1, 0, 3) \in \nC^8\) . Compute \(\W_8\cvec{c}\) by the procedure, showing both levels, and verify entry \(j = 2\) directly from @def-dft-matrix .

title: Exercise (B3: A product of polynomials by convolution)
content: Let \(p = 1 + 2x + 3x^2\) and \(q = 2 + x\) in \(\nC[x]\) . What is the smallest power of two \(n\) for which the recipe in the proof of @cor-fast-convolution is valid? Write down the padded coefficient vectors \(\cvec{c}\) and \(\cvec{d}\) . Compute \(\cvec{c} \ast \cvec{d}\) directly from the definition of cyclic convolution, and read off \(pq\) . Show that using \(n = 3\) instead would give the wrong answer, and identify which coefficient wraps onto which.

title: Exercise (C1: Splitting into three)
content: Let \(n = 3m\) with \(m \ge 1\) , let \(\omega_n = e^{2\pi i/n}\) , and for \(s = 0, 1, 2\) let \[ \cvec{u}^{(s)} \coloneqq \W_m\bigl(x_s,\ x_{3+s},\ \dots,\ x_{3(m-1)+s}\bigr) \in \nC^m . \] Prove that for \(0 \le q \le 2\) and \(0 \le i \le m-1\) , \[ (\W_n\cvec{x})_{qm+i} = \sum_{s=0}^{2} \omega_3^{qs}\,\omega_n^{is}\,u^{(s)}_i , \] where \(\omega_3 = e^{2\pi i/3}\) . Deduce a recursive procedure for \(n = 3^p\) , and show that its cost \(C_3\) satisfies \(C_3(3m) \le 3C_3(m) + 12m\) and hence \(C_3(3^p) \le 4p\,3^p = 4n\log_3 n\) . Hint for (a): imitate the proof of @thm-fft-factorization , splitting the index \(k\) by its remainder modulo \(3\) and using \(\omega_n^3 = \omega_m\) and \(\omega_n^m = \omega_3\) .

title: Exercise (C2: The fourth power of the transform)
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) and let \(\R_n \in M_n(\nC)\) be the permutation matrix with \((\R_n)_{jl} = 1\) when \(j + l \equiv 0 \pmod n\) and \(0\) otherwise, so that \((\R_n\cvec{x})_j = x_{n-j}\) with the subscript read modulo \(n\) . Prove that \(\W_n^2 = n\,\R_n\) . Deduce that \(\W_n^4 = n^2\I_n\) and \(\F_n^4 = \I_n\) , and that every eigenvalue of \(\F_n\) lies in \(\{1, i, -1, -i\}\) . Deduce a second proof that \(\W_n^{-1} = \tfrac1n\conj{\W_n}\) .

title: Theorem 24.12.2 (The Cost of the Fast Fourier Transform)
content: Let \(C(n)\) be the number of operations the procedure above performs on an input of length \(n = 2^p\) , with \(p \ge 0\) . Then \(C(1) = 0\) , \[ C(2m) = 2C(m) + 3m - 1 \qquad (m \ge 1), \] and the solution of this recurrence is exactly \[ C(2^p) = \tfrac32\,p\,2^{p} - 2^{p} + 1, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad C(n) = \tfrac32\,n\log_2 n - n + 1 . \] In particular \(C(n) = O(n\log n)\) .

title: Theorem 24.12.1 (The Radix-Two Factorization)
content: Let \(n = 2m\) with \(m \ge 1\) . Then \[ \W_n = \B_n \begin{pmatrix} \W_m & \O \\ \O & \W_m \end{pmatrix} \P_n . \] Equivalently, for the unitary Fourier matrices, \[ \F_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\,\B_n \begin{pmatrix} \F_m & \O \\ \O & \F_m \end{pmatrix} \P_n . \]

title: Definition 24.13.1 (Arithmetic cost of a matrix product)
content: Fix a field \(F\) and \(n \ge 1\) , and treat the \(2n^2\) entries of \(\A, \B \in M_n(F)\) as indeterminates . A straight-line program is a finite list \(g_1, \dots, g_N\) in which each \(g_t\) is either one of the \(2n^2\) indeterminates, or a constant of \(F\) (an input step ), or \(g_r + g_s\) , \(g_r - g_s\) , or \(g_r g_s\) for some \(r, s < t\) (an arithmetic step ). Each \(g_t\) is then a polynomial in the indeterminates. The program computes the product if for every \(i, j\) the polynomial \(\sum_{k} a_{ik}b_{kj}\) occurs among the \(g_t\) . Its cost is the number of arithmetic steps, and \[ M(n) \coloneqq \min\{\,\text{cost of a program computing the } n \times n \text{ product}\,\} \] is the arithmetic cost of the \(n \times n\) product over \(F\) .

title: Definition 24.13.2 (The exponent of matrix multiplication)
content: The exponent of matrix multiplication over \(F\) is \[ \omega \coloneqq \inf\bigl\{\,\tau \in \nR : M(n) = O(n^{\tau}) \text{ as } n \to \infty \,\bigr\} . \]

title: Example (A small entry lost entirely)
content: Work in binary arithmetic with \(53\) -bit significands, rounding to nearest, so that \(u = 2^{-53}\) . Verify the hypotheses of @thm-strassen-not-entrywise-stable for \(\varepsilon = 2^{-27}\) , and say what each algorithm returns for the \((2,2)\) entry of the product of \(\A = \B = \diag(1, 2^{-27})\) .

title: Example (Seven products on integer data)
content: Multiply \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\B = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 \end{pmatrix}\) by @thm-strassen , with blocks of size \(1\) , so that each \(\P_k\) is a number. Check against the classical product.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State how many arithmetic operations @def-matrix-multiplication uses for the product of two \(n \times n\) matrices, separating multiplications from additions. Define the exponent \(\omega\) , and state what is proved about it in this section. True or false: @thm-strassen shows that \(M(2) \le 7\) . Justify your answer. Which properties of \(m \times m\) matrices does the proof of @thm-strassen use? Say what would go wrong if the identity had needed two blocks to commute. State the difference between the error bound of @prp-classical-product-entrywise and that of @prp-strassen-norm-bound , and say for which matrices the difference matters.

title: Exercise (B1: Seven products by hand)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . Compute \(\P_1, \dots, \P_7\) of @thm-strassen with blocks of size \(1\) , assemble the four entries, and check the answer against @exm-matrix-multiplication . Hence state how many multiplications and how many additions you performed.

title: Exercise (B2: One block, one level)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \] partitioned into \(2 \times 2\) blocks. Compute \(\P_3\) and \(\P_5\) of @thm-strassen , hence the \((1,2)\) block of \(\A\B\) , and verify it against the block formula \(\A_{11}\B_{12} + \A_{12}\B_{22}\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Counting the recursion)
content: Let \(n = 2^{p}\) . How many multiplications does the recursion of @thm-strassen-cost perform, as a function of \(p\) ? How many does the classical recipe perform? Using \(T(n) = 7n^{\log_2 7} - 6n^2\) , compute \(T(n)\) and \(2n^3 - n^2\) for \(n = 8\) and \(n = 64\) . Hence say, for these two sizes, which recipe uses fewer operations.

title: Exercise (C1: Would twenty-three products for three-by-three beat Strassen?)
content: Suppose a ring identity multiplies two \(3 \times 3\) matrices with \(q > 9\) multiplications of combinations of entries, together with some fixed number of additions, and is used recursively on \(3 \times 3\) block matrices. Show that the recursion performs \(q^{p}\) multiplications on matrices of size \(n = 3^{p}\) , and deduce that it gives \(\omega \le \log_3 q\) . You are given that such an identity exists with \(q = 23\) ; this is a result of Laderman, which is not proved here. Determine whether recursing on it beats @thm-strassen-cost . Justify your answer. Determine the largest \(q\) for which such an identity would beat @thm-strassen-cost . Hint: compare logarithms to a common base.

title: Exercise (C2: Where the entrywise bound really fails)
content: Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\A = \B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \varepsilon \\ \varepsilon & \varepsilon \end{pmatrix}\) . Compute \(\A\B\) and \(\lvert\A\rvert\lvert\B\rvert\) exactly, and identify the entry of \(\A\B\) that is smallest as \(\varepsilon \to 0\) . Compute \(\P_1, \dots, \P_7\) exactly, and find which of them is largest as \(\varepsilon \to 0\) . Suppose \(\varepsilon, 2\varepsilon, 1 - \varepsilon, 1 + \varepsilon, 1 + 2\varepsilon\) and \(2\varepsilon^2\) are representable, and that the model rounds \((1+\varepsilon)^2\) to \(1 + 2\varepsilon\) and \((\varepsilon - 1)(1 + \varepsilon)\) to \(-1\) , each time losing a trailing \(\varepsilon^2\) . Determine \(\widehat{c}_{22}\) , and the least constant \(c\) for which \(\lvert\widehat{\C} - \A\B\rvert \le cu\lvert\A\rvert\lvert\B\rvert\) can hold at the \((2,2)\) position. Hint: with \(\varepsilon = 2^{-27}\) in \(53\) -bit binary arithmetic, both roundings are what rounding to nearest does.

title: Exercise (C3: Only the products recurse)
content: Suppose someone proposes an identity that multiplies \(2 \times 2\) matrices with eight multiplications but only two additions, and recurses on it. Write down the recurrence for its operation count with \(T(1) = 1\) , and solve it exactly for \(n = 2^{p}\) . Hence determine the exponent it gives, and compare with @thm-strassen-cost . Explain in one sentence what part of an identity the exponent depends on.

title: Proposition 24.13.4 (The classical product has a small entrywise error)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(\nR)\) have representable entries, let \(nu < 1\) , and let \(\widehat{\C}\) be the product computed by @def-matrix-multiplication , each entry as one inner product taken in the natural order. Then \[ \bigl\lvert \widehat{\C} - \A\B \bigr\rvert \ \le\ \gamma_n \lvert\A\rvert\lvert\B\rvert \] entrywise.

title: Proposition 24.13.1 (The exponent is at least two)
content: \(M(n) \ge n^2\) for every \(n \ge 1\) , and therefore \(\omega \ge 2\) .

title: Proposition 24.13.5 (Strassen’s two-by-two product satisfies a norm bound)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_2(\nR)\) have representable entries, put \(\alpha = \max_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij}\rvert\) and \(\beta = \max_{i,j}\lvert b_{ij}\rvert\) , and let \(\widehat{\C}\) be the result of evaluating @thm-strassen with \(m = 1\) , each \(\P_k\) as written and each of the four combinations left to right. If \(6u < 1\) , then \[ \max_{i,j}\bigl\lvert \widehat{c}_{ij} - (\A\B)_{ij} \bigr\rvert \ \le\ 12\,\gamma_6\,\alpha\beta . \]

title: Theorem 24.13.2 (Strassen’s identity)
content: Let \(F\) be a field, let \(m \ge 1\) , and let \(\A, \B \in M_{2m}(F)\) be partitioned into \(m \times m\) blocks, \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} \A_{11} & \A_{12} \\ \A_{21} & \A_{22} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B = \begin{pmatrix} \B_{11} & \B_{12} \\ \B_{21} & \B_{22} \end{pmatrix}. \] Define seven products \[ \begin{aligned} \P_1 &= (\A_{11} + \A_{22})(\B_{11} + \B_{22}), &\qquad \P_2 &= (\A_{21} + \A_{22})\B_{11}, \\ \P_3 &= \A_{11}(\B_{12} - \B_{22}), &\qquad \P_4 &= \A_{22}(\B_{21} - \B_{11}), \\ \P_5 &= (\A_{11} + \A_{12})\B_{22}, &\qquad \P_6 &= (\A_{21} - \A_{11})(\B_{11} + \B_{12}), \\ \P_7 &= (\A_{12} - \A_{22})(\B_{21} + \B_{22}). && \end{aligned} \] Then, with the same block partition of \(\A\B\) , \[ \A\B = \begin{pmatrix} \P_1 + \P_4 - \P_5 + \P_7 & \P_3 + \P_5 \\ \P_2 + \P_4 & \P_1 + \P_3 - \P_2 + \P_6 \end{pmatrix}. \] Only seven products of \(m \times m\) matrices occur on the right, where @thm-block-multiplication asks for eight.

title: Theorem 24.13.3 (The cost of the recursion)
content: Let \(n = 2^{p}\) with \(p \ge 0\) . Applying @thm-strassen recursively, with the \(1 \times 1\) case done by a single multiplication, multiplies two matrices in \(M_n(F)\) with exactly \[ T(n) = 7n^{\log_2 7} - 6n^2 \] arithmetic operations. In particular \(T(n) = O(n^{\log_2 7})\) and \(\omega \le \log_2 7 = 2.8073\ldots\) .

title: Theorem 24.13.6 (Strassen’s algorithm has no useful entrywise error bound)
content: Work in a model as in @def-floating-point-model , and suppose the set \(\cR\) of representable numbers contains a number \(\varepsilon\) with \[ \varepsilon > 0, \qquad 1 + \varepsilon \in \cR, \qquad \varepsilon^2 \in \cR, \qquad \fl\bigl((1+\varepsilon)^2\bigr) = 1 + 2\varepsilon . \] Put \(\A = \B = \diag(1, \varepsilon)\) . Then the \(\widehat{\C}\) of @prp-strassen-norm-bound has \(\widehat{c}_{22} = 0\) , while \((\A\B)_{22} = \varepsilon^2\) . Consequently, any constant \(c\) for which \[ \bigl\lvert \widehat{\C} - \A\B \bigr\rvert \ \le\ c\,u\,\lvert\A\rvert\lvert\B\rvert \] holds entrywise for this \(\A\) and \(\B\) must satisfy \(c \ge 1/u\) .
